Dublin Core:Description:
William Pitman Jones to Messrs. Blackwood, Preston, 12 August 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
St. Thomas' Parsonage | Preston | August 12. 1857. The Revd. W. P. Jones 951 would be very much obliged to Messrs.
Blackwood to inform him if there will be any more Parts of Scenes of Clerical Life, Janet's Repentance. Parts 1 and 2 of that allude to his deceased Brother, 952 who died 23 years ago last December, and he is utterly at a loss to conceive who could have written the statements or revived what should have been buried in oblivion. W. P. Jones with his only surviving sister had his attention drawn to the Paper by a clerical friend who knew all the Parties alluded to, most if not all of whom have long been in Eternity. If Messrs. Blackwood will oblige Mr. Jones by an answer they will confer a kindness on him.

1 Mrs. Bugden and Mrs. Charles  Hennell conducted a school for children from three to seven years of age. Chapman's daughter Beatrice had been a pupil there in May and June 1851, and Mrs. Bugden wanted his son Ernest also. Though their father favored the plan, Mrs. Chapman preferred to have the children at home. An advertisement of the school in the Leader, 17 July 1852, p. 692, shows that it was planned on "progressive" lines; obedience is enforced "by appealing to the understanding and the sympathies, by directing attention to the natural consequences of conduct, and by fostering a love of excellence . . . and while the teaching of dogmatic creeds on the assumption of their unquestionable truth is scrupulously avoided, as prejudicial to the due exercise and development of the intellectual faculties, the utmost endeavours are made to educe and strengthen those elements of character which are the foundation of true religious feeling. Knowledge is made attractive. . . . For reference, etc., apply to Mr. John Chapman, Publisher, 142, Strand."

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 28 March 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Joseph Munt Langford^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 28 March 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. 28 March 1860.
My Dear Sir
We have received your letter about the subscription of the Mill yesterday. It is very satisfactory so far as it has gone, and we think there will be another 500 from the East and other outlying parties. With regard to Mudie, we cannot bind ourselves not to publish a 12/ edition until a twelvemonth is past, or till any other time. We have no power to do so from our agreement with the author. We do not however think that it will be advisable either for author's or publisher's advantage to publish a cheaper edition until the three volume one has had it's full swing, but when this will be we could not fix just now. From the author's reputation and its own merits we have little doubt that the demand for The Mill will be great and immediate. We published the 12/ edition of Adam Bede sooner than we think we should have done for our own interest, having then only the comparatively limited sale of the author's previous work Clerical Scenes to guide us. We cannot however see that Mr. Mudie suffered by our doing so; the large numbers he took of the 12/ edition showed that he had not near enough of the 3 vol. edition wherewith to supply his readers. On referring to our books I see he had 1500 of the 3 volume edition Adam Bede, 235 of which were taken in May. The 2 volume edition was published in June; he took 250 immediately and another 250 a week later and 400 in July and August. Looking therefore both to the inconvenience to the author and ourselves of coming under any engagement as to the time of publishing a cheaper edition and to past effects in a similar case, upon Mr. Mudie's interest of such an edition, we do not think he has any reason to ask us for such a guarantee as he requires. We should be glad to meet his wishes and oblige him in any way we could, but a guarantee would tie us up in a way that might not only be inconvenient in the present case but as a precedent in future ones.
We are going to press immediately with another 2000, 522 and I have little doubt but that The Mill will find the Printing office work for some time. Fortunately we have got the new cylinder machine working beautifully as well as another Platen within the last month, otherwise we should have been in a fix.
Mr. Simpson I am glad to say appears to have got quite over the attack in the eyes. He is still complaining a little of weakness however. We are very sorry to hear of poor Mr. Sheard's death. 523 It is melancholy, just, poor fellow when he

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to John Blackwood, London, 21 April 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to John Blackwood, London, 21 April 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Albemarle Street | London W | April 21/75.
My dear Uncle
I am very annoyed to find that my letter of Monday did not reach you yesterday morning as I sent it off from here in ample time for the extra stamp post. . . . I lunched with the Lewes' and found them both rather seedy I am sorry to say. George Eliot looked especially so and Lewes afterwards told me that she had been very unwell and I was quite shocked and distressed to see her looking so aged and haggard but she cheered up and both were very pleased to see me.
I thought the sales of Middlemarch were good enough to take her a note of them and she was extremely happy at seeing them so good still. We have sold over 1200 since January 1st and the number for April is already greater than that of March. She thanked me most cordially for bringing such bright news, and I replied that I hoped she had equally good to give me about the new novel. She at once hung her head low and said "Oh no, it is detestable I think, but Mr. Lewes will tell you all about it when you smoke your cigar in the garden" -- which he did.
Of course his opinion was quite the reverse and he said it was perfectly charming and all about English Ladies and Gentlemen and scene laid in Wiltshire. I got the title of it from him in great confidence and as a secret to be told to no one but you, not even Mr. Langford. It is Daniel DeRonda, and as Lewes rolled it out in a deep bass sounding voice he said "Does it not sound very grand?" I then learned that whole of Volume I was in a complete state and part one of the next volume. I suggested could I not take it down for you to read quietly before coming up, as you would then be well able to talk it over with Mrs. Lewes and give her encouragement to go on, and Lewes thought it a capital idea. As for trusting it to the Post that was not for a moment to be thought of. "What would we do if it were lost and it could never be rewritten?"
When she joined us Lewes proposed it as my suggestion very nicely; if you had seen her face of horror and fright and meek expression you would have been startled. It was one of the most striking scenes I have ever seen and for a minute or two she would not speak. She seemed just to tremble at the idea of the M.S. being taken from her as if it were her baby; and by degrees she assented, and I am to go on Sunday or day before I start North for it. . . .
Lewes was also very strong upon the Inkerman Volume and described it as quite the most wonderful literary performance of its class he had ever read. They walked half way back with me and we had altogether a most pleasant chat. . . .
Best love to all.
Ever your affectionate nephew
William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 8 June 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 8 June 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
June 1859.
My dear John
I send you the calculation for Scenes of Clerical Life uniform in two volumes with Adam Bede. Also a calculation for it in one volume of the same size. This I do not think will do -- it leaves so small a profit and will not make a nice volume. I think the two volumes should do, but after the subscription for the two volume edition of Adam Bede we shall be able to judge better. Slip leaf announcing this edition of Clerical Scenes should be put in every copy of the other book, Mr. Simpson says. This should be got ready in London.
There is another question: should the price be 10/6 or 12/-. I am rather inclined for the latter -- of the former edition I see we only printed 1000 -- having at first agreed with the author for only 750. Until yesterday I thought the number had been 1500. The author got from Maga for it 'a3262.10 and for the separate publication 'a3180 ('a3120 for 750, 'a360 after that number should be sold). The total profit estimated was 350 allowing 'a350 for advertising. If we give 'a3100 for a 2 volume edition at 12/- of 1500 and 'a350 when the whole or nearly so are sold, I think it will be a handsome offer, but if you feel confident about the 1500 going off I would make the 'a3150 certain. . . .
Yours sincerely
W. Blackwood
P.M.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 20 June 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 20 June 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
June 1859.
My dear John --
Mr. Simpson thinks we ought to get ready another 163 edition of 2000 of Adam Bede, and that this is Langford's opinion too. By the latter's letter to me of Friday 2000 were accounted for as gone here and in London and I thought the remaining 1000 would keep us in hand for a time. However as it will take 3 weeks to get an edition ready with comfort to the printing office it is a matter for consideration to go to press at once, especially as 112 pp. of the last are still in form and keeping them up interferes with the new edition of Clerical Scenes. If the demand has been continued today in London I should think we are quite safe in another edition.
With regard to the Poysers at the Seaside 164 Simpson is not very anxious. He does not think favourably of it commercially. I have rather the feeling that the Poysers are so good as they stand in Adam Bede that it would be a pity to weaken the effect of that unique work by extending as it were one section of it. Altogether I doubt whether such a thing will be for the author's advantage in the end; at the same time there is no doubt it would take, and if the author is bent on it we would be wrong not to go into it heartily, but I certainly would not press it in any way. . . .
ever yours affectionately
W. Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 18 October 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 18 October 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edin. 18 October /59.
My dear John
I send you a letter from G.E. I am rather sorry to see the change of signature. On the whole I think you may be as well without the new tale for Maga. It is evident there is going to be no secret about the authorship now which is one reason for its not appearing there to which considerable weight may be due: and another is the author's strong feeling about the advantage to be gained by having it brought out at once with the eclat of its being known to be by the author of A.B. Feeling sure that we are right as to the mode of publication we recommended I would not, were the author's position different, mind about pressing our ideas on him. But considering how that position may possibly affect the new book I think we might be placed in disagreeable circumstances by doing so.
Simpson is to have a careful comparison of 3 volume edition and 2 volume made and all the rates shown to me. . . .
Ever yours affectionately
W. Blackwood. . . .

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 14 June 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 14 June 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
June 1859.
My dear John . . .
I send you a very curious letter from a man who supposes he is the original Amos Barton. I think he ought to have some acknowledgment. He writes like what one would almost have expected from Amos and I shall be curious to hear what G.E. says [of] it. Some old clergyman 157 wrote from the neighbourhood of either Liverpool or Manchester about his brother being the original of one character in Clerical Scenes, but that was in Janet's Repentance I think. I have been trying [to find] some trace of our correspondence with him but can't. I have hit upon a capital letter from G.E. however pointing out very beautifully upon how slight a foundation people build up these theories. It was written with reference to Newdegate's confidence about the incidents in Gilfil being all taken from his grandfather's history. 158 Aytoun came to town yesterday afternoon. He is tolerably well and is writing he says.
Ever yours affectionately
W. Blackwood.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 1 December 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 1 December 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh, 1 December 1859.
My dear John
I have been thinking over G.E's letter a good deal as you may suppose in the course of the day. On the whole I think it puts things fairly enough and that he wishes to continue to publish with us. How far that wish will lead him to accept a reasonable and moderate offer from us in preference to an extravagant one from another quarter I am not so clear about.
In saying that your offer stultified the reasons he gave for not publishing in Maga he overlooks that you said we would give him more for it there than in any other way of publication. I think we would have done so but I would not have it now for Maga. Any failure or fancied failure of it in that case would be most disagreeable. Our practice of never giving an author's name in Maga should be strongly dwelt on and our reason for it. It will soothe his feelings. With regard to A.B. Junr. and our neglect of his wishes we have some cause of complaint against him that he did not show more confidence in our judgment in the matter 'aband did not give us credit to believe that'bb. Neither in honor nor justice could we allow any injury to arise to G.E. from the wretched thing that we could prevent, and he might have given us credit for common sense and knowledge of our business enough to know when we were called upon to come before the public.
The dropping of the incognito is the most serious part of the business and will, I feel satisfied, affect the circulation in families of any future work. 411 Then there is the danger of G.E. coming before the public in his own name from some crotchet or another. I really think we should have some understanding with Lewes about this. Altogether it is a tangled kind of business, and though I feel that we should continue to publish for her as long as we have confidence in her other writings, we shall always, I am afraid, have disagreeables attending it in some shape or another. I think too very strongly that we should not bind ourselves until we have seen the new work.
Aytoun has given me back good St. Stephens; 412 he says it is not at all bad, better in fact than anybody else could have done it, but doubts whether it will tell. Of course we can't give any suggestions.
Hoping you had a pleasant journey and find a pleasant houseful at Arbury,
Ever yours affectionately
W. Blackwood.

411 Langford wrote John Blackwood  23 November 1859 about a conversation with Mr. Watson of Nisbet's, who declared that the revelation of GE's identity had affected the book. He had read a MS written by a lady to the women of England aiming to show from internal evidence that Adam Bede was written by a woman of loose morals! Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to John Blackwood, [Edinburgh,] 5 October 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to John Blackwood, [Edinburgh,] 5 October 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
October 1859.
My dear Johnny
There is an order from Paternoster Row for more Adam Bede. We have just 450 to meet it. I expect we are safe to go to press with 2000 more. We have only about 'a3400 in Coutts at present. I would not pay G.E. however before the money is due, which is not till end of this month. I have always thought we ought to give him a handsome sum (in addition to that already promised) for the 12/- edition. I thought however it would be done in a much handsomer manner after the bargain was settled for the new novel. I am still of that opinion, and think whether he negociates with anybody else or not we should, when there is no question betwixt us about a new novel, send such a sum as we think right and say that one reason for delaying to say anything about it before was that we felt a delicacy in doing so while negociating about another book. This has been my feeling, and it is much stronger since his letter, which I do not like. Indeed I thought the terms in which he acknowledged the intelligence of our intention to pay 'a3400 more not gracious. However neither that nor his last letter affects my idea of what we ought to pay him for Adam, though it makes it a less pleasant duty.
Ever yours affectionately
W. Blackwood.
John Blackwood, Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GHL, London, 16 May 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, London, 16 May 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
May 16/68.
My Dear Mr. Lewes
I have given Mr. Langford special instructions about not letting a single copy of the poem out of our hands until the 25th and am also letting them know your wishes at Edinburgh. I daresay you will have observed that we are advertising it for that day. In a letter from Mr. Brown 762 (our press proof reader) received this morning he writes me as follows, and as I think it will interest and please Mrs. Lewes, I quote him at length.
"I am reading Fedalma over again in its perfected form and am more and more struck with its matchless depth and power. Of course it is impossible to say how that mysterious reading public, which buys Charles Dickens by the ten thousand for the thousand of Romola or Felix Holt, will take it, but if Fedalma does not, with the better and more thoughtful part of it, place George Eliot as high among poets as she already stands among novelists, my opinion of the reading intellect of the age will go down to zero. So far as printing etc. goes it promises to be a very handsome book." For Mr. Brown this is tremendous strong.
Hoping you and Mrs. Lewes are better, believe me
Ever yours truly
William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 9 March 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 9 March 1859
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. Edinburgh 9. March 1859.
My dear Lewes . . .
Pray tell George Eliot when you see him that Adam Bede is selling in a most satisfactory way. Orders continue to come in both here and in London for it every day. Two days ago Mudie had another 100 making his total 700. In the circulating libraries the subscribers are all yelling for it and the librarians are not sufficiently philanthropic to take the proper means for adequately meeting the public appetite. Professor Simpson, whom of course you know by reputation if not personally, speaks as enthusiastically of Adam Bede as did Dr. John Brown, and I think the author must be gratified to learn the high opinion entertained of his work by such a man as Simpson.
I had so high opinion myself of Clerical Scenes that I thought the movement in the sale of Adam Bede would have begun earlier than it did in London, from the Author's reputation from the former work, but though it has been a little longer in commencing than I anticipated yet I feel very confident now that it will equal our most sanguine expectations. As you know how high these were both on my brother's part and my own from the hold the book had taken upon us I need say no more. Desiring to be kindly regarded by George Eliot Believe me
Yours Truly
W. Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes, Esqr.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 9 March 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 9 March 1859
Text: Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
5 George Street, Edinburgh 9. March 1859.
My Dear Lewes
We received yesterday the inclosed letter from Mr. Hargreaves 426 one of poor Johnston's executors. From it you will see that Johnston, short time as he lived after the completion of the Chemistry of Common Life, 427 had corrected a copy which has been only now sent to us. This delay is most provoking as from the glance I have given through the annotated copy, Johnston appears to have gone about the work systematically and to have collected many more interesting facts and illustrations for his various chapters which would have added greatly to the interest and 'e9clat of a new edition both from their intrinsic merit and as being the last corrections of the Author.
We send you this corrected copy and will feel obliged if you will look through it and give us your opinion as to whether any of the new matter can be given in an appendix or whether the whole should be reserved for another impression. All that has been done appears to me merely additional explanation and illustration, not correction of statements or opinions, so that we feel we can with perfect good faith reserve it. Nearly the whole of your edition is printed off so that it would be a very heavy sacrifice to cancel it. When we purchased from the executors about three years ago all the author's interest in this and his other works, we specially noticed to them the necessity there would be for corrected editions and how our having to calculate upon this was a matter we had to take into consideration in making our offer. We also inquired generally about the papers Johnston had left. We never thought therefore of applying again to them on the subject when we proposed to you to edit the Chemistry. With the writer of the inclosed we have not had correspondence but with his coexecutor Mr. Shields 428 we settled everything in the most friendly way about the estate and have occasionally corresponded since, so that we can only look upon our not having [had] sooner put into our hands the corrected copy as an unfortunate oversight.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 31 May 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 31 May 1876
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh May 31/76.
My Dear Mr. Lewes
I have the pleasure of announcing the safe arrival of another batch of Deronda and I have instructed Printers to try and have proofs ready to post you tomorrow. I am very anxious to read this thrilling portion which I could not resist from running my eye through.
Mr. Simpson is attending to your wishes about the Casts of the Woodcuts for your new Volume. Mr. Simpson has also handed me the enclosed cheque for £100 from the proprietors of the Melbourne Argus 487 for permission to print Daniel Deronda in its columns. They remitted cheque for the additional £100 last month which makes payment in full of the arrangement made by Mr. Simpson on your behalf and is now discharged by us by enclosed cheque for £100 on Coutts and Co. Hoping both cheques will reach you safely believe me
Ever yours truly
(Signed) William Blackwood
P.S. When my Uncle has got his Oxford anxiety off his mind I have no doubt you will see him often and speedily. This is the day and a nice "Derby day" for Jack too. He will know result of exam tomorrow.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 25 September 1858
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh 25 September 1858.
My dear Lewes
I am sorry to find on inquiry that no reply has yet been sent to Tr'fcbner. It has been partly my mistake owing to a confusion arising from my brother's absence of a conversation I had with Mr. Simpson on the subject after his return from London. We will write on Monday and hope no injury will happen from the delay to G.E.'s interests.
The prospectus 402 is highly approved of by us. I send you a proof. We announce the work as preparing for publication in this number of Maga, but reserve the prospectus to a later period -- probably on 1st November -- we will issue it.
Yours truly
Wm. Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
Send us back Tr'fcbner's letter if you can lay hands on it. It was not returned to us.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 19 September 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 19 September 1871
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. | September 19/71.
My Dear Mr. Lewes
My Uncle wrote to you yesterday enclosing a specimen page for Middlemarch, but it did not please quite and Mr. Simpson and I have been laying our heads together to design another. 367 We have we think hit upon one more adapted for the scheme and which also does not disturb the original calculations of outlay and income though it bulks more. I send you specimens by Book Post and the part will contain 214 pp. which quantity with the quality ought surely to satisfy the public they have got their money's worth. If any other shape or type strikes you as better will you let me know and we will endeavour to carry out your wishes as far as is possible.
I also send you by Book Post a specimen Book from which you will most likely be able to select the colour for the paper cover. I think the one you thought of was a delicate lilac shade and very pretty it would look.
My best regards to Mrs. Lewes and I trust she is recovering from her severe indisposition.
Ever yours truly
(signed) Wm. Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 19 July 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. | Edin. 19 July 60.
My dear Lewes,
I have to apologise for not having forwarded the inclosed to you sooner after your return. I trust the contents are not such as will have suffered by keeping. I was delighted to hear of your and Mrs. Lewes's return to this country in renovated health and spirits -- and both determined for writing! I don't think I have any literary news to give, no special feature in sales of the Physiology or the Mill on the Floss to record, though the former moves steadily and there is still a little demand for the latter. More than 6,000 copies of a guinea and a half novel sold is a success which I am pretty confident has not been attained since the days of the Waverley Novels.
With kind regards to Mrs. Lewes, believe me
Yours very truly
W. Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes, Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 18 March 1859
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh 18 March 1859.
My dear Lewes
We have printed off No. 4 without Digestion and Indigestion. We are not sure however that the public may not grumble at such a thin 6d worth.
Try and keep the parts as near to forty eight (48) pages as possible. There are numerous practical inconveniences, and expense too, attending the variation in size of the numbers, and at the same time I see the unsatisfactoriness to the author in particular of issuing the subjects in so disjointed a form as the taking in of 8 introductory pages of a new subject at the end of an old one merely to make the part of the required number of pages. Still purchasers look so much to quantity as well as quality that Mr. Simpson thinks they won't be satisfied with 40 pp. for their sixpences one month although they get 60 the next. The stupidity of the public in this way is hopeless.
With the original issue of Johnston's Chemistry we looked only to the completeness of the parts and in consequence had to vary the price of each. This we found very troublesome and hurtful to some extent to the sales as the dealers said their subscribers grumbled at the variation in price. It would be a considerable convenience to us if you could keep us well ahead in the printing office with copy. It would also leave time for considering any difficulty about extent of a number.
Yours faithfully
(signed) W. Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
Inclosed is a letter from Williams and Norgate. We do not concur in Mr. Tauchnitz's opinion that he cannot expect such a success for A.B. in Germany as a less English novel would have and think he ought to give a good deal more than he gave for Clerical Scenes. Let us know what G.E. thinks he ought to have.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 16 May 1878
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh | May 16/78.
My dear Mr. Lewes
I heard from Mr. Langford that he had the pleasure of meeting you and that you had been making enquiry about the Cabinet Edition of Mrs. Lewes's works. On reading it I felt very guilty for not having written to you or Mrs. Lewes some news of the sales since my Uncle saw you and reported, but my omission arose not from having forgotten but from the press of work requiring immediate attention I have had during my Uncle's absence abroad. However Mr. Simpson has presented me with a state of the sales and I can no longer postpone enclosing it to you which I do with pleasure as we consider it highly satisfactory.
The sales too of the other editions have been keeping steadily up to the average which under the terrible depression and dulness of trade is very assuring that they do not clash with one another, that there was a decided want for the Cabinet edition and that it was brought out about the right period.
When may we look forward to seeing or hearing of another fascinating book from Mrs. Lewes to give the series of her books another fresh start as well as delighting the public with something to read and think over? I hope before long that my Uncle on his homeward journey will be gladdened by hearing of it from yourselves in person when he halts in London. I expect him to get there early next month and one of his first pleasures will be I know to see you and Mrs. Lewes. My last reports of him have been much more satisfactory and he had got back to Florence, the change there from Rome having benefitted him greatly. All during his stay in Rome he had been ill having caught cold on the journey there. But I trust that when he gets home he will find he has derived more benefit from his travels and rest from work than he did when away.
What are your summer plans? Hoping this finds you and Mrs. Lewes pretty strong and well and with kind regards believe me
ever yours sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 12 March 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: From the Major. Extract published: III, 33, n. 6.
5 George St. 12 March 1859.
My dear Lewes
Thanks for your note about Johnston's Chemistry. I am glad to find your opinions coincide with our own here that it is better to reserve altogether the author's additions for another impression.
The rest of the article on "Food and Drink" is rather short for the next number of the Physiology and we want 8 pp. more to make it of sufficient bulk. Will you be good enough to let us have them as soon as possible. You have had the proof of Digestion [and] Indigestion for some days I believe. I am glad to tell you the Physiology is selling very satisfactorily. A good feature in the sale is that number 1 is constantly asked for.
John has "Only a Pond." 431 It will be Sunday reading for him, I have little doubt. He is off to golf, for his Saturday's amusement. Langford writes with his usual philosophical calmness, in the middle of a letter filled with details of little consequence, which has just come, "Mudie has just made up his number of Adam Bede to 1000. Simpkins have sold their subscribed number and have had 12 today. Everyone is talking of the book." Your allusion to G. E's new tale excites strong interest.
Yours truly
W. Blackwood.
A copy of Mr. Tate's pamphlet 432 has come to us for G.E. I send it you though I daresay he will not care to see it. John will be in London probably the end of next month or beginning of May.
G. H. Lewes, Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 12 July 1878
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh | July 12/78.
My dear Mr. Lewes
We propose with your approval using in our new Series of "Tales from Blackwood" two of your stories Falsely Accused and Metamorphoses 102 and in case you have any alterations to make, I send you the sheets from Maga containing them. I think you should give your name to both, and will you fill it in as you wish to be designated unless you had rather not own them. I am glad to say that the new series promises to do well and is sustaining the reputation the first achieved.
You will be very pleased to hear that I have most satisfactory and cheering accounts of my Uncle's health since he went to Strathtyrum which I trust will continue and that you and Mrs. Lewes will find him in good force when you give him the pleasure of your visit. And by the way when is it coming off? Recollect days shorten much after this month and after middle of August it begins to get chillier with us here North. Even now when we are having lovely fine days it gets cold and chilly in the evenings and you cannot sit out there as you do in England.
Our good and faithful friend Simpson's retirement has made a sad and terrible blank here and I doubt if we shall ever find such another "Von Moltke" in our line, and a more devoted adherent you could not find. He bad us good bye on Tuesday and very full our hearts were when we parted and next morning he started for London and North Germany. How he will get on without "45" to come to and think about puzzles us, but we hope for the best and that he will have much enjoyment and comfort in his retirement from business life.
A half yearly statement of sales of Mrs. Lewes' books is being prepared and I hope soon to have the pleasure of writing with it. Will you present my kind remembrances, and hoping you are enjoying the fine summer.
Ever yours sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 7 October 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinburgh | October 7th 1879.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am happy to tell you I had a much better and satisfactory report of my Uncle last night both from himself and my Aunt. Much of his discomfort and trouble has been caused by indigestion and tendency to asthma and a very strict diet has been prescribed him. I trust he will attend to it.
What answer shall we send to enclosed regarding Theophrastus Such? Your other works have I think been mostly all translated into French already. We have never before had any communications from the writer of it but if you entertain his proposals would first make enquiries about him in London.
We are having lovely Autumn weather now and some of the Scotch harvest will be got in pretty well.
I hope you duly received our letter of the 3rd with enclosures. We have better reports of sales from London this morning and Simpkins ordered 156 "Mill on the Floss" on Saturday and 22 Theophrastus went off during end of week. We shall soon have to reprint "The Sayings." Are you agreeable to Mr. Maynes [i.e. Main's] adding to it from Deronda and Theophrastus Such; both are I think admirably suited for it and it will be a labour of love to him. With best regards and hoping you are enjoying St. Martin's Summer,
Ever Yours Sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 7 August 1878
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh August 7/78.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
The printers were to have had the enclosed specimen page ready for me yesterday to send in my letter to you but they did not keep their promise. It is what we propose adopting for the two volumes of poetry 109 in your Cabinet edition and is I think very pretty and [chaste.] I shall be glad to hear if it meets with your approval. It is a somewhat finer type than what is used for your prose works but it is the same size in reality and in poetry it is desirable to have it sharp and fine. In this form it will run to same number of pages as in the edition now selling and will so make a handsome Volume. The other Volume will take some planning and scheming to swell it out to the required length unless you have any other poems you wish to insert in it. 110 Will you kindly let me know as to this at your early convenience?
We are pushing on with the printing of the other volumes of the Edition so that we may have it ready complete by Christmas as we look forward to the real sale beginning when people can have it in sets. The monthly publication will nevertheless be continued until the edition is complete. I think you wish proofs of both poetry Volumes to be sent you as ready.
As I have not [Von Moltke] now to write you about these details I have to trouble you and I hope I have made them sufficiently clear and believe me
ever yours sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 6 May 1880
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. Edinburgh | May 6 1880.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
The news you send me in your very friendly and cordial letter of yesterday did surprise me but I am very happy to hear it and I wish you heartily much joy and happiness. From what you tell me of Mr. Cross
I am sure he will be to you all that you could desire and his family is I know an exceedingly clever and nice one.
It is rather strange my hearing this news of your future happiness from you this morning as for some days past you have been often in my thoughts. I had written to Langford asking him to send me some news of sales and in reply heard that during the last month we sold nearly 1600 volumes of the cheap editions of your works which considering business is very dull I think is very good and comforting. I wish he had sent me the particulars but he did not do so.
I thank you for your kind wishes for myself and I am happy to say I have been feeling much better lately and the strain of work is coming easier to me as time passes and the days become brighter. I shall be very happy to write to you in the old way when you return in August and hoping you will enjoy your stay abroad and with all good wishes for your happiness believe me
Always yours sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 5 May 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 5 May 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh 5 May 1859.
My dear Sir
I enclose two letters for you. That from Mr. Anders had in some unaccountable way fallen aside and was laid on my desk two days ago only by a clerk. I opened it stupidly without looking at the address for which I beg to apologise. His account of the way in which his letter got into the Times is not very credible. You will be glad to hear that the sale of Adam still goes on to admiration. We published another edition, the 3d, of 500 129 copies on Monday and have disposed of almost 400. This makes a total sale of over 3000, a result which should assure even your self distrusting spirit of the value of your work. It is not however the mere extent of the circulation of Adam Bede which you may regard with pleasure. Widely as the work has been read the appreciation which it has received from those best qualified to judge of its merit must be still more gratifying to its author. You have had ample proof of this in the letters which we have had the pleasure of forwarding to you, and I can add, with much satisfaction, the assurance that we have equally favourable opinions from all who read the book.
I have tried to recover the numbers of the "Leader" and "Critic" which contained the remarks about the secret of authorship, but unsuccessfully. They were foolish and impertinent; attempting to prove that the public had a right to know who was the author of any book and therefore that such as Mr. Anders were justified in stating their beliefs. The articles were contemptible and any notice of such things would only gratify the creatures who had written them. My brother has read with great admiration the M.S. you sent a few days ago and will write himself shortly.
Yours sincerely
W. Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 October 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Lansdowne Cres[cen]t | October 30th 1879.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I have been much gratified and comforted by receipt of your very kind and beautiful letter of 28th about your old friend my dear Uncle of whose sudden death I sent you the painful news in a very hurried note yesterday. I was sent for the day after I wrote to you and found my much loved Uncle rapidly sinking with marks of the approaching end visibly portrayed on his beautiful face, and he was unable to talk clearly the mind having become confused. But he knew me quite well and looked so pleased to see me and said, "I am glad you have come I am very ill" and then the thought could not be further expressed or disappeared from him. It was very sad and painful for all of us, but he breathed his last very peacefully and painlessly and it was a great happiness to look upon the gentle and beautiful expression his face took when death relieved him. I had to come over last night to make the necessary arrangements for the last earthly duties, and I had to leave my Aunt and Cousins very heartbroken and stunned. The funeral is fixed for Monday next and then all will be taken from us of the one we all admired and loved for his many manly and noble traits.
I was sure you would be very pained at the news I had to give you last Sunday but I did not think the end was so close at hand then or I should have written to you sooner. I was very vexed not to be able to be more with him last week but I had to be here to attend to Maga and other pressing business matters which he understood perfectly.
I wish so much I could have given him your loving message and about the last business talk I had with him he spoke much of you, and as to your suggestion about The Sayings he remarked "We will overcome the difficulty, Willie, by making a supplementary Volume and removing the poetry into it or not as Mrs. Lewes likes." I intended to have written it to you in that last letter but I was so harassed with grief that I stupidly forgot it and it haunted me often.
The London papers of to-day have just come in and I know you will be grateful as we are in reading the notices about him and to see that justice is being done to his sound and acute literary insight and other genial characteristics. The great liberal Newspaper of Scotland has come out nobly about him and by post I have sent you a copy as I thought you would like to see what his political opponents here thought of him. The Times, Standard and Daily Telegraph all write very delightfully and his sorrowing widow and children will read them with gratifying comfort but what a loss for us all. I hope and trust that I have not wearied you by this long letter and thanking you warmly for your anxious thoughts about the valued lost one and us all. Believe me dear Mrs. Lewes
Always yours sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.
P.S. I forgot to say that my Uncle on Monday expressed a strong desire to see Mr. Langford but alas before he arrived on Tuesday he was too ill and he never saw his beloved esteemed Master and friend until he saw him dead. Having had him with me was an immense comfort and help to me, my Uncle must have felt a presentiment that I would require an old friend by me with his old forethought.

Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 28 May 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinb. | May 28/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I inclose the London Subscription List of Theophrastus as far as completed and I hope it will please and cheer you. It was quite a fillip to say to my Uncle this morning and he agrees with me in reprinting to the extent of 1500 which will about exhaust the stock of paper we have in hand for it. Would you oblige by sending me a telegram in answer to my querie about printing words Second Edition on title page if you have been unable to write to day as we are very anxious of not checking the sale in any way by not having copies in stock to supply all orders. We are trying to have this reprint ready on Saturday.
We have received payments of £10 from Bohn of Haarlem for right to translate Theophrastus into Dutch, and £25 from Dr. Lehman into German. I have now the pleasure of enclosing you cheque for the two amounts. We have not yet heard from Messrs. Harpers about their payments but hope to do so shortly. Congratulating you upon the successful start of "Theophrastus Such"
Believe me for partner and self
Yours very sincerely
William Blackwood.
P.So. On reading my letter I see I have omitted to mention how favourably my Uncle is progressing and last evening he sat up for several hours and passed a very fair night. I think and hope to see him out of his bedroom in a few days.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 25 March 1880
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letterbook. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. Edinburgh | March 25/80.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I have been wishing to write to you for many days past but with getting Maga to press and attending Committees of our Conservative Candidates for the City and County my time has been fully occupied and business has been rather neglected. However as I feel it is the duty of every patriotic man to do his utmost to defeat Mr. Gladstone and those who agree with him I hope you will pardon the delay.
I am glad you overcame your compunctions as to giving me trouble about the Statement of your works for the last year and when I saw that for 1878 I am not surprised at your giving it the preference and I do not know why our bookkeeper prepared the one for 1879 in a different form. Your wishes for the future will be attended to and I hope to have the pleasure of sending you as many more as satisfactory statements as the enclosed amended one for 1879. The sales for this year have so far opened well and are very encouraging. You were kindly anxious on our behalf about the stock on hand of Theophrastus but I had no fears and I am happy to tell you that the stock on hand is now reduced to about 35 copies, if as many, as I have had no return of it from Pater Noster Row since last month.
I was very glad to hear a good report of your health from Mr. Langford and he would tell you we had finished our heavy and anxious task all pleasantly. It was indeed a relief to have it finished but as I have a very uphill task before me the anxiety and strain of the work makes life very different for me to what it has been. I hope you think the Magazine is keeping up to the old mark. I was very pleased at getting Palander's Narrative 376 and "the Saturday" of last week made a very good article out of it for their own columns and called attention to the paper in "Blackwood." The new number will be ready to post you tomorrow if not to-night but it is rather political. I often wonder if you would be disposed to write something for old Maga and I should be so pleased if you would. With kindest regards and hoping this finds you well believe me
Always yours Sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 23 November 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letterbook. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinburgh | November 23/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
Your last letter was so kind and considerate and so like your usual warm thoughtfulness that I cannot sufficiently thank you. I do feel overwhelmed with all my duties and responsibilities but every one is so kind that I hope to overtake what is necessary without injurious delay.
Your suggestions about the new supplement to "The Sayings" are all very sound and practicable and your wishes will be attended to. Any exuberances on the part of Mr. Main, from whom we heard yesterday, will be curbed.
I am going to London tomorrow for a few days about some business matters and I hope you are now strong enough to [allow] me the happiness of going to see you and although our conversation cannot fail to be very sad and painful [it] may prove to be a great relief to us both to talk of those who have gone from us and on whom we have leaned so very much. Would either Wednesday or Thursday between 12 and 1 o'clock suit you? My address will be 106A Jermyn Street (Miss Williamson) where I have procured rooms as the [house] in Arlington Street -- where I have been in the habit of going is full.
I am sorry you have dropped the old familiar form of "Mr. William" in writing to me and if you do not mind I had much rather you returned to it. It will I think and hope be less painful to you to write to me and I should feel happier and more at [ease] under it.
Looking forward to shaking you by the hand again soon, believe me Dear Mrs. Lewes
Always yours Sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 23 May 1860
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. Edinburgh | 23 May 1860.
My dear Madam
I have just received your letter of the 18th to my brother John, who is at present in London, and as I know he cannot write you tomorrow, being bound for the Derby, 543 I shall endeavour to give you the best account I can of the progress of the Mill on the Floss, that your very unnecessary anxiety about it may be relieved as soon as possible. First as to tangible proofs Mudie took his third thousand, a day or two, I think it must have been, after my brother wrote you. The whole six thousand have been out of our hands for some time, and though there were still copies in the Row, we went to press with another five hundred, 544 which are now just ready to send to London, not, I am pretty confident, before they are wanted. Mr. Langford has not sent us any account for some time of how stock stood with the wholesale houses in the Row, but unless Simpkins have still copies there can be none worth mentioning. All the reviews and notices of the book with exception of those of one or two obscure newspapers have been most favourable, and to crown the whole the Times came out on Saturday 545 with a very good one too in which justice is done to your genius. I hope a copy will reach you with this as instructions were sent Mr. Langford yesterday on the subject and will be again today with your address at Florence. The Times reviewer I think leaves the impression on the reader that the characters in the book are harder, more disagreeably selfish than you have drawn them, and he is wrong I think in saying that the interest in the story is less in the Mill than in Adam. I have heard different opinions on this point, but I think the interest one feels in Maggie is intense, and if one pauses in the story it is only in consequence of the excellence of the scenes through which it is conducted. All our friends are loud in their praise of the book.
I am delighted to hear you have been enjoying your sojourn in Italy so much and have benefited in health by it. Lewes too notwithstanding your reference to headaches, will I hope return much refreshed by travel and change. The horrible winter, which you left this country in the possession of, continued to within the last ten days, when summer came upon us at one stride. I never saw so rapid and beautiful a change in the scenery of this northern climate. Ten days ago grass and trees were alike brown and bare. Now the former is green and thick and the trees covered with blossom and fresh leaves. It has reminded me of the change in India when the first fall of rain comes after the hot winds have hidden all vegetation with layers of sand, where it has not burnt it up, and the verdure comes fresh in a night. Certainly we have a claim for a fine summer if an eight months continuous winter gives it.
The Physiology is doing very well, tell Lewes, and we hope it is taking a fine hold of the public. With kind regards to him Believe me, My dear Madam,
Yours truly
W. Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 May 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 May 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinburgh | May 20/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I have the pleasure of enclosing you cheque for £50 being payment from Baron Tauchnitz for right to reprint in his series "Impressions of Theophrastus Such" which we received from his London agent this morning. I wrote yesterday to Herr Bohn at Haarlem accepting his offer £10 for right to translate it into Dutch and to Dr. Lehman offering to accept £25 on your behalf to translate it into German. I have no doubt that he will arrange with a publisher to pay that sum. My Uncle thought you should not accept less. I am thankful to say he still continues to recover although still confined to bed. And I shall be very pleased when I am able to report to you of his being able to leave his bedroom.
I inclose lists of those to whom presentation copies of Deronda were sent and will you add or delete as you think necessary or wish. We thought better to delay any advertising until near publication and in a few days we shall come out with a burst. From what Mr. Harper wrote me we quite expect him to remit £50 on receipt of the early sheets and we should hear from him soon with draft for that amount.
Believe me always yours truly
William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 September 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 September 1874
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinr. September 16/74.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I have not had the pleasure of writing to you for a long time because I had nothing to trouble you with [in] a letter beyond what my Uncle had told you. Now however the inclosed Treasury order for a small sum of money on Colonial Sales of Foreign Editions of your works gives me the opportunity, as it requires your signature as George Eliot as well as our own to get the money. We have not had one for a very long time and I suspect the late Government must have pocketed several sums. It is some time now since we heard any news of you and Mr. Lewes and I have often wondered how you have been liking your Country quarters. I hope well, and that the air and quiet life have suited you both.
I have had a very jolly summer and am now well and sound though I have never been away from here for more than ten days and that twice only, but business has been lively and my Uncle's health and spirits have been better than I have seen him for several years. Long may he continue so I trust. I think he told you about my doings with The Fife Light Horse Yeomanry and how the Colonel, that mighty Nimrod Jack Thomson, and self and others had suffered from effects of sun, but it had splendid results and made me a new man, so I expect to enjoy some good hunting this coming season.
I am very happy to tell you that Middlemarch goes tripping along most gaily and the 2000 reprinted at end of July are all gone but a dozen or two and we have just reprinted another 2000 the first batch of which goes to London tomorrow. Jubal and Spanish Gypsy have also been selling well since last reported along with your other novels for the season of the year. I hope that your new work has been making as good progress in your hands and that we shall soon be hearing something more from you about it. . . . Post hour is up so I must conclude and with best remembrances to Mr. Lewes, believe me
Always yours sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 July 1878
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh July 16/78.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
The Birthday book is now ready for binding and all but the colour of cloth was arranged for before our good old friend Simpson left us. As I know you are very particular about such matters I send you specimens of what we think will least offend you and yet be very attractive to the retail bookseller and his customers. The designs for side and back stamp are very novel and will not I hope startle you too much, but from its nature and for its purpose it required to be very ornate.
We shall be glad to have it back with your approval as soon as convenient as I have delayed in sending it off thinking you would be here very soon, but I hear no word of your Northern visit. I hope you are not breaking down in your good intention of coming to visit my Uncle in his Fife home. From your last letter to him you indicated I might have some sales to report to you and I have now the pleasure of enclosing statement for last six months. They are pretty good but dulness of trade has told on them as it has on everything else I fear.
My Uncle I rejoice to tell you continues regaining health and strength steadily from all the accounts I get and they are all enjoying the lovely weather we are having. Hoping it will be kind to you when you come North and with best regards to Mr. Lewes from whom I expect to hear
Ever yours sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 May 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 May 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinburgh | May 14/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
My Uncle came home on Monday with, I am distressed to say, a very sharp attack of bronchitis upon him. All last night and yesterday he suffered a great deal but I am thankful to say that he was a great deal easier and better when I left him about an hour ago and I trust that the improvement will continue. The bitter cold wind that there was all last week at St. Andrews has struck into him and he ought never to have exposed himself to it but he would not listen to Mrs. B's advice and warning. It is most vexatious as he had been so very much better and the attack will I fear greatly weaken him, but if we get the inflamation lessened his recuperative powers are wonderfully good yet and I hope he will soon be about again and able to start on his London visit.
He quite agreed with me about accepting Baron Tauchnitz' offer on your behalf for £50 as we are not likely to have a sale abroad that would be so advantageous. Accordingly I have written to Mr. Williams 235 accepting offer. Van Druten declines our terms for translation and Bohn reduces his offer from £20 to £10 as it is not a story. I inclose the letters and one from Dr. Lehman in answer to a former one that I replied to. I rather like the tone of Dr. Lehman's letter and if he is a publisher and agrees to offer a liberal sum I should advise your accepting it. 236 Bohn's offer you will I suppose decline although I fancy his translation would be Dutch.
By book post I have at last the pleasure of sending you specimens of proposed binding some of which will I hope meet with your approval. We like 1 and 2 we like best, and you must only return the one you select and if you desire any alterations will you let us know? Could you please return it tomorrow?
I am happy to tell you that Mudie has written from Rome ordering 500 to start with and our traveler took orders for 55 in Oxford yesterday which is very good.
Ever yours sincerely
William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 13 February 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 13 February 1880
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letterbook. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. Edinburgh | February 13/80.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I have the pleasure of enclosing Bank order £784-10-8d being amount due to you on your works at this time as per accompanying statement which I hope you will find all correct. If there is any point on which you desire explanation do not hesitate to ask me and I will do my best to make it clear. The sales of both the Cabinet and Cheap editions are most satisfactory and from the reports Mr. Langford has sent you and me I trust another as good year is before us.
How rejoiced your friend my dear Uncle would have been to have written to you with enclosed and it fills my eyes with tears thinking over it that he is no longer beside me to talk over some of the joys of the business. I am rather behindhand in sending you this statement but you know full well the cause of the delay and I feel sure you will excuse it.
I was very much touched by the affectionate way you spoke of me to Mr. Langford who is here now and told me of it soon after his arrival. I thank you sincerely and trust you will continue to find me worthy of the regard. We are getting on with our heavy task and duty and when he returns to London he will call and tell you all. I was very happy to hear from him you were keeping so well in health, and hoping this continues to find you so believe me with best regards
Always yours Sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.
P.S. The new edition of the Sayings has just been brought up to me and by book post I have the pleasure of sending you a copy. I hope it will please you. Should you wish some more sent you just let me know. Mr. Langford asks me to present his best regards to you.
W. B.

Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 13 August 1880
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. Edinburgh | August 13/80
My dear Mrs. Cross x x x x. In May and June business was terribly dull and even your works were not selling freely but last month things have revived I am glad to say. Before Mr. Langford went away for his holiday on the 29th of July he sent me a memo of the sales for that month and I enclose copy 466 from it of your books and of his assistant's from 29th to August 7th both which I hope will be interestingly agreeable to you. I think we have no cause to be dissatisfied. We have still copies in stock of Theophrastus and as there were a good few in the hands of the trade we thought it advisable to postpone publication of it in the Cabinet form until October although should we be sold out before then we would supply orders from Cabinet edition when asked for. Kindly excuse this long letter and believe me Dear Mrs Cross
Always yours Sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.
P.S. I was very happy to be able to enroll Charles in the Brotherhood of Maga and I hope you liked his first contribution. 467
(sig.) W.B.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 13 August 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 13 August 1878
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh August 13/78.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I am glad you troubled me again about the specimen page of Spanish Gypsy as I should have been vexed afterwards had not both you and Mr. Lewes been quite satisfied with its appearance. I suspect Mr. Lewes had been comparing it along side of present edition of Spanish Gypsy which is printed on a toned paper and accordingly this specimen page would look white and ghastly. I suppose you do not wish it printed on a toned paper for Cabinet Edition as it would not then be uniform. However I have had some proofs pulled on the Cabinet Edition Paper from different types and under separate cover I send two for selection. The page marked II is printed from the same type as the prose works of the Cabinet Edition. That marked I is printed from the finer faced type which from its sharpness and clear outline printers consider well adapted for poetry. The specimen page previously shown you was printed rather light in the colour which also might have caused you to feel it as not easy to read. Of course to my sharp and young eyes still the sharp freed type seems best but we shall be very glad to adopt whichever you or Mr. Lewes prefer.
I am sorry that the binding of the birthday book has been completed and we only delayed its publication as business had got so bad and we thought a book of that peculiar nature would have a better start in October. I quite join in your condemnation of the binding but we had to consider a colonial class rather as likely to be its largest buyers and cater to their taste accordingly.
As I know you would be anxious and fretting yourself about the D. Deronda I wrote off at once but it is always a pleasure to me to write to you. You are always so considerate to save one trouble and I wish some other authors showed as much consideration for their publishers who imagine they have nothing to do but attend to their bantlings.
Always yours sincerely
(signed) W. Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 12 January 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 12 January 1880
MS: Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Endorsed: Letter about "Theophrastus" Jan. 1880. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
January 12/80.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
In terms of our amended agreement of October 3/79 for [Theophrastus] I have the pleasure of enclosing you cheque £400- in full of the copies printed as stated to you at that date. We have still 97 copies in stock of this 10/6 edition but I have little doubt they will gradually disappear from our shelves as Mr. Langford reports to me that we sold 38 in London during December and I am only annoyed to find that the Scotch sale has so fallen away as we have only sold 3 since September. I cannot quite make it out as our sales at first here were particularly good and the book was so very popular all over Scotland. I hope that by Easter or just after that we shall be able to make a start with the Cabinet edition of it.
On looking through some letters laid aside by my good Uncle I found the enclosed the other day and it was I suppose the original "copy" of Title page for Theophrastus and you may like to preserve it along with the rest of the M.S.S. I was very happy to hear a good account of you from dear old Langford last week and your cordial reception of him pleased and gratified him much. It was also gratifying to me to hear from him of the deep interest that you take in my future welfare and your warm anxiety for me in the onerous duties I have to perform and I thank you very heartily as encouragement from you is very reassuring.
I have had a nasty attack of influenza which has made me very useless and miserable since New Year's day but I am getting better now and hope to be quite fit for that horrible valuation the details for making which will be all ready about end of the month. I shall not fail to let you know when I am well through it. Mrs. John Blackwood and her daughter came over last week and are wonderfully well but are daily feeling more and more conscious of the change that has come over their life. Your kind expressions were very comforting to them. Believe me
Always Yours Sincerely
William Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
P.S. Many thanks for your prompt answer to Professor Miklejohn's wishes. W.B.
P.S. On rereading my letter I see I forgot to mention to you that the yearly statement of Sales of your works is in course of preparation and as soon as it is ready I hope to write to you with checque for the Royalties due.
W.B.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 June 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 June 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh June 11/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
My Uncle was very pleased at receiving your most kind and sympathetic letter and he hopes soon to write you again himself. Yesterday he got downstairs to the drawing room and is no worse for the change of air and scene and I trust now his convalescence will progress a little more rapidly although we should be very thankful to see he has thrown off the attack as well as he has. He is very cheery on the whole and my little news about "Theophrastus" quite brightens him up, and to-day I had some very good sales to report to him, Mr. Langford having written to order 500 copies to be sent off by to-day's Steamer as Mudie had sent for another 100 yesterday and during the day they had sold other 44 copies which left them with only 87 copies in stock at Paternoster Row. As I anticipated this demand we had sent off 200 copies on Monday which they would receive this morning and we have other 250 coming in from the Binder [To Ship] this evening so they would not run short to-day.
We have ordered paper to reprint again as soon as we deem it advisable and I shall take care that the corrections you wish made are attended to. Your letter with them was not in time for the second edition the number printed of which was 1575 and from enclosed Memo you will see half the edition are sold. I congratulate you heartily on the success and I hope it is cheering you as much as it does my uncle and whatever the reviewers may choose to write about it we have the more substantial proof that the public are well satisfied to receive such an admirable work from you.
We think we like "The Times" review the best of any we have seen. 269 When you have time to write we shall be glad to hear how you are and if you are deriving benefit from the country. Believe me
always yours sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 10 February 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 10 February 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. Edinburgh | 10 February 1860.
My dear Madam
The M.S. of the 2d volume of the Mill on the Floss came safe to hand this morning. I take this opportunity afforded in acknowledging its arrival to express to you the pleasure with which I have read that portion of the book which is already in proof. I have been delighted with it. The Dodson family are all very good. I was going to say I am divided betwixt Mrs. Pullet [and] Mrs. Glegg; when I think however of Mrs. Tulliver in her quiet helplessness I begin to doubt whether she is not as good as either. Mrs. Pullet, Mrs. Tulliver, and the bonnet afford I think as fine a comic scene 477 as I ever saw. I don't think I am mistaking the word saw, for the description is so good and easy and natural that I really think I did see Mrs. Pullet turning slowly round like the lay figure and Mrs. Tulliver's awe-struck admiration. Maggy is very good and I expect a great deal from her yet, in which I feel pretty confident I shall not be disappointed. Tulliver and his sister too the scene between, both affecting and humorous. 478 Altogether from what I have read I can with truth assure you that I think the Mill on the Floss will not disappoint the most enthusiastic reader of Adam Bede. I beg to be kindly remembered to Lewes and believe me My dear Madam
Yours ever truly
W. Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, [? November 1880]
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, [? November 1880]
Text: Blackwood Letter Book.
My dear Mrs. Cross
It is a long time since we have heard from one another and I feel the fault lies on my side but it is not from my not thinking of you as I have daily intended for weeks past to write you but some matter of business more urgent than another seemed to crop up day after day and made me postpone my letter to you. When I last heard from you you had not been very well and had gone to Brighton for some bracing air which, I was glad to learn from a letter you wrote to either Mr. Langford or Mr. Henderson shortly after, had done you much good and I trust the improvement continued and that this finds you strong for the short and sunless winter days. I suppose you will have left Witley and are now settled in Cheyne Walk for the winter and I hope are liking it.
Your kind words and sympathy with us in our heavy sorrow were very comforting and gratifying and sorely have I felt my gallant and warm hearted brother's death. 558 Every mail continues to bring us fresh particulars of how he was wounded and killed and how much he was valued which keeps opening up the wound although it makes the memory of him a proud satisfaction to us. Poor fellow he was wounded early in the fight in the inside of the thigh which disabled him from riding as the day wore on, then in the ankle and finally a sabre cut on the head killed him when fighting with the brave 66th in the garden enclosures. But I must not inflict you with more harrowing details of the sad disaster and our grief.
Now to business matters. I am very happy to tell you that although business in general has been terribly dull your books have been selling capitally and I enclose you memo of last month's London sales which will interest you. Mr. Langford also writes me that they have been doing equally well during this month. Theophrastus in the 5/- form has not however started as well as I expected and the London subscription was 620 and between Glasgow and Dublin and here we disposed of about another hundred I daresay. But I have no doubt there will be a continuous dropping sale which should we have any new work from you to bring out is sure to give it a fresh impetus and I hope I may soon hear from you that there is something on the stocks.
You will I expect be deeply interested in Laurence Oliphant's forthcoming work "The Land of Gilead," 559 and your acceptance of a presentation copy will give me pleasure. I shall also be sending you the first Volume of our Philosophical Classics next week and I hope you will be pleased with the way Mr. Mahaffy has done Cervantes. 560 The series will not I fear be so popular as our Ancient Classics but yet I hope it will do fairly well. I wonder if you will read Endymion. 561 I have read the first volume and it amused me greatly and I long to get at the second this evening.
Looking forward to a letter from you soon and hoping this finds both you and Mr. Cross well believe me
Always yours sincerely
William Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: William Blackwood to GE, [Edinburgh], 30 December 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
William Blackwood to GE, [Edinburgh], 30 December 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letterbook. Hitherto unpublished.
December 30th 1879.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I am rather puzzled how to answer enclosed from Professor Meiklejohn 356 of St. Andrews University as I do not recollect of any like application having ever before been made to us, but you are more likely to recollect and how it was received. If Professor Meiklejohn was one of the young and very promising professors at St. Andrews I should have been inclined to advise your declining his request unless a payment was made by him or his publisher, as these compilations are regular robberies and I am greatly surprised to learn that he is engaged in such a work. Another reason and rather a selfish one that inclines me to ask you to accede to his wishes is that he is engaged upon another work of totally different character and which one of my friends, a brother professor, has advised him to bring to us for publication and I am anxious to secure it but do not let this reason influence you in your decision and I only mention it to you that you might not think hereafter I had not been frank with you in the matter when you saw his name in our list of publications. Moreover we can easily decline the request if you do not approve of it without giving him any grounds of ill feeling towards either you or ourselves.
I had intended writing to you for some days past but one pressing matter or another has obliged me to postpone it from day to day. It was a great pleasure to me to hear that the binding of the Manuscript of Theophrastus was all right and your cordial letter of thanks was very welcome. That interruption in your talk with General Hamley about me and my present responsibilities was annoying but I have no doubt our good friend will be soon calling upon you again and you may then be able to end your talk. Your remarks on easily written criticisms will be very useful to me and I shall try to avoid having such criticisms as you so aptly describe in pages of Maga. It was very good of you to trouble to write me and such sound advice and I trust Maga may benefit from it.
I was happy to hear your good report of your own health. I trust it continues. Mrs. J. Blackwood and her family are all better although she is feeling her desolation terribly. What a sad year this dark and heavy one now about to close has been for us all -- surely the incoming one will be a little brighter. With all kind greetings and good wishes of the season, believe me
Always Yours Sincerely
(signed) William Blackwood.

George St. Edinburgh | October 3/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
As my Uncle is far from well and has been told by his medical adviser to quit his desk he sends me the enclosed letter to forward to you and desires me to write you the business one he was unable to overtake yesterday.
The accompanying memorandum will show you that 6190 copies have been printed of "Theophrastus Such" of which there seems to have been about 350 on hand when the balance was prepared, but reckoning these as sold which they will be leaves, after deducting Presentation Copies and 25th books, 5828 to be accounted for to you which at the lordship of 3/- per copy fixed upon would make £874.4.0d but as the sales have gone much beyond our expectation we propose to increase your payment to one thousand pounds (£1000) which will we hope prove satisfactory to you and of this thousand we now enclose draft on London for £600 the rest we shall pay in January next. However he is pretty cheerful and I hope soon to send you a better report of him. I trust that you continue well yourself and that you have been able to enjoy the week of fine weather we have had. Believe me for Partner and self
