Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 28 October 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 28 October 1876
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews October 28/76.
My dear Lewes
I had much pleasure in receiving your Letter which leaves me little doubt that we shall arrange about the work to the satisfaction of all concerned.
I am not surprised that you put the question about the contingency of an additional £500 on the sale of 2000 sets mentioned in my letter making the offer ten years ago. 550 Some time back I said to Willie who had copied it "Why you must have made a blunder in copying; I intended twenty thousand sets," and I never doubted that I had so written. Now it turns out that the blunder is my own, but how such a blunder could have escaped both myself and copyist I cannot understand. I meant not an average sale per year but an average sale of the volumes overhead in that number of years for which 2000 would have been an absurdly inadequate figure. Simpson and Willie both think now they must have taken it up as a yearly average and that seems to be your impression.
Anyway the mistake is clearly mine and I ought to suffer. I would not grudge it a bit especially on books with which we have been so successful but I see that this £500 will sweep up the whole publisher's profit on this long transaction and the idea running in my head that we could afford to pay £500 when we had sold 20000 sets was obviously a fair one. In regard to what you say of the success, admirable and recuperative as the sales have been since the publication of Middlemarch, you will see that the total number sold is still some 8000 volumes short of the numbers on which we based our estimate. You should have heard from me sooner but I was perplexed when I saw by your letter that
I must have made a stupid blunder and I had to communicate with Edinbr. to see whether they could clear it up there.
ever yours truly
(Signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
October 25/77.
My Dear Lewes
We now beg to make the following offer for the library edition of the Works of George Eliot now in preparation in nineteen volumes to sell nominally at 5/- per volume. On the 17 prose volumes we propose to pay a lordship of 1/1'bd on each copy of every volume sold after the first 500, and on the two volumes of Poetry, The Spanish Gipsy and Jubal, a lordship of 1/6 and 1/8 respectively on the same condition of a first free sale of 500 copies.

yours most sincerely
John Blackwood

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 21 July 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 21 July 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
July 21/66.
My Dear Lewes
I think this is about the date you mentioned as likely to catch you at Aix la Chapelle and I hope it will find both of you there well and still enjoying your trip.
I do not know that I ever saw a Novel received with a more universal acclaim than Felix -- the verdict of the Press has amply confirmed all that you and I thought of it. The sale has not yet been so great as I expected, but Mudie had an additional 250 in the beginning of this week and there are other symptoms that the sale is going on. I am not sure as to the exact sale but I think there are about 4400 disposed of. Doubtless the War has affected us, as for a book so admired and universally talked about I would have expected a couple of thousand more to have been gone by this time. 502
I had an amusing illustration the other day of the impossibility everyone feels of reading the book quickly. The chief hair dresser in
Edinburgh, a young female of much shrewdness and a tongue like a Mill Clapper, while pouring forth her praise said, "But do you know, Mr. Blackwood, it has cost me about 5/- at 3d a night from my library to read Felix and enjoy it rightly." I shall give her a copy by and bye for her second reading.
The gigantic events on the Continent occupy all minds and the echo must have come very near you at peaceful Schwalbach. I begin to have a hope that the French Emperor may be checkmated and that we are going to have at last a great united Germany, fit to cope with France. Nothing could have been more unscrupulous and unjust than Prussia's conduct, but only such make conquests. Look at Napoleon or Frederick the Great. Scruples never stood in their way, and men like Carlyle fall down and worship them.
I cannot help feeling desperately sorry for my old friends the Tedeschi. 503 What a feeling it must be for a country to have a noble army like that scattered and smashed in no time. One feels ashamed of caring as much as usual about one's own small concerns in presence of such a calamity to a Nation which, whatever its defects, was in the right in this quarrel.
I have been here almost entirely since I left London, but I go to Edinburgh on Monday to get the Magazine through press. We have delightful weather. I have been busy at Golf. Tell Mrs. Lewes that I do not think she could have been otherwise than pleased with almost every remark I have heard about Felix. Hoping to hear from you soon, I am
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 2 July 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 2 July 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | July 2/68.
My Dear Lewes
I had the pleasure of receiving your letter from Petersthal and I think this should reach St. M'e4rgen about the time you proposed being there. I am glad to hear Mrs. Lewes is so well and enjoying the Black Forest. The sale of the Gypsy was going on very speedily all last week and I think there is now towards 1500 disposed of. There is a good deal of difference of opinion among the reviewers, some apparently suffering under the qualms which assailed me when I came to the turning point of the story. Still they all seem to be of opinion that something big is born into the world. I had to run up to London last week and I found a great many whose opinions I would have cared for were keeping the book to read when they got to the country -- Lord Lytton among the number.
I left London the night before last, passed yesterday forenoon in Edinburgh, and came on here in the evening. It was a hot fatiguing journey and I was said to be looking done, but this morning I am fresh as possible and am off to the links for a grand match which had been arranged in the prospect of my arrival.
Did you get a copy of Kinglake? 784 I intended that you should do so. Send for it when you return if you have not already got it. There has been a large sale and I seem to have hit the right number to print with it as well as the Gypsy which is lucky. None but a real expert can appreciate how much of great work there must be in such matters.
This place is looking lovely and the delight of the change from the heat and bustle of London is inexpressible. Our thermometer however is 74 in the shade.
Give my best regards to Mrs. Lewes, from whom I hope to hear one of these days. My expedition to London quite prevented from taking up The Earthly Paradise but I shall now have quiet for it. The more I see of London the more I am convinced that people read nothing there, at least during the season. I shall write again soon with any news.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 18 September 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 18 September 1871
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | September 18/71.
My Dear Lewes
I have had over several specimens of page for Middlemarch but none that pleases me. The enclosed is I think the right size of paper but I am clear for having less in the page. An opener page will make the book bulk more like the money to the buyer and, is also of importance to the reader when the matter is so fine and so close as in Middlemarch. The increase of bulk will make a slight difference in our Estimates but a mere bagatelle of no importance for either of us in comparison with the probable advantage to the book. By some mysterious oversight Willie has not brought me the Advertisement but doubtless it will turn up tomorrow.
I am as pleased as a child with Mrs. Lewes and you liking my speech so much and thinking you heard me. I had the feeling myself that nobody could have said what I did, and said it so truly.
We had a most glorious Highland Expedition, the weather being simply perfect. My greatest pleasure however was seeing the way my boy entered into the Glories of Ben Lomond and Stobinian. One evening when we were gazing at the Mountains he exclaimed, "By Jingo, Papa, after I shot 366 that partridge I thought of asking you to let me remain at home to shoot, but now I am awfully glad that I came." He is frightfully backward in everything but I would rather have heard that little speech than have seen him do the best latin verses that ever were compiled.
Ever Yours Truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, London, 28 May 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, London, 28 May 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 40.
Jermyn St. | May 28/57.
My Dear Lewes
Yours of the 24th with the touching address of Rosa Cottage reached me today. I wrote to you about a week or ten days ago addressing to St. Heliers and requesting on the cover that if you were not at the Capital of Jersey, the Postmaster should endeavour to find out a maniac answering to your name hammering rocks and dissecting Sea weeds on the shore. I have no doubt the note has reached you and if not you will find it at the Post office, St. Heliers. As far as I recollect there was nothing in my letter except compliments to George Eliot and also to you upon the opening of your new Sea Side Studies.
I am sorry that in moving south I find a still broader piece of water than the Tweed between George Eliot and myself, but I am so confident of his merits that I am content to wait for the confirmation which preconceived ideas of intellect derive from personal acquaintance.
Any one really reading the last part of Gilfil will I think be affected by the cry of love pervading it. That little girl's face comes before me with wonderful distinctness. When I expressed a doubt about the dagger matter[?] I did not mean that it should be, as George Eliot supposed I intended, 874 a dream that "I dreamed in my bed" (a phrase of my precocious infant 20 months old) but a passing dream or thought in the mind not carried the length of actually getting hold of the dagger. I think now however that the author was quite right in his plan.
I have seen a good many literary men since I came up to Town, but I cannot say that I have had anything like literary conversation, but I daresay I shall gather a tolerable idea of the general interest in George Eliot before I leave.
My brother who sent me your letter from Edinburgh will I daresay have sent your Magazines all right, but in case of accidents I send another copy from this. In his note he maintains that Aytoun admits that he was quite wrong in his estimate of the powers of the author of Scenes of Clerical Life and expresses great admiration for the conclusion of Gilfil.
Shall I pay the honorarium into your account?
Hoping soon to hear from you and also from G.E. with the next Tale, I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
I hope you will be able to read this note. An interesting discussion about Derby and Oaks etc. has been going on at my back all the time I have been writing.

MS: Copy in Blackwood's hand, National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Burlington May 26/73.
My dear Lewes
Thanks for your letter which is very handsome and like a gentleman as I expected. I cannot tell you how much it hurts and worries me to have caused you this contretemps, but it will not I trust be any practical loss. Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, London, 24 May 1873(2)
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to Ghl, London, 24 May 1873
Text: Copy by J. M. Langford, National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: Copy, To be copied into private letter book all three letters. W.B. Been copied. W.B. Hitherto unpublished.
The Burlington, Cork St. | May 24/73.
My dear Lewes
I am sorry to say your book 791 grates upon me more than I expected and I have been hesitating for some time whether to say anything to you on the subject but the more I think of it the less I am reconciled to it. I knew quite well that I should not agree with you but I did not expect that the difference between us would have been very wide.
The tone at the commencement assumes too much on your side and apart from the question of your being right or wrong I really think is a mistake. For instance the assumption on page 2 that those are the most weighty thinkers who believe that the world would be better without religion to me is an impossibility and the skit in foot-note early in sheet two about God as an author 792 is neither good for argument or taste.
I am quite aware that most publishers would not object or give weight to their own feelings in this case and God forbid that I should be responsible for all that I do publish, but I do take a very keen interest in all the books we send forth especially when they are the work of a friend and I had rather not publish when I could not heartily enter into the matter and wish you success. Would it put you much out to have another publisher now? Our relations are always so pleasant that I most reluctantly propose this and I have put off and put off writing from day to day.
Commercially of course I would hold myself responsible for our agreement -- should there be any difficulty, which I do not think there would as I believe many would be happy to publish.
I do not myself think that the book will do any harm even in my sense of what would be harm. To me it has rather done good in making me feel how innate is the belief in God and I hope with others. It is as I read that I do not agree with you. Perhaps I mistake what you are driving at. -- To me you seem to give no weight to mind and feeling in the matter. Why do you believe in or love anybody? You can give no scientific reason for so doing.
I am very vexed to write making any difficulty about the book but at all events it is best to be frank with you. 793
Always yours truly
J. B.

My dear Lewes

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, London, 23 May 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, London, 23 May 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: John Blackwood, p. 42.
The Cavendish, Jermyn St. | May 23/58.
My Dear Lewes
I have been paying some visits, and since I came to London a week ago the whirl of engagements has left me no leisure, or rather energy, to get through more than the daily proofs and M.S.S. which every day supplies. This must be my excuse for not sooner answering your pleasant note from Munich, where I am glad to hear that George Eliot and you find so much to interest and amuse you. You are well entitled to a hearty welcome from the Germans and it is to the credit of the Goethe and pipe loving race that they are so cordial. By all means send the Translation from Liebig's Lecture 1137 for the Magazine, unless you think it could appear more advantageously in some other form. I think however that it will suit the Mag. and that will be the best way of making it known in England.
My silence as to the sales of Clerical Scenes and Seaside Studies prevented, I am sorry to say, your having no good news to give. Inclosed is Mr. Langford's mem. of the state of sales in London. It is aggravating but we cannot compel the brutes to buy. As to the Sea-side Studies I have no doubt the edition will go off as the season gets on. We are advertising and I think some copies are gone since this mem. was made out a week ago.
In regard to the Clerical Scenes I am still confident that we will do [them] in a cheaper form, and tell G.E. that I am satisfied the great point is gained, viz., that degree of reputation which ensures a market and readers for the author's next work. The book is talked of everywhere and I am excessively surprised that the sale has not been greater, although to a certain extent I understand it. The following will perhaps interest and amuse G.E. I was smoking my cigar and watching the betters in the enclosure in front of the Stand on the Derby day when I was accosted by Newdigate, 1138 the member for Warwickshire, who after some talk on politics etc. said, "Do you know that you have been publishing a capital series of stories in the Mag., the Clerical Scenes, all about my place and County." My disbelief availed nothing. He knew the author, a Mr. Liggers. This is I think the same unfortunate patronymic that the Manx Cat selected as the author's.
Liggers has not acknowledged the authorship but Newdigate said he had written to him accusing him of it but saying that the stories were told with so much delicacy, good taste, and good feeling that no offence could possibly be taken. Oldinport he said was old Sir Roger Newdigate, and he could send me a key to the whole characters. 1139 The date he considered about the beginning of the present century although more recent characters were introduced. The perfect conviction of Newdigate in the truth of his surmises was very curious, and G.E. must write me a line with a message to him. Newdigate is a capital specimen of an honest high minded English gentleman and Squire, and his opinion is excellent evidence as to the existence of the qualities he attributed to the Tales.
I went to the Isle of Wight to the Revd. J. White, 1140 as I think I told you I intended. Great fun we had, White being one of the most humorous of men. We had one delightful day at Freshwater with Tennyson 1141 whom I had never met before. He was exceedingly pleasant and took Mrs. Blackwood and me a walk nominally of 3 miles which lasted 3 hours at a good pace.
Of literary men the chief specimens I have seen since coming to Town are Bulwer, Thackeray, Warren, 1142 and A. Smith. Bulwer is in great form and I do not think he cares much whether he is to be a Cabinet Minister or not. I hope he will, as I think he has the best head in the House of Commons. I never met any one whose views were so clear and statesmanlike. Very few have any idea what a shrewd practical man he is and how ready to consult the opinions and wishes of others.
Thackeray's daughters had a soir'e9e last night and to be out of the way of the preparations the venerable man dined with us. He says he cannot get ahead with the Virginians and was desperately pushed with the last number, having written the last 16 pages in one day, the last he had to spare. The last two numbers are, I think, better than their predecessors, but he must improve much or the book will not keep up his reputation. He spoke of the Clerical Scenes in the usual terms of praise. By the way Bulwer, as also his son, 1143 a very clever young fellow, spoke in the highest terms of your articles.
The indefatigable Albert 1144 seems pretty well done at present, and no wonder. Fancy playing on that confounded horn and telling the same stories for two thousand nights. He will be greatly the better of his trip to China and I doubt not he will popularise China and give the public a clearer idea of the Chinese than we have hitherto derived from the Tea Chests and three fellows in pigtails crossing the bridge on the old blue plates.
How does Adam Bede get on? Let me know if you wish me to remit or pay into a banker here the honoraria for your Magazine papers.
With best regards to G.E.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
Ministers are now pretty safe for the Session unless Dizzy 1145 commits some absurdity.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, London, 10 June 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 395.
Arlington St. | Piccadilly June 10/76.
My Dear Lewes
I got "The End" today. Grand, glorious, and touching are too mild words for this last book. In fact criticism and eulogism are out of place. I feel more than ever what I have often said to critics: "Bow and accept with gratitude whatever George Eliot writes." 496
The situation of Gwendolen and Deronda is so new too and oh so delicately handled. I felt inclined to burst into the room and prevent Lapidoth from stealing the ring, 497 but the great author knew better and shut the door on the beast for ever.
Give her my best love, respect, and congratulations. It troubled me to see her sitting pale and tired in her carriage at the door yesterday. 498 and I fear I did not say half what I wished to say, but Mrs. Lewes sees every thing and would I trust see what I felt. No wonder she felt tired and unwilling for company, but I earnestly hope that the change across the Channel is already beginning to tell for good.
I intended to have gone to Scotland on Monday, but Delane who has been very ill presses me so earnestly to come to see him at Ascot for a couple of days that I cannot leave without seeing my old friend and companion. So if you write to me address here.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
My guardian angel "Henry" had brought me some note paper which is so much thinner than my own that I find I have written on two sheets of it.

John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 7 March 1864
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 7/64.
My Dear Lewes
Inclosed is a statement of the position of the works of George Eliot as at January /64 and I wish for all our sakes I had a more flourishing account of sales to show; indeed you would have heard from me long ago if I had been able to give cheery news. Adam you will see goes on and Silas slightly but the Mill is very stationary. I hope Mrs. Lewes and you are well and with best regards to her believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 7 July 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 7 July 1862
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh July 7/62.
My Dear Lewes
I could not get Mr. Trollope's Tuscan Chronicle 91 read in London but I have now gone through it carefully and am sorry to say I cannot make use of it. The story is well and clearly told and there are some capital touches but it seems to me too much of a bald horrible chronicle in which none of the characters interest one, not even poor Catarina although she is almost the only one of the lot whose murder would affect one much. The Princess has no remembrance of past happiness destroyed by Catarina to give any one a vestige of sympathy with her in her fiendish revenge, and it is a wonder "Jacopo" did not wind up her "comedy" by murdering her. The story being true does not much matter to the reader unless perchance it had happened recently in Manchester and I think the weight of the infernal denoument he had selected prevents Mr. Trollope from extracting the interest and amusement from the minor characters which his knowledge of the period would have enabled him to give. I regret that I cannot express a more favourable opinion of anything written by Mr. Trollope as independantly of his literary reputation what I had heard of him from you both and also from others very much disposed me to enter into correspondence with him.
I intended to have spoken to you when I called about the review of the Miserables 92 but you were poorly and I could not get to Blandford Square again at the time that suited Mrs. Lewes and you in the afternoon. The passages you quote from Victor Hugo in the beginning of the paper gave me such a turn against him that I felt indisposed for any review of him. Claude Frollo's complaissance to the charms of Esmeralda is so supremely disgusting that I think I would at all events suppress it. The paper is a good one but I do not much fancy it as
Victor Hugo's theories inspire me with a stronger feeling of disgust than you express. I may however like it better at a second reading and in type. I was rather glad to see that Notre Dame did not interest Goethe as I am in this case in the same boat with that great chief.
I hope that you are better and that Mrs. Lewes is well and getting on happily with her work.
Always Yours Truly
John Blackwood.
P.S. I send Mr. Trollope's M.S. by book post.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 7 December 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 7 December 1857
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh | December 7/57.
My dear Lewes
I am very glad to find you entering so keenly into the Editing of Johnston's Chemistry of C. Life and the way in which you propose to handle the book satisfies me that you will do it well.
I quite agree with you that your second plan is the best -- viz: to incorporate the corrections and new matter with the text. The other common plan of constantly putting Editor or Brackets breaks the narrative and interrupts the Reader. In your preface you can give some idea of the extent to which the corrections and additions go.
Do not hurry yourself inconveniently as we have stock to go on with for a time but I will write you again as to the time when we think it would be advisable to begin publishing. I think we shall reissue the work in parts.
My brother is at 38 Jermyn Street but I daresay he will drop you a line. He is only in town for a week and I doubt not very busy.
I am delighted to know that George Eliot is going on with spirit and any report of progress will be very acceptable.
I feel quite friendly towards the old clergyman who was so deeply affected by Janets Repentance -- oddly enough the next letter I opened after yours was from another old clergyman, 352 a correspondent of my own, who said that "Janets repentance was exquisite." This gave me pleasure as the writer is a man of good taste and highly accomplished. My pleasure was shortlived as the next paragraph went on to say, "I must write out my own parochial reminiscences." This gave me a spasm as I more than doubt his power of writing anything like a good story, and I know he will be down upon me with his M.S.
G.E. is too diffident of his own powers and prospects of success. Very few men indeed have more reason to be satisfied as far as the experiment has gone. The following should be a practical Cheerer. When I was away in England my brother got more sanguine than we had been about the Clerical Scenes and increased the impression from 750 to 1000. This will necessitate a change in the sum to be paid to the author for the Edition and I propose that we should pay a further sum of Sixty pounds (£60) when 750 copies are sold.
Ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
I had nearly forgot to say that I think an Index will be desirable for your book. If you can do it without serious trouble you could do it best yourself but I daresay we could manage it here if you were indisposed. Give my regards to G.E.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 6 October 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 6 October 1858
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland. Brief extract published: II, 488, n. 1.
Edinburgh October 7th 1858.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of enclosing a cheque £20 in acknowledgment of your excellent little treatise on Animal Heat. 403 It is really very good.
The prospectus of the great work 404 reads most appetisingly; you are quite an artist at the construction of such things. Towards the end of this month my tent will be permanently pitched in Edinburgh. I shall then have calculations made and make the best proposition I can to you for our joint interests in the Physiology of C. Life. My brother and I are in great hopes that it may be a permanently successful book and no efforts shall be wanting on our part to insure that very desirable end. You are doing your part admirably.
George Eliot would I daresay show you what I said of Adam Vol. 2. It is very difficult indeed to judge of a second volume as one does not read it with the eager curiosity with which one opens the first, or the rapid haste with which one rushes on to the finish, as for example had Vols. 2 and 3 been before me I am sure that I would have read them in less time than I took to Vol. 2 by itself. There can be no mistake about the merits however and I am not sure whether I expressed myself sufficiently warmly. But you know that I am not equal to the abandon of expression which distinguishes the large hearted school of Critics.
I am only here for a couple of days and driving through as much as I can. At St. Andrews we had a visit for some days from Stanfield and Roberts, 405 two excellent men as well as great artists, and I expect the former will give you some idea of the ancient city of St. Regulus 406 on the walls of the Academy next year. You ask whether the excitement of Golf can equal that of Mollusc hunting; I can only say that it transcends anything else that I have tried and all Golfers are of the same opinion. When the game comes to a crisis the boldest hold their breath for a time. I have seen the best of us pale and the voice affected among others gallant Sir Hope Grant 407 a first rate Golfer. Excuse this outbreak and with best regards to G.E.
Believe me
I am yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

January 6/73.
My Dear Lewes
I inclose two bills at 6 and 9 mos. for £1097-16-11, each being half yearly settlement for Middlemarch as per former and accompanying memorandum. You will see that I have only taken half of the discount allowed to Smith off your amount. In some way or other I have very little doubt we would have allowed him 5 per cent discount.

John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 6 April 1859
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh | April 6/59.
My dear Lewes
I think you are mistaken about Owen as I have frequently observed that people generally have a notion that he has done a great deal but nothing like precise knowledge of what it is. That you are mistaken in thinking yourself unfitted for reviewing his discourses I feel certain. You are quite the sort of man to do the thing. The papers in Quarterlies do not much matter.
By the way when you see him ask if in his present state of existence he will ever be able to review Keith Johnston's Physical Atlas. He said he would do so, some years ago but I fear he will always be too busy.

Ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
This is a lovely summer day and I grudge consummately not being in the country.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 5 November 1857
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh November 5th 1857.
My dear Lewes
I have just put your interesting paper on Phrenology 345 into the printing office. The only part where I would seriously object is when you seem to put Phrenology on the same platform as Medicine. I do not think you exactly intend to do so, but any difficulties can be obviated by putting the paper in the form of a letter. Phrenology has not, and never will, discover anything so useful to humanity as an humble black draught or seidlitz powder.
I like the whole of the Illustrations and the charge seems exceedingly moderate. The drawings have a genuine look which is a great thing. The book reads well and I begin to be sanguine. I should like to publish in December but this will depend on your returning the proofs for Press. Do not hurry yourself when you have such a man as Owen to consult and advise with.
Do you know much about Chemistry? I want to find a man who possesses a competent knowledge of science and at the same time writes a pleasant popular style to edit Johnston's Chemistry of Common Life. 346 Poor Johnston's own style was admirably clear and readable and this I have no doubt was the main cause of the wonderful success of the book.
I have once or twice spoken to Lyon Playfair 347 on the subject and he was to have called upon me about it. But as it is a long time ago and he has never come, I consider myself entirely free of him. The impression he made upon me, moreover, was that of not being qualified for the work, "more sound than sense" about him, as we say in Scotland. Of course this is all between ourselves.
Ever yours truly,
Sig[ne]d John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes, Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 4 February 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 4/59.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque 'a314-14/- in acknowledgment of Falsely Accused. 11 It is interesting and curious, but by no means I think one of your first class papers.
You will probably have been to the Row to hear about Adam Bede. Mudie attempted to beat us down, taking only 50 at first, but finally succumbed, taking 500 at our terms 10 per cent off sales, to which I think he is entitled when he takes so large a number. The other subscription was not good, about 'ab250'bb 230 in all when Langford wrote yesterday. Tell G.E. that I am neither surprised nor disappointed by this. As I have often explained before, I felt distinctly that by Clerical Scenes a reputation with readers and men of letters was made, but not a public general reputation, so the orders for the book would not be in the hands of the Row houses, which is the only guide they have in subscribing. When the reviews begin to appear and people who have read the book begin to talk about it the movement will take place.
We are leaving nothing untried to get up the steam by sending copies to the Press in all directions. I have no doubt I shall soon have the pleasure of writing to tell G.E. of the favourable private opinions I hear of the Carpenter. He will be interested and amused by the following. Mr. Simpson had taken a set of the sheets home with him and his brother, a Cabinet Maker, 12 read them with great admiration. He maintains that the writer must have been bred to the business or at all events passed a great deal of time in the workshop listening to the men. This is a curious tribute to one phase of the life-like reality which pervades the whole book. We have not got copies here yet, but I suppose they will arrive tomorrow.
If you can think of anything of the light and lively order for the next number of the Magazine I shall be glad to hear. I quite approve of putting your name to the new edition of Johnston.
Let me know what you think of the article [on] Carlyle 13 in the present number of the Mag.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 4 August 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 4 August 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: John Blackwood, pp. 40-41.
Edinburgh | August 4/57.
My Dear Lewes
I came from the country 945 today and very soon after I arrived I had the pleasure of receiving your note with the packet from G. Eliot and the Seaside Studies.
I did not know that there was any particular call for me to read Janet at once, but it was an immense relief to turn to her from the other mass of papers lying on the table. Part III is admirable. Although Parts 1 and 2 did not exactly hit my taste, my expectations of what was to come were very highly raised, and they are now in the process of being more than answered. The interest rises very high and the first step to a community of feeling between Tryan and Janet is beautifully and most skilfully managed. Towards the close of the part I was in a horrid funk for poor Janet and like her self felt rather relieved when the door was closed upon her. 946
I am only in town for a day but I shall write G. Eliot with the proof from the country. Address here however.
In the meantime I have the pleasure of making a cheque £44, being £20 in acknowledgment of Seaside Studies Part III and 24£ for Janet Part II.
I am afraid you will find Richmond rather hot and dusty at present but with such relaxations as the occasional eye of a cuttle fish to dissect, I daresay you will be able to rub on.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
I have not yet had time to read your M.S. but I daresay you will excuse my giving G. Eliot the pas.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 4 April 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 4 April 1877
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh April 4/77.
My Dear Lewes
I am greatly troubled to see by your letter to Simpson that Mrs. Lewes is so unwell and suffering. The weather has changed at last today and become quite mild. I sincerely hope that this will help to put her all right and that you will be able to reply to this with good accounts of her. Her pleasant letter last week followed me to North Berwick and came in most agreeably to help the change of air in cheering and doing me good.
My wife, son, and daughter went with me and we had a capital expedition from which I am thankful to say I have come back with health quite restored. North Berwick is a very pretty place with breezes blowing fresh from Noroway but I golfed doggedly on and came in daily hungry as a hunter, a sensation I had not experienced for some months. Fresh air and a change are the best of all restoratives.
My room is furnished now with every conceivable form of book for another edition of the Works of George Eliot and we intended to have a sitting on the subject today but Simpson was feeling poorly and had to go home. My thoughts turn very much to a handy handsome edition in 5/ volumes something like the two volume edition of Felix Holt.
Hoping in your next to hear that Mrs. Lewes is better I am
always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 31 December 1858
Text: Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh December 31st 1858.
My Dear Lewis
I enclose a cheque £100 being the first instalment for the Physiology of Common Life.
We have sent out the first part largely on sale but as yet can form no guess as to the probable sale. Indeed we will not have anything like a fair means of judging for a month or two.
Along with this I send the proof of the next two parts arranged as you proposed. You will see that they rather exceed the quantity we fixed upon for each number, but it is no disadvantage to have the early parts portly.
It is not like so knowing a party as you to suggest so dangerous a preface as that proposed for G.E. The single sentence is fully as doubtful a step as the larger preface.
With all good wishes for the year that is opening upon us, I am
Ever yours Truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewis Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 30 March 1859
Text: Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh | March 30th/59.
My Dear Lewes
I enclose a letter for G.E. with continued good accounts of Adam. I am curious to know how he likes the Magazine paper. I was so overwhelmed with M.S.S. this month that I had nothing for it but to postpone the Ponds which will not become stale by the delay.
Stereos from the cuts in the Physiology are being taken for Brockhaus and duplicates will be done at once from the rest of the cuts. How had we best send these as well as the two copies of the book?
Do you ever see anything of Professor Owen now? I sometimes think of a paper on him and his discoveries. I am afraid you would be too heathenish for me. I was remembered of him today by receiving a sort of Abstract of a lecture of his on the Gorilla 437 one of these confounded monkey tribes so disgustingly like ourselves. I know very little of Owen but what I do I admire very much. Scientific men are so often either too dull or too trifling, but he is entirely free from any of these faults.
ever yours truly,
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 30 April 1858
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland. Extract published: II, 449, n. 8.
Edinburgh April 30/58.
My dear Lewes
I would have written as soon as I heard that you were safely housed in Munich had I not waited until the proof which accompanies this was ready. This first paper on the Blood is technical enough but good, especially in the latter part.
Give my best regards to George Eliot and tell him that he will find me quite ready to meet his wishes by the publication of Adam Bede as a separate work at once. In whatever form the Tale first sees the light I am sure it will be an excellent thing both for the pocket and for the reputation of the author.
I am very anxious to hear how it gets on and shall be delighted to see more of the MS when ready. I would write to G.E. but I am desperately busy, having run myself into a corner for time. This you will readily imagine when I mention that I leave for England tomorrow.
I hope your hunt for Lodging at Munich has proved a successful one and that this will find you very comfortable in the Luitpold Strasse.
I am not going direct to London, having one or two visits to pay which will occupy me until the 10th of May. Let me hear from you whenever you can and I promise faithfully to give you a spell of London news.
Always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
Address to me here.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 30 April 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 30/57.
My Dear Lewes
I inclose proof of Mr. Gilfil part the last. It is very powerful and very affecting. The description of Maynard's feelings is excellent, especially when he rides off to find the lost one after his interview with Daniel. I incline to think that the patois of Daniel and Dorkis. stands too prominently forward in the scenes where the feelings are so highly wrought up. 848 The effect of the farmyard scene is very happy and true. The picture reminds me strongly of the genuine English rural landscapes with which we are all familiar on canvas or in nature. The part altogether strikes sadly in the heart and I should have liked a larger gleam of sunshine before poor Tina passed away, but I see that it could not be. Maynard's exposition of how we sometimes think too well and sometimes too ill of ourselves is excellent, 849 and it is very sound doctrine.
If George Eliot is not with you I suppose you will send this to him. Tell him what I say, and you may mention also that I have some fear that he huddles up the conclusion of his stories too much, but I hardly see how the wind up of Gilfil's sad story could have been more effective or affecting. I hope the successor to Gilfil is well advanced.
I got your note of the 26th yesterday and it caused me still further to reproach myself for not having written to you sooner. How quick the letter must have come. I trust that my letter of 28th will reach you as quickly to relieve your anxieties about your packets. I shall pay cheque for the Seaside Studies into the Union Bank to credit of your account.
I am delighted to hear that you continue to like your isle so much. I am tempted to envy your power of amusing yourself so easily, although
I daresay if you saw me starting for a Golf match you would think my tastes still more simple, if not even childish.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 3 February 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 3 February 1872
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh | February 3/72.
My Dear Lewes
I have repeatedly intended to write you with details and prospects of sales of Part 2 but Langford has been provokingly chary of information on the subject. In note with enclosed Mem. received today he says "there is nothing at present to indicate the progress of the Sale."
The falling off is in the numbers taken by Mudie and Smith and Sons and I would rather have this falling off in that quarter than in any other. The sale of part two will have turned 4000 and that of part one must be something like 5400. My feeling about the book is that you may make your minds easy as to its commercial success, and as to its merits as far as I have read they go beyond what even I had ventured to hope for.
Part two will more than sustain the reputation of Part I and as for Part three it is transcendant. I cannot imagine anything of its kind more neat than the capture of Lydgate. It is done with such fine touches, is so simple and so true. Who does not remember at battledore the effect of stooping at the same moment with a fair friend to pick up the fallen shuttlecock? 459 I remember one case in particular when if the tear had been there as well as the smile I would have been done for at a very early stage in life.
We have fine weather now and I hope Mrs. Lewes and you are both enjoying it and feeling better therefrom. Tell her my firm belief will turn to these Books of Middlemarch over and over, again and again. I find it so with Book one in my own house.
Ever Yours Truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 3 February 1858
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh February 3/58.
My dear Lewes
I had the pleasure of hearing from Mr. Langford yesterday that in addition to the subscription of which I wrote to you on Saturday, Mudie had taken 200 and would take 500 if we would give the extra percentage. I wrote to give it and would have written to tell you the good news had I not thought it probable you might have heard it at the Row. 366
I think very little of the subscription to Books unless in the case of a succession of Books similar in character by the same author. Then the subscribers can really form a good estimate as the orders are up from the country, but in most other cases unless there has been a regular clamour about the forthcoming Book the subscription is no index although it is always pleasant to see it large. A month ago we subscribed about 600 of Lord St. Leonards Handy Book 367 and have since sold 15000!
I have the pleasure of enclosing a cheque £75 being payment in full for the first edition of the Sea-Side Studies as agreed. The cancel does not matter. We take such things as the chance of War.
In making the arrangement for your Book and for Clerical Scenes I should have named a date for payment and I had not intended to pay until six months after publication as is usual, but let me know if G.E. wishes or expects payment at once.
Ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes, Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 29 February 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
February 29/76.
My Dear Lewes
I had a pleasant letter from Mrs. Lewes on Saturday and note from you today and I only wish they contained better accounts of both your healths but I trust better weather and the continued most cheering reception of Deronda will help to put you soon right.
As Mrs. Lewes says she has got a little confused about the total number sold, I have had the memorandum I inclose made up which will be about accurate.
The sale of Book 2 is greatly more than that of Book one at the corresponding date last month and in the course of March I hope he will quite overtake Book 1. Mudie has not yet sent in for the second supply 250 that he took of Book 1 but from the demand on the part of the public Langford feels confident he must have it immediately.
From the state[ment]s you have of Middlemarch you will see that Deronda has already got ahead of his great predecessor.
The impression the book is making is enormous and the small cavillers will only do good by exciting discussion and helping on the overwhelming verdict against them.
On the whole the Critics are behaving very well, and I only wonder those who take little exceptions venture, on the imperfect state of their information, to do anything but cry hurrah over the splendid banquet that is opening before them. If Mrs. Lewes heard the excited speculations over Mordecai among the privileged few here who have read Book V she would be more than satisfied with the impression her wonderful Jew is making. The printers promise Book 6 tomorrow and I hope proofs will be ready to post for you but I am not quite certain.
I am very sorry to see what you say of Lady Lytton's health and also that you do not think him looking very fit. I do hope all will go well with them. A sort of comparative coolness had arisen between him and me, but as I felt that it arose from his being so much in the hands of poor Forster, who was always an unfriend to Blackwoods, it did not interfere with my warm regard to Lytton and his charming wife.
Write soon to tell me how you both are.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 28 October 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | October 28/57.
My Dear Lewes
I inclose proof of the first 48 pages of your book. It is very difficult to form any estimate of the probable demand and we hesitate a good deal as to the number we should print. We incline to try an edition of 1250 as it will require some such sale to give anything like a good return. What do you think?
Until this is fixed and I know the exact cost and appearance of the engravings I have no data to guide me in making you an offer for the edition but in the meantime I understand that we take the whole risk of the publication and divide profits with you when any such arise.
I shall miss the Clerical Scenes much. I shall be curious to see how they tell as a separate book.
I daresay it would have been no use, but I wish I had pressed George Eliot more to curtail or to indicate more delicately the Delirium Tremens scene. 996 It is too naked and the shudder with which one turns from the picture is too much akin to disgust. He does push his Theory of qualifying any description by its truth too far. This scene would be more effective if more were left to the imagination. I intended to send you a copy of Smith's book 997 and he also put you on his list. What do you think of it?
Let me know if you have any subject for an article in view.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 28 November 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 28 November 1857
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh | November 28/57.
My dear Lewes
That you may fully understand the position of "Sea-Side Studies" I inclose our estimate. The only uncertain points are the advertising and engravings. The paper and boarding are what we pay and the printing is what we would charge to the book were it entirely our own property. The Corrections and extras being estimated from the expense incurred in the sheets already sent to press. The 10 per cent Commission is fully required to cover the discounts from Saleprice allowed to the wholesalers the loss of interest etc. on the length of time that must elapse before we are paid for the Edition even supposing the sale to be very rapid. I grudge the £50 in advertising but I do not think we can spend less. You are I see sparing no labour or trouble on the Volume and my brother and I wish to give you so much as we possibly can consistently with having ourselves any fair chance of remuneration on the undertaking.
We now beg to offer you £75 for the Edition or if you prefer to wait and take your chance of the result we will pay you two thirds of the clear profits when these arrive.
I am glad you think you can edit and bring down to the present state of Scientific Knowledge the Chemistry of Common Life and I have desired an interleaved copy to be sent you. If on looking over the Book you think you can do what is required I should like you to set about it as soon you find leisure. I imagine that very considerable additions will be desirable but you will be best able to judge. I cannot of course form any accurate idea of the amount of labour you will require to bestow in re-editing the book but at all events I propose to give you one hundred guineas (£105.) if that sum meets with your ideas.
I would have written to you sooner about this had I not hesitated a little as to whether an Editor with a Scientific reputation was not absolutely necessary but having the work really well done is much more essential than the bubble reputation and I have seen so much of your businesslike conscientious mode of writing that I feel quite confident anything you undertake will be well done.
Enclosed I have the pleasure of sending a cheque £10.10. in acknowledgement of your little paper on Phrenology in France. My brother goes up to London next week and hopes to have an opportunity of making your acquaintance.
With regards to G. Eliot
I am ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 28 December 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland and Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
December 28/75.
My Dear Lewes
It gives me much pleasure to receive your letter today and most cordially do I and all your friends here respond in warm good wishes to Mrs. Lewes and you. I often wish she could hear some of our home talk about Daniel as it might lighten some of her despondent views. We speak of the book and the characters as of realities, and the exquisite selfishness of Grandcourt's complaint that Mrs. Glasher had made him feel quite unwell that morning has so tickled us that a reference to that scene 373 is applied to all unreasonable complaints.
Simpson showed me a comprehensive scheme of advertising and "billing" Deronda and I have no doubt he is carrying it out energetically. He is not here today owing to a slight touch of cold and I am sending him your letter as I know your kind message will be very grateful. I have desired Title pages to be set for your approval.
I have already sounded the glories of Deronda in the Times direction and I have very little doubt they will notice the first part at once.
Inclosed I have the pleasure of sending a cheque £333-1-6d being the royalty for the year on Middlemarch, Jubal, and The Spanish Gypsy as per accompanying memorandum. 374 You will I hope join me in thinking it very satisfactory, especially as regards Middlemarch and the Gypsy. Jubal I think ought to sell more.
I am sorry to hear the Life of Heine is so worthless. The compiler must I think be a literary gentleman who was introduced to me some years ago and wrote submitting a list of a dozen subjects all of which he was equally ready to handle. It would have required an intellectual giant with even a few of the subjects proposed, so I intimated that my hands were full or did not answer at all. I must find you some better book.
This is a fine bright day and instead of golfing I am actually going to drive into the country with my wife to make a Christmas call.
The approach of this season generally makes me very dull as it recals so many so very dear who are gone, but when the time comes I feel as of old and our dinner party on Saturday was very bright. My nephew joins me in all good wishes to you both.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 28 April 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 28/57.
My Dear Lewes
I inclose proof of the New Seaside Studies which from the number of my engagements I could not manage to run this month. The paper is very amusing and not the least amusing feature about it is the enthusiasm with which you set out in such weather on such a journey to pursue your researches into the nature of these living sea weeds.
Your enthusiasm prevents you from seeing the peculiar effect of the analysis of the faeces of the Actiniae and I wish you would delete or alter a portion of this. The quotation from your clinical authority is painfully minute and could not be otherwise than distasteful, especially to ladies who form a large section of the readers of such papers.
It has just come across me that in the month in which I have been since my return home I did not acknowledge the receipt of the conclusion of Mr. Gilfil. Pray make my apologies to the author and tell him that I have been even more than usually busy since my return home. There are most exquisite passages in the part and the pathos is very powerful. As a whole it strikes rather too drearily upon the heart, but I do not see how this was to be avoided.
It is a dangerous thing to let the reader know the upshot of a Tale before he gets to the end of it, and no one could in the circumstances have kept up the interest more powerfully than George Eliot has done. There is a very general tendency to attribute the series to Bulwer, of all people in the world. The notion I daresay has mainly arisen from the fact of Sir Edward having written so much in the Magazine, and when people have any such leading clue as that they flatter themselves by imagining that they detect resemblances of style. There are some touches in Mr. Gilfil which look a little like Sir Edward, but how the mistake should be made about Amos I cannot imagine.
Thackeray spoke to me a good deal about the series and thinks highly of it. He said he ceased to read Gilfil when he came to the mournful picture of the dead wife's chamber. One can understand his feelings on such a subject. 846
The picture of Tina's woe has made a very powerful impression on me and I do not know when I have read anything more painfully touching. Nevertheless I am glad to hear from George Eliot that his next story was to be on a brighter theme. I shall be exceedingly happy to see it and hope it is well advanced. In two or three days I shall write you again with the proof of the fourth part of Gilfil.
Meanwhile I hope you continue to enjoy yourself in the quaint isle in which you have stuck up your temporary tent and I trust this will reach you in safety.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
H. G. Lewes Esq.
I am greatly disposed to have a walk into the biographer of poor Charlotte Bronte, and a friend has proposed a paper to me. There is execrable taste in the book, and I detest this bookmaking out of the remains of the dead which must be so grating to the feelings of all whom the dead cared for. 847

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 26 November 1858
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh November 26/58.
My Dear Lewes
Along with this I send a revise of the first part of the Physiology 409 which Mr. Brown 410 has read and makes one or two suggestions as you will see on the margin.
Your hearty acceptance of our offer gives us much pleasure and the feeling you show will add not a little to our satisfaction, should the book prove a great success, while it increases our anxiety to ensure the same.
Inclosed I have the pleasure of sending a cheque £14.14- in acknowledgement of your delightful little paper on Biot. In regard to the dates of payment to you for the Physiology we propose to pay you one hundred when the first number is published and the rest when it is completed, but if you wish the second payment sooner we will be happy to accommodate you. There is also the pleasant possibility of the sale in numbers going beyond 5000 which would accelerate payments and if it does sell above the 5000 in numbers we would make the payments correspond very much with the date of publication or half yearly.
Let us have the copy back soon for press. Tell G.E. that the sheets arrived safely and are sent to press. I think it is wise to lessen the quantity of the local dialect. We are rather puzzled to get on just at present as "Adam" and "What will He do with it" 411 are printing in the same type and from a want of return of proofs of the last there is about a ton and a half of Type locked up. This difficulty will however be overcome immediately.
Ever yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes, Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 26 February 1869
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 26 February 1869
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. | Edinburgh 26th February /69.
My Dear Lewes
I would with pleasure assent to the proposed arrangement for the simultaneous publication of Lisa in America but I am afraid it would be a breach in our agreement with the American Reprinters of the Magazine to whom we are bound to send early Sheets.
I do not think that letting another publisher have the start of them with Lisa would do the reprint the slightest harm, but they would be pretty sure to make a pretence of it and we have at present quite sufficient difficulty in getting them to pay up. If you can get any material sum from the Americans do not consider me at all, as although I admire the Poem so much I shall not be in the least disappointed although it should be published elsewhere.
It was the knowledge that you were going abroad so soon that made me think you wished the Poem published at once. I hope you will have a famous expedition and a letter or two will be most welcome. I intended to have worked all day but an insinuating Golfer has come in and is carrying me off to the Links at once.
Always Yours Truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 25 November 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 25 November 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 25/76.
My Dear Lewes
I have much pleasure in receiving your frank acceptance of our proposal for The Works and I sincerely hope the result will be a good steady sum to be settled yearly.
Like you I was rather startled when I found we had printed 2000 of Daniel in the 21/form although I have no doubt I had settled or assented to the number. However even if it should hang on hand for a time it will always be good stock and I would not allow it to interfere with bringing out the 7/6 edition when the right time comes.
I am sorry to hear of the three or four errors. Are they worth mentioning in an Errata at the end or a cancel or two? Simpson says he wrote to inquire whether there were any corrections for the reprint and the answer was no. I too remember something of this when we printed for Australia.
The Jews should be the most interesting people in the world, but even her magic pen cannot at once make them a popular element in a Novel. The discussion however goes on and the power she has expended on the despised element will tell and force its way. The fact is that Mrs. Lewes stands on such a pinnacle that the Critics are (unconsciously perhaps) glad to fix upon anything they can possibly mention as a flaw. Great success always bears this penalty with it. Bulwer felt it keenly and so did Dickens and Thackeray in a lesser degree. I remember a very hearty laugh with dear old Aytoun. He was complaining humorously of his treatment by the Press in his maturer years and said "Confound the fellows. They used to make me blush at their praises but now they have found out I am a Sheriff and a Professor they won't leave a literary feather on my back." 566
We have famous wintry weather here now and I hope it is agreeing with Mrs. Lewes and you. My wife and I are alone, our daughter having gone to visit her Aunts in England. It is a sad blank in the house but we have always a good deal to talk and think about.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 25 March 1858
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh | March 25th 1858.
My Dear Lewes
Your preface is capital, really quite a model. I was so much struck with its neatness and clearness that Aytoun, who is a considerable artist at such things, coming into my room, I handed it to him saying, There is a thing that you could not beat in its way. -- He quite agreed with me. -- I shall be glad to see the whole work when you are ready to send it down.
George Eliot will think that I am forgetting him but I am not. I think a good deal about Adam Bede every day. There being no absolute necessity for hurry in the reperusal, I have thought it better both for him and me to delay until I was a little out of my present turmoil of occupation. Tomorrow night the Magazine will be off my hands for the month, and in a few days I shall be able to write at length about the excellent Adam.
I send you the first number of Tales from the Magazine. I thought of starting the scheme ten years ago and delayed for what reason I do not know. It has been much in my mind during the last fortnight and should be a great success. Let me know what you think.
I shall not forget to send you proof of the next part of "Food" in time. When do you intend to start?
Ever yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
I have no recent information from London about the "Studies" or the "Scenes."

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 24 December 1866
Text: Copy in George Simpson's hand, National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh, 24th December 1866.
My dear Lewes
I am quite vexed to hear that you are still so poorly, but I hope that the change to the South will put you all right. Pray take a good spell of freedom from work while you are about it.
People are very fond of writing books to teach others to think, but if some one could teach you not to think for a spell it would be doing you a good turn. I hope however that the sun on the Continent will partially have that effect.
I hope the new adventure with the Novels may be a happy and prosperous one for all concerned. 555
With every good wish of the Season I am always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 24 April 1874
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. Edinburgh | April 24/74.
My Dear Lewes
The specimen copies of Jubal will go to you tonight and Mr. Simpson will write with explanation. Business has been so dull that we have not been hurrying anything on. We have as I told you printed 1500 copies and the lordship we propose to pay is 1/6 on each copy sold. The Advertising must be so heavy on the first edition that it will not bear more than that, even selling at 6/- which is a high enough price for a Volume of the size. I think however that the appreciators of Mrs. Lewes' Poetry do not care much whether they pay 5/- or 6/-.
I hope you are both well and enjoying this fine weather. Some of our days are almost finer and warmer than anything we had except for two or three days last summer.
Willie can walk for a moderate distance now without visible lameness and he can get on a horse again which is a great solace to him and seems to act like a "hair of the dog that bit him." . . .
This is the "Preachings" here this week and Willie has gone to the country otherwise he would join me in best remembrances to Mrs. Lewes. Our intention is to be in London on 17th May and I was selfishly glad to hear that you would still be there.
Ever Yours Truly
(Signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 24 April 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 24/66.
My Dear Lewes
I inclose formal offer for Felix Holt which our previous correspondence leads me to believe will be accepted. I would write a long letter but from various causes I only got the two volumes finished about an hour ago and it is now close upon post time.
I am lost in wonder and admiration of Mrs. Lewes' powers. It is not like a Novel and there may be a complaint of want of the ordinary Novel interest, but it is like looking on at a series of panoramas where human beings speak and act before us. There is hardly a page where there is not some turn of expression, witty or wise or both which one loves to dwell upon, but there is no time to write more.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 24 April 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 24 April 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 52.
Edinburgh | April 24/60.
My Dear Lewes
The magnanimous Mudie is nibbling at a third thousand of The Mill and I have little doubt tomorrow or next day will bring intelligence that he has taken them. The doubt is something about when we are to publish a cheaper edition as to which he is striving to obtain a pledge from Langford which he will not get. Mudie taking this third thousand will reduce the remainder of the 6000 printed to a manageable shape. It is very satisfactory. The worst feature in the sale is that Simpkins has still 300 (a few days ago) of the 500 they took. Hamiltons again however are quite satisfied with the sale of their copies. There are dropping sales to libraries but not such as to be features worth mentioning. The reviews generally have been very favourable and there has been nothing offensive that I have seen.
I have a long critical letter from Bulwer. He objects to many things, but his admiration for Mrs. Lewes' genius is as clear and genuine as could be wished and he places The Mill above Adam. As you do not wish any criticisms while abroad I do not send you the letter; besides it is very bulky, being written on very thick paper and in his widest hand. There has been no review in the Times yet.
Rather better than a thousand have been subscribed of the second volume of The Physiology.
I hope this will find you both well and continuing to enjoy Rome. You will I suppose be thinking of moving soon, and you should go to Naples. The expeditions about there are so perfectly delightful. I have not much news from London, the fight for the Championship 533 monopolising everyone's attention. It is quite comical and I cannot help feeling as keen as possible about gallant little Tom Sayers with his one arm maintaining such a fight. I am satisfied that if he had not lost the use of his right arm he would have polished off the giant. I never saw a prize fight, and I daresay five minutes conversation with the worthy Tom would effectually cool my enthusiasm.
Langford does not say much of the opinions of The Garrick about The Mill but I rather gather that the verdict there is not so universally favourable as about Adam. The knowledge of the secret would make them more critical I daresay. The greatest enthusiast is your friend and index maker Mr. Brown. 534 He did not see any of the book as it went through the press and after he got a copy he came to me next morning wild with delight. He gnashes his teeth if he hears of any one who does not think the book perfect. He is a character who would make you laugh, and his remarks are well worth hearing.
I hope to hear from one or other of you in a few days and with best regards in which the Major joins I am
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 23 January 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 23 January 1860
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh January 23/60.
My Dear Lewes
I inclose proof of Tom Jones which I have read twice with great amusement. You make out a most logical case. At page 2 I think "coarse drollery" is too low a quality to be put forward as Fielding's leading merit. It grated on me a bit in the M.S. and I still feel it in the proof. As it would turn aside his great admirers whom we wish to read the paper I think you should put some higher estimate first. Coarse drollery is too low a term for humour such as his which has made so many generations of us shout with laughter. At page 7 "shallow circumscribed nature" seems to me a phrase which should not be applied to a man who has done so much as Fielding. I think you would improve the paper by speaking of him throughout as an intensely clever fellow and making it more clear that it is only the very high rank given to him among the giants by modern critics that you utterly deny his right to. I hope I did not hurry you with this paper. I said I wanted it this month as at the time I wrote three or four had written to say they would not be ready, but within the last week various papers which will not keep have turned up and if you do not mind I will postpone you for a month. I hate doing this when I had asked a man to do a paper especially on the back of my stumble over Darwin but such things can hardly be avoided some times and I daresay they happen more rarely with me than any other editor.
Will you ask Mrs. Lewes to let me know if she thinks the other volumes of the Mill will be about the same length as the first. The printers calculate that the M.S. received will be about 50 or 60 pages more than the first volume of Adam and if the other volumes are to be of a like length we would put a little more into the page than we did in Adam.
Ever Yours Truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
Return the proof. Thackeray's laudation of Fielding is most ludicrous. In fact throughout these Lectures on the humorists his tone is absurd or insincere. He had the lectures to do and I suppose he did them on the large hearted or the bitterly virtuous view according to his humour.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 23 February 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: John Blackwood, p. 38.
Edinburgh | February 23/57.
My Dear Lewes
When you go to the Scilly Islands I shall hope to hear tidings of you in the shape of M.S. You have much reason to be proud of your Literary Godchild George Eliot. My impression is that Gilfil will be even more generally popular than Amos. There are differences of opinion about Amos and probably there always may be, but there is no mistake about the general verdict being as favourable as we expected.
In his last G. Eliot expressed anxiety to hear Thackeray's opinion. From what Albert Smith said I gather that Thackeray is a warm admirer, but I expect the wandering "puller down of Kings" here erelong 801 when doubtless I shall hear his opinion at full length. By the way there are occasional touches in Amos akin to Thackeray's style of humour and feeling.
The inclosed comment is from an intimate friend of mine, a remarkably clever fellow the Revd G. C. Swayne. 802 You may recollect a paper of his on respectability in the November or December number which I daresay would hit your fancy.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
"I forgot to speak of Amos Barton in my last to you, what a charming tale it is! -- and yet without any straining for effect or incident; it reminds me in its tender simplicity of the Vicar of Wakefield more than anything I have read [in] a long time." 803

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 22 November 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 22 November 1878
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 22/78.
My Dear Lewes
I found your note and Mrs. Lewes' M.S. upon my table today and you may imagine the pleasure the sight afforded me. I sent your note along to Willie to cheer him on his sofa and I almost rose to ring the bell to call up "Simpson" but the news will comfort him at Cannes where he now is.
In spite of this being an exceptionally busy day the very nick of sending the Magazine to press I have read the first chapter of Theophrastus and am delighted with it. How true the remarks on the incompleteness of autobiography 151 both from respect to Self and justice to others. A bad orator showing the weak points of his grammar as Jean Jacques' confessions have their greatest use by unconsciously developing the weak points of his own character 152 is very fine and we all like to keep the scourge in our own hands and not to deliver ourselves up to the candid opinion of our enemies.
Theophrastus' whole picture of himself is delightful and there is something very comic in his mixed satisfaction in seeing his remarks appreciated when appropriated by others. It reminds me of my feelings when I see an article in the Magazine copied without acknowledgment. The egoist looking round the world in vain as he is only looking for some flattering unction to himself is so natural. All must have felt what she says of the right interpretation of doing as you would be done by and watch the wandering attention of a friend when you begin to talk of your own emotions instead of listening to his. Truly we cannot enjoy this world without having something of a cabbage garden in it try as we may. All through the chapter I have lingered with delight over the remarks.
I have sent the bulk of the M.S. into printing office to have quantity calculated with a view to size of page and volume. Can you give me an idea how much more M.S. there will be?
Can you send form for a little slip to be stuck into the Magazine announcing a new work in one volume by George Eliot. As we are to publish so soon it is desirable to announce at once.
Give my best regards to Mrs. Lewes and from this chapter I feel very confident that I may congratulate her. It is so readable, and clear as profound. I am so sorry that I have people dining with me tonight so that I cannot go on reading.
Since I have been in Edin[burgh] I have been fairly well and my wife says this work of Mrs. Lewes will make up for the links which I was missing.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
