Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 22 November 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 22 November 1872
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh | November 22/72.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of enclosing another £100. from Melbourne Argus on account of Middlemarch and £25. from the Dutchman for their Translations. 636 We have acknowledged receipt to them. The Melbourne paper was, I think I told you, a coup de Maitre by Simpson. Give my best thanks to Mrs. Lewes for her kind message which I got over at Strathtyrum. I was very unwell but am now particularly well. In fact I think the illness has cleared off some mischief that had been hanging about me as I have not felt so well and fit for a long time.
I should think from Mrs. Lewes' question about Forster's Biography that she and I would agree about that book. As far as regards others I think that Forster seems to have been perhaps more careful and delicate than might have been expected, but does he see no want of delicacy in publishing all those appeals by Dickens to his judgment? I felt for the man of genius. The letters give me a feeling of regret, almost pain, from the want of dignity and repose in them and in all that life of success and laughter there seems no real happiness or fun. I like Dickens better in this volume than I did in the first and when I read all that strain and unrest I could not help wishing that I might have had him down at Strathtyrum to turn him onto the links. They are a much better rest for the mind than fatiguing walk or wandering about streets.
I was pleased to see the allusion to Clerical Scenes. Your instructions about binding M.S. Middlemarch are being attended to. Yes, send down what you have of corrected proof.
We came over from Fife on Wednesday evening and luckily our last few days were fine. I hope Mrs. Lewes has recovered from her cold and with best regards to her I am always
Yours very Truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
I have gone over the Printing Office. It looks melancholy to see the idle cases and machines and I am sorry for the men. They are most sorry for themselves, but they yield like slaves to the tyranny of the Union. We have found it necessary to declare that we will not take a Union man into our office and we are determined to stand to our ground. It will not put us about much and will do good.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 22 May 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 22 May 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | May 22/57.
My Dear Lewes
Your proof arrived all right and also George Eliot's with a very neat Epilogue to Gilfil. I do not know when I have read anything so powerfully pathetic as this last part of Gilfil. The only possible objection is that it may be almost too painful.
I am very anxious to see the next story. Tell George Eliot that I hope he will be in very great form as he will run along side of a new series by Bulwer and I should like our Clerical friend to come out well in such company. Sir Edward is I think first rate.
I inclose a note from Mr. Archer Gurney. 862 Except seeing his name upon occasional volumes of poetry etc. I do not know anything of him, but I fancy he is a large hearted sort of character. I agree with his remarks except about Sir Edward, 863 who has in his later works shown himself as remarkable for wisdom as he always was for vivacity of style.
I go to London tomorrow and my address there for a few weeks is 38 Jermyn St. Is there any chance of seeing you or George Eliot? I have paid £17. 17/- to your credit with Union Bank in acknowledgment of the New Sea Side Studies.
This note will I hope find you comfortably established at St. Heliers, Jersey where I address it on chance.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 22 January 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 22 January 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | January 22/68.
My Dear Lewes
I was very glad to hear that you had got back after a pleasant and successful expedition to Germany. In probing the nervous system of the human race take care that you do not overwork your own. You do work very hard but it is both nature and habit with you.
Give my best regards to Mrs. Lewes and say that I am ashamed of not having acknowledged her note. I did not see the article in [the] Daily News on the Address to the Working Men and could not get hold of it, but I can thoroughly understand what it was and Piggott's disgust at being supposed to have anything to do with it. The Press go in a string and if I were to publish a paper advocating the abolition of the Monarchy and the equal rights of man it would in the first instance be received as another ebullition of rank Toryism. It is curious how few men of mark and thought there are among the Press and if I were allowed my pick among them (which I daresay I might without any difficulty) I do not think there are half a dozen from whom I would accept a paper. Still it is wonderful with how much ability and even taste the whole thing is conducted.
In spite of the non-attention of the Press the Address has I believe told well and it has been immensely admired. I have had two applications for permission to reprint, which I have granted. Some of our Societies should have applied to me for permission to print it wholesale for distribution.
I intend to be in London early in February so I hope to see you both soon. Your news of progress in the Poem is most welcome.
I never heard of Mrs. Howther whom you found taking the German honours of George Eliot. It is more probably some accidental blunder rather than a female Liggins.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 21 November 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 21/76.
My Dear Lewes
Since I came into Edinburgh I have been looking again into the cost and produce of The Works, and I am disappointed to find as I feared, that the inclosed offer of lordship cannot be much varied.
The printing paper and binding are put in the accompanying statement as cheaply as they can be done and the advertising etc. at a less rate than we have estimated during these ten years. The discounts to the Trade are very large, but we do not see how to lessen them without checking the sale -- as Dickens and other similar works are sold at the same rates of discount. For instance the 3/6 volumes of Dickens are sold by the agent here to the retailers at sale price 2/6 13 as 12 to 6 Mos. Acct. and 2'bd per cent discount, so the Agent must have 10 per cent off sale to cover his transaction.
I am disappointed at the result as I was ten years ago when I calculated the whole matter, but I did not then or now see a better form, and we have all reason to be pleased with the steady increasing sale the books have met in their present shape.
While Middlemarch goes on as it is doing it will not be desirable to make any change there, and it is to be hoped Deronda will follow suit. We are going to bring out the Deronda at 21/- immediately and I hope we have not been rash in printing 2000. 560
When Middlemarch and Deronda have run their course as separate books at 7/6, the plates will readily print on paper uniform with the other works, perhaps as two volumes each and they with Romola 561 may give the whole series a fresh start. By that time too I hope there may be a new book to be reckoned among the works of George Eliot.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 21 February 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 21 February 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Randolph Crescent
February 21/72.
My Dear Lewes
I am happy to tell you that the sale of Middlemarch goes on very steadily. Inclosed is a mem. of sales since the 12th. There is also a regular dropping sale of Book one.
Mrs. Lewes is I hope better and in better spirits. I am sure if she heard the comments in this house on her wondrous work it would do her heart good. I indulged my wife and daughter with a perusal of the sheets of Book III and I have also been indulging myself with a perusal of the whole over again. It is a chorus among us of wonderful, perfect, etc. and each commentator is anxious to allude to the points as if being the first to mention any of them gave a share in the merit. I observe that the only comment the Critics outside can make in the way of fault finding is that this or that character does not appear so much as they could wish. A very high compliment I should say.
My talking so much of home criticism arises partly from my having been confined to the house for the last fortnight. I had not felt well for some time and went on fighting against it, trying to work and varying it with Golf until at last I found I was fit for nothing but bed. The cold and general malaise turned into violent sore throat and I had a very disagreeable bout of it, but as I never fevered at all I have come out of it wonderfully well and strong to the surprise of my Doctor (the successor to dear old Burt who died some years ago) who had never seen me ill before. Indeed I do not recollect being regularly laid up in this way since I was a lad.
I feel quite well now and expect to Golf in a few days.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 21 December 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 21 December 1877
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh December 21/77.
My Dear Lewes
I was delighted to get your note the other day with such pleasant accounts of Mrs. Lewes and I hope the approaching holiday time will find you both well and able to enjoy the congratulations of your friends.
I had a call today from Mrs. Wm. Smith who inquired for and sent most warm remembrances to you both. She is living with a niece and her husband, Mr. Constable, and I am happy to say looks well. I almost hesitated to send the enclosed for Mrs. Lewes as it may be from some "curious impertinent" but from the terms in which it is enclosed have deemed it best to forward it to you.
Thanks for your hint about Souvenirs of Madm. D'Agoult which I have sent for.
The Wars and possibilities of Wars fill one with uneasiness. I hope devoutly that we may be able to steer safely through it all. That France should be so helpless is a great embarrassment to all arrangements. What a strange turn that is when we think of past wars and their History.
Mr. Gathorne Hardy 791 was in Edinburgh for a banquet last week and stayed with us for a couple of days. I am happy to say that our Minister of War is I think a man who may be trusted at the helm. He is a very vigorous able man and also full of life and fun. We were all greatly taken with him.
Willie joins me in all good wishes and believe me
ever yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
Our weather is singularly mild and my wife and daughter are rejoicing in their rides.

MS: Tinker Collection, Yale. The text of the statements is from copies in the Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
December 21/72.
My Dear Lewes
I inclose tables of the sales and state of Middlemarch which make a very pretty show. Of the book in four volumes complete we have you will see sold some 240. As the library stocks must be free to a certain extent I did not expect that we could do much with the complete book at 42/.
The point therefore comes, when should we be at liberty to reduce the price, say to 21/. Our idea is that at that price, using the same plates with thinner paper and narrower margin, we might have a considerable sale. What do you think, especially as to the point when it would be fair to bring out a cheaper edition after the dear one? There is a sale going on just now and the 240 we have sold in cloth are mainly since the subscription, which amounted to almost nothing.
The public mind is about as full of the book as well could be and there is a sale on the separate parts especially the later ones which keeps Mr. Simpson on the qui vive not to run short and at same time not to over print. Today there is a Memorandum to send up to P. N. Row 200 part 8 which indicates the public pressing on the libraries impatient to read the close.
When you have looked over these states I shall send you bill for the balance or pay you gradually in cash as you may prefer. The balance you will see is £2243.2/- but you may remember my speaking to you about giving an extra discount to Smith and Sons which we agreed to grant. This discount I find amounts to £94.16.7 and should I think be deducted from the lordship to be paid to you.
I enclose also statement of The Spanish Gypsy and cheque for the balance £28.4/-.
With best wishes to Mrs. Lewes and you believe me

George Street | Edinburgh.
November 20/67.
My Dear Lewes
The precious M.S. of Part one of the Poem arrived safely today. Tell Mrs. Lewes to make her mind easy. The M.S. is lying on table beside me and in spite of endless matters calling for immediate attention I have been wasting!! my day plunging into and dwelling upon these wonderful pages.
My expression above reminds me of a favourite story of mine which may amuse Mrs. Lewes. Old Hugh Philp 685 the Golf Club maker was as fond of playing the game as any of us and after a keen contest with me one day he said with much energy "It's a nasty enteecing gemm. It takes a man aff his business."
I shall put the "enticing game" into the Printing Office speedily.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 20 January 1876
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh January 20/76.
My dear Lewes
By a letter from Langford today I see that you and he propose we should send Deronda to the weekly press from here on the 25th and to the Daily Press on the 27th, but so many of the weekly are connected with the Daily Press that I do not think it would be safe to make the distinction. So if you agree I propose to post all the Press copies from this on the 25th with a request that reviews should not appear before Saturday. I hope Mrs. Lewes is pretty well and that I shall soon be gladened by the sight of Volume 3.
A very clever young contributor of mine Julian Sturgis 387 has asked me for an introduction to Mrs. Lewes and you but I hesitate about intruding upon her at present. He is an immense favourite of mine and you will I am sure be charmed with him. He is American by birth but I could not point out a better type of what Eton and Oxford can produce than this young fellow.
I had a most amusing letter from Lockhart yesterday and he excuses himself for not having sent Christmas greetings because he did not like to send his "good wishes" without a specimen of his "good works." He will I think be able to take the field with a novel in spring.
ever yours truly
(Signed) John Blackwood.
I wonder that blunder of putting letters into wrong envelopes does not occur oftener.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 20 April 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 20/66.
My Dear Lewes
I am delighted to hear that Mrs. Lewes has so nearly finished her Novel and also much pleased that she should think in the first instance of her old friend as the publisher. 429
That such a Novel as you describe by her will be first rate I have no manner of doubt but it would be against the principle upon which I really enter into and take a pleasure in my own business were I to decide finally on such a matter without having some opportunity of forming an opinion of the book by seeing a volume or so. I think she knows me well enough not to object to this and I would give an answer within a couple of days after receiving the M.S.
As to what my opinion will be I feel nearly certain and the more serious matter is the terms.
I contemplate giving from four to five thousand Pounds for the copyright for five years from date of publication and if this does not come up to your ideas I cannot see my way to anything like a fair chance of making the transaction remunerative by giving more. Of course I understand that it is a novel of the ordinary length in three volumes. I should like of all things to publish another great success by George Eliot and I do hope we may be able to agree about terms.
Will you give her my regards and tell her that I have been thinking so much of her Novel since receiving your note that I have found it very difficult to attend to my ordinary work, of which I have more than enough at this period of the month.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 2 March 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 2 March 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, pp. 393-394.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
March 2/76.
My Dear Lewes
I had to go out of Town this morning and have only time to write a line before post hour to say that I read Book Six last night and have unbounded congratulations to send to Mrs. Lewes. She is A Magician. It is a Poem, a Drama, and a Grand Novel.
One cannot rightly read Deronda while people are talking and moving about, so I did not get fairly begun until I went to my dressing room where it kept me reading, thinking, and admiring until past three a.m. The book is A Work in itself, and I do not wonder at the creator of such work feeling exhausted and nervous, but she may dismiss all anxiety as to what the world will think and feel satisfied that she has transcendently carried out her purpose.
There is no doubt about the marvellous Mordecai and oh that Cohen family! The whole tribe of Israel should fall down and worship her. I must read again before venturing to write to her. When I finished the part at 'bd past three I grudged very much not being able to go with Deronda to see his Mother. The suspense is great.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 2 April 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 41.
Edinburgh | April 2/58.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of sending a cheque One Hundred and Thirty
Five Pounds being £30 in acknowledgment of Food and Drink parts 2 and 3 and £105 your honorarium for editing Johnston.
The additions are not so extensive as I thought you would find necessary, but I am not sorry to see this, as it is the best practical testimony to the merit of my old friend's book, and I am in every way satisfied with the judgment you have shown in adding only what you thought necessary and not cumbering the book with superfluous matter. It must have cost you much trouble and research to satisfy yourself as to what additions were necessary.
The Food and Drink papers are exceedingly good and I read No. 3 (of which I inclose proof) with great pleasure last night. Your tribute to Tripe 1116 quite touched me and I read it aloud in triumph to Mrs. Blackwood. That lady cannot bear the sight of what she irreverently calls the horrid mess and it is only at very rare intervals that I am allowed to see the dish, which is an old and particular favourite with me, especially to supper in my supper days.
The M.S.S. of the two papers on the Blood 1117 arrived safely today and I expect to read them with much interest. I hear nothing but praise of the Seaside Studies. Mr. Langford has not said how the book is moving lately but I shall get the return of Sales for the month tomorrow or next day in time to tell you if there are any pleasant features -- but if you are passing the Row look in and see for yourself.
I have an admirable letter from George Eliot today. 1118 I knew that he would fear to give me a sketch of the rest of the Story lest he should give me a wrong impression and I very nearly said so when I made the request. On the whole I think he is right. What he says of the treatment of a subject being the essence of art is very true and a more elegant rendering of my constant reply to fellows sending lists of subjects for articles, "that any subject being suitable entirely depends upon how it is handled." I shall steal his expression the next time I wish to choke off any anxious enquirer as to the probable acceptability of his proposed "little paper."
I hope to receive the additional M.S. tomorrow in time to congratulate George on its merits before he leaves England.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 19 October 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 19 October 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. The memorandum is in Mrs. Carrington Ouvry's collection. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
October 19/76.
My Dear Lewes
Our ten years' lease of Mrs. Lewes' Works, Adam Bede, Mill on the Floss, Silas Marner, Scenes of Clerical Life and Felix Holt is now nearly run out, and both from personal and professional feeling my anxious wish is that we should always continue to be her publishers.
I have been thinking and talking over with my nephew and Mr. Simpson what we can offer for another lease of ten years, and I hope the following may meet her views and yours, or if not I shall be ready to consider any suggestions for alterations in terms that you may think of to meet contingencies.
I now beg to offer the sum of Four Thousand Pounds (£4000) payable over a term of three years for another lease of ten years of the above mentioned works with the addition of Middlemarch, Romola, and Daniel Deronda. I am not sure from my own letters when the present lease strictly terminates but it does not matter and I would propose to make the new arrangement date from the first of January next with the exception in your favour that the 21/- edition of Deronda should be paid to you by a lordship as in the case of Middlemarch.
From the outward aspect of opinion I do not think we can calculate upon such a sale of Deronda at 7/6 as for Middlemarch. The inclosed Memoranda will show you what the first named five books have done in the past nine years and we have made our estimate of sales on a sort of medium between the sales during the past three years and the whole nine. In the event of your accepting the above offer it is understood that the size and price of the works are to be as before at our discretion. Trusting that we may in some form or other at all events be able to meet each other's views I am ever
yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 19 March 1877
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Randolph Crescent
March 19/77.
My Dear Lewes
You will have been surprised at not hearing sooner from me in reply to your last interesting letter. The fact is that I have been out of sorts and languid and being very much puzzled what to advise about the Novels, I have put off writing from day to day.
I feel that there is too little being made out of those admirable books and we must try something to give a semblance of novelty to a complete edition of George Eliot's Works.
After many talks with Simpson and Willie I think we all point to something very like what you propose viz. a 6/- edition beginning with Romola in the same type as the present edition but printed on larger and finer paper which being adopted with the other volumes would make them like entirely new editions and fully worth 6/- except of course Silas Marner. As long as Middlemarch continues to sell as it is doing it will be advisable to keep it at 7/6 and Deronda the same. These two are so much larger than the other volumes that the difference in price could not reasonably be objected to. Deronda we may I think start at 7/6 in Spring some time. We would propose to cancel the illustrations to the present edition and give in each volume an engraved vignette frontispiece like what we have in Middlemarch. We would continue the 3/6 edition or at all events be guided by circumstances as we found how the two editions worked abreast. The Lifted Veil and Brother Jacob are wonderful Tales but both so desperately painful that I have a scruple in coupling them with Silas. Mrs. Lewes and you however are by far the best judges of this.
The Agent we employed for the Deronda advertiser did not do his work so efficiently as we expected 621 but inclosed I have the pleasure of sending cheque £128-17-3d being the balance to author as per inclosed statement.
I hope Mrs. Lewes and you are both well and getting cheerily through your preparations for moving to the country. I quite look forward to coming to see you in May or June.
For the last day or two I have been keeping to the house owing to cold and general malaise but I hope to be about all right tomorrow.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 19 June 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 19 June 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh June 19/68.
My Dear Lewes
It gives me much pleasure to receive your letter and to hear that Mrs. Lewes and you are well in so delightful a spot as Petersthal seems to be.
I am happy to say that the Poem is going on well. I inclose a mem. of London sales up to 11th, which is the last consecutive statement I have, but from the daily reports from the Row I see that the sale is going on satisfactorily. The Spectator of 6th contained the best review that has appeared. 773 The writer I see had felt some of the doubts which occasionally disquieted me. My doubts ceased long ago, fixed admiration putting them to flight, and I have no doubt that the case is the same with the Spectator reviewer if he has had time to turn again and again to the Poem. It certainly is the case that no review of a book, especially a great Poem which one has thoroughly read, ever seems satisfactory. I inclose a note from Patterson 774 which is about the right kind of thing. It is evidently truly felt and I think Mrs. Lewes would like to have it. I inclose also some letters. 775 There ought to be something made from the setting of the songs to music, and I expect there will be other overtures so the matter can stand until you come home.
I have ordered a copy of The Earthly Paradise as you recommend and am taking it to Fife with me this afternoon.
Willie will drop you a note with the actual sale of the Gypsy in a day or two as Mr. Simpson has written to London for a return of state.
My private friends are enthusiastic about the Poem and I think the feeling grows. A friend of Mrs. Scott Siddons 776 has applied to us in her name as to whether the author would be willing to adapt or have it adapted to the stage. Her friend whom we know well and who lives here is in raptures about the Poem.
With best regards to the great Novelist and Poetess I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 18 November 1856
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 18 November 1856
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 421-423.
Edinburgh | November 18/56.
My Dear Sir
I was very far from intending that my letter should convey anything like disappointment to your friend. On the contrary I thought the Tale very good and intended to convey as much. But I daresay I expressed myself coolly enough. Criticism would assume a much soberer tone were critics compelled seriously to act whenever they expressed an opinion. Although not much given to hesitate about anything I always think twice before I put the decisive mark "In type for the Magazine" on any M.S. from a stranger. Fancy the intense annoyance (to say nothing of more serious considerations) of publishing month after month a series about which the conviction gradually forces itself on you that you have made a total blunder.
I am sorry that the author has no more written but if he cares much about a speedy appearance I have so high an opinion of this first Tale that I will waive my objections and publish it without seeing more; not, of course committing myself to go on with the other Tales of the series unless I approved of them. I am very sanguine that I will approve as in addition to the other merits of Amos I agree with you that there is great freshness of style. If you think also that it would stimulate the author to go on with the other Tales with more spirit I will publish Amos at once. He would divide into two parts. I am blocked up for December but I could start him in January.
I am glad to hear that your friend is as I supposed a Clergyman. Such a subject is best in clerical hands and some of the pleasantest and least prejudiced correspondents I have ever had are English Clergymen.
Oddly enough the paper in Fraser to which you allude was pointed out to me by a friend as being suitable in parts at least for the Magazine. I did not read it, being busy, but I shall look at it now. In the meantime I adopt your suggestion and will be happy to look at any M.S. from Mr. Tugwell other than that which you think will hardly do.
I have not read Amos Barton a second time but the impression on my mind of the whole character, incidents, and feeling of the story is very distinct, which is an excellent sign.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 18 January 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 18 January 1878
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh January 18/78.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque One thousand and Six Pounds 17/7 (1006.17.7) being payment due to author on sales of George Eliot's Novels during the past year as per accompanying Memorandum. The result is I think satisfactory and will I hope come up to your expectations. The sale goes on steadily from month to month and does not show symptoms of falling off which is a great point. Of course while Deronda was in course of publication there was greater movement in the sale of all the other Novels and I hope to see them again stirred up by a similar cause one of these days.
From the London reports I gather that the sales of the Novels are going on satisfactorily since the turn of the Year and on the 12th Langford wrote 250 Deronda sold since January 1. You will see that Middlemarch continues to bring in its argosy gallantly and Adam Bede still keeps proudly ahead in sale. The subscription to first volume of Romola Cabinet Edition was not very cheering but up to present date I see the sales are 611 which is equal to what we calculated on at first. We printed I think 1050. That you may understand the sort of continuous rate of the sale from month to month I enclose copy of the London monthly table of sales. The aspect, take it all together, is I think satisfactory.
I hope this will find Mrs. Lewes and you both well and able to take advantage of the mild weather for walks and drives. My long promised expedition to Rome begins to take form and we intend to be in London at all events next month so I look forward to seeing you very soon.
Everybody wishes peace and nobody is working harder for that than Her Majesty's Ministers so I still hope we may escape War. Those firebrands our men of peace howling about the country that England won't fight seem as if they wished to tempt Russia to aggression and insult and do more harm than the most foolish swaggerer.
My nephew joins me in best regards to you both and believe me
ever yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 18 April 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 18 April 1859
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh April 18/59.
My dear Lewes
George Eliot's contradiction in the Times is exceedingly well put and made me laugh considerably. It will stop all the better class papers from publishing rumours as to the authorship. Inclosed is a letter from a Warwickshire Squire apparently a distinguished member of the Fogie Club. Shall I answer the old foozle? From the tone of his letter I daresay he is not a bad fellow. I would only assure him that George Eliot has no need of pecuniary assistance from any one and that his letter in the
Times ought to stop further enquiry and satisfy Mr. Liggins' friends that they are under a delusion. My objection to a point blank denial from us is that if any one stumbles on the real name a less decided denial from us would be an admission.
Mr. Simpson would I doubt not write to apologize for the mistake in the Printing Office about the return of the Physiology for press. He will keep you regularly informed in future as to the requirements of the press. We had better set a paragraph afloat about your distinguished German Translator. Can you do it in the Athenaeum or any of the other weekly literary gossip columns? If you send a para[graph] to me here I will set it afloat among the Edinr. papers whence it may be copied into the London press.
You ask about Spurgeon. His voice and elocution seem to me to explain his popularity. They are wonderful. As for his matter I certainly shall not go to hear him again. As for doctrine he announced in the most unhesitating terms the miserable hopeless creed of the extreme Calvinists that men are sent into this world preordained to Heaven or t'other place and that no conduct on their part can have the slightest influence on their future fate. I suppose he meant to imply that he was of the Elect but he could not possibly have explained how he was to be so lucky as from his own showing neither his principles nor his conduct could have anything to do with the matter. His stock anecdotes about conversions by the force of his preaching were to me very painful. I did not like to disbelieve the fellow but at the same time the stories did not seem genuine. His converts however seemed generally to have been on the verge of Del. Tre. so may have been affected as he described.
Ever Yours Truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes, Esqr.
I shall use the Pond this month.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 17 March 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 17 March 1862
Text: Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh March 17/62.
My dear Lewes
As the books are not particularly new now perhaps we had better alter our title again. 41 I inclose your revise in case you should think of any alterations. Your remarks induced me to turn to Mrs. Browning's poems again. I think you rate her much too high. She is surely strained and artificial to a degree. Did I ever tell you how I posed good old Mr. Kenyon 42 who had sent me a poem by her for Maga. I replied that doubtless it was a noble poem but I would not publish what I could not understand but would print the poem if he could explain certain lines which I marked. The old gentleman was floored and agreed with me.
Mr. Simpson has returned overflowing with enthusiasm about his visit to Blandford Square.
Always Yours Truly
John Blackwood.
By the way I suppose there is nothing in your remarks about language to clash with my paper last month. Keep me straight about this. How did you like that paper by the way? Any news will be welcome and I will give you a screed in reply.

John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 17 January 1874
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh January 17/74.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of enclosing a cheque £807.11/- being £785.13/- on account of Middlemarch and £21.18/- on account Spanish Gypsy as per accompanying Memorandum.
Nothing could be more satisfactory than Middlemarch and the continued sale of the 21/- edition is a grand triumph.

A bruised ankle and foot is always a tedious thing.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 17 January 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 17 January 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. The statement is in Mrs. Ouvry's Collection. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
January 17/73.
My Dear Lewes
It gives me much pleasure to receive your most friendly letter 711 and to hear that your Great Book "Problems of Life and Mind" is so far advanced. I have no hesitation in agreeing to publish the work and on the terms you propose, half profits, which is in this case I think the best and fairest arrangement.
Thanks for your consideration as to the difference in our opinions, and I feel quite satisfied from what you say that there will be nothing in your book which I or any publisher should decline to publish. Indeed I cannot imagine the cause of real religion being injured by any amount of free and fair discussion such as yours is sure to be. The maulers of plain and beautiful Texts and the dogmatic insisters upon Creeds as to points which no human being can know anything about are more likely to injure the cause of religion than any amount of philosophic speculation as to mind and life.
You have been so long engaged on this Key to all the Mythologies that I am very confident it will be a most instructive book, and I know well how clearly and readably you can put any scientific or philosophic point. If the lamented Casaubon had written it I should have insisted on his publishing at his own risk. By the way did I ever send you Collins' letter about the pathos in the story of Casaubon? If I did not I must fish it out for Mrs. Lewes. The Guinea edition is in progress and we shall get it out as soon as we can. 712
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque £143 being the balance due to Author on Middlemarch advertiser as per inclosed statements. We thought the Advertiser would have a better chance in the hands of a regular canvasser Mr. Watson than with us, and have deducted his commission from our share in the proceeds. The Commission looks large, but he does not get the whole of it as he makes deductions for repeated advertisements and also to other birds like himself with whom he exchanges advertisements.
I have taken the liberty of giving a note of introduction to a Mrs. Thompson 713 to Mrs. Lewes. She has written some pamphlets in an excellent spirit and is rather a remarkable woman. Willie told Mrs. Lewes that she (Mrs. Thompson not Mrs. Lewes) was a Dutchwoman, but that he finds is a mistake. Her husband is an engineer and had large works in Holland; that is her connection with the German flute.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 16 January 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 16 January 1877
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
January 16/77.
My Dear Lewes
By a curious coincidence the inclosed from Mr. Dowden came by the same post as your pleasant letter. I wish he had sent the paper to me and I wonder he did not after my note.
I thought I had sent back The Contemporary to you but it goes by this post certainly. Simpson had not forgot the Advertiser in Deronda, but had to postpone settlement owing to difficulties with some of the advertisers. 595
I feel for you both in the troubles of moving and furnishing but I trust the move will be to a pleasant anchorage for life, and I am sure her heart has always been in the country.
I have some experience of furnishing troubles, of late our house having been re-done up. I had staved off this operation for years telling my wife that "her auld hoose looked better than mony ane's new" but she stuck at it and trained her visitors to remark on the seediness of the fittings, as to which there was some truth after 20 years' service. We have one visitor at present a stern old Scotch country wife who used to take care of the house at Strathtyrum in winter. From the state of the house here there was nothing for it but to put her into the best spare bed room. She remonstrated vehemently against such grandeur saying "Oo I'll just creep in beside onybody." Worthy Mrs. Hunter is 5 feet 9 at least and fully built to match. The idea of her creeping in beside any body utterly upset me and if you saw her would make you roar with laughing.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 15 November 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 15 November 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | November 15/61.
My Dear Lewes
I find as I expected on looking into the calculations upon which our agreement for the 6/- edition of the George Eliot Novels was based that the repeal of the paper duty makes a difference hardly worth considering.
When these calculations were made the paper intended for the Series was estimated at 20/- per ream and the binding in printed cloth like that over the one volume novel by Trollope published by Chapman and Hall and costing 4d. 868
The reduction of duty enables us to buy the same paper at present for 17/4 (or 6'bdd. per lb.) which would make a saving of about 'a34.3.4d on the thousand copies or one penny per book.
Our opinion in which I feel certain you will agree is that we should apply this saving to an improved style of binding. This might, we think, assist the sale, and considering that the volumes will contain no more for 6/- than Trollope's for 5/- the difference of quality should be extended to externals. Over at Strathtyrum I had forgot all about the form of book on which our calculations were based and feel doubtful whether we can venture to make that edition of Silas the same price as Adam and the Mill. It would be so thin a volume, as we would need to make it a book precisely like what it is at present for 12/- which would hardly do. The Scenes I think we may keep uniform in price, but we need not decide on that at present as I propose to begin with Adam. Suppose we start that on the first of January.
In the meantime I am hurrying on the 6/- edition of Silas to be ready as soon as possible. It is being made a handsome foolscap volume to range with the 12/- editions of the other works.
Your expectation of receiving 'bd as much per thousand for the 6/- edition as for the 12/- arose from your not knowing or reflecting that the difference in the cost of producing a foolscap octavo and a post octavo volume could only be very small, the quantity of matter and style of getting up being the same in both cases, so that the 6/- foolscap cannot produce anything like 'bd the profit of the 12/ post.
My offer of the 60 'a3 per thousand is I think a fair one. The only difference I could make would be to take a trifle off the payment for the first 2000 and after that number was sold to pay 'a370 per 1000.
I hope I have made myself clear and if not I wish you to write again that you may feel perfectly satisfied about everything. I think I am quite distinct, for which I deserve some credit although the scorings out testify to the some thirty callers I have had since I began this note.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
P.S. It may strike you that being able to give 'a360 per 1000 for the 6/- Adam we ought to be able to give materially more for the 6/- Silas.
But the offer for 6/- Adam which will be really a cheap book was based on the expectation of a sale to an extent which we cannot reasonably expect for a 6/ Silas which is not cheap, and the difference in the style of getting up makes the difference in the cost of production much less than you would imagine.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 15 November 1858
Text: Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh | November 15/58.
My dear Lewes
We have been making our calculations about the Physiology of Common Life, and on the supposition the work will consist of 18 numbers of about 48 pages like the 1st number, which I now send you, we beg to offer you Two Hundred and Fifty Pounds (£250.) for a first edition of Five Thousand copies. The expenses of advertising and fairly starting this first edition will be so great that supposing 5000 sold there will be only a mere trifle of any profit to us, but our hope and expectation is that the sale will go much beyond that number and the book become a steady property. We therefore propose further that for any numbers we print beyond five thousand we pay you at the rate of Three Pounds (£3) per thousand of each sixpenny number. We base the prospective payments to you on the numbers because we know that the sale in that form will be irregular and the proceeds must first be calculated in that way. Afterwards when the sale in numbers had ceased we would adjust the payments to an equivalent on the volumes.
Should it be thought advisable at any time to alter the size and price of the book, we would make you an offer on the same principle as the second part of our proposition in this letter (viz. the £3. per thousand of each number) by which we wish it to be understood that if you accept our offer we have a permanent interest in the copyright to the extent of two fifths, our calculation being that the £3. per thousand will leave about three fifths of the clear profit to you and two fifths to us or rather more if the book moves fast and the advertising is not necessarily heavy.
We propose to stereotype the book as selling in numbers; the stock would not otherwise be kept square, but when a new and revised edition was called for, we would break up the plates.
I hope this offer will be agreeable to you and independently of all monetary considerations it will give you real pleasure should the book prove, as I trust it will, a great success and a good thing for both author and publisher.
Believe me for self and brother,
Always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esqr
I am perfectly delighted with the article on Biot and will write with proof tomorrow or next day. Your style is as bright as the Frenchman's.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 15 February 1858
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh February 15/58.
My dear Lewes
I enclose the proof of Food and Drink which I shall be glad to have back as soon as possible.
I have read this first instalment with much pleasure although being introductory I daresay it is not altogether so interesting as the other two parts. It will be liked. If on going over the proof you think there are any portions which could in the meantime be left out without disadvantage, reserve these for the book, as at present the paper has rather too much the air of a fragment of a systematic work on the subject for a magazine paper. Follow your own opinion about this however. I cannot tell what is necessary for a ground work for the development of your further views so I speak with diffidence. I see you are generally "I." I think, on the whole, it will be better to stick to the mystic "we." 368
I have no recent intelligence of the Studies or Scenes from London so I suppose Langford has no particular feature to mention.
I was delighted to hear from G.E. that I might so soon hope to see something like a volume of his new Tale. I am very sanguine.
I sent a copy of the Studies to the little Doctor (Simpson) 369 and hear he is going about in raptures about the book. I daresay he will deliver himself of a note by and bye.
I am glad you like the appearance of the book so much. It is I think a particularly handsome volume so much so that when I saw it I felt we had been weak in not making the rascally public stump up 12/6 for it.
Always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 14 October 1859
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh October 14/59.
My dear Lewes
I am happy to tell you that the prospects of the Physiology are very satisfactory. Mr. Simpson did not think it worth while to make any Statement as at Midsummer, and it was not, as a volume has not been published and no results could have been shewn.
The Sales are something like 4000 at least in numbers and about 1800 of the volume are disposed of. We made the price of the volume 6/- as it looked worth that. This makes the profit on the sale in volumes greater in proportion than in numbers and of course we will give you your full Share of the benefit when we see what is the Sale in numbers and volumes.
What are you about for the Magazine? When I went into my library to look for the nature printed volume 479 I found a Balaklava of chairs and tables carried from the drawing room and the bookcases matted up. So that I could lay hands on nothing but J. Lausay. Bradbury will give another copy if you think you would go at that subject at present.
A friend of mine Mr. Patterson has got the Press Newspaper 480 and I suppose enters on his labours almost immediately. He is a very able, well informed man and a good writer. He is also a real good worthy fellow as you could wish to know. I think you might give him a hand with advantage occasionally and I should be glad if you could. Should I give him a note to you or would you adopt the simple process of calling at the Press office where he is to be found although he has not fairly taken possession yet? I know he is anxious to make your acquaintance.
I remain in the country until the end of the month and am only in town for a few days.
Always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esqre

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 14 January 1876
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh January 14/76.
My Dear Lewes
We have today telegraphed to Harper's according to your instructions asking them whether they wished the publication of Deronda postponed until March. We did not do so in Telegram we sent on Wednesday as our doing so seemed merely suggesting this awkward step to them. I hope sincerely they will not propose the delay and if they reflect I hardly think they will.
I am excessively vexed that the proofs had not been sent at the time, but unless Harper's were going to publish long before the end of the month the delay can only cause a very trifling inconvenience. Their note too does not seem to indicate anything more than inconvenience and I think you are troubling yourself too much about the matter.
I do not think you reflect sufficiently upon the extreme danger of a copy getting afloat too early in that country where I suppose it could be reprinted in all directions. However I have sent off part today as you direct. I am sorry they are going to publish Deronda in their Magazine 386 as there will be greater difficulty in keeping it out of this country than if it appeared as an independent publication.
Hoping that this little trouble will blow over pleasantly and not interfere with the launch of the goodly ship, I am
ever yours truly
(Signed) John Blackwood.
Frost has come back upon us and really I think it agrees better with my cold than the milder weather.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 14 April 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 14 April 1873
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh April 14/73.
My Dear Lewes
Will you indicate the points with an eye to which you would more particularly like Prof. Tait 767 to look to the proofs of your book. I know him quite well and I am sure he will be pleased at the application but I should like to be better able to define what you want.
The thousand copies of the Guinea Edition of Middlemarch are gone and we have broken bulk upon another 500 which we printed when we saw that the 1000 were going to run out. Even should this 500 not sell off at once this will always have a dropping sale as the best and most luxurious edition.
We are ready in the Printing Office for more copy of the Problems of Mind. I have read the first few sheets. 768 Your metempirical is an ingenious word but I almost feel the general application of the meaning of the word Empirical will not be got over. It strikes me that you assume too much a general disbelief in religion. At foot of page two you speak of some of the most considerable thinkers desiring the extinction of religion. Now I doubt this altogether. People may think as much as they like and believe as little as they like, but I cannot imagine any man with a real head upon his shoulders wishing to cast mankind adrift without religion of any kind.
Give my best regards to Mrs. Lewes, who I hope is well. I have been laid up as an invalid for the last fortnight but am now quite well. I had been very unwell and the Doctor said I must surrender at discretion and treat myself as a complete invalid. Accordingly I have lived upon slops and drunk nothing stronger than water for the last fortnight. The treatment was severe but I have come out of the fiery furnace wonderfully well.
Always yours Truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 13 March 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
March 13/73.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I inclose a letter apparently from America.
We printed 1000 of the Guinea Middlemarch and it is clearly going out of print. 747 The prompt Simpson has ordered paper "to be ready" but we must be cautious. He would write to Mr. Lewes yesterday about the bulk of the volumes of the Key to all the Mythologies to guide us as to the size of the page. You both live so completely out of the Political world that the Row at Westminster 748 will not affect the Priory. I wish you had succeeded in finding a house at Tunbridge. 749 I am rather advised to take a turn at Homburg or some such place this summer but I do not think I shall have the courage. I do not know what I would do with myself.
My daughter is working very hard, this being her last year before coming out, and I am constantly bumping against signors or monsieurs and the piano goes from morning to night. She sings very well, though. She and a cousin Loo Stewart of the same age seem to be holding much converse on the future. One phrase amused me the other day. Loo, she told us, is much afraid lest she should "fall flat on the world" when she comes out.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 13 February 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 13/57.
My Dear Lewes
Thanks for your letter, and the packet of M.S. from George Eliot. Tell him that I read it all last night and am quite delighted. It is sparkling and witty throughout and he is a perfect master in giving individuality and life to his characters.
I shall be able to write with proof the day after tomorrow. Meanwhile I shall have no fear in starting poor Gilfil before I see the conclusion of the Story. I am puzzled as to how the love part is going to be managed but I shall write of this or any other point when I send the proof.
I am very glad to hear your report of the reception of Amos, which tallies very much with my own experience. Generally contributors introducing friends' M.S.S to Editors assume the character of bores, but you are a noble and memorable exception. Are you going to confine yourself to the character of intermediaire at present. Pray let me know if any subject occurs to you. In haste
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 12 November 1856
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 12 November 1856
MS: National Library of Scotland. Published: Cross, I, 419-420.
Edinburgh | November 12 /56.
My Dear Sir
I am happy to say that I think your friend's reminiscences of Clerical Life will do. If there is any more of the series written I should like to see it, as until I saw more I could not make any decided proposition for the publication of the Tales in whole or in part in the Magazine. This first specimen Amos Barton is unquestionably very pleasant reading. Perhaps the author falls into the error of trying too much to explain the characters of his actors by descriptions instead of allowing them to evolve in the action of the story; but the descriptions are very humorous and good. The death of Milly is powerfully done and affected me much. I am not sure whether he does not spoil it a little by specifying so minutely the different children and their names.
The windup is perhaps the lamest part of the story and there too I think the defect is caused by the specifications as to the fortunes of parties of whom the reader has no previous knowledge and cannot consequently feel much interest. At first I was afraid that in the amusing reminiscences of childhood in church there was a want of some softening touch as the remembrance of a father or mother lends in after years to what was at the time considerable penance.
I hate anything of a sneer at real religious feeling as cordially as I despise anything like cant, and I should think this author is of the same way of thinking although his clergymen with one exception are not very attractive specimens of the body. The revulsion of feeling towards poor Amos is capitally drawn although the asinine stupidity of his conduct about the Countess had disposed one to kick him.
I daresay I shall have a more decided opinion as to the merits of the Story when I have looked at it again and thought over it, but in the meantime I am sure that there is a happy turn of expression throughout, also much humour and pathos. If the author is a new writer I beg to congratulate him on being worthy of the honours of print and pay. I shall be very glad to hear from you or him soon. I do not recollect your note proposing a short paper on the anemones but you may take the unintentional silence as consent. 762
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. MS of statements in Mrs. Ouvry's collection. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh January 12/77.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of enclosing a cheque on the Royal Bank in London for £2215.15.6d due to Mrs. Lewes as per accompanying statement which will I hope be found satisfactory.
The only disappointing element is the sudden check in the sale of Deronda and there can be no doubt that we have made a mistake in printing 2000 of the 21/ edition, but where there is so much to congratulate ourselves upon such a mishap counts for little. There will be a rally in Deronda certainly at least when we come to 7/6 form.
The 88 Middlemarch at 21/ and the 3927 at 7/6 are most satisfactory entries. I am delighted also to see that Jubal and the Spanish Gypsy keep up in sale and this will I am sure please Mrs. Lewes.
At the foot of the statement is appended a note of the stock in hand of the edition of the other novels in five volumes, and on this stock the lordship will fall to be paid when sold. You never I think answered what
I said about the blunder in my letter arranging the terms for this edition ten years ago and I should like to settle that matter in any way you think most just.
I hope the year has begun well with Mrs. Lewes and you and that it may prove a happy one to you in your new abode. Mr. Simpson I am happy to say has got the better of his delicate throat sooner than we had ventured to hope and reappeared here today in full activity.
He joins my nephew and me in every good wish to Mrs. Lewes and you and believe me
always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 12 April 1859
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh April 12/59.
My Dear Lewes,
I inclose you a cheque 'a3130 being a second 'a3100 to account of Phys. of Common Life and 'a330 for G.E. received from Low on account of Adam Bede. I hope the supposed glory of the artful Liggins may betray some unctuous dissenter into a generous act for once in his life. The account of him in the letter to G.E. is delightful. It is very odd how perseveringly rumour has attributed the authorship to this man. You may recollect that on the appearance of the first part of Amos the Manx Cat proclaimed that Liggins was the man and I think this was the name Newdigate mentioned. The Miss Thackerays also wrote lately to my wife crying Eureka "Liggins is the name." He must have claimed the authorship himself although according to my recollection Newdigate said expressly he had not. I hope he will attempt no villainy on the strength of his reputation. If so we must look after him. Some years ago a rascal nearly succeeded in marrying a grl with some money on the strength of being the author of a series in the Magazine. Luckily the lady had an acquaintance, a relative of my brother's wife, who wrote to us for information and we blew the Lothario.
The printers are shouting for copy of the next part of the Physiology. It is too late pray send it down at once.
Ever Yours Truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes, Esqr.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 11 October 1871
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. | Edinburgh | October 11/71.
My Dear Lewes
I return Mr. Main's very striking letters. They are a very curious illustration of how the words of a great author tell in the most over-powering manner in every quarter. The cliffs under which he describes himself reading are very much those up which Edie Ochiltree piloted Sir Henry and his daughter. 379 It is a mercy he was not drowned. Absorbed as he was he would never have observed the water covering the "Ratton's Skerry."
I have had some talk with Willie and Mr. Simpson about Mr. Main's scheme for a selection of Thoughts, Wise and Witty (or some such title) from the works of George Eliot and we are very much disposed to enter into it. We do not happen to have any Arbroath correspondent so that I do not know anything of Mr. Main beyond these letters, but I daresay I shall hear something. The letters and specimen look as if he might thoroughly be trusted with the task.
The plan will be I think to retain a complete [right] over what he extracts and you should see everything either in M.S. or proof. You had better as you propose tell him to communicate with us.
I hope Mrs. Lewes continues to improve.
Ever yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 11 May 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 11 May 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 396.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
May 11/76.
My Dear Lewes
I shall be glad to oblige Messrs. Harper by letting them have proofs of Deronda sooner, although neither from their explanation nor my own knowledge of printing can I understand what convenience it can be to have the proofs more than a month or at most two before hand. The point to be strictly stipulated is no publication before the appearance of the book in this country. Any such forestalling would be a very serious thing.
I inclose a most pleasant statistical table of the sales of Daniel up to the present time. The closeness with which the sale of the successive numbers keeps up to the sale of the first Book indicates most satisfactorily how firm and enduring is the hold that the work is taking. I never recollect a case in which the sale of a work published in a serial form kept so closely up to the first start. Many buy a first part of a popular work from curiosity and then drop it, contenting themselves to read afterwards as opportunity may serve, but Deronda has evidently hooked his fish at the first start and is keeping him steadily on the line all through the run. You will have observed too from the tables sent to you at different times what a steady back sale there has been.
I knew that book IV must tell tremendously. Jews are not generally popular pictures in fiction, but then look how they are served up. They never have been so presented before like human beings with their good and their evil, their comic and their tragic side. In the midst of triumph it is distressing to hear of Mrs. Lewes feeling so feeble. I do hope the expedition to Oxford will do her good. I am looking forward with great pleasure to seeing you both next week, as I am going up to London on Monday but I have to go out of town on Tuesday so that it will be Wednesday or Thursday before I can come to you. A letter written tomorrow or Saturday will still find me here. My wife and daughter are not going with me this time so I am going into bachelor quarters at 14 Arlington St. where the old waiter Henry who took entire charge of me at the Burlington for some 15 years has got a lodging house. 473 I had not been well at all, suffering from that confounded thing called the mucous membrane, but a week at Strathtyrum has put me all right again. Hoping soon to see you both well and flourishing
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
I am puzzling greatly as to how Mrs. Lewes is to wind up in one more book and I am certain the public after reading book 7 will sympathise with me in wishing that there were to be more. Indeed I see symptoms already that the public would gladly have it prolonged to any length she wished.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 11 March 1858
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: II, 439, n. 4.
Edinburgh March 11/58.
My dear Lewes
Tell George Eliot that I think Adam Bede all right, most lifelike and real. I wish to read the MS quietly over again before writing in detail about it and since my return I am so overpowered with business that cannot be postponed that I may not for a little get the mental leisure necessary to do justice to a second perusal. For the first reading it did not signify how many things I might have had to think of. I would have hurried through it with eager pleasure. I write this note to allay all anxiety in the part of G.E. as to my appreciation of the merits of this most promising opening of a picture of life. Is there much more written or is it merely blocked out? Tell George Eliot also that I hear to-day Simpkins have 12 more of the [Clerical Scenes] and I think he may make his mind easy that none of the stock of the book will stick to our shelves.
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque £24 in acknowledgement of Food and Drink pt. 1 and I shall write you about pt. 2 with proof in a day or two.
In spite of all injunctions I began Adam Bede on the Railway and felt very savage when the waning light stopped me as we neared the Scottish Border. I picked up a Cab about Hammersmith and got to town in good time after a very pleasant afternoon at Richmond.
Best regards to George Eliot when you see him.
Ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
P.S. Looking over this note I see I have written the word "hurried" in a way that might be misunderstood. By hurried I mean reading as fast as I can, hurried reading in the ordinary acceptation of the term is impossible with anything of George Eliot's. You cannot skim over his pages.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 11 March 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 11/57.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque £45 in acknowledgment of Parts 2 and 3 of Mr. Gilfil, which hand to the mysterious George Eliot with this note.
I have read over the proof of Pt. III this morning and am deeply moved by the picture of poor Caterina's misery. The painting is so vivid that one sees as it were the woe begone little face, and anyone who has known sorrow will sympathise with her heart and soul in the hopeless wretchedness of her solitary chamber. The air of reality in the whole picture is wonderful.
I have grave doubts about the dagger, 820 beautifully as the impossibility of her using it is indicated. I daresay George Eliot will kick furiously at the base idea of altering a syllable at this point, but I am pretty sure that his dear little heroine would be more sure of universal sympathy if she only dreamed or felt as if she could stab the cur to the heart and I think it would be more consistent with her character than the active step of getting hold of the lethal weapon. I may be wrong however and I daresay many will prefer the dadger. I am puzzled as to whether Capt. Wybrow is dead or not. It is a fine climax to a part.
Wishing you a pleasant expedition and with compliments to George Eliot, I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
By all means let the incognito be kept. Shall I say to anxious inquirers that the Scenes are by one George Eliot of whom I know nothing?

John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 11 January 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
January 11/75.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of inclosing statement 191 of Mrs. Lewes' Works for the past year and a cheque for the balance £864-0-6d. I hope you will both be pleased with the result, which I do think very satisfactory. Middlemarch is a subject for immense congratulation. If you look at the dates of the reprints you will see the pace at which the sale has gone on and I do not hear of any symptoms of flagging yet. No previous experience could have led us to expect such a rapid and extended sale in the 7/6 form and it is most satisfactory to think that the right course has been adopted throughout with this great book.
The steady continuous sale of Jubal and The Spanish Gypsy is well and will I daresay please Mrs. Lewes quite as much as the success of their big brother. The Gypsy is just reprinted. 192
Comparing the statement with that rendered at the same time last year will I think enable you to understand this one, but if you are in the slightest doubt about anything, write.
It gave me great pleasure to receive Mrs. Lewes' truly gratifying expression of good wishes at the turn of the year, and I hope this will find you both well. Your being threatened with gout is hard. Nobody can say of you, "Ye've wrought well for it," which is a consolatory phrase I have heard addressed to myself in early days.
I have got quit of the cold which has been bothering me almost ever since I came from the country. The final remedy was I think Musselburgh, where I went on Saturday. It came on to rain so I did not play but walked for several hours with a greatcoat and umbrella, watching a good match in a deluge of rain. I felt that I could not logically defend my conduct and I was in a horrid fright all night lest I should begin coughing, but I did not.
Willie joins me in best remembrances to Mrs. Lewes and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
H. G. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 10 November 1863
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh
November 10/63.
My dear Lewes
I had the pleasure of receiving your note to-day and am glad to know that you have got into your new house which will I hope do Mrs. Lewes all the good in the world. Have you a garden? Houses spring up so fast about the Regents Park that I hardly know whether to think of you as in the Country or the Town.
I am vexed to hear that your son has failed in his examination and caused you so much anxiety but if he is not too confident I feel pretty sure he will ultimately do well, and a clever active young fellow like him may probably do better on his own hook than in the routine of any government service.
You should have heard from me if I had any good news to give of the sales of the 6/ edition of the novels but a statement will be made out and sent to you after the Turn of the Year. The failure of this 6/ edition is very annoying, and that Clerical Scenes, of which there had been no previous large sale, should not sell in this shape is most astonishing.
What are you both about? I hope G.E. is thinking of something new. With best regards to her believe me
Always yours Truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes, Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 10 April 1876
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh April 10/76.
My dear Lewes
I was greatly pleased to hear from Simpson that there was something due to you on our old transaction The Physiology of Common Life. In 1862 we paid you for all the Stock on hand as you will see by statement rendered at that time. Since then we have reprinted odds and ends of numbers to make complete sets of the book and inclosed cheque £66.5.9 pays for them as per accompanying statement. We have about a thousand complete copies on hand which move slowly.
Mr. Langford, I doubt not, keeps you well posted as to sales of Daniel and they are I think most satisfactory and Books two and three keep so well up with Book one. I confess however that I expected more of a spirt in sale but I think the closing scene of Book Four, I mean the Jewel scene, will set all the world talking. There is immense puzzlement as to what the author is going to make of Gwendolen, which is a good thing and none are more sorely baffled than the Newspaper critics.
While writing to you it occurs to me that I did not reply to Mrs. Lewes' last pleasant letter but I do not think there was any point requiring an answer. However I shall write to her very soon.
We had three lovely warm days but today it has gone back to East wind and snow.
ever yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 1 March 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, 1 March 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 1/59.
My Dear Lewes
I intend to have an article on Adam next month so suspend the Austen 57 and ponder well.
My proposed reviewer 58 says in a note I had the other day, "My notion of reviewing a Novel is, that you should never spoil the interest for those who have not read it by giving a resum'e9 of the plot. That is unfair to author and public."
The reviews in the papers, although not good in themselves, will do good to the book. I expect to be able to report soon that the Bedesman is fairly off and coming in a winner.
Damned presumptuous ass was my mental comment on the reviewer in the Saturday. The idea of G.E. sitting at the feet of Kingsley riled me particularly. 59 Why there is more sense in George Eliot's little finger than in Kingsley's whole carcase. With all his blustering, would-be manliness, I do not look upon Kingsley as a man of power and substance at all. I hope he is not a friend of yours as I have spoken so freely of him. It is a great pity there is not some one to tone and direct the feeling in the Saturday as there is much good writing in it, so much superior to the deplorable stuff in the Athenaeum. The Athenaeum has the best of it in this case however. 60 The Saturday Review has the inconceivable folly to speak of men like Bulwer, Dickens, Thackeray, etc. in a tone of happy superiority that would not be justifiable to the humblest literary aspirant.
I return Mrs. Carlyle's pleasant letter. I wrote her a line with G.E.'s message. Tell said G.E. that I have suppressed the extracts. I agree with his feeling about such comments, but they are not intended for the author's perusal but for that of the fools to whom he alludes.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, [17] December 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Edinburgh, [17] December 1857
MS: Copy, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh December 18. 1857.
My dear Lewes
I have read Hunger and Thirst twice with much interest and I am happy to say that I think the Public will take the series greedily. I would strongly urge you to take out the story of the eating of the Negro Boy. It gives one a turn at the start and my brother who has also read the proof with much pleasure made the same objections to it that I feel. A few sentences descriptive of the horrors of hunger would also ballance better with your introductory sketch of the beneficial effects of the stimulus which by the way is particularly good. Do you not take it too much for granted that a loss of 4/10 on weight from hunger is death to man as well as to animals and do you make sufficient allowance for the fatness or condition of the animal or man at the time the abstinence from food begins? You say nothing of the power of the mind in supporting man under Hunger and Thirst and I suppose nothing definite can be said. In the Black Hole of Calcutta 356 one would be disposed to say that the mental Constitution was an element in carrying a man through.
In the magazine it will be better not to give the series the general Title but it would be a shocking bore if any interloper got a hold of it. Do you think we could take any precaution against this, such as registering the first Paper at Stationers Hall under the Title Phys. of C. Life?
Your preface to Sea-Side Studies arrived today. The index is going on rapidly and a proof will be sent to you when ready. How do the illustrations stand? Shall we order the paper or has the engraver done so? We had better see the plates and paper before they are printed off in case of mistakes.
Ever yours truly,
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esqr.
Return proof as soon as you can.
