Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GHL, Colinsburgh, 2 September 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Gebliston by Colinsburgh | Fife September 2/59.
My Dear Lewes
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque 'a314-14/- in acknowledgment of your paper on the Will. 279
When you write let me know what you think of the other papers in the Magazine if you have read them. I always like to hear your opinion and also G.E's to whom give my best regards. Her friend Colonel Steuart arrived here the day before yesterday with 4 dogs, pointers and setters, two horses and a phaeton, an unexpected but welcome addition to our stud which makes a very lively Menagerie.
The history of the finding of the Pug is beyond price. The Colonel had been quite baffled hunting in vain for three days when he happened to go to Willesden paddocks, where he saw a stuffed Pug. Inquiring at the man in charge where it would be possible to find a live specimen, he was informed that a "gentleman" Mr. Rand in Golden Lane, St. Lukes knew more than any other man in London. The Colonel was off at once to Mr. Rand, who proved to be a carpenter not of the Adam Bede type. After a good deal of fencing he said that the landlord of Knave of Clubs, Club Lane, Bethnal Green had two pugs. The Hansom was forthwith turned on Club Lane where the Landlord was from home and the Landlady, a tremendous slasher, a match for anything short of a prize fighter, informed him that her husband never trusted the key of the cellar where the pugs were kept out of his pocket. The Colonel passed some time in agreeable badinage with this beauty and made an appointment for the following day with the husband. The Landlord of the Knave of Clubs proved a thorough man of business, and the transaction was concluded in the most formal style.
I am not doing the Colonel's narrative justice. I am sure his own account would make you shout.
How does the new Novel get on? Do you think we can start before the end of the year?
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
Are you doing anything for Maga?

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, torwood, 12 August 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, torwood, 12 August 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Torwood by Dunkeld | August 12/57.
My Dear Sir
I inclose proof of Janet's Repentance part III and I beg to congratulate you upon it. It is first rate. At pages 3 and 4 you hit the nail on the head. That passage cannot be too highly praised -- full of sound sense and real religious feeling. The root of the matter is in it.
In spite of the objections I mentioned I had a conviction from the first that Janet would turn out something very wonderful and I could not have anticipated anything more powerfully interesting and exciting than the close of this part. I look with great impatience for the rest of the M.S.
This is a lovely morning for the 12th 950 and I rather grudge not having made arrangements to be on the Hill by daybreak. If I shoot at all it will not be until much later in the Season. There is fishing in these parts but I have either been too busy or too lazy, as I have never taken out my rod. The weather is so fine and the country so beautiful that there is amusement enough without any special pursuit.
Tell Lewes that I shall be able to send him his proof tomorrow or next day. Address to Edinburgh.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Thornhill, 25 December 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Thornhill, 25 December 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Eccles | Thornhill | Dumfries
Christmas Day | 1859.
My Dear Madam
Your welcome note caught me as I passed through London. I am extremely glad to hear that you have abandoned the idea of publication in shilling numbers, and you will never I am sure have occasion to repent your acceptance of our offer. I must not write upon business matters today but will do so when I get home which I hope to do on Wednesday or Thursday at furthest.
This district is the very headquarters of the Scottish national game of curling, that is swinging huge stones at a mark about forty yards along the ice. Yesterday we had a glorious day and I wish you had been there to describe the scene. It was a lovely Loch among the snow clad hills where about sixty as hardy looking fellows as one could wish to have at one's back in a row began to muster immediately after breakfast. They were of all ranks from the laird my host 439 to the humblest farm labourer and all on a footing of the most perfect freedom and equality. Looking at the men lounging about before business began you might have thought them rather a lazy apathetic set of fellows, as unimpressionable as their hard rugged pastures. But when the play began my apathetic friends would have delighted you. With voices hoarse with emotion they rushed frantically about the ice watching their own stone or their adversary's as it slipped along to the goal, and the shouts that arose when a really first rate shot was made might have been heard miles off. I have seen plently of hustle and excitement among the French but their ebullitions are like those of children compared with the fierce enthusiasm of my friends yesterday.
Wishing Lewes and you a pleasant Christmas and much happiness, Believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
Look at the Press this week and you will see our friends of the Saturday Review as pleasantly flayed as you could wish for their insolent attack upon Dickens. 440

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 8 September 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 8 September 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
September 8/72.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
The first hundred pages of Sunset and Sunrise came here last night and instead of going to Church with the rest of the family I sat down and have just finished reading the proof. Dorothea is better than any sermon that ever was preached by man. It is noble. The picture of that bleeding solitary gallant heart alone that night in her dreary chamber is grandly moving. 590 How one longs to help her and how beautifully you let the daylight in.
How skilfully you are unravelling that most tangled skein of trouble. I think I see my way but I am dying to see the sun fairly risen. If the rest of the M.S. was in Edinburgh I would telegraph to the printers never to stop work until it was ready to send to me. I do not wonder at such work upsetting the ordinary routine of life and consequently health. The mere reading of it has made me think with contempt of lunch, the gong for which is about to sound.
Lewes said something about changing the division of the Books. There might be a break at page 194, which would make Book 8 begin with "In Middlemarch a wife could not long remain ignorant that the town held a bad opinion of her husband." 591 How exquisitely those touches relieve the graver parts. The little talk with Tantrip in "the old tone" follows daylight delightfully in Dorothea's room. 592
I do hope this will find you better and the work finished. When I wrote to you yesterday with all the admiration I expressed and felt I was puzzled as to how you could "put your house in order" but now accept from me the first instalment of the hearty congratulations and thanks the world will soon offer to you.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
On thinking over the division of the Books I feel that Dorothea's declaration of standing by Lydgate is so good an opening for what is to be expected in the last book that it is the most appropriate finish for
Book 7, so I would not mind making the one Book thin and the other thick.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 8 August 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
August 8/79.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Willie is away with his Light Horse up about Dundee so may have omitted to tell you that Simpkins having ordered 100 more Theophrastus last week, all doubt about reprinting was removed and another 500 put in hand at once.
I inclose a table of Sales of your works from January 1 to June 30, which I suppose it was intended that I should send on to you and at all events it will not be unrefreshing for you to look at it. We shall send you a cheque for Theophrastus at the beginning of October or sooner if you should wish any of it.
The weather is so far better and I earnestly hope that you are well enough to drive out. Strange to say with better weather I have not been quite so well again, but it is nothing and I daresay I had been walking rather much. Today I expect to be fit for my round of the
Links again, walking not playing. Oliphant writes to me from our embassy at Constantinople. He has been all over Syria and Palestine and sends me some of the first fruits in a M.S. article to be followed by others and also by a book. 309 You and he and Disraeli are all I fancy working to one end.
I had a long letter from Hamley too lately who had fallen [in] with Oliphant when dining at the Embassy on the Bosphorus. Hamley has been acting as our chief commissioner in settling the boundaries of Roumania and Turkey according to the Treaty of Berlin. They have succeeded beyond expectation. . . .
always your truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 7 September 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 7 September 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
September 7/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am so glad to think of you safe and well in England again and to hear that you have both enjoyed and benefited by your expedition. Your walking feats are worthy of Golfers. The details you will have got of the sales of Deronda would I think assist to make your return home pleasant. They are indeed most satisfactory and have I trust come up to Lewes' expectations and yours. The sale in the 4 vols. has not been large, but after such a triumphant run in the Numbers, that was not to be expected in the present form.
The praise of the Chief Rabbi is truly gratifying and the most convincing evidence that your intuitions as to Jewish character are as true as all the world admit them to be when you are painting your own countrymen and women. It is almost impossible to make a strong Jewish element popular in this country and it was perfectly marvellous to see how in your transitions you kept your public together. Anti-Jews grumbled but went on. I could not hear whether Disraeli gave any utterances on the subject.
We have had a wonderfully fine summer here but of late Scotland has been asserting herself and rain, cold winds, and fog have reappeared among us. You give a most enticing description of St. Blazien but St. Andrews Links on a fine day leave no room for envy at least in a Golfer's mind.
We are all very well and regret that the pleasant summer is slipping away from us, but we generally have a fine autumn and there are to be extra festivities at the end of the month, as Prince Leopold 521 is coming to take the chair as Captain of the Club. The discussions at the Club as to how things are to be arranged would make a play. The main difficulty is want of room, as you cannot dine 200 men with a Club room that will only dine 95. Mr. Melville aged 79 has solved this as to the dinner by deciding that senior members are to have the preference. The young ladies wonder whether this is to hold good as to the Ball.
I am writing a line to Lewes and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
I hope the suffering eye lid is better. Such little things do worry. You would have the ardent sympathy of my son Jack, the close of whose holidays have been darkened by the dentist and a swelled face.
I inclose a note which came yesterday from Mrs. W. Smith. She evidently feels the Book. Look at the Wordsworth Strathmore narratives to which she alludes in present month's Magazine. 522 Mrs. Wordsworth is a delicate, still pretty looking woman. How she survived those horrible hardships is a miracle. I never saw a more remarkable case of "the back being made for the burden."

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 7 September 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 7 September 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: John Blackwood, p. 382.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
September 7/72.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am so sorry to hear from Lewes that you are still poorly and I do wish your wonderful Picture was ended, that you might get away to health-restoring Homburg.
How you do paint and dissect Bulstrode's feelings. It is a terrible picture of the attempt to love God and Mammon, for you throw in a touch of reality in the wretch's religion which removes him from the ordinary religious hypocrite of his school. In the struggle that night he, as it were, hardly knew himself that he was committing murder when he gave the brandy. 588 That is the impression you have left I think.
This 7th Book leaves Dr. Lydgate in a terrible mesh out of which it is difficult to see his way unscathed, but with Dorothea to the rescue I was glad to see hope.
The gossiping Middlemarch harpies gathering to the prey is fine. 589 It makes one's flesh creep to think of any good man's character in their hands. My own reflection reminds me of a story. A humorous old bachelor, relative of mine, had retired from business to live about 20 miles from Edinburgh, and one Sunday had out a batch of his old Lawyer cronies. Late at night when they had ably dissected their various acquaintances, the liquor in the dining room ran short. My friend said "Gentlemen, there is the key of the cellar and any of you may go and get up whatever you like, but damn me if I'll leave my character in your hands for five minutes."
My wife and daughter have read Book 7 and are in a great state of excitement. They feel ahead of the rest of the world. We have the most abominable rainy weather. Our harvest prospects are very bad.
With best regards to Lewes and hoping to get good accounts of you soon I am always
yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 5 November 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
November 5/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
It gives me much pleasure to receive your interesting letter and to hear that you have got quit of the cold which our damp wretched autumn had spread so freely.
I quite understand your feeling of wishing to keep up parental relations with your goodly progeny of good works, and I think we shall have no difficulty in arranging a system of lordship to your satisfaction. 554 This is to be our last week here for the season so tell Lewes I propose not to go into the matter until I go to Edinburgh where I intend to be on the 13th or 14th.
The loss of his promising son at Natal must have been a heavy blow to him. It is hard to see the useful and active taken away while bad shillings always keep cropping up from the uttermost ends of the earth.
You need not disturb yourself about reviews of Deronda, while people keep discussing the book like a great historical event about which there is a difference of opinion. The discussion would not exist if the book were not felt and doing its work even among those who most dissent. I always knew that the strong Jew element would be unpopular, but your picture of the Jew family at home did wonders in overcoming the public distaste to a kindly human view of the Jewish character.
This is a glorious day here and the woods are looking beautiful with as many colours as Joseph's Coat. The weather looks too as if it would last and give us a good wind up of the season here.
My wife and daughter are sorrowing that we are so soon to go, and to me the move to Edinburgh is always the mark that another year is gone. We are all well and so are the numerous animals, bar old Tickler the terrier, whose skin and temper show increasing marks of age and irritability. I shall have a good many golf matches this week and tomorrow one of my antagonists is Mr. Whyte Melville now in his 80th year but looking as young as his son. 555
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. andrews, 4 October 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 47.
St. Andrews | October 4/58.
My Dear Sir
You would feel that I could not do otherwise than like the second volume of Adam Bede otherwise I should not have been guilty of so long a silence as to its merits, although my house has been so full of visitors during the last few weeks that I have had the greatest difficulty in finding any time to read, think, or write.
The story is a very striking one and I cannot recollect anything at all of the same kind. I long to see how you will work it out.
You may be sure that I shall sit down to the third volume the moment I get the M.S. and you shall have no cause for impatience to hear from me about it.
Hetty is a wonderful piece of painting. One seems to see the little villain. She is painted in such irresistible colours that I am very sorry for the well intentioned Arthur. One feels that there is no chance of escape for any youth of his age unless he takes to his heels.
I have thought a great deal over the encounter between Adam and Arthur, 1193 indeed I daresay it is pondering over that scene which has prevented me from sooner sitting down to write to you. The picture of Adam's feelings before he gets the fatal glimpse of the scene in the wood is perfection. The point is worked up to with wonderful skill. It is very difficult to imagine what would happen between any two men brought so suddenly into such a total revulsion of feelings and change of relative positions as happens to Adam and Arthur, but on the whole I think you have hit the mark and sustained in a very trying climax the characters of the two men you are drawing. I am ashamed of myself for not feeling more sorry for Adam, but I have no doubt the sympathies will gather round him keenly when the full force of his affliction comes upon him and the tender and stern fibres in his heart of oak fairly begin to struggle.
Mrs. Poyser is excellent as also her husband and the children, or rather child. I am puzzled as to what the wicked old Squire is up to.
There can be no doubt that the book will be successful but the degree of success will depend very much upon the third volume, so I think the best plan will be to leave our final arrangements for publication, number of copies to be printed, etc. etc. until the book is finished. The printing will occupy very little time and it would not save much to begin until you could give your undivided attention to the proofs.
I inclose Mr. Froude's note which is very gratifying. I write him a line embodying your message which will probably bring another outpouring from him.
Give my regards to Lewes when you see him and say that I shall write to him from Edinburgh where I intend to be tomorrow. Hoping soon to congratulate you on the completion of Adam, Believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 4 August 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 4 August 1874
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: John Blackwood, pp. 384-385.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
August 4/74.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I have such good news to give of Middlemarch, Jubal, and also Spanish Gypsy that I write a line to report progress.
Of the 7/6 edition of Middlemarch we printed 3150 in May and 2100 in the latter part of June. The above are all disposed of and we have just reprinted 2100 more of which the first batch went off to Pater Noster Row the other day to supply orders. The success of Middlemarch has also exercized a benign influence on the sale of the other novels.
Of Jubal you are aware that the first edition 1609 copies is gone and we subscribed 247 of the second edition in London. Of the Spanish Gypsy I see we have sold 107 copies between December and July. This is all good and must I think make you turn to a new work with fresh confidence that you are not writing in vain. News of how that work is getting on will be very welcome.
I hope you are both well and enjoying this delightful weather in the country. It is charming here and even my daughter feels that there is enjoyment apart from London gaieties. As we drove through Regent St. to the Railway Station she exclaimed "Oh Papa, don't you wish we were coming in instead of going away? How bright and gay everything is." It was positively a wet foggy day.
Major Lockhart came over to us a few days ago with loud talk of shutting himself up in his room and working. The scoundrel has never been off the Links since his arrival. The other day I played a match with the Whig whip W. Adam 135 just relieved from his weary duties in the House of Commons. When we were a few holes out he exclaimed fervently, "This is a great, glorious, and noble game. There is nothing like it in the world." He was a little ahead of me at the time I think, but we were quite agreed.
In addition to the usual entertainments of the place we had a famous military week the Fife Mounted Rifles drilling in one of the Parks here. Willie turned out with them and their colonel, that mighty hunter Jack Anstruther Thomson, 136 stayed with us. You will have heard of Thomson in former days as Master of the Pytchley and also of the Atherstone. He told me a good one of Newdegate. He (T) had got a fall and broken one of the small bones of his leg. No one of course could be kinder than Newdegate, but when he had got his friend into the most comfortable possible position he began at once about the Jesuits. On which exclaimed the tortured Thomson, "My dear Charlie, you have done everything for me that man can until the Doctor comes and the hounds are running -- pray ride on." I remember him telling me this story long ago and I never can think of it without laughing as it is so characteristic of both men.
All the world comes to St. Andrews and among others we have at present that great Oxford Don the Dean of Christ-church. 137 Liddell's
Greek Lexicon Lewes probably will know and have suffered under. He is a most agreeable old gentleman and along with his fair daughters walked round with Lockhart and me in our match yesterday. For the honour of learning I am happy to say he showed intelligence about the Game.
My son is at home for the holidays and I think you would like him. He has a strong turn for humour which he developes with much gravity.
With best remembrances to Lewes, I am always
yours truly
John Blackwood.
I cannot remember your Country address so must send this into Edinburgh to be posted. Willie is with us and he and my wife are gone out riding and I am now going to walk down to the Club to hear the Golfers retail their day's performances.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 3-4 August 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 3-4 August 1878
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
August 3/78.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
There is a strong feeling of regret and disappointment throughout the house since the receipt of your letter telling that you did not think you could come to us this year. My wife and daughter are very low on the subject and beg you both to reconsider your decision and start for the north. My own opinion is most decided that it would do Lewes good as it would be a thorough change and a change to quiet pleasant places. We have lovely weather (even for Scotland) and there is every prospect of it continuing. I too am leading exactly the life for a man who has been ill, eating fish puddings and all manner of what we used to call Baby's Meat, while for drink I take [lemonade?] strengthened by a change to claret after dinner. For exercise I walk round the links after lunch looking at a Golf Match and after dinner comes a mild cigar round the woods and then with possibly another cigar in smoking room to bed. All I can say for this manner of life is that I came here a month ago feeling it a labour to go up stairs or walk half a mile and now I am quite ready to walk any reasonable distance and sometimes find myself walking up the stairs two steps at a time in the old fashion.
I had almost forgot to mention that I satisfy my business conscience by working about 3 hours after breakfast. Tell Lewes I do hope he will come yet as I sincerely think it will do him good and I need not say it will be a great treat to us. The journey by the Flying Scotchman to Edinburgh is the easiest in the world, 400 miles in 9 hours and you sweep into Edinburgh as the clock strikes seven with Princes St. and the Castle looking splendid in the setting sun. "Ah! We're a Great Nation"!!!!
We had a famous time last week with the Fife Mounted Rifles. Their Colonel the famous "Jack Thomson" of the Atherstone etc. and the inspecting officer, Col. Munger [?] a most pleasant fellow being with us. In the games after the review Willie won the prize for horsemanship which pleased him and his friends. Jack came home upon Saturday. He had been out with the Fife Artillery Militia in which he is a sublieutenant as I thought a little drilling would do him good, and it has. I should like him to make your acquaintance and Lewes.] My wife and daughter ride a good deal but there is also much driving and if the weather is fine the sea makes up for the want of your beautiful trees and vallies. The drives with you must be splendid but almost too hot this summer.
There has been a hot passage at the end of the Session but Ld Beaconsfield's speech tonight and the division last night will wind it up sweetly. Disraeli will be in great form tonight at Guildhall. 108
I had written the first word of this letter yesterday morning when Mr. Main was announced. He was looking well and we had a pleasant luncheon. I told him we would not publish Birth Day Book until October. I did not breath[e] a word of your possibly being here nor have I said a word on that head to anyone as I did not wish invaders.
My wife sends her best regards and earnestly hopes you may yet come, and begging Lewes to consider this the best place for gout imaginary or concealed, I am always
yours very truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 3 November 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 3 November 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 384.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
November 3/73.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
By a message from Lewes to George St. I doubt not you are now established at the Priory for the winter and I hope your stay in the Country has done you both a great deal of good. We go into Edinburgh for the winter on Wednesday and the melancholy packing has already begun. I hear them hard at it outside the door of my room.
When I last heard of Middlemarch the sale was still going on. It has been most satisfactory, but I shall write to you with particulars from Edinburgh.
We are getting the best weather we have had at the close of the Season. The woods are looking lovely and the Golfing green is in rare order. We have had a good many visitors as usual and among others Delane lately. His tale of the blunders through which the Ashantee War had arisen increase our anger at the policy and administration which has sent so many fine fellows to that horrid coast. Wolseley 866 is a friend and correspondent of mine. He wrote the account of his Red River expedition in the Magazine. I had a letter from his wife yesterday. She had heard from him in good health and spirits. He wrote on the 5th from Cape Coast where he had arrived on the 2nd. He is an able man and will, I doubt not, do well, but who can fight with such a climate? I have a great many friends with the force and I wish I saw them well out of it.
I have suffered a good deal this autumn from those horrid attacks of oppression at pit of stomach apparently, which unfit one for anything while they last. I cannot make out what it is but I have always been more or less subject to them. Sometimes worry seems to me to be the main cause of them. However they never affect my strength so I do not think it can be anything very bad.
We had much interest in my daughter coming out which she did at the Golf Ball at the beginning of October. She looked like a little fairy and to see her and her mother dancing opposite to each other was a treat.
With best regards to Lewes and hoping to get good accounts of you both, believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 29 September 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 29 September 1878
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
September 29/78.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Your kind letter is most welcome and it touches me much to think of your cordial feeling about me. I am truly thankful to say that my health has gone on improving all summer and after having been so ill as I was it is an enjoyment to be able to walk twice round the Links without halting and panting behind my old companions as was the case with me when I came here at the end of June. I wish much that your letter gave me a better account of the health of both of you. My friend Mr. Lucas Collins went from here to Braemar and found your friend Andrew Clark there practising what he preached as to Scotch Air. I hope that your Doctor will send you also to Scotland next year. When I get a letter from you it is curious that I feel as if you knew all the ways of this house as well as our most frequent guests and by this time next year I hope you will know them practically. We have had a magnificent summer as to weather and have been very fortunate in our guests despite the blank in our expectations that you were compelled to make. Julian Sturgis was here. He is a fine fellow and talked much of you. I am greatly taken with a little thing he has written this month "Fire Flies." Will you let me know what you think of it and also of The New Ordeal. 135
This has been the Golf Meeting Week as you will see from the Field. Scot's patriotism was rather upset by some Saxons from Westward Ho who beat several of our most famous Golf Champions. Yesterday afternoon however at the close of the Meeting Scotland as usual showed she had "a man as good" by producing "a couple of Lambs" two noble brothers with the purest and most undefiled Scotch accent who beat the Devonshire champions. I walked round with the match trembling for the honour of Scotland. There was an Exodus from St. Andrews yesterday of sorrowing golfers waving their handkerchiefs from every train to their happier friends who were still left upon the Links. This house too was partially cleared but any blank was soon made up by the goodly presence of Principal Tulloch who arrived between 8 and 9 last night. Willie and his sister, Miss Blandford and Jamie White too are still here so it is not exactly a solitude.
My daughter has had her full share of dancing fun at the Inverness Meeting on the previous week where reels are danced madly and here the same kind of thing was going on. I am sleeping so beautifully that I never heard them come in at 4 in the morning although they made noise enough to rouse Abou Hassan. 136 Coming from Inverness on the Highland Line Mary distinguished herself by the polite information she gave to an English Traveller. To his asking the name of the mountains she replied with great sweetness "There are many mountains about here and they have no particular names." Soon after a fellow with an accent in the opposite corner of the carriage remarked to his companion "I never saw Ben Mac Dhui 137 lookin' better." She ought to have been covered with confusion but I fear could not resist laughing.
Jack is well and since he has been in the Fife Militia has a most decidedly military appearance. The Truefit of St. Andrews cutting my hair the other morning remarked "That feather is a sore trouble to Mr. John." I suppose some rebellious hairs on my head made him think of this hereditary taint. My world renowned Caddie from Musselburgh who signs himself "Commonly called Fiery" was over here for the Meeting Week. His parting from me was graceful. "I met Mrs. Blackwood ridin' on her horse. I am ra'al pleased to see ye baith lookin' sae weel."
The news from India is very grave and there is no Peace anywhere. I hope our friend in India has a good adviser along side of him. He is very dependant on that. The short reign of John Forster broke up my intimacy with him and had it lasted we would have come to a quarrel.
Your Books will form part of History so you need not think them small whatever wars may be going on. The sale of the cheap edition of your Novels is going on steadily and for the Cabinet Edition I think we shall have a good demand when we are able to sell it complete. Willie tells me they are ready in the printing office for the additional matter you propose for the second volume of poetry so will you send it to Edinburgh. He joins me in best remembrances to Lewes and you and believe me
ever yours Truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F

John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 29 July 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
July 29/72.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I cannot adequately express my admiration for Book VI. Every book seems to go on becoming what one could not have thought possible -- better than its predecessor.
I dallied for days over this Book, pausing and reading and rereading, and now when I sit down to write to you, instead of doing so out of hand I find myself turning over the sheets of the Book, looking at the different points and wondering what is most perfect, until if I do not take care the morning will be gone and no letters written at all, as has happened to me more than once before. When things please me particularly I sit back in my chair and begin dreaming. Just at the opening of this Book what can be more perfect than Dorothea and Celia, and Sir James' equivocal reply "Not if he had been like Casaubon" 566 has my entire sympathy. There are some truly exquisite touches in those two interviews with Will Ladislaw. 567
Lydgate had very great merit in not taking a stick to Rosamond. You have painted that heartless [one word illegible] obstinate devil with a vengeance. It is a most highly polished picture, painted on the hardest possible bit of panel.
That scene in the Garth family 568 is famous. One feels almost uncomfortably in the thick of it, rather afraid of sticky fingers on one's garments. I have assisted at such scenes.
I was extremely glad to hear from Lewes that you had benefited so much by the quiet of the country, but I wish he gave a better account of himself. If it suits you I quite approve of the plan of only allowing a month between the publication of the last two parts so as to wind up on the first of December. I return Mr. Charles Ritter's most gratifying letter. It is a tribute.
You should have heard from me sooner but I have been sorely oppressed, in fact nearly had my brains blown out with M.S.S. You know that I always walk through the world with people pointing M.S.S. instead of pistols at my head, and on my return I found a tremendous accumulation of revolvers in my room. Our expedition abroad was a great affair, and my daughter's enjoyment of it was a treat in itself. I think Venice and Como (Belaggio) were our greatest delights.
In travelling my wife attempted to read the fifth Book of Middlemarch but failed, saying, "It is utterly impossible to read Middlemarch with your head and heart half out of the window." This is quite so. It requires the most undivided attention. I know that if a line or a word escapes me I find out as I read on that I have missed something and I turn back.
We passed about a week on the Lake of Como, and certainly it is a place where one can enjoy doing nothing. The following incident at the Villa Sommariva 569 will have your sympathy. My daughter exclaimed, "What a lovely lizard," as one glittered along the edge of the path. This attracted the attention of the young Tom Tulliver, our guide, who promptly stamped it out. The young lady forgot her dignity, exclaiming "Oh you little brute," and only checked herself when on the point of seizing him by the collar.
Tell Lewes I am having over the Tables of the sales of Middlemarch and will write to him with the result in a few days. 570
With many congratulations on the success and approaching completion of your labours believe me, Dear Mrs. Lewes
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 28 August 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
August 28/73.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am very glad to hear that you have got safely back and have enjoyed the "saury"[?] and I hope you have both benefited by the expedition.
I shall write to Mr. Main about the extracts from Middlemarch. It strikes me he has made rather too many extracts from so new a book, 834 but I shall look through them.
You will be pleased to hear that the 21/- edition continues to sell steadily. It is very satisfactory.
We have been almost entirely at home except for a run of a week into the Highlands. We went the whole family with nephew and niece, and Hamley joined us at Perth. We had a great deal of rain but it interfered little with our enjoyment, which was very great. The weather here is mixed to use a mild phrase, but it never interferes with Golf.
I am well although just at present suffering from one of those horrid stomach attacks which floor one. With best regards to Lewes, believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 27 July 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
July 27/68.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am delighted to hear that you have got back and are both so well. You have returned just in time to hear that the Poem is nearly out of print and to consider what had best be done. I do not think that it will do any harm to be out of print for a little. We kept the type up and I think the best plan will be to print another little edition of 500 in same form and price. 793 Paper has been laid in to be ready in case of a sudden rush on the book, but I do not see a chance of that now. The sale you will see has gone on in a very steady sort. I rather fear there is a falling off in the last week or so but I have not got a very recent memorandum.
The reviews have not been good. The reviewers have looked perseveringly for faults and shut their eyes to the beauties. This was eminently the case with a most unpoetic gentleman in the Pall Mall Gazette. 794 I do not understand a man with any poetic feeling writing two reviews of the Gypsy without giving way to enthusiasm about the beauty of the language and imagery. However the lad is very well pleased with himself evidently, if he is not in the same frame of mind with the Gypsy.
We have had the most scorching dry weather I ever remember in this country. There is nothing green to be seen anywhere, but the crops are good in spite of the drought. I have as you suppose been leading much my usual life, working and golfing, the sameness of which, although it does not weary, leaves no landmarks to indicate the lapse of time like journies such as you have been making.
We had a visit lately from two young Oxonians, and I could not help thinking that you would have enjoyed seeing the lads full of fun and mischief and enjoying themselves quite beyond their powers of expression. The father of one of them, a very intimate friend and correspondent, had told me they were on a walking tour in Scotland, so I desired them to come to Strathtyrum. Of course they missed their train, owing to some lark and arrived on foot towards midnight with a Bull Dog! a perfect specimen. The butler was terrified and did not wish to let them in until I appeared. The dog, I need not tell you, turned out an angel and was soon on the best seat in the drawing room. My friend's son proved like his father, very clever, and I laughed almost as much as the lads did. At Church they fell in with a friend, "the most popular fellow in Trinity," who had come here having heard that "St. Andrews was a first class place to read." This "devil of a fellow to read" was speedily brought to Strathtyrum, introduced to the ladies golfing ground etc., and I really feel anxious about his studies.
With best regards to Lewes believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Inclosed is a Mem. of some corrections suggested. Have you any?

John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 26 October 1871
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
October 26/71.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Thanks for your kind expressions regarding the death of my brother. He was a most sterling fellow with an immense deal of character about him, such an one as you would have liked. My real moan was made for him some years ago when his health broke, but the final blow tells. I have seen six brothers, all strong able men, go down almost in the prime of life, and I am now the last of seven. Blessed as I am in my own immediate family, I feel that I have no right to repine.
Mr. Main came here the day before yesterday and I am happy to tell you that I was very much pleased with him. He is a little fellow, dark with bright clear-looking eyes. He had been intended for "The Ministry" but it did not suit him, and he left Glasgow without going into the Clerical course. He does a little in the way of teaching, in reading with lads, and has apparently some little means. He seems about 30 and has evidently seen nothing of the world or scarcely, but there is something interesting in his manners and the ladies like him. He bears the mark of enthusiast about with him and you are his particular idol.
He is in the habit of reading your works aloud on the seashore, and when he was telling this at lunch I made my little joke about his having been nearly caught by the tide. He replied "Well, I have no doubt she would have made a fine poem about it, and if she could have sent it after me that would have been something." His accent I take to be a kind of mixture between Arbroath and Glasgow, but the voice is euphonious. He is getting on with his work.
Tell Lewes that I think he should register the Title Middlemarch and Miss Brooke at Stationers' Hall, but Langford will know whether this is necessary or can be done before publication. You will be amused to hear that the General 388 has taken to Middlemarch. He is taking it in small doses at a time, with apparent satisfaction and benefit. This letter has been written under difficulty as the good fellow has been sitting opposite me putting up a packet of pipes to go by post to my nephew George in India, and the process has lasted more than an hour.
I do hope that you are better and with best regards to Lewes I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 23 September 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
September 23/61.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I have the pleasure of inclosing a check One Thousand Pounds 'a31000 making the 'a31600 due to you for the 8000 printed of Silas Marner. 843
Willie was not far wrong in stopping the order previously, as the Scotch Banks charge 21 days interest for remitting money to London, a little piece of plunder kept up from the remote days when it took 3 weeks to travel between the two towns. It is very shabby in my bank to charge it to me, as they regularly sack the 21 days on all the large amount of Sassenach gold that I yearly draw down from London, and their refusal to give the small quid for the great quo excited Willie's ire.
I would have answered your pleasant and most interesting letter of the 12th 844 but I waited daily expecting my coffers in London to be filled, but I suppose the bad times make people slow in paying up their accounts.
I have been seriously considering what you say about purchasing the entire copyright of your novels and am very much disposed for the speculation. It is rather puzzling to say what should be offered in fairness to one party or the other but the first time I am again in Edinburgh I shall make you an offer which will I hope meet your views, and in the meantime I have told Mr. Simpson to be making calculations for cheap editions etc. He rather inclines to the cheap edition at once now, and so do I. The 12/- editions must have cut into the 6/- class passengers.
However I wish to have some further talk with Mr. Simpson and Willie before coming to a definite decision. I think I shall make these two Mahomets come to the Mountain instead of going over to the abominable confusion of 45 George St. I am changing my sitting room there in obedience to the orders of the most imperative of Doctors, my friend Burt, 845 who tells me in plain terms that I and most of the men of business he knows are idiots for passing their days in a close confined room when they can afford a better, so I am now moving to what was the drawing [room] of the house, a magnificent "hairy apartment" as the London lodging house keepers say. It is rather comical that this same despot Burt effected a similar revolution for Murray 846 in Albemarle St. The alterations however are no joke and will hardly be finished until I go home for the winter.
I hope most sincerely that the good effects of the Malvern treatment continue with Lewes and you since your return to London and that I shall soon have good accounts both of health and work. My temptations to idleness here are dreadful. The golfing and shooting are both good and White and Aytoun are staying with us, so that in doors also the fun is irresistible. Lewes got a glimpse of White 847 and I shall bring him to you on the first opportunity. He is as delightful at breakfast as at dinner and keeps us all laughing from morning to night without the slightest strain to himself or his hearers. The beauty of his conversation is the perpetual play of fancy and the sort of give-and-take, and one may delude oneself into the idea that one has said half the good things oneself. Those London dining out conversationalists are my abomination, and he is the most delightful contrast to them.
There goes the dressing bell so I must wind up.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Thanks for your kind inquiries. I am getting all right now and able to Golf. I have stood my little illness so well that I am more confident of my health than I have been for a long time.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 20 July 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 20 July 1871
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
July 20/71.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I have read the second portion of Middlemarch with the greatest admiration. It is a most wonderful study of human life and nature. You are like a great giant walking about among us and fixing every one you meet upon your canvas. In all this life like gallery that you put before us every trait in every character finds an echo or recollection in the reader's mind that tells him how true it is to Nature.
It was a disappointment at first not to find any of my old friends of the former part, 327 all except Lydgate apparently entirely strangers, but as you beautifully express it we never know who are to influence our lives while "Destiny stands by sarcastic with our dramatis personae folded in her hand." 328 The elaborate picture of the formation of Lydgate's character is powerfully relieved by the tremendous French adventure into which the wise young Doctor fell. 329 It would be endless to try to refer to all the happy hits and turns. That sylph caught young and made perfect by Mrs. Lemon is a great success, and I like poor Ned. 330 Where did you hear those horsey men talking? 331 Willie's room at George St. opens from my room and I often hear the mysterious words of wisdom flowing between him and his horsey yeomany friends. You have caught the very tone.
The Farebrother family are delights, a perfect picture. Reading of all the various characters in this second volume -- for it is really almost a volume -- I had quite forgotten Mr. Brooke, but I knew his voice the moment he came into the room 332 at the meeting for the election of Chaplain. There is something uncommonly good about Mary Garth who has her "peculiar temptations" not to accept "good sense and good principle" "ready mixed" and does feel it hard to think that she must be called "an ugly thing" alongside of fair Rosamond. 333
I think our plan of publication is the right one as the two parts are almost distinct, each complete in itself. Indeed there will be complaints of the want of the continuous interest of a story, but this does not matter where all is so fresh and true to life. Each group that you introduce is a complete little book or study in itself. I return the precious M.S. registered. Have you observed how much closer and smaller you are writing? When you can spare the M.S. I should like to have the quantity calculated. I am pretty sure there is equivalent to a volume of an ordinary novel in what I now return.
I got your kind pleasant letter and am very sorry you are not coming to the Scott Centenary but at those sort of gatherings there are always forward vulgar monsters to jar upon one's feelings, so perhaps you escape something. Simpson is quite well again and greatly gratified by your kind message, which I told him to take home to read to his mother. With best remembrances to Lewes I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 2 October 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 2 October 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews October 2nd 1879.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Willie was here last week and I hope the decision we came to about increased allowance to you as explained in accompanying note and memorandum will fully answer your expectations.
When I read Theophrastus I little thought that the book could be of such money value to you but I was thoroughly convinced that it would not lessen the popularity of your name, otherwise I should have felt bound to say so.
That this wonderful success should have cheered you and done you so much good is the most gratifying feature of all and it is perfectly natural. When you next take the field I hope it will be in your lighter vein and the public rush joyously into your arms, not that light is a proper epithet for anything you write.
I am sorry to say I have not been so well of late and my Doctor calling this morning told me to quit my desk. There have been no end of fine golf matches of late but I have been so scant of breath that I could not keep up with them. However I am much stronger and do not feel pulled down by this little check in my progress.
Always Yours Truly
(Signed) John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 2 August 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
August 2/66.
My Dear Madam
I hope this will find you safely re-established in your pleasant home and both greatly the better for your expedition.
I have no particular features to report in the sale of Felix since I last wrote, but there is movement. Mr. Langford will I think be off for his holiday, but if Mr. Lewes is in the Row at any time the clerk in charge will show him how it has gone if he gives this message from me.
Have you ever looked into Hamley's book? 506 It is I think going to be a great permanent success. You know I have always thought him in many respects about the ablest man I ever met and the quickest to make action follow thought. If the occasion arises it will be a good day for the Country if they put him into high command.
Your admirer the female hair dresser is a character. She was the manager for a hair dresser who behaved shabbily to her, and by the advice of her numerous supporters she started on her own account. She had the sense to consult my brothers and Mr. Simpson about all business matters and she is now rapidly making a fortune. Their business consultations would have been rich food for you. She laid before one meeting a long letter of advice from the great Truefitt 507 whose business is worth £7000 a year! This letter was nearly the death of me. A general planning out a campaign was nothing to it. He is a Napoleon in his Trade is Truefitt.
There is the gong so I must close but I shall write soon again.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 18 October 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 18 October 1875
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews October 18/75.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
You will think me very ungrateful for not having at once answered your pleasant and most welcome letter. I got it in Edinburgh when I was in a whirl of business, after which I had to pay a visit in a country house, very pleasant but not conducive to writing, and since I came home on Saturday I have been obliged to sit doggedly at an enormous M.S. about which a friend is coming from the other end of the Island tonight to consult with me. Thank God I have finished the reading and the great pile of M.S. is lying beside me face downwards. However the M.S. was I am happy to say worth reading. I am sorry Rickmansworth did not suit you better, but it is a comfort that the "trip" to Wales has done some good. Your happy phrase of trip being too lovely an epithet for such an expedition reminds me of May cruises in the rainy West Highlands when I devoutly wished myself at Randolph Crescent or Strathtyrum all the time.
I am delighted to hear of the two volumes being ready for the printer and I sympathise with your feeling in taking the "Plate Chest" to your bankers before you started. Who has got such a plate chest? Mr. Simpson was energetic in his applause of the precaution and begged me to tell you that we have a fire proof room at 45 George Street where he would carefully deposit the precious M.S. and dole it out to the printers.
I think Lewes is right about February being the best month to begin publication. The active world of London is then drawing together and although I do not think it greatly matters when such a Ship as yours is launched it is well to have the buzz of talk open at headquarters at once. The main thing of course is not to hurry or harass you. It would be better to begin publication in the dog days than do that in any degree. From the state of progress however in which I am happy to think "Daniel Deronda" is, I see no fear of the start in February being too soon.
You had better send the M.S. as soon as may suit you and we shall return proofs at any time that may be most easy to you for correction. From reading the first volume, which privilege has ever since made me feel rather ahead of the rest of the world, I am quite sure Lewes who has seen more is right, and you may dismiss those fears that so easily beset you as to not having hit your mark. The scope and merits of that first volume are wonderful.
As to form I do not think we can do better than follow Middlemarch only making the publication monthly as the audience are more ready.
I am very glad the Abode of Snow pleased you so much as it will be an immense gratification to the Author to hear of praise from you. How he got over those fatigues is not the least remarkable part of the story as physically he seems to have no more muscle than a jelly fish and he is a queer fish but a very big fish in mind and energy. Some 20 years ago when quite a youngster he wrote a paper for me which indicated genius and I wrote to him saying so and urging him to go on. He became however a kind of wandering waif and only hearing of him vaguely for years I feared he had gone to the bad -- when after many days the prodigal son returned and produced this admirable series of papers.
We are suffering here from very wild stormy weather and I fear it is not over yet. Yesterday at lunch we heard the guns signaling a ship in distress in the Bay and of course my wife and daughter insisted on sallying forth with me. Their two slight figures perched in a hurricane of wind and rain on one of the dunes by the seashore watching the struggling ship would have made a picture. The ship drifted away from us and finally went ashore on a sand bank south of the Tay opposite. All lives were saved.
We intend to remain here until about the 10th of November and I am in hopes of good weather after this fearful week.
Always yours truly
(Signed) John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 17 May 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
May 17/68.
My Dear Madam
I am glad you stated your doubts about the terms proposed for The Spanish Gypsy and I can readily understand your surprise at the larger terms per 1000 that we were able to offer for Silas Marner, but the difference is easily explainable. The calculations for Silas were made for the immediate sale of a much larger number. The printing of The Gypsy for 2000 costs about a third more than Silas, the paper above a third more, the binding above a third more, and the advertising we calculate should be more than double what we allowed for Silas. Our rough calculation was that selling 2000 of The Gypsy the profit to us would be a little over £100.
I confess that I was myself disappointed at the smallness of the result, but on looking into the matter I do not see how much difference could be made in our offer, and I hope this explanation will be satisfactory to you. From the way in which the book is got up it would bear 14/- as selling price, but I do not think it would be wise to make it more than the 12/6.
I have been looking into the Poem very often and I am more and more convinced that you have achieved a great and permanent success. I think I like the opening and the end best, but every other page throughout arrests one and discloses something new each time. I am writing a line to Lewes to whom I will explain how I have not written sooner.
Wishing all success for your debut as a Poet, I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 15 July 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum St. Andrews | July 15th 1879.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I have not heard from you for some time and since I came here I think I have been remiss in writing to you. On arrival here I was greeted by a charming letter from you but I wish it had given a more satisfactory account of your health. I do hope you can now tell of real improvement and freedom from pain.
For some time when I first came here I did not know how the change was going to answer. I got better and worse in a very unsatisfactory way and could neither eat nor sleep, but about a week ago I began fairly to mend and now sleep without opiates or any of the poisonous decoctions on which I was nourished for the previous two months. I am thankful to say I really feel getting well and if the weather would only permit I expect to be walking about stoutly soon.
The splendid success of Theophrastus has been a most satisfactory thing to watch. There are between three and four hundred I think on hand and probably this may prove the last edition we should run at present price, but what a run it has been. How he would have enjoyed it.
We have had two and a half days of continuous heavy rain which have knocked up the last hopes of the Harvest in the Lowlands. I never saw anything like the wind and cold at this season. The day before yesterday looking out of drawing room window my wife and I simultaneously remarked, Why this is exactly the sort of afternoon that reconciles us to going back to town in November.
I have been thinking of the remark you made about circumstances having made writers and we have quite a little collection of such tales in the Magazine. I had a letter to-day from Mrs. Thrupp the wife of Captain Thrupp who told the tale of the wrecking of his ship the Megaera telling that her husband was made a Queen's A.D.C. so the "Poor old Megaera had borne fruit at last." 296 Thrupp proved a capital fellow and as mad about Golf as myself.
The Zulu war is emphatically a useless and a miserable business. An American lady whom we know in Rome says my daughter is reported in America to be the author in Blackwood of the paper on the
Zulu War. You have seen Mary and will be amused like me with the extreme congeniality and probability of the task. I hope Wolseley will finish it soon and thoroughly. By the way I think Wolseley's first serious piece of writing was the account in the Magazine of his own Great Red River expedition. The Spectator reviewing the Magazine said he showed great ignorance of the subject, compared with some friend of theirs, I suppose, who had published a volume on the subject. It was a pity I could not reveal the authorship.
Hoping soon to have good accounts of you and with best remembrances from my wife and daughter, I am
always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 12 October 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 12 October 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
October 12/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
The very kind expressions in your letter of the 8th move and gratify me deeply. Tears came into my eyes, and I read the passage at once to my wife who was sitting beside me when I received the letter. I look upon such expressions coming from you, as the very highest compliment that a man holding the position I do could receive, and I shall keep the letter for my children as a memorial that their father was good for something in his day. You are too good about my poor letters which I always felt to be too meagre and too few but I do look back upon our correspondence with pride and pleasure. Each letter from you is a treat and last summer being pressed for your autograph I turned over a number of your letters, but in each there was a feeling or something that I could not part with or deface by cutting off the signature so my friend went without an autograph.
That one who has risen so high as you have should be the subject of idle gossip is almost inevitable. It is a thing for which the public have a depraved appetite and I say "idle" not evil as I do not think it is intentionally mischievous but why are great authors not to enjoy the privacy of common life? I do not know whether living gossips or posthumous memoir writers make me most savage. It is but little of such idle trash that I hear as no one would venture to speak to me of you with ought but praise and of that I do hear ample store.
You will have heard how Deronda is going on and I think the sales are very satisfactory and equal. The discussion about the book still goes on, especially in private company and the great point is that the book is discussed and disputed over as a reality. We had a good scene the other night. My wife said to a young friend staying with us "Have you read [Daniel]?" the familiar name of the book in this house. He stammered and said "No" and forthwith began to turn over his remembrances of the Book of Daniel. Then he turned out to have been a regular student of Deronda and forthwith an animated discussion of all the characters began. Mr. Simpson says that no one could write a review of the Book to please me unless I did it myself.
About Professor Dowden I fear that I am in fault. The strange thing is that I cannot recollect Lewes giving me the review containing the paper on your works. Did he hand it to me or send it to me? In spite of my carelessness I never almost lose anything and I am writing to Edinburgh to see if it is there. I wrote to Professor Dowden asking him to send me a specimen of what he proposed, but it was after many days that I wrote, and I was not surprised that he did not answer as he had probably gone on his holiday. 545 What you say interests me much in him and I shall now write again.
I have been suffering severely of late from irritation I suppose of the mucous membrane. There is an uncommonly good remark in Norman Macleod's Memoirs 546 about that membrane which he says he has been told "covers the whole of his interior and certainly covers all the rest of the world when there is anything the matter with it." I am now happily quite well and fit both for business and golf which had both been in abeyance for nearly a fortnight. I hope Lewes and you are well and settling down comfortably for the winter. Our season here will be winding up soon and the horrible wet weather reconciles one to the thought of Town. Still we have occasional bright days in the midst of the deluge which is so fatal to the outlying crops.
My wife sends her best regards and hoping that there are many years of pleasant correspondence before us Believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 12 July 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland and Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
July 12/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am delighted to receive your letter from Ragatz and to learn that you have there found a quiet peaceful retreat likely to do you good after your giant labours. You were, I am sure, quite right to abandon the knocking about in Railways, and seek a quiet spot where you can have pleasant walks and rest.
First as to the Book. I think the sale of Book VI is fully up to that of its predecessors, but I send this letter into Edinburgh that Willie may put in a Memorandum of what have been sold since the 30th of June. At that date a Memorandum was made up to show the exact state of matters. It is a very healthy show and will I hope afford you both pleasure.
I propose to pay you in cash now to your Banker's £2000 or on your return home 510 as you may wish and the balance £2052.16/- by Bill at 6 Mos. from 30th June.
On some sudden rise in sale we had, I see, printed rather too many of Book One, but I hope we shall work them all out and any way it will be a very trifling overstock on so large a sale. 511
The public continue all abroad as to what your finale is going to be, and it was great sport to me in London that I could decline all discussion of the Book because I knew so much more than the rest of the world that I would be arguing at an unfair advantage. I used to say accept what you get when it comes and be thankful. Delane said at Ascot, "If I proclaim in the Strand here is the one man who has read the whole of Daniel Deronda, the ladies will tear you in pieces unless you tell them some lies or make a clean breast of it."
There will I know be disappointment at not hearing more of the failure of Gwendolen and the mysterious destiny of Deronda, but I am sure you are right to leave all grand and vague, and the real disappointment of your public will be that their monthly food for interesting thought and speculation is stopped.
I stayed in London rather longer than I intended in order to go to see Delane at Ascot and I am happy to say I found him better than I expected, but he has been very unwell and should take a rest. You may imagine how tired I was of my bachelor life when I resisted the most pressing invitation to stay the week at Delane's and came off to the North after the first day's racing.
My wife and daughter really did not come up to London this time and seem rather pleased with themselves now. They threaten me with an expedition to the Highlands when my heart will be, not there but on the Links. The hardest thing for my daughter to miss in London was an invitation from Lady Salisbury 512 to a small dancing party to meet the Prince and Princess of Wales, which followed me down here. Golf goes on a pace. Tom Morris the ex-champion, of whom you have heard me tell, was invited to Liverpool last week to play a match before the Duke of Connaught. He reports the Prince "a most pleasant frank Gentleman." Old Tom is a capital judge of such matters, and I would rather take his opinion on the point than that of any courtier.
I thought the deaths of Miss Martineau and George Sand would touch you. That generation is indeed wearing to an end now.
The ladies send their best regards to you. The weather is pleasant and they are enjoying their rides.
I am interested to hear that you were at Aix and Chambery, very familiar places once to me. My eldest brother was laid up at Aix with a raging fit of Asthma so long and bad that the Doctors gave up all hope, and many a melancholy hour did I pass by the Lac de Bourget. In despair we carried him into his carriage and drove to Chambery. In the ten miles drive that most fickle complaint left him and he got out at the Hotel du Petit Paris suffering only from extreme weakness.
I wonder if the Petit Paris still exists. I always think of it and Chambery with a blessing.
I have a hope that the deplorable fighting will not spread beyond the Turkish Provinces. The Powers are all afraid and jealous of each other, which gives the best hope of Peace. With best regards to Lewes, I am always
yours very truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 10 September 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
September 10/66.
My Dear Madam
I was glad to receive your pleasant note and should have written to you before had I had anything material to tell. There has been a small sale of Felix going on but nothing much to speak of. We printed 5250 and I think we have about 400 on hand. I wish we could get quit of these but from the slow way the book has been dropping off during the last fortnight I fear we must consider the sale in three volumes as about over. The question I have been debating for some time is the form in which we should reprint. Mr. Simpson at first was in favour of trying a one volume edition but you will see however instead he now leans to what I first thought of, an edition like Adam Bede in 2 volumes at 12/. 527 Lewes and you are both excellent judges and I should like to hear what you think.
The libraries have starved the book, or rather their customers, as is proved by the fact of some of them buying quite recently in small numbers. The next time we take the field together I think we must experiment in a new form, but we can keep our own council about this.
I am glad to hear of Thornton doing well. There is a great deal in him, and the other youngster joining him will be a stimulus and comfort to both. Lads at that time are a great anxiety to fathers. My little boy, whose photograph you have, has not reached that stage yet. He is a very thoughtful looking little gentleman. The other day at our luncheon -- his dinner -- he was sitting with a more than usually meditative countenance apparently solving some of the deep problems of life and at last when he declined red currant tart his mother remarked that if he would eat so much fruit in the garden he would give himself a cholic. "I've got one" was the brief reply. Now one cannot imagine either Gladstone or Mill making such an answer in all their days.
We are going to visit some friends in the Highlands for a few days, but address here. In case you should have forgotten dates I mention that the first instalment for Felix becomes due to you on the 14th or 15th of December.
I hope Lewes is well and that your German Campaign has set you both up for the winter.
Dean Ramsay is our Clergyman and a very dear old friend both of my wife and mine. I sent him a copy of the book as a mark of respect and regard. The poor old man had a frightful catastrophe in his house last spring. A favourite niece was tending him in his dressing room when her dress caught fire and she was burnt to death. I went to see him when I came down from London and almost to my surprise he talked freely of it. He said that the scene was so ever present to his eyes that to talk of it to a friend was a kind of relief. A letter from you will I am sure be a gratification to him.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 10 November 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, St. Andrews, 10 November 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 392.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
November 10/75.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I send proof of the first 256 pages of Daniel Deronda and I know not how to express my admiration. The reading in type transcends even the impression the M.S. had left upon me. In print one can turn back so much more easily to re-enjoy the splendid turns of thought, wit, and expression which adorn every page and had hardly been fully appreciated at the first perusal. Stupendo, that often misused Italian phrase, could never be so rightly applied as here.
That wicked witch Gwendolen is perfectly irresistible, new and yet so true to nature, like all the other characters. Her running mental reflections after each few words she has said to Grandcourt are like what passes through the mind after each move at a game, and as far as I know a new device in reporting a conversation. 329 A cautious speaker will here learn that his pauses may also give his interlocutor an advantage.
Uncle Gascoigne is a perfect picture and echoes all over with human nature. His wife, daughter, and Rex are charming, and I did feel for Rex in his terrible prostration. That morning ride with Gwen 330 is a picture, and I see you could not resist the wish that they might gallop away and be happy together. The witch will I hope be saved ultimately but you alone must decide.
In the drawing room here my wife, daughter, and nephew have been reading the proofs and the sort of exclamations are "splendid," "glorious" etc. Having read so much more of the wondrous tale than they have I am ordered to be reticent in my expression of opinion about the characters but up to this point our agreement is perfect. Mr. Simpson too, who has been reading the proofs in Edinburgh, writes in a perfect ecstasy of praise. That wretch Gwen has evidently taken the veteran bachelor by storm.
The verdict among us all here is that you are fairly outdoing Middlemarch and I need say no more. The finish of every character however briefly touched is perfectly wonderful and I should have liked to have heard Gwen giving the Curate's "Perdition catch my soul." 331
Those sworn "horse coursers," my wife and nephew, suggest that poor Primrose's knees were not likely to have been broken by such a fall as you describe in a field. 332
I remember pausing at the use of the word dynamic in the very first sentence and I am not quite sure about it yet as it is a dictionary word to so many people. 333 I know no other word however that would so powerfully and strictly convey your meaning. I think I see Klesmer at the Archery meeting, 334 and how you have touched off a whole class in Lush. Miss Arrowsmith is charming, but Gwen's comparison of the relative effect of their charms is perfectly true.
Mrs. Davilow is truly affecting and effective in her helplessness and slaving.
I was sorry to hear from Lewes that he was so poorly and I hope his visit to Cambridge has done him good. This is our last week here for the season and we have bright clear frosty weather which makes the Links most enjoyable.
With hearty congratulations, Believe [me], Dear Mrs. Lewes
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
As I finish this letter the rest of volume one comes in so I inclose it also and promise myself the pleasure of reading it tonight. The proof goes in separate packet.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Sponden, 25 May 1859

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Sponden, 25 May 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Sponden | May 25/59.
My Dear George Eliot
Your letter reached me safely here. In looking back upon Adam Bede one of our greatest pleasures will always be the thought that its success afforded us so legitimate a means of showing our sense of its value and of gratifying your feelings. From the accompanying note to Lewes you will see that I hope to shake hands with you very soon.
I look forward to a famous afternoon if it suits you to receive me on Friday.
I wrote Lucas a civil note yesterday. The inclosed from Aytoun 141 to my brother will interest you.
We have lovely weather here but still no rain. This place realises Miss Austen's pictures of an English village and would have afforded rich materials to her or to George Eliot.
As I hope to see you so soon no more at present from
Yours most sincerely
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Aytoun wrote William  Blackwood 19 May 1859: "but unfortunately I brought Adam Bede from town, and having begun it, rather for the purpose of examining the style than reading it deliberately, I was so fascinated that I must needs finish the first volume. I am going (this is a positive fact) to send the other two volumes out of the house, until I have got my article fairly completed.
