Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, London, 8 June 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 8 June 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Jermyn St. | June 8/57.
My Dear Sir
The first part of Janet's Repentance 894 of which I inclose proof rather puzzles me. It is exceedingly clever and some of the hits and descriptions of character are first rate, but I should have liked a pleasanter picture. Surely the colours are rather harsh for a sketch of English County Town life only 25 years ago. The glimpse at the end of the part shows that a powerful and pathetic story is coming and I rather wish you had plunged sooner into it instead of expending so much humour in the delineation of characters who do not seem likely to assist materially in the movement of the Story and who are not in themselves interesting.
The first scene especially I think you should shorten. It is deuced good but rather a staggerer in an opening scene of a Story of Clerical Life. Dempster is rather too barefaced a brute and I am sorry that the poor wife's sufferings should have driven her to so unsentimental a resource as beer. Still it is true to nature. The case is but too common, and I have no right to pass any opinion on this part of the story until I see more of it. I shall be very glad if in returning the proof you can send me a further portion of M.S. as I feel very confident that what is coming will more than dissipate the slight doubts I feel about the popular qualities of this first part.
I greatly regret not being able to give applause altogether unqualified, but I may mention a capital sign that both my brother and I liked it better on the second reading than on the first. For the meantime I feel certain that I am right in advising you to soften your picture as much as you can. Your sketches this time are all written in the harsher Thackerayan view of human nature, and I should have liked to have seen some of the good which at page 10 you so neatly indicate as existing at Milby. 895 When are you going to give us a really good active working clergyman, neither absurdly evangelical nor absurdly High Church?
The Scene at the Linnets 896 is capital. Thackeray is I think rather disposed to claim you as a disciple of his, and I daresay the beautiful touch about the flutter in the female hearts at page 17 is something in his style.
Since I last wrote I have been engaged in a regular series of London dinner parties which is the most knocking up work I know. I wish heartily I were with you in the Channel Islands instead of roasting in Jermyn St. I hear nothing but applause of the power of Gilfil. At Bulwer's the other night I was surprised by Lord Stanley 897 speaking to me most warmly about the series. I would not have thought it in his line. He was astounded when I told him that I did not know who the author was but would let the unknown know what he said.
Tell Lewes that I will write to him [in] a day or two with the proof of Sea Side Studies. The second paper from the hasty perusal I gave it in M.S. seemed to me very good indeed. I am afraid his Algerian friend will not do, but I mean to read him again.
I leave this on the morning of the 15th and go into Derbyshire for a day or two on my way home. If you find your answer will be with me here by the 15th address here, if not send packet to Edinburgh.
If my comments upon Janet disappoint you, consider that I am wrong and attribute my want of appreciation to a fortnight of hot weather and hotter dinners in London.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. Eliot Esq.
P.S. I have paid £22/10 into Lewes' account with Union Bank in acknowledgment of Gilfil Part IV.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 7 June 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cavendish, Jermyn St. | June 7/58.
My Dear Sir
I had the pleasure of receiving your letter and also Lewes'. The sales in Scotland make up the demand for the Scenes to the number you supposed so there is no occasion for gloom, although considering the excellence of the book, the opinion formed of it, and the opinion expressed by the newspapers etc., one would have been inclined to bet that double the number would have been sold by this time.
Still the great point is attained, the reputation made, which will bring your next work an audience at once prepared to admire. You would see too from the number we printed that I did not calculate upon a very large sale. My impression was that the general public were not fairly caught, although by what process I arrived at this opinion I cannot tell as it was quite against my own conviction of the merits of your admirable stories.
I sent a copy of the Saturday Review to Lewes containing a highly laudatory notice. I hope[d] it would reach you as the praise was hearty and the description of the author would amuse you highly. 1149 The secret is well kept and it is of the utmost importance that it should continue so.
How does Adam Bede progress? I long to see more of him -- in a week I hope to be out of this red hot Babel and back in Scotland with famous time for reading.
You will I doubt not see the Revue des Deux Mondes 1150 at Munich.
There is not much merit in the Review, although the sketch of the stories is given with tolerable fidelity and it is a compliment to have a paper of that length on your book in the only good French periodical.
Tell Lewes that I have paid £20 to his account at the Union in acknowledgment of Blood pt. 1. As I write, it flashes across me that the Major (my brother) 1151 may not know or remember that part 2 is among the M.S.S. I left at home, but I write to him about it today.
Your account of Munich tallies very much with my own recollection of the place. With the exception of the Gallery I thought it had neither the merits of Germany nor Italy. Still I think you will find a good many studies for heads in the Italian story you have in view. 1152
London is very hot and very full. People seem too busy to read anything but the newspapers. I am sure Lewes is right in thinking this a bad residence for a literary man. Thackeray would I think do well to select some quiet retreat in the country. With best regards to Lewes, Believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.
I have desired a copy of the Magazine to be sent to you. I wish you to read the article on Religious Memoirs 1153 which I think particularly good.

John Blackwood to GE, London, 6 June 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cavendish | 81 Jermyn St. | June 6 /59.
My Dear G.E.
People are full of our letters and they are highly approved of. Delane 145 whom I saw last night was splitting with laughter and said, "Well if that does not choke the fools off I do not know what will."
Your idea of asking Liggins to write a chapter tickled him especially as also it did Thackeray.

ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 29 June 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cavendish | June 29/59.
My Dear George Eliot
I expected to have seen Delane last night and given him your letter but on calling for him on my way to Greenwich I found a note that he could not go with me. I had therefore no opportunity of asking him to insert either the original or the amended letter. I think you should be very shy of going against his advice and doubtless he thinks he has done enough -- nothing on the subject having appeared in the paper since our letters which were as conclusive as possible.
Remember that the general public know nothing of the way in which we are bothered and the mass of people would think that we were kicking up a disturbance about something for which they cared nothing. 188
Neither the stupid Quirk nor the aggravating Selina Bracebridge 189 have ever said that they had seen a M.S. and neither your friend Mrs. Bodichon nor S.G.O's statements 190 about M.S. were things that we could rely or act upon. Depend upon it that if S.G.O. could have got anything positive about a M.S. being shown he would not have neglected such an opportunity of writing either to me or to the Times.
If you still continue determined on publishing I incline for the original letter rather than the diluted one as the latter is nothing more than we have already said nor indeed in substantials is the original document. What ever you send to me I will send to Delane and he of course will do as he thinks fit. When I gave him the letter on Monday he made no objections to publishing and he must have given the matter some consideration afterwards which shows a friendly feeling towards you on his part. Observe too that if you do not publish now in deference to his suggestion you secure in him a fast and potent friend to expose any more serious and definite attempt at fraud. One of my main objections to the letter is that when you talk of branding as an impostor etc. people will think you are angry instead of treating the idiots with the contempt you feel.
The Major and I propose coming up to see you on Saturday about one o'clock. We would come tomorrow or next day but we have some engagements which make it impossible for us to fix positively. If Lewes is in Town ask him to give us a chance. 191 We dine at home tonight. Confound Bracebridge Quirk Liggins and Co. for making me write so long a note.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 26 June 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Burlington, Cork St. | London, June 26/66.
My Dear Madam
Your pleasant letter from Schwalbach is extremely welcome and I am truly glad to hear that both Lewes and you have benefited so much by the change. I had begun to fear that you had been captured by some advanced pocket of Prussians and did not know where to write.
The chorus of applause upon Felix waxes loud and strong. The "Great British Public" is not yet sufficiently aware of the existence of the book to affect the sale but the expressions of public and private opinions which are pouring forth will I think get at the monster speedily.
The difficulty of making the public know about a book is wonderful, and while I am writing it occurs to me that the real plan would be to hire a hundred fellows to go about London with a placard shouting "Felix Holt the Radical is published this day." This is an id'e9e and if you and Lewes were near to consult I am not sure whether I would not act upon it.
I told you I found Bulwer beginning Felix, and he writes and tells me in conversation that he did not give up until he finished it. His admiration is intense. He objects as I did to the plot qu'e2 Mrs. Transome as being too painful for an inadequate object, but what does it signify, he continued; the writing is wonderful and what is an author unless he is a Great Writer? These are not his exact words but convey the import I think.
Old Mr. Gleig 490 the Chaplain General is enthusiastic especially about Esther, whom he declares he has seen. I was greatly taken with the clear-headed old gentleman on the subject yesterday.
Laurence Oliphant, whom I daresay you have heard me speak of as a great friend and companion of mine, is the man whom as far as I have heard you would most like to listen to on the subject of the book. He goes in for Felix and self-sacrifice, taking up your own intentions in the book.
Had I seen him in time I think I would have asked him to review for me. However my own reviewer has I think done it very gracefully and well -- better and more thoroughly like a gentleman in tone than any of the others although he does not agree with Felix and Esther abnegation[?] of wealth as a means of doing good. 491
The others are the Times of today, which I daresay you will see, the Spectator 492 of Saturday, the Post of today, the Standard, and a lot of others all highly laudatory. In coming out of the City yesterday I called upon Delane and found him with the review in his hand, and he said he would publish it today if there was not a row and a long debate in the House. I went down to the Carlton between 4 and 5 to hear what was going on, and Lord John Manners came up and told me that Gladstone had adjourned the House. I as nearly as possible exclaimed, "I am deuced glad to hear it." You can conceive the comical effect in my mind, and I think I must explain the reason to Lord John if there was anything unusual in my manner.
What the Times reviewer means by talking of the idea in the trial scene being taken from something in a Novel of Charles Reade's passes my understanding. 493 Doubtless it is something that neither you nor I ever saw. Probably the remark was taken from something Reade had said himself at the Garrick but it does not signify a brass farthing. The review will do a great deal of good although I do not think it a first class performance, but I doubt whether anybody could please me quite with a review of Felix. It is nearly always so with a big book when you really know and feel it. I am making a collection of these reviews and will send them to you if you like. At the Saturday Review dinner on Saturday I sat next the reviewer of Felix in that paper, a very nice young fellow named Morley. 494
I shall send Oliphant to call upon you when you return to Town. He is a man you will both like.
I am off to see if I can get into the House to hear Gladstone's explanation. 495 Nobody knows what is going to happen and from what I heard I am satisfied that Ministers were in a state of utter indecision as late as Saturday night.
I am pretty well knocked over with my London life and hope to be off to the North on Friday so address to Edinburgh. With best regards to Lewes believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
Willie is at Torquay on his way to Edinburgh.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 25 May 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: John Blackwood, pp. 391-392.
The Burlington | May 25/75.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Reading the whole and rereading many parts of the first volume of Daniel Deronda has more than confirmed the admiration and delight with which I wrote and spoke to you after my first happy sitting over your M.S. That first night I really felt like a glutton dallying over his feast and not reading at all with my usual rapid stride.
The first scene in the dreary gorgeous German gambling saloon with the gamblers all looking so like each other about the eyes and mouth is to the life, and poor Gwendolen's "enraged resistance" 249 is so true. Her want of early associations with home and the very "stars" a part of it is beautifully touched. 250 Mr. Gascoigne's pleasant easy tone that made the world "a manageable place of residence" 251 is very fine.
Gwendolen seeing Mrs. Arrowpoint's folly and not perceiving that she was showing her own hand to the old lady is so like a clever young creature. 252 I did not know what a hold the mermaid witch had got of me until I felt inclined to kick Herr Klessmer for his criticism on her singing 253 and I did not forgive him until I saw him with his hat "on his hair" 254 when a laugh took away all angry feeling. I knew what must happen to Rex but I was very sorry for him when the blow came 255 and her tears afterwards give me a hope that her creator is going to be merciful to the witch. She is a fascinating witch and I shall not be able to help feeling for her if she does get into "a swamp, satin shoes" and all. She had "no objections to be adored" 256 and was hardly entitled to the feeling. That is a magnificent illustration of yours about circumstances weighing upon characters such as hers like the weather upon the Harvests.
There is something very impressive in the way that fear froze that wild wilful heart on the sudden fall of the pannel and disclosure of that horrid picture. 257
The glimpse of the little blacksmith 258 who came to the help of Rex is a perfect picture. I know the little rascal as well as if I had been in the habit of giving him sixpences for years.
Ladies' necks like "leisurely lilies if they took to motion" 259 is a singularly happy idea. I am afraid there are few necks like that but we have all seen some.
Grandcourt is a most original character and he and Deronda promise to be a grand contrast in your picture. Gwendolen takes Grandcourt up admirably about "pleasures and follies left off" 260 and his sudden fit of numbness when he thinks he is within certain reach of his object is so true to nature.
There is somewhere as passage about false air of daemonic strength in commonplace unregulated people who know not how to direct their force that has made a great impression on me, but if I tried to refer to all the passages that have done that I should never finish my letter, as when they recur to me I turn to the M.S. and pass some time reading them and the context.
You tell the Tale of Deronda's goodness and that of the stray Jewish Maid so straightly and so simply that no feeling of doubt or improbability arises, and I quite agree with Mrs. Mer[r]ick that Miriam's mother must have been good, as "wheaten bread does not come from naught." 261 Sir Hugo is always good and his placid reflections upon good birth like those of a man after a good dinner contrast happily with Deronda's sensitive but terrible fears on that subject. 262 That "grim walled slice of a house" 263 that the Merricks have is a happy and consoling thought in the midst of the wilderness of grim looking small houses that really cons[t]itute London. How often one has looked at them with a kind of shuddering pain as to what life could be to the inhabitants, but you have given an interior that leavens the whole mass.
Again I beg to congratulate you on this most auspicious opening of another immortal work 264 and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, London, 25 May 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 25 May 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cavendish | May 25/60.
My Dear Madam
I got your letter on the morning of the Derby and if the Major in sending it to me had not mentioned that he had given you all news, I would have made myself too late for the National event by sitting down to write you at once -- an amount of devotion which I hope you will appreciate. The Major will have explained that the 6000 are all sold and that we are reprinting 500, which will be ready in a day or two now. These will I think supply the public until we can treat the world to a 12/- edition.
This is highly satisfactory and I rejoice to think that there is every prospect of your making as much by our arrangement as the most speculative publisher was likely to have offered you. That it was the best plan for you in the long run I had no doubt, but I thought it very probable there might be an apparent loss in the individual book. I chuckle considerably over Mudie having to take the 3000. You may recollect that he offered to take that number if we would make the book sell at 21/. Confound his impudence it would have been simply diverting something like 3000 times 8/- from the pockets of author and publisher into his voracious maw.
As to public opinion of the book the cry at first was inferior to Adam, but the tide turned and I think opinions are pretty equally divided between the two. The review in the Times of the 19th May is by Dallas. It is not bad and thoroughly friendly in its tone although I do not agree with the critic in many of his views about the book.
I expect to be in London for a month and although I should like to see you taking a prolonged holiday I fancy I have a chance of seeing you before I go north.
I suppose you will have left Florence before this can reach [you], but I daresay you will have left orders for letters to be forwarded. I would have written to Naples but I was away at St. Andrews when Lewes' letter came and when I got home I felt doubtful whether I would be in time to catch you in that lovely place, as to the charms of which, especially the environs, I thoroughly agree with you. There as elsewhere everything looks troubled and war may break out in any corner of Europe.
I hear that Gladstone has no intention of resigning, saying that he feels bound in conscience to stick to his post, to the intense disgust of Palmerston who is sick of him.
I went to the Derby with Steuart, the discoverer of the Pug. I hope that valuable specimen is in safety. Mrs. Blackwood has called her mare (formerly Meg) Maggie Tulliver. The Mare is a wicked, gay-looking thoroughbred with a tendency to get on her hind legs if ridden by any one but her mistress, with whom she is gentle as a lamb.
Hamley 546 does not believe that fine young woman Maggie Tulliver is dead and will be glad if you will introduce him to the original. We are at last in a new edition of the Clerical Scenes 547 and it moves although nothing like Adam, which I think is also in a new edition 548 in which you have interest although I am not quite certain still I feel pretty sure it is. The fag end of the edition of a book has an unfortunate resemblance to the Widow's Cruise, as White 549 said of one of his books, which like the last edition of the Clerical it seemed impossible to exhaust.
With best regards to Lewes I am
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.
Tell Lewes I hope to see him quite robust when he returns.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 20 May 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Burlington | May 20/75. 10 a.m.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I congratulate you. It is splendid. I could not get settled down to your M.S. until 'bd past 8 and I made a night of it. At first I began to try to read quickly but I found that was even more utterly out of the question than usual with your books and I soon settled down to calm leisurely enjoyment reading line by line and constantly turning back again to make sure that I had got it all. I paused and enjoyed myself so much that although it was 3 o clock in the morning when I went to bed I had only got through 'bd the volume!!!!
I must be off to train and again congratulating you
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 20 June 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cavendish | June 20/59.
My Dear George Eliot
I am perfectly delighted with the opening of the new story. The wealth of illustration and thought is wonderful and the lifelike minute delineation of character could not well be surpassed.
No part in these first 110 pages amused me more than the fellow giving his advice to the Miller about a tutor for his son. 162 Before I came to your explanation I had made up my mind that the man had no immediate object to serve by his earnest unscrupulous advice. I have met with this sort of thing hundreds of times.
You may go ahead with perfect confidence that St. Oggs on the Floss or Maggie will be a grand success. My expectations were very highly raised but these opening chapters really go beyond them.
I propose coming to see you on Thursday or Saturday and will then bring the M.S. Let me know which of those days will suit you best.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, London, 2 June 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 2 June 1871
Text: First draft, National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: Copied into letterbook. Hitherto unpublished.
Burlington Hotel | Cork St. | June 2/71.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Although I expect to see Mr. Lewes [to]morrow I must write a line to tell you how intensely I am delighted with Miss Brooke 285 -- it is filled to overflowing with touches of nature and character that could not be surpassed. If I had made a memorandum of all the happy turns of thought still more happily expressed I would have filled pages with quotations as I read from the old twaddler Brooke, who is to the very life, to the smallest sketch introduced. Every character stands out clear and distinct. I have met old Brookes and curiously contagious creatures they are, if you found yourself talking with an amiable specimen of the sort I believe that at the end of the conversation you would feel as if you had equalled him. I recollect a distinct case of the kind happening to myself and [laughing] immoderately over all I had said while endeavoring to keep pace with my worthy interlocuter. The excellent baronet 286 could not be more angry with Mr. Casaubon or sorry for Dorothea than I am. How she will fare when she wakens to real life is a source of great anxiety to me.
There may not be in this first part what are considered popular incidents but there is overpowering interest in such a picture of human nature and I am much deceived if you are not about to repeat if not excell all your previous triumphs. It was impossible to read your M.S. quickly. If I tried to do so for a page I found some gem was escaping me. With many congratulations I am Dear Mrs. Lewes
always yours truly
John B.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, London, 18 June 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 18 June 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Burlington, Cork St. | June 18/66.
My Dear Madam
I hope this will find you comfortably established at Schwalbach 481 and both of you the better for the change. Favourable symptoms begin to show regarding Felix and the paeans will I am sure wax louder and louder.
The Saturday Review lead the way on Saturday with a very good review which I send to you. 482 The opinions from my private friends have hardly begun to pour in yet, but as far as they have reached me they are what I could wish and I need say no more. My wife, who for so quick minded a person is a singularly slow reader, exclaimed today "Why this is an extraordinary book. On finishing a novel generally one turns quickly to one's ordinary work but one sits and thinks over this." I found Bulwer Lytton yesterday; he had just begun the book which was in his hand, and he could only say, "Opens admirably."
As to sales we have disposed of about 3000 Mudie taking 1500 of these. It will I think be the end of this week or next before there will be a decided move. Mr. Simpson writes to me in great glee that his chief ally in Edinburgh, a most matter of fact master of a school, 483 had finished it 'bd past five that morning and was ready to go on for hours in raptures about the book. With all Simpson's over enthusiastic admiration, he despises Felix personally as a man who would have been of no use at 45 George St. and quotes his own particular henchman Roderick Nicholson from the Isle of Skye as practically a much more estimable and useful character. 484 I shall send you news as I get it and hoping to hear from you soon I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Willie has returned from Torquay but I do not know that Simpson would pronounce him a man fit for work at 45 George St. He left his hat in the Opera box the other night and you may imagine the winks and grins of General Steuart.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 15 June 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cavendish | June 15/60.
My Dear Madam
I fancy this will be about the right date to pitch upon you at Berne so I write although I have not much to say and am falling into that stupid useless do-nothing state which always comes upon me after some weeks of London racket.
My letter to Florence would I think catch you, and since then there are hardly any features in the way of sales to mention except that they are pretty steady although not rapid.
The most notable is that Longmans have had 50 of the Mill, which will help the last 500. There are other small dropping sales, and the sales I mentioned in Clerical Scenes and Adam Bede were in the new editions of both which is pleasant.
I should be puzzled to give you any idea of the opinion formed in London of the Mill, but in all directions I find evidence that the attempt has been made throughout the big city to form an opinion which is quite eulogium enough. There is a great deal of balancing as to the merits of the two books, and I think generally Adam is the most popular but there are quite enough of supporters of the Mill to make the verdict a close divided one, and I have heard nobody worth a farthing who did not think the last book fully worthy of the author of the other.
I have heard a good deal of sort of ex post facto wisdom proceeding from the knowledge of who the book is written by, especially among the small deer of criticism.
Delane spoke of the Mill and used very much my own sort of language saying "God it is a wonderful book. It is no use arguing about it." I have not had an opportunity of sending to Dallas what you said of his review but will do so.
I was very glad to see by your letter to the Major that something had occurred to you in the way of writing although your hint is so vague that I cannot guess the style.
Tell Lewes I have seen a few of the London men but not many. I met the "godlike Forster" 559 at M. Morris'. 560 With that noble franchise which distinguishes him he insisted upon stating to me at some length that he could not turn to the Mill again. He was very impressive and said he had wished to make this statement to me. I told him I could bear it and the fun is I cannot recollect that he gave a single reason for this incapacity to reread the Mill. He must have said something but there could have been no critical remark worth remembering. Understand that he did not mean to be unfriendly or offensive; indeed there was as little of the latter quality about him on the occasion as his singular natural gifts in that way could permit. Of the Physiology I do not think there is anything to report. Thackeray is blooming but I have seen less of him than usual.
I am wearying to get off to the North now but do not expect to do so until the 26th. Is there any chance of seeing Lewes and you by that time? I hope this will find you both in good case and enjoying the glorious scenery.
I should like much to have a photograph of you, and will treasure it very much if you will get one done for me. There are beautiful coloured ones done in Paris and you would be safe from the illustrated papers in a place where you were not known. I suppose you will come home via Paris. With best regards to Lewes Believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, London, 14 June 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, London, 14 June 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Jermyn St. | June 14/57.
My Dear Sir
Your long and interesting letter of the 11th affords me much pleasure as it gives me great confidence that in spite of my objections to this first part of Janet's Repentance the Tale as it goes on will prove one of your best. Indeed the glimpse of what was coming in the last pages left this impression on my mind at first.
I do not fall in with George Eliots every day and the idea of stopping the Series as suggested in your letter gave me "quite a turn" to use one of Thackeray's favourite phrases. There is nothing in the part that can make me "afraid" to publish it. On the contrary no one can read it without being impressed by the ability and truth of the individual pictures, and I only wished to convey my fear that you are wasting power in sketching in so many figures who would not help on or add to the popularity of your story.
From the tone of this first part I do not think that it will be much liked, but you know what ground work you require, and when I have not seen the whole of your M.S. you must always take my remarks as those of one writing to some extent in the dark. I wish much now that I had the rest of your M.S. as I feel sure that it would enable me to write and heartily congratulate you upon a new success.
I liked the religious feeling in Gilfil much, and I am very glad to see what you say on that head in your letter. I feel sure that we shall agree in disliking canters of all creeds and respecting real religious feeling whatever form it takes. Send the proof direct to Edinburgh where I hope to be on Thursday.
I leave this "damned distracting Town" tomorrow morning and, many friends as I have in it, I am not sorry to get away. For the next two days I shall be in a remarkably rural district of Derbyshire and tell Lewes that while there I shall reread his literary Zouave friend's M.S. and write to him on the subject.
Thackeray was here today to say good bye to Mrs. Blackwood and had there not been some other parties in the room I would have read what you said about him, as I do not think it would have been otherwise than gratifying to the old Trojan.
In continuing to write for the Magazine I beg of all things that you will not consider yourself hampered in any way. Of course I will say when I think you are failing to produce the effect you intend or otherwise missing the mark, but unless you write entirely from the bent of your own genius or knowledge or observation it would not be worth my while to make any comments at all.
The cordial tone of your letters gives me great pleasure, and after reading your last I should have liked very much to have shaken hands with you and expressed the hope which I now write that there are many years of happy friendly and literary intercourse before us.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
To the Author of Clerical Scenes.

John Blackwood to GE, London, 14 December 1859(1)
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cavendish | December 14/59.
My Dear Madam
I got back from the Isle of Wight last night. While there I was chiefly and most pleasurably occupied in reading the M.S. you gave me of Sister Maggie. It is a most wonderful portrait gallery and the humour and exquisite touches of nature make one pause upon every page.
At first I was rather afraid that you hung too long over the childhood of your hero and heroine and that there was a want of narrative interest, but the striking merits overpower any feeling of this kind.
I incline to think you are right in your own instinct that the book should be published in a mass. Inclosed I send offer which is based on the principle that we take our chance of selling 4000 in the first instance and that you retain your permanent interest in the success of the book along with us.
I shall bring the M.S. with me tomorrow, and as I expect to see you so soon I write no more at present.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

My Dear G.E.
There is a risk in printing so large a number of Clerical Scenes, as seeing we have not been able to sell 1000 of first edition at 21/- the chances are against 1500 of the 2nd selling at 12/-.

P. N. Row | June 10/59.
My Dear G.E.
You will be delighted to hear that the opening of the subscription to the new edition of Adam Bede 150 is very promising nearly 1000 on the Row. I have ordered some copies to be sent to you and hope you will like the appearance of the book.
On the whole I think our best plan will be to print Clerical Scenes at once uniform in form and price. For such an edition of Fifteen Hundred Copies I now beg to offer you One Hundred and Fifty Pounds ('a3150). I hope this will meet your ideas.
We have hesitated whether to make the book one volume or only to print 1000 in 2 volumes.
We could not make a very neat book in one volume and on the whole we think it best to go for the 1500 in 2 volumes.
If we sell the whole it will be a good thing for us as well as for you, or if it sticks we can well afford to sacrifice the stock and certainly will not grudge it.
Let me know soon if you approve of the 2 volume Clerical Scenes as we should stick a slip announcing it into the new edition of Adam.
I wrote to Mr. Quirk yesterday and sent him your pleasant note about the gravel in his boots. My letter would not help to "boil his peas" and I think L. and you will shout over it.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.
Address to me at the Cavendish. Let me know of any friends whom you may wish to receive copies of Adam.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 9 May 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | May 9/66.
My Dear Madam
Burton was here today and he says that there was no such thing as transportation without hard labour, in this sense that every convict was absolutely a slave. His only chance of anything like freedom was falling into the hands of a singularly kind or soft hearted master. This picture of Convict life is something too horrible to think of, so the best way is to touch as lightly as possible upon it. He says it does not matter how much you blunder and his account of the mistakes that clever fellow Charles Reade had made about prison life 458 was really amusing. His theory is that if you do make a slip nobody will detect it, and I add that everything was possible that you are likely to write.
You will now have received the proof up to end of first volume and as far as I gather the sheets are being read with eager delight, but from my migratory state my own household are not so far advanced as they would otherwise have been. As far as I have read the proofs I find that the M.S. had printed itself on my mind. As I read I find that I remember every word and turn of thought and feeling.
We got back from Strathtyrum last night and leave for Derbyshire on Friday. I intend to be in London on Monday afternoon. I am looking forward anxiously to see you and to hear how the third volume stands and what it is like.
My nephew had the pleasure of receiving your note with the proofs today.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 9 March 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 9 March 1874
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
March 9/74.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Your welcome note with the poems came safely on Saturday and by a mistake between Willie and myself their receipt was not acknowledged.
It will make a most delightful volume and will I am pretty sure be a success. Before sending the "copy" into the Printing Office I have been looking through the Poems. They are truly good and have their meaning. 51 Mr. Simpson got the edition of Keats you mentioned out of the Advocates Library. The look of it took me back to the days of my youth. Do you think we should have the paper so narrow? The type to be used will enable us to submit it to you in both forms, like Keats and a little broader.
Willie is going up to London tomorrow so hopes to see you very soon. He is still very lame but otherwise well. He will be at the Burlington. Mary's ball came off on Friday and was a tremendous success. The Missionary came to see the supper his wife had so efficiently prepared. Gunter 52 could not have beat it. She is the same of whom I told you the story long ago. The clergyman whom we got in to speak to her was one of our best and luckily came from the same part of Roxburghshire where Gipsy blood is a large element. For the ball the artful Mary had secured more dancing men than ladies so that all were provided with partners. She amused me with her description of one of her partners who "held me at arm's length and kicked me all round the room so that I was afraid my ankles were bleeding, but he was so pleasant that I forgave him." This must be a dangerous fellow.
One feature since she came out tickles me -- in the streets I am constantly being saluted by the sort of youngsters whom I remember 30 years ago coming into my room saying "Won't you have a turn, old fellow." Collins has sent me the inclosed photo. of his Lowick Church and Rectory. Isn't it English all over?
I am sincerely grieved about the Lyttons' loss. It will press hard upon them. I hope you will write to him or her. Hoping to get good accounts of you from my nephew, I am always
yours very truly
John Blackwood.
I read Mr. Forster's most outrageous attack upon Lewes' Dickens Article. 53 It looks like an outbreak of bad health and worse temper.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 9 February 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 9 February 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 9/60.
My Dear Madam
I inclose four more sheets of The Mill. I have been laughing immoderately over them. They are far better than I thought. In fact in reading the M.S. I was so eager to get on that I could not have the full enjoyment of the excellent turns of humour and even feared that some might think the narrative dragged, but there is nothing of the kind. You are irresistible. That visit to Mrs. Pullet with her "deputy scraper" bonnet etc. etc. and the domestic scene between Mr. and Mrs. Glegg are grand. 472 The softening of good old Tulliver's heart is beautifully done and Mrs. Moss with her 8 children sorrowing over the lost twins is delicious. 473
The scene of poor Maggie's return from her Gipsy flight 474 is a great stroke of art, that is to say it is perfectly natural.
The Major and the rest of the family here who are reading the sheets are enchanted. I am particularly glad to see the way the ladies are taking to Maggie.
No passage in these sheets occurs to me for comment except the description of Mrs. Moss as a "patient etc. woman." 475 It is excessively good, but as some might take exception to it, I think I would alter it. If I had seen the last sheet before it went to you I would have suggested a modification of Mrs. Pullet's graphic description of the dropsy patient which is very humorous but perhaps strong enough. I reinclose the sheet containing the passage in case on looking at it again you should feel inclined to alter. 476
Tell Lewes that his concluding chapter has arrived all right
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 9 December 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 9 December 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | December 9/58.
My Dear Sir
I inclose cheque £30 being the amount received today from Tauchnitz for the right of translation 1241 in German. Williams and Norgate's was a cheque on a Scotch Bank which would have been charged with commission in London, so I send one of our own on Coutts instead.
It struck me as very possible that a divan would sit upon your signature at Williams and Norgate's so I got another copy of the Vertrag and made them be contented with my signature.
In regard to America for Adam Mr. Langford has seen Low and Co. who wish us to name a price. Shall we say £50, although I doubt whether we will get more than £30. Lewes may as well see Langford about it.
I have been quite vexed about the delay in the printing, but it was one of those unexpected fixes which will arise in the best regulated establishments. I am thankful to say that we have now got a release of Type and your Bedes or rather pearls will be strung as fast as you could wish now. I expect to have the whole in Type by the end of the year so that in reality no time will have been lost.
Sampson Low, 1242 the American agent, asked to see some of the sheets of Adam, but I consider this a farce.
Lewes asked about a new edition of Alison's Physiology. 1243 I am sorry to say that there is no prospect of such a thing, as the excellent old Doctor is shattered by repeated seizures of paralysis. No man ever devoted himself to good of the poor more heartily than he. He abandoned what would have been the leading practise in Edinburgh to toil perpetually in the lanes and wynds of the High St and Cannongate. I suppose L. has the old edition. If not I will give it to him.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.
I was sorry to hear that there had been some prying into your incognito. Keep your secret all you can. I shall do everything in my power to divert suspicion if I see any one getting on the scent.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 8 July 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 8 July 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | July 8/59.
My Dear George Eliot
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque 'a387-10/ being 'a350 received from Tauchnitz for Adam Bede and 'a337-10 in acknowledgment of "The Lifted Veil." The Veil is making very much the impression I expected. All admire the excellence and power of the writing, lovers of the painful are thrilled and delighted, others like me are thrilled but wish the author in a happier frame of mind and not thinking of unsympathising untrustworthy keepers of secrets. 204
Bulwer's copy of the Magazine had by mistake not been sent down to Knebworth. The tale is one of which I should have liked very much to hear what he said. We found the baronet in great force, better I think than I have seen him for some years and full of fun. He told some capital stories. He was great in praise of his Doctor Mr. Todd 205 and when
Lewes gets out of sorts as I know he does occasionally I think he should consult him. Delane too told me that this Todd was the best man in London with no quackery or humbug about him.
The Scenes are nearly ready and I shall soon have the pleasure of remitting to you for the second edition as also for Adam. The Bedesman never tires and we are reprinting as fast as possible.
Among the few here who have observed the paragraph in the Athenaeum contempt is stronger than indignation. It was lucky the low dog showed himself as foolish as he is malignant. The secret does not seem to be out here and all you or we have to do is to keep quiet.
I hope you are going to start on some expedition and I expect to hear from you in great spirits undisturbed by Liggins or any of the other ills that flesh is heir to. I often think of the new Tale and the name of the heroine comes more readily to my lips than St. Oggs on the Floss.
The Major sends his best regards. We frequently talk of our very interesting visit to you. 206
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. Eliot Esq.
P.S. While writing I thought the second instalment for Adam Bede was due at six months from publication instead of nine as I see it is. As I mentioned before however if any furnishings or movings should make an earlier payment desirable it will afford us pleasure to meet your wishes.
I have intrusted the getting of a pug to my cousin Col. Steuart, 207 an excellent fellow, knowing in horses and dogs and a devoted friend of mine. When he said good bye to us at the station he started in a Hansom for Blackman St. in the Borough where there is a dive kept in his early days by Dick Curtis the pet of the Fancy. If such a thing is to be got I doubt not the Colonel will manage it for me.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 8 February 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 8 February 1877
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
February 8/77.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I should have answered your very interesting letter sooner had I not been very busy and also rather unwell, two things which do not suit each other. The last few fine days however have made me much better and we have had a talk here over the Novels.
I most cordially agree with you as to including Romola in the uniform cheap edition of your Works. Smith and Elder's 2/6 edition, which I suppose they are entitled to go on with, will doubtless interfere with the sale, but we must hope the handsome uniform edition will hold its own.
Seeing that there is this cheaper edition and that it would be a little confusing to have Romola 4/ while Adam Bede and the Mill were 3/6 I doubt about going beyond latter price, and perhaps it will be better to meet the difference in thickness partially by putting a little more into the page of Romola which the public would hardly perceive. As to illustrations we are of one mind, and if Mrs. Allingham can satisfy you let us try her. Will you or Lewes speak to her on the subject? Bear in mind that the book will not bear much expense in that way, and I think we should not attempt more than two or three illustrations to Romola.
The two illustrations you justly denounce in Adam shall be burked in future 'abeditions'bb reprints. Silas Marner is such a perfect thing that I incline to keep it a small volume by itself and rather to make the Lifted Veil and Brother Jacob another thin volume. 606 What you say of reading Romola after an interval of ten years is very striking and adds another proof to many I have seen that your books are the permanent work of your heart and will be permanent in the heart of the world. I had a remarkable instance of this in a letter this morning from my dear old friend Mr. Brown, who has so long been chief reader and corrector of press with us and whom I think I introduced to Lewes when he was in Edinburgh. He came into my father's house when he was a boy and has been with us all these 'ab45'bb 47 years and is now about 60 or 61 years old. I am in great grief about him as for many months he has been confined to the house by a most painful illness which threatens to prove chronic in the stomach. It is most touching to see how the true gentle nature of the man comes out in his illness and I have seen him many a time much more impatient and complaining over a printer's blunder than he is in the midst of all his sufferings. It seems a relief to him to write a long letter to Mr. Simpson or some of us here every morning and the following is [an] extract from his letter today which will I am sure affect you. Speaking of a Novel he had been reading he says "George Eliot's I don't rank as Novels but as second Bibles. I think I never enjoyed anything so much. You never think or feel you are reading fiction, but biography told with the most exquisite simplicity, and biography of people into whose minds and hearts you can enter with the intensest sympathy. Such books are worth nine tenths of the Sermons ever preached or published and they must be dull both in mind and soul who can read them without feeling the better for them." I quite agree with him.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 8 April 1879
Text: Copy. National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
April 8/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes.
I am glad to [have] received your letter and to hear that you have reconciled yourself to the publication of Theophrastus before the end of May. I shall write to Mr. Harper and it will give me great pleasure if I can save you any trouble in such negotiations, especially if I can do so successfully in a business point of view for you. In the mean time I think from what you say it will be better to do nothing about translation into German and not to allow Tauchnitz to reprint unless he offers something very considerable. He could bring it out very cheap and it is a sort of book the English would buy abroad, particularly for the Indian market. You have not returned the Title-page or mentioned the form of advertisement you would like. At present I do not propose to stereotype but to begin with a moderate edition say two thousand and to keep the type standing. 215 We could reprint quickly enough to meet any demand.
Thanks for your kind messages about my health which I quite appreciate; indeed it was to please my wife that I had the second wise doctor here. Our weather has gone back again a little but I hope it will be fine enough for Musselburgh tomorrow. Hamley 216 is away to Bulgaria where he is to be our chief commissioner as to boundary, but I do not see what we can do. Kinglake has nearly finished his new volume. It tells of the Winter Troubles before Sebastopol. It is strangely fascinating reading. My Nephew reports delightful weather in London and I earnestly hope that you are taking advantage of it by being out of doors as much as possible. 217 Since I became an invalid I have felt nothing do me much good except the open air.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 8 April 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 8 April 1867
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 8/67.
My Dear Madam
I was glad to receive your pleasant note about the first part of the illustrated edition of the Novels 605 which Mr. Simpson feels as a peculiar grace to himself. The figure of Adam 606 is hard and their making it so sinuous as well as sinewy irritated me, but the accessories are good.
We cannot tell yet how the series is going to do but although the first demand has not been so good as I expected, I hope that it will go on steadily improving. I feel that it should do.
I shall be very curious indeed to see the Spanish Poem or Drama. That it will be very fine I have not a doubt. I intend to be in London some time in May when I hope to find this and your other project taking shape. If any of the M.S. of the Poem is in such a state that you would not mind showing it, I should feel very great interest in looking at it.
I have mislaid Lewes' note and cannot recollect what he wrote about, but I remember that I entirely concurred in what he proposed, whatever that was, and I do not think it required an answer.
In reply to your kind allusion to family arrangements, I am sorry to tell you that my nephew's marriage has been broken off. It has been a sore grief, but as it happened months ago now, the wound is I trust beginning to heal over. There was an objection to the marriage originally in this, that the young lady was doubly Willie's cousin, her father being his mother's full brother and her mother their cousin. If her parents had made this objection at first, nobody could have denied that there was something in it, but to bring it forward after six month's engagement with their entire approval, was a stupid cruel business, harder even upon the girl whom they frightened than it could be upon any man. Willie would have pushed it on, but after such a fear had been put into a girl's head I should have dreaded the result.
I hope Lewes' health continues in the upward state and that he is getting corpulent.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 7 November 1867
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 377.
Edinburgh November 7/67.
My Dear Madam
It gave me very great pleasure to receive your letter and it was most ungrateful of me not to write at once to thank you. I am much delighted with what you say of the Memoir of Aytoun and of the man him-self. For twenty years we were bosom friends and companions, and his death was the break up of as joyous a fellowship as ever existed between two men much engaged in business together. I feel what you say the more as I have been intensely disgusted at the tone of the London Press in regard to Aytoun. I am tolerably well acquainted with the London Press and there is not among them any who for poetry, humour, and real power of argumentative writing can be compared with Aytoun, yet they speak of the dead man with the most lordly contempt. However Lewes and you know the fellows, so I need not say more about them.
In spite of your misgivings I feel very confident that Fidalma is getting on well. I long to see more of her. 678 What would you say to trying some of the drama in type to see how it looked? At present I have no intention of being in London this winter, but there is no saying. I ought to be more in London, but when I am there I find it very difficult to do anything. Driving about in Hansoms cuts the day to pieces, and when I get back to my rooms callers pour in, and by the evening I am only fit for a cigar with the General. To hear you read Fidalma would be a strong inducement to run up to Town, but I think it would not be a bad plan for you to try some of it in type.
Adam Bede goes on steadily but not brilliantly. I must confess to heavy disappointment at the non success of the works as a serial, and I cannot understand it. Next to predicting who will win the Derby I think foretelling how many of a book will sell is about the most difficult problem going.
I had a call today from Theodore Martin and gratified him by reading what you said of the Memoir of Aytoun. While he was with me another friend of Lewes' William Smith turned up. Smith is looking strong for him, and was very glad to hear that Lewes was better.
I agree with you in thinking that Trollope giving up his official situation is a doubtful step, but I hope he has a good retiring allowance. Of shilling Magazines there seems no end. They cannot answer and it is difficult to see how many of them continue to exist.
Disraeli's visit here was a great success. His address to the Working Men was the best thing I ever heard him do. 679 It was thoroughly well done. My printers were all there and were highly delighted.
Do you never think of writing any miscellaneous papers for the Magazine? It strikes me that you could do a first rate address to the Working Men on their new responsibilities. It might be signed Felix Holt. With best regards to Lewes, Believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
Write to me whenever you have leisure.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 7 March 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh March 7/60.
My Dear Madam
I had intended not to read the M.S. of volume 3 as it would be in print so soon but I could not help myself. I took up the first page and of course never halted till it was finished and then sighed for more. 499
I am indeed wearying for the rest and feel the misfortunes impending on Maggie like a personal grief. The moment I saw Stephen Guest and Lucy sitting together 500 I felt that there was the element which I had missed in the probable form of the coming tragedy. This third volume will be perfectly fascinating.
So intensely real is it that I am not sure whether I did not exclaim aloud "Why the devil is she putting poor Maggie into a position where she would be more than human if she did not come to grief." It is a most wonderful performance and I feel satisfied that the interest is coming to a very grand culmination. The second vol. too winds up very beautifully with poor old Tulliver's death. 501 That scene is most effective and affecting.
My nephew Willie 502 writes that from what he knows he thinks 4000 will be too small a number. 503 We will however take care to feed the public appetite.
I hope you will see Willie and that he will be able to report you as well in the midst of your tragic work. He probably may be able to tell that all is finished.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 7 July 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 7 July 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | July 7/57.
My Dear Sir
I inclose proof of Janet's Repentance Part 2. 915 Most graphic and life like your pictures are. Clever and humorous as this part is I feel that the best of the Story is yet to come. Hitherto Janet and Tryan, who ought to bear the chief burden of the interest, do not stand out from your canvas so distinct in form and substance as your other figures.
Your Bishop is doubtless a true sketch, but I wish he had been a better sample of the cloth. Some allusion to the solemn and affecting sight that a confirmation ought to be would not lessen the effect of your quaint and amusing picture of the scene at Milby thirty years ago and would destroy the chance of any accusation of irreverence or wish to make the ceremony ridiculous. 916
The preparations for the reception of the Bishop 917 are capitally sketched, as also Mrs. Jerome with her abominable tea cups. 918 Indeed the part is full of admirable touches. The placard is too long and my impression is that it would be better very much cut down or described in general terms. It did not make me laugh, which ought to be the emotion combined with indignation at the outrage excited by such a document. 919 You show very great skill in exciting the interest of your readers and I am sure most of them will be as anxious as I [to] see the rest of Janet's story. Let me have back proof as soon as you conveniently can.
The Madeleine Smith 920 Trial keeps Edinburgh quite ahead of London at present. The girl will get off. She is a nice young woman but I really doubt whether she did poison the beast and at all events he deserved anything. I wish the dog had died and made no sign, as such exposures do much harm. I should like to hear Lewes on the subject as I think he has rather a turn for the analysis of remarkable trials.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.
I have been giving out George Eliot as the mysterious author. Do not allow any objections of mine to Janet to disturb you. Probably my want of experience of English country life [keeps me] from seeing that the placard is natural in the excitement of a village religious war.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 7 January 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | January 7/58.
My Dear Sir
I inclose memorandum of the subscription to Clerical Scenes as far as it has yet gone. The prospect looks well for the disposal of the edition and I think I shall have the pleasure of making the first and second payments to you at one and the same time.
The Leviathan Mudie was induced to take the 350 by our giving him an extra 10 per cent discount. Do not mention this however as, although we thought it wise to give the discount in this case, as a general principle it is doubtful policy.
We shall not be able to judge for a week or two how the book is really going to take as the subscribers generally are rather more at sea than ourselves and it is only when we know how the books are moving from the shelves of the purchasers that we are able to form a sound estimate of sales.
The review in the Times was a most fortunate circumstance and it was a very friendly act on the part of the potentates of P[rinting] H[ouse] Square. 1050
Mr. Langford, our manager in Pater Noster Row, writes me that he got an early copy off to Lewes and you. Let me know how many more copies you would like or send me a list of friends private or literary whom you wish to receive the book.
Mr. Langford necessarily knows now that the Clerical Scenes came through Lewes, but of course keeps the secret. If L. can look in at P. N. Row at any time Mr. Langford will show him our presentation list in Town and he may suggest additions. He will also be able to show him how the book is going on.
How does the new Tale progress? I think you should be in good feather about it now.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 6 March 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
March 6/79.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
The corrected proof of Theophrastus arrived safely today and I shall send you revise of the whole with both Titles for our joint consideration. Your proof was not pulled on the paper on which we proposed to print the Book and we shall send you a specimen with proper margin. It will be a point with us to make it as handsome a volume as possible and we shall put in such a notice as you may approve as to the time at which we received the M.S. May or June are as good a season as any other to publish.
I am extremely glad to hear that you have been driving out and I hope you will persevere in going out. When I come up in Spring I trust to find you much stronger than at present and your face wearing that look of gentle power and sympathy with every one with which I have so long been familiar.
always My Dear Madam
Yours most sincerely
John Blackwood.
P.S. We sell the Birth Day Book at 3/6 cloth bound and 5/- bound in leather. There were some few copies bound plain morocco but they would be more expensive. The Book takes well but we made the binding too expensive for the selling price.

March 6/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
On Saturday I got the inclosed note and sent the reply, the substance of which I have scrawled on at the end of the note. On Sunday came your note to Mr. Simpson on the same subject. It is a laughable coincidence, and not the least curious thing to me is that I should not only have taken the trouble to reply but have kept a memorandum of what I said. Simpson is writing to you what measures he is taking to stop if possible your corrector's correspondence. 422
The sales during the last three days of last week were most satisfactory, and as we have a note from Mudie today ordering the extra 250 of Book II it is as I predicted overtaking Book I while B. one is still marching on. always yours truly

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 6 January 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 6 January 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | January 6/60.
My Dear Madam
It is a real pleasure to receive such a letter as yours, which I got yesterday. Since then we have all been considering the various Titles proposed, and this morning it suddenly came across me that
The Mill on the Floss would be an appropriate Title and in some respects more appropriate and curiously exciting than any of those suggested. It has too a sort of poetical sound.
The Major and I rather inclined for Sister Maggie, but as the early part of the story is so much about children I think Lewes' objection is valid. Mr. Simpson to whom we showed the proposed titles was for the House of Tulliver or Life on the Floss, but now we all incline for The Mill. The Title however is of no great moment and whatever you fix upon will be best.
It will be as well to advertise in the next number of The Magazine so send down what you think should be said. Mention when you think we may be able to publish. I do not mean this for announcement in the advert[isement] but that we may consider whether we are not giving too long notice of the good things that are coming.
The dates you propose for the payments, viz. 'a31000 at 6 months and 'a31000 at 9 months from date of publication, are quite agreeable to us.
With regard to the Clerical Scenes we have been thinking a good deal, and our proposition is to print another edition of 1000 at 12/- which, placing the book on the same permanent footing as the new novel and the future editions of Adam Bede, will yield you 'a3150.
Looking to Clerical Scenes as an individual book, this is the worst proposition for us pecuniarily that we could make, but considering the large interests both you and we have in the other books, we think it is the wisest course. A 6/- Clerical Scenes would naturally lead to the expectation of a 6/- Adam and that again to a 6/- edition of the new novel, which might be very fatal to the 12/- edition. When we come to have the three books there will really be something to be made out of a uniform edition of them at 6/-. They will help instead of hurt each other.
I fancy the present edition of Clerical Scenes is about sold out, so we should print at once. 451 There were sold in London in December 39 copies and the same number in previous month.
I had no opportunty of asking Sir Edward what he got from foreigners, but something like 150 'a3 from America and 'a375 from Germany strikes me as having been at one time the rate, but now I think it is more. I am however very uncertain. Sir Edward will be very glad indeed to make your acquaintance and also to renew that with Lewes. I am to send the address, which I shall do in writing today or tomorrow. He is looking better than I have seen him for years, although he complains a little of cold on the chest.
I intended to have written to Lewes but as I have got on to a new sheet of paper and have nothing particular to say, merely ask you to tell him that I am greatly amused with his animated interview with Cooke. It will not I fear do any good. A bird like Cooke cannot at any time feel the respect due to a man of genius, however much you may dislike the man or his principles. Inflated too by the success of the Saturday and surrounded by cleverish sharp disappointed men like the Reviewers there, he will consider them the equals of Bulwer, Dickens or any body and entitled to dogmatism accordingly. I am not sorry to pause and consider the Darwin a bit.
The Major sends his regards and believe me,
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.
I am glad the review of Fielding is on the stocks.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 6 December 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 6 December 1867
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: John Blackwood, pp. 376-377.
Edinburgh December 6/67.
My Dear Madam
I inclose proof of your noble Address to the Working Men. 693 I wish the poor fellows were capable of appreciating it. If they were we should be all right, but it will do great good and is exactly what I expected that you would write.
Should there be a preliminary note from me or a note from you to the Editor? I incline for the last, as I know that anything I could say would sound quite discordant beside your perfect English. At foot of first page do you not allow too much weight to the assumption that the franchise makes the working man the master? The allegation in the House was made as a sarcasm by those opposed to the Bill. 694
Your picture of "the ignoble martyrdom of fools" 695 which would be their fate if they allowed the mob and mob orators to mislead them and destroyed the class who have leisure and refinement to think and legislate is perfect. According to my knowledge of working men, which is not inconsiderable, the good among them are thoroughly up to the useless self-seeking character of their own noisy demagogues, and I think you may say something more on that head.
The first part of the Great Poem is now all in type. It is wonderful. I find myself reading and rereading and I feel myself quite incompetent to say all I think of it, especially within half an hour of post time. Shall I send up the proof? You may feel satisfied that Fidalma will add another wreath to your laurels. I really feel that I do not know how rightly to express myself about it.
I think Lewes will shout out, Why has he not sent proof, and I think I would, had I not left it at Randolph Cres[cent]. Willie tells me that he had a most pleasant forenoon at the Priory, and your visitor turned out to be a grand-daughter of my own friend and my father's friend, excellent old Mrs. Hughes. 696
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Edinburgh | April 6/59.
My Dear Sir
By all means send the jeu de melancolie for the Magazine. I think with great pleasure of the new Novel and do not know how I can restrain my impatient curiosity until the middle or end of May, which is I fear about as soon as I can be in Town.
I am glad you like your Reviewer in the Magazine. I selected him very much from knowing him to possess the qualifications you indicate, and I do not know that he ever reviewed a book before. Few Words on Social Philosophy and How to Boil Peas by him. 87 I had corresponded with him for some 16 years and never saw him. I recently got him to come and pay me a visit and found him a capital fellow not very many years older than myself. His own Rectory is in Wales, 88 but for a length of time he has done the duty at Gt. Houghton.
I inclose a couple of letters, the unopened I daresay as eulogistic as my friend Theodore's. I like Martin's note very much.
There will be more money from Clerical Scenes some day, but in the meantime if it will be any convenience to you we will be happy to make a further payment on account of Adam Bede. The sale goes on steadily and we will be cleaned out by the time the new edition is ready next week.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | November 5/57.
My Dear Sir
I inclose the first 16 pages of the Reprint. In looking over the proof the impressions first made upon me by each turn of phrase come so vividly before me that I can hardly believe a twelvemonth to have slipped away since I sate eagerly reading the M.S.
I think it wisest to print a short number but do not let that discourage you. No man can approach to anything like an accurate idea of the probable demand for a book when there are no previous data to go upon, and it is best to err upon the safe side. We shall also be able to keep a large portion of the Type standing so that we will be ready to meet an extended demand very quickly.
You may rely upon my doing the best I can for you, and I should be bitterly chagrined if I thought anyone could fairly do better. The proofs will now follow fast on each other.
What of the new Tale? I shall miss you much each month.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 5 March 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 5 March 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
March 5/79.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
We ordered the two errata on Self and Life to be cancelled and the stereotype plates to be altered so that the mistakes cannot recur.
Your young friends at Natal will be all safe now. 189 I do not think Sir Bartle Frere has sufficiently counted the cost of the war either in blood or treasure. We shall doubtless slaughter those wretched Zulus in any number but that is no satisfaction. One is ashamed to look at the illustrated papers and see the portraits of ourang outangs with whom we are fighting.
There is here at present a young Mr. Conder R. E. who was at the head of the Palestine exploring expedition and wrote the account of what they did. 190 He is sanguine of something being done or rather tried in Palestine and he had heard of Oliphant's expedition. He is at present employed in fortifying Inch Keith with guns which will secure the firth of Forth against all comers. This great National boon which Scotland has prayed for ever since I can remember and long before was secured when Mr. Hardy 191 then War Minister was staying with us last winter. The house at Randolph Cres[cen]t was filled by the meeting. Conder writes a little for me and the paper on the climate of the Levant this month is his. I have reports from the best authorities in Cyprus directly contradicting each other as to the climate and this paper of Conder's holds I think the golden medium. We have very high winds here now but there is something of a soft pleasant air at last.
From what you say I hope your health is indeed better. I wish I heard of the year looking a shade brighter to you. A heavy heart casts a shadow on everything. My nephew is feeling his leg better and hopes to be in London about the end of next week. I am not feeling quite so well today but still I have nothing to complain of only I do not feel fit to run a race and certainly shall never rejoice in that prospect but luckily there is no occasion.
Pray let me hear from you when you can, and believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 5 March 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 5 March 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh
March 5/61.
My Dear Madam
On coming here this morning I found the M.S. of Silas pp. 233 to 308 and of course sat down at once to it. What a picture or series of pictures you place before the reader. It is quite delightful. The association of the old man and the child and its effect upon him is beautifully done, and Mrs. Winthrop is a jewel in every sense.
Silas' attempt to inflict punishment and the "toal hole" 710 quite affected me, as I had a somewhat similar incident this very morning at breakfast. The children were making too much noise (a very trying thing at that time) and I shouted "Silence or you go out of the room" in a voice that might have struck horror into a giant, when the smallest offender replied "Naughty old Reekie" (Smoky, my nickname).
I should have liked to see more of Miss Priscilla, but what there is of her is perfect and Nancy is very natural. The disposal of the reprobate Dunsey and the discovery of his remains 711 is I think the most skilful thing you have done in the way of plot.
I was in hopes at one part that you were going to introduce a clergyman to the help of Mrs. Winthrop and that we should have another picture of character, but I suppose you had not a good one at hand as sometimes happens in this life. The motto giving to some extent the keynote to the story does not I think signify in this case, as whenever the child appears her mission is felt.
You may I am sure make your mind easy about this story and rejoice in the prospect of another success. The M.S. is in the Printer's hands.
I am sorry to see you write so cheerlessly about your health, but I trust to hear soon that you feel all right. There is very little change in my brother since I last wrote. Thanks for your kind expressions of interest in him. The more you knew of him the more highly you would have thought of him.
ever, my Dear Madam yours very truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
Tell Lewes I am very glad to hear he likes Petherick 712 so much. My idea was that by seeing him he might be better able to fill in a sketch of this remarkable specimen. He is a most original character.
