John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 5 December 1877
Text: Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh December 5/77.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
It was a great pleasure to receive your charming and most interesting letter and had I not been going off to Golf I would have sat down and written to thank you at the moment.
The inclosed is the last we have from Mr. Main and I like his choice of extracts. They at all events are undeniable good things for man whatever may be thought of the scheme of such books. To me it will be like another collection of Sayings by you.
Mr. Simpson has attended to the details you wrote about and is thinking over the best form for the Birthday Book. When we get back this specimen from you we shall try it in type.
Tell Lewes I shall be glad to hear from him how you are bearing this gloomy depressing weather. It seems to be worse in London than here where it is bad enough.
My daughter paid a visit to some friends at St. Andrews last week. Her first walk was of course to Strathtyrum where she was rapturously received by the section of dogs left there. In the midst of his gambols the collie jumped clean over her head when she turned to caress another favourite. Otherwise the place looked terribly desolate and wintry.
always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 4 July 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | July 4/60.
My Dear Madam
Your welcome letter from Berne only reached me on Sunday having, owing to the stupidity of mine host of the Cavendish, wandered about Derbyshire instead of coming direct here. Your note today and intelligence from Langford of Lewes' appearance in the Row gives me the pleasant news of your being again well and comfortable in your old quarters at Holly Lodge. I begin to regret that I did not wait in London until you returned as I should have liked a chat with you of all things.
If the grand secret cannot be trusted to writing, I shall still more regret not having had a pleasant converse and luncheon at Holly Lodge. Such a meeting would have refreshed me after five weeks of London turmoil, which is to me nowadays very tiresome.
I inclose Sir Edward's letter. 577 I did not see much of him when I was in Town as he was chiefly at Knebworth and I was unfortunately engaged when he asked me to go there. His health is wonderfully restored, indeed I do not think I have seen him looking so well for the last ten years. The best general point in his criticism is I think in the distinction between the painful and the disagreeable, and it is good to hear the author of Lucretia 578 on that point. I do not by any means expect that you will agree with the application, and I see readily how you can answer what he says about position, but in the main I think the letter is a very good one and gratifying, as the tone of consideration in which the big fellow writes shows how thoroughly he feels that he is speaking about another very big fellow. As to imitation of Dickens, 579 I know there is none and the only involuntary likeness that struck me was in one or two phrases of Mrs. Pullet as in the dropsy case.
The Newspaper reviews would neither amuse nor instruct you so I daresay you are wise in deciding not to look at them.
The Major sends his best remembrances and believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes
Recollect that I am a first-rate hand at keeping a secret.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 31 March 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 31 March 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 31/58.
My Dear Sir
I have again carefully read the 219 M.S. pages of Adam Bede and a very remarkable story it promises to be.
To begin at the beginning the scene in the carpenter's workshop is very lifelike, and Adam's reflections upon Religion are capital as also upon men working without heart in their work, striking when the bell strikes -- the grindstone illustration is happy.
The picture of the cottage preparatory to the sermon is very complete -- the loud talking habit of the rustics truly and graphically described. I did not think you could possibly have managed such an outr'e9 proceeding as Dinah's Sermon with such delicacy and skill -- freedom from cant or offence of any kind. It is beautiful. I think her prayer too much of an address rather than a petition but perhaps this is done as characteristic of her sect. The meaning of the proverb about Chad's Bess should be made clear or it may be taken to imply something more than I suppose it does. 1108 I feel doubtful about the direct address to poor Bess and her throwing down the ear rings. It strikes me that the passage page 53 about the identity of Love, religious feeling, and Love of Art would be better modified a little. 1109
At page 57 some of the remarks about relations are most beautiful and true, but part of the reflections might be softened with advantage. 1110 Adam's dreary night work, the rap of the willow wand, and the brothers carrying the coffin in the lovely morning 1111 most skilfully throw in the shadows, preparing one for the coming catastrophe. The wind up of the first part and Adam's reflections are admirable.
The Vicar is a capital fellow and the visit to the sick room is very touching, 1112 but I wish for the sake of my Church of England friends he had more of "the root of the matter in him." However I hope he is to sublime as the story goes on.
The description of Mrs. Poyser is first rate. The Captain's inquiries as to Hetty walking in the Chase are direct enough. 1113 Dinah and the clergyman are good together and Hetty is certainly very attractive.
Does it not seem inconsistent with the minute reality of the story to say nothing of the Vicar's visit to the cottage after the death.
Lisbeth is a very perfect picture but there is rather too much of her, or rather of her dialect. 1114 The reflections on her emotions after the old man's death are beautifully true. Dinah's soothing influence on her is exquisitely painted -- the influence of real religion and good feeling with no cant or methodism about it. Dinah's is indeed an angel visit. Adam's reflections on hearing her footstep in the house with the illustration of dreaming in sunshine and waking in moonlight are very touching. I should not wonder if Dinah fell in love with the manly fellow.
The Captain's unfortunate attachment to Hetty will I suppose form a main element in the Tragic part of the story. I am not quite sure how far I like the scenes in the wood and I hope things will not come to the usual sad catastrophe!
Is the mysterious stranger who listens to the Sermon the general of the district -- looking at Adam with an eye to a recruit? I suppose he will reappear soon. 1115 There is as you said too much of the dialect but this can be remedied in proof.
The story is altogether very novel and I cannot recollect anything at all like it. I find myself constantly thinking of the characters as real personages, which is a capital sign. It will be very different from anything that has ever appeared in the Magazine and as far as I can at present judge will do well there, but if you will allow me I shall not decide on the form of publication until I have seen more.
When you send down the two other parts you mention will you give me a sketch of the rest of the story?
I look anxiously for more of Adam Bede and believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 31 December 1872
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh December 31/72.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I cannot allow the year to close without expressing my hearty good wishes for you in the opening year and the same for Lewes.
The publication of Middlemarch will be one of the events by which will be remembered. The public mind has been wonderfully exercised by the book and exercised for good.
It is indeed a triumph for you. I was sorry to see by a letter from Lewes to Von Moltke that you had returned from a visit rather out of sorts but I hope this favourable change of weather has done you good. This has been about the best day we have had all through the year. Having some hundred things that I ought or wished to do before the end of the year, I felt that I would probably sit all day doing nothing so I went off to Musselburgh to golf and for the last five hours have been busy in a glorious match which ended all even, the four players finishing in a state of breathless excitement.
There is a little sale going on in the leviathen 42/- and Willie, Von M. and self are much exercised considering what ought to be done. 679 They join me in best wishes and believe me
Always yours Truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
I shall write to Lewes in a few days.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 31 December 1871
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
December 31/71.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I cannot let the year close without writing a line to wish Lewes and you health and happiness in the year which opens upon us tomorrow.
When I came out a little ago I left my wife deep in the "Sayings" with which she is perfectly delighted and told Principal Tulloch who lunched with us that they are undeniable Sunday reading. He had not taken up the volume himself but said his son was raving about it.
Simpkins and Whittakers have each had 25 Middlemarch recently, which looks as if the public were buying. The sale is [word illegible] something over five thousand. The change in the second part is I think an immense improvement and makes it most attractive. Mr. Simpson would acknowledge the third part, which is in the printers' hands.
I intended to have come to see you again before I left London but I could not get it made out. However I had nothing to say but to repeat congratulations on the reception of Middlemarch. Hamley only ran up for an afternoon and could not get to the Priory. This place is dull after Paris and London, but when I am not golfing I am working as hard as can be so it does not signify to me. I have laid down a rule to take two days golf each week and as the regimen is agreeable to me I am likely to stick to it. I found a brother enthusiast for golf in Capt. Thrupp of the Megaera. 429 You would have laughed if you had heard us go at it in the midst of his description of St. Paul. I hope you will like the way the Tale of the Megaera is told in the Magazine. From the way Puck (my daughter) and Jack devoured it I am in hopes the right chord is struck. Jack is away at St. Andrews for a little winter shooting but returns tomorrow. Hoping that you are both well I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 31 August 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 31 August 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | August 31/60.
My Dear Madam
Your letter communicating the Great Secret is truly refreshing and opens up a famous prospect.
Savonarola and his times is a splendid subject for you, and you have such a power of imparting reality to every thing you write that your Romance will not read like Fiction. I expect that you will return Historical Romance to its ancient popularity.
Your fears about not being able to carry out your ideas do not alarm me. Your doubts are better than other men's certainties, as Lord Kames said of the celebrated Scotch Law Book "Dirletons Doubts." 624 The wealth of thought and power of illustration in the Mill give the idea of inexhaustible stores in your mind.
The Major, I am thankful to say, continues to improve steadily, but he is very feeble yet and time will be required to put him all right again. He was much interested by your letter and rejoices with me in the idea of such a series for the Magazine and also in the prospect of publishing another Story of English Life by you. If I could get away from here just now I would come up to London solely for the pleasure of talking about those two novels with you.
My nephew Willie is going with his brother 625 to Southampton on Tuesday and intends to pay his respects to Lewes and you on Wednesday if you are to be at home. The young soldier is a very tidy specimen of what an officer should be, and I would have sent him to you but he is only to be in London on the Monday. A young fellow starting from the midst of a happy family for uncertain duties is always a sombre business, and it is doubly so when the usual mainspring of the house is reduced to his sofa.
I had an idea that the secret was an Italian story and a hope that you might intend it for the Magazine but I was entirely out as to the date of the story.
Is the English Story to be Town or Country?
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 November 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 November 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 30/75.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
You would get proof of all the M.S. we have last week, which brings us to the end of the second volume. I have been reading and rereading and always with increased wonder and admiration. As I read I constantly lean back in my chair to make sure that I am taking in all the beauty of the thought and feeling. It is like inspiration and you may rest assured that you are writing one of the most remarkable Books that ever was produced by man or woman. I know nothing like it.
It seemed hard to be torn away from Gwendolen after she read that "horrible" letter and Grandcourt came down "dressed for dinner," 355 but so exquisitely do you work the other chain of your story that one is speedily as engrossed as ever. Where did you get your knowledge of the Jews? But indeed one might say that of all your characters, so life-like and human are they. That Jew boy 356 is a little marvel and in the midst of their substantial kindliness Mordecai being helped to "the tails" of the whitings 357 is irresistible.
Simpson tells me he sent you yesterday specimens of cover papers which he has gathered in all directions. I rather lean to the pearl grey which he told me is the name of the colour. 358 At home we have constant discussions as to what is going to happen and who Deronda is, all being spoken of as living beings, but I must not tell you of our speculations.
When you are ready we shall be glad to stereotype so as to return type. It seems confoundedly prosaic to mention such things in connection with such a book.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 March 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 March 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 30/59.
My Dear Sir
Along with this you will receive your copy of the Magazine and I hope you will like the Review of Adam. 78
The demand for Adam goes on and we have decided to print a short edition in the present form. 79 Mudie wishes 100 more but Mr. Langford has only given him 50 as the stock is running low. The Magazine
Review is calculated to tell on the circulation more than any puff, however enthusiastic. From what I hear too I expect that there will be Reviews in other influential quarters, so on the whole I think it was best to reprint in the present form.
Tell Lewes however that I perfectly agree with his views about the reprints of books according to their character. Indeed his views are identical with my own.
I had great pleasure in sending the M.S. of Adam. 80 I have kept the M.S. of Clerical Scenes 81 for myself. It makes one large thick quarto volume. It is one of the strongest practical marks of my admiration for the Scenes that from the first I had ordered the M.S. to be set aside for me. It is an inexplicable thing that all the popularity of Adam has not carried off the fag end of the edition of the Scenes. There has been no demand here and Langford has not reported any in London, so it can only be trifling if any there.
This is unaccountable and forms another instance among many I have seen of how impossible it is even with the best means of judging to predicate with certainty what the public will do about a book. The only principle is to publish according to the best of one's judgment nothing but good books, and if the public is sometimes a stupid beast I am happy to say I have found him a most excellent beast in the main.
The Clerical Scenes will sell in a cheaper form along with Adam. I put a query as to what you were doing with the new Tale. I am very anxious to hear about it. I want a Tale for the Magazine and I know I can trust to George Eliot.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot, Esq.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 June 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | June 30/57.
My Dear Sir
I hope you have got your copy of the Magazine and find Janet correctly printed in all respects. 914 Your letters always give me much pleasure, and I wish I could overcome my habitual disinclination to letter writing so as to give myself a fair claim to more frequent communications from you.
As yet of course I have no means of judging how Janet is going to take with the public, but I have no doubt as to the power, ability, and lifelike character of the sketches in Part 1. That too many of the harsher elements of character are painted without relief in this part I still think, but I feel perfectly confident that the continuation of the Story will cause my objections to disappear altogether. The temptations to idleness in this hot weather in Jersey must be very great; nevertheless I hope to see a batch of M.S. very soon.
In the meantime I have the pleasure of paying into Lewes' account with the Union Bank £27 in acknowledgment of Janet Part 1. As I write to Lewes along with this I trust that you will excuse the brevity of this note.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 January 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 January 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: M. Blind, George Eliot, 1883, p. 96, and William Blackwood, II, 437-438.
Edinburgh | January 30/57.
My Dear Amos
I have the pleasure of sending to the care of our friend Mr. Lewes a copy of the February number of the Magazine containing the conclusion of the history of the poor parson. A good many people will be disappointed at finding his history so speedily wound up, but I trust that you will quickly do away with any such regrets by sending me down an assistant and successor who shall eclipse the worthy Curate of Shepperton.
The public is a very curious animal and those who are most accustomed to feel its pulse know best how difficult it is to tell what will hit the bull's eye, but I shall be much astonished if the death of Milly does not go to the hearts of all readers. It is a most touching death bed scene.
Critics are a good deal divided about the first part of Amos, but they generally are about anything of real merit. Some of my friends praise it very much; others condemn. I was rather startled by two of my familiars -- about the best men going -- declaring dead against Amos. They have rather modified their opinions now and I think may probably end by agreeing with me. They were the first men who had seen the Magazine after it was published and finding two such lads against me it required all the self reliance, without which an Editor would be the most miserable dog alive, to make me feel quite easy and satisfied that
I was right. With one of them, Colonel Hamley, 787 I do not recollect of ever differing in opinion before. He thought the Author very possibly a man of Science but not a practised writer. The idea of a man of Science had occurred to me before from some of the illustrations.
I forget whether I told you or Lewes that I had shown part of the M.S. to Thackeray. He was staying with me 788 and, having been out at dinner, came in about eleven o'clock when I had just finished your M.S. and was busy talking about it to Mrs. Blackwood. I said to him "Do you know I think I have lighted upon a new Author who is uncommonly like a first class passenger." I showed him a page or two, I think the passage where the Curate returns home and Milly is first introduced. 789 He would not pronounce whether it came up to my ideas but remarked afterwards that he would have liked to have read more, which I thought a good sign. The Newspapers generally have I think been very favourable, but I do not attach very much weight to what they say until they catch the general echo.
Hoping soon to hear from you with M.S. and, with remembrances to Lewes, I am
yours very truly
John Blackwood.
To the Author of Amos Barton.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 December 1874
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Randolph Crescent
December 30/74.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I must not let the year slip away without writing all good wishes to Lewes and you in that which is now so close upon us. I do hope you are both well and facing the cold manfully. We are all well and happy, bar an obstinate little cough which keeps me off the Ice, as Curling, which next to Golf is the best game in the world, keeps one hanging about in the cold too much. I went out to the ice however yesterday to see my son and daughter skating and they were a neat little pair, though I say it. He is, I am sorry to say backward in all his studies, but he is a clever fellow. He did make me laugh this morning at breakfast. On pretext of seeing whether it would suit the ladies he had gone last night to the minor theatre here and gave a doubtful answer to his sister's question. I asked "Is it low?" "The dresses are," was his brief reply.
Will you look at a story Giannetto which begins the January number of Maga? There is only another part of it, and it strikes me as one of the most perfect stories of its kind I ever read. The writer is a young lady (23) 175 "a leddy o' high degree." In such cases one has usually to exhaust oneself in excuses, and my surprise and pleasure were great when I found this tale so good that I not only agreed to publish it as a little volume, but said I should like the readers of the Magazine to have the first of it. I shall be curious to hear what you think of it.
Pray give me any news of your approaching work and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 April 1877
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
April 30/77.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
After much puzzling and consideration we have pretty well come to the old conclusion that the handiest and most handsome form for your works will be an edition in 19 or 20 volumes somewhat similar to the 2 volume edition of Adam and Felix. We have been further assisted to this conclusion by looking at a set of your novels which had been bound and cut to as near as might be a uniform size to catch the eye of some of your worshippers here. This set I send to you by rail and I think it will look well in the library or drawing room in Town or country.
This continual North East wind has again made Simpson's throat a little rough and he is keeping to the house for a day or two but the inclosed note and calculations will show you that he is busy as usual. The calculations will assist Lewes and you in coming to a decision. The only other form would be the novels in one volume octavo but it is impossible to make that a handy volume to read by the fireside. You will see that Simpson shrinks from making the vols. 5/- but I incline for the five and so does Willie. I expect to reach London by the 10th or so when we can talk over all these matters.
So there is War at last 657 and where it will end none can tell. On coming into the breakfast room the other morning I exclaimed to my daughter "The Russians have crossed the Pruth and entered Jassy. It seems but as yesterday (although 24 years since) that I read these same words in this room, and papa would have gone to the Crimea but he had met Mama and was going to visit some of her friends in Derbyshire." History is repeating itself with a vengeance. It is impossible to say how long we may be able to keep out of the mischief.
This is the Golf Spring meeting week and I am going to St. Andrews for a few days to brace myself for the London campaign. I go en garcon to join some other golfing maniacs in lodgings. I hope this will find Lewes and you well and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 April 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 30/68.
My Dear Madam
I write a line to acknowledge the safe arrival of Book V and the sheets for press.
There is a solemn calm as after a storm in the last book and the parting is pathetic and impressive to a degree.
I have ordered two thousand to be printed, which is I think the number we both thought of.
The correction of the heroine's name to Fedalma will be carefully attended to. The bulk of the slips had already been turned into pages before your first correction of the error arrived. You certainly wrote the name originally Fi and it is a curious case of delusion as once even in book form I observed that you had written it Fi. Our last letters crossed but I shall write tomorrow or next day.
always yours truly

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 April 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 30 April 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 30/66.
My Dear Madam
Your letter gives me great and honest pleasure. Felix Holt is now fairly in the Printing Office and proofs will begin to pour in upon you in a few days. There is always a little delay at starting for calculations of quantity etc.; besides this has been what is popularly called "The Preaching Week" 448 when the Scottish "working man" biennially shows his devotion -- to Bacchus. Not that I mean anything against my own printers, who with rare exceptions are excellent steady men.
I had the manager up to my room to warn him about spacing the dialogue properly. He is a most matter of fact gentleman and remarked "Sir, there is every sign of experience about the Dialogues." I kept my countenance and understood his meaning -- that you had marked the dialogues so distinctly that the compositors could not fall into the mistake of running on. By the way, how admirable your mottoes are. Many of them I imagine to be your own. I see you have left blanks in many cases. Do you mean to fill them up?
I must tell you that when Mr. Simpson took home the M.S. at night his mother, a most shrewd old lady, an Englishwoman, got hold of it and has nearly blinded herself. I went to call upon her yesterday and found her in perfect raptures. There was an additional comical element that she was under the impression that she had rather done something surreptitious of which I might possibly not approve.
I am off bag and baggage to Strathtyrum this afternoon. It is the
Golf meeting week and I am almost as eager for it as my little boy Jack, who for the last fortnight has aroused me in the morning with a statement of in how many days we would be at "the Strath." Yesterday after dinner he suddenly broke out "At this time tomorrow Papa." On the 14th of May I intend to be in London, when I hope to find you and Lewes quite recruited and your work pretty well over.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
I think Lewes will probably be able to make a better arrangement for the right of early sheets for America, and the liberty to translate than we could for you. The transatlantic vultures may be drawn a speck nearer honesty by the desire to propitiate a great author than they would in any business transaction with a publisher. If Mr. Lewes does not know to whom to apply Mr. Langford can give him every information. Tauchnitz may very probably ask for leave to introduce the book into his series of English novelists in our own language, but do not grant him this. It is dangerous.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 3 November 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 3 November 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 48.
Edinburgh | November 3/58.
My Dear Sir
After writing to you on Saturday I fastened upon the 3d volume of Adam Bede 1209 and read the whole of the M.S. that afternoon. I am happy to tell you that I think it capital. I never saw such wonderful effects worked out by such a succession of simple and yet delicate and minute touches. Hetty's night in the fields 1210 is marvellous. I positively shuddered for her, poor creature, and I do not think the most thoughtless lad could read that horrible picture of her feelings and hopeless misery without being deeply moved.
Adam going to support her at the Trial 1211 is a noble touch. You really make him a gentle Man by that act. It is like giving him his spurs.
The way poor Hetty leans upon and clings to Dinah 1212 is beautiful. Mr. Irving 1213 is always good. So are the Poysers, lifelike as possible.
Dinah is a very striking and original character, always perfectly supported and never obtrusive in her piety. Very early in the book I took it into my head that it could be "borne in upon her" to fall in love with Adam. Arthur is the least satisfactory character but it is true too. The picture of his complacent happy feelings before the bomb shell bursts upon him 1214 is very good.
We have been trying pages so as to start with the printing immediately. The extent is not so great as I imagined and I cannot help thinking that our people have rather underestimated the quantity.
Inclosed I send our formal offer 1215 for the book which will I hope come up to your expectations and, congratulating you upon having worked out the climax of your story so splendidly, I am always,
yours very truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 3 February 1860

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 3 February 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 3/60.
My Dear Madam
I have just finished reading the first 96 pages of The Mill, which with another sheet will be sent to you along with this.
Pray make your mind easy and abandon dismals. Your pictures are wonderful. The people are all alive and in the flesh. Mrs. Tulliver is a great creation and the superior wisdom of her husband is as irresistible to me as one touch of it was to even the usually immovable Mr. Riley. 466 Maggie, Tom, and Bob Jakin are delightful, and even the glimpse of the Miller's man 467 brings the worthy fellow perfectly before one. The exquisite touches of human nature are very numerous; in fact it is human nature all over. Yap is a good dog, and Tom calling to him on the moment of his arrival 468 is to the life. The Major is out this afternoon so that I have nobody to turn to and say "Isn't this good etc." which is very hard upon me.
I do not like the word lymphatic applied to Mrs. Tulliver. 469 It interferes with the pleasure one has in looking at her.
I am delighted to hear of the professional compliment to Lewes of the dedication. Should we make a paragraph of it?
Mr. Simpson is attending to your "incisive" message about the Sea Side Studies.
If people generally can go at The Mill again and again with as hearty a relish as I do, you will have a triumph that will put to flight the most obstinate of headaches, and I hope in the meantime you have got quit of that from which you were suffering when you last wrote.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.
Has Sir Edward been to see you yet? I am rather curious for an account of that interview.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 November 1867
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh.
November 29/67.
My Dear Madam
I feel deeply gratified by the kind consideration for my wish shown in your letter today 690 and I am satisfied that what you propose to say and have said to the Working Men will hit the nail on the head and may possibly be of great service. Your doubts are better than other men's certainties, 691 and I will rather take my "chance of your doing" this than ask any one else to try their hand. You have the knowledge of what the working men ought to do and the real feeling towards them which will give a force to your words which no ordinary address could possibly possess. I do therefore earnestly hope that you will go on.
The great Poem is now fairly in the Printing Office. Every line of it nearly "donne 'e0 penser." The beauty of the language and thoughts is something perfectly marvellous.
Willie went up to London yesterday to see his brother 692 off to India, and I have no doubt they will be with you tomorrow or next day if not already.
I write in a great hurry, having been away for a grand pitched Golf match. My chosen mate and I were beat in the morning, but in the end covered ourselves with glory.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 January 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 January 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | January 29/59.
My Dear Sir
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque 'a3400 being the first instalment for Adam Bede in terms of our agreement.
Copies will be with you in the early part of the week, and ask Lewes to let Mr. Langford know how many copies you wish. Do not stint yourself as to these. Send also a list of parties, private or connected with the Press, whom you would like to receive copies. The book is to be subscribed on Tuesday 4 and you shall have early intelligence as to its success.
Whatever the subscription may be I am confident of success, great success. The book is so novel and so true. The whole story remains in my mind like a succession of incidents in the lives of people whom I know. Adam Bede can certainly never come under the class of popular agreeable stories, but those who love power, real humour and true natural description will stand by the sturdy Carpenter and the living groups you have painted in and about Hayslope.
My brother joins me in congratulations and good wishes for a triumph in this case and many more which we think your pen will yet achieve.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 December 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 December 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Text of statement: Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh December 29/68.
My Dear Madam
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque £333.18 in acknowledgment of the first and second editions of the Spanish Gypsy as per accompanying memorandum. The edition's being sold completely off makes the transaction a very satisfactory one. I expected a quicker rush of sales in the first instance, but the gradual nature of the sale is a better symptom.
I intended to have written to Lewes in reply to his obliging note, but something came in the way. We quite agree in what he says of calling each thousand an edition or even giving that title to a smaller number, and although our first edition was 2000, the second being so small brings the proportion very near.
Of the third edition (7/6) we have already disposed of over 800, which I hope this season will clear out of the hands of the Trade so as to let us go on quietly printing a fourth edition. 850
These sales are not what they ought to be, but looking to all that we hear of the fate of others, they give good cause for satisfaction. The newspaper critics have I see got it into their heads that it looks intellectual to admire or rather to praise Browning. I say praise because through all their laboured words and attempts at analogies it peers out that they can neither admire nor read him. I was struck by this and made to laugh in reading reviews in the Saturday and Athenaeum. The words are as laudatory as possible, but it is obvious that the creatures had the utmost difficulty in reading the words of their idol, so how could they admire him? I confess that I am a heretic as to Browning, but perhaps I have not gone at him seriously enough, although I have made several attempts and also read picked extracts with more of attention than admiration. I should like to hear what Lewes and you think of this first instalment of his new Poem. 851
Lewes seems to be getting on famously with his researches and experiments. I can easily imagine the pursuit becoming very exciting. Of your Novels I have not much to tell as they move very slowly. I never was so far out in calculating what a sale would be, but I know I was right as to what it should be. I do not allow the mistake to disturb me in the very least. We shall probably find our public and pull through in some cheaper form.
My nephew joins me in wishing Lewes and you health and happiness in the coming year, and I hope there are many years before us in which as in the past not the least pleasant of our associations and relations will be with George Eliot.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 December 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh December 29/66.
My Dear Madam
I have the pleasure of receiving your acceptance of our offer for the Copyright of Adam Bede, The Mill on the Floss, Felix Holt, Silas Marner, and The Clerical Scenes for ten years from this date.
I shall pay the Thousand Pounds in two instalments of £500 each at the dates you wish, viz. 15th March and 15 June along with the further payments then due for Felix, and I hope devoutly for both our sakes that the contingent £500 may in good time become due to you. Should any change arise in our copyright relations with America it will afford me real pleasure to give you any benefit that may accrue from it.
You may rely upon my making the covers of the parts and volumes neat. The boarding of Felix was a happy combination of and improvement upon a lot of specimen boards that the London binder had sent down, and I think he owes us thanks for making him turn out so neat a book. I am quite pleased that you like its look so much.
I got a cold bath this morning in the shape of two specimen illustrations of Adam. They are both returned as unsuitable. I have written a separate line to Lewes, of whose continued indisposition I am very sorry to hear, but I hope the foreign tour will do good. You should go on to Rome. There is always lots to interest there and now more than ever. With every good wish of the Season, I am always
yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 December 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | December 29/60.
My Dear Madam
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque Thirteen Hundred Pounds (£1300), being £1000 the second instalment for the Mill on the Floss and £150 for Adam Bede and £150 for the Scenes, a thousand copies of each of which were printed last spring. 682 The stock of Adam must be pretty well exhausted, but I am afraid we shall not be able to get through this edition of the Scenes. Next week however I shall send you an exact memorandum of the stock on hand and number printed of all the three books.
There will be £300 to come to you for the 2000 printed of the 12/ edition of the Mill, and this we shall make payable with the last instalment of the 1/11/6 edition, which I think falls due in Spring.
There must have been some oversight in our calculations in giving £150 on single thousands of the 12/- editions as the sale of the whole number will hardly cover the expenses, but on enterprises which have been so happy and profitable to us we are very glad that you should have the benefit of this slight blunder. I would not have alluded to the thing at all did I not feel that my silence would leave you with a wrong impression of the profit really made by the 12/- editions.
These books have been a great and glorious success and many such triumphs may we see together. That the sale of the Scenes should be so far behind the other two books is astonishing, but as I have often said to you, the sale of a book is a thing that no man can calculate with anything like certainty.
I hope this will find you happy and comfortable in your new home and well protected from the weather. The Major joins me in best wishes of the Season and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 December 1856
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 December 1856
MS: National Library of Scotland. Mostly published: Cross, 1, 425-427.
Edinburgh | December 29/56.
My Dear Sir
Along with this I send a copy of the January number of the Magazine in which you will find the first part of Amos Barton. It gives me very great pleasure to begin the number with Amos and I put him in that position because his merits will entitle him to it and also because it is a vital point to attract public attention to the first part of a Series, to which end being the first article of the first number of the year may contribute.
I have already expressed to our friend Mr. Lewes the very high opinion I entertain of Amos and the expectations I have formed of the Series should his successors prove equal to him, which I fully anticipate.
It is a long time since I have read anything so fresh so humorous and so touching. The style is capital, conveying so much in so few words.
Those who have seen the Tale here are chiefly members of my own family and they are all enthusiastic in praise.
You may recollect that I expressed a fear that in the affecting and highly wrought scene of poor Milly's death the attempt to individualise the children by reiterating their names weakened the effect, as the reader had not been prepared to care for them individually but simply as a group -- the children of Milly and the sorrow stricken Curate. My brother 773 says no -- "Do not advise the author to touch anything so exquisite" -- Of course you are the best judge.
I now send proof of the conclusion of Amos in acknowledgment of which and of the first part I have the pleasure of making a cheque £52-10/ -- Fifty Guineas.
If the Series goes on as I anticipate there is every prospect that a republication as a separate book at some time or other will be advisable. We would look upon such republication as a joint property and would either give you a sum for your interest in it or publish on the Terms of one half of the clear profits to be divided between author and publisher, as might be most agreeable to you.
I shall be very glad to hear from you either direct or through Mr.
Lewes, and any intelligence that the successors of Amos are taking form and substance will be very acceptable.
I shall let you know what the other contributors and the public think of Amos as far as I can gather a verdict, but in the meantime I may congratulate you on having achieved a preliminary success at all events. very truly yours
John Blackwood.
To the Author of Amos Barton
I have made the cheque payable to Lewes so that it will require his endorsement.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 29 April 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
April 29/72.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I inclose some memoranda of Middlemarch Book III which show that there is a pleasing movement going on although not so rapid as one could wish.
Mr. Langford has not said anything for some time as to the sale of Books 1 and 2 so I do not know how they are going on.
If Lewes is ever in the City tell him to look in at 37 P.N. Row and L. will show him how the movement is. I hope to see you next week as we intend to be in London on Wednesday 8th May. We are going abroad and taking our daughter with us and only intend to be a few days in London. We mean to go to Vienna and Trieste, then home by North of Italy and Switzerland. I do not know whether my daughter or her mother are most excited. This week is the "May Meeting" at St. Andrews, and we go over to Strathtyrum this afternoon. It is not an Exeter Hall meeting, but one of jolly golfers. I am obliged to go as Captain, but I am anything but averse to the road as it is great fun and the place will be looking lovely.
I took the liberty of giving a note of introduction to you to Mrs. Chetwynd 515 who is anxious to throw herself at your feet. She is a pleasant, accomplished woman and I hope you will excuse the liberty. Also I was so long in answering her note that I think she may have left London before she got my reply. I cannot recollect the name of what she has written.
Hoping to see Lewes and you both well next week, I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
When are we to get any more M.S. I am wearying to see more.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 29/68.
My Dear Madam
I send along with this proof of Book IV. It is truly grand. I do not know when I have been so struck with anything as when "Awful Night" 747 closes in upon Silva driving his misery and remorse in and in upon the wretched man.
The Gypsies wild chant 748 comes in well, and perhaps this night scene is even more impressive than the more exciting one of the death of Zarca, although nothing can be more effective than Silva walking away unharmed but hopeless on every side. 749 Zarca keeping in life to say what he wished to say is wonderfully drawn.

Perhaps we should advertise with the name of the Poem now and
Lewes should get the Pall Mall or any friends in the Press to put in paragraphs as to the approaching event. The Poem bears reading and rereading bit by bit and is greater I think in that way than as a story.
By the way, does not the word Baron come in awkwardly in one of the beautiful arias. 750 It seems prosaic in the wild melody.
Willie is going up to London in the beginning of next week and will see you soon. I hope to hear from him that you are well and not suffering from your poetical fatigues. It must be most exciting work.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 28 October 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | October 28/57.
My Dear Sir
I fear you will think me rather dilatory in answering your last letter. The explanation is that the past week has been what are called "The Preachings" 993 here which cut so seriously into business hours that there is no time in the Printing Office for anything but works of necessity and mercy, foremost among which of course I reckon The Magazine.
I have now however had a regular calculation made of "The Scenes" and see that they will make 2 post 8'b0ree; volumes of about 400 pages each to sell for 21/. The page will be rather sparser than I like but that cannot be helped. I wish the Series had been long enough to make the statutory 3 vols. as that would have afforded time to fix your reputation more firmly and familiarly in the public mind and given the reprint a better chance of a start at first. With this view I would have suggested a prolongation of the Series had I not thoroughly agreed in the opinion that you require a broader canvass and freedom from the trammels of your Clerical Title.
The chances of a permanent or extended sale for the Scenes must be in one volume at a moderate price, so we propose to make the first edition a short one of 750 copies and for this I beg to offer you £120. According to our calculation this is a little less than 'bd the clear profit supposing we sell the whole edition, which of course is no certainty. We have hesitated whether to make the edition 1000 994 but on the whole we think the short number the best plan as it is a desperate nuisance to be stranded with 4 or 500 copies of a book which we feel would sell better in a cheaper form.
As to the copyright of the book I wrote before publication 995 commenced saying I should consider that we had an interest in it to the extent of one half, and as a general principle this is what I think we are entitled to unless in the case of authors of very firmly established reputation whose works are sure to command an audience and an extensive sale in what ever form they are published.
I did not recollect that Lewes had mentioned your wish to retain the Copyright, but I at once agree to it and in the event of future editions, of which may there be many, I daresay we will have no difficulty in arranging about them as pleasantly as we have been able to settle everything in our intercourse hitherto.
Inclosed I have the pleasure of sending a cheque £30 in acknowledgment of the last part of Janet. I shall miss the series very much but I trust soon to see you in the field with your new Tale. Pray let me know if you begin to make way. Believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.
P.S. Your motto is very applicable. Has it not been used before as a motto? I hope to be able to write to Lewes today with a sheet of his book but if I do not, I shall tomorrow.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 28 November 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | November 28/59.
My Dear Madam
In reply to your note I beg to say that I cannot recollect any expression of mine which implied anything like disinclination to continue to act as your publisher and the expectation of not continuing to do so arose from your recent letter 407 which changed both my brother's mind and my own.
I am glad you have written this note as it shows there has been some misapprehension on your part and it gives me the opportunity of trying to put an end to it as also of being frank with you.
I was very much annoyed or rather, I should say, hurt at the tone in which my offer for the new novel was replied to and also at the very dry way in which our conduct in doubling the purchase money of Adam Bede was acknowledged.
In regard to the new Novel other people may take a more sanguine view than I do of what it will produce and to secure a great popular author may offer a sum such as I would neither think it right nor prudent to give. If such offer has been made, I would be the very last man who would wish for a moment to stand in the way of your doing what you thought best for yourself, but I think I should have been told so frankly instead of having my offer treated as if it were not worth consideration at all.
As to the withdrawal of the incognito, you know how much I have been opposed to it all along. It may prove a disadvantage and in the eyes of many it will, but my opinion of your genius and confidence in the truly good, honest, religious, and moral tone of all you have written or will write is such that I think you will overcome any possible detriment from the withdrawal of the mystery which has so far taken place. Believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 28 December 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 28 December 1867
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | December 28/67.
My Dear Madam
In sending the inclosed acknowledgment £25 of Felix Holt's Address I beg to thank you very much for doing this paper, which I feel as a personal favour to myself. The Address is excellent. The only fear is that it may be too good. If the mass could appreciate rightly such words and feelings, what a grand nation we would become. I wrote to Delane about the Address and hope Lewes will have stirred up the Pall Mall Gazette.
We are keeping Christmas very quietly. My little boy had a famous rise upon me on Christmas morning. When I greeted him on coming down he said "When I came into your room this morning, Papa, to wish you a Merry Christmas instead of saying [The same to you, old fellow,] you called [Get out, you little brute.]" The twinkle in the little villain's eye when he exposed my unpaternal conduct was good. The fact was I had just dropped into a particularly balmy slumber and had a vague remembrance of rebuking some disturbance.
The Printers set your Poem very badly and they had no excuse, but it is a strange thing that I find them most frequently at fault with the plainest M.S.S. while with difficult ones they often show great skill. For instance Kinglake's M.S. which was being set at the same time is a very involved one, and he is struck with wonder at the correctness with which it has been set up.
How is the Poem getting on? I hope you are in good heart about it. There is a set of the proofs lying in my dressing room and I take a little refreshing look at them every now and then.
With every good wish for Lewes and you in the coming year, I am
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
When does Lewes think of going to Germany? I intend to be in London early in February and hope I shall not miss him.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 28 April 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 28 April 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
April 28/73.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Very many thanks for your pleasant letter. I should like very much indeed to see your Sonnets on the childhood of a brother and sister. To my eyes of course my children are a pretty and moving sight as they step along together, laughing, joking, and looking gaily to the future.
I like what you say of Kenelm Chillingly greatly. In a few words you say so much and express exactly what I feel about the tone of the book. I too was deeply affected by the closing sentences and I thought even the critics would have been touched by the wind-up in such circumstances, but no, it does not seem to have touched those stern stoics. Your critic in the Quarterly is a heavy man, too wise by half, but he is friendly and means well and such a review does good.
The success of Middlemarch has given a good stimulus to the sale of the Works, and for some time Mr. Simpson has been talking to me about a reduction in price, making Adam Bede 2/6 and so on in proportion, and meeting the change of price so far by a cheaper paper with less margin and also a cheaper binding with the omitting of the blessed illustrations. Will Lewes and you turn this over in your minds and let me know what you think? I am doubtful myself.
As to the effect that such a change of price would have upon the value of the copyrights at the end of the ten years when our lease expires, I do not consider that it would affect the value to any appreciable extent.
The more your books are known the more they will sell, and that I hope will fully balance any possible forestalling of future sales. The question at the end of the ten years will be as it is now, whether we should go in for large sales at 2/6 or be content with the modest sales at 3/6.
The sales have been good and steady but never anything like what we calculated we might hope for. They stand about something as follows: Adam 14500; The Mill 8500; Felix 5800; Scenes 5000; Silas 5300. During the past year and half the influence of Middlemarch has been distinct and Adam has been moving at the rate of something like 2000 copies a year and the others in a like lesser proportion. This is something like a half more than had been selling during the recent previous years.
I hope you are going to get away to the country now. After a long term of bitter east wind we have an attempt at west wind today, but you would by no means call it the balmy west as you hurried past the corner of any of the streets that cross George St. My health I am happy to say is quite restored, and as we go to Strathtyrum on Saturday I expect to be quite robust soon.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 October 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 October 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | October 27/59.
My Dear Madam
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque 'a3400, being the final payment for Adam Bede in terms of our agreement. I wrote to you some time ago that it would not be agreeable to my brother's feelings or mine not to give you a further pecuniary share in the triumph of Adam. Since I so wrote the success has gone on, and instead of 'a3400 we now intend to send you 'a3800 at the beginning of the year.
Adam is indeed a grand success, and it is absurd for the author to bother herself about the absurdities of Liggins' friends. It is easy however to be wise for another in a matter where the feelings are concerned, and I do not mean to deny that I have a very pretty talent for worrying myself even in cases where fully satisfied of the downright folly of so doing. The only whisper I have heard of the matter was a letter the other day from that worthy Quirk, 366 saying he was now satisfied that he had been imposed upon by Liggins. I have taken no notice of his note.
The printers have been sorely reprimanded for the blunders in the recent editions of Adam of which I was sorry to hear. You may rely upon them all being put straight now. The blunders in the "dialect" arise no doubt from the compositors thinking that there is no "dialect" in the world except Scotch.
I am delighted to hear of the progress of Maggie in whom I shall always feel a very keen interest. I wish I were in London to read the M.S. of the first vol. I would not be long about it, although to read your Tales fast is not to do them justice. The first volume of Adam I recollect kept me as busy as possible from London to the Border.
The Major sends his best regards and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
To Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 March 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 March 1877
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
March 27/77.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Thanks for your pleasant letter and I hope the improved health which had begun when you wrote has gone on with you both in spite of the weather, which with us at least is bad as ever.
We all here incline for an edition of your works in goodly octavo. Can you refer us to the edition of Fielding you possess or send down a volume to guide us? It is difficult to get novels of length such as yours into one volume octavo at once portable and with an open readable page. I would be inclined to go in for 10/- volumes if we fix upon 8vo but uniformity in price would not be necessary.
Pretty early in May I certainly expect to be in London and I am very glad to hear that you are still to retain The Priory. You are quite right to feel your way before finally settling in the Country. I am going for a few days change to North Berwick and my wife and children go with me. The weather is most uninviting but as it has rained steadily for four days we are hopeful and as N. Berwick is only 20 miles off we can easily come back. It is a pretty country and there is a Golfing Links.
I am afraid you will think the Magazine review of Miss Martineau 631 too severe but in the main I think it is right. The paper on the French army 632 I have every reason to think as authentic and accurate as such things can be and you will be glad to see that France seems fit for self defence. It is a fearful comment upon all the talk about peace and goodwill among men to see France and Germany more than ever like two great armed camps watching each other.
We lost our good old Mr. Brown about ten days ago. At the last he only suffered from total prostration of strength. My nephew and Mr. Simpson are both well and join me in best regards to Lewes and you.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 January 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 January 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
January 27/79.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I have the pleasure of inclosing Bank Order £777.12.6d being amount due to you on your Works at this time as per accompanying statement. The sales of cheap editions are very satisfactory and the Cabinet or Library Edition 171 is going on steadily. To enable you to understand about this edition you should refer to my letters of October 1877 and last January.
You will observe that very few are sold of the last six volumes of this edition and this arises not from a falling off in sale but because those volumes were not yet published in their usual monthly course at the 31st of December. We hurried them through the press that we might be able to supply complete sets at the end of the year and in this way you will see we disposed of about 100 complete sets. If there is any point on which you desire explanation be sure to let me know and I will make it as clear as possible. Since the turn of the year the sales of the volumes have been extremely good.
Thanks for your kind inquiries as to my health. I am really bearing the weather well. I had a twinge in the knee which was supposed to be gout or rheumatism but turned out nothing but a passing strain of muscle. I got no sympathy and my family said my "action" was worse than Cousin Bill with his broken leg.
Willie joins in best regards and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 January 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh January 27/60.
My Dear Madam
I inclose a letter which came today. From the stamp on the back I am in hopes that the letter may announce a present from the appreciating proprietor of the Fabrique D'Horlogerie.
I think the announcement of The Mill on the Floss looks very captivating. Proofs will be up to you soon now. Let me know whether you would like a good batch at a time or to have them sheet by sheet.
We are not making the space between the lines any closer than in Adam but are going a line or two more in the page. 461 I got Lewes' obliging note about the Tom Jones paper, which I have reluctantly postponed for a month, but the subject is not of a day.
The paper which chiefly interfered with Tom was that on Fleets and Navies by Capt. C. Hamley, 462 who had been unwell and I did not expect him; however by a great effort he had got it done. You should read that paper; it strikes me as wonderfully good even to the unprofessional reader, and naval men tell me they have seen nothing on the subject so sound as these papers.
I hope you are getting on merrily.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 February 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 February 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 27/61.
My Dear Madam
We think there will be no risk in making Silas one volume to sell at 12/ as we can make it a thicker and handsomer book than the ordinary volume of a 31/6 Novel.
For an edition of four thousand copies to sell at this price we beg to offer you Eight Hundred Pounds payable at six Mos. from publication, and payment at a like rate for any number we may sell beyond the four thousand.
Our idea is that 5 or 6 thousand at least should be sold and the only doubt we have is as to how the one volume may affect the library demand, but we think any possible falling off in that quarter is more than made up by the additional chance of the one volume Story finding private customers who never think of buying a 1/11/6 novel.
I hope the above proposition will meet with your approval and that I shall soon have the pleasure of receiving the conclusion of the story, of the character of which I am delighted to hear.
Since I wrote to you Willie and Mr. Simpson have read the M.S. and are in a most pleasurable state of excitement about it. In regard to the printing it will hardly be worth while to begin until the whole is finished or the end fairly in sight unless you wish to have the proofs by you. On consulting the foreman of the Printing Office as to time he said "Oh, we'll blaw it out like a bottle," meaning that the printing would be as rapid as that almost instantaneous process which you may have seen.
Will you send the form of advertisement you would like, as we should begin to blow our trumpets at once.
It is a relief to try to think upon your book or anything as sorrow is pressing hard upon us here. My dear brother's state leaves little or no hope. He is very calm and resigned and suffers little, which is a great comfort.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 February 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 February 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh February 27/60.
My Dear Madam
I send a further batch of proofs which have also gone to Mr. Sheard as far as page 144, 489 which I suppose embraces all that you wish to refer to him about. Except the allusion to the action of a bill in Chancery, 490 which could hardly I fancy be so prompt as you make it, I hardly think there will be any legal point to criticise.
The scenes in these pages are painted with a power and minute finish which is perfectly wonderful. I entered so keenly into the matter and felt so angry at the Dodson sisterhood that I could hardly laugh at their absurdities, intensely comical as they are. I wish you could have given them some touch of feeling to relieve the sensation of oppression. Would it not be possible to give Mrs. Tulliver some trait of feeling for her husband to enable one to sympathise in her woes? The contrast between Maggie's feelings and Tom's is exquisitely done. She is an individual character and no mistake. I begin to regret that we did not stick to our old favourite name of Sister Maggie, but it is no matter. If it was, Lewes and I should have our heads punched.
Mr. Deans' conduct is I think the shabbiest as being less in keeping with his character and position. My old friend Tulliver's difficulties were in reality so small in amount that a man like Deans could have eased him without any great expenditure of breath or coin, but this would have played the deuce with the story.
I am wearying for volume three and hope your labours are well through. Your announcement of the coming tragedy excites me greatly and I am puzzling as to the precise shape it will take.
Sir Edward's deafness is a sad bar to conversation with him. I am glad that you saw him and were favourably impressed with his kindness and sincerity. I have the same opinion of him from long experience.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 February 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 February 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 27/57.
Dear George Eliot
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque £21. in acknowledgment of the first part of Mr. Gilfil's Love Story. Having written to Lewes and you so recently I need not repeat my laudations of Mr. Gilfil.
Yesterday afternoon I read over the proof of part two which I now send to you. I am truly happy to say that it seems to me admirable. When I first read the M.S. the night was so far advanced that my eyes as I drew towards the end were beginning to get weary, and although
I arrived substantially at the same opinion of the merits of Part 2 as I now entertain, I do not know that I fully appreciated all the excellences and beauties of this portion of the Story. On the proof I have marked one or two trifling points for your consideration. very truly yours
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.
P.S. The cheque will require Lewes' signature.
Of your two adverse critics to whom I alluded before -- Hamley adheres to his first opinion but admits that as far as he can judge the public agree with me, of which he is very glad. Aytoun, 810 the other, has not said much but I think he begins to be of opinion that I was right. One of his reasons for not liking Amos was comical enough. "Confound you, you had praised it so much before I saw it that I could not be otherwise than disappointed." There is a good deal in the feeling he alludes to, and I do not know how I was so injudicious as to raise his expectations so highly.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 April 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 27 April 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 27/59.
My Dear George Eliot
The sale of Adam goes on and the 750 are pretty well exhausted now. 500 more are being got ready 115 to supply the public appetite which it is to be hoped will continue healthy and good. We propose also to print at once an edition in two volumes small 8'b0ree; to sell for 12/. Let me know if you wish to make any alterations or corrections.
We did not write to the Times about the Liggins delusion, as we thought our doing so might be misinterpreted as a publishing dodge to reraise the discussion and stimulate curiosity. Also we did not think it wise, as some of the myrmidons of the press do not seem disposed to admit an author's right to privacy, and a sharp protest from us without any immediate call for it might further tempt the fellows to make your case the battle field of the question. That there is such a tendency you may see from the last number of the Leader and the Critic. 116 I think I see Lewes' astonishment and indignation when he read the Leader.
I wrote in the most distinct terms to "the auld sap at Hazlewood" 117 (Atherstone Hall) telling him that you were not Liggins and required assistance from no man. Of course he only shakes his foolish old head and says he knows better. 118
The inclosed came from Sir E. Lytton 119 today and will, I hope, please you. I think more of it than of any of the tributes you have met with, as no one can deny his experience and he is not given to extravagant laudation. He really is a great man, Sir Edward. He thinks and works so much and has such a head to think and work with.
Dallas writes to me 120 that a lot of little Tracts -- "The Fear of the Lord," "Repentance unto Life" etc. -- have come to him from Warwickshire as the Reviewer of Adam Bede. It is rather curious, as he is the writer of a paper in the present number on Tracts. 121
I am in daily expectation of the Tale.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.
This note should have gone to you yesterday but I was interrupted by the conclusive War News 122 and could do nothing but look at maps and discuss and think of the contingencies for the rest of the day. Let me have back Bulwer's note; it is the first I have had from him since his illness.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 26 June 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 26 June 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Randolph Crescent
June 26/79.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I send you a little volume on the ethics and religious aspects of your Works by our late friend John Brown 281 who was as you will recollect with us at 45 George St for something like 45 years. He had written the bulk of it long ago and never told me but I found him completing and correcting it during his last illness. I was so much struck with it and with his perfect devotion to you, which also the queer contrairy chap had if anything rather concealed from me, tempering as it were my admiration, that I got the M.S. from him intending to have it out at once but meanwhile, poor fellow, he died. Then I thought that in the circumstances possibly I had taken too high a view of what John had written and put it aside until his widow recalled it.
I am very much distressed to hear that you have been in so great pain and anxiously hope that you have got over the attack. You will I know bear pain heroically but it hits high sensitive natures hardest. I am getting fairly well again and we mean to be off to Strathtyrum on Saturday. Jack is to meet us with artillerymen at Cupar 8 miles from Strathtyrum. He thought of telling off a guard at St. Andrews Station and escorting us up the Avenue but it would be irregular and discipline is the soul of the British Army.
Our officers are terribly cut up about the poor Prince Imperial's death. 282 British officers are always doing something bold to recklessness and that one of them should desert a dismounted comrade never entered the mind of man. That comrade too a Prince and the guest of the whole British Army there is something incredible in the way the story is told.
Hoping heartily that this may find you better I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
You were quite right we only printed 1000 of 3d edition.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 26 January 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
January 26/72.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
The subscription of Book Two is going on today and as far as I can gather yet it looks well. You shall have details tomorrow. Mr. Langford mentions that Simpkins had 50 Book One yesterday, which is a fine healthy symptom. 454
Two copies of Book Two in its complete form came to Randolph Cres[cen]t last night and there was much enjoyment over them. There is a wealth of thought and expression that is simply marvellous.
Your corrected sheets of Book Three arrived today. I was seated amid a sea of unanswered letters and unread M.S.S., but on the false pretext to myself that I should look to see what alterations you had made, I passed most of the morning revelling in it again. It is beyond praise. I could rival Main in superlatives if I had time but my morning's occupation has thrown me behind hand and I am going to Golf tomorrow.
I hope Lewes is better.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 26 February 1873
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh February 26/73.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am glad you like the appearance of the Guinea Edition which I am in great hopes will do. We have sold about 250 copies. Although the printers did keep us back a bit we could not have ventured to publish the cheaper Edition much sooner.
There is some rule about not having advertisements of books that have been published for more than a few weeks in that particular column of the Times and that may be the explanation of what you allude to, but Mr. Simpson is writing to Mr. Langford who attends to the distribution of the London Advertisements. I am writing to Delane about the review. I am delighted to hear of the substantial compliment to the Spanish Gypsy in Germany.
It gives me great pleasure to send books to you and do not fail to let me know if there are any others besides Lockhart's in that Catalogue that you would like. About Lockhart's Life of Scott I thoroughly agree with you; unlike the other biographer to whom you allude he almost effaces himself too much if that defect were possible in a biographer.
When in London I asked Lewes whether you would have any objection to the republication of The Lifted Veil in a proposed new Series of Tales from Blackwood. He thought you wished to keep it for a volume of miscellanies and I would not wish to interfere with that. Still I should like much to have this striking although horribly painful story to help the start of our new Series and I should consider it as an obligation to be paid for.
In looking over old Magazine stories I have a sort of failing of memory that almost confuses judgment and I asked Lockhart 735 to look over a lot that had been picked out. He asked who the world wrote The Lifted Veil and The Last French Hero and was greatly delighted when he found he had picked on one by you and another by Hamley.
I read the Veil over again and my impression is that now the feeling of admiration for the power of the Story is greater than at first when my pain for the poor wretch prevented me from fully appreciating the wonderful skill. 736
Always yours Truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
