Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 26 April 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 26 April 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland, which has also a copy in George Simpson's hand. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 26/66.
My Dear Madam
I most heartily respond to the feelings expressed in your gratifying note and do rejoice in resuming old relations with you. It quite takes me back to the days when Adam Bede won the Derby.
The more I think over these two volumes of Felix Holt the more I am impressed. Every individual or group of individuals says something to the purpose. I paused over every page as I read lest I should lose some of the exquisite flavour.
As I turned page after page passage after passage struck me as one that I would quote with admiration when I wrote to you about the book, but it would take a longer letter than I ever wrote to give even a sprinkling of these gems.
Mrs. Transome and her maid 432 are a perfect picture, and the description of the managing old lady's feelings when her son is so cool and taking the reins out of her hands and all her hopes are blasted 433 is so painfully true. What a group are the old minister, Esther, and Felix in that dingy little house with Mrs. Holt like a comic chorus in the background! 434
I am charmed with Esther and desperately anxious about her future.
I enjoyed her turning the tables on her mentor by laughing at his French accent. 435 How often one sees that sort of thing. It is like the House of Commons the other day laughing at Bright for talking of the Pittchley. 436 How the obstinate young radical did not fall at Esther's feet when she "tut her finger" 437 passes my comprehension. That is a touch beyond all praise. Jermyn's mistake of trying to soothe another by praising himself is good. 438 Who has not occasionally when consulting a friend under a difficulty been cheered by a lucid explanation of how much more cleverly he (the friend) would have arranged matters?
Your side scenes are inimitable. One assists at them and is present in the servants' hall, the public, and in that saddler, the smell of whose leather is associated with the idea of a pleasant gossip. 439 The smell of the leather and the feathers in the old golf ball maker's shop is associated in my mind to this day with elevating talks about "the great game" although for 20 years the golf balls have been made of gutta percha. That retired London tradesman 440 is a jewel, and it is marvellous how you invent all those life-like conversations of the town worthies of every degree.
Mr. Chubb with his id'e9e and croyant faire son 'e9loge in explaining his sordid views to Felix is fine. 441 When you mentioned the death of a possible beneficiary affecting an entail I thought you must have been consulting a lawyer, and I am glad to hear that it is so.
I say nothing about the plot as I think it is wrong to hazard speculations to an author (unless in conversation perhaps when false impressions can be corrected on the spot), but I need not tell you how anxiously I look for the upshot of the Drama in the third volume. I am uneasy as to what Mrs. Transome has done. Poor Felix is in a terrible fix at the end of the 2d volume and you pile up the evidence against him to such an extent that it is difficult to see how his innocence is to be satisfactorily proved. However you wield the wand of an enchanter. I inclose a slip which according to Lewes' suggestion I insert in the forthcoming number of the Magazine. I found the ever thoughtful Mr. Simpson had provided paper for the purpose. I burst out laughing when he told me he had done so. My nephew and he have been reading bits and are in a high state of delight. The former I think has nearly finished. I hope you will approve of my quoting the motto in the advertisement. 442 I think it gives the key note beautifully.
I am sorry to hear from Lewes that he is poorly. The east winds in Edin[burg]h at this season are not conducive to health and I have been very much out of sorts myself for the last six weeks, but Doctor George Eliot has done me a world of good. If I do not write you a long letter of criticism my silence is not "barren." I am "brooding over the full nest" of good things in Felix Holt.
Again congratulating you and hoping that the resumption of our old relations may be a source of pleasure and profit to all concerned, I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
I had nearly forgot to say how good your politics are. As far as I see yet, I suspect I am a radical of the Felix Holt breed, and so was my father before me. 443

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 25 February 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 25 February 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Randolph Crescent
February 25/72.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
It gave me much pleasure to receive your interesting letter yesterday and I am happy to say the sales of Middlemarch continue. Simpkins had a 100 Book Two upon Friday which looks like the demand from out and out purchasers.
Do not disturb yourself about Book III being thin -- there is the matter of volumes in it. That capture of Lydgate 466 is worth a volume. Besides the acute Simpson is using paper for the part which will make it bulk about the same as the others. This will amuse Lewes who I hope is better.
I fear it is going hard with poor William Smith, and it would be very kind if Lewes could go down to see him. I had not heard that it was heart, but felt from his wife's letters and his that he must be very ill. My wife's sisters, Miss Blandfords, are at Brighton and they report him very cheerful and pleasant as usual but looking very weak indeed.
Send down Book IV at once and we shall get it into type immediately. I am most eager to see it.
I quite agree with you about Mr. Main. He is not like an ordinary "gusher" at all. 467 He does pour forth certainly, but he gives a reason for the faith that is in him.
I am now quite well. Better indeed I think than I was before the illness. I shall not however I believe feel all right until I have been to Golf, which the weather at present is against.
Hoping to hear from you with M.S. almost immediately, Believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 25 December 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 25 December 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | December 25/58.
My Dear Sir
What you say by way of Preface is excellent in itself and I cordially sympathise with your feelings, but I decidedly advise against the publication of such a preface. It might raise a nest of hornets about you. Consider that probably one half of the small deer who will sit down to review you are constantly guilty of the very crime you reprobate and would consequently come to the book with highly irritated feelings after seeing themselves so justly shown up.
Lewes is almost as knowing and experienced about such things as I am, so that I attach great weight to his suggestion, but I am sure I am right. I have read the first volume in print and am delighted to tell you that I am more confident than ever. Your characters are wonderfully individual and lifelike.
I am not sure but what Mrs. Poyser is the most perfect picture. She makes me chuckle uncommonly. While laughing over her quaint reflections on Hetty's want of feeling, I was positively affected at the illustration she gave of Hetty's supposed strong indifference to the child she had handled from its cradle. 1245 In the third volume her passage at arms with Bartle 1246 is a wonderful performance.
The second volume I have not yet begun as I wish to let the proofs accumulate so as to read it more in a mass. I had more doubt about the latter half of second volume than any other part of the book. I often think of the Italian Story of which you told me you had the idea in your head. 1247 I look to it for the Magazine. Do you ever think of reviewing or writing miscellaneous papers. Your preface would come in capitally in a review.
Give my regards to Lewes when you see him and with every good wish of the season, Believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq. 1248

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 25 April 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 25 April 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Str. Edinburgh | April 25th 1879.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
It gives me great pleasure to receive your letter and I am quite gratified that my letter to Mr. Harper should meet so thoroughly with your approbation. I too would have proposed that he had given a round sum but I do not think that we could do otherwise than accept his offer which will I hope turn out well.
I am glad that you mentioned the discrepancy which naturally struck you between the 2/- for the 5/ parts of Middlemarch and Deronda and the 3/ for the 10/6 volume. The difference arises in this way that the preliminary expenses advertising etc. are in proportion larger in starting the one volume than the four volume book, also as you will see Theophrastus is much larger and handsomer than a volume of Deronda but mainly the difference proceeds from our calculations being necessarily based upon a much smaller sale.
Yesterday was what is called the Fast or preaching Thursday here and bitterly cold and gloomy it was. To-day we are almost rejoicing in not exactly a pleasant rain but certainly a softer air.
I rejoice to think of your getting away to the country and I look forward with much interest to seeing you in May.
Jack has gone to St. Andrews for the preaching week and I daresay is perfectly indifferent to the weather.
Always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 24 November 1878
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Randolph Cres[cen]t | November 24/78.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am so vexed to hear that Lewes is so unwell again. The intelligence in his last note was so healthy that I almost forgot to express the sympathy I felt with his ailments. I hope this will find him pretty right again.
The Printers calculate that Theophrastus will make some 266 printed pages like the inclosed and this with the breaks for chapters will make quite a thick enough volume. We can easily put less in the page if you desire it.
You will see that Parliament meets so soon that we cannot be out before but the moment we get the word from you it will be in type "right speedilie". Do you remember our old printing office manager when I told him to get up Silas Marner quickly replied "I'll blaw it up like a bottle."
I am reading with greatest pleasure. Your idea of advert[isement] is much my own.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 24 March 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 24 March 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinburgh | March 24/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I inclose proof of Theophrastus Title page and I quite agree about the single title "Impressions" and saying simply by George Eliot. The motto is rather too long for a title page and perhaps it had better be printed on the opposite leaf but we can try it on the title page.
When you made the arrangement with Harpers for Daniel Deronda did you send them any idea of the nature of the book, and did you correspond with any individual in the house or simply address the Messrs. Harper? I think I should explain to them that this is not a novel, and perhaps send them the contents, which are very attractive.
Our Australian friends will be disposed to do what they can for Theophrastus, although as you say the book does not seem greatly adapted for the bush, but there must be many a solitary fellow there who will be glad to ponder over the words you so gracefully lay before your reader. I can quite imagine translators mauling your language, and when in Theophrastus they are not guided by any story they are more likely to miss your fine points than in a novel.
I was struck by seeing the death of Strodtmann whom you mention in to-day's paper. I have an intimate friend at Berlin, Paul Lindau 204 who is a high official there, Legationsrath whatever that may be. I know him very well and as you do not in any way wish to be mixed up in the matter I think of handing it over to him and telling him to make the best he can of it, but give me some idea of what you have previously received. Lindau's brother is at the head of the German Press and between them their interest seems very powerful. In writing to America I should tell them when we intend to publish and I hope you are reconciling yourself to the appearance of the book in the end of May or beginning of June.
I trust that you have thrown off your headaches and [are] not suffering from such bitterly cold weather as still blows a half snow upon us here.
Always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 24 February 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 24 February 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinburgh | February 24/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
Mr. Charles tells me [you] are amissing in your copy of Theophrastus Such so I inclose sheets 8 to end. I am sorry to see in his note that you are obliged to have your medical 'abmen'bb friends about you, but I anxiously hope that it is more as friends than professionally that these good advisers come to see you. Do not allow the proofs to disturb you but I think they may prove a useful distraction. Let me know exactly in what terms you would like the book announced.
The weather is I understand nearly as bad in London as here so even if well enough you will not be able to get out much. To day it is snowing with us and melting nearly as fast as it falls so that the streets are almost impassible with slush. In spite of the weather I am pretty well and have got quit of a horrid swelled face. My Nephew, although the bone of his leg has knit well and straight, is still suffering a good deal of pain from the muscles and thinks of trying a change in London next week. I hope he will, as the change is likely to be the best thing for him after his long confinement.
Fortunately we have no friends in South Africa where it is very anxious work. But will I think be all right. It will remind you of poor Thornton and Natal. What a state Lewes would have been in.
The weather has kept me off the golfing green but I hope soon to have my club in hand again. The Ladies have only been able to ride twice during the last three months and my son who expected to have a little hunting is very solemn upon the weather. He comes to 45 George Street this winter.
Laurence Oliphant whom you always take an interest in has gone out on an expedition to Palestine. There is a cry H.E.P. to Jerusalem and I imagine that Oliphant is in some manner there forerunner of work in these parts. Hamley has gone to see Rome for the first time. Lockhart has I imagine started for the continent to avoid our spring. He is very well I am happy to say.
We have a paper on Novels in the forthcoming number of the Magazine. And I hope you will like the remarks upon your works. 182 Hoping to hear from you soon with better accounts of yourself and spirits I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 24 February 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 24 February 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Brief extract published: John Blackwood, p. 393.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
February 24/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
The revise of Book V was sent to you last night and the Printers will soon have proof of Book VI ready. Book fifth is very wonderful. There is a feeling of thunder in the air that inspires awe, and I do not think the boldest critic that ever dashed off daily and weekly reviews would go in at it lightly. Grandcourt is hateful and one reflects with grim satisfaction that the Furies have entered his house.
Poor Gwendolen, her penance has begun. One sees now why you brought out so strongly that element of nervous terror in her character.
The gravity of the Book is admirably relieved by the touches you throw in. Sir Hugo's little attempts at mild humour and the perfect description of the old abbey 401 tell famously. Then the little house at Chelsea is so true to itself when the mighty Klesmer appears to decide the destiny of Mirah. 402 Of Mordecai I feel that it would be presumptuous to speak until one has read more, and I daresay that puzzling and thinking over that phase of the Tale has been the cause of my not having written to you sooner.
I suspect we would need to get back a Titian to put him and Deronda on canvas as you have done them upon paper. 403 There is something excessively quaint in the conjunction of two such extremes of Jewish nature as that little Jacob and Mordecai. 404 I am determined to enjoy Book VI quietly at home, so did not look into the M.S. beyond a page or two before sending it into the printing office.
Mr. Langford writes that he is keeping Lewes informed of the subscription for Book Two and I think it is very satisfactory. Here the numbers are about equal to what the trade had taken at first of Book One and bought since, which is satisfactory. Willie would I daresay tell you that I had a pleasant letter from Mr. Alden, 405 the Editor of Harper's Magazine. You may probably have heard from him since he had read Book One. He seems to wish the Books earlier than the date Lewes named, which was to be in their hands a month sooner than the date of publication of their Magazine. There is no objection if they can keep them safe, but a month does seem plenty of time.
With many congratulations and good wishes, I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 23 February 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 23 February 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 23/59.
My Dear Sir
I return Professor Owen's letter 38 and inclose an effusion from Dr. John Brown, also one apparently from the Sage of Ecclefechan, which I should like to see.
Professor Owen is very distinct and expresses himself like a man accustomed to weigh what he says. There is however one ambiguous expression. By "peculiar among" does he mean peculiar to or singular among. I think I told you in the early days of Clerical Scenes that my suspicions pointed to the distinguished Professor as the author. There is, too, a resemblance in the hands, which by the way was very striking on the envelope addressed to you, more so than in the note itself.
I sent Dr. J.B. [an] extract from your letter which I knew would glad his heart. Your note was more in his than in your own usual style and I amused myself thinking that you must [have] unconsciously or for fun adopted it for him.
The real demand for Adam will I think begin within the next week or ten days. I hear nothing but laudatory expressions of opinion. One may interest you. Our celebrated preacher Mr. Caird 39 was to call by appointment to make Mrs. Blackwood's acquaintance. He did not appear, but arrived an hour or more after his time and said his best apology was to confess the truth that he had been so fascinated with Adam Bede as to forget time altogether. He spoke most warmly of the book, thought you too hard upon Hetty.
There have not been so many reviews yet as I should have expected but it is not a book to pronounce in a hurry upon. I send a portfolio containing such as we have collected, which please return. The best I have seen is that in the Edinburgh Courant.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 22 March 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 22 March 1860
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 22/60.
My Dear Madam
I inclose proof of the conclusion of the Mill. No words of mine can convey any feeling of the greatness of the success you have achieved. I wish I had time to write you a long letter but I daresay I would only maunder, repeating superlatives upon superlatives of admiration. This book is a greater triumph even than Adam and you may make your mind easy about all Critics. Any mean creature that may venture to carp will only dispute himself.
The greatest lovers of all ending happily must admit that Providence was kind in removing Maggie. She could not have been happy here and she will not be forgotten by others besides Lucy, Phillip and Stephen. I was pretty well prepared for the end but would not have been so knowing had I not been aware that a flood was coming.
I have been occupied nearly all day in the [word illegible] work of trying to reduce a long proof of that famous fellow Speke to something like grammar, and you may conceive the contrast it was to turn from your M.S. to his rugged sentences.
Of course Lewes or you will send a list of presentation copies and all instructions you wish attended to. Also the address to write to you which I suppose will be Poste Restante, Rome.
A very early duty and pleasure with me will be to read the whole book on consecutively. It is perfectly astonishing with how few words you have managed these last chapters and yet how complete they are. Not a word could be spared nor a word added without disadvantage, especially in that inestimable meeting between Lucy and Maggie.
With all my heart congratulating you and wishing you well believe me
ever yours truly,
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 22 April 1879[2]
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Str. Edinburgh | April 22nd 1879.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I enclose Telegram received to-day from Mr. Harper which is I think very satisfactory and I send him by this mail the sheets of Theophrastus. I send you a copy of what I wrote to him, of which I hope you will approve. If I had attempted to give him more of an idea of the Book I must have slipped into criticism to which I did not feel equal and I was determined not to mislead him.
In one of your letters you mentioned that there were some thoughts you wished particularly to bring out and I should like much to have some of these guiding hints from you when you have leisure to write. We have written to our Australian friend who has agent in this country but have not yet heard in reply.
The weather continues very trying but I have resolved to go to Strathtyrum for a week at the end of the month and I have felt better and stronger ever since I came to that resolution so I do not think there can be much the matter with me. After we have been at Strathtyrum we propose to go to London for a short time.
I hope you are continuing to be able to get out into the country and are picking up some strength. Many people inquire how you are and all in a nice spirit of anxious sympathy.
The telegraphic news from Africa has been coming in all day. In the main the intelligence is satisfactory but there is heavy loss to ourselves and no satisfaction in killing these savages.
always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
Copy of Harper's Telegram.
Send Theophrastus Such immediately will pay Author ten per cent Royalty advancing fifty pounds.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 22 April 1879[1]
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Str. Edinburgh | April 22nd 1879.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
In Mr. Lewes' note sending the M.S. of Theophrastus he mentioned 10/6 as price of volume so we considered that settled, and it looks the natural price for such a volume in this country.
Since I wrote to you I have changed the first impression from two thousand to three thousand as I think the first demand should go beyond 2000 and I hope it may exceed the larger number. While the selling price is 10/6 we propose to pay you by a lordship of 3/- on every copy sold reckoned 25 as 24. I hope this offer which is in proportion with our recent arrangements for your works will meet your ideas but if not we shall be happy to meet your wishes by any other arrangement you may fancy.
My nephew joins me in best wishes and I write separately as to other matters connected with the work.
always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 22 April 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 387.
Randolph Crescent
April 22/75.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Willie tells me he has had a long and most interesting visit at the Priory, the only drawback to which was that you were complaining of not feeling well and being depressed. I have seen that depression on you before at periods when other authors would have been crowing and flapping their wings without the solid reason which I am sure you have for doing so. I am quite elated at the prospect of Willie bringing down so large a portion of your new Novel and I feel your sending the M.S. to me in this way as a thing to be proud of. Curiously enough I was walking about with Theodore Martin yesterday when talking about you and Lewes; he mentioned how devoted the Queen was to your works, especially Adam Bede. 236 So I told him how you had given me the M.S. of first volume of Adam with strict injunctions not to read it until I could do so quietly at home and how I utterly disobeyed orders by peeping into the first pages on the top of the omnibus where Lewes deposited me at Kew and fastening upon it the moment I left King's Cross next morning until I finished my reading with delight before I reached Newcastle when night was setting in.
This is what is called Preaching Thursday here, and Edinburgh is not a lively place to me when 45 George St. is shut up, and although my wife and daughter have been affable and kind they evidently feel me a sort of intruder.
I shall go now and have a walk into the country which is beginning at last to look bright and spring like. I hardly expect to be up in London until after the middle of May. One reason of my detention strikes me as peculiarly ludicrous. Our old butler who has been with us for 15 years is leaving us, and it is thought that I should be here when his successor comes. Now I am utterly useless about household affairs and would be most justly sat upon if I attempted to lift up my voice on the subject. With best regards to Lewes
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 22 April 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 22/68.
My Dear Madam
It gave me much pleasure to hear from you today and also to receive Book IV of The Poem, which will speedily be returned to you in type. Along with this I send by Book post the three first books put into pages.
I have been reading them a good deal and the dirty state of the outer pages is owing to frequent transits between this and my dressing room, as I always brought them back here thinking I might hear from you any day of your return.
It is a grand poem and one cannot dip into any page without being arrested by the beauty and power of thoughts and lines. I like books 2 and 3 greatly better than I did on the perusal in M.S. I feel too more reconciled to Don Silva's fearful bolt off the course, as I do see you had from the first drawn his character so mixed
"that each today May seem a maniac to its morrow." 743
"A lion's whelp" but "unstable as water." 744
There is difficulty in getting over his character so as to keep up the interest of the story.
Fidalma's
"What the Zincala may not quit for you I cannot joy that you should quit for her" 745 puts the thing beautifully.
I am sorry to hear that you have brought back headaches with you but I hope soon to hear from you that they are gone and to see part of their absence in the shape of M.S.
With best regards to Lewes I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
I have of course been looking into Book 4 today and I see Silva and Fedalma are left in a terrible climax. Zarca's death and dismissal of Silva to misery are fine.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 22 April 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Randolph Crescent | April 22/66.
My Dear Madam
The Telegraph will I hope have told you of the safe arrival of your M.S. I know you will be anxious and I cannot deny myself the pleasure of writing you a hasty line to say that I think I may congratulate you with all my heart although I have only been able to read about 80 pages. It is impossible to read it hurriedly but I shall "make a night of it."
The opening picture is perfectly beautiful and so distinct. The description of Transome Court 430 has the vivid power of an old ballad. One has a feeling of oppression as one walks up to the Hall door. The characters stand out like living individual beings and one dwells upon the descriptions to feel all their beauty. The first thing that made me burst out laughing was the parson's reflections after his nephew left him. 431
I am "breaking the Sabbath" but I think even a puritan would forgive me. I agree with the worthy old Scotch Clergyman, a devoted Curler, who after finishing the service said from the pulpit, "My bretheren, there is no more harm in saying than in thinking it; if the frost holds I'll be on the ice at 10 tomorrow."
I have a lot of Magazine work which I cannot possibly postpone tomorrow so I may probably not write until Tuesday.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 21 October 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 21 October 1862
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | October 21/62.
My Dear Madam
By the memorandum you got you would see that we printed 3000 of the 6/- edition of Adam Bede and of these there are still about 900 on hand. They are pretty sure to go however, and I have now the pleasure of inclosing you a cheque £180 in acknowledgment of this edition being at the rate of £60 per thousand as agreed upon.
Of The Mill on the Floss seeing the state of sales we only printed 1500 in the 6/- form and we propose to publish this next month as I do not think it would be worth while to delay any longer.
I wish I had a more cheering account of sales to give you but everything is very dull this year and we have less reason to complain than most people.
I am still living in the country but the weather is so broken that I think we shall come to Edinburgh for the winter next week.
It is a long time since I have heard from you but I hope you have been getting on well and are strong and not allowing your work to bother you. Lewes also is I hope in good case and doubtless busy as usual.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 21 November 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 21 November 1877
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 21/77.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I inclose proof of The "College Breakfast Party" which I should have written with before, but the subject of this striking dialogue is not one on which I feel well qualified to write or speak although I daresay I have thought as much as most people about it.
Were I to attempt to criticise the conversation of Hamlet and his friends 768 I fear I should be as much puzzled as any of the interlocutors, but one does not require to be a philosopher or theologian to appreciate the poetical beauty of the thoughts and language. There are lines without end for quotation and the whole picture is characteristic of the Youth of the present day who are given to beating out their brains upon what it is not granted to them to understand.
What a comment upon most sermons is your concluding line. They do indeed "leave the soul in wider emptiness." Confident divines do not allow their lips to be sealed as Hamlet does. What form of publication do you think of?
Simpson is writing to you about the omission of the Motto 769 in the 7/6 edition of Deronda for which he has visited the printing office justly and severely. The edition I am happy to say is going off well and we have only some 400 left of the 5250 printed.
The Cabinet edition of the novels is going to be a beautiful book and we shall be happy to meet Lewes' suggestion of increasing the lordship after the sale of 2000 copies by making it after that number are sold 1/3 on each of the 17 volumes and 1/7 and 1/10 on each of the other two volumes.
Smith and Elder's cheap edition will be a formidable competitor to our 3/6 edition of Romola, but we shall print it in that form like the others.
How have you been since you came back to Town? The weather has been very trying but I hope you have not suffered from it and have been able to take advantage of the occasional fine days for walking.
We left Strathtyrum about a fortnight ago, and as usual there was weeping and wail at leaving the country. "It's awfu' dull when ye're away" was the pathetic farewell of the gardner's wife to my wife and daughter, and her words found an echo in their hearts. However we are pretty cheery in Town and I hear of various ongoings contemplated. The weather makes one think more of the unfortunate wretches on both sides in Bulgaria and Asia Minor. It is too horrible.
With best regards to Lewes and hoping to get good accounts of you I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
P.S. I had nearly forgot to send the inclosed from friend Main. What do you think? We are willing to undertake the book if you approve. 770

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 21 March 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | March 21/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
Revise of the whole of Theophrastus is sent to you to-day and I hope you will find it all correct. Mr. Allardyce has a few queries marked on proof. I incline to put in a petition in favour of George the III about whom there was a great deal of good and he fought well with his troubled brain. The book requires such very close and attentive reading that I almost wish you had put in a heading for each page.
I am very much touched by your note to my Nephew and I am sure he will appreciate your kindly feeling to him.
In regard to date of publication I think it would be a pity to delay beyond May or June. The explanatory [note] as to when the M.S. was received will be conclusive as to when the book was written and the longer delay would be more than likely to cause the surmise you dread of your recent work. But indeed you need not fear any such [thing?] in any unkindly sense as no one will be brute enough to be otherwise than glad to see any publication from you which may possibly divert your thoughts.
Always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 21 December 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | December 21/66.
My Dear Madam
After many consultations and much dubiety the opinion we have formed here is that the best plan will be to try the cheap illustrated edition of your Novels in sixpenny numbers of which Adam, The Mill, Scenes, Silas, and Felix would make 30, ultimately to form four volumes selling at 3/6 each.
That Lewes and you may understand the matter as well as I do, I inclose our calculations of cost sales and results and some sheets stitched together to show the size of the proposed sixpenny part. We would use the stereotype plates of the present 6/- edition of Adam, The Mill, Clerical Scenes, and Silas.
Whether we are right in our estimate of probable sales is a thing that no one can tell. Thirty thousand is a large number to put down for Adam Bede, and it is a very great chance whether we do sell so many, but I think we should. The sale of Felix is put low in the estimate as you have no interest in that for so many years. The gain attending the result of the adventure if successful is much less than I hoped for, but the Printing, paper etc. are put at cost price, the Printing I think at less than we should have to pay if we were not Printers. The discount to the Trade is very heavy, and the "less ten per cent" marked in the estimate is not a commission to the publisher but is a discount that we know we should have to give to all who deal in Number publications in any quantity. With reference to your suggestion that we should buy up your interest in the works for ten years, the puzzle to me is what to offer you in fairness to both parties. 551
I am willing to give you One Thousand Pounds (£1000) for your interest in these works for the time above mentioned, or if you prefer it two thirds of the profit upon Adam Bede, The Mill, Silas Marner, and The Scenes, we to be allowed to work the publication in what form and at what price we choose. Further if you accept the first proposition we would pay you Five Hundred Pounds (£500) more should the edition now proposed prove a success, i.e. sell at any time during the next five years within an average in Numbers and volumes of two thousand sets of the Numbers and at the prices set down in the accompanying estimate. Should you prefer the two thirds of profits we would charge a commission of 5 per cent on the sales.
I thought that I could offer you a larger sum and I much wished to do so, but looking the matter fairly in the face as a speculation, I do not see how I can make much change in what I have said above, although I shall be glad to meet your wishes in any way I can. The 6/- editions of the works have been a disappointment. They produce so little that they are hardly worth considering.
Mr. Simpson has had various consultations with what are called the "Number Men," i.e. men who sell the weekly and monthly publicacations in large numbers, and they are strong for the sixpenny Numbers of our series. He (Mr. Simpson) and I had both heard much but vaguely of large sums given for copyrights to sell in cheap editions, so he inquired what was the most successful series and his informant, the chief Number Man here, replied Chapman and Hall's 2/- series worked much by Smith and Sons. He accordingly brought home a volume of the series and the inclosed calculation 552 gives the result of the adventure. I do not see how the system can pay.
I return "Brother Jacob" 553 and send with him "The Lifted Veil." They are both as clever as can be, but there is a painful want of light about them and my advice is against including them in the recognised series of your works. I remember the Lifted Veil was published when Adam Bede was in the full blaze of fame, and I thought it better not to accept Lewes' kind offer to put your name to it in the Magazine, which I believe no other editor of a periodical would have done. My opinion has not changed yet.
By the time the sixpenny series was finished the copyright of Romola would have reverted to you and the state of the sales of the series would show pretty plainly what it would be worth to you or to us. We would most probably bring out each book complete in the volume before the issue in Numbers was completed.
My nephew joins me in hoping that Lewes is better and with every good wish of the season Believe me,
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 October 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 October 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 379.
Edinburgh | October 20/68.
My Dear Madam
I am happy to tell you that the second edition of the Gypsy is so nearly out of print that we ought to proceed with a reprint at once.
We have been considering what shape we ought to throw it into and think that a page like the inclosed, which will make a handsome volume of about 416 pages to sell at 7/6, is about the thing to do now. Of this we would propose to print a thousand 821 and then stereotype, paying you a lordship of 1/6 on every copy sold.
The sale is very gratifying, especially considering the number of hostile criticisms, and I am in great hopes that the Poem is working its way into the knowledge of the general public. Whether it is not too refined ever to reach the point where a cheap edition with a view to a vast sale one cannot tell, but at present we certainly do not think it would be wise to try that plan.
We propose to settle with you for the first and second editions at the turn of the year, but if you have expected the payment sooner it will be quite the same to us.
You will now I suppose be fairly settled in London for the winter, and I hope you are both well and strong. Are thoughts of writing in your mind? We still linger in the country but will break up from Strathtyrum at the end of the month. It always makes me melancholy to leave the country, but I intend to have ten days of it yet.
Tell Lewes that I have a review of his book 822 in forthcoming number which I hope he will like. I daresay I do not require to tell him who is the writer. Look at the beginning of a story called Doubles and
Quits 823 in the next No. It is not in your line, but I should like to hear what Lewes and you think of it.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes
The inclosed specimen page will best give you an accurate idea of what the size of the book will look. It will be a volume like the small edition of Aytoun's Lays. 824 I think I must have given you a copy of that; if I have not tell Langford to send you one.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 May 1862
MS: National Library of Scotland. Published: John Blackwood, p. 80.
Edinburgh | May 20/62.
My Dear Madam
I am of course sorry that your new Novel is not to come out under the old colours but I am glad to hear that you have made so satisfactory an arrangement.
Hearing of the wild sums that were being offered to writers of much inferior mark to you, I thought it highly probable that offers would be made to you, and I can readily imagine that you are to receive such a price as I could not make remunerative by any machinery that I could resort to.
Rest assured that I feel fully satisfied of the extreme reluctance with which you would decide upon leaving your old friend for any other publisher, however great the pecuniary consideration might be, and it would destroy my pleasure in business if I knew any friend was publishing with me when he thought he could do better for himself by going elsewhere. We have had several most successful enterprises together and much pleasant correspondence and I hope we shall have much more. 68
In a few days we go to Derbyshire where we leave the children with their aunts and intend to move on London about the end of next week. I hope therefore to see you soon and trust I shall find you in good health and spirits with your work progressing.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 March 1867
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 20/67.
My Dear Madam
Along with this I send formal note and order for £2166.13.4d and I now write to say how glad I am to hear that you have got safe back after an expedition so successful and pleasant in every way. I only hope that the abominable weather will not throw Lewes back again. A howling northeast wind and sleet in St. John's Wood must be a painful contrast to the sunshine at Grenada, but a comfortable English house and fireside is not to be sneezed at.
I intended to have sent along with this a copy of the first part of the cheap edition of the novels, but Mr. Simpson has not yet got an impression of the cover and illustration thrown off to please his critical eye. The cover I think you will like, as it seems to me neat. The first illustration seems to me the worst of the lot, but some of them are really very good. I found it was no use fighting with the illustrators and that they must be allowed to have their own way in choice of subjects, and they assert that figures are the only things to tell. Some of the illustrations will, I doubt not, give you "a turn" but on the whole they are much better than I expected, and Mr. Cooper 602 has certainly spared no pains or trouble.
The 12/- Felix has, I am sorry to say, done very little. Our next adventure, I think, we must try some innovation in form of publication. This library system I feel to be a false one. 603 It fosters the production of mediocre novels, but of a really good book each copy is made to do duty some hundred times over. I have told Mr. Simpson to make the arrangement with Tauchnitz for the republication of Felix.
I am curious to hear about your work connected with Spain. Is it a Romance?
You once talked to me of a short work on home life something on the scale of Silas. Has that ever taken any shape in your thoughts? I observed the letter in the Pall Mall correcting the Edinburgh Review as to the law in Felix Holt.
I am amused with your view of Mr. Reeve. He is a very singular instance of the success of self satisfied mediocrity. I remember Oliphant and I one night speculating at the Cosmopolitan, when Reeve was sitting opposite to us, smiling complacently as usual, as to what could be the secret of his permanent success and position in life. We could hit upon no theory, unless it was his imposing Paunch.
Politics at present are worrying me, but as all are agreed that Reform must be, I think Household Suffrage is the best business, the most likely to be permanent.
I hope your cold is better in spite of the weather, and with best regards to Lewes, in which as also to yourself my nephew joins, Believe me, Dear Madam
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 March 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 March 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 20/60.
My Dear Madam
Your second last chapter 511 arrived safely today and will go out in proof to you along with this. I must write you a line of congratulation without waiting for the last chapter, which I hope to see on Thursday morning. The Mill on the Floss is safe for immortality.
Of course in spite of Lewes' strict injunctions I fastened upon these two last chapters the moment I secured them. Nothing short of a point of honour would have restrained me.
Bob Jakin's attempt to convey his sympathy to Maggie 512 is beyond price. Never surely were pathos and exquisite humour more beautifully combined. Bob is the prince of packmen and a gentleman. In his reply to Dr. Kenn 513 he will have the ardent sympathy of every one who has groaned under the inforced idleness of a dull sermon, and who has not?
I do not envy the man who can read the scene where Lucy appears and falls on Maggie's neck 514 without being affected to tears. It is overpowering and touching and beautiful and is moreover exactly what was wanted to relieve the reader's feelings as well as Maggie's. The skill too with which it is indicated that dear Lucy's is a sorrow which may not be without hope like poor Maggie's is very fine.
I early foresaw that good Dr. Kenn would play a part and he comes in most happily. The illustration that his effort to put Maggie's character in the right light was as hopeless as a struggle to change the shape of bonnets 515 made me burst out laughing. Aunt Glegg is great. Several times in reading these last chapters I have found myself start from my seat and walk to the Major's adjoining room exclaiming "By God she is a wonderful woman." The exclamation was irreverent, quite superfluous, and has a rude sound but I felt impelled to speak and the emphasis conveyed volumes of heartfelt admiration, so I hope to be excused.
I await with trembling impatience the Catastrophe.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.
Mr. Simpson, I am sorry to say, is confined to the house with cold in the eyes but I inclose copy of a Mem. he left for me which will show you our plans for the publication of the book.
I must tell you one of his. He came to me in fits of laughter over Mrs. Tulliver's notable expedition to bring old Wakem to her side. 516 He has just had a precisely similar case. With great skill he was arranging to get a deceased bookbinder's business carried on for the benefit of his widow and family when all his plans were knocked on the head by the poor woman thrusting herself in and confiding all her hopes and fears to the very man on whom he was working, viz. her late husband's foreman, and he accordingly has done her. I daresay however that our arms will be long enough to protect this Scottish Mrs. Tulliver to some extent. I have called the chapter received today the second last as Lewes seemed to indicate, but I hardly think it possible as you have so much work before you.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 February 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 20 February 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 20/60.
My Dear Madam
I inclose another letter from Geneva. The "quelque importance" will I fear only apply to "Adele Roch." Volunteer correspondents rarely see that what is of importance to them may be totally uninteresting to the person whom they take the liberty of addressing.
I went out of town on the day the last proofs were sent to you, otherwise I would have written you a line. I had nothing however to say except that I had read to the end of the volume with continued delight. Tom's life at Stelling's is perfect. 483 It is perfectly wonderful how you have been able to realise the boy's feelings. Men will read it like reminiscences of what they themselves felt -- suffered. Uncle Pullet makes me laugh uncommonly, and my boy is generally addressed as "Young Sir" now. 484
I read the M.S. of volume 2 with keen interest. The darkening of old Tulliver's days and the whole scene drearily settling over the Mill form a very pathetic picture. I shall be glad when sunshine brings Tom more back to young life. I wish noble Maggie had a more goodly lover, 485 but I doubt not you are as right as can be, and she does not seem really in love. The ground is beautifully laid for the third volume and my expectations are great.
Mudie's threatened op[p]osition will melt under the sense of his own interest. It is quite natural that he should wish to have the book at a cheaper rate and his proposition is a good sign.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 2 May 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | May 2/68.
My Dear Madam
The Poem will make one very handsome volume of some 360 pages and our idea is to make the price 12/6 at which price it will not look dear. For the edition of two thousand copies we propose to give you Three Hundred Pounds and in the event of reprinting, a lordship to you of 3/- per copy for all copies beyond the 2000 sold at the same size and price. I hope this will meet Lewes' ideas and yours. Anything that could be offered for the copyright would be too little in the event of (what I hope for) a real permanent success, and too much if the Poem missed fire.
The sale of 2000 ought to be a certainty, but there are no certainties in publishing. I am writing a line to Lewes so I say no more, but I hope we may have frequent occasion to adjust your lordship in many various editions and that it may prove as fruitful as a lordship on a coal mine.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 2 January 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 2 January 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | January 2/60.
My Dear Madam
From various causes I did not get home until Friday night.
Inclosed I have the pleasure of sending a cheque Eight Hundred Pounds, being the extra acknowledgment for Adam Bede of which my brother and I beg your acceptance. We propose also when the current edition of Adam is exhausted to place that work on the same footing as Sister Maggie, giving up our exclusive copyright for the remaining portion of the four years. We hope this may turn out a matter of some importance to you and think it likely as, if Maggie is a hit, the chances are that there will be uniform cheap editions of the old work and the new running off before the 4 years are out.
In regard to the payments for Maggie, our intention was to make them at six, nine, and twelve months from date of publication. It would fall rather heavy on us to make so large a payment so long before there could be any return to us, but if you had any object in wishing a portion of the money on publication we would meet your wishes.
My brother joins me in all good wishes for you in the opening year, and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
October 19/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Along with this I have written to Lewes with a proposal for renewed lease of your works which may I hope prove agreeable to your views. 549 At all events I am ready to meet any suggestions for alterations as I am bent upon continuing your publisher as well as friend through life.
We have a long career of successive triumphs to look back upon and I hope there is much yet before us.
It must be some 21 years since Amos Barton was published, and although during that long term of years we have had our share of sickness and sorrow, I dare venture to say we are as little decayed in thought and feeling as most people.
always yours truly

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 19 November 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 19 November 1874
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, pp. 385-386.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 19/74.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
When I got back from the Country last Thursday I found a most alarming pile of letters and packets of manuscript of all kinds awaiting me, but your pleasant dispatch with its most welcome news leavened the whole mass. 161 I do long to see that "Slice of M.S." which has passed into the "irrevocable." Lewes and I are both I believe good critics but it is very plain sailing when we have works such as yours to comment upon.
You will be glad to hear that Kinglake has returned for press nearly the last sheet of his Inkerman volume. It is a splendid series of pictures and will take us all back to the Crimea. In writing to him I told the good news of your novel with a sort of explanation of your mode of composition and I cannot resist copying for Lewes' delectation if not for yours his truly graceful and powerful comment. He says, "Another novel from Mrs. Lewes is really a national blessing! Why don't critics have illuminations for news so grateful instead of making believe to [rejoice] at some absurd [birth-day] or the accession of another Lord Mayor? What you tell me of the intellectual fermentation from which works like Middlemarch result is very interesting and makes me envy the process of disciplined thought which after the [simmering] passes all at once into [the irrevocable.]" There speaks a Master of English and I feel ashamed to go on with my own disjointed sentences.
We are shaking down into town life now and the stair carpets are down. I mildly suggested that they might have been laid down before we came but was sternly asked what effect the innumerable packing boxes and workmen's feet would have upon them. I retired. The leaving
Strathtyrum was as usual a melancholy business and we had to leave behind Tickler, the favourite old Terrier, for whom a visit to his usual sanitarium, the keeper's lodge, was declared necessary. He was heard swearing violently as we drove through the lodge gate to the railway. Meanwhile we are not without dogs, as that rascal Jack brought down a fox terrier with him from school and left it with us. It is a perfect demon of mischief. Its first act was to tear my own copy of the monthly Magazine and then it tried to apologise to me by utterly demolishing a Cornhill. From its supposed great value it is not allowed to go into the streets yet and occupies its leisure with insane attacks upon a bear skin rug in the library. It will finish the work my nephew's rifle began in the Himmala&ytilde;a. I see I cannot spell the word in any known form although I am printing it every month. Have you read the Abode of Snow 162 -- not that it is by my nephew? I wish it was.
With best regards to Lewes and hoping to hear from you soon, I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 19 November 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 19 November 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 19/73.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I wrote to Mr. Main as inclosed and have accordingly settled that there shall be no preface to the second edition of the Sayings. 886 I did not mention your opinion as I thought the knowledge of it would make the suppression of his little effusion still more agonising to him.
Along with this I send some sheets of the proposed one-volume edition of Middlemarch, which will now be sent to you regularly. I hope Lewes and you will like the look of the page.
Willie continues to mend steadily but it is a very slow process. The truth of your thoughtful reflection as to how much worse the accident might have been received a sad confirmation. The very next day the hounds were out a friend received a kick which smashed his ankle. Mortification ensued and the poor fellow died on Saturday.
I do not like the look of this Ashantee bush fighting at all. The risk of our officers being picked off is very painful. I see one of the Correspondents says "The present inclination of the Houssas is to run away when they are fired at." 887 I suspect the Correspondent shared the emotion.
How little attention the terribly grave state of matters in France is attracting in this country! Edinburgh is more occupied with a confounded Water Bill and London with that beastly Claimant than with the infernal drama that is going on across the Channel. I have interesting letters from Paris but no one seems to know what to expect and hardly what to wish for.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
The proofs are not on the size of paper that will be used for Middlemarch.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 19 February 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 19 February 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh
February 19/61.
My Dear Madam
I have read the M.S. you have sent of Silas Marner with the greatest admiration. The first 100 pages are very sad, almost oppressive, but relieved by the most exquisite touches of nature and natural feelings hit off in the fewest and most happily chosen words. I wish the picture had been a more cheery one and embraced higher specimens of humanity, but you paint so naturally that in your hands the veriest earthworms become most interesting perfect studies in fact.
The child found on the hearth replacing the poor weaver's lost treasure is a beautiful idea and is I hope to be the medium of restoring the unfortunate Silas to a more Christian frame of mind. How perfectly you paint the poor creature quite at sea when his simple faith was cut from under his feet.
The conclave at the Rainbow 700 is beyond price and no one but yourself could have done Mrs. Winthrop. She is perfect. Nancy Lammeter is very good and her toilette in presence of the Miss Gunns 701 is screaming, but Priscilla is my favourite; she promises to be a truly rich bit of character. I cannot help feeling sorry that you have done for the only one of the Cass family who had anything about him to redeem the breed. 702
My only objection to the story is the want of brighter lights and some characters of whom one can think with pleasure as fellow creatures, but this may come in the sequel of the story and in the meantime the touches of nature, the humour, and the power and precision are as wonderful as in anything you have ever written. Are you sure you will be able to wind up in the space you allot to yourself? I should almost doubt it.
Shall we calculate upon a post 8'b0ree; volume to sell at 12/- and make a proposition upon that basis, or is there any chance of your matter extending to what would make two smaller volumes? We can get the whole into type in a very few days.
Congratulating you upon your unfailing powers, which seem as inexhaustible as ever, believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 18 May 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 18 May 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | May 18/59.
My Dear George Eliot
I feel quite ashamed of my long silence and Lewes' reminder this morning added to my remorse by telling me that I had caused you to postpone an excursion. 131 I have been "awfully" busy and occupied about many things but I was determined to write today although I had not heard of you.
I inclose proof of the Lifted Veil. It is a very striking story, full of thought and most beautifully written. I wish the theme had been a happier one, and I think you must have been worrying and disturbing yourself about something when you wrote. Still, others are not so fond of sweets as I am, and no judge can read the Lifted Veil without deep admiration and the feeling that it is the work of a great writer.
I very much dislike the revivifying experiment at the end and would strongly advise its deletion. 132 I cannot help thinking that some of our excellent scientific friend's experiments on some confounded animal-cule must have suggested it.
The Magazine is still in such a dreadful state of size that it will suit me better to postpone the Veil for a month 133 so we will have plenty of time to talk it over.
I leave this tomorrow and intend to be in London on Wednesday the 25th and will find my way to Wandsworth on as early a day as you may be able to see me. I do long to have a talk with you and personally to congratulate you on your triumph.
I have no very recent information from London, but there is no doubt that the third edition (520 copies) will all be disposed of, and there is an excellent prospect for the 12/ edition of which I inclose a specimen sheet.
It is a great triumph and apart from all commercial considerations my brother and I take the keenest personal pleasure in the success. You know enough of us to feel that we will not forget to whom that success is owing, and on the principles we have acted upon in similar cases we will not rest satisfied without making you some acknowledgment beyond the letter of our agreement, although we do leave Mr. Liggins in penury. We propose therefore to give you an additional sum of ('a3400) Four Hundred Pounds towards the end of the year when the returns from the book will be coming in to us.
As I am leaving tomorrow, you may guess that my desk is a painful memento of work not sooner attended to, so Lewes will excuse my [not] writing for a day or two. If you write within the next few days address care of Revd. J. Blandford, Sponden near Derby, where we are going to leave the children with their adoring Aunts.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.
Although I have not been writing to you lately I have been writing about you, or rather Liggins. I will bring up the correspondence which will, I think, make you laugh. 134 Keep your secret.

My Dear Madam

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 18 February 1874
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
February 18/74.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
The sudden political convulsion made letter writing difficult to me, not that it is ever very easy. It is a wonderful change and I hope we are now in for a quiet steady government, able to attend to the business of the Country without being forced to count the votes of extreme sections.
I was truly glad to hear that the continued sale of Spanish Gipsy pleased you so much and it continues to move as I see in London there were 31 sold in December and 12 in January. Middlemarch holds on its course, 99 in December and 85 January. The political excitement is succeeded at home by that of a ball which we are going to give in honour of my daughter's first year. It is most amusing to see her opening the notes and registering her numbers in the most methodical way. I call it the Butterfly's Ball.
Our Cook who had been with us for 14 years recently left us and married a Home Missionary. She was a great artist and great favourite and my feelings towards the Missionary were not particularly friendly. There must however be good about him as she writes in great glee that with her husband's warm approval she is coming from Glasgow to help to cook the supper for Missie's Ball.
Mrs. Trollope came down from London last night to pay us a short visit. She is looking well and gave a very amusing account of her experiences of American and Australian travelling. Anthony seems to be flourishing and hunting. What an indefatigable fellow he is.
I hope the new work is taking form in your mind and partly on paper. I long to hear about it.
Do you read the Magazine much? I like greatly to hear what Lewes and you think of anything in it.
Willie is getting better but is still very lame. However his health is good. We are rather in the cripple line as my boy has got his collar bone broken in a foot ball match but is mending all right. After the accident he played on to the end of the match which was not a good thing, but I daresay he did not know what had happened and thought much more of the match than of his own pain.
Hoping to hear that Lewes and you are well, I am always
yours truly
John Blackwood
How do you like Lytton's Fables. If by any chance I have not given the order to send you a copy write and let me know.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 18 February 1869
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh February 18/69.
My dear Madam
It gave me much pleasure to receive your letter 29 and poem. I have read the simple tale of Lisa's love first in M.S. and then in type with increased admiration. The complete story is told in beautifully clear and simple language. Such lines as "Eyes that could see her on the summer's day might find it hard to turn another way" 30 have a wonderful effect.
I will never give a fancy price for anything to appear in the Magazine. Indeed I do not think that an article from one of the Apostles would much affect the sale. Believers in Blackwood's believe that every article is written by the best possible person for the subject and the knowledge that such is actually the fact will not convert miserable unbelievers. However I think you are entitled to extra consideration and I beg to offer you £50 which I hope you will think handsome.
I am delighted to hear of a Novel of English Life having taken such warm possession of you. When do you think it will take form? I hope you will be able to manage the expedition abroad and that it will do you both good. My Nephew has quite recovered from his cold, at least he is going out to Lockhart's at Ashiestiel to hunt tomorrow.
Always Yours Truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 September 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 September 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
September 17/73.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I am happy to tell you that the 21/ 4-volume edition of Middlemarch still goes on selling, but the divan here, chiefly Mr. Simpson, are strongly of opinion that we should be ready with a cheap one-volume edition to present to the public when the demand for the 4 vols. flags although still keeping that edition on sale. 841 The proposition is that the one-volume edition should be on paper the size of the 2-volume edition of Felix Holt and with a page and type somewhat similar to the cheap one-volume edition of Lorna Doone, in which shape Middlemarch would make about 640 pages. For illustration we propose a first-rate drawing of a fancy English village by Berket Foster 842 to be engraved in steel in the best style by Jeens 843 as a vignette on Title page.
The first two thousand of such an edition would about pay expenses, but we propose to pay you a honorarium of £50 for that and for every copy sold beyond the 2000 we should pay you a lordship of 1/6 per copy, the selling price nominally to the public being 7/6 and this lordship would, we calculate, be fully two-thirds of the profits at least.
The artist and engraver have been sounded and if this plan and proposal are agreeable to you we would proceed with the edition at once so as to have it ready to bring out at the right time. It might be a success and is about as feasible as anything I can think of, but you (especially Lewes) are capital judges and may suggest something else. The inclosed extract from a letter from Collins 844 is a curious coincidence and may amuse you.
I hope you are enjoying the country in spite of the weather.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 November 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 November 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 17/75.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
In regard to the division of the parts you are by far the best judge and I lean to what you now propose which would make the first volume end with the close of Mirah's story and the explanation of Deronda being at Leubrunn which draws this whole tale and dramatis personae together. 338 As it stands the first part ends very well with the introduction of Grandcourt to Gwendolen but is of course more complete after the Archery Ball 339 and as a windup to the second part Mirah's most touching narrative to dear old Mrs. Meyrick is necessary to waken up the full interest in the little wanderer.
Practically if there is to be a difference in the thickness of the volumes it is well that the two first should have the preponderance, and in this case unless I am utterly mistaken by the time the public have reached the third volume they will be too happy to take and pay for whatever you give. Divide as you think best without regard to the outward aspect of the volumes. I enclose 180 pages more and I think I need only say that my admiration has gone on at a fastly crescendo rate. The interest goes on and on mounting and then it is a series of perfect little dramas. Every touch makes a picture.
I do not like to remark upon particular beauties, as when I turn back over the leaves I see that I would be omitting to comment upon something equally good in the next page. The only plan would be to mark with a pencil as one read but that would interrupt the pleasure and after all it would only be a running bene bene BENISSIME. The point to which I have read you will see is the wondrous scene where Gwendolen accepts Grandcourt. 340 You kept me uncertain up to the last moment as to whether it was to be Yes or No. I had not the heart to tell her to say No and send the bright creature to be "looked over" by Mrs. Mompert and all the hopeless gloom she foresees so clearly. This feeling in my mind proves I think the surpassing skill of your workmanship.
My wife and daughter have not yet had an opportunity of reading this part and I am very curious to see how it strikes the ladies but I think I can guess.
To return to business details we think here that the first part should be published about the 15th of January so as to give the Newspapers time to speak out before the meeting of Parliament.
On another point there is a difference of opinion among us. Mr. Simpson holds strongly, and my nephew inclines, for an interval of two months between the four first parts at any rate, as it takes the public a long time to digest and fully appreciate the value of such food and talk to their neighbours about it as we found with Middlemarch. I on the contrary am in favour of only one month's interval as our audience is much more ready than it was for Middlemarch and I am afraid of the two months giving the Librarians a better opportunity of starving their supplies.
There can be no better judge of such a point than Lewes. Will you ask him also to write to me with form of advertisements which should begin to appear now. Should we let loose any gossiping paragraph? I am not fond of such things but it will be done in spite of us and as the name Daniel Deronda does not give the idea of such a thorough picture of English life we had better put them on the right and most popular scent.
We left Strathtyrum on Monday with weeping and wail in spite of the weather which had been most eccentric. On Saturday to make the most of her last day my daughter skated in the morning and in the afternoon rode on nice soft roads. We had a fortnight of hurricane and rain, then a week of bright clear frost and afterwards a hurricane which only lasted 24 hours. The tides were exceptionally high and the sacred links were invaded. On the Sunday afternoon we walked down to look at the sea which was coming in grandly. Of course all the dogs accompanied us on this farewell walk and one of the little terriers barking and splashing gallantly through the shallow water surrounding the (usually) small burn which crosses the links went headlong into the burn itself. The scene would have amused you. I have heard many a golfer swear at his ball getting into this burn but I am sure [no] direr oath than Tory's (the pet's name) when he found himself suddenly heels over head in four feet of water. However he struggled gallantly up the walled side of the burn and saved me from walking in to the rescue.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 January 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 January 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
January 17/72
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
It suddenly flashed across me last night that by some unaccountable oversight I had not written to you to say how perfectly delighted I was with the third book of Middlemarch. It is beautiful all over and I could not do justice to my feelings without going over nearly every sentence and dwelling upon it. I do not know what to admire most in it. Every turn is perfect. Poor Mrs. Vincy all mushed up, Rosamond working up to Lydgate, with the winding up scene in which he is done, are pictures indeed, which the back ground of young Plymdale, his mother, and Mrs. Bulstrode just fill up. 439
The higher parts where Dorothea and her surroundings come in are beyond praise. The General will swear at you for not disposing of Casaubon in that fit. 440 Mrs. Waule is a darling. In fact the three dramas going on at the Vincys, at Lowick Manor and at Stone Court are not only perfect pictures but in the most delicious contrast.
Even the pen of Main will I think drop speechless from his hand when he comes to this third Book. I felt all this so strongly when I read the proof that I seem to have been under the impression that I had written or said it to you, and the sheets coming into my hands last night made me start when I realised the fact that I had not.
All who have spoken to me about the Sayings are delighted. I remonstrated strongly with Main about the unnecessarily unmeasured tone of Preface, but like all enthusiasts he was obstinate and as I thought Lewes had seen it I did not press the matter further. It would be cruel to hint to him that you agreed with me, but it would be a good lesson as I could see he never reflected that on such a point I was about the most practised adviser that could be found. 441
I was very sorry to hear from Lewes that your expedition to Weybridge had not done your health good. The weather was mild too and I was in hopes of hearing of your return to Town quite vigorous. The weather here has been very unsatisfactory neither fit for Curling Golfing nor Hunting and very unwholesome. The Doctors say they never had so much sickness in the Town. I have been exceptionally busy and even less than usually disposed to work. Give my best regards to Lewes. I am quite ashamed to find a request in his note to which I forget to attend, but have now given orders about a copy of Brougham. Hoping that this will find you much better,
I am always yours truly
John Blackwood.
