Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 January 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 January 1863
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | January 17/63.
My Dear Madam
I think towards Easter will be as good a time as we can select to publish the 3d volume of the collected 6/ edition of your works, putting Silas and the Scenes into one volume. 130 Have you corrected copy to send down?
Of the Mill at 6/- there are about 950 sold including 200 to Australia so I think we shall only print 1000 of the next volume in the first instance. This edition is stereotyped, so that if there is a run on the three volumes when published together we will be ready to meet it. Of the 6/ edition of Adam there are about 650 on hand.
This 6/ edition is not doing what we hoped, and I see that up to midsummer last we had spent 85£ on advertising it (and only Adam was published at that time) so we are not neglecting it in that way indeed. The proposition is too heavy, as much as we had calculated on a sale of 5000. I wish I had a more flourishing account of sales to give but we must hope that the 3 volumes will go together.
A stupid blunder was made, of which so far you will be glad to hear, in reporting the impression of Silas 6/- at 1500 instead of 2000 which was the actual number printed, and as if that were not mistake enough there was a counter blunder, a portion of the stock on hand had been overlooked, as I find there are now 870 on hand. The last blunder had rather prevented the first from striking us at once. Mr. Simpson, who is generally so very accurate, is annoyed at the mistake in the impression and thinks he must have put it down for the number of the Mill printed. 131
There have been about 100 of Silas sold since midsummer and I fear we cannot calculate on many more in the present form when the cheap edition with the Scenes is announced but I hope it will drop a little still.
I have desired copy of Mill to be sent to you but it was too bad of you not to remind Mr. Langford of his oversight when you knew you could have as many copies of any of your books as you like at any time.
With remembrances to Lewes, believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
I find we have a corrected copy of Scenes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 April 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 17 April 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 394.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
April 17/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Proofs of Book Seven go to you by this post. I can hardly venture to speak about it and as for criticism, I should as soon think of regaling you with comments upon one of the great Greek Tragedies. This Book is so powerful as to be very terrible. What a pain must have been Deronda's in that interview with his mother 450 and how directly and simply does the language bring it home to the reader.
I was nearly as uneasy as Deronda while Gwendolen went on with her confession. 451 The words of old Elspeth in the Antiquary came irresistibly to my mind: "An' Murder tirlit at the door if it cam na' ben." 452
No wonder Deronda felt "worn" 453 at the close of the interview. I can hardly imagine any one reading without being carried away and feeling upset, and what must be the strain of thinking and writing out such a scene. Much as I know of the conscientious pain and anxiety you go through in the construction of your great works, I never felt more deeply and sympathisingly with you in your labours than I did last night in reading this Book 7 of Daniel, and it was for the second time, as I had not been able to resist reading the M.S. before I sent it into the Printing Office. But the glory is great and I trust the labour with this work is nearly over.
I think I hear and see Lewes over the proofs and hoping this may find you well and happy, I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
P.S. I must tell you I sent for a Hebrew Dictionary to look up the word tephillin 454 but to my shame I could not make out the letters and the dunderhead of a German who compiled the book had not given a relative table of English and Hebrew letters.
You were quite right as to Lush saying he would "take odds." He was not in such a happy and sanguine state as to say he would lay odds, but as to that you are the only judge, as you alone knew his exact feelings.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 March 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 March 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
March 16/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Sales for the last day or two have been steady but hardly worth reporting and the mute eloquence of the enclosed note touched me so much when Simpson laid it before me with a smile that I said I would send it to you. From the memo. there are purchases, obviously for buyers of the book, not for mere library readers. Book Two is coming up hand over hand upon Book One and must now be between two and three hundred of its predecessor.
Critics both public and private amuse me by their complaint that they do not quite understand Gwendolen. Did they wish you to lay down a chart of her character and fate on the first page? Did they ever fully know any human being at a first meeting or even after years of acquaintance? The objection is in reality the highest compliment, being in fact the plainest confession of the interest excited. I hope you have both enjoyed your expedition to the country 423 and returned with renewed health and spirits. The weather has I fear been against you. We have frost and snow here today, but Willie has gone out to hunt and I saw other maniacs passing the window in red coats as I was dressing.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 March 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 March 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | March 16/59.
My Dear Sir
I think I may now fairly congratulate you upon being a popular as well as a great author.
We printed 2090 65 of Adam Bede and with the aid of the insatiable Mudie we have disposed of upwards of 1800, so a second edition is now a certainty. 66 The question is in what form should it be: 2 volumes small 8'b0ree; 12/ or another short edition in the present shape. The two vol. 12/- must be the form one day even as intermediate to a people's edition for which I have a strong inclination so I think we had better set about printing the two volume edition at once to be ready. If the dregs of the first edition go off very quickly I suppose we must treat the public to another 3 volume edition. 67 Let me hear what Lewes and you think.
Your triumph is a great one and I do heartily rejoice in it. The sale is nothing to the ring of applause that I hear in all directions. The only qualm that ever came across me as to the success of the book was that really to enjoy it I required to give my mind to it and I trembled for that large section of Novel readers who have little or no mind to give, but now I think the general applause is fairly enlisting even noodles.
I was delighted by an allusion in one of Lewes' notes to your being engaged in a new Tale. 68 Pray let me hear about this. Inclosed are a couple of letters from worshippers 69 I suppose.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 February 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 February 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 16/57.
My Dear George Eliot
I inclose proof of the first part of Mr. Gilfil with which I am very greatly delighted. The proof fully confirms the impression made by the M.S. The first eight pages in particular are bright, lifelike, and witty as may be. Many men write well and tell a story well, but few possess the art of giving individuality to their characters so happily and easily as you in both these stories. I think Mr. Gilfil is likely to be more generally popular than Amos and I have no qualms in starting him without seeing the conclusion.
On the proof I have made some marks in regard to which I shall be very glad if you agree with me. The last marks affect 'abrather seriously'bb the plot of the story but I think my objections may be obviated without any serious alteration of the plan. It is not a pleasant picture to see a good fellow loving on when the lady's heart is openly devoted to a Jackanapes, and I am a little puzzled as to how you are to bring the excellent Gilfil out 'abunless'bb without making him too abjectly devoted a lover for a man of character. I think the objection would be readily met by making Caterina a little less openly devoted to Wybrow and giving a little more dignity to her character. Understand that I by no means object to her; on the contrary I think that she promises to be most interesting and I look with great anxiety for the picture of her half-broken heart turning to Gilfil. I hope she finally rejects the insufferable Wybrow -- but I must not speculate upon your plot, and if I am wrong in my opinions about the demeanour of Caterina with Wybrow recollect that I write to some extent in the dark.
I have not been able to get part 2 into type yet but I read it with very great pleasure and I do not recollect of any passage that moved my critical censorship unless it might be the allusion to dirt in common with your heroine 797 and the cool proceeding of Wybrow at the close of the part. 798
Let me have back proof as soon as you can, and with many congratulations on your success believe me very sincerely yours
John Blackwood.
To the Author of Clerical Scenes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 April 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 April 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinburgh | April 16/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
I inclose proofs of Title page and I think you will agree that the motto looks best upon the opposite page. When put on title page there seems too much printing and the main title does not seem sufficiently prominent. I also inclose proof of what I have thought of as the publisher's note as to the time when we received the M.S. 222 My only thought of course is to put it in the way that will be most agreeable to your feelings and I am equally afraid of saying too little or too much so I wish your advice.
The accompanying letter came from America to-day. My nephew came home yesterday looking all the better for his London expedition and the lameness nearly gone. We went down to the club together to lunch and as he remarked it was the first time we had walked together for six months. Our cold weather still continues but there are glimpses of the sun to-day so we are hopeful of better things tomorrow.
Always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 April 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 16 April 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | April 16/59.
My Dear George Eliot
You must now I think have good news enough to cheer even your most desponding spirit.
Lewes did mention that neither he nor you saw the Times regularly, but I had given so strong a hint that I did not doubt one or other of you would be on the look out.
The review is by Dallas and does him great credit. The authorship should not be named as the Times people very sensibly do not like their reviewers to be known.
It appeared most opportunely and the effect on the second edition was instantaneous. Mr. Langford who has been bewailing my recklessness in printing 750, now writes wildly to send up the whole impression. What the exact sale is I do not know. I fancy over 400, but Lewes who has been in the Row will have seen. The demand seems so brisk that we have given orders to reprint again. There is about a volume in type.
Mr. H. Anders, rector of Kirkby is a singular specimen of officious ignorance. I wonder the Times inserted the letter. Mrs. Blackwood says there was a Mr. Anders, a surgeon at Newark, who attended her grandmother and family. 106 This Anders had a son, a clergyman, who was suspended for two years for some little transgression. We think this must be our beauty. But who in the world is Liggins? He must have ability of some kind to impose upon so many people.
Langford tells me that you have sent in a contradiction -- which is right and it will, I doubt not, be most neatly expressed. I hope you have taken care of the hand. There is evidently a perfect fever about the author's life now.
I read with great pleasure the expression in your last letter as to the "quiet joy" you experienced in your success. I long to see you and congratulate you on your triumph.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 15 October 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 15 October 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | October 15/57.
My Dear Sir
I inclose proof of Janet. I have read this last part both in M.S. and Type with the deepest interest. The pathetic interest is very great and gathers strongly round Janet in spite of the unpoetic nature of her weakness and temptation. It was a bold choice of a plot and some will object to such a feature in a heroine, but there is no more common agent of human misery and trial than drunkenness, and consequently there can be no more legitimate material for the writer of Fiction. There is an air of reality about the whole story and that is in itself about the greatest of all merits.
I was a little puzzled when I came to the climax about the bottle of brandy but you have rearranged it beautifully and it contributes to the air of truth. 984 Should there be so much of Dempster's delirium? 985 I daresay the effect would be lessened if it was shortened. Tryan's death is finely painted and I think few can fail to be affected by the closing scenes of the good man's life. 986
Along with this I send you a copy of all the parts of the Clerical Scenes in order that you may make any corrections you wish for the reprint. We should begin it soon.
I rejoice to think that you are going to devote your powers to a Tale on a great scale. With a larger canvass your exquisite little sketches of character will all come into full life and take their legitimate share in the story.
It will give me much pleasure to hear anything about this new story and to know how soon there is any chance of it being transferred from your head to paper.
Return the proof of Janet as soon as you can. Very probably I shall begin the number with her this month.
With compliments to Lewes I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 October 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 October 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | October 14/59.
My Dear George Eliot
I inclose a letter which came today.
I am happy to tell you that Adam Bede still goes on selling and we have ordered another edition of 2000 to be printed. 349 It is a grand success and a deserved one. The Clerical Scenes too are moving so that I think we shall soon be through the 1500.
I regret very much that you should allow yourself to be so disturbed by an old fool like Bracebridge. After his two letters to me I would not have allowed myself to attach any more weight to his opinions and reasonings than to those of any poor creature under restraint. Quirk's mode of appealing to your feelings was most unjustifiable and indicates a narrowness of mind, inquisitiveness and a total absence of delicacy which would seem incompatible with the charitable good feelings which you tell me the man really shows. No whisper of your persecutions has reached me. I fancy I have choked the crew off.
Newdegate was with us for a day not long ago and like a gentleman as he is said not a word on the subject beyond an incidental praise of your books.
The Major and I are very sorry indeed that you cannot entertain our proposal for the new Tale. I hope Maggie gets on as gloriously as she promised.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 November 1867
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh.
November 14/67.
My Dear Madam
As far as I can remember nothing has ever leaked out from our Printing Office and the chances of publicity being given to the birth of Fidalma by a portion of her being put into type is hardly worth considering when the advantages on the other side are so obvious. There will always be rumours about what you are doing and I cannot tell you how often I have heard of your being engaged upon different works, and my simple statement of "Well I think I would have heard of it" is looked upon as a publisher's diplomatic utterance.
My advice is in favour of getting what you have ready of Fidalma into type -- then we can all coolly judge. The Printers will have no difficulty in setting the duplicate versions of occasional passages. They were I think distinctly marked in the M.S. but it may be as well to put the second of any of these alternative passages with "or" before it. In the Printing Office at present I have two more volumes of Kinglake 683 in type, and with Fidalma too the office would really be big with fate. Kinglake is wonderful and will I think make as much row as his first volumes. His style is enchanting and he does paint a picture.
I am excessively anxious that you should do an Address to the Working Men as I am thoroughly convinced that no one could do it so well. When the new Reform Bill comes into operation the working man will be on his trial and if he misconducts himself it will go hard with the country, but at all events his class would be the greatest sufferers. My own impression is that whatever swaps 684 and blockheads may have the suffrage there is intelligence and power of wealth enough to keep the country pretty straight. Do consider the matter and I shall be really obliged if you can give me an Address to the Working Man with which to begin the January number.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 January 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 January 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 399.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
January 14/79.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
It comes home to my heart to see your hand again, and your considerate note in the midst of your heart-breaking trouble is so like you.
Do not allow the proofs of "Theophrastus Such" to concern you in the least, the type can wait your perfect convenience. I had it set up that the proofs might be ready to your hand when you were able to turn your thoughts that way. It is all in type now and I shall complete your set of proofs tomorrow.
I have been reading it all with great interest, and it does make one think. In the circumstances perhaps it does make me think more gravely than I otherwise would have done. There are so many things too that make one feel where one's own shoe pinches, especially in the weaker points of character. It brings us all in a kind of a way to the Confessional.
I could not at first make out what H.E.P. 165 meant until Mr. Allardyce 166 suggested that it must be the old gathering cry of Peter the Hermit. He guessed this too before he had read that Essay. He has read them all now and I am glad to observe that he feels no want of individual interest and that Theophrastus is to him a real entity throughout.
Willie's leg is nearly mended now and he moves about the room with sticks, although he cannot venture into the streets yet. My wife and daughter are well and often speak of you. I am really very well and mean to take my first day's Golf tomorrow if the weather is at all fit. I tremble to think of your health in the midst of your suffering.
It has given me great pleasure to observe the tone of good feeling and sense in Charles Lewes' letters.
At this season the position of your Works has of course been looked into and the returns of sales in the opening year come from London. My first sensation was what a pleasant table they would have made to send to him so I need not tell you they are looking well. God bless and comfort you.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 December 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 December 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
December 14/75.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I was very sorry to see by a note from Lewes to Simpson that in the change of weather you had caught a bad cold, but I hope the steady continuance of the milder weather has put you all right again. 361 It has enabled me to golf and my wife and daughter to ride, both things conducive to the family health and happiness.
I often wonder how you are getting on with the Great Book and I never venture to ask how far you have got with your wondrous tale of human life.
Mr. Langford evidently felt so left out in the cold while we were all full of Daniel that I told Simpson to send him a copy of the sheets for private perusal. He returned them to me with an excellent rapturous letter which may be summed up in his own statement that when he finished the second volume he felt inclined to "rush up to the Priory and throw himself on his knees before you." The idea of the tableau is amusing, but the same genuine feeling will be shared by many, so great is the mastery of the book.
Mr. Simpson has arranged with the Australian paper but could not get them above the £200.
You will be glad to hear that Middlemarch is going on selling and there is also good life in The Spanish Gipsy and Jubal.
Hoping soon to get good accounts of your health, believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
A two volume 8'b0ree; life of Heine 362 has been sent to me and I propose to send it to Lewes if he has not got a copy. I inclose a poetic letter from Lockhart to me which may amuse you and has intensely delighted the golfing world. 363

Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 December 1868
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh December 14/68.
My dear Madam,
I was shocked to hear of the secondary place in which you had found The Spanish Gypsy in lists of advertisements. I called up Mr. Simpson and you would have laughed and sympathised with the gleam of triumph in that able administrator's eye as he exclaimed "Why, I altered that in the copies of the list that I sent out" and rushing off brought me back the country paper I send to you where you will see the Gypsy heads the list. The thing had arisen from the list being one of Christmas presents when illustrated books are usually put at the head of the list. The enclosed are the ordinary forms of advertisements that we are sending out. I am happy to tell you that we have sold upwards of 700 of the new edition which is very satisfactory. It shows that there is a steady demand.
I am very glad that Lewes and you like Doubles and Quits and your applause has delighted the Author and his wife. He is a great ally and companion of mine and for several years I have been looking at things he did and urging him on, telling him I was sure he would succeed, so I have a sort of double pleasure in his success. He is of literary blood, being Captain Lockhart, Nephew of John Lockhart, 848 and lives at Ashiestiel, the lovely spot where Sir Walter Scott was so happy and wrote so much. He is full of fun and I shall bring him to you the first time we are in Town together. Are you writing anything?
With best regards to Lewes and hoping you are both well I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | December 14/57.
My Dear Sir
I inclose proof of Title page which I shall be glad to have back by return with any thing else that you may wish to go into the book. As I write I recollect that you sent a motto from Fielding. I have stupidly allowed it to fall aside but if you still fancy it send down another copy and it can be printed yet. I thought I had sent it into the Printing Office but they say no.
We shall probably subscribe the book in London on Thursday or Friday 1037 and the earliest intelligence of the result will be sent to you. It will give me real pleasure if I can send you good news but a bad subscription will not cast me down at all.
I hear a great many favourable opinions of the Scenes 1038 and, what is more to the purpose, I know that they are good, but I see that you understand the difference between a general and a literary reputation and it is impossible to say whether that general buzz which is the precursor of a large sale has arisen about the book.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 April 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 14 April 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street Edinburgh | April 14/79.
My dear Mrs. Lewes
Your letter last week gave me real pleasure. I rejoice to think of you getting out to walk in the quiet lanes beyond the houses and I had sat down to write congratulating you on our having some return of the spring at last when the snow began to batter against the windows again and we have had it more or less with us ever since.
I wrote to Mr. Harper last Wednesday and I hope I may prove a successful negotiator. I sent him the contents to show the nature of the book and a leaf to show him the size and number of pages. On looking at the motto again I found it so appropriate that I wish I had sent it to him, but it can follow and I have been trying its effect on the title page. I shall send it to you in a day or two also note stating when we received the M.S.
This return of winter has made me feel rather out of sorts for the last few days but in spite of the east winds I took a long walk yesterday afternoon with my doctor and he congratulated me most heartily upon the state of my pulses after the exertion.
Thanks for your valuable message to Julian Sturgis which I shall convey to him in some form as he is a fine fellow and will be highly gratified, being a devoted worshipper of yours. My nephew has been paying a visit in Derbyshire for a few days, but I expect him home to-night. You will not I think be disappointed with Mr. Kinglake's volume. My son Jack is sitting with me busy reading some M.S. adventures in Australia which are very well told. He sends his respects. Believe me
Always truly
John Blackwood.
I said to Harper that we proposed to publish towards the end of May.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 13 March 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 13 March 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
March 13/72.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I intended to have written to you the day after I read Part IV but I went to Golf instead of working and the East Wind nearly caught my throat again.
Part 4 is graphic to a degree in every sketch and detail. Every individual character stands out as clear and finished as can be, although it may be seen but for a moment. The Frog-faced gentleman 474 becomes at once a thing of flesh and blood as much as the Tichborne Claimant. If Mrs. Garth had given Caleb a thump on the side of the head when he proposed to take Fred Vincy as his assistant, 475 she would have been perfectly justified, but it is in perfect keeping with the old fellow's character.
It could not well be such an attractive picture as Book III which will I think fairly bring down the House, but there is nothing more exquisite anywhere than that touch at the end where Dorothea is so thankful that she had not given way to her irritation. It is so true and so beautifully put. 476
The inclosed is I think the last report we had of Sales which will show you how it has been going on. There are sales since. I was disappointed to find the Scotch Sales so small as you will see on the small memorandum. Still it is all very satisfactory. A young fellow Donnithorne belonging to one of the regiments here dined with us the other day and I as nearly as possible informed him that I was well acquainted with his family and I could not for some time recollect the origin of the confusion in my mind. 477
I am tearing through proofs for post time and work in a desperate hurry. I trust Lewes and you are well.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 12 December 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
December 12/76.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
It gives me the most sincere pleasure to learn by Lewes' letter today, 570 that you have bought a place in the country which seems likely to suit you both in every way.
Most heartily do I congratulate you and hope that this permanent anchorage in the country may be a long continued source of health and happiness to you such as I should ever wish your home to be. My nephew joins in congratulations and it will be a labour of love to Mr. Simpson to hasten the preparation of the statements of your books from knowing the happy end to which the results are to be applied.
The Magnate correcting you about Grandcourt and Gwendolen walking into a room arm and arm 571 amused me but after all I half think that at the date of the story you are right. The custom of the husband following the wife into a room resulted from the overflowing skirts etc. of the ladies. My wife has a favourite story of her uncle Canon Guthrie 572 who was also Vicar of Calne having been told jokingly by the Marquis of Lansdowne that it was no longer the custom for husbands to come in with their wives on their arm. This would be about 30 years ago and the change must have been new then, as the Canon was as punctilious a church dignitary as ever I saw and both he and his wife thoroughly members of the best stamp of society all their lives which made the joke against them in their nieces whom they told the story.
I am glad you like the appearance of the new edition of Deronda. Do you not wish copies to give away. As yet I fear it is not doing much but I shall let Lewes know. With all good wishes I am
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 October 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 October 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | October 11/61.
My Dear Madam
You would guess from my not writing sooner that I was puzzling over the amount that I should offer you for the entire remaining copy right of "The Scenes" Adam Bede, The Mill, and Silas.
I now beg to offer Three Thousand Pounds ('a33000) payable in the course of a couple of years from date of publication of first volume of reprint.
I wished to make the sum larger but I cannot see my way to making it answer within any reasonable term of years.
The profit on the very cheap editions, even calculating upon enormous sales, is very small, and how these cheap publishers manage is to me inexplicable. I have no objections to show you our calculations if Lewes and you would like to look at them. If the sum I have mentioned does not come up to your expectations I shall be sorry, but I am sure you will give me credit for wishing to give as much as any prudent man would. 856
Tell Lewes I got his paper on Buckle 857 on coming here yesterday afternoon and have sent it into the printing office. From the tone of his note and seeing his M.S. I do hope he is better. His critique on the Magazine papers in his previous note did savour of dyspepsia; at all events I did not agree with him, but judges often do differ. Did you read the Chronicles of Carlingford? 858 I have not seen his lad 859 yet but Willie tells me the home influences with you have had a decidedly good effect upon him. We all like him.
We have been in great griefs at St. Andrews owing to the fearfully sudden seizure and death of Lord Eglinton. 860 He dined with us on the Saturday and was as always delightful -- happy himself and making all about him so. On the Tuesday he was golfing all day as usual and we were all laughing and talking over the prospects for the Medal on the following day. That evening he dined at a neighbouring house -- in his usual spirits until he dropped in the hall while pulling on his greatcoat and never spoke again.
When I repaired to the usually gay scene on the links next morning I could hardly resist crying aloud when I heard of the Catastrophe. I had received a great deal of kindness from him and had a very warm feeling of affection and respect for him, admiring his frank manly character with all my heart. He was indeed a very fine fellow and a very able clear-headed man.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes
I go back to Strathtyrum tonight but address here.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 November 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 November 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
November 11/73.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I was very glad to receive your pleasant letter and especially to observe the paragraph about your simmering towards another big book. That this simmering will boil up to the right point I feel very hopeful. There are as good fish in the Sea as ever came out of it, and those really studying and loving Middlemarch will feel that the proverb applies to your mind instead of harking back to that great book as a climax.
I inclose table showing the very gratifying sale of the 21/- Middlemarch for which I propose to send settlement after the turn of the year. Beyond this table of printed and sold there are 500 printed on which we are just beginning to break bulk. 875 We do not think that this 500 will be exhausted before it will be fair to bring out the one-volume edition, but from the way the sale has gone on we consider that it will always be desirable to keep on a 4-volume edition. The sheets of the one-volume edition will begin to be sent to you for correction tomorrow, I think.
Have you and Lewes seen Mr. Main's preface to the second edition of your Sayings? It seems to me that our friend puts the case rather too strong in favour of his compilation as compared with the Works. I am sure he does not intend what his words may seem to convey, but will Lewes and you look at the points where I have put a query?
We got back to Edinburgh last week and you will be sorry to hear that I found my nephew laid up from an accident in the hunting field. When he was addressing himself to a fence, a beast on a runaway brute galloped bolt against him and caught him on the ankle. Fortunately the bone is not broke but it is [a] terrible bruise and necessitates confinement to bed or sofa for some time. The shock to the general system at first was great but now his general health is all right and Doctor says he is going on as well as possible.
It is very hard and very provoking. It was only his second day of the season.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 January 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | January 11/60.
My Dear Madam
I am delighted to hear that you expect to be ready so soon with the new Novel. If we are to be out by the end of March we should begin to print very soon, so whenever you can spare some M.S. it will be well to send a volume down. I long to see the rest.

Tell Lewes I hope to receive the Fielding paper in time for the next number.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
In the Advert[isement] I am doubtful about saying in March, as I hardly think you can be ready.

Edinburgh | February 11/59.
My Dear Sir
I am delighted to tell you that the murmur of opinion regarding Adam Bede which begins to reach me is as favourable as we could possibly wish.
My own family and immediate connections are enthusiastic, and it is most pleasant to hear their remarks as I see the book is being really felt as it should be by them. I chuckle as much as if I were the author myself when I hear some passage which had struck and moved me long ago enthusiastically lauded.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 December 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 11 December 1867
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | November 701 11/67.
My Dear Madam
In case of any slips I inclose revise of Felix Holt's Address. It is a most delightful and refreshing contrast to the fustian usually addressed to the wearers of that article. The real sound advice is delivered with the right feeling in the tersest and best language. The only fear is its being too much above your audience, but I do not think it is so to such a degree as to prevent its telling most forcibly. At top of proof you will see I have deleted the words delivered and a meeting of. Do you think this should be so? Keep whatever title you deem best.
I am quite ready to accept all that Felix Holt says, and I think the Address comes more dramatically without any introductory words from me. I hope the six proofs of the precious Poem arrived safely.
It was my intention to write to you a long letter with mention of my favourite lines and ideas, but between the first most striking line that catches one
"On the Mid Sea that moans with Memories" 702 to the last most touching one there are such multitudes of lines and thoughts calling for reflection that I shall never have time or confidence to say what I think ought to be said.
The whole scene and conversation in the Hostelry is a picture which one can dwell upon for any length of time. To how many a Spruch-spr'e4cher does your inimitable phrase "mournful prophet of high drollery" 704 apply. After the bright Fidalma bursts upon the scene one speedily feels her connection with the Gipsy, whose robes, not he, lose their grace when they fall from him. The contrast in the Gipsy King's case reminded me somewhat of Thackeray's best bit of satire in drawing Louis 14th with and without his robes. 705
Fidalma's explanation of the feelings which prompted her to dance is splendid. 706 I feel for the Duke when he gets her letter. The letter is a marvel. 707 Surely never note contained so much, not even in a Postscript. Yet how simple and touching the words are.
Of the alternative passages put for consideration I think that in almost every case the expressions in the text are the best.
How far a Poem which requires the reader to pause and dwell so much at every step to feel it aright will be popular with the mass is a thing that no man can tell, but there is no question that it is a grand thing.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.
I would have written to Lewes but have nothing particular to say. Tell him I hope he is not working too hard. I desired the copies of his book to be sent and I have no doubt they would reach you along with the proofs.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 10 January 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | January 10/61.
My Dear Madam
Your pleasant letter was very welcome. Thanks for what you so handsomely propose in regard to the current edition of the Scenes but we must take our chance with it.
I inclose memorandum of the numbers printed and stock on hand of the three books. The stock on hand of the Mill 3 vols. was swollen by our taking back some unsold copies in the hands of one or two of the Row Houses. From the length of time that had elapsed they were not entitled to this, but it was better to do it than to cause bad feeling and it would have been hard enough upon them.
I am sorry to hear that your health is not quite what could be wished, but I hope the breaking up of the frost will allow you to get exercise and become quite strong soon.
I would have written to you sooner but waited in hopes of being able to send the table of the Physiology along with the inclosed, but it is not ready yet, some details having to be queried to London. Tell Lewes that Mr. Simpson rather funks sitting down to write to him details of his objections to the little Physiology, 684 but he will try his hand when he is a little less busy.
I am glad to hear that his paper 685 is in a state of forwardness and hope to see it in a day or two.
Have you been working and on what? Pray let me hear. A letter from you is generally a cheering one, and I had very great pleasure in taking your last to the Major when I went to see him, which I usually do at one o'clock. He is still, I am sorry to say, confined to the house.
There has been no serious return of illness but he does not gain strength as we could wish. However he is decidedly better than last few days.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 10 February 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | February 10/58.
My Dear Sir
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque £120 being the first instalment for the reprint of Clerical Scenes, and from the state of the sales I think the other payment for the edition will be at your service when you wish it. I have not heard lately from London about the book from which I infer that there is no particular movement, but I fancy the sale must be towards 800.
After the fine start I thought we should have got through the edition at once, but there is no call to feel disappointed. On the contrary the sale is a good sale and you will recollect that when we proposed to reprint my impression was that the series had not lasted long enough in the Magazine to give you a hold on the general public although long enough to make your literary reputation. Unless in exceptional cases, a very long time often elapses between these two stages of reputation -- the literary and the public. Your progress will be sure if not so quick as one could wish.

always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 10 February 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 10 February 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Brief extracts published: William Blackwood, II, 439.
Edinburgh | February 10/57.
My Dear George Eliot
Each morning as the pile of letters is laid upon my groaning table I look through the heap for a packet from you. It would be a monstrous pity not to come to time with No. 2 of the series and I hope the M.S. is either on the way or will be dispatched in response to this. Do not of course hurry yourself to the detriment of the story; the perfecting of that must always be the first consideration, but it would be a serious disadvantage to baulk the public expectation now fairly raised.
I am delighted to be able to tell you that Amos seems fairly to have taken with the public. I could not explain the exact symptoms of popularity but to me they are literally unmistakeable. They reach me in different ways and an occasional objection I look upon as by no means a bad sign, showing as it does that people are thinking over and discussing the story.
Nearly all of my own immediate friends are loud in praise. The impression among them seems to be that you are new to writing fiction. They mean this as a compliment implying not rawness but that invaluable quality freshness.
Of all people in the world I have a letter from the excellent Albert Smith, 791 perfectly enthusiastic about Amos. He describes himself as having been more moved than he thought possible, and from his account the luminaries of the Garrick generally seem to have mingled their tears with their tumblers over the death bed of Milly. It will be great fun if you are a member of that society and hear yourself discussed. I sympathize with your desire for the incognito, although I hope to break through it erelong as far as regards myself.
In regard to scientific illustrations neither Hamley nor I meant that you used them too much. We merely alluded to a sort of precision of expression or illustration which gave us the idea that the writer was accustomed to scientific definitions.
I rarely forget handwriting which I have once seen and your hand has all along struck me as being in some way or other familiar to me. When I got your last letter I caused a Clerk to turn up some letters 10 years old as I was forcibly reminded of the hand of Captain George Warburton 792 (a brother of Eliot) an old correspondent of mine. I found a remarkable resemblance but not identity, nor does Amos seem to me anything like what that good artillery man would or could write.
I am uncommonly anxious to see No. 2, and when I get it will not allow grass to grow at my heels until I read it and let you know what I think.
With regards to Lewes from whom I expect to hear soon I am
yours very truly,
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 1 November 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 1 November 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | November 1/60.
My Dear Madam
I inclose proof of the title page New Edition of the Mill. What shall we put upon it New Edition? or 4th Edition? It is the 4th edition as we printed first 4000 then 2000 and then 550. I incline for simply new edition in the first instance and then we might advertise the numbers afterwards, although that is not a favourite plan of mine nor do I think it does any good.
We propose to bring out the new edition in the course of the month and to advertise at once. There has not of course been much demand of late for the Mill. I have not yet seen return of the sales for October but in the previous months Adam was most satisfactory, and there was also a modest sale of the Scenes.
I long very much to hear how your two new schemes are taking shape in your head. As to both these Novels I feel as sanguine as possible. Whatever the most carping or malevolent critic might say of the Mill, no one in his senses could venture to deny the power and the extraordinary fertility of the author's resources. I only hope you will not overwork or bother yourself with doubts as to future triumphs, of which no author has so goodly a store in prospect.
Tell Lewes I have his note and am clear for the paper on Uncivilised Man and Animals. 654 I am sure he will make a capital thing of such a theme and I hope he will set about it. when here he suggested the idea of a Theatrical Article from you at Christmas and I hope you will enter into the idea as you might do a first-rate thing about London theatres and audiences and the process of acquiring the requisite experience would be a diversion. I shall write Lewes soon with proof of his transmitted paper. 655 He seems to be getting on famously with the Physiology for schools.
I am sorry he does not report your health as being quite perfect but
I hope this will find you quite restored. The Major you will be glad to hear goes on steadily improving. He joins me in best regards, and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood
Mrs. M. E. Lewes
I came back to Edinburgh for the winter two days ago and was not sorry to do so as the weather is very bad.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.

May 1/74.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Mr. Simpson has I doubt sent you an elaborate explanation about the paper, the quality of which is very provoking. Like Lewes I thought at first the copies might not have been fully pressed., It is to be hoped that only experts like ourselves will feel the thing. I send you a list of presentation copies of Jubal that we are sending out, and there are some we have not sent, thinking you might wish to send them yourself. Suggest any others you think of.
I was glad to see from Lewes' note that you were both well and both writing. I hope this means writing books not letters. Simpson was so engrossed about the paper catastrophe that he did not observe the expression about both writing and I had a laugh at him.
We are going over to Strathtyrum tomorrow for a week in a sort of Pic Nic fashion. It will do me good before going to London. There was not a bad one at Randolph Cres[cen]t the other day. A little housemaid grounded an application for a rise of wages on the rise in the price of every thing!! Her mistress said "Why Mary, what have you to provide yourself with? You rather give a reason why I should reduce wages."
always yours truly

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 1 April 1879
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George Str. Edinr. | April 1/79.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
I got your touching note and it is impossible not to sympathise with your feelings and hesitations in sending a new work into the world for the first time after the loss of your dear husband and right trusty adviser.
The little incident you mention 210 of finding the crumpled leaf reminds me of various conversations with him by which I knew his anxiety that you should not read stupid or vulgar criticism.
Theophrastus most certainly had his full sanction and apart from that I can vouch from his own fervent expressions how thoroughly he who knew you best felt that your works were above criticism and incapable of being made better by the assistance of any human being.
I would have written to you last week but the return of the bitter weather had rather caught me up and I was not feeling fit. On Saturday however I had a consultation with two wise doctors and I am sure it will give you pleasure to know that the verdict upon me was the most satisfactory I have had for many a long day. The weather is now much milder at last and has I hope enabled [you] to get about a little and take some joy in the first taste of the coming spring.
always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 1 April 1874
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 380.
George Street, | Edinburgh.
April 1/74.
My Dear Mrs. Lewes
Along with this I send the rest of the Revise of your Poems. My idea is to make the Impression 1500. What do Lewes and you think as to price of the little volume? I daresay 5/- is the right thing. We have not said anything about Terms of publication but I propose to offer you either two thirds of profits or a lordship on each copy sold when we have settled the selling price.
I have had a copy of the proofs lying in my dressing room and have been reading and rereading the Poems at night. They are very beautiful. There is a solemn cadence and power, almost a warning voice about them all, which becomes very impressive when thought over. You must have been thinking if not writing Poetry all your life, and if you have any lighter pieces written before the sense of what a great author should do for mankind came so strongly upon you, I should like much to look at them. Turning over the leaves of the revise I see you have removed the dates which stood originally at the end of each Poem. Something should be said as to previous publications of the Poems. Do you intend a preface or should something be said in contents indicating the facts of previous appearance? Mr. Simpson is very anxious to hear whether he has met your views as to handiness of form etc.
I expect Willie home tomorrow night and hope to get good accounts of you both from him. He has been seeing no end of people and must I fear be rather knocked up. He has been much with the Ashanti Warriors. Indeed during the turmoil of receptions and reviews Brackenbury has half pitched his tent at the Burlington as being more handy than his own home at Shooters Hill. Brackenbury's History of the Expedition 68 promises to be both interesting and very curious. He has Wolseley's consent to publish everything.
We have had such a fine winter that we began to brag over Italy and all the rest of the world, but during the last few days we have winds and rain, which tell that Scotland is Scotland still.
We do not think of going up to London until the middle of May. Will you still be there at that time?
always yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F

John Blackwood to GE, Edinburgh, 1 April 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh April 1/68.
My Dear Madam
I had the pleasure of receiving your note today and the corrected sheets and slips of the great Poem arrived safely at the same time. They are sent into the Printing Office and will be revised by the time you get back to the Priory.
I read parts two and three in type since I came here. They are full of beauties but I think you said you would like best to hear from me when I had seen the whole. This I am happy to hear that I so probably shall soon, and it is delightful to think of publishing towards the end of May. We ought to put forth some announcement now in order to set people talking and expecting. What form would you suggest? Should we give the Title or have it vaguely a Poem by George Eliot? On the revises I see you have made the title The Spanish Gipsy. I thought you intended to call it Fidalma, but the other title better expresses what you mean to illustrate.
I was very glad to learn that you were both enjoying yourselves at Torquay. It must be lovely there in this wonderful weather. Even here it is positively warm and every one is going about without a greatcoat, which is a rare state of matters in these parts. We shall probably pay for it with a snow storm in the merry month of May.
I came home soon after I saw you but I have been abominably busy and only had one day of Golf. Tomorrow however is the Golf meeting which begins at 12 and ends about the same hour after dinner, so I shall have enough of it for one day. The conversation (when the exigencies of the game permit speech) during those 12 hours will be entirely of golf -- this match and that match.
Best regards to the Mollusc hunter and believe me
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Edinburgh | April 1/61.
My Dear Madam
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque Thirteen Hundred and Fifty Pounds (£1350) payable to you for the Mill on the Floss as follows.
First of this is a £1000 for the 5th and 6th thousand of the edition at 1/11/6 and second £300 for the 2000 printed of the 12/- edition. The odd £50 is for the unfortunate 500 printed beyond the 6000 in the original form, of which 500 only about 100 have been sold. 729

They will hear of this blunder from Mr. Simpson. This leaves about 400 on hand in the original form and we propose gradually to use those up as waste in our own establishment so as not to let any of them come before the public in so humble a light, keeping however a few copies to meet any possible demand.
This being my first day at regular work for a week I am very hard pressed, so do not attempt to write you a longer letter but acknowledging your last which it was really a pleasure to read, Believe me
ever yours truly
John Blackwood
Mrs. Lewes
I shall read the paper in MacMillan.

John Blackwood to GE, Colinsburgh, 26 September 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Gebliston | September 26/60.
My Dear Madam
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque One Thousand Pounds being the first instalment for the Mill on the Floss in the terms of our agreement. 641
If you are housebuying or doing anything for which money is wanted, we shall be happy to make the other payments at an earlier date to suit your convenience.
There are the 500 copies beyond the 6000 to be settled for also, which leaves £2250 still to be paid to you.
When Lewes comes down I shall have some talk with him as to when we should publish the cheap edition of The Mill. There are still copies on hand and more lingering about the Row than I like, but we shall not hesitate to sacrifice those whenever it seems judicious to bring out the cheap edition.
The Major is still decidedly an invalid but gathering strength by air and exercise at Innerleithen, where I hope to find him pretty nearly all right tomorrow. As I have a line to write to Lewes I make this note short.
always Dear Madam yours very truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Colinsburgh, 24 July 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Colinsburgh, 24 July 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Gebliston 227 House | Colinsburgh, Fife | July 24/59.
My Dear George Eliot
I am glad to hear of your safe return and rejoice to think that you can so well afford to laugh at and despise all the Dixons in the world.
From what you and Lewes say I feel confident the new novel will go on swimmingly now and the more I think of what I read of it the higher does my opinion rise.
The gallant and indefatigable Colonel has secured a Pug and the best way to get it will be for Lewes to write a line to Langford to bring it to you or to say that he will call at P. N. Row for it. The animal is I believe under charge of Mr. Cherry 228 the veterinary of the Mounted Police, and I believe a squadron of that vigilant body is in daily watch over it, as the dog is well known to the Fancy and the responsibility of seeing to its safety has nearly crushed the Colonel. I do not think
Jhansi 229 or any other of his campaigns ever weighed so heavily upon him. He spent three days in Bethnal Green on the quest amid a very singular variety of ruffians, and when he brought it off in triumph he passed two hours at the house of a friend in the City lest the cabman should carry intelligence to Bethnal Green as to where the treasure was to be found.
The Colonel, I need not say, is a character as well as an excellent fellow and I think I must send him up to you some day to give his narrative which I am told occupies two hours.
I hope the dog will turn out what you want and justify the superhuman exertions of the worthy Colonel. If you knew him as well as I do you would sympathise with the fits of laughter which his adventures with the dog have caused to all of us.
One of his schemes for securing the safety of the animal when he was prostrated by hearing that you had gone abroad and could not receive the dog at once was to go himself with it down to Dorchester where he keeps his horses, and he also made an attempt to get a friend of mine who was coming down to Edinburgh to bring it with him to me. I trust Mr. Cherry and the Mounted Police have been able to protect the creature. I have ordered a photograph to be sent to me. We have been here for the last ten days and very enjoyable it is. I do not intend to be much in Edinburgh until November.
Tell Lewes I will write him soon. This is written in the drawing [room] full of people, your note having only reached me today, and I hear one of my brothers suggesting that a tray with the elements of natural conviviality should be brought up at once (a little earlier than usual) this being Sunday evening.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Colinsburgh, 21 September 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Colinsburgh, 21 September 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Gibliston | September 21/59.
My Dear George Eliot
I wish to have your new novel for the Magazine as from what I read of the story I feel confident that it will be admirably adapted for publication there. Publishing in that form we will give you at least as much as we would for it to publish in any other way.
In such a case it is very difficult to make up one's mind 316 as to what it is right and prudent to offer and my brother and I have been puzzling over the matter.
Our intention is to offer you Three Thousand Pounds for the right to publish the tale in the Magazine and for the copyright for four years after the completion of its publication there. 317
We hope that this sum will meet your views. The prospects of the book are great but there is no certainty under the sun. Who would have supposed that Clerical Scenes, admirable as they are, would not have been carried off in thousands by the flood tide of Adam's popularity.
In the Magazine we would not put any author's name, and it would be great fun to watch the speculations as to the author's life. 318 The style would be to me easily recognisable but no one, especially of the puffing writing and publishing order, would suppose that we would throw away such an advantage as putting the magic words by George Eliot at the head of a series of papers. In the long run however ours is the wisest course, as nothing equals the excitement of uncertainty.
If the above offer is satisfactory to you we would settle the matter after seeing the next batch of M.S. and arrange the dates of payment.
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Colinsburgh, 15 August 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Colinsburgh, 15 August 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 56.
Gebliston by Colinsburgh | Fife August 15/59.
My Dear George Eliot
I have the pleasure of inclosing a cheque 'a3200 for the second edition of Clerical Scenes. 256 I have not heard anything of the sales since the subscription but I think we must get through our edition. The Tales are so good and Adam Bede as you will have heard goes on gloriously. 257
How is the new Tale? 258 I long to see more of it. Every bit of what I read is distinctly before me now.
I am enchanted that the Pug proves a success. His portrait is very engaging. We have four little dogs here and four more entirely useless animals it would be impossible to find.
For the last few days we have had a very interesting visitor Captain Speke 259 lately from the Mountains of the Moon and what he believes to be I think with good grounds the fountains of the Nile. He is a fine manly unaffected specimen of an Englishman. He is very innocent of literature having since he went to India at 17 been devoted to wild sports and geographical discovery.
He has gone through dangers and suffering enough to disgust any ordinary man with the mere thought of Africa but he is determined to go back and carry out his discovery and has got a grant for the purpose. His reply to my remonstrance against his going again was unanswerable.
"Fancy my disgust if any vapouring boasting brat of a Frenchman went and got the credit of this discovery for France."
I hope to hear from you soon with good accounts of the new Novel and believe me
ever your truly
John Blackwood.
George Eliot Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to GE, Arbury, 2-4 December 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to GE, Arbury, 2-4 December 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Arbury December 2/59.
My Dear Madam
Your letter reached me yesterday morning a few minutes before starting for this place. There has been a misunderstanding on both sides and I am glad you have so written that I hope it can be cleared away and leave nothing but our long continued and cordial correspondence to think of. I am much vexed that anything I may have said or left unsaid should have hurt your feelings for a moment.
From not referring more specifically to your letter from Weymouth when I made our offer I suspect I had not your letter beside me, and our offer, subject to any modifications we might mutually agree upon, was more than we would have proposed as a certainty separate from publication in the Magazine. I cannot think what I said in any way depreciatory of the new novel as my proposition showed my confidence in it by wishing to publish in the way which would most surely make it stand on its own merits and by which the publisher ran the greatest risk. As to proposing that the Tale should be anonymous in the Magazine, it is our usual custom and is I think the wisest plan. We departed from it in the case of My Novel and What Will as they were a sort of series and Sir Edward wished Pisistratus to be prefixed to them. 413 I now see how with your susceptibilities painfully excited by your persecution the proposition might fall disagreeably upon you and I wish I had said more than I did in explanation.
I regretted the partial removal of the incognito but I never thought of ceasing to be your publisher on that account nor did I dream that such an idea would ever occur to you. 414 As to the effect of the spread of the secret on the new book there must be, and I know there are, different opinions. My opinion is that George Eliot has only to write her book quietly without disturbing herself about what people are saying and she can command success.
As to our not writing to the Times I think Lewes and you might give the Major and me more credit for knowing when it is worth while to speak on a matter of business affecting your interests or our own. I had written to Lewes twice expressing my opinion that it was better to let the rubbish die a natural death and adding that I would consult legal and literary friends whom afterwards I found still more strongly of the same opinion. I thought that the book had so died, and Lewes might have written to me further after my first notes as you were so bent on doing something. You have no idea what a bitter pill it was to me to write a civil note to that hound the editor of the Athenaeum, and I do not think you could have refrained from laughing had you heard the expletives with which the composition of the note was accompanied. I wrote it because I thought it might satisfy you and, the advertisement giving the ground, it seemed the most natural place for attaining the object without causing a fuss which I am sure it was desirable in every way to avoid.
I intend to be in London on Monday night and will be free on Wednesday or Thursday as may best suit Lewes and you. If we cannot agree in our opinions as to a fair sum for Maggie possibly we may arrange some plan for a certain payment in the first instance and further instalments according to the sale of the book.
It gives me pleasure to know from your last letter that I was mistaken as to the spirit of your reply to our offer and to think that your feeling is the same as my brother's and my own, that a connection which has gone on so pleasantly and advantageously to both parties should not be broken if it can be avoided.
December 4. The above was written on Friday when I found myself too late for the post, but my note to Lewes would warn you that you could not hear from me at once.
I need not describe this fine quaint old place to you, of all people in the world. Our hosts are very kind. Newdegate who is, as I daresay you know, tolerably persistent, insisted on my hunting yesterday. I had not hunted for some 10 years and intended merely to look on, but of course when the noise began forgot all prudence. However I was splendidly mounted and came to no grief, enjoying it much. Today I am stiff as a post horn and like Mr. Squeers can hardly hold a pen in my hand. 415 Our hosts are very kind people. 416
Address to me at the Cavendish, Jermyn St. and believe me, Dear Madam,
always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: John Blackwood to Charles Lee Lewes, Edinburgh, 9 December 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to Charles Lee Lewes, Edinburgh, 9 December 1878
Text: Copy in Blackwood Letter Book. Hitherto unpublished.
George St. | Edinburgh December 9th 1878.
My Dear Charles Lewes
I intended to write to thank you for kindly anticipating the wish I ventured to express that you should write to tell me how Mrs. Lewes was and now I am further obliged by your note of Saturday.
The blank pressure upon her must be terrible, but that she would bear up stoutly I knew if her physical health would only hold. The wear and tear of body and mind must try her sorely.
I am truly glad that she has got so good an aide as you to whom she could naturally look and who has grown up with the affection and respect which intercourse with her must always inspire.
Time will I trust bring her consolation and you will already feel as if you had lived a lifetime since your father's death. Although the loss is ever present I have always observed that after the great separation has taken place an enormous space of time seems to speedily to have elapsed. I suppose it is the total change in the whole train of thought that makes the time as well as the loss seem so vast.
I suppose his writing with and posting the Theophrastus was about the last business of his busy life and there is something solemn and fit in it. The M.S. is not long so that its standing in type will not matter and I propose setting it so as to be ready when she is able to turn her thoughts that way.
Write to me when you have time and tell me all you can of her.
Always yours truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
Charles Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John Blackwood to Charles Lee Lewes, Edinburgh, 31 December 1878
Text: Blackwood Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
George St. | Edinburgh December 31/78.
My Dear Charles Lewes
You should have heard from me sooner had I not been confined to the house partly from the weather and more from a confounded pain in the back which made anything but sitting in an easy chair at the fire irksome. However it is nothing and I seem all right now.
I enclose a formal note which will I doubt not enable you to settle any enquiries as to succession duty on Physiology of Common Life and Seaside Studies. Among your father's papers you will probably find an elaborate statement as to the Physiology of Common Life rendered on 10th April 1876.
I was greatly troubled to see by your letter that Mrs. Lewes was still so very poorly and it will be a real relief if you can give me a more favourable account of her. The Weather here has been very trying but now it is soft and mild and I hope she may be able to get into the Garden.
Will you give her my wife and daughter's warm regards as well as my own and with full wishes to yourself in the new Year I am
Always yours truly
John Blackwood.
Charles Lewes Esq.
P.S. I have got the bulk of Theophrastus and send you a proof. 476

John Blackwood to Alexander Main, Edinburgh, 13 November 1873
Text: Copy by George Simpson, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | Edinburgh November 13. 1873.
My Dear Sir
On looking at your preface to the New Edition of George Eliot's Sayings I see two passages (See copy of proof at page 496) which would never do and these I have marked. They are not sound nor are they just to her.
I am sure that nothing could be farther from your thoughts than to say that the teaching of her, the most condensed and unsermonising of Writers, could be best and most easily approached from a Volume of Extracts such as yours, but that is how these passages may most naturally be interpreted. There was a preface to the first edition and my advice is merely to add to it the fact that the second edition is further enriched by extracts from Middlemarch with the Author's consent. 882
It is a lucky thing I looked at this preface and indeed I might not have done so as I thought you were submitting everything to Mrs. Lewes.
Yours very Truly
(signed) John Blackwood.
Alexr Main Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: John and William Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 25 October 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
John and William Blackwood to GHL, St. Andrews, 25 October 1877
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Strathtyrum | St. Andrews | N.B.
October 25/77.
My Dear Lewes
The calculations of cost and produce of new edition of The Works of George Eliot have been sent over to me and I now beg to inclose formal offer for this edition.
I knew that the profits on it must be small unless the sale went beyond what we could reasonably hope for, but it was necessary to have such a standard edition round which I hope to see the more popular editions cluster and flourish.
You will see that we do not propose the lordship on each volume to commence until it has reached a sale of 500 copies and the reason for this is that it will take a sale of some 750 copies to pay the preliminary expences stereotyping etc.
With a somewhat similar edition of Lytton's works we had a painful warning to be cautious but in this case although a large sale cannot be looked for at first, my hope is that there will be a quiet but steady sale which will gradually bring in a steady little income. The book will I think be as handsome as well could be and form I hope a permanent and creditable presentment of George Eliot's Works.
Willie sent me Mrs. Lewes' charming letter to him and I rejoice to think that her stay in your country home has done you both so much good. For her sake I shall always think of that lovely place with pleasure and gratitude. The constant temptation to wander out of doors is the great thing in the Country but the dear old Priory has its pleasantnesses too and I hope this will find you comfortably established there for the winter. The Books, Friends, and other comforts not exactly such as The Bailie sighed for in "the Saut Market" will make some amends for the woods and walks of Witley. Our weather has been so sadly broken that I should have been frightened to press Mrs. Lewes to come here at this season. We had nearly continuous rain for a month at what should have been our midsummer. In the midst of it my daughter gazing gloomily out of the window exclaimed "We might as well be in Edinburgh." This disparaging allusion to the Town which contains 45 George St. and 3 Randolph Cres[cen]t rather riled me, but in the circumstances I let it pass. Since that deluge we have had broken weather but some very fine days and I hope your last days in the country have been as bright as it has been with us today.
I am very pleased that you like the translation of the Jewish Rabbi's tribute to Deronda so much. To me it reads as a very striking and original pamphlet and I hope the press will take it up.
I have been very remiss in correspondence of late but I have been constantly thinking of writing to Mrs. Lewes or you. The fact is I knew that this edition would not afford such a sum as I should like to give the author for any edition of her works and that worried and made me put off writing. You however know as much about paper and print as I do and have also I think our calculations for printing etc. and will not I hope be disappointed.
ever yours truly
John Blackwood.
G. H. Lewes Esq.
P.S. My Uncle has sent me this to forward to you and told me to add anything that he had omitted to allude to in his letter. The only point that occurs to me is as to the edition of Romola published by Smith and Elder at 2/6. I think my Uncle's understanding was that their edition was or is to be withdrawn as it would not be pleasant to have it run in opposition to our editions at 10/- and at 3/6. Their stereotype plates of it would not I suppose serve for our reissue but should they not be transferred to us? Please give my best thanks to Mrs. Lewes for writing me so charming an answer to my letter, and I hope to send her a further memo of Deronda sales beginning of next month. Mrs. Lewes is quite right in supposing that the kind of holiday I like is commencing now and I have already had two or three cheering gallops.
W. B.

James Thomson to GE, London, 20 June 1874
MS: Alderman Library, University of Virginia. Hitherto unpublished.
Tachbrook St., S.W. | 20 June '74.
Dear Madam,
In my note of Thursday I omitted to qualify, as I intended, the general statements by the distinct admission, of what however is in all likelihood quite obvious, that the poem in question was the outcome of much sleepless hypochondria. I am aware that the truth of midnight does not exclude the truth of noonday, though one's nature may lead him to dwell in the former rather than in the latter.
Pray pardon me for troubling you on so small a matter.
Yours very respectfully,
James Thomson

Dublin Core:Title: James Thomson to GE, London, 18 June 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
James Thomson to GE, London, 18 June 1874
MS: Alderman Library, University of Virginia. Hitherto unpublished.
Tachbrook St. | Pimlico, S.W. | 18 June '74.
Dear Madam,
Having been absent for several days, I am only now able to thank you for your very kind letter, 111 for your generous expression of praise, and for your yet more generous trust, though this I fear will prove to be misplaced.
I have no Byronic quarrel with my fellows, whom I find all alike crushed under the iron yoke of Fate; and few of whom I can deem worse than myself, while so many are far better. I certainly have an affectionate and even joyful recognition of the willing labours of those who have striven to alleviate our lot, though I cannot see that all their efforts have availed much against the primeval curse of our existence. Has the world been the better or the worse for the life of even such a man as Jesus? I cannot judge, but on the whole I fear considerably the worse. None the less I can love and revere his memory. A physician saves a life, and does well; yet perchance it were better for the patient himself and for others that he now died. But it is not for me to introduce such thoughts to you.
I ventured to send you a copy of the verses (as I ventured to send another to Mr. Carlyle) because I have always read, whether rightly or wrongly, through all the manifold beauty and delightfulness of your works, a character and an intellectual destiny akin to those of that grand and awful Melancholy of Albrecht D'fcrer which dominates the City of my poem.
I cannot conclude without expressing to you my gratitude for many hours of exquisite enjoyment. I am, Madam, with profound respect,
Yours sincerely,
James Thomson
(B.V.).

Taplow House | Bideford | 26 September.
Sir,
A shadow holds out a hand to me. I try to take it and it fades away. Who are you? I do not ask from curiosity. You send me your book. I tell you how much it has affected me and I express my hope that the George Eliot who has touched me so keenly may allow me to know in him something more than the writer of the volumes on my table. You send me no answer. 1190
Keep yourself to yourself if you please -- but I should value your acquaintance beyond that of most men if I was so happy as to possess it.
Yours
J. A. Froude.
