Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Walter Cross, Rickmansworth, [17 September 1875]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Walter Cross^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Walter Cross, Rickmansworth, [17 September 1875]
MS: Yale. Envelope: J. W. Cross Esq | Weybridge Heath | Weybridge | Surrey. Postmarks: RICKMANSWORTH | C | SP 18 | 75; B | WATFORD | SP 19 | 75; WEYBRIDGE STATION | SP 20 | 75. Hitherto unpublished.
The Elms, Rickmansworth | Sunday.
My dear Nephew
From aunt and self all good wishes rest upon the new Firm! 310 I won't say may you get your deserts as that may be a whipping; but may you be as prosperous as rational desires can prefigure!
I wish I could give better accounts of Madonna; but this low lying Thames Valley is decidedly enervating, and added to her depression of spirits, it has counteracted even the splendid weather we have had of late. We shall only stay one day in town and then start for the Welsh Mountains. Perhaps their bracing air (and complete idleness) may set her up for the winter. Nor can I give much better accounts of your's truly. Our life is so unvaried here that there is absolutely nothing to write about except health! Yes, by the way, there was one variety the other day in the escape from what might have been a serious accident. Madonna was coming to meet me at the Watford Station on my return from town, 311 when a runaway horse in a brewer's cart, dashed up against ours -- broke our shaft and strained the springs but did no other damage! When I learned about it you can imagine "the turn" it gave me. Madonna was perfectly calm throughout, and not really frightened.
It is sad to hear of dear Emily not getting strong again. Why is love so little therapeutic? and why are nice people so seldom strong?
Charles and Gertrude are at St. Moritz and write rapturously of the Engadine and the weather. Our dearest love to all
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Walter Cross, London, [22 February 1877]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Walter Cross^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Walter Cross, London, [22 February 1877]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
My dear Nephew
Your loving and suffering aunt -- who begs me to say that she was not too subdued by pain to enjoy the sweet perfume of the flowers you sent, and the sweet feeling which moved the sender -- is of the opinion that the 2000 £ 612 had better be invested without any risk -- so we leave you to choose the most favorable Scotch and English Debentures.
Dr. Clark says there is no sort of doubt that all her late discomfort and present pain arise from the renal calculus. The dear man came up last night after his late dinner and long day's work to see her and this morning Mrs. Clark called and left some fine Scotch oatmeal for gruel. Clark hearing that she wished for Scotch oatmeal exclaimed to think of the hundreds of Scotchmen who if they heard George Eliot wanted oatmeal wouldn't hurry up with sacks of it to her door! And so his wife was the buglewoman of the Scotch corps!
My gout decidedly better and to-day the aunt is in less pain. Altogether it has been a much milder attack than the former ones.
Yours ever
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Stuart Blackie, Richmond, 19 December 1855
Dublin Core:Subject: John Stuart Blackie^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Stuart Blackie, Richmond, 19 December 1855
MS: Yale.
Park Shot | Richmond | 19 December 1855.
My dear Sir
Your letter gave me great pleasure: to be praised by a man of genius is worth endless columns of newspaper laudation. I am the more sensitive to your's because I have long been an admirer of your powers.
I really think your Faust is worth retranslating, in spite of the terrible labor which translation of such a work must involve. 270
Yes, the liaison with the Frau von Stein did become more than platonic, as you will see I quietly indicate in one passage; 271 but I was forced to keep that part in a subdued light because the British public would have gone into fits at the open avowal. His letters leave no doubt of the fact.
Thanks for the Sonnet. -- I was glad to hear of Sch'f6ll. What an excellent creature! And Saupe also. Though I speak German so badly that I am amazed Sch'f6ll should have entertained any hopes of the book. However the Germans seem delighted. Varnhagen has written to me in the highest terms about it. He has recommended its translation, but before he did so I had already concluded a treaty with Duncker of Berlin who will employ a very competent translator. 272 The book has met with far more success than I ventured to hope -- 900 copies have been sold in six weeks. But sale is only one kind of test. The approbation of men like yourself is far more valuable. Your good word will have great influence in Edinburgh.
If any suggestions occur to you which would enable me to improve a second edition they would be very gratefully accepted by
Yours very faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
I have been much interested in your pamphlet. 273 But will Auld Reekie be moved?

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Simon, Shottermill, 25 May 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: John Simon^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Simon, Shottermill, 25 May 1871
Text: Copy made by Edwin Mallard Everett.
Brookbank Cottage | Shotter Mill | nr Petersfield | 25 May 71.
My dear Simon
Dr. Payne 32 who is a candidate for a post at your Hospital wishes me to say a word in his favor, and although I cannot speak as one having authority I can't refuse to bear conscientious testimony to the real worth and ability concealed under his modest and unimpressive exterior. You will be the best judge of his qualifications -- professionally -- I can only say that I believe him to be a thoroughly good man with honest work in him. That is a kind of man rare as you know!
We are here amid lovely scenes and, what is more precious, intense solitude. Lord Houghton laughs at us for our St. Simeon Stylites kind of existence, and many other friends marvel that we can run away from London with all its season gaieties and our very [curious] wish to bury ourselves in the country. But you can understand it.
I am hard at work -- digging at the foundations of things with but a distant prospect of reaching the artesian well. Meanwhile it gives life a purpose and the afternoon ramble a keener edge of enjoyment. Remember me to Helps whom I suppose you see often and whom I never see now.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Sibree, Jr.^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Sibree, Jr., Richmond, 2 April [1856]
MS: Indiana University.
Park Shot | Richmond | April 2.
My dear Sir
Our friend Miss Evans has spoken of you in such terms that I should be very glad if our mutual interests could establish an arrangement. I have three boys, from the ages of thirteen downwards, whom I should like to place under your care. But I should warn you that my project is to take the two elder boys to Germany in about another year, if my means admit of it, so that it is very possible their stay with you would be shorter than would enable you to do full justice to yourself. If however you are not indisposed to take them with that contingency, and if the terms which would remunerate you are such as a literary man, who has to look closely to his expenditure, can afford to pay, it would be gratifying to me to know my boys were in such excellent hands.
The two eldest are at present at the Bayswater Grammar School. 286 The youngest is at home 287 and is very backward, because for some years his health was delicate, and I did not like his being at school. The elder boys are clever, and eager to get on. They are already tolerably grounded in Latin, and French, and have commenced German.
An answer at your earliest convenience will oblige,
Yours very truly
G. H. Lewes.
John Sibree Esq.

Text: The Letters of John Fiske, ed. Ethel Fiske Fisk, New York, Macmillan, 1940, p. 268.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday.
My dear Mr. Fiske 867
Yesterday an American called here stating that he had an introduction from you. I was out, but I write now to beg you to decline all applications for introductions. We are forced to see so many more people than is good for our health, and therefore wish as much as possible to limit our circle. It is only in case of people exceptionally interesting, like yourself, that we willingly enlarge our circle. I was obliged in politeness to ask your friend Mr. [Jeremiah] Curtin, 868 when I met him with you; but habitually I never ask strangers to come. You understand this, don't you? It is not unsociableness but feebleness.
Ever yours truly,
G. H. Lewes.

867 John Fiske (1842-1901) was assistant  librarian at Harvard 1872-1879. In reply to a letter, GHL had written him that they were rusticating but would like to see him on their return to town. By chance he met Fiske and his friend Curtin at Tr 'fcbner's shop in Ludgate, 21 October 1873. (GHL Diary.) In a letter to his wife Fiske describes GHL as old and feeble looking, weazen and little, and ever so homely. "But when he opens his mouth to speak, he becomes transfigured in a moment. . . . His manners are fascinating beyond all description, and he took my heart captive at once. I never before saw a man who seemed so full of the divine indescribable something that makes a man different from common men -- and all this in spite of his homely and meagre and puny physique. I don't wonder that he captivated George Eliot; I think he is just the man that any woman who had an eye for the spirituelle would fall in love with." (The Letters of John Fiske, pp. 260-261.)
868 Jeremiah Curtin (1840?-1906),  American folklorist, a classmate of Fiske's, Harvard 1863, who had studied for six years in eastern Europe and was spending a year collecting folklore in the British Isles.

GHL to John Dennis, London, 10 May 1866
MS: Yale.
The Fortnightly Review, | Office -- 193, Piccadilly.
0 May 1866.
My dear Dennis 707
If any expression of my belief in your scrupulous conscientiousness and punctuality in discharge of all duties devolving on you can be of assistance to you as a candidate for the editorship of the periodical you speak of I shall be happy to give it. I set my face against testimonials in general, because they are commonly insincere, and are mostly written without any knowledge of the qualifications of the candidate. But I have had you assisting me in the [Fortnightly Review] so long and with such entire satisfaction that I do not hesitate to express my belief in your doing well whatever you undertake. So satisfied have I been that I should greatly regret losing your services, though of course I would not for a moment stand in the way of your taking a more advantageous position.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Chapman, Dresden, 23 July 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: John Chapman^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Chapman, Dresden, 23 July 1858
MS: Medical Library, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
B. Waisenhaus Strasse | Dresden | 23 July 1858.
My dear Chapman
Here we are deliciously settled in a magnificent suite of rooms looking on a pretty all'e9e where nothing but sky and trees, and promenaders are to be seen, and birds to be heard -- carriages not having the right of way -- and for this we pay 18/- a week! Is it not to make the mental mouth water? We quite regret that we can only stay here till the end of August, for the lodgings are so charming, the place so agreeable, and the pictures in the gallery so divine that it will be heartrending to tear oneself away.
Munich we left without any regret, unless it was to leave so many kind and illustrious friends. Polly, although very popular, did not enjoy Munich; but I learned so much there from Liebig, Von Siebold, Bischoff, Harless, 1164 and others that the place will be ever memorable to me. Polly saw Strauss the day before we left, and was much pleased with him. He called while I was at a meeting of physiologists to whom Jacubowitzsch 1165 showed his 50,000 preparations of the spinal column!
On leaving Munich we had an exquisite tour through the Tyrol, down the Danube to Vienna, where we stayed three days, and called on Hyrtl, 1166 the great anatomist whose injections are the marvel of Europe. He was very friendly, and quite pleased to show Marian preparations which no woman -- not even his wife -- had ever expressed a wish to see. From Vienna we went to Prague -- the most splendid city in Germany -- where we stayed a day -- and then came through the "Saxon Switzerland" to this place, having had an intoxicating draught of beauty -- lakes, mountains, and valleys such as will long live in the memory.
She has not been well since we left, and in Munich was for one week in bed, but here at Dresden she seems in capital condition and will I trust continue so.
I have nearly finished the article on German novels, 1167 but unless you much wish to have it before, I should prefer keeping it till our return on the 1 Sept. because meanwhile I may have fresh books to add, or modifications to make. If however you want the paper earlier I will send it when required. As far as I can guess it will run to six or eight and twenty pages, but extract type puts me out, and it may be much less.
Let us hear all about you and anyone else in whom we are interested. Spencer I suppose is at Treport. Do you know anything of the new Quarterly that is to be published by Bentley? 1168 My authority is Galignani. Have you heard from the Calls? Where are the Lintons? "These be questions!" -- Polly who is writing in the next room shouts, in answer to my question whether she has any message to send "only my kindest regards."
Ever faithfully yours,
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Chapman, [London, 18 July 1853]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Chapman^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Chapman, [London, 18 July 1853]
MS: University of California, Los Angeles. Endorsed: G. H. Lewes | July 18th 1853.
My dear Sir
I confess to having been annoyed by your proposal (though your last removes the annoyance) and for these reasons: --
It was I who indoctrinated you with the advantage and necessity of limiting your contributors, and have -- in my own case -- always written within the limits -- allowing you indeed to cut out and even materially injure my contributions (as in Mad. von Kr'fcdener 174) although during 10 years contributing to the Edinburgh I never was limited at all and in the British and foreign Review have had even 70 pages when I wanted it. 175 I still maintain the principle of short articles. But brevity is a relative term, and to limit a paper such as the one I scheme would be to stultify it; therefore from the first I declined to think of limits. It has cost me a great deal of severe thinking, patient research, and even dissection; it is a subject, I conceive, of the very highest importance and I do not intend that it shall suffer from any procrustean tyranny. I mean to write an essay not a volume; if the essay extend beyond the limits which would be advisable in a review under any circumstances, I shall enlarge it with more illustrations and publish it as a volume; but the space it will occupy as an essay or article I do not know.
It will not be ready for the October number in any case. This proposition however I will make. Should the article extend beyond 60 pages (I don't think it will reach 50, but it is impossible to say -- and my object in this, as in all cases, is brevity for the sake of effect) you are at liberty to decline it, and I will then do something else with it. 176 The only reason I have for wishing any understanding at all about it is that if written for publication in a Review it will be written in the plural editorial form, and written with more uniform brevity of illustration and citation. As it is historical as well as expository you can imagine how such a condition would operate -- a phrase taking the place of a section in a book.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

My dear Blackwood

On a second reading I find it -- as two friends also do -- a very remarkable production, eloquent and highly interesting even to outsiders. By the way tell Lockhart that his opening number 721 kept me in one gurgle of delight -- so very different from the constant grating of "A Woman Hater"! Jonas Lie also was pleasant. Now we are reading Mad. D'Agoult's M'e9moires 722 -- not for her sake but for the sake of her daughter Mad. Wagner.

"Describe the Horse."

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Witley, 6 August 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Witley, 6 August 1878
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
August 78.
My dear Blackwood
The cordial urgency of your letter excited a strong impulse in me to decide on starting at once for Strathtyrum. But second thought, third thought, and all succeeding thought made it less and less feasible, till this morning we came to the final decision that it was not to be ventured on. You do not realize my state. The parallel you suggest of your own is not exact. You came back to your peaceful home. I shall leave mine to undertake a journey most formidable (even when we are in condition we have lately been unable to stand long railway journeys, and should be forced to reach Edinburgh in three stages) and at the end of it have the excitement -- pleasurable yet to me very telling -- of some days of friendly intercourse. I do not feel capable of bearing either the one or the other. You can do your three hours work of a morning. If I could even read an amusing book for three hours I should consider myself strong enough to come. But I can't work at all, and can't read for more than an hour. Walking is what I do best -- (no, sleeping is my forte!) -- even listening to Mrs. Lewes reading soon wearies me.
Now when I say that I have been forced to avoid all intercourse with friends -- have not even had the children on a visit -- and could not bring myself to go up to London either for the marriage of a friend or a bit of important business -- you will understand how formidable appears the prospect of a journey to Scotland, much as I should enjoy it! I dare say much of this is imaginary -- but it is part of my malady and imaginary evils are very real in certain states. Much also is certainly not imaginary -- I mean the effects of railway travelling and the excitement of visiting. The other day we drove to Haslemere but when we reached the bottom of Tennyson's hill, courage failed and we turned home again.
Abbotsford and Strathtyrum must therefore be unvisited this summer; but be assured that our disappointment thereat is great, and that we look forward eagerly to better luck next year.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, Godalming | (Telegrams to be addressed:
Witley Station) | Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
I write instead of telegraphing, because there is more to say than can be conveniently put into a telegram.
Any day will suit us, that is most convenient to yourself; only Wednesdays and Saturdays are in this respect the best that on those days we get our Fish from London! Barring that, one day is the same as another.
Then as to trains, which may not be very convenient for you. If you can spare us a long day -- which however with your press of London friends and engagements may not be easy -- there is a train which leaves Waterloo at 11.30 and reaches this 12.43. We dine at 1.30 and you could then lunch or dine with us, rest during the heat of the day, have a delicious drive in the cool, back at 7.30 or so to supper, and home by the 8.25 train. But if you can't spare all this time, there is a train from Waterloo at 2.35 reaching this at 3.54. We could then dine at 6.30 and you return by the 8.25; or if you came by the 11.20 and lunched with us you could return by the 4.13, or 7.5.
These are the alternatives -- choose the one which best suits your engagements and be sure of a hearty welcome whichever it is!
This place is Paradise. Or it would be if Madonna were only free from pain, and the bloom only return to her cheek.
Let us know when to expect you -- and with kindest regards to Mrs. Blackwood and the fair Ebonina. 711 Believe me
Yours ever
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Weymouth, [6 September 1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Weymouth, [6 September 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
East Street | Weymouth | Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
Your letter, with the checque, was sent on to me here where we are rusticating and zoologizing, and I hope getting up some health to stock us for the autumn and winter. We tried North Wales, and then ran across here; and although Weymouth does not turn out what we wanted, we made a discovery yesterday which will repay all. G.E. is in high spirits, having found a Mill and Millstream to his heart's content; and we are going to hire a laborer's cottage for a day or two, and live a poetical primitive life, the results of which will appear in Maggie -- who by the way becomes more fascinating than ever, and Tom more intensely boyish.
We really must see the Colonel and hear the history from his own mouth -- nay he ought to see Pug -- for I venture to say that hitherto he has not seen that noble beast -- but only a larval form! The Pug he saw was the Pug of the Knave of Clubs. Since his introduction into literary society he has developed an aristocratic audacity and refinement, not to mention originality of genius, of which he before had no gleam. He was un Pug incompris, in Bethnal Green. Seriously, he is 100 per cent more lively and handsome than he was when we had him. I don't think he could have fallen into more admiring hands: he makes us shout with laughter continually; and we miss him terribly -- for we dared not bring him away with us.
I haven't seen Maga, and can't therefore give any opinion of its contents, except that "I am given to understand" it is peculiarly brilliant and profound in the metaphysical department! No, I am not doing anything for that respected periodical; but I have got a French book which may be available. You were to send me some book about Sea Weeds Nature printed 280 -- but that will do when I return which will be very shortly. Indeed our movements are so uncertain that unless you write within the next week, you had better address to Wandsworth.
Adam follows us about everywhere. By the way your friend Quirk has turned up again and this time with a pointblank question to G.E. begging to know if it were true that she was the writer! We were naturally indignant at this repeated proof of his want of delicacy but as he had attended her sister in her final illness, and spoke in her name, we were unwilling to let him go quite unanswered so I wrote to say that "I was not aware Mr. Liggins had ever directly claimed the authorship; but even if he had the word of honorable and responsible men emphatically denying that he was the author, was enough for all sensible people." He is evidently intensely annoyed at having Liggins no longer to patronize as the author; and at the Coventry people all turning their backs on Liggins. I told him his letter overstepped the bounds of etiquette and that I only answered him at all because of Mrs. Lewes's sister.
Before we left town there was an American Literary Agent 281 who offered 'a31,200 for a story in one small volume, to be published in the Century a New York newspaper; but we wished America might get it! To-day a letter has come from the editor of a "Parish Magazine" 282 -- and really G.E. was almost more likely to be tempted by that audience than by the New Yorkers. Indeed he is so interested by the letter, that he begs me to enclose it for your perusal -- but you must not forget to return it when you write. The first volume of Maggie is ended or nearly, but he is going back to insert fresh details and passages. But of that he will write probably after our cottage experience. With his best regards believe me,
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.
G.E. says will you please write a polite note to Erskine Clarke and say that although he sympathizes very strongly with his efforts, his cooperation is impossible from want of leisure.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 5 February 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 5 February 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 44.
Holly Lodge | Wimbledon Park | Wandsworth
February 1859.
My dear Blackwood
Your letter with the checque arrived this morning, for which thanks.
GE was both greatly amused and greatly gratified at the Cabinet Maker's verdict. Having already been a clergyman of puseyite tendencies and large family, he is now a carpenter and doubtless will soon be a farmer and methodist. It is a great compliment when a writer's dramatic presentation is accepted as actual experience.
The subscription is surprisingly small -- less than that of "Clerical Scenes" -- but if the book is not a hit I will never more trust my judgement in such matters.
E. thanks you for the promise to send him any private opinions which may be agreeable. Perhaps also you will send the "Times" should that "publication" notice the carpenter. E. does not see the "Times" -- nor do I, though I did see the notice of Seaside Studies by accident, and hope some good may come of it. Have you seen the notice in the "Edinburgh"? I hear there is one of the "Physiology" in the "North British." 14
We are in the moil and turmoil of moving into our new house -- of which the address is as above, but shall not be settled there till Thursday so that proofs or letters may come to Richmond till Wednesday. Apropos of proofs I haven't yet received that of Food and Drink part III -- I hope my m.s. arrived safely.
In answer to your question about a light article what say you to the notice of Miss Austen, about which we spoke during our pleasant walk on the banks of the Thames last year? If you would like that, please ask Langford to get me Bentley's edition of Miss Austen's novels, and send them to Wimbledon. 15
I have not had time to go to the Row, nor to read a line of Maga, nor indeed to do anything but worry myself with upholsterers, land-lords, and other organisms. My frogs mutely reproach me for neglect. My microscope gathers the dust of disuse. My hand forgets its cunning, and does nothing but write checques and open purses. In short, life is a very dilapidated, fragmentary, chaotic, impossible thing just now. "Would it were done."
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Holly Lodge | 27 December 1859.
My dear Blackwood
A dismal Christmas and a miserable New Year to you! May Maga perish; and Maggie not "repay perusal"! Voil'e0!
I suppose you got Mrs. Lewes's letter 489 addressed to the Cavendish? She is now in deep water (and deep feeling) and is sailing away at a steady rate.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 26 March 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: How are stereos. to be sent? How are the 2 copies to be sent? Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Wimbledon Park | Wandsworth | 26 March 59.
My dear Blackwood
I thought myself lucky when the news came that the m.s. of the Bedesman had not gone the way of the m.s., but of course never had any idea of receiving it in that superb shape -- c'est faire noblement les choses, Monsieur! and I wish your good nature could have had the gratification of witnessing the pleasure with which G.E. turned over the pages, and recalled the feelings with which they were written.
By the way I suppose you saw or heard (as I did) that Adam Bede was quoted in the House of Commons the other night -- that looks like popularity indeed.
I have received a letter from Brockhaus, the German publisher who is to issue a translation of the Physiology, and he wants to know whether you would let him have casts of the woodcuts, he to pay the expence thereof. If there is any objection to this say No because he can well afford to get the illustrations done in Germany; but if there is no objection it would be an economy to him.
He also says that it will be necessary for you to send two copies of the work -- one for Leipsig and one for Berlin -- to secure copyright. If you need any agent in this matter he will act for you, but he supposes you must already know how this is to be done, as you have done it with other books. What answers shall I give? Kind regards to the Major. Believe me
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 25 August [1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Saturday 25 August.
My dear Blackwood
Your checque and letter arrived in due course.
I am glad you like Mad Wits. At present I am preparing a paper of a more popular character -- "Seeing is Believing" -- with a view to make people understand the difference between a fact and an inference. It is with especial reference to the monstrous folly of Table-turning and Spirit-rapping which has revived -- and which the "Cornhill Mag." has the immorality (I can call it nothing else) to assist by a paper in its favor, although Thackeray does not pretend to believe it. 617 People imagine that the "respectability" of a witness is a guarantee that he saw what he relates; whereas in truth he relates a great deal more than he saw, than was possible for any one to see. He saw the table move, but he did not, and could not, see that "no physical force, could have moved it" -- that is pure inference, and is based on his ignorance as to how the table was moved.
My paper embraces the various aspects of evidence, and only takes table-turning as one sample. Would you like it for Maga?
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 20 April [1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | 20th April.
My dear Blackwood
If you could set afloat a paragraph to my disadvantage I have no doubt that Mr. Hempworth Dixon 111 would cordially open the columns of the "Athenaeum" to the same; but to no other. Nor have I any relations with the pressgang here, nor any wish to cultivate them, certainly not to ask them to do anything for me. If you think the Edinburgh Papers might advantageously be employed in this matter you can turn a sentence somewhat to this effect. "In spite of their numerous works in all branches of science the Germans are always ready to honor those of foreign writers. The well known firm of Brockhaus at Leipsic announces a translation of Lewes's Physiology of Common Life; and we understand that the celebrated Professor Victor Carus 112 has offered to be the translator. This is a great compliment to our country-man."
Pray let me see a proof of the Pond.
Enclosed is a letter from G.E. I agree with him that the Liggins myth is getting so serious that it would be very desirable for you to step in; and by saying that you don't intend to answer other questions that will save you in future.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 17 March [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 17 March [1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Wimbledon Park | Wandsworth. 17 March.
My dear Blackwood
Your letters are a succession of surprises. The success surpasses all expectation formed by E. or myself. It is intensely gratifying -- not merely as success -- but in a purely moral and literary point of view -- showing that truth will move even the unthinking public as well as the thoughtful and feeling public. I confess I had never any doubts about the success of the book among the best readers; but it was always dubious how a work which flattered none of the reigning tastes or prejudices would be accepted by those who are led by these tastes and prejudices. The effect upon G.E. has been almost sad, instead of joyful -- but the sadness lies near joy -- and you will understand the effect on such a nature.
Respecting the edition or editions, as I am referred to, I suggest this. By all means print the 2 volumes at 12/ -- that will be ready, and is certain to be wanted sooner or later. But as printing small editions is very expensive -- a ruinous proceeding in most cases -- I should only do that if the demand made it imperative. My view of the case is this: with a history, or biography, which is purchased by private persons, there is an obvious unfairness to the purchasers of the first expensive edition, in rapidly bringing out a cheap edition -- or rather there is the appearance of unfairness, since in point of fact a publisher is at liberty to affix his own price. But in the case of a novel, almost exclusively purchased by the libraries, this does not obtain. The libraries prefer three volumes, and they never take a copy more than they are forced to take. Many libraries can't afford 31/6, which would gladly give 12/- and thus accommodate subscribers. Then too private persons gladly purchase a book which has delighted them, if at 12/-. Voil'e0!
As you say nothing more about the "Food and Drink" question (mooted by the Major) I conclude you have settled to stint the public of the 8 pages in consideration of previous and succeeding excesses! 72
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 17 August [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 17 August [1859]
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 56.
Holly Lodge | Southfields, Wandsworth | August 17th.
My dear Blackwood
The proof I return to Edinburgh, as the shortest route.
Owen 466 I will ponder on; and Nature's Seaweeds -- with the materials from Bradbury 467 -- may turn out a practicable article. It is true I know as little as possible about seaweeds, for one who has had so much to do with them. But what then? Is a reviewer called upon to know anything? doesn't he know everything in virtue of his egotism? If facts fail him, is there not the moral consciousness out of the depths of which he can construct immense wisdom? "Base is the slave who knows"! 468
Your picture of your daily life is suggestive of pleasant hours; but I see you don't turn the dogs to account. Four dogs! my dear fellow, how can four dogs be without attraction? I would rather hear Mrs. Blackwood's opinion on that point, not believing in your ability to edit a dog. Perhaps the dull dogs have wearied you with too many contributions to make you appreciate justly the genus dog. When you have seen Pug your mind will be more expanded, your sensibilities heightened. Till then believe me
Ever your canine
G. H. Lewes

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | August 16.
My dear Blackwood
By this post goes the article. 611 It is short, but contains all that I had to say on the subject, and I hope will not be uninteresting.
The statement of the sales of Physiology is beyond my expectation. Now that there is real hope of the medical students taking to it, the sale is likely to be steady for some years. The balance will be acceptable forthwith.
Mrs. Lewes will go over the Mill and see if any corrections are needed. Except misprints there is little I think to alter.
Pug is not blind after all. It was only a cold in his eye.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 10 August 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 10 August 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | 10 August 1860.
My dear Blackwood
I did not think I should be ready for this month, but as you are in danger of running short you may count upon me. It shall be done. I have had my holiday now and propose to make Maga's back creak with my weight!
Rejoice with me, as I know you will, that my oldest boy has come in at the head of the poll -- although one of his competitors was 23 years of age, and another had already been in a situation. I don't know whether I told you he was to compete for a place in the Secretary's office of the Post Office? 608 He is now launched -- and off my hands. Both his mother and myself are naturally very joyous thereat. We have him still with us, and until he marries hope always to have him.
Laurence will no doubt gladly make you a copy of the portrait. When I see him tomorrow I will ask.
What a sight that review must have been! Arthur's Seat and sunshine would be enough to make even the awkward squad look splendid but such a corps and such a crowd of spectators may well have made the perfervidum Scotus tingle!
Schmitz I saw in London. He has daughters growing up and does not therefore take puberty into his family circle.
We are looking forward to the Major's visit. I wonder whether the "great secret" will be really a surprise or not.
Mrs. Lewes sends her kindest regards to both and Believe me
Ever yours
G.H.L.

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 1 March [1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Wandsworth | 1 March.
My dear Blackwood
Harpers have agreed to give 300 'a3 for the early sheets on condition of the work not being published here till 10 days after delivery to them of the last sheet -- as they can have the last sheet when it is sent to us for correction, this will not I presume delay you a single day. Tauchnitz has also agreed to give 'a3100 for the reprint in Germany.
Will you ask Mr. Simpson to take these matters in hand, and see that the sheets be sent to Sampson Low as they are worked off -- and to Williams and Norgate volume by volume? The American people are ticklish to deal with and unless they get their sheets regularly and in time, they may object to pay. I have a written stipulation from Sampson
Low that no portion shall appear in America until the whole is published here.
Maga is capital.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 1 April 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, 1 April 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Holly Lodge, Southfields | 1 April 1859.
My dear Blackwood
I don't know how far my heathenism might be an objection to my writing an article on Owen and his Discoveries, but I know that my ignorance would be a very formidable objection against such an attempt. Indeed there are very few men in England at all competent; the paleontologists are not sufficiently versed in comparative anatomy and the anatomists seldom know enough of paleontology.
Moreover I doubt whether an interesting paper could be written on Owen at the present time; all that would interest the public has been told over and over again -- quite recently in the North British and Quarterly Reviews. 438 I so greatly admire and like Owen, that I would rejoice at all honor he might anywhere receive; but I don't think he affords you or me a chance just now, of expressing more than a general admiration.
If you will tell Langford to put himself in communication with Tr'fcbner on Brockhaus's affairs (Tr'fcbner acts as his agent) I will write to Leipzig today to send them word to that effect. 439 I concluded that "Ponds" had swamped you, by my not getting a proof.
Should the "Thunderer" 440 nod and shake Olympus, please remember we don't see that majestic person. I observe the West. Rev. has a long article on "Adam Bede." The more the merrier. Plus on est de fous et plus on rit. 441
By the way I must tell you of an honor which has come to your physiologist -- Victor Carus, 442 a celebrated German Anatomist, has offered to translate the "Physiology" for Brockhaus. That will have good effect on our public, when known, meanwhile it is a pleasant tribute.
Ever faithfully yours,
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [7 February 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: Febr. 7/60. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Wandsworth | Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
Proofs of the "Mill" go by this post, and the first day I go into town I will take the m.s. of volume 2. The first proofs read delightfully tempting I think; and Mrs. Lewes strengthened and encouraged by your letter thinks so too. There never was so diffident and desponding an author, since the craft first began! -- By the way -- you ought to know -- who was the first author? and who reviewed him? and what did his copyright fetch?
I also send proof of "Physiology" and the final chapter with Preface. How will you manage the preface in those sets when the first volume has already been sold? I feel a pang at parting with this work, although I can't help rejoicing at the thought of its being safely brought to an end. It has occupied two years -- not to mention the previous years of preparation.
Sir Edward has not given any intimation of himself. Probably he has forgotten all about it.
The dedication was gratifying but one can't paragraph it.
The story of the "Mill" gets more intensely interesting with every chapter and the third volume is a novel in itself. Mrs. Lewes begs her kind regards to be sent to you and the Major, and believe me
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [6 August 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
You who know everybody in Edinburgh, can doubtless help me to a decision in the following matter.
My second son, aged 16, is about to leave Switzerland in October and I intend him to spend a final year at the High School, Edinburgh under Schmitz's 599 own eye. But for this it is necessary to find some family where he could be received at a not too high a sum, and where besides his board and lodging, he would find some man willing and capable of looking after him in every respect except that of tuition. I want him to have the advantages of family life; and at the same time to have someone over him to replace me.
I have already heard of one place which might be suitable; but before concluding I should like to run down to Edinburgh, and see for myself the kind of person to whom I was entrusting the boy. In this case it would be an advantage for me to have two or three to choose from. Do you know of anyone -- NOT Calvinistic -- but Episcopalian and gentlemanly -- who would be likely to undertake such a charge? Perhaps Mr. Simpson does?
I hope you will not be golfing or rusticating when I do come to Edinburgh. I have so much to tell you -- "the secret" -- among other things. I suppose you saw the impertinent Athenaeum on the Physiology? 600 It was lucky however they were not more impertinent and objectionable -- I dare say they were afraid.
I shall be getting to work soon on Great Wits Mad Wits, but have had all my time occupied with preparing my eldest son for his competitive examination -- and am only just free.
Mrs. Lewes begs her kindest remembrances to you and the Major. She is in grief because Pug's eye (always threatning) has at last become completely covered with cataract.
She is sitting to Laurence for her portrait, and I hope it will be a success. It is to be the same style as his portrait of Thackeray (you know the one -- that published by Smith and Elder?) and as it was Laurence's own express wish to draw her, because he felt he could, I have some confidence in the result.
[Unsigned]
Mr. Simpson has never written about the binding of the Mill on the Floss.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [5? March 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: March/60. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
Thanks for the Mem. though 'tis not so bright looking as I had hoped; but I will hope that the publication when complete may not only pick up again, but become a permanent "good thing." I hear such strong testimonies of it from the profession and from young medicals that I begin to look to them as the chief source of sale. I would rather the settlement took place when your books are finally made up. Enclosed is a list of "presentations."
Mrs. Lewes is getting her eyes redder and swollener every morning as she lives through her tragic story. But there is such a strain of poetry to relieve the tragedy that the more she cries, and the readers cry, the better say I. She is anxious to hear your opinion of the part you have got; although she knows you don't like disagreeable and uncomfortable situations.
Maga certainly fears no rival -- nor need she: a schooner may sail faster than a frigate but for serious work the frigate is the craft.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [4 January 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Wandsworth | Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
First about Darwin -- I am half through the paper, but your doubts give me pause. Although I don't think it will turn out in any way objectionable, yet it is perhaps safer to wait a month or two, and see how the public generally accepts the book. At present it has been treated by the Press with great respect and the National Review seems to think that only very narrow bigots indeed can see any danger in it. Meanwhile I will set to work with Tom Jones. 447
Oh yes, I enjoyed "the Last French Hero" 448 and had a shrewd guess as to its military author. It will serve to illuminate the garbage of France and do some good I hope. A glance at St. Stephens 449 made me exclaim Aut Bulwerus aut Diabolus. Apropos of the Bart., did you ascertain what sums he got from America and Germany? We have to answer applications from both, and should like to have a guide, if possible -- not to ask more than is likely to be given, and not less.
Ponder on these titles.
Sister Maggie. (That sounds rather like a child's story)
The House of Tulliver or Life on the Floss.
The Tulliver Family or Life on the Floss.
Maggie Tulliver.
The Tullivers.
It will be well now to begin announcing it in lists -- if not the title at any rate the fact of a new novel being in the press.
I had the satisfaction yesterday of making a clean breast of it with Cook 450 'e0propos of the Saturday Review and its tone towards men of genius and eminence. We got very warm, and I told him of the growing execration in which the journal was held by all kinds of readers. There will probably be no alteration, but at any rate I have "said my say." I wish Mrs. Poyser could have tackled him and had her say out. The night before last a scene was read to me between Bob Jakin and Mrs. Glegg which would have convulsed you, I think. But you will soon have volume 2 in your hands, I expect; and may chuckle over it in private. The book decidedly improves as it goes on.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
Don't forget to send word about Bulwer's price if you know it.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [30 April 1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [30 April 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
Your letters with the checque, for which thanks, arrived this morning, and excited various feelings of pleasure and curiosity. But oh! wildly chimerical supposition, that we see such papers as the "Critic" and "Leader" (the very name of the last, has long been a sore to me). The only papers we see are the Athenaenum and Saturday Review, and for the rest of the pressgang are content to remain in ignorance of all their wisdom. Nevertheless you have roused my curiosity, as to what I am to be indignant at, and I should be glad if you could send me the slips of the Critic and Leader containing the offensive paragraph. The curs! to pretend that an author has no right to privacy. 127 He has no right of course to balk their tittletattle; it would be to rob them of their bread.
The good news of the book is delightful; but you will hear from the author.
Did I tell you I had seen Owen and spoken to him about Keith Johnston? He said he remembered his promise and had made some preparatory jottings, but was terribly busy just now. I think if you were to drop a line in a week or two, he might be brought to the scratch.
I am, and have been for some time, very far from well; and the day before yesterday alarmed Mrs. Lewes by fainting suddenly without the least provocation, a most absurd proceeding!
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
Will you tell Mr. Simpson that as there are to be 18 parts of the Physiology volume 1 will close with part 9 "Why we are Warm."
I feel much tempted to write a satirical letter on the subject of the right of a newspaper man to publish any secret he may ferret out. Will Maga receive such? My idea is a letter to the editor written in indignant remonstrance against this squeamishness which would deprive me of my most telling paragraphs. As I have no ideas, and no knowledge, how can I get a living except by reporting the conversation, the gossip and the flying rumours of clubs and coteries?

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [3? August 1859]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Southfields | Wandsworth | Wednesday.
Most costive of correspondents!
We have been expecting daily to hear from you for more than a week, and in spite of my experience of you, when in the country, I was na'eff enough to go on expecting. "In the days of Innocency Adam fell" 244 [two words deleted]
Firstly: By this post I send you a short article -- the one I spoke to you about -- which I should be glad if you can get in this number, 245 as I want to use a part of it for the Physiology in October or November and don't want the two to appear too close together. Hating copying extracts as much as -- you hate writing letters -- I send the volume with it for the printers.
Secondly: What about Owen? You were to write. The book 246 has come, but I am in the dark.
Thirdly: Pug is transcendent in ugliness ( -- un beau laid!) -- and in tyranny over G.E. -- in gustativeness, and general selfishness. Stupid as a beauty; but very gentle, and affectionate. The laughter is Homeric and inextinguishable, excited by his odd looks and ways; and the anxiety is diminishing. G.E. pets him above petting.
Fourthly: We were pleased to hear of such good subscriptions, 247 and hope to hear of continuous streams of a misguided public pouring towards 37.
Fifthly: As I have nothing to answer in your nonwritten letter I can't answer it but "subscribe myself" for as many copies as you please.
Yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [28 February 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
Your letters and checque arrived this morning; and the proofs I suppose will come this afternoon. Will you please "put on the steam" with the printing now, as in a few days the greater part of the 3rd volume will be sent. I don't know whether I ever explained to you our object in having the printing done in advance -- we want to reach Rome by Holy Week and in fact want to be there as soon as it is possible, so that no sooner is the last sheet corrected than off we start without even waiting to see the book out. To effect this it will be necessary that all should be printed off by the time the last few sheets are sent, so that not a day will be lost in delays.
I have got so many matters to settle that I shall not be able to write any more articles before returning to work.
Your enjoyment of Maggie is a cheering sign. I think so much character, life, and at the close so strong an interest of story must carry the book at least everywhere where Adam went.
We shall be delighted to see your nephew.
Mrs. Lewes begs me to add her kind regards and that she was very much pleased with your note but has no time to say anything this morning. No more proofs need go to Sheard.
I suppose the Physiology and Seaside Studies will be out before we start?
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [28 April 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Holly Lodge | Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
The checque arrived yesterday while I was in town. Many thanks. But you make me uncomfortable about your printers shouting for copy. More than a fortnight ago I sent back the revise of Digestion and Indigestion, which will appear in May. The two next parts in revise have also been sent to me, and I return one by this post. Is it possible that you have not received Digestion? I should be much obliged to Mr. Simpson if he would keep me regularly informed respecting the progress and wants of copy and proofs. I won't be behind hand; but I like to retain copy and proofs as late as possible in order that the book may have the benefit of the very latest discoveries, or revision. The whole m.s. is done; but is constantly being altered, and added to; and this will be the case as long as there is a chance left.
I am exceedingly happy to find that the book is producing an impression among eminent medical men, and that the articles in Maga were much talked of, and have been quoted by the profession. This must affect the general public. If we can secure a reputation sale will inevitably follow.
A letter from Algiers today 449 informs us that "there is a work which seems to have convulsed English society" (of the higher class) and accordingly it has been sent for by our correspondent. She says it is "Adam Bede." Do you know of such a book?
Ever faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Holly Lodge | Wandsworth | Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
Proof goes by this post. If it is any convenience to you by all means do not hesitate to postpone the appearance of Master Jones -- he will keep; and as I shant be able to do any thing for the next number it won't interfere with me.
Mrs. Lewes begs me to tell you that according to your calculations the 1st volume of the Mill will be 10 pages more than the 2d volume of Adam Bede; in which case the 2d volume of the Mill will be about 10 or 15 more than the first volume of Adam; the third volume will probably be of the same length. Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [24 October 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
Proof goes to Edinburgh by this post. Of course you have seen that Blackguard Newby's advertisement? 362 What can be done? From two people who spoke to me on Saturday I learned that one concluded Adam Bede Junior was by George Eliot and the other by Liggins. These ideas will of course obtain currency in the provinces, and will damage the next work. As the title of Adam Bede is copyright, and as no one can have a right to publish a sequel to a living author's work surely Newby might be stopped by a letter threatening legal proceedings? At all events it ought to be tried. Do see to this matter at once. Newby must either give up the publication altogether or he must announce the name of the real author of his book and state that it is not G. Eliot. In haste, and hot indignation
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [22 November 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
By this post I send the corrected copy of Seaside Studies -- the corrections are in pencil but I presume they will do as well as ink. On reflection I decide against "Only a Pond."
I was it appears under a mistake respecting Clerical Scenes. But the fact is that observing it to have for some weeks dropped out of the advertisements I concluded it was on its last legs, and on consulting the books Langford told me that the edition seemed to be gone. Your revised and precise statement of course banishes that pleasant fiction. 400 At the same time I do not understand why we should not be anxious to get the edition sold as quickly as possible, and a new one to follow it -- although Langford did some time ago say that he would rather the edition did not go off before Christmas -- why, I omitted to ask him. If the new one has to wait till after Maggie, the postponement is likely to be a long one. Surely it is better to produce it before the new one is the talk of the town, than soon afterwards? To push a book and sell it as fast as possible is the very purport of publishing. If the public won't buy they won't -- and one must content oneself with reflections on their taste. If they will, they should have every chance.
I consulted Mr. Sheard, 401 the attorney, yesterday about Newby and he, while advising no legal proceedings on account of the uncertainty, thought it desirable that you should issue a cautionary advertisement, which would to some extent check the rumour, very rife, that George Eliot is the author. You would be surprised if you knew the "intelligent people" who have no suspicion it is not George Eliot's.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [22 July 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Friday.
My dear Blackwood
We came back last night, driven from Switzerland and warned off Holland by the intense heat. Except the sight of the boys, and the beauty of Lucerne, the trip was not worth the fatigue and time and money. The weather was such as Sydney Smith declared would drive one to take off one's skin and sit in one's bones. 214
Among the pile of letters were two from you, pleasant as usual, with the checques, and a thrilling prospect of a Pug.
Don't call my dear Jane Austen old Sarah -- how would you like to be called Jim? 215
Respecting Owen I forgot to say that I had given up the idea. I haven't the requisite knowledge for such an article. But if you like I will write a paper on his new Classification of Mammalia 216 -- that is to say a paper on Classification generally 'e0propos of his new book published by Parker (send it me) in which I can say something generally of his labors. But the first paper I do must be on the Voluntary and Involuntary Actions, as I shall want that for the Physiology.
G.E. is writing to you. Pray give my compliments to Mrs. Blackwood and kind regards to the Major.
Ever hurriedly yours
G. H. Lewes.
Paris is in a fever about Adam Bede. Even at Hofwyl -- five miles from Berne -- with only half a dozen English boys -- I heard of it; for on telling my second son I had brought him a novel all three shouted "Is it Adam Bede?" 217
In spite of the fatigues of the journey Mrs. Lewes feels greatly benefited by the trip, and will rock the cradle of the new "little stranger" with fresh maternal vigour.

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [21 November 1859]
Text: B. C. Williams, George Eliot, New York, Macmillan, 1936, pp. 166-168; corrections have been made from facsimile of first page of letter on p. 167. Reprinted by permission of the Macmillan Co. Endorsed: Octr or Novr | 59.
Holly Lodge | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
In a letter just received from Dickens 399 there is this story about "Adam Bede, Junior," which he says "I have at first hand and know to be true." A scavenging wretch in the employment of Mr. Newby goes to a certain Librarian to subscribe the book. Librarian says he considers it a dishonest proceeding and will have nothing to do with it. "Dishonest!" says the Scavenger, "how do you know by whom it's written? How do you know it is not by Miss Evans?" Librarian replies, "All I know is I will have nothing to do with the book or you either." But behold! the Librarian's subscribers attracted by the advertisement, demand the book, and because he is under contract to supply them with all new books he is obliged to order it, and has ordered it!
This, as you may suppose, has deeply annoyed us; and I cannot help expressing my regret that, if you thought it advisable to treat Newby with silent contempt, you did not inform me of it, that I might have taken some steps in time.
It is now too late for anything but a letter in the Times and they will, I suppose, insert one from you, not only undeceiving the public, but characterizing Newby's proceedings. An advertisement will be overlooked; a letter will be read and talked about.
Yours in haste
G. H. Lewes.
We feel that Mrs. Lewes's interests are compromised by silence on such a point.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [21 April 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
By this proof goes the post or this post the proof, which is it? Your dithyramb on Ignorance amused us. But are we not all dreadfully ignorant? As for myself I live intellectually from hand to mouth -- I forget even my own discoveries after a little while, and of course don't remember the wisdom of others. I know a good fellow, a charming woman, a good book, a good cigar, a good dog (no, all dogs are good), but on most other points I get hazy.
Talking of good books it is really gratifying to see our confidence in Adam Bede so confirmed. Two out of every three people I meet speak to me about it; and it is excessively amusing to hear each person give a version of the letter in the Times and what it meant.
You must prepare for a surprise with the new story G.E. is writing. It is totally unlike anything he has written yet. The novel will be a companion picture to Adam Bede; but this story is of an imaginative philosophical kind, quite new and piquant. As usual he is unwilling to believe that anyone will see anything in it.
What you say of Spurgeon exactly tallies with the notion I had formed of him from reports.
I shall go and see Owen tomorrow or Sunday, and will probe him about Keith Johnston.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [2 September 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
Your letter with checque arrived in due course. Seeing is Believing you will have in very good time, for I must get myself free to continue house hunting. "Oh! that mine enemy had let his house and hadn't found another." Then I have the visit to Edinburgh hanging over me as a dreadful necessity. Instead of enjoying it as I should have enjoyed it had my mind been disengaged from houses and furniture and worry I shall be in a state of remorse all the time. But I don't like sending the boy without seeing where (for seeing is believing you know!)
We shall certainly be at home on Wednesday to receive your Nephew, and only regret the cause which deprives us of the pleasure of seeing his father at the same time!
With our united kind regards to him and yourself, Believe me
Ever yours
G. H. L.

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [19 February 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
The proof dispatched to-day is ready for press. I don't need to see a revise, so that Mr. Simpson, if he wishes it, may be out at the beginning of the month.
I had the first part of the German translation by Prof. Carus yesterday: it looks very tempting in teutonic type, and the translation seems admirable from what I have read. But of course the honor of having so eminent a translator would make one inclined to be indulgent even were the translation inferior.
Mrs. Lewes wishes me to ask you to send duplicates of the next batch of proofs -- those of the opening of volume 2 -- to Mr. Sheard | 3 Cloak Lane | Cannon St. | he having promised to see that her law is all right. She is as fidgety about minute accuracy as if she were on oath.
We are reading Oliphant's book 482 and are greatly interested by his account of the Japanese, though not a little indignant with the gratuitous disregard of feelings, prejudices, and rights displayed by the English in the Chinese quarrel. Even on Oliphant's showing 'tis a deplorable case -- such as between man and man would excite universal reprobation.
Maggie is coming rapidly to grief.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [18 November 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: Novr/59. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Friday.
My dear Blackwood
I hope the paragraph to which you refer, 393 but which I have not seen, and only heard of accidentally, (it was probably the good office of some friend) has stopped the blackguard. Not having heard from you after you said you were to consult your legal friends, I concluded that you were taking some active measures, and would let me know the result.
Langford tells me the Clerical Scenes are all gone. We must see about a new edition in time for Christmas. I presume you do not contemplate another at 12/. Ought it to be 7/6 or 6/? and how many would it be prudent to print?
I am correcting Seaside Studies for the new edition. When do you propose issuing it? Are the plates copied? Shall we add "Only a Pond?" "These be questions!"
Maggie goes on gloriously and Mrs. Lewes does not suffer herself to be much bothered by external things. Pug grows in extenso, but not in intelligence. He is certainly not bound to be more fascinating than he is already.
What days these are for furious speculation in the periodical world! My precious time is occupied with declining offers on all sides -- every one imagining that he can seduce George Eliot, simply because he (the everyone, not G.E.) wants that result!
Mrs. Lewes begs me to add her kind remembrances to the Major and yourself and believe me
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
I have been unable to see Mr. Patterson yet, but I shall try today. Not that I can do anything for him.

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [18 January 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Wandsworth | Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
Herewith goes Tom Jones, which I hope you will like -- I have rather exaggerated the praise in order not to raise too great a hubbub. 459
Yesterday I consigned to the shoulders of Langford the onerous responsibility of volume 1 of the Mill. The second will come when you have advanced some way with the printing. Please keep the m.s. for yours truly!
You will be pleased, as I was, to learn that Dr. Daubeny 460 has been delivering a Lecture at Oxford on "Animal Nutrition with reference to Lewes's Physiology of Common Life" -- this has been printed in the Gardener's Chronicle. In it he takes up the cudgels for Liebig against me, but is throughout very courteous and complimentary and strongly recommends the book to the students. Rejoice Mr. Simpson's heart with that!
Ever yours faithfully

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [15 October 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: Octr/59. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
It is very pleasant to hear satisfactory news of the Physiology, and the sale in volumes seems to promise. By the way as the Medical Schools are now opening in England and Scotland would it not be desirable to have some extra advertizing with a view to catch the students? It is not easy to get that class of purchasers; but once got 'tis a good and renewing public.
I shall be very happy to make Mr. Patten's 350 acquaintance, although I fear I shall not be able to render him any assistance. The state of my health, and the absorption of my time in scientific pursuits, put a great check on miscellaneous writing of the journalistic kind.
It is owing to my health that you have not sooner had a paper I am concocting on "Another pleasant French Book," 351 but I hope to send it you in a few days. Bradbury on Sea Weeds will keep till the Commission has sat on Balaclava.
Mrs. Lewes begs me to send her kind regards, and say she will write to you in a few days. She is delighted of course with the good news. Maggie grows slowly into womanhood -- and since she is to rival Adam -- she had better take her time, and not be outgrowing her strength. I have just heard the first volume over again, not bit by bit as heretofore, but en masse; and my admiration increases with familiarity.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [11 April 1859]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Wimbledon Park | Wandsworth | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
Mrs. Lewes and I have only just returned from the Isle of Wight whither we made a rapid flight in search of health, I having been unable to work for a week. Your letter with its enclosures awaited us.
Since you seem to have set your mind on my doing an article on Owen I will ruminate the matter and see whether I can do it historically; for dogmatically I don't feel at all competent. I will ask him about Johnston 96 the first time I see him.
By this post I send you the review of Miss Austen, in case it may happen to be more convenient for you to put it in next month; but I should prefer the "Ponderings" to take precedence, as this is the time ponderers ought to "ponder well." 97
Moving into my new house has so much exceeded my calculation of expences that it would be a great convenience to me if you would make the second payment for the "Physiology" shortly. You were kind enough to say that this second payment might be anticipated, if wanted; but I had no idea of being in any want of this convenience.
G.E. has a delicious bit of myth for you; but he shall give it himself. How you can drink your wine from the skull of Liggins, and yet wear a smug face before the whole world is one of the mysteries of our time! What a chance for Adam -- to become a contributor to the "Eclectic"!
By the way you were to tell us what you thought of Spurgeon.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
A letter has just come from Brockhaus of Leipsig wishing to know what the exact cost of each cast of the illustrations of Physiology will be. He has I fancy some vague idea that I meant the cuts themselves, when I mentioned casts; but at any rate please let me know the price that I may satisfy him.

GHL to John Blackwood, Wandsworth, [10? July 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
I have now made a clearing in the forest of correspondence which had sprung up for me during absence and am ready to set to work again -- as you may suppose after three months and more during which pen has not touched paper except for a rare letter. Have you any subject to propose for Maga? -- any book in my way you would like reviewed? There is only one subject I can think of at present and that is the connection of great wits with mad wits 591 -- but it wants turning over, and if you think it promises I will turn it over while finishing the bit of work I undertook before quitting England -- viz. the editing of the modern dramatists for Brockhaus. 592
Pug you will rejoice to hear, is in high feather, and has actually developed a bark! For the rest I find the world much as I left it.
I intend making another descent on Langford shortly to get news of the books. Kindest regards to the Major
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, St. Mary's, [27 March 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
St. Mary's | Scilly Isles | Friday.
My dear Blackwood
The pursuit of zoology under difficulties in March gales has brought me here at last. Weatherbound at Penzance I have been eyeing the sea and sky with wistful glances; and for four days remained with corded boxes and without change of linen, to be tumbled about on the Atlantic at last in rare style. The place however is enchanting; quite surpassing all my expectations; and it promises good material, both Maga-wise and animal-wise. The weather is perfect, or would be if a little warmer.
I'm hurrying with letters to catch the post which only goes out twice a week so having given notice of my whereabouts to the best of editors I break off with
Ever truly yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, St Mary's, 26 April 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
St. Mary's | Scilly Isles | 26 April 1857.
My dear Blackwood
I have been anxiously expecting to hear from you, lest either of my parcels should have miscarried. I sent one from G. Eliott; and a paper on Seaside Studies -- both let me hope reached you in all safety. If the seaside paper is printed in Maga this month, please not to send me a checque here, because as I have to endorse it, the sending to and fro is riskious. If it is no trouble to you I should prefer your paying in the amount to my account in the Union Bank of London, 4 Pall Mall East, 845 which will save all risk.
I continue delighted with this place, and have been very fortunate with my animals, novelty and beauty being well represented in my vivarium. Early next month however -- about the 10th I think -- I shall take flight for Jersey and there George Eliot will be with me, engendering new clergymen, I hope.
Maga is "taken in," even here! If that isn't popularity I don't know what is.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, St Mary's, [3 May 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: June 1857. Hitherto unpublished.
Scilly Isles | Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
I am not at all sorry you deferred the article. 851 The sight of the proof and the extra time given for No. 2 are decided advantages. I shall cut out the objectionable faeces altogether. But you must confess it is an awful wet blanket on a writer's shoulders, that terror of lady readers, and what they will exclaim against. I am tempted to exclaim with Charles Lamb "Hang up the ladies! I will write for antiquity." 852 The passage you object to about giving way to desires was playful but I perceive it may be misinterpreted and shall change it altogether.
I have sent proof and letters to G.E. He will be much pleased with them. You cannot think how shy and diffident he is, and how much it takes to persuade him that what he writes is worth anything. Not a common failing with us scribes, is it?
I strike my tents on the 11th for Jersey. When settled there I will let you know.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Shottermill, 7 May 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Shottermill, 7 May 1871
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Shotter Mill | nr Petersfield | 7 May 1871.
My dear Blackwood
Here we are quietly settled for the summer and I hope you will be able to run down and see us (station Haslemere) some day and get out of the vortex of London.
Meanwhile here is something for you to turn over in your mind, and come prepared to discuss. Mrs. Lewes finds that she will require volumes for her story, not 3. I winced at the idea at first, but the story must not be spoiled for want of space, and as you have more than once spoken of the desirability of inventing some mode of circumventing the Libraries and making the public buy instead of borrowing I have devised the following scheme, suggested by the plan Victor Hugo followed with his long Mis'e9rables -- namely to publish it in half-volume parts either at intervals of one, or as I think better, two months. The eight parts at 5/- could yield the 2 £ for the four volumes, and at two month intervals would not be dearer than Maga. Each part would have a certain unity and completeness in itself with separate title. Thus the work is called Middlemarch. Part I will be Miss Brooke.
If in a stiff paper cover -- attractive but not bookstallish -- (I have one in my eye) this part ought to seduce purchasers, especially if Mudie were scant in supplies. It would be enough to furnish the town with talk for some time, and each part thus keep up and swell the general interest. Tristram Shandy you may remember was published at irregular intervals; and great was the desire for the continuation. Considering how slowly the public mind is brought into motion, this spreading of the publication over 16 months would be a decided advantage to the sale -- especially as each part would contain as much as one ought to read at a time.
Ponder this; or suggest a better plan!
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
Thanks for Ferrier. 282

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Shottermill, 21 August 1871
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Shotter Mill nr Petersfield | 21 August 1871.
My dear Blackwood
Last night Mrs. Lewes read to me what she has written of part III -- "Dorothea Married" 352 -- and my delight in it not only confirms the expectation of a great success, but also confirms my belief in the desirability of bi-monthly publication. This being decided, and since we ought to publish the first part at Christmas -- to be out before the Americans with whom our arrangement has been made -- it is now time to settle about the terms of publication.
Since the plan is novel and may not realize all that one hopes from its novelty the choice is open to you to speculate or not as you think fit. Assuming that the work will consist of 4 volumes to sell at 40/- if you propose to take the risk we should be willing to part with the English right only, for 4 years (which would bring it into your other term of copyrights) for the sum of £6,000 -- payable in the course of 1872-3 in any instalments you may think fit.
Or if we take the risk we should require a royalty of 2/- per copy sold, on each 5/- part, in the original form, and an equivalent royalty on copies in cheaper editions. Half yearly accounts.
We ought to sell 10,000 at this cheap rate, because soon the Libraries will find it more profitable than ordinary novels since they will have 8 volumes to distribute in lieu of 4. But no one can tell.
Were we not lucky to have escaped the festival 353 which seems to have been a failure? The more so as the weather here was delicious and we have got into that charming house opposite our cottage, so that creature comforts have permitted work to go on quietly and successfully.
We return to the Priory on the 1st September. Not to shoot partridges but far wilder birds known as "readers in general" who are not at all particular.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.
