Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Schwalbach, 30 June 1866
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
Schwalbach 30th June 1866.
My dear Blackwood
I have asked Mrs. Lewes to let me answer your pleasant letter 712 because I wished to give you a [bit] I overheard as we crossed to Calais. Seated beside me on the deck was a nice elderly lady (English) before whom stood a superb crinoline (also British) imparting her views on things in general and at last sliding into literature. The following is verbatim:
Crinoline: Have you read [Armadale] yet?
E. L. Not yet.
C. It's very clever! Such well drawn characters! I like Wilkie Collins.
E. L. I see we are to have a book by Adam Bede soon.
Crinoline, impressively, Yes, but I'm sorry she's gone into that!
E. L. gently, What, the radical?
C. Yes, I don't think politics good in novels.
E. L. Nor I. But she has such a beautiful mind I feel quite confident of her whatever she may take up.
Crinoline apparently not sharing this sentiment or by a specific levity of mind wafted to other subjects, I lost my interest in the conversation.
It was with great difficulty I got sight of the Times review, 713 for although the paper is taken in at the hotel, the particular half sheet had been taken away. However I went to a salon de lecture and read it &unknown;feeling&unknown; and am entirely of your way of thinking respecting it -- a poor performance but a good puff. The stupid allusion to the trial scene he ought to have been warned off by the very fact that the similarity, if similarity there be, exists between F. H. and Reade's last novel 714 -- now it would be too impudent for an author to borrow an incident from a work so very recent. As you surmised she had never seen the work she is supposed to have taken her suggestion from. Reading the Times once more convinced me of the wisdom of her practice not to read criticisms favorable or unfavorable. This she has -- with very rare exceptions -- steadily adhered to since Adam Bede. I read them, when they fall in my way and tell her about them; and that is enough. The best testimony is the sale. If there is a large body of readers there is certain to be among them readers to whom the book speaks, and the influence of what she writes is secured.
The weather here continues magnificent -- hot, but not too hot, with an occasional shower to relieve the air and brighten the green. Our daily explorations of the country round about only increase our delight in the place, and if climate, idleness, good living, and the waters can help us to flesh we shall come back obese. We leave this on the 5 or 6th for Schlangenbad, where it is possible that we may stay ten days or a fortnight and then take a flying look at the gaieties of Wiesbaden. I dare say you will not have occasion to write again just at present, but a letter addressed to Bonn by the 21st or Aix la Chapelle by the 23rd (I mean reaching those towns on those dates) would perhaps convey some agreeable intelligence and certainly be very welcome because it is in your hand.
Mrs. Lewes in giving me the post of secretary on this occasion begs me to thank your particularly for the interesting details of your letter. She values Bulwer's expression of opinion all the more as she happens to know that he is sincere in his expression about other writers.
I know Oliphant and once hoped to have him as a colleague in the Fortnightly. Morley also I know slightly and like what I have seen of him.
Our routine here is this: we rise at 6 or a little before and after tub and apology for toilet step out on to the promenade (at the foot of the hotel) drink the sparkling and delightful water, listen to the band, and walk about till 8. Breakfast, book and cigar, occupies till 9'bd. Then we go out into one of the several woods or to some point de vue -- sometimes taking a book with us -- but oftener not -- and walk, and sit, and muse and talk while "Idlesse in her dreaming mood" 715 lets the hours roll noiselessly by till 1. Then another glass of water and siesta till dinner. We always dine alone in our apartment having a strong disinclination for table d'h'f4tes and the people met thereat. After dinner at 3, coffee, cigar, and a nap prepares me for the promenade (and more music and more water) at 6-8. Here we observe the swells and crinolines -- not a word have we spoken to one of them as yet, a charming deprivation we owe to dining alone. When the music ceases we ramble in the evening sunlight till tea and bed beckon us home. [Thus runs the round of life from hour to hour.] 716
Every yours faithfully
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Rickmansworth, 29 July 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Rickmansworth, 29 July 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Elms | Rickmansworth | Thursday 29 July 75.
My dear Blackwood
Mrs. Lewes' correspondents are of course not grateful to me for relieving her of her task of writing them. But unless I did so her valuable time and strength would have to be largely used up; and as we don't put racers into Hansom cabs so we mustn't let writers do the work of correspondents.
The Deluge has passed; our river running so quickly at the end of the garden has not overflowed its banks and floated us into Space (with G.H.L. 'e0 l'instar de Caesar holding aloft her Commentaries!) 295 but like a sober, well-conducted river has kept the even tenor of its way so that we have not had to make a raft of our dining table. While the deluge lasted, Mrs. Lewes continued getting stronger, but now has taken a chill, which affects her throat 296 -- I hope not seriously. Meanwhile the Commentaries have been developing into deeper and deeper interest. It is true I am snubbed for being [cockaloop] about them, and for not adopting the despondent view of other people -- but on that subject my estimate of the estimate of other people is that it isn't worth two peas!
Your account of Cheneys 297 was not exaggerated, and we were willing to take on your authority the character of the beer. But Cheneys is only one of the lovely drives hereabouts -- they have but the one defect of being too hilly, and of not having enough of wild country and commons.
I'm glad you agree with the dramatic criticisms -- a subject on which a d -- d deal of nonsense is written and spoken. -- We were so pleased with your picture of the dogs, and the arrival of "the boy." 298 Mrs. Lewes begs me to say she thoroughly sympathizes with you there, and that we both think a deficiency of scholastic brilliancy the smallest possible defect where there is good honest heart and brain -- those are the levers of this world! This is how we have felt about our own boys.
We are complete hermits here -- not a soul have we seen or spoken to. I had to rush up to town one day to a garden party at Lady Airlie's because the Queen of Holland had expressed a wish that I should be presented. I hope her majesty found the interview more interesting than I did! -- Except that, and twice rushing to the Priory to get books (it's no use taking down a bookcase -- one never thinks of the right books!) my days have been passed in the most delicious peace and uniformity and work has advanced proportionately.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, Rickmansworth, [11 September 1875]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Elms | Rickmansworth | Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
You were kind enough to say you would send Mrs. Lewes The Abode of Snow 309 -- if it has not already been sent to the Priory will you please order it to be sent here?, as she wishes to read it aloud of an evening.
The book gets on slowly amid usual depression. Her health does not improve and when we leave this -- on the 22d -- I propose taking her to Wales for a complete holiday in hopes that rest and bracing air may set her up.
I am hard at work and tolerably well. What superb weather we have at last. You must have too many letters to write for me to wish for any reply to this unless you have something special to say.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 6 November [1856]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 6 November [1856]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Published: Cross, I, 417-419.
Park Shot | Richmond | 6 November.
My dear Sir
Did you get my last letter proposing an article on Sea Anemones? and did your "silence give consent"?
Meanwhile I trouble you with a m.s. of "Sketches of Clerical Life" 756 which was submitted to me by a friend who desired my good offices with you. It goes by this post.
I confess that before reading the m.s. I had considerable doubts of my friend's power as a writer of fiction; but after reading it those doubts were changed into very high admiration. I don't know what you will think of the story, but according to my judgement such humour, pathos, vivid presentation and nice observation have not been exhibited (in this style) since the "Vicar of Wakefield" -- and in consequence of that opinion I feel quite pleased in negotiating the matter with you.
This is what I am commissioned to say to you about the proposed series. It will consist of tales and sketches illustrative of the actual life of our country clergy about a quarter of a century ago; but solely in its human and not at all in its theological aspect; the object being to do what has never yet been done in our Literature, for we have had abundant religious stories polemical and doctrinal, but since the "Vicar" and Miss Austen, no stories representing the clergy like any other class with the humours, sorrows, and troubles of other men. He begged me particularly to add that -- as the specimen sent will sufficiently prove -- the tone throughout will be sympathetic and not at all antagonistic. 757
Some of these, if not all, you may think suitable for Maga. If any are sent of which you do not approve, or which you do not think sufficiently interesting, these he will reserve for the separate republication and for this purpose he wishes to retain the copyright. Should you only print one or two he will be well satisfied; and still better if you should think well enough of the series to undertake the separate republication.
He calculates the present story will make two parts for Maga. 758 Believe me
Ever truly yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 6 August [1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 6 August [1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | 6th August.
Dear Blackwood
Magas and the double checque arrived in due course, for which thanks. I shall send your letter to G.E. with the [filthy lucre.] 947 It will please him to have pleased you, for he was immovably and disagreeably possessed with the idea that you didn't like the story. Genus irritabile! Now in my buoyant confidence I am most immovably possessed with the idea that you do like the papers I send you -- or else you wouldn't publish them pour mes beaux yeux -- and I try in vain to give him some of my hopefulness, but Nature is too strong. She has made him diffident, and d'e9fiant (the French, not the English word of that aspect) of praise; and no sooner does anything not praise come than he says "There, you see I was right!" So he will hug your letter, for he is obstinate in cleaving to what he has written, and really thinks it fine though he can't think others will think so.
Richmond is not Jersey, tant s'en faut; neither, however, is it London. I went to see Ristori in Medea 948 and although I got a headache, I got it cheap. What a superb creature it is! Did you fall in love with her? I was disappointed with her Lady Macbeth -- the first part I saw her in -- but Medea surpassed all expectation.
Are you coming to London? I hope it won't be towards the end of this month, as then I shall have run away to Switzerland to see my boys, whom I have not seen for 12 months. As you are a father, I needn't say more. Ever my dear Blackwood
Yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 5 September 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | 5 September 1858.
My dear Blackwood
We reached home considerably knocked up having come from Leipsic without stopping on the way. Your letter with the checque (for which thanks) was laid aside, and I did not get it till last night.
I will see Mr. Simpson and consult with him about the C.S. and give him also the 2d volume of Bedesman to take back with him. We are not a little curious to hear your impressions thereof.
In spite of Maga's willingness to take more of the chapters on Physiology, and in spite of the advantage there is in having them printed first -- as a sort of rough draft to work from -- I think that the paper which goes herewith, and the one on [Sleep] 1188 (to be written) are all that we had better print, in order to preserve a sufficient quantum of novelty.
If there is time I intend preparing a paper 1189 for the British Association of Science this year under Owen's presidency. I wish to give that official publication to some very astounding results I got at in Munich; and in the book I can then refer to that official publication. If there is not time, I must come out without

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 5 February 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 5 February 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | February 5th 1858.
My dear Blackwood
The checque for 75 £, 1081 with the pleasant news arrived in due course. I had no conception that it was your custom to pay six months after publication although as you do not get your money till 12 months after the plan is fair. G.E. says he also understood his arrangement to be on date of publication and made his calculations on that basis.
How very handsome [Sea-Side Studies] looks! I do not remember anything in better taste, or more genuinely attractive. It almost tempts me to read it myself -- which is the utmost stretch temptation can reach after I have once dismissed proofs.
G.E. is again [down in the mouth] because his book does not sell and all his old misgivings come over him in spite of Dickens's letter which raised his spirits for a time. I preach a sanguine philosophy, but half the prosperity of a sermon lies in the audience, and here my audience is painfully deaf. If you hear of any good critical notices mention them when you write. They will make his new story (which I think surpassingly fine) evolve itself more pleasantly.
By this post I send you part 1 of Food and Drink. There will be three parts 1082 I find: the two to come being occupied with examination of the various articles used by man, with dietetic explanations and practical hints. I have done all three parts, but retain the two last in case of additions suggesting themselves. With kind regards to your brother Believe me
Ever truly yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 30 November [1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 30 November [1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Park Shot | 30 November.
My dear Blackwood
Your letter -- checque -- and Johnston arrived this morning. I am so much pleased with the liberality of your proposals and the confidence you express that I can only hope both will meet with the right return.
I have never contemplated any but the slenderest money result from [Sea-Side Studies,] but as to a poor man every addition to the banker's account is important, I shall be quite pleased to get 75£ for the edition -- and not less so to hear you have got as much for your trouble and risk.
Johnston is a task which I shall set about con amore. When I see my way clear I will write to submit my plans. No time shall be lost.
It will give me great pleasure to make the acquaintance of your brother, and I hope his stay will be long enough to allow of his giving us a day among the lingering autumnal tints of Richmond Park.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 30 January 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | 30th January 58.
My dear Blackwood
Now I know you approve the method of Johnston 1074 I shall finish in comfort. Send me back Vol. 1, however, as occasional touches may be added, unless you want to begin printing.
My next paper on Food and Drink 1075 will be sent off in a few days. Such a collection of facts and arguments has not I believe been made before, even by erudite Germans.
G.E. is pleased with the good news, as he always is with anything in that direction. I agree with you that having secured the admiration of the best judges that of the public must follow. It was six weeks before Jane Eyre showed any decided movement in the way of sale. 1076
Faraday has written a letter 1077 which G.E. treasures beside that of Dickens. Has the [Spectator] or [Examiner] pronounced? Rigid secrecy as to authorship will help the interest in the book, as well as preserve E's cheerfulness.
I shall be anxious to hear what subscription there is of Sea-Side
Studies -- and I should be hopeful about it, if a public were secured to begin with. With kind regards to your brother
Believe me, ever truly yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 3 January 1859
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
Park Shot | Richmond | 3 January 59.
My dear Blackwood
I returned yesterday with one eye bunged up and vision imperfect in the other, from cold -- (not drink, nor fighting) but able nevertheless to read your letter and its enclosure viz. the first instalment (may there be many!) of the Phys. of Common Life.
By this post I send you a paper I have drawn up about a German criminal trial which greatly interested me. If you think it as interesting as I do you will put it in Maga -- if not send it me back. 415
When you see Aytoun pray tell him how much gratified I am by his flattering notice of my Goethe. 416 Quotation is one of the pleasantest testimonies a brother author can pay, when that brother is himself of eminence. May Aytoun's shadow never grow less!
Ever faithfully yours,
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 3 April 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | 3 April 1858.
My dear Blackwood
I am hurrying to London, but pause to acknowledge forthwith the receipt of the checque of 135 £ for Johnston and Food and Drink -- for which many sincere thanks. I did not expect the Johnston before it was due; but just now it comes in most agreeably, and I can't help feeling how friendly and thoughtful it was of you to send it.
I will give G.E. your message. You are the right sort of person to deal with him, for you perceive his Pegasus is tender in the mouth, and is apt to lay back his ears in a restive ominous style if even the reins be shaken when he is at work. Some people's Pegasus seems to have the mouth (as well as the pace,) of a cart horse; but your thoroughbred -- all bone and nerve -- requires other treatment. Ever my dear Blackwood
Yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 2 February 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | 2 February 1858.
My dear Blackwood
I am disappointed with the subscription. I should have thought the booksellers would by this time have had more confidence in me, but probably they felt sceptical of my vitality in so new a direction as zoology, the more so as many trashy tank books have been published of late. However if the book be really a good one, as I believe, it will make its way when known; though I fear slowly.
My banker's balance has been seriously drained this month by the schooling account of my boys, and I should feel obliged by your sending me a checque. You must deduct therefrom the expense, whatever it may be, of that alteration I suggested, because the fault was wholly mine in making the statement, and in justice I ought to pay for the same.
I have sent Langford a list of some eminent names to whom the book may with effect be sent. G.E. of course is included among private friends -- he having as you may suppose been duly indoctrinated not to say overwhelmed by
Yours ever faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
Would it not be well to send one to Prof. Simpson -- and one or two leading men in Scotland?

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 17 November 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | 17 November 1858.
My dear Blackwood
Alex. Dumas, in one of his many lawsuits thus addressed the Judge. Un jour M. V'e9ron v'eent me voir et m'offrit cinq franc la ligne pour mes romans. C'est un homme de relations charmantes.
This eulogy of V'e9ron must have been very appreciable to those who remembered how Dumas would write pages in this style.
Monsieur?
Eh bien!
Vous croyez . . .
Si fait.
Pourtant . . .
Et il se t'fbt. 1220
Five francs the line would be remunerative on this reckoning. Although Physiology is not so remunerative as romans (if I [it?] were I know who would be physiologists). I have always said of you what Dumas said of V'e9ron -- c'est un homme de relations charmantes! and your liberal offer for the Physiology of Common Life (a formal acceptance of which is enclosed) considering how great a risk there must necessarily be in such a work assures me that I was quite right to leave the matter wholly in your hands, our previous relations having been so charmantes, that I was certain to be paid as much as there was any warrant to expect.
But you do not mention the when. Now as the book will take eighteen months before it is finally published, and as I am obliged to calculate some time beforehand what my income will be, I should be glad if you will tell me, when next you have occasion to write, at what period, or periods, the first edition will be paid for; in order that I may arrange accordingly.
Yesterday I placed the concluding portion of the m.s.s. of "Adam
Bede" in Langford's hands, who undertook to forward it in the next parcel.
By the way I have not seen any proofs of the illustrations. Do you print them, or does Mr. Branston? 1221 I must have a set of proofs.
Please ask Mr. Simpson to do me the service of critically reading the proofs and marking any word or passage which is not perfectly clear. He, or you, queried the phrase alimentary canal, in the Hunger and Thirst. I should never have suspected any possible difficulty here; but as soon as his pencil directed my attention to it, I saw that "digestive organs" would be better. As I want every one to understand me, no criticism can be too minute or too trivial -- if he can take so much trouble. I need scarcely add that any pencillings you may have time to make will also be of service.
With kind regards to the Major Believe me, my dear Blackwood
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 13 September 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Park Shot | Richmond | 13 September 1857.
My dear Blackwood
I have shown Monti all the drawings which will serve as the illustrations of our book, and which will give a specimen of each animal spoken of in the text. His estimate is that for 7 plates 8vo containing 28 figures the whole expence -- including printing of a 1,000 copies -- would be about 30£ -- not more perhaps less. Woodcuts would cost at least 3 times that sum. We have arranged that the effect of transparency shall be given to the delicate transparent animals, by drawings of white on a black ground. Woodcuts cannot do this. 329
I have suggested 8vo for the sake of the plates; but if you think post 8vo would be better, because cheaper, I do not think much difference in expence of plates would accrue -- perhaps we must then have 8 plates instead of 7 -- the number of figures running the same, the extra expence of one plate would not be more than 30/- I fancy.
I shall be glad to know how much the printed matter will make, as in revising it I find myself tempted to make large additions, but must restrain myself within limits of a portable and cheap volume.
One of the Aquarium makers 330 told me he was often asked by customers whether the papers in Maga would be reprinted, and he urged me to do so, not knowing that the thing had been already contemplated.
Are you drenched? Do the lanes require ferry boats? Do you swim instead of a walk? We have a deluge here.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 13 March [1858]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | 13 March.
My dear Blackwood
By a strange coincidence G.E. was with me when your letter 1097 arrived with its checque (for which thanks) and he was greatly relieved and inspirited by your approbation, for with his customary misgivings he had no belief in anybody's feeling the sort of delight in his personages he feels, or in any one (I, of course, counting as nobody!) liking the story. Your hearty letter made him quite comfortable and he will doubtless write with fresh confidence -- till the next desponding fit comes. Simpkin's rational demand for more copies has also not been without effect.
He bids me say that no more is yet written; although all is laid out; but before he goes away he will send m.s.s for another part. 1098
We are glad to know you got your cab, as we had some misgivings lest, giving us more of your time our pleasure in the river-stroll and chat might have frustrated some other engagement. We were so pleased at the chance which brought you to town, since our absence in May would have prevented a meeting for a long while.
With kind regards to your Brother, Believe me
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 12 January 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | 12 January 59.
My dear Blackwood
Troublesome as I find the reading of proofs I think it decidedly advisable that I should see those of the Chemistry. Moreover when I drew up the imports, it was of course for 1857 and these must now be cancelled, and 1858 substituted. 2 That alone would render it desirable I should see proofs or have back the original.
Respecting my own proofs I am much obliged to Mr. Brown 3 for taking the trouble of reading them and making queries; only I should be glad if he would make them when he sends the revise and so save me a third dispatch.
What you say of Adam Bede quite falls in with my own experience and has greatly cheered G.E. who is prone to despond. I feel in reading the proofs the same emotions and shed the same tears as over the m.s. This is a good sign. Indeed the perfect truthfulness of every page has from the first assured me that the success of the book must be enduring.
Respecting publication G.E. says that if 1 February is the earliest day on which it can conveniently appear nothing more is to be said; but in his opinion every day that can be gained before the rumour may chance to reach critical circles would be in his favor.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, 1 April [1858]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Park Shot | Richmond | Thursday 1 April.
My dear Blackwood
By this post I dispatch two articles for future use -- the best of the series hitherto, I think. The others will be written under the inspiration of the Munich pictures. We start on Tuesday.
Do you observe the "Studies" are quoted in two articles of Frazer this month? One by Kingsley, 385 and the other by Broderip. 386 Owen tells me the latter is so charmed with the book that he is meditating an article for the Quarterly on it -- that would be luck!
I had got thus far when your letter arrived. No, I do not know who the whelp of the Literary Gazette 387 is, although I suspect. At any rate he places himself out of court not only by the obvious animus, but by the deliberate falsification of which he is guilty: it was this which made Owen mention the article to me -- otherwise I should not have seen it. The Literary Gazette is printed for private circulation otherwise I should expose the writer. Before the book appeared I heard that there was to be an attack on it -- and as the book treads on the corns of some naturalists it is but reasonable to expect they will cry out -- with eloquence or abuse as may be.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Park Shot | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
By this post I send Hunger and Thirst, which is not much altered, and only elucidated here and there. Unless you want the m.s.s. I prefer keeping it by me and sending it part by part in order to add anything if need be. The book is however nearly all done; though I am rewriting for the fourth time the difficult chapters on the Nervous System; and shall perhaps rewrite them again before they go to press. One can't be too particular -- and I want the book to be permanent.
I have been so occupied with experiment and dissection for many months 1207 that I begin to want the relaxation of a little literature. Would you like an article on Biot's M'e9langes for Maga? it gives biographical accounts of Laplace, Newton, Lagrange, Galileo, -- and some pleasant semi-scientific papers. There are some anecdotes and passages which would make a popular article I think. 1208
The letter you sent to George Eliot was not from an admirer he tells me, but from the editor of the Military Spectator begging for a copy of the "Scenes" to review in that "widely circulated journal." G.E. asks me to mention it to you -- you will know whether there would be any use in sending a copy.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [9 March 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
By this post you will receive the third part of Eliot's story. It improves greatly, I think, as it goes on. The interest of the story becomes exciting; and the subtle truth in delineation of complex motives is better than anything he has yet done in that way.
I can't leave this till the 13th or 14th. Printers and publishers are as you know remorseless. The German publisher of the "Life of Goethe" has written for [additions and corrections] for a second edition of the I volume of the translation 819 -- a second edition called for before the second volume appears! -- and so I have to rake up that matter and read the books which have appeared during the last year.
Pleasant as second editions are, it is not pleasant to have to return to one's work, which one had fancied dismissed for ever. I don't envy you the having to read M.S.S first and then the proofs a little while afterwards.
I haven't looked at Maga yet. Thank you for sending it.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [8 October 1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [8 October 1858]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | Friday.
My dear Blackwood
The checque for Animal Heat 1199 (for which thanks) and the Prospectus (enclosed) arrived this morning.
I am glad you are hopeful about the book. I put my whole soul into it and expect it will be a property to us, for it has no real rival. I am ready to go to press whenever you please; indeed almost all the new chapters -- about one half of the whole work -- are done; and those already printed are revised, expanded, and improved. There is nothing but illustrations to wait for, and tell Mr. Simpson, for his especial gratification that I have contrived to get two into the first chapter -- which is all the better as none can possibly come in in the second and third. I don't think I shall want more than 15 altogether; but acting on his advice I will squeeze in as many as possible, while keeping clear of the "unpleasant."
If the book should be a hit, I have another scheme -- "The Zoology of Common Life" -- the fish we eat, the animals we domesticate, the animals we eat and which eat us, the insects which annoy and the insects which enrich us. A glorious field and inexhaustible! What do you think of it? However that is all looming in the distance.
My paper was read by the great Owen himself at the British Association 1200 -- and he replied to some objections. It was pronounced "most valuable" by the chairman, and will doubtless do good although the
Times did spoil my advertizement by calling me G. A. Lewes. That puts me in mind of poor R. H. Horne 1201 who went nearly distracted because when he played Shylock one night at Sadlers' Wells (because I had done it) found to his horror that the walls were placarded with the announcement of Shylock by Mr. R. J. Horne. This comes of having initials!
That is a delicious touch in your note 1202 about the largehearted critics -- an awful race. E. was extremely gratified by the praise and the kind of praise in your letter. When you see the third volume -- the bulk of which will be dispatched he says in a few days -- bringing the tragedy to a close, I shall be much surprised if you do not rush even into large-hearted emphasis, only that it will be sincere emphasis and not mere typography. -- I know nothing like it.
I advise him to send you the m.s. which concludes the tragedy, because on the effect of that will depend the kind of success with the public. But he is disposed to wait till the whole is completed before sending you any. What do you think? If you agree with me write him word. After the winding up of Hetty's story nothing but peaceful sunshine and happiness will come -- like the fifth act of the Merchant of Venice when R. H. Horne has left the stage.
Your dithyramb on golfing stirs my desires. "Thou almost persuadest me to be a golfer." Who knows but some day I may develope in that department too -- and write you a book the "Golfing of Common Life"?
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [7 November 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [7 November 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: II, 395.
Park Shot | Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
Your suggestion about turning the paper on Phrenology into a Letter is very good and obviates all difficulties.
My knowledge of Chemistry is almost exclusively in the direction of Organic Chemistry, but as this is the ground occupied by Johnston 348 I feel able to undertake the editing of his book, so as to bring it up to the present state of Science. Pray observe that I construe the passage in your letter as a suggestion rather than a proposition on your part; and it is in that spirit I reply to it. I feel that, if called upon, I could do the work, and say so. But I should not like my name to appear. It is doubtful whether any but a very attractive name would be of much service to a book so popular and so respected; but it is certain that mine, not being that of a chemist, would be of no value whatever.
Having answered explicitly for myself, let me add that if you can alight upon a good man who will do the work well and put his name to it, there will be every reason to place it in his hands.
What number do you propose to print of "Seaside Studies,"? and at what price?
I am sorry to say "Thorndale" does not greatly interest me, in spite of my old regard for the author. Some years ago I dare say I should have read it with pleasure; but the age of doubt and vacillation has passed and I want something solid, or seeming solid whereon to stand and look about me. The book is charmingly written, but I think its structure a mistake. Don't tell him so, however. If the public likes it, he won't believe me; if the public doesn't like it, he will find out the mistake fast enough.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [7 May 1856]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Park Shot | Richmond | Wednesday.
My dear Sir
It is gratifying to find you like the story on rereading. It is but a slight affair, but from the variety of incident may perhaps be amusing. I have however determined on completing it in this third part (which I send by this post) because unless a story has a good backbone of interest and character, the shorter the better. Now the defect of my story, as it seems to me, is the defect of the original play from which I altered it, viz. that neither hero nor heroine have sufficiently marked character. 288
I wanted to do something novel with Victor -- something out of the ordinary hero type -- a semi-humbug. But nuances are not fit for the stage; and require even in a novel more patient development than this character seemed to me to be worth.
I quite agree with you that Nicotte and Goulard are the most interesting and have thrown the burden on their backs.
Ever truly yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [5 December 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
I wish to submit to your judgement the two plans by which the editing of Johnston 1021 may be executed. The ordinary plan is that of leaving the text unaltered, and placing the corrections in footnotes, signed Ed. Instead of this I suggest that the corrections, which will be very numerous, should be made silently in the text; the editor keeping as much out of sight as possible, and only making a note when a difference of opinion seems called for -- as for instance when Johnston adopts the current doctrine but the editor thinks it right to indicate that other authorities hold another view.
By this plan it seems to me the book will be far more readable. Controversial notes distract attention and call attention to the editor, who ought really to be in the background. But of course on this plan the reader will not see the amount of alteration in the new edition. When I add that the corrections are mostly of a physiological nature -- the mistakes arising from the author treating physiological subjects on chemical principles, which from Liebig downwards has been the cause of a flood of hypotheses and errors -- you will I think agree with me that the less obvious the editorial alteration the better.
What an admirable and interesting book it is! I do not wonder at its great success.
I am at work collecting material and shall allow nothing to interrupt me in getting on. If you are in any hurry to reprint, I can send you the parts as they are finished.
G. E. has come to stay at Richmond and is writing his new story with a fresh influx of confidence (much needed) from having heard of a rector of a large parish having "cried like a child" over Janet's Repentance. If a few more rectors would be equally tearful I think E. would at last really begin to believe in his power.
Have you thought of an index for Seaside Studies? I think there should be a minute one made because the book contains such a mass of details.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [29 October 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Park Shot | Richmond | Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
The proof, letter and checque for G. E. 338 arrived this morning. Will you please ask the printer always to send me duplicates of the proofs that I may send them to Owen and other pundits for correction when needful?
About the edition I think you had better wait till the plates are ready, some of which I expect daily, as they will give you an idea of the aspect of the book. If Kingsley could sell 3 editions of Glaucus 339 which had nothing whatever new in it, nothing of his own except the preaching, we ought to be able to get off 1250, but it's a horrid bore having a weight of unsold copies on one's shelf.
I have written a paper on "Phrenology in France" 340 which will make the phrenologists all the more savage because they must see that I am not indisposed to recognize such truth as they really have achieved. If you like to print it, and if you would prefer the personal pronoun instead of the impersonal "we," I can make that alteration in proof. If you don't like it, there's no harm done; so I send it on the chance.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [27 December 1858]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: Mr. Lewes's arrangement will be adopted. Revise will be sent on Thursday.
Park Shot | Richmond | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
By this post go the proofs of Parts 2 and 3 of Phys. On reflection I think it eminently desirable to preserve the original divisions; that is to say, to make part 2 include the whole of the 1st section, and begin part 3 with section 2. It is true that part 2 thus becomes longer than the other -- and longer than we ought to give for sixpence but that will be made up by the shortness of part 3. 414 The advantages are these. There is a completeness given to each number. There is so much argumentation in the early portions of part 2 that unless it be carried off by the details of the close, I fear our unphilosophical subscribers (and we shall have but a poor list if we only include the philosophical) may find it uninteresting. Finally we get an illustration in the second part and that keeps up the idea of an illustrated work. The only disadvantage is the matter of length. Perpend!
I am just starting for Vernon Hill to spend my usual Christmas week with Helps; but shall be back again on Saturday. Remember me kindly to your brother, and With heartiest wishes -- Christmassy and other -- Believe me
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [23? August? 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: Sep. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
G.E. has sent back his proof altered, and I now send it on to you, with nothing further to add except that I think the alterations improvements. What you say 958 about the hacknied nature of the clergyman's story is perfectly true; and it appears all the more hacknied because the rest of the tale is so entirely original; but the vaguer such a story, the more hacknied it would necessarily appear; details give an air of reality, and I could have wished G.E. had been more detailed.
I don't know how you find Janet's story affect people in general, but to me it seems singularly powerful and pathetic. My sympathies are not easily enlisted on the side of an Evangelical curate and a woman with "spiritual" weaknesses; nevertheless Tryan affects me, as if the real man were before me, and Janet redeems her weakness by her goodness. One feels the want of a larger canvas so as to bring out those admirable figures, Old Mr. Jerome -- the Linnets -- and the rest; but that is the drawback in all short stories.
By the way G.E. begs me to ask you not to draw a checque again for George Eliot, as it will be revealing to his banker who George E. really is.
I am hard at work revising and adding to Sea-Side Studies. In your estimate don't leave out the paper on Sea Anemones which will of course find its place.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [22 November 1856]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Published: Cross, 1, 423-424.
Park Shot | Saturday.
My dear Sir
Your letter has greatly restored the shaken confidence of my friend, who is unusually sensitive, and unlike most writers is more anxious about excellence than about appearing in print -- as his waiting so long before taking the venture proves. He is consequently afraid of failure though not afraid of obscurity; and by failure he would understand that which I suspect most writers would be apt to consider as success -- so high is his ambition.
I tell you this that you may understand the sort of shy, shrinking, ambitious nature you have to deal with. I tried to persuade him that you really did appreciate his story, but were only hesitating about committing yourself to a series and your last letter has proved me to have been right. Although, as he never contemplated binding you to the publication of any portion of the series to which you might object, he could not at first see your position in its true light. All is, however, clear now. He will be gratified if you publish Amos Barton in January, as it will give him ample time to get the second story ready, so as to appear when Barton is finished, should you wish it. He is anxious, however, that you should publish the general title of "Scenes of Clerical Life" -- and I think you may do this with perfect safety, since it is quite clear that the writer of Amos Barton is capable of writing at least one more story suitable to Maga, and two would suffice to justify the general title.
Let me not forget to add that when I referred to "my clerical friend" I meant to designate the writer of the clerical stories, not that he was a clericus. I am not at liberty to remove the veil of anonymity -- even as regards social position. Be pleased therefore to keep the whole secret -- and not even mention my negotiation or in any way lead guessers -- (should any one trouble himself with such a guess -- not very likely) to jump from me to my friend.
I heard yesterday from an American publisher that there was some thought of reprinting "Sea-Side Studies"; but I believe I have put a spoke in that wheel by holding out the prospect of an enlarged and improved series. Kingsley's little book 765 seems to have had such success, that we may fairly hope, I think, to find a good public if we give them a good thing. What an amount of virtue in that if! Believe me
Ever faithfully yours
G. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [2 December 1858]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
Is there a copy of Hunger and Thirst 1239 ready for me to send to Germany? If so, please let me have one forthwith.
G.E. is very uncomfortable about the delay in printing. He thinks -- and I agree with him -- that mystery as to authorship will have a great effect in determining critical opinion, and although when once a success has been made, the knowledge of the authorship cannot affect it, it might have a prejudicial influence if the rumour to which he alluded in his letter to you should spread -- as spread of course it will. The evil consequences of the mystery being disclosed before the book appears seem to him, and to me, far greater than any disadvantage of contemporaneous appearance with "What will he do with it" 1240 -- the more so as that book having already been for 18 months in the mouths of men, will necessarily be less of a novelty, less talked about, than if it were now first appearing. Under these circumstances don't you think it very desirable to crowd all sail? Your own experience must have shown you the immense advantage there is in a mystery about authorship. Let the public [know] that Smith and not Brown wrote a certain book, and although both Smith and Brown are entirely unknown to the said public a certain charm is lost. When Jane Eyre was finally known to be a woman's book the tone noticeably changed. Not that I believe in the possibility of anything adventitious permanently hurting a good book, but there is always something temporary in the success of a novel, and one may as well secure all adventitious aids.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M

MS: National Library of Scotland.
Park Shot | Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
I have brought out my meaning more distinctly towards the close of the article. But I cannot see anything to alter in the passage about Medicine which, as a science, 349 is, I assure you, in a state not less chaotic than Phrenology; but gains, and deserves, greater respect than Phrenology because its pretensions are humbler.
As I said before I prefer leaving all publishing arrangements to your experience, necessarily so much better a guide than any opinion of mine. Nevertheless as a suggestion I would say let 10/6 rather than 12/- be the price of the book, if that will pay a decent profit. 350 Not being a work which people must have, the cheaper it is the greater will be the sale; and 10/6 seems to me as much as any one would like to give.

Yours very faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

My dear Blackwood
I am truly glad that you like the idea of the series which it will be a real pleasure to me to write. This first part is by no means a fair specimen of the interest that can be thrown into the subject.
I will cut out the negro-eating as you both dislike it; although as a rule I always prefer a specific to a general statement. 357

Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [15 November 1856]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: Cross, I, 421.
Park Shot | Saturday.
My dear Sir
I have communicated your letter to my clerical friend, who, though somewhat discouraged by it, has taken my advice and will submit the second story to you when it is written. At present he has only written what he sent you. His avocations, he informs me, will prevent his setting to work for the next three weeks or so; but as soon as he is at liberty he will begin. 763
I rate the story much higher than you appear to do from certain expressions in your note, though you too appreciate the humour and pathos and the happy turn of expression. It struck me as being fresher than any story I have read for a long while, and as exhibiting in a high degree that faculty which I find to be the rarest of all, viz. the dramatic ventriloquism. At the same time I told him that I perfectly understood your editorial caution in not accepting from an unknown hand a series on the strength of one specimen.
I have another paper sent to me by another friend -- the Rev. George Tugwell -- who is mentioned in Sea-Side Studies as the gentleman so honorably known to the Anemones of Devonshire, and whose recent book on Sea Anemones is much praised by the critics. 764 He is a pleasant writer and might I think be a contributor you would approve. Perhaps you read a paper of his I sent to Frazer a little while since on Science at the Sea-Side?
His present paper is "Wanderings on Exmoor." It is very slight, but agreeably written; contains some descriptions, three legends, and discursive reflections. I do not feel sufficient confidence in it to send it to you without hearing that you would like to see it. If I were an editor I think I should ask the writer to try again; and perhaps on that ground you might like to see it, or shall I suggest to him to try again, proprio Marte?
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [13 December 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Park Shot | Richmond | Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
Can you lend me a copy of Stephens's Book of the Farm, 353 in which I suspect there will be a few details useful for me to know? If you haven't got a cut copy I will go to the Brit. Museum and look at it there.
When I had the pleasure of a visit from your brother I mentioned to him the scheme of a "Physiology of Common Life" which has taken shape in my mind to replace the systematic work on Physiology for which I have been several years making collections. I propose to do for Life what Johnston has done for Chemistry -- and to explain popularly yet according to the latest results of science what is known of Hunger and Thirst -- Food and Drink -- Digestion and Indigestion -- Respiration and Suffocation -- The Blood and its Circulation -- Poisons and Poisonings -- The Moral and Physical Qualities We Inherit from Our Parents -- Sleep and Dreams -- Our Senses and Sensations -- etc.
I propose to publish articles in the Magazine on these topics first, and to enlarge and alter them afterwards. In the first article 354 -- sent by this post -- you will see a specimen. It contains an amount of facts and cases which have never been assembled before in any work that I am acquainted with.
One or two of the topics -- such as Digestion -- have been touched on by Johnston, but my treatment will be not only more exhaustive than his, but will be strictly physiological, and include the unpleasantness so familiar to many which cluster round the disturbances of Digestion.
What do you say to the scheme? If you think we had better publish at once without first appearing in Maga, that also can be done; but there are many advantages in having the work in type, as it were, before beginning the serial publication.
I have been commissioned by my friend Mr. Max Schlesinger 355 of 4 King William St., Strand, to tell you that whenever you publish any work likely to find a sale in Germany, Holland, or Russia, if you will forward him a copy he will notice it in his London Letter, which he contributes to 60 of the principal German papers. His notice will not be a review, but will take the form of literary news -- in fact it is a splendid advertisement which not only appears in his 60 papers, but is copied by a variety of other journals. He announced my "Life of Goethe" in that way, and I had immediately two offers from publishers for the sale of the German translation -- and two for the English reprint. It is of no use sending books not likely to have a foreign sale. But Alison -- Johnston -- Aytoun -- and my book would I think benefit by such advertisement. However, I have explained the matter, and leave it to your judgement.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Richmond, [11 February 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | Wednesday.
My dear Sir
By this post you will receive an instalment 793 of Eliot's new story, which I think even better than the first part of [Amos Barton]; though in a different way. I don't know whether you will have confidence enough to begin printing before seeing the conclusion, but I advised the first instalment being sent to you in order that no break should occur in the publication of the series, if you wished it.
I intended writing to you some days ago to report what I had heard of [Amos Barton] -- it is not much but it is unanimous, and from typical readers, namely foolometers and men of intellectual eminence. I read the first part aloud one evening at Vernon Hill. The women were charmed. Helps said it was "pestilently clever," and John Major, 794 a clergyman, was very much pleased with it. Owen "does not remember when he has read a better story" and Mrs. Owen thinks it "very clever."
By the way turning to my own paper, 795 Owen, in spite of being controverted in it, thinks it masterly and convincing, as he told both Mrs. Owen and myself. The other evening at Carlyle's, Dr. Carlyle was speaking of Goodsir 796 as the most eminent man in Edinburgh now, in science, and added "He has been writing a very striking series of papers in Blackwood lately." I pricked up my ears; and on inquiry found he meant my papers. We laughed at this; but I thanked him for the very great compliment.
I am panting for the Scilly Isles, and every gleam of sunshine makes my uneasiness greater; but printers -- rightly named diabolic -- keep me proofbound inland, and I shall not be free till the end of the month; but early in March I take wing. After Scilly, I think of Guernsey and Brittany -- in the two latter places I have great hopes of having the company of Eliot. And if these three places do not furnish interesting papers, so as to permit a future Book, I shall be disappointed.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
I have not thanked you for Maga -- a very interesting number. Before this was sent off to the post your letter to Eliot came in. I have dispatched it, knowing the extreme pleasure it will give that sensitive doubting fellow. You would never believe the work I have had to make him credit his own genius. He (very judiciously!) looks up to my critical opinion as oracular; but in spite of confidence in me he is so diffident of himself, that I had to bully him into acquiescence with the fact that I had discovered a genius. I cackle over my hatched chick; and so may you.
You will see that the main part of your letter is already anticipated. I think he ought, and will, break through the anonymous with you; mais patience! cela viendra! I have suggested it more than once and when I am no longer here to act as go-between he must, I think, become his own literary Agent.

Elversley | 9 August.
My dear Blackwood
Your bill for 1434 £ and cheque for £100 arrived in due course. Mrs. Lewes begs me in thanking you to say that the success has been quite as great as she ever expected and much greater than the book deserves. The crescendo of admiration ought to tell upon the sale in volumes, for many people refuse to read it in parts.

Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Redhill, [13 July 1872]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Redhill, [13 July 1872]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Elversley, Red Hill | Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
Welcome back again to home, Maga, and golf -- I dare say you are glad enough to be again under the shadow of your penates after the excitement and whirl of the last weeks. It is so with us. An [outing] has its highest relish by a reflex from home.
You will rejoice to hear that our retirement from London excitement has been an immense success -- at least as far as Mrs. Lewes is concerned -- and I am much mistaken if Parts VI and VII do not show the benefit. She got stronger at once and is enjoying the complete solitude and hopes to finish her book by September when we shall take a real holiday.
What think you of publishing VII and VIII at monthly intervals so as to have the whole work completed for December? Part VI would then appear in October when people are returning and VII in November and VIII in December. Christmas would thus have the whole world of Middlemarch to enjoy -- if it needed that!
I have not been so well down here -- I came down with troublesome head symptoms and didn't get over for some time. Now I am the worse for a little imprudence having been seduced up to town to dine with the Irish Chancellor and some other interesting people, 560 and having to pay in headaches for my entertainment! It is all the more provoking as I am [bursting] with ideas -- and want to give them birth. The shadow of old Casaubon hangs over me and I fear my "Key to all Psychologies" will have to be left to Dorothea! 561 -- Isn't the Garth Family a gem?
The enclosed letter 562 gave her and me so much pleasure and her so much encouragement that I am tempted to send it you. Main has already seen it. Send it me back -- or rather when you write to her don't forget to enclose it.
Mad. Bodichon wrote to her the other day that Judge Fitzgerald 563 told her at the opening of the Dublin Exhibition he was struck with the attention of the Archbishop 564 to the interior of his hat which at first he took for devout listening to the speeches, but on close examination saw he was reading something, and as this was so intent he was prompted to look also into the hat, and found the Archbishop had Middlemarch there laid open -- what a much better way of listening to [opening speeches]!
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Ragatz, 17 July 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Ragatz, 17 July 1876
Text: John Blackwood, pp. 396-397.
Hof Ragatz, 17th July 1876.
Your pleasant and welcome letter found us both greatly improved in health and spirits by our stay here. Mrs. Lewes is quite another woman, and is recovering her colour and contour -- not before they were wanted. Her appetite is good, and we walk four hours amid the woods and up the easy mountain-sides -- bathe, eat, read, and idle -- "letting the world fleet by as in the golden time." 513 Not a single word have we exchanged with any one above the rank of a waiter or shopkeeper -- and don't miss the "charms of society," about which some people talk so glibly as indispensable to existence. In the woods of a morning she has taken to instruct me in Hebrew, 514 and we waken the echoes with our laughter sometimes at my blunders and attempts at Israelitish eloquence!
Mrs. Lewes desires her very best remembrances to all (with especial thanks to Willie for his agreeable note), and hopes you have been enjoying your trip into the Highlands. I have had some notion of going there too when we come back, and visiting the Brit. Association at Glasgow, but this is at present very vague.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Petersthal, 23 June 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Petersthal, 23 June 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Petersthal June 23rd 1868.
My dear Blackwood
Your letter with its enclosures acted like a tonic! I believe Mrs. Lewes was fast lapsing into the private opinion that you and I were the only people likely to care about the poem, and when Patterson's enthusiasm reached her it gave her confidence in the possibilities of future works -- at least for a time! It is indeed a fine augury when one superior soul can be stirred as Patterson's evidently is; and we both regret he could not carry out his idea of reviewing it for the Brit.
Quart. Unlike the Times critic he has felt the significance and grandeur of the work -- nor is he so wise as to find out "influences of Browning!" -- (a discovery due I believe to the fact that the critic met Browning at our table). 777
With regard to making a drama of the [Spanish Gypsy] tell Mrs. Siddons that no one thoroughly acquainted with the stage and the poem would fail to see that it was eminently suited for an opera (and I hope will take that shape) but as eminently unsuited for an acting play. To put it on the stage would be to spoil the poem -- and it could not be shaped into an effective drama. 778 I say that "as one having authority." 779
With regard to the proposal of Messrs. Hutchings and Romer 780 of Conduit Street if you have not already informed them of Mrs. Lewes's absence perhaps Mr. Simpson would drop them a note to that effect. When we return we can resume the matter.
Will you ask Langford to get a copy of the poem bound in russia somewhat as the Queen of Holland's copy of [Adam Bede] was bound 781 and let it be at the Priory on or before the 25 July? Mrs. Lewes wants to make a present as soon as she gets back.
We continue enchanted with this place and intend exploring the Black Forest to see if there are more such spots. Both our bodies and both our souls are manifestly the better -- her's would have been more manifestly so had she not been troubled with toothache which is depressing. Our next permanent abode will be St. M'e4rgen | bei Freiburg | im Breisgau | where a letter will be acceptable on the 7 July if you have any news to send.
The delightful sound of the dinner bell -- (and on y dine tr'e8s bien!) -- all the more welcome after a four hours ramble through the woods interspersed with snatches of rest and poetry read aloud -- cuts the thread of my discourse sharp off, but not before I have said all essentials.
Mrs. Lewes begs me to add her very kindest regards and to say your letters always do her good, you seem always to pick out just the most agreeable details.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Petersthal, 15 June 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Petersthal im Schwarzwalde | Monday 15 June 1868.
Dear Blackwood
I got your note just before leaving Baden and in consequence went over to the Rooms to get a look at the [Times] critique which I thought a wretched affair and a complete evasion of the task; but as an advertisement it had its good points. Evidently the poem has laid no hold upon the writer, nor was he prompted to say a word about its nature, but only to [knock off an article] in the readiest manner.
The weather after having been lovely for three days at Baden got cold and continuously wet again so that partly from fatigue with the grandeurs and the stupid gambling and partly from not feeling well we were glad enough to get away and find ourselves in this Earthly Paradise "unknown to Murray." The weather is perfect, the scenery ravishing, life all peace and poetic suggestion, and the food excellent -- if we don't pick up again under such circumstances it will be our fault. We take Morris's poem into the woods with us and read it aloud, greedily looking to see how much more there is in store for us. If ever you have an idle afternoon bestow it on the "Earthly Paradise."
We shall stay here certainly till the 26th so if you write on the 22 or 23rd you will be able to send us news from the Saturday papers -- and I hope another such a slip as the one you sent to Baden showing a movement in the sale. Any good news will act like a tonic. We left London before Maga appeared so did not see it. Willie told me you were not quite satisfied with it. But one never is satisfied with a criticism of a book one thoroughly knows. -- "Unqualified praise and all extracted" -- that is the only criticism which satisfies!
Mrs. Lewes is in her bath and I occupy the leisure moment in writing letters. I know what she would wish me to send in the way of messages -- and send them!
Ever yours
G. H. L.

GHL to John Blackwood, Paris, [13 June 1876]
Text: Copy by Edwin Mallard Everett.
Paris, Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
You will be glad to hear that our journey here was effected without fatigue, though the gaieties have been a little too much for our weakness and deposited a headache in both of us -- but that's of no consequence and we start tomorrow for Dijon and thence to the quiet of Aix and Chamb'e9ry.
Your letter was a great pleasure to her -- we read it in the post office and then went to the Champs Elys'e9es where I couldn't resist reading the proofs -- and made myself icy more than was necessary before entering the Salon. Such a Salon! 4000 frames of theatricality, lubricity, and commonplace, with some score of good pictures -- portraits and landscapes.
The weather which was winter when we arrived has become splendid and summery, which also makes Paris so brilliant. Tonight we close our gaieties with L''c9trang'e8re -- we were last night at the Fran'e7ais and the night before at the Od'e9on, 340 but now unless the open air theatres of Italy I don't fancy we shall have any more theatricals.
Madonna sends her very best regards to you and Willie.
Ever yours,
G. H. L.
I send the proofs in duplicate in case one should miss.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 9 June 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 9 June 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Luitpold Strasse | Munich, 9 June 1858.
My dear Blackwood
It was very kind of you to send the "Saturday," although Langford had already done so, and G.E. begs me thank you for it. Have you seen the article on the Clerical Scenes in the Revue des Deux Mondes? The number has not yet reached Munich so that we are uncertain as to whether its tone be flattering or the reverse. I assume the former. E, of course, the latter.
The weather has become splendid since I last wrote -- rather too splendid, indeed, in these shadeless streets; and has tempted us into little excursions more advantageous to health than to the progress of work. 'c0propos of work, Liebig has changed his mind about that Lecture of his, and wishes it not to appear. It is very tiresome, this shilly shally, but on the whole I am better pleased not to have to translate the lecture; though I was willing to undertake it for him, because he has been so very kind to us. That indeed must be said of everybody here.
I have been expecting daily to hear from you with the proof, and hope it has not been lost or missent. But perhaps you are not contemplating the insertion of the paper on the Circulation in the next number 1154 and that may be the cause.
Are you still broiling in London streets, and London parties? I don't envy you. Even in old London days I always pined to get away as soon as the sunshine appeared, and now it is incomprehensible to me how those stay there who are not forced. De gustibus!
Can you spare me a couple of copies of Seaside Studies for Liebig and von Siebold -- the latter of whom will quote it in the new edition of his "Comparative Anatomy" -- they are both much interested by the discoveries therein described and I should like on all accounts to present them with a copy. If my request is not unreasonable perhaps Langford will send the parcel per Continental Parcel Delivery Co.
G.E. begs to be most kindly remembered. And believe me
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 5 May 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 5 May 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland.
5 Luitpold Strasse, Munich | Wednesday 5 May 58.
My dear Blackwood
Herewith goes the proof of "Blood." I agree with you, in rereading it, that it is a little trying to the general reader, especially without the diagrams which would make it more intelligible; but, en revanche, every reader who is at all interested in the subject will find there a mass of interesting matter, such as he cannot easily get elsewhere. The next paper being purely historical 388 will not have the same obstacle to its popularity.
You do not say how the books are selling, so in your promised letter of gossip let that form an item. The more widely [Seaside Studies] is known the greater acceptance will Physiology of C. L. find, and it is as a [Herald] or [forerunner] that I regard the book.
We are in very comfortable lodgings here, and dine at the table d'hote like princes for 1/3 each, exclusive of wine. Munich contains enough to occupy us a month in mere "seeing," if we were bent on nothing else; but having our daily work to do we find it difficult to get the art and sights "done." Besides this we have the distraction of friends. The "Life of Goethe" has made so great an impression in Germany that its author finds himself in clover, everyone seeming to vie with everyone else in showing attention.
Some of the people here have world-celebrated names -- Liebig, Kaulbach the painter, and Martius 389 the traveller -- others, of smaller fame, are even more interesting. Liebig is charming, however, and we get on famously. He is at this moment absorbed in a new process, he has invented, of making mirrors with silver backs, instead of quicksilver. He has gone with me through the whole process, and the result is astounding: when you look in one of his mirrors and place an ordinary German mirror beside it, you seem to be looking at a living face and at a corpse. Liebig has also communicated to me some new discoveries in Agricultural Chemistry; but declares he has given up Physiology in despair. Tant mieux! Kaulbach we do not much admire although he is assuredly the greatest of their painters; he has given me a proof of his [Madhouse] which has a terrible Hogarthian power; and one of his new cartoons strikes us as fine -- but on the whole, our impression is that a man of remarkable talent has been ruined by German criticism.
The opera is very bad; the tenor outrageous, and the prima donna utterly German. But the orchestra is first rate, and the stalls only cost 2 francs each! The theatre also is poor so that we have not been there more than once.
E. begs his kind regards and believe me ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 28 May 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Luitpold Strasse, | Munich | 28 May 1858.
My dear Blackwood
The pleasure of hearing from you was somewhat damped by Langford's enclosure. It seems particularly hard that books which -- especially the C.S. -- excite such unusual admiration, should nevertheless make so little progress in the market. Of course every author thinks his book good, and worthy of an exceptional sale; but I am not the author of C.S. and yet I scarcely know any book of the kind to put above it. Upon all those who read it it produces a deep impression; but the public seems quite content to leave it unread. It is my unshaken confidence in the merit of the book that makes me agree with you in the certainty of its ultimately doing well, in a cheap form; for it is a book to buy. About my own book I have never been very sanguine or only so at times, when I thought of the public there is for such a book, and the amount of new matter which it contains. Yet though not very sanguine, I am very anxious that it should sell.
The Manx Cat has miauled to some purpose! It is well that Liggers, or any one else, should be the supposed author; because the more confidently such reports are spread, the more difficult will be the detection of the real culprit.
"Adam Bede" gets on steadily and vigorously. 1147 As it is not to appear in Maga, the new edition of C.S. (whenever you think it desirable to bring one out) will be the best possible advertizement it can have. If "Adam" does not produce a profound sensation I will hold my tongue as critic for ever after, and say that I have grown "out of joint with the time." 1148
Liebig is going to assist me in some experiments on Animal Heat; and altogether I find my studies here very profitable, unfortunately my health does not let me work as much as I could wish.
It was an agreeable surprise to hear that the Bulwers liked my articles. But the word [articles] (when one thinks of articles in general and how they are written) applied to papers, in which a mere parenthesis often costs days of labor and sentences sometimes compress the results of years, the word [articles] I say has a sort of implied compliment, indicating that the d -- d hard writing has been easy reading. Don't forget to warn me whenever I am getting dull or technical.
Yes, please pay into the Union Bank of London 4 Pall Mall East, any monies that may from time to time be due.
E. has given you all the news.
Believe me, ever faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 28 June 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 28 June 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Luitpold Strasse | Munich 28 June 1858.
My dear Blackwood
I have just returned from Switzerland 1157 where I have been to see my boys and had the delight of seeing them in splendid health, very happy, and making progress. On my return I found your pleasant letter, and the two copies of [Seaside Studies,] for which thanks. Your advice about the Tyrol had already been anticipated in petto. We start on the 6th for Salzburg, and after a breath of Alpine scenery go to Vienna, Prag, and Dresden, staying at the last named place a few weeks. If you have any proof to send me and do not despatch it by the 2d, please address it Dresden poste restante.
We shall leave our friends here with real regret. It is they who have made our stay memorable and advantageous. The place itself -- especially the climate -- we shall quit with great cheerfulness. We have had tropical heat, and now suddenly great coats are in requisition! G.E. suffers from the climate, but works on with untiring energy. We have puzzled ourselves greatly to divine the reason why Mudie 1158 has never advertized "The Scenes" among his works, although many works very far less significant, and of which he must have taken fewer copies are named in every list. As he doesn't know the author it can't be personal whim -- is it to you? E. of course takes it as a sign that Mudie doesn't think much of the book. I utterly scout that idea. He sends his kind regards. And believe me
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
I have been doing some capital work in the laboratories of my friends here, 1159 where an extensive apparatus and no end of frogs are at my disposal! When government establishes a physiological Institute professors (and amateurs) can work in clover.
I stopped a day at Zurich to see Moleschott, 1160 who invited some celebrities to see me, and I had quite a little ovation. My portrait has been published in one of the German periodicals, with a biography which I should like to see -- one always learns something new in such memoirs! This portrait -- as well as the [Goethe] -- had reached Zurich, so that when I presented myself at Moleschott's his wife, who first said he was not at home, suddenly recognized me, and seizing me by the hand dragged me triumphantly to her husband and we had a "tremendous recognition" as Forster said when he met Leech 1161 in the Strand.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 18 June 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 18 June 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Luitpold Strasse, Munich | 18 June 1858.
My dear Blackwood
Herewith proof, and an article on Respiration and Suffocation.
Thanks for Maga. We both especially admire the article on Religious Biographies both in tone and style; and indeed the sight of the familiar face is quite pleasant here. The German reviews we carefully avoid.
What a poor article that is in the Revue on the Clerical Scenes! but nevertheless one calculated to have some reverberations in England, and do good to the author's reputation, and aid the sale of the cheap edition. I see you are advertizing "Seaside Studies" with a "courage worthy of a better cause" -- and hope that when the people go to the coast they will exhibit a more lively desire to possess that invaluable work. By the way that scrap from the Daily News excites the most ludicrous images in my mind. I see myself in Academic cap and gown smilingly strewing "the path of learning with flowers" (sea anemones I suppose?) at once affable and pedantic, pottering and big wiggish -- but above all unsaleable! A mild watering pot of Science, a zoologist who has taken to the "hat trick" of the wizards, and from the intestines of a mollu[sc] keeps incessantly producing bouquets which he scatters among his "overflowing audiences" (three men in the pit, and one box order.) -- that is the hero of the Daily News criticism.
G.E. begs his kindest regards and believe me,
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
