Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 15 May 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, 15 May 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland.
5 Luitpold Strasse, Munich | 15 May 1858.
My dear Blackwood
I wrote to you the other day with the proof so that this morning I need only dispatch the bit of "business" which prompts this letter. Liebig gave a Lecture here, on the Identity of the Physical Forces, which was very popular, owing to its clear exposition of facts only known to the learned. He has given me the Lecture, and communicated to me the 12 new "Letters" which he is preparing for the new edition of his "Chemical Letters." The Lecture he wishes me, if possible, to make known in England; and he has been so very kind that, much as I dislike translating, I have gratified him by the promise that I would translate it for him. My first thought is for Maga. 390 Would you like to have it? Not having been published, even in Germany, and having Liebig's name attached, might be sufficiently attractive for you -- but unless you would really like to have it, pray don't on my account entertain the idea. Only tell me. I merely wish to give you the first offer.
I find writing here very difficult so much time is absorbed in seeing and discussing. What with Art on the one hand and Science on the other, my brain is like Buridan's ass 391 between water and hay, uncertain which to attack first; except that that stupid young Edward died before he could make a choice whereas I am more likely to die from choosing too much.
E. sends kind regards, And believe me
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, [14 April 1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Munich, [14 April 1858]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Luitpold Strasse | Munich | Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
We reached this place on Monday and have only just settled into our lodgings, the search after which seemed as little promising as that of the philosopher's stone. Imagine yourself in a semi desert of brick and mortar every other house appearing to be a palace (though most of them have lodgings to let) and with no better guide to vacant rooms than a scrap of paper pasted against a post (generally a long way off) informing you in illegible pot hooks that "a solid gentleman" can find elegant rooms at such a place. In full persuasion of your solidity, you trudge to the spot indicated, and after being first sent here, then there, and finally back again you come perhaps to a dog kennel, or spitoon, which you are not ambitious of making your residence. The amount of damns I have bestowed on the worthy German during the last few days is scarcely worth alluding to. Enough that we are settled at last, and with some prospects of comfort and the certainty of cleanliness; and here perhaps we shall remain some time.
Our journey was like every other journey except the two days at N'fcrnberg, which was one protracted oh! Were you ever there? If so, you will understand our rapture; if not, I don't think any description bearing the marks of sanity would convey a proper feeling of the pleasure we received. E. was all entoozymoozy -- having never seen anything of the kind before. Who knows but some day we may have a N'fcrnberg novel, as the product?
I couldn't get to Paternoster Row, so that I am still innocent of the news -- bad or good -- which there awaited me. When you write 1119 let us know what a misguided public has been induced to order. E. sends kind regards and believe me, My dear Blackwood
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
I have 20 letters to scribble -- perhaps they're all as legible as this.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 9 October 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 9 October 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
October 1861.
My dear Blackwood
By this post I send you the paper on '91Buckle'92 which I think had better not be kept any longer lest some of the points should be taken up by others and so give an old rechauff'e9 air to the paper when it appears. I hope you will agree with me that it is policy as well as justice to praise Buckle at the outset seeing how he is flayed throughout the rest of the paper. But if you don't like to commit Maga to so much admiration I can alter it in proof, with a letter from "Scalpel to the Editor? and so make praise and blame more personal.
Does not this moist warm muggy weather incapacitate you from Golf -- and not capacitate you for work? I feel as if one had the Turkish Bath gratis.
Mrs. Lewes is very well and buried in musty old antiquities, which she will have to vivify. I am a sort of Italian Jackal, hunting up rare books, and vellum bound unreadabilities in all the second hand book stalls of London. Sometimes I have great success -- the other day paid 3/- for a little book I despaired of getting because in Libri's sale 854 it fetched five guineas and as it consisted of about [a] hundred small latin poems, you may imagine its rarity.
In the course of these searches for her I alight upon some treasures for myself -- queer Middle Age books of science. By the way just to finish this sheet I will quote you a passage from one of them, -- Van Helmont, 855 -- which you will admit is only too good for Maga: "Hath any one with his excrements defiled the threshold of thy door, and thou intendest to prohibit that nastiness for the future, do but lay a redhot iron upon the excrement, and the immodest sloven shall in a very short space grow scabby on the buttocks; the fire torrifying the excrement, and by dorsal magnetism driving the acrimony of the burning into his impudent anus."
There's more of the like kind but nothing quite so good.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 8 January 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 8 January 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Wednesday 8 January 73.
My dear Blackwood
I had only time yesterday, owing to visitors, to dispatch a postcard acknowledging receipt of your two letters with the bills for 1097.16.11. (for which and for your sharing of Smith's discount many thanks) and I now write to say that we are quite willing to accept your proposal of 5/ a copy for the 21/ edition.
I think this edition ought to be hurried out as soon as may be for these reasons: As far as I can gather there is a ground swell beginning which will rapidly affect the libraries and we ought to be ready for the top of the wave. To drop metaphor, I heard only yesterday sufficient indication that the book is being talked about in various influential quarters. Thus one gentleman 700 told me there was an animated discussion in the smoking room of the Athenaeum and while he was saying this up came Pigott who said he had just left Partridge 701 who told him that at the Academy dinner Bishops and Archbishops were enthusiastic -- I went on to the London Library and there saw Sir James Alderson 702 who had been staying at Hatfield (Lord Salisbury's) and there Middlemarch was the subject of much discussion. Now these three very different sources imply a general interest. But the Libraries will be able to finesse with their copies unless there is the inducement to them of a cheaper edition in the same number of volumes.
I think therefore it should be expressly advertised as "The Guinea Edition." We both think a plain cover desirable. Could it not be made to range tolerably with the 12/- edition of the works? Same color and almost same size?
The Times is only of use as an advertisement and if it came out with our advertisement of a guinea edition might help us.
If you don't take a flight in the [Flying Scotchman] I will write you a programme of the Key.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

March 1861.
My Dear Blackwood,

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 5 August [1861]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 5 August [1861]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
Tuesday 5 August.
My dear Blackwood
I returned the day before yesterday from Spa where by good luck I found Bulwer whose society made a most agreeable addition to that agreeable place. He was more fascinating to me than all the princesses, countesses, Barons, and travelling English I met there. We were constantly together and had fine talks. I brought over a parcel from him for you which was dispatched by yesterday's post.
The trip did me great good and I have come back "my soul in arms and eager for the fray." 827 Mrs. Lewes, who had never been away from me for a week before, since we were married, did not bear the absence so well; but she has brightened up again and is hard at work -- though with the usual fears and apprehensions.
By the way, when you sent me the list of sales some time ago you said that if I looked in upon Langford he would tell me what had been the sales since Christmas. I never contrived to find him in and wrote to him. He replied that Mr. Simpson would send me word when the accounts were made up -- in a few days. But Mr. Simpson has forgotten all about it -- please jog his memory.
What delicious weather! I suppose you are at Strathtyrum?
You will be glad to hear that Thornie has passed -- he was 38th on the list which out of 270 is very well. It is an anxiety the less for us.
Mrs. Lewes begs me to send her kindest regards and believe me
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 31 January 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
January 1861.
My dear Blackwood
Your pleasant letter with its pleasant cheque arrived this morning. I think it will be better to separate the two spontaneous articles, or else people will fancy they have read one when the other is spoken of. Combustion will be popular.
I am trying to induce Mrs. Lewes to run down to Hastings next week in the hope that a sniff of the sea may do us both good. She can't be torn from her work, which by the way, advancing slowly advances with intense interest. It is very original and striking. She thinks it may in all probability be ready for Easter, because she thinks it will not be more than one volume; but that the gods must decide.
It is very kind of you taking notice of my boy and I am much gratified that he produces a favorable impression. The young bear wants licking into shape, but there is real power in him.
Give our kind regards to the Major and tell him I quite agree with him about the bread and butter.
Ever faithfully yours
G.H.L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 27 December 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 27 December 1875
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 75.
My dear Blackwood
I hope it isn't a mocking sound in your ears to be saluted with "a merry Christmas." It is in ours; unless we are understood in Froissart's phrase as taking our pleasure "moult tristement." Mrs. Lewes has been much out of sorts and overpowered with gloom and apprehension which no [reasoning] has power to dispel. But she is getting better again. I have had a diffused sense of the universe being a vague headache. Fortunately we have accepted no invitations, so that we need not be troubled by [festivities.] [Deronda,] advances very slowly -- but superbly. By the way we have not seen a proof of title page and motto 367 -- will you order it to be sent? It should appear with part I.
I suppose you will now begin to advertize energetically; and if the Times could be persuaded to notice the 1st part that would be worth 50 £ of advertizing. [Middlemarch] they did not notice until their notice came too late for any good effect. They used always to notice Thackeray and Dickens's first numbers.
Your advertizing agent might soon begin to canvass for Part I. A good show would help to make the part look more important. 368
The life of Heine you were kind enough to send me I couldn't read. I looked into it here and there, but read blockhead and blunderer in very [round text,] and so closed the volumes with a sigh. It was a task to have tested high abilities. Why do the dull dogs always lay hold of subjects specially demanding wit and lightness of touch?
Mrs. Lewes begs me to remember and add her kindest regards to Mrs. Blackwood, Miss Blackwood and Willie as well as to her [old friend J. B.] Nor should good Mr. Simpson be omitted.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, 25 November 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 72.
My dear Blackwood
Your letter and the checque for 100 and Bill for 25 £ from Melbourne and Holland duly arrived.
We were indeed pleased to hear that you had shaken off your indisposition and were now in good case to face -- empty printing offices and empty authors! Would you take on a Union Man for Maga -- as a contributor?
You seem exactly to feel with us about Forster's Life of Dickens which is surely a lasting injury to his friend whom it presents in a constant state of rouge and footlights.
Mrs. Lewes has got rid of her cold -- but is suffering now (silently, as Mrs. Casaubon would) under an oppression of marital m.s. with no permission to "omit the second excursus on Crete." 639 However she is doing as well as could be expected, and yesterday got through her visitors (18 of them, mostly women) with great spirit. 640
[Everybody] seems greatly agog as to how Middlemarch will end and Mrs. Lewes feels perfectly sure that everybody will be disappointed. The book seems to have produced a profound impression on all who like it. Sunday week a West End clergyman alluded to it in his sermon on the Prophet Hosea in these words: "Many of you no doubt have read the work which that great teacher George Eliot is now publishing and have shuddered as I shuddered at the awful dissection of a guilty conscience. Well, that is what I mean by the prophetic spirit." 641 Plucky, wasn't it? I quote Rogers and say "But the man is right, you know."
By this post I send you all the revise proofs we have. In two parcels.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 25 May 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 25 May 1873
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday 25 May 73.
My dear Blackwood
If you read my letter which first proposed your publication of the [Problems] you will remember how strongly I expressed the sense both Mrs. Lewes and I had of the possible objections, and my assurance that I should entirely sympathize with your refusal. But I wished on personal grounds to give you the refusal -- and I thought it possible that in the present state of opinion even the widest speculative differences might not have interfered. We were both surprised and pleased to find you ready to overlook all speculative differences, and after you had read the pages you would object to, it was still open to you to have stayed the further printing, and saved me the very great inconvenience of some three months delay. I am indeed very glad that you have finally decided as you have done. It would have been very painful to both of us had the work been published and you had -- when too late -- expressed your feelings on the subject. Now there is no harm done beyond the wasted time, and the announcement of the book as about to be published by you.
Let us therefore consider the whole project at an end -- treat it as if it had never been; and let me have the m.s. and any proofs that may be ready as soon as practicable.
But now this matter is finally disposed of let me rectify your very strange misconception of my position. I took no notice of it in your letter accompanying the first proof because I thought you had read and written hastily and that a glance at the pages would dispel your misconception. This appears not to have been the case. Look again at pages 2 and 3. You will see first that I do not say those are the most weighty thinkers who believe religion at an end -- and that I could not have implied it, since I declare myself to hold the opposite view; secondly that the whole of page 3 is a summary of arguments against this view, and an expression of my own adhesion to such arguments. How you missed such plain statements I cannot imagine -- probably because you started with a preconception. Thus you say I assume too much on my side at the commencement -- the fact being that I assume nothing, but am simply recording what are the two views held by philosophic speculators.
I add this rectification simply for the sake of disabusing your mind of a complete misconception -- when you add that I "seem to give no weight to mind and feeling in the matter" the misconception of my views is beyond rectification. I can only despair of my power of exposition!
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.
This will of course make no difference. We will meet without reopening the subject -- having decently buried it. When shall you come up? Or will you take your chance some afternoon about 5? We are almost always in at that hour.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 23 October 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 23 October 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 76.
My dear Blackwood
We have been duly pondering your liberal offer for another ten years lease of the novels, but the various considerations which present themselves keep us in a fluctuating state, and we must have another week before finally deciding. In any case be assured that we are as anxious as you can be that the books should continue to appear under the old flag. Mrs. Lewes begs me to add that she is quite sure there will be no difference in our views whatever the ultimate arrangement may be.
You are quite correct as to the termination of the old lease in December. Only one doubt remains which I wish to put before you, namely whether we are to have any of the contingent advantage notified in the old agreement? Your proposal was either 2 thirds of the profit -- or 1000 £ with 500 £ contingent on success "should the edition prove a success i.e. sell at any time during the next five years within an average of 2000 sets." Well, during the first five years that success was not achieved, but was it not during the next five? Does not the sale of copies in those five years -- and of 73,398 in the whole ten years -- pretty well accord with the notion you had of a success? Perhaps you have already considered this point; perhaps not; at any rate I bring it before you just as it lies in my mind.
Yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 22 November 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 22nd 76.
My dear Blackwood
We quite agree to your proposal.
Mrs. Lewes would have been glad to know that you were going to issue the 21/ edition of D.D. as she wished to correct three or four errors -- however it is too late now, and we must wait for the 7/6. But I am a little surprised that you did not content yourself with risking 1,000 -- as the types were ready to reprint a second 1,000 if needed -- for I have grim doubts of your getting through with the 2,000£. There seems to be so general a sense of disappointment -- so much deadness to the Jewish element -- that my only hope for a large sale until the public has learned to get over its first disappointment is in the Jewish public and they can only, I fear, be caught by the cheap edition. (Don't allude to the disappointment in any letters to me -- she only knows that Judaism is unpopular not what is said otherwise about the book.) 565 I remember that [Romola] was received with a universal howl of discontent -- and now it is the book most commonly placed at the head of her works -- or at any rate after [Middlemarch.] If Deronda is the book I take it to be we shall see a revival or rather a reversal of opinion. Curiously enough in America it seems to have surpassed [Middlemarch.]
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 20 August 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 20 August 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
August 61.
My dear Blackwood
Are the charms of golf all engrossing or has your letter been tampered with by some inquisitive postman? This is the 20th and not having heard from you makes me dubious.
Willie will have told you that I have finished the paper on "Buckle's Scientific Errors" but detain it, till after your review of volume 2 appears. Mine is solely devoted to an expos'e9 of his blunders in science and doesn't touch any other point.
I am half way through a paper "Discoverers in Science: Marshall Hall," but my health continues so bad that I doubt whether I shall be able to finish it in time for this month. If you don't receive it by the 25th you may conclude I am not up to the scratch.
We dispatched Thornton to Switzerland this morning and the house will now resume its quiet, much to Mrs. Lewes's benefit. She allows herself to be preyed upon dreadfully by the boys -- she can't say No.
"The Book" is slowly crystallizing into what will be a magnificent programme. Until quite lately I thought she would relinquish altogether in despair, her singular diffidence being exaggerated in this case. But now I think it will really be written. If only I could see the first chapter!
What delicious weather! I long so to run away and be at rest on the coast.
Ever yours faithfully,
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 2 September [1871]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 2 September [1871]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September.
My dear Blackwood
Home again and not sorry once for a while to enjoy the [comforts of the saut market.]
My arrangement with America is very simple and cannot in the least interfere with England. The advance sheets are to be sent to Osgood and Co. who will begin to print in their weekly paper at such a time as will allow their last instalment to be out before Part 1 reaches America. That is to say although we publish Part 1 in England a fortnight before they publish their last weekly instalment of the same, they will have the advantage of really being before the other Americans, though not before us. Only two copies of the paper come to England, one to me. These are posted. The slight advance in point of time given to them though of great importance to them will be of none to us. If they waited till we published in England before they began to publish they would of course be forced to print it as we do all at once. It is to give them their weekly advantage that the plan has been devised; and they pay for it.
As respects terms I think prudence rightly suggests that you should not take the risk when the adventure is so novel. But I also think that in that case the alternative I proposed is the only proper one. If the adventure is a failure your modified proposal would leave you at a disadvantage. If a success it would leave us at a disadvantage. Since the expenses are certain to be more than covered, my plan leaves us both a risk only of diminished profit, with the chance of a good one.
Mrs. Lewes begs her kindest regards and says Mr. Simpson did not send The Speech -- or it did not come!
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 2 July 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 2 July 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
July 1861.
My dear Blackwood
I couldn't help laughing at the passage in your letter relating to Mrs. Blackwood's priority. It is the way of wives! They will think our best thoughts before us. Mes hommages 'e0 Madame, et dites lui ou je me trompe fort, ou elle est bien capable d'avoir souvent de ces priorit'e9s l'e0.
It would indeed be a great gain to Thornie if he could catch something of Willie's savoir faire. He wants rounding.
Lucky people to be out of the smoke and in the country! But everything has its compensation and I reflect (with gratitude) that if I am in London -- I haven't a pile of '91contributions'92 to oppress me. Alas! the series 803 is quashed. I feared it would be so, and so it is.
Yes, I have already read the articles you refer to and think all three first rate. I didn't understand Thackeray's sneer 804 to apply to Aytoun; it is most untrue, as well as uncalled for, since it is notorious that Aytoun's greatest poet was Homer -- not I believe a gentleman of the Caledonian persuasion, though we don't know where he was raised. The fact is, Thackeray is so soured by the want of success which his writing of late has had, that he is sardonic and bitter against all who are successful -- even against his friend Trollope, I hear! -- I too have somewhat itched to '91remonstrate'92 with him, in the tone of the remonstrance with Dickens; but I fear it would be of no use. He has said his say and done his work; very admirable work too!
Mrs. Lewes continues very well and I continue very much autre chose. She is buried in the middle ages and I am yapping amid mad dogs.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.
I shall send Du Chaillu 805 through Langford.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 2 April 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland.
16, Blandford Square, | N.W.
Tuesday 2 April 61.
My dear Blackwood
Your two letters with their checques have just arrived and I intend saving this post to acknowledge their arrival.
The trifle I had "in hand" was an experiment of which you must judge -- viz. the turning of an old unacted piece of mine into a lively story. As just such an experiment was the fortunate commencement of a connection with you, 531 which has been most agreeable and profitable, I was seduced into repeating it, the more so because I have long since cut the theatre and its affairs. I don't know what you will think of the story. 532 It seems amusing and lively to me; but it may smack too decidedly of its origin; so don't be under any misgiving about returning it, if you don't take to it.
Murray advertizes De Chaillu's book for April. As before hinted, I should like to review it, since it will be full of natural history stories. 533 I'm afraid if we go to Italy I shall not be industrious enough to write; but be assured that if I write at all, it will be for you.
I can sympathize with your swelled cheek. Some three or four years ago I was a martyr to it and it always indicates an anarchical condition of Schleswig Holstein, as you remark.
Mrs. Lewes will write, I suppose tomorrow, meanwhile she bids me send her kind regards. I think we go to the Proph'e8te tonight -- that is if Langford has a box. 534
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 19 January [1878]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday 19 January.
My dear Blackwood
Your most welcome letter with accounts and checque arrived this morning. Satisfactory? I should think so! The total surpasses our expectations and the details are curiously interesting. Why [Silas Marner] should lag so far behind the others is a perpetual puzzle to me because it is the one book which everybody praises without reserve and which always rises when G.E. is mentioned. The vitality of the poems is also a pleasant sign.
We envy you the expected visit to Rome. Have you any dreams of a Hat? Dean Stanley 14 amused us the other day by describing a coherent dream he had of having been elected Pope, and was puzzled as to the name he should assume. Paul seemed most suitable as a Protestant but he reflected that he would then be Paul VI, and six was a fatal number with Popes. -- [Cardinal Blackwood] would sound well -- but oh! the shrieks of Auld Reekie at his stockings!
Mrs. Lewes is pretty well, but troubles with decoration and furnishing at the Heights are soon to begin.
I have begun [Marmorne] 15 and fancy it is going to turn out something original and good. Otherwise I have not been reading anything lighter than an anatomical periodical (not the liveliest of literature!) Anthony Trollope is back again 16 and called here on Tuesday in all his native force and goodness.
Mrs. Lewes begs to be kindly remembered to you and the family.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

January 73.
Dear Blackwood
Your cheque for 143 £ arrived to-day and your very welcome acceptance of my proposal about the Key to all Mythologies. Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 18 April 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
8 April 1866.
My dear Blackwood
Mrs. Lewes is finishing the novel which has been so long delayed by the state of her health, and will in all probability be ready to publish it by the end of May. She wishes it to appear all at once, and the printing to be so far advanced that the last sheets may be set up as soon as written. It is therefore necessary that the question of publication should be settled forthwith, and she would not like to make any arrangement until she had heard your views on the matter, if you are disposed to make her an offer for the entire right for 5 years; without your seeing the m.s. which would involve too much delay.
It is a novel of English Provincial Life just after the passing of the Reform Bill in '32. I need not say that the political tone is as dramatic and impartial as her tone has been in all her writings, and that the fact of the story moving amid political scenes which form its background will only render it more interesting to all parties.
Let me hear from you as soon as you conveniently can and believe me
Yours very truly
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, 15 April [1861]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: Jan. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
April.
My dear Blackwood
I am pleased that you like Mrs. Beauchamp. 747 I could not form a fair opinion myself, because that which is effective on the stage often fails in print.
Du Chaillu I fear will not be out in time for me to take with me; but it can be kept till my return in July, if you like. I take with me a learned book on our lacustrine ancestors -- the people who built towns in the lakes -- and were very strange beings indeed. A learned Genevese 748 has made a vast collection of ornaments, utensils, and fragments of various kinds which enable him to restore something like an image of these antique races and their ways. The book will make I think a very interesting paper, and I hope to write it at Florence and will send it you from there.
There can be no need for anxiety as to Maga; at any rate as far as my poor pen goes you may count upon its best, and abundance in quantity. I thought the story would be welcome after so much science; in science I have three or four subjects in petto.
Mrs. Lewes is writing so I leave to her to say everything else.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
P.S. Address post restante Florence -- we shall be there by 1 May. If anything particular should occur -- poste restante Nice or Genoa will catch us by 25 and 28 April. But Florence is safest.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 14 November 1869
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 14 November 1869
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Sunday 14 November 1869.
My dear Blackwood
On our return home last night we found the letters from you and Willie. Immediately after the funeral I took Mrs. Lewes away to a farmhouse in Surrey where we could be sure of perfect solitude. She needed it greatly, for she was terribly shaken by the climax of our six months anxious watching. She had lavished almost a mother's love on my dear boy, and felt almost a mother's grief. I was better prepared, having never from the first held much hope of his recovery, and for the last three months having almost ceased to wish it, since it could not have been more than recovery into a state of constant helplessness and pain. In the deep peace of the country she has become calm, though still very sad. A beautiful image remains to us; a sweeter purer nature than his can seldom be met with; and we look back with peculiar satisfaction at the fact that never once did we discern the slightest trace in him of anything mean or unworthy.
Now we are back again we may get to work, and help by that to learn endurance. You would have been shocked to see her when we left and delighted to see her when we returned so great was the improvement.
She begs me to thank Willie for his kind letter and to send her kind regards to both of you.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, 13 January 1877
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 77.
My dear Blackwood
With the unusual gleam of sunshine this morning came your gleam of a letter with its checque and statement. The sales -- except D.D. at 21/- are indeed very satisfactory -- those of the Poems the most gratifying to G.E. The 88 copies of the 4 volume Middlemarch leads one to hope that D.D. will also in time get run off. Why the Jews don't come in I don't understand.
There is only one omission I notice in the statement, and that is of the advertisements in D.D.
If I forgot to say anything respecting your blunder in arranging terms for the copyright it was because after your explanation the whole thing passed out of my mind. I had not only interpreted your letter but had misinterpreted the figures of the statement of sales.
Apropos of forgets I mean to convict you of forgetting to send me back the Contemporary Review, with Dowden's article as well as of clearing up that story -- if it ever was cleared up.
We are both tolerably well but troubled in our minds with the prospect of furnishing and moving.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, 11 August [1861]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
August.
My dear Blackwood
Your checque arrived in due course. Respecting the publication of the "Mill" we think it will be more prudent to wait till October -- no one buys at this period, and the start is important.
I have observed for several months that Smith 828 does not exhibit any of the novels either at London Bridge or Waterloo. I don't suppose that he has sold all his copies (if so he might replace them) but if he keeps them unseen they stand a poor chance. Does your traveller ever jog their attention to such points? When idle men waiting for the train run their eye over the bookstall they are tempted to buy what they see, and not to ask for what they don't see.
The lovely weather seems to have departed again!
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, 10 January 1876
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 10/76.
My dear Blackwood
I observe that you have not billed the Contemporary or Fortnightly Reviews; the former has become a very important organ circulating among probable buyers of Deronda, and I think that in the next number at any rate a bill might be inserted with effect 381 -- better late than never! Mrs. Lewes is better again, and the third volume is oh! so grand! 382
I think of reproducing some half dozen of the illustrations which appeared in the [Physiology of Common Life] in my 3rd volume. 383 Would you object to let Tr'fcbners have casts of them? I haven't quite determined the point, nor the figures to be chosen; but I should be glad to have the casts if you see no objection.
I believe you bind the proofs of Mrs. Lewes's books? I am preserving them for you.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, 1 May [1866]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, 1 May [1866]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Fortnightly Review | Office 193, Piccadilly.
May.
My dear Blackwood
From the postscript of your letter today I infer that you have understood to your disadvantage our arrangement about "Felix Holt." We meant all rights whatever during five years to be included, and not simply the copyright in England.
From America you ought to get £300 (that was the sum given for "The Mill" by Harper). From German translation about £30. From French £20. I quite agree with you about Tauchnitz; unless he paid a handsome sum he ought not to have it -- but perhaps he had better not have it at any price likely to be paid. 450
I have given our friend Lehmann a letter to you about the German translation. He wants to purchase it for his brother 451 and will give as much as any one for it.
If you wish it I will apply to Sampson Low about the American right, though I think Langford could play off Harper against Ticknor better than I could as I shall be away and can't carry on the war by letter. 452
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.
N.B. Don't give any Frenchman permission unless he comes with a distinct offer from a publisher. You will be beset by translators.

Friday.
Dear Blackwood
Io triumphe! The last pages were dispatched yesterday -- and thrilling they were! But the delight of seeing her free from the terrible strain is inexpressible. Yours ever

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [9 January 1869]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Dear Blackwood
Tom Trollope in a letter just received begs me to ask you whether a story entitled [Plagassian] 3 which he sent you for Maga some three months past has reached its destination. Not having heard from you he fears the post may have played him false. He says he doesn't wish to hurry you in reading or deciding on the story but only to know that it has reached you safely. Let me know as I have to write to him -- and if it has arrived I should be glad also to be able to intimate your decision to him.
I have just had sorrowful intelligence from Thornton which I am sure you will sympathize with. 4 The poor fellow has stone in the kidney and his sufferings are so great that I have written to him to come over to England and have the best advice and perhaps go through an operation. The vision of him haunts me incessantly.
Ever yours faithfully,
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [7 December 1867]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
My dear Blackwood
Your approbation of the Poem has given Mrs. Lewes fresh life and hope (she needs such stimulus to counteract her terrible diffidence). Please let us have half a dozen proofs for correction.
I should like an extra copy of Maga for January. Don't you think a hint to Delane might possible get a leader in the Times on Felix's address? I will poke up the [Pall Mall.]
Mr. Simpson will kindly keep the m.s. of the poem for me to have it bound like the others when complete.
I am deeply immersed in researches on the nervous system and intend running over to Germany as soon as the weather will let me, to work in the laboratories of the great anatomists there. I should like to have three or four copies of the [Physiology of Common Life] to take there if you can spare them.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [5] January 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
432 January 72.
My dear Blackwood
We returned last night from Weybridge where we had spent the opening week of the New Year with our friends the Cross family -- in the hope that the hospitality, fresh air, and rest would set Mrs. Lewes up she having been in an ailing condition for some time. We enjoyed the visit but alas! it did her no good and she is now under Sir H. Holland's care. We had Jowett, Bowen 433 (the junior in the Tichborne case on whom Coleridge mainly relies), Sandars, 434 and had charades, lots of fun, and some delightful olives -- but all to no purpose as I said!
Going down I found that at the Waterloo Station all the copies of Middlemarch were gone -- and a friend told me he wanted to buy one ten days ago at the London Bridge Station but there were none to be got. I suppose one couldn't stir Smith up to look after his stalls? 435
Main's book is very handsome and the inside is amazing even to me.
Mrs. Lewes thinks there may be some material for her in [Brougham's Life,] 436 and would be grateful for a copy of it.
How does golf get on this weather? sloppy? And you? and Willie? Not that you are expected to answer these questions unless you have to write about something else.
Yours ever
G. H. L.

433 Charles Synge Christopher Bowen  (1835-94), M.A. Balliol College, 1857, was elected a Fellow while still an undergraduate. He was an intimate friend of Benjamin Jowett, who became Master of Balliol in 1870. His close association with the Attorney General Sir John Duke Coleridge (1820-94), began during the trials in the Tichborne case, 1871-74. Bowen and his wife were frequent visitors at the Priory after October 1871.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [5 November 1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [5 November 1860]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Harewood Square.
My dear Blackwood
At last I have got through my task of rewriting the Physiology, 660 which has been a great pleasure to me as well as hard work, for I felt all along that the right manner had been got hold of, and I think the book will be the most intelligible as well as the most interesting that has yet been published on the subject.
The size of the woodcuts renders it necessary that the new book should be printed in the same form, as the Phy[siology] of C[ommon] L[ife] and as the matter is not much in quantity, it would perhaps be advisable to use the same type. This would make a volume of 240 or 250 pages which might sell at 3/6. But on such points you and Mr. Simpson will be better able to decide.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, [5 March 1870]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank | Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
I am forced to suspend work altogether for a time and so we are going to Germany for a couple of months to see if the relaxation will restore me a bit. 131 We start on Monday week. If the last year's accounts are not made up in time to send before that it will be as well to keep them back till our return in May.
The holiday will do Mrs. Lewes good also I hope.
In haste yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Relation: 131 GHL, not yet recovered from the  painful experience of Thornie's death, suffered prolonged headaches and felt languid. 17 February 1870 he "fainted in bed before going to sleep," and felt queer and rather numb in the extremities next day. GHL to John Blackwood, London, [4 November 1875]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
She was much pleased to hear that the second reading was not a falling off. She is decidedly better in health since our return, but proceeds very slowly and despondingly with volume 3. Non fit aliter!
As to terms, yes, the old Middlemarch both price and lordship. May the success be as great! 326
I am curious to hear how volume 2 will affect you and whether you find a crescendo of interest.
I am going to Cambridge next week to work in the Physiological laboratory 327 -- but have a wretched account to give of myself. Nervous exhaustion has for some weeks entirely prevented work and I am only now feebly beginning again.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [31 May 1873]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
I am glad to think that arrangements have been made as to printing which prevent any loss having occurred, 198 and hope that the loss of time may be in some degree lessened by encreased energy in future. I sent back the six sheets yesterday.
When the guinea edition of Middlemarch was first contemplated we both thought it a risk and neither you nor I imagined that we should sell more than 500 copies at that price. On such a supposition your proposed royalty was quite acceptable; but now the event has turned out so very differently, and the rapid sale of 1500 has so pleasantly disproved our calculations ought not the royalty to be encreased?
We were sorry to miss seeing you yesterday -- all the more so because after all we did not have to run down to Chislehurst, the gentleman having written to postpone our visit till Monday. 199
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Saturday.
Dear Blackwood

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.

Dear Blackwood
Your inspiriting approbation came when Mrs. Lewes was in a very desponding mood, and rescued her -- for a time! She clings to the idea that since the poem has laid hold of you it will not wholly fail with the public. Nous verrons. I think it prudent not to print more than 2,000 at first and as I presume you will keep the type standing we shall soon see how it is likely to go.

I should like to see your Dogbook -- it may be serviceable to Ben. 752
I asked the Pall Mall to put in a paragraph.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, [29 October 1876]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
The more we ponder your proposal the more we feel that a royalty is the most satisfactory arrangement for all parties. It is not that we are in any way dissatisfied with the sum you propose; but that we would rather be relieved from the sense that the arrangement might turn out disadvantageous to you; and also that we should like to have free command over editions and prices.
The Jews seem to be very grateful for Deronda -- and will perhaps make up for the deadness of so many Christians to that part of the book which does not directly concern Gwendolen. When the cheap edition is issued we shall perhaps see the effect of this Jewish sympathy. The Jews ought to make a good public -- as the doctors did for Middlemarch.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [29 December 1875]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Wednesday
My dear Blackwood
Your checque and agreeable letter arrived this morning. The sales are indeed satisfactory and promise for Deronda, who I suspect will have a much larger public. The Jews alone would constitute an energetic propagandist party, for never have they been idealized and realized so marvellously before.
Since I wrote Mrs. Lewes has been better. But 'tis a frail vessel of Venetian glass! Your amusing account of Stigand is just what might have been conceived. But I must tell you that I am far too deeply engrossed with nerve centers to pay attention to anything else -- my strength is small and it is all absorbed by my work. It is rarely I can even read Maga!
Yours ever
G. H. L.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, [28 March 1873]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Dear Blackwood
I send you such a letter as you may send to Tait and will put him in possession of what is asked of him. 171 The type and aspect are all that could be desired. Please ask Mr. Simpson to order the m. s. to be sent along with the proofs.
[Kenelm Chillingly] 172 arrived this morning. May it prosper! The Times notice was not a good one for those who read carefully; but the mass don't read, they glance.
Every American mail continues to bring gushing testimonies about Middlemarch. Mrs. Lewes is not the thing and longs for quiet and the country. On Sunday we had 23 at our gathering from 1.30 to 6.30. -- Darwin, Kinglake, Grant Duff, Clifford, Joachim, Roundell, Browning, and some [swells.] 173 We went to bed at 9!
We hope the new edition 174 continues in demand. Does not this delicious weather rejoice your heart? Kind regards to Willie.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.
Here comes more m. s.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [28 June 1861]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [28 June 1861]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
June 1861.
My dear Blackwood
I have read Du Chaillu but have so very little confidence in his veracity that I cannot make an article on the book -- especially as it is now rather a worn subject. How much may be true and how much make up one cannot say; but the book has not the ring of personal experience.
What say you to Mad Dogs! a subject I have for some time had in petto and for which a recent French publication will furnish a peg. Popular superstition makes these July and August months the great periods for hydrophobia, and the article would have a sort of 'e0propos. My purpose is to clear up some of the current errors on the subject and show what can be done as preventive.
How about Buckle? I have been unable to write ever since I came home; but am feeling better today, and therefore ready to scheme papers.
Mrs. Lewes is buried in old quartos and vellum bound literature which I would rather not read; but she extracts nutriment, I have no doubt. She is very well. Don't forget to get a copy of Pug's photograph taken that the disconsolate family may occasionally recal him.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood, Esq.
Isn't it too bad of the Cornhill continuing to take up my subjects and titles? This month they have "Food" -- and of course people imagine I am furnishing a rechauff'e9 of my physiology.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [28 January 1876]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Friday.
My dear Blackwood
You are quite right about sending to Dailies and Weeklies at the same time. Indeed your proposition was exactly the one I submitted to Langford, though not on your grounds. There must be no favoritism shown.
By the way, indisposed as I am to look at criticism I should be glad to see what the dailies except the Times say of the first part -- if Mr. Simpson will kindly send them. Mrs. Lewes is but so so and gets on slowly and anxiously, but I hope soon to send you volume 3.
Although we are rather shy of making new acquaintances unless they are really pleasant we should of course be glad to see any one of whom you speak so favorably as of Mr. Julian Sturgis. If he will come some Sunday he will be welcome.
Enclosed my list of presentation copies. My sister in law's address I will forward you by post, when I get it. The letter missent to you was to ask her where she had moved to now her son is appointed chemist to the Wellington College. 391
Langford tells me that we shall see Willie shortly. Perhaps he may take back the precious m.s.!
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [27 February 1877]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [27 February 1877]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
For the last month I have been laid up by an attack of rheumatic gout, and as soon as I began to get about again -- though feebly -- Mrs. Lewes was laid low by a return of her old malady. She I am happy to say seems decidedly on the mend now, but has had a bad time of it. 613
In my wearisome seclusion from work and friends I read Dowden's article on Middlemarch and Deronda with intense gratification -- it made me regret the contretemps which had prevented his carrying out his idea of a book, and I dare say he might still be induced to resume that idea if you thought fit to nudge his elbow a little.
I also read Romola again with fresh delight. Mrs. Allingham is unable to undertake the illustrations, and we should both prefer the republication without anything more than a frontispiece.
I have been "dallying with the faint surmise" 614 of a new and uniform edition of the works of G.E. to begin with Romola -- to continue with Silas Marner -- with Brother Jacob and Lifted Veil. Each volume to be six shillings (except Silas -- Middlemarch and Deronda) -- the type of the present edition would do very well but a larger margin and a new cover, would disguise this. My belief is that the public is always attracted by a novelty -- be it only that of the binding! -- and that six shillings would be just as freely paid as 2/6 by a great many people. This need not interfere with the cheap edition. The main difficulty is about Deronda. When do you think we ought to issue the 7/6 edition? It would of course be made to range with the edition I speak of.
While Mrs. Henry Wood, Miss Braddon, Wilkie Collins 615 etc. sell their novels at 6/- surely G.E. may expect a public?
I send the corrected Romola by post. With our kindest regards to you and yours believe me
Yours ever
G. H. L.
Dublin Core:Creator: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Publisher: George Eliot Archive, edited by Beverley Park Rilett. https://GeorgeEliotArchive.org
Dublin Core:Contributor: MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Dublin Core:Relation:
613 Friday, 23 February 1877 GE had  a visit from Mrs. Burne Jones. "But after dinner while about to take my nap I was alarmed by her violent screams in the drawing room and rushing in found her hysterically screaming and sobbing -- not from pain but strange and excessive irritation in the kidneys. She quieted and then felt as if she had taken chloroform. As the evening advanced she got better and before bed time became quite chatty." 27 February GHL reports "Polly very much better." The next day "the old pains in kidneys" had returned. (GHL Diary.)
614 Lycidas, line 153 reads "false surmise."
615 Ellen Price Wood (1814-1887), author  of East Lynne, 1861; Mary Elizabeth Braddon (1837-1915), author of Lady Audley's Secret, 1862; William Wilkie Collins (1824-1889), author of The Woman in White, 1860. All three were prolific writers, publishing a new novel almost every year.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [27 February 1876]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [27 February 1876]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
I was very sorry to find from your last that you did not take cordially to Mordecai -- sorry because I think it on the whole one of the greatest of her creations, (and of course one likes to have one's admiration reflected in the admiration of others) -- but mostly sorry because I knew it would damp her. It has cast a gloom over her already desponding mind; she feeling that the public will in general share your imperfect sympathy. All along this has been her vision of the effect which this presentation of the Jewish ideal would have; and I have vainly combated it. But whether it is liked or disliked do it she must and will.
The great success of Part I and the confidence exhibited by the booksellers ought to encourage her, but doesn't. She knows that her gloom is foolish, but this knowledge can't displace the feeling. What a blessing a little of the author's self satisfaction would be to her!
Last night we dined with the Lytton's to say good bye. Poor Lady Lytton is far from well and Robert is certainly not in a promising state for India and official work. 411
I have been laid up with severe lumbago, which is now gone at last. 412 Mrs. Lewes is better again, but until volume four is finished one can't hope for more than a slight improvement.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [26 November 1860]
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
0 Harewood Square | Monday.
My dear Blackwood
By this post goes the article on [Uncivilized Man] -- with one of the volumes for extract. 520 The paper is short -- let me hope [sweet] also. -- When I proposed it I thought the books (which I hadn't read) would have furnished better details. But so few men have eyes to see!
Mrs. Lewes, who has been very low and poorly is better again and at work. She is writing magnificently and as usual can't be made to believe that it is worth reading! It was pleasant to see the [Mill] in the two charming volumes. 521
Our kind regards to the Major.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.
The greatest of German physiologists 522 (whom I don't know) has just sent me a book of his -- which shows that the [Physiology] is held of some account abroad.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [26 April 1874]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [26 April 1874]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday | (Before the guests come)
My dear Blackwood
Your proposal is quite acceptable and accepted; and your intimation of being soon in town makes the beer bottles lively in expectation!
We have got our country house for the summer; but don't emigrate until June.
We are both flourishing and both writing. This lovely weather would be too enchanting were there not a dark cloud of suspicion behind it in the shape of certain east wind and probably snow. Willie once more on horseback is a "good line in the bills."
Mrs. Lewes is uncomfortable in the belief that the paper which the poems are printed on is that of the specimen volumes sent for the boarding; but I assure her that they are proofs and that W. B. and Sons are more inclined to err on the side of too good a paper than too poor a paper. After all, I say to her, it is what is printed on the paper, not what is the paper printed on which she ought most to regard.
You see how the heat diverges my pothooks. When the score or more guests 78 have come and gone I shall probably go to bed!
Ever yours
G. H. L.

GHL to John Blackwood, London, [25 February 1869]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Dear Blackwood
We start on Monday -- will you therefore please by return of post let me know whether we can sell Ticknor and Fields the early sheets of Lisa, as I want to conclude this before starting. I forgot in writing to you that this was just the pressure of the end of the month, and did not therefore say [drop me a line yes or no.]

Yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [25 April 1866]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [25 April 1866]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
In enclosing the formal acceptance of your offer let me tell you what a cordial your letter was to the drooping spirits of Mrs. Lewes, who as you know never believes there is any good in her books until somebody she can rely on (I count for nothing!) tells her so. Your first letter gave her a glass of moral champagne. The letter of this morning repeats the dose. You convince her that you have entered into the spirit of her book. When the lawyer 705 whom she consulted (and who was evidently almost as much struck by her mastery of the law of Real Property as by anything else) told me he thought it would have a greater success than any of her previous books, she concluded that to be mere friendly politeness, though she knows he is an enthusiastic admirer. But you have (for a moment) given her confidence.
Isn't it altogether a most original book? so unlike novels? -- Though the drama of the 3rd volume, will, unless I am a bad prophet, lay hold of even those frivolous readers who care only for story.
It is a great pity that it isn't quite ready for publication just in the thick of the reform discussion so many good quotable [bits] would be furnished to M.P's. 706 However the subject will not grow cold. She expects to be entirely finished by the end of May; so as to appear at the beginning of June. -- Would it be too late to insert a slip into Maga this month announcing it for June -- with the title?
I am suffering from one of my bilious attacks which makes correspondence and everything else laborious -- so if this is a little incoherent you know the cause.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
Your telegram arrived three hours after your letter. The old story!

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [23 May 1876]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
We have no objection to offer; but you can understand how very reluctant Mrs. Lewes would be to say a word in favor of such a scheme, 485 or of anything else that tended to her glorification. When you have read his article you will best be able to judge of the advisability or non-advisability of the proposal.
Mrs. Lewes was so poorly after the dinner on Thursday at the Portsmouths (though she enjoyed it greatly) that she determined not to risk the Oxford visit and I wrote to Jowett to say as much, but happily about 12 on Saturday she felt so much better that she agreed to go, and has come back certainly none the worse for the lionizing.
We have friends on Wednesday and Thursday -- and on Saturday we go to the Philharmonic. I know of no other movements; but tell you of these lest you should be contemplating a run up on those days.
Yesterday we had a long letter from the Viceroy full of hope and energy, but with bad news of his health. To-day I met Salvini at dinner. 486
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [22 November 1875]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [22 November 1875]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday.
My dear Blackwood
The question of division into parts has greatly [exercised] us latterly but finally we have come to a decision and abide by that already existing in the proofs. Accordingly I telegraphed this morning to cancel Mrs. Lewes's letter of yesterday. 348
"George Eliot's New Story of English Life -- Daniel Deronda -- will appear in Eight Monthly Parts. The first part to be published on February 1."
That is the kind of announcement I should suggest, but leave you and Mr. Simpson to improve on it. I don't know how the gossip paragraph should read. It may as well say that the new book like [Middle-march,] is a story of English life but of our own day, and dealing for the most part in a higher sphere of Society. 349
We are so pleased that Klesmer has laid hold of you. The coincidence of your experience is very interesting -- only last night I was telling Madonna that I thought she was doing a real service to many a misguided girl and youth in thus plainly setting forth the arduousness and difficulties of a career so facile in imagination.
Yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [22 February 1869]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [22 February 1869]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Monday.
My dear Blackwood
I have just returned from the city not a little puzzled how the misunderstanding about the poem arose, because if you did not get Mrs. Lewes's letter, Mr. Simpson must have got mine. I hope it has not put you to any serious inconvenience!
When in the city I saw Tr'fcbner who says Ticknor and Fields of Boston would give Mrs. Lewes a good sum for permission to print the poem in the Atlantic Monthly simultaneously with its appearance in Maga if you would not object to the entrance into England of the 250 copies which the Atlantic subscribers would receive in due course i.e. a fortnight or so after the appearance in Maga. This was done with a poem of Swinburne's and a novel of Charles Reade's and I do not suppose that coming so long after Maga and in so small a way there would be any objection, but I should like to be sure from you on the point before selling the proofs. 35
My desire is to publish in the May number. This will give us plenty of time for revision, and will bring the poem out "in the season."
Mrs. Lewes read it aloud to our son Charles last night and was highly gratified by the effect. I wish Maga's subscribers could hear it so read!
Hail, sleet, and snow made the city not lovely this morning. I was breakfasting with Sir Henry Holland and Lord Dufferin 36 otherwise I should not have put my nose outside the door.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [22 December 1872]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [22 December 1872]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: 22 December [1872]. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
My dear Blackwood
The accounts look better than I anticipated and if the Times would only give us a lift with its advertisement the rest of the 4 volumes would perhaps go off.
Touching the cheaper edition -- whenever you think the time arrives at which it may fairly be issued -- I am puzzled about the price. 21/- seems to me prohibitory except to the Libraries; and 12/- which would place it within reach of private purchasers seems too low a price for 4 volumes; and yet it would be impossible, I suppose, to print the 4 in two even on very thin paper; and it would certainly be desirable to save the expense of reprinting now we have the types. What says Von Moltke about the 21/? -- Might it be brought to range with the old 6 shilling a volume edition of Adam Bede, and only charged 3/ a volume? or is the size (and type) too dissimilar?
We will bear Smith's discount. But there will be the advertisements in each part to account for; and Asher ought to be sending in some money now. If it is equally convenient to you we should like a bill as before payable at midsummer.
Are you coming up to town at Christmas or thereabouts? I want to talk over the [Key to all Mythologies] with you. 670
Letters and testimonies from all sides come pouring in showing how deep an impression the book is making, so that one cannot but look forward to a continued sale, though 42/- must "give pause."
Mrs. Lewes begs me to send her thanks for the cheque and her best wishes to you and yours (not forgetting Willie) for Christmas and onwards!
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.
On reconsideration 12/ is impossible at least for some time yet. Purchasers would feel less aggrieved at 21/- than at so considerable a reduction as 12/. Perhaps the 21/- edition might be issued soon if announced as on thinner paper -- with the 42/- edition still to be had. This is not unfrequently done: two editions, one large on fine paper and one on common paper are legitimate; and thus one would avoid that [sense of injury] which might be urged by those who had bought the more expensive, unless they were told that they had bought the most elegant -- and elegant it is.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [21 November 1878]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
The parcel which goes by this post would have been sent a week ago but I have been in bed. A fluctuating sickness with much malaise and headache as a sort of general state has closed with a nasty attack; but the storm I hope has now passed by. 149
Of the parcel itself I say nothing except that it is the work of the last few months and is not a story. 150 Your impression on reading it will therefore have no bias. How it affects you we shall be glad to hear.
There is more to come, but we should be glad to know how many pages you estimate the present instalment would make, and we wish the volume to be out before the opening of Parliament. A 10/6 handsome volume. Either I or Mrs. Lewes will write more fully after hearing from you. She is pretty-well, but has been horribly anxious about me.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Monday.
My dear Blackwood
Tait's suggestions will be immensely useful -- I have written to thank him for the trouble he has taken in reading the proofs 181 so carefully and expressing himself so unreservedly. Even when I do not adopt his corrections they are useful. I happened to have had a great mathematician and a great scholar 182 with me yesterday and they both endorse my [insoluble] and reject [insolvible.] The book will gain greatly by such a revision!

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [18 November 1875]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [18 November 1875]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Thursday.
Dear Blackwood
I agree with you entirely on the question of monthly rather than bi-monthly issues. But although there would be some advantages in issuing number 1 on the 15 or later of January -- (though announcing it for the 1 February) yet I have doubts as to whether that would interfere with the American reprint. I suppose they must not publish on 1 January -- if we only come out on the 15th -- and if we come out on the 15th we do not give them the fair start for February 1. As it is a question of 1500 £ 342 you will see that it is worth considering. If there is no objection to their appearing on January 1, then it might be well to anticipate the opening of Parliament by a few days. But on consideration the 15th seems to me too early since it will make six weeks between 1 and 2. The newspapers might have their copies earlier than the public.
I have read and reread the parts with a view to decide as to their divisions and come to the decided conviction that the present arrangement is on the whole the best -- except that I throw the last five pages of volume I on to the opening of volume II. 343 At each close there is a strong expectation excited -- the best of all closes. The end of the scene in Mrs. Meyrick's moves me so that I can't patiently read the few pages which follow -- they come as anticlimax but would open volume 2 quite pleasantly.
We are so pleased that you continue to like the book. It gets better and better and what it will be at last!
Yes, the gossipping paragraph will be good as advertisement and a hint as to the subject will serve to correct that absurd rumour about American life. 344 It takes so much advertizing to make the public alive to the fact of a new work's existence so that a little preliminary notice is always good.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.
Antaeus it is said recovered his lost vigour whenever he touched the earth. I seem to have recovered some of mine on handling my old friends the frogs -- I was at work in the Cambridge laboratory last week, and now I can write of a morning!

MS: National Library of Scotland.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
My dear Blackwood
A Hungarian Professor writes me word that he has translated the Physiology of Common Life and found a publisher but wants my permission (which of course is gladly given) he also wants to preface it with an account of my works and has not got the Sea-side Studies. Would you kindly order a copy to be sent through a Leipzig bookseller to him through L. Cs'e2thy Company | Debreczin, Hungary. His name is Prof. Ladislaus Dapsy.

These bitter winds! This horrid snow! This horrid slush! Mrs. Lewes is writing to you so I shall presume all the necessary details will be given or will have been given by her.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

I am very weak and in want of some change; and as Mrs. Lewes can't be seduced to leave her work I am going to Belgium for a fortnight and hope the Spa waters will restore some vigour to my stomach. Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood

As from all appearance the poem is likely to go on selling don't you think it would be polite and fair to call every 1,000 a new edition? Absurd as the motive is people are influenced in their desires to possess a work by the knowledge that a great many other people possess it, and I often hear the number of editions referred to as proof of excellence. GHL to John Blackwood, London, [14 January 1876]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Friday.
My dear Blackwood
Mrs. Lewes has been greatly worried about this Harper business, because they will not unreasonably feel that we have not acted up to our promise. Giving so exceptionally large a sum for early sheets they had a right to expect to have their convenience consulted and I promised them the sheets as soon as they were ready. Nor was there any valid reason for not letting the sheets go; and I cannot explain how the prompt and considerate Simpson disregarded my last letter to him on the subject wherein I explained why Harpers wanted the sheets earlier and that I wished them to be sent. Even now, neither he nor you have mentioned the date at which they were dispatched -- so as in some sense to relieve Mrs. Lewes's anxiety. You both merely say the sheets have been sent. Nor do you say whether you have asked Harpers if they wished publication postponed. This is absolutely important to keep to our contract -- otherwise the sheets may have arrived too late or not at all -- and we should then have no claim whatever on them. I should like the postponement as little as you but it would be the only fair course. Please telegraph to me on the two points of date and postponement.
Will you also please have Part II sent at once, and make a note that each succeeding part be sent off on the 20th of each month -- thus giving them a full month in advance?
As we are in this state with Harper's we must not issue the book before the 20th and press copies 25th. Otherwise it will reach America too soon. We have determined not to reprint at all in Germany until our sale in parts has been exhausted, namely in October next.
Will you send a copy to Main? I haven't included him in my list because Mrs. Lewes said you always sent to him.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [14 December 1861]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
First let me say how grateful we feel for your thoughtful kindness to our cub. Grin indeed? I should think he would grin at such a proposal, and I envy him his enjoyment. In every way it is a most satisfactory idea to us.
We were also not a little pleased at the news of your expected visit, and hope to see much of you.
I thought Maga looked uncommonly promising, but as yet I have only read the Month with the Rebels 894 which is extremely interesting. I must tell you that for the last two months I have scarcely read anything but Aristotle's scientific writings and they are not lively, I pledge you my word, especially as there are no translations to help one faster over the ground. But it is a stern bit of duty I am going through, and it absorbs all my reading time, except just the hour before dinner when I look over the Times and Maga. In one of those pauses I shall look at Clutterbuck 895 -- (I didn't read No. 2 for reason above named) because I have considerable reliance on your judgement.
I am the more pleased that Maga should be in force because the Cornhill has become utterly unreadable. Thackeray is less mangy and therefore more interesting than he was; but his contributions ought to have their posteriors brought into relation with Mrs. Beecher's toe.
Polly is still deep in her researches. 896 Your presence will I hope act like a stimulus to her to make her begin. At present she remains immovable in the conviction that she can't write the romance because she has not knowledge enough. Now as a matter of fact I know that she has immensely more knowledge of the particular period than any other writer who has touched it; but her distressing diffidence paralyses her.
This between ourselves. When you see her, mind your care is to discountenance the idea of a Romance being the product of an Encyclopaedia.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [13 February 1872]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday.
Dear Blackwood
Your letters always welcome and generally cheering could not have come at a time when they were more needed; for partly from health and this damp damnable weather, she is in one of her most depressed moods. Reading [Felix Holt] the other morning made her thin with misery, so deeply impressed was she with the fact that she could never write like that again and that what is now in hand is rinsings of the cask! How battle against such an art of ingeniously self tormenting?
We were pleased to see that so many more of Part II were taken by some of the booksellers, though the considerable falling off in Smith and Mudie's subscriptions looks bad. 460 At three principal Railways -- Charing Cross, Waterloo, and London Bridge -- there were no copies of Part I to be had some weeks ago, so that if Smith hasn't sold all his stock it must be in a great measure his own fault.
I am disappointed at the Times and some other papers holding back -- evidently intending to notice the book when complete -- but then their advertisement (which is all they can give) will be of little use. Drolly enough the editor of the [Academy] 461 wrote to me some time before Part I was out begging for early sheets that his reviewer might not be hurried. I replied that Mrs. Lewes rigorously abstained from all and every thing that could seem like currying favor with the press, and that early sheets couldn't be sent. Whereupon not only has the [Academy] had no notice of either Part -- but has not even mentioned its appearance among literary intelligence -- though if Swinburne has a cold, Rossetti goes to Scotland, or Morris comes to a new edition -- it is duly chronicled! Was not Fanny Kemble's phrase a good one "the press gang"?
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.
