Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [13 August 1868]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [13 August 1868]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
Taking up my [Daily News] this morning I was agreeably surprised to find the very sympathetic and in some aspects excellent review of the [Gypsy,] and the guess I make as to its authorship accounts for the lateness of its appearance. I infer the writer to be one of the Eton Masters named Johnson 806 whom I don't know but know of and I know he occasionally reviews for the D.N. Pigott is away so it can't be by him. If it is Johnson the praise is the more valuable.
Last week I spent at Oxford at the Medical Association and not the least of my pleasures there was to hear the deeply reverential way in which men of eminence spoke of Mrs. Lewes's genius and the evidence they gave that her work had profoundly entered into their souls. Paget, 807 the great surgeon, and some lesser medical men spoke of her as the greatest genius -- male or female -- that we could boast of. The [Gypsy] I find deeply affects all men except reviewers, and I pity the man it does not affect.
It is interesting to know that [Aurora Leigh] 808 -- (I have seen Chapman and Hall's book, so this can be relied on) was thus printed and disposed of: November 1,000 copies, January a second 1,000 printed, and August 750. But we have sold 2,000 in little more than 2 months; nevertheless it is risky work printing large editions and I am better satisfied at the idea of 250 being printed.
I bought a third microscope on my way through Paris, and the nervous systems of my [humble] relations will have to pay the penalty thereof. I am as hard at work as this enervating weather will permit.
You were kind enough to say you would send Kinglake 809 -- a book not to be refused -- and as we neither of us have read (only dipped into) the 2 first volumes I shall make bold to beg these also that we may read the whole.
We were much amused at your account of your midnight visitors -- and the Bulldog who was an angel -- as all uncontaminated-by-man-bulldogs are!
[The rest of this letter has been cut away.]

Text: John Blackwood, p. 381.
The Priory, North Bank, | Regent's Park, Thursday.
My dear Blackwood,
Talk of tonics, you should have seen the stimulating effect of your letter yesterday respecting [Miss Brooke]! Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [11 March 1873]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
The great Work bears the title Problems of Life and Mind; and the first batch thereof goes by this post registered. 150
I think it should be a volume resembling Hamilton's Lectures 151 -- but as there will be no marginal headings we may have a broader line. It will be desirable to make it as cheap as one can, by using a thin paper; but it ought also to look libraryish and handsome -- as all your books do.
I am quite ready to keep the press going but don't send more m.s. at a time than is needful because I have often revisions to make -- Casaubonlike.
Your news about the sale of the guinea edition is cheering, and unexpected. The Times review 152 is very well written but not specially remarkable I think. Others -- because it is in the Times? -- seem to think it a grand affair; and one or two friends cannot understand that Mrs. Lewes should not read that.
Port Royal Logic 153 arrived and was welcomed. We have just returned from Tunbridge looking after a country house -- found what we wanted and found it already let! 154
Mrs. Lewes begs to be kindly regarded by both of you.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [11 January 1868]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [11 January 1868]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
I have returned after a most successful visit to Bonn and Heidelberg, where spending the whole day in the anatomical theatres and the evening over the microscope I learned more in two weeks than I could here have learned in twelve months. Nothing could exceed the kindness and attention shown me -- all the scientific men seem to know (directly or indirectly) both [Seaside Studies] and the Physiology; so that besides their interest in the biographer of Goethe they were disposed to show all their material to a confr'e8re. The weather was bitterly cold and travelling at this season made me regard myself as a [Martyr of Science] fit for a new edition of Brewster. 720 I came back to find Maga (both copies) had been whisked away by eager son and mother, so I must wait till tomorrow before I read Felix in full costume.
The poem advances with increasing power and a new instalment will shortly be sent you, if health does not interrupt. We are both so delighted at your appreciation of it -- to her especially it is a support.
I am going to beg for a couple of copies of [Seaside Studies] to send to my German friends. By the way at Heidelberg I was asked if George
Eliot was Mrs. Lewes and on my affirming that, I was shown the Museum Catalogue in which her works are headed thus: George Eliot (Mrs. Howther) [Adam Bede] etc. etc. etc. etc. No doubt Mrs. Howther was one of the disclosed Unknowns of whom we used to hear in the Liggins days. How droll it is to look back on those days!
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.
Kind regards to Willie.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, London, [10? April 1872]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [10? April 1872]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
Your letter and the cheque for 500 £ arrived in due course. 506 Whatever plan of payment is most convenient to you will be acceptable to us.
We rejoice that there is no falling off in the subscription; and although (privately) I confess to a great disappointment at the result of our plan, the libraries especially having not come out as I expected they would considering they practically get the book at half price, and private persons being far more reluctant to purchase than I had looked for, yet we are both enormously gratified at the success of the plan in its deepening the impression on the minds of worthy readers by keeping the characters longer before them and not being gulped down four volumes at a sitting!
The fact is the public has got out of the habit of buying books owing to its reliance on libraries; and I believe had the price been 2/6 we should not have sold 500 more. As an illustration, I heard last week that a wife of an immensely rich manufacturer who knew Mrs. Lewes in early life and is immensely fond of bragging among her acquaintance of the fact of this old friendship, and might therefore be calculated on as a purchaser, so far from buying the book, has twice borrowed the numbers from another friend, rather poor, who does buy them! 507 Again, a lady who made Mrs. Lewes's acquaintance on the ground of her intense admiration, and whose husband is one of the richest men in all England, 508 told me that she wanted a friend of hers very much to read Romola "so I drove to Cawthorn's 509 to get it for her; but it was out; and Cawthorn told me that there was now such a run upon the early books that every one of his 30 copies of [Romola] was out; so I drove away disappointed." Thus, not only did it never occur to this lady that 2/6 would buy the book she wanted her friend to read, but it never occurred to her that such a reflection must strike me when she narrated the episode. She relied on the Library. Buying books was not in her habit. What is one to do in such a state of things?
Poor Smith! We are deeply pained. His poor wife, who worshipped him, one dreads to think of her suffering! Perhaps the last letter he ever read was one from Mrs. Lewes. 510
We hope Willie's young frame doesn't feel these changes of weather as our old ones do! Remember us both to him.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.
The advertisement of that English Dictionary 511 of yours makes my mouth water -- and in pursuance of the good habit of not buying, I shall ask you to give it me!

GHL to John Blackwood, London, [10 May 1866]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
You come up on Monday. Will you lunch here at 2 on 2'sday? 459 I hope you can, because Wednesday is my day in town; but if not Tuesday let it be Thursday.
"Baron Tauchnitz" 460 saw the announcement in the Pall Mall and is in a flutter. He wants to know conditions and if he can have early sheets. I referred him to you. In your place I should ask him £500. He probably won't pay that sum -- but no matter -- and if he will it will cover the disadvantage of his reprint.
Mrs. Lewes is looking forward to seeing you. Your letters lighten her depression which is very great just now, partly health, but mainly anxiety about her book. She can't persuade herself or be persuaded that what is not written will be up to the mark.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

The Priory, | 21. North Bank. | Regents Park.
Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
We returned last night from a visit to Jowett at Oxford where from Saturday we have been in one continuous excitement of talk, and are proportionately knocked up. 202 Among a heap of letters was yours with a perfectly satisfactory explanation and a delicious burst about golfing which amused us much. Ever yours faithfully
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, London, [1 December 1875]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Wednesday.
My dear Blackwood
We both think the cover chosen quite perfect and the lettering exactly what Mrs. Lewes wished. Let the back correspond in style and plainness.
Your admiration is very cheering to her, and I must add that your taking so heartily to the Jewish scenes is particularly gratifying to me, for I have sometimes shared her doubts on whether people would sufficiently sympathize with that element in the story. Though I have reflected that [as] she formerly contrived to make one love Methodists, there was no reason why she should not conquer the prejudice against the Jews.
You are surprised at her knowledge of the Jews? But only learned Rabbis are so profoundly versed in Jewish history and literature as she is -- and this will not only make a Rembrandtish background to her dramatic presentation, but I suspect will rouse all the Jews of Europe to a fervor of admiration for the great artist who can -- without disguising the ludicrous and ugly aspects -- so marvellously present the ideal side of that strange life. Lydgate in Middlemarch conquered all the medical profession -- and Mordecai will in like manner conquer all the Jews. What a stupendous genius it is! I have heard of several of our great surgeons expressing their astonishment how any one not bred to the medical profession and practising in the country could have painted such a picture as Lydgate -- and yet her direct knowledge has been very slight.
I return proofs of the first volume for press. My fourth reading has intensified my admiration and I begin to think that the book will be a great success even for her.
Ever yours
G. H. L.
Have you seen Trollope's first part? 359 And do you think we ought to adopt as wide a margin to look handsome or keep to the old size for the sake of uniformity?

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Ilfracombe, [19 May 1856]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Ilfracombe | Monday night.
My dear Sir
Only this afternoon, after post time, did my box arrive, thanks to the G. W. Railway which has taken exactly a week to send it!
Your letter, proofs, and the checque arrived in due course. I have found your criticism always so just that I am disposed to accept it even against my own judgement -- for on reading the proof 289 this evening I do not feel that the story reads like a play -- at least not so much as I thought it would. It is too curt and hurried; indeed I was afraid of getting lengthy and have fallen into the opposite extreme. This it is perhaps which causes your objection -- and this is an objection. However, as I said before, the story is an unambitious one, and if it amuse the reader its object will be gained. Part I seemed to do this -- at least those readers I heard of, and as no one knew the story to be mine, I had their unbiassed opinion.
I have tried to remedy the curtness as far as a few minor sentences would do so, and dispatched the 2nd Part to your brother. I quite agree with you about Lestang giving way too soon -- but there again I dreaded prolonging the episode. I have not ventured on altering it.
As you have probably stopped the checque, according to my last note, (though I see it would not have been paid if stolen) I shall not present it till I hear from you. 290 By the way my initials are G. H. not H. J.
I don't know whether you are familiar with this lovely coast? It is an enchanting spot; with hills and valleys to employ painters for a life time, and rock pools to make every naturalist's heart thrill with expectation. I have already been very fortunate -- alighting upon some rare species, and on animals I long wanted to put under the microscope. I haven't opened a book yet, and shall do my best to be as idle as possible.
You don't say when you will return to London for a prolonged stay -- but I hope it will be in the Autumn, as I shall not leave the seaside till August or the end of July and then I take my two eldest boys to Switzerland, so that before the first week in September I shall not be back -- yet I should like to spend one evening with you.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, 24 May 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: John Blackwood, pp. 39-40.
Rosa Cottage | Gorey, Jersey | 24th May 1857.
My dear Blackwood
G.E. and I are comfortably settled in this pleasant fishing village, where the lanes and landscapes will enable him to meditate on man -- and clergymen -- while the shore furnishes me with food for dissection and experiment. We are both delighted with Jersey; and intend receiving fresh inspiration therefrom -- of which you will bear the burden! I am in clover. The shore is amazingly rich, and the brother-in-law of our landlord is the owner of a fishing vessel, and with him I propose interrogating Nature in her submarine recesses. 870 The weather is perfect, and French wines, duty free, help to "fleet the time carelessly as in the golden age." 871
Although we have all the advantages of "the capital" -- 4 or 5 miles off -- we are here remote from all the noise and moil of civilization -- among delicious valleys, lanes, and a rocky coast which has orchards down to the very edge of the cliffs. The only drawback is want of books. By the way will you give orders for Maga to be sent here, and not to Richmond, for the delay in such a place as this becomes felt -- and the sight of Maga will be quite cheering.
If you are not too busy when you write to pause for gossip, Eliot would be pleased to hear some pros and cons about Mr. Gilfill. In London he had the satisfaction of the anonymous, and enjoyed the surmises which are ventured on there, respecting the authorship. The stories seem to be frequently discussed there. He begs me to send his kind regards and to say he shall soon be writing to you with his new clericus. Believe me
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, 2 June 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, 2 June 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Rosa Cottage | Gorey, Jersey | June 2nd 1857.
My dear Blackwood
What say you to another new Contributor from my circle? By this post I send you a charming paper which has just reached me from Algiers. 878 It is only too short. But if you print it I dare say my friend will give more, on a future occasion. If you don't happen to like it send it me without delay.
Many thanks for Maga who is doubly appreciated here among a dearth of books. Bulwer will be a great card! Eliot's new story promises to be first rate.
I shall send you No. II of Sea-Side Studies in a few days. Having made a startling discovery, I thought before promulgating it I should do well to get a scientific friend 879 to repeat the experiments and confirm them. He has done so and I am now ready to write. If we are to have a book out of these papers there must be a due admixture of solid and serious matter.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
We return to London early in July and I hope you will still be there. Not only should I like to see you for my own sake, but I would organize a quiet dinner and persuade our excessively umbrageous friend to peer from beneath his umbra, join our party and show himself to you in the flesh. He is so gratified with your treatment of him that I marvel he has not revealed himself already.

GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, [20 June 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Jersey, Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
If it is not too late I wish you would insert the following sentence in my paper. At that passage where I am speaking of the paradoxes presented by fishes, find some available place to wedge in this: --
"And although in general Fish are neither vocal nor eloquent, there are many of them capable of uttering sounds: there are Fish that snarl, Fish that grunt, like a pig, and Fish that send forth the cuckoo's note. Aristotle knew this, and Johannes von M'fcller has recently explained the mechanism whereby it is accomplished." (M'fcller's Archiv f'fcr Anat. 1857 p. 269.)
I think the passage will best come in just before the close where I speak of Fishes, bisexual and metamorphic. 323
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, [19 July 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Jersey, Sunday.
My dear Blackwood,
You have been so uniformly agreeable in editorial relations with me that I should be sorry indeed, if any inconvenience arose from my papers; and beg you will decide respecting the publication of No. III next month entirely according to your own convenience. As a mere memorandum I would suggest that the interruption of a series is always undesirable, and peculiarly does this apply just now when people are flocking to the coast and are more likely to take an interest in marine articles than at any other time. But you have doubtless weighed that consideration, and I repeat, if there are other papers of more temporary interest, or if you wish to oblige their writers, don't let me stand in the way, but decide as your own judgement and wishes incline, assured that I shall entertain no doubt of the propriety of the decision.
Your bits of Madeleine Smith amused me much. What utter deadness of moral feeling! -- she is so unmoral that she produces in me the effect of a wild beast. I should like to "anatomize her and see what breeds about her heart." 932
George Eliot has not left. Indeed it is owing to his resolution of staying here till next Friday 933 that I am not already in Richmond. On Friday however I make "positively last appearance" on the sands of Gorey.
G.E. begs me to send his kind regards. We were both amused with the divination of the Manx Seer and his friend Liggers. 934 Quel nom! How can you wonder at the anonymous being desired, when its removal would disclose a somewhat antique Liggers who had sown wild oats in Manx society, and was now subdued to the grave proprieties of Maga. Liggers would look well on a title page! Liggers's New Novel. | The Manx Cat. | By Joshua Liggers. | 3 vols. £1.11.6d.
"In the Manx Cat the brilliant Liggers has produced a work which may vie with the finest productions of his pen." Sun.
"In the Manx Cat Liggers shows a master hand." Observer.
"We were the first to recognize the genius of Liggers. The Manx Cat may go forth with our recommendation." Athenaeum.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
Proof goes by this post.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, [14 June 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, [14 June 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Rosa Cottage | Gorey, Jersey | Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
The proof 902 goes with this. It is highly gratifying to me to find you pleased with these papers; because if an intelligent reader, not specially interested in Zoology can find pleasure in them, 'e0 fortiori may we expect the numerous amateurs of zoology -- and I will add the serious students -- to be interested. I have great hopes of a successful republication, and rejoice that we did not reprint the first series which was too slight except for temporary amusement.
I was in raptures with "Janet's Repentance" when Eliot first read it to me and declared it would be the finest thing he had written. Your letter therefore considerably staggered me, as I have much confidence in your judgement; accordingly I reread the part with a critical eye to detect the objections you spoke of. In vain! Two readings have left me in the dark. Either you or I must be under a profound misconception of the effect likely to be produced. I agree with you in thinking the description of the town and its inhabitants the least successful part of what is printed -- but I agree with Eliot that it was necessary to paint the locale for the truth of the story. Only in such an atmosphere could such a story move freely and naturally. Dempster seems to me a marvellous creation -- Dr. Johnson turned rascal, or rather dissolute. 903 Janet is a striking figure, too. And when I think of my ignorance of clerical life and squabbles, yet find myself so interested in this story, I feel that all persons better informed must be greatly moved.
Much do I regret your leaving town before our return. I had set my heart on breaking through the incognito, and bringing you and Eliot together, feeling sure that if you once saw and conversed with him and found the sensitive, shrinking, refined creature he is, you would have your opinion of your new contributor considerably modified. Is there any chance of your being in town in the Autumn?
You must like my Algerine friend on reperusal. The wretched scrawl in which he writes 904 may have prejudiced you; but the style and matter are surely fresh and picturesque. You see I stand up for my friends! But then I don't thrust my friends upon you, unless they first convince me it is for "your good." I used to be caned for "my good" when a boy -- and didn't like it. Perhaps you are equally recalcitrant? My Algerine friend is a lady -- whose name is already known to you, for Maga has been respectful to her. 905
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, [12 July 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Gorey, [12 July 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 39.
Rosa Cottage | Gorey, Jersey | Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
You want to know what I think of the Smith case. In one word I would say that it is very lucky for that miserable girl that her victim was a Frenchman and she a Scotchwoman. Under any other circumstances she must have been hanged. A more hideous case it would be difficult to find. I cannot feel the slightest approach to sympathy with her. I see absolutely no trace of goodness in her. From first to last she is utterly bad. As to Angelier's having corrupted her -- in the ordinary sense of the word, he did -- that is he gained her consent to what she seems far from reluctant in granting; but for all other [corruption] she seems to me more capable of corrupting him. Not that I have any sympathy with him. But he had good feelings. She has none.
While, however, the evidence against her is overwhelming and even the jury only returns a verdict of not proven 927 -- a moral condemnation though a legal acquittal -- I must say the masterly defense of the Dean 928 was enough to shake a jury. It is one of the finest specimens of forensic argument I remember. Admirable in tone as well as masterly in legal acuteness. From the first I feared lest the last proof could be adduced; and the Dean takes up a strong position in showing the absence of such proof.
The sympathy felt for this girl is to me thoroughly incomprehensible. I understand the profound sympathy felt for her family. But it is clear the Dean believed her guilty -- the judge summed up dead against her -- the evidence in her favor was of itself a tacit avowal -- yet the audience cheers her acquittal! Unless that cheer meant a condemnation of capital punishment altogether, it has a hideous sound in my ears.
Entre nous let me hint that unless you have any serious objection to make to Eliot's stories, don't make any. He is so easily discouraged, so diffident of himself, that not being prompted by necessity to write, he will close the series in the belief that his writing is not relished. I laugh at him for his diffidence and tell him it's a proof he is not an author. But he has passed the middle of life without writing at all, and will easily be made to give it up. Don't allude to this hint of mine. He wouldn't like my interfering.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
By the way I have not had my copy of Maga this month. One came for G.E. which he carried off.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Florence, 28 May 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Florence, 28 May 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Florence 28 May 1861.
My dear Blackwood,
Mrs. Lewes's last letter will have reached you shortly after you wrote yours. She is now lying down with a headache from heat and fatigue after an expedition we have paid to Pistoja in search of Tuscan antiquities and I cannot better employ my time than in thanking you for your prompt and pleasant letters. The opinion of such a man as White about Silas was as you anticipated, highly valued, indeed all expressions of sympathy and appreciation are both delight and stimulus to her.
She is "drinking in" Florence, and as far as the old past life can be restored she will, I am certain, restore it, if only from that wonderful intuition with which genius throws itself into all forms of life. As I often tell her most of the scenes and characters of her books are quite as historical to her direct personal experience, as the 15th century of Florence; and she knows infinitely more about Savonarola than she knew of Silas, besides having deep personal sympathies with the old reforming priest which she had not with the miser. Why is it that Shakspeare makes us believe in his Romans? Certainly not from any of those "solid acquirements" which would have made him a valuable contributor to Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography, and earned the respect of the "Saturday Review."
The weather is very hot, and yet with occasional cold winds which keeps us both, especially yours truly, in a most disordered and disorderly condition. That however is not the reason why I have carried out none of my grand resolutions about articles; quite other! Had you seen the stock of paper and pens I brought with me, and could you but see the amount used thereof, you might draw some conclusions as to my industry which would not be flattering, and would be false. Idle? Not I. Only I haven't been working.
However now we are not far off Blandford Square, and then -- By the way as you have postponed your visit so long we shall in all probability see you in town, if you come; since we contemplate being back by the 16th or thereabouts and you will hardly stay less than three weeks in London. Though why a man who has a charming place in the country for summer must come rushing up to hot, noisy, gossiping intellectual London, I can't see. In this case perhaps egotism will make me see that a run up to London must be pleasant for you (because it will be pleasant for us to have you), but in any other case --!
We were glad to hear that Thornie made a pleasant impression. We are naturally very anxious about their development (which with boys is always an inscrutable mystery) and every indication that it is going on satisfactorily is cheering. Mrs. Lewes is as anxious about them as if they were her own boys; and it would interest you to see her with the eldest, who worships her, and thinks no treat equal to having her all to himself for an evening to make, and be made much of. Among the many blessings that have come to me late in life this of seeing the perfect love between her and the children is one of the greatest; perhaps because it was one of the rocks ahead. Having had no domestic life for many years I now have such domestic happiness as can be given to few.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
We shall go to Berne by the 6th or 7th in case you should have anything to write about.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Earlswood Common, 23 June 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Earlswood Common, 23 June 1874
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cottage | Earlswood Common | Red Hill | Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
I see you have brought out Flint's Philosophy of History 112 -- if the book is yours I should very much like to have a copy.
We are greatly enjoying our sweet monotony of existence -- never seeing a soul -- but working like negros. Mrs. Lewes is fairly now at her new novel, and that means [going on.] She is continually receiving some gratifying testimony about the poems. How are they selling? By the way what strange fancy possesses Langford to advertize Middlemarch separately as if it were a new book and relegate the poems to the list of old ones? Surely this is not the way to [catch the public eye]? --
The weather has been horrid of late -- cold winds and rain -- but the country is so lovely here that we have resolved if possible to find a retreat for our old age in this region.
I wish you could get some one of your metaphysical contributors to attack my Problems. A good rattling attack would call the attention of metaphysicians far more than a eulogy, and no one seems disposed to gratify me in that way.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Dresden, 19 July [1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Dresden, 19 July [1858]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Waisenhaus Strasse | Dresden 19 July.
My dear Blackwood
After an exquisite journey through the Tyrol, down the Danube, a stay of three days at Vienna and one day at Prag, we are here comfortably settled and ready for work once more after the holiday. 1163 We left Munich with ungrateful alacrity; and carry away no pleasant memories of the place, although so many of the people! I do not regret the time given to it for it has been extremely beneficial to me, but I never want to see Munich itself again. Dresden, as you know, is the most habitable of German towns, and our lodgings front the Johannis All'e9e, to which we pass out, and there the perpetual sight of green foliage and the pleasant sound of birds presents a striking contrast to our Munich prospect of tall blank houses, with not handsome Bavarians lolling out of the windows and asthmatic soprani and bellowing bassi singing through the summer day.
E. says he has seen so much beauty this last fortnight, and such fine works that he feels it shameful not to have spent less time in Munich, and more in the Tyrol or elsewhere. The Bedesman ought to profit by such a journey; whether any glimpse of beauty will irradiate my Physiology may be more confidently questioned. It was so very amusing to find myself thinking of "nerve cells" amid the grand mountains, and of physiological processes on the shores of a lake. But after all the two went perfectly well together.
I have a heap of letters to write and send this only to give you our address for the next six weeks. Is it as hot with you as it is and has been with us? But you run off to St. Andrews I suppose and get the breezes. I wish Dresden had a coast!
E. begs to be most kindly remembered and believe me, my dear Blackwood
Ever truly yours
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

(GHL Journal, 12 July 1858.) After a whole night on the train they reached Prague, where they visited the "Jews' quarter," the "alte Friedhof," and the Synagogue. "The Jew who showed us over the Synagogue explaining everything and reading a bit out of the old parchment copy of the Books of Moses was a very decent quiet man for whom I felt quite a liking." (GHL Journal, 16 July.) At the Friedhof (the Jewish burial ground) they saw a lovely dark eyed Jewish child, "which we were glad to kiss in all its dirt." (GE Journal.) The next morning they went to Dresden, stopping at the Hotel de Pologne while looking for lodgings.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, Dresden, 16 August 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Dresden, 16 August 1858
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Waisenhaus Gasse | Dresden 16 August 58.
My dear Blackwood
By this post the proof goes to Edinburgh. The following is the list of subjects for the Physiology:
*1 Hunger and Thirst
*2 The Food we eat
Digestion and Indigestion
*4 The Blood and its Circulation
*5 Respiration and Suffocation
Why we are warm and how we keep so
Feeling and Thinking in relation to the Nervous System
Sleep and Dreams
The qualities we inherit from our Parents
Life and Death
Those marked * have already been printed; 3, 6, and 7 are written; and 8, 9, and 10 I never contemplated publishing in Maga.
Perhaps, however, Maga has already had enough of physiology and we may cry Hold! 1175 -- Even those that are printed will have to be enlarged on republication, and by enlarging them I shall be able to make them more readable to "those that run." The necessities of space hampered me in Maga: each subject was really too much for an article and could only be got into one by compression. Moreover in republication there will be the advantage of illustrations (most of which by the way can be repeated from Johnston).
Have you heard any grumbling or yawning remarks about those which have already appeared? and did the yawners specify what parts were tiresome? Tell me any thing of this kind, that I may stop the future mouths!
G.E. is vastly pleased to hear of a revival of the clerical interest. 1176 White neck-cloths forever! Bedesman is in training, and will make a splendid run if he does not win the Derby. I have faith in that horse and will back him to any reasonable amount.
E. begs his kindest regards to his best and most encouraging of jockeys, and says he will let Bedesman show some of his paces directly we return to Richmond (NB. this will be the 1 September) when E. will also write to that successful and cheering jockey.
I am also glad to hear that "Studies" have so much of life as is implied in movement. It will be deuced hard if the book doesn't sell, considering how some books sell with nothing new in them at all.
We live like Hermits here. Not a soul will I see and our society is strictly limited to Raphael, Titian, Correggio, Veronese, and the other "gents" of painting. In Munich we had too much society; it was pleasant but prevented work; and as it is not easy for me to know one family in these small places without being forced to know a great many more I have resolved on complete seclusion. It is amazing how well one can do without "society"! When the mind is occupied, and the affections engaged, "the world" becomes a visionary kind of entity -- a sort of playhouse into which one feels tempted to go now and then for an hour, halfprice to see what is going on; but where one has no desire to remain.
So you are golfing again? I must learn that golf, some day to ascertain what its fascinations are. Do you really think it as thrilling as molluscs? How many days could you spend doing nothing else? That is the test. In Munich I made the acquaintance of a Russian anatomist who for six years daily has done nothing but make preparations and observations on the Spinal Chord -- and with 50,000 preparations he couldn't convince me of the truth of his "discovery." What say you to that?
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Dorking, [29? March 1863]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Dorking, Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
Mrs. Lewes, who I am sorry to say continues far from well, and has been ailing for some months, wishes me to say for her that she thinks the better title page will be
Scenes of Clerical Life and Silas Marner without the additions of subtitles either as to the Scenes or as to Silas. Would it not also be better to have the distinction of type more marked on the second page? At present the titles of [Scenes] and [Silas] too closely resemble the separate names of the scenes.
Her work gets on but slowly owing to the combination of feeble health and strong misgivings. You know her tendency that way; years and success rather increase instead of diminishing it.
I have been much better of late, and next month shall run over to Switzerland to see my youngest boy. We return to town tomorrow. Mrs. Lewes begs me to add her kind regards. And believe me
Yours ever faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Dorking, [27 April 1862]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Dorking. Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
We have been here for a fortnight enjoying the quiet and the beauty of the country: and I have been picking up some vigor; but unhappily Mrs. Lewes has not been so fortunate. I hope, however, that another week will tell upon her; after that we must be home again well or ill. You may imagine how indifferent her health has been when I tell you she has only written about 'bc of a volume since 1 January.
If no one has anticipated me I should like to write a paper on Victor Hugo's new Romance. 56 I must tell you that although admitting his power -- nay genius -- he is too intensely French for my taste; and the article would show up his tinsel and antithesis without remorse. I shall run up to London on Wednesday for a day or two, so your reply can go to Blandford Square and I will get the book and bring it down here, if you approve the project. Of course you will be up in May, as usual, and we shall then see you.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, Boulogne-Sur-Mer, 28 October 1872
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Boulogne Monday 28 October 1872.
My dear Blackwood
We are here awaiting a fine day for crossing and a little recruitment of our somewhat damaged strength. On Wednesday we hope to be at the Priory again, and hope there to have a line from you or Willie to say the revise we despatched from Strasburg reached Edinburgh in safety.
We were driven away from Homburg by the fatigue of acquaintances and sought refuge in the delightful quiet of South German towns where no grandeurs were visible. Fortunately the weather was delightful and what with good living, 616 quiet, and quiet amusement we managed to pick up considerably. But unluckily we travelled all night from Strasburg to Paris, which set us both wrong, and Paris was not the place to set us right again. I got to loathe its splendours and frivolity and we came here for a breath of the sea and an aspect of real human nature, however inelegant, so unlike Boulevard nature!
I dare say when we get back again the good effects of our holiday will manifest themselves, but at present they belong to the class of hopes rather than realities.
The rain is now pouring down with a quite English vigour and the sky is as gloomy as London. Fortunately we have grand apartments; (there being scarcely any one in the hotel) which after the pokey holes of Paris seem more like home, and we have books in abundance. Mrs. Lewes begs her kindest regards and believe me
Yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Saturday.
My dear Blackwood

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, [Richmond, 4 September 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, [Richmond, 4 September 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Friday.
My dear Blackwood
I came back yesterday morning after a delightful trip, 962 and after the greatest pleasure a father's heart can feel, in seeing my boys robust in health, greatly improved, and perfectly happy. Janet No. IV awaited me, and having read it I dispatch it by this post together with the last Sea-Side Studies. The conclusion is not so amusing in matter as I could have wished; but if the substance be a little severe, the discovery therein announced will be sufficiently startling to excite the attention of all philosophic readers -- and if the paper should be thought uninteresting it is a consolation to know that it will be the last.
I am much pleased that you concur with me respecting the illustrations and I will get from Monti 963 an exact estimate of the expense. I shall alter the papers considerably, and remove the purely magazinic portions, without touching what is popular and gilds the scientific pill. The additions will be mainly directed towards making the book useful to seaside visitors, so as to have a permanent value. There is no book which really instructs the student in many of the indispensable trifles -- and from my own experience of the want of such information I hope to be able to save others much of the trouble and annoyance I felt in not knowing where to look, and how to set about my work.
The additions will not add much to the quantity already printed, when the excisions are taken into account. But until I set about altering I can't say with accuracy how much new matter there will be. Believe me,
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
Last night I saw G.E. to whom I gave your letter and checque. He wants to close the series with Janet. But as he is to write to you today on the point, I need say nothing, except that his reasons for closing seem to me valid, bearing all things in mind.

GHL to John Blackwood, [Richmond, 3 January 1858]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Sunday.
My dear Blackwood
I came home last night from Helps's hospitable and delightful mansion where Christmas has been very jolly, 1046 and my arrival was saluted by your very pleasant letters and very liberal enclosure. The approbation of men like Simpson 1047 is indeed gratifying; and your unexpected increase of the honorarium was a practical compliment which had an eloquence of its own.
G.E. has a fine bit of luck in that notice in the Times, and the encouragement will materially help him in his new story. Though the critic is I think quite solitary in preferring [Gilfil] to [Amos] and [Janet]
I was interested by what you said of Stephens 1048 ( -- whose Book of the Farm by the way I have not thanked you for sending, which was the more ungrateful as the book is really very useful) and I shall be glad to make his acquaintance.
The index seems admirable and will be a real addition to the book. 1049 I have written to Monti about the illustrations which were promised a month ago and told him to send them without further delay.
Wishing you and your brother many pleasant new years Believe me
Yours very faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, [London, 9 May 1876]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, [London, 9 May 1876]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
What do you say to the enclosed proposition. It was made some time ago but I declined, not seeing what convenience it could be to Harper to have proofs he was unable to use, and if he had proofs a month in advance that was surely ample. In spite of what I send he returns to his point. We don't care two straws about having the money paid all at once, though we should like to oblige him, if it involved no risk or inconvenience to you and us. Consult on this and let me know the result. Send me a sentence I can copy for Harper.
Part IV seems to have drawn blood everywhere. How could it fail? The Jewish element has also been more generally popular than we expected. I am curious to see how volume 3 will be received.
Mrs. Lewes continues very feeble, despondent and incredulous of being able to finish effectively. She gets on slowly with part VIII. In a few days I shall send you the early chapters to have them set up so that no delay may keep us in England. I long so to get her away!
We are going to Oxford on the 20th on a visit to Jowett. This is always delightful, but very exciting and I fear it will help to delay the completion.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to John Blackwood, [London, 7 September 1871]
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, [London, 7 September 1871]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Thursday.
My dear Blackwood
If I thought there could be the least damage to the effect in England I should sacrifice the sum (£1200) willingly; but not only do I concur with you that a little tittilation of the public curiosity will do good rather than harm, I do not believe there is any chance of that good; since if we publish as agreed on, only two weekly parts could reach England (or newspapers containing accounts of the two parts) before we publish. It takes at least a fortnight to come from Boston here. If they begin printing on the 4 November and we publish on the 1 or 5 December, only what has appeared on the 4th and 11th November could get over here. So you see the good which might accrue is reduced to a minimum.
I think it would be well to advertize in Maga next month.
As it is eminently desirable to get the printing through as soon as possible I will send the m.s.s. of part I when you tell me whether it would better be sent direct to Edinburgh or to you at Strathtyrum.
We have added on to the end of part I that portion of part II which closes with the scene at the miserly uncle's -- a capital bit to end with; and this new arrangement not only pitches the interest forward into part II and prepares the way for the people and for Dodo's absence from part II, but also equalizes quantities better, though making part I rather longer than II which however is desirable.
By the way a thought strikes me. Would it not be well to have an advertisement sheet bound up with each part -- as Dickens and Thackeray had with their parts? (though not of course on the covers). This would not only bring in some hard cash, it would help to make the volume look bigger for the 5/- which in British eyes is a consideration not to be neglected.
Mrs. Lewes is not at all well -- depressed in spirits and in liver -- I hope to see a favorable turn soon, but perhaps gestation is more favorable when so much emotion accompanies it. 359
Ever yours
G. H. L.
We both thought the [speech] capital and heard your accent in it. Though I suppose a good skinful of wine preceeded?

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, [London, 30 September 1871]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday.
My dear Blackwood
I am disappointed at your not taking the same view of Main's proposal as we do. It seemed to me one likely to deepen and extend the reputation of the works by bringing distinctly before people's minds what they only see indistinctly, the marvellous wealth of thought and feeling which the works contain. And Main's keen appreciation -- as shown in his letters -- seemed an augury that the work would be done well. But perhaps your are right in wishing to know more about him. Can you get to know more?
Mrs. Lewes improves, though the improvement is not so rapid as might be wished.
Please send back Main's letters when next you write.
I have enjoyed the rereading of Middlemarch greatly -- being in a perpetual gurgle of laughter all the while. I think it will be a coup; and that the scheme will turn out satisfactory.
Do you intend remaining at Edinburgh, or are you only going for a flying visit?
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, [London, 29 September 1871]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
My dear Blackwood
First read the enclosed correspondence which is sent you as the most fitting introduction to the final letter. Having read that you can return to this.
Mr. Main's letters have been a source of extreme gratification and sustainment to Mrs. Lewes -- not because of their enthusiastic praise (which is not more than she is constantly receiving without its producing any effect) -- but because of the real insight and appreciation of her meaning on points where most critics and admirers seem to have been dead.
It is in consequence of her sense of having a real appreciator in Mr. Main that she and I both think most pleasantly of his proposal to collect the Wise and Witty Sayings of George Eliot (what do you think of that title which just occurs to me?) which he would assuredly execute not only con amore but con spirito. The book ought not only to be a good speculation in itself but a treasure to readers. If you approve of the scheme I will ask him to write to you direct on the subject.
Mrs. Lewes's health improves -- though slowly -- and fluctuates more than I quite like. She is so impatient to get back to Dodo!
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. L.

GHL to John Blackwood, [London, 10 September 1872]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Tuesday.
My dear Blackwood
How pleasant that ring in your letter! and how useful it would have been while she was in her agonies of depression and disbelief! However now all is over except the comparatively easy pages of winding up, and I hope we shall send the final sheet on Thursday so as to be able to start for Homburg on Saturday.
Surely Dorothea is the very cream of lovely womanhood? She is more like her creator than any one else and more so than any other of her creations. 593 Only those who know her (Dodo -- or her creator) under all aspects can have any idea of her.
I think the present division most effective and it matters little about the length of the part.
What a first rate story that is about "leaving the character in friendly hands."
You will hear from us when we are settled. Our kindest regards to Mrs. Blackwood and the young travellers.
Yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to John Blackwood, [London, 1 February 1876]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Tuesday.
Dear Blackwood
By to-day's mail registered I send Part 6 for printers to begin on; part 7 will follow in a few days.
I hope -- in fact I am sure -- that you and Mr. Simpson are highly gratified with the brilliant start of D.D. And as to the grand idea of the placards I am almost tempted to carry it further and walk down Bond Street with one pinned on my brow as a phylactery!
Mrs. Lewes was horribly depressed on Saturday, feeling as she said "quite guilty and that every one would be despising her feeble performance." However Willie's cheering news and assurances and the Times 395 and other voices revived her spirits yesterday. I hear nothing but a chorus of praise and delight -- but that of course. I take good care that nothing comes to her ears or eyes that would sound or read like objection, being so well aware of how she would lay hold of it as proof of her forebodings being justified. And I don't let her see even the enthusiastic criticisms, for many reasons.
Will you please ask Mr. Simpson to put down on my list of presentation copies the name of E. S. Pigott | 28 South Bank | N.W. and send him No. I? My sister in law has not yet sent me her address, so I can't give Mr. Simpson that.
I am curious to know how the third volume will strike you.
We were so pleased to hear of your being yourself again and so sorry to hear that Mr. Simpson still suffers from his bronchial affection.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: James Thomas Fields^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to James Thomas Fields, London, 8 May 1870
MS: Huntington Library. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank. N.W. | 8 May 1870.
Dear Mr. Fields
We returned yesterday from a trip to Vienna, and while there my friend Robert Lytton read me some of his new poems -- a collection of Fables of a novel and I think attractive kind. After which he consulted me about the publication; and as his poems have, I believe some sale in America, we agreed that if the [Atlantic Monthly] would like to have les premiers of some, or all, before they appeared in England, it would be all pure gain to him. I offered to be the channel through which the proposition might be made; and that you might more distinctly appreciate the kind of Fable he has attempted, I suggested that he should submit three of them to you -- one very short -- the other two of moderate length. He has written twenty which will make a small volume. When you have read them and decided as to their publishability in the Atlantic perhaps you will make me the channel of an offer for as many (or all) of them as you may wish. 173
Mrs. Lewes and I regretted not seeing more of you and your charming wife (to whom are sent the sweetest messages compressible in a parenthesis) but we understood your fatigue, and the calls upon you in your hurried visit. We have just gone through the same at Berlin and Vienna and have come back heartily wearied of being lionized -- though it's ungrateful to feel so when everyone is so kind.
What do you think of [Jubal]? Remember me kindly to Mr. Osgood 174 and Mr. Ticknor and believe me
Very truly yours
G. H. Lewes.
T. J. Fields Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to James R. Quirk, Wandsworth, [20 August 1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: James R. Quirk^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to James R. Quirk, Wandsworth, [20 August 1859]
Text: Copy owned by Mrs. Michael Womersley. The date is supplied from another copy in the possession of Miss Dorothy Evans. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Wimbledon Park | Wandsworth | 19 August 1859.
Revd Sir
Mrs. Lewes -- formerly Miss Marian Evans, has received a letter from you, which under ordinary circumstances would have been left unanswered -- since I am sure you will perceive on reflection that it oversteps the bounds of etiquette in such matters; but as the friend of her late sister you have an extra claim upon her courtesy. 269
I am not aware that Mr. Liggins has ever positively stated himself to be the author of "Scenes of Clerical Life" or "Adam Bede"; but if he has done so -- if he has deliberately and knowingly caused it to be believed that he in any way contributed a single sentence to those works, I, who am perfectly cognizant of the whole history of their authorship, have no hesitation in saying he is an impostor. Nay, even on the supposition that Mr. Liggins had positively claimed the authorship, it would be clear to most minds that the positive and explicit denial of his claim made by honorable and respectable men like the Messrs. Blackwood, would suffice to settle the question.
I remain, Revd Sir
Your Obedient Servant
G. H. Lewes.
To the Revd J. R. Quirk.

GHL to Jabez Hogg, Witley, 28 June 1878
MS: University of California Los Angeles.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
June 78.
My dear Mr. Hogg
It was very kind of you to think of me and had I been in town I should for your sake have gone to hear your prot'e9g'e9, but the concerts to which alone I am seductible by now are those of my own wood -- nightingales at night, finches, thrushes, blackbirds by day. The roar of London is happily distant now and the heat of society exchanged for the delicious warmth of nature!
We were both knocked up by London gaieties and Royalties and have said adieu to all for another five months.
Yours very truly
G. H. Lewes.
When last I heard from Ripley his sight had almost recovered its healthy state.

GHL to J. R. Osgood & Co., London, 7 September 1871
MS: Gordon N. Ray.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank | Regents Park.
September 1871.
Gentlemen
In reply to your letter of the 18 August apropos of Canada we shall be much obliged to you if you would make all the necessary arrangements, paying us 200£ additional as you propose. 47 This will save us trouble.
Mr. Blackwood is so very uneasy about our arrangement lest extracts should creep into our newspapers before we appear here that Mrs. Lewes has been for some time on the point of asking you to rescind it. But I think on due consideration of the case both our interests may be served by your publishing larger weekly instalments 48 than you proposed -- and indeed I think on a revision of the matter you will see that 'bd a volume ought only to occupy 5 weeks in publishing. This was your original estimate -- viz. 30 weeks for 3 volumes. If you can manage this -- while you will have the undisturbed priority -- the book not appearing in America until your last weekly instalment also appears -- we shall be tolerably secure against more than an extract or two since if you begin to print on the 4 November and we publish on the 1st December our part can't reach America till the 15th or later when you would have completed your publication; but on the other hand we could only have received in England the two numbers you had printed.
Can you therefore manage to publish each part in 5 or at the utmost 6 numbers? Please let me know about this.
Yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
Messrs. James R. Osgood & Co.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to his Sons, Wandsworth, 10 November 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: his Sons^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to his Sons, Wandsworth, 10 November 1859
MS: Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Extracts published: Paterson, pp. 77-78.
Holly Lodge, Southfields | Wandsworth. S. W. | 10 November 1859.
My dear Pups
Let me first tell you how much gratified both your mother and I were to hear good accounts from Dr. M'fcller of you, especially that you Thornie had decidedly improved. Next let me beg Charley to inform Dr. M'fcller, with my best remembrances, that I yesterday called on Messrs. Scott and Co. on his and my business. And now having discharged this purpose of my letter, I will tell you what news there is.
You have heard I dare say that Mr. Thackeray is about to edit a new Magazine. Well, as soon as he had begun to make arrangements, he wrote to me to ask me if I would help him. I replied that I should be very willing indeed, if I saw clearly that I could do so, and if the payment was tempting. Whereupon Mr. Smith, the publisher, drove here in his carriage, and made me a tempting offer, which I accepted. I am going to write a book for him "Studies in Animal Life," which will appear as a series of articles in the Magazine, and then be republished like the "Seaside Studies." So you see my hands are full, just now.
Yesterday I dined with Mother. Agnes was there. From her I learned that Vivian had had the Meazles; Edmund 374 was still away with the coast guardsman at Goring; and the baby was very poorly. Captain Willim has been suffering severely from the gout, several chalk stones having come from his foot! Imagine that! Mother was in good spirits, but very feeble. On my way I met Mrs. Edward Chapman -- do you remember her? She used to live at Brompton, and had little girls and a boy whom you used to play with. She asked after you, kindly; and after Charley's whiskers.
To-day we are going to have Charles Dickens to dinner. He is an intense admirer of your mother, whom he has never seen; and we expect a very pleasant dinner, at which two such novelists will gobble and gabble!
I suppose you got the '91Two o'clock in the Morning'92 which I sent; but you mustn't expect books to be sent by the post in future it's too expensive. Did you also get the Scotch newspaper, I sent, containing an account of the British Association at which my paper was read before the
Prince? Mother was in great pride yesterday because Mrs. Abronson had told her that the ex-royal family of France admired my "Life of Goethe" very much, and made many inquiries about me. Dear mother! she thinks the admiration of royalty so much more complimentary than the admiration of other mortals: a feeling I do not share.
What weather have you had lately? It has been terrible with us; such gales and storms as I can scarcely remember. But now it is bright and autumnal again.
Your mother is hard at work on her new book.
There was a blackguard who wrote a book called "Adam Bede Junior" -- and advertized it as a "Sequel to Adam Bede" -- but I think the indignation of the press will have made him withdraw it. This annoyed us at first because, we thought, the people in the provinces would believe the book was by George Eliot; and as it was certain to be trash -- no man of any talent condescending to such frauds -- George Eliot would have had to bear the disgrace of having written it.
Pug grows fatter and more fascinating every day; but his intellect does not develope. He is decidedly no genius and will never set the Thames on fire nor even the Wimbledon ponds.
Your mother sends her love and kisses to you all; and I say "ditto to Mr. Burke." God bless you my dear boys, and love ever
Your loving
Pater.
My regards to Dr. and Mrs. M'fcller.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to His Sons, Naples, 6 May 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: His Sons^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to His Sons, Naples, 6 May 1860
MS: Yale.
Naples Sunday 6 May 1860.
My dear Pups
We left Rome on Sunday last and have been vastly enjoying the lovely weather and incomparable scenery of this place. To see Naples and die -- is the proverb. We are seeing Naples, but have no immediate intention of dying either hair or whiskers, for all the proverbs in Europe. It is in vain to hope to squeeze into a letter all or half that we have seen at Rome and this place; but I will just jot down a few items and leave your vivid imaginations to fill the picture.
While at Rome we visited Frascati, and ascended, by the aid of jogging donkeys, to Tusculum 505 -- or rather to the ruins of that ancient and famous site, which Roman History and Horace have doubtless made familiar to you. It is a lovely spot, with an exquisite view of the campagna, and all the hills -- Mount Algidus, Soracte, Monte Cavo, the Alban hills, Castel
Gandolfo etc. From thence we saw the Lake Regillus. On another day we went to Tivoli, 506 famous for its beautiful waterfalls, its Temple of the Sybil, and its scenery. The morning was lovely when we started but we had not traversed much of the Campagna before it grew threatening and cloudy, and on reaching Tivoli (through a beautiful grove of olive trees) down came the rain, which had been coming down almost daily all the time we were at Rome -- and down it poured while we explored the valley and gazed at the waterfalls. But disagreeable as the rain made the expedition, there was so much beauty, that we enjoyed it on the whole very much.
Here at Naples we have visited Pozzuoli, Baiae, Cumae, Misenum, Posilippo, and Pompeii. The day at the last named place was one I shall never forget. Imagine the delight of finding yourself in the long silent streets of the ancient city so recently dug up -- the very marks of the Roman chariots on the pavement being still as they were worn away nearly 1800 years ago -- and the signs on the shop fronts reminding you of today. Everywhere at the end of each street you see the rich hills around, and the deep blue sky above. The houses, Temples, Forum, and Theatres, are many of them in excellent preservation, the paintings and arabesques on the walls being often well preserved and very graceful. All the utensils and objects have been removed into the Naples Museum, where we have examined them with intense interest, but they would have added greatly to the effect if they could with safety have been left where found. For example in the baker's shop they found a loaf with his name printed on it, an oven, yeast, etc. But these must be seen at Naples now.
Tomorrow we start for Salerno, Paestum, Amalfi, and Sorrento, and shall start for Florence on Tuesday week, so you must address your letters to Florence, Poste Restante.
I hope, dear Charlie, you have not forgotten to let your hair grow, and that we shall find you blooming. And you too, Bertie, must present yourself to your mother in splendid condition. As for Thornie -- but I have a special postscript to address to him in answer to his last letter.
Well Thornie! in the first place I have to "pick a crow with you" about that gun story. I was sorry to find that you did not appreciate what I said about its not being right, and only replied to what I added as a secondary reason, about its not being prudent. I thought that the mere mention of its not being right would have sufficed. You must bear in mind that so long as you are an inmate of Dr. M'fcller's house, so long you must conform to his rules and wishes, and any attempt to evade or violate them is morally wrong. For observe, suppose an accident should happen -- of course you intend to be very careful, but accidents constantly happen even with men -- and then consider what an injury you would have inflicted on Dr. M'fcller, merely, because it was at his school that a boy was shot! Dr. M'fcller would really have been blameless, but the responsibility would nevertheless be borne by him, and people would say he ought to have taken care that no gun was kept by boys.
Enough of this unpleasant topic, and now for stamps. 507 Enclosed you will find a complete set of Neapolitan stamps which I got at the post office (one of them stamps this letter) but you misled me about the Roman stamp of uno soldo. I inquired at the Post and they had only 'bd baj. or 2 quattrini which I had already sent you. The one you say was received by a boy must have come from one of the Roman states, as uno soldo is not Roman, but means a sou or bajoso. If I can pick up any of the stamps you mention be sure I shall.
I am surprised to hear that the books have not arrived yet. I would advise you Thornie to drop a line to Dr. E. Brockhaus, Leipsig saying that Tr'fcbner undertook to forward it to him for Hofwyl in March last, and asking him if he has addressed it on to Bern, and to whom.
And now dear boys it is time to dress for dinner, but as I have pretty well exhausted my budget I can afford to end this. Your mother sends showers of kisses -- she is very well -- but I am only so, so. God bless you my dear boys
Ever your loving
Pater.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Herbert Spencer, Richmond, [9 March 1856]
Dublin Core:Subject: Herbert Spencer^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Herbert Spencer, Richmond, [9 March 1856]
MS: University of London.
Park Shot | Richmond | Sunday.
My dear Spencer
And so you have become a hewer of wood and drawer of water? 281 Is that the exodus of philosophy? It explains what in English life has hitherto been an obscurity to me, viz. the venerable old men who occupy themselves breaking stones on the Queen's highway -- they are all ex-thinkers, broken down by large discourse of reason, decrepit with scepticism, used up from cerebral excitement. I shall take off my hat to the next I see; and ask him whether he has made any annotations on the Biog. Hist. of Phil. which invaluable work he will of course know by heart.
But now about you. Do you get good wages? Is your beer included? Do you cut your fingers, and occasionally hack your toes? -- not that cutting hurts -- at least not me; for I am by no means contemplating letting myself out as an ablebodied labourer. My function in life is to be ornamental.
We were amused by your asking if I had anything to do with the Lion article 282 (which indeed I had -- it was written in a hurry to stop a gap for J.C.) because you knew my "weakness" for dancing before lions. Marry come up, weakness! You might have called it strength which your unfeline weakness couldn't sympathize with. -- There's a young lioness in the Z. Gardens just now more kissable than the loveliest Circassian in the Sultan's harem. Perhaps you think that a weakness? Do you never dance before noodles, and shall not I dance before majestic lions? --
Do not fail to come here, when you lounge to London. We shall most likely have a bed for you, at any rate you can get one near, and then we will have such reminiscences!
As you must not reason, and 'e0 fortiori not excite yourself over the Reasoner, I content myself with enclosing you this cutting from that exhilirating publication. Marian pictures to herself you "entering the arena of public controversy" with Mr. T. Cooper, 283 and discussing the principles of Psychology in presence of the whole society of Secularists. It would be pleasant.
[NB. In case the sagacious Psychologist should not think of it -- when you come here if Mr. Lewes should happen to be out, mind you ask for Mrs. Lewes!]
I have been cutting up Brodie's Psych. Inquiries in the Saturday, which gave me an opportunity of again bringing in your "Principles." 284 I hope the book sells. If it can get a decent nucleus of a public it is sure to make its way; all that surrounds the nucleus being as you know a sell.
My budget is at an end. Marian too heady to write begs her kindest remembrances.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

281 In the winter of 1856 Spencer  retired in search of health to a farm house at Brimsfield, near Painswick, Gloucestershire. "By far the best exercise I have found yet is grubbing up tree-stumps and splitting them into pieces for burning," he wrote. (David Duncan, The Life and Letters of Herbert Spencer, [1908], p. 80.)
282 "Lions and Lion Hunting," Westminster  Review, 65 (January 1856), 205-217. GHL wrote: "We were once embraced by an affectionate young lioness, who put her paws lovingly round our neck, and would have kissed our cheek, had not that symptom of a boldness more than maidenly been at once by us virtuously repressed." (p. 216.)

Holyoake in the Reasoner, 2 March 1856, though praising Cooper's courage, commended to his attention "the greatest book of the year on the side of free thought," Spencer's Principles of Psychology, and urged him to address himself to refuting Spencer, in whom he would find a foeman worthy of his steel. In a letter to the editor (9 March 1856, p. 75) Cooper wrote: "`Mr Herbert Spencer,' you hint, `is a foeman certainly worthy of my steel.' Be pleased, my friend, to leave me to my own sense of duty. I do not see that I am bound to fight either Mr. Spencer, whom I never saw -- and who, most probably, would deem the challenge arrogant and absurd -- or any of the numerous correspondents who have sent me their challenges."
284 In a slashing review of Benjamin  Brodie's Psychological Inquiries, 3rd ed., 1856, Saturday Review, 1 (22 March 1856), pp. 422-423, GHL calls it "indeed, a poor book. . . . Such being our opinion, we should obviously be doing the book an injustice if we tested it by the standards of Mr. Alexander Bain's Senses and the Intellect, or Mr. Herbert Spencer's Principles of Psychology."

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Henry George Bohn, Ilfracombe, 8 June 1856
MS: Yale.
(Copy)
Runnymede Villa | Ilfracombe.
June 8th 1856.
Dear Sir
Your letter has greatly surprised me. I send you a literal copy of the memorandum drawn up by your son, and you "think there must be some mistake in my recollection of what was intended between us." Surely you cannot have read my letter with &unknown;very&unknown; attention?
Then again as to the delay. I spoke frequently to your son about the work being in progress and occasionally even to yourself, long before the m.s. was in your hands.
The reprint of the old translation was agreed on by us, and you gave me the volume for that purpose. The only difference being that if my Introduction and extracts from the other works occupied too great a space, it was not to be printed entire, but some portions of it abridged. As however I deemed it necessary that the work should, if possible, be entire, I have so contrived it.
You forget that the 75£ covers not only cost of editing but the translation of the Ethics, which is entirely new and has never been translated before.
&unknown;I confess not to understand one passage in your letter where you allude to there being no "signed agreement," as I cannot suppose an honorable man thinks a memorandum less binding than a regular bond.&unknown; You may remember that when Spinoza was first entertained and Mr. Kelly was to translate &unknown;it, I&unknown; the works I asked 50£ for the editing alone; and declined to accept less. Subsequently we talked the matter over, and arranged to get the whole of what was necessary in one volume for 75£; and this is what your son records in his memorandum.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Henry Danby Seymour, [London], 13 January 1865
Dublin Core:Subject: Henry Danby Seymour^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Henry Danby Seymour, [London], 13 January 1865
640
Text: Printed letter enclosed in letter to Lord Houghton, 6 February 1865, Trinity College, Cambridge.
[Private and Confidential.]
13th January, 1865.
My Dear Seymour,
Allow me to submit to you and our friends a brief statement of my conception of the proposed Review. It is needless to enter upon the details; the principles are the most important, and they alone can justify the scheme: --
It is clear that important political changes, both at home and abroad, are slowly but inevitably approaching. Any periodical which can acquire commanding influence with the intellectual classes will have a great part to play. We must first aim at influence -- a large circulation will follow. To gain this two things are necessary: we must address ourselves to various interests; and we must secure the best services of the best writers.
Besides the many political and social topics which will constantly solicit attention, there are the topics specially interesting to the Literary, Philosophical, Artistic, Financial, Manufacturing, Military, and
Sporting classes, which we should keep steadily in view, making ourselves, as far as possible, the well-informed and authoritative organ of each class. I do not mean that we should rival the Sporting Magazine or the Banker's Magazine; but that our treatment of subjects interesting to Sportsmen and Bankers should be such as would attract these classes while giving variety to our pages. The publication once a fortnight, and our wide connection, should enable us to do this.
The spirit of the Review ought to secure excellence as well as variety. Keeping ourselves untrammelled by the limitations of a party, or a sect, we shall give expression to every idea which justifies itself by its tendency towards Progress and is consistent with Order -- in conformity with the poet's estimate of our country, as one
"Where freedom broadens slowly down 641 From precedent to precedent."
The writers will be asked to express their own opinions, not the opinions of the editor. At present it is notorious that most of the able writers contribute to several journals of different parties, and are rarely, if ever, allowed to express their most cherished convictions with perfect sincerity, because they have to maintain "consistency." I propose to remove all such editorial restraints. The responsibility of selecting the writer and the subject is all the editor should assume; that done, he should throw all the responsibility of each article on its writer. By this the Review would gain greatly in force and authority, and would never be called upon to answer for a consistency to which it avowedly made no claim. By this also no one contributor would be implicated in what was written by another. The example of La Revue des Deux Mondes shows with what admirable success diversity in opinions may co-exist with a general policy. Unless we had the intention of becoming the organ of a party it would be unwise, in losing the intensive force of limitation, not to avail ourselves to the utmost of the extensive force of a large and liberal range.
Such latitude of course demands that the articles shall be signed. There are many obvious advantages in keeping certain political communications anonymous; but in most other cases -- especially where the personality of the writer or the individuality of his views gives a relief to his contribution -- the signature should appear. It will be an earnest of sincerity. It will give authority to praise and dignity to attack. It will give the writer freedom to a sense of serious responsibility, without which freedom is apt to become anarchy. It will lessen the insolent asperity and the culpable carelessness of criticism. In avowing that the opinions expressed are truly nothing but the opinions of an individual, to be valued as such, it will remove the false prestige which too often belongs to judgments that would be disregarded were the judges known.
I am aware of all the objections that have been often urged against the practice of signing articles. It is unnecessary for me to answer them here; the fact that I think it an essential part of our scheme shows that I think its advantages greatly outweigh its disadvantages. Let me simply add that it will be a great temptation to many important writers who would otherwise refuse their aid.
In allowing great latitude of opinion and great diversity of opinion, the only difficulty will be in fixing the limits beyond which it would be fatal to pass. If I rightly understand the temper of the public we address it is one which, while yearning for greater freedom of discussion, would never tolerate a negative or aggressive spirit in reference to the fundamental principles of Government and Religion. Our motto, Progress and Order, must inspire us. We have no ism, Theological or Political, to advocate. But we shall claim for Theology, Philosophy, and Science their perfect independence, each pursuing its own serious course. In the Church, and out of it, there is the agitation of a deep unrest which is daily becoming wider, and which is exasperated by the want of freedom; serious discussion on such questions must arise, and we cannot disregard them. Our course is plain: -- we must take no side; we must espouse no party; we must open our pages to various opinions, vigilant only as to their agreement with our motto -- Progress and Order.
Believe me, my dear Seymour,
Yours very truly,
George Henry Lewes.
H. Danby Seymour, Esq., M.P.
