Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Homburg, 8 August 1873
MS: Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Extracts published: Paterson, pp. 164-165.
No. 6 Schwedenpfal | Homburg, Hesse, | Friday, 8 August 73.
Dearest Boy
Our letters have been unfortunately directed. Yours was sent on to me from Geneva to Frankfurt, and glad we were to get its news of you and Gertrude and Blanche! The long silence made the anxious little Mutter anxious; yet we knew not where to write to you, not having heard from Hofwyl.
We stayed 18 days at Plombi'e8res and have regretted ever since that we left it. No place ever did the Mutter more good in a short time, though I was languid and out of sorts all the time owing to perpetual chills. I suppose this was mainly due to my weak state but partly also to the fact that we lived in a wooden chalet, hot in the hot weather and icy cold in the cold, and always damp. I left town with a nasty aural catarrh which has never left me but has had several relapses just as it seemed departing. One day last week the pain was dreadful and I feared not only permanent deafness but some organic injury. However, the pain has vanished and only the buzzing and slight deafness remain. The Mutter also took cold the day before we left Plombi'e8res and our week at Luxeuil -- another bath in the Vosges -- was disturbed by that.
From Luxeuil we went to Nancy -- a charming place where we should have stayed more than a day had it not been on the eve of the Prussian evacuation 824 and the Mutter's dread of crowds drove us away. From there, to Strasbourg and to Frankfurt where we stayed 5 days in order that we might attend service at the Synagogue (for Mutter's purposes).
It was terrifically hot and not interesting to us who had often been to Frankfurt. We came on here last Saturday at 7 in the morning, I having looked through the Kurlist to see that there were no acquaintances. But the first day turned up a Capt. Maxe whom I had met at Lady Amberley's, and yesterday morning Lady Castletown, 826 who spent the greater part of the day with us bringing the ill news that the Wigans also had arrived! Mrs. Eustace Smith 827 called -- and that is all we are at present likely to see. We avoid the Kursaal -- dine and lunch apart -- keep from the promenade, and trust thus to avoid every one except Lady C. whom we like too well to want to avoid. The pure air here and the gentle breeze which always blows even on the hottest days, the waters and our quiet living will I hope set us up during the next week. On Saturday next we begin our journey home but we shall take it in very easy stages and not arrive till towards the end of the month.
A line sent to us here with all family news will be very welcome. Mutter is now at her bath and I utilize the leisure to scribble this -- hitherto I have been too indolent and languid even to write my diary, usually done in two minutes, but so easily left undone.
Love to Gertrude and kisses to Blanche from
Your loving
Pater.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Homburg, 10 October 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Homburg, 10 October 1872
MS: Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Extracts published: Paterson, pp. 161-163.
Homburg Thursday 10 October 1872.
Dearest Boy
Your pleasant letter came like added sunshine to the sunshine of our sky. The weather has been very variable and today le temps est 'e0 l'eau very decidedly, 610 but we have had some exquisite days and on the whole cannot complain. The autumn tints are unusually varied and brilliant, and Darby and Joan enjoy their long solitary walks all the more as a contrast to the tumult of cackle in the Kursaal. The Wigans 611 (whom to avoid we employed the strategy of a Von Moltke, and whose proffered hospitalities after vaguely postponing I point blank declined as "among the impossibilities") have departed at last. But Lady C. after three days at Baden Baden so much regretted the loss of the Mutter's society that she wrote to say if we were going to remain she should return to Homburg; and this she did, bringing Lord C. and Mrs. W. with her. 612 She is a very dear creature and I like her more and more.
But unhappily there are other grandeurs here who want to get hold of us. The Countess Usedom 613 (wife of Bismark's predecessor) has succeeded
Except a visit to Frankfurt to do some shopping I don't think anything out of the programme has occurred since I wrote. Les jours se suivent. We continue to like Homburg very much and propose returning when the gambling is at an end. It has done me some good, and the Mutter also, but not so much as if we had been here earlier in warmer weather which would have permitted our passing the day chiefly in the open air.
From all I hear you have had worse weather in England, so that we congratulate ourselves on being out of it. Gertrude and Blanche have not suffered? Our love to them and to Margaret. The kiss was duly transmitted to the Mutter. Do thou likewise pay the debt!
Ever your loving
Pater.

Lady C. gave curious sketch of her early life." (GHL Diary, 6 October 1872.) The following day Lady Castletown walked with GE in the Park, and they dined with "Lord and Lady C, Mrs. Wingfield, and a Mr. Williams. Went afterwards to concert. Smoked a cigar with Lord C. in the billiard room and we all adjourned to the gambling saloons -- Miss Leigh, the `Destroying Angel' etc. -- wearied of the ignoble spectacle we soon came home. Read one of F. W. Robertson's Sermons."

Sir John Malcolm, Governor of Bombay 1827-31, was the 2d wife of Karl Georg Ludwig Guido, Graf von Usedom (1805-84), Prussian minister to Florence in 1870, later Director of the Royal Museum at Berlin. Paterson reads the name "Vidome." "Dined with Lord and Lady C. and Countess of Usedom and Hildegarde at the Belle Vue." (GHL Diary, 8 October 1872.) The next day when they were at the Castletowns' "Countess of Usedom came in to say that Hildegarde would play to us this afternoon; so Polly, Lady C, Mrs. W. and I called there and sat two hours with the lovely creature while she played Lohengrin and Tristan and Ysolde and talked with enthusiasm about Wagner, Music, and Art. Mrs. Wingfield then poured forth confidences to Polly." They talked with Hildegarde till 9. They called on her 11 and 12 October. On the latter day GHL notes that they dined with Lady C. "after taking leave of Countess Hildegarde, who promised to come and see us in London." There is no indication that she ever did.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Harrogate, [20? September 1864]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Harrogate, [20? September 1864]
Text: Paterson, pp. 140-141, where it is dated July 1870.
Benwell House, | Low Harrogate
Dearest Boy,
You will be glad to hear that Harrogate promises to be a success. We are both better and should the weather only continue as fine as it has been we have little doubt of coming back set up. We have abundance of open air and exercise, and the walks here are lovely. I will tell you what we did yesterday, and it will serve as a specimen. Up at half-past six. At seven went to the Pump-room to take our glass of water (which, by the way, is not very good) and then took a spanker in sun and wind till eight. After breakfast read our books (I enjoying "Don Quixote"; your mother her Spanish history) till half-past nine, when your much expected letter came (together with letters from Mrs. Congreve and Mrs. Taylor to the Mutter). We then set out for a glorious walk. At twelve we again took our water -- listened to the orchestra in the pretty grounds of the Pump-room where young ladies were promenading, playing croquet, etc. Lunch at one, books again till three, when we went to a concert of the Huddersfield Choral Society -- glees badly sung, so we left. A third glass and a third walk -- dinner at half-past five, tea at half-past seven, then read The Times and read aloud to the little Mutter.
We leave on Friday and pass the night and next morning at Peterborough, the cathedral of which attracts us.
Mutter looks from her Spanish to waft you a kiss.
Ever your loving
Pater.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Granada, 18 February 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Granada, 18 February 1867
Text: Paterson, pp. 125-128. The events described in the 3d and 4th paragraphs occurred 22-23 February. Two letters may have been combined in this text.
The Alhambra. | Monday, February 18, 1867.
Dearest Children,
The address will tell you that the dream of many years has been realised and that the Mutter's more recent, but more intense longing to see this place has become a fact. To think of Granada with its plain, its mountains, and above all this Alhambra being no longer a name but a picture! Under such a sky and in such a climate the least interesting of cities and of sights would become glorified; but here it is a sober fact that the very earth has a splendour of colour and a poetic halo such as of itself would be enchanting. The "red hill" (Alhambra) it is truly named, and we have rooms in the very garden of the palace, with the snowy mountains seen from our window.
From Malaga we took the diligence to Granada -- sixteen hours 587 -- but we had the coup'e9 to ourselves, and the first part of the way was so grand and various that it was pure pleasure. The diligence is drawn up these mountains by a team of ten mules and the steepness of the ascent renders it necessary to go very leisurely, so that we have time to gloat over the scenery. One quite fairy-like effect was the sight of Malaga in the distance lighted up, as of course it is in the evening, but seemingly for our benefit. Four or five times as the road wound round the mountains we caught a sight of this lighted town some fifteen hundred feet below us. When the moonlight came we had marvellous effects!
Our week at Granada was a perfect one, the weather continuing its transcendant character, with sunsets one sees once in a lifetime elsewhere. We tore ourselves away -- though not before it was time, and on this ground: you know I never write my name legibly or in full in the hotel books, wishing to preserve the obscurity of nobodies. But at Granada, there being only two Frenchmen in the hotel 588 I wrote my name legibly for the sake of acquaintance or others who might come afterwards. The next day the hotel began to fill with English and Americans. It was whispered round at once who we were, and the attention of the guests was flattering but boring. One very pretty American woman, to whom "Romola" was a sort of Bible, made the Mutter write her an autograph. 589
We saw life in various interesting shapes -- in a potter's family 590 up in the mountains -- in gipsy quarters -- and we struck up a friendship with the captain of the gipsies 591 -- he has 3,000 under him, and is a blacksmith of genius. He introduced us to his wife. From Granada we took diligence to Martos and rail to Cordova 592 -- our first great disappointment -- all its ancient splendour vanished -- the deadest of dead cities.
Of the Alhambra I will not say a word. The effect is indescribable the bliss extreme. We are in a delightful house 593 (all the servants being part of the family) with a kitchen where one might live even if one had English notions of cleanliness, with baby and a little trot, bright eyes and simple kindly manners, good food and transcendant weather. Dinner announced.
Your loving
Pater.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Florence, 5 May 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Florence, 5 May 1861
MS: Yale. Published: III, 411-412, with many omissions and revisions.
Florence Sunday 5 May 1861.
My dear Boy
It did the hearts of the tired Mutter and Pater good, last evening, shortly after reaching the hotel, to get your long and pleasant letter. We had swallowed some tea, and said deux mots to a thin beefsteak, not by any means juicy, when, as I learned the post would be open for an hour, I trotted out in the rain, and quickly came back bearing letters from "the boy," and from Blackwood -- that from the latter containing the best of news about [Silas] namely that the "Row" is buying furiously, that every one speaks admiringly, and that the edition is 7,500 copies, or was on the 24th last month.
I presume that on Monday after writing to us you received the darling Mutter's long letter which she wrote at Nice, while I enjoyed a sick headache. Therefore from that point shall be resumed the history of our very long, very delightful, and very expensive journey here. Writing to you brought us up to the hour of table d'h'f4te. After that we went to the French theatre, and saw Le P'e8re Prodigue which was prodige-ux! We came away disgusted at the end of the third act; disgusted with the piece, and with the audience which did not rise against it in protest. 540
On Friday we started by vetturino (one always says by vetturino, though why one should go by coachman and not by coach is not clear) for Mentone which we reached at noon. The carriage was as comfortable and elegant as a private carriage in England and the horses good. The road was a succession of pictures, winding up the mountain passes, with the snowy Apennines as a grand line on one horizon, and the Mediterranean, "deeply darkly beautifully blue" 541 on the other; through groves of olives, and orchards of orange trees and lemon trees bearing their golden fruit; the day being transcendant, bright, warm yet not sultry, and with no dust. At Mentone we had half a day of delicious rambling among the orchards of oranges, sitting "under the shade of melancholy boughs," 542 reading our books, and planning to have a lovely place of our own, some day, wherein Pater would rear his own peas, his own pears, and his own frogs -- leaving filius to do the hard work of digging etc. We dined at 6, and -- as usual -- were in bed by 'bd past 7.
Saturday we had another exquisite day, but much longer en route. We stayed two hours to lunch and repose at San Remo where we saw palm trees in blossom, a thing I once saw in Kew Conservatory, but never before in the open air. But palms here are abundant. The aloe is on this coast a common hedge weed; and the cactus grows freely in many places. We reached Oneglia, an uninteresting place at 'bd past 4 -- dined and went to bed early, as a step to getting wealthy and wise.
Sunday the route to Savona was less beautiful, but even less means much beauty; the day also was cloudy, though mild. Monday we got to Genoa by 2 o'clock having stopped to lunch en route. We were so enraptured with Genoa last year that I feared lest a second visit should be a disappointment. But a "thing of beauty is a joy for ever, its loveliness increaseth" 543 (as I remark to Mutter respecting my own beauty) and our stay at Genoa was again intoxicating (not alcoholic). At the hotel where we stayed there was Garibaldi's Col. Peard 544 -- his "Englishman" of whom you doubtless often heard. We had been very much struck by his appearance before we learned who he was, and after learning it we saw him no more. At Genoa, where we stayed Monday and Tuesday, we went to the opera and heard Verdi's Attila bawled with great vigour. The "scourge of god" 545 was represented by a basso with the shortest arms and the most obtrusive stomach, I ever saw, doch war es immer nicht der Held! 546 The Mutter conceived a violent passion for him. The tenor labored under a deficiency of voice and a redness of nose. The prima donna was a vigorous little fat jewess, not bad at all.
Mutter sternly resisted Genoese velvets, and Genoese bracelets, so that we bought nothing at Genoa but a few volumes of Italian lit[erature] and history. 547 On Wednesday, May 1 when we ought to have been here had we not taken this delicious but lengthy route, we started again with our vetturino, through a lovely country, still coasting the Mediterranean, remember that! staying at a charming place (Camogli) to lunch, and reaching Sestri at 5, in time to enjoy a ramble by sunset after dinner, and to get to bed well tired. Next day we got to Spezia which is very beautiful -- I mean the bay and Carrara marble mountains which rise on one side of it. We were here in time for a delicious ramble along the sands; and we did not quit till 'bd past 12 the next day, when we started on a much less interesting route to Pietra Santa; and yesterday got thence to Pisa, where we stayed four hours, and for the third time were thrilled by the marvels of the place.
During the last part of the journey Mutter has not been quite well, and yesterday was positively ill. But today she seems only languid, tired and with a slight cold. It is cold and raining so we have not been out today, and are languidly vegetating in the hotel, 548 rather unsettled as to our future settlement. We are too expensively lodged at present, but tomorrow I shall look about. Meanwhile address poste restante -- and prepay; as we shall do in future; for I find that letters not prepaid are charged double. I have scarcely left room for the Mutter's p.s. so will only say God bless you, my dearest boy.
Ever your loving
Pater.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Florence, [31] May 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Florence, [31] May 1861
Text: Paterson, pp. 98-100.
Florence. | May 30, 1861.
Dearest Boy,
Mr. Trollope 774 has returned and has seduced us into prolonging our stay for another week, in order that we may witness the great national festival of regenerated Italy on Sunday; and on Monday make an expedition to the monasteries of the Val d'Arno -- the Camaldoli and La Verrica [Verna]. Does the word Camaldoli excite any thrill in you? It does in us, and in most of those who have read romance. The Mutter is looking forward to a great treat in going there. But in spite of this delay in starting we shall not be much behind the time we stated for our arrival home, as we shall make up by journeying rapidly.
Since our last we have witnessed a solemn and interesting ceremony, in honour of the devoted youths who fell in 1848 fighting for Liberty. The large church of Santa Croce was arranged with banners, catafalques, tablets and black crape, which gave it a festal yet solemn air. The aisle was filled with troops, the reserved seats with officers and high functionaries, and the reserved seats on each side with the invit'e9s (among whom were il Signor Lewes e consorte). Every altar was ablaze with wax candles. Two fine bands, one military, and a large but loud chorus performed a requiem and some other pieces. After about an hour of this we had Padre Angelico, a famous preacher, who preached a politico-religious sermon with affecting eloquence and most impressive oratory. He is old and blind, and it was intensely interesting to the Mutter, as you may imagine, to sit and look at his face and hear him uttering brave, wise words to the Florentines. Altogether this is the religious ceremony which I have most thoroughly enjoyed; generally they have been wearisome and rather exasperating, but this was grand throughout and had a real feeling in it.
Also since I wrote we have discovered two open-air theatres to which we have been four times, 775 and intend going as often again as may be. At one there is a really fine melodramatic actress, 776 one who would draw all the town if in Paris or London. At the other there are two good actors. To-night 777 we are going to see Goldoni's "Bottega del Caff'e8," the comedy you began to read with the Mutter. Don't you wish you could be with us? Dinner is just about to be put on the table and I have nothing more to say except God bless you.
Mutter sends many kisses.
Ever your loving
Pater.

GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Earlswood Common, 17 August 1874
Text: Paterson, pp. 166-167.
The Cottage, | Red Hill. | August 17, 1874.
Dearest Charles,
I went to the Priory the other day 140 and found there the Diploma of Foreign Membership to the Hungarian Academy which the President had sent me, stating in his letter that my "highly distinguished scientific merits have caused" me "to be admitted among the celebrious Foreign Members." The tribute is pleasant and the honour of a kind some men run after, but I cannot feel as elated as I suppose I ought.
The little Mutter has been variable in health and I do not get strong as I hoped and expected, yet getting through my work steadily enough. I must tell you of the continued sale of "Middlemarch" and the poem -- the cheap edition sold over 5,000 copies in two months and is going on as brisk as ever. Our love.
Ever your
Pater.

GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Earlswood Common, [17 June 1874]
Text: Paterson, pp. 165-166, dated 18 June 1874.
The Cottage, | Earlswood Common, | Red Hill.
Thursday, June 18, 1874. 109
Dearest Charles,
You will be glad to hear what report we have to make of this place after a fortnight's trial. It is worth going through the London racket to realize the bliss of perfect seclusion, and the long days of sunshine (moral and physical). We are both beginning to turn the colour of berries and propose "putting on flesh" before we leave. The cottage is very comfortable but we are out of doors many hours of the day, either strolling in the garden or on the common, or driving. The long spaces of uninterrupted work are good for the "Foundations" which are being laid with concrete. 110
"Middlemarch" has to be reprinted and "Jubal" is rapidly approaching that pleasant state.
We have two dogs here -- one a dear brown spaniel very like Dash -- the other a Skye terrier all hair and irritability, his yapping takes away from his fascinations and I am going to try to get him removed.
The Mutter says she has nothing to send but her love and a wish to hear how Gertrude and the children are.
Ever your loving
Pater.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Biarritz, 11 January 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Biarritz, 11 January 1867
Text: Paterson, pp. 123-125.
Hotel d'Angleterre, | Biarritz. | January 11, 1867.
Dearest Children,
Your letter came whilst we were at lunch and Charlie's picture of the delicious London climate made a fine background for our imagination; we who had just come in from sitting on the rocks with our books -- the Mutter reading a little and the Pater confining his studies to the waves. 566 I will take up our story at Bayonne. 567 Saturday was a memorable day. For the first time I felt thoroughly satisfied at having taken this long journey -- the air was delicious, soft and summery -- so warm that roses are blowing in the open air and the Mutter had to buy a parasol. At this period London was covered with snow! Our first visit after a delighted glance at the streets was to the Cathedral. We ascended the tower, and never was a toilsome ascent of several hundred steps more repaid. The view of the Pyrenees was enchanting, not simply from the lines of the mountains and the snowy peaks but also from a peculiar combination of sky effects. The town below, the river winding silently through the plain and the background of mountain kept us in a series of detonating "Ohs!" till the custode must have formed some suspicion of our sanity. 568
We then explored the town. It is more than half Spanish and so picturesque that it may be called a succession of Prouts. 569 The costume of the Basque peasant -- a graceful cap, a red sash and a loose jacket -- and the oxen yoked to every cart, helped the general effect of coloured houses and jalousies (mostly buff houses with rich brown or green shutters). The streets narrow, the gables effective, the faces handsome and good-humoured. We sat by the river for half an hour's silent, dreamy enjoyment.
Sunday we had a farewell glance at the town and then set off in torrents of rain for Biarritz, having the coup'e9 to ourselves. Here we have three good rooms and a large antiroom, so that privacy is undisturbed. We took lunch the first day at table d'h'f4te to see what it was like and one trial was enough -- there was only a German baron and an English curate, and a very little of the latter and "sour English wife" goes a great way with us. And the place! What shall I say of the place? Hyperbole must be largely drawn upon to express our rapture in this marvellous coast. The stormy grandeur of the Bay of Biscay is something surpassing anything we have seen. The huge rocks seem to have been storm-torn from the coast and flung about in fury; and one understands how they were wrenched away and afterwards scooped and hollowed into caverns and arches by these tremendous waves that incessantly dash upon the coast, throwing up their spray to a height of 20 or 30 feet. Then the mountains -- and such sunsets! and the miraculous lights in the sky and over the sea. The effect upon us both has been prompt and immense -- the Mutter burst out laughing yesterday at my fat face.
We rub up our Spanish, I suddenly calling upon the Mutter to utter without hesitation a Spanish word or phrase for any English one I may suggest. In this way we are preparing ourselves for Spain.
God bless you my dearest Chicks. Mutter sends her love to you and all.
Pater.

GHL to Charles Lee Lewes, Berlin, 29 March 1870
MS: Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. On same sheet as 28 March 1870. Hitherto unpublished.
March.
Dearest Boy
Your letter with its news was very welcome. What you did was rightly done and I wish you would complete it by sending back Carter Blake's verses simply saying that I am abroad. Your resolution about Ben Rhydding 143 is one I am most pleased to hear. I did not like to urge it too strenuously on Gertrude but always felt it was eminently desirable.
The Mutter and I have come to the conclusion that the Music of the future is not for us -- Schubert, Beethoven, Mozart, Gluck or even Verdi -- but not Wagner -- is what we are made to respond to. 144 Lucca as Cherubino is enchanting and if she plays it while you are in London don't miss the chance. When next you write address care of Honble. Robt. Lytton, British Embassy, Vienna unless you should have occasion to write so as to reach this by the 5th -- the day on which we shall probably start -- (but it is not certain). We stop at Prague on the way and so break the journey besides resuming our acquaintance with the picturesque capital of Bohemia.
Mutter sends love and kisses.
Ever your loving
Pater.
You will deliver the kisses to Gertrude from both of us, and get her to pay you in kind.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Holte Bracebridge, Wandsworth, 29 September 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Holte Bracebridge^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Holte Bracebridge, Wandsworth, 29 September 1859
Text: Copy, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Wimbledon Park | Wandsworth | 29 September 1859.
Sir
You appear to have completely misunderstood the feeling animating us. We were never in the least disturbed by the idea of Mrs. Lewes's literary reputation being affected by the stories you were so industrious in circulating.
The case is this. Upon mere report, or surmise, you believe that Mr. Liggins is the author of Clerical Scenes and Adam Bede. When that is denied by the author, you choose to entrench yourself behind the absurd position that Mr. Liggins must have collected materials or furnished suggestions for those works; and you persist in that after my letter to Mr. Quirk, which admitted of no equivoque. When finally I write to you pointing out that by this persistence you accuse Mrs. Lewes of baseness and falsehood -- you evade that part of my letter altogether.
Moreover you state that certain characters in Adam Bede are portraits of certain persons; and that Mrs. Lewes had access to her aunt's journals and notes of sermons. An unequivocal denial comes -- and you evade that also. You cite instances of other writers having drawn "portraits"; but suppose any one should choose to identify some odious or ridiculous person in a novel with "Mr. Bracebridge of Atherstone," would you like that? And suppose the author were an acquaintance of yours, what would be his vexation at having a meaning ascribed to him which was never in his mind?
To prevent all possible mistakes and all further correspondence on this exceedingly disagreeable subject, Mrs. Lewes wishes me to ask you the following simple questions: -- 1. Do you still believe, and continue to inform people, that Mr. Liggins had anything whatever to do with the works in question?
If you do believe this, will you state the evidence on which you reject her positive denial of any acquaintance with Mr. Liggins, or with any notes or materials he may have collected?
Do you still maintain that Mrs. Lewes meant to represent the persons you have named, in the characters of Adam Bede?
Do you still maintain that she has seen the journals and notes of sermons, you mentioned?
Awaiting your replies to these questions I remain Sir
Your obedient Servant
G. H. Lewes.
C. H. Bracebridge Esq.

In fact the house hunting has so much occupied us the last fortnight or three weeks that little other work has been done."

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Holte Bracebridge, Wandsworth, 19 September 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Holte Bracebridge^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Holte Bracebridge, Wandsworth, 19 September 1859
Text: Copy by GE; another copy in a different hand has supplied heading, date, and a few words in brackets. Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Wimbledon Park, | Wandsworth, S.W.
September 1859.
Sir,
Mr. Bray has forwarded to Mrs. Lewes your two letters to him about "Adam Bede."
I have no doubt that you, having been imposed upon, have been actuated by benevolent motives, but I think that on reflection you must see that your continued rejection of the explicit statements of honourable men, and your persistence in maintaining a belief for which you can have really no evidence, is the more inexcusable because you thereby imply that the Messrs. Blackwood, Mrs. Lewes, and myself are deliberate liars. For equivoques such as you imagine, are lies.
Further, I am compelled to call your attention to the fact that you are placing yourself in a very responsible position by disseminating falsehoods (unintentional, yet positive falsehoods) respecting Mrs. Lewes and her works.
As to Mr. Liggins, whom you declare (authority not stated) to have been once "well acquainted" with Mrs. Lewes, I have to assure you, on her authority, that she never exchanged a single word with him; she is doubtful whether she ever saw him: if she ever did see him it must have been in her childhood and at church. Nor did she ever see a line of Mr. Liggins's writing.
As to Mr. Liggins's share in the authorship, or in having "collected materials" for either of the works, it is false -- false in every possible respect -- and only persons ignorant of how works of art are created could believe in it.
You have been so positive and explicit about the places and characters in Adam Bede that you will no doubt hear with surprize that Mrs. Lewes never saw some of them; and of the rest, while like every other artist she has used the materials which have come within her own experience, it is unequivocally false to say there is a single portrait among the characters in Adam Bede. She knew her uncle and aunt, it is true, and greatly loved and respected them; but it is because she knew them that she can solemnly declare that Seth and Dinah are not portraits of them -- they only resemble them as good and pious people of the same sect resemble each other. The Journals and sermons of which you speak, if they exist, she never saw, never heard of.
So much for what seems your strongest case. I will now take the weakest, but one which will suffice to show how these inferences as to portraits have been drawn. The successor to Mr. Irwine, you say, is Mr. Henry Hake. Now there are more than a thousand Evangelical clergymen who might with equal justice be named as the original. Mrs. Lewes had not Mr. Hake in her mind at the time, nor indeed any other individual man. The name of the Poysers has induced you to "inquire of the Poysers." Mrs. Lewes never saw anyone of that name. Suppose I were to go into Scotland, and find out a Mr. Deans, and repeat as facts respecting Scott and the Heart of Midlothian what Mr. Deans in idle gossip or conjecture might tell me -- what would be your opinion of my sense?
I beg you once for all to understand that these statements are to be accepted literally, and not to suppose, as has hitherto been the case, that any covert meaning is reserved. In saying there are no portraits in Adam Bede, I mean that Adam, Dinah, Seth, Lisbeth, Mrs. Poyser, Hetty, Mr. Irwine and the rest are creations out of combinations of varied experience, just as Hamlet, [Falstaff,] Parson Adams, Jonathan Oldbuck, or Edgar Ravenswood [were creations of their authors,] the materials in each case being of course suggested, but only suggested, not given, as in biography, history or portrait painting.
An occasional nucleus of incident, is in like manner, taken from what did once occur -- for example, Mrs. S. Evans did visit a poor girl in prison -- but then, Mrs. Evans is not Dinah, nor is that poor girl represented in Hetty. Indeed, the very fact upon which you insist, that the materials must have been collected a long time ago, because the people whom you suppose to be drawn, and the incidents you suppose to be adopted belong to a period far removed from our own day, would suffice to show how little the author can have adhered to any actual story, or characters. But the whole supposition of a "collection of materials" is to any one versed in literature sufficiently absurd.
If, because a certain trait in a character resembles or suggests what is known of a real human being, we are rashly to jump to the conclusion that the author meant that particular person by that particular character; any one with sufficient curiosity, and leisure, might draw up a list of portraits and places in every work of fiction that appears. Busy inquiry among relatives and friends (all extremely gratifying to the author and his family, of course) would furnish a large crop of such foolish identifications. It is notorious that "everybody" said his mother was Mrs. Nickleby, and every Yorkshire schoolmaster was Squeers.
The "Scenes of Clerical Life" and "Adam Bede" proceeded entirely from Mrs. Lewes's own mind; the former was commenced in 1856, the latter in 1857. No one's notes, sermons, journals or collections, had anything whatever to do with those works. Indeed you must, on reflection, perceive that in your inexplicable persistence in proclaiming Mr. Liggins to have had a share in these works, you are not only implying that we are liars, but that we are guilty of the baseness of seeking to deprive Mr. Liggins of that share of credit to which you think he has a claim, and of that pecuniary assistance which a belief in his claim would warrant. Such implications as these require an apology. They require also that you should state in plain terms the evidence (not the mere surmise) upon which you make them.
I need not characterize the attempt to pry into private matters, and to circulate the surmises founded thereon. But as you have from the first been very active in circulating statements which you are now informed, on the best authority, are erroneous, I must call upon you to do all that now remains in your power in the way of retractation of those statements to everyone to whom you may have made them. I remain, Sir,
Your obedient Servant
G. H. Lewes.
C. H. Bracebridge Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Edward Apple^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Edward Appleton, London, [6 February 1871]
MS: Mr. J.H. Appleton. Endorsed: Lewes. Feb. 6 1871.
North Bank | Monday.
My dear Sir
I have availed myself of almost all your suggestions -- quoted some of your criticisms and modified the passages to meet others. 14 One or two points are left untouched because to discuss them would have led too far. Many thanks to you for the trouble you have taken.
May I suggest to you the desirability of your not only completing your translation of the Prop'e4deutik but rendering it available to English readers by numerous annotations of an explanatory kind? It is a work for which you are peculiarly fitted and would be a real service to the public. Stirling's book is even less intelligible than Hegel; but you have the power of re-thinking in English what Hegel has thought -- and that is what is most wanted.
I am very much disgusted with the result of my labors now I see them in proof. What is clear enough in my own mind does not stand out clearly in my exposition. I ought to have begun by an exposition of the Phenomenology, and passed onward from that. But it is now too late.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.
C. Appleton Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Bray, Wandsworth, [23 March 1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Bray, Wandsworth, [23 March 1860]
MS: Yale.
Holly Lodge | Friday.
My dear Bray
We start tomorrow morning and hope to be in Rome by Palm Sunday.
Knowing your real regard for Marian there is one point on [which] I wish to speak. You know how Gossip Report -- liar that she is -- busies herself with every one who has the misfortune of being famous; and you may imagine how eagerly people cite "friends of many years" as the authorities, for their legends. Unhappily friends -- when biographical -- have as little chance apparently of being accurate, as the merest strangers; yet who would question their authority, when the fact stated seems simple and patent? When George Combe, for instance, cited you as the authority 502 for saying that Marian was "self-educated" and a "farmer's" daughter the facts were simple -- and the authority seemed indisputable. Again it has come to our knowledge that you have said that Marian, when young, was "a regular boy," and joined in all boyish games -- and this was adduced as a reason why she could paint the psychology of boys so wonderfully as she has done in her new novel! I should have thought that any one who knew her as a woman would see that so timid a creature was little likely to have been a tomboy -- at any rate the fact that she "had been" one, was quite new to her. These points are trivial, but I mention them as samples of the liability to error, which even the oldest friends fall into; and it is only necessary I am sure to hint that unless she is to be gratified by seeing them in print, and hearing them in the reported gossip of the day, her friends should carefully abstain from any biographical statements -- of which they have not clear and immediate knowledge.
I am sure you will not misunderstand this appeal. It is open to every one to mention likings and dislikings, and personal details of which they have unequivocal knowledge; but biographical statements are different; and when they are made, those who made them must expect that their authority will be cited, and that the reports will finally reach the ears of the unhappy subject.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles Bray, London, [February 1866]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles Bray, London, [February 1866]
MS: Yale.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
My dear Mr. Bray
Your discovery is a very old friend with a new face -- and the new face one not presentable in scientific circles. I have no time if I had the desire for discussion of the various hazy conceptions and misconceptions of your pamphlet, 696 but with regard to the new face on [the discovery] which is to bridge over physics and metaphysics, let me point out this glaring logical error.
Mental force you first declare to be force [conditioned] by the brain. You then suppose this force can exist apart from its conditions -- floating free of brains like a bird in the air. Now the a.b.c of logic affirms that this force when no longer conditioned will no longer present the qualities it presented when conditioned -- i.e. the force which became mental under cerebral conditions will cease to be mental when those conditions on which its mentality depends are removed, it will assume its [unconditioned] state. Ergo the idea of emanation of mental states to form a thought atmosphere, is tantamount to the emanation of spectral brains spectrally active -- which for those who believe in spirits and rappers may be acceptable enough, but for those who are to follow the methods of science is an [unpresentable] idea.
Stripped of this illogical notion of a thought atmosphere away from the conditions of thought, your hypothesis is the old materialistic hypothesis clouded with the term of many meanings [Force.]
In a word while I sympathize with the pleasure you must have felt in weaving these speculations, I cannot but regret that you should have wasted money in printing anything so crude, and am quite sure you will get no man of science to pay the slightest attention to it.
Yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Charles And Thornton Lewes, Weimar, 27 September 1854
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles And Thorn^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Charles And Thornton Lewes, Weimar, 27 September 1854
MS: Yale.
Weimar | 27 September 1854.
My dear Boys
I suppose you will be glad to hear from Papsy as he would be glad to hug you! Here I am in the capital of the Grand duchy of Weimar, about which you, Thornie, know something already, I have no doubt -- or soon will. It is a very queer little place although called the "Athens of Germany" on account of the great poets who have lived here; one of them, the greatest of all, you know already by the portraits and little bust in our house -- I mean Goethe. I am writing his Life, which work brought me to Weimar, to seek for materials. Fancy a little quiet town without cabs, omnibuses, very few carts and scarcely a carriage -- with no gas lights for the streets, which are lighted (in winter only) by oil lamps, slung across the streets on a cord. These, which are rare, give so little light that when ladies go to the theatre they take a servant with them to carry a lantern. -- But though the town is quiet and queer, it it very agreeable as the Park is within five minutes walk of even the most distant parts, and the Park is something like Kensington Gardens with a river running through it, and with rocky paths and winding ways.
As my poor head continues very bad, and prevents my working I walk a great deal; and take little journeys to Jena, Berka, Wartburg, Ilmenau etc. 221 At Jena I visited the field of battle where Napoleon thrashed the Prussians so terribly. At the Wartburg I saw the room where Luther lived so long, as Squire George; they show his inkstand, chair, footstool, and the spot on the wall made by the Inkstand which Luther through at the devil's head, when the devil came to tempt him. You know the story, don't you? I saw there portraits of Luther, of his mother and father; and a magnificent collection of ancient armour which would have pleased you more than anything else.
The other day the Grand Duke 222 sent word that he should be glad to see me at his summer palace. As I had never paid a visit to a crowned head before I felt very uncomfortable lest I should not behave myself according to strict etiquette. How should you have felt, Charley? -- However the Grand Duke at once made me feel at home, and except that I called him "Royal Highness," I did not behave otherwise than I should to any gentleman whom I might visit for the first time. He was very kind to me, and begged me not to hesitate to ask him any service I might desire. He has a just regard for the English. When the Grand Duchess 223 comes to Weimar he is to present me to her.
The last week I have been roaming through the Thuringian forests -- splendid forests of solemn pines and brilliant beeches -- with wide stretching valleys and mountains of the loveliest aspects. One day I lost my way, taking a wrong path, and had a terrible roundabout before I got right again. 224
I heard of your accident, dear Thornie, and of the clever way in which you swallowed the tooth -- I suppose to give your stomach an extra weapon for all the extra food thrust into it -- eh? And you too, dear Charley, I heard of. May I continue to hear good reports of both of you (but no more tooth swallowing) and that you are getting on well with your studies.
Give my kind remembrances to Mr. and Mrs. Pearce 225 and kiss each other for me -- the only way I know of sending a kiss so far.
Your loving
Pater.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Arthur Helps, Richmond, [17 February 1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: Arthur Helps^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Arthur Helps, Richmond, [17 February 1858]
MS: Nuneaton Public Library. Endorsed: G. H. Lewes Esqre | Feb. 1858.
Park Shot | Richmond | Wednesday.
My dear Helps
I have just finished a careful and delighted reading of [Oulita,] 372 noticing numberless improving touches, but especially noticing the finish and grace of the poetry. Had you devoted your whole life to the "accomplishment of verse" 373 I do not see how you could have acquired a more exquisite sense of melodic expression and descriptive felicity. Dramatically I should still have many objections to make, even to the writing which is often too reflective -- by which I mean that one sees the author peering through the eyes of his people, and glancing sarcastically or meditatively on life and manners. This, which is permissible in a poem, will have a distracting effect on the stage. Perhaps however it is my knowledge of the author which makes me detect his echos in the voices of his persons. Note therefore if any one less familiar with your thoughts makes the same objection. Possibly if we knew Shakspeare we should have that fault also to add to his numerous errors of excess.
I hope there will be some good criticism evoked by Oulita. Although for the most part, owing to the [d -- d ignorance of the drama] which flourishes in our island, my expectations are but moderate.
I wish I could see you to tell you a delicious story about John Forster. Here is one about Lemaitre the actor. 374 When Atala Duch'eane left him in disgust at his ill treatment he presented himself at her mother's. [N'ayez pas peur] he said to her [je ne viens pas pour enfoncer ma botte dans votre derri'e8re -- je viens vous demander un coin pour pleurer Atala!] -- Is not this mixture of brutality and sentiment delicious?
Yes, my book is a great success; it is not only selling well, but it has drawn forth from Sir Henry Holland, Simon, 375 Huxley, Carpenter, Harvey, 376 Sharpey 377 and others the warmest recognition of its scientific value; and this considering who is the writer is very surprising. Simon says [had it been the work of one who had done nothing else all his life, it would be very remarkable.] -- Voil'e0!
Love to all. Let me see you before I flit.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Arthur Helps, London, 21 February 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Arthur Helps^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Arthur Helps, London, 21 February 1861
MS: Nuneaton Public Library. Published: Correspondence of Sir Arthur Helps, ed. E. A. Helps., 1917, pp. 243-244.
16, Blandford Square, | N.W.
1 February 61.
My dear Helps
The gods were not propitious to me yesterday and would not let me see you. I came to congratulate you (if you wished it) on the completion of your arduous and important book 527; though I have some doubts whether it ought to be all congratulation for I think you will sadly miss the companion of so many years. One never likes to say finis. In spite of the trouble and vexation I dare say you already begin to feel a void left. Nor am I at all sure that your readers compound for the idea of not having more such volumes, or the poor reflection that at any rate the work is complete. The only satisfactory reflection is that we shall have other works, -- and the more because they won't be so expensive of time as this was.
I hope you are in tolerable strength and spirits. I don't ask you to write and say so, knowing your faint fondness for letters. -- By the way, if ever you don't want a solitary dinner and don't want the bore of a club, please drop in here at 'bd past 5 and take what you find; or come in for an hour some evening when you feel sociable and not too tired to talk. We are always at home; and there is no one, literally no one, whom we both see with such pleasure. -- On the other hand if you don't like moving after the fatigue of the day we won't reproach you for not coming.
I long for these dreary months to be over, and pant for Italy once more.
I was with Carlyle the other day -- grimmer than ever. 528
Yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to Alfred Tennyson, Witley, 18 June 1877
MS: Tennyson Research Centre, Lincoln. Mostly published: Alfred Lord Tennyson, A Memoir, 2 vols., 1898, II, 192.
The Heights, Witley, Godalming.
June 1877.
My dear Tennyson
We have just read [Harold] (for the first time) and [Mary] (for the fourth) and greatly wished you had been here to read certain scenes, especially that masterly interview between Harold and William, 371 or that most pathetic close of Mary. 372 It is needless for me to say how profound a pleasure both works have given us. It is not, however, to carry the coals of applause to your Newcastle that I scribble these lines, but to inquire whether there is a hope of your being at Blackdown this summer and of our seeing you? 374
We should be glad to hear that Mrs. Tennyson was better -- and news of yourself and the "boys" would be welcome to
Yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, Rickmansworth, 22 July 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, Rickmansworth, 22 July 1875
MS: The late Arthur Pforzheimer. Hitherto unpublished.
The Elms | Rickmansworth, Herts. | 22 July 75.
My dear Main
We concluded from your silence that you were on your walking tour. 287 It was quite well that you hadn't my book 288 in your knapsack, for it would have been quite unworthy of its porterage. It is a mere trifle -- reprints of papers written between 1851-67.
You need not send me the [Theory of Knowing] (though thanks for the intention) the author sent it me on its publication. 289
In spite of the vile weather we have had during the last fortnight, the peace of our country life has had a most beneficial effect on Madonna, who begins to look like her own sweet self again, and is hard at work on a glorious book -- which she is as dejected over as usual! We see no one -- absolutely no one; but read, write, drive and ramble in sweet security and unvarying happiness.
I ran up to town the other day for a garden party at Lady Airlie's where I was to meet the Queen of Holland, who had expressed a wish to see me. The interview was flattering, of course; but not interesting. The cock having scratched up an uneatable pearl reflected that a simple grain of millet ferait mieux son affaire. I agreed with the cock -- a single ganglionic cell -- well isolated -- would have pleased me better than the biggest crown in christendom. I am hard at work on the [Physical basis of Mind,] with ever increasing clearness, and consequent enjoyment. We shall stay here till the end of September, and then most likely go somewhere to the coast as I have a few questions to put to the molluscs.
We were not a little startled and interested at the revelation of your chance phrase "my sisters" -- we had no suspicion of there being such tender belongings. How reticent you have been about yourself!
You may be interested to know that my son Charles has an article in the new number of the Edinburgh Review on the education of Pauper children. 290 To our great satisfaction he has not gone into feeble literature but from time to time has written in the Spectator and such on social subjects.
Madonna sends her kindest regards.
Ever your faithful
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, Redhill, 31 May 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, Redhill, 31 May 1872
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
Elversley, Park Road | Red Hill, Surrey | Friday 31 May 72.
My dear Main
Your letters, always so cheering in their fervour and their keen sympathetic insight, seem particularly suited to the tone of mind which our summer solitude induces, and yesterday we had both a real pleasure in your last. It was high time to get away from London and its turmoil, for Mrs. Lewes was no sooner getting a little stronger than some other excitement was sure to come to destroy the good again. We propose to live like hermits, we refuse to go into Society even to go into other people's houses (though I am not absolutely excluded -- only making the rule a convenient excuse for not going oftener than I like) and yet somehow what with this desire of people to come and see her, and what with our desire to have pleasant people round us, we do endure far too much social excitement to permit of work being properly carried on. Lords and Ladies, poets and cabinet ministers, artists and men of science, crowd upon us on Sundays -- very delightfully -- but we as hosts have to pay for the pleasure -- and they even flow into the week days, so that what with one thing and another les jours se suivent et ne se ressemblent pas, whereas here seeing no one les jours se ressemblent and one morning takes up the thread of yesterday. She is already the better for this change and I hope three months' peace will see her at the end of Middlemarch and then we shall be off to the Continent for a real holiday.
In return for your pleasant bit of news about "Romola" let me tell you something about the "Sayings." A very sweet creature and dear friend of ours, Mrs. George Howard, 526 (the future Lady Carlisle) who was much set against "the idea of the Sayings" and has been thoroughly converted by possessing the book, asked me the other day to tell her about you. She was sure "he must be a dear fellow: such a fine mind is seen in the choice of the extracts."
I may also tell you -- quite in private of course -- what I think will please you almost as much as it did me: Mrs. Cowper Temple told Mrs. Lewes that she had copied passages from "Romola" into her New Testament. This is strong measure from an English woman, and a devout one, but it shows how deeply the wisdom and beauty of that work has penetrated.
Cuc0u257 dwu257 llu259 du275 r not Cu257 dwu259 llu257 der is the right accentuation. "The opportunity for pronouncing wrongly if you liked" reminds me of a mot of one of my German friends. I was walking with him in the Thiergarten of Berlin and expressing my annoyance at not being able to remember the gender of some noun. "Sometimes I say der and sometimes das," said I. He smiled and said "Choose one of them, whichever you like, stick to it, and although you will be wrong, you will at least be consistent: it is die."
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, Redhill, 28 August 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, Redhill, 28 August 1872
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
Elversley 28th August 72.
My dear Main
Our boxes are packed for our return to the Priory and I snatch half an hour of unoccupied fatigue -- I can't say rest -- to answer your last. Your view of the change in G.E.'s style agrees pretty well with mine only it exaggerates the difference. But then I am not properly placed to appreciate the change which to me must have been so gradual. She and I were delighted at the idea of your reading to your blind friend. How I envy you the pleasure! And seeing a thought dawn on his face till the face becomes all eye! We hope the book will be finished by the middle of next month -- then complete rest will set her up.
You asked me not to forget you in case any literary employment should present itself -- be assured I shall be on the alert. Meanwhile it strikes me that you may earn a few pounds presently by writing up your walking tour into a Magazine paper. 585 "Lost in the Glens" would be an attractive title leading the reader through a series of pictures and poetic musings and winding up with your adventure. This if told simply and picturesquely would be pleasant reading; and a walking tour may be made the vehicle of any amount of musing and meditation -- as it is usually the occasion of such. If this plan pleases you work it out carefully and I will do my best to get it in some good Magazine when I come back from the Continent. It might be an introduction for you to an editor. You will hear from Mrs. Lewes before we start. Meanwhile, believe me
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, Redhill, 25 June 1872
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
Elversley, Park Road | Red Hill, | 25 June 1872.
My dear Main
The passage relating to yourself in the enclosed letter is so delightful and will assuredly delight you that I send the whole letter on; you will like to read it all. Send it me back.
At the close of your last there was a passing mention of your having studied Mathematics which suggested to me that perhaps you might like to undertake a work which I schemed some weeks ago intending to find some ingenious and idle person to execute it. The notion is this: De Morgan 546 contributed all the mathematical articles to the Penny Cyclopaedia and very valuable they are; now if these were extracted as they are, with the intercalation of biographies of the great mathematicians and mathematical physicists also from the Cyclopaedia and also mostly written by De Morgan the whole might make a compact Mathematical Dictionary of great utility, Hutton's being now out of date.
The work would only be selection and intercalation -- unless you chose to add anything of your own -- and I daresay Bradbury and Evans would pay well for such labor if I spoke to them about it. Shall I speak to them on your behalf? Would you like to employ your leisure in such hack work? Be perfectly frank about it, for my desire in the matter is simply to benefit the public by presenting material in an accessible form, and benefit any writer who would happen to like such employment.
Mrs. Lewes is visibly improving in health and writing, writing, writing -- ye gods! How she is writing! But you must not ask her for letters just now -- her correspondence falls on me -- and her friends must be content with reliance on her thinking of them.
I think Blackwood will be much pleased to hear of the "Sayings" becoming a breviary. I shall tell him of it when he returns, which must now be shortly.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, Redhill, 19 July 1872
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
Elversley 19 July 72.
My dear Main
I fear there is no chance of Bradbury and Evans undertaking the Dictionary and as the copyright is theirs we must let the matter drop. I am sorry for your sake and the public's.
You will be glad to hear that my son Charles is a happy father at last. His first baby was born strangled, and the poor wife has been grieving ever since for a substitute which she has got at last in the form of a healthy vigorous girl. It is a great comfort to us as you may imagine.
You will soon be dandling Celia's baby in your sympathetic arms. But Book VI will I think surpass all its predecessors and Book VII promises to be equally strong. Mrs. Lewes is not quite so well as she was at first -- the sudden changes of temperatures affect her injuriously -- but she still continues to be vigorous at her work. And I am better too.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to Alexander Main, Redhill, [6 August 1872]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
Elversley Tuesday.
My dear Main
Your silence raises unpleasant misgivings in our minds respecting the state of your health, or the state of your post office -- we trust the latter.
Some weeks ago I wrote to tell you that B. and E. were not apparently disposed to undertake the mathematical work -- also that my son Charles was at length a happy father. Did this letter reach you? And did you reply? If so, can you remember the date in order to attack the P. O. for its negligence.
Mrs. Lewes you will regret to hear has not been well lately -- a whole week wasted in headache and malaise. She caught a chill and this shifting weather prevents her getting better. Today however she is looking up again and is at work.
Ever yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, London, 5 December 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 5 December 1872
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 1872.
My dear Main
In return for your ever welcome "screed" I send you a rare sample of moral judgment. A lady known to Mrs. Lewes declared to another lady that she couldn't get to sleep at night thinking of "poor Bulstrode and all that had fallen on him after sitting up to tend on that wretch. . . . and I don't believe it was the Brandy that killed him. . . . Well, now Bulstrode has nothing left but Christ!" Isn't this just the sort of touch George Eliot would have invented? To me it is strangely significant. 1st of the profoundly real impression the book makes. 2nd of the profoundly immoral teaching that passes for religious. Here is a pious woman so utterly blinded by the fact of Bulstrode's piety that it prevents her from seeing what Bulstrode himself sees, the guilt which that piety has not prevented. In real life where motives are hidden and deeds admit of many explanations, we would expect the mere fact of piety to lead judgment astray, and make people seek for any but a criminal explanation; but there we see that in the face of the clearest evidence, and the sinner's own confession, the guilt is not believed in!
Curiously enough an orthodox West-End preacher, the Rev. Stanley Leathes, 650 quoted this very picture of Bulstrode (in his sermon on Hosea) as a striking illustration of the "true prophetic spirit."
Among the pleasant tidings that have reached Mrs. Lewes she places foremost the declaration of Sir James Paget that not only is there no medical detail which is erroneous but that in some respects the insight into medical life is so surprisingly deep that he could not understand how the author had not had some direct personal experience -- it seemed to him that there must have been a biographical foundation for Lydgate's career. 651 When I told him that she had never even known a surgeon intimately, and had no acquaintance in any degree resembling Lydgate, he said it was like "assisting at the creation -- a universe formed out of nothing!" While the medical men are surprised at the medical fidelity the lawyers are expressing their astonishment at the ingenuity and correctness of the Law. And all of us wonder at the insight into Soul!
Dorothea is now busily engaged in going through the collections for that "Key of all Psychologies" which hangs over her husband. How many "excursus on Crete" she will have to omit one shudders to think. If she knew I was writing to you she would send some loving message -- imagine it sent and believe ever in
Yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 31 August 1873
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday 31 August 73.
My dear Main
Back at last! You will have understood from our silence that your letters were not forwarded. Indeed no one knew where we were, nor did we often know from day to day where we should be. Our plan of a planless journey was thoroughly carried out. It was not a great success however. Mrs. Lewes benefited somewhat, but not very much, and I not at all -- a succession of chills and sore throats followed me everywhere. Now we are only passing through London and on Thursday or Friday go to our house in the country. Blackbrook | Bickley | Bromley, Kent.
Mrs. Lewes wrote off at once to Blackwood giving permission about the sayings from "Middlemarch." I suppose you have nearly finished the printing of Johnson by this time. When I am at Blackbrook I must write the preface.
My own book is nearly printed, some 70 or 80 pages more will complete it.
From your letter I gather that M. Ritter did not come to England but my servant told me a French gentleman had called, without leaving a card. When I asked if his name was Ritter she said yes. I don't attach much value to what she may have remembered in the way of names, and hope M. Ritter did not come.
Yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 29 November 1871
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 1871.
My dear Sir
Both your letters arrived in due course -- indeed there was but the remotest chance of their missing. Here in London the post is unexceptionable.
By this time I suppose you have made the acquaintance of Dodo and are over head and ears in love with her -- I am at any rate -- and I won't believe you are rebellious to her charm, until I hear you say so -- if then!
It is pleasant to think of you and your poetical friend reading the "Life of Goethe" -- although the book is so far from me now as to be more like the writing of a stranger. I have many associations, painful and pleasant, which make it peculiarly interesting to me, though I would rather not read it. Among the pleasant associations there is that of the generous acceptance of it by the German nation. Not only has there been some fifteen thousand copies sold -- (not for my benefit!) but it has made me friends all over Germany. It was written when I was in such a precarious condition that very often I was forced to set down the pen lest I should fall from my seat -- the swimming in my head being so bewildering. But enough on this subject!
Mrs. Lewes continues well and is vigorously at work again. She desires her kindest remembrances. Believe me
Yours truly
G. H. Lewes.
Alexr. Main Esq.

MS: Morgan Library. Envelope: Alex. Main, Esq | West Mary St. | Arbroath | N.B. Postmarks: LONDON-N.W. | 5 | SP 26 | 71; ARBROATH | C | SP 27 | 71. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 1871.
My dear Sir
Mrs. Lewes you will be sorry to hear is too weak to answer your letter 370 -- she is only now recovering from a sharp attack which for two or three days kept me very anxious. However she is now fairly on the way to recover again and it was a real gratification to her -- as to me -- to receive your letter with its "happy thought." Some years ago a lady suggested that [texts] should be selected from the works to hang up in schoolrooms and railway waiting rooms in view of the banal and often preposterous bible texts, thus hung up and neglected. Your idea is a far more practical one, and executed by one like yourself who has shown such real and unusual insight, it would I think be both a treasure for readers, and a good speculation for the publisher. We should like Blackwood to publish it, and with your permission I will propose it to him; or perhaps it would be better if I gave you a letter of introduction to him which you could send with your own proposal in full. It would be desirable that you should deal directly with him. What title do you propose?
Thoughts and Sentences in Prose and Verse
Selected from the works of George Eliot By A. Main. does not seem a bad title. 371 [Beauties] at any rate must be avoided.
Should you adopt some sort of classification of subjects? This is but a hurried scrawl. I wished however not to lose a post.
Very truly yours
G. H. Lewes.
A. Main Esq.
We should be glad of your photo -- if you have one. Enclosed is mine. Mrs. Lewes has not had one done of her -- her shrinking from publicity has made her refuse all overtures.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, London, 26 March 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 26 March 1873
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 73.
My dear Main
Reflecting on what means I had of furthering your views, as expressed in your last, the idea occurred to me that you might carry out an old scheme of mine with profit to yourself in many ways. The scheme is this:
"Boswell's Johnson," although one of the most delightful of books to skip, is rarely read, because of its bulk and tedious "connective tissue." If a new work were founded on it taking in not only all the truly good bits of Boswell, but also those of Mrs. Thrale etc. and leaving out all that in these writers never was interesting and much that has ceased now to have interest, and retelling in simple, brief, intelligent language the story of Johnson's Life, so as to paint a picture full of moral significance and literary interest, the thing would surely succeed and would be well worth doing.
Now I propose that you should do this. Your aim and title is to be "Life and Conversations of Dr. Johnson, founded on Boswell, Thrale, etc." You will have to throw Boswell overboard entirely, taking simply the facts he has collected, and giving the best bits of the conversation (without his comments) in their chronological order. Your own labour will be confined to rewriting the connecting narrative, and rearranging the matter. The whole must be compressed into one volume 8vo. of about 450 or 500 pages. You must not dissertate but narrate, and so contrive the narrative and the conversations as to bring out the moral picture. If the book were a mere abridgement of "Boswell" it would not do. The public would always prefer the original though refusing to read it. But Boswell is an excellent quarry.
It is because I felt convinced that you could do this conscientiously and effectively that I expounded my views at full length to Chapman and Hall who said if I would write a preface to the book they were willing to engage in it. 759 I had a long debate with them about the terms, not liking that you should take anything more in the shape of risk than the risk of getting less than a definite sum. Half-profits -- especially when profits are vague -- did not seem to me to meet your case. I accordingly induced C. and H. to agree to terms which appear to me fair to both and what may ultimately prove very good for you. At any rate the book if well done will be the forerunner of others for you. Enclosed is C. and H.'s formal offer. You had better write to him (Chapman) a formal acceptance.
Mrs. Lewes and I both hope that you will find this an agreeable and profitable bit of work. She is somewhat better than she was but until summer comes and with it country repose I don't expect any great change. I am unusually well and horribly busy.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
Alexr. Main Esq.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 21 October 1871
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 71.
My dear Sir
I fear that Mr. James Blackwood's sudden death will have prevented your visit to St. Andrews to see Mr. John Blackwood. However the scheme is all safe now and only minor details remain to be arranged.
Touching the size -- I think it best to reduce the extracts from "Adam Bede" rather than from the other works because that has been so much more widely read and reread.
Curiously enough before your letter came I was going to mention Jubal and Armgart to you. The former I consider one of her very finest works, brief though it is and we were both pleased though not surprised to see how it had laid hold of you. It is a pure myth -- and a myth of her own creation too, which few readers suspect. The fact is, it reads so like an old Saga that no suspicion arises as to its origin. -- What a passage that is about Death! 385 It was written under the shadow of a great grief, when our second boy in his 25th year passed away from us after six months of frightful agony.
Mrs. Lewes continues to mend, and has even got to work again, though feebly. She begs me to assure you that her silence is no defect of sympathy -- which assurance, I assure her, you assuredly do not need!
Yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 21 February 1872
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 72.
My dear Main
Mrs. Lewes interrupted me in my reading of your last to exclaim "Really this is a case to apply the conventional phrase and say if I can only find one reader who understands me I shall be content" -- so that the works may be said to have been written for you! But when I came to that passage in which you refer to what I said in the paper on Dickens respecting preliminary praise being done away with subsequent blundering, we both protested that such an allusion never could apply to you -- for one of the great pleasures of your letters has been precisely this absence of the too common tendency to scratch one when one doesn't itch!
It is pleasant to hear that the "Sayings" are already beginning to sell. I feel confident they will ultimately reach a very large sale. Already some friends of ours have got at the trick of making a present of it to proper readers, and this will spread.
I will ask my son for a photograph of himself and send it you but of her alas! there is nothing and will be nothing. Some day you will come to London and see her in the flesh, I hope.
I wish some of your hopefulness and Blackwood's could be communicated to her respecting the parts that are still to be written and those that are ready to appear: but she is incorrigibly sceptical, diffident -- or rather confident on the negative side -- feeling profoundly convinced that nothing will be worth printing. The more emphatic the testimonies to the parts that have already appeared the greater seems to her the ground for despair over the unborn!
Ever truly yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 20 December 1871
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 71.
My dear Main
It was a kind prompting which moved you to send that very welcome bit of news, which has cheered and strengthened her not a little. I don't know whether I told you that she does not read criticism on her works, favorable or unfavorable, -- not because she is less sensitive than others but because she is more, and does not think it right to occupy her mind with such necessarily distracting details. But she is proportionately delighted at all such evidences of influence as your letters have conveyed -- and these have reached her from all parts of the world, so that now in spite of her extraordinary diffidence and self-questioning, she begins to feel that her life has indeed not been unavailing. Unhappily the habitual tone of her mind is distrust of herself, and no sympathy, no praise, can do more than lift her out of it for a day or two; but by repetition the curing influences tell, for they become massed, and as we psychologists say they enable her to apperceive the fact that her books are something more than mere amusements.
We shall welcome the "little stranger" as a real Christmas child, and hope you will reap the full credit for your own share in the work -- a work which could not have been executed except by one who to loving insight added literary taste. I was so easy to go wrong in such a matter, that Mr. Blackwood was justified in his hesitation.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.
Alexr. Main Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 2 January 1876
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 76.
My dear Main
May the blessed sun shine on you through the year! It won't -- but never mind -- let the moral sun shine instead.
Your friends here have but a poor account to give of themselves. It has been an unfortunate year for both of us as regards health -- (in
every other respect we have nothing but blessings) and we have not had the advantage of a recuperant holiday. Wales under an umbrella was not bracing!
The great book proceeds slowly but superbly. She has not yet finished the 3rd volume, and is in the usual gloom of despondency and diffidence which is not more than momentarily lightened by my and Blackwood's admiration.
Your Glasgow enthusiast interested me and I felt inclined to say with Spontini 379 when Berlioz praised him hyperbolically, "Il a du talent -- comme critique!"
We had a most charming letter from M. Ritter a little while ago, in which to our surprise he speaks of you as a correspondent from whom it is difficult to get a word! I fear he will be sadly put out when he finds that no reprint of Daniel Deronda will appear in Germany until the end of the year. We don't fancy English tourists supplying themselves with Tauchnitz or Asher's editions.
I am getting on slowly with the "Physical Basis of Mind" 380 -- condensing the mass of material and trying to put it into a shape intelligible as well as interesting to the general reader.
Have you seen the new periodical Mind? The article by Pattison on philosophy at Oxford is very valuable and extremely well written. Altogether for a first number the periodical presents a most hopeful aspect. Mrs. Lewes sends her best wishes.
Ever yours
G. H. L.
