Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, London, 2 January 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 2 January 1873
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 73.
My dear Main
Lying ready, stamped for postage, is Mrs. Lewes's New Year's letter to you, and lo! your plaint of silence arrives. 688 She occupied herself last evening, while I was dining out, in assuring you of our real regard -- and all this time you were tormenting yourself with fantastic fears and thick coming fancies due, let us hope, to indigestion of Christmas cheer! -- due at any rate to an abnormal susceptibility. Be this a lesson to you! And in future be assured of this -- which (if you knew me better and my "brutal frankness") would need no assurance -- that whenever you say anything I do not like I shall certainly explode on you.
We have returned from our visit to that Scotch family I told you of before, whose fervent love and admiration of Dorothea equals your own, and of whom Prof. Sellar declared that the first article of their religion was "I believe in Mr. and Mrs. Lewes." But even their warmth could not drive out the effects of a chill, and Dorothea is still confined to her room with neuralgia and sore throat. I am glad to hear the "Sayings" are so lively. 689 A new edition will soon be called for; and I think the demand will be a permanent one.
It is pretty to think of you reading aloud to your mother. For some years my mother used to watch for my visits like a girl watching for her lover: she would sit at the window for hours before my regular time, and with the first glimpse of my "wide-awake" in the distance she would exclaim to her maid "There he is" -- and be happy for the rest of the day. You can imagine how I look back on those days and what a comfort it is to me to think that I never allowed other attractions to rob her of her one remaining joy. My father died when I was two years old, and with my mother were bound up all my early recollections. We lived together till I married. Her belief in me, and pride in me, you may estimate when I tell you that secretly she thought not of what a prize I had secured, but of the prize Dorothea had secured!
But I am getting garrulous, and as I suppose Mrs. Lewes told you of our grandchild's christening on the 20th there is nothing more but to say believe me
Yours ever
G. H. L.

GHL to Alexander Main, London, 17 April 1877
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 77.
My dear Main
The article is very interesting but I have queried one place where there is a d'e9faut de la cuirasse. I hope you will find assimilable food in the volume. The printing has been very tedious.
We have been both invalids. For three weeks I was laid up with rheumatic gout, and no sooner did I get about again than Madonna had another attack of her old enemy -- and that is eight weeks ago yet she is not free. We shan't get down into the country before June -- if then -- the workmen will not have left the house. But I look forward to five months quiet and country air as a restorative for both. I am impatient to begin "Feeling and thought."
If Madonna is well enough we are going at the end of May to Cambridge for a visit. These visits to the universities are always interesting though very fatiguing. When I see Knowles 640 -- if I see him -- I will mention your paper. We are plotting a symposium for the XIX Cent[ury] "on the dread and dislike of science." 641 Mrs. Lewes sends her kind regards.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 16 April 1872
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday 16th April 72.
My dear Main
Charles yesterday brought me the enclosed photo for you. The delay in sending it arose from his stock having been exhausted.
The other day a very celebrated man and great admirer of G. Eliot told me that his dislike to books of extracts had made him feel almost savage at the announcement of the "Sayings," but that happening to take it up at the house of a friend he was so much struck with it as forthwith to order it. "Since then it has been my companion." He made many inquiries about you -- and now you may like to know his name -- it is Owen Jones.
Your letters gave me great pleasure, as you will have supposed; I seem to hear an echo of my own youth in them every now and then; and when I don't hear that I am interested to see the young soul impregnating with its passion the thought of favourite writers. What especially strikes me in your letters is that the fervor never leads you wrong; which fervor is apt to do, in spite of its sharpening the insight, for it sometimes leads to over-seeing and over-refining. I was particularly pleased with the passage in your letter the other day about Heaven; and in the one today about Dickens and Little Nell. I too abominate Little Nell!
As to the "report" you mentioned -- thank you for not letting it come under her eye. (By the way, your first letter arrived at breakfast and the second 513 three hours after -- so if you remember the times you posted both you may always send to me with good chance of her not seeing the letter) -- But for itself I have this to say. Newspapers can neither make nor mar -- therefore I pay very little attention to them; and unless the question touched one's personal honour or sense of duty nothing that could be said would extort a contradiction from me. We have both of us ill-wishers -- and besides these there are the careless scribblers -- Let both scribble what they please! For your own private ear I may say that although the sale has been less by two or three thousand than I expected it has been very large and quite up to Blackwood's expectation; and as to other success we can't judge -- all those who come near enough to us to be allowed to speak of the book are naturally of the public for whom it is intended. What the outsiders think or say I neither know nor care.
Ever yours faithfully
G. H. Lewes.

GHL to Alexander Main, London, 13 October 1875
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
Wednesday 13th October 75.
My dear Main
On our return home your letter smiled at us amid a pile of circulars and notes. The return was from Wales, and not M'fcrren -- so you see the papers have been as accurate as usual, and our interview with the Archbishop must have taken place in the presence of a "Special Correspondent." 321 I had hoped the mountain air would brace us both -- but we had little sun, and gales in lieu of "air," blustering day and night, and diversified with storms, so that our journey was a mull and made us long for the "comforts o' the saut market." Now we are fixed for the winter and ready to resume work, not indeed as strong as one could wish, but yet well enough to jog on.
Among the letters was the enclosed which I thought would interest you on account of your share in it. Send it me back. Madonna is always deeply gratified by such evidence that her work has not been in vain. I have too many letters to write to expatiate.
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, London, 13 March [1874]
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 13 March [1874]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March.
My dear Main
You are right in supposing I should be gratified by your sympathy. I have also been interested by your acuteness in respect of Clifford and Hutton. 57 The latter is really too feeble. My disappointment was great.
I was prepared for and wished for a strong opposition from him -- but I hoped it would be strong. The first edition was so nearly sold out that Tr'fcbner asked me to prepare a second when the elections suddenly intervened, and for three weeks not a copy was sold; since then the demand has revived again and we calculate on getting out no. 2 in May.
But what will interest you more is that Mrs. Lewes has at last consented to send a volume of poems to press -- including reprints of Jubal, Armgart, Agatha, and Lisa, besides some lovely new things of small length. She does not get strong however, and I look forward to our quiet retirement during the summer to set her up. I continue flourishing -- very hard at work getting my second volume recast and getting daily clearer in my laborious effort to determine the homologies of the Brain and Spinal Cord.
The day before yesterday Mrs. Lewes committed the rare excess of dining out -- a thing not done twice a year. But Lady Colvile seduced her with Joachim, Piatti, Strauss, and Agnes Zimmermann -- such music heard in private was not to be resisted; so we had a delightful dinner and a glorious evening. But headaches had to be the price all next day!
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, London, 1 March 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, 1 March 1876
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 76.
My dear Main
Your sympathy is so genuine and the insight which springs from sympathy so unerring that in spite of its hyperbolical expression it cheers and strengthens Mrs. Lewes -- too much given alas! to despair and doubt. All the ringing chorus of praise which echoes from afar does not stifle her doubt; but is nevertheless very pleasant to her. The success of Deronda already seems to surpass that of Middlemarch and I am persuaded that it will increase with each monthly part. To my mind it is the greatest work she has done.
She is still in very feeble health I am sorry to add, and there seems no chance of her getting better now till the book is finished and we get away to the Continent. I also have been laid up with severe lumbago, headache and liver and the "Problems" have been getting on slowly in consequence. The third volume will not be sent to press until the autumn because I want it to have the benefit of her reading before printing it. Two things I hope this volume will effect -- namely a sweeping away of much superstition respecting the nervous system, and a final quashing of the automaton theory.
I am glad you liked [Animal Studies." I have not looked at it since it was published -- now several years ago -- but it was written with almost as much gusto as "Seaside Studies" -- the book of all my books which was to me the most unalloyed delight.
We went last Thursday to hear Liszt's Oratorio 414 -- mainly out of regard for Liszt; but partly also out of curiosity as to this specimen of the music of the future -- so in spite of its being an evening concert we went and suffered (physically) in consequence. Then to add to the ill effect we dined out on the day after at the Lyttons, to say good bye to them, before they go to India. We are very fond of them both; and so far were glad to have a last farewell; but dining out doesn't suit us, and we have both been limp since.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [8 January 1874]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Dear Main
You will lay up a store of uneasiness in life if you do not learn to "take much for granted" -- and do not get into your head the fact that other people are not so impatient as yourself. Here you have been uneasy because of not hearing from us about the "Sayings," and we have had other things to do than even to look into the book! -- Nay if we had looked into it can't you realize what a burden our necessary correspondence is and how we shirk all unnecessary writing, so that we should have waited until writing to you on other points to mention anything about the "Sayings."
I heard at Chapman's last week that Johnson would be subscribed this week.
That was a pleasant sentence from Ritter -- he is one of the readers worth having.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

GHL to Alexander Main, London, [7 March 1875]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
Sunday.
Dear Main
Your two letters were very interesting, and your story about the Lectures immensely significant. Mrs. Lewes was very poorly when yours to her arrived. She has had another attack of stone -- the pain of which is excruciating -- and leaves her weak and fluttering, but she is now again getting into her usual state, and will no doubt improve after this.
Don't expect to hear from us unless we have something special to communicate -- letter writing is so onerous -- but be sure of our constant regard.
Yours ever
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, London, [31 October 1871]
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [31 October 1871]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday.
My dear Sir
Admirable! The effect is beyond my expectation. I like the classification and the mode of printing the dialogue. The title-page is perfect. I have deleted a few passages which are rather unimportant or common property, and have inscribed one favourite bit of mine in Bartle Massy's sayings.
You will rejoice to hear that Mrs. Lewes is now fairly herself again and at work. Last week we went on a four days visit to some friends (and worshippers) in the country -- a beautiful English family (only it happens to be Scotch!) such as makes one proud of one's country and hopeful of the future. In their pleasant circle she found a bracing tonic and has come back invigorated.
While your collection of sayings astonishes by their wealth I am still more impressed by the wealth when I think of the many passages omitted. Not that I wish these to be inserted; by no means; all cannot be given; but as I read, and remembered, for the first time I realized the fact of the superabundance of thought and emotion which the works contain. Yet so simple is the stream from which they flowed that you will, I think, find no poverty in the book now about to appear -- every page there is as full as if it were a first work. You will observe many more elisions from the first part than from the others. The reason is that it is desirable to make a strong impression in the early pages, and not to weaken it by scattering it over small sentences.
I sympathise with your impatience so much that I have this morning set aside my own work to go over the sheets in order that you might have them again by return. It would be hard indeed when you had shown so much energy and enthusiasm if we who are deeply indebted to you for it did not show something of the same impatience.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.
Alex. Main Esq.

GHL to Alexander Main, London, [31 January 1876]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
My dear Main
If the editor does not print both your articles 393 it will assuredly not be because they don't deserve it -- they are admirable -- but because he hasn't space for them. On the first topic he has a note from me, (at his request) in answer to Bain, and as we take the same line he may think yours superfluous carrying of coals to the Newcastle dep'f4t.
In a letter from Ritter we received the other day he plaintively remarks that you haven't written since May last. Now this book is appearing I daresay you will feel the impulse to s'fog'e1rsi on it to him.
Yes, what you say about Mrs. Lewes's happiness in her work is true -- the pain is there but it is delicious pain after all; and the deep feelings she creates in others react upon herself and make her prize her power.
Tomorrow you will have the "Spoiled Child." 394
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Alexander Main, London, [30 November 1874]
Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [30 November 1874]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday.
My dear Main
We have returned from our continental trip in fairly good condition, and I am hard at work on the final proofs of Volume 2 while Mrs. Lewes advances with her new work. You need be under no anxiety about her beginning to publish until the whole is complete -- or at least so much of it that no probable interruption would occur.
After leaving the country house we paid a visit in Cambridgeshire then went to Paris and through the Ardennes (visiting Sedan) to Brussels, going almost nightly to the theatre and leading a very holiday existence. The weather was transcendent. On our return home we started again for a tour through Wiltshire having long promised ourselves a sight of Salisbury plain and Stonehenge. This was a delightful tour though the weather was often wretched.
I have not seen Picton's book, 169 though your words about it will give it an interest for me should it fall in my way. I have too much to read for my own purposes -- and in a quite different direction -- to look after other people's speculations.
Reading the proofs of Vol. 2 is very dispiriting. All seems so dull and incomplete. One wishes to have the whole thing rewritten -- a wish checked by the knowledge that even then it would produce just the same effect! It is only by the response of other minds that one can ever feel lasting satisfaction. All I can console myself with is the consciousness that I have done my best to condense into a few chapters the best results of years of meditation. But it is not only the prosperity of a jest half of which lies in the hearer 170 -- the prosperity of all writing half depends on the reader. The listener seldom brings any prepossession which will disturb the effect of the jest -- but generally the reader brings his views, theories, superstitions to disturb the effect of a proposition.
Mrs. Lewes bids me send her affectionate remembrances.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [29 September 1871]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Friday.
My dear Sir
By this post I have written at some length and with due emphasis to Mr. Blackwood, and await his reply before sending you the proposed introduction. It seemed more delicate to say what I could say in favour of your scheme, and your ability to execute it, in a private letter than through a letter of introduction, in which moreover all praise wears a constrained official air. I have little doubt that he will gladly enter into the affair.
Mrs. Lewes gains strength though more slowly than could be wished.
The title which now suggests itself to me as better than "Thoughts and Sentences" (rather formal) is "Wise and Witty Sayings from G.E.": that is both descriptive and attractive. What think you?
We are sorry not to have your photo. Even when the photo is bad -- as mostly they are -- it serves to give imagination a steadying point. However I daresay we shall see you in the flesh some day.
Yours very truly
G. H. Lewes.
Our eldest boy -- (a married man of 29, but still our "boy") was much gratified by the perusal of your letters. He takes his mother's influence to heart, for he completely worships her.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [26 May 1873]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Monday.
My dear Main
Our fruitless efforts to get a suitable house for the summer have all but decided us to go abroad and try the effect of mountain air and a German Bath for Mrs. Lewes's recruitment -- much needed I am sorry to say. We go to Oxford on a visit to Jowett on the 7th (we were at Cambridge last week, and it would have done your heart good to see the silent worship of some of the best young men there) and then shall decide where we are to pass the summer. If we decide to remain I will let you know but I do not think that in any case I can undertake to look over your M.S. I feel quite assured from what I saw that you have done what I could have wished; and you had better lose no time but send it at once to Chapman and ask him to get on with the printing so as to be ready by October.
I am at present more than usually bothered -- not only by those business arrangements about a new house for the autumn to be settled, lawyers seen, etc. but I have to get a new publisher for my "Problems" -- Blackwood has taken the alarm, and stopped the printing. Although this bothers me by the waste of three months which it involves I am not really sorry for the change of publisher. B's views on philosophy and religion are too diametrically opposed to mine for perfect comfort in such arrangements. -- This makes no alteration in our friendship though I think he has not acted with his usual considerateness and sagacity. Mrs. Lewes was as usual pleased with your letter. Perhaps we shall see Ritter in Switzerland.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [22 December 1873]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | Monday.
My dear Main
I felt sure of you! -- After writing I made three attempts to see Chapman and finally succeeded not only in seeing him but in getting his promise to send you the money at once. Keep him to it!
I love your friend for that mot of his "George Eliot has become a necessity."
The Problems seem eminently promising -- 800 copies having been sold already and only the shabby notice in the Athenaeum and the good one in the Sat[urday] Rev[iew] as yet. 901 The pleasantest thing I have heard about it is that people not versed in such subjects find it clear and interesting. Mrs. Lewes heard yesterday from Miss Hennell who said her sister had read the book and found "she was the bigger for it -- she knew not why."
Your wishes have run in company with our plans -- we are to spend Christmas with that Scotch Family, where the young men and women call us uncle and aunt and I believe love us as such. Mr. Sellar says of the girls (his cousins) that their religion begins with the credo "I believe in Mr. and Mrs. L."
A Merry Christmas to you and may Johnson meet with the welcome it deserves!
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [20 January 1874]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday.
Dear Main
As you seem unhappy about some attack or other I must write a word of advice. Brace yourself to meet all attacks and all complaints by the consideration that no book ever was or will be written up, or written down by critics -- it stands or falls by its own vitality: and all the buffets of adverse winds, all the puffs of vanity, leave it just what it is. Consider, there is not a single cell but is opposed by the forces of this whole universe -- yet it resists them as long as it has life -- and succumbs as vitality ebbs. If you reflect on the treatment which some of the greatest works have received, the abuse heaped upon the purest and wisest, you will see that if adverse opinion had the power to obstruct truth the world would be in a sad plight.
Don't look at what is said about your work, but do your work honestly and carefully. I haven't seen the Saturday 17 and shall probably not see it -- certainly should not go out [of] my way two yards either to see or avoid it.
I can't promise to read your book for some time yet, I am so busy in other ways nor do I think Mrs. Lewes will be able to do so. But if we thought it a masterpiece that wouldn't alter the fact -- and if we thought it rubbish hundreds of others might think it a masterpiece -- and they are its real public. A beef steak is not food for a cow or a camel, but very good food for us and Christian dogs.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [19 February 1874]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
My dear Main
At last I can give you my opinion of the Johnson, which is very much the opinion of Mrs. Lewes, my son, and a few candid friends who have spoken to me about it. I haven't seen a single newspaper notice, so I can only tell what is thought in our private circle. First then we all agree that the story is very well told and the condensation very well made. But there is a chorus of objection against the excessive showmanship of the commentary -- the framing and glazing of the pictures, with the obtrusion of superfluous indication as to their merits. One reader said he was in a perpetual state of irritation at your not allowing him to enjoy a good thing but insulting him by pointing out that it was good. Again I think the excessive use of quotation (against which I warned you) gives a patchy and made up look to the book especially as so many of the quotations are threadbare from frequent use. Further your delight in italics and small caps is objectionable -- it is like a man raising his voice and thumping on the table to enforce opinions which ought to carry their own force. As a rule italics always give a small appearance unless very specially or carefully employed and small caps is mere loudness not force.
These are defects which you will not fall into in future work and I therefore rely on the sterling qualities of the book as evidence that you may do a good book not open to the criticisms which diminish the effect of this one.
Mrs. Lewes has had a bad attack (it is feared of stone) since I last wrote; between five and six hours of agony. But she has had no pain now for a fortnight, and seems on the way of getting into condition. I am unusually well and very hard at work. I don't know whether you can see the "Academy" in your town -- if so look at Prof. Clifford's review of the "Problems" 36 in the number for February 7th and you will see a review which has gratified me more than anything else written about my book before. Pages of laudation would be trivial compared with such appreciation.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [19 December 1873]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | Friday.
My dear Main
I have known too well the worry of money cares not to sympathise with you! There was no stipulation with C[hapman] about time of payment, but I certainly thought he would pay on publication, and I will try to see him and arrange that it shall be so. You may be quite sure of getting your money -- but equally or almost sure that C. will be as dilatory and unbusinesslike in that as in all other matters. You may write half a dozen letters and get no money and not even a reply! Don't mind that -- continue to write until he answers! 896
Meanwhile as I should be sorry to think of your not being able to enjoy your holiday and being otherwise hampered for want of a few pounds I send you herewith a small loan, which you can send back when you get the last instalment (if it is paid in instalments) from Chapman. You won't mind accepting this temporary aid from me, I am sure; and for your sake I hope it will be but for a short time. In haste
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.
We are neither of us flourishing -- in fact under doctors hands adopting a new regimen.
Cheque dated 22nd for safety.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [12 October 1871]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
My dear Sir
At last a letter from Edinburgh! Here is the important passage (I must tell you that to give B. an idea of your capacity, when he seemed hesitating, I sent him your letters) --
"I have had some talk with Willie and Mr. Simpson about Mr. Main's scheme, and we are very much disposed to enter into it. We do not happen to have any Arbroath correspondent, so that I do not know anything of Mr. Main beyond these letters, but they, and the specimens, look as if he might thoroughly be trusted with the task. . . . You had better, as you propose, tell him to communicate with us." This is very satisfactory.
Now as to hints: It would not do I think to suggest so large a volume as you contemplate. Let Blackwood decide on that point. The scheme you propose (he has not seen that letter) of classification seems excellent -- but if carried out to the extent you mention it would I fear defeat its purpose. Reading extracts is fatiguing work; and the volume should be a small one, both on account of price and portability.
Mrs. Lewes has reserved her rights in Romola.
You had better tell Blackwood that you propose submitting the extracts to Mrs. Lewes for her approval. Remember "Clerical Scenes" is the first of the series.
Curiously enough I also had thought of the word tender for the title -- only placing it first -- "Tender, Wise, and Witty Sayings." Mrs. Lewes though still very weak is decidedly improving and I hope in a few days she will be at work again. You must not expect to hear from her, however. Indeed even when she is in her usual health (never very good at the best) letter writing is such a crux, that I take from her all but the indispensable part of her correspondence.
Yours very truly
G. H. Lewes.
A. Main Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, London, [12 February 1875]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Friday.
My dear Main
I should be glad if the second volume contains any real food for you -- mystical or non-mystical. We have observed with some surprise (not suspecting you of philosophic studies) a keen insight in such matters -- probably here as elsewhere insight comes from sympathy, as, according to my doctrine, all cognition is primarily emotion. Certainly no one ever really understood an opinion until he had learned to see it as it presented itself to the mind which formulated it. I shall send you Vol. 2 in a few days. You would have had the first had I thought it likely to be so much to your taste.
Mrs. Lewes is pretty well and hard at work -- despairing over it, of course, -- aliter non fit liber -- at least with her. I am and have been for some time supremely happy in my work, having got away from hated metaphysics into dear Biology and Psychology. If ever you see a duck painfully picking its way over the stones, and then, when it has reached the water, complacently wagging its tail, and turning round its head with an air of calm content at finding itself once more in its element, think of me as I was during the last two years, and as I am just now. If I wag my tail a little, don't call it conceit so much as Elemental Complacency! Mrs. Lewes told me when I wrote to you to send some pretty message from her -- and I send it. You remember Quintus Fixlein in Jean Paul 213 who was all his life occupied with a work on Errata, which contained important moral conclusions, he said, and -- advised the reader to draw them.
Ever yours
G. H. L.

GHL to Alexander Main, London, [10 April 1873]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
My dear Main
Go on and prosper! The two chapters read very well -- I haven't compared them with Boswell but only tried them as the ordinary reader will. Except a few deletes and a few changes of expression which I have marked in pencil there is nothing to suggest in the way of alteration. Yes -- there is one thing -- avoid as much as you can the habit of small quotation -- I mean familiar scraps like "seriously inclined." They give a journalistic made-up air to writing. Good quotations lighten up a page.
Ever yours in great haste
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: Alexander Main^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, Earlswood Common, 8 September 1874
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cottage | Earlswood Common | September 8. 74.
My dear Main
I quite agree with you about Tyndall's speech, and think Huxley's open to quite as much objection: both as to matter and manner. 143 I could not help regretting that my second volume was not out, or just about to appear; for I believe many readers would see in it how baseless were the exultations and the tribulations founded on the supposed reality of atoms. As to the Unknowable, I have a regular crusade against it, though I don't expect to be more listened to than any other unpopular teacher. What a strange perversity of speculation is that which makes men declare we cannot know a given thing because we do not know something else!
For once the round of the papers was not a fiction respecting Mrs. Lewes. She is writing what I believe will be a glorious book. I can't say the country has done her so much good as I had hoped -- still she is stronger. As for me, I have had a worse time of it than in town and my rewriting (not revision alas!) of Volume 2 has been much delayed in consequence.
We go back to town on the 25th and then start for the Continent where we shall probably remain till November. But our movements are uncertain.
It is very delightful to both of us to think of you and Ritter returning with such zest and satisfaction to the works you know so well.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. L.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, Earlswood Common, [2 August 1874]
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cottage | Earlswood Common | Red Hill | Sunday.
My dear Main
We had rightly divined the reason of not hearing from or seeing you, and were glad for your sake that you had made the choice. Your account of the trip reassures us; there is a health of enjoyment from every line.
Our stay here has been delightful in its solitude and the beauty of the country; but has not been so beneficial to our health as might have been expected and was wished. Mrs. Lewes although better on the whole, has had no little malaise, and is not strong. She is hard at work however. My headaches and dyspepsia have been rather worse if anything since we left London -- but I also am working hard and that may have something to do with it!
The revision of my second volume has turned out to be a rewriting of it -- I hope to its advantage; and there is still much to be done. Therefore I do not think we shall leave England this autumn -- or only for a week or two if at all. We stay here till the end of September.
As you are a lover of Wordsworth you will delight in Dorothy's Journal. 132
Ever yours truly
G. H. L.

GHL to Alexander Main, Blackbrook, 27 October 1873
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
Blackbrook, Bickley. | 27th October 73.
My dear Main
I think it would be very graceful of you to acknowledge your debt to the Cowden Clarkes in the way you propose, and I think they will be pleased. 860
The Problems will not appear until the 15th November. A Russian publisher has paid £50 for the advance sheets for translation of this volume and he must have a fair start. 861 Besides November is a better month than October; and I presume your Johnson will also appear in November. Have you seen the paragraph about it which I enclose from the Athenaeum? 862 It will do you service.
I am gratified to find that the Reflex Theory has proved suggestive to you. In the Problems (not those soon to appear) it will be worked out in great detail.
You will be glad to hear that we are both somewhat stronger, and return to the Priory on Friday next. Tomorrow we spend the afternoon with the Darwins. 863
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Alexander Main, [Redhill], 17 August 1872
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Hitherto unpublished.
August 72.
My dear Main
You don't know what a relief to our anxiety was brought by your first letter! Your silence seemed only interpretable as caused by illness -- and it made us feel how near you had become to us! The idea of your being away did keep anxiety in check -- but then we said "Surely he would have letters forwarded?"
Mrs. Lewes keeps in a shaky state -- there is no hope for strength now, until the book is finished, but that will be I trust in about three weeks. We leave this for the Priory on the 28th.
Your appreciation of all the points in Part V is as usual keen and sympathetic. By the way you are one capable of solving a doubt which has been raised. An old friend of hers -- her translator into French -- writes to say that Middlemarch is more difficult in style than Felix Holt, and Felix was more so than Silas or Adam. Now is this because he is getting older and his faculties less alert, or is it the fact that there is any appreciable change? We of course cannot see it -- we do not see the changes in our person so obvious to others -- but if it is there you surely will perceive it.
Thank you very much for mentioning the Contemporary Review. I should probably never have heard of it -- for Mrs. Lewes's friends all know that she abstains from reading criticisms on her works and therefore they abstain from alluding to them. I was delighted with the article -- moved to tears in fact -- and read some of the passages to her much to her comfort and sustainment.
Ever yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Text: C. L. Graves, Life and Letters of Alexander Macmillan, Macmillan, 1910, p. 346.
The Heights, | Witley, | August 26, 1878.
I feel sure you will be glad to know the pleasure Mrs. Lewes has received from the first three instalments of your series of English classics. 132 She has read them aloud to me, and although Scott is to her an almost sacred name, she was so delighted with Hutton's largeness of feeling and sympathetic insight that, as she told a lady yesterday, "she was in a glow all the time she read it." Stephen's Johnson also gave her great pleasure. The Gibbon was of course a less attractive subject, but it is on the whole admirably done.
We have seen scarcely any one except Tennyson, who has read his new drama and some other poems to us. Not a trace of age in the old poet! The drama is full of fine dramatic power.

Dublin Core:Subject: Albert Druce^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Albert Druce, London, 13 April [1874]
MS: Miss Elsie Druce. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April.
My dear Druce
Letters such as yours are the best rewards an author can get. I must suppose that my exposition has been faulty in some respect since you misapprehend me about universality and necessity. I certainly did think they were stated in terms of experience, and refer you especially to 'a7'a7 167-183 to show that I am not converting a postulate of practice into an axiom of reason. The experience which tells us that a thing is what it is, tells us that it must be what it is universally so long as the conditions are unaltered. That is the only universality and necessity I recognize and I especially decry the metempirical uniformity of Nature or universality which is not the uniformity of uniform conditions, the universality of conditions universalized.
Give our love to your wife and our hopes that the sea breezes are cooperating with Problems in giving vigour to your constitution.
Yours ever
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL to Albert Cohn, London, [10 December 1873]
Dublin Core:Subject: Albert Cohn^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Albert Cohn, London, [10 December 1873]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1873. Lewes. London, December. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Friday.
My dear Sir
The guinea edition of [Middlemarch] continues selling, so I suppose you also find the sale in parts too good to be interrupted by the cheap edition of which you threw out a hint in a letter which I got just as I was starting for the continent. We may, however, as well come to some arrangement if possible, so as to be ready when the sale in parts has ceased or become too small to be worth consideration. Send me your views on this point.
Are you to be in town this Christmas? If so I wish you would bring me a fur coat. For walking the fur coat is too warm and heavy in any winter we have here; but for our open carriage one would be a great comfort, and the London prices are outrageous because few Londoners wear such things. In Berlin they abound and as you would be certain to know of a good and trustworthy shop where they could be bought at a reasonable price, and as what would fit you would fit me, I should be greatly obliged if you would execute a commission for me to that effect, and bring the coat with you, if you are coming, (wearing it on the way if convenient) or send it by some safe channel.
What would be the price of a good, light, coat. I don't want a [swell] affair -- but I should like a good fur and a light coat. Will you ascertain the prices and let me know? Excuse my putting you to this trouble -- if you can -- and believe me
Yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Adolf And Fanny Stahr^^M,F
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to Adolf And Fanny Stahr, [London], 1 September 1870
Text: Aus Adolf Stahrs Nachlass, ed. Ludwig Geiger, Oldenburg, 1903, pp. 314-315.
September 1870.
Dear Friends
Stahr's Sturmglockenrufe 929 awoke response in the peaceful Priory, as you can well believe. The translation of Prestige should be painted in letters of gold!
This morning I read Frau Fanny's well-timed protest against the favouritism shown to French prisoners by those who wish to give their French an airing and although we do not refuse our sympathy with suffering French still on all accounts the Germans must have the first place -- and this would be so even were my wife and I not specially bound by many a grateful thought to German friends and to the German people. It is the memory of the many kindnesses we have received at German hands, especially in dear Berlin, that prompts us to send the accompanying trifle towards the relief of German sufferers -- wounded or orphans -- to be applied as you will best know how to apply it, either in private aid, or to merge in public efforts. Any banker will cash the checque for you, but you must first write your name on the back. As we are certain that Frau Fanny will be active in many good works, we feel that she can best decide in what direction our small contribution can be best applied. The English subscription is already over 50000'a3 and goes on vigorously. But it is for French and German alike.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL to [?], London, 8 November 1872
MS: Princeton.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regent Park.
November 72.
Dear Sir
Mrs. Lewes (George Eliot) is so much occupied just now that I relieve her, whenever practicable, of the labour of correspondence; and she is the more desirous that I should reply to your question, because she has a very slight experience on which to found a judgment, and I have had a tolerably large experience.
My advice is by all means not to throw yourself on Literature for a living. Very splendid talents and wide knowledge are often incompetent to secure bread and cheese and except in the department of journalism there is but a perilous outlook for any one who has not already proved that his talents are commercially valuable. Now it seems to me that this question you can decide for yourself. Assuming that your present employment is intolerable to you and that you have a strong bent towards Literature, I would urge you to ascertain decisively whether editors and publishers are willing and eager to pay you for your writing? If they are you can form some estimate of your probable success when you devote your whole energies to Literature. Meanwhile you can do what hundreds of others are doing, viz. cultivate Literature in your leisure hours, and try by your production to encrease your income and find a footing for yourself on the shifting sand of periodicals. To give up any honorable employment on the vague chance of success in Literature is what all rational men would advise against. 118 You must not confound your hopes and wishes with the condition of success. It is for you a question of pounds and shillings and pence not of literary activity -- and that question you, like every one else, have the means of settling, by simply offering editors and publishers what you have written. Believe me both editors and publishers are for their own sakes eager to accept and pay for whatever promises to be commercially valuable; and no one will accept work that does not seem to promise such commercial advantage.
Yours truly
G. H. Lewes.

Dear Sir,
Mrs. Lewes never reads articles written about herself. I have read what you were good enough to send, and, in reply to your question, beg to assure you that every single detail in it is imaginary -- birth, parentage, education, and history are not distorted or exaggerated, they are totally wide of all resemblance to the facts. GHL to 'e9Mile Mont'e9gut, Wandsworth, 1 December 1859
Text: Revue de litt'e9rature compar'e9e, 49 (September 1975), 77.
Holly Lodge, Southfields
Wandsworth, Surrey, 1 December 1859.
My dear Sir
Knowing your admiration of "Adam Bede" -- on which you wrote so exquisite an article -- I am tempted to renew our long interrupted correspondence, to ask you if among your literary acquaintances you know of any one who would be competent to translate it properly, and willing to undertake the task. George Eliot is Mrs. Lewes -- so you see I have an interest in the matter. We have already had several applications but it is of consequence to get a good translator, and I think you would be very likely to know of one. A work which has had greater success than Bulwer or Thackeray have ever achieved, and which in less than nine months has sold 10,000 copies, must surely be a good commercial speculation for a French publisher; and if a good translator could be found we are willing to sell the right of translation for 1,000 francs.
I have not seen Carlyle since he [left for] Scotland; but Pigott [we had] with us the other day and we talked of you and the Revue des Deux Mondes. I suppose you know he has sold the "Leader," -- is now one of the editors of the "Daily News."
When fate brings me to Paris, I shall hope to [see you]. If you [come to] London, [don't] forget me.
Ever faithfully yours
G. H. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Weymouth, 5-16 September 1859
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday 5th.
After breakfast we rambled out and the weather was so tempting that we resolved to give up the morning to a walk up the Wey. Having made our way, in rather a roundabout manner and some trespassing to Radipole, we there went all over a Mill which was kindly shown us by the Miller. This was the very thing for Polly who has a Mill in her new novel and wanted some details. We were so delighted with the spot that we enquired about lodgings thinking a day or two might pleasantly and profitably be spent near the mills (there are five within three miles) and the stream. A laborer seemed willing to let his cottage, which we found very clean, and quite comfortable enough. We left him to ask his wife, and then rambled about. Came home at 2 -- dined. Polly read Layard 289 aloud, and we went out for a stroll, and our letters. Tea. I then rewrote the finale to my article, and some letters.
Tuesday 6th.
Read Schr'f6der van der Kolk; 290 went to the post for letters and found a large packet there. Wrote to Blackwood, the Major, and Nurse; 291 rambled; read Athenaeum and lunched. After that we walked to Radipole and were much put out at finding the laborer's wife decidedly opposed to letting her cottage. We sat with a little old woman whom we were told might possibly let lodgings and had a little talk with her; then wandered along the river to another Mill which we went over; and came back very tired. In the evening Polly cont[inue]d Layard; I, the Excursion. Read Schr'f6der.
Wednesday 7th.
Read Schroeder van der Kolk; lounged about the beach. Examined a serpula under the Microscope; but felt too unwell to do any work. After lunch we had a ramble on the Cliff. In the evening went to the Theatre and saw the Hunchback 292 performed in true provincial style.
Thursday 8th.
Read Schroeder van der Kolk. The proof of Feeling and Thinking 293 arrived, and correcting it was occupation for the whole morning. Rambled on the cliff and read Blackwood. In the evening we walked on the Parade to hear the band. I read the Excursion aloud, and Schr'f6der van der Kolk to myself. --
Friday 9th.
Read K'f6lliker: Gewebelehre. 294 Rambled on the sands and had a talk with Mr. Barnes the Kensington tax gatherer. Came in and began to rewrite "The Mind and the Brain." 295 After lunch we went across by Steamer to Portland Island and went to see the Breakwater now in course of construction. After dinner Polly continued Layard.
Saturday 10th.
Read Moreau Psychologie Morbide. 296 Continued "The Brain and the Mind." At 1 o'clock we took the rail to Dorchester, desirous of ascertaining whether the river Frome would suit Polly's purposes. Had lunch at an inn and learned from the landlord that there was no footpath and that the stream was insignificant. We then rambled through the meadows by the side of the stream which is deliciously clear, showing the weeds and waterplants beneath in great beauty and as the day was lovely we enjoyed our ramble greatly. Dorchester a very pretty quiet town with chesnut avenues and trees along the turnpike roads reminding us of Germany. Came back by the 'bd past 5 train. After dinner Polly cont[inue]d Layard and I read Ernest Renan Essais de Morale et de litterature. 297
Sunday 11th.
Read Moreau. Polly's head being troublesome we resolved to give up the morning to fresh air, and walked along the cliff and sands to Portland Island. Returned, lunched, and then went on the Esplanade. Read the papers. After dinner Polly cont[inue]d Layard and I Renan.
Monday 12th.
Read Moreau: Psychologie Morbide. Went out marketing and [bought] both a hare and brace of partridges. Then returned and continued the Mind and the Brain. After lunch we hired an open carriage and went to Upwey, a lovely village, the source of the Wey, which we visited and should have found it enchanting had it not been beset by a crowd of small boys and girls with glasses of water which they thrust upon us with unmistakeable demands for backsheesh; and even when they got it would not retire but stood gaping round us all the while. The spot is however a study for a painter. The whole village remarkably pretty. On my return found a long letter from Dr. Inman 298 on my proofs of Feeling and Thinking -- it dispirited me to find that even he had quite failed to seize my meaning which I had taken such immense trouble to make clear to every understanding. It is a bad presage of what the public will think! -- In the evening Polly cont[inue]d Layard, and I, Renan.
Friday 16th.
This morning we left Weymouth for home. Started by 8.20 train and reached Holly Lodge 3.40. Found letters from Charley, Spencer, Mr. Quirk, Chapman, etc. Baker was there to meet us and Pug somewhat sceptical at first but finally acknowledging us. Unpacked and set things in order for tomorrow. After dinner read Aurora Leigh aloud and Once a Week to myself.

GHL Journal, Wandsworth, 9-10 November 1859
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Wednesday 9th.
Read Gegenbaur, Grundz'fcge der Vergleichenden Anatomie 375 and finished the rough draft of my first chapter of "Studies in Animal Life." My new Microscope is a great treasure, and will induce me to work even more than before. Went into town. Met Mrs. Edward Chapman, who seemed very glad to see me and asked after Mrs. Evans Lewes, speaking of "Adam Bede" with the usual rapture. Looked in at Bailliere's and bought some books. Dined with Mother. Agnes there. Mother in a high state of pride and delight because Mrs. Abronson had told her that the ex-royal family of France had read the "Life of Goethe" and admiring it very much asked all sorts of questions about me.
Thursday 10th.
Read Gegenbaur Vergleichende Anatomie. Began the rewriting of Chapter 1 of "Studies in Animal Life." After our walk, did a little microscopy and then went to the station to meet Dickens who dined with us. He reminded me that it was three and twenty years ago since I first went down to Twickenham to see him, Eheu! fugaces! 376 We had a delightful talk about all sorts of things, and I walked part of the way home with him and then turned into the Congreves where we 377 had a discussion on George Stephenson, the Religion of Humanity etc.

GHL Journal, Wandsworth, 29 April 1859
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
On Wednesday after my dinner sleep I went up into my dressing room feeling quite as usual, when suddenly, without any premonitory symptoms I fainted away. I must have fallen senseless, and the shock must have for a moment revived me, since my fall, which brought me against the bath, made a terrible booming noise which startled Polly, and made her call out to ask what I was doing. I answered '91I am fainting'92 -- and then again became unconscious. Now I remember distinctly feeling that I was going to faint, and that she spoke to me and I answered; yet she could not have spoken until after I had fallen, as my fall alarmed her. This has left me very weak and giddy ever since, and quite unfit for work.

GHL Journal, Wandsworth, 27 October 1859
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
On Thursday 27 October I had a visit from George Smith 363 of Smith and Elder in consequence of a correspondence between Thackeray and myself, in which I agreed to cooperate in the forthcoming "Cornhill Magazine" if terms and subject suited. Smith evidently wishes to nouer des relations and proposed a series of papers on Natural History which might afterwards form a volume. I agreed to consider his proposal, and he drove me into town, where I called on Smith and Beck, and exchanged my old Microscope for one of their First Class Instruments. Beck was at Aberdeen and heard my papers read at the "British Association." 364 He gave an amusing description of the "row" they excited, and told me that Allen Thomson 365 and Huxley both defended me. I expected the papers would create a disturbance, but hardly expected these eminent men to stand up for me. The proposal of George Smith becomes very seductive and I have almost decided on accepting it. One of my regrets at the idea of finishing the Physiology was lest I should not find a paying scientific subject to take its place.

GHL Journal, Wandsworth, 27 May 1859
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Today Blackwood dined with us. He brought an amusing correspondence about the authorship of Adam Bede, which is the great literary mystery of the day. It appears that subscriptions of money have actually been set on foot [for] Liggins the supposed author. Blackwood urged that the secret should stedfastly be kept, at least until after the next book. He also advised against our idea of putting Charley into the publishing business. After dinner we walked with him through the park and wood to Putney Station where he departed and we walked home.

Monday 23rd.
Since the 30th of last month, when we reached Holly Lodge, I have been busy with arrears of correspondence and with arrangements for Charles. Among the two or three people I spoke to about him was Anthony Trollope, and of him I only asked information, yet he most kindly interested himself and wrote to the Duke of Argyll 598 for a nomination to compete for a vacancy in the Post Office -- which was granted on Friday last. We have been much occupied training Charley for the examination, and I have dictated to him every day. Yet in spite of this work and distraction I have finished my Introduction and Memoirs of the Dramatists for Brockhaus: £50 easily earned!

Wednesday 2nd November.
Read Leuret: Anat. Comp. du Syst'e8me Nerveux, 371 and continued the rewriting of my chapter on the Spinal Chord. GHL Journal, Wandsworth, 15 November 1859
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Tuesday 15th.
Read Gegenbaur and finished "Studies in Animal Life I." 388 Dickens having written to ask Polly if she could on her own terms write a story for "All the Year Round" we have turned the matter over and almost think it feasible. Today I went by appointment to see Lucas and Evans who wanted me to write a novel for "Once a Week" on my own terms; but having agreed with Polly that it was desirable I should not swerve from Science any more, at least just now, I declined. They then asked me to contribute articles on my own terms. 389 After this they approached the subject of a story from Polly, and wanted to know whether her new novel was in the market. I told them I thought it unlikely that she would publish in "Once a Week" and that she felt bound to give Blackwood the refusal; but they assured me that whatever Blackwood offered they would give more. We parted on the understanding that they were to make an offer.

GHL Journal, Wandsworth, 1 March 1860
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Thursday 1st. Yesterday I had a busy day in town. First I went by appointment to Tr'fcbner who wanted me to write a preface to the translation he proposes to issue of Humboldt's letters. 492 But as I object altogether to the system of preface writing, I acknowledged the compliment and declined. Promised him, however, to read the book and give him my opinion on it, and on the necessary omissions. He then went with me to Appleton's agent 493 who is very anxious to secure the early sheets of "The Mill on the Floss." He said he could give as much as 300 'a3 if he were protected against Harper's reprinting the book; but I could not take that risk, so I went to Sampson Low, Harper's agent, who agreed to give 300 'a3 without any conditions. This is 100 more than he offered some 'abweeks'bb days ago. -- Called on Langford and on Lucas, smoked a cigar with the latter, who again returned to the charge about my writing a novel for "Once a Week" and made me promise that if I should change my mind, and think of writing one, he should have the refusal of it. Went to Williams and Norgate, who have been trying to bargain for Tauchnitz, offering only 80 'a3 for the right of reprinting "The Mill" in Germany; but I stood out for 100 'a3 and to that they now agree. This morning read Whewell's "Philosophy of Discovery" 494 -- which, singularly enough, he has sent me. Wrote several letters, and worked at "Animal Studies."

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Vienna, 8-17 April 1870
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Vienna, 8-17 April 1870
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Friday 8th April.
Reached Vienna at 8.30. Robert Lytton came to meet us and while his man looked after our luggage conducted us to the apartment he had secured for us in the R'f6mischen Kaiser -- very spacious and quiet, on 1st floor. (11 florins a day however). Breakfasted, slept for an hour, washed, and took a ramble, but the place so altered that I could not find myself in it again until meeting F'fcrstenberg 147 we got at last into the Graben and Stephans Platz. Went into the Cathedral, but the cold was so great that even this grand interior could not arrest us long. Back to the hotel, lunched, and read B'f6rne [Skizzen.] 148 Dined at the Lyttons. In the evening Prof. Gompertz 149 and his wife came in. Arranged to go with him tomorrow to Meynerts. 150 Mrs. Lytton very charming.
Saturday 9th.
Polly's cold turned last night to severe hoarseness and this morning it was still so bad that I wrote to Lytton to put off our going with them to Count von Beust's 151 private theatricals this evening. As all the Court and all the fashion of Vienna will be there, it is a disappointment. But the risk too great. Read Stahr's Ein Winter in Rom. 152 Prof. Gompertz called and took me to Meynert who had been summoned by telegram. We then went over to Stricker 153 who showed us some new apparatus he was inventing, a new immersion lens 15. by Hartnack 154 under which we examined the muscle of Hydrophilus, still waving and contracting. Saw a frog whose semicircular canals had been destroyed. Ray Lankester 155 came in. Back to Hotel and found Lytton with Polly. When he left we went to Dehnes and had coffee and thence to the Belvidere -- portraits finer than I remembered. Giorgione, Velasquez, Titian. Home and read B'f6rne. Dined with the Lyttons. Mrs. Erle 156 the only one present. Polly too unwell to go to Beusts so we came home, changed our dress, and rambled in the starlit streets.
Sunday 10 April.
Another superb day. Wrote to Mother. Rambled then went to the Lichtenstein Gallery. Marvellous Rembrandt -- portrait of a plump pleasant gentleman in a velvet cape, with hat half shadowing his face. The modelling and flesh painting surpasses anything I remember of his. Portrait of Wallenstein and many others by Vandyck, Rubens, etc. Disappointed now with Rubens' [Assumption.] Home and read Stahr Ein Winter in Rom. As we were finishing luncheon Mrs. Lytton called. Accompanied her home. Lytton then proposed that we should drive in the Prater and I went to get an open carriage for that purpose but none to be had, so he, Polly and I walked in the Volksgarten. Came back tired and read the Times. Dined at Lyttons. A most delightful evening. Villers, 157 the Saxon charg'e9 d'affaires, nephew of the old translator of Kant, speaking German and French with equal elegance and felicity, conversation like champagne, and manner very amiable. Klackzo 158 also a lively well-informed man. Conversation always general and easy. Many bons mots and stories.
Monday 11.
The weather less fine to-day, cloudy at times and threatening rain. Read Stahr Ein Winter in Rom. Went to the Irrenhaus and had a long talk with Meynert on the brain; arranged to go there tomorrow to see his preparations. Gompertz walked home with me. Lunch and rambled in the sun and through the streets, shopping. Polly's cold still too bad to permit of galleries or other visits. Read Jean Paul Kazenberg's Bad Reise. 159 Dined at Lyttons. Polly's throat bad.
Tuesday 12 April.
Read Stahr's Ein Winter in Rom. Went to Meynert and spent the whole forenoon with him over his preparations. On coming back found M. Villers with Polly. He sat nearly an hour and then she had a light dinner, her cold being too bad for her to dine out or stir out today. I hunted in vain for a pretty brooch for her. Dined at Lyttons. Present: Mr. Jay, 160 the American plenipotentiary minister (seemingly quite commonplace), Prof. and Mrs. Gompertz, and F'fcrstenberg. Villers came in during the evening. Very gay and pleasant. Lytton brought a message from the Princess Hohenlohe, 161 very desirous of seeing us.
Wednesday 13.
Read Meynert: Ursprung des R'fcckenmarks. F'fcrstenberg called to see Polly's throat -- slight ulceration which needs great prudence. Went with him to the Apothecarie and bought a spirit lamp. Went to Lytton and talked to him about his Fables, 162 and about Polly. Came home and found Mrs. Gompertz with her. Lytton called. Then Mrs. Lytton who brought tickets for the Feet Washing tomorrow. 163 Called on the Princess Hohenlohe. She very cordial; sent for the children to show me, but only the young Prince 164 in. Stayed all the rest of the day in the hotel. Dined there. In the evening went over the Brain with Polly.
Thursday 14.
Polly's throat too bad to think of our going to the [Feet Washing.] This is the second chance we have missed of seeing the Empress. F'fcrstenberg called. Bought oil silk for compress. Read Meynert. Went to Stricker: protoplasm of toad's egg, hyaline, without granules but amoebaform movements. Came home and found Gompertz with Polly. Had lunch while Polly dined. Mrs. Lytton and children called, bringing some barleywater. Lesson on the Brain to Polly. Wrote to Mother. Dined at Lyttons: Prince and Princess Ahrenberg, 165 Gr'e4fin Kolonitsch, 166 and a Hungarian baroness whose name I missed. The countess a handsome genial, very fat, woman talked well. The princess very lively, smoked cigars. The prince quiet but placed his mot 'e0propos. At 10 o'clock left them to go to a party at Gompertz: hot rooms blazing with light, diamonds and pink dresses. Felt very weary of being introduced to women who all said the same thing. Bettelheim sang superbly the Erlk'f6nig and a song by Schumann. Slipped away with F'fcrstenberg when supper began.
Friday
Good Friday. Polly's throat rather better. My headache came on and towards evening became horrible. Dined with the Lyttons alone and said goodbye. I lay on the sofa after dinner and slept. Very sick when we got away.
Saturday.
Bad night, but head got better towards morning. Took leave of the Gompertz -- Polly with me. Went to Bank. The Lyttons came to say goodbye once more. Lunched. F'fcrstenberg came and took me to Leidesdorf 167 and Meynert. Dined at hotel and packed up.
Sunday 17.
Splendid morning. Great trouble in getting our slow waiters to move rapidly enough to get off in time. F'fcrstenberg was at the station having kindly spoken to the Inspector to secure us a coup'e9 alone. Said goodbye to him, and glad enough to say goodbye to Vienna which has completely changed its character and for me lost all its old charm. The sunshine quickly gave place to rain and hail. Reached Salzburg at 5.30. Hotel Nelboeck -- quite cheered to find ourselves in a comfortable hotel, with friendly landlord and waiters after the splendid discomfort of Vienna and Berlin. The ravishing views from our windows also an important advantage; especially after the noisy dusty streets. Excellent dinner of trout, venison, beef, and mahlspeise, all of the best, and the waiter anxious for us to eat more. Read Times over my cigar.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Thun, 13 July 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Thun, 13 July 1868
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
We left Petersthal on the 1st with many regrets and resolutions to come back some future summer. Although I had preserved my incognito by declaring myself, when asked, to be the relative of the Mr. Lewes I could not resist revealing the fact to a very pretty, cultivated and charming girl whom I sat next to a[t] dinner during the last week, the daughter of the Austrian Consul at Helsingfors. 787 I stipulated that she was not to betray me until after our departure; but although the secret had only to be kept two days it was too much for her and about an hour before our departure the news had run over Petersthal. The Landlord seemed overwhelmed with the "honor his establishment had received"; several gentlemen and ladies came to express their enthusiasm and to beg my card; and all the guests assembled to see us off, waving handkerchiefs and bowing. It was very pleasant. Our drive to the Appenweier station delightful. Thence per rail to Freiburg -- Z'e4ringer Hof, capital room -- supper, ramble, and bed early.
At Freiburg we stayed two days, made agreeable and memorable by the acquaintance of Funke, Weismann, Ecker, Kussmaul, Manz, Frau von Hillern, etc. 788 Polly came in for her share of lionizing here. Funke showed us Helmholtz's Sirene and Vocal tuning forks. Manz some retina preparations. Weismann his insect develop[ment] preparations and some others. Ecker the Comp. Anat. Museum.
From Freiburg we took a carriage and drove to St. M'e4rgen (four hours). The first evening ravished us with the beauty of the place, but the next day Polly was ill in bed, and the day after it was cold so that we could not sit about in the open air. Walked to St. Peter however, and made other charming rambles, especially to a peasant's house -- a memorable visit -- in company with the Gr'e4fin Baudisin and her daughter. 789 But after four days we were forced to depart -- the want of indoor accommodation and the fatigue of having people to talk to outbalancing the manifold attractions of the place.
Came back to Freiburg and next morning (Thursday) started for B'e2le. Hotel de la Couronne -- good. There saw the Holbeins and called on His 790 who gave me a morning to his embryological preparations. Reached this place, Thun, (Hotel Freienhof) on Friday evening. We have been here <four> three days greatly enjoying the walks and the quiet and the sunsets. We intended starting for Interlaken this afternoon but continuous rain prevented us. Tomorrow, if fine, we depart.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Schwalbach, 4 July 1866
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Wednesday 4th.
The last week has not been so agreeable. Since Friday there has been occasionally a thunderstorm, and since Sunday only gleams of sunlight interrupted with fierce rain. Yesterday three families fled from the hotel in a panic because a Dr. here had foolishly told them they had better escape while they could, a great battle at Frankfurt being inevitable. After ordering carriages and driving away as far as Ems they met English travellers on the road who pointed out to them the absurdity of their fears and that even should a battle be fought Schwalbach was as safe a place as they could find. Whereupon they returned to the old quarters. Their panic without absolutely communicating itself to us caused us to consider what were the conditions and whether it would not be better to place ourselves out of all danger of an interruption of the route. We decided however on remaining, or rather on going to Schlangenbad as originally proposed. -- The rain has greatly interfered with our enjoyment of this place though we have walked as much as before, and the walks are surprisingly varied and beautiful.

GHL Journal, Richmond, 29 January 1859
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
As Polly was not well we went into town to pay our long contemplated visit to St. Paul's which I have not entered since I was 8 or 9 years old. The inside is much inferior in effect to the outside -- the wretched statues, and the partition probably destroy much of the effect. We then went to a wholesale warehouse in Watling Street and bought our carpet and rugs. After which we walked up Fleet Street and the Strand to the Bankers, and bought a watch, which is to be Polly's present to Charlie. Then we bought an elegant teacaddy and came home thoroughly tired.

Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Richmond, 12 February 1859
MS: Yale. Extracts published: George Eliot and John Chapman, pp. 101-102.
Wrote to Blackwood's clerk 18 and to Dr. Chapman who again has annoyed us with his indelicate conduct about the authorship of Adam Bede, which, in very emphatic and distinct terms, I have denied on Marian's behalf. She was reluctant that I should do so; but the very existence and possibility of anonymity would be at an end if every impertinent fellow could force you either by confession or implication to admit the truth of his questions. Therefore I hold a man in no respect forfeits his truthfulness in denying questions put to him as to anonymous writing, unless those questions be in themselves warrantable, and not simply curiosity; and if the thing is to be denied at all I am for distinct, effective denial rather than equivocation. 19
Polly and I went into town about more shopping; on our return found the "Statesman" had a review of "Adam Bede" which much disgusted me, and somewhat disheartened me. It was laudatory throughout; but the kind of laudation was fatal. "One of the best novels we have read for a long time." The nincompoop couldn't see the distinction between Adam and the mass of novels he had been reading. This made me fear that Langford might be right, and that the public would not discriminate a work so truthful and artistic. However before dinner there came a letter from Blackwood full of real encouragement, speaking of the enthusiasm excited in his private circle; and sending also a little story by Dr. John Brown (who "raves" about Adam) called "Rab and his friends." This Polly read aloud after dinner -- a charming bit of sympathetic painting, the hero of which is an old mastiff, and the heroine an old Scotch woman with a cancer. -- She then read Scott's Life till 11.

Monday 15th.
Our enjoyment encreases. The beauty of the place with its varied and ravishing walks, its agreeable water and baths, good food, and perfect repose, added to the soft bergluft and the perfect weather make life without a wish. We rise at 6. Drink waters and walk till 7. Breakfast in open air. Ramble and read Morris's [Earthly Paradise] 772 -- Bathe, drink, ramble. Table d'h'f4te at 1. Cigar and rest till 5; walk till 7. Light supper, brief ramble and bed at 9. To-day my headache prevented my bathing so during Polly's bath I wrote to Blackwood and journalized.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Paris, 29-31 December 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Paris, 29-31 December 1866
MS: Yale. Extract published: Kitchel, p. 240.
Saturday 29 December.
After breakfast did shopping, rambling, and picture seeing. Back to the hotel and stretched myself on the bed for an hour's rest. At 'bd 6 we went to dinner at Mad. Mohl's -- present L'e9once de Lavergne, 557 Jules Simon, 558 de Lom'e9nie, 559 Prof. Scherer 560 and his wife, Lanfrey 561 and a M. Gigot, 562 a young Catholic advocat. Liked Scherer very much; Jules Simon commonplace. The dinner agreeable and the talk lively but sadly wanting in individuality or distinction.
Sunday 30th December.
The streets yesterday and to-day horribly crowded; every one buying 'e9trennes; the boulevards like a fair with booths on each side. We left Barbara's letters at Mad. Mohl's and then went to the Louvre where we met Woolner. He went to the sculpture room with us and explained certain technical excellencies of the statues. We arranged to dine with him and Clark, 563 but found ourselves too tired as we were going to the theatre. Dined at the hotel -- capital dinner. Went to Th'e9'e2tre Lyrique expecting to hear Richard Coeur de Lion and Rigoletto and found to our disgust Richard not to be given but instead a wretched opera comique -- Cartouche. Even Rigoletto not so well cast as last year.
Monday 31st.
Breakfasted with Mad. Mohl. Renan, Woolner, and the Duchesse di Colonna 564 the only guests. Renan very much like a Belgian priest in aspect -- broad, coarse, suave, agreeable, commonplace; he talked just as the thousand and one Frenchmen talk -- inconsiderately, superficially. He interested me by what he said of Littr'e9; 565 of Comte he talked the usual nonsense. I could not help probing him when he was talking about Kant, and finding that, as I expected, he only knew Kant at second hand, and that inaccurately. He pressed me to go and see him -- don't think I shall. The duchess a charming apparition. Pretty, very graceful, a sculptor of genius (I hear) and an individual mind, I perceived. She talked a good chat with Polly and pressed me to go and see her when we revisit Paris -- which we shall.
Stayed till 2 -- a most interesting morning; but the rain poured in torrents and no cab to be had! At last a messenger sent to Mohl took us in his cab as far as the Palais Royale and there we walked under the arcades till the rain ceased after which we had a horrid walk through the overcrowded muddy streets to our hotel -- packed up, dined and started for Tours at 7.15. Arrived at the station we found passengers were not deposited at Tours by that train, so we went to Orl'e9ans. Hotel du Loiret very primitive; had a fire lighted and got to bed.
