Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Naples, 4-5 May 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Naples, 4-5 May 1860
MS: Yale. Extract published: Kitchel, p. 200.
Friday 4 May.
Yesterday at dinner a Russian and his wife to whom I have occasionally chatted proposed that we should join them in an expedition to Pompeii, and as that would lessen the expense, we agreed, in spite of our disinclination to join parties. The day began most brilliantly and though it clouded over at one time, was on the whole splendid. The drive to Pompeii, through P'f3rtici, Torre del Greco, and Torre dell' Annunziata is very interesting; but the first thrill on entering the silent streets of Pompeii surpasses everything in the way of thrilling emotions at ruins. It was wholly different from what I had pictured it, and far more solemnly affecting. The long streets with the marks of the chariot wheels worn on the stones, the signs of shops, the constant view of the distant mountains, the similarity, amid so much dissimilarity to our modern life in the various indications still preserved, produced strange sensations. I longed to be rambling among the streets by the light of evening, unaccompanied by guides, undisturbed by the occasional glimpse of a visitor with "Murray." We were fortunate in having chosen a day and an hour when but a very few persons had arrived, and those few only crossed our paths now and then, so that on the whole we had the streets much to ourselves. The chief mosaics, pictures, all the utensils, and with a few exceptions all the statues have been removed from the houses and temples and collected in the Museum. This robs Pompeii of one great attraction. The Forum is grand, the Basilica very impressive, and the Amphitheatre and Theatre are so well preserved that a perfect idea of their construction is formed without any architectural knowledge.
It was curious to see the schoolboy like tendency in these Pompeians, to ornament their bedrooms with pictures of hideous obscenity. The phallus outside the lupanar is very well, and innocent enough; but hideous suggestions of amorous donkeys and satyrs with naked women seem anything but fit ornaments for bedrooms -- or indeed any other rooms. Noticeable amid the profusion of ornaments of all kinds everywhere -- mosaics, arabesques, pictures, statues, columns etc. is the great elegance of taste displayed. I imagine the predominance of the color red (chocolate red) would have been monotonous; and indeed the similarity of one house to another must have very much destroyed the effect of any one; but remembering one was in a provincial city, and that not important, it gave a vivid idea of the luxury and elegance of the lives led by these people. After 4 hours and a half we were thoroughly exhausted and went to the Hotel Diomede (a miserable restaurant) and had a lunch of bread, butter, Swiss cheese and Capri wine. Back to Naples by 'bd past 5.
Saturday 5th May.
Went to the Museo Borbonico to see the ornaments and utensils found at Pompeii and Herculaneum. This was an extremely interesting sight. Besides the cameos and ornaments (a few of the cameos of exquisite workmanship, and the one large Medusa nearly a foot broad unique among cameos -- for size, not for beauty) there were objects quite touching -- the linen of a wash wrung as if just wrinced, the loaf of bread with the baker's name printed on it, the silk, thread, ropes, keys, walnuts, oil (some still liquid) bottles, lens, mirrors, urns very similar indeed to our tea urns, the children's playthings, the letters for the shopfronts, surgical instruments, cooking utensils, in fact all the familiar objects of familiar life. These interested us so much that we bought a large volume of engravings of the chief objects.
Wrote to Agnes. Received a letter from Blackwood containing checquered news about the "Mill on the Floss." The sale is about 5,600 -- immense, but I gather that the general talk about the book is less favorable than it was about Adam. The disclosure of the authorship would have much influence in that direction, which would be increased by the fact of the book being a '91second book.'92 Moreover I doubt whether it is intrinsically so interesting as '91Adam.'92 Neither the story nor the characters take so profound a hold of the sympathies. Mais nous verrons. It is early days yet.
We then drove to the fortress of St. Elmo which commands the town from a great height. After waiting there an hour, till the commandant had dined, we were allowed to ascend the platform of the castle, and had a superb view of the bay, the city, and all the country round. The weather was delicious, and we gazed out upon the calm deep blue sea and at Vesuvius and the chain of mountains all round with a sort of yearning to be for ever living among them, without any of the intellectual strife and vicissitude of English life.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Lucerne, 13-16 July 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Lucerne, 13-16 July 1859
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Kitchel, pp. 190-191.
Wednesday 13th.
Up at 4. Started at 5 for Zollikofen, 211 which was reached at 10. Found the boys awaiting me, and looking in splendid condition. After a hot walk through the wood and along the dusty road a little lemonade and quiet chat in the shade with Dr. and Mrs. M'fcller and the boys was grateful enough. We then went to the Inn where I unpacked and distributed the presents I had brought. Dined at the school. Coffee and fruit in the drawingroom, followed by cigar in the shade. The boys then accompanied me to the wood and there lying on the moss I unburthened myself about Agnes to them. They were less distressed than I had anticipated and were delighted to hear about Marian. This of course furnished the main topic for the whole day. -- Came back and heard Charles play -- surprised and delighted with his progress. Took tea at the school. Cigar and chat as we watched the sunset over the Bernese Alps. Bed at 9.
Thursday.
Up at 5. Boys came to breakfast, after which we all set off to walk to Berne, by way of Reichenbach -- a delicious walk had the sun, dust, and horseflies been less obtrusive. At Berne I called on Prof. Schiff, 212 and had a long interview with him discussing points of nervous physiology, and witnessing some experiments. I then lounged through the town to the Platteforme where the boys were to be and took them to the Hotel to dine. After dinner returned to the Platteforme for coffee, cigar, and ices. Came back to Hofwyl by train at 5. Took tea with the school. Music singing and chatting. Bed at 9.
Friday 15th.
Up at 5. The boys came and in the cool of the morning we rambled about the wood and grounds. Charles played with his master Mozart's duett for piano and violin, very well. Went with the school to bathe. Dined; and got the whole school a half holiday, which made me popular. Spent the day as usual in talk, and rambling. Our talk mainly about the domestic changes, and future arrangements. In the evening music. Bed at 9.
Saturday 16th.
Up at 4. The boys accompanied me to the station and said a painful goodbye. Reached Lucerne at 10. Long chat with Polly about the boys. Rambled with her and went to see Thorwaldsen's Lion 213 -- which greatly disappointed me having very little that was truly leonine about it. After dinner Mrs. Congreve called and sat with us. We then accompanied her to her rooms, took tea there, and went out with the three to see the sunset -- a delicious walk and superb view. Back at 9 to supper.

Thursday 8th.
Read Pliny. Continued my Aristotle. Monday 10th.
Worked at Middle Ages. 228 In the evening we went to the Adelphi, having a private box sent us, to see Miss Bateman in Leah. 229 While wondering at the badness of the piece and the success it has with the playgoing public, I thought of writing one for Helen Faucit and amused myself with sketching a plot. The idea laid hold of me, and during a sleepless night, I made out the skeleton of the whole five acts. In the morning I suggested to Polly that she should do the piece. She rather liked the suggestion, and when I had written out the barest possible outline of my plot, I read it to her. She thought the subject a good one, and one that she could work out. So I wrote to Helen Faucit to arrange a meeting next Sunday that I might learn from her, before Polly begins, whether she is prepared to return to the stage if a good play were ready for her.

MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Tuesday 8 April.
Read Rohault's System of Natural Philosophy and was interested to find him anticipating the dynamic theory of heat, and in his own person colorblindness. Continued my rewriting of Aristotle.
George Smith called with a proposition to publish Polly's novel in weekly numbers at 6d with one plate. He also spoke to me about the editorship of the Cornhill Magazine which Thackeray has resigned. 48 I declined taking any responsible position, but agreed that if he would edit it responsibly, get a subeditor, and some other adviser of whom I approved, I would act as consulting editor. He is to think over the proposition.
Polly and I then went to the Society of Antiquaries to see the collection of autographs of celebrated Englishmen, with their portraits. This was very interesting -- especially some of the portraits; and Scott's M.S.S. of Peveril of the Peak and the Black Dwarf. In the evening we went over to the Marylebone Theatre to see Webster in the Dead Heart 49 -- wretched piece; but he was good.

Saturday 6th October.
On Thursday night (27th) Thornie arrived from Switzerland and stayed with us till Sunday night when I took him by mail train to Edinburgh where he is to attend the High School for ten months. At Edinburgh I stayed till Thursday morning, making all arrangements about Thornie's classes, and residence in Mr. George Robertson's family -- with the whole of which there is every reason to be satisfied, as far as one can judge beforehand. I also did a great deal of visiting, saw Goodsir who showed me over the anat[omical] museum, Simpson, Laycock, 643 Blackie, Rogers, 644 the geologist, Dr. MacVicar, 645 the Schmitzs, Lankester etc. Blackwood gave us a dinner at the Hotel at which Rev. James White, Simpson, Stephens, 646 James and Willie Blackwood were present. With Blackwood I talked over proposed books of Lives of the Elder Naturalists (to appear in Maga) and Physiology and Chemistry for Schools (abridgements of mine and Johnston's books) 647 as well as some articles for the Magazine. Yesterday I went into town and Langford gave me a letter to Laurence 648 of Old Jewry Chambers, who is to be our solicitor. With him I consulted about investments, and he took me to his stockbroker, who undertook to purchase 95 shares in the Great Indian Peninsular Railway for Polly. For 1825 £ she gets 1900 £ worth of stock guaranteed 5%. Saw Mrs. Nutt and Tr'fcbner and came home very tired to dinner. To-day wrote to Blackwood making a proposition about "The Physiology for Schools" -- and several business letters.

Sunday 5 May.
We went this morning to hear Congreve deliver the opening Lecture on [Positivism.] 611 Lord Houghton, Trevelyan, 612 Butler Johnstone, 613 Lord and Lady Amberley, 614 Mrs. P. Taylor, Beesly, Harrison, etc. there with some sixty or seventy others. Introduced Lady Amberley to Polly; she wanted us to go back and lunch with her; but this was against rules, so she is to come to us next Sunday. Chat with Forman and Miss Sella. 615 The Theodore Martins, Beesly and Rallston 616 came in the afternoon.
Monday 6th May.
Continued the writing of my Prolegomena. 617 Called on Shirley Brooks 618 -- out but found his wife in. Dined with Morley at the Garrick. Browning, Forster, FitzJames Stephen, Beesly, Meredith, Greenwood, Macmillan, 619 Trollope, and three or four others there. Browning told us that when Tennyson heard Wordsworth was about to publish the [Prelude] he said he knew one line must be in it somewhere and it was:
One Mr. Wilkinson, a clergyman. 620
Home at 12.
Tuesday 7 May.
Finished my Prolegomena! Had a long ramble in the Park. Dined at the Amberleys -- Lord and Lady Russell, 621 Lady Airlie, 622 Sir J. Bowring, W. E. Forster, Prof. Frazer, 623 Dr. Hanna, 624 Crompton, 625 and several others at dinner and in the evening. Lady Amberley more charming than ever, but her sister Lady Airlie even pleased me more -- perhaps because her talk was mainly about Polly, whom she seems thoroughly to appreciate. Lord Russell talked to me about Spain. Home at 12.

GHL Journal, London, 27 February 1862
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Kitchel, pp. 213-214.
Thursday 27 February.
Finished the rough draft of my Aristotle.
George Smith called bringing with him the whole of the proofs of Animal Studies. In the course of our chat he made a proposal to purchase Polly's new work for £10,000. This of course includes the entire copyright. It is the most magnificent offer ever yet made for a novel; and Polly, as usual was disinclined to accept it, on the ground that her work would not be worth the sum! Moreover she felt it impossible to begin publication in April or May -- the period when Smith wishes it to begin to appear in the [Cornhill Mag.] Unless she sees her book nearly completed and such as she considers worthy of publication she objects to begin printing it. I went down to Smith to tell him of her difficulties. He was much put out, April or May being the months when the Magazine will stand in need of some reinforcement as Thackeray's story is quite insufficient to keep up the sale. Smith then proposed to print her story of Brother Jacob, written in 1860, if it can be split up into three numbers, and thus tide over the three months; and then to commence in August or September with the new work. She has consented to let him see the story to see if this arrangement will do. If not some other proposal will be made by him.
Met Dickens in Regent St. He turned back to walk some way with me, and I turned back again with him. Pleasant talk. Bought Villani Historie Fiorentine for Polly. In the evening Beethoven, singing; and read my proofs. We had sent both our servants to the theatre, Amelia never having been to one, and sat up for them. Their expressions of delight on returning home were very amusing. It is a real pleasure to give pleasure to such excellent people.

Wednesday 26th. On Monday we moved out of Holly Lodge, sending the greater part of our chattels to the Pantechnicon. It was a wearisome day and we were glad to get to bed a little after 8. We lunched with the Congreves. On Tuesday our books three bookcases and such goods as were needed in the new home arrived and had to be set in order. This occupied us till past three; we then took Pug out for a smell airing in the Park and were much pleased with the prospect of walks before us. To-day after breakfast we gave the finishing touch to our arrangement of books. I wrote some letters and pottered.

GHL Journal, London, 25-30 December 1864
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Christmas Day.
Last night we had a delightful family party: Mother and Lizzie, Gertrude and the aunts, Miss Marshall and Bertie, who is home for a holiday and who delights us with his manifest improvement, and his general amiability. We acted charades and sang both before and at supper and were very merry. Today Dr. Stummer called in the morning; Bessie Parkes and Isa Craig in the afternoon. We dined alone; the boys dining out and our Christmas dinner postponed till Tuesday.
Yesterday I received a charming letter from Trollope who I feared would be very much disgusted with me for having withdrawn from the editorship of a new Fortnightly Review which he wanted me to take and which I had accepted rather imprudently, seduced by the prospect of a good income and pleasant work. But my fears lest it should be too much for my health, and disturb our domestic habits, have made me resign. 300 This is the second editorship I have declined since my return from Malvern. A third position, namely that of adviser to George Smith in the conduct of the Pall Mall Gazette, an evening paper, I have accepted, because it entails no responsibility, very little work and that purely consultative, and is paid for at the rate of £300 a year. This helps to replace, in some degree, my loss of the Cornhill.
Friday 30 December.
Wrote a review of Southwood Smith for the Saturday. 301 Went down to Smith to consult about a prospectus of the Pall Mall Gazette and other matters. Then went to dine with Danby Seymour 302 to meet Trollope, Oliphant 303 and Chapman, with whom we were to discuss the Fortnight[ly]. I have given a provisional adhesion to the proposal of my editing this, they offering me a subeditor and every facility.

Christmas Day.
Bertie came home from Scotland for a few days on the 22nd and delighted us by his great improvement moral and physical, and by the evident interest he displays in farming. Our Christmas dinner was a quiet affair, quieter than usual from the fact that both Charles and I were out of sorts. We played whist in the evening. In the morning I called on Owen Jones and Dallas, where I heard of Thackeray's sudden death. 216 In the afternoon on Mother (whom I found laid up with diarrhoea) and Nursie.
Yesterday had an interesting visit from a young poet Robert Buchanan, 217 who four years ago sent me some m.s.s. for my advice, and whom I advised to refrain from publishing for 3 years. He has waited 4, and now his volume of Undertones appears, and seems to have some success. He stayed lunch with us, and made a favorable impression. I pointed out a subject to him, and told him if he would take pains with it, I would get it inserted in the [Cornhill.] I hope I shall be able to assist him, for he has a hard struggle to live, and seems a man of high and noble aims.

Monday 20th.
Today Charles and Gertrude were married. The day was remarkably brilliant, but piercingly cold from a bitter and fierce east wind. No one was invited to the wedding except Polly and I, the Aunts, 325 Gertrude's mother and sisters; yet there were many people in the Church. We went back to Church Row and had a quiet and pleasant talk with them all. The young couple started at 'bd past 1 for Folkestone on their way to Italy. Happier prospects never smiled upon a marriage. Polly and I then called on Mother. Drove home and were quiet and cozy together all day.

GHL Journal, London, 2 October 1864
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Sunday 2nd.
Yesterday afternoon we returned from a three weeks outing which was rendered necessary by my debility and dyspepsia, and by Polly's general malaise. . . . All the time we were away did nothing but rub up my Spanish and read Don Quijote. Polly also began Spanish and as[k]ed to read pages aloud to me. I read Tennyson Idylls to her occasionally. On our way back stopped at Peterborough for night and half the day. The Cathedral not comparable to that of York, but the facade with its three arches one of the most exquisite we have seen. -- Ben in a state of irrepressible rapture on our arrival!
With this month ceases my consulting editorship of the Cornhill Magazine began May 1862 . . . the diminished and constantly diminishing circulation no longer permitting the Magazine to be at such an expence which could be spared. I regret the loss of the income very much, the more so because the duties were so light and agreeable but on the other hand it is a tie loosened. When I was very poorly, before going to Harrowgate, George Smith strongly urged me to try horse exercise. I took four lessons at a riding school and went away before they could be prolonged. The exercise seemed to stir up my liver into unpleasant activity -- but perhaps that was too brief a trial. I am doubtful about resuming it.

GHL Journal, London, 19 October 1867
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday 19 October.
On Monday at the meeting of the London Library Committee Herbert Spencer proposed that we should take a walking expedition into Surrey, and on Wednesday morning I put a night shirt, comb, and toothbrush in my pocket, and we started per rail for Weybridge. Arrived at the Inn we found friends of his -- the Cross family 675 -- just leaving it, after a fortnight's stay there, driven there by the burning down of their own house. I was introduced to them and received like an old friend -- they knowing my books well and worshipping Polly. After a chat we set off for St. George's Hill. The day superb; the tints of Autumn ravishing; the scene a constant surprise and delight. Back at 4 thoroughly but pleasantly tired. Wrote to Polly. Slept for 'bd an hour. Dined and spent the evening till 12 with the Cross family -- laughter and talk. 676
On Tuesday started per rail for Guil[d]ford, but the train carried us on to Basingstoke and we lost 3 hours thereby. Back to Guil[d]ford and walked across the Hog's Back to Farnham -- reached The Bush, good inn, very tired and very hungry. After dinner looked through the Times and went to bed at 'bd past 8. On Wednesday after breakfast we went to Waverley, and as Spencer knew some of the Nicholson family 677 we were permitted to explore the exquisite grounds; then went to the ruins of the Abbey, and ascended Crooksbury Hill -- a hill of Scotch firs -- from which charming views. Descended on to the wild heath, and thence into the Godalming Road. We paused at a little Inn to have a glass of ale and cigar and then walked on to Godalming -- reaching it at 3. The Angel. A lovely day and an exquisite walk. Dined and home by rail.

April.
My forty sixth birthday. A day which naturally sets the mind into retrospects, not always the most cheerful attitude.
Since the last entry nothing noticeable has occurred. We have been twice to Dorking and I shall take Polly there again on Monday, leaving her there during my trip to Hofwyl to see Bertie. Of work, Aristotle, and some investigation into Roman history -- especially under the Empire, have principally occupied me. I have written a paper Was Nero a Monster? 151 as a result of the latter, having been deeply impressed with the untrustworthiness of all the historians.
I have also seen Sir Chas. Nicholson 152 and had his advice about Bertie, whom we are thinking of sending to Australia as a farmer in a few years, when he has learned enough and is old enough.
I have also made it up with Susanna; or rather have had the long misunderstanding partially cleared up, and the estrangement removed. Have seen her several times, and Polly will see her on my return from Switzerland.

Saturday 17th.
This last week has been a busy one. Polly one evening read several chapters of Romola to George Smith, in order that before finally making any proposals he should know the kind of work it was to be. He dissuaded us from the notion of a serial, believing that it would not tell in small portions. He wishes to publish it in the [Cornhill Magazine,] but in considerable instalments -- of 45 or 40 pages each number, with two illustrations. He is to send a proposal on that basis. 65 Besides this I have been a good deal occupied reading proofs, and arranging matters for the Magazine. On Wednesday we went to the New Philharmonic and tonight we go to the opera to see Rigoletto, G. Smith having given us his stalls.
Another incident in the week has been a severely painful one to both of us. Anthony Trollope came to lunch, and heard with surprise that Charley was back in his old office, not having any advancement. He inquired into the cause, and wrote me a kind, candid, but painful letter 66 telling me that the boy was not doing well, was careless, slow, and inefficient. This completely upset me, and brought on a bilious attack.
On Wednesday we hired a Brougham for the day; went to the Printroom of the British Museum to see Italian portraits of 15th cent. Did shopping. Sent up for Mother, who came to lunch with us. Took her to the Zoological Gardens. Had two puppy bears taken out of the cage to play with, and suck my fingers!

"Before the appearance of the first part Mrs. Lewes said that she found that she could not properly divide the book into as many as sixteen parts. I took exception to this alteration of our arrangement, and pointed out that my offer was based on the book being in sixteen parts, and that my calculations were made with regard to the MAGAZINE being able to afford a payment of so much a number. We pointed out to her that the publication in the MAGAZINE was ephemeral, and that the work would be published in a separate form afterwards and be judged as a whole. Friday 15th.
To-day as I had to lecture this evening at the General Post Office on "Life from the Simple Cell to Man," I interrupted the writing of my article on Recent Natural History Books, 697 on which I have been recently engaged, and rewrote the notes for my Lecture. Polly and I then went to the Zoological Gardens. After dinner Charley and I started for the Post Office. In Mr. Scudamore's 698 room where we waited I was surprised and delighted to see Herbert Williams whom I have not seen for two and twenty years. We talked over the old student days when we used to sit up reading, writing, and drawing, and making our coffee at 2 in the morning. The Lecture was very well attended, and was immensely successful. The audience never manifested the slightest inattention or want of interest. Trollope, Yates, and Turner 699 complimented me afterwards, but the real compliment was in the attention of the audience. Having never handled chalk and a diagram board before I felt a little anxious as to how I should succeed; but it went quite well. Home to tea and found Polly immensely rejoiced at the success, and not a little relieved at having this one cause of anxiety the less -- dear creature!

Tuesday 13 June.
Breakfasted with Lord Houghton: present the Bishop of Minnesota -- the pleasantest American I ever met. 345 Ranke, the historian of the Popes, 346 who seemed pleased to know the author of the Life of Goethe and promised to write for our Review, Arrivabene, Clark, 347 Sir J. Sat with Polly for two hours in the garden discussing her novel and psychological problems. Called on Bell to see about a series of papers on Town Life of the Restoration. Went to Her Majesty's -- Cherubini's Medea 351 -- very fine, large, and simple. Titiens, 352 not equal to Medea but sang well.
The Fortnightly Rev. at present a great success and I rather like the work. I continue to do a good deal for the Pall Mall Gazette and earn £60 a month by it.

GHL Journal, London, 12-14 May 1865
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
May 12th.
Sat to Watkins 337 for my photograph. Dined with Spencer at the St. George's Hotel, Albemarle St. -- present Huxley, Tyndall, Hooker, 338 Masson, Bain, an American (Prof. Youmans), 339 and ourselves. Got Huxley, Tyndall and Spencer to promise contributions to the Fortnightly.
Saturday 13 May.
The First Number of the Fortnightly appeared. We went to the Royal Academy. Charles and Gertrude dined with us and the Aunts came in the evening.
Sunday 14 May.
Wrote letters. Spencer came to lunch. In the afternoon Lord Houghton, Crompton, Beesly, FitzJames Stephen, Warren, Bagehot, and Mr. and Mrs. Martin called. 340 Kept up talk and tea from three to 7! We then packed up, for our start to Eastbourne to-morrow.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, London, 10 January 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, London, 10 January 1868
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Friday 10 January.
On Wednesday night returned from a fortnight's run to Bonn and Heidelberg. 719 The visit was in many respects eminently fruitful and instructive besides being very pleasant in spite of the bitter cold. Max Schultze was kindness itself and with him I spent the greater part of the time at Bonn, discussing microscoping etc. Pfl'fcger also showed me some interesting experiments and gave me three of his works. Boll, Rindfleisch, Preyer, Veit, R'fchle, Bernays, Mrs. Klinglemann, also seen. Dined out each day, and supped out also. The Preyer family very agreeable.
At Heidelberg I saw Helmholtz, Kirchoff, Zeller, Gervinus, the three Arnolds, Wundt, Friedrich, Hoffmeister, Kopp, and several less distinguished men. The elder Arnold three days in succession went over his preparations of the Brain with me -- most instructive. Friedrich also showed me a case of Ataxy -- without the slightest loss of sensibility.
Found my [Seaside Studies] and [Physiology] universally known to the men of science and the [Goethe] still continues to be read by everyone.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, London, 1-7 June 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, London, 1-7 June 1866
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Kitchel, 238-239.
Friday 1st.
Yesterday Polly finished Felix Holt. The sense of relief was very great and all day long suffused itself over our thoughts. The continual ill health of the last months, and her dreadful nervousness and depression, made the writing a serious matter. Blackwood (who is overjoyed at her return to him and who pays £5,000 for the copyright during five years) thinks the book superior to Adam Bede. I cannot share that opinion; but the book is a noble book and will I think be more popular than the Mill. She went into town with me and did a little shopping; and in the evening Owen Jones came and smoked till 12.
To-day I worked at Roger Bacon -- for the new edition of my Hist[ory] of Phil[osophy] and went with Polly to see Mother. After lunch we had the brougham and did a deal of shopping.
Saturday. 2nd. To-day read the last proof of Felix Holt -- which has been at press during the composition of the last volume (written in 6 weeks) and latterly the printing has overtaken the writing. -- Continued Roger Bacon, and finished it. Blackwood and his Nephew called to express their great delight in the windup of Felix Holt. After lunch I went to the Zoological Gardens alone to hear the band. On the way met Bulwer who stopped the Brougham to have a long chat about the Fortnightly Review, Felix Holt, and the present state of parties.
Sunday 3rd. Read Kant. Called with Polly on Mother and Nursie. Forman, Dr. Baetche, and Deutsch 473 the afternoon visitors. After dinner Bain called and stayed till 11 discussing philosophical questions. Together we groped our way to some explanation of the organic differences between the receptive and active intellects. He began by remarking how men of active productivity were almost always men of small receptivity; and too impatient to be doing, were almost incapable of learning. I suggested that in them the reflex was more direct than in the receptive natures: an idea or emotion rapidly discharging itself in a result or action, instead of exercising a wide reflex on the sensibilities and awakening a complex ideal precursor to the act.
Monday 4th. Read Kant and Motley's United Netherlands. 474 Went to the office. Trollope, Dennis, Bain, and Mad. Bodichon to dinner. Bain startled us by his antichristian onslaught, and Trollope amused us by his defence. One bit of Bain's convulsed me with laughter. He was arguing against the principle of self sacrifice being insisted on as a point of duty, and referring to the contrast between the early Christians and Butler, 475 the former in the fervor of converts accepting the idea of sacrifice with enthusiasm, the latter never daring to hint that every sacrifice would not be [repaid.] "Such was Butler's view of what man in the 17th century required. Not that I agree with him. I think that in all centuries there have been men quite ready to abandon all idea of compensation, ready to give their sixpence with no thought of getting it back." The Scotch accent gave this an exquisitely droll effect.
Tuesday 5th. Read Kant. Took leave of mother. Blackwood and his Nephew came to lunch. Went to the opera: L'Elisir d'amore -- Patti, Mario, Romoni, Faure. 40 minutes before we could get the Brougham!
Wednesday 6th. Preparations for departure. Made all arrangements at the office. Trollope takes my place. On my way home met Dickens who walked home with me. Curious stories of dreams, etc. One night after one of his readings dreamt he was in a room where everyone was dressed in scarlet (after glow of the scarlet opera-cloaks) and a lady standing just before him he stumbled against her; apologized; she turned and said "My name is Napier"; face perfectly unknown; name unknown. Two days after he read again and before beginning Miss Boyle entered his little room accompanied by a lady in a scarlet cloak desiring to be introduced to him. "Not Miss Napier?" he said jokingly -- "Yes, it was a Miss Napier."
During the railway accident in which he had a narrow escape he saw a bride lying dead in one of the carriages; she had excited his interest on board; husband looking for her; Dickens led him to other carriage and gradually prepared him for the sight. No sooner did he see her corpse than he rushed round a field at the top of his speed, his hands above his head, and then dropped fainting. -- Another man described his sensations on finding himself in the ooze of the river: he thought the moisture was his own blood, but he crawled out and sat down to wipe his face -- the fact being that Dickens saw him get out and run up and down a plank for half an hour before sitting down to wipe his face; of this he was unconscious. 476 Albert Smith unconscious of all that had passed for 48 hours previous to his epileptic attack.
Charles and Gertrude came to say goodbye; but I was suffering from a terrible sick headache and had to go to bed after dinner.
Thursday 7. Head still very bad. Final preparation. Started at 8.30 for Dover. The train made my head worse. Lord Warden; comfortable room.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, London, 1-13 November 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, London, 1-13 November 1863
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
November the 1st.
Since last entry life has been full of worry. The Priory has been one great source: owing partly to builder, painters etc. and partly to the old woman whom we put in to take care of it. Owen Jones kindly undertook to decorate the drawing room and dining room for us, and has made a very exquisite thing of it; only in the pursuit of artistic effect, he has drawn us into serious expence, sacrificing our drawing room furniture, and causing new furniture to be bought. We move in next week.
Besides the house there has been great trouble about the boys. Bertie is in Scotland learning farming. 201 Thornie at last shipped off to Natal, well equipped with funds, outfit, and letters, to seek a career for himself there. I spent three days with Bulwer at Knebworth, discussing colonial plans, and owing to what he said gave up my idea of Vancouver's Island. -- At Knebworth there were Ernst and his wife (very charming), Louis Blanc and his brother Charles, Herbert Wilson, Robert Lytton, and Dr. and Mrs. Wagstaffe. Very agreeable visit.
The new edition of the Life of Goethe which I had reluctantly allowed Nutt to have was put to press and after about three parts of it were ready his shuffling made me take it away and place it in the hands of Smith and Elder; who have also begun to print Aristotle. -- For the new edition of the Goethe 2,000 copies at 15/- I received 250 £.
Thursday 13th November.
On Monday week began moving into the Priory. It took us the whole week to get the things in and the books on their shelves, though, even now they are not arranged, only put up, and the drawing room is still uninhabitable. Besides the trouble and vexation incident to moving we have had extra annoyances. The tuner was sick over our elegant drawing room paper, which Owen Jones had decorated, and over the carpet! This obliges us to have fresh paper made, as there are no remnants of the old, and it was originally made for us. -- Polly having imprudently left her purse in the drawer of her dressing table, one of the workmen stole it. Still, in spite of annoyances, we are highly delighted with the house now we are in it, and hope to continue so. The idea of removal is too formidable.
To-day finished correcting proofs of the Goethe. Those of Aristotle are also in progress.

Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, London, 1 March 1862
MS: Yale. Extract published: Kitchel, p. 214.
Saturday 1 March.
Began the revision and rewriting of the Life of Goethe.
George Smith called. On examining his engagements he finds it impracticable to delay the publication of Polly's new work in the Magazine till August or September. This project is therefore finally abandoned. But he is very anxious to publish her book and we discussed the plan of a sixpenny serial, also of publishing the book at once at 6/. On these points he is to make calculations and then make a new proposal.
Although I regret the loss of such an opportunity of £10,000, I am just as well pleased that Polly should not be hurried and flurried, by being bound to appear at an earlier date than she would like.
In the evening George Scharf, Burton, Spencer, Desmond, Pigott and Redford came. Kept it up till past 12 very pleasantly with talk and music.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, London, 1 January 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, London, 1 January 1864
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
January 1.
In a literary sense the past has been the least productive year I can remember, and yet, thanks to the Cornhill Magazine, mainly, my income has reached a higher point than ever it did before -- £1083. Except a few articles for the C.M. and the Saturday Review, I have done nothing but revise and correct proofs of the Life of Goethe and the Aristotle, (the proofs of the latter being nearly finished) and write rough drafts of the chapters on Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Archimedes, and Pliny for the History of Science.
In a domestic sense it has been a checquered year. Much trouble about the two boys; much bother about the new house; continued happiness with the best of women.
Yesterday I walked to Kensal Green to attend Thackeray's funeral. He was found dead in his bed the other morning -- aged only 52. There was a very large gathering -- between 1000 and 1500 people; among them most of the literary and artistic celebrities. Theodore Martin drove me home, and came in to be introduced to Polly. Owen Jones then called, and we walked with him in the Park. In the evening we played whist, which we have taken to, since Bertie has been home. This evening Bertie goes back to Scotland.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, London, [22] August 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, London, [22] August 1863
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Kitchel, pp. 220-221.
Saturday 21.
Since the last entry [18 April 1863] many things have occurred, mostly painful, which deserved a record. Polly has finished [Romola] which has been flatly received by the general public though it has excited a deep enthusiasm in almost all the 'e9lite. 185 Tennyson, Browning, Coleridge, 186 Monckton Milnes, Trollope, 187 and others speak of it with unbounded admiration. The Rev. F. D. Maurice has written to her two letters which are among the most exquisite things I ever read. His sister, Archdeacon Hare's widow has also written with great fervor, and asked Polly to go and see her.
We spent 10 delicious days of quiet at the Isle of Wight and a week at Worthing. Bertie and Thornie have come home. Thornie has failed to pass his second Indian Examination, and refused to go through the two years' ordeal again. Indeed he refused for a long while to choose any other career, having set his mind on going out to Poland to fight the Russians. The idea of his enlisting in a guerrilla band, and in such a cause was too preposterous, and afflicted us greatly. But for some time we feared that he would set us at defiance and start. Finally, he consented to join Bertie in Algiers and learn farming. He then went to Switzerland for a holiday and is there now. Meanwhile a petition is being got up to enable all the rejected candidates to have another trial for India. With what success I know not; nor am I sure Thornie will consent even to try again.
The Algerine scheme has fallen through, and I must look out for a Scotch farm for Bertie.
We have bought The Priory, at North Bank, for £2,000 for 49 years. But owing to the state of the funds we lost 90 £ on selling out. -- To-day we went over our house with Harris the builder to see about alterations. I have finished Aristotle and the new edition of the Life of Goethe.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Geneva and Paris, 26-28 June 1860
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Tuesday 26.
Charley accompanied us henceforth having bid adieu to school forever. We went to Geneva which we reached at 8 o'clock after tea, drove to the D'Alberts'. It was a great delight to me to see how truly they loved and prized Polly and we spent an exciting evening with them.
Wednesday 27.
After breakfast the D'Alberts called in a carriage and took us out for the day. After driving about we went to the Museum 566 to see the pictures, called on Calame who showed us his atelier, and there we got his two fine etchings. After lunch, M. D'Albert, Charley and I went out to see Reading-Room etc. and I broached the subject of Thornie's residence in Geneva to him, and was glad to find that it seemed practicable, and that he would undertake the charge. After dinner we had a delightful drive in the country, returning by the side of the lake.
[Thursday 28.]
Went shopping with the D'Alberts. Dined with them, and started at 2 for Paris which we reached next morning at 6.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Florence, 3-6 June 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Florence, 3-6 June 1861
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday 3 June.
At 7 this morning Trollope came, as agreed on, with the carriage and we started for Prato Vecchio which we reached at 2. On the way one of the horses fell and cut his head severely. At first we thought him dead; it was with some difficulty he was got up again. -- At Prato we ordered some coffee, and with the cold food we brought with us, had a tolerable luncheon. At 3 we started for Camaldoli. Polly mounted on a well trained poney which also carried the portmanteau. I occasionally took her place, and thus alternately walking and riding, we got to Camaldoli about 'bd 6. The views were lovely; and when after crossing a space of arid hills -- like a vast mud sea hardened into rock -- we came upon the delicious valley of Camaldoli which was seen in the tender evening light we felt it worth any amount of fatigue.
We were received by a very handsome, graceful young friar (Cistercian 778 order) who attended on us till the Padre Foresteraio came. He brought us wine and cold water, and said we should dine at sunset. As my throat was still bad and cough troublesome, they sent for their Padre Speziale, a thin, active, lively old man of nearly seventy -- quite like a comedy apothecary -- who with great volubility and benevolence first gave us a Lecture on the Cause of Cough and its Cure (sounding as if fresh from Hippocrates) and then departed to prepare me a calming potion. Which turned out very agreeable and very efficient. At supper (an excellent one) the Padre Foresteraio, a stout genial man over fifty sat by us and chatted. His delight when Trollope gave him a prime cigar was worth witnessing! T. slept in the monastery; and it was arranged that I might sleep with Polly in the cowhouse where the ladies are sent to sleep. This was about a mile higher up the hill, and we went there accompanied by a boy and his lantern. Capital beds; perfect cleanliness.
Tuesday 4th.
Up at 6. From our windows the prospect was enchanting -- made one long to live in the peaceful valley. Walked to the Foresteria and breakfasted. We there saw the Padre Superiore -- an elegant and intellectual man, also very handsome and full of the most suave courtesy. They took us with pride to see their saw mill, and we then started for the Sacro Eremo: 779 an ascent of about 1'bd hours, through delicious wood of firs, and beeches. Polly had to remain outside looking down the valley while T. and I went over the monastery, and saw the separate houses, each with its four rooms and little garden. The monks only dine together 13 times a year, and are allowed to speak 3 days in the week. We looked over their good Library. The Padre hearing that a Signora was outside, instantly got his straw hat and came out to see her and conduct her to an elevated point from which she might see the monastery. He was very gallant. He seemed perfectly healthy and very happy. He said there was "no remorse there as is in the world." We then walked (I rode) along the hilltops to the Casotto having exquisite views all the way, through woods of pine, beech, and chesnut, -- one whole mountain side covered with asphodels -- and descended once more to the Foresteria where we dined well. The Padre who followed us about like a dog again enjoyed his cigar with us, and then took T. and me over the monastery. Looked over the strangers book, Wordsworth, 780 and Sismondi, 781 among the names inscribed. The usual amount of folly and egotism from unknown noodles. At 'bd past 3 we started for Bibbiena which we reached at 7. En route Polly's horse fell on the edge of a precipice, but she was neither hurt nor shaken. I who saw her fall felt very sick and faint from the shock.
Wednesday 5 June.
Up at 'bd 6 and after breakfasted walked (as before) to La Vernia. 782 Quite different landscape. The heat was intense and the fatigue at last overpowering. While waiting to be admitted we cautiously drank and washed our mouths out at the well. At last the padre (Franciscan order) appeared. Very civil and prevenant, but the Franciscans are quite another guess kind of friars, much lower in type, taken from the poorest classes. After a good dinner we went over the monastery and saw the marvels. Then reposed awhile and chatted (N.B. all the journey we have had fine talk with Trollope, who is a most loveable creature) till we thought ourselves able to ramble among the rocks and beeches and pines of this lovely place. This fairly knocked me up. My pulses fluttered so with fatigue I could scarcely get along. After coffee Polly rode down to her sleeping place and T. and I talked enthusiastically about her over our cigars. We slept in the monastery. Beds very rough -- but weariness will snore upon a flint -- and we were weary.
Thursday 6 June.
Up at 6. Dismayed to find a pelting rain, with no prospect of cessation, and a three hours walk before us, with no '91change'92! After breakfast and adieu to the monks we descended the steeps of La Vernia, and called for Polly who was still in bed, thinking we should not start such weather. While she dressed and breakfasted we stayed warming and drying ourselves by kitchen fire. Then began our descent to Bibbiena through mud and clouds -- rain fine but steady. About halfway down the rain abated; and we reached Bibbiena without much damage. After a second breakfast we started in the carriage for Pontassieve, through rain and mist, and then through the most furious winds. Dined there and home to Florence by the evening lights. Bed at once.

Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Florence, 21-22 May 1860
MS: Yale. Extract published: Kitchel, pp. 200-201.
Monday 21st May.
This morning while reading about Savonarola it occurred to me that his life and times afford fine material for an historical romance. 540 Polly at once caught at the idea with enthusiasm. It is a subject which will fall in with much of her studies and sympathies; and it will give fresh interest to our stay in Florence. . . .
Tuesday 22nd May.
Went to Baptistry, sat there some time in the cool. Then went to the Accademia della Bella Arte -- the collection of early Tuscan painters of extreme interest. . . . These were all we had time to study, except a very striking portrait of Savonarola by Fra Bartolommeo. From this we went to St. Marco, and Polly remained in a room where the great Fra Angelico -- Crucifixion -- may be seen by ladies while I went over the monastery and took notes for her. In the cells I saw several frescos by Angelico, among them a bambino of ideal beauty, and in another a Virgin (in the Coronation of the Virgin) more graceful in attitude and in the flow of drapery than anything I remember. In the chapel beside Savonarola's rooms there is a much defaced Mother and Child by Bartolommeo, the child more lifelike and noble than any but Raphael's Sistine children. The Crucifixion is the largest and finest of Angelico's works. We then spent some time in old booksellers shops, and bought Savonarola's poems. Lunched and went to the Post -- letters from Thornie and Mrs. Congreve. Went to the
Uffizi to see pictures and statues again. Bought Perrens's Vie de Savonarola. 541 After dinner drove to a print shop and bought engravings of Fra Angelico; then drove for two hours and a half amid the lanes and orchards of this charming place. Read Kugler, 542 went to caf'e9 for ices, and returned to read.

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Florence, 20-26 March 1869
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday 20
March. Rain again and torrents! After seeming to hold out no hope of a clearance, it became sufficiently trifling for us to go out and have a look at the Cathedral, Baptistry and Tower, which seemed even more lovely than memory had pictured. This hour of mitigated weather was the only one during the day; all the way to Florence the rain and wind were violent and incessant. Tom Trollope was at the station waiting for us. His villa a nobleman's mansion both in grandeur and costliness.
We stayed from Saturday till Thursday evening with the Trollopes, having enjoyed but little of the old sights, because Polly's sore throat and headache kept her almost a prisoner. Nothing could be kinder than our hosts. I went with them to a party at Miss Blagden's [22 March] -- and Polly was strong enough to accompany us to a s'e9ance at the Laboratory when Schiff 39 exhibited the instrument for measuring the rapidity of thought [23 March]. Mrs. Schiff agreeable. Left by train on Thursday at 'bd 9 and reached Naples on Friday at 7 p.m. Hotel de Geneve. Tea and bed.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Biarritz, 21-23 January 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Biarritz, 21-23 January 1867
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday 21st.
Started at 9 for Pau; agreeable English family (MacKinnan) in the train. Reached Pau at 2. Hotel de France -- only a room au troisi'e8me to be had. Went to the coiffeur and had hair cut -- badly -- then called on Mrs. Lehmann 572 -- out. Rambled along the Park and Terrace with beautiful view of the Pyrenees not unlike the view from Berne platform. Fierce storm came on. While waiting under an arcade for shelter amused by watching the market people -- the pigs and cattle.
Bought La Estrella by Fernan Caballero and a pocket French and Spanish Dict. Dined at the table d'h'f4te, and went to Mrs. Lehmann to tea. Chat and music till 10.
Tuesday 22 January.
After a light breakfast had a delicious walk along the Park and sat under the castle to bask in the sun -- weather superb. At 12 went to Mrs. Lehmann to lunch, and left Polly with her while I went to call on Savage 573 and his wife: found him very poorly, hating every place he went to with the true invalid's impatience. He was very grateful to me for the visit. After chatting an hour with him returned and walked with Polly and Mrs. L. in her delightful garden with the grand panorama of the mountains. Then we left her and went through the town, on to the place where the soldiers were exercising and the band was playing. Dined with Mrs. L. cozily.
Wednesday 23 January.
Went over to Mrs. L. to say goodbye. Walked with her in the garden and she finally walked with us to the station. Bayonne at 3 -- Biarritz at 4. Went out to see sunset. Polly felt headache coming on, went to bed early.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Biarritz, 10-11 January 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Biarritz, 10-11 January 1867
MS: Yale. Extract published: Kitchel, p. 243.
Thursday 10th.
Polly had her warm bath, and on the sands afterwards she opened to me her secret desire of going from Barcelona to Granada. The idea quite fired me and it was almost resolved on. To prepare ourselves bought a Spanish conversation book and grammar; and taking the former in my pocket, as we walked I asked her words and phrases over and over again to impress them on our minds. This gave a new and amusing variety to our walks besides being a most efficient mode of learning to speak. Came back to lunch and found a letter from Charles and Gertrude; the latter telling of Susanna being £55.10 in debt and urging me to release her from it at once. -- Continued our Spanish exercise. No sunset to-day, the sky overcast.
Friday 11th January.
Read Comte. Wrote to Charles and to Susanna sending her the checque. Spanish exercise. The weather boisterous and rainy. It cleared towards sunset, but there was no flame in the western sky.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, Antwerp, 10 June 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, Antwerp, 10 June 1866
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Sunday 10th.
Up at 8. After breakfast changed our room to a large and cool salon, donnant sur la rue. In our ramble last night we saw an affiche announcing that the Mystery of the Birth and Death of our Saviour was to be performed by the Oberammergau people. As we have long wished for such a chance, our first visit this morning was to the bureau to secure stalls. The man kindly took us into the theatre and there we chose our seats. High Mass at Cathedral. Effect of the music dreamy and delightful. Rubens's Descent was uncovered during service. Called at Post Office and found three [Pall Mall Gazettes] awaiting me. Home and read them. -- Went to the Museum. Rubens glorious: especially the Crucifixion and Adoration. Vandyke feeble and false in his religious pictures and wonderful in his portraits -- they are as individual and forcible, as his historical heads are general and feeble. Same remark applies to De Vos whose portrait of the Custode of the Royal Academy is singularly effective. Van Eyck's Adoration of the Lamb now reunited and restored -- or else there is a copy of the scattered parts presented to the Academy. Smoked a cigarette in the garden of the Museum, under the branching shade and walked leisurely home, to read Kugler, and potter till dinner. Dined alone once more. Coffee and cigar in our room.
At 8 went to theatre. The performance surpassed our expectations. It was all pantomime, but that of the Christ both expressive and noble. A handsome tall man with fine sensitive nostril straight brow, black hair, and good figure. Action fluent and unconventional or at any rate unstagey. Nothing uneasy or seeking for effect. Nor did he once drop the mask. The others were all as bad as bad actors can be. The dresses those of a small provincial theatre. The stage was arranged with black baize on wings and centre forming a dark background for the pictures, a tree or seat occasionally occupying the foreground. The Adoration of the Shepherds with a doll lamb that baa'd when its head was moved was followed by the Flight into Egypt: a pretty picture of Virgin on a pasteboard donkey, and well taught infant who kissed her and comforted her: Joseph handsome. The entry into Jerusalem showed Jesus on the pasteboard donkey addressing the palmbearers. The adieu to friends and mother at Bethanie a good piece of acting -- really touching. Same with the weeping over Jerusalem and Judas conceiving the idea of betrayal. The Supper was a poor representation of Da Vinci. The agony in the garden good acting -- Before the high priest more of dramatic effort but as Christ has little to do the effect feeble; a murmur of horror ran through the audience at seeing Christ smitten by the soldier. Judas conventional in his remorse. Peter denying Christ well managed. The flagellation very effective. Pilate asking for his release and the people demanding that of Barrabas bad -- especially the Barrabas who tried to give a comic turn to his release. The bearing the cross and meeting with Veronica very powerful; so also the nailing on the cross which had a horrible reality about it. The death on the cross not so good. The Descent imitated (badly) from Rubens. The entombment and Resurrection old pictures.
The performance lasted till 'bd past 10. An organ accompanied the scenes and greatly aided the effect. The audience hushed and intent during each scene, but the effect purely momentary, for they were gabbling, laughing, and jesting noisily directly each scene was over.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, ,4-9 April 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, ,4-9 April 1864
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday 4th.
This morning delighted with the arrival of a long letter from Thornie, written in the highest spirits, and showing a manly determination to work out some career for himself, after a thorough survey of the conditions. We then ordered the brougham and drove to Leighton's to see his pictures before they are sent to the Exhibition. Much interested by his sketches especially of babies. Shopped. Called on Fred Chapman 251 and saw Browning there.
During the last week we were in Scotland; starting on Sunday night and arriving in Glasgow on Monday morning in time for breakfast. Glasgow hideous and noisy; but we enjoyed the Cathedral and its crypts; and also Helen Faucit's acting in Cymbeline, Much Ado, and Romeo and Juliet. We were in the same hotel as the Martins and saw a great deal of them, liking them more the more we saw. But the smell of paint in the hotel, the east wind, and the noises together kept me in a perpetual state of headache and sickness.
On Friday we left Glasgow for Symington, and were disappointed at not finding Bertie at the station. Took the train to Thankerton, and were walking towards Hillhead when Bertie overtook us in the poneychaise. Much pleased with the farm and with Mr. Stodart. Went all over it; saw Bertie weave at the loom of one of the cottagers; dined at the farm; and were driven by Bertie over the hills through a blinding snowstorm to the station. Reached Carlisle at 'bd past 7. Slept there, and returned home on Saturday.
Saturday 9 April.
Worked at Middle Ages. After lunch we had the Brougham and calling for Owen Jones drove to the South Kensington Museum to see the collection of Mulready's 252 pictures and sketches. Very interesting to observe the progress of one mind through many changes of taste and fashion. His studies up to the very last were those of an ambitious and aspiring student. Looked at the Indian Courts Owen has decorated, and at some of the ancient specimens of ornamentation. Then drove in Hyde Park and home to dinner, Owen with us, who also accompanied us to Covent Garden to see La Favorita and the new prima donna Lagrua, 253 a fine actress but not a great singer. Mario acted finely and sang -- without voice. The opera heavy.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, ,26 March 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, ,26 March 1857
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Thursday 26th.
At six this morning the man came to call us to say the packet was out of harbour and awaiting us. Hurriedly dressing and without time for breakfast away we went. Glorious morning. The sun red in the east; the sea calm. On getting on board the Yacht Ariadne, which is the packet boat, we found no tea or anything possible for breakfast, so we munched our biscuits and made the best of it. Presently the rain came on, and we descended to our cabin and got into our berths. Only ourselves as passengers. The swell and roll of the Atlantic soon produced a terrible commotion, and we lay sick, at times semidelirious, icy cold, and with pain in the intestines of a very unpleasant kind. Nevertheless between intervals -- when lucid -- I mentally wrote passages in my contemplated article for Blackwood, and reproached myself for the cowardly twinges of remorse extorted by suffering. At length about 1 o'clock we got into the Sound. The sun was shining brightly and the aspect of the Scilly Isles surpassed all my expectations. We got on shore and took lodgings at the post office -- 14/- a week with 1/6 for fire. Rooms large but low, and comfortably clean. After tea and toast which greatly restored us, we went out and rambled over the Fortification Hill. The weather was beautiful and the prospect full of promise. The place seemed to be the very place we wanted. Unpacked our boxes and arranged books. Then took another ramble. Went early to bed.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, ,15-18 March 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, ,15-18 March 1857
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Sunday 15th.
Started at 9 in the evening from Richmond on our zoological expedition. Slept at the Great Western Hotel, where we were very comfortable and the next morning started at 10 for Plymouth by Express. Arrived at 'bd past 5. The Globe Hotel. -- Went out for a ramble while a chop tea was being prepared. Got to the Hoe and had a view of the sea and Mount Edgecombe. After tea Marian read Cranford aloud.
Tuesday 17th.
After breakfast rambled about the town and bought a basket. At 'bd past 10 started outside the coach for Truro. A Scotch sailor and a stout benevolent traveller interested us much; also a vulgar pretentious surgeon who laid down the law on physiology in an amusing manner, I drawing him out by feigned ignorance; also a young girl, a peasant, with unabashed hearty manners and pretty Devonshire face. The drive to Bodmin very pretty. Between Bodmin and St. Austel the drive was wild and drear, but interesting from its mining traces and the porcelain clay works. One of the passengers explained the method of extracting and preparing the clay, and from our seats we could follow all the principal episodes. Reached Truro at 6 and at 'bd past per Rail to Penzance reaching it at 8. The Union Hotel. After a chop tea we retired much fatigued to bed.
Wednesday 18th.
When the Boots called us this morning and announced that it was raining hard, and the wind was due west, we resolved not to cross, but to wait a few days at Penzance. After breakfast the rain still pouring Marian read Cranford aloud. We then went in search of lodgings, and by a strange infatuation fixed upon No. 1 Marine Parade, and repented thereof when too late. Nautical lodgings with cases of stuffed birds, a [sailor's departure] and a [sailor's return] ornamenting one side of the wall; a portrait of the late husband, proprietor of the Brig Triton (which was correctly misrepresented entering the harbour of Marseilles) graced the other side: a genuine lodging house portrait by a Bad Master, representing a blackhaired mariner on a mahogany background, with general uniformity of complexion and no expression. Silhouettes in black of son and daughter. Everything rickety in the house. Bedpole fell as I drew aside the curtain. Teapot with wobbley top; fender without rests; chairs with yielding backs etc. We resolved to stay no longer than was absolutely necessary. As it continued raining all day we stayed in. I wrote some letters and read Draper's Physiology. In the evening Marian continued Cranford.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Journal, ,[11]-18 May 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Journal, ,[11]-18 May 1857
MS: Yale. Brief extracts published: Kitchel, p. 174.
Monday 18th.
This day week we quitted Scilly. There was a dead calm which prevented our starting at the appointed time, so that we had to hang about without books or occupation, walking on the Hill, and reading newspapers till 1. At two we started, and after a very calm passage reached Penzance at 'bd past 10. Not sick, nor even nauseous. We went to Dingley's Private Hotel -- very comfortable. Next morning after breakfast I called on R. Q. Couch, 856 the Naturalist, who showed me his drawings and collections, and gave me several of his papers. He interested me by his talk. M. and I then went for a walk through fields and lanes, relishing the greenery and trees, after Scilly. In the evening Couch called and sat three hours chatting very pleasantly.
On Wednesday morning at 7 we started by Omnibus, outside, for Falmouth which we reached at 'bd past 10. After a wash, and a lunch we walked to the castle; basked on the rocks; came slowly back, buying Miss Austen's [Emma] and [Sense and Sensibility.] I called on Cocks, 857 the naturalist, a character and a guy. He is old now, not unlike Jervis, 858 wearing a black skull cap, green spectacles, and wool over his teeth. He twaddled furiously, and said nothing sensible or interesting. Came home and amused Marian by imitations of him.
On Thursday morning at 8 we left per Steamer for Plymouth: horrible fog all the way, in consequence of which we nearly ran down two boats, and very nearly ran ashore. Reached at 'bd past 1. Went on shore and dined. Started again at 6 for Jersey which we reached on Friday morning at 10. Very calm passage.
Friday 15th.
The first aspect of St. Helier's was quite novel to me. I had not seen it since 1829, 859 and the place was of course much changed; except the Fort and Elizabeth castle nothing wore a familiar aspect till I got to the Royal Square, and then the old boyish feelings came back. The Square seemed so much smaller! Broad St., the theatre, the market, and a few other places were revived; but for the rest the place seemed as much changed as I. Why should I have expected to find it otherwise? 860 We went to the Union Hotel in the Square. After lunch we set out to buy boots, get hair cut, get letters, and look for lodgings. We walked all the way to St. Aubin's without finding anything quite suitable, as to money and zoological requirements. Came back in the 'Bus.
Saturday 16th.
After breakfast took the Omnibus to Gorey. The ride very pretty. The contrast between Scilly and the smiling richness of the fields and orchards here very refreshing. Took lodgings at Rosa Cottage, 13/ a week for three rooms and attendance. Went back to St. Helier's bought wine, brandy, groceries, paper, map etc. hired an easy chair, and a bath; dined at the Hotel and had a fly to carry us here, where we unpacked our things and went tired to bed.
Sunday 17th.
Walk on the sands after breakfast. Wrote letters. Delicious walk; sat on Castle hill and M. read Emma aloud. In the evening a long walk on the sands to St. Clements. Spoke with a fisherman and engaged him to bring me refuse from the trawl. 861
Monday 18th.
Walk on the sands. Revised my Sea-Side Studies No. II and journalized. After lunch, an exquisite walk in the vale of Queen's farm. At all times such a place would be charming but after Scilly, its rich uplands and clustering trees were inexpressibly delightful. There was a pool overhung by oaks and ash trees, -- on the opposite side with a meadow of buttercups, a white winding path on our side, and on the surface a mass of white flowers looking like snow, and in the depths a small forest of shrubs -- the pool brought back boyish days with a sweet reminiscence. -- In the evening Marian read Emma aloud.

Friday 22 June 1877
Since the last entry 714 life has moved on its regular routine, the weather transcendent, the work successful. Dublin Core:Title: GHL Diary, Witley, 20-23 August 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Diary, Witley, 20-23 August 1878
MS: Mrs. Robert Nuttall. Hitherto unpublished.
Tuesday 20 August 1878
Sch'fcle. Vol. IV. Lawn Tennis. Mrs. Congreve to lunch. Walk with Polly when she left. Archiv f'fcr Psychiatrie. Gibbon. 124 Jacquemont. 125
Wednesday 21 August 1878
Sch'fcle. Vol. IV. Godalming. Archiv. At 6 Tom Trollope and his wife came on a visit. Pleasant reminiscences and talk.
Thursday 22 August 1878
After a chatty breakfast we all took a walk to Hambledon Church and home by the wood. Then Mrs. Rudd showed us over the school. 126 After lunch we went to Tennyson who took us to the spring and then read two of his new poems; most interesting visit. The Du Mauriers to dinner. Singing.
A cardinal going to the window one fine July morning exclaims: Non dies per vantarmi, ma oggie bellissima giornata!
Mrs. Thistlethwaite at a country house with Gladstone. As the party returned from Church she suddenly asked "Where's Gladstone?" "Stayed for Communion." "Has he? D--n it, then I'll take it too!"
A child delighting in some delicious pears exclaimed, "I could eat a million of them!" "Non, il n'y a que Dieu qui pourrait en manger un million!"
Du Maurier when he lost sight of one eye consulted a Belgian oculist -- a cold, hard, catholic, who although knowing he was a poor student, took the largest fee each time, and after some weeks examined the other eye, and said, patting an Italian greyhound as he spoke: "You seem a courageous young man, and I may tell you that one day when I told a young man what I am going to tell you, he blew his brains out at my door. Your other eye is going, and I advise you to seek some employment in which eyesight will not be much needed." He then made evident signs that the interview was ended, took his fee, and pulled off his skull cap to bow him out. 127
Friday 23 August 1878
Chat at breakfast and walk on Sand Hill. The Trollopes left at 11. Walk. Drove to Guildford -- splendid afternoon. I read Morrison's Gibbon aloud. Archiv f'fcr Psychiatrie.

Monday 12 August 1878
Both had bad headaches this morning. Read Sch'fcle. 119 At 'bd past 10 started in a fierce storm for Tennyson's, leaving Polly at home as too unwell. Mrs. Greville and myself were the only visitors, and after lunch I read his not yet finished drama of A Becket on which he was anxious to have my critical opinion. 120 Greatly interested by many scenes of it, though I had some serious doubts which I did not express, and some doubts which I did. These he asked me to write down and send him that he might not forget them. Mrs. Greville drove me home; found Polly in bed with sick headache. Sat with her all the evening.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL Diary, Six Mile Bottom, 4-7 October 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Diary, Six Mile Bottom, 4-7 October 1876
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Wednesday 4 October 1876
We went on a visit to the Halls at Six Mile Bottom. M. Scherer 535 was the only visitor today. He took a long walk with us -- superb sunset.
Thursday 5 October 1876
Today our party was encreased by the Sidgwicks, a German, and Dr. Paget 536 (the latter only to dinner). After lunch we drove to New-market to visit the stables of a trainer. Saw Kisber, the winner of the Derby and Grand Prix -- a beautiful creature. Other horses -- dogs -- and the trainer himself a refined Bambridge 537 who said the Baroness Rothschild, 538 whose picture he showed us, was a beautiful skinned lady! He treated Polly with great deference, always styling her My Lady and much struck by her having pointed out a defect in the build of Kisber. 539
Friday 6 October 1876
Today Mrs. Higford Burr 540 joined the party and at dinner Dr. and Mrs. Humphry. 541 Very pleasant. I played Lawn Tennis with the Sidgwicks after lunch and read Heyse, Die Kinder der Welt. Dr. Paget told us of an auctioneer who was kicked down stairs and at the bottom shook his fist exclaiming "Another kick, sir, and you'll rouse the lion in me." One day at Church he [knocked down] the preacher "tub and all" for 5/6.

Came home at 4 to find several letters and parcels. . . .

Dublin Core:Description:
GHL Diary, Six Mile Bottom, 25-27 October 1877
MS: Mrs. Ouvry. Hitherto unpublished.
Thursday 25 October 1877
Horrible weather all day. Reached Six Mile Bottom at 5. Party to dinner -- music in the evening.
The difference between Universalists and Unitarians. The one think God too good to d--n people, the other think themselves too good to be d----d.
Three men on a raft being swept down Niagara. "Can no one sing a hymn?" "No." "Nor a prayer?" "No." "We must do something religious -- let's make a collection."
An old man left his property to his nephew but with a life rent of it to an old woman of 80, bedridden. When the will was read the Nephew rose and said "I take ye all to witness that I'll bide the Lord's time."
A Frenchman entered the hotel salon at Chamouny declaring he had just made an expedition up Mont Blanc. "Vous avez fait l'ascension?" "Je crois bien!" "Jusqu'au sommet?" "Pas pr'e9cis'e9ment jusqu'au sommet -- mais jusqu'au Montanvert."
A very merry party on board a Cunard Steamer. Plenty of stories told; one man never smiled nor made a remark. The capt. asked him why this was. "Why you see, sir, I'm a liar myself."
Friday 26 October 1877
Sedley Taylor 751 came to Halls, and played and read at the Penny Reading which Hall got up for the farm servants etc. I recited [Chesnut Horse], [Garrick and the Cock] and the Frenchman at the station. Lawn Tennis. Read Deronda.
Saturday 27 October 1877
Johnnie, Sedley Taylor, Prof. Stewart 752 etc. guests. great fun and interesting talks. Lawn Tennis. Deronda.

Left at 10 for Shrewsbury and found I had left my Guide Book behind, so as soon as dinner was ordered at the Raven went to Telegraph for it. GHL Diary, Oxford and London, 8-10 June 1878
MS: Mrs. Robert Nuttall. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday 8 June 1878
De Quincey. Vol IV. Went on our annual visit to Jowett: but the Holiday 79 made such a tremendous congestion at the Railway that we were two hours late and lost our portmanteau -- or rather on our arrival it did not arrive. With vague promises of its being sent on by next train we were forced to be content. It did not arrive till Sunday about 5.
Lord and Lady Abercrombie, Sir James Lacaita, 80 Wm. Sellar and his eldest daughter staying in the house. At Dinner the Bishop of
Limerick, Wallace the Hegelian 81 and several others. I took down Mrs. Wallace.
Sunday 9 June 1878
An exciting day. At breakfast beside the guests a Mr. Nash 82 -- lawyer at Manchester -- and an undergraduate. Then I called on Pattison and smoked a cigar with him and her till 1. After lunch Polly accompanied me to the Pattisons -- the Huttons and Appleton there. Talked with Mrs. H. Evening service at Magdalen. The Master walked with us. Large dinner party and people in the evening.
A farmer showing his fattened pig to the parson and thinking it right to say something pious exclaimed. Ah! sir, if we were only as well prepared to die!
The Master of Trinity 83 when his conduct was obliquely criticised by one of the junior men replied "We must never forget that none of us are infallible -- not even the youngest."
A man fussy at a funeral was asked [Who are you?] "I am brother of the corpse."
Lord Leitrim, 84 who was shot recently by a tenant, one day talking about the shooting of landlords to one of his tenants said "Well, why don't they shoot me?" "Bedad, sir, its because what's everyman's business is no man's."
The Bishop of Limerick told of an Irish priest having dragged a drunken man off the rails on which he had lain to sleep just before a train passed. The priest tried to impress on him the providential nature of his escape and when the man looked at him with a drunken stolid stare, said Can't ye say a prayer, can't ye express thankfulness? The man roused himself and thundered forth "To hell with the Pope."
Neville 85 the actor told Jerrold's repartee of rowing in the same boat but not with the same skulls -- as "not with the same oars." On being laughed at for his mistake he said "Well, a boat is rowed with oars, who ever heard of its being rowed with skulls?"
Monday 10 June 1878
The Empress of the French 86 was coming to lunch and the Master wanted us to stay, but we declined, and came home by 2 o'clock. Shortly afterwards the Blackwoods called. Dined at Sir H. Thompson's. 87 I took Mrs. Arthur Lewis 88 down. Henschel played and sang till 11.30.

MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday 1 May 1875
Wundt. 238 Finished revision of Problem I. Went to Oxford on a visit to Jowett. Bowen and Lord and Lady Lansdowne the other guests, but at dinner and evening, each day there were several interesting people. 239
Lord Ramsay, Sir H. Maine, Henry Smith, Cannon Liddon, Lady Claud Hamilton and her daughter, Mr. Abbott (paraplegic), Mr. Esquith, Mr. Tatton, Mr. Symonds, Mr. Gore, Two Japanese, Mrs. Pallavicini, Mr. Roper, and others. Very pleasant talk and some good stories. . . .
Sunday 2 May 1875
Called on Henry Smith, Rolleston and the Pattisons -- at the latter house saw Nettleship, Neubauer, Jefferson, Mills, Thursfield, etc. Went over the Museum with Rolleston rapidly.
Monday 3 May 1875
But this morning at 4 Polly awoke me with the painful news of a fresh attack of her stone. The pain lasted till 6.30 Then she got better and we came home.
Tuesday 4 May 1875
Polly became very unwell at night though without return of the pain. She stayed in bed all day. I sat with her and wrote letters. London Library and called on the Calls whom I drove in the Park. Then sat the rest of the day with Polly.
Wednesday 5 May 1875
Polly better this morning but not well enough to get up. Read Wundt, Menschen und Thierseele. Problems. Walk in Park. Dr. Clark came to see Polly at 3. Went to Chemist's and drove in Hyde Park. Found Polly up on my return. Read Scott's Poems to her. D'fcntzer Charlotte von Stein. 240

GHL Diary, London, 8-13 May 1869
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday 8 May 1869
Mill's Analysis. 64 Went to Mother. Thornie came home. Dreadfully shocked to see him so worn; but his spirits good and he listened with pleasure to the music.
Sunday 9 May 1869
A dreadful day -- Thornie rolling on the floor in agony. 65 Paget 66 came in the evening and examined him. Up 4 times in the night to give him morphia etc.
Monday 10 May 1869
Went into town, and got a prone couch for Thornie. All day nursing him. He quiet, but suffering from the morphia given yesterday. Mr. Roberts 67 (surgeon) called to see him.
Tuesday 11 May 1869
Thornie passed a quiet night without pain. Went to Mother, and into town to get a new pillow for Thornie. Nursed him all day. In the evening he got excited talking about his African experiences and singing Zulu songs. Made anxious about him. Mr. Roberts called.
Wednesday 12 May 1869
Thornie had another quiet night. Read Mill -- looked over some parts of [Problems.] Went into town and spent the rest of the day with Thornie.
Thursday 13 May 1869
Another quiet night -- there is a [break in the clouds.] Read Mill and went to see Susannah; found her out. Barbara and Owen Jones called. Fields, American publisher, called and made proposition about uniform edition of George Eliot -- also offered 300 £ for a poem (Agatha) to appear in Atlantic.

Friday 20 April 1877
Cabanis. 643 Notes. Morning concert at F. Lehmann's: Paul Viardot, Hausmann and Henschel played a trio of Schumann. Fra'fclein L'f6we sang and Henschel sang superbly. Sat next to Mrs. Goschen and her daughter and had pleasant chat. Saturday 21 April 1877
Headache from the dinner! Polly's cold very bad. Unable to do anything. Charles called to ask if he might come here for a week while his house was being set in order.
Sunday 22 April 1877
Headache contd. Polly worse -- sick and headachy. She did not come down. Cabanis.
Johnnie and Eleanor, Charles, Barbara, Miss Greatorex, 648 Miss Rintoul, Alice Helps, Leslie Stephen, Du Maurier, Knowles, Mrs. Orr. Balzac [Correspondence.] 649
Monday 23 April 1877
