Tuesday 24 April 1877
Cabanis. Polly up to breakfast. Notes. Johnnie called to say Mrs. Stewart 653 would buy the Heights if we were disposed to sell. Balzac [Correspondence.] Lubbock Origin of Civilization. Charles came.

Charles, who is staying with us for a week, breakfasted with me. Cabanis. Notes. Park. Went to the Conversatione at the Royal Society. Talked with Darwin, Tyndall, Harrison, Burden-Sanderson. Home by 11.

Kussmaul. Vol IV. We went to the Telephone office to have the Telephone explained and demonstrated. Chat with Kate Field and Col. Reynolds. 33 Park. Simon on [Cancer.] 34 Lecky. [Cosmos.]

Tuesday 15 May 1877
Caird. 672 Wagner Rehearsal. Talked with Mad. Wagner, Frau Materna, and Norman Grosvenor, who walked through the Garden with us. After lunch called on Chapman and George Smith. Revue Positive. Brehm, [Thierleben.] 673

GHL Diary, London, 13-17 September 1872
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Friday, 13 September 1872
This afternoon we started for Six Mile Bottom, the estate which Hall has recently inherited. Polly very unwell, was quite knocked up by the time we arrived. Found there Mrs. [Cross], Emily, Florence and Johnnie Cross, Albert Druce, and Mr. Patterson.
Saturday, 14 September 1872
Went over the estate, and visited farms, etc. In the afternoon drove out. Saw the pheasants fed. Ferocious bull-mastiff belonging to the Keeper! A Mr. and Mrs. Lethbridge came to dinner.
Sunday, 15 September 1872
Today besides various rambles and a drive we paid a visit to a wealthy farmer -- Nash -- a sort of Martin Poyser -- with a hearty wife and a lovely daughter of the Dudu 595 type. His house and gardens were perfect. Taken over the place and shown the dogs, fowls, horses, barns, etc. Then came in and had tea; and drove home in the setting sunlight. Augustine G[o]ulden. 596 Music and chat after dinner. Mrs. Cross accompanying Polly into her bedroom caught fire with her widow's streamers at the candle. Fortunately it was soon put out, and no great damage done, but Polly had a slight hysterical fit from the shock.
Monday, 16 September 1872
Polly awoke with dreadful headache and sickness. This delayed our departure till the midday train. Reached home at 5; she very unwell. Went early to bed.
Tuesday, 17 September 1872
Polly somewhat better. Corrected proofs of [Middlemarch] and wrote to Mr. Cyples 597 who has dedicated a work to me which he sent. Slept at Dover.

Wednesday 10 April 1878
Tito Vignoli. 40 Vol IV. Revue scientifique. Johnnie Cross gave dinner at the Devonshire club: -- Sidgwick, Hall, Bridges, Walter Morrison, 41 Alex Sellar, 42 and Henry James. 43 Capital talk and stories. Walked home at 12 in a downpour.
Mat Arnold when at College bathed in a river in front of a village. The clergyman came to remonstrate. Mat quite naked waved the towel gracefully and with quiet seriousness said, Is it possible that you see anything indelicate in the human form divine?
Lord Ernest Bruce at a ball at the Tuileries was made uneasy by the attentions of the Emperor to his wife. Saw them disappear from the ball room. Followed and was pulled up by a sentinel. On ne passe pas monsieur. Mais permettez, permettez. On ne passe pas. Cette dame, je suis le mari. Raison de plus!
Thursday 11 April 1878
Tito Vignoli, Saggio di psichologia. Vol IV. Went to Hampstead to see Margaret's Pictures. 44 Revue Scientifique. Macaulay on Frederick the Great. 45
Friday 12 April 1878
Tito Vignoli. Vol IV. Music party at the Grosvenor Gallery: Joachim, Piatti, Strauss, Hall'e9 and Mad. Joachim. Large group of acquaintances. Dined at Tennysons: Lord Acton and Annie Thackeray and husband. In the evening large party: the Monteagles, 46 Garnett Wolseleys, Cowper

Saturday 13 April 1878
Spencer. Vol IV. Concert: Schumann's quintett, Chopin Serenade for violin cello and piano. Beethoven's Kreutzer. Joachim, Piatti, Strauss, Krebs and Frl. Janotha 47 (first appearance). Mad. Joachim sang.

Both had headache. Tr'fcbner.
Lord Acton, Sir Garnett and Lady Wolseley, Mrs. Priestley, Kate Field, Moritz, Mr. and Mrs. Gurney, Smith, Thompson, Mr. and Mrs. Liebreich, Mr. and Mrs. Cox, Frl. Redeker, Dr. Simon, Mrs. Lankester, Ray Lankester, Shadworth Hodgson, 48 Croom Robertson, Henrietta Rintoul, Alice Helps, Mrs. and Miss Busk, Mad. Moscheles, 49 Mrs. Felix Moscheles, Kegan Paul -- 27 People. Redeker and Liebreich sang.
A Frenchman looking at a half-naked 'e9plor'e9e Mary Magdalene exclaimed "Oh! si c'est l'e0 l'amour divin, je le connais!"
Monday 15 April 1878
Spencer. Vol IV. Park. Looked through Le Diable 'e0 Paris. 50 Cerebrale Zust'e4nde. Polly not well enough to read aloud.
Tuesday 16 April 1878
Spencer. Mrs. Congreve to lunch. We went to a music party at Leighton's: Joachim, Piatti, Hall'e9, and Janotha. Mad. Joachim sang. Talked to the Chief Justice, 51 the Percy Wyndhams, Mignon, 52 A'efd'e9, 53 Millais, Mrs. Ponsonby etc. Home at 6.30. Polly read her m.s. Gavarni Les Fourberies de Femmes. 54
Wednesday 17 April 1878
"Brain." Vol IV. Went to see the Turner Drawings some very fine; most of them uninteresting; more like confectionary than Nature. Park.
Fierce hail storm -- thunder and lightning. Kosmos. Green's History of England. Claude Bernard La Science Exp'e9rimentale. 55
Thursday 18 April 1878
Birthday spent very quietly. Walk in Park and drive to Willesden. Read Kosmos and the Village on the Cliff. Polly read Green's Hist. of England aloud.
Friday 19 April 1878
Headache prevented all work. After lunch we went to see the Calls, on the way picked up Browning and drove him in the park. Heavenly day, mild as June. Sigismund [Kind und Welt.] 56 Annie Thackeray [The Village on the Cliff.] 57 Green Hist. of England.
Saturday 20 April 1878
Horwicz Analysen. Vol IV. Tremendous rain. Cleared about 3 when we drove in Park and walked in Kensington Gardens. The Village on the Cliff. Green Hist. of England.
Letter from Lytton. At the ceremony of his unveiling the statue of Lord Canning at Calcutta after his speech an old judge approached him with tears in eye and voice and said "Poor Lord Canning, if he could but have lived to see this day." 58
Sunday 21 April 1878
Horwicz. Polly had walk with me.
Miss Scott (of Girton), Mr. Sanderson, 59 Oscar Browning, Mr. Hoare, Mr. and Mrs. Allingham. Green's Hist. of England.
A little girl praised for her accurate account of the Fall slipped her hand into that of the praiser and looking up in his face said "I know why Adam and Eve were sent away -- because he ate the peel."
Lady Colvile overheard a rough exclaim "Once a Jew always a Jew: give me Beaconsfield."
An American said of the Rajahs "Those fellows have no more idea of time than a sitting hen."

She talks like the best part of her books, the parts where she analyses without dissecting, the parts out of which compilers get her `wise, witty, and tender' sayings. She is wonderfully thoughtful, even in trifles. She shut up George Lewes when he tried to talk about her. She does not seem vain. She adores Charles Darwin because of his humility. GHL Diary, Cambridge, 19-21 May 1873
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday 19 May 1873
Went to Cambridge on a visit to Myers. 785 At lunch there was Mrs. Huth 786 and her daughter, H. Sidgwick, Gurney, Jebb, etc. Trinity Library and music in the chapel. Tea. Then to the boat race. Brilliant day but very cold. Dr. Phelps 787 and his wife. At supper several of the fellows. Home at 12 knocked up.
Tuesday 20 May 1873
Breakfasted with Sidgwick. Capital talk. Took a walk with Polly behind King's till lunch. After lunch went to a choral festival in King's Chapel. Anthems etc. Tea. Boat race. Supper. Hallam Tennyson, and the two Balfours. 788 Good talk till 'bd past 11. 789
Wednesday 21 May 1873
Breakfasted with Myers: Sidgwick, Mrs. Huth, Jebb, Gurney. We went over the University Library. Started at 1.30. Home to find quantity of letters.

GHL Diary, Blackbrook, 5 September 1873
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
This morning we started with the three servants for Blackbrook and found on arrival that our goods and chattels had not been sent on from Railway and would not arrive till tomorrow! Found the house also wretchedly provided with necessaries -- not a blanket nor a brush -- and most of the things broken or dilapidated. The weather was gloomy and cold and our spirits were considerably damped. We resolved not to make this our home, and if possible to get released from the yearly engagement.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL and GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 9-10 July 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL and GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 9-10 July 1860
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Wandsworth | 9 July 1860.
My dear Miss Hennell
To be frank with you, I did not contemplate reading your book -- it lay so completely out of my present studies. But the notice in the Westminster, and especially what Marian told me of it, as she read on, made me determine to put other things aside and attack it at once. This morning it was finished and I will now tell you in all sincerity that I think it a remarkable and interesting work -- to some minds it will probably be intensely interesting. It shows great industry, and intellectual activity, and is likely to be fruitful in suggestion to many inquiring minds. Its moral tone is high and some of its ideas are of great importance. If I were now exercising the critical function there are many isolated passages which I should quote with emphasis and comment.
On the other hand I must own to an utter inability to seize your meaning both in the general scheme and in many particular passages. You have worked out for yourself a scheme; but what that is you fail to make intelligible to me. I do not say that I agree or disagree -- simply I do not understand. As it has been my lot to read many obscure books, and often to fail in seizing their meaning, or even to make clear to myself a meaning, I have learned in some measure to understand why your book is so obscure. Briefly it is on these accounts: --
In the first place you do not throw your thoughts into the form of propositions. There is assertion -- aper'e7u -- eloquence -- but little or no proposition, and never dependent propositions. If you, who have your own scheme clearly before you, would take the trouble to express it in a series of dependent propositions, you would perhaps make it clear to others. It would be a good exercise for yourself, and in the event of a new edition would serve as a valuable introduction or resum'e9. All, or almost all the vagueness and seeming contradiction might then vanish.
In the next place your mode of presentation is so excessively abstract that only the clearest diction could render it other than wearying and perplexing. Spencer is abstract enough in all conscience, but no one complains of not understanding him: his illustrations are concrete and his style is clear. Whereas your style (excellent in some pages) is often so wordy, involved, and vague that the meaning is lost as in a mist. There are paragraphs which read like a translation from a language into which one cannot retranslate them. Not to keep to uninstructive generalities I will particularize two or three examples of unintelligibility.
You offer the following as a definition -- it is to me Chaldaic: -- "Every framing of a theory is the setting up of a god to govern the idea" -- perhaps so; but one asks what idea? how governed? the definition may be irresistible -- when once it is understood. p. 252 What Spencer is made to say of Bacon -- utter darkness! p. 270 You are endeavouring to express an important idea -- I have read and reread the page to myself and to Marian and the only meaning I can extricate is so trivial that I am sure it is not what was in your mind. Try that passage on some one else! p. 308 "The setting in . . . centre." This sentence reads like one of my quizzical aphorisms in the '91Orphic Fragments.'92 p. 353 is the announcement of one of the great conclusions of your book. I can make nothing of it except 'abthat very'bb the superfluous remark that man's first conception of the Infinite was his first conception of God -- and that the emotions have likewise been rendered objective. What is the "literally external station"? -- It is the frequent use of ordinary words (like this "literally") in unintelligible connections which makes so many passages hazy.
You will remember that I speak under the confession of not having seized your scheme, when I say that there does not seem any new idea or principle, and I should like to learn what it is and where expressed, since it has escaped me. Nor do I at all understand your reconciliation of Feuerbach and Spencer; -- in reading the West[minster] Rev[iew] I imagined a way in which you might have united them, but that way is not the one I imagined you to have found, so that all is mist once more. After this you must not be surprised if Call has "misrepresented" you.
There is only one point more which need be noticed and that is the carelessness, almost culpable, with which you speak of Comte. It is not wise -- it is not right -- to speak of great writers without having previously read them; and it is obvious that you cannot have read Comte or you would not commit such a glaring mistake as to accuse him of not taking the element of History into account. Just run through his '91Cathechism'92 586 (it is the smallest book and therefore I refer to it) and you will find that many of the best ideas in your book have been thoroughly and persistently expounded by him; and indeed with regard to History I venture to say that no philosopher has ever laid so much emphasis on it, no one has more clearly seen and expressed the truth, that the past rules the present, lives in it, and that we are but the growth and outcome of the past.
But I must break off. Had I not a real personal interest in Marian's friend, and a real respect for the mind which produced such a work as "The Thoughts," you must be sure that I should not interrupt my pressing avocations to write so long, and I fear so unpleasant a letter. If it is unpleasant, reflect how much easier it would have been for me to have written a general compliment as to what I did admire, and speak vaguely about the rest. But as "The Thoughts" will not be your last book I thought it more friendly to be frank.
Ever truly yours
G. H. Lewes.
[In GE's hand]
I must amuse you, dear Sara, by telling you of a gentleman who has elected himself into a too-frequent correspondent of mine. He advertises himself in the Athenaeum 587 as the author of "numerous works highly spoken of by the press"; the works, I imagine, are little known to any but the press who spoke highly of them. I put this as one of the many cases in point to confirm what I say to Cara.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL and GE to Charles Lee Lewes, Shottermill, [10 August 1871]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL and GE to Charles Lee Lewes, Shottermill, [10 August 1871]
MS: Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Endorsed: Aug. 10. 71. GE's part published: Paterson, pp. 157-158; the postscript about Tennyson has been added from 27 August.
Shotter Mill | Thursday.
Dearest Boy
I hope this heavenly weather is beneficial to Gertrude though I fancy it is perhaps too hot for her. Greatly as we enjoy it, it does not seem to have strengthened either of us. I have had two headaches with sickness this week, and the Mutter ails vaguely. Perhaps it is the sudden change.
The enclosed letter I think you will like to see. Keep it till our return. It is from a Scotch Lecturer who wrote first to ask what was the right pronunciation Rom&obreve;la or Romuc0u333 la. In his Lectures he called it Rom&obreve;la, and was frequently taken to task for a false quantity. The Mutter briefly replied and lo! this expression. 345 It pleased me very much to see such gratitude.
We seem to be in the way of gratitude. I have received from Russell Lowell 346 and from Mrs. Gilchrist, strange acknowledgments. They do one good.
Will you on Saturday or Sunday look in at the Priory and see if Browning's poem [Balaustion] 347 has come and if so post it to me? Also ask Grace if she will want any money or anything, as I don't want to come up unless forced. The days here are so delicious.
Mutter sends love to both ditto from Pater.
[In GE's hand.]
Dearest Boy,
Since Pater has left a blank page, I will use that and the quarter of an hour before dinner 348 in writing to you -- just a word of love and chat.
I have often thought of you sitting or rather standing in your City office on these fine days -- as you said -- and enter into the longing for more freedom. But I am composed on account of you by the reflection that happiness depends much more on "must do" than on "may do." Of the two evils it is unspeakably the less to want a little more freedom, than to have more than one knows what to do with. All that reads like very confused English now I have written it -- but here is the servant come to say dinner is ready, so you will understand the source of bad style.
Afternoons, we enjoy our quiet the more because we have escaped being miserable at Edinburgh. I am pretty well -- for me, in spite of Pater's report that I am "vaguely ailing," which sounds like a general description of life. Dear Pater has been a sad sufferer for two days but he is enjoying himself again now.
I am writing a big book and thinking that I shall never finish it. Love to Gertrude from her and your loving
Mutter.

Dublin Core:Title: GHL and GE to Charles Lee Lewes, Milan, 5 June 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL and GE to Charles Lee Lewes, Milan, 5 June 1864
MS: Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Extracts published: Paterson, pp. 114-115.
Hotel Gran Bretagne. Milan 5 June 64.
Dearest Butor
On reaching Milan last night at 9 I found your two letters, one sent on from Venice and one addressed here. While the Inn was getting ready for Mutter's weakness -- tea -- I read them aloud to her, and we were both delighted to hear how you had been enjoying yourselves while we have been in a state of perpetual delight (mitigated somewhat by my continued ill health, which though better since I left Venice on the 28th is still very far from the thing. However headaches have quite vanished and the little Mutter continues vigorous).
We left Venice under one of the most magnificent sunsets ever seen by mortal eye. Padua, where we stayed Sunday and Monday did not preserve its former glory -- perhaps because this time we saw it after the matchless Venice; however we had delicious weather and the art there is immensely interesting, especially Giotto's chapel, built and painted entirely by himself -- a rare gem. There was a very good theatre there also with a company from Rome. We went twice and enjoyed it. 265 On Monday morning we went to Verona; this was a great delight to us. It is one of the most picturesque and interesting cities we have seen, and we did not half see it on our former hurried visit. There were drawbacks of much rain and much society (fleas); but we stayed there till Friday at 10, and then went to Brescia, a very quiet and lovely place, at the very foot of exquisite mountains which make a verdant wall on one side while on the other stretches the vast rich plain of Lombardy. Friday and Saturday were actively occupied in seeing all that is to be seen, and last night after a delicious journey under the most enchanting lights of Italian summer afternoon and evening we got here.
We left the painter at Venice, he not being able to tear himself away so soon, and wishing to make some sketches. He is to join us here tonight. We shall then spend Monday in looking again at our favorite pictures; and on Tuesday start for Como, Lago Maggiore, St. Gothard, Lucerne, Strasbourg, Paris, and the picturesque Grove Road! 266 How long precisely we shall take in getting through these lovely scenes I can't say; but I hope not many days after the 15th. I shall of course write again; but don't whisper to Grace and Amelia that we are contemplating extending our absence beyond the 15th as in that case they will put off the cleaning, which the Mutter is anxious should be thoroughly done.
I conclude from your letters that dear Grandmamma has not been to Cheltenham yet. I hope health has not been the cause of her postponement. Ben seems to be enlarging the circle of his acquaintance: query? Will contact with dogs of an artistic society elevate and refine him? If one Butor, why not two? Strange that no letter has come from Thornie. I suppose you wrote to Bertie with my permission to buy a saddle? Send him my letters.
This is written after breakfast while the Mutter is resting and as she has now completed her toilette, I leave her to send her own love. Give mine to all and believe ever in the love of
Your feeble
Pater.
[In GE's hand.]
Dearest Chick! Mutter is delighted to think of you as enjoying many pleasures in her absence. She is wonderfully well and strong, and life would appear singularly jolly to her just now if the little Pater were as well as she is. Greetings to Grace and Amelia and much love from
Mutter.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL and GE to Charles Lee Lewes, Florence, 5 May 1861
Text: Paterson, pp. 88-91. GE's postscript revised from the MS in Mrs. Ouvry's collection.
Florence. | Sunday, May 5, 1861.
My dear Boy,
It did the hearts of the tired Mutter and Pater good, last evening, to get your long and pleasant letter. We had swallowed some tea and said deux mots to a thin beefsteak, not by any means juicy, when I trotted out to the post in the rain and quickly came back bearing letters from "the boy" and from Blackwood; that from the latter containing the best of news about "Silas," namely, that the "Row" is buying furiously, that everyone speaks admiringly, and that the edition is 7,500 copies, or was on the 24th of last month.
You will have received the darling Mutter's long letter from Nice, therefore I take from that point and resume the history of our very long, very delightful and very expensive journey here. On Friday we started by Vetturino (one always says by vetturino, though why one should go by coachman and not by coach is not clear) for Mentone, which we reached at noon. The carriage was as comfortable and elegant as a private carriage in England and the horses good. The road was a succession of pictures, winding up the mountain passes with the snowy Appennines as a grand line on one horizon and the Mediterranean "deeply, darkly, beautifully blue" 758 on the other, through groves of olives and orchards of orange trees and lemon trees bearing their golden fruit. At Mentone we had half a day of delicious rambling, planning to have a lovely place of our own some day, wherein Pater would raise his own peas, his own pears and his own frogs -- leaving filius to do the hard work of digging, etc. Saturday we had another exquisite day; we stayed two hours to lunch and repose at San Remo, where we saw palm trees in blossom. Sunday the route to Savona was less beautiful, but even less means much beauty. Early to bed as a step to getting wealthy and wise. Monday we got to Genoa and our stay was again intoxicating (not alcoholic), we were as enraptured as we were last year. We went to hear Verdi's Attila bawled with great vigour at the Opera.
Mutter sternly resisted Genoese velvets and Genoese bracelets, so that we bought nothing at Genoa but a few volumes of Italian literature and history. We stayed at a charming place (Camogli) to lunch, slept at Sestri, next day we got to Spezia, which is very beautiful -- I mean the bay and Carrara marble mountains, and yesterday got to Pietra Santa and thence to Pisa where we spent four hours and for the 3rd time were thrilled by the marvels of the place. During the last part of journey Mutter has not been quite well and to-day she is languid with a slight cold. I have scarcely left room for her p.s. so will only say God bless you.
Your loving
Pater.
[In GE'S hand.]
Enter Mutter (with her nose running and her feet well muffled). 759 She imagines herself kissing her dearest Grub and says that she is delighted to hear of his having passed the time industriously and pleasantly. Glad, too, to hear of poor Empson's 760 reprieve. No doubt he will be wiser in future. The only thing in all the letter (about yourself) that makes me sorry is that you should heat yourself with running. Is that wise? Your letter was just what we wanted -- full of particulars. Write us another like it very soon, and tell me how Grace and Amelia are and whether you are quite comfortable en m'e9nage. Remember me to poor Nursie and say I hope to hear she is less suffering than when I saw her. Tell me, too, whether Miss Allen (your "funny little thing") has yet called for the little book wrapped up in newspaper which I left for her on the drawing-room table. I am afraid of some mistake about it and you know it is very precious, being the children's 761 present to Mrs. Bodichon. Take M. d'Albert's letter out of the envelope and send it to me. He sometimes sends no envelope; in that case enclose it with one of yours. Pater has been pretty well until to-day, but now he has a bad sore throat. We talk of you very often and I think of you still oftener. The two months will soon be gone, alas -- like other months.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GHL and GE to Charles Lee Lewes, Dresden, 23 August 1867
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Paterson, pp. 131-133.
Waisenhaus Gasse, Dresden
August 1867.
Dearest Boy
Your letter which awaited us here was eminently acceptable in its pleasant news -- that about Hardy 669 being foremost, as you may imagine.
My previsions about Ilmenau were most charmingly falsified, and instead of staying only one week we stayed two, and left it with many regrets, not having half exhausted the matchless walks through the pine forests, on every side. The weather was continuously lovely, not too hot, the sun being tempered by the delicious mountain air in which I spent the greater part of the day, greatly to my benefit. I soon lost all my unpleasant symptoms, and felt stronger than I have felt since Spain. Our daily programme was this: At 6.30 we rose; after breakfast the little Mutter retired to her room where she sat reading and writing till 12. I meanwhile sauntered in the woods or climbed one of the heights, taking my note book with me to jot down any thoughts (not many) that might occur. Then I came back and fetched Mutter for our warm bath -- after which a stroll and at 1.15 table d'h'f4te (we found one trial of having our dinner sent to us enough). This lasted till 'bd past 2 in a low, hot, crowded room, noisy with noisy Germans of a small shopkeeping class. But the food was excellent, and the length of time over dinner was good for digestion so that consoled us for the weariness. Then we walked back to our lodging and had coffee and after my cigar (sometimes followed by a nap) the Mutter read aloud till 5 when we started for our evening walk, always beautiful but sometimes very fatiguing. We usually got back by 8 -- then supper at the hotel -- trout or venison every day and light Rhenish wine. Then a cigarette while the Mutter read the Pall Mall aloud and bed soon after 9.
We left Ilmenau on Tuesday -- the hottest day yet -- and came on at once to Dresden, where to my disgust I find it exceedingly difficult to get lodgings for so short a time as a month. I spent two whole mornings in hot and wearisome search, and although we at last lighted on the very thing we desired, it is still somewhat uncertain whether we shall be able to get into them before Tuesday (NB address as above) and the hotel though comfortable is in so noisy a situation that sleep is difficult, and unless the windows are closed we can't hear each other speak. We have twice been to the Br'fchlsche Terrace where the evening open air concerts remind us of old days; and this evening we were to have gone to the opera to see Wagner's Fliegende Holl'e4nder but unfortunately it is postponed. I shall write more details in my next. The Mutter wishes to add a word so I leave her space. Love to all
From your loving
Pater.
P.S. Just learned that we can get into our lodgings in the Waisenhaus Gasse No. 5.B. on Monday next. A most charming first floor all to ourselves!
[In GE's hand]
Dearest Boy
I must break my usual silence to tell you of my hearty joy and sympathy in your joy at Hardy's recognition of your efforts. I like the news better than any other you could have sent us about yourself, for I am chiefly ambitious for you that you should make yourself felt as valuable in your business -- after that, in any other good work. But John Mill's Logic would not have been an excuse for his doing his work at the India House badly.
Little Pater looks gloriously well, and has enjoyed our travel greatly. Give my best love to all your three guardian angels. You have more than your share. Also to Aunt Susanna when you see her, with congratulations on her having got through the horrors of removal. Always your
Mutter.

GHL and GE to Charles Lee Lewes, Avignon, 21 April 1861
Text: Paterson, pp. 83-84, dated 24 April.
Avignon | April 21, 749 1861.
My dear Boy,
Although this is written under difficulties (too long to be explained) I just scribble a line to say that so far we have arrived safe and sound. We reached Paris at 'bd past 11 and turned in thoroughly tired. We did not get up till 8 because Breakfast could not be got before 9. Our day in Paris was pleasant enough, spent in rambling about, seeing the pictures at the Luxembourg Palace and visiting P'e8re la Chaise. 750 We got here at 12 and by paying 20 francs extra had a coup'e9 all to ourselves so we had slept tolerably well. After breakfast we went out for a long and delicious ramble of three hours -- we left the cold of winter in Paris, and find ourselves in the heat of summer here, roses and iris in full bloom and lilac disappearing. We saw among other things the tomb John Mill has erected to his wife who died here -- very touching. 751 We saw also a rustic dance, very interesting indeed. The people are remarkably healthy, happy and good looking, que c'est une f'eate!
To-morrow morning we go to Arles, and having spent some hours at that curious old relic of Rome, we shall reach Toulon in time for bed unless anything happens.
The sweetest Mother is very tired but remarkably well and says she must add six words to this, so I leave her space.
Ever your loving
Pater.
Mutter's Autograph.
Die Mutter thinks of her dear Boy very much and loves him better than ever now she is at a distance from him.

We were both much affected by this visit." (GHL Journal, 21 April.)

Dublin Core:Title: George Smith to GE, London, 3 May 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
George Smith to GE, London, 3 May 1864
MS: Yale.
45, Pall Mall, S.W.
May 3rd 1864.
My dear Madam
It was only yesterday that I clearly understood from Mr. Lewes that I was to regard "Brother Jacob" as a present from you. 615 I can hardly tell you how much I was touched and gratified by your kindness. The gift is a princely one in value, and it comes to me at a time when it is even more than ordinarily valuable; but you will I am sure understand me, when I say, that it is not chiefly on that account that I am pleased at receiving such a present from you. I hope that I may regard it as an indication of your satisfaction with the manner in which our business relations have been conducted as well as of your feeling of personal kindness towards myself. And I value your good opinion so highly that such an expression of it is deeply gratifying to me.
Wishing you and Mr. Lewes perfect enjoyment of your trip I remain My dear Madam
Your very faithful and obliged
G. Smith.
Mrs. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: George Simpson to William Blackwood, Edinburgh, 9 May 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Simpson to William Blackwood, Edinburgh, 9 May 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
George Street | 9th May 1868.
My dear Sir
I do not admire the cases for the Spanish Gypsy, they could hardly be plainer, and all one pattern in different colours. Our idea was to have the Book externally as nice looking as we have made the inside -- fit for a Drawing-Room Table, and not merely what would do for the Circulating Library which is all that these cases are fit for. I think there should be some gold on the outside and it would be worth while to give the ornamentation a Spanish or Morish style.
It appears to me that when we have a Book to publish that we know to be a first rater we should let it be seen that we appreciate it by doing the best that can be done for its externals. So I hope the question of binding will be reconsidered. I return 2 of the Cases, keeping one as Mr. Blackwood may wish to see it.
Master Jack has come into my room enquiring for you in his usual familiar style and utterly amazed to hear you had been a week in London.
A want of consideration on your part certainly not to have communicated your movements to the venerable Gentleman!
What a privilege you had in getting into the House on Thursday to be witness of a scene you will never forget. 759 How wild the rascals must be. Surely sensible people must be disgusted at the recent exhibition of the cloven foot among them, the blackguard demagogues.
No letter from Strathtyrum today. Too busy of course this week to think of anything but the noble game.
I must not trespass on your time writing me so often, but thank you heartily for what you have been good enough to tell me. I am my dear Sir
Yours faithfully
Geo. Simpson.
I sent complete copy Gypsy to Ticknor and Field yesterday by order of GHL!

Dublin Core:Title: George Simpson to William Blackwood, Edinburgh, 21 May 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Simpson to William Blackwood, Edinburgh, 21 May 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | 21st May 1868.
My dear Sir
You will be glad to hear your Uncle is so much better. He is most unreasonable in expecting to get well all at once for the treatment was severe -- a cruelty! but he bore it heroically and must have been in first rate condition to have pulled through so easily.
You come down upon me pretty strongly about my dissatisfaction with the case for Gypsy, but I bear it with the most severe indifference, for I feel I am right in condemning the back, especially the side. I should not like to let GE get a glimpse of it.!
A Spanish or moorish style is not necessarily a heavy style. (Look at Lockhart's Spanish Ballads), 764 and if we had accepted the back we could not the side for there is no correspondence of style between them, except perhaps that little brute of a centerpiece, which is very ugly. Mr. Langford says I cannot answer her question as to when we will ship the Sheets. He never put the question but told me he would subscribe it on Monday, and I hurried forward a thousand to get packed off to day, by Rail. I have telegraphed this to him and that the price is 12/6 to which Mrs. Lewes agrees in a pleasant letter received this morning. 765 I would send you copy, but this is Queen B Day and I am alone.
I have not either been asked what colour I think George Eliot will like best. You told me you preferred the brick dust colour. 766 I liked it, but did not say anything about it till I heard more of the design. There is no time now to send us designs. I hope you and Mr. Langford will decide upon that.
She regrets so short a time has elapsed between the time she was able to let us first announce her work and publication, for the Public she finds are hardly yet aware of its being forthcoming. They are going away next week. Your uncle did well to hold fast by his first offer merely showing how much more expensive in the getup this Book was than Silas Marner, in Printing, Paper, Binding, and Advertising. So 3/- per copy on what is sold or £300 on 2000 copies remains the same as it was [The rest of this letter has not been found.]

Dublin Core:Title: George Simpson to William Blackwood, Edinburgh, 19 May 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Simpson to William Blackwood, Edinburgh, 19 May 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | 19th May 1868.
My dear Sir
I was glad to have your Uncle yesterday in a fair way to speedy recovery and in good spirits, but "Ase' Bell" says he must not travel by Rail all this week so I must struggle through as I best can. . . .
You can I think be useful at present in London in hurrying out Kinglake and in seeing how the Sub[scriptio]n, Presentation Copies, advertising etc. of it and of GE's poem is done. What is the hitch about Kinglake? Why can we not publish at the beginning of the month?
I am very much disgusted with the Ornamentation for the Spanish Gypsy. The Book is heavy and tasteless and common place. The gilt side is simply stupid, and not worth criticising for it won't do. The back might suit a volume upon the Architecture of Spain. Something very much simpler, light and graceful should be done. The sight of this would I suspect give George Eliot a sick headache.
I cannot understand how Burn 763 should have so far missed his mark. He is in general so apt at hitting the right style for a book. I have sent the Cases back to Mr. Langford with a description of what I want him to counter with Burn for an amendment. I am my dear Sir
Yours faithfully
Geo. Simpson. . . .

Dublin Core:Title: George Simpson to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 3 November 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Joseph Munt Langford^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Simpson to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 3 November 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Confidential
Edin. November 3 1859.
My dear Sir
When the time came to make an offer to GE. we all had the matter under consideration. The Major thought a good sum to accord with a payment of so much per 1000 sold. Mr. John said he was determined to have it, so much would it help Maga to have it in her pages, and he wrote us from Gibliston that he would offer a sum that he thought could not be refused for the same number of years I believe as we had A.B. that sum was 'a33000. A reply came immediately couched in very stiff terms, stating that GE had determined to keep the new work in his own hands.
Mr. John had said that of course he had no doubt of the success of a second work by the same hand, although there was always a risk, for he instanced the Scenes of Cler. Life as an example of another Book equally good in many respects and yet how far short it had fallen of the public favour.
Some allusion was made in GE's letter to this expression of Mr. John's, but which I cannot recollect precisely, it may be that GE's sensitive nature has recoiled at this, or which I think more likely his disposition is inordinately greedy and he expects some wonderful price from a Routledge or Smith Elder and Co.
Mr. Blackwood made no reply, and lately having occasion to remit the second pay[men]t of AB. took occasion to say how grateful he was to see the continued popularity of the Book and reminding GE of the additional Sum we had voluntarily added to the stipulated price some months ago when we found the work more popular than at first we had expected, now had the pleasure of saying that another bonus would be added of the same amount viz. 'a3800 + 400 + 400.
The acknowledgment for this was even more cold and insensible than the letter first alluded to. Not a single expression of gratitude or acknowledgment of Mr. B's handsome conduct. The result is that both Mr. John and Major B are utterly disgusted and I do think would now decline the new book if it were offered them. Mr. John has been most thoroughly hood-winked. His enthusiasm about GE was extraordinary, and his feeling of sympathy for his unfortunate position most heartfelt, but I must say the reaction is very great.
All this time Lewes has said never a word, which looks queer. He is corresponding about other things but says nothing about GE. Read me the riddle if you can, but address to my house 5 Lothian Road, when you write about it.
I have told you all not knowing how much you knew before but depend upon your not mentioning even to your bosom friend what I tell you, but I do think you should now know considering your position towards Lewes. John would I daresay have written to you about [it], but he is excessively sore on the subject and I am really sorry for him.
What do you think of the sum offered? I thought it handsome, but I am sure he would have give more rather than lost it, but what do you also think of the house continuing to publish by a party held in small estimation by People like Mr. Brown of Longman and Co.
G. S.

Dublin Core:Title: George Simpson to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 19 November 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Joseph Munt Langford^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Simpson to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 19 November 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh 19th November 1859.
My dear Sir
There was a very awkward letter from Lewes today. He and his friend are evidently in a fix. I fear L is not highminded. His conduct in this matter is most disingenuous. He makes a great fuss about no notice being taken of the Publishers of Newby's Ad[vertisemen]t and says that the paragraph in the 'abCourt Journal'bb Daily News is not his, which I would swear it to be, and that he does not think any one has seen it. Mr Blackwood told him that he had consulted the lawyers here and was assured by them that no prosecutable offence was committed but still Lewes urges us to move in the matter. Why should we? what further interest have we in the author's productions?
He makes an absurd remark just the sort of thing the Ladies have such a knack of doing. After saying that he is pestered on all hands to contribute to new Magazines etc. he adds that "numerous attempts are also made to seduce George Eliot"! I say no wonder when Mr. Lewes has shown them the way.!
He says you tell him Clerical Scenes is O.P. and urges a 5/ ed[itio]n for Christmas. What a muff! No cheap edition of it or AB should be talked of till the new Novel is published, and we must have our hands totally cleared of the present Edition for which we have paid handsomely. 394
He also asks if we are preparing the Plates for Sea-side Studies. I have not, nor have Messrs B., heard that this must be done afresh. Are the old ones not to be recovered? I do not think you should speak to him about them, but tell me if you cannot hear of the artist who did them, and I shall set about getting them reproduced at least expense.
I wish you had told him what Mudie has said. 395 I am sure you are right that the secret was published by him to gratify his vanity, but I think the penalty will be enormous.
I am quite enrag'e9 that Mr John did not write you earlier. I urged him till he got obstinate, but he now regrets it, I see. He was indeed so disgusted that it was natural he should be unwilling to approach the subject.
The title of Thackeray's Magazine conveys to me the idea of Banks Stockbrokers, and Assurance Companies not of Literature, How lucky for Macmillan that this has at once realised a perfect failure. Had it gone on dubiously they might have been led into a heavy loss. Of course they will stop in time.?
I asked the same question as you do when I looked at the article on Tennyson, 396 for I was disgusted at seeing it almost verbatim of what I saw said elsewhere, the Major tells me it is a new Contributor a Lady in the N. of England and that when about to return it he was so struck with its originality and right feeling that he read it again and urged Mr. John to insert it. I should like to hear what you say of it. I am my dear Sir
Yours faithfully
Geo. Simpson.
Mr. Langford.

Dublin Core:Subject: Joseph Munt Langford^^M

George Simpson to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 16 November 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
November 16. 1859.
My dear Sir
I am sorry to see my suspicions confirmed by your note of yesterday. G.E has sold herself to the highest bidder. I said very early that he was an avaricious soul, but even with this failing if he had known what dealing with Gentlemen was I think he would have explained the matter to the Messrs B. before accepting the offer of another party. I have no doubt the tempter is that fallen angel C.D. You remember his early letter to GE immediately after publication of Adam Bede.! I should like at your convenience to know confidentially your own views on the subject.
I am happy to hear you found Mr. Kipling so much better than I expected to hear. I hope he will get round again and be spared for many years enjoyment of the reward of his early hard work. I am, my dear Sir
Yours faithfully
Geo. Simpson.
Mr. Langford.

Dublin Core:Title: George Simpson to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 12 November 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Joseph Munt Langford^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Simpson to Joseph Munt Langford, Edinburgh, 12 November 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh 12th November/59.
My dear Sir
Thanks for the sight of enclosed which I think prove that [at] the date they were written no unpleasant feeling possessed the mind of the writer towards any member of the firm. My own notion is that the motive is insatiable greed, and with such a disposition it is most unpleasant to deal.
Pray take no notice of my communication, for in reply to a remark of mine that you should be informed, Mr John answered very impatiently as if he were disgusted with the affair and did not care to have anything more to say about it or the parties, and this after he had said he would write you. The Major is thoroughly out of conceit at them.
Be prepared to advise whether cheap Edition shall be 6/, 5/ or 2/6. I am hankering for another 2000 in 2 volumes as a Library Edition 'e0 la Bulwer.
A Reverend Gentleman who had Miss Evans as a pupil is in Edinburgh just now enlightening the fashionable circles with her early history and that of Amos Barton, and it was this Clergyman's house where the Meetings of Clergy were held referred to in A. Barton. 383 He by the bye gives proof that there is no want of invention in the mind of the author of A Bede, for he says that while A Barton is truly painted from the Life, also the Polish Countess and her protector, the wife Mrs Barton is purely imaginary.
I am very sorry to hear of Mr. Kipling's state of health. What a distressing position for his Wife! How sadly sickness must have changed this once happy circle to which you could always come with a certainty of cheerful welcome.
Thanks for your kind message to my Mother. She is wonderfully well and desires to be kindly remembered to you. I am my dear Sir
Yours faithfully
Geo. Simpson.
Mr. Langford.

Dublin Core:Title: George Simpson to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 30 May 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: John Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Simpson to John Blackwood, Edinburgh, 30 May 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Edinburgh | 30th May 1866.
My dear Sir,
You will be anxious to know how the printing of Felix Holt is going on. Vol. I is gathering. Vol. II is on the Machines up to Sig. K. 467 and the whole of it will be on to morrow. Vol. III one-half of it will be printed by Saturday afternoon.
We had a small instalment of M.S. yesterday barely making 16 pages and have not sent it out in proof, expecting more according to Mr. Lewes' promise to day, but which has not arrived.
I see the Advertisement very well displayed in the Monthlies.
As soon as last revise is returned for press we shall let you know when we can undertake to ship to London. Meantime, now the Magazine and Periodicals are off, I am watching progress and seeing that no hitch occurs. One Machine broke its Crank shaft yesterday and 3 "Printer" Boys ran off to Sea on Monday but that I could not help.
Mr. William will doubtless have told you with what joy I heard of his happiness. 468 I cannot imagine a choice that would be more agreeable to yourself, and I feel assured the union will be a source of great comfort and satisfaction to your families. I have long wished in my heart to see him well mated, and I now hope to see him and her enjoy years of happiness as perfect as can be realised on this Earth. . . .
With respectful remembrances to Mrs. Blackwood, I am my dear Sir
Yours faithfully
Geo. Simpson.
John Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: George du Maurier to Charles Lee Lewes, Hampstead, 1 December [1878]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Lee Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George du Maurier to Charles Lee Lewes, Hampstead, 1 December [1878]
MS: Balliol College, Oxford. Hitherto unpublished.
New Grove House, | Hampstead Heath.
December 1.
My dear Lewes,
I cannot tell you how grieved and shocked I was today at hearing the sudden news of your father's death; I had not even heard of his illness, and so little suspected anything wrong that on my way to the Priory I was actually rehearsing a song which I hoped to sing to him this afternoon! Sad and strange to say, I had only just learnt the words ('fcber alle[n] gipfeln ist ruh) from the life of Goethe which he was kind enough to give me some time ago and which I only finished this week! -- I like to think how much he has been in my thoughts lately, and I realise in great distress of mind that I have lost a good friend whom I shall always remember with warm gratitude and affection.
I have been trying to write to Mrs. Lewes to express the sympathy my wife and I so deeply feel -- but I cannot find words to do so now, in the freshness of her great bereavement, and fear to intrude on her grief. We can only think and talk of her, and you must kindly convey to her for us the message of our earnest and heartfelt condolence.
And with you also, my dear Lewes, we sincerely grieve, knowing how warmly attached you were to your father and how great his loss must be to you. Believe me always
Yours very sincerely
George du Maurier.

Dublin Core:Title: George Croom Robertson to GHL, London, 2 March 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: George Henry Lewes^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Croom Robertson to GHL, London, 2 March 1877
MS: Draft of letter, University College, London.
Lorton Terrace, | Ladbroke Road W.
3. 77.
My Dear Mr. Lewes
We are very sorry to hear about Mrs. Lewes and hope she will soon be quite well again.
Many thanks for the preface. It may not be possible to print it in full, but what is given shall be in your own words. You need not be deterred from asserting your claims by anything I have said in the supplement hurriedly tagged to my little paper, read months ago to the Metaphysical Society and which Knowles would have to be printed. In adding the supplementary remarks a short time ago, I had in view, besides odd essays like Clifford's and Pollock's, chiefly Leslie Stephen's new book, 358 which I have read since the paper was written and which has certainly struck me as saturated with the notion of the overshadowing influence of society. Maudsley 359 also has a number of passages (though plainly inspired by Comte) which point the right way. Even in Spencer, I have in the last few days come across a passage which is worth looking at -- Psychology II. 'a7 493. And for myself I may say that anything there is in this paper -- and there is more implied than could be set forth -- has been taking shape in my mind for quite a number of years past. But I regret that when it did seem to me in writing, first to remark on Mill etc. and then to mention you, I did not look up your first volume and do more justice to your emphatic statement of the position as fundamental in psychology.

Dublin Core:Title: George Combe to John Chapman, Edinburgh, 7 December 1851
Dublin Core:Subject: John Chapman^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe to John Chapman, Edinburgh, 7 December 1851
Text: Copy in the hand of Robert Cox, unsigned, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh | 7th December 1851.
John Chapman, Esq.
My dear Sir
I have been knocked up by cold at Manchester, and employ Mr. Robert Cox 54 as my amanuensis. I inclose for your perusal a letter dated 8th instant which I have considered it necessary to write to Mr. Lombe. Be so good as read it and seal it with a seal different from your own; and send it to the post office without delay.
In announcing the names of the Subscribers to the Review you looked at the matter only from your own point of view, and did not consider how the announcement might affect your supporters. The Review has the reputation of being the organ of infidelity, and at an evening party in Edinburgh last week, a lady called out to Mrs. Combe, "So Mr. Combe has subscribed 'a320 to the Westminster Review!" This could do me no harm; but Mr. Robert Chambers, 55 if he had subscribed, might have been seriously injured by the announcement of his name as the saints are watching every opportunity of convicting him of a leaning to infidelity. My conviction is that several others of my friends have been deterred from coming forward by the announcement of the names. Now, however, that the error has been committed, I advise you before taking any further step in relation to the subscribers, to wait till you see the effect of your letter and mine on Mr. Lombe.
I would again very respectfully recommend to you to use Miss Evans's tact and judgment as an aid to your own. She has certain organs large in her brain which are not so fully developed in yours, and she will judge more correctly of the influence upon other persons of what you write and do, than you will do yourself.
I return the copy of your letter to Mr. Lombe, which I think is quite correct, and called for.
[No signature]

Dublin Core:Title: George Combe to John Chapman, Edinburgh, 5 March 1854
Dublin Core:Subject: John Chapman^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe to John Chapman, Edinburgh, 5 March 1854
MS: Copy in Combe Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh 5th March 1854.
John Chapman Esq.
My dear Sir
I am favoured with your letter of 3d March, and beg to remark that, according to my recollection, I told you that the act abolishing Transportation had been passed; that new prisons must be built, new modes of discipline instituted, and that as the convicts would be liberated after a few years confinement, there would be a public interest excited, as soon as the nature of the act was known. All this information I derived from Mr. Perry, medical inspector of Prisons, before the Act was printed for the public, or its probable effects known; and I communicated it to you and asked you whether you would wish to have an article on the subject in your January number, which would probably anticipate the other Reviews. You said you would be glad to have it. I certainly said that I should be willing to write it; but apparently you thought that I suggested the article to gratify some wish of my own; I, on the other hand, being conscious only of a friendly desire to aid the Review by furnishing an article on a subject of public interest which, it appeared to me, no other person was likely to supply. Your view, I am willing to allow, may have been as natural to you, as my own was to me; and here was a mistake for which neither of us was to blame.
I never hinted a complaint of your postponing the article from January till April, until you proposed again to postpone it till July, and then I could not help saying that I thought that you should have given me the earliest possible notice of your wish to postpone it, to set me at liberty, whereas you allowed me to toil on, and proposed postponement only after I wrote that I had finished it. Perhaps you did not know sooner; but no explanation was given me to that effect.
In regard to the delay between the slips and the proof, and the difficulty of reducing the Pamphlet to the size of an article, I was wholly in the dark, until your letter of the 3d March explained the former, and the moment I got a proof I removed the latter. -- Miss Evans informed me that her official connection with the Review had ceased on 1st January, but I imagined that she continued to take an interest in its affairs, and that from her knowing more of Phrenology than you professed to do, the arrangement by which she agreed to edit the pamphlet and judge of its suitableness for an article, would be equally beneficial to you and me. When she expressed her difficulty in reducing it, which she did before a proof was sent to me, I said that I could not judge whether I could to it myself, until I got a proof. When one came, I instantly saw that the thing could be done, and did not lose a post in saying so. I may add that when the M.S. was sent to Miss Evans in January I was sleepless and confined to bed for weeks, rising only for a few hours in the evening, otherwise I should have probably saved her the trouble I imposed on her.
You will perceive from this statement that your proposal to delay inserting the article till July came upon me quite by surprise, and that while you assigned the delay in preparing it, as your reason for the postponement, I felt that I was wholly guiltless of that delay, and that on your side alone it had arisen, imagining, as I did, that you and Miss Evans were co-operating in the matter. With these explanations, I leave the matter in your own hands. Insert or reject the article as suits your own convenience. I see no reason for your paying me £20, and do not ask or wish you to do so, because I wrote the article with the desire to aid the Review; but if you are of a different opinion, I leave this to your own decision also.
I remain

George Combe to John Chapman, Edinburgh, 28 November 1851
Text: Copy, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh 28 November.
John Chapman Esq.
My dear Sir
I am truly sorry to hear of so much bad health in your domestic circle, and hope that it may soon cease. We send our sympathies to the sufferers. 53
I have received, and now send you, another letter dated 20 November from Mr. Lombe, which please return. I have written to him today that in my opinion he cannot be made liable for the debts of the Review by your announcing "a donation" from him of 'a3200 a year. But, as you have apparently gone too far in making the statement general in place of particular, I think that you should write to him calmly, renouncing all claim to 'a3200 a year for general purposes, and that you accept of his gifts for particular articles as he proposes. I have told him that you may have made a mistake, but could have had no intention of either "cheating" or "lieing." These are opprobrious terms, but they are not addressed to you.
[No signature]

Dublin Core:Title: George Combe to John Chapman, Edinburgh, 2 March 1854
Dublin Core:Subject: John Chapman^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe to John Chapman, Edinburgh, 2 March 1854
MS: Copy in Combe Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh 2d March 1854.
John Chapman Esq.
My dear Sir
Your letter of the 28th February reached me only this morning. Before answering it, I must refresh your memory on a few points which you, in thinking of your own interest and convenience, seem to have forgotten. -- You expressed a desire that I should furnish you with an article on prison discipline for the January number of the Review: and I agreed to place it in your hands on the day named by Miss Evans, 1st December, and on your own terms, as to pecuniary remuneration, or rather non-remuneration. -- At the sacrifice of my health and convenience, I had the article ready by the day named; and wrote that it was at your command. You wrote to me begging that, for your convenience, it might stand over till April. -- I felt that it was one-sided to leave me to labour, at every cost, to keep faith with you, while you coolly consulted your own convenience, and bid me wait; but making every allowance for your necessities, I did not express what I felt, but assented frankly to your proposal. -- I was then desired to send the M.S. to London by a certain day in January. I availed myself of the interval in working up my materials into a full exposition of the subject for a pamphlet, and wrote to you offering as much of it as you chose to print for an article in the April number, and you were satisfied with my terms. The M.S. was delivered to Miss Evans two days before the day specified for its being sent. If delay in setting it up and sending me a proof ensued, this was no fault of mine. No proof reached me till 23d February nearly 7 weeks after the M.S. was delivered in London. I immediately wrote that I could make it into an article, and desired you to send a proof to be cut down. You lost two posts in sending it. It reached me on 28th February at 9. a.m. and by one o'clock on the same day, I wrote to you that I had gone over it and reduced it to 35 pages and would reduce it to 32 if you could not afford to give 35. -- But after putting me to all this trouble, I then, on the 2d March, receive a letter from you, dated 28 February, requesting me to postpone its insertion till July!
Now, there has never been a delay of one hour on my part: I have made health, convenience, and every consideration in money, give way to meet your wishes: the whole disappointments have arisen from your own style of managing business: But your style does not suit mine. I have borne as long as my patience would hold out; and now I have done. You may do as you please about inserting or not inserting the article; but it shall not wait till July. The pamphlet shall be published as soon as it can be completed: and here again my interest is sacrified to your convenience. Had I known that you were to delay sending me a proof till you could not insert the article, I should have printed the pamphlet here, at less expense, in a neater form, and saved Miss Evans a world of trouble.
By this evening's post I shall return to Miss Evans the proof with all my corrections, and the proof cut down for the Review, and you can do precisely as you please in the matter; but you will excuse me for never again subjecting myself to this kind of treatment. I remain, My dear Sir
Yours faithfully
Geo. Combe.
II, 144:11 George Combe to John Chapman, Edinburgh, 2 March 1854
MS: Copy in Combe Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh 2 March 1854 | 4 p.m.
John Chapman Esq.
My dear Sir
Your letter to me dated 1 March reached me after mine to you of this date was posted for our morning mail. Had it arrived sooner, it would have saved me writing, and your reading that letter. However, I do not regret that it has gone; because I wish you to know that when I make an engagement, I make every possible exertion to fulfil it; and that I expect corresponding treatment from others.
I send you the remaining sheets revised; and to-morrow I shall send the reduced proof to Miss Evans. Your proof to me was paid correctly; but if Dr. Browne's was not, the 1/- worth of stamps sent by you will pay his double postage. In no case, could it have paid both his and mine. I have written him on the subject.
The reasons why I wish my own publisher's names inserted was that it will save opening a new publishing account; that it will save us all trouble attending to advertising, sales, etc. for they do all that most attentively without my needing to prompt them; and lastly, it will save separate advertisements, for they will add it as a line or two to my other advertisements.
You may order 500 copies of the pamphlet to be thrown off and I wish a complete copy for my own use as soon as it is thrown off. -- The top line at present is a sheer waste of paper and type; but it would be expensive to alter it now, otherwise it might be withdrawn from the pamphlet. I shall send a table of contents, and also advertisements to go at the end of it. These and the title page may stand over, till the decision of Sir James Clark is known, unless the Title is already part of the first sheet, in which case it may go to press. I remain, My dear Sir
Yours sincerely
Geo. Combe.

Dublin Core:Title: George Combe to GE, Edinburgh, 3 March 1854
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe to GE, Edinburgh, 3 March 1854
MS: Copy in Combe Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edinburgh | 3 March 1854.
Miss Evans -- 21 Cambridge Street
My dear Miss Evans
My heart is grieved at the annoyance and trouble I am giving you, but it is in a good cause. Mr. Chapman has agreed to insert the article in the April number and I now send you the Proof, with the Passages to be kept in and omitted to constitute the article, marked by me in pencil on the margins. You will soon judge whether the article will read continuously; and you can have little difficulty in adding a few connecting sentences if necessary. -- I presume that you will get a clean proof with all the corrections made. I have made corrections on this proof on pages 62 and 92, which please transfer to the corrected proof, in so far as that on page 62 is not already there. Page 62 is not in it, and is necessary to avoid cavilling.
I have written to Mr. Perry, and you will not wait for him or any of the others longer than suits Mr. Chapman's convenience. I shall run all risks rather than incommode him. I shall write also to Sir Jas. Clark explaining how things stand, but this need not interfere with the action of himself and friends, for the pamphlet will not be published for a month, and their opinions, if given, can be thrown off with the title page, and table of contents, which I now send. There will also be some advertisements at the end, which I shall send. I have ordered 500 copies of the Pamphlet to be printed. I regret that I cannot give it to Mr. Chapman as publisher, but I have told him so.
With our united kindest regards, I remain, My dear Miss Evans
Sincerely yours and obliged
Geo. Combe.

Dublin Core:Title: George Combe to GE, Edinburgh, 17 November 1853
Dublin Core:Subject: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe to GE, Edinburgh, 17 November 1853
MS: Copy in Combe Letter Book, National Library of Scotland.
Edin[burgh] | 17 November 1853.
My dear Miss Evans
The accompanying article 182 is the text of my lucubration for the Review; which is now far advanced, and will be in your hands by the first of December. I shall have it revised by Rob. Cox and James Coxe M.D. before sending it to you. You and Mr. Chapman may feel quite at ease about rejecting it, if found too phrenological and technical, for I shall print it as a pamphlet and distribute it, if you reject it, and thus my labour will not be lost. I expect this result: so you will not disappoint or annoy me in the least by an adverse decision on the part of the Review.
I have had several letters from Sir James Clark lately. At my suggestion, he is working, and with some prospect of success, towards inducing Lord Palmerston to consult physiologists in his forthcoming prison building and prison discipline, instead of parsons and military officers. Conceive, then, my judgement of the discretion which introduced that long paragraph of conglomerated nonsense from the British Review into the Leader, 183 on Phrenology, with approval, and with a piece of fresh nonsense added. The ignorance of the writer of the extracted lines is equalled only by his self-complacency.
I do not know who is now the Editor of the Leader and, therefore, have no personal reference when I ask him whether there will be more phosphorus in one part of the same man's brain, than in another? and so that his small organ of Causality, for instance, shall have so much phosphorus, as to make him a second Bacon, while his large organ of Self-esteem shall have so little, as to render him a second Moses in meekness? 184 That is the practical question in deciding on the relative strength of the mental powers of a man. Besides, would not Iron be as good as Phosphorus for the purpose in hand in the Editor's remarks. It is deplorable to see the Leader's bending backwards on the science through which only certain and selfconsistent progress in all interests emanating from and resting on the mind of man, can be made.
We are both well and unite in kind regards to you. I remain, My dear Miss Evans
Yours sincerely
Geo. Combe.

Dublin Core:Title: George Combe to Charles Bray, Edinburgh, 15 November 1854
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe to Charles Bray, Edinburgh, 15 November 1854
MS: Copy in National Library of Scotland. Extract published: Haight, George Eliot, p. 166.
Private
Edinburgh 15 November 1854.
My dear Mr. Bray --
An intimate friend of Mr. Lewes's in this city, wrote to him begging of him to contradict the reports of an improper connection with Miss Evans. He gave ample explanations about his wife, denied that Miss E. had written to Miss Martineau; but in regard to the main question, he said that he is not answerable to his correspondent for his conduct. He has written in precisely similar terms, in answer to a similar request, to Mr. Carlyle. The conclusion, then, is irresistible that the reports are too true. -- They are spread everywhere, and we now meet them in society. We are deeply mortified and distressed; and I should like to know whether there is insanity in Miss Evans's family; for her conduct, with her brain, seems to me like &unknown;insanity&unknown; morbid mental aberration.
I have no right to dictate to you, but I esteem you too much not to state frankly to you my convictions. T. Hunt, Lewes, and Miss Evans have, in my opinion, by their practical conduct, inflicted a great injury on the cause of religious freedom. "The Leader" has become disagreeable to Mrs. Combe and me as the recorded thinking of minds that can act in such a manner, and when my subscription expires I shall give it up. "The greatest happiness of the greatest number" principle, 234 appears to me to require that the obligations of married life should be honourably fulfilled; and an educated woman who, in the face of the world, volunteers to live as a wife, with a man who already has a living wife and children, appears to me to pursue a course and to set an example calculated only to degrade herself and her sex, if she be sane. -- If you receive her into your family circle, while present appearances are unexplained, pray consider whether you will do justice to your own female domestic circle, and how other ladies may feel about going into a circle which makes no distinction between those who act thus, and those who preserve their honour unspotted?
I again assure you that it is in deep sorrow that I write these lines, and that love and respect for you and yours, alone prompt me to unburden my mind to you in this manner.
With our united kind regards to you, Mrs. Bray, and Mrs. 235 and Miss Hennell, I remain, My dear Mr. Bray,
Yours very truly
Geo. Combe.
I think that Mr. Lewes was perfectly justified in leaving his own wife, but not in making Miss Evans his mistress.
Chas. Bray Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: George Combe to Charles Bray, Charlton, 24 July 1852
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe to Charles Bray, Charlton, 24 July 1852
MS: Draft on verso Bray's letter, 20 July 1852, National Library of Scotland.
Charlton, 24 July 1852 Answered thus:
If a practical scheme can be found for preserving the Review in the hands you mention, I should contribute 'a3100 and ask friends to join in raising 'a31000 but your scheme is not a practical one. Mr. C. is insolvent in his general business and the Review is still a source of loss, in my opinion of 'a3400 a year. To &unknown;take&unknown; give Mr. C. 'a31000 would be simply to cover his general deficiencies perhaps for 2 years, when it would be all lost, and the persons to whom the Review was conveyed would be liable for its debts, and when Mr. Chapman again stood still they would be called on to pay those claims and take the whole concern into their hands.
If by re-imbursing Mr. C. in the 'a3350 paid by him for the Review, disconnecting it from his general business, and applying the 'a3650 remaining of the 'a31000 to it, it might be carried on for 2 years, and I should be ready then to allow him to buy it back on refunding the 'a3350 and intermediate loss; but this would leave no remuneration for him and Miss Evans as editors. If they were paid 'a3100 a year each, the loss would be 'a3600, and the 'a31000 would suffice only for one year. Were the Review taken out of his hands entirely we should lose the advantage of his connection. In short I do not see any way to a practical solution of the difficulty.

Dublin Core:Title: George Combe Journal, London, 15 September 1854
Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe Journal, London, 15 September 1854
MS: National Library of Scotland.
John Chapman and the Westminster Review.
Dr. Hodgson writes to me that Mr. Courtauld, John Chapman's friend and patron, has paid him (Dr. H.) Chapman's debt to him £ in full to avoid calling another meeting of creditors, or forcing Chapman into Bankruptcy.
There is truly a great deal more of benevolence than of conscientiousness and discriminative intellect in the world. Mr. Courtauld is sacrificing his money apparently from the best of motives, to uphold Chapman as the organ of advanced opinions, without any perception of the inadequacy of the man to accomplish the end in view. Chapman is deficient in business talent, in conscientiousness, in knowledge, and in sound practical sense; he is a dreamer and a schemer; his leading motives are ambition and the love of the new; and his chief talents are a capacity for plausible talk, rendered easy by large Secretiveness, Love of approbation, and Wonder, acting unrestrained either by Causality or Conscientiousness. Great efforts making to preserve the Westminster Review in his hands; and this, in my opinion, is an error in judgment. He is morally and intellectually incapable of taking the lead in the philosophy, religion, &unknown;practical&unknown; social economy, and science of the 19th century; and yet this is what he aims at. He must be editor as well as publisher; in short the great oracle of liberal opinions. He will fail again in a few years. He has much good nature, but ill directed.

Dublin Core:Subject: U
Dublin Core:Description:
George Combe Journal, Coventry, 29 August -- 1 September 1851
MS: National Library of Scotland.
August 29 1851.
Coventry. Mr. Bray -- Miss Evans
We travelled from Liverpool to Coventry by rail and found Mr. Charles Bray waiting for us at the station, and went with him on a visit to Rosehill, close on the Town. He introduced us to his wife and her sister, the two sisters of the late Mr. Hennel the author of the work against Christianity as a Revelation; and to Miss Evans, the daughter of a farmer. The whole party are superior and interesting persons. Mr. Bray is a Ribbon manufacturer about 40; a Phrenologist and a convert to the natural Laws, with an excellent intellect, bilious, nervous, lymphatic and sanguine temperament, excellent coronal region, but great Comb[ativeness] and Destruc[tiveness] and very deficient Concentrativeness. He is proprietor of the Coventry Herald, which he uses as the organ of the new philosophy and its applications, so far as public opinion will allow him to go.
Miss Evans is the most extraordinary person of the party. She translated Strauss's work "Das Leben Jesu" from the German, including the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin quotations in it, without assistance; and it is said to be admirably executed. She has a very large brain, the anterior lobe is remarkable for length, breadth, and height, the coronal region is large, the front rather predominating; the base is broad at Destruc[tiveness]; but moderate at Aliment[iveness], and the portion behind the ear is rather small in the regions of Comb[ativeness] Amat[iveness] and Philopro[genitiveness]. Love of approb[ation], and Concentrativeness are large. Her temper[ament] is nervous lymphatic. She is rather tall, near 40 43 apparently, pale and in delicate health. She is an excellent musician. She read the Letters of Henry Atkinson on new organs in his and Miss
Martineau's Book, 44 and we discussed them. She shewed great analytic power and an instinctive soundness of judgment. We had a great deal of conversation on religion, political economy, and political events, and altogether, with the exception perhaps of Lucretia Mott, 45 she appeared to me the ablest woman whom I have seen, and in many respects she excells Lucretia. She is extremely feminine and gentle; and the great strength of her intellect combined with this quality renders her very interesting. Mrs. Bray also is a superior and accomplished woman, extremely modest and unpretending. Her sister plays well on the piano forte and is full of vivacity, with rather a large head, but the anterior lobe is not large.
September 1.
We visited Mr. Bray's ribbon factory, and saw a large apartment filled with looms weaving by steam. We saw a workman weaving a ribbon for the Queen on a Jackard loom, most beautifully flowered and about 5 inches broad. He is the best weaver in Mr. Bray's employment, but very drunken. He has a small brain, a small, but regularly formed, anterior lobe, Individuality, Form, Size, and Weight being predominantly large. His temperament is bilious nervous. He had been off work drinking for 6 days, and received notice that, unless he weave 2'bd yards a week, he shall be held as having resigned his employment. This is an example of a small brain with a special combination of certain organs fitting a man for a certain employment, or rather not operating as a disqualification.
