Dublin Core:Title: GE's Draft For J. Chapman to J. Martineau, Coventry, 29 August 1851
Dublin Core:Subject: J. Martineau^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE's Draft For J. Chapman to J. Martineau, Coventry, 29 August 1851
40
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Draft of a letter to Mr. Martineau.
August 29, 1851.
My dear Sir
The application to you for an article on Christian Ethics and Modern Civilization was indeed not only by a general sense of your ability to treat such a subject, but more especially by the perusal of those passages in your recent article on the Creed of Christendom, 41 in which you briefly but forcibly exhibit the conviction that the moral teaching of the New Testament is inadequate and partly inapplicable to the needs of the present day, that Jesus himself, on the shewing of the synoptical gospels, was under the influence of serious error, and that the religious theory of Paul was based on the official destiny of Christ and not on his moral character.
The future Editors of the Westminster desire that the article in question should contain an impartial inquiry into the moral spirit and code of the primitive Christians as embodied in the New Testament, conducted on true principles of critical investigation and with entire freedom from conscious or unconscious predisposition to accommodate the phraseology of the Gospels and Epistles to the expression of modern ideas, or to use them with an esoteric meaning. The object of the article should be, not to sustain an argumentum ad hominem against the professor of Christianity by making the term cover as much truth as possible, but to ascertain in all simplicity what the New Testament writers really believed and meant to teach, what was the moral influence of their belief on themselves, and how far a strict conformity to their teaching in the present day would correspond with our modern ideal of individual and social life. The Editors believe that the moral perceptions are greatly confused &unknown;and the religious advancement retarded&unknown; by the vague reverence for Christ and Christianity which, owing to our national backwardness in critical science, has been countenanced by some of our most candid and recent writers on religious topics; hence their wish that the questions -- what are Christian Ethics? and How far are they available for our actual wants and in accordance with our highest conceptions? -- should be treated by a mind which to adequate critical knowledge unites thorough directness of purpose and deep sympathy with the onward movements of the age.
An article such as they desire would show that Jesus contributed no new element to ethics, that the emphasis which he gave by his teaching and life to certain true principles was partly counteracted by his misconceptions concerning his own mission and the divine government in general derived from his Jewish culture, and by the false views and expectations which he consequently communicated to his followers, and that the beneficial effect of his character on Christendom has been chiefly due to the substitution of the ideal for the historical. It would discriminate the character of the Pauline development with the moral bearing of its dogmatic elements, from that of the simple Christian school. It would place in strong light the vein of asceticism in the Christian system, leading to such monstrous results in the early centuries of the Church and causing perpetual offences against conscience in simple minds of our own day, its subordination of domestic and social duties to an impractical enthusiasm and the egotistic seeking for '91salvation'92, its depreciation of the present life [about 8 words deleted] especially as regards the culture of the intellect and taste, and its passivity towards political and social abuses -- all which had their foundation first in the dualistic theory -- the antithesis of God and the world, and next in the expectation of Christ's immediate return. The writer's strictures would extend over many other particulars of Christian theory and practice, for example the creation of doctrinal belief into the condition of fellowship, 42 but the main point would be to shew that the faith and life of the early Christians were entirely based on the idea of the special and the exceptional, whereas the essence of modern advancement is the recognition of the general and invariable, and this must henceforth be the standpoint of an effective religious and moral theory. The article, however, while shewing what Christianity has not done and cannot do for us, should do full justice to the positive side and endeavour clearly to define what we really owe to Christianity as a stage in the religious development of the race.
These few hints will enable you to decide whether the Editors may hope for the valuable aid of your pen on the above subject.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Fanny [Mrs. Henry] Houghton, St. Mary's, 3 May 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: Fanny [Mrs. Henry] Houghton^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Fanny [Mrs. Henry] Houghton, St. Mary's, 3 May 1857
Text: Typed copy made for Miss Elsie Druce, Yale.
St. Mary's, Scilly Isles | May 3rd 1857.
Dear Fanny,
Thank you very fervently for sending me Sarah's letters about Chrissy, 314 which both reached me together, last night. I have suffered a great deal from the long intervals that have elapsed between the letters I have received. Until yours came I had not heard since the 22nd when I received a letter from Isaac written on the 19th saying that Chrissy was worse and in great danger! But I can well understand that both he and Sarah have their hands and minds too full to retain a very vivid recollection of those at a distance. Poor Sarah has had a terrible trial.
You too, dear Fanny have had your special trouble; now, I trust being rapidly alleviated. I am grieved both for Henry's sake and yours that his general health is so delicate.
Thank you for your kind question about my health. I can say nothing good of myself in that respect. For several months I have been very ailing and have found my necessary work difficult. But I hope to get strong again with care and not become a troublesome invalid. My writing prospers, which is a great happiness to me, and opens a brighter prospect than I have ever had in my life before, but everything depends on my health.
I do not understand your allusion to Isaac's having said that he had received no answer from me. I have always answered punctually every letter that required answering. But the postal communication hither and back again is terribly slow -- only twice a week.
You have not sent me your address, so that I am reduced to the magnificent vagueness of [Leamington] as a direction. I hope you are the only Mrs. Henry Houghton there.
Once more, dear Fanny thank you for writing to me and taking some of the load off my heart. It has been a heavy load indeed, but I do not like to write useless words about such things.
With kindest remembrances to Henry, I am always, dear Fanny,
Your affectionate sister
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Alexander Main, London, 28 December 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Alexander Main, London, 28 December 1871
Text: Main's copy owned by Mr. John R. Sprunt. Mostly published: Cross, New Edition, pp. 480-481.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 28. 71.
Dear Mr. Main
Your gift -- what gift can be more precious than the patient care which helps to save the seed of one's soul from perishing? -- has come 428 to brighten a Christmas in which my large share of good has been somewhat dimmed by bad health. One of the memorable events of this closing year to me will always be the acquisition of you as a known friend -- a friend of the only sort I now desire much to acquire: one who takes into his own life the spiritual outcome of mine. Let it be a memorable year to you in this light -- that you have given me a lasting source of encouragement in those often-recurring hours of despondency which, after cramping my activity ever since I began to write, continue still to beset me with, I fear, a malign influence on my writing. I don't suppose I could assure you of anything better for you to know, than that you have planted something to be a sweet shade and fruit for your elder fellow-traveller.
I have been looking through the [Sayings] with that sort of delight which comes from seeing that another mind underlines the words one has most cared for in writing them.
In one sense the book is marvellously new to me -- since I had forgotten the greater part of what I had written. In another sense it is rather startlingly familiar -- namely, that I find my old self (meaning my past self) very much like my present self. If there is any progress, I fear it is downhill.
I think that I have not yet seen any passage which I am sorry not to have had left out, and I have confidence that I shall not be less completely satisfied with the selecting mind when I have made further acquaintance with the work. Always with gratitude
Yours most sincerely,
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: William R. Shedden-Rals^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William R. Shedden-Ralston, London, 4 April 1878
MS: Pennsylvania State University.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 4. 78.
My dear Mr. Ralston
We knew of your illness while you were still laid low in Paris, and were so far comforted about you as to learn that you had a mother's tendance. 435 We saw the announcement of your return, and though I remembered well your pretty project about Switzerland and did not like thinking that you had been obliged to renounce it, I hoped and imagined that your health was restored. It is a sad disappointment to learn that you are still a sufferer -- and from a complaint which we too, between us, have had enough bodily hints of, to experience a lively fellow-feeling with a friend who is more severely afflicted.
It is some relief for you that you are able to write, but I feel that your days must be trying -- I hope the nights are less so.
Your letter is a welcome assurance at least that you believe in our caring about any good or evil that befals you, and we are both heartily wishing that we may soon hear of the good after this smart visitation of evil.
Always, dear Mr. Ralston,
Yours very truly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: William Macilwaine^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Macilwaine, London, 30 July 1868
Text: Cross, New Edition, p. 433.
The author of [The Spanish Gypsy] begs to thank the Rev. W. MacIlwaine 798 for the care he has kindly shown in sending her a list of errata, which would have been acknowledged long ago but for her absence on the Continent.
Some of the passages marked by Mr MacIlwaine for revision were deliberately-chosen irregularities, but others are real oversights in the correction of the press. These will be thankfully attended to in the immediate reprint, and the suggestion of them is the more acceptable because the author is at present unable to give the work any close revision.
George Eliot adheres strongly to the principles, -- 1, That metrical time must be frequently determined in despite of syllable-counting; and 2, That redundant lines are a power in blank verse. But the principles may be true, while her particular application of them is often mistaken. She hopes always to keep in mind that distinction between strong theory and feeble practice.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Macilwaine, London, 10 August 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: William Macilwaine^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Macilwaine, London, 10 August 1868
Text: Cross, New Edition, pp. 433-434.
From one of the poems which you have kindly sent me, I gather that you knew intimately the late Dr Craik, 804 who was also one of Mr Lewes's earliest and most revered friends. Those who have such a reverence in common are not quite strangers.
I am sincerely obliged to you for your expressions of sympathy, which are the more valuable to me now that I know them to have come from one of long experience.
I assure you I shall not cease carefully to study the great medium of verse, bearing in mind, however, that what are called laws in the "art which nature makes" 805 were at one time undiscovered possibilities, and that some such possibilities may yet lie in store for watchful spirits.
It seems to me that Milton wrote his grand verse partly in virtue of such hopeful watching -- such listening for new melodies and harmonies with instructed ears. He is very daring, and often shocks the weaklings who think that verse is sing-song.
Believe me, my dear sir, gratefully and sincerely yours
[M. E. Lewes.]

GE to William Cross, Witley, 18 September 1880
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
September 18. 80.
Dear Brother
Why will you not come and see us? You are dreadfully proud. Johnnie goes to town on Monday, but on Tuesday he will be at home. Can you not come to lunch and dinner? And then we will take you a glorious drive -- always supposing that the rain will allow us. If Tuesday should be a wet day, take another.
We are grateful to Florence for warning us about the woman in the Chelsea house. I too had smelt the gin, and we had been wondering how soon Anna could spare the trustworthy old servant whom she had recommended to us as a temporary housekeeper. Gin-drinking seems an inevitable attribute of women who are [put in] to take care of houses.
You and Florence will perhaps be too busy about the future house to spare the day for lawn tennis. But if not, you can arrange with Johnnie when you come here. Love to Florence.
Your affectionate Sister
M. A. Cross.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
August 9. 78.
My dear Mr. William
I think that the specimen page of [The Spanish Gypsy] is quite satisfactory. As to the [Jubal] volume, there will, I hope be added matter enough to save you from difficulty as to the size. I should like to see the proofs.
Your saying that the printing is being [pushed on] alarms me lest the corrected copy of [Daniel Deronda] which I send by today's post should be at all too late. I could have sent it four months ago, but I thought it better to reserve it till it was actually wanted, lest there might be any mislaying. I also send a corrected copy of [Jubal,] to be printed from.
It is important that the corrections in [Deronda] should be carried out perfectly, since this edition is to last, and I shall be much obliged to you if you will send me word whether my corrected copy has arrived in time.
I assure you, we find your execution of von Moltke's business very zealous and punctual. Mr. Lewes, with his usual indulgence, insists on answering the letters of which I get the benefit, but you must believe in my tacit sense of obligation.
Yours always truly
M. E. Lewes.

GE to William Blackwood, Witley, 3 September 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: Cross, III, 376-377.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
September 3. 79.
My dear Mr. William
I am much obliged to you for writing me your letter of pleasant news. It is wonderful how Theophrastus goes on selling in these bad times, and I have only to hope in addition that the buyers will be the better for it. Apparently we shall get through this last edition before Christmas, and then perhaps you will think of adding the volume to the Cabinet edition.
I am especially rejoiced to hear that your Uncle is better again, and I trust that Strathtyrum is sharing our sunshine which will be the best cure for him as for me. I am getting strong and also am gaining flesh on my moderate scale.
It really makes a difference to one's spirits to think that the harvest may now possibly be got in without utter ruin to the produce and unhappy producers. But this year will certainly prove a serious epoch and initiate many changes in relation to farming. I fear from what I have read that the rich Lothians will have to be called compassionately the poor Lothians. 314
By the way, if you happen to want any translation done from the French and have not just the right person to do it, I think I can recommend a Miss Bradley Jenkins of 50 Cornwall Road, Westbourne Park, as one who has an unusually competent knowledge of French. We sat side by side on the same form translating Miss Edgeworth into French when we were girls. I have not seen her for many years, but I know that she has been engaged in a high order of teaching and I have lately heard from her that she is anxious to get work of the kind in question. She already spoke French well when we were pupils together, and she has since been an unintermitting student. But who has work sufficient for all candidates?
I wonder, talking of translators, how the young Mr. Ferrier is going on -- who translated Kaufmann's pamphlet on Deronda. What Mr. Blackwood told me of him interested me about his future.
Oblige us all by not falling into another accident when the next hunting season comes and believe me
Yours very sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights | Witley | October 18. 77.
My dear Mr. William
It was pleasant to see your nice handwriting again. Thanks for the copy of the subscription list, which seems encouraging.
The parcel of (4) copies 747 is come, and I am well satisfied with the sobriety and clear lettering of the volume. The compact form is very welcome to me for my own behoof. Naturally, we did not bring copies of my own books in our small cargo, and I have often been wanting a "Deronda".
We are rather sorry to think that we shall be in the murky air of town again on the 30th., the air here entering into one's consciousness as some mysterious source of good spirits. I hope you will happen to be on a visit to England next year during the time of our [villeggiatura,] so that you may come and see our beautiful bit of country.
On the 25th we move from this house to leave the servants time for emptying it of our [bits o] things' and getting them in order in their old places at the Priory. So that after the 25th proofs or anything else should be addressed to me in London.
Yes, we are having delicious autumnal skies -- a sharp air, though, and our share of the storms blowing off our tiles with a thunderous sound that made us imagine the chimney was falling.
I hope that, in spite of the unkind season in the North, you have been having some pleasant holidays. But I imagine that the sort of holiday you care most for begins in November.

Thank you for sending me the new specimens of type. I think with you that the sharper faced No. I. is very elegant, but Mr. Lewes declares decidedly and strongly for No. II -- the type of the Cabinet prose, and I would rather abide by his preference than have the smaller gratification of pleasing myself.
For the volume of miscellaneous poems, there will be (retaining the present page of 20 lines) enough additional matter to make the volume about 300 pages, 121 which I see from the volumes of [Scenes of Clerical Life] will be a suitable size to run with the other works.
Do not write on purpose, but when you have to write to me again, pray tell me as nearly as you can when you shall want the additional pages for the Jubal volume.
We have certainly to pay for all our other happiness, which is a Benjamin's share, 122 by many small bodily miseries. Mr. Lewes continues ailing and I am keeping him company with bilious headache. [Rejoice, O young man, in the days of thy youth], 123 and keep a reserve of strength for the more evil days. Especially avoid breaking your neck in hunting. Mr. Lewes did once try horseback some years ago, but found the exercise too violent for him. I think a Highland Sheltie would be the suitable nag, only he is very fond of walking, and between that and tennis he tires himself sufficiently.
I shall hope by and by to hear more good news about your uncle's health.
Ever yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Blackwood, Witley, 12 June 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, Witley, 12 June 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Published: Cross, III, 365-367.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
June 12. 79.
My dear Mr. William
I was beginning, with my usual apprehensiveness, to fear that you had no good news to tell me, since I did not hear from you. And I should have gone on fearing till tomorrow morning if I had not happened to drive to Godalming and ask for the second post. We only get one post a day at the benighted Witley, so that if you want me to get a letter quickly it must be posted early at Edinburgh.
I am heartily glad to know that the invalid is going on well and I trust that the softer air we are having now will help him forward.
Theophrastus seems to be really welcomed by the public though not by the Athenaeum, 270 the only paper I see besides the Times. But I think I have known other books succeed in impressing the public without the sanction of that "literary organ."
Mr. Blackwood will be amused to hear that one gentleman told Charles, or implied, that Theophrastus was a higher order of book and more difficult to write than a novel. Wait long enough, and every form of opinion will turn up. However poor Theophrastus is certainly not composed of [chips] any more than my other books.
Another amusing bit of news is that the other day Mrs. Pattison sent me an extract from the Livret of the Paris Salon, describing a picture painted by a French artist from [the Lifted Veil] and representing the moment when the resuscitated woman, fixing her eyes on her mistress, accuses her of having poisoned her husband. I call this amusing -- I ought rather to have said typical of the relation my books generally have with the French mind.
Thank you for sending me the list of orders. It does interest me to see the various country demands. I hope the movement will continue to cheer us all, and you are sure to let me know everything that is pleasant, so I do not need to ask for that kindness.
The weather is decidedly warmer and Tuesday was a perfectly glorious day. But rain and storm have never let us rest long together. I am not very bright and am ready to interpret everything in the saddest sense, but I have no definite ailment.
My best regards to the convalescent who I have no doubt will write to me when he is able to do so. But I am only one of many who will be glad to hear from him. Believe me
Always yours truly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Blackwood, Witley, [July 1877]
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, Witley, [July 1877]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extract published: John Blackwood, p. 398.
The Heights, | Witley | Godalming.
My dear Mr. William
It was a very harmless breach you committed in opening my American letter, which happens to be one that I should have liked you to read. A young lady of New York 733 expresses much gratitude for being saved, by reading Daniel Deronda, from marrying a man whom she could not love, but whom she was disposed to accept for the sake of his wealth, but she is so far from being absorbed by this momentous personal matter that she goes on to be still more effusive about the [enjoyment and instruction] she has had from the Jewish elements in the book, and thinks the scene on the Bridge the best in the book -- [flashing through one with a sort of electric sympathy] etc. Tell your uncle that America is the quarter of the world for "appreciative butter."
We were not very expansive on business when he was with us, but I think we settled what was needful in two questions and answers. First, we agreed that the 7/6 ed. of Deronda had better be deferred till Autumn, and secondly, that it would be well to carry out the last-approved conception of a complete edition of the works (7/6 per vol., novels 2 vols. each).
But it would also be well, before anything irrevocable is done, that Mr. Simpson should just write me word of the general plan. For in looking over the list of volumes designed, with Mr. Blackwood in London, we made a supposition as to the division of the shorter works, which may have been forgotten, and unfortunately I have not brought down the paper of statements about which we were consulting.
I also agreed with Mr. Blackwood that Romola should be included in the 3/6 edition, as well as in the 7/6.
I fear we tired your uncle with too long a drive over our hills, which are like a bit of Scotland dropped into the midst of Southern pastures and hedgerows. I am glad to hear that he enjoyed the day nevertheless -- as we did. Perhaps if we keep this spot, you too will run the risk of being tired in the same way. Mr. Lewes unites with me in best regards.
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
I have corrected copies of [The Lifted Veil] and [Brother Jacob] which I will send when they are needed.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Blackwood, Wandsworth, 24 August 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, Wandsworth, 24 August 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | August 24. 60.
My dear Major Blackwood
A week ago Mr. John Blackwood sent me word that you were about to begin the printing of a cheaper edition of "The Mill," and that I could make any alterations, if I chose. There is only one I want to make, but as it is on p. 50 of the 1st volume it is very likely too late for me to mention it. Instead of "close by the brink of the Ripple," at line 11 I wish to be read, "at the other end of the Mill Fields." 616
Mr. John Blackwood, at the same time, gave us the hope that we should see you at the end of this month. I hope we shall not be disappointed.
Two people who see literary society have teazed me with questions about the sale of the Mill, as if they had not noticed the advertisement: I wish the lettering of the advertisement could be managed so as to prevent this sort of ignorance, or rather of ignoring. Will you be kind enough to suggest this to Mr. Simpson's typographical judgment? I am naturally jealous for "The Mill," which is my youngest child, and don't like that those who depreciate it themselves should suppose that everybody else shares their partialities.
This is really saddening weather -- is it not? -- with the harvest time so close at hand.
Ever yours truly
Marian E. Lewes.
Major Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, Wandsworth, 16 February 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | February 16. 60.
My dear Major Blackwood
It is very pleasant to know that you like my old-fashioned Dodsons. The comedy inevitably diminishes as the lives of Tom and Maggie advance, but I suppose no book without its share of tragedy ever took a strong hold on the public mind.
Looking into the Clerical Scenes, the other day, I found an awkward misprint at p. 95. volume II: "prepare an oration," for "prepare an ovation." 480 Will you be so kind as to ask Mr. Simpson to note this, for the benefit of the printers?
Mudie seems to be beginning a small warfare against us, as I dare-say you have heard from Mr. Langford. 481 There had need be some authors and publishers strong enough to resist his tyranny, which threatens to thrust poor books down the throats of the public, and to strangle good ones. I remain, my dear Major,
Yours very truly
Marian Evans Lewes.
Major Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 7 May 1866
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 7. 66.
My dear Sir
Thanks for your kind letter which came with the proofs last week. If I were capable of being much cheered just now, your expressions of interest in Felix Holt would contribute to the effect. But I am in that state of utter distrust and anxiety about my work which is usually the painful accompaniment of authorship with me until the last word of the last page has been written. Still it does gratify me to learn that your uncle, Mr. John Blackwood has thorough satisfaction in the renewal of our business relations which have always been made doubly agreeable to me by high regard for him.
Will you be so good as to say to Mr. Simpson for me that I believe I have underlined the brief bits of epistolary correspondence in the first and second volumes as if they were to be printed in italics after the fashion of the old novels. But this is undesirable now that people are unaccustomed to it, and therefore I will beg him to let the printer know that he need not notice my interlineations. 456
Today, just before we left Dorking I got the letters from Sir A. Alison and Mr. J. Hill Burton, 457 which Mr. John Blackwood had enclosed for me, and am much obliged to him for making the inquiries. I remain, my dear Sir
Yours very truly
M. E. Lewes.
William Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 6 August 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 6. 68.
My dear Sir
Thanks for your letter and for the list of sales. I suppose it is too late now to hesitate about the reprint, but on seeing the reduced sales of the last fortnight and learning that there are still 70 copies on hand, I am inclined to think that we might have done without any more of the dear edition, since the return of the publishing session is not so very far off, and the publication of a cheap edition will be desirable. However, Mr. Lewes is possibly right in his judgment -- one can hardly say more about any judgment in the matter of book-sales -- and 250 is a prudent number.
Mr. Lewes is at Oxford among all the Dons of physic who are assembled there. He went by most courteous invitation and writes me word this morning that his visit is full of interest. 801
It is not possible for you, without the useless pains of examining closely, to conceive the silliness of many things that are said by reviewers who are in the helpless condition of judging without a precedent. They fling about phrases about the caesura etc. with a marvellous foolhardiness -- very much as if a man were to try and make gibberish pass for Greek without inquiring beforehand if any one of the company happened to know that ancient tongue. 802
I can imagine the glory of being on the great moors with an unbroken sky above you. Perhaps you are sharing the rain which is falling vigorously this morning, and may introduce a time of less unrelenting heat.
We saw a gentleman so like you when we were abroad that Mr. Lewes and I both exclaimed at the same moment -- "Mr. William Blackwood!" I hope he is not a double who will bring you into unmerited disgrace.
Always yours truly
M. E. Lewes.
The demand for the graver sort of books (not novels) is often so slowly continuous, that perhaps we may fairly hope a quiet ratio to go on through the next months.

Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 5 November 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
November 5. 61.
My dear Sir
I am very much obliged to you for relieving me from all possibility of anxiety about my corrected copies. Of course, after the fashion of authors, I hold my manuscript to be among those precious things peculiarly liable to casualties in this perverse world.
Your uncle gives us a pleasant picture of his enjoyment in being once again with his brother and playmate, Major Archibald Blackwood. There are few things sweeter than these revivals of early memories. I hope we shall know something of the same sort with our boys, if they ever go far away from us.
Apropos of boys, we are sincerely obliged to you for thinking of Thornie at all, and only hope he will not bore you. Young gentlemen of seventeen have often immense resources for boring their elders. 866
Mr. Lewes, I am glad to tell you, keeps up his improved health and enjoys the mornings over his desk. I have not yet got clear of the effects of a wretched cold, which is a common trouble to London people just now; and either the cold, or a keener perception of fact, makes me feel myself one of the most stupid people in existence -- which is not agreeable, as long as one's resignation is not perfect. 867
I want to get well, that we may go and see Fechter in Othello, a wish you will understand, if you saw him in Hamlet when you were in London.
Mr. Lewes unites with me in kind regards.
Ever yours truly
M. E. Lewes.

May 5. 80.
My dear Mr. William

Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 4 November 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, 21 North Bank | November 4. 79.
My dear Mr. Blackwood
I have delayed writing to you again because, intensely occupied as you must be, I was unwilling to make one more correspondent whose letter you would have to open.
Thank you for sending me the [Scotsman.] The article it gave on my dear lost Friend does credit to the management of the paper. The articles in the [Times] and [Athenaeum] were also good. I am continually thinking of the blank that is made for you both in your personal and public life, and of the anxiety you must be undergoing as to the way in which your Uncle's important work can be carried on, your own time having been quite sufficiently absorbed hitherto, I imagine, by your own department of duties.
I write now about the question of the [Sayings], because I think that by doing so I may save you the trouble of writing a letter. The plan of a supplementary volume seems to me objectionable and not likely to answer. I have been examining the actual volume, and it seems to be capable of sufficient compression by substituting a thinner paper -- still fine and tinted, but as thin, for example, as that of Matthew Arnold's Selections from Wordsworth, which form quite a small volume though of only 100 fewer pages than the [Sayings]. 341 And the addition of Sayings from Daniel Deronda and Theophrastus Such ought not to be considerable. Pray prune any too great exuberance in this supplementary selection. With this alteration of paper, the new volume would probably not be so thick and heavy even as the present edition. 342
If you concur in my proposition do not think it necessary to write specially in order to tell me so. I want not to occasion you trouble but would save you from it.
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

GE to William Blackwood, London, 31 December 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 31. 79.
My dear Mr. William
I think there is no objection to your giving the desired permission to Professor Meiklejohn, on the condition mentioned -- namely that the extracts should be few and not exceeding six pages. Dr. Abbott and Professor Seeley introduced (with my permission) several well-chosen extracts in their [English Lessons,] and I think that such indications from scholarly and tasteful men are really useful to the works from which they are taken.
Our weather here during Christmas week was hideous, purgatorial. I am a little less well perhaps in consequence of our long sunlessness and want of clear air, but the ailment is only slight.
Yes, I trust that the coming year may bring us both reasons for contentment in our life even though it is hardly possible that it should be otherwise than anxious and fraught with effort. This world is not one in which any but the quite youthful can be without regretful memories and importunate forebodings. But we must muster our courage and, as much as we can, rejoice with those who have good reason for rejoicing. I feel very much for Mrs. Blackwood, knowing well that in proportion as she is not called on to act even in a mournful way, she must be more and more conscious of the change that has come over her life.
I shall be glad to hear when you have got well through the horrible [valuation] and other brambly passages.
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

GE to William Blackwood, London, 3 May 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 3. 79.
My dear Mr. William
A very handsome translated edition of my works sent me from Holland is, I see, published by Van Druten. Hence he is a man to deal with. The difficulty is to know whether he and Bohn of Haarlem want the early sheets for the same purpose or purposes, in which case I suppose it would not be according to usage in Holland to send early sheets to both. If Van Druten wants to translate and Bohn to reprint, it would clearly be well to accept B's offer and send terms to Van Druten. 232 I suppose that Bohn knows the size and character of the book, since he makes an offer without inquiring. I see that I had £40 from Holland for Deronda, so that £20 for Theophrastus would be in handsome proportion.
You will have received my letter enclosing one from Tauchnitz this morning. If you and Mr. Blackwood think that any offer for a continental edition is to be entertained, the offer should be a very handsome one. Published at this time the German reprint would have a great sale among the wandering English, and I should think you send a certain number of a new book to Germany and Switzerland, for we found foreigners taking in even so expensive a book as the English edition of Deronda.
We have a cruel wind here with the sunshine, and I get endless headache. I hope you are all more fortunate.
Always yours truly
M. E. Lewes.
I should be glad to see the cover and lettering.

GE to William Blackwood, London, 24 September 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: Cross, III, 58-60.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 24. 68.
My dear Sir
Your letter gave an additional gusto to my tea and toast this morning. The greater confidence of the trade in subscribing for the 2d edition 814 is on several grounds a satisfactory indication, but, as you observe, we shall be still better pleased to know that the copies are not slumbering on the counters but having an active life in the hands of readers.
I am now going carefully through the poem for the sake of correction.
I have read it through once and have at present found some ten or twelve small alterations to be added to those already made. But I shall go through it again more than once, for I wish to be able to put "revised" to the third edition, and to leave nothing that my conscience is not ready to swear by. I think it will be desirable for me to see proofs. It is possible in many closely consecutive readings not to see errors which strike one immediately on taking up the pages after a good long interval.
We are feeling much obliged for a copy of Kinglake, which I am reading aloud to Mr. Lewes as a part of our evening's entertainment and edification, beginning again from the beginning.
You are less fortunate than we are, if your fine weather has departed. This week we have had perfect autumnal days, though last week when we were in Yorkshire we also thought that the time of outside chills and inside fires was beginning. We do not often see a place which is a good foil for London, but certainly Leeds is in a lower circle of the great-town-Inferno.
Always yours truly
M. E. Lewes.
If there were no good reason against it, I should like the colour of the next edition of the S. G. to be changed for a deep mellow red, 815 like Munro's Lucretius 816 or Col. Hamley's "Operations of War."

November 22. 61.
My dear Sir
I think the advertisement and specimen pages are perfect. 870 The utmost simplicity is the only thing that is distingu'e9 in these days. There is only one thing that I shrink from on my own behalf more than from a puff -- namely, a preface in which the author informs the public either that they have not done justice to his work or else that they are very praiseworthy for admiring it.

Marian E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Blackwood, London, 20 October 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 20 October 1871
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 20. 71.
My dear Mr. William
I had just been thinking that this morning I would at last write to thank you for your kind letter and inquiries, when there came to us the sad announcement of your loss. 382 I do not like to think how many family losses your uncle Mr. John Blackwood has had to go through even since I have known him -- though indeed our acquaintance now stretches over fifteen years. We have been reflecting that probably the end in this case may have seemed less sudden to you than to us, who had not heard of any change since the first recovery.
Ever since death was in our own house we have become much more sensitive to like trials befalling our friends -- knowing how much deeper they cut, especially in those who are no longer young, than any outward show implies.
I have been in the receipt of all sorts of kindness for the last month without making any sign of gratitude, and I am getting strong enough to be rather ashamed. Your letter did me all the more good because you considerately desired me not to answer it on paper; but I gave it a long answer in my head. I cannot boast of great vigour yet, but I am able to take up my writing with more or less effect every morning.
Mr. Lewes unites with me in begging you to offer to Mr. Blackwood, and to accept yourself, our earnest sympathy and regard. Believe me always
Yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
William Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Blackwood, London, 2 October [1867]
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 2 October [1867]
MS: National Library of Scotland, 3112, fol. 300. Endorsed: 1867. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Wednesday. October 2.
My dear Sir
I wonder what you have been thinking of me all these weeks during which your letter has lain here unopened, and your kind present of grouse unacknowledged! I hope that your charity has suggested some shadow of the fact, namely, that I have been in the depths of Germany whither my letters have not followed me. I really felt ashamed of writing to your uncle to tell him that we were running away again in search of health, but I have sometimes felt fidgetty lest some letter should come from Edinburgh, which required an answer. Our son opens Mr. Lewes's letters, but leaves mine unopened, only describing their physiognomy to me when they seem likely to be of importance.
Your kind intention in sending the grouse was not wholly frustrated, for our cook sent them to Mr. Lewes's mother, an old lady of eighty who still enjoys a bit of game more than all other eating. And it is also very pleasant to me on my return to find that you had thought of me.
I went abroad rather unwillingly but Sir Henry Holland said travel was the right thing for Mr. Lewes's dyspepsia, so I submitted to that raison majeure. We revisited with great delight some spots where we had been thirteen years before, but the unsettled life has sadly hindered some work that I should like to carry on uninterruptedly. But pray tell your uncle from me that I have nevertheless made some progress since he was here. My easily disturbed health makes me wofully dependent on outward conditions for my power of working -- the mere presence of pen, ink, and paper will not suffice for me.
We reached home only last night, and I found some rather amusing requests awaiting me, from unknown correspondents. One asks me what terms she should propose to a publisher for the novel she is writing, and a young lady at school in Scotland sends me some of her school exercises to read, that I may deliver my opinion on her powers!
I conclude that you are at Edinburgh again by this time, and I hope you have laid in a stock of robustness for the winter. Mr. Lewes unites with me in kindest regards and I am
Always yours truly
M. E. Lewes.

GE to William Blackwood, London, 18 March 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21 North Bank | March 18. 79.
My dear Mr. William
I trust you will not interpret it as a sign of slight regard if I ask you to communicate with me by letter only at present. I have not yet received any friend male or female -- except three gentlemen who are helping me to carry out a plan I have at heart. 198 You will think this weakness -- and so it is. This week for the first time I am going to see a lady friend, 199 but people have been so good to me, my obligations for their kindly expressed sympathy are so mountainous, that I am afraid to break my silence and my solitude lest by showing gratitude to some I should seem ungrateful to others.
Will you kindly send me the specimens you mention? -- and since you write letters with so much ease and clearness, will you send me a note of any suggestions for my guidance?
Would it not be desirable to defer the publication till October?
I like to think that you walk now without pain or difficulty. You have had a long and trying discipline.
Shall you remain in London more than a week?
Always sincerely yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 17 December 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 17. 79.
My dear Mr. William
The M.S. of Theophrastus came yesterday afternoon in its beautiful fragrant binding which corresponds with the Deronda and Middlemarch. I feel very much your kind attention to this matter among your many cares and am greatly obliged to you.
General Hamley came to see me last Sunday and while we were alone we began to talk of you and your present responsibilities, but before we had ended our talk some one else came in. 348 He is only one of the many excellent friends you possess, whose sympathy is likely to be practically useful. Among the good auguries I should desire for Maga would be the avoidance of easily written criticism -- a writing about and about, in place of giving an account of books. I think that mere criticism unless it be of the very highest order is the least beneficent of all writing, stimulating the practice of ignorant lazy judgment apart from any genuine impression. Excuse this gratuitous delivery of opinion. I am led to it by my constant conviction that the perpetual swallowing of criticism instead of knowledge is the curse of the time -- no better than the Tartar fashion of swallowing a paper prescription instead of curative juices.
Thank you for mentioning that Mrs. John Blackwood is a little better. I am wonderfully well, considering the sharp transitions of the weather. I hope you will keep strong and be able to send me good news of yourself.
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 15 May 1879
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 15. 79.
My dear Mr. William
I am grieved to hear of Mr. Blackwood's new attack. Pray tell me how he goes on.
Since Theophrastus is sure to be translated when the copyright expires
(I speak from observation and experience of the German appetite for translating) we may as well allow it to be translated now. Dr. Lehmann gave Mr. Lewes £20 for the right to translate "Actors and Acting." Mr. Lewes purposely put that price on the right as high enough to hinder the translation which he did not care to have made. Hence I should think £25 would be a fair enough sum -- if Mr. Blackwood and you do not judge otherwise. Paetel gave me £100 for translation of Deronda, but I see Duncker only gave £30 for the translation of Middlemarch. Of course, the publisher having to pay the translator as well as other expenses, he cannot afford anything like what should be given for the right of reprinting. I wish to be reasonable in all things, but the reading of my books has spread greatly in Germany of late years, and you know that there is no effective reduction of prices to the public in consequence of one's asking less than a publisher or translator is willing to give.
I see the Dutchman Van Druten gave me £25 for the translation of Middlemarch but £40 for the translation of Deronda. Certainly £10 for the one volume of Theophrastus is not out of proportion to those prices. But I don't mind about it. It might be as well to accept it, unless there were a chance of a better offer after the appearance of the Book. Just as you think wise. I suppose Harper is to send at once the £50 promised in advance. 237
The covers are just come by a later post. I choose the grey with the gilt centre. But I think that the stamping on the underside should be also black, with a black centre. 238 The stamping on this grey cloth shows no shadow and looks poor without the black. I see one of the other covers has a centre on both sides, and looks the better for it. The lettering is very good.
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

My dear Sir
I am delighted to get the fresh proof this morning, and the assurance that I need not be fidgetty about occupying type. 778

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 14 February 1880
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 14. 80.
My dear Mr. William
I am much obliged to you for the account and the accompanying cheque which have come to me this morning. Our letters crossed, you perceive, and I feel as if I ought to apologize for having asked you to order me a copy of the new [Sayings] now that I see you had spontaneously done so. I thought it quite natural that the matter should not have occurred to you. I like the colour of the cover, and the volume is not at all clumsy.
The sales seem to me very satisfactory, and I think we have reason to be glad that the Cabinet edition was undertaken. But the scheme of the account is not quite so clear to me as usual -- at least my stupidity has not yet made out the total number distributed, as distinguished from the number on which Royalty is paid. 373 It is interesting to me to compare each year with the preceding in this particular of distribution, quite apart from money. I have no doubt that all would be clear enough if my head were clearer, so do not trouble about the matter. I had a simple statement of sales sent me with a letter from your dear Uncle on the 15th of July.
The prosperity of our editions in the last year is the more marked because of the general depression of trade. I hope for the world's sake and not for ours only that this year will be one of less calamity.
I shall expect with much interest a visit from Mr. Langford on his return to town. Please give my kind regards to him and believe me
Always yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 14 December 1880
MS: National Library of Scotland.
Cheyne Walk, | Chelsea, S.W.
December 14. 1880.
My dear Mr. William
I thank you with much feeling for sending me the well-judged volume in memory of your dear Uncle. 562 I have read through it this morning, and I should not have believed beforehand that a selection of Obituary Notices would give me so much satisfaction. They are sober and truthful and, I imagine, only inexact in some minor details. It is really to the credit of our press that such a volume would be a trustworthy authority to a writer who wished to give a full history of our literature and its personnel in the last quarter of a century.
My experience and affection say a hearty amen to all the praise of your Uncle's character contained in this volume. I feel that his death was an irreparable loss to my mental life, for nowhere else is it possible that I can find the same long-tried genuineness of sympathy and unmixed impartial gladness in anything I might happen to do well. To have had a publisher who was in the fullest sense of the word a gentleman and at the same time a man of excellent moral judgment, has been an invaluable stimulus and comfort to me. Your Uncle had retained that fruit of experience which makes a man of the world as opposed to the narrow man of literature. He judged well of writing because he had learned to judge well of men and things, not merely through quickness of observation and insight, but with the illumination of a heart in the right place -- a thorough integrity and rare tenderness of feeling.
When you write to me again I should be very glad to hear news about your Uncle's family, especially his son. I finish hurriedly in order to send this to the post.
Yours always sincerely,
M. A. Cross.

GE to William Blackwood, London, 13 January 1880
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 13. 80.
My dear Mr. William
I am very much obliged to you for your letter enclosing a cheque for £400, being the remainder of the sum finally awarded to me for the 4 editions of [Theophrastus Such.] But your punctuality makes me more anxious than I should have been on my own account that the 97 copies still on hand should be completely disposed of. I will be hopeful, however, since the public seems well disposed towards me. Mr. Langford told me that 1000 volumes of the cheap edition had been sold since New Year's Day. This is encouraging for us.
I must also thank you for the handsome present of Burton's [History of Queen Anne] 363 which came last night. It is a book that I desired to possess. I admire the getting up greatly. And it was very good of you to send me the little title-page -- but I no longer care for the scraps of my writing. It was my other lost self that cared for them. It would have been a pity, though, that the MSS of Theophrastus should have been missing from the row of Russia backs, for Mr. Lewes had set his mind on their going after our death to the British Museum. 364
The demon of Influenza was particularly spiteful to fasten on you, who so much need health and strength just now. But if you live in the sunlessness that we are enduring here it is no wonder you cannot be well. I have escaped marvellously hitherto with no more serious suffering than headache and depression. But there have been many mornings in which I have written and read by candlelight -- indeed whole days which have thus been turned into night.
Yes, I shall be rejoiced to hear that the valuation has been well got through and that your mind is lightened of that load. It was a satisfaction to know that Mr. Langford had undertaken the task, for I knew that you preferred his doing so.
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 12. 79.
My dear Mr. William
I will accept Tauchnitz's offer (£50.) if your Uncle sees no objection. It is not, I suppose, much out of proportion to the £250 he gave me for Deronda. As to what happened about Romola, it is quite irrelevant to the present state of things. And, as you observe, the hinge of the question is the sale of the cheap reprint to the travelling English -- also, I think your Uncle mentioned the export to India.
I wish, of course, to do what will be commercially the wisest, and as you have a knowledge of such relations which is not accessible to me, I must ask you to assist me with your judgment. One would not reject fifty pounds and the advantage it represents of additional distributions among Continental readers without solid reasons. But it would certainly be less objectionable to have a cheap reprint appearing in October than now, just when people are looking forward to their summer journeying.
It is still very cold here, though bright, and I am putting off going to Witley till next week.
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, London, 11 March 1868
MS: National Library of Scotland. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 11. 68.
My dear Sir
The Revise reached me quite safely yesterday. The specimen pages look very handsome, and the length of 28 lines will prevent undue thickness in the volume.
It is necessary to have patience in the printing of a poem, which is properly subjected to a more frequent and fastidious revision than a prose work. I think I am less troublesome than I hear of other authors being with regard to proofs and alterations, and the printing off of these earlier sheets at present is very much to be deprecated. Mr. Lytton 725 had a whole volume of poems in print by him to metamorphose as he chose, a long while before he published. But I shall certainly not linger unduly, and the sooner I can have the proof of the second batch of M.S. (which Mr. John Blackwood told me he had forwarded to Edinbro') 726 the better will be my advance, for when I see what I have done as a whole, I am helped to conclusive determinations. Now I have no copy (beyond fragments) of the M.S. in your hands. I do not remember having made any serious accusation against the printers: I only laughed at the drollery of some mistakes, such as "doff all your I sir."
We are going to the coast next week to try and get some health for me and some zoologizing for Mr. Lewes, who desires his kind remembrances to be offered to you. His "hunting" begins, you see, when yours ends.
Always sincerely yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Blackwood, Florence, 27 May 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, Florence, 27 May 1860
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: Cross, II, 230-231.
Florence | May 27. 60.
My dear Major Blackwood
I am much obliged to you for writing at once, and so scattering some clouds which had gathered over my mind in consequence of an indication or two in Mr. John Blackwood's previous letter. The "Times" article arrived on Sunday. It is written in a generous spirit, and with so high a degree of intelligence, that I am rather alarmed lest the misapprehensions it exhibits should be due to my defective presentation, rather than to any failure on the part of the critic. I have certainly fulfilled my intention very badly if I have made the Dodson honesty appear "mean and uninteresting," or made the payment of one's debts appear a contemptible virtue in comparison with any sort of "Bohemian" qualities. So far as my own feeling and intention are concerned, no one class of persons or form of character is held up to reprobation or to exclusive admiration. Tom is painted with as much love and pity as Maggie, and I am so far from hating the Dodsons myself, that I am rather aghast to find them ticketed with such very ugly adjectives.
We intend to leave this place on Friday (3d) and in four days after that we shall be at Venice -- in a few days from that time, at Milan -- and then, by a route at present uncertain, at Berne, where we take up Mr. Lewes's eldest boy, to bring him home with us. We can hardly manage all this before quite the end of the month, and I should like to receive a letter from Edinburgh at Berne (Poste Restante). In the unlikely case of any important reason for writing soon, Milan would be the address that would find me by the 'ab14th or earlier'bb 12th.
We were both very glad to hear your favourable report about the "Physiology," and I am happy to tell you that the author's personal physiology is also in a more promising condition than when I last wrote. We are particularly happy in our weather, which is unvaryingly fine without excessive heat. There has been a crescendo of enjoyment in our travels, for Florence, from its relation to the history of modern art, has roused a keener interest in us even than Rome, and has stimulated me to entertain rather an ambitious project, which I mean to be a secret from every one but you and Mr. John Blackwood.
By the by, Mr. Lewes, before we left home, requested Mr. Langford to send a copy of "The Mill on the Floss" to Holly Lodge. The last report we heard was, that the copy had not arrived. Will you be so kind as to repeat the request on our behalf? Possibly Mr. Langford may have thought our absence a reason for not sending books; but we have left a friend there who is anxious to read the book, and will have no other means of getting it.
Any news of the "Clerical Scenes" in its third edition? Or has its appearance been deferred? The smallest details are acceptable to ignorant travellers. We are wondering what was the last good article in "Blackwood," and whether Thackeray has gathered up his slack reins in the "Cornhill." Literature travels slowly even to this Italian Athens. Hawthorne's book 550 is not to be found here yet in the Tauchnitz edition!
Mr. Lewes unites with me in kind regards, and I am always
Yours very truly
Marian Evans Lewes.
Major Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, [Wandsworth], 6 May 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: Cross, II, 107-108.
May 6. 59.
My dear Major Blackwood
I enclose a correction for the two-volume edition of "Adam" -- which I unhappily forgot until this morning.
You must not think me too soft-hearted when I tell you that it would make me uneasy to leave Mr. Anders without an assurance that his apology is accepted. "Who with repentance is not satisfied" 130 etc. -- that doctrine is bad for the sinning, but good for those sinned against. Will you oblige me by allowing a clerk to write something to this effect, in the name of the firm? -- "We are requested by George Eliot to state, in reply to your letter of the 16th, that he accepts your assurance that the publication of your letter to the Reviewer of "Adam Bede" in the "Times" was unintentional on your part."
Thank you for telling me the drift of the "Leader's" folly. I feared it might be something demanding a denial.
Yes -- I am assured now that "Adam Bede" was worth writing -- worth living through long years to write. But now it seems impossible to me that I shall ever write anything so good and true again. I have arrived at faith in the past, but not at faith in the future.
A friend in Algiers has found me out -- will "go to the stake on the assertion that I wrote Adam Bede" -- simply on the evidence of a few extracts. So far as I know, this is the first case of detection on purely internal evidence. But the secret is safe in that quarter.
I hope I shall have the pleasure of seeing you again during some visit that you will pay to town before very long. It would do me good to have you shake me by the hand as the ascertained
George Eliot.
Major Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, [Wandsworth], 6 June 1859
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: Cross, II, 111-112.
June 6. 59.
My dear Major Blackwood
I shall be much obliged to you if you will accept for me this amended offer on Tauchnitz' part. 144
The "Liggins business" does annoy me, because it subjects you and Mr. John Blackwood to the reception of insulting letters and the trouble of writing contradictions. Otherwise, the whole affair is really a subject for a Moli'e8re-comedy -- "The wise men of Warwickshire," who might supersede the "Wise men of Gotham."
The letter you sent me was a very pleasant one from Mrs. Gaskell, saying that since she came up to town she has had the compliment paid her of being suspected to have written "Adam Bede." "I have hitherto denied it: but really I think, that as you want to keep your real name a secret, it would be very pleasant for me to blush acquiescence." "Will you give me leave?" I hope the inaccuracy with which she writes my name is not characteristic of a genius for fiction, though I once heard a German account for the bad spelling in Goethe's early letters by saying that it was "genial" -- their word for whatsoever is characteristic of genius.
Yours very sincerely
George Eliot.
Major Blackwood.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Blackwood, [Richmond,] 4 February 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, [Richmond,] 4 February 1857
MS: National Library of Scotland. Extracts published: Cross, I, 429-430, as to John Blackwood.
February 4. 57.
My dear Sir
Thank you for your last kind letter, fulfilling your promise to let me know something of the criticisms passed on my story. I have a very moderate respect for "opinions of the press," but the private opinions of intelligent people may be valuable to me.
In reference to artistic presentation, much adverse opinion will of course arise from a dislike to the order of art rather than from a critical estimate of the execution. Any one who detests the Dutch school in general will hardly appreciate fairly the merits of a particular Dutch painting. 790 And against this sort of condemnation, one must steel oneself as one best can. But objections which point out to me any vice of manner or any failure in producing an intended effect will be really profitable. For example, I suppose my scientific illustrations must be a fault, since they seem to have obtruded themselves disagreeably on 'absome'bb one of my readers. But if it be a sin to be at once a man of science and a writer of fiction, I can declare my perfect innocence on that head, my scientific knowledge being as superficial as that of the most "practised writers."
I hope to send you a second story in a few days, but I am rather behind-hand this time, having been prevented from setting to work for some weeks by other business; and having, since then, been retarded by a bilious attack -- surely one of the worst among the [calamities of authors.]
I shall be glad to know if people think the better of [Amos] from reading it to the end -- and even if they think the worse, it will be better for me to know it.
Whatever may be the success of my stories, I shall be resolute in preserving my incognito, having observed that a nom de plume secures all the advantages without the disagreeables of reputation. Perhaps, therefore, it will be well to give you my prospective name, as a tub to throw to the whale in case of curious inquiries, and accordingly I subscribe myself, best and most sympathizing of editors,
Yours very truly,
George Eliot.
W. Blackwood Esq.
Lewes is very encouraging, and has heard good reports, but perhaps he will tell you of them, as he said he was going to write to you.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to William Blackwood, [Richmond, 4 January 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: William Blackwood^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Blackwood, [Richmond, 4 January 1857]
MS: National Library of Scotland. Endorsed: January 1857. Mostly published: Cross, 1, 427-428, as to John Blackwood, to whose letter of 29 December 1856 it is a reply.
My dear Sir
Your letter has proved to me that the generous editor and publisher -- generous both in word and in deed -- who makes the author's path smooth and easy, is something more than a pleasant tradition. I am very sensitive to the merits of cheques for fifty guineas, but I am still more sensitive to that cordial appreciation which is a guarantee to me that my work was worth doing for its own sake.
If the "Scenes of Clerical Life" should be republished, I have no doubt we shall find it easy to arrange the terms. In the meantime, the most pressing business is, to make them worth republishing.
I think the particularization of the children in the deathbed scene has an important effect on the imagination. But I have removed all names from the [Conclusion,] except those of Patty and Dickey, in whom, I hope, the reader has a personal interest.
I hope to send you the second story 781 by the beginning of February. It will lie, for the most part, among quite different scenes and persons from the last -- opening in Shepperton once more, but presently moving away to a distant spot and new people, whom, I hope, you will not like less than Amos and his friends. But if any one of the succeeding stories should seem to you unsuitable to the pages of Maga, it can be reserved for publication in the future volume, without creating any difficulty.
Thanking you very warmly for the hearty acceptance you have given to my first story, I remain, my dear Sir,
Yours very truly,
The Author of Amos Barton.
W. Blackwood Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: William Allingham^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Allingham, Witley, 26 August [1877]
MS: Parrish Collection, Princeton. Published: Cross, III, 313-314.
The Heights, | Witley, | Godalming | August 26.
Dear Mr. Allingham
I hope that this letter will not find you at the old address but that it may be sent on to you in some delicious nook where your dear wife is by your side preparing to make us all richer with store of new sketches.
I almost fear that I am implying unbecoming claims in asking you to send me a word or two of news about your twofold -- nay fourfold self. But you must excuse in me a presumption which is simply a feeling of spiritual kinship bred by reading in the volume you gave me before we left town. 738 That tremendous tramp -- "Life, Death; Life, Death," makes me care the more, as age makes it the more audible to me, for those younger ones who are keeping step behind me.
It is a burthen to write notes, but let us bear it in turn. With affectionate remembrances to your wife,
Always yours truly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: William Allingham^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to William Allingham, London, 8 March 1877
MS: Privately owned. Published: Cross, III, 303-305.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 8. 77.
Dear Mr. Allingham
Mr. Lewes feels himself innocent of dialect in general and of Midland d[ialect] in especial. Hence I presume to take your reference on the subject 618 as if it had been addressed to me. I was born and bred in Warwickshire, and heard the Leicestershire, North Staffordshire and Derbyshire dialects during visits made in my childhood and youth.
These last are represented (mildly) in [Adam Bede.] The Warwickshire talk is broader and has characteristics which it shares with other Mercian districts.
Moreover dialect, like other living things, tends to become mongrel, especially in a central fertile and manufacturing region attractive of migration: and hence the Midland talk presents less interesting relics of elder grammar than the more northerly dialects.
Perhaps unless a poet has a dialect ringing in his ears, so as to shape his metre and rhymes according to it at one jet, it is better to be content with a few suggestive touches, and I fear that the stupid public is not half grateful for studies in dialect beyond such suggestions. I have made a few notes, which may perhaps be not unacceptable to you, in the absence of more accomplished aid.
We hope soon to hear that Mrs. Allingham is as flourishing as Baby.
Mr. Lewes is pretty well again, and for the last fortnight I have been taking his place as the household invalid.
Yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
The vowel always a double sound -- the y sometimes present, sometimes not: either a'e4l or ya'e4l. Hither not heard except in C' moother addressed to horses.
Thou never heard. In general the 2d pers. sing. not used in W. except occasionally to young members of a family and then always in the form of thee i.e. 'ee. Can't pron. Cawn't. For the emphatic nominative Yo, like the Lancashire. For the accusative Yer, without any sound of the r.
Not year but 'ear. On the other hand with the usual [compensation] head is pronounced yead.
"A gallows little chap as e'er yer see."
Heres to yer, Ma'e4ster. Sa'e4me to yo.
Never V.
The demonstrative those never heard among the common people (unless when caught by infection from the parson etc.).
Self pron. Sen.
The f never heard in of, nor the n in in.
Perhaps, however, these imperfect indications may only determine you to reject all but the faintest signs of dialect in your well-to-do farmers who have been to London.

GE to William Allingham, London, 13 February 1877
MS: Yale. Published: Letters to William Allingham, ed. H. Allingham and E. Baumer Williams, 1911, pp. 177-178.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 13. 77.
Dear Mr. Allingham
I don't know how far Mrs. Allingham may be able to think of business just now, so I address you on a subject which directly concerns her, that you may communicate or reserve it according to circumstances.
Mr. Blackwood is going to include [Romola] in the cheap edition of my books (Smith and Elder having only the right to continue its publication in the one format which they have finally chosen), and as that edition has unhappily made for itself the precedent of [illustrations] it is needful to get for [Romola] two drawings from the story and a vignette for the title-page, in correspondence with the other volumes.
I mentioned to Mr. Blackwood my wish that, if it were possible, the desired drawings should be executed by Mrs. Allingham, and he has asked me to ascertain for him whether she can consent to undertake this minor work and also whether her professional charges would come within the publisher's economical calculations for a 3/6 book.
If Mrs. Allingham wished to avoid the subjects chosen by Mr. Leighton, I trust that it would not be impossible to find two additional scenes sufficiently pictorial. Miss Martineau 607 I believe made a pretty thing out of Romola finding little Lillo on the sunshiny pavement. But her picture was not memorable enough to make a reason against repeating the subject.
However, on all these points Mrs. Allingham is the only proper judge, if she chooses to trouble herself about the matter. There is no immediate hurry for the drawings, as the book has to be printed.
We are full of sympathy with you under that exasperating affair of the [Echo.] 608 It is certainly worse to have letters forged for one than opinions. But this latter injury happens to people every week. The other, I should have thought, might be brought under the head of libel by a sufficiently ingenious judge.
Always yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Walter W. Skeat, London, [1872?]
Dublin Core:Subject: Walter W. Skeat^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Walter W. Skeat, London, [1872?]
Text: English Dialect Society, A Bibliographical List, Part I, London, 1873, p. viii. 72
It must be borne in mind that my inclination to be as close as I could to the rendering of dialect, both in words and spelling, was constantly checked by the artistic duty of being generally intelligible. But for that check, I should have given a stronger colour to the dialogue in "Adam Bede," which is modelled on the talk of N. Staffordshire and the neighbouring part of Derbyshire. The spelling, being determined by my own ear alone, was necessarily a matter of anxiety, for it would be as possible to quarrel about it as about the spelling of Oriental names.
The district imagined as the scene of "Silas Marner" is in N. Warwickshire. But here, and in all my other presentations of English life, except "Adam Bede," it has been my intention to give the general physiognomy rather than a close portraiture of the provincial speech as I have heard it in the Midland or Mercian region. It is a just demand that art should keep clear of such specialities as would make it a puzzle for the larger part of its public; still, one is not bound to respect the lazy obtuseness or snobbish ignorance of people who do not care to know more of their native tongue than the vocabulary of the drawing-room and the newspaper.

Christmas Day.
My dear Vivian,
Your Uncle and I were both very much pleased to have the pretty cards by which you conveyed your good wishes to us. Rosa Cottage | Gorey | Jersey | June 13. 1857.
My dear Sir
I have just received your letter written to me by my brother's request, and I willingly reply to it at once by a statement of the facts concerning which you desire information; the more so, because I anticipated the probability of my having to correspond with you as joint Trustee under my Father's Will.
My brother has judged wisely in begging you to communicate with me. If his feelings towards me are unfriendly, there is no necessity for his paining himself by any direct intercourse with me; indeed, if he had written to me in a tone which I could not recognize (since I am not conscious of having done him any injury) I must myself have employed a third person as a correspondent.
Mr. Lewes is a well-known writer, author among other things, of the [Life of Goethe] and the Biographical History of Philosophy. Our marriage is not a legal one, though it is regarded by us both as a sacred bond. He is at present unable to contract a legal marriage, because, though long deprived of his first wife by her misconduct, he is not legally divorced.
I have been his wife and have borne his name for nearly three years; a fact which has been known to all my personal friends except the members of my own family, from whom I have withheld it because, knowing that their views of life differ in many respects from my own, I wished not to give them unnecessary pain. Other considerations, however, have at length determined me to inform them of my circumstances and of the responsibilities for life, which I have undertaken.
It may be desirable to mention to you that I am not dependent on any one, the larger part of my income for several years having been derived from my own constant labour as a writer. You will perceive, therefore, that in my conduct towards my own family I have not been guided by any motives of self-interest, since I have been neither in the reception nor the expectation of the slightest favour from them.
Mr. Lewes, as I have already stated, has an account at the Union Bank of London, Charing Cross Branch, 4 Pall Mall East. I have requested that any money due to me may be paid to his account there, because, as we are frequently out of England and away from town, the transmission of cheques is attended with much inconvenience. I presume that I have a legal right to appoint the payment of interest due to me to any person I may choose to name. But if there is any point necessary to be taken into consideration, which I have overlooked or of which I am ignorant, you will be good enough to set me right.
I have satisfaction in communicating with you in this case, rather than with anyone else, not only because you kindly undertook, from friendship to my Father, to become my trustee, but because I learned from him that it was owing to your considerate suggestion that some provision was made for me during the first year after my Father's death. 901 I daresay you have forgotten the circumstances, but I have always remembered gratefully that instance of thoughtfulness on my behalf, and am glad to have an opportunity of acknowledging it. I remain, my dear Sir,
Yours very faithfully,
Marian Lewes.
Vincent Holbeche Esq.,
