Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 21 May [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 21 May [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Extracts published: Cross, II, 110-111.
Holly Lodge | May 21.
Dear Sara,
That is a very charming plan -- for you to have country lodgings near us. I think it is possible you might get them at Wimbledon, which is within half an hour's delicious walk of us. I don't think there is a single case of "Apartments to let" in South Fields: I should be more sorry for that, if I thought the quarter would suit you for the railway; but it is a fatiguing ugly walk to the Wandsworth station from us -- we always go to Putney, when we can. It would not do to write and ask the Congreves about letting you their house for a week. Mr. Congreve is not at all a man to be free and easy with: he internally resents everything like a freedom, looking very benignant all the while.
I see the Rehearsal takes place on the 18th, so I suppose you will not want your lodgings till the last week in June? When does the bon'e2 fide festival 138 begin? The Wimbledon lodgings could not be taken long beforehand, I dare say, but we will look round the village and see and inquire. The Wimbledon station lies conveniently, and I fancy you will be at Sydenham in 5 or 10 minutes from it. Wouldn't that be just the thing? I'm so glad the Festival happens just at the time we shall be at home again. We are waiting now for some business interviews, and then, after next week, when we may reasonably hope that it will not be still raining, we are going for a long country ramble by the river side.
I lay in bed with wet towels on my head yesterday while Mr. Lewes spelt out your letter to me. This morning I am brisk again. You see, we take it in turns to be ailing and nurse each other -- so our life is pleasantly varied. You all seem to be well in health, and that is more than the half of happiness, in spite of "wenches" and printers. Dr. Chapman writes that he saw Mr. Bray the other day looking "wonderfully well," -- certainly an enviable mode of exciting the world's wonder.
But I do enter into Cara's worry all the more, because I shall hardly find it in my heart to rejoice in the Wimbledon lodgings or anything else, if she fails to come. I should like to see her once more on this side Jordan, and as I am not likely ever to visit Coventry again, her flight hither is my only chance. It is surely nearly six years since I saw her!
We don't think of going to the Festival, not for want of power to enjoy Handel -- there are few things that I care for more in the way of music than his choruses performed by a grand orchestra -- but because we are neither of us fit to encounter the physical exertion and inconveniences. Are there any reserved seats at the Festival -- i.e. any purchasable by us canaille? We are going on Wednesday evening to hear Acis and Galatea 139 -- our first attempt at a musical treat since we came back to England. It is a cruel thing, the difficulty and dearness of getting any music in England -- concerted music, which is the only music I care for much now. At Dresden we could hear thoroughly enjoyable instrumental music every evening for two-pence, and I owed so many thoughts and inspirations of feeling to that stimulus.
Mr. Lewes's Physiology of Common Life has sold 7000 a number already, which is a great encouragement and happiness to him, and he has had pleasant letters from people thanking him for it. Such things, even when mitigated by dyspepsia, make life worth living.
Let us know anything that we can do for you, in the way of getting lodgings -- or in any other way. Affectionate feelings to you all from
Yours always
Marian E. Lewes.
Have you an autograph of Dr. Elizabeth Blackwell's? I think it worth keeping for those who keep any.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 2 July 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 2 July 1860
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 256-257.
Holly Lodge, S. Fields | Wandsworth | July 2. 60.
My dear Sara
I opened your letters and parcel 569 a little after one o'clock on Sunday morning, for that was the unseasonable hour of our return from our long, long journey. Yesterday was almost entirely employed in feeling very weary indeed, but this morning we are attacking the heap of small duties that always lie before one after a long absence.
It is pleasant to see your book fairly finished after all delays and anxieties -- but I will say nothing to you about that, until I have read it. I shall read it the first thing, before plunging into a course of study which will take me into a different region of thought.
I was almost surprized to see you date from Ivy Cottage, for by some blundering process of thought (our thoughts about others are always more or less a continuous blundering) I had got it into my head that you would all be settled at Sydenham. 570 I hope the letting of the house is in every way a fulfilment of Mr. Bray's intentions and wishes, which I had wrongly interpreted. I should have liked to hear some more decidedly cheerful news about material affairs -- houses etc. -- but in default of that I throw all my feeling into joy at Cara's satisfaction that she has done a useful piece of work, and gets a kind recognition as the doer. 571
We have had an unspeakably delightful journey -- one of those journies that seem to divide one's life in two by the new ideas they suggest and the new veins of interest they open. The sweep of our travels was wider than we had ventured to plan beforehand: over the Mont Cenis to Genoa, first; then by sea to Rome, where we stayed exactly a month; then by sea to Naples, which, with Paestum, Amalfi and Sorrento, kept us a fortnight; back again by sea to Florence, and, after another fortnight spent there, to Venice by way of Bologna, Ferrara and Padua. After Venice we considered ourselves merely on our way home, but the way has been a slow one, for we set out from Venice on the thirteenth. We took Verona, Milan and Como, on our route over the Splugen to Zurich, where we staid for a physiological day with Professor Moleschott, and went on to Bern and Hofwyl with parental purposes, of course; bringing away our eldest boy Charles, who has a downy lip and chin and a back broader than his father's. From Berne we went to Geneva and spent two days with my old kind friends the D'Alberts -- a real pleasure to me, especially as Mr. Lewes was delighted with "Maman," as I used to call Mde. D'Albert. She is as bright and upright as ever: the ten years have only whitened her hair, a change which makes her face all the softer in colouring.
We have lived in entire innocence of newspapers since we have been away, so that a letter from Mrs. Bodichon telling us of her father's death two months ago is only one of the many changes that we have to learn. We had not even known the state of the weather in England until we met a family at Milan who had just come across the Alps. Until we left Venice we had had unbroken sunshine for six weeks: the clouds and rain that had been almost constant during our stay in Rome kindly said goodby to us at Naples where fine weather is quite indispensable to enjoyment. In Rome there is so much to be seen under roofs, that bad days pass over unregarded.
Mr. Lewes was not at all well when we set out, and continued ailing for many weeks, but he is as well now as people with feeble digestion can expect to be.
I have given you this bare matter-of-fact history, because your imagination will make out a more truthful picture with that skeleton or nude figure once correctly drawn. For the rest of my mind is too full of cares and duties of a serious prosaic kind for me to be very expansive just now.
Unchanging love and sympathy in all good and evil fortune to all three friends, from their sincerely affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 19 February 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 19 February 1859
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1860. Extracts published: Cross, II, 82-84.
Holly Lodge | South Fields | Wandsworth | February 19. 59.
Dear Sara
Your letter was doubly pleasant after the long cessation of such batches of interesting gossip. You have the art of writing just the sort of letters I care for -- sincere letters, like your own talk.
We are tolerably settled now, except that we have only a temporary servant, and I shall not be quite at ease until I have a trustworthy woman who will manage without incessant dogging. We have the hope of getting the phoenix we want next week. 21
Our house is very comfortable -- with far more of vulgar indulgences in it than I ever expected to have again; but you must not imagine it a snug place, just peeping above the holly bushes. Imagine it, rather, as a tall cake, with a low garnish of holly and laurel. There was a house after my own heart at Mortlake, which we were kept in suspense about for some weeks -- a place where I should have liked to think of living and dying; but it turned out at last to have a premium affixed to the lease, which made it too expensive for prudence. As it is we are very well off, with glorious breezy walks and wide horizons, well-ventilated rooms and abundant water. If I allowed myself to have any longings beyond what is given, they would be for a nook quite in the country, far away from Palaces crystal or otherwise, with an orchard behind me full of old trees and rough grass, and hedgerow paths among the endless fields where you meet nobody. We talk of such things sometimes along with old age and dim faculties and a small independence to save us from writing drivel for dishonest money. In the meantime the business of life shuts us up within the environs of London and within sight of human advancement, which I should be so very glad to believe in without seeing.
Among my household cares I have had time to think now and then of your book 22 which has been giving you so much happy labour, and to imagine you reading it to the reticent John Sibree -- terribly chary of praise that could commit himself. But who that reads the newspapers would desire praise when they can get criticism? Every fool gets praise: the little real criticism there is in the world is given only to the writers capable of making an impression.
I was sorry to see that rather tradeswoman-like advertisement of Isa Craig 23 as a writer in the Eng[lish] Woman's Journal, and a poem "in our present number which we are proud to include in our paper," and wished when I read it that Bessie had a hypercritical friend at her elbow. As to the Ode on Burns, I thought it very creditable as a bit of prize poetry, but the principle of prize poetry is so bad that nothing of a high character can be expected to come out of it. I should think Isa Craig, as an industrious energetic young woman, is much more admirable than her poetry.
Pretty Arabella Goddard 24 we heard play at Berlin -- play the very things you heard as a bonne bouche at the last -- none the less delightful from being so unlike the piano-playing of Liszt and Clara Schumann whom we had heard at Weimar, both great, and one the greatest.
Thank you for sending me that authentic word about Miss Nightingale. I wonder if she would rather rest from her blessed labours or live to go on working. Sometimes, when I read of the death of some great, sensitive human being, I have a triumph in the sense that they are at rest, and yet along with that, such deep sadness at the thought that the rare nature is gone for ever into darkness and we can never know that our love and reverence can reach him, that I seem to have gone through a personal sorrow when I shut the book and go to bed. I felt in that way the other night when I finished the Life of Scott aloud to Mr. Lewes. He had never read the book before, and has been deeply stirred by the picture of Scott's character -- his energy and steady work, his grand fortitude under calamity, and the spirit of strict honour to which he sacrificed his declining life. He loves Scott now as well as I do. 25
Mr. Lewes thanks you for sending the story of the Pholax, 26 not the less because he knew it before, being frightfully "up" in that kind of information.
Give my love to Mr. Bray and thank him for his letter which told me what I wanted to know. He surely has been close to our present home, for I believe Mr. Richard Congreve 27 lives near us -- how near I am not quite sure, but he was mentioned to us by our landlord as a gentleman who visited with no one in the neighbourhood -- which eccentric course we had declared our intention of following. Amusingly enough, said landlord, Captain Rivers, and his wife, had begun to recommend the place by saying, "We visit with every one about here, and there are very pleasant soir'e9es." Oh! we exclaimed, in horror, "Pray tell '91every one'92 that we don't visit and don't desire to be called on." Whereupon Mr. Richard Congreve was cited as an encouraging proof that we might be as isolated as we desired. He takes pupils, however, and I should imagine is not in the interesting state of destitution that Mr. Bray's enthusiastic sympathy gave us the idea of. We have met a pleasant-faced, bright-glancing man whom we set down to be worthy of the name Richard Congreve. I am curious to see if our ahnung will be verified.
No more at present, except love to Cara, and all blessings to all, from the heart of
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 16 June 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 16 June 1859
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | June 16. 59.
Dear Sara
I made almost sure of a letter from you this morning telling me at least where you would lodge at Sydenham -- but no letter is come.
I don't want to be a troublesome friend, too urgent with my propositions; but if you would like to see me, I am anxious you should understand that I will leave nothing undone on my part to further our meeting under the most propitious circumstances. I only wish we had so little business and so many bedrooms that you could have made our house your home.
If you approve, and, having lodgings at Sydenham, would let us know where they are, we should set off by an early train on Monday, reach Sydenham at 10.20, and spend the time with you in the gardens or elsewhere till we took our places. And I hope I need hardly say, that any time you could give me at our own house, away from more attractive pleasures, would be a welcome treat to me. Mr. Lewes waits to carry my letter to the post. I hope it will be in time to catch you before you set off. But I think your disinclination to letter writing must be getting to the point of serious disease.
Ever yours
Marian. 160

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 15 August [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Extracts published: Cross, II, 128-129.
Holly Lodge | August 15.
Dear Sara
I see nothing at all objectionable of a personal kind now, either in the notes or the text. 253 Print is a great help to one's power of judgment.
I showed Mr. Lewes the note in which you speak directly of your Brother, 254 and he sees nothing that is likely to create objection in the substance though he thought the expression a little awkward. I think you might possibly see some improvement to be made in the sentence I have marked as "not quite clear": obscurity very often lies in the reader's apprehension chiefly, but the slowest of apprehensions is the best criterion for a writer to judge himself by. I have re-read the whole proof, and feel that every serious reader will be impressed with the indications of real truth-seeking and heart-experience in the tone. The style seems to me laboured, and laborious to read, but I dare say when you are farther from the shore you will handle the oar more easily. Beginnings are always troublesome, "misy pantos" as Bulwer would say 255 (I like to follow great models). Even Macaulay's few pages of introduction to his "Introduction" in the English History are the worst bit of writing in the book. I don't mention the style in the spirit or with the pretensions of a critic, but because a remark of that kind is often a useful suggestion in correcting the press. It was no trouble to me to read, so don't talk as if it had been.
Ever yours
Marian.
I don't know specially what is Feuerbach's title, but in a case of personal address, you couldn't be wrong in calling him Doctor. Every German calls everybody Doctor "till further notice."

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 14 November [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Extract published: Cross, II, 141-142.
Holly Lodge | Monday, November 14.
Dear Sara
I sent you word of Mrs. Gaskell's letter to remove from your mind any unpleasant impression you might have of her from my cursory mention of her in a previous letter -- not to re-open the subject of people's sayings and doings about me, which I wish to be closed forever. Don't, please, tell me more at any time, of what Miss Martineau or any one else has said or done about me. 384
The Liggins affair is concluded, so far as any action of ours is concerned, since Mr. Quirk (the inmost citadel, I presume) has surrendered, by writing an apology to Blackwood, saying he now believes he was imposed on by Mr. Liggins. As to Miss Martineau, I respect her so much as an authoress, and have so pleasant a recollection of her as a hostess for three days, that I wish that distant impression from herself and her writing to be disturbed as little as possible by more personal details. Anything she may do or say or feel concerning me personally is a matter of entire indifference: I share her bitterness with a large number of far more blameless people than myself.
It can be of no possible benefit to me or any one else that I should know more of these things, either past, present or to come. "I do owe no man anything" 385 except to write honestly and religiously what comes from my inward promptings, and the freer I am kept from all knowledge of that comparatively small circle who mingle personal regards or hatreds with their judgment or reception of my writings, the easier it will be to keep my motives free from all indirectness, and write truly.
So no more gossip of that sort, dear Sara; but as much as possible about yourselves.
But before eternal dismissal of Quirk and Co., perhaps I am bound to tell you, in answer to your inquiry, that the words of the letter you inquire about were these, and these only.
"My dear Sir,
(Enclosed is) or I enclose the copy of the letter. I hope Mr. Quirk is feeling a little gravel in his boots this morning. I am fond of Liggins, compared with Quirk.
Ever yours truly
George Eliot."
I don't know whether it belongs to the style of sarcasm that is felt to be cutting by authoresses in the north to call a man an "ass" -- but, you perceive, I cannot claim the credit of having adopted it.
Of course you will be careful not to let Miss Martineau infer that you have ever mentioned my affairs to her by any request of mine, or that, except to defend myself from imputations of baseness, as in the case of Mr. Bracebridge, I have ever taken the attitude of a claimant or plaintiff.
And now let the curtain drop, or at least let me go out of the theatre and hear no further report of what goes on there. Ever, dear Sara,
Your affectionate
Marian.
P.S. I think I never thanked you enough for the sensible, admirable letter you wrote to Miss Carter. 386

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 11 November 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 11 November 1859
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 140-141.
Holly Lodge | November 11th. 59.
Dear Sara
A very beautiful letter -- beautiful in feeling -- that I have received from Mrs. Gaskell today, prompts me to write to you and let you know how entirely she has freed herself from any imputation of being unwilling to accept the truth when it has once clearly presented itself as truth. Since she has known "on authority" that the two books are mine, she has re-read them, and has written to me apparently on the prompting they gave in that second reading. Very sweet and noble words they are, that she has written to me. I wanted you to know that good of her, and I can tell you along with it, that I am thinking of you the oftener because our sister-birthdays are so near. I hope yours will be marked by much satisfaction in the ending of your work -- which it will nearly date, will it not? But don't you force yourself to write to me unless you are inwardly moved to do it: this Blatt of mine needs no answer, and is only like the wafted kiss we are content to give when our friend's back is turned. Kind remembrances all round,
Ever thine
Pollian.
If you care to know, I can tell you, the article on Rousseau was Mr. Call's (in the Westminster). 381 Mr. Herbert Spencer dined with us a fortnight ago, on his return to London -- looking "spry" and cheery -- but not apparently nearer the obtainment of that Government post 382 which is to give him freedom for writing the eleven volumes at present imprisoned in his brain.
Yesterday, Mr. Dickens dined with us -- on his return from the country. That was a great pleasure to me: he is a man one can thoroughly enjoy talking to -- there is a strain of real seriousness along with his keenness and humour.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 10 October [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, 10 October [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Extracts published: Cross, II, 135-137.
Holly Lodge | October 10.
Dear Sara
It is pleasant to have to tell you that Mr. Bracebridge has been at last awakened to do the right thing. This morning came a letter 342 enclosing the following to me:
"Madam, I have much pleasure on receiving your declaration that" etc. etc., 343 "in replying that I frankly accept your declaration as the truth, and I shall repeat it, if the contrary is again asserted to me."
This is the first symptom we have had from him of common sense and of any acquaintance with what gentlemanly feeling demands. I am very thankful -- for it ends transactions with him.
Mr. Lewes is of so sensitive a temperament, and so used to feeling more angry and more glad on my behalf than his own, that he has been made, several mornings, quite unable to go on with his work by this irritating correspondence. It is all my fault, for if he didn't see in the first instance that I am completely upset by anything that arouses unloving emotions, he would never feel as he does about outer sayings and doings. No one is more indifferent than he is, to what is said about himself -- but when anything once takes hold of him he is as nervous as a fragile woman, and now that his health is so delicate he has to suffer a good while from what would otherwise be a transient agitation.
We are hoping to see Mr. Bray this week -- are we not right? Tell him he can't take us wrongly any day either at 1 o'clock, (lunch-time) or at half past 5 (dinner). I am much obliged to him for his good plan of sending the paragraph to various provincial papers. 344 No more about my business, let us hope, for a long while to come!
Haven't you almost done your printing?
The Congreves are settled at home again now -- blessing us with the sight of kind faces -- Mr. Congreve beginning his medical course. 345 With love all round
Ever thine
Marian.
Miss Hennell.
Delicious confusion of ideas! Mr. Lewes, walking in Wandsworth, saw a good woman cross over the street to speak to a blind man. She accosted him with, "Well, I knew you, though you are dark!"

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, [9 January 1860]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Jany 10. 1860. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Monday.
Dear Sara
Lord Macaulay is going to be buried, and bets are pending. "The bearings o' this remark lies in the applications on it." 454 For which wait until you have answered the following question. What book in all the world do you most long to possess -- of an expensive and less accessible sort? 455 Boswell's Johnson, or C. Lamb's Works, or all Tennyson, or Sir William Hamilton's Metaphysical Works, or Carpenter's Physiology, or Craik's Dictionary, or what? or what? or what?
Answer me quickly, but carefully -- on your conscience.
Ever thine
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, [5 December 1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, [5 December 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Dec. 6. 1859. Extracts published: Cross, II, 149-150.
Monday Evening.
Dear Sara
I'm glad you have had pleasure in the acting. In opposition to most people who love to read Shakspeare I like to see his plays acted better than any others: his great tragedies thrill me, let them be acted how they may. I think it is something like what I used to experience in old days in listening to uncultured preachers -- the emotions lay hold of one too strongly for one to care about the medium. Before all other plays I find myself cold and critical, seeing nothing but actors and "properties." When we were at Weymouth we went to the tiny theatre there to see the Hunchback, 429 for my especial instruction and amusement, since I had never seen that clap-trap drama. Such a Julia! a nurserymaid in dingy white satin. I like going to those little provincial theatres. One's heart streams out to the poor devils of actors who get so little clapping and will go home to so poor a supper.
Please to thank Mr. Bray for his letter, but remind him that he did not answer my question -- how much we owe for Bentley. When you write again, pray tell me: I don't like to have these things on my memory.
One of my pleasures lately has been hearing repeatedly from my Genevese friends, M. and Mde. d'Albert who were so good to me during my residence with them. M. d'Albert had read the "Scenes of Clerical Life" before he knew they were mine, and had been so much struck with them that he had wanted to translate them. One likes to feel old ties strengthened by fresh sympathies.
The Cornhill Magazine is going to lead off with great spirit, and promises to eclipse all the other new-born periodicals. Mr. Lewes is writing a series of papers for it -- "Studies in Animal Life" -- which are to be subsequently published as a book.
It is quite as well that your book should not be ready for publication just yet: February is a much better time than Christmas. I shall be one of your most eager readers -- for every book that comes from the heart of hearts does me good, and I quite share your faith that what you yourself feel so deeply and find so precious will find a home in some other minds.
Cara's anxiety lest her prime minister 430 should resign is a trial I can understand. I hope it implies that the home government has been going on smoothly of late. I wonder how Harriet is now. It is a long while since you told me anything about her -- indeed I think I have not heard at all whether she prospers in her independent lodgings. Not that I impose on you the task of writing letters to answer my dilettante questions. "Am I on a bed of roses?" I have four children to correspond with -- the three boys in Switzerland, and Emily at Lichfield. With love to Cara,
Ever your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, [30 December 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Dec. 30. 1859. Extracts published: Cross, II, 150-151.
Holly Lodge | Friday.
Dear Sara
I don't like Christmas to go by without sending you a greeting, though I have really nothing to say beyond that. We spent our Christmas day with the Congreves, shutting up our house and taking our servant and Pug with us -- and so we ate our Turkey and plum-pudding in very social joyous fashion with those charming friends. Mr. Bridges, 441 who was there, told us that Dr. Chapman's business is to be turned into a Limited Liability Cy; but I dare say you know all about that, and have been asked to take shares.
What a touching picture that is of Harriet with her friend! 442 -- giving her the bed and the best bits. I am sorry to hear about the change of lodgings, though, for I fear that will cause you extra anxieties.
I dare say, you are having young parties and inventing Christmas shows, which you do so well -- as befits a house where there is a blooming young face, in its early teens. We shall have our young face next Christmas -- and we are meditating a flight to Italy when my present work is done, as our last bit of vagrancy for a long, long while. We should only stay two months, doing nothing but absorb; and then we should return through Switzerland and bring Charlie home with us.
I don't think I have anything else to tell, except that we, being very happy, wish all mortals to be in like condition, and especially the mortals we know in the flesh. So you will understand that our hearts are saying "a happy new year to you" when you come down on Sunday morning. Human happiness is a web with many threads of pain [in] it -- that is always sub auditum. "Twist ye, twine ye, even so" etc. 443
Ever your faithful
Marian.

Thursday.

Your title is very good I think -- far better, "in Theology and Philosophy" than "Theological and Philosophical works." 347
"In," I think, is better than "on" -- more precise. Works on "ologies" do in strictness view the subjects as wholes -- whereas you refer chiefly to works which concern themselves with branches or departments of those "ologies" -- is it not so?
Very glad to have quite a definite prospect of seeing our friend. 348
Ever thine

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, [11 April 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Adam Bede. April 11. 1859. Extracts published: Cross, II, 99.
Holly Lodge | Saturday Evening.
Dear Sara
We are just come home from the Isle of Wight! Whither we rushed in desperation after Mr. Lewes had suffered days and days from a burning head and burning mouth -- the symptoms, as the doctors tell him, of debility and indigestion. He hoped that a sniff of the sea breezes, idleness and change of scene might serve as a better tonic than doctors' stuff, and they really seem to have done him good, though we have been absent only four days. 94
The very day you wrote we were driving in an open carriage from Ryde to the Sandrock Hotel 95 -- taking in a month's delight in the space of five hours. Such skies -- such songs of larks -- such beds of primroses!
I am quite well now -- set up by iron and quinine, and polished off by the sea-breeze. We are not yet quite settled with our new servant, but hope to be so in a few days.
Among the huge heap of letters lying ready for us tonight was one from Mrs. Call, saying Mr. Call is going to Hofwyl shortly -- to see and inquire, I imagine, before determining about Frank. Very wise.
What news of your new book? Not stagnating, I hope, under the languors of Spring. I have lost my young dislike of that season, and am as glad of it as the birds and plants are.
Mr. Lewes has read Adam Bede, and is as dithyrambic about it as others appear to be so I must refresh my soul with it now, as well as with the Spring tide. Mr. Liggins I remember as a vision of my childhood -- a tall black coated genteel young clergyman-in-embryo.
Ever thine
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Tunbridge Wells, [27 July 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 26. Hitherto unpublished.
Pelham House T. W. Wednesday.
Dear Sara
I hope you are enjoying repose in your nest after your flight. Any news of you and your fellow birds will be acceptable. I shall be glad to hear that Cara is well -- free from tooth and head ache -- and that Mr. Bray is happy in his editing etc. Is Harry come or coming back?
I am jolly; much the better for the air of this lovely place, which is growing into my affections. There is one of the prettiest of villages near here -- Southboro' -- with smooth-shaven green and wooded slopes and nothing ugly within sight or hearing.
I am rather longing for some sea-breezes however, and may run off to Hastings or St. Leonard's which lie temptingly in a line with the station here. The frightful expense of this place is one motive for leaving it. The Bournemouth party is gone to Stonehenge 350 this week.
With love to all, ever dear Sara
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Torquay, 22 March 1868
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 35.
Carclew | Torquay | S. Devon March 22. 68.
My dear Sara
I don't know whether you have ever seen Torquay. It is pretty, but not comparable to Ilfracombe, and like all other easily accessible sea-places it is sadly spoiled by wealth and fashion, which leave no secluded walks and tattoo all the hills with ugly patterns of roads and villagardens. Our selfishness does not adapt itself well to these on-comings of the Millennium. We came here for lack of courage to take a longer journey, and because we needed the certainty of finding comfortable accommodation. 729 And Mr. Lewes is very happy with a room quite consecrated to microscopy and dissection.
I was very glad to hear both from Miss Marshall and Mrs. Call that they thought you looking well and bright. And Cara seemed to have drunk at the fountain of Jouvence since her previous visit. So I think of you both very cheerfully, except that poor Harriet's increasing infirmities must be an increasing anxiety for you. I brought down Miss Collet's "Confession of Faith" 730 with me (by permission) and have been reading it with much interest, because of the evident desire to be truthful which inspires it all through. But I think she is wise to keep it in manuscript.
Mr. Morley asked Mr. Lewes to write on Darwin for the Fortnightly Review, so, having something that he wanted to say on Darwin and Darwinism, he is finishing two long articles on the subject: -- the first will appear in the next Fortnightly. 731
I am reading about savages and semi-savages, 732 and think that our religious oracles would do well to study savage ideas by a method of comparison with their own. Also I am studying that semi-savage poem, the Iliad. How enviable it is to be a classic. When a verse in the Iliad bears six different meanings and nobody knows which is the right, a commentator finds this equivocalness in itself admirable!
Farewell. You see, I had nothing to say, but I wished to make a sign that I had received your note.
Ever yours
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Tenby, 29 June 1856
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 408-410.
Bridge Street | Tenby | June 29. 56.
Dear Sara
Good, sweet thing for writing to me! My first impulse was to answer your letter forthwith, but on second thoughts it seemed wiser to wait until our arrival here, that you might know our address.
Yes, indeed; I do remember old Tenby days, and had set my heart on being in the very same house again. 717 We saw a ticket in the window and turned in, but alas! it had just been let. It is immensely smartened up, like the place generally, since those old times, and is proportionately less desirable for quiet people who have no flounces and do not subscribe to new churches. It looks -- I mean Tenby looks insignificant in picturesqueness after Ilfracombe, but the two objects that drew us hither, zoology and health, will flourish none the worse for the absence of tall precipices and many tinted rocks. The air is delicious -- soft but not sultry, and the sands and bathing such as are to be found nowhere else. St. Catherine's Rock with its caverns is our paradise. We go there with baskets, hammers and chisels, and jars and phials, and come home laden with spoils. Then there is Monkstone Point, where we mean to go and explore pools and crevices, and Caldy Island, where Gosse 718 tells us there are treasures to be found. Altogether, we are contented to have been driven away from Ilfracombe by the cold wind, since a new place is new experience, and Mr. Lewes has never been here before.
To me there is the additional pleasure -- half melancholy -- of recalling all the old impressions and comparing them with the new. I think of all dear Mr. Hennell's jokes -- the delicious one about Mr. Bray's nearly committed blunder of pouring the beer instead of the cream over his tart -- "Lor! how Cara would have caught it!", and his notion of economising by eating a double quantity of fowls "because they were so cheap." We went into the market yesterday, but the Fish-women with whom Mr. Bray was an especial favorite, are no longer there. The Fish market is moved to a subterranean place near the quay. Everywhere new houses and smarter shops -- everywhere signs that we are twelve years (or more?) older than when we all landed from the Bristol Packet, feeling rather naus'e9abondes, and thinking the town looked rather dingy. We arrived by coach from the Narberth Road station, but we got down at the White Lion, which I recognized, with its low windows and view of the quay. How nice it would be if some packet would land you all -- Mr. Bray and Cara, you and Nelly -- once more! I suppose Frank 719 too is of your family, though you have not mentioned him for a long while.
I understand your wish to have as much of Rosehill as possible this year, and I am so glad that you will associate a visit from Herbert Spencer with this last summer. I suppose he is with you now. 720 If so, give him my very evil regards, and tell him that because he has not written to us, we will diligently not tell him a great many things he would have liked to know. We have a project of going into St. Catherine's caverns with lanterns some night when the tide is low about 11, for the sake of seeing the zoophytes preparing for their midnight revels. The Actiniae, like other belles, put on their best faces on such occasions.
Two things we have lost by leaving Ilfracombe for which we have no compensation -- the little zoological curate, Mr. Tugwell, who is really one of the best specimens of the clergyman species I have seen, and the pleasure of having Miss Barbara Smith there for a week sketching the rocks and putting our love of them into the tangible form of a picture. 721 We are looking out now for Mr. Pigott in his yacht, and his amiable face 722 will make an agreeable variety on the sands.
Write me word how you enjoy your visit to Ravensbourne, 723 and in general, bear in mind that any little scrap of your writing is welcome.
I thought "Walden" (you mean "Life in the Woods" don't you?) a charming book, from its freshness and sincerity, as well as for its bits of description. 724 It is pleasant to think that Harriet Martineau can make so much of her last days. Her energy and her habit of useful work are admirable. It was a nice picture for me, too, to think of your soothing George Combe with music. 725 Best love to all.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Tenby, 29 July 1856
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Tenby, 29 July 1856
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 412.
Bridge Street | Tenby | July 29. 56.
Dear Sara
Glad to hear, at last, some news of your Essay 733 -- hoping to hear more and better by and bye. I didn't like to think that your labour would be thrown away except so far as it must do good to yourself by clearing up your ideas. Not that your ideas were muddy, but the last degree of clearness can only come by writing.
Mr. Chapman wrote me word that he had seen you and that you were looking "exceedingly well" which was the best augury to me that you would enjoy your visit. 734 And you do seem to have made good use of your time.
I have been so vexed that I have written twice without remembering to thank Mr. Bray for the Herald containing his sparkling description of the Fancy Ball. Give my love to him and tell him I hope it will be a long, long time before he is a "decayed gentleman" in any other than a purely metaphorical and dramatic sense.
Mr. Pigott is with us just now, 735 and we are meditating a nocturnal visit to St. Catherine's caves with him. Our visit to Tenby has been very useful zoologically, but we are not otherwise greatly in love with the place. It seems tame and vulgar after Ilfracombe.
Mr. Lewes has written a very nice paper (in my opinion) describing our "Seaside Studies," which is to appear in the August "Blackwood." 736 I don't think you see Blackwood, or it might amuse you.
Do you care about Monckton Milne's autograph? I send it you for the chance.
We are to be at 8 Park Shot, Richmond, on August 8th.
You see, I had nothing to say. But the penny post justifies letters with nothing in them. Love to Cara
Yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, St. Mary's, 27 March 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, St. Mary's, 27 March 1857
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
St. Mary's | Scilly Isles | March 27. 57.
Dear Sara
At last! After waiting all Wednesday with our things packed up, we were called at 6 yesterday morning, and went on board by the early sunlight, beautiful to see. I represent what followed by x x x x x x according to the approved method, and recommence my narrative at 1 o'clock p.m. when we landed under a bright midday sun -- the sea, blue as the Mediterranean, plashing quietly among little violet-coloured islands. St. Mary's is the largest of them -- just like what one fancies Ithaca. We expect at every turn to meet a priggish young Telemachus, only there is little chance of our "lifting up our hands to the richly prepared meal." 823 However, we have every comfort -- roomy, well furnished lodgings, a quiet accommodating landlady, who is moreover mistress of the Postoffice, and every prospect of finding what we came for -- zoophytes and molluscs and annelids -- for there are all sorts of coast, boulders and sands and creeks. The weather is delicious, and we are going out presently on our first expedition, armed with chisels and baskets. We enjoy the prospect of quiet work here immensely, and are not likely to move for the next month or five weeks. Send me a letter full of gossip -- all about family and house matters -- a picture of you all in the new home. I suppose you are in it by this time.
George is hurrying me to have done and get ready to go out, so no more to-day -- but another day, when we are quite experienced in Scilly life.
Ever your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, St. Mary's, 16 April [1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, St. Mary's, 16 April [1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1857. Extracts published: Cross, I, 441-442.
St. Mary's, Scilly | April 16.
Dear Sara
I was particularly pleased with that notice in the Athenaeum. 837 It is quite a white crow for their short reviews rarely give any idea of the character of a book, and moreover I feared, from their usual avoidance of theology, that they might not mention yours at all. But it was really a just and sensible account of the matter in hand, which is precisely the rarest thing to be met with in newspaper reviews. Better than all newspaper notice is what Harriet Martineau tells you about her nephew. Let that impression be made on four or five readers who live in the world, and the edition will soon be sold; which is a shorthand way of saying that you will have influenced many minds and achieved your greatest object in writing.
Looking back on your unanswered letter about "Design," I do not feel impelled to write anything on the subject. My remark on the paragraph in your book had a purely practical object -- that of calling attention to an obscurity arising, if not from the stupidity of the reasons, probably from an excessive curtness of exposition which you might remedy. I shudder at entering on such great subjects in letters; -- my idle brain wants lashing to work, like a negro, and will do nothing under a slighter stimulus.
You were quite right in your divination. Mr. Lewes does nothing for the Leader now he is away, and it is not a little relief to see no quarterlies and heaps of magazines insisting on being read in a hurry. Mr. Chapman has sent us the Westminster, but we have lent it to a rubicund surgeon 838 here, who has not yet returned it, and so are still in the dark on the "Law of Progress." 839 The number looks rather heavy, but there are at least two articles which can hardly fail to be valuable -- the German Theology, by Wilson, 840 and the "Law of Progress."
We are enjoying a retrogression to old-fashioned reading: -- George buries himself in big physiological books, German French and English, with broad pages spreading like a prairie, unbroken by paragraph or quotation; I rush on the slightest pretext to Sophocles and am as excited about blind old '8cdipus as any young lady can be about the latest hero with magnificent eyes. 841
But there is one new book we have been enjoying -- and so, I hope, have you. The "Life of Charlotte Bronte"! Deeply affecting throughout: -- in the early part romantic, poetic as one of her own novels; in the later years tragic, especially to those who know what sickness is. Mrs. Gaskell has done her work admirably, both in the industry and care with which she has gathered and selected her material, and in the feeling with which she has presented it. There is one exception, however, which I regret very much. She sets down Branwell's conduct entirely to remorse, and the falseness of that position weakens the effect of her philippics against the woman who hurried on his utter fall. 842 Remorse may make sad work with a man, but it would not make such a life as
Branwell's was in the last three or four years unless the the germs of vice had sprouted and shot up long before, as it seems clear they had in him. What a tragedy -- that picture of the old father and the three sisters, trembling day and night in terror at the possible deeds of this drunken brutal son and brother! That is the part of the life which affects me most. 843
I have looked with anxiety for a letter from my brother, on each of the two post days since he wrote last, but nothing has come. I try to think that Chrissey must be going on well, but I am very uneasy.
I can't imagine how you have room for all the family including a servant, in the cottage -- still less visitors, who it seems are a necessary appendage, wherever you may be. Surely there must be some additional bedrooms built, since I saw the place! It is difficult to believe that "Memento Mori" is really dead. But perhaps superfluous people do die, sometimes.
We have wonderful descriptions from Barbara Smith of the glorious scenery and strange picturesque life she finds in Algiers. 844 It really seems an easy way of bringing the tropics near to one's imagination, to take that short journey. In less than a week's easy travelling you are among palms and Arabs and wild horses and lions and panthers, and I don't know what beside. She dashes down sketches with her pen and ink, making arrow-heads to indicate the bark of Jackals!
Tell me any news you hear about your book, and about other things too when you are inclined. You know you live in the thick of the world and [Society] compared with us. Best love to Cara and to the gas-lighted-content-radiating-nap-after-dinner-taking-leg-rest-enjoying- and ever-by-Pollian-remembered-affectionately-presiding genius of Ivy Cottage. And love, also best, to you, dear successful author, from your old friend
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, St. Leonard's, [4 June 1848]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, St. Leonard's, [4 June 1848]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 4, 1848. Extracts published: Cross, I, 188-189.
Victoria Hotel | St. Leonard's | Sunday.
My dear Sara
I wait and wait for a better mood, in which, poor moon that I am, I may shed on you some gentle, peaceful light, instead of thrusting my cold dark orb between you and the [lux alma] which is just now shining on you from Cara's and other friendly eyes. 738 But the better mood does not come, and if I were silent longer you might fancy that it was because I was [full rich and reigning as a king without you.]
Alas for the fate of poor mortals which condemns them to wake up some fine morning and find all the poetry in which their world was bathed only the evening before utterly gone -- the hard angular world of chairs and tables and looking-glasses staring at them in all its naked prose. It is so in all the stages of life -- the poetry of girlhood goes -- the poetry of love and marriage -- the poetry of maternity -- and at last the very poetry of duty forsakes us for a season and we see ourselves and all about us as nothing more than miserable agglomerations of atoms -- poor tentative efforts of the Natur Princip to mould a personality. This is the state of prostration -- the self-abnegation through which the soul must go, and to which perhaps it must again and again return, that its poetry or religion, which is the same thing, may be a real ever-flowing river fresh from the windows of heaven and the fountains of the great deep -- not an artificial basin with grotto work and gold fish.
I feel a sort of madness growing upon me -- just the opposite of the delirium which makes people fancy that their bodies are filling the room. It seems to me as if I were shrinking into that mathematical abstraction, a point -- so entirely am I destitute of contact that I am unconscious of length or breadth, and by the time you see me again, I shall have lost all possibility of giving you any demonstration of a spiritual existence -- like a poor sprite metamorphosed into a pomegranate seed or some such thing. But I am wasting this "good Sunday morning" in grumblings.
A thousand blessings on you all, whether at Woodford or Clapton. I wish it were given to mortal love to waft a delicious scent as of thyme or violets as a most gentle assurance and remembrancer of its existence to the beloved ones at a distance. If it were so, you all might walk in a perpetual springtide odour. My feet are so cold I must go and walk.
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, St. Leonard's, [18 August 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Aug. 18. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 310-311.
Spa Cottage | St. Leonard's.
Dear Sara
For the first time in my experience I am positively revelling in the Prospective! I have been dying with laughter over one passage in the article on Shakspeare which was made for Herbert Spencer and which I long to quote to him. "No doubt there is some reason why negroes have woolly hair (and if you look into a philosophical treatise, no doubt you will find that the author could have made out that it would be so, if he had not, by a mysterious misfortune, known from infancy that it was a fact) -- still one could not have supposed it oneself." 362 James
Martineau transcends himself in beauty of imagery in the article on Sir W. Hamilton, 363 but I have not finished him yet.
Yesterday it rained sans intermission, and of course I said cui bono? and found my troubles almost more than I could bear -- but today the sun shines 364 and there is blue above and blue below -- consequently I find life very glorious and myself a particularly fortunate diabolessa.
Lady Boothby (Mrs. Nisbett) 365 is here -- is building a house on a hill and shews her fine form and very withered but still suggestive-of-prettiness face (highly rouged) on the parade every day. (There is a bit of news to interest Mr. Bray.) Mr. Brooks, 366 a member of Parliament, is her friend and supplies her with £800 a year whereby she lives at ease. The landlord of my lodgings is a German -- comes from Saxe-Weimar, knows well the Duchess of Orleans, and talked to me this morning of Mr. Schiller and Mr. Goethe. A propos of Goethe, there is a most true, discriminating passage about him in the said article on Shakespeare. 367 Mr. Goethe is one of my companions here, and I had felt some days before reading the passage the truth which it expresses. Love to all.
Thy affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Scarborough, 26 September 1864
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, II, 389.
Scarborough | September 26. 64.
Dear Sara
We migrated on Friday last from delightful Harrogate, pausing at York to see the glorious cathedral. The weather is perfect, the sea blue as a sapphire, so that we see to utmost advantage the fine line of coast here and the magnificent breadth of sand. Even the Tenby sands are not so fine as these. -- Better than all, Mr. Lewes, in spite of a sad check of a few days from troublesome eingeweide, is strengthened beyond our most hopeful expectations by this brief trial of fresh conditions. He is wonderful for the rapidity with which he "picks up" after looking alarmingly feeble and even wasted.
We paid a visit to Knaresbro' the very last day of our stay at Harrogate, and were rejoiced that we had not missed the sight of that pretty characteristic northern town. There is a ruined castle here too, standing just where one's eyes would desire it on a grand line of cliff -- but perhaps you know this place. Its only defect is that it is too large, and therefore a little too smoky, first on the northern side and then on the southern or eastern, but except in Wales or Devonshire I have seen no sea place on our English coast, that has greater natural advantages.
I don't know quite why I should write you this note all about ourselves -- except that your goodness having helped us to the benefit we have got, I like you to know of the said benefit. We return home on Friday or Saturday. 288 You will write me news of yourself and all at home before very long?
Ever yours
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 9 October [1856]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
Richmond | October 9.
Dear Sara
I think the first part of Objection II 749 in both its forms is entirely without validity. First, what do you mean by the word uniform? If you mean by "a uniform plan" -- a plan, no one part of which defeats, or is incongruous with, another part, I do not see how this plan must necessarily exclude the coexistence of a race of creatures who are immortal with another race of creatures who are mortal. The conception of an all-wise Being does not compel us to suppose that he would endow all his creatures with the same duration of existence any more than with the same power of vision.
But if by "a uniform plan" you mean a plan that is persisted in, you have first to prove that the gift of immortality to man was an afterthought, before you can bring the Christian position within gunshot of your logical formula, that "a plan not uniform is not the best possible." The withholding of immortality from the brutes is not a proof that God "did not care for them," until you have shown that existence without immortality is a curse to them. In either case, however, "uniform" is a wrong word, and the clause -- "should reign through all his works" seems to imply that you use the word in the sense of congruous or consistent and not persistent.
I think we have not the slightest 'e0 priori ground for supposing that an all-wise Being would not will "man to be of an essentially different nature from other creatures." The 'e0 posteriori argument, that he has not willed it, is the only firm standing-ground, but this you introduce in a slight and subordinate way. I think you should keep the two species of argument distinct.
A priori arguments against Revelation have always seemed to me extremely weak. But I conclude that you are not speaking entirely from yourself, on the Infidel side, but are stating the argument advanced by Infidels? Is it so?
The second part of Objection II. 750 is rather confused in its first sentence. Do you mean that Revelation came in place of "those instinctive impulses" etc. -- or that there was given to man, in place of those instinctive impulses etc. an independent, godlike power of his own. The sentence must be differently turned somehow.
I am unable to speak with any advantage on the Objections, because I don't know your plan, and what may be coming next. But it appears to me that they cannot be consistently classed as "against Revelation in general." Revelation in general is the idea of revelation abstracted from any particular system claiming to be a revelation, but your Objection III. 751 at least, is specifically against the Hebrew Revelation. You must make it clear whether you mean by the God of Revelation, a God who reveals himself, or the God supposed to be revealed in the Scriptures.
The 'e0 priori arguments against revelation in the abstract should come first, and be quite distinct from the others. Then should come the 'e0 priori arguments against the Hebrew and Christian scheme -- Fall of man, confinement of Rev. to one people, etc., etc., and then the 'e0 posteriori arguments. But I am writing hurriedly, from an imperfect knowledge of your plan and an imperfect consideration of the subject.
Pray understand that I do not offer my criticism as worth more than the suggestions of a reader who may help you to guard against the cavils of other readers.
No more just now, because it is working time.
Ever thine
Pollian.
Do not hesitate to ask me about anything in which I can possibly be a criticometer.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 8 November [1856]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
Richmond | November 8.
Dear Sara
The following is a note on the meaning of the word Islam, copied from Smith's Gibbon 759 v. VI. 222. "Islam is the verbal noun or infinitive, and Moslim, which has been corrupted into Musalman or Musulman, is the participle of the causative form of salm, which means immunity, peace. The signification of Islam, therefore, is, to make peace, or to obtain immunity, either by compact, or by doing homage to the stronger, acknowledging his superiority, and surrendering to him the object in dispute. It also means simply to surrender. In the Koran, it signifies in most instances to do homage to God, to acknowledge him as an absolute Lord, to the exclusion of idols. Sometimes, however, it occurs in this book in its technical meaning as the name of a religion."
Mr. Lewes does agree with you that "the right method of science is to learn (or rather to inquire?) how things exist and not why."
Still, so far as my logical faculties will help me, your passage on "design" remains self-contradictory. Either you hold that it is legitimate to infer creative design from observed relations, or you do not hold that position. If you hold it, why do you say that "to pronounce on the final causes of things is beyond the sphere of human reason"? since every inference of creative design involves the affirmation that a final cause is discerned. If you do not hold it, why do you unnecessarily use the words design, designed etc. -- when they misrepresent your meaning? And what is the fitness of the terms "the eye was designed to see," if you only mean by them that there exists a certain relation between light and the eye, which issues in vision?
On the other hand, if you mean by this "affirmation" what the terms convey, namely, that there is a Being who has the same relation to the eye as a piano maker has to a piano, why do you appear to range yourself with the antagonists of Natural Theology, since you admit its fundamental principle?
According to your definition of science, there can be no true knowledge of things except in their evolution -- their dependence on observed antecedents, yet you directly fly off from that position into an anthropomorphic assumption as to the origin of things.
Again if God "designed the eye to see," he surely designed every particular kind of eye and all its relations. How could He design any eye without designing its forms? I cannot conceive what is the bearing of your distinction between those two positions.
Mind, I am not contending against any one position in the extract. I am only stating my inability to see its logic.
Apart from all these objections I must suggest that the phrase "Design of Creation" is equivocal. It may mean "the final cause of the universe as a whole" and is more likely to suggest that idea than what I imagine you mean, namely, the final causes of things considered individually.
Herbert Spencer is coming to dine with us tomorrow, having come back from Paris weary of solitary sightseeing. 760
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 6 October [1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 6 October [1858]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: '58. Brief extracts published: Cross, II, 64.
Richmond | October 6.
Dear Sara
Your letter came in time. Dr. Chapman announces that he will visit us tomorrow.
Thanks for the verses on Buckle. 1194
I'm afraid I feel a malicious delight in them, for he is a writer who inspires me with a personal dislike -- not to put too fine a point on it, he impresses me as an irreligious, conceited man.
Do not guess at authorship -- it is a bad speculation. I have not written a word in the Westminster. The article on German Novels is Mr. Lewes's, and my only contribution to it was reading the novels aloud after dinner. 1195
He very industriously translated and condensed the M'e4dchen von Treppi, 1196 though that sort of work is extremely irksome to him.
Tell Mr. Bray he need have no qualms of conscience about Buckle. We are glad that the volume should be doing service, not at present needing it ourselves.
We understand that there is a very unjustifiable treatment of Miss Parkes's pamphlet -- "Remarks on the Education of Girls" in the [National.] A misrepresentation -- so we are told -- of a passage in the part on [mental training] as if it were a recommendation for girls to read impure literature. 1197 There is not a purer minded creature in the world than Bessie Parkes -- not a woman more removed from vulgarity or laxity in all serious relations of life, and every just-minded person should enter a protest against this wanton mode of affixing a stigma on a writer who is clearly in earnest, whatever mistakes she may make in style or ideas. I mention it to you that if you see the National or hear any reference made to it you may be on your guard against accepting its representation.
I am sorry for Dr. Chapman's poverty which presses on him I fear, in a way to prevent a successful editing of the Review.
The article on Newman 1198 -- whose, I don't know, but my mind turned to Mr. Call as the writer -- is very industrious, but too impersonal and ex officio to inspire a strong interest, and it is a sad mistake to give the whole series of his books, flying from Spiritual religion to the Translation of Horace etc. -- as if it were intended to be a puff of Newman's writings from beginning to end. Happily the tone is too much that of a dissident expositor for the notion of a puff to exist in the minds of those who really read the article. But unfortunately the majority of people form their opinions without that preliminary. Long ago, I had offered to write about Newman but gave it up again.
Ever yours
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 6 November 1858
MS: Yale. Address: MIss Hennell | Ivy Cottage | Radford Road | Coventry. Postmarks: LONDON S.W. | 8 | NO 8 | 58; COVENTRY | NO 9 | 58. Hitherto unpublished.
Richmond | November 6th. 58.
Dear Sara
Do not be too much astonished at the sight of these grimy papers. They are autographs -- such as collectors of autographs value. Mr. Lewes has been looking through a large collection of old letters tonight, and it struck me that it was worth while to rescue these from the fire that you might have the chance of seeing whether they will be real additions to your store. One or two of them you are likely enough to throw away -- either having a specimen of the same hand already, or not caring to have a specimen at all. But Thierry, De Tocqueville, Comte, and all "that description" of great personage, I think are likely to be new and desirable to you.
I heard good news of you yesterday from Mr. Spencer, who dined with us after a walk in our glorious Park.
I will say a "God bless you" for a birthday greeting now, lest I should forget to do it at the right moment. This last has been a memorable year to you. I hope it has had much sweetness in it as well as some sorrow.
Ever your loving Friend
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 5 November [1856]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 5 November [1856]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | November 5.
Dear Sara
Mr. Lewes has read your passage on Design and finds a difficulty in expressing his opinion on it because he does not know the plan of your book. If you are simply expressing the view you yourself adopt, you are of course at liberty to say that "The right method of science is to discover how things exist and not why." But he reminds you that the position would be denied by the majority even of great scientific men. There is one objection, however, which applies to the whole passage whether meant as a statement for others or for yourself; namely, that you begin by denying the validity of inferences as to design, and then proceed to affirm their validity. Kant and everyone else who rejects the design argument would deny that "to say the eye was designed to see is a safe affirmation." Again, Mr. Lewes says he doesn't see the bearing of what you say about the different kinds of eyes. Perhaps if you reconsider the passage by the light of these cavils, you will be able to bring out your meaning better. I can see no flaw in the extract from the preface. It is perfectly clear.
I'm so sorry you should be teazed with the procrastinations and uncertainties of Mr. Baillie. 755 But don't let your determination to publish depend on him. Work honestly done must not be shut up in a drawer. Some good will come of it.
I was so glad to see Mr. Bray looking beamingly happy and healthy. Best love to Cara.
Yours,
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 4 September 1858
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday September 4th. | 8 Park Shot Richmond.
Dear Sara
On the other side you see Liebig's autograph, 1178 in which probably you will discover his character and manners.
We arrived at our beloved Richmond on Thursday, after a prosperous but fatiguing journey of two days and a night from Leipzig, where we spent a day and dined with the mighty publisher Brockhaus 1179 and spent an evening with Victor Carus, of Thierisch-morphological celebrity. 1180
Any good news about you and yours at any time will be acceptable. I retain the copy of your Journal till an opportunity occurs of sending or giving it you otherwise than through the Post.
Ever your affectionate
Marian Lewes.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 29 November [1855]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1855. Extract published: Cross, I, 388.
Richmond, November 29.
Dear Sara
I am so glad to hear that you are happy in your children. 645 I shall be interested in everything you can tell me about Frank's development under your care. What provision is there for poor Lizzie Bray 646 now?
Thanks for the report of Dr. Lankester's lecture 647 which I return because it is so neatly pasted together that you will like to keep it.
I have just finished a long article on Heine for the W.R. 648 which none of you will like. En revanche, Mr. Lewes has written one on Lions and Lionhunters, 649 which you will find amusing. Mr. Ch. applied to him in the eleventh hour, in distress because some expected articles were not forthcoming.
The joke you inquired about in one of your letters is imbedded in a play which would have appeared at the Olympic before this but for a terrible illness of poor Mrs. Wigan. 650
Ever your affectionate
Marian.
No news of your "Essay" 651 yet?

It seems as if I never should be free of bother and misunderstanding about this unfortunate piece which was written for him when we were at Worthing and Richmond, rehearsed, altered, rehearsed again and finally returned on my hands. This spring he again wanted to have it. I offered to sell him the piece to do what he liked with provided my name did not appear, and no application was made to me about alterations. He kept it some time and then returned it, not being able to make immediate use of it. About six weeks ago he again applied for it, accepted my terms; and now wants me once more to alter it and alter my terms. I agreed to do both. GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 27 March [1858]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1858. erratum in Cara's letter 27 for 26. Extract published: Cross, II, 16.
March 27.
Dear Sara
I should so like to have your Journal, 1100 if you could rummage out the copy for me. I remember how good it was, I should like to read it to Mr. Lewes. He has heard your interesting letter, and you may be sure has felt all that becomes an author when he perceives that he has had an appreciatory reader. He doesn't mind about your keeping the passage from the old edition of the Biog[raphical] Hist[ory]. The modification you propose will prevent any one from supposing the old edition to be the final one.
I enclose a letter which will interest you. It is affecting to see how difficult a matter it often is for the men who would most profit by a book to purchase it or even get a reading of it, while stupid Jopling of Reading 1101 or elsewhere, thinks nothing of giving a guinea for a work which he will simply put on his shelves.
Yes, Isaac Taylor, who has just published "The World of Mind," is the Isaac Taylor, author of the Nat[ural] Hist[ory] of Enthusiasm. 1102 I dare say by this time there is a want of fatty particles in his brain.
I think you have misunderstood about the "shamming dead." Mr. Lewes, I think, makes it clear enough, if you look again, that he thinks the phrase merely an untenable anthropomorphism. But no more, for I have pins and needles in my feet. I shall write from Munich.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 26 January 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 26 January 1857
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | January 26. 57.
Dear Sara
We have both been wretches with disordered livers and work standing still in consequence, for the last week. 782 That is the reason I have not written to you before.
We shall not leave here before your book is out, I dare say, so that you need not send us the sheets, especially as we are now so busy that we could not attend to them. Should you like me to review it for the Leader or Mr. Lewes? He forbids me to do any reviewing now, so I never write for the Leader, and have given up for the future the Cont[emporary] Lit[erature] in the W[estminster] R[eview]. 783 But your book is exceptional, and I should like to do what you wish. We are glad to hear that you have decided on the lower price. Even Trench's books, which are about the same size, are sold for 3/6. -- and he is the greatest of great guns among rich book-buying people. 784
I agree with you that Mrs. Phillipson's pamphlet 785 was beneath the dignity of the W[estminster] R[eview]. But I was annoyed at her attributing the criticism to Mr. Lewes and wished to deny for the Westminister reading public in general that he has anything to do with the Contemp[orary] Lit[erature].
Herbert Spencer is settled in London again 786 and beginning to work a little -- with benefit to his health, so far. He was interested to hear that you had gained the prize. I'm sure we know no one that will be tempted by Mr. Baillie's advertisement, so I return it at once.
I was going to write more, but George is equipped to walk out in the rain and carry this to the post. So Goodbye and God bless you dear Sara.
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 25 February [1856]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 25 February [1856]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1856. Extract published: Cross, I, 391-392.
Richmond | February 25.
Dear Sara
You are indeed a valuable coadjutor. I have sent your sheets 676 to Miss Barbara Smith and asked her to write to you.
What you tell me of Harriet Martineau interests me very much. I feel for her terrible bodily suffering, and think of her with deep respect and admiration. Whatever may have been her mistakes and weaknesses, the great and good things she has done far outweigh them, and I should be grieved if anything in her memoir 677 should cast a momentary shadow over the agreeable image of her that the world will ultimately keep in its memory. I wish less of our piety were spent on imaginary perfect goodness, and more given to real imperfect goodness.
You seem to be under a little misapprehension about the Leader. There has been no change in Mr. Lewes's relation to it since we came from Germany. He has never, since then, had anything to do with the editorship and the majority of the literary articles have always been written by other hands. 678 I merely mentioned the matter because we wish it to be generally known. Responsibility for other people's writing is an undesirable dignity or indignity. For example, Mr. Robert Chambers wrote to complain of an allusion to him and his brother in the article on Miss Murray's book 679 -- an article which we both disliked extremely. However, R. Chambers had perceived that Mr. Lewes was not the writer.
An uninteresting explanation this, but accuracy is a good thing. Mr. Lewes does not remember Mr. Coleman. In haste
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 24 December [1856]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 24 December [1856]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | December 24.
Dear Sara
Magnificat anima mea! But a little pang of vexation mingles with my rejoicing namely, the very mesquin amount of the sum which Mr. Baillie is to hand over, after making you wait all this time. I had somehow or other got it into my head that the prize was £100. I have just been reading your letter to Mr. Lewes, and as his opinion about titles and prices is worth having, I write you word of it at once, as a contribution towards your grounds of decision. He says, by no means put Sara, but S. S. Hennell. He thinks that Sara would do harm. Again he objects to the word "popular," and suggests either "Exposition of the Arguments between Christianity and Inf[idelit]y" or, "Christianity and Infidelity, an exposition of the arguments on both sides." For my own part, I don't much like the latter, but I agree with Mr. Lewes in disliking Mr. Baillie's title. 772 As to price, George decidedly votes for the 5s/. and boards. He thinks a paper cover for a philosophical book a bad augury.
I'm glad you have Mr. John Sibree at hand, as a book of reference. Still more glad am I that you have read and delighted in Aurora Leigh. Such books are among the great blessings of life.
Mr. Lewes is just gone. I am thankful for him to have this little change, for his head has been worse of late, and he enjoys a visit to the pleasant hearth of Vernon Hill, more than anything else away from home. Love to Cara.
Ever your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 22 September 1856
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | September 22. 56.
Dear Sara
Shouldn't you like an autograph letter of Currer Bell's? I hope to get you one by and bye, when Mrs. Gaskell returns the letters that have been sent to her. 745 Meanwhile, lest anything should prevent that, I send you some addresses which show her handwriting well enough.
How are you these fine Autumn days? Tell Mr. Bray I hope he won't allow them to pass by without paying his visit to Richmond -- where we will welcome Mrs. C. Hennell or any other friend of his that he likes to bring.
We went to the theatre on Saturday -- for the first time since we came from Germany, to see Dillon, the new actor, reputed to be very fine in Belphegor -- Lemaitre's fine part of Paillasse. 746 The acting is very so so, but the dramatic conception of Paillasse is one of the finest I know, and tell Mr. Bray, if he wants to see a piece that will make him cry, he must go to the Lyceum.
A curious thing happened the other day. Mr. Lewes has lately published in Frazer, two essays on Dwarfs and Giants, one historical, the other physiological. 747 The rule in Frazer is to put your initials to your articles unless there is a reason to the contrary, and accordingly these essays were signed G.H.L. A few days ago, came a letter from George Combe addressed to G.H.L. Esq. care of the Editor of Frazer, expressing very high admiration of the physiological essay, enquiring if the writer had published any other works on physiology, and saying that this essay seemed to him to contain much sounder views than he usually found in works on physiology. He didn't seem to have a suspicion that G.H.L. was G. H. Lewes! Mr. Lewes returned him a brief answer, telling him that his approbation was very flattering. We thought it better for him to answer the letter -- but I fear Mr. Combe would be rather disappointed to find out whom he had been praising, Mr. Lewes being his favorite aversion, as a "shallow, flippant man." However, we should all of us pass very different judgments now and then, if the thing to be judged were anonymous.
By the bye, have you all done with the Baden Powell? If so, perhaps Mr. Bray will bring it up with him when he comes.
Parker is going to publish a library edition of the "Biographical Hist[ory] of Philosophy," and Mr. Lewes has just begun the task of revising and enlarging it. It is to be in one stout volume octavo. 748
There are some scraps of news, such as I have to tell -- written with the thoroughly interested view of getting some from you in return. Especially about your own health. I am glad to hear Cara's has been so good lately. Give my love to her and Mr. Bray. Nelly, I should think, has forgotten me, and is growing into a tall young lady.
Ever yours
M. E.
