GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 22 November [1856]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
November 22.
The portrait is very beautiful, dear Sara, and I think it a treasure. Yet greedy thing that I am, I long for one of Cara too.
Do you know, I had never thought of 'aby'bbour birthdays! I have such an un-anniversary-keeping mind. But you always think of things that give opportunities for feeling and doing what is kind and pretty.
Mr. Lewes is distressed that he didn't know about the birthday too, that he might have put something into my slippers this morning. Ah how much I have to be happy and thankful about every fresh birthday. Life seems worth twice as much to me now as it was even last November. And the assurance of your constant love becomes more precious as all other things become more precious when we have a brighter light within to see them by.
Ever your loving, grateful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 21 September 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 21 September 1857
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 464-465.
Park Shot, Richmond | September 21. 57.
Dear Sara
Mr. Rands 966 writes like a sensible tasteful man, whose good opinion must be valuable to you, such a man as one might expect in the author of the "Reading Raids" and "Tangled Talk." We are quite glad to know who wrote those pleasant papers, the solitary things one could read in Tait. Mr. Lewes used to notice them with admiration in old days, when he wrote the Literary Summary for the Leader. But Mr. Rands must be grateful to some other critic for revising his "Chain of Lilies," for Mr. Lewes hardly writes one article in three months for the Leader, and particularly wishes its literature may not be imputed to him. He seems to have forgotten all about Cronippus, and unfortunately has not by him the numbers of the Leader in which his letters on Butler appeared. 967
I hope you are not reading the old edition of the Hist[ory] of Phil[osophy], for it is not at all a fair representation of the author now, and it is really cruel, after all the trouble he has had in castigating and completing it, that any reader should not have the benefit of his work or not give him the benefit of judging him by his latest revision. I wish we could send you our copy, but he can't spare it. I'm sorry, too, that we have either sold or mislaid the last edition of Baden Powell, 968 so that I can't tell you what he says of Feuerbach.
We have not seen Mr. and Mrs. Call 969 yet, but we are going to dine with them by invitation on Wednesday. We didn't know they were come home until we received a pleasant note from Mrs. Call; and Mr. Chapman, who came to see us a week ago, was also in the dark on that subject. He is grown so stout, that he looks like an elder and coarser brother of his former self.
Mr. Lewes was only absent ten days, and came back greatly comforted to have found the boys more improved than he had ventured to hope in one year. They can speak German quite well, and, what is better, their dispositions seem to be under a favourable influence. They are happy and ruddy, and picking up all sorts of practical knowledge as well as school learning. Altogether, we are very thankful for Hofwyl.
The days are very peaceful -- peacefully busy. One always feels a deeper calm as autumn comes on. I should be satisfied to look forward to a heaven made up of long autumn afternoon walks, quite delivered from any necessity of giving a judgment on the Woman Question or of reading newspapers about Indian Mutinies. 970 I am so glad there are thousands of good people in the world who have very decided opinions and are fond of working hard to enforce them -- I like to feel and think everything and do nothing, a pool of the "deep contemplative" 971 kind.
Tell Cara she little thinks what success some of her witticisms have in my keeping. Do you remember her joke about "the Egyptians talking in beetles"? I told it Mr. Lewes, and we often recur to it with a hearty laugh. I like to think of the journey to Stratford in this nice weather, and of the Flowers 972 rich and content. Some people do prosper -- that is a comfort. The rest of us must fall back on the beatitudes -- "Blessed are the poor." That is Luke's version, you know, and it is really on the whole more comforting than Matthew's. 973 I'm afraid there are few of us who can appropriate the blessings of the poor [in spirit.]
Mr. Bray, I suppose, is going to take the field against the "Working Women," 974 if I am right in my inference from the letter he wrote to Mrs. Bodichon. Something will come out of the battle, whoever is right.
We are reading one of the most wonderful books in French, or any other literature -- Monteil's [Histoire des Fran'e7ais des divers 'c9tats] 975 -- a history written on an original plan. If you see any account of it, read that account.
I must go. It is feeding time.
Ever thine
Marian.
Mr. Lewes desires me to say that he particularly begs you will not quote the old edition of his History of Philosophy, when you bring out a new edition of your book. He repudiates that old edition. He suggests, by the way, that you can probably procure the new edition at the Library of the Mechanics' Institute in Coventry. The "Sea-Side Studies" are to come out in the course of a month or two. 976

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 20 October 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 20 October 1857
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 467.
Park Shot | October 20. 57.
Dear Sara
You are the best correspondent in the world, for you always write to me when you have a nice little budget of news to tell me.
I'm very glad to know that Mr. Bray read his paper and had the satisfaction of feeling that his work was effective. I looked through the Athenaeum report for it in vain, and feared that he might not have been able to read it after all. I shall be glad to receive a copy.
"Open to conviction" indeed! I should think so. I am open to conviction on all points except dinner and debts. I hold that the one must be eaten and the other paid. These are my only prejudices.
I was pleased with Mr. Call. 989 He is a man one really cares to talk to -- has thoughts, says what he means, and listens to what others say.
We should quite like to see him often. And I cannot tell you how much I have felt Mrs. Call's graceful as well as kind behaviour to me.
Your praise of the Biographical History of Philosophy is very pleasant reading to me, because I know it represents your real feeling. That sort of testimony is worth half a dozen newspaper critiques. We have not seen the one in the Spectator, 990 for we never see that oracular journal, and never look out for reviews. When the Biographical History originally came out in Knight's edition it was hardly noticed at all -- Mr. Heraud, in the Athenaeum, said it was written from the transcendental point of view!! and dismissed it in three lines. 991 Yet you see it has sold better than most books that have the laudation of the press and is a text book at Oxford, of all places. Encouragement for all authors who have something to say and know how to say it. Some months ago, before the new edition came out, Mr. Lewes had a letter from a workingman, -- at Leicester, I think -- who said that he and some fellow students met together on a Sunday to read the book aloud and discuss it. He had marked some errors of the press and sent them to Mr. Lewes for his new edition. Wasn't that pretty?
I suppose you see the "National," when you like. The article on the "Ultimate Laws of Physiology" is Herbert Spencer's, 992 as indeed you will see at a glance, if you don't know it already. The whole number is interesting and certainly more fascinating than the Westminster Review, though that too is good this time.
I've no news to tell you, except that we are both much better than we have ever been since our sudden transition from sea-breezes to London haze. You give no sanitary report. I hope that means that you are well. Best love to Cara and Mr. Bray.
Ever your loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 2 March 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 2 March 1858
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 15-16.
Richmond | March 2. 58.
Dear Sara
We spent a very pleasant couple of hours with Mr. and Mrs. Call last Friday. 1091 It was worth a journey on a cold dusty day to see two faces beaming kindness and happiness. I was very glad too to shake hands again with Miss Marshall, 1092 who is mixed up with many grateful memories in my mind. She had her bonnet on before we left, ready to go and see that things were in order in her new house.
We don't migrate till the first week in April 1093 when, one hopes, the wind will have changed its mind. Yes, I know you have been at Munich. When you write again, try and think of what you liked best there, that I may associate you with it. I dare say we shall see Salzburg, but we don't form more than general plans beforehand. Perhaps we may go to
Dresden, perhaps not: we leave room for the impr'e9vu, which Louis Blanc found so sadly wanting in Mr. Morgan's millennial village. 1094
You are among the exceptional people who say pleasant things to their friends, and don't feel a too exclusive satisfaction in their misfortunes. We like to hear of your interest in Mr. Lewes's books -- at least I am very voracious of such details. I keep the pretty letters that are written to him; and we have had some really important ones from the scientific big-wigs about the "Sea-Side Studies." The reception of the book in that quarter has been quite beyond our expectations. Eight hundred copies were sold at once, in the first subscription, so there is a good chance of a second edition being wanted before the year is out. There is a great deal of close, hard work in the book, and every one who knows what scientific work is, necessarily perceives this; happily, many have been generous enough to express their recognition in a hearty way.
I enter so deeply into everything you say about your mother. To me that old old popular truism "We can never have but one mother" has worlds of meaning in it, and I think with more sympathy of the satisfaction you feel in at last being allowed to wait on her, than I should of anything else you could tell me. I wish we saw more of that sweet human piety that feels tenderly and reverently towards the aged.
We had heard that Francis Newman wrote the Rel[igious] Weakness of Prot[estantism] but had not heard so favourable an account of its reception. Dr. Chapman has been announcing a visit to us repeatedly since the appearance of the Review, but we have not yet seen him. He is, I dare say, overwhelmed with anxieties and occupations, just now that he is entering his new house in Albion Street.
Do you know that Miss Parkes is the editress of the Englishwoman's Journal, which you see advertised? Co-editress, at least, with Miss Hayes. 1095 She gave me the first number the other day when I called on her at the office. It is just middling. Her own first paper on the Profession of the Teacher, has some good stuff in it: I can't help crying over the stories of those superannuated governesses. If you haven't seen the Magazine I will send it you. Bessie has talent and real ardour for all goodness, but I fear Miss Hayes has been chosen on the charitable ground that she had nothing else to do in the world. There is something more piteous almost than soapless poverty in this application of feminine incapacity to Literature.
I can't be very sorry that Nelly should have measles now. For I remember how very ill I was with the disease, when I was several years older than she is, and I suppose the older one is, the more one suffers from those inevitable things.
Give my love to Mrs. John Cash, and tell her I shall rejoice in her joy when she has got safely through the terrible hour.
We saw such a fine photograph of Livingstone the other day -- just what one would expect him to be. It is a thousand pities, there is that hideous one at the beginning of his book. 1096 And beside it we saw a portrait of Bulwer! Fancy the contrast. Bulwer looks more of a sham even than his novels. Love to all,
From thine always,
Marian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 2 March 1857
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, I, 433-434.
Richmond | March 2. 1857.
Dear Sara
I began -- oddly enough, you will perhaps think -- by reading through the "Answers of Infidelity," those being the most interesting part of the book to me. Some of your own passages I think very admirable, -- and one of them made me cry, which is always a sign of the highest pleasure writing can give me. But in many of the extracts, I think Infidelity cuts a very poor figure. Some are feeble, some bad, and terribly discrepant in the tone of their thought and feeling from the passages which come fresh from your own mind.
The disadvantage arising from the perpetual shifting of the point of view, is a disadvantage, I suppose, inseparable from the plan, 811 which I cannot admire or feel to be effective, though I can imagine it may be a serviceable form of presentation to some inquirers. The execution I do admire. I think it shows very high and rare qualities of mind -- a self-discipline and largeness of thought, which are the highest result of culture. The "Objections of Christianity," which I have also read, are excellently put, and have an immense advantage over the "Answers of Inf[idelit]y" in their greater homogeneity.
The first part I have only begun, and glanced through, and at present have no other observation to make than that I think you might have brought a little more artillery to bear on Christian morality. But nothing is easier than to find fault -- nothing so difficult as to do some real work.
Mr. Lewes did not make a [mistake] about Isaac Taylor. 812 He read aloud to me that passage which you call [poor,] feeling it to be very eloquent, and I agreed with him. I was afraid you would be distressed for Mr. Baillie, but you must expect people to be provoked into severity by the tone of those advertisements.
Don't let your soul be moved by newspaper criticisms. If you knew well what sort of books the Spectator praises, in those short notices, you would not care about its blame. 813 It is only as a question of sale that such notices are at all important, and even in that light, they can't stop the sale of a book that really lays hold of the readers' minds. One person who has admired and enjoyed tells another, and by and bye Athenaeum, Spectator and Co. are forgotten. On the other hand, no dithyrambs of "Mr. Gigadibs" 814 can make a bad book successful.
Neither Mr. Lewes nor I can see the logicality of that passage about the eyes as an argument against design. Herbert Spencer is coming to dine with us to-day, and I shall ask him to use his spectacles to it. But since we are not absolute blockheads, I think there must be an imperfection in the statement.
This note is scribbled under difficulties of head, and George is shaking the table with wrapping up parcels, 815 so that I had better leave off before I reach the climax of utter unintelligibility.
We never see proofs of the [Leader,] so you must not be surprized at false concords in Latin, 816 or any other exquisite infelicity.
Ever thine
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 19 February [1856]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1856. Extracts published: Cross, I, 390-391.
Park Shot | February 19.
Dear Sara
I was so glad to have a little news of you. I should like to hear much oftener, but our days are so accurately parcelled out among regular occupations that I rarely manage to do anything not included in the programme, and without reading Mrs. Barbauld on the Inconsistency of Human Expectations, 665 I know that receiving letters is inconsistent with not writing any.
If you can let me have the petition next Sunday or Monday it will be soon enough. I suppose you have received the revised edition with the clause about the husband being responsible for the wife's debts. 666
We are in happy ignorance of the Spectator's remarks, 667 for we never see that paper. Apropos of papers, have you seen any numbers of the Saturday Review, 668 a new journal on which [all the talents] are engaged?
It is not properly a newspaper, but -- what its title expresses -- a political and literary Review. The Duke of Newcastle 669 is at the bottom of it, and it has the first requisite of a journal -- money. Mr. Lewes has written some admirable articles for it, and among the rest, (you will be glad to hear) one on Herbert Spencer's Psychology -- not yet printed, however. 670 It is a much shorter and less interesting account of the book, than he gave in the Leader, but as the Sat. R. is not to be heterodox, he was necessarily g'ean'e9. By the way, if you should happen to hear any one imputing articles in the Leader to Mr. Lewes, be so good as to say that he only writes the summary and occasional reviews, and that he has nothing to do with the editorship. Sometimes there is one article of mine in, sometimes one of his, but rarely more.
What are you doing now? We are delighting ourselves with Ruskin's 3d volume, 671 which contains some of the finest writing I have read for a long time (among recent books). I read it aloud for an hour or so after dinner -- then we jump to the Old Dramatists when Mr. Lewes reads to me as long as his voice will hold out, and after this we wind up the evening with Rymer Jones's Animal Kingdom, 672 by which I get a confused knowledge of branchiae and such things -- perhaps on the whole a little preferable to total ignorance. These are our noctes -- without coene for the present, occasionally diversified by very dramatic singing of Figaro etc. -- which I think must alarm "that good man, the clergyman," who sits below us.
Do you know that Mr. Chapman has let his house in Blandford Sq. for a year, and that Mrs. C. is living in lodgings at Redhill, Mr. C. devoting himself body and soul to his medical studies? 673 But I dare say you hear much more news of that sort than I do. I was very sorry to hear from Mr. C. that poor little Ernest has a tendency to scrofula, which makes it necessary to take him into the country.
We have been half laughing, half indignant, over Alison's new volume of his Hist[ory] of Europe, in which he undertakes to give an account of German literature. 674 For an impudent exhibition of ignorance and imbecility, it surpasses anything I have seen -- even Mr. S. C. Fullom. 675 It is deplorable to think how many people will spend their money on his huge volume of rubbish and fancy they are making a valuable addition to their library.
Doesn't this heavy weather make your brain heavy? It does mine, and inclines me to leave off writing. So, with love to all I say goodbye. Ever dearest Sara
Your affectionate
Marian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 19 August [1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1857. Extracts published: Cross, I, 464; George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 98.
Park Shot | August 19.
Dear Sara
What a pleasant surprize -- the date of your note this morning! I write at once, because if you are to fly away again in that sparrow-like way after only peeping at the sea, I must make haste and catch you. I do hope, though, that you will find it do you so much good, you will decide on staying longer than a week. 954
Dr. and Mrs. Bodichon came a few days after you left us. We think the essential is there -- that he is a genuine, right-feeling man. They are wisely going to America for a year, and I hope in that time he will learn to speak English, so as to be an "organ" better fitted to this "medium" of English life than he is at present. 955
We went to see Rosa Bonheur's picture 956 the other day. What power! That is the way women should assert their rights.
It has often occurred to me since I left you, that you may have misunderstood what I said about publishing your book with Mr. Chapman. I should not like you to be under the mistake of supposing, that I would not go out of my way to do him any real service -- for example, I would write an article for his review rather than for any other, though that other might give me a few more guineas. But self-defeating actions do no one any good. And for you to publish with him would in my opinion, be an action of that kind. 957
On one other point, too, do not misunderstand me. Writing is part of my religion, and I can write no word that 'abdoes not clothe my [deep?] faith.'bb is not prompted from within. At the same time I believe that almost all the best books in the world have been written with the hope of getting money for them. God bless you.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.
Mr. Lewes sends his kind remembrances. He takes Bertie to Hofwyl next week.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 18 January 1856
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 18 January 1856
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 389-390.
Park Shot | January 18. 56.
Dear Sara
Thank you for your kind attention in sending us the Herald containing your notice of the "Goethe." 658 I am glad to see that the paper is "lengthening its cords and strengthening its stakes," as the dissenters say when their chapels are enlarged. I see too that Mr. Bray is, as usual, manfully fighting for what he believes to be the right against magnates and friends. 659
Miss Leigh Smith has sent me a copy of a Petition 660 to be presented to Parliament praying that married women may have a legal right to their own earnings, as a counteractive to wife-beating and other evils. I don't know whether you and Cara will think the object worth attention, but if you do, I will send the paper for your signature. The petition is well and soberly drawn up, and has been signed by Mrs. Gaskell, Harriet Martineau, Mrs. Jameson and the et ceteras. So you will be in good company, if you care about that. I dare say Eleanor Cash 661 and some other friends of yours will be willing to sign.
Apropos of Harriet Martineau, have you seen that she has brought out a pamphlet on the Factory question fiercely vituperating Dickens? 662 It was intended originally as an article for the Westminster, but Mr. Chapman was obliged to reject it on account of its personality. I hope this will not prevent her from writing again in the W.R., for her articles are generally valuable. Do you see the National Review? The article on Atheism 663 takes up, in a gingerly way, Herbert Spencer's book, with an acknowledgement of its power.
I believe there have been at least a thousand copies of the [Goethe] sold -- which is a wonderfully good sale in less than three months for a 30s. book. We have a charming collection of letters, both from remarkable acquaintances and remarkable non-acquaintances expressing enthusiastic delight in the book -- letters all the more delightful because they are quite spontaneous and spring from a generous wish to let the author know how highly the writers value his work. But alas! when one has the headache, nothing seems delightful, and we are both half dead with it today. Nevertheless I have been doing a morning's work, and I can't be contented to shut up my desk without writing to you, begging you to make due allowances for a note written under difficulties.
I was so glad to hear of your successful Bazaar, and quite able to understand how it had absorbed you. If you want some idle reading, get "The Shaving of Shagpat," which I think you will say deserves all the praise I gave it in the Leader 664 -- if indeed you have not already had it.
I wish I could think of news, but my head obstinately refuses to suggest anything worth telling, so accept the will -- that miserable assignat -- instead of the deed.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 17 January 1858
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 6-7.
Richmond | January 17. 58.
Dear Sara
Your letters are always seasonable whether it is the new year or the old or the middle-aged. "A pretty letter," Mr. Lewes said, when I read it to him. We can sympathize as to the sore throat having had colds ourselves the last few days, but being otherwise in good condition.
I fear many people will share your opinion about the article on the Religious Weakness of Prot[estantis]m; I don't know who wrote it. I confess it is very repugnant to me, though I abstained from saying so to Mr. Chapman, because I pity the sorrows of an editor. I have long ceased to feel any sympathy with mere antagonism and destruction, and all crudity of expression marks, I think, a deficiency in subtlety of thought as well as in breadth of moral and poetic feeling. The article on Shelley 1060 is a perfect puddle for an unfortunate editor to have fallen into. Can anything be more feebly foolish or foolishly feeble than that stuff about the [blood-red hand of the baronet covering up atheism] and that false sarcasm on the same page about a m'e9salliance? I have not, of course read the article -- I have only dipped in here and there, but a mere taste of an undone cake made with rancid butter is enough.
Mr. William Smith, the author of "Thorndale," is an old acquaintance of Mr. Lewes's -- I should say an old friend, only I don't like the too ready use of that word. Mr. Lewes admires and esteems him very highly. 1061 He is a very accomplished man, a bachelor, with a small independent income -- used to write very effective articles on miscellaneous subjects in [Blackwood.] I shall like to know what you think of [Thorndale.]
How could you waste your pretty eyes in reading [White Lies]? 1062 Surely they are too precious to be spent on the inflated plagiarisms of a man gone mad with restless vanity and unveracity.
Herbert Spencer dined with us last week, and I had a talk with him about his monetary article, 1063 which interests me strongly. It is better written than his things have been of late, probably because it was written more rapidly. He cleared up several questions for me, and inclined me to think that he must be in the right. But I have not time at present to think of the subject except in a scrambling way. Apropos, I don't know whether you look out for Ruskin's books whenever they appear. His little book on the Political Economy of Art 1064 contains some magnificent passages, mixed up with stupendous specimens of arrogant absurdity on some economical points. But I venerate him as one of the great Teachers of the day -- his absurdities on practical points do no harm, but the grand doctrines of truth and sincerity in art, and the nobleness and solemnity of our human life, which he teaches with the inspiration of a Hebrew prophet, must be stirring up young minds in a promising way. Mr. Lewes has been enjoying a week's holiday at Vernon Hill, and was very pleased to find Alice Helps 1065 the eldest daughter there, a girl of seventeen, become an enthusiastic student of painting under Ruskin, and stoutly battling against the falsity that paints what the painter does not see. The two last volumes of Modern Painters 1066 contain, I think, some of the finest writing of this age. He is strongly akin to the sublimest part of Wordsworth, whom, by the bye, we are reading now with fresh admiration for his beauties and tolerance for his faults.
I hope we shall see Mr. and Mrs. Call again before we leave -- we shall certainly make an effort to do so.
Couldn't you write a much better article for the Westminster than most of the contributors? Why don't you? Though, indeed, I think I should rather urge you to rest and take life easily.
Our present plans are: -- to remain here till about the end of March, then to go to Munich, which I long to see. We shall live there several months, seeing the wonderful galleries in leisure moments. Our living here is so much more expensive than living abroad that we save more than the expenses of our journeying, and as our work can be as well done there as here for some months, we lay in much more capital in the shape of knowledge and experience by going abroad.
I have nothing else to say, except love to Cara and Mr. Bray. When you write again, tell me how poor Annie Whittem is -- also if Mrs. John Cash has more than one child. If you can remember that I have asked the questions, which I confess it is unreasonable to expect.
Ever your loving
Marian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 16 October [1855]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1855. Extracts published: Cross, I, 396-397.
Richmond October 16.
Dear Sara
Herbert Spencer is no longer at Tr'e9port. According to the latest news, he is in England, "moving along the coast," 634 but we are ignorant of his precise whereabouts. It is a pity for him not to have your nice notice of his book 635 just now, before tributes have become numerous. We were amused to see the British Quarterly 636 (in its short reviews) belauding a book so utterly destructive of its own theology. That is the only notice, besides yours, that I have seen at present.
I am very glad you find the book so precious to you, and I shall take the first opportunity of telling H.S. what you say, if indeed you will not tell him all yourself which you might do without scruple, if you enjoined him not to reply. As soon as I learn his address I will let you know it.
I agree with you that it is a pity he did not explain how and why he considers Phrenology "comparatively unimportant"; 637 indeed the whole of the latter part of the book has suffered greatly from the haste with which it was prepared for the press. But why you should object to his speaking of Sir William Hamilton's 638 contributions to a theory of perception as "valuable" I am unable to conceive. Sir W.H. has been of service to him as well as to others, and instead of repressing acknowledgments of merit in others, I should like them to be more freely given. I see no dignity or anything else that is good in ignoring one's fellow-beings. H.S.'s views, like every other man's views, could not have existed without the substratum laid by his predecessors. But perhaps you mean something that I fail to perceive.
Your bit of Teleology is very fine. Here is a delicious Hibernicism in return. In a treatise on Consumption, sent yesterday, the writer says, "There is now hardly any difference on this subject -- at least I feel none." 639
I do not know who wrote the article on Drunkenness in the W.R. Mr. Chapman's is an interesting and valuable article, and has cost him immense trouble. It is a sad pity that wretched article on the Newspaper Press 640 should have been admitted. Still, on the whole, the number is equal to the National.
What a family you will have with Nelly and Frank and the little Noels! Your life will be quite noisy and bustling. Ours has no incidents, except such as take place in our own brains and the occasional arrival of a longer letter than usual. Yours are always read aloud and enjoyed. Mr. Lewes says "Miss Hennell writes such nice letters." Yesterday we had two from the Princess Wittgenstein 641 telling us about Liszt and dear old Weimar -- also pleasant to read though aristocratically illegible. Nevertheless our life is intensely occupied and the days are far too short. We are reading Gall's Anatomie et Physiologie du Cerveau, 642 and Carpenter's Comparative Physiology aloud in the evenings, and I am trying to fix some knowledge about plexuses and ganglia in my soft brain, which generally only serves me to remember that there is something I ought to remember and to regret that I did not put the something down in my note-book. For "Live and learn," we should sometimes read "Live and grow stupid." Love to Cara and sympathy with her cold.
Ever yours
Marian E.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, 13 December 1857
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 477-478.
Richmond | December 13. 57.
Dear Sara
I hope you are looking forward to a placidly happy Christmas -- for I suppose you would prefer that to a merry one. I have an impulse to send you that wish, though I have not yet got any news to tell you as an excuse for writing. You know all public affairs better than I do, and I know no private affairs except our own. These are very prosperous just now, making a sunshine in a shady, or rather a foggy place. 1032 It is a great happiness to me that Mr. Lewes gets more and more of the recognition he deserves; pleasant letters and speeches have been very numerous lately, especially about his Sea-Side Studies which have appeared in Blackwood and are soon to appear -- very much improved and enlarged -- in a separate volume. His head is nearly well now, and he works vigorously.
Herbert Spencer, you see, has made his new avatar. His volume of Essays came to us by post this morning, looking very handsome. 1033
Dear Carlyle writes, 'e0propos of his "Frederic" -- "I have had such a 14 months as was never appointed me before in this world, -- sorrow, darkness and disgust, my daily companions; and no outlook visible except getting a detestable business turned off, or else being driven mad by it." 1034 That is his exaggerated way of speaking, and writing is always painful to him; but he has been specially tormented by the short-comings of German commentators and book-makers, on whom he has depended as authorities. Do you know he is 62! I fear this will be his last book.
Tell Mr. Bray I am reading a book of Riehl's -- "The Family" -- forming the sequel to his other volumes. 1035 He will be pleased to hear that so good a writer agrees with him in several points about the occupations of women. The book is a good one, and if I were in the way of writing articles, I should write one on it.
There is so much to read and the days are so short! I get more hungry for knowledge every day, and less able to satisfy my hunger. Time is like the Sibylline leaves getting more precious the less there remains of it -- that, I believe, is the correct allusion for a fine writer to make on the occasion.
Write me some Christmas news of you all when you have nothing better to do. Mr. Lewes who is "a-squinting through his glass," 1036 as the girl at Scilly said of him, sends you his kind regards and anticipatory Christmas wishes. Love to all in Ivy Cottage.
Ever yours
Marian.

Richmond | October 11. /58.
Dear Sara
Dr. Chapman came yesterday, in spite of the weather, and in spite of a bad headache, poor man! It was quite easy for me to speak about the article after your last letter, and I made myself sure of his mind on the subject. The negative seems to be a decided and unconditional one, not founded on any disagreement with the views contained in it, but on the opinion that the form given to the views is not such as to make them telling in a Review. The defect he alleges is a want of fusion: -- the connection of the ideas advanced in the different portions of the article is not made sufficiently evident. It appears that he presented the article to Mr. Wilson 1203 of Oxford (an excellent judge) for the sake of having his criticism, and I imagine that Dr. Chapman is expressing Mr. Wilson's opinion. I asked him point blank if he would insert it gratuitously, and he said "No."
I felt deep compassion for him yesterday. His health seems to be threatening again, and the load of anxieties he has to carry about his neck, while he is making efforts so strenuous and in many respects so disagreeable that few men would have the courage for them! That hideous Martineau-correspondence 1204 gave me almost a sick-headache only to think of. He seems to have enjoyed his visit to Coventry, and gives me a pleasant idea of you all. It is good to me to get a glimpse of you through other eyes. In haste, ever
Your loving
Marian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 7. 1856. Extracts published: Cross, I, 395.
Richmond | Sunday.
Dear Sara
Thank you for taking the trouble to write me a full account of matters so interesting to me. Your description of Pegg and Co. 693 is so graphic that it would have made me laugh if it had not been near making me cry. O dear dear -- I hope you will be able thoroughly to enjoy this last precious summer on the pretty lawn where it is one of my pleasures on sunshiny days to think of you all strolling about or seated on the bearskin.
We are very thankful for the Hofwyl 694 circular and have almost decided to send the two eldest boys there. But it is necessary to weigh all things carefully before coming to a determination, as, not being either swindlers or philanthropists, we don't like to incur obligations which there is not a reasonable certainty of our being able to meet.
I am much obliged to Mr. Bray, too, for sending Mr. John Sibree's letter. Mr. Lewes had already received an answer from him declining his proposition, but we were interested to read his very characteristic letter to his sister, which proved to Mr. Lewes that I had given him a correct description of the man.
We are headachy this morning and so are keeping Sabbath in Mr. Bray's fashion -- enjoying the sunshine and reading the newspapers. I wish you saw the "Saturday." With best love to all,
Ever yours affectionately
Marian.
Tell Mr. Bray, Herbert Spencer is coming to town to stay for some time -- if indeed he is not already on his way here. 695 I conclude his letter was partly a joke. I have written this letter with the steel pen you sent me -- for which thanks.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [5 September 1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [5 September 1858]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. 5. 1858. Extract published: Cross, II, 64.
Park Shot | Sunday.
Dear Sara
You have surely been thinking me the shabbiest of mortals, to send you that curt note at the back of the autograph without saying one word about your interesting letter which you sent to bid me welcome home. Unless, as Helps says, you have employed your imagination in the service of charity, and conceived the possibility of my not having seen your letter at the time I scribbled said shabby note; which was the fact. For our good landlady had placed carefully before us a pile of letters, all of which we should have been content to wait for until the day of judgment, when the writers of unnecessary letters will doubtless receive their reward, and had with equal care locked up in her desk the two letters we should have been glad to see -- yours and another, equally agreeable in its way, since it contained a cheque for £40. I need not enter into details -- you foresee of course that I got your letter just when mine was gone to the irrevocable Post. Not that I am going to make you the least amends now -- only to thank you and tell you how pleasant it was to read your letter aloud after dinner.
Your account of Spurgeon 1184 tallies with all I had conjectured from newspaper accounts and from one or two of his printed sermons which I have read -- also with his portrait. The only thing that shook me with a doubt in his favour was Ruskin's testimony; but Ruskin is a man of strange whims.
There is a sad beauty in what you tell me of Edward Bache. I never saw him after he was grown up, but I remember his sweet mother and the expression of her face perfectly. I did not know of her death. 1185
Will you not write to the author of Thorndale 1186 and express your sympathy? He is a very diffident man, who would be susceptible to that sort of fellowship, and one should give a gleam of happiness where it is possible. Mr. Lewes has no autograph of his, not being a preserver of letters.
I shall write you nothing worth reading for the next three months, so here is an opportunity for you to satisfy a large appetite for generous deeds. You can write to me a great many times without getting anything worth having in return.
Mr. Lewes has suffered a good deal from his head during our absence, but he has been better the last week or two. In all other respects we are faring well.
Yours gratefully
Marian.
I was affected by reading of George Combe's death in Galignani, and Mr. Bray, I am sure must be still more affected by the good and able man's death. For good and able he was, with the utmost that severity might make of his weaknesses. -- Robert Cox, I suppose, will write a Memoir of him. 1187

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [5 March 1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 5. 1857. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 434-435.
Richmond | Thursday.
Dear Sara
I think I wrote very brusquely and disagreeably to you the other day, but the impertinence was altogether in the form and not at all in the feeling. I always have uncomfortable sensations after writing objections and criticisms when they relate to things I substantially admire. It is inflicting a hurt on my own veneration.
I showed the passage on the eye, p. 157, to H. Spencer, and he agrees with us that you have not stated your idea so as to render it a logical argument against design. You appear to imply that development and gradation in organs and functions are opposed to that conception, which they are not. I mention this because, in a second edition, 817 you may see the desirability of altering or expanding the statement.
I had written thus far when your letter came. Please to thank Mr. Bray on my behalf for acting as a steward of my forgotten property. I am very much obliged to him for disposing of it to such advantage.
As to your passage on "design," I suppose you are aware that we all three hold the conception of creative design to be untenable -- we only think you have not made out a good case against it. Mr. Spencer read with interest and admiration your excellent passage quoted in the Leader.
Thank you for sending me some news of Harriet Martineau. I have often said lately, "I wonder how she is." I have a wretched headache, so no more at present from
Your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [24 November 1856]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [24 November 1856]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Monday.
Dear Sara
I feel as if I had written very selfishly in my hasty notes to you and Cara the other day -- all about myself and my own feelings, and no word about what, nevertheless, I do care for -- you and your feelings.
I have looked so much at the little portrait since it came, and have thought how far I have been from valuing enough the dear soul that looks out from it. We are so long in this life before we learn even a little of the sacredness and preciousness of the things that are given to us. Now, on looking back to the days we have passed together, and the conversations in which you have told me something of your thoughts or of your griefs, I feel what a poor, narrow cup I held out to receive all that, and how often I wounded when I might have helped you, if I had only had a larger and more reverent heart. The cup would be a little larger now -- for after all it was not a hard porcelain cup, but one with petals that the sun has opened a little. But now we are separated, and I shall never be able to make up for my past failures. There is so little we can make up for! We repent of our errors towards one friend, and that helps us to behave better to another, but rarely to the one on whom we have learnt our lesson.
All this is scribbled hastily between washing bills and literature. It says very imperfectly what I want to say -- but it relieves my mind a little.
We are very full of our own affairs both pleasant and unpleasant just now, and that helps to make my letters bare and dry.
You must read Aurora Leigh. 766 I wish I had seen Mrs. Browning, as you have, for I love to have a distinct human being in my mind, as the medium of great and beautiful things.
Ever Thine
Marian.

But in this, her longest and greatest poem, Mrs. Browning has shown herself all the greater poet because she is intensely a poetess."

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [24 February 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [24 February 1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 24. 1857. Extract published: Cross, I, 432.
Richmond, Tuesday.
Dear Sara
The two copies of the book arrived this morning. Many loving thanks for my peculiar copy. We are delighted with the appearance and getting up of the volume -- so much more imposing and dignified than Mr. Bray's intimations led us to expect.
You will at least have a candid critic in Mr. Lewes 804 who is one of that minority amongst mankind that find it impossible to say or write what they do not believe, either for a friend or against an enemy. I am the more inclined to think that I shall admire the book, because you are suspected of having given undue preponderance to the Christian argument, for I have a growing conviction that we may measure true moral and intellectual culture by the comprehension and veneration given to all forms of thought and feeling which have influenced large masses of mankind -- and of all intolerance, the intolerance calling itself philosophical is the most odious to me.
We shall not be able to move until the end of the first or second week in March, when we start for the Scilly Isles to proceed from thence to Guernsey and from Guernsey to Brittany -- to be away probably till after the beginning of July. Don't you envy us the sight of romantic Brittany? No you don't -- you are only glad that two fellow-sinners can have the pleasure.
We saw Ira Aldridge 805 at Worthing in some scenes of Shylock, Macbeth, and Othello, and we cannot help marvelling at your admiration. He seemed to us pitiably bad. But Shakspeare moves one through the worst actor that can pronounce English.
I rejoice to hear of the prospective happiness of two such excellent people as Kate Martineau and Elinor Cash. 806 I have seen hardly anything of Miss Cash, so of her I speak by faith and not by sight, but in Kate Martineau I have felt the presence of genuine good-will and feminine gentleness.
What weather! if it would but continue. 807 But
"How sad a sight is British sunshine To him whose thought can pierce beyond an hour."
I shall have many thoughts of the migration you will be accomplishing at the same time that we are accomplishing ours. 808 Those thoughts can hardly be without a pang of regret, for I have not yet reconciled myself to imagining you all in the cottage, instead of in the pretty green drawing room and comfortable red dining room. But Mr. Bray's face looked so happy and sunshiny in the prospect of the change, that one feels sure he will be a great centre of content radiating cheerfulness to all the planets that around him shine. 809
How is Cara through all the vicissitudes? My best love to her and to the radiating centre. Ever dear Sara,
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [23 November 1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 24. 1857. Extracts published: Cross, I, 474.
Richmond | Monday.
Dear Sara
The chinks of my time yesterday 1015 were so filled up with things I was obliged to attend to -- proof-readings etc. that I couldn't write to you. But I didn't forget to think of you gratefully, as we walked in the mild sunshine and looked at the purple and gold along the river.
Sometime, I do mean, if I can, to send you an ugly photograph, since-you desire it, having perhaps a savage pleasure in perceiving how "the individual withers." 1016 I didn't give your letter to Mr. Lewes or tell him it was my birthday, for except you, I don't like anybody to say anything about it or make a fuss and congratulate me. Anniversaries are sad things -- to one who has lived long and done little.
Herbert Spencer dined with us the other day -- looks well, and is brimful of clever talk, as usual. His volume of [Essays] 1017 is to come out soon. He is just now on a crusade against the notion of [species.] Next to that his indignation with government interference about Jointstock Banks seems to be the dominant interest. 1018
We are reading Harriet Martineau's history 1019 with edification, and otherwise feeding our souls, which flourish very well notwithstanding November weather. What of your Antichrist? 1020
Ever thine
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Richmond, [2 October 1858]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oct. 2. 1858. Hitherto unpublished.
Richmond | Saturday.
Dear Sara
I had a letter from Mrs. Call the other day in which she said incidentally that Dr. Chapman was staying with them, so I dare say we shall not see him for a week or so. I will willingly ask him that question, but as it is rather an awkward one, I must have some knowledge that will enable me to ask it adroitly. Can't you tell me what is the subject, and just hint the treatment?
I am all alarm and anxiety about the penny paper. The other, of course, is not given up? What worry and care Mr. Bray must be having -- and Cara can't help sharing it. She may well be thin. My love to her and tell her I don't value her a bit the more for not writing to me -- on the contrary.
That is a delicious picture of poor Harriet! 1191 I wish I could run in with you some day and hear her talk. I remember so well that description of the Clerus at the Asylum, which she gave us one day when we were all seated snugly in the drawingroom at Rosehill.
The "mysterious stranger" 1192 is certainly thrilling to look at. It seems ludicrous that we take the opera glass to look at him -- and see him much the better for it. I am not at all inclined to think contemptuously of him as a mere "flocculus."
We have had the pleasure of seeing our interesting friends Dr. and Mrs. Bodichon, who are soon to go away to Algiers again. She means to buy a house and garden there, and reside there the greater part of the year. I am delighted with her husband on a nearer acquaintance. He seems to me a gentle hearted, noble spirited man, and they are as happy together as -- we are. They have been the only people we have seen since we came from Germany. Dinner is come.
Your loving
Pollian.

Park Shot | Saturday.
A great improvement, dear Sara, and I can't help being glad that I sent my perhaps brusque criticisms, not having time to say that "I begged leave respectfully to differ from you."
Miss Barbara Smith and her father and sisters are going to Algiers! in the hope that this extreme application of [change] will complete Bella's recovery. 752

When Herbert Spencer comes to town, I will let Mr. Bray know his address, and then he can write to him according to any revised and amended edition of an invitation that may suggest itself. Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Penzance, 24 March [1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1857. Hitherto unpublished.
Penzance | Tuesday, March 24.
Dear Sara
I can't help being a little glad at your anxiety -- it shows you care about me. We are still at Penzance you see, and have not yet trusted the Atlantic with our crazy bodies. The boat only goes to Scilly twice a week -- Wednesdays and Saturdays -- and last Wednesday we were both so knocked up by our journey, that we dare not incur the extra sea-sickness threatened by the delays of an obstinate west wind. So we took lodgings, praying for a better wind on Saturday. But on Saturday it blew a hurricane, and now our hopes, or rather our fears, all turn on to-morrow. The weather has been just what we wanted every day except those on which the packet has sailed. 821 It is clear we are important persons, the state of the wind having evidently a relation to our movements.
But we make the best of a bad business, and are so much stronger than we were last week, that only the very worst weather will prevent our crossing to-morrow. In the meantime, we explore the charming walks round Penzance, and learn by heart all the hedgerow beauties of March in this country. 822
Our letters, sent to the Scilly Isles, have only come back to us here, this morning. I hope you have not been wondering much that yours was not answered earlier. The Ariadne is a capital yacht, warranted not to be a wreck, so don't be in any fear about us. But I will let you know of our arrival as soon as possible. Ever, with love to all,
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Niton, 21 June [1863]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Niton, 21 June [1863]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 21, 1863. Extracts published: Cross, II, 355.
Post Office, Niton | Sunday, June 21.
Dear Sara
Your letter telling that the Sydenham house is let for a good long space was a welcome addition to our sunshine this Sabbath morning. For in this particular we seem to have been more fortunate than you, having had almost constant sunshine since we arrived at Sandown on Tuesday evening. 165
This place is perfect, reminding me of Jersey in its combination of luxuriant greenth with the delights of a sandy beach. You see we are at
Mrs. Blythe's, recommended to us by Mr. Bray and Miss Marshall. Unfortunately for us, her best rooms were all occupied, but we have a tolerable sitting room and bedroom, and don't mind making shift a little for a week. At the end of our week, if the weather is warmer we shall go on to Freshwater for our remaining few days. But the wind at present is a little colder than one desires it when the object is to get rid of a cough, and unless it gets milder, we shall not venture to go to Freshwater but shall go back to Shanklin.
I imagine you pleasing yourself with your tiny photos. That little one you gave me, in a frame, is a very good one for some points of your face and expression to any one who knows you, but in general strangers would imagine you quite a different person from that small-featured delicate-faced thing you really are, if they saw nothing but your photographs. As for Cara, they alter her face much as the moon is altered when it looks very large, white and weightless, hanging low in the sky.
I am enjoying the hedgerow grasses and flowers with something like a released prisoner's feeling -- it is so long since I had a bit of real English country when I could give myself up to it without distraction. No more now. With love to all
Your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Munich, 17 April 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Munich, 17 April 1858
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 28-29.
Luitpold Strasse | Munich | April 17. 1858.
Dear Sara
We got into our lodgings last Tuesday, and on Wednesday when we were seated on our sofa, taking our after-dinner coffee, I read aloud your journal. So you see, you have made part of our thoughts in this far-off new place.
We arrived here on Sunday night from N'fcrnberg -- that town of towns -- and of course the first thing to be done on Monday morning was to look out for lodgings. We walked ourselves weary all round by the Englischer Garten and the streets leading from the Ludwig Strasse, till we began to think it a hopeless business. That private mode of advertising which is common in Germany, seems to attain its climax here; for the only intimation you get of lodgings to be let is on small bits of paper covered with small German manuscript and pasted up at street corners as remote as possible from the place in question. At last, Mr. Lewes bethought himself of going to Oldenburg, 1120 the publisher, to whom he had an introduction, and he turned out to be an unostentatiously kind man, who was ready to take a great deal of trouble for us without making the smallest fuss. He took us to two H'f4tels Garnis -- places where you get lodgings and attendance and coffee and nothing else -- but they were too grand and comfortless. Then we took to reading notices again, and trudged along no end of streets all in vain, till we couldn't, for shame, trouble our benevolent German any longer. So after our one o'clock dinner we set out again by ourselves and at last found "zwei elegant m'f6blirte Zimmer," where there has been an immense expenditure on wax and china ornaments and the least possible outlay in basins. We have two time-pieces under glass shades, several crucifixes also under glass shades, several bouquets of artificial flowers under glass shades, a Schranke with glass doors crammed full of the most brittle and tiny articles to be found in the German shops, selected apparently for their brittle-minuteness, and seventeen bad pictures. These are the chief advantages of our lodgings. As secondary ones, we have a very clean old maid as our landlady, and a goodnatured ruddy dummes m'e4dchen for servant; we have a clean Abtritt(!) and two very large gilt framed mirrors hung in dark corners.
Our only discomfort of a serious kind, is that our box of books dispatched a fortnight ago is not yet arrived. We only want that to make us feel quite settled. Mr. Lewes has introductions to some of the best people here -- von Siebold, 1121 and Bodenstedt 1122 and eminences of that sort -- and Oldenburg is going to introduce him to Liebig, 1123 who is now one of the University professors here. So I dare say we shall have quite as much society as we shall care for.
We have been just to take a sip at the two Pinacotheks (the new one devoted to modern art is just finished) and at the Glyptothek, have bought our catalogues, and glanced here and there at the chief attractions. At present the Rubens-Saal is what I most long to return to. Rubens gives me more pleasure than any other painter, whether that is right or wrong. To be sure, I have not seen so many pictures and pictures of so high a rank, by any other great master. I feel sure that when I have seen as much of Raffaelle, I shall like him better, but at present Rubens more than any one else makes me feel that painting is a great art and that he was a great artist. His are such real, breathing men and women -- men and women moved by passions, not mincing and grimacing and posing in mere apery of passion! What a grand, glowing, forceful thing life looks in his pictures -- the men such grand bearded grappling beings fit to do the work of the world, the women such real mothers.
We have just glanced round the Glyptothek, and looked at the original Sleeping Faun, of which I had seen an excellent copy at Berlin, at your great Apollo, the Medusa head, 1124 and the Venus of Cnidos; but the cold marble floors are not so comfortable now as they will be in warm weather, and enthusiasm, I find, though of the warmest "description" will not warm one's feet. So we hurried out, promising ourselves many another visit by and bye. Amongst the modern pictures Kaulbach's seem to me quite the best -- I don't know what we shall say to Cornelius here, but at Berlin I saw nothing that gave me a great idea of him.
The general aspect of Munich is distasteful to me. The buildings are generally huge, expensive and ugly, and one feels everywhere that the art is something superinduced by royal patronage. Such a contrast to N'fcrnberg! I see by your journal that you didn't come to Munich by way of N'fcrnberg -- the more's the pity. We staid there only twenty-four hours, and I felt sad to leave it so soon. There one sees a real mediaeval town, which has grown up with the life of a community as much as the shell of a nautilus has grown with the life of the animal; and the result is just as beautiful. No uniform barrack-like lines of houses there. Every house has a physiognomy -- there is no end to the varieties which the vista of every street presents -- but it is a variety like Nature's, showing general unity presiding over an endless play of individual variety. A pity the place became protestant, so that there is only one Catholic church where one can go in and out as one would. We turned into the famous St. Sebald's for a minute, where a Protestant clergyman was reading in a cold formal way under the grand gothic arches. Then we went to the Catholic church, the Frauenkirche, where the organ and voices were giving forth a glorious mass, and we stood with a feeling of brotherhood among the standing congregation, till the last note of the organ had died out.
I can understand the effect you must have experienced from being set in a different key to your companions. The gentleman 1125 you mention once said to me, "I think Mannheim the most delightful of German towns." I have never seen Mannheim, but since then I have read Riehl's description of it, and know just what sort of place it must be. That is enough to tell me how much sympathy you must have had.
I am miserable physically for the first time since setting out, having caught a Schnupfen or Schleimfieber, which gives me a headache and a general sense that life is a thing which smells badly and has a nasty taste.
Mr. Lewes sends his kind regards. By the bye, did the "lady" present herself only at Ivy Cottage? Love to all from
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Munich, 14 June 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Munich, 14 June 1858
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 44-45.
Luitpold Strasse | Munich | June 14. 58.
Dear Sara
My thoughts were very often with you in conjectures not far from the truth, before your letter came. 1155 It is a long while since it came -- for I have been very poorly and have not had energy to put a letter on paper, though I have been sometimes writing one in my mind. Words are very clumsy things -- I like less and less to handle my friends' sacred feelings with them. For even those who call themselves [intimate] know very little about each other -- hardly ever know just how a sorrow is felt, and hurt each other by their very attempts at sympathy or consolation. We can bear no hand on our bruises. And so I feel I have no right to say that I know how the loss of your mother -- [the only person who ever leaned on you] -- affects you. I only know that it must make a deeply felt crisis in your life, and I know that the better, from having felt a great deal about my own mother and father and from having the keenest remembrance of all that experience. But for this very reason, I know that I can't measure what the event is to you, and if I were near you I should only kiss you and say nothing. I cried over your letter and felt myself with you in all you were telling me about. People talk of the feelings dying out as one gets older -- but at present my experience is just the contrary. All the serious relations of life become so much more real to one -- pleasure seems so slight a thing, and sorrow and duty and endurance so great. I find the least bit of real human life touch me in a way it never did when I was younger.
I hope this letter will be sent to you at Ramsgate. That is a very nice place to take Harriet 1156 to -- it is so full of innocent enjoyment to counterbalance the hoops and the vanity of a watering place. 'abWhat a precious sister you are to her. I don't know any one else who could have fulfilled that duty so bravely and generously as you have done.'bb Cara, I dare say, is like you, worn and in need of rest and change. I hope she means to allow herself some by and bye. Give my best love to her and divide between you twenty kisses.
Mr. Lewes has been suffering a good deal for the last fortnight from his old trouble of singing in the ears and deafness, which often obliges him to leave off work. I am quite well again now, and better pleased with the heat than most people can be; it saves me the trouble of walking after breakfast to warm my feet.
Whenever you can spare me half an hour to tell me something about yourself, you will be doing a good deed.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

1156 Harriet Hennell had been brought  from Northampton at the time of her mother's death and taken back there 2 June, after a brief holiday. Sara wrote in reply to this letter 27 June 1858: "My immediate business is settling Harriet in a lodging of her own at Northampton. I have engaged a couple of rooms for her in the house of a very respectable old couple -- the husband calling himself Revd from casually officiating as a Baptist minister, but whose impoverished circumstances make them glad of pecuniary aid. And in a fortnight I am going to Northampton to take the rather hazardous step of taking her away from the Asylum, though the power of restoring her there is still, unknown to her, retained. . . . We did not go to Ramsgate after all -- she would not muster courage for it, and it would have been unwise to press it." (Yale.)

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Munich, 10-13 May 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Munich, 10-13 May 1858
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 34-39.
Luitpold Strasse, 15 | Munich | May 10th 1858.
Dear Sara
I write to you again so soon because I want you, whenever you have a spare moment, to tell me how all has been going on with you for the last month -- how Mrs. Hennell is, and what sort of spirits and health you are in yourself.
Our life here is very agreeable -- full of pleasant novelty, although we take things quietly, and observe our working hours just as if we were at Richmond. People are so kind to us that we feel already quite at home, sip Baierisch Bier with great tolerance, and talk bad German with more and more aplomb. The place, you know, swarms with professors of all sorts -- all gr'fcndlich, of course, and one or two of them great. There is no one we are more charmed with than Liebig. Mr.
Lewes had no letter to him -- we merely met him at an evening party 1126 -- yet he has been particularly kind to us, and seems to have taken a benevolent liking to me. We dined with him and his family yesterday, and saw how men of European celebrity may put up with greasy cooking in private life. He lives in very good German style, however, has a handsome suite of apartments, and makes a greater figure than most of the professors. His manners are charming -- easy, graceful, benignant, and all the more conspicuous because he is so quiet and low-spoken among the loud talkers here. It is touching to look at his hands, the skin begrimed and the nails black to the roots. He looks best in his laboratory with his velvet cap on, holding little phials in his hand and talking of Kreatine and Kreatinine in the same easy way that well bred ladies talk scandal. He is one of the professors who have been called here by the present king, Max, who seems to be a really sensible man among kings -- gets up at five o'clock in the morning to study, and every Saturday evening has a gathering of the first men in science and literature, that he may 'abgather'bb benefit by their opinions on important subjects. At this "Tafel-rund," every man is [required] to say honestly what he thinks -- every one may contradict every one else -- and if the King suspects any one of a polite insincerity, the too polished man is invited no more. Liebig, the three poets -- Geibel, 1127 Heyse, 1128 and Bodenstedt, and a Professor L'f6her, 1129 a writer of considerable mark, are always at the Tafel-rund, as an understood part of their functions; the rest are invited according to the King's direction. Bodenstadt is one of our best friends here -- enormously instructed after the fashion of Germans, but not at all stupid with it. Like all the best men here, he is a North German, and has not acquired the Bavarian habit of spending his evenings at the Kneipe, drinking beer, smoking tobacco, and trying to talk down his companions. That is the understood mode of life for all genuine Bavarians, however cultivated, and you may imagine what is the character of the women dabei. It is quite an exception to meet with a woman who seems to expect any sort of companionship from the men, and I shudder at the sight of a woman in society, for I know I shall have to sit on the sofa with her all the evening listening to her stupidities, while the men on the other side of the table are discussing all the subjects I care to hear about. And the stupidity of a Bavarian woman --
I think I was going to say that the stupidity of a Bavarian woman has not the virtue even of German cabbage -- it is not copious, liberal, abundant -- it is stingy, feeble, barren of propositions. But there [are] exceptions to this dreadful description. And happily there is such a colony of North Germans among the educated people that one hopes there may be a gradual modification through their influence.
Mr. Lewes is in a state of perfect bliss this morning. He is gone to the Akademie 1130 to see wonders through von Siebold's microscope and watch him dissecting. We were at his house last night to meet a party of celebrities, and, what was better, to see the prettiest little picture of married life -- the great comparative anatomist (von Siebold) seated at the piano in his spectacles, playing the difficult accompaniments to Schubert's songs, while his little round-faced wife sang them with much taste and feeling. They are not young -- von Siebold is grey, and probably more than fifty, his wife perhaps nearly forty, and it is all the prettier to see their admiration of each other. She said to Mr. Lewes, when he was speaking of her husband, "Ja, er ist ein netter Mann, nicht wahr?"
We take the Art in very small draughts at present, the German hours being difficult to adjust to our occupations. We are obliged to dine at one! and, of course, when we are well enough, must work till then. There is no moving for two hours afterwards, and then all the great public exhibitions are closed -- except the churches. There must have been a great deal built and completed since you were here -- the colossal Bavaria and the Ruhmeshalle 1131 -- the Basilica and the Ludwigs-kirche, the one full of frescoes by Hess, 1132 the other of frescoes by Cornelius. 1133 But alas! I cannot admire much of the modern German art. It is for the most part elaborate lifelessness. Kaulbach's great compositions are huge charades, and I have seen nothing of his equal to his own Reineke
Fuchs. It is an unspeakable relief, after staring at one of his huge pictures, the Destruction of Jerusalem, for example, which is a regular child's puzzle of symbolism, to sweep it all out of one's mind -- which is very easily done, for nothing grasps you in it -- and call up in your imagination a little Gerard Dow that you have seen hanging in a corner of one of the cabinets. Kaulbach himself is not much liked here: some are jealous, of course, for he has made a very large fortune, while others who think themselves equal to him are in poverty, getting no royal orders to execute; others have been offended by his whims etc. etc. -- At Munich, as well as in London, one must listen with a grain of scepticism. We have been to his atelier, and he has given us a proof of his Irrenhaus, a strange sketch which he made years ago, very terrible and powerful. He is certainly a man of great faculty, but is, I imagine carried out of his true path by the ambition to produce "Weltgeschichtliche Bilder," which the critics (German) may go into raptures about. His "Battle of the Huns" which is the most impressive of all his great pictures was the first of the series. He painted it simply under the inspiration of the grand myth about the spirits of the dead warriors rising and carrying on the battle in the air. Straightway the German critics began to smoke furiously that vile tobacco which they call AEsthetik, declared it a "Weltgeschichtliches Bild," and ever since, Kaulbach has been concocting these pictures, in which, instead of taking a single moment of reality, and trusting to the infinite symbolism that belongs to all nature, he attempts to give you at one view a succession of events, each represented by some group which may mean "whichever you please, my little dear."
I must tell you something else which interested me greatly as the first example of the kind that has come under my observation. Among the awful mysterious names hitherto known only as marginal references, whom we have learned to clothe with ordinary flesh and blood is Prof. Martius 1134 ("Spix and Martius"), now an old man, and rich, after the manner of being rich in Germany. He has a very sweet wife -- one of those women who remain pretty and graceful in old age -- and a family of three daughters and one son -- all more than grown up. I had suspected that Frau Martius was a Catholic, yet it seemed to me, from the Professor's Wesen, impossible that he could be a Catholic too. So the other night, I asked the charming Frau, and learned that she is
Catholic, that her daughters are Catholic, and her husband and son Protestant, the children having been so brought up according to the German law in cases of mixed marriage. I can't tell you how interesting it was to me to hear her tell of her experience in bringing up her son conscientiously as a Protestant, she herself being a Catholic all the while, and then to hear her and her daughters speak of the exemplary priests who had shown them such tender fatherly care when they were in trouble. They are the most harmonious affectionate family we have seen, and one delights in such a triumph of human goodness over the formal logic of theorists.
But I go on scribbling in a meagre way what is present in my own imagination, forgetting that this bit of paper will carry no picture to you. Goodbye, and God bless you -- Love to all.
Your affectionate
Marian.
I was sorry to hear there was anything in Mr. Call's article 1135 that you didn't understand. I admired it thoroughly. On the other hand I did not admire Dr. Chapman's part, 1136 and was obliged to tell him so, when he sent me the proof. However, he cut off the last few pages, which were the most objectionable. There are several misstatements in his part. But it is well that readers differ. We all get admired in our turn.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Meriden, 24 December [1850]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1850. Hitherto unpublished.
Meriden | December 24th.
All Christmas blessings to you dear Sara. The other morning as I was lying in bed I had a clear revelation of my own deficiencies towards you, and of the justice of your feelings. This, like all other self-insight comes too late but it is an irresistible impulse to tell you of it. I hope you got home without railway misadventures. 906
Ever thine
Pollian.
Mr. Slack refuses to print the answer to Dr. Beard! 907

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 9 October [1851]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 9 October [1851]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1851. Extracts published: Cross, I, 263-264.
Strand | October 9.
I wish, dear Sara, you could see Miss Bremer's Albums full of portraits, flowers and landscapes, all done by herself. A portrait of Emerson marvellously like -- one of Jenny Lind, of Oersted 1026 etc. etc.
Last night we had quite a charming soirée -- Sir David Brewster 1027 and his daughter; Mr. Kay, the brother of Sir J. P. Shuttleworth, and author of a work on popular education 1028 you may remember to have seen reviewed in the Leader; the Ellises, the Hodgsons and half a dozen other nice people. Miss Bremer was more genial than I had seen her -- played on the piano and smiled benevolently. This morning at breakfast, she told me a very pretty story -- all the prettier for her broken English ([The young man had to make his fate.]) Altogether I am beginning to repent of my repugnance. She did intend to stay another week, but now fears she must leave on Sunday. 1029
Mr. Kay approves our Prospectus in toto. He is a handsome, fine-headed man, and a [good opinion.] We are getting out a circular 1030 to accompany the Pros[pectus]. I have been kept down-stairs by Mr. Mackay for the last two hours and am hurried, but it was a necessity to write [ein paar Worte] to you. Mr. Mackay has written an account of his book for the Catalogue. I have been using my powers of eloquence and flattery this morning to make him begin an article on the Development of Protestantism. He says [Thank you] and asks me what books I recommend him to read!!
I trust to you to send me word about Cara's health because, you know, she [tells such lies] about herself.
Miss Bremer has just been telling us of a little girl in America who asked her Mamma if Sunday was not a very strong day -- since all the rest were weak days.
Tell Mr. Bray I made a conquest of a fat clergyman and a thin student last night. Mr. Ellis was more agreeable -- really witty. He and Mrs. Ellis particularly cordial to me inviting me to visit them without ceremony. -- I love you all better every day, and better the more I see of other people.
Your affectionate
Pollian.
Write all of you and tell me everything. The properest of phrases to Mr. Noel that will express hearty friendship, and kisses to all the children. I am going to one of the Birkbeck schools. 1031

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 9 March 1863
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, II, 349-350.
Blandford Sq. | March 9. 63.
Dear Sara
I think we must not grumble any more about our health just yet for we are hardly worse off than our neighbours. I suppose poor Miss Marshall's affliction is neuralgic face-ache -- piteous to think of. And Mr. Bray's, of which I learn for the first time from your note, is perhaps like something Mr. Lewes has been having from irritable teeth. I remember old troubles of that sort. I feel for all mortals with ailing bodies.
We have had a week at Dorking, 139 returning a few days ago to welcome Charlie home after his holiday -- not to see the procession, which I should have liked well enough to see if I had had more strength of mind and body to endure being driven through crowded streets and sitting at a window with people who would have a long while to stare at one before the procession came.
Poor Mr. Congreve, after his severe attack of sciatica, is trying to quicken his recovery by a stay at Peter Hall. 140 Mrs. Congreve writes that he seems to be the better for the change. She says, they hear nothing about the Coventry distress, and I am hoping that it is somewhat diminished, since Mr. Bray wrote last about it.
That scheme of a sort of Philosophic Club that I told you of 141 went to pieces before it was finished, like a house of cards. So it will be to the end I fancy, with all attempts at combinations that are not based either on material interests, or on opinions that are not merely opinions but religion. -- I think I have no news to tell but such as is in the newspapers. Doubtless you have been interested in the Colenso correspondence, 142 and perhaps in good Miss Cobbe's Rejoinder to Mrs. Stowe's Remonstrating Answer to the Women of England. 143 I was glad to see how free the answer was from all tartness or conceit. Miss Cobbe's Introduction to the new edition of Theodore Parker 144 is also very honourable to her -- a little too metaphorical here and there, but with real thought and good feeling in it. With best love to all,
Ever yours
Pollian.
