Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 9 March 1854
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | March 9. 1854.
Dear Sara
Pray keep the M.S. another week. By the week after next I shall have a large parcel for you which I hope Mr. Bray will not object to carry. You know the German fashion of writing 'fcber= und wider= nat'fcrliche, ausser= und 'fcber=weltliche etc. Do you prefer the innovation of introducing this abbreviation into the English, or the awkwardness of repetition? 442
I am rather surprized that Mr. Noel should "speak slightingly" of Feuerbach, since when he came to England with Dr. Springer 443 he brought a smaller work of Feuerbach's "Das Wesen der Religion" 444 containing the same fundamental ideas as the "Wesen des Christenthums" and expressed great anxiety to have it translated. But perhaps he was speaking in Dr. Springer's sense just then. Au reste, Mr. Noel is not a reading man and, I know, has no clear idea of the contents of Feuerbach's works. But that does not hinder him (Mr. Noel) from being a man of strong sense, of real kindliness and large experience of life especially of life among distinguished people and in remarkable places. I am glad you have had some pleasure in his lecture 445 and society.
I am exceedingly well now and enjoying existence as an imperfectly developed stunted creature may. I like my independent life in lodgings better and better, and want nothing but a little more money. Miss Barbara Smith has lent me some of her pictures, of which I am very fond, to ornament my room with and suggest some prettier ideas than I can extract out of dingy walls and curtains. I am often longing for a little more of "le superflu, chose si necessaire" 446 -- much oftener than I remember that half the things I have are "le superflu" for the majority of mankind.
I must tell you a characteristic trait of Herbert Spencer. I happened to say in reference to a criticism I had given of a passage in his article on the Universal Postulate, which passage he expunged in consequence, that the better form for the axiom which is the basis of the syllogism as explained by Mill would be -- "Things which have the same fixed relation to the same thing have the same fixed relation to each other." Mill gives "Things which co-exist with the same thing" etc. The next day he came to tell me in intense delight how important the suggestion was to him in his work on Psychology -- how it had given him just the bridge he wanted etc. -- and that he should put a long note in his book explaining how he came by the idea. Is he not a dear bit of conscientiousness and scrupulosity? 447
Mr. Lewes has just come in and put into my hands the enclosed letter from Gerald Massey, which shew Mr. Bray. Be it noted, that the "letter" G. Massey refers to contained the question -- when was Mr. L. going to review G.M.'s book, as he (G.M.) meant to advertise in the Leader. Also, that Mr. Lewes has been very kind to Gerald Massey as an author. 448
I have no time to say any more. I fear you can't read even this.
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 9 April 1866
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 424-425.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 9. 66.
Dear Sara
Don't think any evil of me for not writing. Just now, the days are short and art is long, to artists with feeble bodies. If people don't say expressly that they want anything from me, I easily conclude that they will do better without me, and have a good weight of idleness, or rather bodily fatigue, which puts itself into the scale of modesty.
I am grieved to see that you write of Cara's cold as if it were something of unusually long standing. Give my best love to her and tell her I like always to believe that she is extant though the only proof is that I hear nothing to the contrary.
We are always the same -- happy in everything except our livers and stomachs. Yet, in spite of these, I feel a growing cheerfulness -- I torment myself less with fruitless regrets that my particular life has not been more perfect. The young things are growing, and to me it is not melancholy but joyous that the world will be brighter after I am gone than it has been in the brief time of my existence. You see my pen runs into very old reflections. The fact is I have no details to tell that would much interest you. It is true that I am going to bring out another book, but just when, is not certain.
A lord's son, 421 who comes often to see us, interests us greatly by giving us an idea of what many of his class are suffering from this calamity of the cattle-plague. 422 He has been working hard among the poor beasts and their owners in Cheshire. His father doesn't expect to have any rent for 6 years, and now this young man is wishing he knew how to get his bread!
Mr. Spencer was with us yesterday -- very cheerful and running over with argument as usual.
Always yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 9 April [1864]
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, II, 381-382.
April 9. 63.
Dear Sara
Yes! I am come back from Scotland -- came back last Saturday night. But engagements are so constant now, that I shall hardly see Cara at Sydenham except by some lucky chance. How is it you are not there?
I thought the whole household was to migrate to Sydenham, and was about to write thither to inquire whether and when you were coming to London. Cara had spoken of a journey to Liverpool as a project of yours -- and that was the only thing that made me doubtful whether you would come to Sydenham.
I was much pleased to see Cara so wonderfully well and cheerful. She seems to me ten times more cheerful than in the old days. I am interested to know more about your work which is filling your life now, but I suppose I shall know nothing until it is in print -- and perhaps that is the only form in which one can do any one's work full justice.
It is very disappointing to me to hear that Cara has at present so little promise of monetary results from her conscientious labour. I fear the fatal system of half-profits is working against her as against others.
We are going to the opera tonight to hear the Favorita. It was the first opera I ever saw (with you I saw it!) and I have never seen it since; that is the reason I was anxious to go tonight. This afternoon we go to see Mulready's pictures -- so the day will be a full one.
I have not been well this week and have been preoccupied with visitors 254 -- else I should have written to Cara.
Ever thine affectionately
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 8 February 1861
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1861. Extracts published: Cross, II, 286-287.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
February 8. 61.
My dear Sara
Miss Marshall called yesterday and I delivered over to her the "Strauss letters." 691 I have not read them since you gave them to me, years ago, and I would rather not know what is in them since I have not the right to destroy them. The knowledge would only give a more definite repugnance to the idea of their falling into other hands after your death.
I have destroyed almost all my friends' letters to me, simply on that ground -- because they were only intended for my eyes, and could only fall into the hands of persons who knew little of the writers, if I allowed them to remain till after my death. In proportion as I love every form of piety -- which is venerating love -- I hate hard curiosity; and unhappily my experience has impressed me with the sense that hard curiosity is the more common temper of mind. But enough of that.
The reminders I am getting from time to time of Coventry distress 692 have made me think very often, yearningly and painfully, of the friends who are more immediately affected by it, and I often wonder if more definite information would increase or lessen my anxiety for them. Send me what word you can from time to time, that there may be some reality in my image of things round your hearth. Give my best love to Cara and Mr. Bray, and tell Cara I often have a longing to write, and yet feel a letter hardly justifiable with so little to say as I have.
We have been anything but brilliant in health since we saw you, but in other respects are as flourishing as possible. I was rather glad you escaped the long-legged gentlemen who came the next Saturday after your visit; but Mr. Spencer, longest-legged of all, was sorry not to have seen you. 693
Ever yours
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 7 December 1866
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, II, 446-447.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 7. 66.
Dear Sara
I am quite ashamed that we talk of our movements so long beforehand as to lead our friends into continual mistakes. We are not gone, or going, just yet. Mr. Lewes has still a month's work to do, 544 and he is obliged to take frequent intervals of ch'f4mage. Thank you for sending me that old letter of '57 which I had quite forgotten. But it is rather saddening to know that the new edition of the History will be still further beyond the purchasing reach of the men referred to in the letter: I believe it is to cost a guinea, being in two large volumes. The copyright has never been in Mr. Lewes's hands, and he works at the book for love, not for money; the £150 which he receives for revision bearing no appreciable proportion to his work. 545 The book-trade in this country is in a sad condition, in many ways, especially in the enforced dearness of good books.
We have been to Tunbridge Wells for a week, 546 hoping to get plenty of fresh air and walking in that sandy undulating country. But for three days it rained incessantly!
No, I don't feel as if my faculties were failing me. On the contrary, I enjoy all subjects -- all study, more than I ever did in my life before. But that very fact makes me more in need of resignation to the certain approach of age and death. Science, history, poetry 547 -- I don't know which draws me most. And there is little time left me for any one of them. I learned Spanish last year but one, and see new vistas everywhere. That makes me think of time thrown away when I was young -- time that I should be so glad of now. I could enjoy everything, from arithmetic to antiquarianism, if I had large spaces of life before me. But instead of that, I have a very small space. Unfeigned, unselfish, cheerful resignation is difficult. But I strive to get it. Tell Cara, with my love, that I believe in her unwritten letters.
Always yours affectionately
Pollian.
My affectionate remembrances to Mrs. J. Cash when you see her.

The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 7.
Dear Sara
Thanks for your delightful picture of Harriet 386 with her cats and her cups and plates. George and I enjoyed it.
I don't see the Spectator, but Mr. Congreve, who does, told me of the notice, 387 which struck him as complimentary. The Spectator, though it has not a great circulation, holds so good a rank among the weekly papers that a respectful notice there is worth a great deal of slipslop from the Mr. Bludgers 388 of the "Dailies." Not that any notice is good for anything except as an advertisement. And for that purpose abuse often does better than praise.
It is worth your while to send for the last Fortnightly to read an article of Professor Tyndal's "on the Constitution of the Universe." 389 It is a splendid piece of writing on the higher Physics, which I know will interest you.
A propos of the feminine intellect, I had a bit of experience with a "superior woman" the other day which reminds me of Sydney Smith's story about his sermon on the Being of a God. He says, that after he had delivered his painstaking argument, an old parishioner said to him, "I don't agree wi' you, Mr. Smith; I think there be a God." The result of my conversation with my superior woman was a letter two days after which showed the same sort of satisfactory comprehension. Our talk had been about the Future Life and the necessarily higher character of motives that were not personal.
We are going to hear the Israel in Egypt tomorrow. 390 Best love to Cara, and keen sympathy with Mr. Bray under his pain. For shame of you to have any worries with your beautiful teeth! I have no time to write much, but am always
Your loving
P.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1865. Extracts published: Cross, II, 396-397.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 6.
Dear Sara
I suspect you have come to dislike letters, but until you say so, I must write now and then to gratify myself. I want to send my love, lest all the old messages should have lost their scent, like old lavender bags.
I wonder how poor Cara's patient 312 bears the winter with its rapid alternations from severity to mildness, and how Cara herself is under all vicissitudes.
Since I wrote to you last we have actually been to Paris! A little business was an excuse for getting a great deal of pleasure, 313 and I, for whom change of air and scene is always the best tonic, am much brightened by our wintry expedition, which ended just in time for us to escape the heavy fall of snow.
We are very happy, having almost recovered our old t'eate-'e0-t'eate, of which I am so selfishly fond, that I am beginning to feel it an heroic effort when I make up my mind to invite half a dozen visitors. But it is necessary to strive against this unsocial disposition, so we are going to have some open evenings.
There is great talk of a new periodical -- a fortnightly apparition, partly on the plan of the Revue des deux Mondes. Mr. Lewes has consented to become its editor if the preliminaries are settled so as to satisfy him.
Ecco! I have told you a little of our news, not daring to ask you anything about yourself, since you evidently don't want to tell me anything.
I did not trouble Mr. Bray with special thanks for the Phil[osophy] of Health, but I was not the less obliged.
I hope at least you are pretty well, dear Sara: not harassed with cough or any other winter maladies.
Ever yours affectionately
Pollian.

MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge St. | February 6.
My dear Sara
Thank you for your observations. I have not been able to look into the M.S. yet, but when I do I shall consider all your suggestions. Will you have the kindness to return me the M.S. you now have as soon as possible? -- that is, of course, when you have read it. I enclose six stamps, that you may send it as a pamphlet, with the ends open, by post.
I shall send you Feuerbach's Preface soon. I wish you could have the German at the same time to amuse you. It is very curious that while his text is -- for a German -- concise, lucid and even epigrammatic now and then, his Preface reads like a caricature of the faults of German writing generally, one sentence is nearly a page and a half long! 436 I have done my best to save this from appearing in the English, but I wish you to pay particular attention to the Preface and to mark everything which seems odd and does not flow easily -- as it is very important that this preface should be read.
Ever your loving
Pollian.
It is such a comfort to have at least one person who can appreciate one's work. The dreariness of giving such a translation to Mr. Chapman who neither knows what is in itself good English nor what is the difficulty of truly representing German!

MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 321-323.
Blandford Sq. | December 6. 61.
Dear Sara
Thank you for that pretty bit of news. I shall delight in thinking that your Christmas will be cheered by such companionship.
Miss Marshall came to see us yesterday. That is always a pleasure to me, not only from the sense I have of her goodness, but because she stirs so many remembrances. The first time I saw her was at Rufa's wedding, and don't you remember the evening we spent at Mrs. Dobson's? How young we all were then -- how old now! She says, you are all under the impression that Mr. Lewes is still very ailing. Thank all good influences, it is not so. He has been mending ever since we went to Malvern, and is enjoying life and work more than he has done before for nearly a year. He has long had it in his mind to write a history of science -- a great, great undertaking, which it is a happiness for both of us to contemplate as possible for him. And now he is busy with Aristotle, and works with all the zest that belongs to fresh ideas. Strangely enough, after all the ages of writing about Aristotle, there exists no fair appreciation of his position in natural science. 878
I am particularly grumbling, and disagreeable to myself, just now, having been teazed with a slight cough that would not be shaken off, and now that is better, feeling constant Hemicrania and pain in the side -- all debility, I have no doubt, and carrying no consequences except those of present discomfort and depression. The way in which a slight cough affects me makes me think all the more of you, who have to suffer so frequently and severely from a cough. I think no one bears physical pain so ill as I do, or is so thoroughly upset by it mentally.
I must tell you a story which Mr. Wilkie Collins told us about Bulwer the other night. 879 I don't know whether you are reading "The Strange Story," 880 which from its air of lofty science along with representations of preternatural power, is, in our opinion of rather unwholesome tendency for popular reading -- and indeed would be wicked if it were not done by Bulwer in perfectly good faith, as it is. He is quite caught by the spirit of the marvellous, and a little while ago, at Dickens's house, was telling of a French woman who could raise the dead, but only at great expense. "What," said Dickens, "is the cause of this expense in raising the dead?" "The Perfumes!" said Bulwer, with deep seriousness, stretching out his hand with his usual air of lofty emphasis. -- I feel as if I ought not to tell you this, for if you repeat it to anybody else, I don't know what sort of monstrosity it may be turned into by the time it gets to the fifth narrator. I ought also to tell you, by way of balance to this absurdity, that Bulwer has behaved very nicely to me, and that -- quite apart from that personal question -- I have a great respect for the energetic industry with which he has made the most of his powers. He has been writing diligently in very various departments for more than thirty years, constantly improving his position, and profiting by the lessons of public opinion and of other writers.
I'm sorry you feel any degeneracy in Mr. George Dawson. There was something very winning about him in old days, and even what was not winning, but the reverse, affected me with a sort of kindly pity. With such a gift of tongue as he had, it was inevitable that speech should outrun feeling and experience, and I could well imagine that his present self might look back on that self of 21-27 with a sort of disgust. It so often happens that others are measuring us by our past self, while we are looking back on that self with a mixture of disgust and sorrow. It would interest me a good deal to know just how Mr. Dawson preaches now.
Charles is come back from Hofwyl now, and settled to work again -- but with a weight on his mind -- and on ours too -- about his box from which he parted company on the journey, and which contains almost all his earthly goods -- music, dress suit, new shirts, journal, a ring which his grandmamma gave him, and presents from his Hofwyl friends.
Mr. Spencer is coming to lodge in Harewood Square 881 close by us, but as we exclude visitors except on a Saturday we shall not, I dare say, see the more of him. He is very delightful when we don't get on art and classical literature -- subjects on which there is a great gulf fixed between us. I don't mind it when we are alone, but I am always uneasy for him when I see he is boring other people. For, to my thinking, it is more pitiable to bore than to be bored.
I am writing on my knees with my feet on the fender and in that attitude I always write very small -- but I hope your sight is not teazed by small writing. Give my best love to Cara and sympathy with her in the pleasure of grasping an old friend by the hand, and having long talks after the distance of years. I know Mr. Bray will enjoy this too -- and the new house will seem more like the old one for this warming.
I should have been sorry for you to come to London in this dreary season. Come in Spring instead.
Ever your loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 4 January 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 4 January 1872
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank | January 4. 1872.
My dear Sara
I hope that you have drawn the true inference from my three days' silence, namely that I have been away from home. We returned this afternoon -- rather earlier than we had intended, that I might consult Sir Henry Holland, my "inwards" having got all wrong again. This want of health would have hindered me from much enjoyment in seeing you just now, as it has hindered me from having much pleasure in a visit to some good friends in the country. I imagine, from what your letter tells me of your intentions, that you must already have got back to Coventry, so I shall send this scrap thither. Your sketch of circumstances at Ravensbourne implies that you have had to help others to be cheerful instead of being cheered by them. But this kind of sympathetic exertion is often more curative than mere reception -- only there is the troublesome winter cough! To bear that well seems to me almost an excuse for doing nothing else.
I am glad to hear a better account of Mr. Bray, which is at the same time a better account of Cara, if she has not broken down at the end of her nursing.
Please give them my love and greetings. I do earnestly hope that this year has comforts rather than anxieties in its lap for you all three. I suppose we must all of us accept a mixture of the anxieties, for those who are perfectly happy otherwise get their lungs or livers out of order.
Always, dear Sara, your affectionate
Pollian

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 4 February 1869
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 4 February 1869
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 4. 1869.
My dear Sara
Mr. Bray wrote to me on business about a week ago, but said no word about you, so that I was quite in ignorance of your movements.
I shall be most glad to kiss you after our long, long separation by time and space. Will it not be a better plan than the one which Miss Carter 16 kindly proposes, for you to come straight to us and occupy Charlie's old bed for a night? -- Come to us if possible in time for luncheon (i.e. at 'bd past 1) on Thursday the 11th, dine and sleep at our house, and then have an easy drive to the Euston Square Station the next morning. You see, dear Sara, I cannot ask you to stay more than one night, for, to have a visitor staying with us would be a perturbation of our lives which, under present conditions, we cannot endure. The fact is, we are brutally inhospitable, and I beseech you to understand that I treat you according to our rule and not as in any way an exception.
Pray write as soon as you can and fix the details, because, if my plan suits you, we will ask Mr. Spencer to dine with you. 17
I have been rather good-for-nothing lately, but Mr. Lewes has been buoyed up by some interesting inquiries which possess him wholly. We are going to Italy at the end of this month, unless Mr. Lewes's mother should be too ailing to part with him. Always
Your faithful
Marian.
If you do not like my plan, I will meet you wherever you choose.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 4 December 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 4 December 1880
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Cheyne Walk, | Chelsea, S.W.
December 4. 1880.
My dear Sara
I did absolutely, totally, and up to the arrival of your letter, forget my custom of writing to you in November! I would not beforehand have believed that such oblivion was possible to me while I retained my rational and representative faculties. But so it was, and I think that you would enter with some compassion into this lapse if I could possibly paint to you all that has been going on inwardly and outwardly for me at this epoch. Certainly I have in no way deserved that you should write me one of your charming letters as of old -- perfect letters that tell one what one wants to know without asking. But with my usual perversity of dwelling on what is least pleasurable, I find myself noting especially the [boiling] of your head, and the deafness, and the feebleness of dear Cara's eyes. O dear, I find an excuse for speaking ill of this planet when I hear that my friends have so many infirmities to struggle with. These things touch one's imagination more than the wrongs done by the tyrant of Thibet. The death of Annie Whittem 500 affected me with a pang of memory. I had never seen her since she was a most interesting
I wish you did not find yourself so repelled by Herbert Spencer's writing. He has so much teaching which the world needs, and with all systems one is justified in doing what Goethe mentions satirically in relation to dramatic or other art as the universal practice of audiences -- "If you give them a whole they will straightway take it to pieces. Each seeks what is adapted to him." 501
About Mozart, I am at one with you when I think of him in comparison with Handel, Beethoven and Schubert and some more modern composers -- that is, I feel his kinship to the Italian [sugared] view. But I find him, Haydn, and the Italians a welcome rest from more searching music.
About Cara's rheumatism -- is it at all an indication to think of hopefully, that many years ago, I had a beginning of rheumatism in my wrists? But it has never got worse, and for long spaces of time I have hardly felt it at all. I wish I could believe that her visitation of it is not worse than mine, but I fear it is rather severe since it keeps her awake.
Thank you, dear Sara, for taking the trouble to write when I am sure it is rather trying to you to do so.
Your ever affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 30 July 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 30 July 1861
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, II, 311-312.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
July 30. 61.
Dear Sara
Since I make my moan to you about my griefs, I ought to tell you when they are at an end, lest you should have the least bit of a causeless ache for me. Mr. Lewes has been much better, and in fair working order, for the last ten days or a fortnight, and I might have written to you cheerfully and thanked you for your suggestion of the aerated bread sooner than this, if I had not been preoccupied with various little affairs.
Thornie, our second boy is at home from Edinburgh, 823 for his holidays, and I am apt to give more thought than is necessary to any little change in our routine.
We had a treat the other night which I wish you could have shared with us: we saw Fechter in Hamlet. 824 His conception of the part is very nearly that indicated by the critical observations in Wilhelm Meister, and the result is deeply interesting -- the naturalness and sensibility of the Wesen overcoming in most cases the defective intonation. And even the intonation is occasionally admirable; for example, "and for my soul, what can he do to that etc." 825 is given by Fechter with perfect simplicity, whereas the herd of English actors imagine themselves in a pulpit when they are saying it.
Apropos of the pulpit, I had another failure in my search for edification last Sunday. Mrs. Bodichon and I went to Little Portland St. Chapel, and lo, instead of James Martineau there was a respectable old Unitarian gentleman preaching about the dangers of ignorance and the satisfaction of a good conscience in a tone of amiable propriety which seemed to belong to a period when brains were untroubled by difficulties and the lacteals 826 of all good Christians were in perfect order. I enjoyed the fine selection of Collects he read from the Liturgy. What an age of earnest faith, grasping a noble conception of life and determined to bring all things into harmony with it, has recorded itself in the simple pregnant, rhythmical English of those Collects and of the Bible! The contrast when the good man got into the pulpit and began to pray in a borrowed washy lingo -- ex tempore in more senses than one!
Ever yours
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 30 August 1864
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 30. 64.
Dear Sara
Certainly punishments are not fairly distributed in this world. I, who scarcely ever put off answering a letter, did put off writing to you till yesterday, and of course addressed my letter to Harrogate. And now for my immediate direct punishment I find this morning that you were already at Coventry. While wretches who never care to answer letters --
However in the hope that you will get that scrap of a letter from Harrogate I will not repeat what I said therein, but tell you in reply to your question about Charlie, that we don't expect him to be married till next year. Gertrude is going for this next month with her aunts into Brittany, and Charlie's holiday will not happen till next April, May or June.
I am so pleased to hear that you have enjoyed your outing. With best love to Cara
Ever your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 30 April 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 30 April 1864
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, II, 382-383.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 30. 64.
Dear Sara
Only think! next Wednesday morning we start for Italy. The move is quite a sudden one. We need a good shake for our bodies and minds and must take the Spring-time before the weather becomes too hot. We shall not be away more than a month, or six weeks at the utmost. Our friend Mr. Burton, the artist, will be our companion for at least part of the time. He has just painted a divine picture -- better than Millais' Huguenots -- which is now to be seen at the Old Water-Colour Exhibition. The subject is from a Norse Legend, but that is no matter -- the picture tells its story. A knight in mailed armour and surcoat has met the fair tall woman he se[cretly] loves on a turret stair. By an uncontrollable movement he has seized her arm and is kissing it. She, amazed, has dropped the flowers she held in her other hand. The subject might have been made the most vulgar thing in the world -- the artist has raised it to the highest pitch of refined emotion. The kiss is on the fur-lined sleeve that covers the arm, and the face of the knight is the face of a man to whom the kiss is a sacrament. 258
How I should like a good long talk with you! From what you say of your book that is to come, I expect to be very much interested in it. I think I hardly ever read a book of the kind you describe without getting some help from it. It is to this strong influence that is felt in all personal statements of inward experience that we must perhaps refer the excessive publication of religious journals.
I am wondering whether Cara is still at Sydenham or has returned to leave room for the tenants. My best love to her and Mr. Bray -- and wishes for poor Nelly's perfect health. Mr. Lewes waits to take my letter -- so I will only say good-by dear Sara.
Your ever affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 3 October 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 3 October 1862
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square | October 3. 1862.
Dear Sara
Where are you? I fear I must have written to you from Little Hampton under some misunderstanding of your letter received there. The sad fact was, that after I had given your letter a first hasty reading as breakfast was beginning, Mr. Lewes snatched it up along with his own letters and carried it away, and though I asked him for it very shortly after, he could not find it. 110 Such magical disappearances are effected now and then by the sleight of hand of some spirit that doesn't rap. The consequence was that I wrote under the impression that you were coming to town about the middle of September to stay a month. I begin to think now that I made a wide mistake, and am anxious that you should not attribute any stupidity in my letter to some other cause than the true one. I could not have seen much of you in any case, as it is my plan now to avoid any other distraction than that of our family talk and walks, but I am truly sorry if I have missed the pleasure of kissing you and hearing something about you from your own lips, by reason of that unlucky snatch at the letters.
We are going to take a second and last look at the Exhibition (the pictures only) tomorrow, feeling that such an opportunity is not likely to come again in our lives. Best love to all from
Yours ever
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 3 February [1862]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 3 February [1862]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 332.
Blandford Sq. | February 3.
Dear Sara
I am wondering rather impatiently whether you could not tell me that your sprain is nearly well, and the half belief I have that you would have told me so if you could, makes me anxious lest you should be still lying a prisoner in these mild days. Though alas, I can do you no good, in that sad case.
I was taken to see my Pantomime just on the last day of its performance -- Saturday, 16 having been hindered by ailments from going earlier. How pretty it is to see the theatre full of children! For we went in the day-time, in child fashion. Ah, what I should have felt in my real child-days, to have been let into the further history of Mother Hubbard and her Dog!
I am scribbling at night and don't pretend to write for anybody's satisfaction but my own. If you can tell me any good news, do. Or if telling bad news is any relief I consent to hear it.
Ever yours
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 29 September 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 29 September 1866
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 29. 66.
Dear Sara
Your words of kind feeling for us all were very sweet. The trial is all the greater to poor Gertrude because she had looked forward to her maternity with more than the usual share of serious joy, and she was so well and vigorous to the last moment beforehand, that we were all full of hope. The little one was a fine child, too, and died only from an accident during its birth. 536 We reckon it a great alleviation for Gertrude that she never even heard it cry. She is so precious to us that all regret seems merged in relief at the promise of her speedy recovery. Sometimes it requires an effort to feel affectionately towards those who are bound to us by ties of family, but it is as easy to me to love Gertrude as it is to love the clear air.
You write as if you were rather depressed, dear Sara. Is it not the weather, which affects everybody, and is really a cause of melancholy in its far-off as well as immediate results? I have often wondered whether you had lately seen Harriet and am glad to know that you are at ease about her.
Alas -- for the empty houses! Best love to Cara -- I wish such a true message were of any use to her. You see, I have disobeyed you about writing -- obeyed rather my own impulse which is always that of answering whenever I can.
Yours lovingly
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 29 January 1872
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 150-151.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 29. 72.
Dear Sara
I do lead rather a crawling life under these rainy fogs and low behaviour of the barometer. But I am a little better on the whole, though just now overdone with the fatigue of company.
Your account of yourself does not at all satisfy me, but I hear all round that this winter is one of unusual sickness, though the mild unhealthiness of the weather is less fatal to the old than the severe frosts. But which is kinder? -- the weather that kills, or the weather that keeps uncomfortably alive?
To hear of Mr. Dawson coming to lecture at Coventry is a revival of old memories. How changed he probably is from the slim mercurial dark-haired creature whom I heard in his twenties!
We have been to hear Coleridge addressing the jury on the Tichborne trial -- a very interesting occasion to me. He is a marvellous speaker among Englishmen, has an exquisitely melodious voice, perfect gesture, and a power of keeping the thread of his syntax to the end of his sentences, which make him delightful to follow. We are going some other day, if possible, to hear a cross-examination of Ballantyne's. 456 The digest of the evidence which Coleridge gives, is one of the best illustrations of the value or valuelessness of testimony that could be given. I wonder if the world which retails Guppy anecdotes 457 will be any the wiser for it! With love,
Ever your faithful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 28 October [1865]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 28 October [1865]
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, 11, 412-413.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 28.
Dear Sara
I am sorry to say that I cannot tell you anything of the Congreves. About a week or ten days ago, Mr. Congreve wrote to say, that they had a hope, and that he should let me know as soon as it was wise for Mrs. Congreve to see me. Since then I have heard nothing.
The best compensation for not seeing Cara is to know that a Tenant was the cause. With these "auction winds" 378 one is apt to think visiting at a stand-still and expect nobody. I dare say that in the open country you get a good deal of pleasure out of the autumnal tossing and leaf-shedding.
I have read Mr. Masson's book on "Recent Philosophy." 379 The earlier part is a useful and creditable survey, and the classification ingenious. The latter part I thought poor. If, by what he says of Positivism, you mean what he says at p. 246, I should answer, it is simply "stuff"; he might as well have written a dozen lines of jargon. There are a few observations about Comte scattered here and there, which are true and just enough. But it seems to me much better to read a man's own writings than to read what others say about him. Especially when the man is first-rate and the "others" are third-rate. As Goethe said long ago about Spinoza, "Ich immer vorzog, von dem Menschen zu erfahren wie er dachte, als von einem andern zu h'f6ren, wie er h'e4tte denken sollen." 380 However, I am not fond of expressing criticism or disapprobation. The difficulty is, to digest and live upon any valuable truth oneself.
The handsome volume, in its pretty green, is come to me. I am glad to have it in that portable form rather than in sheets, and I shall return to it with all the advantages of convenience. Always
Your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 28 August 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 28 August 1864
MS: Yale. Published: Cross, II, 386-388.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 28. 64.
Dear Sara
I am distressed to find that I have let a week pass without writing in answer to your letter, which made me very glad when I got it. Remembering you just a minute ago I started up from Max M'fcller's new volume, 282 with which I was consoling myself under a sore throat, and rushed to the desk, that I might not risk any further delay.
It was just what I wanted to hear about you -- that you were having some change, and I think the freshness of the companionship must help other good influences. Not to speak of the "Apologia" which breathed much life into me when I read it. Pray mark that beautiful passage in which he thanks his friend Ambrose St. John. 283 I know hardly anything that delights me more than such evidences of sweet brotherly love being a reality in the world. I envy you your opportunity of seeing and hearing Newman, and should like to make an expedition to Birmingham for that sole end.
My trouble now is George's delicate health. He gets thinner and thinner. He is going to try what horseback will do, and I am looking forward to that with some hope.
Our boy's love-story runs smoothly and seems to promise nothing but good. His attraction to Hampstead gives George and me more of our dear old t'eate-'e0-t'eate, which we can't help being glad to recover.
Dear Cara and Mr. Bray! I wish they too had joy instead of sadness from the young life they have been caring for these many years. 284 When you write to Cara or see her, assure her that she is remembered in my most affectionate thoughts, and that I often bring her present experience before my mind -- more or less truly, for we can but blunder about each other, we poor mortals.
Write to me whenever you can, dear Sara. I should have answered immediately but for sickness, visitors, business etc.
Ever thine
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 27 March 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 27 March 1874
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 229-230.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 27. 74.
My dear Sara
I can imagine how great an encouragement you feel from the enthusiasm generously expressed in Mr. Cupples' 62 letter. It is always an admirable impulse, to express a deeply felt admiration, but it is also possible that you have some grateful readers who do not write to you. I have heard men whose greatest delight is literature, say that they should never dream of writing to an author on the ground of his books alone. 63 I don't remember that I have ever heard where Mr. Cupples lives or other particulars about him, unless indeed I am right in conjecturing that he is the friend of Stirling, the polemical meta-physician. 64
Poor Mr. Francis Newman must be aged now and rather weary of the world and explanations of the world. He can hardly be expected to take in much novelty. I have a sort of affectionate sadness in thinking of the interest which in far-off-days I felt in his "Soul" and Phases of Faith, and of the awe I had of him as a lecturer on mathematics at the Ladies' College. How much work he has done in the world, which has left no deep, conspicuous mark, but has probably entered beneficently into many lives!
I think, from your first prompting to ask me to return the copy of Mr. Cupples' letter, that it may probably be of use to you, so I return it, for I habitually think of death as so near that I see all documents in the light of things left behind for others, rather than kept for myself.
I hope you are well, and not yet exhausted of the refreshment you got from your visit to Ravensbourne.
Your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 27 March [1862]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 27 March [1862]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 338.
Blandford Sq. | March 27.
My dear Sara
I congratulate you on being out of London, which is more like a Pandemonium than usual. The fog and rain have been the more oppressive because I have seen them through the medium of Mr. Lewes's almost constant discomfort: I think he has had at least five days of sick headache since you saw him. But then, he is better-tempered and more cheerful with headache than most people are without it, and in that way he lightens his burthen.
I think we have not seen anyone whom you know -- except the Noels who came on Saturday evening. Mrs. Noel told me the sad story of her having lost her little family treasures of pearls and likenesses etc. There is something very genuine and sweet-natured in her manners.
I am gratified by your having felt "Beata": it was originally a shorter story written for "All the Year Round," and rejected (for reasons one can imagine under the necessities for circumspection in the editor of a "family" periodical). 43 The rejection was a very fortunate one, for it caused the writer to expand the story into a book, and the public has recognized its merit.
Have you noticed in the Times Mr. Peabody's magnificent deed? -- the gift of £150,000 for the amelioration (body and soul, I suppose) of the poorer classes in London? 44 That is one pleasant association to have with an American name.
We went yesterday into No. 5 45 to look at two pictures in oil, which Mrs. Bodichon has sent over. They are the first oil pictures she has painted with the intention of exhibiting. One is a very grand scene in Algiers, and is finely composed. Of course, she is not yet at home in her material as she was in her accustomed water colours.
My "gentlemen" would doubtless send kind remembrances if they knew I was writing.
Ever your affectionate
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 26 November 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 26 November 1862
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 342-343.
Blandford Sq. | November 26. 62.
Dear Sara
I was very glad to have your letter lying ready for me when I went down to lunch. I wanted to know what it tells me -- that you are feeling comfort in being settled at home again. But I can't help regretting that your visit to London was not made in a brighter time and that you had not more variety. You must come again the sooner, when I hope I shall be less pre-occupied, and better able to make little plans for your being with us under more comfortable circumstances than those of eating a miserable make-shift dinner of our poor luncheon and then trotting off immediately.
I too thought of our twin birthdays, and remembered with much gratefulness the pretty letters I have had from you at those epochs. I wish I knew that this birthday has found you happier than any that went before. There are so many things -- best things that only come when youth is past, that it may well happen to many of us to find ourselves happier and happier to the last. -- I almost believed you would be gone to Miss Julia Smith, but I dare say you will be glad to have an interval between visits.
You will be interested to know that there is a new muster of scientific and philosophic men lately established, for the sake of bringing people who care to know and speak the truth as well as they can, into regular communication. Mr. Lewes was at the first meeting at Clunn's Hotel on Friday last. The plan is to meet, and dine moderately and cheaply; and no one is to be admitted who is not "Thorough" in the sense of being free from the suspicion of temporizing and professing opinions on official grounds. The plan was started at Cambridge: Mr. Huxley is president, and Charles Kingsley is vice. If they are sufficiently rigid about admissions the club may come to good 117 -- bringing together men who think variously, but have more hearty feelings in common than they give each other credit for. Mr. Robert Chambers (who lives in London now) is very warm about the matter. Mr. Spencer too is a member.
That look which you interpreted into an expression of a "shock" at your words in relation to the last named philosopher, 118 must really have expressed a stomach ache; for I remember I was in a state of malaise that morning, and I am sure I was not "shocked" at you. The impression left on me after our conversation was not that you had said anything unbecoming, but rather that I, as usual had been too ready to find fault with the excellent champion of heterogeneity. I get a little impatient sometimes with his contentment in abstractions, and allow myself to look at the seamy side of an old friend's mind more than is kind or right. On those great, great subjects that your letter refers to, it is more likely that a short conversation will darken than clarify mutual understanding, when meetings are rare, and the memory of the past is constantly thrusting itself forward as knowledge of the present. But I should think we are very near to each other in our sense of needs, and also in our enjoyment of certain sympathies.
Mr. Congreve came to have a long chat the other day, and I was pleased to find that he had been for a week to Oxford, where he was very cordially received by the men of the liberal party, in spite of his heresy. <I should think> Few people outside the University can imagine how much an Oxford man gives up when he leaves an Oxford clique for conscience's sake. 119
Mr. Lewes sent your "Buddhism" today by post. Thanks for it. If I had not been dull of sense, I might have found it on the table, when you wanted it. We <went> have been to a "Monday Pop" this week, to hear Beethoven's Septett, and an amazing thing of Bach's played by the amazing Joachim. But there is too much "Pop" for the thorough enjoyment of the chamber music they give. With love generally,
Yours ever
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 26 December 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 26 December 1867
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 28-29.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 26. 67.
My dear Sara
Thanks for the pretty remembrance. You were not unthought of before it came, but a mucous membrane out of sorts has of late made it difficult for my thoughts to pass into expression. Now, however, I rouse all my courage under the thick fog to tell you my inward wish -- which is, that the New Year as it travels on towards its old age may bring you many satisfactions undisturbed by bodily ailment.
Mr. Spencer was here yesterday and told me of your letter about the worm. I imagined you well, stooping to investigate and checked suddenly by the sense of a Coventry lady's severe eye on you.
Mr. Lewes is going tomorrow on an unprecedented expedition -- a rapid run to Bonn to make some anatomical researches with Prof. Schulze 712 there. If he needs more than he can get at Bonn he may go to Heidelberg and Wurzburg. But in any case he will not take more than a fortnight. The weather is not encouraging but he has been much better lately, and the scamper, with the intense interest of a great subject in his mind, will be likely to do him good.
Public questions, which by a sad process of reduction become piteous private questions, hang cloudily over all prospects. The state of Europe, the threat of a general war, the starvation of multitudes -- one can't help thinking of these things at one's breakfast. Nevertheless there is much enjoyment going on, and abundance of rosy children's parties. 713 I dare say you have had one.
Please offer my loving greetings to Cara and Mr. Bray.
Always your faithful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 26 December 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 26 December 1863
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 372.
The Priory, N. Bank | December 26. 1863.
Dear Sara
I should have written to you before but that I was uncertain whether you had left Lea Hurst. But one great charm of your correspondence is that you give one a perfect sense of freedom about it, instead of seeming to exact answers in punctilious regularity. I don't suspect that you are getting angry with me when I don't write; and that saves me from any uneasy association with the thought of you. For I get less and less inclined to write any but the briefest letters.
Thanks for the pretty story about your Leicester visit. My books seem to get so far off me when once I have written them, that I should be afraid of looking into "The Mill"; but it was written faithfully and with intense feeling when it was written, so I will hope that it will do no mortal any harm.
I am indulging myself frightfully, reading everything except the "current literature" and getting more and more out of rapport with the public taste. I have read Renan's book, however, which has proved to be eminently in the public taste. It will have a good influence on the whole I imagine; but this "Vie de J'e9sus" and still more Renan's Letter to Berthelot in the Revue des deux Mondes 218 have compelled me to give up the high estimate I had formed of his mind. Judging from the indications in some other writings of his I had reckoned him amongst the finest thinkers of the time. Still his Life of Jesus has so much artistic merit that it will do a great deal towards the culture of ordinary minds by giving them a sense of unity between that far-off past and our present. I have witnessed this effect in our own Charlie, who is now reading Strauss on the strength of the interest which Renan created.
I wonder what you are most enjoying now -- what subjects your mind is dwelling on. But I deserve to know nothing about you, for I have no patience to write more than these scribbling notes about nothings. Nevertheless I do care about everything that affects you, and shall share all the good that I can know of as befalling you in this coming year.
I am, as ever, a person who feel and talk a great deal, and do very little to correspond. Not a rare character, but your loving friend
P.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 26 December 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 26 December 1862
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, 11, 346-347.
Blandford Sq. | December 26. 62.
Dear Sara
It is very sweet to me to have any proof of loving remembrance. That would have made the Book-marker precious even if it had been ugly. But it is perfectly beautiful -- in colour, words and symbols. Hitherto I have been discontented with the Coventry Book-marks, for at the shop where we habitually see them they have all got "Let the people praise Thee, O God" on them and nothing else. But I can think of no motto better than those three words. I suppose no wisdom the world will ever find out will make Paul's words obsolete "Now abide" etc. "but the greatest of these is Charity." 123
Our Christmas too has been quiet. Mr. Lewes, who talks much less about goodness than I do, but is always readier to do the right thing, thinks it rather wicked for us to eat our Turkey and plum-pudding without asking some forlorn person to eat it with us. Last year we invited a poor little governess 124 -- but she had to dine with her mother at Hackney. And this year we invited a poor shrivelled-hearted bachelor who shall be nameless, but he too had a filial duty. 125 I'm afraid we were glad, after all, to find ourselves alone with "the Boy." On Christmas Eve a sweet woman, 126 remembering me as you have done, left a beautiful plant at the door, and after that we went to hear the Messiah, at her Majesty's. -- We felt a considerable minus from the absence of the Organ contrary to advertisement, nevertheless it was good to be there. What pitiable people those are who feel no poetry in Christianity! Surely the acme of poetry hitherto is the conception of the suffering Messiah -- and the final triumph "He shall reign for ever and for ever." The Prometheus is a very imperfect foreshadowing of that symbol wrought out in the long history of the Jewish and Christian ages.
Poor Mr. Congreve has had, as we learned from Mr. Harrison the other night, 127 a severe and long attack of sciatica, not yet surmounted -- a very sad explanation of a five weeks' silence in Mrs. Congreve, who is worn with anxiety and nursing. Mr. Lewes and I have both been in miserable health during all this month. I have had a fortnight's incessant malaise and feebleness but as I had had many months of tolerable health it was my turn to be uncomfortable. You say nothing about your cough, so I hope this mild weather is tempering that grievance -- which must be terribly wearing, shaking head and chest. I speak of the mild weather, but it occurs to me that I must not imagine other places so oven-like as London with its million fires and smoke canopy.
Apart from health, we are brim-full of happiness and have so many good things that we seem to be preparing for the state of Dives. As I have not heard from Mr. Bray about the Coventry distress I am hoping that it is milder than he expected.
If my book marker were just a little longer I should keep it in my beautiful Bible in large print, which Mr. Lewes bought for me in provision for my old age. He is not fond of reading the Bible himself but "sees no harm" in my reading it.
He has just finished reading Russell's American Diary 128 which is intensely interesting -- full of strange pictures. Some one told me on oracular authority that if I had to be born again, I ought to pray to God to be born an American. I should sooner pray to be born a Turk or an Arab.
Farewell, dear Sara. Give my love and best wishes for the coming year to Cara and Mr. Bray. I am always yours affectionately
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 23 November 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 23 November 1864
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, II, 391-392.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 23. 64.
My dear Sara
I believe I have thought of you every day for the last fortnight, and I remembered the birthday -- and "everything." But I was a little cross because I had heard nothing of you since Mr. Bray's visit, nor even seen Miss Marshall so that I could inquire about you. And I said to myself "if she wanted to write she would write." I confess I was a little ashamed when I saw the outside of your letter ten minutes ago, feeling that I should read within it the proof that you were thoughtful and mindful as ever.
Yes, I do heartily give my greeting -- had given it already. And I desire very much that the work which is absorbing you may give you some happiness besides that which belongs to the activity of production. But do go to Lea Hurst, because you are always the better for change.
It is very kind of you to remember Charlie's date too. 293 He is as happy as the day is long -- and very good -- one of those creatures to whom goodness comes naturally. Not any exalted goodness, but everyday serviceable goodness such as wears through life. Whereas exalted goodness comes in brief inspirations and requires a man to die lest he should spoil his work.
Mr. Lewes is much better and is enjoying himself "in his skin" again, according to the German phrase.
I have been ill, but now am pretty well -- with much to occupy and interest me, and with no trouble except those bodily ailments.
I could chat a long while with you -- but I restrain myself, because
I must not carry on my letter writing into the "solid day." Best love to all.
Ever your faithful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 23 November [1877]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 23 November [1877]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
November 23.
My dear Sara
I enjoyed your letter greatly. Thank you for the exertion you undertook for my sake. I thoroughly appreciate the effort it requires to give oneself forth in a letter, and I hardly know how I should get through my life with decent regard to gratuitous correspondents' feelings if Mr. Lewes did not come to my rescue and do most of my [answering] for me.
But I want to tell you that you must not interpret H. S's indifference to your ideas and authorship as any special negation towards you because you are a woman. He has, whenever it was possible, shown just the same blank towards Mr. Lewes, who certainly has more claims on him as an older friend 'abwho was'bb very generous to him in the days of his obscurity. With regard to not reading books or listening to ideas, I must again plead for him, as I have done before, that he is not a reader, and that his mind both "spontan'e9ment and syst'e9matiquement" rejects everything that cannot be wrought into the web of his own production. 779 He has this in common with many productive minds. And you must not regard him in the light of a person who will be moved by sympathies. We have long given up vain expectations from him and can therefore enjoy our regard for him without disturbance by his negations. He comes and consults us about his own affairs, and that is his way of showing friendship. We never dream of telling him our affairs, which would certainly not interest him. I write this only to prevent you from retaining the belief that he has any specially ignoring or contemning disposition towards you either as to your personality or your womanhood.
Your description of your astronomical pleasures at Llandudno makes us envy you. We have never seen Saturn's ring, nor Jupiter's moons -- [nor nuffin] -- except the wondrous eclipse of the moon which exhibited itself to perfection in front of our drawing-room window. 780
I am rather amazed at your enjoyment of [the New Republic.] To me it was a hateful book. But the Master of Balliol who is chiefly insulted is my particular friend.
Your loving
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 23 June [1864]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1864. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 23.
Dear Sara
We are returned 267 you see, but before I say anything about ourselves I want to know what is the state of your poor Nelly's health. I feel unable to write at length, until I know whether there still exists the special cause of sadness among you that Cara's note made me aware of just before we started.
Will you send me a few lines to tell me as much as you can first about the common household and then about yourself? Until I know that you are not in heavy trouble, it is impossible to write gossip about our own affairs. Ever, dear Sara
Your true and loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 23 April 1874
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, III, 230.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 23. 74.
Dear Sara
I am very glad to know that you and Cara have been comforted by finding Harriet in comparatively cheerful circumstances. It is of more importance that she should have her prospective delight in Cremation than that we should settle whether the hope is premature.
Give my love to Cara and tell her I shall long for some news of Paul Bradly -- which I am sure she will not fail to give me.
We have fixed on our country house for the summer and shall go to it at latest by the beginning of June. How glorious this opening Spring is! At this moment even London is so beautiful that I come home filled with the Park landscapes and see them as a background to all my thoughts.
Your account of Mr. George Dawson is rather melancholy. 73 I remember him only as a bright vigorous young man -- such as perhaps his sons are now. I imagine it is his fortune or rather misfortune to have talked too much and too early about the greatest things.
Miss Beedy's account of the way Mr. Spencer arrived at his present point of view 74 is not quite correct, I think. His opinions, I should say, do not take date from his acquaintance with Mr. Youmans, or with any facts about American women.
We have a second granddaughter -- a little Maud 75 to pair with Blanche, and in all respects we are faring as well as mortals can do -- who are no better than we are, I mean, organically and morally better.
It would surely be the more satisfactory alternative that the Sydenham tenant should stay on, and that Cara should have no trouble of mind or body about a second house.
Always your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 22 November 1879
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 384-385.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 22. 79.
My dear Sara
I am very grateful to you for your kind letter. News about you all had been much desired by me, but I have now so many business letters to write that I am apt to defer such as are not absolutely necessary.
The careful Index is a sign of your effective industry, and I have no doubt that it will be a great help to yourself as well as to your readers. One very often needs an index to one's own writings.
As to health this premature winter is not encouraging, but I hope you will all keep yourselves snugly warm and avoid [passive cold] -- the demon against whom Dr. Andrew Clarke always warns us. I am writing in the yellow twilight of a London fog, from which you are happily free. And the snow which is so hideous in town remains beautiful in the country. It grieves me to learn that Cara's eyes are troubling her so cruelly. I remember that in old days they used easily to smart after working in the evening.
My chief objects are quite completed now. The Dr. Roy appointed to the Studentship is held by competent persons to be the most hopeful of our few young physiologists and was absolutely in need of monetary help to save him from being forced to give up his researches. And there is a volume of 500 pages (the last) of Problems of Life and Mind ready to appear next month.
I am quite recovered from the ailment which made me good for little in the summer, and indeed am stronger than I ever expected to be again. People are very good to me, and I am exceptionally blessed in many ways, but more blessed are the dead who rest from their labours, and have not to dread a barren useless survival. Best love to all from
Your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 22 November 1876
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 296-297.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 22. 76.
My dear Sara
I am sadly disappointed to find that you have been, and are, suffering so much, Cara's last account having suggested a more cheerful picture of you. Any one who knows from experience what bodily infirmity is -- how it spoils life even for those who have no other trouble -- gets a little impatient of healthy complainants strong enough for extra work and ignorant of indigestion. I at least should be inclined to scold the discontented young people who tell me in one breath that they never have anything the matter with them and that life is not worth having -- if I did not remember my own young discontent. What a pity that you did not get to Penmaenmaur before the bad weather set in! When I think of your cough and trouble of breathing, it makes my own ailments seem small -- I imagine so vividly the distressing effect on your head. It is a comfort that Cara is comparatively strong. Please tell her that I want to be [posted up] in her affairs by another little noteful of news.
We are perfectly happy, save and excepting the old headaches and other newer infirmities incident to our advancing years. 562 Mr. Lewes is getting his third volume through the press -- it turns entirely on the physiology of the nervous system -- though he can't work half so long as he used to do, he works with much enjoyment, reviving quickly after a crushing headache or an attack of lumbago. It is remarkable to me that I have entirely lost my personal melancholy. I often, of course, have melancholy thoughts about the destinies of my fellow-creatures, but I am never in that mood of sadness which used to be my frequent visitant even in the midst of external happiness. And this, notwithstanding a very vivid sense that life is declining and death close at hand.
Perhaps it will amuse you to know that our friend Mr. Spencer, who used to despise biography as the least profitable occupation of brain, is now busily collecting the materials of his own family and personal history! 563 The Spencer family is really interesting. H. S's father was a strong, peculiar character, and there seems to have been a strain of mental force through former generations.
We are waiting with some expectation for Miss Martineau's autobiography, which I fancy will be charming so far as her younger and less renowned life extends. All biography diminishes in interest when the subject has won celebrity -- or some reputation that hardly comes up to celebrity. But autobiography at least saves a man or woman that the world is curious about from the publication of a string of mistakes called [memoirs.]
Apropos -- you will not think me blasphemous if I pass to the memoirs of Jesus Christ. I remember you used to possess a volume containing the apocryphal gospels. If you don't use it, will you lend it me for a few months? I shall be very grateful.
It would be nice if we could be a trio -- I mean you, Cara and I -- chatting together for an hour as we used to do when I had walked over the hill to see you. But that pleasure belongs to "the days that are no more." 564 Will you believe that an accomplished man some years ago said to me, that he saw no place for the exercise of resignation when there was no personal Divine Will contemplated as ordaining sorrow or privation? He is not yet aware that he is getting old, and needing that unembittered compliance of soul with the inevitable which seems to me a full enough meaning for the word [resignation.]
I wish I had more news to tell you about people whom we know in common. Madame Bodichon is still, I think, at the coast with Miss Julia Smith, to whom she is a very loving, duteous niece. What a pretty delicate little old lady that aunt was the last time I saw her! With best love to Cara. Always, dear Sara,
Your faithfully affectionate
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 22 November 1871
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, III, 144.
November 22. 71.
My dear Sara
Thanks for the pleasure of reading Mr. Cupples' 406 letter. He writes like an accomplished man and I think that his sympathy weighs well.
I shall hope to hear if you do move to Ravensbourne. Three lines are enough to relieve one from total darkness. Please give my tender love to Cara under her pressure of coal-carrying. Alas for the heavier trouble of Mr. Bray's bad health! We who are getting old together have the tie of common infirmities. But I don't find that the young troubles seem lighter on looking back. I prefer my years now to any that have gone before. -- I wish you could tell me the same thing about yourself. And surely writing your book is on the whole a joy to you -- it is a large share in the meagre lot of mankind.
All hail, dear Sara, for the morrow! 407 How many sweet laughs -- how much serious pleasure in the great things others have done -- you and I have had together in a past islet of time, that remains very sunny in my remembrance. I am certainly the better for having been your
Pollian.
If you can think of it when you are writing to Tr'fcbner's, and will consent to exchange instead of mere acceptance will you let me have the last two Parts you have issued? 408

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 22 November 1869
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Envelope: Miss Hennell | 3 Barr's Hill Terrace | Coventry. Postmark: LONDON-N.W | X | NO 22 | 69. Endorsed: About a month before Jubal appeared. 115 Jubal is dated 1869. The "Choir Invisible" 1867. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank | November 22. 69.
My dear Sara
The view you express in the paragraph marked with your penstroke is entirely mine. I must found my belief not on what is glorious for this one or that one, but on what is probable for all. One cannot but feel tenderly towards the yearnings of individual sufferers, but theoretically speaking, it seems to me that the conception of religion as chiefly valuable for the personal consolations that may be extracted from it, is among the most active sources of falsity. The test of a higher religion might be, that it should enable the believer to do without the consolations which his egoism would demand. And this test, I imagine, coincides with what you have written in the first half of p. 256.
Misprints in an advertisement are particularly cruel, and that was a nasty one. I do enter with fellow-feeling into your vexation. Mr. Lewes has a singular faculty for remembering what is advertised, and what forms the common or exceptional material of Book-catalogues. It comes of his diligent, hungry search in his days of youthful penury, when he dined on a sausage in order to buy a longed-for book.
Your good wishes for me, dear Sara, tend to fulfil themselves. It is already a chief blessing, that others wish us well.
Ever your grateful
Pollian.
I don't like making statements about other people's opinions, but to prevent mistake, I had better say, that I believe Mde. Bodichon's sentiments are not at all in agreement with Miss Cobbe's, so far as I know these. 116

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 22 November 1867
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 25.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 22. 67.
Dear Sara
Yes, indeed -- when I do not reciprocate -- "chaos is come again." 686 I was quite sure your letter would come and was grateful beforehand.
It was very pleasant to have Cara with us for [the] good part of a day. I was rather proud of Mr. Lewes's being so well then, but alas, since that evening he has had five days of continuous headache! However, a better interval has come, and we live in hope that the alternations of a cold east wind and mugginess will not be perpetual.
Cara told us about the piano next door to you. No two people on earth could feel more sympathy in such misery than we do. The millennial prospect of some day getting away from the terrace 687 and going to Ivy Cottage is something to dwell on as a relief.
There is a scheme on foot for a women's college, or rather university, to be built between London and Cambridge, and to be in connection with the Cambridge university, sharing its professors, examinations and degrees! "Si muove." 688
I suppose you will not move until you have finished your volume, 689 but then you will surely try a little change.
Always your loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 22 November 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 22 November 1866
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 445-446.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 22. 66.
Dear Sara
For a wonder, I remembered the day of the month and felt a delightful confidence that I should have a letter from her who always remembers such things at the right moment. You will hardly believe in my imbecility -- I can never be quite sure whether your birthday is the 21st or the 23d, and whether Charlie's is the 23d or the 24th. 540 I know every one must think the worse of me for this want of a retentiveness that seems a part of affection, and it is only justice that they should.
Nevertheless I am not quite destitute of lovingness and gratitude, and perhaps the consciousness of my own defect makes me feel your goodness the more keenly. My mind dwelt on you yesterday, and I had some cheerful thoughts about you because Mr. Bray had told me that you had Miss Carter 541 with you and enjoyed that companionship greatly. I shall reckon it part of the next year's happiness for me if it brings a great deal of happiness to you. That will depend somewhat -- perhaps chiefly -- on the satisfaction you have in giving shape to your ideas. But you say nothing on that subject.
I have been telling Mr. Lewes that it is my birthday, and at that news he smiled through the sad look of head-ache as he lay on his pillow. It is the second morning that he has been unable to get up to breakfast, from the presence of that horrible demon, who has taken possession of his poor body as a penalty for our entertainment of a gentlemen's party on Tuesday. A little extra excitement -- or a morsel of mutton fat -- will lay him prostrate for days. But before Tuesday he had been much better, was very bright, and wrote regularly for many mornings together.
However, I am comparatively at ease now he has given up his editorship and has nearly finished his History. He will be able then to think of nothing but what he likes best, and we shall probably go southward. His successor in the editorship is Mr. John Morley, a very accomplished man, and I hope he will be able to keep up the Review in the same spirit -- but that is a point in which you are not interested, since the Fortnightly is a stranger to you. 542
We knew about Faraday's preaching, but not of his loss of faculty. I begin to think of such things as very near to me -- I mean decay of power and death. But I find age has its fresh elements of cheerfulness.
Those dreadful, always-getting-empty houses! My love to Cara and congratulations on the large tolerance which enables her to read Dr. Bodichon. 543
Bless you, dear Sara, for all the kindness of many years, and for the newest kindness that comes to me this morning.
I am always your affectionate
Pollian.
I am very well now, and able to enjoy my happiness -- one has happiness sometimes without being able to enjoy it.
