Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 14 September 1865
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 14 September 1865
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, II, 409-412.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 14. 65.
My dear Sara
We came home again on Thursday night -- this day week -- after a month's absence in Normandy and Brittany. I have been thinking of you very often since, but believed that you did not care to have the interruption of letters just now, and would rather defer correspondence till your mind was freer. If I had suspected that you would feel any want satisfied by a letter I should certainly have written. I had not heard of Miss Carter's death, 370 else I should have conceived something of your state of mind. I think you and I are alike in this, that we can get no good out of pretended comforts, which are the devices of self-love, but would rather, in spite of pain, grow into the endurance of "all naked truths." So I say no word about your great loss -- except that I love you and sorrow with you.
Dear Sara, you do not doubt that I love you? The circumstances of life -- the changes that take place in ourselves -- hem in the expression of affections and memories that live within us and enter almost into every day, and long separations often make intercourse difficult when the opportunity comes. But the delight I had in you, and in the hours we spent together and in all your acts of friendship to me, is really part of my life and can never die out of me. I see distinctly how much poorer I should have been if I had never known you. If you had seen more of me in late years you would not have such almost cruel thoughts as that the book into which you have faithfully put your experience and best convictions could make you "repugnant" to me. Whatever else my growth may have been, it has not been towards irreverence and ready rejection of what other minds can give me. You once unhappily mistook my feeling and point of view in something I wrote 'e0 propos of an argument in your "Aids to Faith," and that made me think it better that we should not write on large and difficult subjects in hasty letters. But it has often been painful to me -- I should say, it has constantly been painful to me, that you have ever since inferred me to be in a hard and unsympathetic state about your views and your writing. But I am habitually disposed myself to the same unbelief in the sympathy that is given me, and am the last person who should be allowed to complain of such unbelief in another. And it is very likely that I may have been faulty and disagreeable in my expressions.
Excuse all my many mistakes, dear Sara -- and never believe otherwise than that I have a glow of joy when you write to me as if my existence were some good to you. I know that I am, and can be, very little practically, but to have the least value for your thought is what I care much to be assured of.
When we got home I found Miss Marshall's card, and wrote to her. She has answered me from Folkstone, telling me the grievous effect of that sun-stroke on her sight, which used to be so strong. I am glad she is out of London, for the heat is peculiarly languor-giving here. Perhaps in the cooler part of the autumn when your book is out of your hands, you will like to move from home a little and see your London friends?
Mr. Call writes that he and his brother have a difficult executorship for their sister's children. He has sent an article on Apollonius of Tyana for the Fortnightly 371 -- which, I suppose, you do not see.
We are feeble wretches as to our health -- but otherwise all is well with us. Our traveling in Brittany was a good deal marred and obstructed by the Emperor's f'eate 372 which sent all the world on our track towards Cherbourg and Brest. But the Norman churches, the great cathedrals at Le Mans, Tours, and Chartres 373 with their marvellous painted glass were worth much scrambling to see.
Always your old
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 14 July 1862
MS: The Carl H. Pforzheimer Library. Envelope: Miss Hennell | 3 Barrs' Hill | Coventry. Postmarks: LONDON-N.W | 11 | JY 15 | 62; COVENTRY | 9 | JY 15 | 62. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square | July 14. 62.
Dear Sara
I am not such a stony-hearted woman as you have taken to imagine me -- caring for nobody's sympathy. I am really glad to know that
Romola interests you -- only don't make up your mind about anything that is to come, else whatever it is will disappoint you. Of necessity, the book is addressed to fewer readers than my previous works, and I myself have never expected -- I might rather say intended -- that the book should be as "popular" in the same sense as the others. If one is to have freedom to write out one's own varying unfolding self, and not be a machine always grinding out the same material or spinning the same sort of web, one cannot always write for the same public. I forewarned the proprietor of the Cornhill on that point, read a large portion to him, and made him fully aware what the book was to be -- but he is confident and happy -- so I am acquitted of all scruple or anxiety except the grand anxiety of doing my work worthily. Alas, I want to do something very much better than I ever can do it -- if fasting and scourging oneself would make one a fit organ, there would be more positive comfort.
I am much pleased that you like Mr. Leighton's illustrations, for he has suffered an artist's agonies at the misrepresentation -- (it is almost that) which the engravers have made of these two first drawings. I have the photographs taken from his drawings, which you will see are far superior to the wood-cuts. He is an invaluable man to have because he knows Florence by heart. 95
I am just now rather sad at the prospect of parting with Mr. Lewes for ten days or so. 96 He has become so weak from a terrible attack of indigestion, that some change seems absolutely necessary as a tonic. Erasmus Wilson thinks he has taken the Turkish Baths too zealously, and that the over action in the skin has thrown the liver into a state of comparative inaction. I feel it on the whole a duty to keep close at home and not run the mental risk of any distractions -- but of course I shall be in a fidget till he comes back.
We thought Cara looking as pretty and well as possible. I hope she thoroughly enjoyed her visit to London -- as we did her brief peep at us. 97
We heard from Mr. Call the other day, very pleasantly, but he said nothing of a visit to London.
I am writing unconscionably ill, in the twilight. Farewell.
Ever yours
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 14 January 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 14 January 1862
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 331.
Blandford Sq. | January 14. 62.
Dear Sara
I am grieved to think of the sprain. Pray let me know, when you can, that it is better, for I have a dread of the possible persistence attributed to sprains.
I hope you are able to enjoy Max M'fcller's 12 great and delightful book during your imprisonment. It tempts me away from other things. I have read most of the numbers of Orley Farm, and admire it very much, with the exception of such parts as I have read about Moulder and Co., which by the way, I saw in glancing at a late Spectator, the sapient critic there selects for peculiar commendation. 13 There is no mistake an author can make but there will be some newspaper critic to pronounce it his finest effort. Anthony Trollope is admirable in the presentation of even, average life and character, and he is so thoroughly wholesome-minded that one delights in seeing his books lie about to be read. Have you read "Beata" yet -- the first novel written by his brother at Florence who is our especial favourite? Do read it when you can, if the opportunity has not already come.
It is very good of you to remember poor Charlie's missing trunk or trunk "gone-a-missing." Alas, we are still wishing -- hardly hoping -- that it may not be utterly lost. Our last effort has been to inquire through a Railway authority here who has an agent in Paris, and we should have done more wisely if we had had recourse to him first instead of writing to foreign friends and foreign officials.
You have never told me what impression Mr. Spencer's book 14 makes on you as it proceeds. I am anxious to know whether the elaborate proof of generalities which are accepted as soon as stated will not cause some of the later numbers to be wearisome for the majority of readers. I hope not, for it is touching to see how his whole life and soul are being poured into this book and into keeping himself well that he may write it. The very watching against disease is becoming a disease in itself. He has had his father in London lately, and the old gentleman, seated upright on a small chair, looks almost the younger of the two. 15
I am going to be taken to a pantomime in the day-time, like a good child, for a Christmas treat, not having had my fair share of pantomime in the world. Farewell -- let me know about the sprain, and think of me always as
Your loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 November [1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 November [1860]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1860. Extracts published: Cross, II, 278-279.
Harewood Square | Tuesday, November 13.
Dear Sara
I understand your paradox of "expecting disappointment," for that is the only form of hope with which I am familiar. But drive away the expectation if you can, for I don't see how it is possible that I should not be in London when you come, if I am extant at all; and you must not sit down with any reasons for not coming, since you need the change for health's sake. I can't help wishing that I could offer, and that you could find it altogether agreeable to accept, a thorough home with us during your stay. But Mr. Lewes find it so incompatible with the quiet prosecution of his work to have any visitor staying in the house, that I could not urge it in justice either to him or to my friend. The prohibition extends to every one, and has no special relation to you. He will hear of no one for more than one night, except my niece Emily, whom I hope to have for a week during these Christmas holidays. I myself should feel the additional excitement of a resident visitor a thing to be avoided in the case of every one who was not in a peculiar sense a friend; but it would be very sweet to me to show perfect hospitality to any one of the small number who could come under that class.
I should like, for your sake, that you should rather see us in our own house than in this; for I fear your carrying away a general sense of yellow in connection with us -- and I am sure that is enough to set you against the thought of us. There are some staring yellow curtains which you will hardly help blending with your impression of our moral sentiments. In our own drawing room, I mean to have a paradise of greenness.
I wish you could try and read Herbert Spencer's book 661 before you come, because I shall ask him to meet you, and the knowledge of what it contains would add to the pleasure of conversation with him. I think the first part superior to anything he has done before, and he says he feels the same himself: it is less barely intellectual -- the considerations are larger.
Talking of books, I have lately reread your "Thoughts" from the beginning of the "Psychical Essence of Christianity" to the end of the Hist[ory] of Philosophy, and I feel my original impression confirmed that the "Psychical Essence" and the "General Review of the Christian System" are the most valuable portions. I think you once expressed your regret that I did not understand the analogy you traced between Feuerbach's theory and Spencer's. I don't know what gave you that impression, for I never said so. I see your meaning distinctly, in that parallel. If you referred to something in Mr. Lewes's letter, let me say once for all that you must not impute my opinions to him, nor vice versa. The intense happiness of our union is derived in a high degree from the perfect freedom with which we each follow and declare our own impressions. In this respect I know no man so great as he -- that difference of opinion rouses no egoistic irritation in him, and that he is ready to admit that another's argument is the stronger, the moment his intellect recognizes it.
Thank Mr. Bray for his letter on the spirit-rapping. I am glad to see him contributing his quota to the exposure of that odious trickery. Mr. Lewes lately wrote an article ("Seeing is believing") in Blackwood 662 on the subject. I hope Mr. Bray knows that Sir David Brewster, in the "Times" 663 long ago, contradicted the report that he gave his adhesion to Mr. Home and his spirits.
It was not head-ache that I was suffering from when Mr. Bray called, but extreme languor and unbroken fatigue from morning to night -- a state which is always accompanied in me psychically by utter self-distrust and despair of ever being equal to the demands of life. But I went to Erasmus Wilson after he left, and between bluepill and hydrochloric acid I find myself getting stronger in body and mind.
We should be very pleased to hear some news of Mr. and Mrs. Call. I feel their removal from town quite a loss to us. Love to Cara and thanks for the "Physiology."
Ever yours
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 May [1867]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 May [1867]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 17-18.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 13.
Dear Sara
I like to think of you all resting deliciously at Shanklin in this spring time -- Cara and Mr. Bray with no house on their minds and all three of you enjoying "the fine nature," as our hostess at Scilly used to say. I cannot sit with you on the sands, but I scribble a little note which I hope will seem like a morning smile and greeting.
Mr. and Mrs. Call dined with us on Saturday. I fear they were neither of them well, and found it an exertion to come to us amongst other friends. But to us it was a pleasure to see them again; they are both, I think, all the more loveable for the years, and have not been injured (morally) by the worrying cares which have unhappily fallen to them.
Yesterday, we went to the second of a course of lectures which Dr. Congreve is delivering on Positivism, in Bouverie Street. At the first lecture, on the 5th there was a considerable audience -- about 75, chiefly men -- of various ranks, from lords and M.P.'s downwards, or upwards, for what is called social distinction seems to be in a shifting condition just now. Yesterday the wet weather doubtless helped to reduce the audience, still, it was good. Curiosity brings some, interest in the subject others, and the rest go with the wish to express adhesion more or less thorough. It remains to be seen whether Dr. Congreve's mode of lecturing will secure a continuous attendance on the part of experimental comers. 627 But he has now a great opportunity.
You remember the brilliantly healthful appearance of my dear good friend Madame Bodichon. She has had a severe illness -- an attack of Algerian fever, and is still in a very delicate state. But she has been able to get as near her English home as St. Cloud where she is staying in careful quiet, with Miss Parkes as her guardian angel.
I am afraid you have ceased to care much about pictures, else I should wish that you could see the exhibition of historical portraits at Kensington. It is really worth a little fatigue to see the English of past generations in their habit as they lived -- especially when Gainsborough and
Sir Joshua are the painters. But even Sir Godfrey Kneller delights me occasionally with a finely conceived portrait carefully painted. There is an unforgettable portrait of Newton by him. I think Cara would like to see this exhibition very much if she happens to be in town again before it closes. We have been to see nothing else yet, and have been keeping ourselves as quiet as possible. With best love to all
Ever yours
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 June 1870
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 June 1870
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, III, 113-114.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 13. 1870.
My dear Sara
Our programme, of which I told you, is disturbed. Dr. Reynolds advises Mr. Lewes to leave London again and go to the bracing air of the Yorkshire coast. So we must pack again! I am unwilling to go without letting you know, because I had hoped that some journey of yours might bring you to London, and I had said that we should be here till the beginning of August. But the Internal Order proposes and the External Order disposes -- if we are to be so priggish as to alter all our old proverbs into agreement with new formulas.
If you or Cara should have any occasion to write to me, a letter addressed to this house will always reach me, with the words "to be forwarded" on the cover.
Dickens's death 196 came as a great shock to us. He lunched with us just before we went abroad and was telling us a story of President Lincoln having told the Council on the day he was shot, that something remarkable would happen, because he had just dreamt for the third time a dream which twice before had preceded events momentous to the nation. The dream was, that he was in a boat on a great river all alone -- and he ended with the words "I drift -- I drift -- I drift." 197
Dickens told this very finely. I thought him looking dreadfully shattered then. It is probable that he never recovered from the effect of the terrible railway accident. 198
With love, always dear Sara
Your faithful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 July [1864]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 July [1864]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Envelope: Miss Hennell | 3 Barr's Hill Terrace | Coventry. Postmark: LONDON-N.W. | 3 | JY 13 | 64. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | North Bank, | Regents Park.
July 13
Dear Sara
Your letter interested me deeply. I can't help thinking very often of the time when Nelly was a bright little child, playing with Fly on the lawn. That part of her life, I think, was really joyous -- and how much you did for her then! I used to feel your elevation above me continually in the attitude of mind you showed about Nelly's education and your sense of your relation towards childhood generally. These are the lasting things -- the true thoughts, the true feelings, the good deeds, which live in others even when they have gone quite away from the mind in which they were born, so that sometimes the man or woman who is sitting in desolation is doing the office of a glorified Saint for those who remember. Surely that is a strange perversion into which men's minds have been led by long and various causes -- to think that unless life can be made perfect, unless the prospects of humanity can be made to appear the very best, strong moral motives are gone! As if the very absence of that highest security were not a more urgent reason for at least diminishing the pressure of evil, for worshipping the goodness and the great endeavours that are at least a partial salvation, a partial redemption of the world? 277
The other day, Miss Marshall called on us, to our great pleasure, and so certified to me what I was in doubt about -- that she will go on living in London. I was very glad of that, and I hope now to see her oftener than of old, when she had imprisoning duties. 278
I have been reading Newman's Apologia pro Vita Su'e2, 279 with such absorbing interest that I found it impossible to forsake the book until I had finished it. I don't know whether the affair between him and Kingsley has interested you, or whether you have shared at all my view of it. I have been made so indignant by Kingsley's mixture of arrogance, coarse impertinence and unscrupulousness with real intellectual incompetence, that my first interest in Newman's answer arose from a wish to see what I consider thoroughly vicious writing thoroughly castigated. But the Apology now mainly affects me as the revelation of a life -- how different in form from one's own, yet with how close a fellowship in its needs and burthens -- I mean spiritual needs and burthens. At the end there is a beautiful letter written by our old acquaintance Dr. Ullathorne, Bishop of Birmingham, 280 intended as a public testimony to Newman's active life since he entered the Catholic Church.
Yesterday we went to see Holman Hunt's picture which he has been labouring at intermittently of course for five or six years. He calls it the Afterglow in Egypt, but the chief thing is what the afterglow shines upon -- a Nubian girl carrying a bundle of gleaned wheat which has attracted a flight of pigeons towards her. One pigeon clutches the bundle and pecks there -- the others are about her feet. She and the wheat and the pigeons are so much physical life and beauty ripened under the rich sunlight. It is a bit of existence, not of action, and is painted with immense elaboration, yet with shortcomings in the midst of elaboration that prevent it from being a triumph. That is always rather a sad thing to say when there has been so much study, so much hard work, so much heroism as must always go to the doing of anything difficult. But Inspiration is a rare incalculable thing -- it will flash out sometimes in a mere bit of sky and water and weed, and leave you only to wonder at its absence in a picture where all sorts of rare and beautiful things have been brought together and studied with immeasurable pains.
How your story about Harriet amused me! Mr. Lewes is nearly the same with our bull-dog as Harriet with her cat. "Ben" is master of us all, and the most momentous subject must be deferred if Ben wants a stick thrown for him.
My best love and deep sympathy to Cara and Mr. Bray. Write again on the first movement of your will that way.
Ever thine
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 April 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 13 April 1861
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 297-298.
Blandford Sq. | April 13. 61.
Dear Sara
I was going to write you a farewell before our departure for Italy. We start on the 19th and shall be away two months or perhaps less. Our route will not extend beyond 'abFlorence'bb Tuscany, and we shall come back through Switzerland, to see Bertie, who is now brotherless in his school life. Charles, meanwhile, will keep house here, and work like a nigger at his music, as we are going to give him the privilege of having lessons from Brindley Richards 740 while we are away.
We went to hear Beethoven's Mass in D last night, 741 and on Wednesday to hear Mendelssohn's Walpurgis Nacht and Beethoven's Symphony in Bb 742 so that we have had two musical treats this week; but the enjoyment of such things is much diminished by the gas and bad air. Mr. Lewes and I both feel that London privileges of this sort are not worth the purchase to easily perturbed people like ourselves. Indeed our long addiction to a quiet life in which our daily walk amongst the still grass and trees was a f'eate to us, has unfitted us for the sacrifices that London demands. But, for everything except health, I can answer your possible questions comprehensively by saying that we have all sorts of blessings.
I thought Holyoake 743 had renounced the term "Atheist" long, long ago: I have often [heard] Mr. Lewes speak of his having done so.
Mr. Spencer is gone to Derby for a month or two to give some companionship to his father, who has been much out of health lately. He has bought a microscope, and is going to work at it, which I hope will be an agreeable variety in his brain labour.
Major Robert Noel tells us that his brother 744 is expected from
Greece. I trust Cara and Mr. Bray are able to look forward with some pleasure to seeing their old friend, in spite of clouding anxieties.
Don't think about reading Silas Marner, just because it is come out. I hate obligato reading and obligato talk about my books. I never send them to any one and never wish to be spoken to about them, except by an unpremeditated spontaneous prompting. They are written out of my deepest belief, and as well as I can, for the great public -- and every sincere strong word will find its mark in that public. Perhaps the annoyance I suffered from Mr. Bracebridge and Co. has made me rather morbid on such points, but apart from my own weaknesses, I think the less an author hears about himself the better. Don't mistake me -- I am writing a general explanation -- not anything applicable to you.
God bless you. Love and goodby to all.
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 12 June [1854]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 12 June [1854]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | June 12.
Dear Sara
On looking at the clean sheets of F[euerbach] I see many things to regret -- at least in the three first chapters, but they are merely matters of typography and punctuation. The Introduction wants a few more italics, and the notes are printed on a different plan from the one adopted in the third chapter and pursued through the rest of the work. I don't wonder at this, considering that my usual fallibility was increased by more than my usual headache and other evils when I was looking at the earliest proofs. The consequences must be borne, like all other consequences.
Mr. Bray passed yesterday with me -- very pleasantly to me, but he was hindered from his intended evening walk in Kensington Gardens by a visit from Dr. W. Smith 486 and Mr. Pears who took tea with us.
Much love and gratitude to you, dear Sara, for your sympathy and encouraging words -- a great debt which I can't pay. The money debt I send in stamps.
Ever your true
Pollian.
You will like to read the enclosed. Please return it. I enclose a stamp that you may do so without spending a penny which it is not worth.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 12 July 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 12 July 1861
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 308-310.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
July 12. 61.
Dear Sara
Your letter gave me a pleasant vision of Sunday sunshine on the flowers and you among them with your eyes brightened by busy and enjoyable thoughts.
Yes! I hope we are well out of that phase in which the most philosophic view of the past was held to be a smiling survey of human folly, and when the wisest man was supposed to be one who could sympathize with no age but the age to come.
When I received your Monday packet, I was fresh from six quarto volumes on the history of the monastic orders, 814 and had just begun a less formidable modern book on the same subject -- Montalembert's "Monks of the West." 815 Our reading, you see, lay in very different quarters, but I fancy our thoughts sometimes touched the same ground.
I am rather puzzled and shocked, however, by your high admiration of the articles on the Study of History in the Cornhill. I should speak with the reserve due to the fact that I have only read the second article; 816 and this, I confess, did not impress me as exhibiting any mastery of the question, while its tone towards much abler thinkers than the writer himself, is to me extremely repulsive. The writer is not Mr. Hinton 817 (who, you know, writes the physiological contributions) but Mr. Stephen, 818 a barrister -- the son of Sir James Stephen, and formerly one of the critical corps belonging to the Saturday Review. Some time ago, as we learned from his friend Mr. Fawcett, 819 he was dismissed from the Saturday, and has since written regularly for the Cornhill.
Long ago an article appeared in the Sat[urday] on Sir W. Hamilton's doctrine of contradictory inconceivables which both Mr. Lewes and I thought admirable, and we were told that it was Mr. Stephen's. It was written with a touch of graceful humour which I have not recognized in anything else pointed out to me as his. Such writing as -- "We should not be called upon to believe that every crotchet which tickled the insane vanity of a conceited Frenchman was an eternal and self-evident truth" -- is to me simply disgusting, though it were directed against the Father of Lies. It represents no fact except the writer's own desire to be bitter, and is worthily finished by the dull and irreverent antithesis of the eternal truth and infernal lie.
I have just been reading the survey of the Middle Ages contained in the 5th volume of the Philosophie Positive, 820 and to my apprehension few chapters can be fuller of luminous ideas. I am thankful to learn from it. There may be more profundity in Mr. Stephen's exposition than I am able to penetrate, or possibly the first article may contain weightier matter than the second. Miss Dobson 821 shares your admiration of them, according to Miss Marshall, who called and had a chat with me yesterday.
Mrs. Bodichon is near us now, and one always gets good from contact with her healthy practical life. It is a comfort to know that her sister Mrs. Ludlow is very well at present. Mr. Lewes is gone to see Mrs. Congreve and carry his net to the Wimbledon ponds: I hope he will get a little strength as well as grist for his microscope.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian.
I quite agree with you -- so far as I am able to form a judgment -- in regarding Positivism as one-sided; but Comte was a great thinker, nevertheless, and ought to be treated with reverence by all smaller fry.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 12 August 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 12 August 1861
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, II, 313.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
August 12. 61.
Dear Sara
Mrs. Bodichon had heard (through the Carters) of the vacant rooms, before I saw her in sufficient privacy to mention the matter. She is more likely than any one else to find out the right persons for that cheap and pleasant accommodation, and she promises to bear it in mind -- a promise which means more with her than with the common run of people.
The regret I have at your leaving the pretty cottage which I knew, to go to one which I don't know, 829 is softened by the reflection that Cara and Mr. Bray will be the happier for reducing their expenses within the needful limit.
That doctrine which we accept rather loftily as a commonplace when we are quite young -- namely, that our happiness lies entirely within, in our own mental and bodily state which determines for us the influence of everything outward -- becomes a daily lesson to be learned, and learned with much stumbling, as we get older. And until we know our friends' private thoughts and emotions we hardly know what to grieve or rejoice over for them.
London is very hot and close; but it is a satisfaction to know that this must be a corn-favouring time. Don't infer a revolution in my character from the appearance of my handwriting. I am writing with my paper on my knee, for the sake of sitting at the open window. With best love to all
Ever thine
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 10 June 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 10 June 1863
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, II, 354.
Blandford Sq. | June 10. 63.
Dear Sara
In a general routing of papers such as comes after a release from preoccupying work, I have alighted on an autograph of Montalembert which I put by for you two years and more ago. I don't know whether your zeal as a collector is still alive: if it is, Montalembert is one of the men who will be historical, and is therefore worth a place in your book.
I had cut off the signature, not meaning to send you the letter. But, on second thought, it may amuse you, in the dearth of variety at Coventry, to see what the brilliant Frenchman happens to say in English about an English book. You can read the letter and then burn it -- don't put it away without that -- and the signature may go among your autographs.
I trust you can tell me now that your head is better than when Cara wrote. How impossible it is for strong people to understand the way in which bodily malaise and suffering eats at the root of one's life! The philosophy that is true -- the religion that is strength to the healthy -- is constantly emptiness to one when the head is distracted and every sensation is oppressive.
We intend to have a run to the Isle of Wight next week -- to take a carriage and go round the island, and so get a breath of freshness before Thornie comes to demand our presence at home.
At a little gathering we had on Saturday Miss Marshall and Mrs. W. Marshall joined us, and the latter delighted us very much with her excellent piano-playing.
Don't write to me unless you feel the prompting. Only when you do, I shall be glad to know something more of you than my own rather sombre imaginations.
Ever yours affectionately
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 10 February 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 10 February 1874
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday Evening | February 10. 74.
Dear Sara
Oh what a picture that is which you have been so good as to give me of Harriet! -- how deeply pathetic, and yet almost happy from the rays of affectionate goodness both in her and in her poor friend Ann! I am quite grateful to you for taking the trouble to write me the narrative, and I quite share your comfort in the sense that Harriet is now in kind keeping and sure to have the needful tendance.
I have read both the newspaper slips. Your letter to the Examiner 22 is much milder than I expected, and hardly makes apparent the severe objections you mentioned to me. But I am not sorry that there should be a little boiling of the peas shot at poor Mr. Spencer just now, for he is running the gauntlet in rather a fatiguing way between Cambridge men who are criticising his physics and psychology, and historians who are criticising the [Sociological Tables] on which he has already spent £500, in the hope that he is doing the world a service. Perhaps you do not see [the Academy,] which has been regenerated and has started on its new life with great vigour: it is in this periodical that the [Tables] have been discussed. 23 Then there is Moulton, 24 a Cambridge mathematician, who is carrying on a venomous as well as harassing attack in the British Quarterly; and there are various bitings and snappings of metaphysicians in other directions. Such are the delights of philosophical celebrity -- of a better sort however than those of poor Dickens, as they are painfully revealed in this third and last volume of his Life. 25
I have been almost constantly an invalid during the last seven weeks or more, and last week I had quite a new form of an ailment which Dr. Andrew Clarke is inclined to dignify with the name of lumbar neuralgia. The pain was very trying while it lasted, but happily it came on in fits and after a few hours would leave me suddenly like a cast out daemon. However, I have now been free for several days and am cheerfully hoping that the enemy will not return.
The dirty Christians 26 are very dilatory too, but I suppose we must allow for an immense amount of pressing business in which dear Cara's story seems to lie like one pebble in a heap as seen from the Secretary's point of view, he having painfully to dispose of the heap pebble by pebble. I have been thinking of it almost daily, and have been tempted to the irrationality of writing to ask her whether she had had any news of it.
Your handsome green volume 27 has been duly sent to me -- but only the other day. The paper-covered parts are pleasant to hold, but not so good for reference. Thank you for this extra gift.
Do you know that the [Examiner] is now the property of Mr. Peter Taylor? -- who, by the way, is one of the minority of returned Liberals, keeping his old seat for Leicester. Surely the Mr. Jackson you mention must be the son of Peter Jackson? But who is [old Sam Carter]? 28 However the story you tell of his behaviour is very pretty.
I am not yet quite up to my ordinary pitch of strength, and find my inevitable letter-writing a little too much for me. But I am very glad of the occasion which has made me scribble this to you the last thing before going to bed. I read your account of Harriet to Mr. Lewes, who has entered into it very keenly. Best love to all from
Your ever affectionate
Pollian.
I return the slips, lest you should not have any duplicates. Mrs. William Smith has written a very interesting memoir of her husband (the author of Thorndale) which is appended to his Essays on Knowing and Feeling originally published in the Contemporary. 29

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 10 August 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 10 August 1866
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, 11, 436-439.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 10. 66.
My dear Sara
When I read Mr. Bray's letter I felt it to be a perversity in things that you should all three have made a long stay at Sydenham precisely during my absence. But I must grumble at nothing, since I have had a delightful holiday, and find my double self very much the better for it.
Mr. Bray will wonder less that Mr. Lewes could be so long away when he knows that he had arranged the programmes of all the numbers beforehand, save for such circumstantial demands as Mr. Anthony Trollope undertook to meet; and that there is always on the spot a subeditor
(Mr. Dennis) 512 who has the unfailing interest of a shareholder in the proprietorship of the Review. Mr. Lewes is much better, and I am quite well -- "looking," Grace says, "just like my portrait," from which I conclude that my face has some of that "fleshiness" which Cara found objectionable.
Please to understand that this account of our condition is an advance which you are expected to repay by an equivalent account of yourself and belongings.
We made a great round in our journeying. From Antwerp to Rotterdam, The Hague, Leyden, Amsterdam, Cologne. Then up the Rhine to Coblenz, and thence to Schwalbach, where we stayed a fortnight. From Schwalbach to Schlangenbad where we stayed, till we feared the boats would cease to go to and fro, and in fact only left just in time to get down the Rhine to Bonn by the Dutch steamer. From Bonn, after two days, we went to Aix; then to dear old Li'e8ge, where we had been together thirteen years before: and, to avoid the King of the Belgians, ten minutes backward to the baths of pretty Chaudfontaine, where we remained three days. Then to Louvain, Ghent and Bruges, and last of all to Ostend, where we waited for a fine day and calm sea until we secured -- a very rough passage indeed. Ought we not to be a great deal wiser and more efficient personages, or else to be ashamed of ourselves? Unhappily this last alternative is not a compensation for wisdom.
I thought of you -- to mention one occasion amongst many -- when we had the good fortune at Antwerp to see a placard announcing that the company from the Oberammergau, Bavaria, would represent that Sunday evening the Lebensgeschichte of our Saviour Christ at the Th'e9'e2tre des Vari'e9t'e9s. I remembered that you had seen the representation with deep interest, and these actors are doubtless the successors of those you saw. Of course we went to the theatre. And the Christ was, without exaggeration, beautiful. All the rest was inferior and might even have had a painful approach to the ludicrous, but both the person and action of the Jesus were fine enough to overpower all meaner impressions. Mr. Lewes, who, you know, is keenly alive to everything "stagey" in physiognomy and gesture, felt what I am saying quite as much as I did, and was much moved. 513
I forgot what was your exact route to Cologne, and how far you saw the Belgian towns, besides Antwerp. To me, these towns remain superior in interest to anything in Holland. Rotterdam with the grand approach to it by the broad river, the rich brick of the houses, the canals uniformly planted with trees and crowded with the bright brown masts of the Dutch boats, is far finer than Amsterdam. The colour of Amsterdam is ugly: the houses are of a chocolate colour, almost black (an artificial tinge given to the bricks) and the woodwork on them screams out in ugly patches of cream-colour; the canals have no trees along their sides, and the boats are infrequent. We looked about for the very Portuguese Synagogue where Spinoza was nearly assassinated as he came from worship. But it no longer exists. 514 There are no less than three Portuguese Synagogues now -- very large and handsome. And in the evening we went to see the worship there. Not a woman was present, but of devout men not a few, curious reversal of what one sees in other temples. The chanting and the swaying about of the bodies -- almost a wriggling -- are not beautiful to the sense, but I fairly cried at witnessing this faint symbolism of a religion of sublime far-off memories. The skulls of St. Ursula's eleven thousand virgins seem a modern suggestion compared with the Jewish Synagogue.
I know you have been at Kissingen, so you are very well acquainted with the nature of the German Bath, and can imagine the sort of life led at Schwalbach and Schlangenbad. Our life was led chiefly in the beech woods which we had all to ourselves, the guests usually confining themselves to the nearer promenades. The guests of course, were few in that serious time, and between war and cholera we felt our position as health-and-pleasure-seekers somewhat contemptible.
The Congreves dined with us yesterday. They intend to settle in London -- a great sacrifice to duty -- as soon as they can sell their present house. The delightful relief of having got through the medical examination has made a young man again of Dr. Congreve.
Our Gertrude expects to have her baby at the end of September and is remarkably well. And we have found no greater domestic calamity on our return, than the distortion of our white blinds and curtains by cleaning, and the extortions of a wicked gardener's bill. I wish Mr. Bray did not hint at vexations of this latter sort for him too. We enter thoroughly into his need for quiet above all things. I fear age is making us too impatient of our fellow-men's society.
There is no end to what one could say, if one did not feel that long letters cut pieces not to be spared out of the solid day. I think I have earned that you should write me one of those perfect letters in which you make me see everything you like about yourself and others. Best love to all.
Always your
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 1 January [1863]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1863. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | Thursday January 1.
Dear Sara
The beautiful mark is a little too long for my Bible, but that can be remedied. It will be treasured there till I die. The little one also will go into a sacred book with the odour of devout centuries in it. Mr. Lewes's mother is coming to lunch with us and my head is so infirm that I am afraid of asking it to do anything. So I will only say, all blessings for 1863!
Ever yours
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 1 August 1862
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | August 1. 62.
Dear Sara
I ought to have answered your kind inquiries before, since I can answer them joyfully. I have had the most promising letters every day from the first arrival of Mr. Lewes at Spa, and now the blessed end of the fortnight is come, and he is to be at home again tomorrow at eight, "feeling strong," he tells me. Spa has proved just the right sort of place -- with a pretty country and pleasant idleness in the way of occupation, to prevent invalids from wishing for books or work. "Healthful play" is the business of the place. Mr. Lewes found Bulwer there, and the companionship has been agreeable. The weather must make all life away from towns paradisaic, and to me, you may imagine, it is rather difficult to understand how you can want to travel away from leisure and green fields.
Have you noticed in the Times -- what has been a sad grief to the Congreves lately -- the death (by suicide) of Mr. Winstanley, 99 formerly one of Mr. Congreve's pupils -- a man of wealth thoroughly attached to Comte's system of philosophy and religion? On many grounds it is a trial for the Congreves. He had always been subject to fits of melancholy. With best love to all
Ever yours
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [September 1865]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
My dear Sara
Mr. Lewes prefers the larger title page, and so did I, before referring the matter to him. But the size of the volume is rather the question than the comparative appearance of these two title pages [three lines torn away.] I shall be sure to read a great deal of them before seeing you.

Ever your

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [March 1854]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Sara
I fear you will be very weary of your task, but I must entreat you to continue it. As we shall begin to print soon, I shall be glad if you will return the sheets I now send by post in 6d. parcels as you get done with them. I forgot to tell you that I have agreed with Mr. C. to have no variation of type beyond occasional italics, so you need not trouble yourself about any underlining.
To save you from fidgeting about the s. and p. in the references I must tell you that Feuerbach habitually puts p. (for pagina) in his references to German works, so I leave it as he puts it. If it will not be much more trouble to you, please to put the punctuation, additional capitals, and any thing about which you are quite sure, in ink. Every stroke of the pen you can save me is so much charity.
I send you the original of the Preface to amuse you with the long-winded sentence pp. ix and x. I feel your reading of Feuerbach as a real act of friendship to me -- but it is something still better than that -- a contribution towards the perfecting of a mental product, to be reckoned with improving crops of wheat and all other real human work.
Pollian.
Feuerbach's sentences are too uniformly short. Would you weave them together at all, or leave the style intact?

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [January 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: To S. S. Hennell, Jany 17. 1854. Hitherto unpublished.
My dear Sara
It has struck me while writing this morning that you may some times mistake Feuerbach's habitual amplification, which I think it necessary to preserve, for a "whichever-you-please-my-little-dear" of my own, and so play the devil by crossing out what should be kept in. By the bye, let all your crossings be in pencil and then there will be no danger. This word to the wise will suffice. You will now be awake to the distinction. Pray get rid of as many dashes as possible. What I put in are always
Feuerbach's. Here is a story for you. Carlyle, meeting FitzBall 431 said, "How is it I never see your name as a dramatic author now?" "Oh" (very much through the nose) "I'm comfortable now; my mother's dead." That mustn't be put in the paper or told to any one. But it will make you all laugh for three minutes -- not a trifling boon in this world.
Your faithful
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [8 November 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 1853. Brief extract published: Cross, I, 316.
Cambridge St. | Tuesday.
Dear Sara
Thanks many for both your letters. It must be that tremendous conscientiousness of yours on the hunt for duties that makes you read through the Co[ntemporar]y Lit[erature] of the W[estminster] R[eview]. However it is to be worth reading in future -- done on a new plan -- the Foreign Lit[erature] blended with the Eng[lish]. J. Martineau is to do the Theology and Philosophy, Huxley the Science and Froude the History!! 391 I am afraid, though, that this will not be a very tempting programme to you.
Pleasant Mrs. Mackay came on Sunday morning and invited me to meet Dr. Elliotson tomorrow. Her husband has made his call this morning, looking frightened as to the eyes and clean as to the collar. He is full of the book on Christianity and I hope will really get it done before long. 392 I always like to see him and talk to him. He seems so kind -- so full of good-will towards one.
Have you known the misery of writing with a tired steel pen which is reluctant to make a mark? If so, you will know why I leave off.
Ever your loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [8 February 1862]
MS: Yale. Endorsed. Feb. 8. Extracts published: Cross, II, 333.
Blandford Sq. | Saturday.
Dear Sara
Mr. Spencer has made an arrangement with Williams and Norgate, but it would be useless for you to think of them, as they rejected Mr. Spencer at first, and were only induced to accede to his proposition by Mr. Huxley's recommendations. They are not, you know, in the midstream of publishing. 20
Mr. Lewes thinks the best thing you could do would be to go to
Trubner 21 whom he knows very well and likes. There is one drawback, which deterred Mr. Spencer from arranging with him: it is, that you will have 15 per cent deducted for commission. The reason is that T. employs a country traveller, who charges 5 per cent on all copies disposed of to country booksellers; Tr'fcbner himself taking the usual commission of 10 per cent. This extra 5 per cent would of course not be deducted in the case of copies ordered directly from the publisher by private persons. The extra charge is a pity, but Mr. Lewes thinks that, under all the circumstances, you would do better to put up with it than to seek among other publishers. Tr'fcbner is a clever and very hearty German, with a good deal of culture. The doctrinal aspect of your books would be of no importance to him either personally or commercially.
Apropos of your previous letter -- we shall not, I think, go abroad this spring. I am wondering whether you and Cara could spare me, for a few weeks, the Tempest Music and any other vocal music of that or of a kindred species? I don't want to buy it until our singers have experimented upon it. Don't think of sending me anything that you are using at all, but if said music be lying idle, I should be grateful for the loan. We have several operas: Don Giovanni, Figaro, the Barbiere, Flauto Magico -- and also the music of Macbeth, but I think that is all our stock of concerted vocal music.
Ever yours
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [7 May 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: May 8. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge St. | Sunday.
Dear Sara
I am obliged to apply to you again, for I have no one else whom I can ask to give me their impression. Until the last two days I had resolved to omit the 2d 3d and 4th sections in the appendix 463 because they are abstract and Germanized "to a degree" and might repel the reader from the appendix, which contains a great deal of important and accessible matter. But I shrink from omission, so I have determined to ask you for your opinion. You who come to the thing fresh with your brain unfatigued will be better able to judge of the effect on ordinary readers -- or rather extraordinary readers who will get so far as the appendix. I will not be affected and make apologies for asking you to read such fearful scribble etc. I know your Herz und Vernunft both will make the task endurable.
The printers will want the appendix soon, so of course I shall be glad to have these sheets again as soon as possible, but do not hurry so as not to satisfy yourself completely.
The laxity of Feuerbach's language is particularly tiresome in the 2d 'a7. I am obliged to translate sensation in one place and emotion in another. 464 Notice whatever is incomprehensible to you.
Your loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [7 March 1864]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [7 March 1864]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 7. 1864. Extracts published: Cross, II, 378-379.
Monday Morning.
Dear Sara
Thanks for thy letter. I felt it long since I had had news from you, but my days go by, each seeming too short for what I must do, and I don't like to molest you with mere questions. I have been spoiled for correspondence by Mr. Lewes's goodness in always writing letters for me where a proxy is admissible. And so it has come to be a great affair with me to write even a note, while people who keep up a large correspondence and set apart their hour for it find it easy to cover reams of paper with talk from the end of the pen. I shall write to Cara, having happily written the Sydenham address in my "Where is it?" 234 -- the only means with me of remembering a London address.
You say nothing of yourself, which is rather unkind. We are enjoying a perfect t'eate 'e0 t'eate, Charlie being gone for this month of March on his holiday journey, of which the goal is to be Munich this year. On Friday 235 we are going to hear the Judas Maccabaeus and try if possible to be stirred to something heroic by "Sound an alarm."
I was more sorry than it is usually possible to be about the death of a person utterly unknown to me, when I read of Maria Martineau's death. 236 She was a person whose office in life seemed so thoroughly defined and so valuable. For an invalid like H[arriet] M[artineau] to be deprived of a beloved nurse and companion is a sorrow that makes one ashamed of one's small grumblings.
I am glad to know that you felt the story of David Gray. Friend "Bob" 237 told us the other evening, that he (Bob) had once for three whole weeks never gone to bed, writing a 2s volume for bread and onion, hardly for bread and meat. He just dozed off in his chair, and then went at his work again.
Mrs. Congreve writes me word that her husband is the better for their travel, though not yet just the thing. I was sorry to know of how Walter Congreve's 238 illness interrupted his apparently prosperous career. O dear O dear when will people leave off their foolish talk about all human lots being equal? as if anybody with a sound stomach ever knew misery comparable to the misery of a dyspeptic.
Farewell, dear Sara. Be generous, and don't always wait an age in silence because I don't write.
Ever your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [31 March 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 31. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | Friday.
My dear Sara
As much M.S. as you can send me by Monday morning I shall be glad to receive, as I want to send it to the printer. I have made up my mind that no one will read the book, still less understand it. If you are tired of it, pray say so, for there is no necessity that you should bore yourself with it if you find it a labour.
Pray thank Mr. Bray for his note. I was so stupid as not to think of the foreign Bradshaw or I would not have troubled him.
To-morrow night 450 the opera opens with William Tell -- and I go! Ask Mr. Bray if he doesn't envy me? He enjoyed William Tell so last year. Best love to Cara and all spring pleasures to you every one.
Your loving and grateful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [31 January 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Jany 31 | 1852. Extract published: Cross, 1, 270, as part of [21 January 1852].
Strand | Saturday.
Dear Sara
Mrs. Chapman said she should charge Mrs. C. Hennell last night with a message of invitation to you. I am sure she will be heartily glad to see you and so will Mr. Chapman. Just now we are in rather uninteresting circumstances -- Mr. C. up to the ears in a business affair all about Bookselling and discounts, 18 which things grate horribly on my ears -- and the weather is generally detestable, so that hardly any going out can be done.
Mrs. Chapman is going to Leamington for a week on business, and I remember you said that you should not like to be here when she was out. I say all these things, not to prevent you from coming now if you feel inclined, but just to let you know how the land lies. To me it will be a pleasure to have you, -- come when you will.
We are going to Mr. Mackay's tonight, but I am in a miserable state of languor and low spirits in which everything is a trouble to me.
I must tell you a bit of Louis Blanc's English which Mr. Spencer was reciting the other night. The petit homme called on Thornton
Hunt, I think, and said "I come to tell you how you are. I was at you the other day. But you were not." 19 Best love to all
Your faithful
Pollian.

Chapman maintained that the Association had no authority over the price of imported books, which at this time he announced he would sell at cost plus a small commission. He was summoned before the committee of the Association, which canceled his membership. Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [30 August 1852]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [30 August 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Aug. 29. 1852. Extract published: Cross, I, 289.
Strand | Monday.
My dear Sara
I celebrated my return to London 172 by the usual observances -- that is to say, a violent headache and sickness. The headache is not yet gone, and of course I am in the worst spirits, under the influence of blue devils alias blue pill, and my opinion of things is not worth a straw. I tell you this that you may know why I only send you this scrap instead of the long letter which I have in petto for you and which would otherwise have been written yesterday.
Mr. Chapman says that Mr. Bray meant to come to London to-day if he obtained an affirmative from Mr. Flower 173 about another of these miserable loans. I loathe the very mention of them.
Love to all. I shall write very soon.
Your loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [3 June 1854]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [3 June 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 3. Brief extract published: George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 87.
Cambridge Street | Saturday Morning.
Dear Sara
Thanks in the first place for the better news about business. It is a ray of sunshine to me this morning which finds me on the whole in a cloudy state.
The printers have been so dilatory with Feuerbach, that I am only just going to correct what I think will be the last sheet but one. I am sorry to find that they have put into italics all the large type of the latin quotations in the appendix, which I had not thought of giving directions about, and Mr. Chapman shudders at the expense of alteration. 481 Perhaps there is an advantage in typographical emphasis in Latin -- it may help to attract or to fix the reader's attention.
How came you to imagine that I did the Belles Lettres in the West[minste]r? Mrs. Sinnett did them as usual -- and she begs Mr. Chapman not to take this work from her at present, as the loss of it would make a serious deficit in her income. I am glad to tell you that one of her daughters is engaged to young Ellis, only son of Mr. Ellis of Champion Hill. 482 One likes to think of the rich and the poor coming together.
I went to the Strand last night and found Mr. and Mrs. Chapman already in the bustle of their double removal. 483 A well-to-do brother of Miss Tilley's is come from Australia and will do something for her, I hope.
Mr. Lewes is still suffering from his head and is ordered to go into the country again. He sets off on a visit to Oxford this morning and from there he will go to Malvern to see Mr. Bray's acquaintance, Dr. Balbirnie, 484 of whom I have not a pleasant recollection.
Brain and legs and fingers all move heavily with me. I do nothing well but idling, and the consciousness of this is like a garment of lead about me. If I could only fancy myself clever, it would be better, but to be a failure of Nature and to know it is not a comfortable lot. It is the last lesson one learns, to be contented with one's inferiority -- but it must be learned. In haste ever
Your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [3 April 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 4. Hitherto unpublished.
Thanks, dear Sara, for the M.S. I have a headache today in spite of a ramble in Hampstead Heath yesterday, so I am unable to look over it -- that is, the M.S. Certainly I think it quite worth while to send you the rest, and shall only be delighted to do so. But I was afraid of tiring you. The last part will soon be all ready for you -- but after that comes the appendix.
I am going to hear William Tell tomorrow. Vivian has not been well so he abstained from the opera on Saturday. 451
Pray don't impute the Orphic sayings to Alcott. 452 Mr. Lewes dictated the greater number of them to me, as they bubbled up amidst the most careless talk.
More another day. Love to all.
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [29 November 1860]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Envelope: Miss Hennell | Ivy Cottage | Radford Road | Coventry. Postmark: LONDON N | 4 | NO 29 | 60. Hitherto unpublished.
Harewood Sq. | Thursday Morning.
Dear Sara
We always lunch at 'bd past one, and at that time are ready to see visitors. But immediately after lunch, if the heavens permit, we prepare to go out of doors, and usually remain out from 2 till 4. I hope you can come to us on Monday -- in time for dinner, at 'bd past 5 if not earlier, and we will either go to the Monday's concert at St. James's Hall, where there is fine instrumental music, 665 or we would stay at home, whichever you liked. Mr. Lewes is writing to Mr. Spencer to ask him to come and dine with you here on Wednesday. We give him the latest day, because being a great diner-out, he may have engagements. So please to reserve Wednesday for us, until you hear from me what is Mr. Spencer's answer.
You have happily hit on the week before the hustle of moving begins. I do hope you have also hit on a week when there will be less rain and fog than we have been living in lately.
Ever yours
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [29 April 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 30. Extract published: George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 81.
Cambridge St. | Saturday.
Dear Sara
I have yet another service to beg of you -- a very great one. It is to read as quickly as you can the portion of the appendix which I send you by today's post, and to tell me how far it will be necessary to modify it for the Eng[lish] public. I have written it very rapidly and have translated it quite literally so you have the raw Feuerbach -- not any of my cooking. I am so far removed from the popular feeling on the subject of which it treats that I cannot trust my own judgment. With the ideas of Feuerbach I everywhere agree, but of course I should, of myself, alter the phraseology considerably. Before I do this however, I want you to tell me what I must leave out. Mind, I want to keep in as much as possible. 462 Send it me back as soon as possible, and don't think of the style but only of the matter and the crudity of expressions. In great haste,
Your ever grateful
Pollian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 28. 1854. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | Tuesday.
Dear Sara
I am full of regret for having written you such a dismal note yesterday. I was feeling "desperate" just then, as Miss Parkes would say, but cold and headache both took a favourable turn later in the day -- I ate a good dinner and am at work again this morning, hoping that the cough will soon take its flight from me and wing its way across the Baltic to the Emperor Nicolas. 440 So don't spend undue commiseration on me. I have no time to say more.
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [28 April 1867]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [28 April 1867]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 29, 1867. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday.
My dear Sara
Thanks for your kind note. It was only from Miss Marshall I heard that the Coventry house was to be let and that consequently you were all three to migrate. Since then I have been hoping to see both you and
Cara, thinking it possible that you might intend to make a little stay in London after the arrangements at Sydenham had been completed. But I thoroughly understand how you can neither of you make a journey into London for the sake of brief interviews.
I am anxious to know where you are all going -- to some pleasant place I hope -- and when you are settled perhaps you will send me a scrap to save me from entire ignorance.
What weather we have had 609 -- in London, at least, for I imagine the country weather always more endurable. We have felt the return to damps and glooms rather heavily. Still, we have comforts on our hearth, molecular physics and all other great subjects, and must not complain with a lot so much better than that of the people in Ratcliffe Highway 610 and elsewhere.
We shall meet again, sometime, I trust, before we are too old to recognize each other. God bless you all, and farewell -- not a long farewell.
Always yours lovingly
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [27 February 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 27. 1854. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | Monday Morning.
Dear Sara
The reason I have not written to you is that I have had almost constant headache and mal-aise for the last fortnight or more so that the grasshopper has been a burthen 437 -- that is, it would have been if this had been the season for grasshoppers and I within hearing of their chirping. Now I have a cold which I am afraid is turning into a cough. The worst of it is that I can't get on with work, which is eminently needful.
I send you sixpennyworth of M.S. by today's post. If you can manage to read it and send it back by Mr. Noel, 438 so much the better. But I would rather you did not hurry over it. Perhaps Mr. Bray will be coming again soon. Send me word of the parcel's safe arrival, for I should go more hopelessly mad than Carlyle if I had any of my work to do over again. 439
I have given your letter to Mr. Chapman.
Thank you very much for writing yesterday, dear Sara. There are few people who can be generous enough to give even a letter. You see I gracefully leave your gift unreturned -- a sort of delicacy at which I am particularly au fait.
Ever your faithful and grateful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [26 October 1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [26 October 1860]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oct. 29. 1860. Hitherto unpublished.
Harewood Square | Friday.
My dear Sara
When Louis Blanc saw Mr. J. Morgan's Transparencies, he said "Tr'e8s beau; mais il y manque l'impr'e9vu." 652 That element is so abundant everywhere except in Mr. Morgan's Utopia, that there is no saying absolutely what will have become of us in "three weeks or a month." But "sauf l'impr'e9vu," we shall be where we are, and very glad if you will retire out of the world to us as often as you are inclined to do so. Harewood Square adjoins Blandford Square and is within reasonable distance of "everything," so that it is an excellent place to dine and rest in, and go out again from, to any evening engagement.
I say no more, because I don't know what friends you may have made arrangements with, and Mr. Lewes and I have a great horror of perpetually changing pre-arrangements, unfulfilled expectations, and all such waste of human energies. We are almost always at home and almost always alone, so that when you are inclined, as I said, to come out of the world, rest in an easy-chair and warm your toes at a good fire, you will find what you want with us. -- I am much comforted to have a hint that business is looking up a little. My love to all.
Ever your affectionate
Pollian.
While I have been writing to you, Mr. Lewes has been seeing a solicitor about a house, 653 and made one step nearer taking it. But in any case we shall not move till the December quarter, I believe.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [26 April 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 26. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | Wednesday.
Dear Sara
Thanks for your last letter. Happily I need not decide on the motto 459 until the last.
I shall not be able to send you the appendix, I believe; indeed how I shall get to the end of it myself I don't know, for I have been almost constantly ill for the last ten days and all head work is literally an agony -- or wrestling -- to me. There are some passages which you disappoint me very much by not understanding and I should like to write to you about them, but I haven't strength or spirit to do it. I am too entirely without hope about the book to be sensitive. The press will do nothing but abuse or ridicule it -- which for those who know what "the press" means, as I do, is not of the slightest consequence to one's own view, but must always affect a publisher's. I dare say Mr. Chapman will think his case pitiable, but if he knew the amount of phosphorous it requires to translate such a book (which he does not) he would think it still more pitiable to have only two shillings a page for it. 460
Give my love to the married couple who are celebrating their wedding day 461 in sackcloth and ashes. Tell Mr. Bray I wish he would write to me and let me know how things are really going on. For you all, I desire immense things, but for myself nothing seems desirable but to get out of this headachy world or rather to take my headachy body out of it and make room for a more healthy existence.
Ever yours affectionately
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [25 November 1853]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [25 November 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 22. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, I, 317-318.
Cambridge Street | Friday Morning.
Dear Sara
Sundry hindrances external and internal have prevented me from fulfilling my desire to write to you. Chiefly an uncomfortable state of body -- indeed I am now writing on my knee because I don't feel able to sit up at the desk. But you know that my life is a perpetual werden. I have not the less felt all that your letter said. Thank you for it dear, and for all the helpful love you have given me for the last ten years. I begin this year 402 more happily than I have done most years of my life. "Notre vraie destin'e9e," says Comte, "se compose de resignation et d'activit'e9" -- and I seem more disposed to both than I have ever been before. Let us hope that we shall both get stronger by the year's activity -- calmer by its resignation. I know it may be just the contrary -- don't suspect me of being a canting optimist. We may both find ourselves at the end of the year going faster to the hell of conscious moral and intellectual weakness. Still there is a possibility -- even a probability -- the other way.
My ailments and the fog together have prevented me from going to Blandford Square 403 to see Robert Noel and his wife and to Mrs. Wedgewood's 404 where H. Martineau is staying. I have not seen H. M's Comte yet -- she is going to give me a copy -- but Mr. Lewes tells me it seems to him admirably well done. I don't know whether you noticed the article on Mahomedanism and the Greek Church extracted from the Daily News, in the Leader 405 of last week. That was hers, and I think it excellent. [Seven words deleted.] James Martineau tells Mr. Chapman that he shall never write another book on theology! Don't you think that a good sign?
I told Mr. Chapman yesterday that I wished to give up any connection with the editorship of the Westminster. He wishes me to continue the present state of things until April, but admits that he is so straitened for money and for assistance in the mechanical part of his business that he feels unable to afford an expense on the less tangible services which I render. I shall be much more satisfied on many accounts to have done with that affair -- but I shall find the question of supplies rather a difficult one this year, as I am not likely to get any money either for Feuerbach, which, after all, Mr. Chapman I think will be afraid of publishing in his Series, or for "The Idea of a Future Life," for which I am to have "half profits" = 0/0!
Herbert Spencer writes me word that he has had an attack of palpitation of the heart -- but is quite recovered. 406 I am going to quote to him a passage I found in Sainte-Beuve which just fits him. "Quand j'ai dit qu'il n'avait jamais eu de passion et d'exc'e8s, je me suis trop avanc'e9; il a eu un exc'e8s de raison."
Give my love to Cara and thank her for her kind letter. I shall write to her soon. Love to Mr. Bray too. Tell him to send me word of any new phase in matters of business, and any leader as brilliant as the last I saw.
Ever your loving
Pollian.
I hope you will appreciate this bon-mot as thoroughly as I did -- "C'est un homme admirable -- il se tait en sept langues!" 407

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [25 June 1864]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [25 June 1864]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 25, 1864. Extracts published: Cross, II, 384-385.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday.
Dear Sara
Your letter has affected me deeply. Thank you very much for writing it. It seems as if a close view of almost every human lot would disclose some suffering that makes life a doubtful good -- except perhaps at certain epochs of fresh love, fresh creative activity, or unusual power of helping others. One such epoch we are witnessing in a young life that is very near to us. Our "Boy," Charles has just become engaged, and it is very pretty to see the happiness of a pure first love, full at present of nothing but promise. It will interest you to know that the young lady who has won his heart and seems to have given him her own with equal ardour and entireness, is the granddaughter of Dr. Southwood Smith 274 -- the granddaughter whom he adopted when she was 3 years old, and brought up under his own eye. He left her to the care of the two Miss Gillies 275 -- (you have heard of Margaret Gillies) and these two elderly women dote upon their Gertrude, which is one good testimony to her character.
She is very handsome, and has a splendid contralto voice, which was educated for some time with the idea of her having a professional career -- an idea since given up. Altogether "Pater" and I rejoice, for though the engagement has taken place earlier than we expected or should perhaps have chosen, there are counterbalancing advantages. I always hoped Charlie would be able to choose or rather find the other half of himself by the time he was 23 -- the event has only come a year and a half sooner. This is the news that greeted us on our return! We had seen before we went that the acquaintance which was first made eighteen months or more ago, had become supremely interesting to Charlie, but his father suspected that it would "come to nothing," and that she being four years the elder was not likely to fall in love with our crude bit of human goodness. But parents are not judges in these matters. Altogether, we rejoice.
Our journey was delightful, in spite of Mr. Lewes's frequent malaise, for his cheerful nature is rarely subdued even by bodily discomfort.
We saw only one place that we had not seen before, namely Brescia; but all the rest seemed more glorious to us than they had seemed four years ago. Our course was to Venice, where we stayed a fortnight, pausing only at Paris, Turin and Milan on our way thither, and taking Padua, Verona, Brescia, and again Milan, as points of rest on our way back. Our friend Mr. Burton's company was very stimulating from his great knowledge not of pictures only but of almost all other subjects. He has had the advantage of living in Germany for five or six years, and has gained those large serious views of history which are a special product of German culture and this was his first visit to Italy, though he is not less than 6 or 7 and 40! So you may imagine his eager enjoyment in finding Italy beautiful beyond his hopes. We crossed the Alps by the St. Gothard and stayed a day or two at Lucerne -- and this again was a first sight of Switzerland to him. But his life too has been saddened by much trouble, and his health is miserably delicate. He paints with his left hand, having had his right shoulder intrinsically injured when he was a child, and his wrist is contracted inward by the palm[?].
Best love to Cara and Mr. Bray, and sincere fellow-feeling in all their trouble.
Thine ever
Pollian.
That bit of literary gossip you have seen in a newspaper is like most such gossip false. The foundation for it is only a trifle 276 which I wrote 3 or 4 years ago, and have just given to Mr. Smith because he wanted something for his forthcoming number of the Cornhill, and his [two words illegible] to Mr. Lewes [over the editorship?] is so [considerate?] that I am willing to shew him any sign of appreciation.
