274 Thomas Southwood Smith (1788-1861)  began life as a Unitarian minister and physician, practicing both professions until his work on sanitary reform demanded all his time. He was one of the projectors of the Westminster Review, to which in 1824 he contributed "The Use of the Dead to the Living," advocating facilities for dissection. The body of Jeremy Bentham was left by will to Smith for dissection. (DNB.) His daughter Caroline was married in 1835 to James Hill, by whom she had five daughters; the second, Gertrude, was born 28 July 1837. When Hill fell into financial difficulties in 1840 she was adopted by her grandfather, on whose death she and her sisters were left to the care of Mary and Margaret Gillies, who had been Mrs. Hill's bridesmaids. See C. E. Maurice, Octavia Hill, 1914, p. 10n and passim.
275 Mary and Margaret Gillies lived at  Hillside, Highgate -- "the one an embodiment of peace and an admirable writer, but whose talent, like the violet, kept in the shade; the other, the warm-hearted painter." (Mary Howitt: An Autobiography, ed. Margaret Howitt, 2 vols., Boston and New York, 1889, II, 30-31.) For an account of Margaret Gillies (1803-87) see John H. Lloyd, The History, Topography, and Antiquities of Highgate, Highgate, 1888, p. 350, and Records of the Manor, Parish, and Borough of Hampstead, ed. F. E. Baines, 1890, pp. 391-392.
276 "Brother Jacob," Cornhill, 10 (July  1864), 1-32. Written after her return from Italy in 1860, the tale was originally called "Mr. David Faux, Confectioner." (GE Journal, 27 September 1860). In her Journal, 7 February 1862 GE wrote: "The other day Mr. G. Smith called and offered me 250 guineas for my story of the Idiot Brother, which George mentioned as lying by me. I am not quite certain yet whether I shall accept." After the comparative failure of Romola in the Cornhill, GE sent it to Smith as a gift. His letter thanking her, 3 May 1864 is at Yale.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [25 June 1853]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [25 June 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 25, 1853. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday Morning.
Dear Sara
If there are some opinions in the 1st article of the Rev[iew] which give you pause, pray mitigate your concern by reflecting that they are contradicted in the 2d. So of the 3d and 4th, and I daresay there are sundry other pretty discrepancies in the remainder to accommodate differing tastes and theories. I hope to have the benefit of your criticism both by letter and by Herald.
When I was reading your congratulations that my teeth were "settled" I was racked with pain, and the next day I had the tooth which Mr. Barclay had stopped taken out by another dentist -- a man with [bowels] who will risk giving chloroform. I was quite unconscious during the extraction and only began to protest that I would not submit to the operation when the tooth was lying on the table before me.
This affair hindered me from dining at Sir J. Clark's again to meet the Combes and the Pulzskys 336 -- for which I was more sorry than for the loss of most dinings-out. On Wednesday evening Mr. and Mrs. C. 337 and I went to Blandford Sq. to meet Mr. R. Noel, who was more agreeable than I ever saw him before. Tell Mr. Bray that Mr. N. spoke very admiringly of him and inquired about him with much interest. He called on me the next day with Mrs. Jameson 338 twice and I was unfortunately not in. Vexing that, for I wanted to see Mrs. J., and this is the third time I have missed doing so.
I am going to hear Berlioz' new opera tonight 339 -- an [experience] I have looked forward to with great expectation.
What do you mean by saying that you fear the Whitby trip will drop through? Surely not. Business is not disappointing? I take tea with the Combes tomorrow and am to see the Pulzskys at whom I am a little frightened -- she being a genius and he an encyclopaedia.
Love to the good friends who think it worth having -- and even if not -- love.
Your faithful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [23 August 1863]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [23 August 1863]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Envelope: Miss Hennell | 3 Barr's Hill Terrace | Coventry. Postmark: LONDON-N.W | 10 | AU 24 | 63. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | Sunday.
Dear Sara
I confess it was a relief to me to know how you have been occupied this last month, 188 for I had begun to fear that your silence meant bad health or bad spirits -- if the two are separable. I can well understand that you are weary -- what weariness can I not understand, when I am often, from bodily languor, weary even of blessings?
You must get to the sea. I had a week of the breezes at Worthing, and came back last Tuesday with new courage to the inevitable town life. I never needed, never yearned after, a long holiday of travel, as I do now, but a complication of circumstances, half of them important duties, are likely to forbid our getting away even in the Autumn. One is ashamed to talk of denials which would cut up into luxuries for a dozen of one's neighbours, and whenever I grumble I feel that the disposition to grumble is my worst misfortune.
You are right in saying that Romola is ideal 189 -- I feel it acutely in the reproof my own soul is constantly getting from the image it has made. My own books scourge me.
I value very much your assurance that you are "satisfied." The various strands of thought I had to work out forced me into a more ideal treatment of Romola than I had foreseen at the outset -- though the "Drifting away" and the Village with the Plague 190 belonged to my earliest vision of the story and were by deliberate forecast adopted as romantic and symbolical elements.
A very deep delight, which I think you will share with me, has come to me in the (to me) unexampled beauty of Frederick Maurice's conduct towards me. I should think there are very few men living who would do just as fine a thing as he did in writing a certain letter which you shall see some time. I don't like the thing talked about, because it seems as if I cared to tell it for my own glorification, and I can say quite genuinely that I rejoice more in the deed itself than in the fact that my personality is concerned in it. I think everything we admire profoundly has that sort of effect. The contemplation of whatever is great is itself religion and lifts us out of our egoism. The pity of it is that one perpetually sinks back behind the dust-heaps, seeing nothing great. -- Mr. Maurice's sister, the widow of Julius Hare, long imprisoned in her room by terrible chest ailments and loss of voice has also written to me with womanly tenderness.
These things entre nous. I tell them you because I know you feel an interest in certain relations between conduct and religious belief which have been much urged on my notice by the experience of the last eight years.
Of course you have been interested in the picture of "Mr. Buckle in the East" given in Fraser -- and have noticed Mr. Glennie's letter, 'e0 propos of it, in this week's Athenaeum. 191 And perhaps you have felt inclined, as I have, to be a little impatient at the "fuss" made about Renan's book, as well as Colenso's doings, by an English public which supposes that these men are finding out new heresies. However, such impatience is unreasonable.
We have had much disappointment and anxiety from Thornie's failure in passing his examination. His colleagues in failure have agitated and got up a memorial to Sir Charles Wood against the injustice done them in making the examination final (contrary to precedent) after it was too late for them to take an additional year for study before passing the initiatory examination last year. There is strong confidence that the memorial will succeed, and if so, we hope Thornie will be prevailed on to "go at" his Sanscrit and Law again for another year.
Bertie is also at home now, awaiting a destination, or rather a preparation for one, probably in a Scotch family where he will learn farming. Over and above these delays and difficulties, we have the prospect of moving into our new house -- I fear, not till after the beginning of October.
Such is our life just now. A little while ago, I felt ill, and exaggerated these small crosses. But now I am stronger and perceive how little I have really to bear, how much I have to enjoy.
A letter from Mrs. Congreve last night told me that Mr. Congreve's troublesome pains have returned, making them dread the winter. A sad sequel to his hard work at medical study. I am expecting news of Cara's book -- though probably it will not now be published till November. Love to all.
Your affectionate
Pollian.
I think the most about the last page of your letter, though I have written nothing about it. That sketch of a life's experience is painfully true.

189  "I say Romola is pure idealism --  very, very beautiful, -- because she lies so outside of, so altogether above my own experience. A being who could be so loved, and so wanted, as you show her, is so utterly blissful to my conception, that, if not envied, she must be worshipped as a beautiful saint.  

"You make me feel a craving desire that I could paint, as you have painted Romola: one that by the very eagerness of her desire for human fellowship never succeeded in obtaining it; one who, feeling intensely that the only salvation from her own inner sins and sorrows was in loving communion with fellow beings, yet felt herself for ever rejected as exactly the nature that is not capable of communicating that which really makes her a blessing to others; one whose most earnest efforts to get out of self are always a most desperate flinging back upon self -- simply because that all endeavors to cling must always be an encumbrance. It is only those who want nothing for themselves, that can really be wanted by others. And therefore I feel, that in Romola you have painted a goddess, and not a woman."

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [22 October 1853]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [22 October 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oct. 22d. 1853. Mostly published: Cross, I, 314-315.
Cambridge St. | Saturday Morning.
Dear Sara
How are you? I am reading "The Religion of the Heart" 380 and am far more pleased with it than I expected to be. I have just fallen on two passages with which you will agree.
"Parker . . . is full of the poetry of religion; Martineau equally so, with a closer style and incessant eloquence of expression, perhaps a perilous superabundance of it as regards the claims of matter over manner; and his assumptions of perfection in the character of Jesus are so reiterated and peremptory, that in a man of less evident heart and goodness, they might almost look like a very unction of insincerity or of policy, -- of doubt forcing itself to seem undoubting."
"Hennell's Christian Theism is one long beautiful Discourse proclaiming the great Bible of Creation, and reconciling Pagan and Christian Philosophy."
To-day is an exceptional day -- that is, a fine one. I am hoping for a row (pron. ro) on the Serpentine, which is really almost as good as a lake.
Good Sir James Clark stopped me in the Park yesterday as I was sauntering along with eyes on the clouds, and made very fatherly inquiries about me, urging me to spend a quiet evening with him and Lady Clark next week -- which I will certainly do; for they are two capital people, without any snobbery.
I don't expect you to write after what you said -- I would rather not be associated with boredom in any form, so I will be content to have no letter and be liked a little the better in consequence.
Ever your faithful
Pollian.
Will you tell Cara that I left a small gold brooch on the table in my room with my Father's hair in it? Love to all.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [21 January 1852]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [21 January 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Jan. 21. 1852. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 268-270.
Strand | Wednesday.
Many thanks, dear Sara for the critique. 2 It is amusing enough to compare the diverse and contradictory opinions given by people and journals on every single article in the Review. Mr. Johnson 3 agrees with you in having an antipathy to James Martineau -- therefore won't read the article. Herbert Spencer has tried and can't. Crabbe Robinson thinks it splendid -- is shocked that the article on France should be in the same cover, 4 whereas Mr. Hodgkin 5 of the Economist -- a great man though you may not know it -- thinks the [Ethics] good for nothing, and the article on France the best of all.
I have brought the James Martineau affair 6 to a satisfactory termination. I convinced Mr. C. that he had expressed himself in a way calculated to mislead and that he owed an admission of this to J. M. He got up early one morning to write this with a renewed request that J. M. would accept the supplementary cheque which had been refused -- was taken ill, unable to write, and finally asked me to write for him, he signing the letter. Yesterday came a very kind reply, accepting the cheque, which I had requested him to do in justice to Mr. C., and very graciously acknowledging Froude's compliment which I had sent him. Of course, there was the quotation "Laudari a laudato viro." 7 So ends the affair, Mr. C. having saved his colours. "C''e9tait une grande affaire, ce crise drole."
Harriet Martineau called on Monday morning, with Mr. Atkinson -- very kind and cordial, but unhappily not able to stay long enough to dispel the repulsion excited by the vulgarity (I use the word in a moral sense) of her looks and gestures. Mr. Atkinson wrinkles up his forehead horizontally and draws in his lips -- has a good anterior lobe, but I should think it is not well fed with blood. I honour Harriet Martineau for her powers and industry and should be glad to think highly of her. I have no doubt that she is fascinating when there is time for talk.
We have had two agreeable soir'e9es. Last Monday, I was talking and listening for two hours to Pierre Leroux 8 -- a dreamy genius. He was expounding to me his ideas. He belongs neither to the school of Proudhon which represents Liberty only, nor to that of Louis Blanc which represents Equality only, nor to that of Cabet which represents Fraternity. Pierre Leroux' syst'e8me is the "synth'e8se" which combines all three. He has found the true [pont] which is to unite the love of self with the love of one's neighbour. He is, you know a very voluminous writer. George Sand has dedicated some of her books to him. He dilated on his views of the origin of Christianity -- Strauss deficient because he has not shewn the identity of the teaching of Jesus with that of the Essenes. This is Leroux' favourite idea. I told him of your brother. 9 He moreover traces Essenism back to Egypt and thence to India, the cradle of all religions etc. etc. with much more which he uttered with an unction rather amusing in a soir'e9e t'eate-'e0-t'eate. "Est-ce-que nous sommes faits pour chercher le bonheur? Est-ce l'e0 votre id'e9e, d'eetes moi." "Mais non -- nous sommes faites, je pense, pour nous d'e9velopper le plus que possible." "Ah! c'est 'e7a." He is in utter poverty -- going to lecture -- autrement il faut mourir -- has a wife and children with him. He came to London in his early days, when he was 25, to find work as a printer -- all the world was in mourning for the Princess Charlotte, "et moi, je me trouvais avoir un habit pomme-vert." So he got no work, went back to Paris, by hook or by crook founded the "Globe" journal, knew St. Simon, disagrees with him entirely as with all other theorists except Pierre Leroux.
We are trying Mazzini to write on Freedom v. Despotism. 10 Don't tell, of course. Froude is too busy translating the "Wahlverwandschaften" for Bohn 11 to do anything for us worth having. We have received an admirable article on "The New Puritanism" i.e. physical puritanism, from Dr. Browne the chemist of Edinburgh which I think will go in the next number. 12
I am afraid there is nothing to interest you much in this hasty scribble, but somehow the scum on the surface is all I can give anyone this morning. I have a sore finger which makes it a bore to write.
Thine
Pollian.
Love to Cara. I hope to hear from her on Monday morning.

Blandford Square, | N.W.
Wednesday.
Dear Sara
I am grateful to you for your letters. They are just what I want, and prevent me from feeling so far away from you, and so shut out from your lives, as I have sometimes felt.
Mr. Lewes got through his Lecture with perfect ease, and I have been all the happier since the task has been done.
My niece Emily did not come at Christmas -- the weather was too discouraging for a long journey. But if we are at home at Easter, I think she will come for a week then. Her father's brother is very kind to her, and I think he and his wife contemplate taking her into their family; for her aunt told Emily that she need not think of being a governess, as there were plenty of friends to take care of her. I should have been inclined to have her with me a good deal, but our boy puts that out of the question. At present she is still at school, at Lichfield.
I am glad to hear that Mr. Maurice 704 impressed you agreeably. If I had strength to be adventurous on Sundays, I should go to hear him preach, as well as others. But I am unequal to the least exertion or irregularity. My only pleasure away from our own hearth is going to the Zoological Gardens. Mr. Lewes is a fellow, so we turn in there several times a week, and I find the birds and beasts there most congenial to my spirit. There is a shoe-bill, a great bird of grotesque ugliness, whose top-knot looks brushed up to a point with an exemplary deference to the demands of society, but who I am sure has no idea that he looks the handsomer for it. I cherish an unrequited attachment to him. Best love to Cara and Mr. Bray. One touch of biliousness makes the whole world kin 705 -- I dare say there was a close resemblance in our experience.
Ever thine
Pollian.
I should think it was not an advertisement that Mrs. Cash saw but one of those newspaper paragraphs which appear without the slightest authority. I know of no advertisement, at present. 706

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [2 October 1864]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oc. 2. 1864. Extracts published: Cross, II, 390-391.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday Morning.
Dear Sara
If I had not written too hastily and carelessly to you from Scarbro' I should have told you that I received your nice letter addressed to Benwell House, giving me hints about the things to be seen in the neighbourhood of Harrogate. A little drawback in George's health prevented us from making any expedition except the little one to Knaresbro', and after our ten days at Harrogate he thought he should like the change to Scarbro'. But we register Harrogate among the places to be revisited.
It makes me very, very happy to see George so much better, and to return with that chief satisfaction to the quiet comforts of home.
I have had a fit of Spanish history 289 lately and have been learning Spanish grammar -- the easiest of all the Romance grammars -- since we have been away. Mr. Lewes has been rubbing up his Spanish by reading Don Quixote in these weeks of idlesse, and I have read aloud and translated to him, like a good child. I find it so much easier to learn anything than to feel that I have anything worth teaching.
I hear and read with deep interest any details about Nelly, and am always grateful to you for taking the trouble to write me any.
All is perfectly well with us, now the "little Pater" is stronger, and we are especially thankful for Charlie's prospect of marriage. We could not have desired anything more suited to his character, and more likely to make his life a good. But this blessing which has befallen us only makes me feel the more acutely the cutting off of a like satisfaction from the friends I chiefly love.
Ever, dear Sara your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [2 November 1851]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 3. 1851. Extracts published: Cross, I, 264-265.
Strand.
Dear Sara
I have been quite laid up for the last day or two or I should have written you a word or two yesterday.
I must tell you a good story Miss Bremer got from Emerson. Carlyle was very angry with him for not believing in a devil and to convert him took him amongst all the horrors of London -- the gin-shops etc. and finally to the House of Commons plying him at every turn with the question "Do you believe in a devil noo?" Miss Bremer left this morning. She is to have £300 for the English edition of her book on America and Mary Howitt £150 for translating it! 1046
There is a severe attack on Carlyle's Life of Sterling in yesterday's Times 1047 -- unfair as an account of the book but with some truth in its general remarks about Carlyle. Perhaps Mrs. Hennell has her copy of the Life with her and so you may see it.
Mr. Chapman had the heartiest, most friendly letter possible from Geo. Combe yesterday -- he will write for the April number. 1048 There is an article evidently by James Martineau in the Prospective which you must read -- [On the Unity of the Logical and Intuitive in the ultimate grounds of religious belief.] 1049 I rather think the article on Polemical Fictions, with [Yeast] at the head, must be John Sibree's -- ask his sister. 1050
I am reading with great amusement (!) J. H. Newman's Lectures on the Position of Catholics. 1051 They are full of clever satire and description. My table is groaning with books and I have done very little with them yet -- but I trust in my star which has hitherto helped me to do all I have engaged to do. Pray remember to send by Mrs. C.H. (since she has been kind enough to say she will bring it) the M.S. translation of Schleiermacher's little book and also the book itself. 1052
I suppose I shall see Mr. Noel on his way southward in a day or two. I have no news worth telling -- and you don't want any -- having such a party.
Love to all -- to thee especially this week, dear Sara.
Tell Mr. Bray this story. When Bentley gave a dinner to the writers in his Miscellany on its first being started, there was a discussion about the title. [Let it be the Wits' Miscellany,] said one. [But if it were not witty?] said another. [Then,] said Bentley, [suppose we call it Bentley's Miscellany.] [No, d -- it,] said Douglas Jerrold. [Don't go to the other extreme.] 1053

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [18 September 1865]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. 18. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Monday.
My dear Sara
I think your new title a great improvement, and quite the best of all. I quite understood from your previous titles that you regarded Faith as having a tap-root of its own, and was not without a sense that "subjection" might not be an acceptable word. But "subjection" has not, I think, etymologically and classically the absolute meaning sometimes given to it. Man is in subjection to the external world, though he also to a certain extent controls it. But your own new edition is much better than anything I had thought of, both for precision and brevity.
I am very glad to hear of the projected journey to Ramsgate, and all the more, that it is not to happen till a month hence; for the places at the coast are too crowded now to be comfortable.
Mr. Spencer is just come back from Scotland 375 in great force. He has been much more assured about his health during the last year, and has been more like his old self -- full of delightful talk and with amiability in his eyes.
Thanks for your double letter, dear Sara. You have made your feeling quite clear to me.
Ever yours,
Pollian.
Mr. Lewes thinks the new sub-title very good.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [18 November 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 3. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, I, 315.
Cambridge St. | Friday.
Dear Sara
When I wrote the other day I had not read your nice little notice of Leigh Hunt's book. 396 I think you have characterized it very justly -- at least all the praise you have given it is appropriate, but of course you have charitably suppressed a great deal of disprobation which is equally just. I can't help laughing at the imbecility of that pious dictum -- that if Shelley had lived till now he would have been a Christian -- that is, he would have been old woman enough for it by this time.
We had a pleasant evening at Mr. Mackay's on Wednesday, Dr. Arnott 397 my especial favorite being there. I was considerably surprized at the sight of Dr. Elliotson -- I had expected a tall graceful man. He is rauh and stumpy in person and abrupt in manner. But Mrs. Mackay says he is the "best man living." He expressed considerable indignation about Carpenter's article -- not unjustly I think -- because it blinks all the facts of mesmerism. 398 Mary Marshall was there. She seems very sadly out of health. I saw old Mrs. Atkinson the other day -- a really fine old woman, full of the sweet milk of human kindness.
Mr. Lewes was at Cambridge about a fortnight ago, and found that Herbert Spencer was a great deal talked of there, for the article on the Universal Postulate as well as other things. Mr. Lewes himself has a knot of devotees there who make his history of Philosophy 399 a private text-book.
Miss Martineau's Comte is out now. Do you mean to do it or Mr. Lewes's? 400 We can get no one to write an article on Comte for the next number of the Westminster -- Bain, 401 our last hope, refusing.
I dare say this gossip is not very interesting to you, but a headache this morning inclined me to fill up ten minutes by writing it.
Ever thy loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [17 May 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: May 17. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | Wednesday.
Dear Sara
I hope you have not thought me ungrateful for not writing before this to thank you for your last kind service. The fact is, at the end of last week I felt regularly "done up" both in body and mind, so I have sent them word at the Leader office that they must expect nothing from me this week, 465 and I am idling about, looking at pictures and Nature -- in Kensington Gardens. 466 I am terribly out of spirits just now and the pleasantest thought I have is that whatever I may feel affects no one else -- happens in a little "island cut off from other lands."
The proof-reading of Feuerbach is really a pleasure to me and opens up afresh to me what there is of truth and beauty in the book. I find scarcely any need of italics -- hardly one instance in 20 pages. I am more and more convinced that a good style not only does not require them, but excludes them. But at present I intend to have the first sentence or par[agraph] in every 'a7 of the appendix in italics, just to indicate what is the text of the 'a7. 467 In the original there is no numbering of the different parts in the appendix.
On Monday I went to look at the French pictures among which is that unforgettable Francesca di Rimini of Ary Scheffer's. 468 It surpasses one's expectations from the engraving. I could look at it for hours. There is nothing at the Royal Acad[emy] to affect one in the same way -- or indeed at all. I never was less interested in the exhibition there. But perhaps this was owing to my mood and my aching legs. I have been there ever since breakfast time this morning and am come back in a miserably uninspired state -- which is rarely the case with me after seeing pictures.
I had a very kind letter from Mr. Combe the other day, and it really did me good. Kindness becomes more and more precious to one in proportion as one learns not to expect it.
There is enough about myself to last for the next three months. How are you? What are you enjoying or not enjoying? I hope Mr. Bray will have imbibed some good hope for trade by his visit to London, and so put you all in spirits to receive the Combes. 469 Love to you all from
Your ever affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [16 September 1865]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. 16. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday.
My dear Sara
Just sitting down to my desk, I have read your letter. The second title expresses fully what you mean, and without, I think, any liability to be mistaken. It indicates a stand-punkt which, I feel sure, is shared by a good number of minds, who are likely to have their interest roused by your advertisement or title page. Still the title is cumbrous, and I should like if possible to compress it, or, as Carlyle says, to squeeze some water out.
I am going to walk with Mr. Lewes to Erasmus Wilson's before 12 o'clock and then I will discuss it with him and tell you the result. But I can say at once that you must cross out the "its" before "aid," and read "admission of aid from thought." How far would it be worth while to consider the substitution of -- "a Faith that is shaping itself in conscious subjection to Thought" --? But I am good-for-nothing at title pages, and will consult George, who is clever at them.
An account of | Present Religion | as | a Faith shaping itself in | conscious subjection to Thought. 374 o'clock. Mr. Lewes rather shudders at your second title -- begs you not to place an obstacle in the way of your book by anything so awkward and cumbrous -- thinks my suggestion as to the sub-title acceptable, but would utterly abolish the words "an account of" which are of no use. He does not approve of Present religion. He thinks Modern Religion or the Religion of the 19th century would be better -- but I confess I don't like these and hardly think they will satisfy you.
I believe I can say nothing else now, but if anything occurs to me worth mentioning I will write again. A title to works of this sort is always a difficulty.
Your affectionate
Pollian.
The Religion of Today is better than Modern Religion, I think.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [16 October 1865]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oct. 16. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday Morning.
Dear Sara
I rejoice to think that you have probably had two days of sunshine, but here it is again foggy and damp this morning. I get this pleasure out of the London sky -- that I can suppose every one who is away from it to be better off in point of weather.
The last time I heard of dear Miss Bury 377 (it was by a letter from Mr. Congreve on Wednesday) she was still in a doubtful state, and I am full of anxiety about them. I have not been to Wandsworth because Mr. Congreve thought it better for me to keep away. I cannot of course wish them to write, for their bodies as well as minds are overweighted. I dread the effect on Mrs. Congreve's delicate frame. She and Mr. Congreve did the nursing entirely till Miss Julia Congreve joined them, and there is another invalid -- a servant, I imagine -- in the house.
Tell Cara, with my best love, that I hope she will be able to indulge me with a sight of her as she passes through town again. She and Mr. Bray can perhaps at least lunch with us on their way to some other of the many persons they are obliged to think of when in London.
I have given due attention to your letter, my dear Sara. You do not expect me to be in accordance with it.
Always yours affectionately
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [15 May 1870]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: May 16, 1870. Mostly published: Cross, III, 104-105, dated 16th March 1870.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday Morning.
Dear Sara
Cara has told me 175 about your republication of "the Inquiry," and I have a longing to write -- not intrusively I hope -- just to say "thank you" for the good it does me to know of your being engaged in that act of piety to your brother's memory. I delight in the act itself and in the satisfaction which I know you have in performing it. When I remember my own obligations to the book, I must believe that among the many new readers that a cheap edition will reach, there must be minds to whom it will bring a welcome light in studying the New Testament -- sober, serious help towards a conception of the past, instead of stage lights and make-ups.
And this value is, I think, independent of the opinions that might be held as to the different degrees of success in the construction of probabilities, or in particular interpretations. Throughout there is the presence of grave sincerity.
Cara gives me a not uncheerful account of your health and working, but I would gladly have a word or two directly from yourself, when you can scribble a note without feeling me a bore for wanting it. I should hold such a thought on your part as quite innocent, and consistent with much friendliness, for people who write many letters without being forced to do so, are fathomless wonders to me. But you have a special faculty for writing such letters as one cares to read, so it is a pity that the accomplishment should lie quite unused. I wonder if you have read Emerson's new Essays. I like them very much.
Ever, dear Sara, lovingly yours
"Marian" Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [15 February 1869]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 15, 1869. Extracts published: Cross, III, 78.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday Morning.
Dear Sara
I have looked back to the verses in Browning's poem about Elisha, 27 and I find no mystery in them. The foregoing context, for three pages, describes that function of genius which revivifies the past -- that past which is not totally forgotten and cannot therefore be said to be quite dead. Man, says Browning (I am writing from recollection of his general meaning) cannot create, but he can restore: the poet gives forth of his own spirit and reanimates the forms that lie breathless. His use of Elisha's story is manifestly symbolical, as his mention of Faust is -- the illustration which he abandons the moment before to take up that of the Hebrew seer.
I presume you did not read the context yourself, but only had the two concluding verses pointed out or quoted to you by your friends. It is one of the afflictions of authorship to know that the brains which should be used in understanding a book are wasted in discussing the hastiest misconceptions about it, and I am sure you will sympathize enough in this affliction to set any one right, when you can, about this quotation from Browning.
You had a bright day for your journey home, and I hope you will enjoy your home life, for some time to come, all the more for having been away from it. This is usually the best result of visits. With love to all
Yours always
Marian.
I forgot to tell you that in two young men named Payne, who visit us -- one, a physician of promise, the other a clergyman who writes a great deal -- I have discovered second cousins of Miss R. Franklin's, whom I have often heard speak of their mother, once Eliza Dyer. 28

GE TO SARA SOPHIA HENNELL, LONDON, [13 OCTOBER 1851]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 262-263.
Strand | Monday.
Dear Sara
I have read your dear letter twice, and shall read it again.
Mrs. Chapman quite enjoys Miss Bremer's society now, and all the world is doing its devoir to the great little authoress.
I went to the Ex[hibition] on Saturday to hear the final God save the Qu[een] and the three times three 1032 -- [C]était un beau moment,' but headache, headache! [9 lines deleted.] <Miss Tilley is coming back today.>
Mr. Greg thought the Review [well done, and in a kindly spirit,] -- but thought there was not much in it -- dreadful true, since there was only all his book. I think he did not like the apology for his want of theological learning -- which however was just the thing most needed, for the Eclectic 1033 trips him up on that score.
Went to Mr. Mackay's yesterday with Mr. C. Mr. M. will give us £200 -- Mr. Woodfall 1034 also £200. Miss S. Hughes 1035 £20. No circulars have yet been sent out.
Newman's article on Direct Legislation 1036 is already come. We can get no one to write on the Peerage.
Carlyle was very amusing the other morning to Mr. Chapman about the Ex[hibition]. He has no patience with the Prince and [that Cole] 1037 assembling Sawneys from all parts of the land till you can't get along Piccadilly. He has been worn to death with bores all summer, who present themselves by twos and threes in his study, saying "Here we are," etc., etc.
The [Thin student] is no such thing but a beneficed clergyman who admires Strauss, discusses the Immortality of the soul, and preaches [extrumpery] to his poor Dorsetshire parishioners, who have seen nothing beyond their native hedgerows. Love to all. In haste
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [12 October 1867]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [12 October 1867]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oct. 12. Extract published: Cross, III, 22-23.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday.
Dear Sara
Mr. Lewes will take the first opportunity of inquiring about the Railway Shareholders' Association, and I will let you know any result immediately.
Before I got your letter I was about to write to you and direct your attention to an article in the forthcoming (October) number of the Quarterly Review, on the Talmud. 670 You really must go out of your way to read it. It is written by one of the greatest Oriental scholars, the man among living men who probably knows the most about the Talmud, and you will appreciate the pregnancy of the article. There are also beautiful soul-cheering things selected for quotation.
This being said, I proceed to scold you a little for undertaking to canvass on the Women's Suffrage question. Why should you burthen yourself in that way, for an extremely doubtful good? I love and honour my friend Mrs. Taylor, but it is impossible that she can judge beforehand of the proportionate toil and interruption such labours cause to women whose habits and duties differ so much from her own. She would have understood the case if you could have briefly explained it.
I hope the separation from the undesirable Mr. Taunton has been achieved without anything very unpleasant. Best love,
Thine ever
Pollian.
It just occurs to me that Mr. Charles Potter (he clearly not being Mr. T. B. Potter) is Mr. Herbert Spencer's friend, 671 a man of high moral character. I will ask the immortal philosopher, whom I am sure to see shortly, perhaps tomorrow.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [12 March 1862]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 1862. Extracts published: Cross, II, 337-338.
Blandford Sq. | Wednesday.
Dear Sara
We returned from our flight into the country yesterday -- not without a sigh at parting with the pure air and the notes of the blackbirds for the usual canopy of smoke and the sound of cab wheels.
I shall leave you to choose the time you will give us. 40 I am not going out again, and our life will have its old routine: lunch at 'bd past 1, walk till 4, dinner at 5. You cannot come inconveniently, if you do not come before 'bd past one.
Ever your affectionate
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [12 February 1866]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [12 February 1866]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 12, 1866-80. Extracts published: Cross, II, 423-424.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Monday.
Dear Sara
Thanks for your kind letter. Alas -- we had chiefly bad weather in the country, and the latter part of our time I was pulled down by a bilious attack. George, whose state is of more importance, was a little benefited, but only a little. He is too far "run down" to be wound up in a very short time. We enjoyed our return to our comfortable home, and perhaps that freshness of home was the chief gain from our absence. You see, to counterbalance all the great and good things that life has given us beyond what our fellows have, we hardly know now what it is to be free from bodily malaise.
The symptoms you mention seem to me to be alarming in a constitution like Mr. Bray's. Let me know when he is freed from them again, for even if they indicated nothing seriously wrong, they must be distressing to bear. Palpitations are horrible.
After the notion I have given you of my health, you will not wonder if I say that I don't know when anything of mine will appear. I can never reckon on myself. 417
Our Bertie is gone into Warwickshire, to be under the tutelage of a Mr. Hollins of Snitterfield near Stratford on Avon. He was much pleased to see a country less black, and people a little less harsh, than he has been used to in Scotland. Yet Scotland was a better preparation for roughing it in a colony. Best love to all from
Yours ever
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [11 July 1863]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [11 July 1863]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 11. 1863. Extracts published: Cross, II, 356-358.
Blandford Sq. | Saturday.
Dear Sara
I have often been feeling the want to write to you since we came home, but constant languor and hemicrania from the new heat have made me shirk all exertion not imperative. And just now there are not only those excitements of the "season" which even we quiet people get our share of, but there is an additional Boy to be cared for -- Thornie, who is this week passing his momentous examination. We returned from our Isle of W[ight] excursion last Monday week: both of us frightfully sunburnt and somewhat strengthened, and I happily with no more than an insignificant remnant of cough which is now quite gone. Tell Mr. Bray that Mrs. Blythe desired me to present her "duty" to him and his family.
Your picture of things at home is cheering. Nelly's health or want of health 167 must affect you all strongly. It is difficult to resign oneself to the drooping of young things whose life makes half our own reason for wishing to live. I don't mean that any single girl or boy has all that weight in our lot, but our hopefulness for the many is apt to vary with what befals those who are close to us.
Apropos, a pretty thing has happened to an acquaintance of mine, 168 which is quite a tonic to one's hope. She has all her life been working hard in various ways as housekeeper, governess, and several et ceteras that I can't think of at this moment: a dear little dot about 4 ft. 11. in height, pleasant to look at and clever; a working woman, without any of those epicene queernesses that belong to the class. Her life has been a history of family troubles, and she has that susceptible nature which makes such troubles hard to bear. More than once she has told me that courage quite forsook her -- she felt as if there were no good in living and striving; it was difficult to discern, or believe in, any results for others, and there seemed none worth having for herself. Well! a man of fortune and accomplishments has just fallen in love with her, now she is 33 -- it is the prettiest story of a swift, decided passion, and made me cry for joy. She is so much above vulgar feeling about such things, that she was not at all sure at first that she would have him, "splendid match" as he is; but now she has accepted and yesterday Mrs. Bodichon and I went with her to buy her wedding-clothes. Barbara has for years been her best friend, and it is her school that this clever little curly-haired woman has been managing. The future husband is also 33 -- old enough to make his selection an honour, fond of travelling and science and other good things such as a man deserves to be fond of who chooses a poor woman in the teeth of grand relatives: brought up a Unitarian, just turned Catholic! Last, not quite least, he settles £150 a year on his future mother-in-law. If you will only imagine everything I have not said, you will think this a very charming fairy tale.
We are going this evening to see the French actress 169 in Juliet, who is astonishing the town. Last week we saw Ristori, the other night heard the Faust, and next week we are going to hear the Elisir d'Amore and Faust again! So you see we are trying to get some compensation for the necessity of living among bricks in this sweet summer-time. I can bear the opera better than any other evening entertainment, because the house is airy and the stalls are comfortable: we both feel now that we are too old to find pleasure in bad air and with cramped limbs. The opera is a great, great product -- pity we can't always have fine Weltgeschich[t]liche dramatic motives wedded with fine music, instead of trivialities or hideousnesses. Perhaps this last is too strong a word for anything except the Traviata. Rigoletto is unpleasant, but it is a superlatively fine tragedy in the Nemesis -- I think I don't know a finer.
Best love to Cara, and tell her I rejoice to think of her being so far on in her work. We are really going to buy the Priory after all: 170 -- she would think it very pretty if she saw it now with the roses blooming about it.
Ever yours lovingly
Marian.
You know, of course, that there is to be another number of Romola? 171

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [11 February 1854]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [11 February 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 11. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge St. | Saturday.
Dear Sara
I ought to have thanked you before this for sending me the M.S. but too much for the day has been the evil thereof. Cara too has made me her debtor by sending me the extract from the Scotsman. Thank her for me.
I don't think a translator is bound to reproduce the occasional offensive defects of taste in a writer. I confess I have not gone on that principle of damaging faithfulness. Indeed I have felt it necessary in the part you have read to omit a whole sentence. I could not do otherwise -- and indeed German sarcasm may be fairly said to be untranslateable. I think you would agree with me if the whole case were before you, but it is impossible to say what one wants in a letter. I hope your head is well.
Your faithful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [10 July 1854]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [10 July 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 10. 1854. H. Spencer. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 325.
Cambridge St. | Monday.
Dear Sara
It seems very ungracious to say so, but it is the fact, that I am vexed Feuerbach has been noticed in the Herald, and especially that anything has been said about me.
As to Mr. Noel's criticism, 493 I must reply, in the first place, that as the book has been advertised under that title for a year and he has frequently seen me and spoken of Feuerbach within that time, it is rather extraordinary that he should have reserved his criticism until the book has appeared. In the second place, it is quite true that Feuerbach's work might justly be called a Natural History of Christianity, but it is not true that that is what he means by Wesen. "Essence" is perfectly correct both as a translation of that word and as a representation of the gist of the book. Moreover, anyone who has read Feuerbach, which depend upon it Mr. N. has not, will be aware that this title corresponds perfectly or rather uniquely to the author's mode of statement.
I am going to pack up the Hebrew Grammar, the Apocryphal Gospels, and your pretty Titian, to be sent to you. Shall I despatch them by Rail or deposit them with Mr. Chapman to be asked for by Mr.
Bray when he comes to town? I shall soon send you a good bye, for I am preparing to go to "Labassecour." 494
This morning I feel very much as I (suppose) I should if I had been standing on my head for an hour, having paid for a visit to the Crystal Palace 495 and the luxury of French Chocolate by a headache yesterday. What a creation it is! (The C.P. not the headache). Shakspeare, our Navy and the Crystal Palace are the three most eigenth'fcmliche things we have produced.
Herbert Spencer's article on the Genesis of Science 496 is a grand one. You must read it. He will stand in the Biographical Dictionaries of 1954 as "Spencer, Herbert, an original and profound philosophical writer, especially known by his great work x x x which gave a new impulse to psychology and has mainly contributed to the present advanced position of that science, compared with that which it had attained in the middle of the last century. The life of this philosopher, like that of the great Kant, offers little material for the narrator. Born in the year 1820 etc."
Vivian's head is not likely to be up to the pitch of Feuerbach, so it will fall to the lot of some other non-leading attach'e9 of the Leader. 497 I have not had a copy yet!
Ever your affectionate
Pollian.
The Cosmogonical Principal was in the advertisement.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, London, [1 October 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oct. 1st. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 313-314.
Strand | Saturday Evening.
My dear Sara
I meant to write to you today in time for tonight's post, but I have been busied about my lodgings all afternoon. I am not going to Albion St., but to 21 Cambridge St., Hyde Park Square.
You will have seen by the papers that Savill and Edward's printing office was burnt down yesterday morning. 373 The W[estminster] R[eview] narrowly escaped the fate of the Leader, the Lit[erary] Gazette and poor Dr. Vaughan's 374 elaborate article on the Religious Tendencies of the Age, intended for the next number of the B[ritish] Quarterly.
I hope you will be pleased with our present number. If you don't think the Universal Postulate 375 first-rate, I shall renounce you as a critic.
Why don't you write grumbling letters to me when you are out of humour with life, instead of making me ashamed of myself for ever having grumbled to you? I have been a more good-for-nothing correspondent than usual lately -- this affair of getting lodgings, added to my other matters, has taken up my time and thoughts. But I don't deserve to be punished for this by your not writing to me for the next six weeks.
I have promised to do some work tonight and tomorrow for a person is rather more idle than myself, so I have not a moment to spare.
Ever your loving
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Littlehampton, 12 September 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Littlehampton, 12 September 1862
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 340-341.
Beach Hotel, | Little Hampton | September 12. 62.
Dear Sara
Imagine me -- not fuming in imperfect resignation under London smoke, but -- with the wide sky of the coast above me and every comfort positive and negative around me, even to the absence of staring eyes and crinolines.
Worthing was so full that it rejected us and, to our great good fortune sent us here. Mr. Lewes is just gone back to town to send Thornie on to Edinburgh to his Sanskrit studies, 106 and I shall have perfect solitude till Monday. I am not sorry to have it for that brief space.
We were pleased to hear that you had seen Mr. Spencer. We always feel him particularly welcome when he comes back to town: there is no one like him for talking to about certain things. But I am sorry to find that he gave you a poor impression about his health. To me those future unabsehbare volumes would be misery and madness; but I think they brighten the prospect of life to him.
You will come and dine or walk with us whenever you have nothing better to do, in your visit to town. I take that for granted. We lie, you know, on the way between the Exhibition and Mr. Noel's. 107
I don't know when we shall return to B[landford] Square. That will depend on the weather. We may be here a fortnight longer. We may leave in a week.
You ought to see the collection of Pictures at the Ex[hibition]. I regret that we have only been once. Much love from
Your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Limpsfield, 12 August 1870
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Limpsfield, 12 August 1870
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 118-119.
Park Farm | Limpsfield | Surrey | August 12. 70.
Dear Sara
Thanks for letting me have some share in your enjoyment of the waves and the sunsets. It is really something added to the cheerfulness of the sunshine over our Surrey fields, to know that you are at your old beloved Penmaenmaur, and in company which I know you like -- better, perhaps, than any other.
We too, you see, have come back to a well-tried refuge 209 -- the same place that soothed us in our troubles last October -- and we especially delight in this deep country, after the fuss which belongs even to quiet watering-places such as Cromer, Harrogate and Whitby, which are, after all, "alleys where the gentle folks live." We went to all three of these places in succession, and when we were at Harrogate I was constantly on the verge of writing to you, to remind you how we were originally indebted to you for a description, nay, a little plan of the place. 210 But I abstained, doubting whether it did not teaze you rather than please you to have notes which might hang about your mind as things to be answered. Harrogate, like all places which keep in fashion, is much increased by house-building, but it has the charm of being a place where the company is too mixed, in consequence of the serious need to get health from the air and waters, for the arrangements to be of the detestably luxurious, exclusive sort. Mr. Lewes found great benefit there, his pulse rising from its thread-like t[r]ickle of 58, to a good 70.
Whitby was a rather unfortunate sequel, the weather being first sultry, then cold, then misty. We paused a week in London on our way here, where we have been since Monday, and all the good effects of
Harrogate seem to be reappearing after a temporary check. Mr. Lewes is able to vary his mornings now by revising his History. His ailing, which caused our second flight from home, was a relapse -- surprizingly rapid -- into the state of nervous weakness, which hindered him from all interesting work before we went to Germany in March. It is always attended with obstinate dyspeptic headaches. But I am in good hope now that he may have a fair time of freedom from these trials.
And you too, dear Sara -- for, believe me, I represented to myself very vividly what you told me in your former letter of that weariness which all our poor bodies get, when they have stayed a long while in this world, and of the impossibility that solitary travelling was to you. But now I read your letter this morning, I feel that there is a good chance of your going back to Coventry with refreshed strength and courage. It seems just the sweetest way in which you could have got the change, to have it come unexpectedly through the affectionate effort of a friend.
We are excited even among the still woods and fields by the vicissitudes of the War, and chiefly concerned because we cannot succeed in getting the day's "Times." We have entered into the period which will be marked in future historical charts as "The period of German ascendency." 211 But how saddening to think of the iniquities that the great harvest moon is looking down on! I am less grieved for the bloodshed than for the hateful trust in lies which is continually disclosed. Meanwhile Jowett's Translation of Plato is being prepared for publication, 212 and he has kindly sent us the sheets of one volume. So I pass from discussions of French lying and the Nemesis that awaits it, to discussions about rhetorical lying at Athens in the fourth century before Christ. The translations, and Introductions to the Dialogues, seem to be charmingly done.
Also, we are reading Froude's picture of England under the Tudors, 213 which he rather timidly insinuates than maintains to have been a time when Englishmen were far nobler and more unselfish than now. So, you perceive, we get plenty of contrast with that agitated Now, which is the main interest even in this far-away village. I don't quite know when we shall return to Town -- probably in September.
Perhaps you have not heard of the death of Miss Mary Gillies, a most gentle-minded, refined woman -- the elder of the two sisters whom
Gertrude has cherished, and been cherished by, with devoted affection. She was aged 70, and had been ailing for a long while. Always, dear Sara,
Your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Harrogate, 15 September 1864
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 388.
Benwell House | Harrogate | September 15. 1864.
Dear Sara
You see, the trouble you so kindly took for us was not in vain. We journeyed hither on Tuesday, and found the place quite as pretty as we expected. Empty lodgings were not abundant on a first evening's observation, so we perhaps too hastily "took up" with these. 285 However we seem to have alighted on nice clean simple folk, who make us comfortable enough. Our situation, on the rise of ground near the Sulphur Well, going towards Miss Cushman's lodgings (not alas! vacant) is far from equal to that of your Diamond House. But the great merit of Harrogate is, that one is everywhere close to lovely open walks. I think I saw Mrs. Higginson 286 at the window, the evening of our arrival -- at least it was a lady with a head and profile strongly resembling Harriet Martineau's, though, so fallacious is human argument, to you who know the facts, that very resemblance may prove that the face was not Mrs. Higginson's.
Your plan has been a delightful reference for Mr. Lewes, who takes it out of his pocket every time we walk. At present, of course, there is not much improvement in health to be boasted of, but we hope that the delicious bracing air -- and also the chalybeate waters, 287 which have not yet been tried -- will not be without good effect. The journey was long and made a day of irregularity in diet etc. that was sure to upset any one in so delicate a condition as George's. How hideous those towns of Holbeck and Wakefield are! It is difficult to keep up one's faith in a millennium within sight of this modern civilization which consists in "development of industries." Egypt and her big calm gods seems quite as good. We both thank you, dear Sara, for helping us hither.
Ever your loving
Pollian.
You know, I shall be glad to learn anything about the Coventry Home.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Griff, [11 April 1850]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April? 1850. Mostly published: Cross, 1, 251-252.
Griff | Thursday.
My dear Sara
Will you send the enclosed note to Mrs. C. Hennell? I am not quite sure about her direction, but I am anxious to thank her for her kindness in inviting me. Will you also send me an account of Mr. Chapman's prices for lodgers 897 -- and if you know anything of other boarding houses etc. in London will you tell me what you can? I am not asking you merely for the sake of giving you trouble. I am really anxious to know.
O the dismal weather and the dismal country and the dismal people. It was some envious demon that drove me across the Jura 898 to come and see people who don't want me. However I am determined to sell everything I possess except a portmanteau and carpet-bag and the necessary contents and be a stranger and a foreigner on the earth for ever more. But I must see you first -- that is a yearning I still have in spite of disappointments. My love to Mrs. Hennell.
Ever your faithful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Gorey, 22 May [1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Gorey, 22 May [1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1857. Extracts published: Cross, I, 448-449.
Rosa Cottage | Gorey | Jersey | May 22.
Yes, dear Sara, I had your letter at Scilly, with the little plan of the cottage, telling me just what I like to know. I suppose you have been keeping house for the last week during Cara's absence -- almost like the old times when you and Mrs. Hennell were in the cottage alone, only you have not had Pollian to drop in and ask you to take a walk with her over the hill. But you have had something better for company in your walk, I dare say -- perhaps meditations about a new book which shall be brought out when the Prize Essay has reached a second edition, or pictures, that you are dreaming of now the weather is bright and the hedgerows in blossom.
Such hedgerows in this island! Such orchards, white against the green slopes, and shady walks by the woodside, with distracting wild flowers that Miss Catlow 864 never says anything about, just because they are the very flowers you want to identify. We enjoy the greenery and variety of this bushy island all the better for our stay on bare Scilly, which we had gone to and fro upon till we knew it by heart.
This Gorey is a very retired spot -- a fishing place, about four miles from St. Helier's, with plenty of rich people's houses about to make it a point for omnibuses and tradesmen's carts. Our little lodgings are very snug -- only 13s/. a week -- a nice little sittingroom with a work-room adjoining for Mr. Lewes, who is this moment in all the bliss of having discovered a parasitic worm in a cuttle-fish! It is painful to think of the inequality of human lots! I dare say, now, your acquaintance with parasitic worms is of the "most meagre description."
Today, it is raining, after a long spell of fine weather, so I find a few minutes to write to you. Otherwise, now we dine at 5 our afternoons are almost exhausted in rambling. I hope to get up my strength in this delicious quiet, and have fewer interruptions to work from headache than I have been having since Christmas. Mr. Lewes is going on very well, and bears the "hunting" and the bilious sea-breezes better than he did last summer.
I wonder if I should have had the happiness of seeing Cara, if I had been at Richmond now. I would rather see her than any one else in the world -- except poor Chrissey. Give my love to Mr. Bray and tell him
I read the leader he sent me with much interest, and wish him God speed in his battle against ignorance and folly. 865 I like to think of him and Cara enjoying the pictures and other pleasant things to be seen in London just now. Where and when shall you go for your holiday?
I imagine you very vividly sitting by the piano in the lumber room and beating time as inexorably as a metronome. Does Nelly promise to play well? -- Do you ever see the Miss Franklins now? And who are the gentlemen about to marry Kate Martineau and Elinor Cash? Those are bits of gossip I should like to know, when you can think of them at the right moment for writing them.
Tell me when you have read the life of Currer Bell. Some people think its revelations in bad taste -- making money out of the dead -- wounding the feelings of the living etc. etc. What book is there that some people or other will not find abominable? We thought it admirable -- cried over it -- and felt the better for it. The article on it in the Leader -- Th. Hunt's, I dare say -- did not give a sufficiently high idea of its interest. 866
We read Cromwell's Letters again at Scilly, with great delight, and Mr. Lewes wrote an article on them which you will see in the Leader. 867 That and the one on the Oxford Essays 868 is all he has done in that way.
I have nothing to say, but a letter is pleasant either as an accompaniment to one's breakfast, or as idle reading after dinner. So I feel sure you will like to have this "nothing that I so plentifully give you." 869
Ever your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Gorey, [14 July 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Gorey, [14 July 1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 17. 1857. Hitherto unpublished.
Rosa Cottage Gorey | Tuesday Evening.
Dear Sara
I do answer your letters because there are things I want to say.
First, we shall be at Park Shot, Richmond again, on the 16th 929 July. If, as is very likely, the rest of the house should be full, we can make you a comfortable bed for a night in Mr. Lewes's dressing room, which is in fact a bedroom as soon as there are sheets on the bed. I don't ask you to stay with us because, as we have no superfluity of rooms or of time, that would hamper us in our work. But it would be a real delight to me if you could take us in your way to or from the Carters. 930 I say just the truth, because you used always to like that.
Secondly, I have written to Mr. Holbeche, my Father's trustee telling him the whole truth as far as essentials -- that our marriage is not a legal one though we both regard it as sacred, why Mr. Lewes cannot contract a legal marriage, how long it is since I have been his wife and borne his name, and why I have withheld the fact from my family. I dare say I shall never have any further correspondence with my brother, which will be a great relief to me. So now there is nothing to be concealed from any one, and the greatest service my friends can do is to tell the truth in contradiction to false rumours.
No more now, because it is evening and we are going to carry the letters to post.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Geneva, [26 October 1849]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Geneva, [26 October 1849]
MS: Yale. Address: Sara. Endorsed: 1849. Extracts published: Cross, I, 237-238.
Geneva Rue des Chanoines 107.
Liebe Gemahlinn
I trust you have thrown off the sackcloth with which you had clothed yourself when you last wrote to me. If it were not always presumptuous for us to pronounce for another in such matters I should say that you are excessive in your self-humiliation. I share your respect for Mr. Hennell's admirable judgment and feeling but from all that both you and Cara have told me for the last 2 or 3 years I am convinced that both have been intensified and narrowed in their action to a morbid degree, and that you are doing yourself wrong when you bow to his dicta as a vox Dei. 868 But no more about matters which I dare say have ceased to occupy you.
Cara has told you by this time how happily I am situated. I like my town life vastly and shall like it still better in the winter. There is an indescribable charm to me in this form of human nest-making. You enter a by no means attractive-looking house, you climb up two or three flights of cold dark-looking stone steps, you ring at a very modest door and you enter a set of rooms snug or comfortable or elegant. One is so out of reach of intruders, so undiverted from one's occupations by externals, so free from cold rushing winds through hall-doors, one feels in a downy nest high up in a good old tree. I have always had a hankering after this sort of life and I find it was a true instinct of what would suit me. Just opposite my windows is the street in which the Sisters of Charity live 869 and if I look out, I generally see either one of them or a sober-looking ecclesiastic. Then a walk of five minutes takes me out of all streets within sight of beauties that I am sure you too would love, if you did not share my enthusiasm for the town. I have to write to Rosehill again today about the newspapers so I have scribbled a little bit to you to make the postage pay for a little more, but I have not another minute having promised to go out before dinner, so dearest take my letter as a hasty kiss just to let you know how constantly I love you -- how the longer I live and the more I have felt the better I know how to value you. That is at least one redeeming point in your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Foleshill, 9 October 1843
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Foleshill, 9 October 1843
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, I, 121-124.
Foleshill October 9th 1843.
Lieber Gemahl, 484
The first thing I have to say to you is to entreat that you and Mrs. Hennell will not perplex yourselves for a moment about my accommodation during the night. 485 I am so well now that a hearthrug would be as luxurious a couch as I should need and I defy anything short of a kettledrum or my conscience to keep me awake after a long day. So pray let me take what happens to be at hand and remember that the only fear I have about the matter is that I may be inconveniencing Mrs. Hennell by my presence at a time when she will be crowded with friends and feelings.
The subject of your conversation with Miss Dobson 486 is a very important one, and worth an Essay. I will not now inflict one of mine on you, but I will tell you as briefly as possible my present opinion which you know is contrary to the one I held in the first instance. 487 I am inclined to think that such a change of sentiment is likely to happen to most persons whose views on religious matters undergo a change early in life. The first impulse of a young and ingenuous mind is to withhold the slightest sanction from all that contains even a mixture of supposed error. When the soul is just liberated from the wretched giant's bed of dogmas on which it has been racked and stretched ever since it began to think there is a feeling of exultation and strong hope. We think we shall run well when we have the full use of our limbs and the bracing air of independence, and we believe that we shall soon obtain something positive which will not only more than compensate to us for what we have renounced, but will be so well worth offering to others that we may venture to proselyte as fast as our zeal for truth may prompt us. But a year or two of reflection and the experience of our own miserable weakness which will ill afford to part even with the crutches of superstition must, I think, effect a change. Speculative truth begins to appear but a shadow of individual minds, agreement between intellects seems unattainable, and we turn to the truth of feeling as the only universal bond of union. We find that the intellectual errors which we once fancied were a mere incrustation have grown into the living body and that we cannot in the majority of causes, wrench them away without destroying vitality. We begin to find that with individuals, as with nations, the only safe revolution is one arising out of the wants which their own progress has generated. It is the quackery of infidelity to suppose that it has a nostrum for all mankind, and to say to all and singular, [Swallow my opinions and you shall be whole.]
If then we are debarred by such considerations from trying to reorganize opinions, are we to remain aloof from our fellow-creatures on occasions when we may fully sympathize with the feelings exercised, although our own have been melted into another mould? Ought we not on every opportunity to seek to have our feelings in harmony though not in union with those who are often richer in the fruits of faith though not in reasons, than ourselves? The results of nonconformity in a family are just an epitome of what happens on a larger scale in the world. An influential member chooses to omit an observance which in the minds of all the rest is associated with what is highest and most venerable. He cannot make his reasons intelligible, and so his conduct is regarded as a relaxation of the hold that moral ties had on him previously. The rest are infected with the disease they imagine in him; all the screws by which order was maintained are loosened, and in more than one case a person's happiness may be ruined by the confusion of ideas which took the form of principles.
But it may be said how are we to do anything toward the advancement of mankind? Are we to go on cherishing superstitions out of a fear that seems inconsistent with any faith in a Supreme Being? I think the best and the only way of fulfilling our mission is to sow good seed in good i.e. prepared ground, and not to root up tares where we must inevitably gather all the wheat with them. We cannot fight and struggle enough for freedom of enquiry and we need not be idle in imparting all that is pure and lovely to children whose minds are unbespoken. Those who can write, let them do it as boldly as they like, and let no one hesitate at proper seasons to make a full confession (far better than profession). St. Paul's reasoning about the conduct of the strong toward the weak in the 14 and 15 chapters of Romans, is just in point. But I have not said half what I meant to say. There are so many aspects in which the subject might be presented that it is useless to attempt to exhaust it. I fear I have written very unintelligibly, for it is rather late and I am so cold that my thoughts are almost frozen.
Your affectionate
Mary Ann Evans.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Foleshill, 31 October [1844]
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, I, 127-128.
Foleshill. October 31st.
My dear Sara,
How shall I thank you for sending me a little remembrance after my own heart of your trip to Germany? The "Andenken" will be figuratively kept in lavender.
Pray tell Mrs. C. Hennell that no apology was needed for the very good translation she has sent me. 537 I shall be glad to avail myself of it to the last word, for I am thoroughly tired of my own garb for Strauss's thoughts. I hope the introduction etc. will be ready by the end of November when I hope to have put the last word to the first volume. I am awfully afraid of my own translation and I want you to come and comfort me. When will that be? I am relapsing into heathen darkness about everything but Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Heaven has sent "leanness into my soul" 538 for reviling them I suppose. This lovely autumn! Have you enjoyed its long shadows and fresh breezes? Give my love to all, dear Sara, and believe me ever
Your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Foleshill, 3 November [1842]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Foleshill, 3 November [1842]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1842. Extracts published: Cross, I, 116.
Foleshill | November 3.
My dear Sara,
I have been as slow to write as they tell me I am to speak, and that for two reasons -- first, because bien-séance requires that we do not run up to kiss people who bow to us at the other side of the room, and next because I have been musing on many things and have been in high displeasure with myself, have thought my soul only fit for Limbo to keep company with other abortions, and my life the shallowest, muddiest, most unblessing stream. Having got my head above this slough of Despond, I feel quite inclined to tell you how much pleasure your letter gave me -- it was so bright and good and loving, like yourself, you dear one. I think of you more and love you better than ever, and could almost turn Guebre 450 and worship the sun for giving me a sight of my favourite glance.
I have had many pleasures since you wrote in the society of Mr. Hennell and Miss Brabant. 451 You wish to know what conception or misconception I may happen to have about the character of the latter. The first empfindung was unfavourable and unjust, for in spite of what some caustic people may say, I fall not in love with every one, but I can now satisfy your affection by telling you that I admire your friend exceedingly; there is a tender seriousness about her that is very much to my taste, and thorough amiability and retiredness, all which qualities make her almost worthy of Mr. Hennell.
I read your [Confessional] with pleasure and not unfruitfully. Reason seeks not for a release from penalty -- if the result of that penalty be purification, but this cannot apply to the doctrine of Forgiveness as presented by Christianity. According to that, forgiveness is synonymous with the enlargement of the spirit from the prison of darkness and enmity to God. The punishment to be shunned would be unmixed evil to the individual and to choose unmixed evil is impossible to the human mind. You observe in your note that [some persons say that the unsatisfied longing we feel in ourselves for something better than the greatest perfection to be found on earth is a proof that the true object of our desires lies beyond it.] Assuredly this earth is not the home of the spirit -- it will rest only in the bosom of the Infinite. But the non-satisfaction of the affections and intellect being inseparable from the unspeakable advantage of such a mind as that of man in connection with his corporeal conditions and terrene destiny, forms not at present an argument with me for the realization of particular desires. 452
That huge Gryphon necessity that robs us of all the gold we dream of obliges me to stop short, for I only allow myself the time from tea to the departure of the letter bag to write. My love to all I know. I had a world more to say, but perhaps you are fortunate in being rescued from the trouble of reading another half sheet of scribble.
Ever your true and loving
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Foleshill, 29 January [1843]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Foleshill, 29 January [1843]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1843. Mary died March 16. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 117.
My dear Sara,
It has been love for you and not the want of it that has prevented me from teazing you of late with morsels from the [infinite deal of nothing] 469 that makes up my thought and feeling. I did not like that you should have to think of writing to me when you might do something pleasanter. But I cannot help wishing to tell you now that you are in trouble and anxiety how dear you are to me, and how the recollection of you is ever freshening in my mind. I hope soon to hear that you are released from your watchings and that Miss Hennell is enjoying ease after these sad blisterings which would be worse than disease if they had not hope for their companion. You have need of all your cheeriness and energy, and if they do not fail I think it almost enviable as far as one's self is concerned not of course when the sufferer is remembered, to have the care of a sickroom, with its twilight and tiptoe stillness and helpful activity. I have always had a peculiarly peaceful feeling in such a scene. But this is all idle, and I will not rob you of any more minutes. Do not suppose that I fancy myself worth thinking of because I have reminded you of me -- I have only indulged myself. Tell Mr. Hennell if you think of it that I have been flattered with the hope of seeing him for long, long weeks and am not resigned to disappointment. Give my kindest remembrances to Mrs. Hennell and to him. I am going to obtain news at Rosehill and shall beg for the conveyance of my note. Ever, my dear Sara,
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.
Foleshill | January 29th.
