Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Dover, 16 March 1855
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Dover, 16 March 1855
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 380-381.
Sydney Place | Dover | March 16. 1855.
My dear Sara
It has been very pleasant to me to think of you ever since I had your last letter as happy in work which I feel sure will be useful in some way or other even if it does not win the prize. 576 Mr. Lewes was particularly interested in your letter and thought your characterization of the Archbishop and Co. admirable. Pray let me know as soon as there is any issue connected with the essays.
I dare say you will be surprized to see that I write from Dover. We left Berlin on the 11th and a friendly fit of sea-sickness enabled me to rejoice at the sight of the British cliffs on Wednesday. I have taken lodgings here for a little while, until Mr. Lewes has concluded some arrangements in London, and with the aid of lovely weather am even enjoying my solitude, though I don't mind how soon it ends. News of you all at Rosehill -- how health and business and all other things are faring -- would be very welcome to me, if you can find time for a little note of homely details.
I am well and calmly happy -- feeling much stronger and clearer in mind for the last eight months of new experience. We were sorry to leave our quiet rooms and agreeable friends in Berlin, though the place itself is certainly ugly and am ende must become terribly wearisome for those who have not a vocation there. We left all our sight-seeing till the last week and so had a very large bite at pictures and statuary by crowding them all into three or four days.
Berlin, to be sure, has not many riches of this sort, but I increased my acquaintance with the modern German painters by our visits to three private galleries 577 and to the New Museum where Kaulbach is employed in painting the frescoes on the grand stair-case. There is a figure of the Deutsche Saga 578 which I should love you to see. I at once compared it with Michael Angelo's Sybils. It certainly satisfies one better in the colourless cartoon than in the finished painting, for Kaulbach seems greater in conception than in execution. He is also at work on some illustrations of Shakspeare, and we saw the originals of two from Macbeth. 579 They are very Germanesque, but still, finer than any other attempt at Shakspeare illustrations that I have seen. One of them represents the moment when Macbeth is girding on his armour and receives the news of his wife's death. The spirits of those he has murdered are hovering in the air above him and amongst them of course is Banquo with his children. This group of childish spirits, looking on in chubby composedness while their murderer is torn with contending passions, is the best bit of the picture. The Macbeth is too demoniacal -- not Shakespearian. But I am forgetting that my words are not likely to call up the idea of the picture in your mind. We went again and again to the New Museum to look at the casts of the Parthenon sculptures, and registered a vow that we would go to feast on the sight of the originals, the first day we could spare in London. I had never cast more than a fleeting look on them before, but now I can in some degree understand the effect they produced on their first discovery.
Apropos of Greek art, should you like to add an autograph of Liszt's to your collection? If so I can send you one.
Dover looks very lovely under a blue sky. The cliffs with the soft outline of the hills beyond, looking, as Kingsley says, like the soft limbs of mother Hertha lying down to rest, and the town with its blue smoke, made a charming picture under the afternoon sun as I walked up the castle hill. But here as everywhere else "man is vile," 580 cheating one out of sixpences and making one feel misanthropic in spite of oneself. My lodgings, however, are very comfortable and I have a nice quiet woman to wait on me. I think I have earned a little news about you now, and please to remember that it is for the sake of that I write. Ever, dear Sara,
Your affectionate Friend
Marian Evans.
Love to all.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Dorking, 23 April [1862]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Extracts published: B. C. Williams, George Eliot, New York, 1936, p. 198, dated 1863.
Parsonage House | Station Road | Dorking, | April 23.
Dear Sara
Mr. Lewes's words 'e0 propos of M'fcller are contained in an article entitled "A Box of Books" in the April (this current) number of Blackwood. 50 The article on Buckle's Scientific errors to which you refer, was also written by him. 51
I am NOT the author of the Chronicles of Carlingford. They are written by Mrs. Oliphant, author of "Margaret Maitland" etc. etc. etc. 52 A little reflection might, one would think, suggest that when a name is precisely the highest-priced thing in literature, any one who has a name will not, except when there is some strong motive for mystification, throw away the advantages of that name. I wrote anonymously while I was an unknown author, but I shall never, I believe, write anonymously again. I have not read the "Chronicles of Carlingford" but from what Mr. Lewes tells me, they must represent the Dissenters in a very different spirit from anything that has appeared in my books. And on this ground -- namely, the desire only to be responsible for views and feelings that one really shares, and again, to prevent others from being made responsible for one's own doings -- quite apart from the monetary question, I should not, without important reasons, put forth anything that was not virtually declared to be mine.
Mrs. Cash's statement is a fair specimen of the value carried by such ex post facto memories in relation to authorship. I can recall no "revelations" she ever made to me. And certainly no dissenting life I ever came in contact with in the provinces, could furnish an example of a dissenting minister being invited to visit her by a lady of title on a first interview in a shop. 53
But it is an ordinary weakness of human nature for each reader who happens to have a little personal knowledge of an author, to suppose that his book must be capable of thorough explanation by that personal knowledge. For example, an old acquaintance of Mr. Lewes's who has never seen me, told him he might well like Adam Bede the best of my books, because there was so much of his own character in Adam! Surely the force of human folly can no further go in this direction. But no number of mistakes seems to make people more modest in such matters. Unhappily the conceit is too often backed up by a little dishonesty: for example, Dr. Chapman, after learning from a private source 54 that I was the writer of Adam Bede, and on that ground pronouncing in the W. R. that it was probably a woman's work, allowed the writer on "The Mill" to begin his article with an assumption of superior acuteness in the Review as the first detector of that fact! And the very people who quarrelled on behalf of Liggins were those who turned round and said they saw the proofs of a woman's hand.
But Requiescat in pace. You know I do not willingly encourage these ghosts of the past to haunt me -- that I do not willingly write or speak about my books. And I should tell you by way of interesting you in Mrs. Oliphant, that she is a widow with a family of six children 55 and does a perfectly stupendous amount of work of all sorts -- translation and article writing and everything literary. I am glad to think you enjoy the retrospect of your outing. Love to all, from your affectionate
Marian E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Dorking, 1 May [1862]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
Parsonage House | Station Road, Dorking | May 1.
Dear Sara
I fear I wrote rather peevishly and irrelevantly to you the other day. Pray pardon it. I was not at all well, and three years ago, after the appearance of Adam Bede, my nerves were so jarred on the subject of my authorship, that I have never recovered the injury. The only remedy is the one I habitually observe -- to fling the subject as far away from me as possible and avoid either hearing or speaking of it. I only hope that when, in a moment of feverish headachiness I transgressed my own rule, I did not write anything which, from want of explanatory knowledge concerning my inward experience, you might misinterpret into irritation against you for your innocent and really sympathetic inquiry. When I give myself time to think, there is nothing I more scrupulously shun than such sending of enigmas by post.
For the rest, I shall be much obliged to you if you will take any opportunity that occurs of contradicting the report that I am the author of Mrs. Oliphant's stories. And, in general, you may be sure that whenever a fiction is mine it will bear the name of George Eliot, or at least be formally and officially announced as written by George Eliot. I am under no external pressure to write anything which there is no strong internal reason for me to write, and rather than publish anything with a precipitation which would deprive me of my inward warrant, I have refused the highest price ever offered for fiction. You will therefore be undisturbed in future by guesses and rumours which urge you, in your friendly sympathy, to send for back numbers of magazines, and groan over the effort to see all the virtues you desire in them. Of course every writer who produces an effect on the public suggests to others a choice of subjects or of manner which is a more or less conscious imitation and in some cases the inevitable result of a certain affinity.
I hope I have cleared up whatever my last letter left dark, and I am always your self-reproving affectionate friend
M. E. L.
We return to Blandford Square Monday.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Conway, 29 August [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Corrected proofsheet enclosed. Hitherto unpublished.
Conway | August 29.
Dear Sara
I got your letter only this morning -- almost too late, I fear, for my answer to be of any use. We set off on Thursday night from London. 273
Mr. Lewes and I do not feel the strong repugnance you describe Cara as feeling to the personal references in the marked passage, 274 but we think the threefold occurrence of "to me" unnecessary. I can't see any need for the clause which I have included between pencil brackets, and, in the succeeding clause do you mean to say that the view started in this work seemed to you to strike others with the impression etc. or that it struck you with that impression? If the latter, as the concluding clause seems to imply, surely the "to me" is misleading. "Truthfulness" is a personal quality, is it not? and cannot be properly used to express the quality of being true in an impersonal object i.e. a statement or exposition. Your brother was "truthful" in the expression of his opinions, but his opinions were "true" or the contrary.
I cannot give you our permanent address at present, for we have been so unfortunate as to be obliged to take temporary lodgings here -- a sad disappointment. You did not -- could not over-rate the beauty of Penmaenmawr, but you underrated the difficulty of getting lodgings there, for we could get absolutely none. I never turned my back on a place with more regret. There is a lone house on the beach near Abergile that we are now in suspense about; if we don't get that we shall try Penmaenmawr again after the lapse of these few days.
But I don't wait a post before writing, in order to obey as nearly as possible your wish that I should write by return. In haste
Ever yours
Marian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Broadstairs, 16 July [1852]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 285-286.
Broadstairs | July 16.
Dear Sara
I thought of you last night when I was in a state of mingled rapture and torture -- rapture at the sight of a glorious evening sky, torture at the sight and hearing of the belabouring given to the poor donkey which was drawing me from Ramsgate home. You will hear from Miss Field that her sister Alice has joined her.
I had a note from Miss Florence Nightingale yesterday. I was much pleased with her. There is a loftiness of mind about her which is well expressed by her form and manners. My talk the evening Miss Carter was at Mr. Chapman's 143 was chiefly with Miss Nightingale and Mrs. S. Smith. I have so profound a faith in your likings, if not in your dislikings, that I am quite sure any unfavourable impression about your Hilary is the sign of a want in me rather than in her. Had she been a person whom you had not prepared me to respect, I should have thought her rather affected and the least bit snobbish -- that is thinking of her conventional rank and afraid lest you should overlook it. I was the more surprized at this that her friends seemed so entirely the reverse. I am far more agreeably impressed with Barbara Smith -- one of the tabooed family 144 -- who is Bessie Parkes's intimate friend.
Glad you are pleased with the Westminster. I do think it a rich number -- matter for a fortnight's reading and thought. Lewes has not half done it justice in the Leader. 145 To my mind the Niebuhr article is as good as any of them.
If you could see me in my quiet nook! I am half ashamed of being in such clover both spiritually and materially while some of my friends are on the dusty highways without a tuft of grass or a flower to cheer them. A letter from you will be delightful. We seem to have said very little to each other lately. But I always know -- rejoice to know that there is the same Sara for me as there is the same green earth and arched sky when I am good and wise enough to like the best things.
Ever thine
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Bishop's Teignton, 5 August [1851]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Bishop's Teignton, 5 August [1851]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1851. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 257.
Bishop Steignton | August 5.
Dear Sara
I am grieved indeed if anything might have been written which has not been written to allay your anxiety about Cara. Her letter yesterday explained what has been the matter. The fact is, I felt in a difficulty. The illness would have been trivial in a strong person, and Dr. Walker 990 thought there was no cause for anxiety. But I know so well Cara's unfitness to endure pain, her sad want of latent strength, that I was alarmed. Still I felt it would be wrong to communicate to you an alarm which a few days might prove to be needless. I thought it a duty just to let you know that she was not well, and I knew her own handwriting would be pleasanter to you than any other. She is, I trust, getting on fast enough to warrant our setting off from here on Monday. I have been talking to her this morning about the going to London or to Rosehill. She seems to prefer London, as the journey she says is less terrific than the idea of getting to Birmingham late in the midst of a hubbub. A glance or two at the Exposition she thinks would do her no harm. I believe this is what she really feels and that she was not governed by thoughts for other people.
Today we are all going to Teignmouth. She is going in a carriage, of course, and seems to like the idea of sitting by the waves. Her poor face is very pale, but I think she is really getting on. Her illness is a pure accident, for which no one is to blame. She has been guilty of no imprudence since she has been here that I am aware of, made no extra exertion nor run any risks. The weather was as miserable as possible for some days and I think this house must be unhealthy in damp weather, but now the sun is shining gloriously and all things are tolerably promising. I am going to walk on before the rest and have a bath.
Ever your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Berlin, 9 January [1855]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, Berlin, 9 January [1855]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1855. Mostly published: Cross, I, 364-367.
Dorotheen Strasse, Berlin | January 9. 1854. 565
Dear Sara
I ought to have enclosed a letter to you in the one I sent to Mr. Bray, but the fact is our days are so accurately parcelled out that my time for letter writing is rather restricted, and for every letter I write I have to leave out something which we have learned to think necessary. I am so uneasy under the sense of having said nothing to you in reply to your letter, that I sit up tonight to scribble you a note which I shall enclose in a letter to Mr. Chapman.
We have been to hear Fidelio this evening -- not well executed, except so far as the orchestra was concerned, but the divine music positively triumphs over the defects of execution. One is entirely wrapt in the idea of the composer. Last week we had Orpheus and Euridice and I heard for the first time at once an opera of Gluck's and Johanna Wagner. 566 It is one of the glories of Berlin to give Gluck's operas, and it is also something of a glory to have "die Wagner." She is really a fine actress and a fine singer; her voice is not ravishing, but she is mistress of it. I thought of you that evening and wished you could hear and see what I know would interest you greatly -- I refer rather to Gluck's opera than to Johanna Wagner. The scene in which Orpheus (Johanna Wagner) enters Tartarus, is met by the awful shades, and charms them into ecstatic admiration till they make way for him to pass on, is very fine. The voices -- except in the choruses -- are all women's voices, and there are only three characters -- Orpheus, Amor and Euridice. One wonders that Pluto does not come as a Basso, and one would prefer Mercury as a tenor to Amor in the shape of an ugly German soprano -- but Gluck willed it otherwise and the music is delightful. The scene in Elysium is immensely absurd -- Ballet girls dance in the foreground and in the background are Greek shades looking like butchers in chemises. But the worst of it is, that instead of letting it be a tragedy, Euridice is brought to life again and we end with another Ballet girl scene before Amor's temple.
I am reading a charming book by Professor Stahr -- who is one of our acquaintances here -- Torso: Kunst, K'fcnstler und Kunstwerke der Alten. 567 It feeds the fresh interest I am now feeling in Art. Prof. Stahr is the futur of Fanny Lewald, 568 the novelist. He is a very erudite man, and what is very much rarer amongst Germans, a good writer, who knows how to select his materials and has above all a charming talent for description. We saw at his house, the other night, the first portrait of Schiller which convinces me of a likeness to him. It is the copy of a miniature which has never been engraved. 569 The face is less beautiful than that of the ordinary busts and portraits; but is very remarkable -- the eyes blue, the complexion very fair (the picture was taken in his youth) and the hair sunny. He has the long "goose-neck" which he describes as belonging to Carl Moor in the Robbers, 570 and the forehead is fuyant, in correspondence with the skull. The piteous contrast there is between the anxiety poor Schiller is constantly expressing about a livelihood -- about the thalers he has to pay for this and the thalers he has to receive for that -- and Goethe's perfect ease in that respect! For the History of the Netherlands 571 he got little more than 15s. per sheet.
I am very much interested in Professor Gruppe as a type of the German Gelehrter. He has written books on everything 572 -- on the Greek drama -- a great book on the Cosmic Systems of the Greeks -- an epic, numberless lyric poems etc. -- he has a philosophical work and a history of literature in the press -- is professor of philosophy at the University -- has invented a mode of staining paper beautifully for bookcovers -- is enthusiastic about Boar-hunting, and has written a volume of hunting poems -- and ich weiss nicht was. Withal he is as simple as a child. When we go to see them in an evening, we find him wrapt in a motheaten grey coat, once a great coat, now converted into a schlafrock, and a cap on his head. Then he reads us a translation of one of the Homeric hymns, 573 and goes into the most na'efve impersonal ecstasy at the beauty of his own poetry (which is really good). The other night he read us part of an epic which is still in MS. and is to be read before the King -- such is the fashion here. 574 And his little wife, who is about 20 years younger than himself, listens with loving admiration. Altogether, they and their two little children are a charming picture.
We have been to Rauch's 575 atelier. He is now occupied on a group representing Moses with his arms held up by Aaron and Har. It is very interesting to see the original little clay model -- the marvellous expression given in that rough way. My back aches and it is nearly 12 o'clock. Best love to Cara.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, 440 Foleshill, 30 August 1842
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, 440 Foleshill, 30 August 1842
MS: Yale. Endorsed: I first saw her July 1842. Brief extract published: Cross, I, 115.
Foleshill August 30th 1842.
My dear Sarah,
Next to the pleasure of seeing your dark eyes beaming on me was the very unexpected one of having a note from you. I will not tell you how often that little note has been read, and how I have delighted in the thought that there are beings who are better than their promises beyond the regions of waking and sleeping dreams. According to your own theory you ought to love me the more for letting a week pass without thanking you instead of following the impulse that would have led me to write on the very evening that your kind words [I do not forget you] reached me. But I begin to think that cold dignity is only becoming to wise people and suits me about as ill as would the Lord Chancellor's wig; so I shall go on being sentimental and Liebsehnende 441 in defiance of the march of reason and propriety. And by the bye there ought to be a few straggling animals of the old formation in the early strata of the new, a few spectral clingers to the memory of the old régime in the era of political regeneration, so I shall do for a specimen of an almost extinct species and in that character manage to secure a place in the cabinet of people that can like a thing for its curiosity.
And now, O most unreasonable Sarah mine, you ask me to tell you all about myself, when you send me not a word of yourself. Do I not live with myself and tire of myself until I have no need of metaphysics to make me believe that there is nothing certain but that self exists? And you after all your philosophical lectures to me, would keep me on a spot where I have already pirouetted until I am giddy, until I am one of the most egotistical speakers and writers in this world of egotists.
Thank you a thousand times my friend of the dark eye, as the Indians would call you, for destining your Autumn picture for me. Are you not beginning to enjoy the mists and calm, slow decay? I have a world more to say, but I am too modest to send a note more than twice the size of yours, and you have had quite enough copper coins for once. All good angels attend you, my Sarah, love peace and hope, and now and then a thought of your affectionate
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth], 19 May 1859
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, II, 109.
May 19. 59.
Dear Sara
You live -- all of you -- and "make no sign," 135 which is far more inexcusable than dying with the same omission. Why do you all collapse into utter silence? I hope, because you have a great many other friends that you are very fond of writing to. I have never heard yet whether Cara is comfortable with her servant. I am, at last. And what are you all doing? Is Mr. Bray swearing at May, because it is wet and cloudy, as I remember he did many years ago? Is he building his new house at Sydenham? Are you all happy, or all miserable, or neither one nor the other, but middling?
Are you coming to town this season? We have no spare bed in our own house but we can get you one for a night in Mr. Congreve's, which is empty of all but servants. Mr. and Mrs. Congreve kindly begged me to make that use of their room, during their absence, which in other respects is a loss to us (they are gone into France until September). Mrs. Congreve is a sweet woman, and I feel that I have acquired a friend in her -- after recently declaring that we would never have any friends again, only acquaintances who are obliged to conceal their nasty feelings and make themselves civil. I allude to friends of another calibre than yours.
I had a terrible alarm three weeks ago in Mr. Lewes's fainting and falling with his head on the edge of his bath. Happily his dressing gown collar protected his head from injury, and the event had the good effect of making him go to Mr. Simon 136 and be stethoscoped. Simon pronounced him sound in heart and lungs -- only suffering from debility -- the one cause of all his symptoms.
We were sorry that Mr. and Mrs. Call had a disappointment about Hofwyl. Frank, it seems, is too delicate for ordinary boys' diet and treatment, and Mr. Call objected to the religious instruction, a point on which we differ from him.
Do write and let me know that you think of
Your affectionate
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth], 15 April 1859
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, II, 99.
April 15th 1859.
Dear Sara
Send the proof, 99 by all means. I shall read it with pleasure. But hurl that detestable title to the Domdaniel 100 where Dr. Doran 101 and his books will assuredly go, along with all books and authors who deal in alliterative titles. I would carefully not open a book with such a title. Lest you should despise my opinion, I have asked Mr. Lewes to write his, which I know is of the same complexion.
The contemplated servant did not come, as we found her character unsatisfactory, so we have still our scatter-brain Caroline, and Mr. Lewes is "making himself into four," in writing answers to advertisements and other exertions which he generously takes on himself, to save me. A model husband.
The iron I took was assisted by quinine -- a prescription of Erasmus Wilson's, 102 not Mr. Spencer's. Mr. Spencer has urged several specifics for his friends since the iron. They are required now to take nux vomica on pain of his contempt -- the ground therefor being that he took it himself and got a bad cold by it -- also, that he drank an extra cup of coffee in consequence. 103
Yours affectionately
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth,] 6 August 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth,] 6 August 1860
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 267-268.
August 6. 1860.
Dear Sara
If Cara values the article on "Strikes" in the W[estminster] R[eview] she will be interested to know -- if she has not heard it already -- that the writer is blind, from having been shot in the eyes by his Father, when they were out sporting together, not more than two or three years ago. 601 I dined with him the other week, and could hardly keep the tears back as I sat at table by him. Yet he is cheerful and animated, accepting with graceful quietness all the minute attentions to his wants that his blindness calls forth. His name is Fawcett, and he is a Fellow of Cambridge.
The writer of the "Physiological Riddles" is a Mr. Hinton, 602 son, I believe, of a Baptist minister of considerable note among Baptists, with whom I breakfasted in my early teens after hearing him speak at a public meeting. Our attention was first drawn to Mr. Hinton the younger by an article in the British and For[eign] Medical Review, 603 which struck Mr. Lewes as quite marvelously similar in style to Mr. Spencer's writings, and which Mr. Spencer himself felt to be so alarmingly near to his own speculations on Organic Form that he hastened to publish these in the same Review (last year, I think). After this, Mr. Lewes met Mr. Hinton, and found him a very agreeable young man.
A propos of Mr. Spencer, he was in London, after all, and had been there for three weeks -- as we learned by his sending us a letter and proposing to come and see us. He seems to be in very good spirits about his publication by subscription -- the American list of subscribers being a large one. 604 I do hope it will answer in every way, and I only wish he had adopted this plan earlier.
I don't know what verses on Pan by Mrs. Browning you refer to. 605 I have seen none expect some very fine ones on the same subject written by her many years ago. (But I haven't read the Cornhill).
It is really worth a Jubilate to get your essay on Antichrist published at last, without expense, after all the study and trouble you gave to it. I didn't know that you had ever been obliged to be severe on the "silly gentleman." 606 Certainly we would like all silliness to take as harmless a turn as his must have been admitted to take, even if you had not written for him -- and, as it is, there are many people who are bound to thank him for one of the most useful compact books for people who are at once inquiring and busy. You have never told me how the sale of "Infidelity and Christianity" goes on now: I should expect it to continue selling steadily, if quietly.
I am sitting for my portrait -- for the last time, I hope -- to Lawrence, the artist who drew that chalk head of Thackeray which is familiar to you. He is a very interesting man -- with plenty of sadness in his life, like the rest of us.
Mr. and Mrs. Congreve have been paying a visit of two or three days to Combe Hurst with Mr. and Mrs. Clough 607 for their host and hostess, -- nearly after the fashion of your visit five years ago. -- There is gossip, in grateful return for yours.
Ever yours faithfully
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth, 27-28 August 1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth, 27-28 August 1860]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Aug. 27. 60. Extracts published: Cross, II, 268-271.
My dear Sara
I am very sorry that anything I have written should have pained you. That certainly is the result I should most seek to avoid in the very slight communication which we are able to keep up -- necessarily under extremely imperfect acquaintance with each other's present self.
My first letter to you about your book, 618 after having read it through, was as simple and sincere a statement of the main impressions it had produced on me, as I knew how to write in a few words. My second letter, in which I unhappily used a formula in order to express to you in briefest phrase my difficulty in discerning the justice of your analogical argument, as I understood it, was written from no other impulse than the desire to show you that I did not neglect your abstract just sent to me. The said formula was entirely deprived of its application by the statement in your next letter that you used the word "essence" in another sense than the one hitherto received in philosophical writing on the question as to the nature of our knowledge; and the explanation given of your meaning in your last letter shows me -- unless I am plunging into further mistake -- that you mean nothing but what I fully believe. My offensive formula was written under the supposition that your conclusion meant something which it apparently did not mean.
It is probable enough that I was stupid, but I should be distressed to think that the discipline of life had been of so little use to me as to leave me with a tendency to leap at once to the attitude of a critic, instead of trying first to be a learner from every book written with sincere labour.
Mr. Spencer lunched with us, as I think I told you, before his departure for Scotland, and was in very good spirits at the aspect of his subscription list. We spoke of your book, and as far [as] I was able to gather, he was in the same position towards it as myself -- except that he had not read it through. He implied that he found in it much ingenious thought, and especially an admirable moral spirit, but had, so far as he had looked into it, found some difficulty in seizing your meaning and in perceiving the consistency of certain phraseology with previously stated propositions.
Will you tell Mr. Bray that we are quitting our present house in order to be nearer town for Charley's sake, who has an appointment in the Post Office; and our time will be arduously occupied during the next few weeks in arrangements to that end. So that our acceptance of the pleasant proposition to visit Sydenham for a while is impossible. We have advertised for a house near Regent's Park, having just found a gentleman and lady ready to take our present one off our hands. They want to come in on quarter day, so that we have no time to spare.
Mrs. Congreve, who has just returned from the neighbourhood of Coventry, brought me the sad news, which you confirmed, of continued and even heightened distress there. One can't think of the effect of the rain on one's own pleasure -- the thought of the heavy suffering it is likely to cause for those whose lives are so far less pleasurable than ours at the best of times, urges itself before every other. It is piteous to see the laid corn, and then hear the rain pouring in the still night!
I have been reading this morning for my spiritual good, Emerson's "Man the Reformer," 619 which comes to me with fresh beauty and meaning. My heart goes out with venerating gratitude to that mild face which I daresay is smiling on some one as beneficently as it one day did on me years and years ago.
I forgot to tell you that I 'abmet'bb saw Miss Frances Carter 620 at Mrs. Bodichon's some time ago. Her sickliness and deformity attract a sympathy which her manners do not encourage. I spoke to her of you but she said you were "Alice's friend." Perhaps the unengaging manners are only another outside trial that Nature has laid on her -- misrepresenting her inward self.
Do not write again about opinions on large questions, dear Sara. The liability to mutual misconception which attends such correspondence -- especially in my case, who can only write with brevity and haste -- makes me dread it greatly, and I think there is no benefit derivable to you to compensate for the presence of that dread in me. You do not know me well enough as I am (according to the doctrine of development which you have yourself expounded) to have the materials for interpreting my imperfect expressions.
Tuesday. How comforting to see the sun again for the third day! I add a few lines this morning to say, that I have told you as well as I could the gist of what Mr. Spencer said about your book, because you appeared to ask me; but pray do not write or say anything to him on the strength of my report. He would perhaps prefer that you should only have his opinions when he has been able to read you more fully, and his health has been of late so barely sufficient for his own work, that I fancy he will want as much of his time as possible while he is in Scotland to be given up to pure relaxation and oblivion of difficult questions. You know, he is at no time a great reader -- perhaps I should say, he is the minimum of a reader, except for special purposes of his own.
I think you would spare yourself some pain if you would attribute to your friends a larger comprehension of ideas, and a larger acquaintance with them, than you appear to do. I should imagine that many of them, or at least some of them, share with you, much more fully than you seem to suppose, in the interest and hope you derive from the Doctrine of Development, with its geometrical progression towards fuller and fuller being.
Surely it is a part of human piety we should all cultivate, not to form conclusions, on slight and dubious evidence, as to other people's "tone of mind," or to regard particular mistakes as a proof of general moral incapacity to understand us. I suppose such a tendency to large conclusions about others is part of the original sin we are all born with, for I have continually to check it in myself.
Ever yours with old affection,
M. E. Lewes.
My love to Cara and Mr. Bray, and joy in their joy over the "insides." I wish there were no sorrowful outsides for me to share their pain in them. Ever yours, M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth, 27 June 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 1859. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Sara
Just a special word or two to you. I don't know whether you quite understood that I read that part of the M.S. introducing your brother's work, 177 very carefully, and I think I should even on many reperusals, retain the opinion I expressed -- namely, that it is desirable for you to introduce the book so that the reader may understand you at once to have selected it as the best exponent of a particular phase of thought -- without having his attention diverted from that main point by a word which looks like a plea, eulogy or vindication. I should not be disposed to contend for my view very strongly, because I am rather morbidly averse to anything that can be mistaken as a sign of a personal reason for a critical judgment. But whenever I think over the matter, it bears the same aspect to me, except that I have recently thought there might be a note briefly indicating that Mr. Hennell's independent inquiries had led him to results which in Germany had been the outcome of a whole era of critical inquiry. But wouldn't that note come best -- not at the beginning, but where you have arrived at the statement of these results?
After all, I don't think I am a good judge, and I feel strongly that the suggestion Mr. Lewes made should not worry your mind. Unless you felt a disposition at once to fall in with it, I don't see how you could model your book on another person's ideas. A suggestion sometimes becomes our own idea immediately, opening a new possibility to us. If not, it is better to forget it.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth, 24 June 1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Wandsworth, 24 June 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 24. 1859. Mostly published: Cross, II, 114-115.
Dear Sara
There is always an after-sadness belonging to brief and interrupted intercourse between friends 165 -- the sadness of feeling that the blundering efforts we have made towards mutual understanding have only made a new veil between us -- still more the sadness of feeling that some pain may have been given which separation makes a permanent memory. We are quite unable to represent ourselves truly -- why should we complain that our friends see a false image?
I say this, because I am feeling painfully this morning that instead of helping you when you brought before me a matter so deeply interesting to you, I have only blundered, and that I have blundered, as most of us do, from too much egoism and too little sympathy. If my mind had been more open to receive impressions instead of being in over-haste to give them, I should more readily have seen what your object was in giving me that portion of your M.S., and we might have gone through the necessary part of it together on Tuesday. 166 It seems of no use to write this now -- and yet, I can't help wanting to assure you that, if I am too imperfect to do and feel the right thing at the right moment, I am not without the slower sympathy that becomes all the stronger from a sense of previous mistake.
Dear Sara, believe that I shall think of you and your work much, and that my ear and heart are more open for the future because I feel I have not done what a better spirit would have made me do in the past.
Yours,
Marian.

Dear Sara
It was worth your while to write me those feeling words -- for they are the sort of things that I keep in my memory and feel the influence of a long long while.
Chrissey's death 74 has taken from the possibility of many things towards which I looked with some hope and yearning in the future. I had a very special feeling towards her, stronger than any third person would think likely.
The eldest girl 75 writes me very nice, simple letters -- grave and womanly, but in her own words, and not in borrowed sentences. The eldest boy 76 is almost of age -- finishes his apprenticeship this April. The second 77 is being well educated at Ewell College. The eldest girl is between 14 and fifteen -- old enough to take care of her one little sister.
No more now -- dear Sara. I will write when my thoughts are happier.
Ever your affectionate
Pollian.
Miss Hennell.

Tuesday Morning.
Dear Sara
We both like your literal title "Thoughts in aid of Faith" very much, and hope in spite of temporary "mushing" to see a little book under that title before the year is out -- a book as thorough and effective in its way as "Christianity and Infidelity." Rewriting is an excellent process frequently both for the book and its author, and to prevent you from grudging the toil, I will tell you that so old a writer as Mr. Lewes now re-writes everything of importance, though in all the earlier years of his authorship he would never take that trouble.

I mourn for Cara's disappointment, and shall trust to you to give me the pleasure of knowing that she has got a satisfactory substitute for "Jane's cousin." We have a new servant at last who is promising. 107
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday | November 15.
Dear Sara
I think I see your point of view, and of course the important point is, not that I should agree with you, but that you should do your opinions no injustice in the expression of them. It was entirely with a view to that result that I wrote my last letter. Discussion about such opinions is quite out of the question in letters.
I am distressed that your thoughtfulness in sending me an envelope all ready has been frustrated by some mischance. This morning I can't find it anywhere. I have had a little bilious attack the last few days and so am in a feeble condition of brain and limb.
Ever thine
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Richmond, 9 November 1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 9. 1857. Extracts published: Cross, I, 470-471.
Monday.
Dear Sara
It was just one of your pretty actions to send the Spec[tato]r, which I return. The article 1004 is not what one cares to see, because the writer has evidently not that sort of knowledge which would enable him to make any valuable criticism or suggestion. One is glad to have one's book spoken well of by papers of good circulation, because it is possible, though not certain, that such praise may help the sale; but otherwise it is hardly worth while to trouble one's self about newspaper reviews unless they point out some error, or present that very rare phenomenon, a true appreciation, which is the most delicious form in which sympathy can reach one. I have just read your letter to Mr. Lewes. He sends his kindest regards, and thanks you for your offer of sending him the Psych[ological] Journal, 1005 but unless there were any point in it which would suggest to him a necessary reconsideration or correction, he would rather not see it.
I hoped you were nearer the end of your first edition than it has turned out. Still, I should think the book has not done ill as publishing goes. It has surely not been out more than half a year? and you may reasonably hope that another half year may carry off the 180.
It is quite news to me that Henry Pears has so long been in the army. 1006 How should I ever hear any news if it were not for you? But you don't let anything thrust me out of your loving care to give me pleasure -- not even when you have the excuse of being occupied, as I know you must be, with Harriet, 1007 in addition to your daily doings for others.
We had a visit from Mr. Chapman last Sunday, accompanied by his brother 1008 whom I had never seen before. The brother is really an interesting man -- tradesman-like in person and manners, but impressing one as having true refinement in intellect and feeling. It was a trait I always liked in Mr. Chapman that he admired his brother -- and I think the admiration is well-founded.
I suppose you have read the [Virginians.] We groaned over the recurrence of the everlasting type -- the old lady courted for her money and fond of champagne. It is unfortunate the 1st no. 1009 should be so far from promising.
My love to Cara and Mr. Bray, though they never make any sign of remembering me.
Everything goes well with us and we make no bad blood. Some of the sweetest in my system goes to feed the feeling that you are very good and very dear. Doubtless, very naughty and hateful also, to some people or at some moments, but then that is all hidden from me, like the other side of the moon.
Ever your loving
Pollian.
I have forgotten to say, that it seems a fixed idea in your mind and Mr. Bray's that Mr. Lewes knows nothing of Phrenology and writes about it in sublime ignorance of what phrenologists say. He must be ignorant indeed not to know that "a great portion" of the brain is assigned to the animal functions. A propos of a philosophical discussion, we lately re-read the chapter on Phrenology, 1010 and I detected no misconception of phrenological data. Not that this is any proof of there being no misconception. But one so gross as that you mention could hardly have escaped me. I know the attitude of Mr. Lewes's mind towards Phrenology and I am sure it is free from any unphilosophical desire to make out a case. But so much sectarian feeling usually arises in discussions on the subject that I confess the associations of the word are not agreeable to me. The last refuge of intolerance is in not tolerating the intolerant -- and I am often in danger of secreting that sort of venom.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Richmond, 5 September 1856]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. or Oc. 1856. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Sara
You don't know how much I think and feel about your cough, and all the weary weakness and discomfort you have been feeling through the Spring and Summer. Those are just the troubles that people pass by so carelessly -- "she is not very well," "not strong," which means generally that life is very hard work.
We have had a letter from Herbert Spencer in which he says that he very much enjoyed his visit to you and that "the people at Rosehill know thoroughly how to treat their visitors."
In default of a clergyman, can't you get some pious, sensible woman to listen to your Christianity? 744 But I should think you are hardly in any danger of misrepresentation after all your reading of orthodox writers. I shall expect your Essay with a great deal of interest, for contrary to the general, I like reading what my friends write and finding out a great deal more about them than one can ever know in any other way. We mortals have such a knack of shutting up our best selves quite away from each other, as well as our worst. Don't say you don't expect me to answer your letters. I know I often answer very stupidly and briefly, but I do not shew myself altogether ungrateful. I am just now at the end of my paper and time. By and bye I shall be able to write more.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Redhill], 29 May [1872]
MS: Coventry City Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 29.
My dear Sara
I am quite able to enter into the troubles of sore throat and inflamed gums -- they have been visitants of mine on the slightest pretext for the last year or two; but your wearing cough is a trouble which I am less experienced in. I hope that you are all finding relief from the pleasant change in the weather.
We have taken a house for a few months and have been in the country now for the last week, but we don't want any one to know our address, as we desire perfect quietude. We rejected some pleasant places, because they were in the neighbourhood of friends.
Cara was kind enough to send us a card giving the address of the Mote at Ightam, 524 which we had heard of before as having been inhabited by the Hensleigh Wedgwoods, 525 last summer, I think. It is very picturesque, they say, but it is inconveniently out of the way for us, under our present arrangements. Please to give Cara my love and thanks for the unacknowledged card.
We have two of our own servants with us and on the whole are very well off, though the pictures in the drawing room are chiefly such as one would pay to be rid of.
Don't you long for some persistently warm months? It seems as if summer were being withdrawn from our temperate zone, and really our mildest weather -- that in which one is least persecuted by winds -- often comes from November to Christmas.
It would interest me whenever you write again to hear how Harriet is now. It is long since you gave me any account of her, and I should be glad to know that she is not an increasingly anxious subject of thought to you. Always, dear Sara
Your affectionate
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Redhill], 1 August 1872
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, III, 165-166.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 1. 72.
My dear Sara
I was glad to get better news of you all three, having been often wondering whether you had quite got over the spring ailments. And it is a comfort to know that poor Harriet goes on quietly. But alas what tragedies you imply in your words about Lizzie and Harry -- 'abhow much better (it seems as if) it would have been if the marriage that produced those two poor victims had never happened'bb!
The death of that honoured, good creature, Mr. William Smith, touched us particularly, because of the perfect marriage bond which had made the last eleven years of his life unspeakably precious both to him and his wife. Mr. Lewes offered to go to Brighton to see him, but he was so reduced, so very feeble in body though he kept to the last much brightness of mind, that Mrs. Smith feared for him the excitement of seeing friends who came specially from a distance. She came to see us in the first fortnight of her widowhood 571 on her way to their old abode near Keswick, and I have since had a letter from her. Her life at present is little more than a submission to mental anguish, but she tries to be cheerful with a young niece who is her companion, and by and by I hope her sympathetic nature will find some useful objects of interest. She is a fine, strong woman -- very charming in her manners; and her devoted admiration of her husband, who was little appreciated by the coarse successful people of the world, was always delightful to witness.
We have borne the heat tolerably well. Mr. Lewes is better, but I have gone back a little, and have just had a very nasty little bilious attack, which is very inopportune. Mr. Lewes stands over me, saying, "Don't write more now; say your husband forbids you." He wants to take me out of doors. So I must obey.
Gertrude has got a little daughter. The last bulletin was very good, and we are full of joy for her sake. Her sister is going to be married to the eldest son of Rev. Frederick Maurice. I meant to gossip much longer. But goodbye, dear. With love to all
Your
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [London, 4 April 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 4. 1853. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday.
Dear Sara
Delighted with your letter this morning -- especially with your appreciation of the article on Bunsen. 305 The writer on Thackeray is Theodore Martin (Bon Gaultier), 306 the husband of Helen Faucit.
Pray read the article on Schopenhauer 307 next -- I think it one of the best.
Did I tell you that Mr. C. paid £20 for an article which we were obliged to throw away? One had need to have £700 to spend on every number as they say the Editor of the Edinburgh has. -- Bad news about the American Copyright this morning. People think it will not pass the Senate. 308
Mrs. Follen and Miss Montgomery have just called -- so have Dr. Samuel Brown and his wife -- he looking like a ghost, but very cordial notwithstanding my editorial crimes. 309 I have had headache for three days and "don't know which end I stan' on," as poor Mary Hammond used to say. I had a charming letter from Harriet Martineau this morning which I will send you by and bye.
Best love to Mr. Bray and Cara. Tell the former that I had not time to do more than glance down the columns of the Herald before H. S. took it away, and he was going the next day into Derbyshire. 310 I will tell him what to look at, if he has not yet found it out.
I am sadly dispirited by long headache -- and I dare not think of a holiday at Rosehill to refresh me, because I could not be in Warwickshire without going to my sister and I don't feel equal to that just now.
Ever your faithful
Pollian.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [London, 29 June 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June. Brief extracts published: Cross, 1, 284; George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 48.
Tuesday Morning.
My dear Sara
Mrs. S. Smith 130 had called on me before she received your letter of introduction, and Miss Florence Nightingale with her. I like them both, especially Mrs. S. Smith, who has more freedom and simplicity than any undistinguished woman of her age I ever saw. By freedom and simplicity, I mean non-subjection to "formulas." They came again last night with Miss Carter, 131 your Hilary -- and Madame Mohl, 132 whose make-up was certainly extraordinary, but I suppose she is a superior woman. We had quite a constellation, a beautiful American authoress, Miss Sara Clarke, alias Grace Greenwood, 133 being the greatest star.
I went to Kew yesterday on a scientific expedition with Herbert Spencer, who has all sorts of theories about plants -- I should have said a proof-hunting expedition. Of course, if the flowers didn't correspond to the theories, we said, [tant pis pour les fleurs.] 134
Mr. Chapman begged me to accept a dozen catalogues that I might present them to you and Mr. Bray, and I did not refuse, so you must do me the honour etc. Miss Parkes has introduced me to Barbara Smith, 135 whose expression I like exceedingly. I hope to know more of her.
Can you send me Miss Field's 136 address at Ramsgate? but don't say that I asked for it, as I should like to be free either to see her or not.
I go to Broadstairs on Saturday. I am sadly in want of the change, and would much rather present myself to you all when I can do you more credit as a friend.
Ever your loving
Pollian.
Write, some of you.
I wrote Miss Julia Smith etc. on the Catalogue as you desired.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: May 31. 1853. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday Morning.
Dear Sara
Condole with me. I find Foxton's article detestable, and quite enough to damn the Review. I think we shall be obliged to offend him by declining it. 323 So much for bad news. For good, I have nothing better than that the [Society for the Conversion of the Jews] has converted one Jew during the last year and has spent £4400.
Mr. and Mrs. Combe are at Kingston, and I am going to dine with them there (at Dr. Cox's) 324 to-morrow. That is to say, if the lumbago, which seems to have succeeded the influenza, will let me.
I hope you are in better condition than I and are at this moment enjoying a trudge backwards and forwards "to earn an appetite."
Your affectionate
Pollian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 28. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 307.
Monday Morning.
Dear Sara
On Saturday I was correcting proofs literally from morning till night -- yesterday ditto -- so I have been unable to earn my week's penny-worth. The Review will be better than I once feared, but not so good as I once hoped.
I send the enclosed autographs in the hope that one or two of them may be worth putting in your collection. I suppose the weather has chilled your charity as well as mine. I am very hard and Mephistophelian just now, but I lay it all to this second winter. 300 We had a pleasant evening last Wednesday -- Lewes, as always, genial and amusing. He has quite won my liking, in spite of myself.
What do you think of the last Vagabond Letter? I am extremely glad not to be acquainted with Yseult 301 -- she is only a degree less insupportable than the Vagabond himself.
Love to the other dear creatures.
Ever your faithful and loving
Marian.
Of course Mr. Bray highly approves the recommendations of the Commissioners on Divorce. 302

MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 28. 1853. Brief extracts published: Cross, 1, 309.
Tuesday.
Dear Sara
Pack up your trunk and come to London on Friday (or Thursday if you can) and then on Saturday we will go to Ockley near Dorking, where are staying Miss Julia Smith, 340 Barbara Smith and Bessie Parkes.
They invited me and Mrs. Chapman to go to them and I am sure they -- at least Miss Julia Smith -- would be more pleased to see you than either of us. I had a packet of invitations this very morning and it struck me that here was just the thing to make it worth your while to come to London and see the Exhibition and do other pleasant things. My only fear is that you may hesitate to leave the two children. 341 But surely Mrs. C. Hennell and Cara might manage with them, for a week.
I would not be an expensive journey for you -- only the railway to London and back. Don't say nay, but come like a good Gemahlinn.
I shall write to the Ockley party to-day 342 and tell them of the probability that they will see you.
Your affectionate
Marian.
Mrs. Chapman writes to invite you by the same post.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. Mostly published: Cross, I, 291-292.
Saturday.
Dear Sara
We shall make a respectable figure after all -- nine articles and two or three of them good, the rest not bad. The Contemp[orar]y Literature, too, is rather better done this time. The Review has been selling well lately, in spite of its being the end of the quarter. We have made splendid provision for January -- Froude, 185 H. Martineau, 186 Theodore Parker, 187 Sam. The Autumnal freshness of the mornings makes me dream of mellowing woods and gossamer threads. I am really longing for my journey. 189

Ever thine
Pollian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 1852. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Sara
These are very shabby autographs which I send you, but as Mr. C. is an amateur of autographs himself, I find it difficult to get even these. J. S. Mill, C. Knight, Theodore Parker, 124 and R. M. Milnes, "our good Richard," are the names.

Ever thine, in haste,

Monday.
Dear Sara
I did not forget and meant to have written, but on Saturday afternoon 1063 I was teazed, and then came Mr. Spencer to ask Mr. Chapman and me to go to the theatre -- so I ended the day in a godless manner, seeing the Merry Wives of Windsor. 1064

Yesterday we went to Mr. Mackay's, Dr. Brabant being there. All blessings on thee, dear Sara.
Thy faithful
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [London, 21 April 1852]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [London, 21 April 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 21. Extracts published: Cross, I, 275-276.
Wednesday Morning.
My dear Sara
I am lost in amazement at your letter and cannot rest without writing an answer before I do anything else, though alas! that answer cannot reach you till tomorrow.
It is perhaps vain to inquire what fancied foundation Mr. Bray may have had for his assertion about me. I hope it is enough to say that he was never more completely in error. If there is any change in my affection for you, it is that I love you more than ever, not less. I have as perfect a friendship for you as my imperfect nature can feel -- a friendship in which deep respect and admiration are sweetened by a sort of flesh-and-blood sisterly feeling and the happy consciousness that I have your affection, however undeservedly, in return. I have confidence that this friendship can never be shaken -- that it must last while I last, and that the supposition of its ever being weakened by a momentary irritation is too contemptibly absurd for me to take the trouble to deny it. I am not conscious of having felt even that transient irritation towards you for a long, long time on my own account. I have admitted to Mr. Bray that I perceived what it was in you that frequently repelled him and chilled his affection for you, but as far as I can remember, I have chiefly to repent of having been too severe upon him rather than upon you in relation to this matter.
As to your whole conduct to me from the first day I knew you, it has been so generous and sympathetic, that if I did not heartily love you I should feel deep gratitude -- but love excludes gratitude. It would be a sad day indeed for me in which I was "alienated" from you, for I should never replace you. It is impossible that I should ever love two women better than I love you and Cara -- indeed it seems to me that I can never love any so well, and it is certain that I can never have any friend -- not even a husband -- who would supply the loss of those associations with the past which belong to you.
I have been interrupted two or three times, and I feel that I have not written as I should have liked. But, dear Sara, do believe in my love for you and that it will remain as long as I have my senses, because it is interwoven with my best nature and is dependent, not on any accidents of manner but on long experience which has confirmed the instinctive attraction of earlier days.
No more this morning -- for I am busy, but I will write again soon.
Marian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: May 13. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday.
Dear Sara
Headache again this morning -- the evening and the morning being the fifth day 91 of it, so I take unkindly to letter writing as to everything else. I spent Thursday and Friday at the Taylors, at Sydenham, thereby missing something better of course -- namely seeing Fonblanque 92 at Mrs. Parkes's. Mrs. Sidney Hawks, formerly Miss Ashurst, 93 came to Mrs. Taylor's on Friday and smoked her cigarette with a charming non-chalance. Harriet Martineau has sent us an article on Niebuhr 94 (don't tell). By the way she is a perfect lady in her letters and in little matters of detail, so far as I have seen, and shews to advantage compared with her brother.
Yesterday we dined at Mr. Johnson's at Shacklewell. Your Adonis Mr. Badler was there. There is a charming drawing hanging up in the dining-room -- The Pleiads -- a group of female forms, of course, with a star on each of their heads. I liked it particularly. Can't you do something of the same sort?
I'm so glad to hear that your cold is on the wane.
Ever thine
Pollian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: Jan. 10. 1853. Extract published: Cross, I, 302.
Monday morning.
My dear Sara
Pray do not lay the sins of the article on the Atomic Theory 260 to poor Lewes's charge. How you could take it for his I cannot conceive. It is as remote from his style both of thinking and writing as anything can be. The real author is Dr. Samuel Brown. It is amusing enough that Miss Martineau writes by the same post as you: "Dr. Brown's article is the beauty of the whole. Exquisitely beautiful his articles always appear to me; and he is the poet of scientific history." For my own part I dislike the article extremely, but I have had so much unpleasantness about it already (with Dr. Brown himself) that I have not patience to discuss it any further. I confess, however, that I don't see why you call it "vulgar."
I have read your notice of Esmond 261 -- but, you know, I can't change my opinion without getting a fresh impression from the book itself. Pray thank Mr. Bray for the paper.
I am thinking of paying another visit to my sister by and bye, and then I hope I shall manage to see you all. In haste, dear Sara
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Gorey, 5 June 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Gorey, 5 June 1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: about her marriage. June 8. 1857. Extracts published: Cross, I, 461.
Dear Sara
The news from Virtue and Co. 888 is very satisfactory, and I should think the edition will have moved off by the end of the year, for every purchaser of a cheap book like that begets two or three other purchasers. High priced books are lent; but cheap books are bought. I quite approve of your disinterring that strange beast, but I really give the preference to the wonderful Cydippes that we found yesterday floating in the sunny sea -- tiny crystal globes with delicate meridians of cilia, and long streamers spreading behind them as they float. I feel every day a greater disinclination for theories and arguments about the origin of things in the presence of all this mystery and beauty and pain and ugliness, that floods one with conflicting emotions.
Didn't you like the conclusion of Herbert Spencer's article in the W[estminster] R[eview]? There was more feeling in it than we generally get in his writing. 889 By the way, I dare say you have heard that he has made the acquaintance of the Miss Carters. 890 He seemed much pleased with them. Do they write to you often now? And have they not been interested in your book? Miss Julia Smith, I should think, would value it very highly. She seems to be relied on above all people by Barbara Smith as a friend ready to give help and sympathy under all circumstances.
Barbara has written us such descriptions of the splendour and romance to be found in Algiers, that we can't help envying people who can [do the Tropics] in miniature by going thither in 5 days for £12! Miss Parkes was there a little while, and is now I believe in Italy with Mrs. Jameson. I am so glad to think of her travelling with people who have hearts and souls, for the Savile Row establishment is not richly provided with those commodities. Alas! What skeletons there are in houses where things look so enviable! 891
We are reading [Aurora Leigh] for the third time with more enjoyment than ever. I know no book that gives me a deeper sense of communion with a large as well as beautiful mind. It is in process of appearing in a third edition, and no wonder. My head is getting so bad, that I must make haste to say what I have to say and be content to send you the shabbiest letter.
I have written to my Brother and my two sisters, telling them that I have changed my name and have a husband. Fanny has already answered me in a very kind letter. I have not yet heard from my Brother. I feel satisfied to have done this, for they are now acquainted with what is essential in my position, and if any utterly false report reaches them in the first instance, their minds will be prepared not to accept it without reserve. I do not think Chrissey will give up correspondence with me in any case, and that is the point I most care about, as I shall still be able to help her as far as my means will allow.
The "rumours" you mention have I dare say come through the Smiths and Mrs. Pears 892 -- friendly head-shakings and regrets which are meant in the best spirit. I have kept the subject so long before my mind, and have learned to see how much of the pain I have felt concerning my own family is really love of approbation in disguise, that I look calmly on the most disagreeable issues. If I live five years longer, the positive result of my existence on the side of truth and goodness will outweigh the small negative good that would have consisted in my not doing anything to shock others, and I can conceive no consequences that will make me repent the past. Do not misunderstand me and suppose that I think myself heroic or great in any way. Far enough from that! Faulty, miserably faulty I am -- but least of all faulty when others most blame.
Ever thine in headachiness
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Geneva, 4 December 1849]
MS: Yale. Excerpts published: Cross, I, 240-241.
[On the same sheet with the preceding letter.]
Dear Sara
It is three weeks since you wrote the letter which I have received only this morning -- the pleasant visit to Chetham [?] is past and you are by this time at Rosehill, 872 which after all is only an exchange of pleasures. How do you look? I hope that bandeau of silvery locks is not widening too fast on the head I love so well -- that the eyes are as bright as ever. Your letter tells me they will beam as kindly as ever when I see them once more. Never make apologies about your letters or your words or anything else. It is your soul to which I am wedded, and do I not know too well how the poor soul is doubly belied, first by the impossibility of being in word and act as great, as loving, as good as it wills to be -- and again by the miserable weaknesses of the friends who see the words and acts through all sorts of mists raised by their own passions and preoccupations. In all these matters I am the chief of sinners, and I am tempted to rejoice in the offences of my friends because they make me feel less humiliation.
Mrs. Follen is the authoress of that pretty story [The Log Cabin,] 873 is she not? I am quite satisfied to be at Geneva instead of Paris -- in fact I am becoming passionately attached to the mountains, the lake, the streets, my own room and above all the dear people with whom I live. I have scribbled so fast and so horribly you will hardly be able to read what I have written but your imagination is sure to substitute something better than the reality.
Thy faithful spouse
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, May? 1846](3)
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 142-143.
Tuesday.
My dear Sara,
As I believe that even your kindness cannot overcome your sincerity I will cast aside my fear that your wish to see me in your own home is rather a plan for my enjoyment than for yours. I believe it would be an unmixed pleasure to me to be your visitor, and one that I would choose among a whole bouquet of agreeable possibilities -- so if Mrs. Hennell will really not feel it an annoyance to have an inmate so unloveable except to her loving-in-spite-of-people's-faults-and-deficiencies daughter Sara and perhaps a few others, I will say that (Father permitting and being well and happy) I will indulge myself and accept the good that the heavens and you offer me. I am miserably in want of you to stir up my soul and make it shake its wings and begin some kind of flight after something good and noble, for I am in a grovelling slothful condition, and you are the only friend I possess who has an animating influence over me.
I have written to Mr. Hennell anent the title-page and have voted for critically examined 624 from an entire conviction of its preferableness. When I returned the prefaces to you I intended to put in a note telling you to ask Mr. H. about the translation of Kalt-bl'fctigkeit, but I forgot all about the matter on coming to fold the sheets up again after an interval. I rather prefer sang froid myself, but I have no particular anxiety about it and if Mr. H. concurred with you in thinking cold bloodedness better I should be more disposed to distrust my own taste than yours and his conjoined -- no very great modesty either, you may say. 625 Please to express to Mrs. Hennell my sense of her kindness in tacitly concurring with your invitation and tell her that I am induced to accept it from my knowledge that she is chiefly gratified by the fulfilment of your wishes.
Ever Thine
Mary Ann.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, May 1849]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1849? Published: Cross, I, 193-194.
Thank you beloved for a sight of our blessed Saint Francis's 790 letter. There is no imaginable moment in which the thought of such a being could be an intrusion. His soul is a blessed yea. There is a sort of blasphemy in that proverbial phrase "too good to be true." The highest inspiration of the purest, noblest human soul is the nearest expression of the truth. Those extinct volcanos of one's spiritual life, those eruptions of the intellect and the passions which have scattered the lava of doubt and negation over our early faith are only a glorious Himmalayan chain beneath which new vallies of undreamed richness and beauty will spread themselves. Shall we poor earthworms have sublimer thoughts than the universe of which we are poor chips -- mere effluvia of mind -- shall we have sublimer thoughts than that universe can furnish out into reality?
I am living unspeakable moments and can write no more.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, May 1845]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 130-131.
My dear Sara,
I am alarmed to hear that you are all going to the coast 554 without my having any intimation that Mr. Parkes has fulfilled his promise. I begin utterly to despair that Strauss will ever be published unless I can imitate the Revd Mr. Davis 555 and print it myself. I have no confidence in Mr. Parkes and shall not be surprized if he fail in his engagement altogether -- at the very best, if we go on according to the rate of procedure hitherto, the book will not be published within the next two years. This seems dolorous enough to me, whose only real satisfaction just now is some hope that I am not sowing the wind. 556 It is very laughable that I should be irritated about a thing in itself so trifling as a translation, but it is this very triviality of the thing that makes delays provoking. The difficulties that attend a really grand undertaking are to be borne, but things should run smoothly and fast when they are not important enough to demand the sacrifice of one's whole soul. I have not time to write another word. In great haste
Thy loving
Mary Ann.
Mrs. Hennell once told me that Dr. Brabant had translated the Conclusion 557 and that I might possibly have a sight of his translation. Will you inquire about this for me? I should be unpardonable if I neglected any help.

MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, I, 141.
I think on the whole, my fidem Achates, that [the Lord's Supper] is better than [the Sacrament.] My objection to it was the awkwardness of saying "Jesus instituted the Lord's Supper." It reminded me of who was the father of Zebedee's Children? But I think the grand consideration that there are many sacraments -- 7 Romish and 2 Anglican -- must carry the day against the Sacrament.
I wish we could get the book out in May. Why not? I suppose the binding could not be all got through. The printing and writing I should think might be managed in time.
Shouldn't I like to fleet the time away with thee as they did in the Golden Age -- after all our toils to lie reclined on the hills (spiritually), like gods together, careless of mankind. 605 Sooth to speak idleness -- and idleness with thee is just the most tempting mirage you could raise before my mind's eye -- I say mirage because I am determined from henceforth to believe in no substantiality for future time, but to live in and love the present, of which I have done too little. Still the thought of being with you in your own home will attract me to the future for without all controversy I love thee and I miss thee.
Pollian.

MS: Yale. Published: Cross, I, 136-137.
My dear Sara,
As Mr. Bray tells me that you were disappointed not to have any new M.S., I send you to-day the conclusion of the chapter you are reading, and unless you find anything of importance to be rectified, you need not return this to me, but may forward the whole to the Printer as soon as you have read it.
I am not altogether satisfied with the use of the word Sacrament as applied specifically to the Abendmahl. It seems like a vulgarism to say, the Sacrament, for one thing, and for another, it does not seem aboriginal enough in the life of Jesus: but I know of no other word that can be substituted. 603 I have altered passover to paschal meal, but to pascha is used in the New Testament of the eating of the lamb, par excellence. You remember in the title of the first 'a7 in the Schluss which I had been so careless as to omit, the expression is "Nothwendiger Uebergang der Kritik in das Dogma." Now Dogmatism will not do, as that would represent Dogmatismus. Dogmatik is the idea I believe
I have had a miserable week of headache, but am better now, and ready for work, to which I must go.
Thine lovingly,
Pollian.

Dear Sara

MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 1848. Extracts published: Cross, I, 169.
[The first page of this letter is missing.]
Your body changed into wavy grass indeed! As if it would be long before I should be turned into toad-stools -- or some other poisonous fungus.
I am reading G. Sand's Lettres d'un Voyageur with great delight, and hoping that they will some time do you as much good as they do me. In the meantime I think the short letter about Lelia 683 will interest you. It has a very deep meaning to my apprehension. You can send back the pages when you have duly digested them.
I am quite missing the pleasure I should have had in talking over Mr. Dawson with you. 684 I once said of you that yours was a sort of alkali nature which would detect the slightest acid of falsehood. You began to phiz-zz directly it approached you. I want you as a test. I now begin to see the necessity of the arrangement (a bad word) that love should determine people's fate while they are young. It is so impossible to admire -- s'enthousiasmer of an individual as one gets older.
I shall go to Rosehill to-morrow to know how it is you are sad -- if indeed the sadness have a special outward cause. Moreover I shall quarrel very violently with Mr. Bray for his horrid indifference to any feelings but what concern himself.
Pollian.

Cara sposa
Father's tongue has just given utterance to a thought which has been very visibly radiating from his eager eyes for some minutes -- "I thought you were going on with the book --" so I can only bless you for those two notes which have emanated from you like so much ambrosial scent from roses and lavender.
