Tuesday Morning.
Beloved Achates,
I have been idle, and have not done a stroke to the prefaces, but they shall be sent as soon as possible. Thanks for the copy of the Latin preface and letter. They are in preconceived harmony with my ideas of the appropriate. 618 I do not quite understand what you mean about the two first volumes being completed. Are then the prefaces and index to be printed immediately before the rest of the 3d volume? 619 It would be very stupid for a reviewer to see the 2 first volumes and no more.
The friend of whom I spoke is Miss Jenkins 620 whom you will remember as Mrs. Whittem's governess. This is quite a secret, and must above all not be mentioned to Cara or Mr. Bray, as Miss J. would be extremely hurt to find that her little project was known. She merely asked me for the sake of information on the subject. She is clever, but whether clever enough to trust to her brains alone for a living I dare not venture to say. She poor girl evidently has the utmost repugnance to the life of a governess. She is good and conscientious, but rather utopian and freakish. She thinks she could sit from morn till noon, from noon till dewy eve, 621 translating German or French without feeling the least fatigue. I shall tell her that I have asked the opinion of one friend, who thinks the speculation h'f6chst prec'e4r, and shall I not say that that friend has had experience which warrants her to pronounce teaching better work for the soul than translating? There are not even the devil's wages for a translator -- profit and fame. She says she wants neither, but only food and clothing.
Once more, this is for thy private ear. In great haste,
Thine gratefully and lovingly
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, April? 1846](4)
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Achates,
I have no doubt that Paschaabend must be translated the evening of the Passover, and I think if you look at the passage again you will see that it would make nonsense of it to translate eve of the passover. "Je mehr das letzte mit ihrem Meister gehaltene Mahl den J'fcngern 'fcber alle Paschamahle gegangen sei, desto weniger sei ihnen auf die Zeit desselben, ob es am Paschaabend selbst, oder einen Tag fr'fcher gehalten worden war, angekommen." 617 Now the only question as to the time of the meal is whether it was eaten on the evening of the 14th Nisan i.e. not the eve of the passover, but the commencement of the Passover itself, or on the evening of the 13th Nisan, which would be what Strauss calls the Vorabend des Pascha.
The synoptists say that the last supper was taken at the proper time for eating the passover -- John intimates throughout his story that it was taken on the evening before (Vorabend) that of eating the passover. "Paschaabend selbst" expresses the representation of the synoptists, and the eve of the passover was not the proper time for eating the Paschal meal. I am tired and hurried, but if I have not made the matter clear, your own logical faculty will do it.
The perpetual recurrence of the stiff expression Paschal meal is very ugly, and I think passover might properly have been used interchangeably for the eating of the Paschal lamb, especially as it is so in the quotations from the New T. and as [feast of the passover] is the best way of indicating the Gesammtheit of the passover -- but this is not of much consequence. I have been hindered, and shall not be able to send the next parcel before Thursday or Friday. Do you think Mr.
Chapman is advertising sufficiently? I hope he is not so penny wise as to economize in that particular.
Thine
Pollian.
Do not ask anybody about the meaning of Paschaabend because the nature of the subject is the only evidence.

MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Dearest A.
A young lady of my acquaintance 616 is so judicially blinded as to think translation and nothing but translation would be an easier life than that of a governess. She has asked me if it be possible for a person to get regular employment in this way. I do not suppose any scheme of the kind is practicable, and so I told her, but I promised to enquire for her. Her idea is that she could live in London and get her bread by turning German and French into English from morning to night. I wish you would be so good as to get a decided verdict against any such plan from an authoritative quarter that I might get the maggot out of her brain. Please do not mention the matter except for the sake of the inquiry, as she begged me to be secret.
Thine.

Beloved Achates,
I have considered the subject of division, or rather the division of the subject, and I am decidedly for beginning the third volume with the history of the Passion i.e. the third Part. The transfiguration and entrance into J[erusale]m extend over only 40 pages, and they would make no great difference either way.

Beloved Achates,
Have I really written exegesists? I can hardly believe it because this travesty of the right word seems as if it were quite strange to my eyes and hand. Thy
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 9 February 1849]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 9th, 1849. Mostly published: Cross, I, 197-200.
Dear Sara
My life is a perpetual nightmare -- always haunted by something to be done which I have never the time or rather the energy to do.
Opportunity is kind, but only to the industrious and I alas! am not one of them. Else I might write to you oftener, if indeed you would thank me for doing so. I have sat down in desperation this evening though dear Father is very uneasy and his moans distract me, just to tell you that you have full absolution for your criticism 775 which I do not reckon of the [impertinent] order. I wish you thoroughly to understand that the writers who have most profoundly influenced me -- who have rolled away the waters from their bed raised new mountains and spread delicious valleys for me -- are not in the least oracles to me. It is just possible that I may not embrace one of their opinions, that I may wish my life to be shaped quite differently from theirs. For instance it would signify nothing to me if a very wise person were to stun me with proofs that Rousseau's views of life, religion, and government are miserably erroneous -- that he was guilty of some of the worst bassesses that have degraded civilized man. I might admit all this -- and it would be not the less true that Rousseau's genius has sent that electric thrill through my intellectual and moral frame which has awakened me to new perceptions, which has made man and nature a fresh world of thought and feeling to me -- and this not by teaching me any new belief. It is simply that the rushing mighty wind 776 of his inspiration has so quickened my faculties that I have been able to shape more definitely for myself ideas which had previously dwelt as dim [ahnungen] in my soul -- the fire of his genius has so fused together old thoughts and prejudices that I have been ready to make new combinations.
It is thus with G. Sand. I should never dream of going to her writings as a moral code or text-book. I don't care whether I agree with her about marriage or not 777 -- whether I think the design of her plot correct or that she had no precise design at all but began to write as the spirit moved her and trusted to Providence for the catastrophe, which I think the more probable case -- it is sufficient for me as a reason for bowing before her in eternal gratitude to that [great power of God] 778 manifested in her -- that I cannot read six pages of hers without feeling that it is given to her to delineate human passion and its results -- (and I must say in spite of your judgment) some of the moral instincts and their tendencies -- with such truthfulness such nicety of discrimination such tragic power and withal such loving gentle humour that one might live a century with nothing but one's own dull faculties and not know so much as those six pages will suggest. The psychological anatomy of Jacques and Fernande in the early days of their marriage 779 seems quite preternaturally true -- I mean that her power of describing it is preter-natural. Fernande and Jacques are merely the masculine and the feminine nature and their early married life an everyday tragedy -- but I will not dilate on the book or on your criticism for I am so sleepy that I should write nothing but b'eatises.
I have at last the most delightful "de imitatione Christi" with quaint woodcuts. 780 One breathes a cool air as of cloisters in the book -- it makes one long to be a saint for a few months. Verily its piety has its foundations in the depth of the divine-human soul.
Thine Ever
Pollian.
Do not suppose that I mean this as an answer to your criticism or that I do not understand it.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oc. Mostly published: Cross, I, 149-150.
How art thou, my sweet Sara? I am truly yearning for a word from thee specially to myself. All the world is bathed in glory and beauty to me now 635 and thou sharest in the radiance. Tell me whether I live for you as you do for me and tell me how gods and men are treating you. Monday Evening.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 5 November 1846]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 5 November 1846]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1846. Extracts published: Cross, I, 148-149.
Just been to Rosehill, dearest Sara, and read your letter of this morning. Thank Mr. Chapman for his kind offer and assure him that I shall have much pleasure in accepting it. Do you think it worth my while to buy the Prospective for the sake of Wicksted's Review? 639 Is there anything new in it? Do you know if Mr. Chapman has any unusual facilities for obtaining cheap classics? Such things are to be got handsome and secondhand in London if one knew but the way. I want to complete Xenophon's works. I have the Anabasis -- and I might perhaps get a nice edition of the Memorabilia and Cyropaedia in a cheaper way than by ordering them directly from our own bookseller. But all this is very selfish and troublesome, and do not teaze yourself with it except when you want something to do or say.
I begin to be of your and Cara's opinion anent Dr. B. 640 You are my own best plainspoken friend and generally judge better for me than I can judge for myself. I hope Rufa knows the contents of my letter to you. Pray convince her and every one concerned in the matter that I am too inflatedly conceited to think it worth my while to run after Dr. Brabant or his correspondence. If I ever offered incense to him it was because there was no other deity at hand and because I wanted some kind of worship pour passer le temps. I always knew that I could belabour my fetisch if I chose, and laughed at him in my sleeve. Even that degree of inclination towards mock reverence has long since passed away and ridiculous as it may seem to every one else, I looked on my renewal of a correspondence with him as a favour conferred by me rather than received. I shall certainly take an opportunity of certifying him on which leg the boot was. You see I am getting horridly vulgar as well as proud.
Do not judge too harshly of the L.L. 641 on a first interview. I am quite glad to hear of prettiness associated with learning and heresy. Is there genius too? If so, the gods are getting kinder to mortals.
I have been reading the [Fawn of Sertorius.] 642 I think you would like it, though the many would not. It is pure, chaste, and classic beyond any attempt at fiction I ever read. If it be Bulwer's he has been undergoing a gradual transfiguration, and is now ready to be exalted into the assembly of the saints.
You must write to me, do -- there's a dear soul. Keep a bit of paper lying ready to scribble on for me. The Professor's letter 643 transmitted through you, gave me infinite consolation -- more especially the apt and pregnant quotation from Berosus. Precious those little hidden lakelets of knowledge in the high mountains, far removed from the vulgar eye, only visited by the soaring birds of love.
Thine entirely
Pollian.
Thursday.

This learned personage has come over to England with the single purpose of getting his voluminous writings translated into English. There are at least twenty volumes, all unpublished, owing to the envious machinations of rival authors, none of them treating of anything more modern than Cheops, or the invention of the hieroglyphics. The respectable professor's object in coming to England is to secure a wife and translator in one. But though, on inquiry, he finds that the ladies engaged in translation are legion, they mostly turn out to be utterly incompetent, besides not answering to his requirements in other respects; the qualifications he looks for in a wife, besides a thorough acquaintance with English and German, being personal ugliness and a snug little capital, sufficient to supply him with a moderate allowance of tobacco and Schwarzbier, after defraying the expense of printing his books. To find this phoenix among women he is sent to Coventry on all hands.  

"In Miss Evans, so she runs on, the aspiring professor finds his utmost wishes realised, and so proposes to her on the spot; thinking that it may be her last chance, she accepts him with equal celerity, and her father, although strongly objecting to a foreigner, is induced to give his consent for the same reason. The lady's only stipulation is that her future husband shall take her out of England, with its dreary climate and drearier inhabitants. This being settled, she invites her friends to come to her wedding, which is to take place next week."  

In reply Miss Hennell wrote as from Professor B 'fccherman, the letter mentioned here, "declining the engagement because she was not ugly enough after all." "It was the most capital thing I ever saw," Mrs. Bray wrote her sister. "The hieroglyphics sent her into fits over and over again." (Bray-Hennell Extracts, 4 November 1846.) Berosus was one of the fictitious authors the professor quoted. Cross took the passage seriously, thinking it alluded to Strauss.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 4 March 1846]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 4 March 1846. Extracts published: Cross, I, 142.
Beloved Achates,
Will it not please thee to have some more manuscript in company with the requisite scrap of German, that, if necessary, it may be returned by Mr. Bray, and so the proceedings be quickened, or shall I wait until the 25th? 597 Send me word in the next extra-blatt attached to a proof.
The last 100 pages 598 have certainly been totally uninteresting to me, considered as matter for translation. Strauss has inevitably anticipated in the earlier part of his work all the principles and many of the details of his criticism, and he seems fagged himself. Mais courage! the neck of the difficulty is broken, and there is really very little to be done now. If one's head would but keep in anything like thinking and writing order! Mine has robbed me of half the last fortnight -- but I am a little better now and am saying to myself Frisch zu! The crucifixion and the resurrection are at all events better than the bursting asunder of Judas. 599 I am afraid I have not made this dull part of Strauss even as tolerable as it might be, for both body and mind have recoiled from it.
Anything heard of Strauss's preface yet? The 3d volume might begin with the Transfig[uratio]n 600 if the symmetry of the volumes be a preferable consideration to the proper division of the subject, and I think it is true the latter could not be observed in the two first volumes. Thank you dearest, for all your love and patience for me and with me. I have nothing on earth to complain of but subjective maladies. Father is pretty well and I have not a single excuse for discontent through the livelong day.
Thy
Pollian.
I was pleased on the whole with the two 'a7'a7 on the devils. 601

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 4 February 1849]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 4 February 1849]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 4, 1849. Extracts published: Cross, I, 196-197.
Sunday Morning.
Out, hyperbolical fiend! talkest thou of nothing but music? 766 An exquisite little morceau of connubial torture, I suppose. Never tell me that thou knowest not -- at least the devil that prompts thee knows -- that I have not touched the piano for nearly two months until this morning when, Father being better, I was determined to play a mass before the piano is utterly baked out of tune again. Therefore avaunt! thou strumming and warbling devil -- get thee to some fat Quaker and torment him in the guise of a hurdy-gurdy boy.
Your letter, dear love, was brought to me in bed and I managed to read it in spite of unutterable headache. Every scrap of paper (out-taken the musical ones) is a little winged angel to me, seems to fondle me and fan me with its soft dove-like wings. Therefore write, asking for nothing again, 767 like a true disciple of Jesus. I am still feeling rather shattered in brain and limbs, but do not suppose that I lack inward peace and strength. My body is the defaulter -- consciously so. I triumph over all things in the spirit, but the flesh is weak and disgraces itself by headaches and backaches and vomitings.
I am delighted to find that you mention Macaulay, because that is an indication that Mr. Hennell has been reading him. 768 I thought of Mr. H. all through the book, as the only person I could be quite sure would enjoy it as much as I did myself. I did not know if it would interest you. Tell me more explicitly that it does.
Think of Babylon being unearthed in spite of the prophecies! 769 Truly we are looking before and after 770 au jour d'aujourd'hui, as Monsieur Bricolin says. 771 Send me the criticism of Jacques, 772 the morn's morning, 773 only beware there are not too many blasphemies against my divinity.
Paint soap bubbles -- and never fear but I will find a meaning though very likely not your meaning. Paint the crucifixion in a bubble, after Turner 774 and then the resurrection -- I see them now.
There has been a vulgar man sitting by while I have been writing and I have been saying parenthetical bits of civility to him to help out poor Father in his conversation, so I have not been quite sure what I have been saying to you. I have woful aches which take up half my nervous strength. Brothers and sisters coming this afternoon -- therefore believe that I love thee or I should not have written even this today.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: Jan. 1846. Published: Cross, I, 137-138.
Dear Sara,
I do pity you with the drunken Christmas workmen, keeping you in this uncomfortable interregnum. 590 But do not go distraught -- the spring will really come and the birds -- many having had to fly across the Atlantic which is farther than you have to go to establish yourself.
I could easily give the meaning of the Hebrew word in question, as I know where to borrow a lexicon, 591 but observe, there are two Hebrew words untranslated in this proof. I do not think it well to give the English in one place and not in another where there is no reason for such distinction -- and there is not here, for the note in this proof sounds just as fee-fo-fum-ish as the other, without any translation. I could not alter the troublesome, because it is the nearest usable adjective for schwierig, which stands in the German. I am tired of inevitable importants and cannot bear to put them when they do not represent the German.
I have an invitation to refuse -- just come.
Thine in haste
Mary Ann.
Wednesday.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 30 April 1847]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 30/47. Extract published: Cross, I, 155.
Friday Evening.
My dear Sara
My strong conviction about my ménage was quite right. I find painters all behind hand, and sisters and brothers besetting me. But it is one of my pleasantest thoughts now I am come home that you said and therefore I am sure felt, that you would have liked me to be with for a day or two. Thank you for that and every other loving word or look you ever gave me.
I did so long to see you after hearing Elijah just to exchange an exclamation of delight. Last night I had a perfect treat too, in I Puritani. 661 Castellan was admirable as Elvira, and Gardoni is a seraph. N.B. -- I liked the Ballet less -- another sign of age. Love to Mrs. Hennell,
Thine
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 29 April 1845]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 29 April 1845]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 29, 1845. Extract published: Cross, I, 129-130.
My dear Sara,
Let me assure you for the last time that I never stickle for a word or a phrase unless it express an idea that cannot be equally well conveyed by another. I like as if quite as well as as though and lastly as well as finally -- indeed, rather better. I must have been stone blind to have left the tau out of Christos and apostles 552 and I am truly sorry that you have to correct so many stupid omissions. I am relying a little on the idea that your eye will detect the want of points etc. and I do not therefore consider these matters as minutely as I should otherwise have done, but I will attend to my figures, that is, my Roman letters, for chapters and I will put s. in the notes except when the quotation is from a Latin work. 553 I decidedly agree to the fs and ffs if you think we are great enough to create a precedent. If you think any of my future manuscript too untidy for the printer only mark it to that effect, and I will re-write it, for I do not mind that mechanical work, and my conscience is rather uneasy lest the illegibility of my hand should increase materially the expense of the publication. Do not be alarmed because I am not well just now -- I shall be better very soon and I am not really disgusted with Strauss. I only fancy so sometimes, as I do with all earthly things.
Pollian.
Do not wait until you have something particular to say before you write again. Your letters cheer me greatly.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 25 September 1845]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 25 September 1845]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. 25. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 134-135.
Thursday.
My dear Sara,
I am delighted with the proof -- the type and everything else are just what I wished. To see the first sheet is the next best thing to seeing the last which I hope we shall all have done this time next year. I have never yet been able to learn whether the volumes are to come out separately or all at once. Some time when you write to Rosehill or to me, do send me word. I see the Greek notes are given in the Introduction just as they are in the original. Will it not look rather queer to begin with giving Greek and then to alter the plan? I have been thinking over the matter of the notes and it seems to me that when, as is generally the case the substance or the leading idea contained in them is given in the text it would look very ungeschickt to translate without at the same time giving the Greek, since Strauss's object is to verify his assertions rather than to give information by the quotations at the foot. 578 What thinkest thou?
There is a very misty vision of a trip to the Highlands haunting us in this quarter. The vision would be much pleasanter if Sara were one of the images in it. You would surely go if we went, and then the thing would be perfect. 579 I long to see you, for you are becoming a sort of transfigured existence, a mere ideal to me and I have nothing to tell me of your flesh and blood self but sundry very useful little pencil marks and a scrap of Mrs. Bray's notes now and then. So if you would have me bear in my memory your own self and not some aerial creation that I call by your name you must make your appearance. Ever dear Sara
Your true and affectionate
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 25 April 1849]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 25th '49. Hitherto unpublished.
Wednesday.
Dearest Sara
The sweet pictures 789 came to me when I was in bed with miserable headache and sickness, and it was not until yesterday that I could bear even to look at anything. I should have sent you word of their safe arrival and warm welcome last night, but when I had walked home with Cara I found that the letter-bag was gone. Dear Sara -- you always know what will give me the most pleasure in the world -- I thanked you with delicious happy tears -- the only tears almost that I ever shed now. I could hardly believe it was a waking fact that any one loved me well enough to speak to my heart in that sweet way. If I am thought worth putting into a coffin I should like my little pictures to go with me.
I am not at all well today so I will not try to write long or I should only write miserably. You know that Father is much worse?
Ever your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 23 November 1848]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 23, 1848. Hitherto unpublished.
Mother Nature -- who by the bye is an old lady with some bad habits of her own -- like other great names does her work by deputy and so gets both credit and discredit that don't properly belong to her. The vulgar may not know it, but she in fact leaves the creation of her plants her animals and her homunculi to a whole herd of sprites and genii some of whom make but laughing work of it. Now over a quarter of a century ago 762 there was a very young sprite who forsooth having turned out some respectable toads and a few indifferent lemurs and marmosets must fain try his hand on a human article and one 22d of November he presented to Dame Nature at her evening levee a rough though unmistakeable sketch of a human baby. The Old Mother had been rollicking all the autumn in the vintage and wanted no less than a winter's sleep to sober her. Being rather cross-grained in her cups she was in no humour to make the best of a bad business so she said, What have we here? in such a snappish tone, flourishing a bunch of nettles all the while, that the poor little Prometheus of a sprite began to look very snubbed. "A pretty piece of work I should have to patch up this thing into a human soul and body that would hang together! Here," she called to one of her Vishnu-sprites, "smother it at once to save further harm." Thereupon the poor spriteling fell a crying that his first Homunculus was to be sent to limbo without having one chance given it. So some of his brother genii who were bringing in their day's work were touched with pity, and began to intercede for him and his Homunculus. "See mother," said they, "we have brought you many gentle maidens and high-browed, 763 brave men. We will make them to be friends to this poor bratling if you will only spare it, and they shall love and cherish and guard its poor rickety soul." "And see," said one hard-working sprite, "some Novembers ago 764 I brought you a dark-haired maiden and she shall be to this little one as a sister and her dark eye shall beam on the wandering one with love to soothe and grave warning to reclaim." And so Dame Nature heard the intercession and the brother-sprites kept their word. For the poor sketch of a soul was found by the dark eyed maiden and those other bright and good mortals and they pitied and helped it, so that at last it grew to think and to love.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 23 June 1848]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 23, 1848. Mostly published: Cross, I, 190-191.
Dear Sara
All creatures about to moult or to cast off an old skin, or enter on any new metamorphosis have sickly feelings. It was so with me, but now I am set free from the irritating worn-out integument. I am entering on a new period of my life which makes me look back on the past as something incredibly poor and contemptible. I am enjoying repose strength and ardour in a greater degree than I have ever known and yet I never felt my own insignificance and imperfection so completely.
My heart bleeds for dear Father's pains, but it is blessed to be at hand to give the soothing word and act needed. I should not have written this description of myself but that I felt your affectionate letter demanded some I-ism, which after all is often humility rather than pride.
You are ever with me as Spiridion was with Alexis and Angel. 754
Pollian.
Paris, poor Paris alas alas. 755

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 21 February 1848]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Sara
Thrice welcome will you be on Thursday even at the distance of Rosehill from me, and still more welcome when you come to me and let me nurse you after all these trying scenes and thoughts. 700 I have faith that they are to be an introduction to more lasting quiet than you have had for a long while and so I comfort myself in hearing and reading of them.
If you can think of such a matter when you are packing will you put Salvador in your box for me? I want to see him again very particularly, but I am ashamed to ask you to do anything for me at such a time. Perhaps you have returned it to Woodford. If so, of course I do not suppose I can have it.
Farewell until next Friday!
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 20? May 1846]
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, I, 143-144.
Dear Sara,
See what it is to have a person en rapport with you, that knows all your thoughts without the trouble of communication. I am especially grateful to thee for restoring the [therefore] to its right place. I was about to write to you to get you to remonstrate about this and the "dispassionate calmness," which I did not at all like but I thought you had corrected the prefaces, as the marks against the Latin looked like yours, so I determined to indulge my laissez-faire inclinations, for I hate stickling and debating unless it be for something really important. I agree with you that coldbloodedness would have been better than insensibility, 626 sed quod scriptum scriptum est.
I do really like reading our Strauss -- he is so klar und ideenvoll but I do not know one person who is likely to read the book through, do you? I have a woful pain in my eingeweide and can hardly comprehend the use of my oracular tongue. Next week and we will be merry and sad, wise and nonsensical, devout and wicked together!

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 20 September 1842]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 20 September 1842]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. 1842. Hitherto unpublished.
Tuesday.
My dear Sara,
I saw yesterday for the first time the beautiful Autumn picture, which Mrs. Bray had detained for the sake of contemplating it a little while. It is, like many other things that fall to my share, quite too good for me, and I cannot help regretting, much as I shall value and try to appreciate the gift, that I should rob your portfolio of so lovely a specimen of your taste and power. It is a scene after my own heart; I should like to be a Hamadryad among such woods and have my feet in such peaceful water as you have painted. I fancy I could manage to live in an old oak and drink out of the palm of my hand as well as the old cynic did in his tub, but it must be when the [lights are [burnt] dead and all but me departed] 445 from my little life's banquet, for though I can forego spoons and carpets, I would not willingly say good bye to the loved and the loving. You must have thought me strangely insensible to your kindness, never to speak of the very nicest present you had sent me; my ignorance of its arrival is the explanation. I shall soon go to Mrs. Bray to read what you have permitted me to share, like a blessed little Houri that you are! May my paradise be peopled with such.
Tell Miss Hennell we have had another evening with Dr. Ullathorne, 446 whom I wish you had seen. I love to "interrogate a picked man of countries," 447 and he is one who has shivered among ice-bergs, been broiled between the tropics, and seen the wonders and beauties of the old world and the new.
Mrs. Hennell 448 tells me you were well when she left home, and to me that is news worth hearing. I am in a hurry now as I was when I wrote last, but I will chat a little more leisurely with you soon, that is unless you impetrate me to desist from teazing you with my nothings. [Rien faire] generally merges into "faire des riens" and that is my case. Those favourites of the skies who are living their "glorious hour of crowded life" 449 are the only beings who have no temptation to act and talk folly. I look ever with new delight at the representation of your back in my pretty little picture. May I one day have the face to kiss again! Love to Miss Hennell. Ever, my Sara,
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.

MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, I, 134.
My dear Sara,
As I have been obliged to lose two days this week, and shall have to give a third to my teeth I do not think it worth while to wait for the week's harvest, so I send you last week's, with the part you returned by Mrs. Bray's parcel. I am glad you sent it. Thank you for all little notes thrust in between the proofs. They are very refreshing in this valley of Baca. 585 I am never pained when I think Strauss right -- but in many cases I think him wrong, as every man must be in working out into detail an idea which has general truth, but is only one element in a perfect theory, not a perfect theory in itself. I have not another minute.
Thine.

GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 1845](1)
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Dec. Extract published: Cross, I, 135.
Dear Sara,
I have not the German of 'a7 81. I gave you from 'a7 64 to 84. I cannot therefore alter the passage which you have copied and which I have just this moment had the misfortune to drop into the pie. Nor can I decide about the note 12. I think I remember that the "uninterrupted agony of God" 580 refers to the words "My Father worketh hitherto etc.," and I fancy they are an addition of my own to make the reference clear, but of course I cannot judge anything about the matter without the German. Hellenistic 581 you may venture to put instead of Greek. The only meaning of Doppel-G'e4nger 582 is a double-sighted person, i.e. one who sees more than is visible to healthy organs. You must not alter that. Please to tell Mr. Hennell that [habits of thought] is not a translation of the word particularismus. This does not mean national idiosyncrasy, but is a word which characterizes that idiosyncrasy. If he decidedly objects to particularism ask him to be so good as substitute exclusiveness 583 though there is a shade of meaning in par[ticularis]m which even that does not express. It was because the word could only be translated by a circumlocution that I ventured to anglicise it.
I am very much hurried to-day, being obliged to go out, so that I have been obliged to answer you hastily. Be so good as to make yourself quite sure as to what German you have.
Thine,
Mary Ann.
Sunday.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 18 February 1847]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 18 February 1847]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 18, 1847 | 1847-April 1850. Partly published: Cross, I, 153-154.
Dearest Lalla, 652
Lying in bed this morning, grievously tormented, your Heliados visited me and revealed itself to me more completely than it had ever done before. How true that "it is only when all portions of an individual nature or all members of society move forward harmoniously together that religious progress is calm and beneficial"l 653 I imagine the sorrowful amaze of a child who had been dwelling with delight on the idea that the stars were the pavement of heaven's court and that there above them sat the kind but holy God, looking like a venerable Father who would smile on his good little ones -- when it was cruelly told, before its mind had substance enough to bear such tension, that the sky was not real, that the stars were worlds, and that even the sun could not be God's dwelling because there were many, many suns. These ideas would introduce atheism into a child's mind, instead of assisting it to form a nobler conception of God -- (of course I am supposing the bare information given and left to the child to work upon) -- whereas the idea it previously had of God was perfectly adapted to its intellectual condition and formed to the child as perfect an embodiment of the all-good, all-wise, and all-powerful as the most enlightened philosopher ever formed to himself.
Thou wast very good for writing to me so soon. I have no doubt that your having gone home at the call of all sorts of heavenly voices will be a source of satisfaction to you. 654
Mr. Bray will carry to London Dr. Brabant's Spinoza. Will you be so kind as to send it forward to Devizes, paying the carriage, for which Mr. B. will settle with you.
Best love to Mrs. Hennell.
Thy
Meine.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 18 December 1845]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Thursday Evening.
My dear Sara,
It was pleasant to see a little scrap from you this morning as a proof that you are safe at Clapton. 586 I am not writing to-night out of affection, though there is good store of it prompting thoughts of you many times in the day. I am writing to tell you how vexed I am to see the indistinctness of the Greek in the proof. It makes my eyes ache to look at it, and if it be equally faint in the final impression I think it must be considered a great defect in the getting up of the work. Look for example at p. 371 in the proof of to-day. 587 One had need be Alexis 588 to read it. It may be owing to some cause which is removed in striking off the sheets, for I observe a good many faint places in the English. If not, do make a fuss about it, for it seems to me a very important point.
Not a word more to throw at a dog. So said Rosalind to Celia and so says one to thee, who loves thee as well as Rosalind did her Coz -- 589

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 15? March 1843]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 15? March 1843]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 1843. Extract published: Cross, 1, 117-118.
My dearest Friend,
You had my sympathy before you asked for it, and you have a large share of my thoughts. 478 You are right in believing that experience has taught me to understand your trial and I know that in the present stage of grief your comfort must come to you from within and not from without -- all the eloquence of friendship reaches no farther than the ear. Let feeling have its course, and there will not fail to be seen a green tract of peaceful joy after the streams of sorrow. We always find that our stock of appreciated good can never be really diminished. When the chief desire of the eyes is taken, we can afford a gaze to hitherto unnoticed possessions, and even when the topmost boughs are lopped a thousand shoots spring from below with the energy of new life. So it will be with you, but you cannot yet look beyond the present, nor it is desirable that you should. It would not be well for us to overleap one grade of joy or suffering -- our life would lose its completeness and beauty.
I am afraid of writing for I know not what may have occurred since yesterday. Only let me remind you of the single duty you are apt to forget -- care of yourself for the sake of others. I wish I could be helpful to you, and I long for a time when I can prove by more than words that I am wholly yours.
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 14? September 1846]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 14? September 1846]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. Hitherto unpublished.
Dearly beloved spouse,
Thou art a good one for writing me a wee note so soon. I have seen your letter to Cara too, and now I am ever and anon with you in spirit, sitting by the little table in your own room, or lying on the couch enjoying these beautiful autumn days. That dear unmanageable male unit in our quaternian has been so ill that I have thought of nothing but Cara and him for the last three or four days. 632 He is getting better I hope -- I am going to spend the day with them for the sake of reading to him when he can bear it.
Take care of yourself my precious friend and keep up the fat you gained at Rosehill. 633 If you do not soon reappear, there will be nothing for you but the slightest possible residuum of Mr. Jenkins. 634 He is fast getting rid of the mortal coil that envelops his subtler essence, and if you do not make haste back, he will slip through the keyhole of your room and hover about you as your guardian angel. Love to Mrs. Hennell. Write me again.
Thy
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 14 April 1848]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 14 April 1848]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 14. Extracts published: Cross, I, 185-186.
My dear Sara
I am a miserable wretch with aching limbs and sinking spirits, but still alive enough to feel the kindness of your last note. I thoroughly enjoyed your delight in Emerson. 722 I should have liked to see you sitting by him [with awful eye] for once in your life feeling all the bliss of veneration. I am quite uncertain about our movements. Dear Father gets on very slowly, if at all. Whether we shall be able to set out on Monday I do not know, still less how soon we may be on our return. You will understand all this, and the impossibility of my forming any plans for my own pleasure. A day will come when my head will be clearer and my heart lighter, and then I will write to you again. Rest is the only thing I can think of with pleasure now. Love to Mrs. Hennell. Even writing this makes my head swing.
Your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 13 June 1845]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 13 June 1845]
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, 1, 132-133.
My dear Sara,
I have just been looking over some of the revise and reading again your sweet letter to me from Hastings, and an impulse of gratitude and love will not let me rest without writing you a little note though my head has almost done its possible for the day under this intense heat. You do not guess how much pleasure it gives me to look over your pencillings -- they prove so clearly that you have really entered into the meaning of every sentence, and it always gives one satisfaction to see the evidence of brain work. I am quite indebted to you for your care and I feel greatly the advantage of having a friend to undertake the office of critic. There is one word I must mention, -- Azazel is the word put in the original of the O.T. for the scape-goat. 570 Now I imagine there is some dubiousness about the meaning and that Strauss would not think it right to translate scape-goat, because from the tenor of his sentence he appears to include Azazel with the evil demons. I wonder if it be supposed by any one that Azazel is in any way a distinct being from the goat. I know no Hebrew Scholar, and have access to no Hebrew Lexicon. Have you asked Mr. Hennell about it?
It was sadly disappointing to me to have no more quiet intercourse with you in London 571 -- but we shall find time. Your letter describes what I have felt rather than what I feel. It seems as if my affections were quietly sinking down to temperate and I every day seem more and more to value thought rather than feeling. I do not think this is man's best estate, but it is better than what I have sometimes known.
Where do you think we, i.e. Mr. and Mrs. Bray and I, went last night, wishing that you were with us? To Birmingham to see Macready act Brutus! 572 I was not disappointed on the whole, and it was a real treat, notwithstanding a ranting Cassius and a fat, stumpy Caesar and a screeching Calpurnia. I am coughing myself into such heats that I cannot write any more. Ever, dear Sara,
Your affectionate
Pollian.
Friday.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Foleshill, 12? April 1846]
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, I, 140-141.
Beloved Achates,
I have been guilty of the most unpardonable piece of carelessness for which I am stretched on a rack of anxiety and mortification. In the proof (the one which begins p. 385) that came on Thursday I unwittingly drew out a 'bc sheet with the blotting paper, and did not discover the mistake until Saturday morning when about to correct the last proof. Surely the printer would discover the absence of the four pages and wait for them -- otherwise I would rather have lost one of my toes 612 or all the hair from my head than have committed such a faux pas. For there were three very awkward blunders to be corrected. Maintaining had been put for maintains, making nonsense of a whole sentence -- in for is in an important passage -- and later theologians instead of the latter theologian which is worse than all because it would be taken for a mistranslation instead of a misprint. 613 All this vexation makes a cold and headache doubly intolerable and I am in a most purgatorial state on this "good Sunday." 614 I shall send the proofs with the unfortunate 'bc sheet and an explanation to-night to Mr. C. 615 -- and prithee do thou inquire and see that the right thing is done. It is all right anent the volumes.
The tears are streaming from my smarting eyes, so fare well.
Thine entirely
Pollian.
Sunday.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Edinburgh, 12 October 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oc. 12. Extract published: Cross, I, 294.
My dear Sara
I am in your debt I don't know how many letters deep, and I cannot ever say, [Have patience with me and I will pay thee all] 201 -- I can only ask for full and free forgiveness. Of course all the letters I send to Rosehill are addressed to you as much as to the others, but I feel that your share in the weekly dispatches to me often demand a special answer, and if my pen were as ready as my thought, you would often have such an answer.
We shall soon be face to face and not talking to each other through letters darkly, so I reserve all I have to say till then. Glad, however, that you liked the article on the Ox[ford] Com[missio]n. Froude himself had the good taste to strike out the Boanerges passage at the end. 202 Those who know the article on Whewell to be Mill's generally think it good, but I confess that to me it is unsatisfactory.
The sun does shine here, albeit this is the 12th of October. I wish you could see the view from Salisbury Crag!
Your loving and longing-to-see-you
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [East Sheen], 17 June 1855
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
June 17. 55.
Dear Sara
Have you heard any news about your Essay yet? And what else of your doings and leavings undone? It seems to me a long time since I had a word from you, and I don't know whether you want to hear from me.
I send you an autograph of Bulwer's which I think you will like. That of Varnhagen was not so contemptible as it looked for it shews a perfect German handwriting. He always writes just in that way, and I would send you a copy of verses he wrote for me, only that it would be a slight to his memory if I gave them away.
Are you enjoying summer and the lawn and the bearskin, as usual? -- Without an inundation of visitors? Always, dear Sara
Your affectionate
Marian.
I write the news for all in the letter to Mr. Bray.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [East Sheen, 28 July 1855]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [East Sheen, 28 July 1855]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 28th 1855. Hitherto unpublished.
Saturday.
Dear Sara
You did me good by telling me about that journey to the Crystal Palace. But I know that fine natures take their finest actions as a matter of course and like no fuss made about them. So I shall say no more.
Indeed, I did not in the slightest degree admire the advertisement of the National. 620 It was too transparent a piece of malignity to be clever. Pity a conscientious newspaper critic! Imagine yourself with three or four quarterly reviews and as many magazines to give a judgment on in one week and with a real anxiety in your mind to say nothing unfair. Then after you have deprived yourself of other reading in order to be able to speak of these reviews with adequate knowledge, imagine one editor telling you that you have taken no notice of the best article -- another writing to say that you have praised one quarterly (not his) far too highly and that in his opinion it is very dull -- while a third impales you in an advertisement. And all this after you have avoided saying all the good you think of your friends, and all the evil you think of your non-friends, lest you should be unconsciously biassed by the personal.
Mr. Lewes is totally indifferent to such things but I am thinner skinned and feel for him.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [East Sheen, 13 September 1855]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. 1855. Hitherto unpublished.
Thursday.
Dear Sara
Thanks, late and brief, for your letter which came the other day with Cara's. I am so preoccupied with finishing work and with prospective ideas of packing and removal that I can write no letter worth having. However, as you are interested in Herbert Spencer, it will perhaps be worth knowing to you that we have heard good news of him. He writes us word that his health is already much improved by his stay at Tr'e9port, a place on the coast, and he wants us to meet him in Paris next month. But neither our inclination nor our pocket says yes, so we content ourselves with not seeing either him or the Exhibition, 628 and shall go to seek polyps and health at Worthing.
I wonder if Frank 629 is yet come to you, and if you are all rested from your visit. I was sorry to miss you that last day that you called. Our walk had beguiled us further than usual -- indeed I think it was the day we had a boat on the Thames and were obstinately resisted on our return by the spring tides which, as the Boatman said, "tries a fellow, them does."
The smallest detail about you thankfully received by
Your affectionate friend
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Coventry, 26 March 1850]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Coventry, 26 March 1850]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 1850. Extract published: Cross, 1, 251.
Dear Sara
No -- I am not in England -- I am only nearer to the beings I love best. I try to forget all geography and that I have placed myself irretrievably out of reach of nature's brightest glories and beauties to shiver in a wintry flat. I am unspeakably grateful to find these dear creatures 892 looking well and happy in spite of worldly cares, but your dear face and voice are wanting to me. But I must wait with patience and perhaps by the time I have finished my visits to my relations, you will be ready to come to Rose Hill again. I want you, dear, to scold me and make me good. I am idle and naughty -- on ne peut plus -- sinking into heathenish ignorance and woman's frivolity -- remember you are one of my guardian angels.
Will you send me word of the address of the gentleman who has a collection of Turner's pictures which he opens weekly to the public? 893 I want M. D'Albert to see it. I mean the collection from which you stole my soap-bubbles. I was ill in London after our rough passage from Calais, and unable to move from the Hotel -- I should have thought my sickness much harder to bear if I had known there was a possibility of seeing you and going to Mr. Chapman's. More next time
From your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Berlin, 22 November 1854]
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell, [Berlin, 22 November 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sara. 1854. Extract published: George Eliot and John Chapman, pp. 84-85.
My dear Sara
I have kissed the pretty little white S. 556 again and again and shall put it in a sacred place. Thank you for it, and for the noble, affectionate words in your previous letter, which I fear my answer did not shew me fully to appreciate. But I assure you they had their due effect and are kept in my memory amongst my most precious things.
Of course I wrote Miss Hennell and not Mrs., but I am nevertheless indebted to the latter for the trouble she took. I am very glad you liked the article on Mde. de Sabl'e9. Mr. Lewes thought very highly of it, and so did some other good judges, but I feared that Mr. Chapman did not approve it, as he has said no word of satisfaction about it, and though he had been urgent on me to write for the Review before, he has made no proposition to that effect since. I have not seen the Westminster, but Mr. Lewes has seen it at the Library here. He told me about the notice of Feuerbach, which appears to be rather stultifying to Mr. Ch. as publisher of the Series. I am very sorry for Mr. Ch. Whatever may have been his mistakes I think he must have been hardly used by Dr. Hodgson and J. Martineau. But I am acquainted with no details.
There is an article in the Edinburgh by Herbert Spencer -- "Railway Morals and Legislation" 557 -- which I think you would like to see. I had a nice long letter from him the other day, telling me all about his late travels. 558 Imagine his indignation when, in reply to his entreaty to be corrected when he made mistakes in French, he was told that he made no mistakes!
We are going to the theatre tonight to see Emilia Galotti. 559 Dessoir, 560 the actor, presents us with tickets whenever there is an interesting representation. Last evening we went to Gruppe's, 561 and had a peep into the int'e9rieur of a German Professor of very moderate income. The simplicity with which people receive their friends here is delightful. No agonies about appearances, no grand dinners and suppers, but instead of them heartiness and intelligence.
I should be very glad to have my pen employed in something that would yield immediate profit, and there are plenty of subjects suggested by new German books which would be fresh and instructive in an English Review. But I cannot bring myself to run the risk of a refusal from an editor. Indeed I cannot for several reasons make any proposition at present. So I am working at what will ultimately yield something which is secured by agreement with Bohn. 562
Ever your loving
Marian.

558 Spencer spent August at Tr 'e9port  on the French coast and some time in Paris and Jersey. GE received his letter 16 November 1854 and answered it the 21st. (Journal.)
559 Lessing's tragedy was first produced  in 1772.
560 Ludwig Dessoir (1809-74) became  a leading actor of the Berlin Court Theater in 1849, playing many Shakespearean parts. He had been in London with the German company at the St. James's Theater in July 1853, but GHL, who mentioned him not uncritically in his reviews, had probably not met him at that time.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Sara Sophia Hennell and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 6 October 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Sara Sophia Hennell and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Sara Sophia Hennell and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 6 October 1861
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1861. Extract published: Cross, II, 317.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
October 6. 1861.
Dear Sara and Cara
It is at least half as good as the sea-breezes, to know that you are both enjoying them. And we must be content with that good, for the journey to Penmaemawr is too formidable to be undertaken at the end of all the other journies we have made this year. Else, I should have liked it very much -- mountains, methodists and all -- but chiefly the opportunity of being with you both in a freedom for quiet intercourse which cannot often recur. I am glad to have the vision of Penmaemawr as it is, so that I can imagine a very probable picture, with your two dear little figures, each with a well-known walk, making brief foot marks on the fine stretch of sand.
'abThat is very good news about Mr. and Mrs. Call. It seems very sad to me that a love like that between [Rufa] 850 and you should be nearly severed, and I should like to know whether you and she are knit together again.'bb There is a point of disgust or discovery of discordant principle which one feels must make a full stop, and call for a Finis in friendship or acquaintanceship -- and yet I have often felt the superiority of a large tolerance which will hardly allow any ground for complete alienation from the once known and once loved, and am a little uneasy at any breach which is voluntary on my own part.
We are enjoying a great, great pleasure -- a new grand piano; 851 and last evening we had a Beethoven night. 852 We are looking out for a violinist: we have our violoncello, 853 who is full of sensibility, but with no negative in him -- i.e. no obstinate sense of time: a man who is all assent and perpetual rallentando. -- We can enjoy the pleasure the more, because Mr. Lewes's health is promising. He has a pull with the oars for an hour every day now, and finds that variety of muscular exertion rapidly invigorating.
Send me word when you get home, and tell how you feel braced and cheered for the coming winter. Always
Your affectionate
Marian.

GE to Samuel Laurence, London, 8 April 1861
MS: Yale. Endorsed: George Elliot. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
April 8. 61.
My dear Sir
I have mentioned to Mr. Lewes your wish to exhibit my portrait at the Royal Academy, and he has stated to me -- what he had not stated before -- namely, his reasons for originally stipulating with you that the portrait should not be exhibited, or exposed to the risk of being copied. These reasons are entirely unconnected with you, or with the character of the likeness: they would apply to any portrait of me, by any artist whatever, and they are reasons which, now that he has fully stated them to me, I feel to be as strong as they appear to him.
I must therefore decline to give my consent that my portrait should be exhibited anywhere beyond the doors of your own atelier. 735 I remain, my dear Sir
Yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
Samuel Lawrence Esq.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Samuel Evans, Griff, 26 February 1840
Dublin Core:Subject: Samuel Evans^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Samuel Evans, Griff, 26 February 1840
MS: Yale. Address: Mr. S. Evans | The Mill Houses | Wirksworth | Derbyshire. Postmark: Illegible. Hitherto unpublished.
Griff February 26th 1840.
My dear Uncle,
I beg you will not consider my tardiness in answering your kind letter a representation of my feelings towards you and my Aunt; these would have led me much earlier to tell you how welcome news of you was to me and my Father, but circumstances have so occupied my body and mind that I have not before been at liberty to write to you. I grieve for my dear Aunt's illness more on your account than on her own, for a spirit so well fortified as hers will sustain bodily infirmity, and even enable her to glory in that tribulation which is calculated to work an increase of patience, experience and hope. Yet I should rejoice to know that her weak frame has ceased for the present to be tried by pain and exhaustion, and that she is able to be again your cheerful companion, busying herself as usual for the good of souls.
Why do you suspect me, my dear Uncle of being inclined to blame the self-denying exertions of one whom I ought to yearn to imitate, in spirit at least, if not in the particular practices by which that spirit discovers itself?
Death appears to have made sad breeches in your circle of Christian friends. Mrs. Joinson 169 looked like a very healthy person when at Griff, to human observation unlikely so soon to be summoned. The little intercourse I had with her gave me such an idea of her character as led me to expect that her end would be peace.
I am very glad Mary is so comfortably situated and almost within an easy walk to you. I hope Elizabeth 170 is well and happy. My dear
Father is quite as well as usual and desires me to send you his love. I cannot give you a hopeful account of my spiritual state, for of late I have been much exposed to temptation from contact with worldly persons, and that traitor within, the love of human praise, has opened the door to too many compliances with what is likely to make me less hungry for heavenly blessings, by enabling me to derive a temporary enjoyment from what is merely earthly. I have great need of your prayers, and I fear not that I shall be denied them. We had your letter after the receipt of the box. To my dear Aunt and yourself I offer my kindest love and thanks for your remembrance of me. May it continue and soon be moved to do so by sending me another letter. With love to my Cousins I am, my dear Uncle,
Your sincerely affectionate
Mary Ann Evans.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Samuel Evans, Griff, 10 August 1840
Dublin Core:Subject: Samuel Evans^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Samuel Evans, Griff, 10 August 1840
MS: Yale. Address: Mr. Evans | Mill Houses | Wirksworth | Derbyshire. Postmark: Illegible. Mostly published: W. Mottram, The True Story of George Eliot in Relation to "Adam Bede," 1905, pp. 133-134.
Griff August 10th 1840.
My dear Uncle,
Remembering the Apostle's declaration that "to be absent from the body is (for redeemed souls) to be present with the Lord," 235 I cannot for her own sake regret that my dear Aunt is so near the very brink of Jordan; 236 I would only pray that her Heavenly Father may, out of His tender consideration for His creatures, who "are but dust," lighten her weight of bodily suffering as far as may consist with His designs of mercy to her soul. Give to my dear Aunt if she should be able to receive it an assurance from me of my warm affection for her, and tell her I humbly resolve in the strength of the Lord to "seek his face evermore," that we may sing together a new song before His throne. For you, my dear Uncle, both my Father and myself truly feel, and I have endeavoured to pray that you may be powerfully sustained under a trial that will indeed bereave you of one who has been as the apple of your eye; but is it not to this end? "That God may be all in all" with you, and that having no earthly prop, you may walk entirely by faith? My Father bids me give his love to you, and tell you that you are passing through what he has already experienced.
We are glad that my Uncle William 237 is able to be at hand to offer you comfort. I trust his health is at least as good as when we were with him. The books belonging to my Aunt which she kindly lent me, I will send the next time I write, as I wish this letter to reach you as soon as possible. It will be a satisfaction to me to hear of your state, and probably one of my cousins will be so good as to write me word concerning you, should you feel unequal to the task. I doubt not, my dear Uncle, that you will evidence the possession of what belongs only to the Christian, "joy in tribulation," and that you will thus glorify the Lord God of Israel even in the fires. Truly the commandments of God are not grievous, for the Apostle sums them up by a "Rejoice in the Lord, and again I say rejoice," and though this may seem a great difficulty when the heart is bowed down and rent in twain by the loss of our earthly gourds, in reality that is the very time when we can best relish the waters that make glad the city of God. "Trials make the promise sweet," such promises as these, "To him that overcometh will I grant to sit on my throne," and "the Lamb that is before the throne shall feed them, and God himself shall wipe away all tears from their eyes."
I am fearful of not being ready for the post so I must say good bye.
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Samuel Evans, Foleshill, 2 October 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Samuel Evans^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Samuel Evans, Foleshill, 2 October 1841
MS: Yale. Address: Mr. Evans | The Mill Houses | Wirksworth | Derbyshire. Postmarks: COVENTRY | OC 2 | 1841. WIRKSWORTH | OC | 1841. Hitherto unpublished.
Foleshill October 2d 1841.
My very dear Uncle,
I have quite enjoyed your letter, and am determined to prove that I have done so by writing in return immediately. I had been for some time expecting to hear from you, and should have done so by my Father, who intended to visit you the last time he was in Derbyshire but that he was detained at Hallam by the election. I am glad to hear a good account of my Aunt's health, and to conclude from your silence about your own that you are free from your old enemy, the rheumatism. I am thankful to tell you that my Father is quite well and appears very comfortable under his change of situation, indeed I feel the ordering of our outward circumstances a special call for gratitude.
My Brother Isaac about whom you kindly enquire seems to have a very suitable partner as far as similarity of taste and domestic habits are concerned, and I think we have reason to hope for his worldly prosperity. You justly observe, my dear Uncle, that this alone is insufficient to give peace. I feel increasingly that nothing but the enjoyment of God's favour, walking in the light of His countenance, and daily progressing in fitness for His presence and the companionship of the saints in light, can give real satisfaction. Our earthly friends disappoint us and often wound us by coldness, and there is in every cup enough of bitterness to make him who drinks it feel the need of patience, faith, and hope.
You ask me about my own state and express a hope that I am running the way of God's commandments. I must answer that I am often, very often stumbling, but I have been encouraged to believe that the mode of action most acceptable to God, is not to sit still desponding, but to rise and pursue my way. I have often occasion to use David's words, "I have gone astray like a lost sheep, yet seek thy servant for I do not forget thy commandments." 369 He who condescends to seek the lost, will not I trust cast them away from his presence when they go to him in the spirit of Job. "What I know not teach Thou me; if I have done iniquity, I will do so no more." 370
I shall look forward to a letter from my dear Aunt, and pray tell her that if there is anything which it is in my power to send her that will be of any use I shall be pleased if she will mention it. We had not heard from my Uncle William of his recent attack although my Brother Robert has just been with us. Pray give my love to my Cousins and tell Samuel and Mary that I hope their little Joseph will prove as rich a treasure as he after whom they have named him. We are not greatly favoured in our Minister 371 -- though we hear the truth, yet it is not recommended by the mode of its delivery. But there may be as much profit reaped by humble endeavours to derive good under disadvantages, as from the highest privileges, and I would rather narrowly examine my own state of feeling than complain of the lack of outward helps. With my best love to Aunt, believe me my dear Uncle
Your affectionate Niece
Mary Ann Evans.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Roland Stuart, Earlswood Common, 21 July 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Roland Stuart^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Roland Stuart, Earlswood Common, 21 July 1874
MS: British Museum. Envelope: Master Roland Stuart | Tobermory | Mull | Scotland. Postmarks: PR | LONDON | 21 JY | 74; OBAN | D | JY 22 | 74; [TO]BERMORY | JY 23 | 1874. Published: Stuart, pp. 23-24.
The Cottage | Earlswood Cn. | July 21. 74.
My dear Roland
Thanks! you are a brave fellow for sending me your Mother's photo, 131 and have given me real pleasure. The likeness is as good as I can imagine any likeness to be. So if you get the shepherd's crook laid about your back for your pretty action, you will bear it the better because you know that you not only had the good motive of giving pleasure, but were successful in giving it.
I hope you are sharing our splendid sunshine amidst your fine scenery, and enjoying your holiday to the utmost. I wonder which is the merrier of the two -- you or your Mother? Please tell that dear Mother that I was very grateful to her for remembering my wish to have a photo of your profile, which I think represents you better than the front face.
You know, you are my adopted grandson, and I am concerned that you should be handsome in all ways -- chiefly in that best way of doing handsomely, as the heroic Roland of these times. Are you practising the winding of the horn among the mountains, so that you may not be behind your predecessor and great namesake in that accomplishment?
We ate the delicious Dinan Cake as if we had been youngsters, though in fact we are aged and, just now, rather ailing. But in all other respects -- pray tell my dear daughter with my love -- we are thoroughly happy and are constantly bearing her in mind and heart.
Mr. Lewes sends his love to you, and I am always, dear Roland,
Your affectionate Friend
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Robert Lytton, London, 26 September 1870
Dublin Core:Subject: Robert Lyt^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Robert Lytton, London, 26 September 1870
MS: Lady Hermione Cobbold.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 26. 70.
Dear Mr. Lytton
The photographs are lovely, and I am grateful. But my gratitude includes some anticipation. I think Mrs. Lytton promised me the complete group -- parents as well as children. Still I should not like to be troublesome, so you must let the fulfilment of the pretty promise depend on your convenience.
I am getting more and more gloomy about the War. It seems as if every one were getting the worse for it (I mean morally worse), spectators as well as agents. In my intense dislike of vague blame, it is always a satisfaction to me when any one will speak who (like Sir Henry Bulwer) 930 is practically acquainted with affairs. If you were here I should ask you whether there is any real authority, any evidence beyond Parisian conceptions for the statement that the other neutral Powers hold back from recognition of the French Republic because they wait for England to take the initiative. I find excellent people, in talking of such matters, as free as savages from the need of any evidence for a statement which falls in with their dominant mood. Those who sympathize with the French believe what is discreditable to the Germans, and vice versa. This is to me the most pitiable weakness, and precisely that slavery of the judgment which it is one end of life-discipline to get rid of. To keep the temper also is an accomplishment which people are fast letting slip in this War discussion. Perhaps the aristocratic regions are more serious than the mid-air we are breathing. After all, one is glad that any public question should be a matter of general interest, and hot temper about them is better than the indifference of philistinism.
Mr. Lewes is going to Tunbridge Wells on this beautiful day to visit some friends 931 of ours who have a country paradise there. I was to have gone with him, but have been entered by a demon of tooth-ache and general misery, and am glad to hide myself from the world like a sick crab. This demon, of course, has written a muddled letter, and not allowed me to guide my own pen.
Mrs. Congreve sent me a note the day you were with us, 932 hoping that it would reach us in time for us to convey her thanks to you for the note you had sent to her.
The demon allows me to feel lovingly, though not to write clearly, and much of that lovingness goes out towards Mrs. Lytton. To her other self also I am always
His affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Robert Evans, London, 3 April 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Robert Evans^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Robert Evans, London, 3 April 1864
MS: Miss Dorothy Evans. Endorsed: "M.A. Letter to Robert on Hy's death 1864." Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 3. 64.
My dear Nephew
When your letter, telling me of a second loss in our family, 244 arrived, I was absent in Scotland, and I only read it on my return home last night. Otherwise, I should much earlier have thanked you for writing to me.
I feel sincerely grieved for your Aunt's -- my affectionately remembered Sister's -- loneliness and trouble. I only hope that her own health has been strong under the watching and anxiety she has had to sustain. Pray offer her on my behalf my love and sympathy: I understand the heaviness of separation after long years of union.
It is a vexation to me that your letter lay so long without being read by me, but I hope this will not fail to reach you, by means of a double address, and so assure you that my silence was not a neglectful one. Yours, my dear Nephew,
Very sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Robert Evans, London, 26 September 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Robert Evans^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Robert Evans, London, 26 September 1874
Text: Copy supplied by Mr. Percival R. Allen. Envelope: Robert Evans, Esq. | The Park | Nottingham. Postmarks: ST JOHNS WOOD N.W | C 3 | SP 26 | 74; NOTTINGHAM | A 3 | SP 27 | 74.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 26. 74.
My dear Nephew
I enter fully into the duteous and affectionate anxiety which prompted the letter I received from you last night, precisely on my arrival for a few days stay in town. The correspondence between me and your Aunt Fanny ceased simply by her ceasing to write to me, the last letter between us having been written by me; 254 at least, I have never since received from her the slightest sign of remembrance. Your good mother has written to me more than once, 255 but there was no word in her letters implying that your Aunt Fanny retained any affectionate regard for me. All that I have heard concerning her is this -- that some (perhaps eight or ten) years ago, she spoke of me with dislike and unkindness, on an occasion in which I think my informant could have made no mistake. But I bear my Father's memory in too deep reverence willingly to dwell on anything painful in the conduct of those who were near to him; also I feel grateful for all goodness shown to me in my childhood and youth, and I have entertained only kind and admiring recollections of my sister.
But from the delicacy manifested in your letter I feel sure you will understand me when I tell you that during the seventeen years in which I have heard nothing from your Aunt Fanny, my connexions and duties, with consequent claims on my time and effort, have been continually multiplying. My strength, never quite equal to the demands upon it, naturally diminishes rather than increases with the increase of those demands, and I am constantly obliged not only to decline invitations but to escape from the pressure of visits and correspondence by retreating into the country out of the reach of all but the most intimate friends. I fear it is too late, my dear Nephew, for your Aunt Fanny and me to meet again. I cannot sustain agitating renewals of past relations in addition to the many social and family duties which have accumulated on me in the intervening years
Life goes on urgently, and those who willingly renounce a friendship cannot after a long lapse of years recover it at a given moment.
I have a keen recollection of all the pleasant affectionate intercourse I had with my sister in my childhood and youth, and especially I bear in mind the tenderness we felt in common for our dear Father. But I have no store of nervous energy, no superfluous time, to make it right for me to encounter the excitement of reviving those memories actively in personal meetings. I am not conscious of having ever, either by word or deed, done anything injurious to my sister, and I have a lively satisfaction in hearing from you of her comfort and welfare. But I cannot respond to your suggestion (made, I am sure, with the best sympathetic motives) that I should reopen communication with your Aunt by writing. My correspondence is very onerous to me, and I must not enlarge it in any way that does not wear the aspect of a duty.
I gather from your very kind and delicate letter that you have not spoken to your Aunt of your intention to write to me, and that your view of her desires is a matter of interpretation. I trust to your evidently good judgment to comprehend my feeling and position without a more lengthy explanation, and also to withhold everything from your Aunt Fanny which might cause her unnecessary sadness. You can assure her with truth that I bear her in sisterly remembrance.
I rejoice to hear of your happy family circumstances. The youngest who bears the dear name "Robert Evans" 256 will I trust, grow up to be a comfort and delight to you. Pray offer my best regards to your Mother when you have an opportunity of doing so. I was deeply touched by that last (I think it was the last) letter of hers to me in which she gave me an account of your Father's death, and I always bear in tender remembrance his uniform brotherly goodness to me.
Believe me, my dear Nephew,
Your sincerely well-wishing Aunt
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Robert Evans, London, 2 February 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Robert Evans^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Robert Evans, London, 2 February 1864
MS: Miss Dorothy Evans, who supplied the text. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 2. 1864.
My dear Nephew
I am much obliged to you for your kind attention in writing to let me know of your dear Father's death.
I share in your sorrow both for the loss and the long and severe suffering which went before. It is a sorrow which I have strong reason to share, for all my memories of your Father were those of unbroken kindness and generous brotherliness on his part towards me. I should like very much to write to your Mother, but I have unfortunately lost her address. Will you offer to her for me my best love and sympathy, and assure her of my deep interest in all that concerns her? If she were ever to come to London, I hope she would let me have the great pleasure of taking her by the hand again. Always
Yours very sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
Robert Evans Esq.
