Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, 3 December 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, 3 December 1877
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, III, 322-323.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 3. 77.
Dearest Mignon
I have been made rather unhappy by my husband's impulsive proposal about Christmas. We are dull old persons, and your two sweet young ones ought to find each Christmas a new bright bead to string on their memory, whereas to spend the time with us would be to string on a dark shrivelled berry. They ought to have a group of young creatures to be joyful with. Our own children always spend their Christmas with Gertrude's family, and we have usually taken our sober merrymaking with friends out of town. Illness among these will break our custom this year, 789 and thus [mein Mann] feeling that our Christmas was free, considered how very much he liked being with you, omitting the other side of the question -- namely, our total lack of means to make a suitably joyous meeting, a real festival, for Phil and Margaret. I was conscious of this lack in the very moment of the proposal, and the consciousness has been pressing on me more and more painfully ever since. Even my husband's affectionate hopefulness cannot withstand my melancholy demonstration.
So pray consider the kill-joy proposition as entirely retracted, and give us something of yourselves only on simple black letter days when the Herald Angels have not been raising expectations early in the morning. I have been putting off too long the writing of this true deliverance, and I feel that to defer what I have to say till Friday for the chance of seeing you then might leave your mind inconveniently hampered with considerations about an arrangement with us.
I am not afraid of your misunderstanding one word. You know that it is not a little love with which I am
Yours ever
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, 28 April 1877
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 28. 77.
Dearest Mignon
To have a loving note from you is the next best thing to seeing you. We both felt it good to have you here 654 in that distant past before I had an attack of Influenza which has stretched out the ten days into a purgatorial period. However, I am better now, and disposed to think that your troubles with your maidens are the stronger appeal to sympathy.
If the Lindsays 655 had not happened to send us tickets for the private view, we should have been most grateful for those you offer us, but now we are supplied.
I wonder what I ought to have for a morning dress to wear at breakfasts and walk out in on visits at Oxford and Cambridge. I have just had a black silk, of the robe species, such as I humbly trust you would approve, for my dinner dress. But I want something less heavy and dust-showing for the day-time. I like plain silk better than anything, but it is hard to get the right colour. These remarks are to give you a faint idea of my heavy private anxieties -- not to urge you into taking the trouble to write me advice.
Our best love to both.
[Signature cut away.]

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, 23 March 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, 23 March 1878
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 23. 78.
Dearest Mignon
Yes, please take two tickets for us. 35 I promised this to Dr. Payne last Sunday. And Mr. Lewes will occupy his place in the flesh. I would beseech you to come round and go with us, only I am uncertain whether we may not have to go to another place beforehand. As to my enjoyment of the Two Grenadiers, it would have been impossible, but for the complete reduction of it to symbolism in my own mind, and my belief that it really touches nobody now as enthusiasm for the execrable Napoleon I. But I feel that the devotion of the common soldier to his leader (the sign for him of hard duty) is the type of all higher devotedness, and is full of promise for other and better generations. [I don't know,] as Mr. Curdle says, [whether I make myself understood.] 36
We shall be very glad to see Mr. and Mrs. Percy Wyndham. 37 That you admire her is a warrant to me of her suiting my taste in many ways.
We are off to our spiritual Pop, and shall post this by the way. Oblige me by keeping well.
Yours ever
M. E. L.

GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, 18 November 1878
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 18. 78.
Dearest Mignon
At last we are in the old place again, but it vexes my soul a little that if you could come to see us on Friday we might not be at home till 'bd past 5, having to do parental duty in seeing our children's new house.
I am unhappy about my husband, who is grievously ailing. This anxiety spoils all joy, which would otherwise be abundant with me in spite of the world's calamities. The newspaper makes me sad one part of the day, but I recover myself and find the air sweet nevertheless. I suppose nobody ever committed suicide because the world was full of suffering, unless he felt the fact through some misery of his own.
Love to all from
Yours always
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, 13 June 1870
MS: Yale. Envelope: Mrs. Burne Jones | The Grange | North End | Fulham S.W. Postmarks: LONDON-N. | 2 | JU 13 | 70; LONDON-S.W | GP | JU 13 | 70. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 13. 70.
Dear Friend
You will cease to think me worth caring for, since all the signs of regard that I give you are unverified words. We are driven away from town again before I have had an opportunity of getting to you as I longed to do. The cause of this second flight is the return of Mr. Lewes's nervous exhaustion. Dr. Reynolds is so far comforting in his opinion, 195 that he declares the symptoms to be those of mere weakness, and recommends bracing air and rest from brain-work as sufficient remedies. We must not grumble at being driven from home in this world of the many homeless. But I would willingly have been stationary till August.
We are to start for Cromer on Wednesday or Thursday. After Cromer, we shall probably choose Whitby, and we shall keep away from London till about the end of July. Then we shall have a peep at our home again, before going to our favourite spot in Surrey. This programme is of no value to you, but I give it because if Fate should send you and the children to the Yorkshire coast and precisely to Whitby, it would be worth while for me if not for you, that you should inquire for me at the P.O. Goodby, dear Friend. The thought of you is much cherished by
Yours affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, 11 May 1875
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, III, 257-258.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 11. 75.
Dearest Mignon
The doctors have decided that there is nothing very grave the matter with me, 244 and I am now so much better that we even think it possible I may go to see Salvini in the Gladiator tomorrow evening. 245 This is to let you know that there is no reason against your coming, with or without Margaret, at the usual time on Friday. 246
Your words of affection in the note you sent me are very dear to my remembrance. I like not only to be loved but also to be told that I am loved. I am not sure that you are of the same mind. But the realm of silence is large enough beyond the grave. This is the world of light and speech, and I shall take leave to tell you that you are very dear to
Your faithfully affectionate
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, London, [14 June 1870]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 14. 1870. Envelope: Mrs. Burne Jones | The Grange | North End, Fulham | S.W. Postmarks: LONDON-N.W | 5 | JU 14 | 70; LONDON-S.W | JU 14 | 70. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday.
Dear Friend
Since I have to sit down to my desk to write other letters, I must indulge myself with saying to you that my words and looks 200 about your coming to Whitby could not have been so cordial as my thoughts, because my face and tongue had on them more weariness from packing than had reached my heart. It will be a real joy to have you and the chicks at Whitby, and I am thinking with delight that you will learn something of my husband's goodness, by seeing him more constantly. I am the Lady Theory, and he is the good Knight Sir Practice, with respect to all sweet virtues.
You must think that I am a terrifically moralizing preaching woman, to keep you at the gate 'e0 propos de bottes, 201 or of a woman whom you don't know, who is therefore still more irrelevant than those familiar boots which have been everybody's starting point. But you will find me anything but too moral on a nearer view, and will rather find yourself in the position of a missionary sent to me, an old sinner at Whitby. At all events come, dear, and you will come to your warm friends.
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, Harrogate, 10 July 1870
MS: Yale. Envelope: Mrs. Burne Jones | The Grange | North End | Fulham | London S.W. Postmarks: HARROGATE | A | JY 10 | 70; LONDON-S.W | K7 | JY 11 | 70. Hitherto unpublished.
Brunswick Terrace | Harrogate | July 10. 70.
Dear Friend
It is now settled that we are to leave this place and go on to Whitby on the 18th. I send you word at once on the decision being made, lest we should lose any chance of having you there, by narrowing your time for resolve or preparation. If nothing has arisen to alter that pretty disposition of yours which made you wish to be where we should be, please ask for our address at the post office when you come, or, if your arrival should precede ours, leave your own address there in readiness for our inquiry.
I am in excellent spirits about Mr. Lewes. Our coming hither has answered gloriously, and he gains strength every day. But the waters are so strongly tonic that it will not be prudent to continue taking them longer than a fortnight, and Whitby will be a desirable change for him. I need say no more now, than that I shall count on seeing those sweet eyes of yours soon after our arrival, unless you write to tell me that something untoward has happened to hinder that pleasure from befalling me. In haste
Always yours affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, Earlswood Common, 3 August 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, Earlswood Common, 3 August 1874
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 239.
The Cottage | Earlswood Common | August 3. 74.
Dearest Georgie
It was sweet of you to write me that nice long letter. I was athirst for some news of you, and though what you send me is not perfectly good, one has learned to be thankful for sma' mercies in this world of dreadful possibilities. That the children are well and a joy to you both, that your health has not quite broken down (of which I had some fear, remembering the terrible fluttering of your heart), and that there is this hopeful journey to Naworth in prospect, is altogether a store of "better-than-might-be's" which make my mind much easier about you than it was in its former ignorance. Life, as you say, is a big thing. No wonder there comes a season when we cease to look round and say "how shall I enjoy?," but as in a country which has been visited by the sword, pestilence, and famine, think only how we shall help the wounded and how find seed for the next harvest -- how till the earth and make a little time of gladness for those who are being born without their own asking.
We are as usual getting more than our share of peace and other good -- except in the matter of warmth and sunshine. Our common is a sort of ball-room for the winds, and on the warmest days we have had here we have found them at their music and dancing. They roar round the corners of our house in a wintry fashion while the sun is shining on the brown grass. Perhaps this touch of extra changefulness in the temperature from one spot to another has helped to bring on again Mr. Lewes's old dyspeptic torments. He has lost too many mornings in headachiness, but that is the only drawback we have felt on our enjoyment of walks and long drives in this lovely country.
I hear his feet, I think, coming to ask -- yes, his feet really ask me to come and walk with him.
We are not certain whether we shall stay here till the end of September, but in any case we shall not be settled at 21 N.B. until the end of October, because our house there wants cleaning, and our servants are here, so we shall have to leave them in London to brush and scour. You will not let me be without knowledge of anything good or evil beyond the everyday mark that happens to you. I am so glad of what you say about the Latin. 133 Go on conquering and to conquer 134 a little kingdom for yourself there. When one sees the foolish and the ignorant happy it is possible to doubt the good of a larger vision, but nobody ever envied narrowness of mind in misery. Always
Your loving Friend
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, Cromer, 26 June 1870
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Edward Burne-Jones, Cromer, 26 June 1870
MS: Yale. Envelope: Mrs. Burne Jones | The Grange | North End | Fulham | London. Postmarks: CROMER | JU 26 | 70; B3 | NORWICH | JU 26 | 70; LONDON-S.W | J7 | JU 27 | 70. Hitherto unpublished.
Albert House | Cromer | June 26. 70.
Dear Friend
I was meditating a letter to you, just when yours came to me, for I wanted to tell you exactly all that could be told about our future movements, so that in as far as your own movements might be determined by ours, you might not be left in an unpleasant state of conjecture. We are to leave this place on the 30th and Mr. Lewes has set his heart on going next to Harrowgate, to try the effect of the chalybeate waters there. We should only stay a fortnight there at the utmost, and possibly we may quit it much earlier for Whitby, which is still our goal. I think Mr. Lewes is a little strengthened, but this place is not inspiriting and the weather is just now very cold, so that though I am clad in woollen, I am as cold as if the woollen were my shroud. I must not depreciate Cromer, however. There are fine sands and the inland scenery has much quiet beauty. The sunsets over the sea and the absence of German bands playing out of tune are "local features of no mean order," as the Athenaeum writers would say.
Still I expect Whitby to be far more various and stimulating, and I do hope that nothing will hinder our all meeting there -- you, the bairns (and possibly the husband?) with us two grandparents. But I hope with some trembling, because of George's health, the conditions which may suit it defying all prophecy, especially with this changing climate. I shall write at once to you on the slightest change of intention, and of course I shall let you know when we have determined on the day of our departure for Whitby, always supposing that you do not set off in advance of us. You will let me know of that, will you not, dear little Epigram? And, in general, you will be faithful, and keep me well-informed about you?
I am grieved to hear that your great painter is ailing still. Tell him that friends of ours, who know Whitby, give us enthusiastic descriptions of the country round it. And they are old Fellows of Cambridge and Oxford, who are not usually vials of enthusiasm. Let us hope that we shall have a rainy week or so for the good of the country, and that afterwards we shall have sunshine for our good at Whitby. Our united love to all. Keep in mind
Yours ever faithfully
M. E. Lewes.

GE to Mrs. Edward Atkinson, London, 29 October 1877
MS: Princeton. Envelope: Mrs. Edward Atkinson | care of Mr. Edward Atkinson | 40 State Street | Boston | Mass. | U.S.A. Postmarks: ST JOHNS WOOD N.W | C 2 | OC 30 | 77; BOSTON | NOV 14 | PAID. Endorsed: Mrs. Lewes (George Eliot) Care of Messrs Blackwood & Sons, Publishers, London, England. Extract published: VI, 413-414.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 29. 77.
Dear Mrs. Atkinson 379
I remember very well the interesting party which the name [Frothingham] 380 recals to me, notwithstanding the many eventful years that now divide me from our meeting at Mr. Chapman's in the Strand. Many kind letters come to me from your side of the Atlantic which want of time and strength for unnecessary correspondence obliges me to leave unanswered, but I cannot allow you to imagine me discourteously indifferent to your friendly recollection of our interviews in old days. That you are the mother of grown-up children is one of the many reminders I am constantly receiving that the larger part of life's journey lies behind me. I trust that the waymarks with you are signs of long-continued happiness, in spite of that infirmity of the eyes to which you refer.
Of Dr. and Mrs. Chapman I rarely hear anything, and the news of his death must I imagine be mistaken, since no public announcement of it has fallen under our notice.
Your request for my photograph 381 it is impossible for me to fulfil, as I have had no such image of myself taken. Requests for autographs and photographs are too numerous for me to answer them without great discomfort, and a sacrifice of time that would hardly be warranted by the value of the result. Hence I resign myself to being pronounced rather churlish by numerous [unknown friends.]
With best wishes for you and yours, I remain, dear Mrs. Atkinson,
Sincerely yours
M. E. Lewes.

MS: The late Dr. Herman T. Radin. Envelope: Mrs. Louise R. Estes | care of Estes and Lauriat | 143 Washington Street | Boston | U.S.A. Postmarks: BOSTON | JUN | 9 | PAID; ST JOHNS WOOD N.W | 8 2 | MY 28 | 74. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 28. 74.
Dear Madam
I value very highly, and I shall bear in mind very gratefully what your letter 97 tells me of the feeling with which you regard my books and, in consequence, the unknown remainder of myself. That my work should have made any happy difference in your life is a joy to me of the kind I most care for, and the modest tone of affection which your letter breathes is very sweet to my inward ear.
We are often out of town for some months together, and the frailty of my health obliges me to limit as narrowly as I can the reception of strangers, but after your letter I will not call you a stranger, and if I am in town when you visit England I shall be much pleased to shake hands with you. But pray remember that the best of an author is, or ought to be, in his books. Believe me, dear Madam,
Yours faithfully
M. E. Lewes.
Mrs. Louise Reid Estes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Coleridge Kennard^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Coleridge Kennard, Earlswood Common, 31 August [1874]
MS: Bancroft Library, University of California Berkeley.
The Cottage | Earlswood Common | August 31.
Dear Mrs. Kennard
A thousand thanks for the trouble you have so kindly taken. Mr. Lewes had just written you a note to say that the prospect of the cloak kept my imagination in too restless a state, when the post brought your letter.
In the choice of a cloth I should have trusted to your judgment more willingly than my own. I hope you will approve my preference for the bronze which I return.
We have been all the happier for the warmth, rejoicing in the prosperity of the harvest as well as in our own bien-'eatre.
The cloak will be very welcome and in wearing it I shall often be reminded of you on your lovely background of the Riviera. I trust that the wintering in that kindly region will be propitious to the health both of yourself and your dear little girl.
Mr. Lewes has been rather ailing this last day or two, but is in better force this morning. He unites with me in best regards to you and Mr. Kennard, who, I hope, knows that we feel much obliged for the pains he took to get us acquainted with Oakfield -- a bit of knowledge which we value.
Sincerely yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Charles S. Peirce, London, 14 September 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Charles S. Peirce^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Charles S. Peirce, London, 14 September 1866
MS: Yale.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 14. 66.
My dear Madam
I do not usually answer letters unless they demand an answer, finding the days too short for much correspondence; but I am so deeply touched by your words of tenderness and by the details you tell me about yourself, that I cannot keep total silence towards you. 718
My consciousness is not of the triumphant kind your generous joy on my behalf leads you to imagine. Exultation is a dream before achievement, and rarely comes after. What comes after, is rather the sense that the work has been produced within one, like offspring, developing and growing by some force of which one's own life has only served as a vehicle, and that what is left of oneself is only a poor husk. Besides, the vision of something that life might be and that one's own ignorance and incompleteness have hindered it from being, presses more and more as time advances. The only problem for us, the only hope, is to try and unite the utmost activity with the utmost resignation. Does this seem melancholy? I think it is less melancholy than any sort of self-flattery.
I want to tell you not to fancy yourself old because you are thirty, or to regret that you have not yet written anything. It is a misfortune to many that they begin to write when they are young and give out all that is genuine and peculiar in them when it can be no better than trashy, unripe fruit. There is nothing more dreary than the life of a writer who has early exhausted himself.
I enter into those young struggles of yours to get knowledge, into the longing you feel to do something more than domestic duties while yet you are held fast by womanly necessities for neatness and household perfection as well as by the lack of bodily strength. Something of all that I have gone through myself. I have never known perfect health, and I have known what it was to have close ties making me feel the wants of others as my own and to have very little money by which these wants could be met. Before that,
I was too proud and ambitious to write: I did not believe that I could do anything fine, and I did not choose to do anything of that mediocre sort which I despised when it was done by others. I began, however, by a sort of writing which had no great glory belonging to it, but which I felt certain I could do faithfully and well. This resolve to work at what did not gratify my ambition, and to care only that I worked faithfully, was equivalent to the old phrase -- "using the means of grace." 719 Not long after that, I wrote fiction which has been thought a great deal of -- but the satisfaction I have got out of it has not been exactly that of ambition. When we are young we say, "I should be proud if I could do that." Having done it, one finds oneself the reverse of proud.
I will say no more about myself except that you must not imagine my position to be at all like Romola's. I have the best of husbands, the most sympathetic of companions; indeed, I have more than my share of love in a world where so many are pining for it. Mr. Lewes, who cares supremely for science, is interested in what you say of your husband's labours; 720 and he is so delighted when anything good or pretty comes to me that I think he is more grateful to you than I am for your generous, affectionate words. Yet I too am not insensible, but shall remain always
Yours in grateful memory
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Charles Meredith, Witley, 7 November 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Charles Meredith^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Charles Meredith, Witley, 7 November 1878
MS: Yale. Endorsed: From "George Eliot." Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
November 7. 78.
My dear Madam
I feel with you most keenly in your affliction under the sufferings of your Son, whose excellence must make the trial all the harder to you. What heroic endurance he has shown! I wish some of our complaining idle young men in this old country could have such examples impressed on them.
Your interesting contribution to Zoology shall be taken the utmost care of. We return to town next week, and Mr. Lewes will at once seek in the first instance to put the drawings and M.S. in the hands of Dr. Allman, the President of the Linnaean Society. 145 These beautiful Sabellae remind us of our old joys in hunting on the coast, when we thought it a great glory to find a specimen of a kind already familiar to the Zoological world. We shall be exceedingly glad if the Dons[?] of our Linnaean Society give you any sort of appreciation of your labour that will be a pleasure to you.
We quite understand, and sympathize with, your disappointment in having the appearance of your work so long deferred. But I trust that there will by and by be some good results which will not come "too late." We are very near Christmas now, and are at the beginning of the busy season for book-selling -- if in this sad time of wars and trade-depression we can count on any briskness of sale. It is comforting amidst the sad news that fill our papers to get signs from you of good works going on in your newer society. What an antithesis the tenderness to animals which is a mark of our times, presents to the persistence in war and the apparent hopelessness that it will be even reduced for the next generation!
Believe me, dear Madam,
Yours very sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
Mrs. Meredith.

GE to Mrs. Charles Lee Lewes, London, 5 July [1867]
MS: Mrs. Carrington Ouvry. Endorsed: /67. Published: Paterson, pp. 128-129.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
July 5.
Dearest Chick
Your letter dated July 1 has just come to me. Pater says "Yes" about the window, but also says, "Of course no step of that sort must be taken until there is certainty about the lodgings."
I had it in my mind to make a bundle of clothes and carry them to you as soon as I could on my return. As I employ Eliza 641 to work for me and help her in that way, it will perhaps be better not to complicate our relations by gifts, and to let those go entirely through your sisters. I have two good dresses which may go to the Bains.
We are enchanted with Niton, and like our good Mrs. Newnham and her cream very much. It is not at all warm here, but the weather is on the whole good.
You are quite right, dear about the translation. 642 It would have been injudicious for Charley to be making himself intimate with foreign idioms just when he is wanting to improve his English.
Best love to the dear older generation. 643 We were talking of them and their virtues at breakfast this morning. So they can reflect, if they will that the good of their lives reaches all the way to Niton.
Pater joins in all love. In haste, dearest child,
Your loving
Mutter.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Gertrude [Mrs. Charles Lee]Lewes, London, 21 December [1865]
Dublin Core:Subject: Gertrude [Mrs. Charles Lee] Lewes^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Gertrude [Mrs. Charles Lee] Lewes, London, 21 December [1865]
MS: Mrs. Edward Hanson. Address: Mrs. Charles Lewes. Endorsed: 1865. Published: Paterson, pp. 118-119.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 21.
Dearest Gertrude
Ever since our Pearl promised me the frieze, 395 I have set my heart on having it in my study, on the Book case. A length of four feet would do to surmount the middle compartment; but I am ignorant of the mechanical requirements -- whether the frieze must be applied to something forming a back, or whether it can be simply superposed. I think the decision had better be deferred until you come and see the book case, so as to understand the conditions.
It has occurred to me since you were with us the other day, that something I said about "Church people" at Canterbury N. Z. was open to misapprehension. Your sister Octavia 396 once said to me "Have you never known any earnest church people?" -- and lest you should be unable to correct the sort of misconception implied in her question, I want to tell you that I was brought up in the Church of England, and never belonged to any other religious body. I care that this should be known, not at all on personal grounds, but because, as I have been, and perhaps shall be, depicting dissenters with much sympathy I would not have it supposed that the sympathy springs from any partiality of association.
As to its origin historically, and as a system of thought, it is my conviction that the Church of England is the least morally dignified of all forms of Christianity i.e. all considerable forms dating from the Reformation; but as a portion of my earliest associations and most poetic memories, it would be more likely to tempt me into partiality than any form of dissent.
What I referred to as dreading in a New Zealand settlement was the peculiar aspect which any religious body assumes when it is quite dominant in a new country, and is not under the stringent criticism of dissidents.
Perhaps all this explanation was needless, but lest it should not have been, I prefer to give it. Best love to all.
Always, dearest Chick,
Your loving
Mutter.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Gertrude [Mrs. Charles Lee] Lewes, Harrogate, 10 July 1870
Dublin Core:Subject: Gertrude [Mrs. Charles Lee]  Lewes^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Gertrude [Mrs. Charles Lee] Lewes, Harrogate, 10 July 1870
MS: Mrs. Edward Hanson. Envelope: Mrs. Charles Lewes | 25 Church Row | Hampstead | London N. Postmarks: HARROGATE | A | JY 10 | 70; LONDON-N. | JY 11 | 70. Published: Paterson, pp. 141-143.
Brunswick Terrace | Harrogate 204 | July 10. 70
Dearest Gertrude
Your letter did not reach us till after the middle of the week, when we had had Charlie's subsequent history of your thoughtful wise care about poor Lizzie. 205 It is a comfort to know how well you and Charles acted on Pater's behalf, and I should think that no other measure as to expenses would be thought of than the one which you suggest to Pater.
I have nothing particular to say; but my heart goes out to you more than usual on dear Aunt Mary's account, 206 so it is easier to me to write to you than to abstain. And you will all be glad to hear that this place seems to be doing wonders for Pater. His pulse is getting strong, his appetite is good, and he enjoys the fresh air and exercise. It is settled now that we are to go to Whitby tomorrow week (on the 18th), as our lodgings are let to others from that day. And probably a fortnights' drinking of the strong chalybeate 207 waters is as much as it would be prudent to take at once.
The weather is delicious now -- warm, but not warmer than we like it to be: on these hills there is almost always a pleasant breeze stirring, and on the slightest pretext the wind is ready to howl round us quite mysteriously, something in the configuration of the ground and houses apparently favouring this melancholy music.
I wish you could share the magnificent strawberries which are brought round here in the market carts, and the abundant green peas. But I hope that the rains have been enough round London to have made fruit and vegetables less poverty-stricken than they were.
I say nothing about the dear invalid, except that we send our love. You know that we care always to have news of her and all of you.
The last sentence in your letter "I am very well," -- was especially welcome. Don't hang too much over dress-making, lest it should cease to be true. We have been a long walk, which has tired my legs, and made my arms sympathize, so I write in a sprawling way, just to say that I am your ever loving
Mutter.

MS: Harvard. Envelope: Mrs. C. Norton | 18 Queen's Gate Terrace | W. Postmark: LONDON-N.W. | A4 | JA 22 | 69. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 22. 1869.
Dear Mrs. Norton 6
I thank you for sending me Mr. Lowell's poems. 7 They could not have come to me in a way more pleasantly memorable than as a gift from you and Mr. Norton, and I expect to enjoy the reading of them very highly.
I am wondering whether your charitable judgment of our climate will wear through many more weeks of fog. I lose one half of my minutes in dwelling on my miserable sensations and the other half in shame that I have not heroism enough in me to triumph over such ills.
Mrs. Pattison 8 did not come on Sunday, after all, so I am glad to think that you got home without too much fatigue -- which you might not have done, if you had waited to see her.
With best regards to all those of your family whom I have had the pleasure of seeing, and whom I hope we shall soon see again, I am
Sincerely yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, 8 July 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, 8 July 1878
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
July 8. 78.
My dear Cara
Some weeks have passed now since you left Sydenham, and I cannot help being anxious to know whether they have brought a tenant. The thought that you would probably have written to tell me the good news makes me fear that there has been no such news to tell, and the sunshine is not so pleasant as it would be without that fear. Do let me know how things are with you in every respect. One is very thankful for the prospect of European peace, but these larger joys want some small personal comforts to give them the complete relish, and the particular comfort I should choose now would be the assurance that your mind is relieved from immediate worry about the year's income.
Mrs. Geddes -- who used to be Emily Bury -- lives near Guildford with her two little girls, and has just had to part again with her husband for three years! He is an Indian judge, you know, and has just had his year's holiday.
Since we came down here Mr. Lewes has been gouty and I have had bilious headache, but we are getting better, I by blue pill and he by taking walks before breakfast.
I trust that this sunshine is friendly to your husband's breathing. He is sure to make the most of each good, and will not be punished in the Dantesque circle of mud, as one who "piange l'e0 dove esser dei giocondo," or even in the fog, with those who say "Tristi fummo nell' aer dolce che'l sol rilume." 96 I fear that I have often deserved those severe ways of being "made to know better."
Sara is flourishing over her proofs, I hope. My best love to her.
Ever affectionately your
Marian.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, 28 November 1880
MS: Yale. Envelope: Mrs. Bray | 3 Barrs Hill Terrace | Coventry. Postmarks: GODALMING | A | 28 NO | 80: COVENTRY | D | NO 29 | 80. Published: Cross, III, 434-435.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
November 28. 80.
My dear Cara
I have thought of you all the more because I have not even heard anything of you for several months. You will wonder less why I have not written as a consequence of those thoughts when I tell you that I have been ill and allowed to do nothing but indulge myself and receive indulgence. I am very well now and am every day consciously gathering strength, so that if I could like giving trouble I should look back on my illness as a great opportunity of enjoying the tenderest watching and nursing. I kept my bed only about a week and have always been equal, except at short intervals, to much reading and talking, so that there is no fair cause for any grumbling on my part. It has not been so bad an illness as that of last summer.
You see, we are not yet at Cheyne Walk, but we are to be settled there by the end of next week. It has been a great business to move the books, and the prospect of that always hindered us from moving from North Bank as we were often otherwise inclined to do years ago. I have had no trouble, but have remained here on my cushions while Mr. Cross has gone early for several mornings running to superintend the removal. He is exceedingly strong and well now, and cuts down a thickish tree in half an hour, with a special axe which he bought on purpose to make a desirable clearance in our little forest.
I received dear Mrs. Cash's card, but I was not at that time well enough to write to her. Will you tell her so, and say that I begged you to assure her of my affectionate remembrance and sympathy.
I think you are quite right to look over your old letters and papers and decide for yourself what should be burnt. Burning is the most reverential destination one can give to relics which will not interest any one after we are gone. I hate the thought that what we have looked at with eyes full of living memory should be tossed about and made lumber of, or (if it be writing) read with hard curiosity. I am continually considering whether I have saved as much as possible from this desecrating fate.
Your too compendious account of yourselves is quite cheering as far as it goes. I was wondering whether the sort of weather we have been having would be favourable or the contrary to Mr. Bray's comfort. Sarah's winter cough will I hope sit lightly upon her this year.
It is difficult to give you materials for imagining my [world.] Think of me as surrounded and cherished by family love -- by brothers and sisters whose characters are admirable to me, who have for years been my friends, and who adore my husband as a sort of father and brother combined. But there is no excessive visiting among us, and the life of my own hearth is chiefly that of dual companionship. If it is any good for me that my life has been prolonged till now, I believe it is owing to this miraculous affection which has chosen to watch over me. Love to all three from
Your ever affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, 26 August 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, 26 August 1878
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
August 26. 78.
My dear Cara
O I am so glad about the House! If the new tenant will only be sensible enough to take it on to the end of your term there will be no more anxiety for you in that quarter. I feel your relief.
Doubtless Mr. Bray and you have laughed at the notion of the "most talented George Eliot" being president of the Perry Bar Institute and being baited by the fact of having had a predecessor in "Irving the actor." 128 I must beg Mr. Bray kindly to send as polite a refusal as possible on my behalf, saying that I have invariably declined invitations to that sort of publicity -- and some have already come from Birmingham.
I grieve to think of our dear Mrs. Pears's suffering. If she ever happens to mention me to you, assure her of my continued, affectionate memory of her goodness to me in my far-off youth.
And poor Rufa, who was so wonderfully well and free from her chronic tormentor, is feelingly thought of by Mr. Lewes as something of a fellow-sufferer. For he has been sadly tormented by gouty twinges and nightly cramps in these latter months. Indeed, we have been unfortunate in health amidst all our delights of country and fine weather. Mr. Lewes came down much out of sorts and until the last fortnight his state caused me great anxiety. He is now better, and I as usual have taken his place as invalid, having had a bilious attack which has only half loosed its hold on me.
I was not very fit to receive visitors -- always an exertion to us, from our hermit-like habits -- but I got better than I expected through a two days' visit from Mr. and Mrs. Tom Trollope (of Florence) in the middle of last week. We took them to see Tennyson, who is in great force under his 68 years and a figure whom you would like to contemplate while he is chanting his poetry -- and so the time passed. But when they were gone I collapsed into hemicrania and nausea, and am this morning for the first time a little freer and in possession of my soul. Hearing from you about the much worse ailments of our friends helps me to think less of my dyspeptic griefs.
I hope Sara will have a fine autumnal time with her friend Miss Carter at Penmaenmaur. I suppose no other sea-place would do her equal good with this to which she has taken an especial fancy. Certainly the mountains there are grand -- only man and his habitations seemed to us rather vile than otherwise. But I remember the wide sands as an attraction, and there at least you don't hear the singing of the Methodists.
Best love to Sara and Mr. Bray, and many thanks to you, dear, for writing me a letter of news which has cheered me.
Always your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, 12 July 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, 12 July 1878
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
July 12. 78.
My dear Cara
Mr. Lewes says that there is not the slightest doubt about the law in the matter of a sold manuscript: it belongs simply to the purchaser. Endless manuscript plays have been bought by managers who have never put them on the stage: but there is no redress for the disappointed author, and no other manager can use the stifled play.
But with regard to your M.S., Mr. Lewes is convinced that it is not in the nature of a publisher to give money for a work and then willingly suppress the work. 101 If Nelson had only engaged to give you half profits or a percentage on sales he might be supposed to be careless in the matter, but he would not lightly allow his payment of £40 (was it not?) to have been made in vain. Hence Mr. Lewes thinks that he may still publish it, and his neglect of letters is a neglect common to many of his tribe. In any case your use of the proof without his concurrence would lay you open to unpleasant consequences. You can only have a right to print by repurchasing.
I am very sorry, for there is a sad lack of reasonable moral teaching, and I can believe that your little book would have taught teachers as well as children. One not improbable supposition is, that Nelson sees a danger of unsaleableness or scandal injurious to his business in a book which might seem to aim at making the world moral without help of clergy. Indeed, that is the only imaginable reason for his suppression of the M.S. after he has paid money for it -- if indeed it turns out that he is bent on suppressing it.
Mr. Jolly's notion is quite [subjective.] The purchase of a M.S. is not a contract to publish, and if it were it would include the repayment of the money as a condition of recovery.
This is the troublesome truth, which you will prefer knowing. Is there anybody of your acquaintance who has had transactions with Nelson and would call upon him for you?
Yours ever lovingly
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, [30] July 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Witley, [30] July 1879
MS: Coventry and Warwickshire Collection, Coventry City Libraries. Endorsed: July 31, 1879. Mary Scampton. Envelope: Mrs. Bray | 3 Barr's Hill Terrace | Coventry. Postmark: GODALMING | C | JY 31 | 79. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
July 31. 79.
My Dear Cara
Excuse me -- but I cannot bear to write to my friends on post cards, unless it be a mere [Yes] or [No] or a date. But I am very grateful for the affectionate anxiety that sent the card, and glad to have some news of you in addition.
I am much better -- get up soon after my breakfast, and am able both to walk and drive without much fatigue. For the last week I have had no pain to speak gravely about and my appetite is good. Sir James Paget writes me this morning 306 that he and Dr. Clark want me to go up to town that they may get another special medicus to consult with them as to possible causes of my illness. But since I have been daily getting stronger and easier since Dr. C. saw me, I am going to write and ask that my power of recovery without all that trouble may be tested a little longer.
My work is not done, you know, as to seeing the final volume through the press, but the printing is going on steadily. This volume will be more than twice the size of [The Study of Psychology.] But you see, as times go in this rainy world, I must not consider myself heavily afflicted.
I am so glad to know that the Sydenham House will not trouble you through the winter.
Love to all from
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 8 March [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 8 March [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | South Fields | Wandsworth | Tuesday, March 8. 61
Dear Cara
Mr. Lewes urges me, reluctant as I am to trouble you any more, to ask you if you can ascertain for me whether Ann Overton is yet engaged. If not, I think it is very likely we might be thankful to engage her, for the new servant, 62 though a good young woman I believe, is frightfully inefficient. From your and Mrs. Wick's description, I think Ann Overton would do very well for us, for we make no excessive demands of any sort. I should of course pay her expenses to Wandsworth, and we would give her 'a312 wages with a prospect of raising them if she remained with us and served us satisfactorily.
It distresses me -- not formally, but really and truly -- that you should be teazed again with my letters. I have been ill in bed with cold and cough 63 (rather better now), and my own feebleness under all exertion makes me estimate at its full value the exertion of others on my behalf.
By the time you answer me, I shall be able to send a positive reply by return of post.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian.
Chrissey writes by her daughter Emily, that she should love to see me, but fears the excitement. She writes herself a few words in pencil this time as if she were weaker -- alas --

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 26 July [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 26 July [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1860. Hitherto unpublished.
July 26.
Dear Cara
Mr. Lewes desires me to tell you that he will order all the numbers of the "Physiology of Common Life" to be sent to the Coventry Herald
Don't think of mentioning to Mr. and Mrs. Call the Hofwyl religious instruction again. They acted on their own impressions and could not properly do otherwise. But it is desirable that other people should not be scared away from a school which is so unusually free from the objections attaching to most continental schools.
Mr. Bray will sympathize with our excitement in the expectation of a real pug dog! Blackwood, determined to procure me one, if possible, set his cousin, Colonel Stuart, hunting in all the dog-fancying regions of London for one, and after infinite pains and adventures the much-desired animal is found. The anxieties of our life are beginning -- we shall now have no peace lest Pug should be stolen. He comes as a substitute for lost friends.
Ever thine
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 24 February [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 24 February [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Extracts published: Cross, II, 85.
Holly Lodge | February 24.
Dear Cara
One word of gratitude to you first, before I write any other letters. Heaven and earth bless you for trying to help me. I have been blasphemous enough sometimes to think that I had never been good and attractive enough to win any little share of the honest disinterested friendship there is in the world: one or two examples of late had given that impression, and I am prone to rest in the least agreeable conviction the premisses will allow.
The advertisement in the Herald is a business-like way of proceeding. Perhaps it would be worth while to mention that the servant is wanted for a lady and gentleman only. I need hardly tell you what I want -- you know it so well: a servant who will cause me the least possible expenditure of time on household matters. Cooking is a material thing, not because Mr. Lewes is epicurean (for he is stupid of palate) but because he is, amongst his other eminences, eminently dyspeptic. I am anxious therefore to have a cook who is not only honest but soup-making and full of devices -- as good a cook as your Hannah of old time. Honesty and cleanliness are the two other emphatic requirements and a not unimportant one is a power of keeping simple accounts -- the spelling ad libitum.
I wish I were not an anxious fidgetty wretch, and could sit down content with dirt and disorder. But anything in the shape of an anxiety soon grows into a monstrous vulture with me, and makes itself more present to me than my rich sources of happiness, such as too few mortals are blessed with. You know me.
Ever your grateful
Marian.
I wrote to Mrs. Call too, confiding in her kindness and her wonderful skill in finding out all that makes life go smoothly.
Since I wrote this I have just had a letter from my Sister Chrissey -- ill in bed -- consumptive -- regretting that she ever ceased to write to me. It has ploughed up my heart.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 23 August [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 23 August [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Mostly published: Cross, II, 130-131.
Wandsworth | August 23.
Dear Cara
Our great difficulty is Time. I am little better than a sick nigger with the lash behind him, at present. If we go to Penmaenmawr, we shall travel all through by night, in order not to lose more than one day, and we shall pause at Lichfield on our way back. If we decide against Pen etc. (which I don't think probable) Lichfield will be a separate journey some time in October.
To pause at Coventry would be a real pleasure to me, but I think even if we could do it on our way home, it would be better economy to wait until the sense of hurry is past, and make it a little reward for work done. The going to the coast seems to be a wise measure, quite apart from indulgence -- we are both so feeble -- but otherwise, I should have kept my resolution, and remained quiet here for the next six months. Ever, dear Cara
Your affectionate
Marian.
They have sold 3000 more of Adam and are printing a 6th Edition!

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 22 February [1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | South Fields | Wandsworth | February 22.
Dear Cara
I have just received the sad news that the jewel of a servant who was to have made us comfortable, has been prevailed on by her mistress (at Bath) to stay again.
Is there Balm in Gilead? 36 In other words, is there a servant in your neighbourhood who would like a place near London? A servant of high character and with the general knowledge of the "general servant." We would give high wages. 37 Alas -- I fear you will say no, or perhaps say nothing at all, which will be equivalent to no. Help me if you can.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 11 September 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, 11 September 1860
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | September 11. 60.
Dear Cara
The contrairiness of things! We shall be obliged to turn out of our house in a fortnight and have not yet absolutely settled where we are to lay our heads. Tomorrow we are going to see if we can come to a final arrangement about the house we desire to take; but at present we are certain of nothing but of hurry and of incessant calls to town. That is one part of the "contrairiness" -- that we can't go to Sydenham before Saturday. The other part is, that we have for some time settled with Charley to meet him at the Crystal Palace precisely on Saturday -- that being the only day on which he has a half holiday, and we want him to see the sights with us before we leave this convenient starting place. And from your letter, I fear there is some obstacle to our seeing you on Saturday? We have appointed Charley to meet us among the Greek Sculpture about 2 o'clock; but if there were any chance of our seeing you any how on that day, I would make any arrangement possible for that end.
Pity us -- "careful and troubled about many things." 629 We shall always be at home in the evening for charitable folks to come and see, if they will do so. It is rather hard that an opportunity of seeing you should happen so inopportunely. Mr. Lewes sends his best regards to you and Mr. Bray and I mine -- that is to say, my sincere affection, which I think is quite the best sort of regard. I shall keep a faint hope of seeing you somehow, until you tell me it is impossible.
Ever yours
Marian.
The house we expect to settle in is in Gloucester Road, near Gloucester Gate, Regent's Park.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, [21 March 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 21st 1859. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Monday Morning.
Dear Cara
I am very grateful to you for your exertions on my behalf -- quite as grateful, though not so glad, as if they had issued in any happy result. We are taking active measures ourselves to procure a new servant, and I hope this week will bring us some auspicious change. Caroline, the Disappointing, is not to be entertained as anything but a (very expensive) makeshift.
My cold is well now, and I am taking a tonic to which I trust for giving me some strength of mind and body in which I am deplorably deficient. Mr. Lewes, too, is more than usually infirm of head 73 [Bottom of page cut away.] me mine. So that we are not in that unctuous and insolent state of enjoyment that must necessarily draw down on us the envy of the Gods -- else one might understand our bad luck with the servant.
[Signature cut away.]
Mrs. Bray.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, [18 September 1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, [18 September 1860]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1860. Extract published: Cross, II, 265, dated July.
Holly Lodge | Tuesday Evening.
Dear Cara
I am sincerely obliged to Miss Marshall for her thoughtful kindness in writing me out a list of the tradespeople near Gloucester Gate. I have laid the list carefully by, for we may go into that vicinity after all; but at present our deliberations and mutations have ended in our taking a furnished house, by way of trial how far we can bear a town residence. We shrank from fixing ourselves in a rather expensive house for three years until we had made this preliminary experiment. We move next Monday, and after that, our address will be No. 10, Harewood Square.
My troubles are all of an entirely superficial kind -- mere miseries of moving; and I only asked for pity playfully. I am ashamed of my readiness to make grievances, when I think of other people's real cares. And I do think of them -- dream of them sometimes. I seemed to be dreaming all last night of you. I can enter so thoroughly into your longing for rest from money cares. It is pleasant to know, at least, that the house at Sydenham is well let. We made our journey thither on Saturday, and the country looked so beautiful under the sunshine that I rather envied the people who could manage to live there. Charley enjoyed the treat very much, but I should have felt the day more fruitful if we could have seen you as well as the superabundant sights of another kind.
Our big boy is a great delight to us and makes our home doubly cheery. It is very sweet as one gets old to have some young life about one. He is quite a passionate musician, and we play Beethoven duets with increasing appetite every evening. The opportunity of hearing some inspiring music is one of the chief benefits we hope for, to counter-balance our loss of the wide common and the fields.
Will you tell Mr. Bray, with my love, that I hope he will not be disagreeably surprised to receive a parcel of old clothes from me, if, in the course of packing, I find any turning up. I sent him a very shabby lot for his prot'e9g'e9s, in the spring.
Do write and tell me, dear Cara, whenever you get a little relieved from present anxieties and annoyances. I can only hear of you in that direct way, and I often spend a good deal of "tissue" in conjecture about you. With love to Sara
Ever yours affectionately
M. E. L.
Will you also tell Mr. Bray that now the strike has ceased I find myself neglecting to read the Herald, so that I need not trouble the official further who sends it to "Miss Lewes." Many thanks for the copies I have had. 631

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, [11 March 1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Wandsworth, [11 March 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1859. Hitherto unpublished.
H[olly] L[odge] | South Fields | Wandsworth | Friday.
Dear Cara
Our rapid post brought me your letter last night, before we went out to pass a late evening with the Congreves. 64
I wish you would help me with your judgment about Ann Overton. You see, as well as I do, all the formidable risks of bringing a servant liable to be made helpless by an inevitably recurring malady, all this long way from her own friends. But Mr. Lewes says, "I wonder if one could learn with some assurance how often the malady has recurred. If there were a good chance of her remaining well for a year or two, the thing might be worth risking." I shouldn't mind even nursing her occasionally if one lived in a Christian neighbourhood, where one knew some not unreasonably dishonest, skilful charwoman. But in this undestroyed Babylon, such things are not to be contemplated. Perhaps we had better wait patiently for some better, or at least some less hazardous chance. What do you think? If yes -- give yourself no farther trouble about Ann Overton. We must manage with our Caroline -- name of good omen, but omens unhappily are superstitious affairs -- for a week or two. Poor girl, she has been saying to me this morning that she has been writing to her friends how comfortable she is, and that she can manage the work much better than we expected! I couldn't find in my heart to destroy her illusion at that moment.
If you should hear of another suitable servant, it may be well for me to tell you that to a really experienced person, who would want nothing but my simple orders, we would give 'a315, and find all her food -- beer, tea and sugar. I mention this last point because the servants here make it an object of inquiry. She would be expected to wash her own clothes, but all the rest of the washing is of course put out.
"Jane's cousin" has a pleasant sound. How well I remember that pretty neat Jane, with her quiet obliging ways!
Ever your grateful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, St. Mary's, 5 April [1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, St. Mary's, 5 April [1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1857. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 449-451.
St. Mary's | Scilly Isles | April 5.
Dear Cara
It was very good and pretty of you and Sara to write to me from the midst of your semi-organized chaos. The smallest details written in the hastiest way that will enable me to imagine you as you are, are just what I want -- indeed, all I care about in correspondence. I shall try to do as you do now, and concentrate my affections on the cottage side of the wall, but alas! it is hard to be contented that the windows and the lawn and the garden walks that once knew you should know you no more. When I saw the little celandine, with its heart-shaped leaves, carpeting the lane-sides round Penzance, I thought of the luxuriance with which it used to grow -- and probably grows now -- under the trees near the garden gate at Rosehill.
I can't think of Mr. Bray's flaring gaslight at his elbow without feeling a little bilious, so I confine myself as much as possible to the vague conception that he has certain new comforts which reconcile him to the new home. You seem to say that Sara's present room is not her old one, 824 'ablooking'bb and I am rather at a loss to imagine how she has stowed herself.
We are more and more in love with these little islands. There is not a tree to be seen, but there are grand granite piles on the coast such as I never saw before, and furze covered hills with larks soaring and singing above them, and zoological wonders on the shore to fill our bottles and our souls at once. Mr. Lewes seems already to have recovered the ground he had lost in health during our last few months at Richmond, and by and bye I hope I shall flourish too, but for some time I have been unusually weak and knock-up-able. Our landlady 825 is an excellent woman, but, like almost all peculiarly domestic women, has not more than rudimentary ideas of cooking, and in an island where you can get nothing but beef, except by sending to Penzance, that supreme science has its maximum value. She seems to think eating a purely arbitrary procedure -- an abnormal function of mad people who come to Scilly, and if we ask her what the people live on here is quite at a loss to tell us, apparently thinking the question relates to the abstruser portion of Natural History. But I insist, and give her a culinary lecture every morning, and we do in the end get fed. 826 Altogether, our life here is so far better than the golden age that we work as well [as] play.
That is the happy side of things. But there is a very sad one to me, which I shall not dwell upon -- only tell you of. More than a week ago, I received the news that poor Chrissey had lost one of her pretty little girls of fever, that the other little one -- they were the only two she had at home with her -- was also dangerously ill, and Chrissey herself and her servant apparently attacked by typhus too. 827 The distressing part of [it is] our being here, away so far out of reach of post and out of possibility of my going to her! The thought of her in this state is a perpetual shadow to me in the sunshine. Best love to all. Ever, dear Cara,
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, St. Leonard's, [3 August 1853]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, St. Leonard's, [3 August 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Aug. 3. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 309-310.
Park Cottage West Hill St. Leonard's.
Dear Cara
Your letter, which only reached me this morning, was just what I wanted, telling me everything about everybody. I must persist in hoping that you will get to the coast in spite of unpropitious appearances. I never felt the delight of the thorough change that the coast gives one so much as now, and I shall be longing to be off with you again in October. St. Leonard's, like other things, has been making progress in the last five years. It joins Hastings now -- houses all the way sans intermission. I am on a delightful hill, looking over the heads of the houses on the main road, and having a vast expanse of sea and sky for my only view.
It gave me quite a pang of distress to read of Mr. Noel's troubles bodily and other. I trust the hand is not less usable for the accident and consequent deformity.
I can only sigh too at the prospect of your having poor Harry 353 back again. But you and Mr. Bray like duties better than I -- selfish sybarite that I am.
I shall be very glad of edification from the article on Russia, by whomsoever written. Pray let me have it.
The lights in your picture -- which otherwise certainly does make the world look rather like a Bochim 354 to me -- are the tea-drinkings in Stoneleigh Park, 355 and I like to think that you are all there this lovely afternoon. The bright weather and genial air -- so different from what I have had for a year before -- make me feel as happy and stupid as a well-conditioned cow. I sit looking at the sea and the sleepy ships with a purely animal bien-'eatre. The person in whose house I am lodging -- a nice honest and, I fancy, Unitarian body, about 40 -- went to school to Mrs. Lalor 356 and has now some little girls from her school passing their holidays here.
I shall be very grateful for any scraps of news about you whenever one of the trio will be benevolent enough to write in spite of their disinclination -- for that is the history of all letter-writing, unless indeed one wants to hear from the other "party." I am not sure that I shall remain long at these lodgings. Love to all. Ever dear Cara,
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Shottermill, 3 August 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Shottermill, 3 August 1871
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1871. Extracts published: Cross, III, 140-141.
Cherrimans | Shottermill | Petersfield | August 3. 71
My dear Cara
Thanks for your little picture of things -- eminently acceptable in place of vague conjectures. I am a bitter enemy of make-believe about the human lot, but I think there is a true alleviation of distress in thinking of the intense enjoyment which accompanies a spontaneous, confident, intellectual activity. This may not be a counterpoise to the existing evils, but it is at least a share of mortal good, and good of an exquisite kind.
You write of the Whittem family as if they were living now in agreeable ease. I am glad to think of that, after the sorrows about Albert. Did you notice that effort to bring the question of Asylums for the discipline of drunkards before Parliament? The plan has long been at work in the United States, and poor Mrs. Stowe has gone through the misery of having a son who needed that discipline. 341 But the English are not likely yet to tolerate such an infringement of the drunkard's liberty.
Are you not happy in the long-wished-for sunshine? I have a pretty lawn before me, with hills in the background. The train rushes by every now and then to make one more glad of the usual silence.
A good man writes to me from Scotland this morning asking me if he is not right in pronouncing Romola, in defiance of the world around him (not a large world, I hope) who will say Romola. Such is correspondence in these days, so that quantity is magnificent en gros but shabby en d'e9tail -- i.e. in single letters like this. Always
Your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Shottermill, 25 July 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Shottermill, 25 July 1871
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Tennyson. Hitherto unpublished.
Shottermill | near Petersfield | July 25. 71.
My dear Cara
Mr. Lewes tells me to say, in reply to Mr. Sibree, that the corrected sheets of the new edition in question have for many months been in the publishers' hands, but the publication has been delayed and is now not likely to take place before October. The account of Hegel has been entirely re-written after new study. Mr. Lewes thinks it highly desirable that so capable a man as Mr. Sibree should undertake the translation of Hegel's Hist[ory] of Phil[osoph]y, which would be likely to keep a lasting place. He has spoken, in the aforesaid new edition, of the exceptional ability shown in Mr. Sibree's former translation. 336
We were delighted to see Mr. and Mrs. Call, and to hear of Frank's hopeful plantation in Germany. They gave us cheerful news of you, and said that you reported Sara also to be very well. I was suffering from headache when they were here, but I am better now. Only, the rain and wind distress me in soul and body. One thinks of the beaten-down corn, and one feels stagnation in one's own liver. Next week we move into the house on the opposite side of the road, which is less quaint and romantic than this cottage, but fuller of comforts.
Tennyson has a house on a hill about three miles from here, and he has found us out. Otherwise, we are in secure solitude and read and discuss and walk to our hearts' content. We shall not be back in town again until September and are happy to have got a new shelter here, as our house will only tomorrow be free from builders and painters and we could not yet lay our heads in it.
I worship Scott so devoutly that I leaped out foolishly with a consent to go to Edinburgh, feeling that I should have a good happy cry at seeing any honors done to his memory. But I am altogether thankful that the step was not irrevocable. The journey and the fuss would have been intolerable to me. Edinburgh will look fine with the crowds streaming along Princes Street, but I doubt whether anything else will be satisfactory.
I wish you had told me some details about Sara. It seems an age since I got any glimpse of her. With best love,
Always your faithful
Marian.
There is a paper-famine just now. 337

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Richmond, 26 November 1858
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Richmond, 26 November 1858
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, II, 72-73.
Richmond | November 26. 58.
Dear Cara
I am very grateful to you for sending me a few authentic words from your own self. They are unspekably precious to me. I mean that quite literally, for there is no putting into words any feeling that has been of long growth within us. It is easy to say how we love new friends, and what we think of them, but words can never trace out all the fibres that knit us to the old.
Mr. Bray's welcome visit 1228 was sadly too short. I have been thinking of you incessantly in the waking hours since he left, and feel a growing hunger to know more precise details about you and to talk with you about these changes in the aspect of things towards you. I am of a too sordid and anxious disposition, prone to dwell almost exclusively on fears instead of hopes, and to lay in a larger stock of resignation than of any other form of confidence. But I try to extract some comfort this morning from my consciousness of this disposition, by thinking that nothing is ever so bad as my imagination paints it. And then, I know there are incommunicable feelings within us capable of creating our best happiness at the very time others can see nothing but our troubles. And so I go on, arguing with myself, and trying to live inside you, and looking at things in all the lights I can fancy you seeing them in, for the sake of getting cheerful about you, in spite of Coventry.
I listen to the project of your spending many months abroad with some trembling, lest the pleasures should not quite counterbalance the discomforts -- especially in regions crowded with rich snobbish English visitors or residents. I should have thought beautiful scenery nearer home -- in Scotland or Wales -- would be found at less cost moral and financial. Towards the English as English, no foreigners have a kindly feeling -- only one of predatory antagonism, and the English abroad are always English who decline to know fellow-countrymen without prestige.
I cannot satisfy my love and anxiety without saying these things, which I had not opportunity to say yesterday -- and indeed the case did not present itself to me at once in all its complications. Mr. Bray's plan of living in a private lodging and providing everything himself, increases every form of difficulty. With the market-people, speaking in South Switzerland a French patois, and in N[orth] S[witzerland] a German patois, the language alone would be a serious obstacle and annoyance. In a boarding-house you would avoid that unpleasantness and twenty others that belong to the isolated plan. And in a boarding house there would be assured civility and endurable society. It is always a hateful office to urge doubts and negatives, but the distinct knowledge Mr. Lewes and I have of what foreign residence is for English people is something that we ought to use honestly for our friends, giving them the truest result we can of our experience. And after all we are only giving you a datum, which you can reject at once if you find it outweighed by others.
You are very much thought of and talked of -- you, individually, dear Cara -- in this chair where I sit, and in the Richmond walks; always with deep regard and tender affection. And so it will be through all changes, till the change that takes me out of this world. That doesn't seem so very far off to one now, the years rolling by so quickly as they do.
Ever yours
Marian.
N.B. No respectable (so-called) lodging house people would take in English lodgers who acted on Mr. Bray's plan.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Richmond, [30 October 1857]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Richmond, [30 October 1857]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 1. 57. Extracts published: Cross, I, 469.
Richmond, Friday.
Dear Cara
How I wish I could get to you by some magic and have one walk over the hill with you again. I often think I see your dear little shoulders and dearer phiz just as they used to come towards me. Letters are poor things compared with five minutes of looking and speaking and one kiss. Nevertheless I do like to have a little letter now and then, though I don't for a moment ask it, if you have no spontaneous impulse to give it, and my words to Sara were rather intended as an apology for sending messages quite gratuitously, than as a complaint. I can't help losing belief that people love me -- the unbelief is in my nature and no sort of fork will drive it finally out.
I fancy you a great deal in your present [Weben und Streben,] with your kitchen apron on one hour, and looking very nice and pretty at your sewing or writing the next. Then taking up the books as you used to do in the evening and picking out some joke or other, at which I see your laughing face as well as if it were only yesterday that I looked at it last.
I can't help wondering you can think of me in the past with much pleasure. It all seems so painful to me, made up of blunders and selfishness, and it only comes back upon me as a thing to be forgiven. That is honest and painful truth, and not sentimentality. But I am thankful if others found more good than I am able to remember.
Mr. Lewes laughed very heartily at your description of Mr. Wise, 1001 which I read to him. We had never heard of him before and wondered who was the anonymous man Mr. Chapman talked of as the proposer of an article on Shelley.
If ever you know of any one who would be glad of some old clothes, too good for servants -- such as would do to make up for children etc. I wish you would ask me to rummage among mine; for now I don't send them to my sister, 1002 I should sometimes have such things, and among all your objects of charity you might be able to find a destination more useful for them than I can.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Meriden, [1 May 1850]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1850. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 252.
Meriden 899 | Wednesday.
My dear Cara
Have you any engagement for the week after next? If not, may I join you on Saturday the 4th and invite M. D'Albert to come down on the following Monday? 900 It appears he cannot stay in England longer than until about the second week in May. I am uncomfortable at the idea of burthening even your friendship with the entertainment of a person purely for my sake. It is indeed the greatest of all the great kindnesses you have shewn me.
Write me two or three kind words, dear Cara. I have been so ill at ease ever since I have been in England that I am quite discouraged. Tell Mr. Bray to write me something at the end of yours. I hope the ribbons have been selling well -- that all things are brightening with the brightening sky. What news have you had from Clapton and from Sara?
If you see a black box of mine come from Griff will you give it house-room until I am with you? I packed up my unnecessary clothes in it.
Dear Chrissey is much kinder than any one else in the family and I am happiest with her. She is generous and sympathizing and really cares for my happiness. But I am delighted to feel that I am of no importance to any of them, and have no motive for living amongst them. I have often told you I thought Melchisedec 901 the only happy man, and I think so more than ever. Mrs. Pears I hear is come to Allesley. 902 I shall go to see her some morning when Edward drives to Allesley. Ever dear Cara
Your affectionate
Pollian.
