Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 8 September 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 8 September 1876
MS: Miss Kate C. Savage. Envelope: Mrs. Bray | 3 Barrs Hill Terrace | Coventry. Postmark: LONDON-N.W | SP 8 | 76. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank | September 8. 76.
My dear Cara
We got back to our nest at the end of last week, and remembering that when I saw you you were not without anxieties, I am anxious to have some news of you. How is Mr. Bray's health? How is everything that touches your comfort?
We are much the better for our travel, which has lain in a direction other than we intended on setting out. When we got to Aix-les-Bains I was taken ill, the heat was already rather fierce in that region, and we felt that it would be unwise to go father south. In order to get on to the cool heights of the Maritime Alps we must have gone into hot depths. So we turned northward and by slow stages got at last to Ragatz, which proved a place of healing and invigoration. The last two months of our absence were spent entirely in the north-east of Switzerland and in the Black Forest -- out of the English tracks. We saw but one acquaintance, and he was a Berlin publisher. 523 It is pleasant to be back in London when "nobody" is here.
I hope that the unusual old-fashioned heat has not been unfavourable to any one of your trio. Every detail about you will be acceptable. I think you are under a promise to tell me honestly of any outside good or evil.
My best love to Sara. It is a pity the spirit moves her so seldom to write letters, seeing that she writes them so charmingly. But I am the last who should wonder at such abstinence. In reading a heap of letters, I am preoccupied with calculating how few I can make my answers.
We shall be so glad to hear that the summer weather has been benignant to Mr. Bray's lungs. Our "often infirmities" 524 make us sympathetic about all bodily ills.
Always your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 8 July 1861
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
July 8. 61.
Dear Cara
It is always worth while to write a word to our friends when we are cheery. Your bright little note came opportunely towards counter-balancing some sadness I feel in the prolongation of Mr. Lewes's constant bodily feebleness and frequent malaise. Your pretty home and garden are a very pleasant addition to the small outlook on the Square gardens, and any good that can ever come to you will piece out my life and make my happiness broader.
I suppose I may answer the circular, although it is addressed to
G. H. Lewes with an exclusive dash under the initials: Mr. Lewes begs that his name may be put down as a subscriber for three copies; 812 and I add a ditto for myself. The separation of names is desirable in making a list of subscribers. Mr. Lewes desires me to tell Mr. Bray, with his kind regards, that he hopes he will pursue Mr. Spencer's prudent plan -- not to begin printing until he has secured a sufficient number of subscribers to cover the expenses.
Tell Sara her letter was very welcome to me: it proved how often our thoughts must be moving in the same direction and dwelling on the same source of joy and comfort. I shall write to her by and by, when I am rather more free. She has been making the most of the advantages that belong to a single state over a married one (there really are some such advantages over and above what St. Paul saw) -- the power of opening the window at any hour of the night without dread of giving a husband sore throat, and the power of sitting up as long as she likes without danger of disturbing his rest. My view of the comet has been "of the haziest description," so that I am consoled by the statement that it has been much less splendid than that of 1858. 813
I am remarkably well in health -- and that makes everything easy except the one trouble of seeing Mr. Lewes poorly. With love to all,
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 7 November [1851]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 7 November [1851]
MS: Benjamin Collection, Columbia. Hitherto unpublished.
Strand | Saturday | November 7.
Dear Cara
Who should be announced yesterday but Mr. and Mrs. Pears? Of course I ran down with open arms delighted. In the evening Mr. Chapman and I went to Dr. W. Smith's 1054 who lives in the Ultima Thule of Regent's Park Villas. The evening was not brilliant, but it was pleasant to sit by Mrs. Pears on the sofa. We have a thorough November morning after a week of really fine clear healthy days. Of course Mr. Bray will write Kossuth 1055 -- how can you expect any other? There is after all a little truth in the spiteful sayings of the Times, about the Political Barnums who are making a show of him -- still we must be glad when humbug takes a good direction. Perhaps that is the utmost one can expect from poor humans.
Mr. Neuberg who has been here some time is an agreeable, intelligent man. He said the other morning, [Do you ever feel stupid? I feel sometimes as if there were a wall built up between me and me.] Is not that just it? All the bright ideas, the fit words and the clever illustrations are on the other side of the wall -- are really there, though people wouldn't believe it. I shall be glad to have another glimpse of Mr. Noel before he sets out on his dreary journey.
You have really been living quite fast lately -- but Mrs. Pears says you are looking all the better -- for which blessing at least I sing my Jubilate.
Write, write, write.
In haste
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 7 May 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 7 May 1868
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, III, 49-50.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 7. 1868.
My dear Cara
The dear green letter was very welcome this morning. Mr. Lewes handed it to me saying that the writing was a certain barrister's of our acquaintance, but I knew it at once as a little fist which I prefer to the barrister's. 756
Yes, I am at rest now -- only a few pages of revise to look at more. My chief excitement and pleasure in the work are over; for when I have once written anything and it is gone out of my power, I think of it as little as possible. Next to the doing of the thing, of course, Mr. Lewes's delight in it is the cream of all sympathy, though I care enough about the sympathy of others to be very grateful for any they give me.
Don't you imagine how the people who consider writing simply as a money-getting profession will despise me for choosing a work by which I could only get hundreds where for a novel I get thousands? I cannot help asking you to admire what my husband is, compared with many possible husbands -- I mean, in urging me to produce a poem rather than anything in a worldly sense more profitable. I expect a good deal of disgust to be felt towards me in many quarters for doing what was not looked for from me and becoming unreadable to many who have hitherto found me readable and debateable. Religion and novels every ignorant person feels competent to give an opinion upon; but en fait de po'e9sie, a large number of them "only read Shakspeare." But enough of that.
Spiritually, we are happy, but bodily, we are wretches. Torquay was beautiful, and the Zoology went on gloriously there. But it lowered Mr. Lewes's pulse, and he has been headachy ever since we came back. I am not headachy, but I am feeble and flaccid and piteous to behold. We are going to Germany and Switzerland in June, but we don't tell our servants because they will begin to wail.
Mr. Spencer returned from Italy sooner than he intended, disappointed in the sanitary effects of travelling. 757 The long railway journeys were eminently unpleasant to him. He is better, however, and talks with much spirit about his experiences, of which you will probably hear when you come to town -- so I will not anticipate any of his matter.
I am much interested and gladdened for Sara's sake that Miss Alice Carter can be so precious a friend to her. It is an especially pretty result of their earlier relation to each other. 758 Give my love to Sara, and "good speed" through the troubles of proof-correcting. I shall revive my acquaintance with her first volume in preparation for the second.
Mrs. Cash sent me her book with a very kind letter about a week or ten days ago. I am rejoiced to find that she looks forward to the possibility of her taking a journey.
Best love all round. You will have the volume at the end of May -- but don't write, because I shall probably be gone.
Always thine
Marian
By the way, should the volume be sent to Sydenham or to Coventry?

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 7 March [1864]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday morning | March 7.
Dear Cara
Sara sends me word this morning that you are coming to Sydenham today. This is to say, what I hope is needless, that any time and whatever time you are able to give us we shall joyfully accept. I abstain from teazing you with special invitations because we are not going away and shall always be ready to receive you, if you will come either with or without notice. With notice I will have a lunch dinner to suit Mr. Bray any day when that will fit into your arrangements.
I am sorry to hear from Sara that Mr. Bray's health is ailing. Yours, of course, is good, you lucky angel. No more now, since more is unnecessary, and you need not write in answer to this unless you can write to say when you will come. But don't make me disagreeable by giving yourself trouble about me.
Ever your
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 7 June 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 7 June 1878
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 327-328.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 7. 78.
My dear Cara
I am so grieved to hear that the Sydenham house must still be a load on your mind. One can only hope that the summer demand will by and by carry it off at least for a few months.
The royalties did themselves much credit. The Crown Prince is really a grand looking man, whose name you would ask for with expectation if you imagined him no royalty. He is like a grand antique bust -- cordial and simple in manners withal, shaking hands and insisting that I should let him know when we next came to Berlin, just as if he had been a Professor Gruppe, living au troisi'e8me. She is less distinguished in physique, but equally good-natured and unpretending, liking best to talk of nursing soldiers and of what her Father's taste was in literature. She opened the talk by saying, "You knew my sister Louise" -- just as any other slightly embarrassed mortal might have done. The only complaint one had to make was that she never sat down till quite late in the evening -- a sore trial to plebeian legs and backs. We had a picked party to dinner -- Dean of Westminster, Bishop of Peterborough, Lord and Lady Ripon, Dr. Lyon Playfair, Kinglake (you remember Eothen -- the formal old gentleman is a good friend of mine) Froude, Mrs. Ponsonby (Lord Grey's granddaughter), and two or three more [illustrations] -- then a small detachment coming in after dinner. It was really an interesting occasion.
We have got through our furniture buying to our great relief -- and now Charles and Gertrude are going to leave Miss Gillies and set up a house of their own -- room being deficient for the growing family. But we shall not have to buy for them, thank heaven, except in the sense of finding the money. 78 We both long for quiet and a farewell to shops which are my abhorrence.
I hope you will have found Sara pretty well by the time you read this, and will feel no other shadow over your life than this of the Sydenham business. But remember everything I said to you.
Your loving
Marian.
We go to Oxford tomorrow, and by the following Saturday we hope that the flitting will have been made.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 6 October 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 6 October 1871
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 6. 71.
Dear Cara
I am getting better now -- many thanks for your affectionate sympathy. The attack has been sharper than anything I have had in the form of illness since I was a little girl. It was gastric irritation which just swept the edges of gastric fever, and I have to be grateful, i.e. patient and contented on the score of my comparatively easy escape. A friend of ours has just had gastric fever lasting for six weeks, and is now so reduced that she cries at everything like a fretful infant.
I think my complaint had nothing to do with brain-work, except so far as this has been diffused over my life at the expense of my bodily capital; for I have not been taxing myself -- indeed for many months I have been too ailing to do more than an apology for a morning's work. We are hoping that this crisis may have delivered me from long-accumulating sources of dyspepsia, for I am certainly going on well now in my eingeweide. But I am as thin as a mediaeval Christ, and Mr. Lewes is exerting his ingenuity to feed me up. He has been housekeeper, secretary and Nurse all in one -- as good a nurse as if he had been trained in a hospital.
Our old servants' going was a shock to me at first. 375 We should never have dismissed them, and we looked forward to taking care of them when they were too old to work. But their oddities were a yoke which we were certain would get heavier with the years, and since they could think of going we are contented now that they should go. To inherit servants from Mrs. Call, who is in all respects an excellent mistress, seems the best fortune that could have happened to us in this matter. But it is difficult for us masters and mistresses to allow enough for the difference between our drawing-room point of view and that of the kitchen. A very good quiet young woman 376 whom we had as nurse for Thornie, soon became an object of dislike and criticism to Grace and Amelia, and they apparently are unable to tolerate any "stranger," though she were hired purely to relieve them from excessive work.
Here is a long spell about myself -- the first letter I have written, and probably the last for a good while. With best love to all,
Your faithful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 6 April 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 6 April 1867
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 6. 67.
My dear Cara
When you come to town to prepare for these much-to-be-rejoiced-in tenants, do try to spare me a day. The Noels surely are gone to Greece by this time, and must have left you more of yourself to bestow elsewhere. You know I love to see you, but I am timid in asking you to come to me, because I have not a comfortable bedroom to give you as your other friends have.
Your letter seemed cheerful as to all things except Mr. Bray's constant headaches, a trouble which one groans to think of for any mortal, still more for an old friend whose life can be thoroughly imagined, pressed upon daily by that terrible weight.
You made the prettiest picture of Sara for me, varying her intense inward life with kind activities. Please give my best love to her and tell her that my bad management of life obliges me to economize letter-writing. People who do twenty times more than I do can write volumes of correspondence, but I am obliged to resign myself to the fact that I can get very little into my days.
Don't write any answer to this letter, except in the shape of a little note when you are in town, to say you are coming to me.
Ever yours lovingly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 5 June 1866
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1866. Extracts published: Cross, II, 431.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 5. 66.
My dear Cara
We start on Thursday! I finished writing on the last day of May, after days and nights of throbbing and palpitation -- chiefly I suppose from a nervous excitement which I was not strong enough to support well. As soon as I had done and read the last page to George, I felt better, and have been a new creature ever since, though a little overdone with visits from friends and attention (miserabile dictu!) to petticoats etc.
Along with your letter the post brought me a very kind one from Rufa, written under the supposition that I must already know of her father's death. 477 It is not wonderful that I was in ignorance, for I have no acquaintances who know anything of our Bath friends.
I can't help being a little vexed that the course of things hinders my having the great delight of seeing you again -- during this visit to town. Now that my mind is quite free, I don't know anything I should have chosen sooner than to have a long, long quiet day with you.
Will you give my best love to Sara when you write to her and tell her that if my hands had been less demanded by all sorts of women's affairs I should have written a parting word of love to her.
After you left me, I had a good deal of regret that in explaining about my sending Mr. Spencer's letter to Mr. Smith I dwelt on that view of the subject which had the aspect of self-justification. In reality, my chief -- my lasting feeling about the matter is, that I am grieved to have made a mistake, and I am convinced that I acted ill-advisedly in sending it without a direct authorization. Pray tell Mr. Bray this, and that I hope my mistake in this affair will not prevent him from trusting me again when there is a chance that I can be of service. It is true, however, that I do not believe there would have been any difference in the issue, if I had not sent the letter.
Bless you, dear Cara. Believe me always,
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 4 December 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 4 December 1863
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, II, 369-370.
The Priory, | North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 4. 1863.
Dear Cara
The book 212 is come, with its precious inscription, and I have read a great piece of it already (11 a.m.) besides looking through it to get an idea of its general plan. See how fascination shifts its quarter as our life goes on! I cannot be induced to lay aside my regular books for half an hour to read "Mrs. Lirriper's Lodgings," 213 but I pounce on a book like yours which tries to tell me as much as it can in brief space of "the natural order," and am seduced into making it my after-breakfast reading instead of the work I had prescribed for myself in that pleasant quiet time. I read so slowly, and read so few books, that this small fact among my small habits seems a great matter to me. -- I thank you, dear Cara, not simply for giving me the book, but for having put so much faithful labour in a worthy direction and created a lasting benefit which I can share with others. Whether the circulation of a book be large or small there is always this supreme satisfaction about solid honest work, that as far as it goes its effects must be good, and as all effects spread immeasurably what we have to care for is kind and not quantity.
I had a note from Sara the other day which gives me a cheerful idea of her condition at Lea Hurst, but I am a shabby correspondent and have not yet answered her, being in ardent practice of the piano just now, which makes my days shorter than usual. Miss Marshall was kind enough to come to our gathering on the 24th in honour of Charlie's 21st birthday. Mr. Lewes agrees with me in liking her very much, so that we wish we could see her oftener. But I fear her life is very arduous just now and am afraid to ask for any of her time and attention.
With love to the Sposo, who I am sure, is enjoying the sight of your book in its finished state,
Ever your grateful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 31 July [1865]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 31 July [1865]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1865. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
July 31. 1856.
Dear Cara
I wish the fact that caused me the satisfaction of hearing from you had been less sad. When you are writing to Miss Marshall, pray give her my love and deep sympathy. I had supposed that the reason of our not seeing her was probably Miss Collett's 361 increased need of attention.
We have been fixed in London through the season -- Mr. Lewes doing a miraculous amount of work, though with health frequently disturbed. All things have been well with us except health. I think
I have fewer troubles than any other mortal, and I feel utterly ashamed of myself that I don't make my life more precious, when I see what is done by dear friends who are not helped outwardly as I am. You, for example, dear Cara. When will there be an end to new worries for you and Mr. Bray? I had imagined all along that poor Harry Bray was dead. 362 And then that worry about Mr. Taunton 363 -- and the little bit of money you get for your close work. O dear, I wish we could find something better for you to do. But every way to work in London is choked by people on the spot.
George had a rather melancholy letter from Mr. Call the other day -- his sister dying leaving him guardian to her children under not very easy circumstances -- himself apparently oppressed in body and mind, and unable to revise an article which he prepared some time ago for the Fortnightly. He said nothing of Rufa, but perhaps you have heard from her.
Thank you for telling me about Mrs. Wansy's 364 annuity. It is a pleasant thing to know, instead of imagining her destitute. Yet, worse than that sort of destitution befalling an energetic woman is what we see in a friend of ours -- a woman who looks healthy but is practically helpless, from hysteria, I suppose, which is constantly creating illusory maladies. After all, the sound body and the sound mind are beyond any other good on the face of the earth. They don't make every one who has them happy, but the unhappiness created by the absence of themis the worst sort of unhappiness.
I hope Sara hears -- what I learn from Madame Bodichon -- that her friend Miss Carter's sufferings are accompanied with wonderful quietude of mind. And it is the same with Nannie Smith, who, you know, has been laid up for several years. These long maladies seem to have conditions that favour complete resignation.
We are not likely to go to "the other end of Europe" this year. A run in Normandy and Brittany for a month is the utmost we can allow ourselves. It is uncertain at what time we can leave, for Mr. Lewes must have two numbers ready in advance.
Ask Sara if she knows that Mr. Grote is past seventy? One likes to hear of cases in which old age can have the pleasures and dignity of labour. Browning is 55, and is now writing a longer poem than any he has hitherto produced. 365 He is as brisk as 35. Ever, dear Cara,
Your loving Friend
M. E. Lewes.
It grieves me to hear that Mr. Bray suffers so much from his cough. My love to him -- if only that could do his cough any good!

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 30 November 1868
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, III, 67-68.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 30. 68.
My dear Cara
It is delightful news that the Sydenham house is let, and that your anxieties are so far diminished. But please remember that what I said refers to any Christmas, or any time in the calendar, which finds us all above-ground. 839
I like to think of your painting the physiological charts, 840 although they tire your eyes a little, for you must be sure that the good of each work is of a kind that goes deep into young lives. "Fearfully and wonderfully made" 841 are words quite unshaken by any theories as to the making, and I think a great awe in the contemplation of man's delicate structure, freighted with terrible destinies, is one of the most important parts of education. A much-writing acquaintance of ours one day expressed his alarm for "the masses," at the departure of a religion which had terror in it. Surely terror is provided for sufficiently in this life of ours -- if only the dread could be directed towards the really dreadful!
It is a very pretty picture that you have made for me of the hour on Sunday morning -- an hour which I have often shared in old days. 842 Tell Mr. Bray he must consider any book of mine that he likes reading as an "allotropic" condition of the old troublesome Marian, and take the later form as some amends for the earlier.
When one has a pain over the left eye and a palpitation of the heart, it is desirable to know that one's life may be some little good or pleasure to others. Always, dear Cara
Yours lovingly
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 3 February 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 3 February 1876
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Lewes on Vivisection. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 3. 76.
Dear Cara
How is it that your sight is troubling you? Unless there is some inflammation, the right glasses would surely make seeing easy to you. Have you taken pains to get the right glasses? Pray when you come to town consult an oculist. Our young Charles, only 33, was slightly short-sighted and used only occasionally a pince-nez. Feeling a little increased trouble in seeing he went to Liebreich, who told him that he was injuring his eyes by wrong treatment and prescribed spectacles which he now constantly wears. I remember that you used years ago to complain of weariness in using your eyes, and I fear that you have suffered for want of the right aids. Don't wear glasses telles quelles but consult about getting the right ones.
Please tell me whether it would be the least comfort and convenience to you if we were to advance the £40 for your "Morals" 396 so that you could await Nelsons' payment without anxiety -- if I understand you rightly in supposing that they have accepted the work. The fact of the Sydenham house having stood empty for a year must have hampered you sadly. I think it is the first time you have been so long unfortunate with the letting or not-letting -- is it not?
Thanks for the little blue-coated Paul Bradley. The illustrations do look a little worse in this form than when one saw them indulgently on the pages of the Animal World. 397 The doggie watching the gap is the least objectionable. The clergyman is of the namby-pambiest "description."
Mr. Lewes gave evidence on the subject of Vivisection before the Committee of Inquiry, and has corrected the proofs for the Blue Book. 398 He thinks it good that there should be a strong check from public opinion, but 'abthinks'bb that hardly any legislative measure on the subject can be taken without doing more harm than good. Your quotation from the [Science Primer] 399 shocks me very much. Mr. Lewes knows Michael Foster, who is in many respects an admirable man -- but men, like societies, have strange patches of barbarism in the midst of their [civilization.] There are facts in almost everybody's habits for which they "have eyes but see not." 400 Let us be thankful for any anointing that will make us see better. But one wishes that the advocates of good would be a little more scrupulous in their modes of advocacy.
Our daughter-in-law and grandchildren are not coming to England -- at least there is no thought of that at present. She was brought up in the colony. And the little boy is still an infant. The little girl is a very lively [Marian.]
With best love to all
Your affectionate
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 3 April 1871
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 129-130.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | April 3. 71.
My dear Cara
I happened today to be talking to a very sweet-faced woman, 262 (the sister of Dr. Bridges, whom I think you know something of,) and she mentioned, 'e0 propos of educating children in the love of animals, that she had felt the want of some good little book as a help in this matter. I told her of yours, and when I said that it was written by Mrs. Bray, the author of "Physiology for Schools" she said, "O, I know that book well." I have made her a present of my copy of "Duty to Animals" feeling that this was a good quarter in which to plant that offset. For she had been telling me of her practical interest in the Infant and other Schools in Suffolk, where she lives.
We have had a great pleasure today in learning that our friend Miss Bury is engaged to be married, to Mr. Geddes, a Scotch gentleman. 263 There is a streak of sadness for her family in the fact that she is to go to India with her husband next November, but all else is bright in her prospect. It is very sweet to see, and think of, the happiness of the young! [Half a page cut away here.]
I am scribbling with an infirm head, at the end of the day, just for the sake of letting you know one proof, in addition doubtless to many others which you have already had, that your pretty little book is likely to supply a want. With best love to all
Yours ever

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 29 May 1874
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 29. 74.
My dear Cara
You must not please grieve me by applying any of the £50 which you earned by writing Paul Bradly to what it was never intended for.
The plan of printing it is good, but you must let me pay for it as my contribution towards the good ends of your Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to (or the protection of) Animals.
I have faith in your affection for me, that you will not set up any difficulty in the way of my doing this small quota towards what you are working for.
We start for our country Hermitage -- The Cottage, Earlswood Common 98 -- on Tuesday next. We take all our servants else I would have asked you whether you could have made use of our house during any part of your stay in town. But the people in charge are not such as would "do for you." With best love to all,
Your faithfully affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 28 March 1861
MS: National Library of Scotland, transferred from the Edinburgh Public Library. Extract published: Haight, George Eliot, p. 459.
6 Blandford Square | March 28. 61.
Dear Cara
I have not been well enough to write to you earlier, and I am not sure that I am quite well enough yet to say just what I mean and feel -- the most difficult and rarely achieved task of "speech-dividing man."
It is perhaps well to exchange a written word now and then, for it is not in my nature to believe in any love that makes no sign. But I know that is a shallow-hearted irreligious disposition, and no words, or deeds either, have any value apart from the faith -- the trust in our friend's goodness -- that interprets them.
I suppose I must lose my memory altogether before I could forget all the tenderness, forbearance, and generous belief that made the unvarying character of your friendship towards me when we used to be a great deal together. I think I was not insensible to these things at any time, but experience deepens our insight into the past, and we feel we never understood or appreciated it thoroughly while it was the present. I should think it quite a chief blessing if that past which lives invisibly, though it has gone away from our outward daily existence, could have some sort of worthy worship in the present. I hardly know what other word to use but worship; for there is no such thing as a return, or a making amends for deficiencies. We can only feel that very great and good things have been given to us, and that they ought to be hallowed for ever more in our speech and actions. So that if ever you can let me be in any way a sharer and helper in trouble as far as our parted lives and duties make that possible, you will be adding something more to what you have already given of trust and kindness.
Mr. Lewes read aloud to me the "Hidden Fires," 529 and I asked him particularly for his criticism. I said, "What should you say if that paper had been sent to you as an editor?" His answer was: "I should say that the writer had a turn for essay and reflective writing, and I should advise her to expand the introductory part." I think he has a wonderfully correct and rapid estimate of writing, and for that reason I venture to send you his opinion. But I think the Welcome Guest ought to have paid you before this. The rule is to pay on publication, for periodical writing; though the rule is not always observed.
Tell Sara, if she has any questions to note -- to ask them, and I will answer. My portrait is still in Mr. Lawrence's hands, Mr. Blackwood being under the sad trouble of expecting the death of his brother, Major Blackwood, so that his coming to town is likely to be deferred. We hear from those who know Mr. Lawrence well that his conduct in this matter is not an isolated instance. 530 Farewell.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 27 September 1863
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | September 27. 63.
Dear Cara
I felt special thanks, though I did not write them, for your words of love written to me from Wales. Sara delights me with her account of your enterprise in climbing the mountains and the good you seemed to get in body and mind. But now I am chiefly concerned to know whether the change of editorship announced in the Coventry Herald, which I found here on my return home yesterday, implies an arrangement which is advantageous to Mr. Bray. I know it is tiresome to be asked questions which one must answer in writing, but I mention my desire for knowledge that, when an easy opportunity offers, one of you may tell me what the said announcement means.
Your book, I imagine, is being reserved until the right time for advertising school books. I shall be one of your first pupils, for I am taking to an eager study of geography in my old age.
Mr. Lewes and I have been taking our beautiful old walks at Richmond, which have such dear associations for us. Mrs. Congreve came to say goodby to me there, before a departure to Italy, Mr. C's health requiring the search for a mild climate during the winter and early spring.
We are plunged just now in affairs that require both thought and action, and were very much in need of the opportunities for long quiet talk that we found under the Richmond trees. Tell Sara I am grateful for every little note of hers -- always full of matter that I care about. But I will not write to her just yet -- not until I am more at leisure, or have something pleasant to tell. Best love to all from
Yours ever
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 27 November [1851]
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, 1, 266.
Strand | November 27.
Dear Cara
I am a wretch today -- head aching ever since Saturday -- draughts and pills for the last two days -- so I write now to save time instead of on Saturday when I hope to be well. So you must understand that I expect a letter on Monday morning. I hope Sara will duly receive her parcel. I gave the commission to Mr. C. Her letter came marked "Too Late."
Carlyle called the other day, strongly recommending Browning the poet as a writer for the Review, and saying "We shall see" about himself.
In other respects we have been stagnating since Monday, and now I must work, work, work -- which I have scarcely done two days consecutively since I have been here. Lewes says his article on Julia von Kr'fcdener 1067 will be "glorious." He sat in the same box with us at the "Merry Wives of Windsor," and helped to carry off the dolorousness of the play by such remarks as "There's the swan preening," 1068 "The swan comes out now and then," and "The play is a farce in five acts. If it were in one act and one didn't see it, it would be very well" etc., etc.
You see I have nothing to tell you, so goodbye, dear deuter. 1069 Love --
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 27 May [1852]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 27 May [1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1852. Extracts published: Cross, I, 281-282; George Eliot and John Chapman, pp. 53-54.
Strand | May 27.
Dearest Cara
Delighted to have a letter from you once again, and to know that the tooth-ache has fled -- without carrying away the tooth, I hope.
You talk of poor Mr. Chapman's laurels -- alas, alas, he is suffering the most torturing anxiety, advertising for a partner in half-despair of getting another kind of aid from Mr. Gardner. (These are secrets of course). The immediate difficulty is how to pay the authorship of the next number of the W.R. -- a sum of £250!
He sits in the shop the greater part of the day now, and is about to part with Mr. Beveridge, as a step in retrenchment. I suppose I am telling you these things on the ordinary principle of consolation -- "You see there are others as badly off as you" -- but I am afraid this is no balm to you good creatures who have the weakness to care almost as much for other people's sorrows as for your own.
The weather is horrid and depresses me more than I have ever felt it before. I look like one of those old hags we used to see by the wayside in Italy -- only a little worse, for want of the dark eyes and dark hair in contrast with the parchment.
My brightest spot next to my love of old friends, is the deliciously calm new friendship that Herbert Spencer gives me. We see each other every day and have a delightful camaraderie in everything. But for him, my life would be desolate enough now, with poor Mr. C. so occupied and so sad -- but he runs away with a great deal of my time.
Kate Martineau called the other day with a friend of hers. I have not been to see the Mackays yet. The Chapmans brought rather a melancholy account of him. They think him rather worse than otherwise for the marriage. 98 I am so grieved to hear that Sara does not get better. What a wretched lot of old shrivelled creatures we shall be bye-and-bye. Never mind, the uglier we get in the eyes of others the lovelier we shall be to each other -- that has always been my firm faith about friendship, and now it is in a slight degree my experience.
Has Mr. Bray described to you Millais' picture of [the Huguenot
Knight]? 99 The face of the woman is never to be forgotten -- I wish you could see it.
The Americans happily are pouring in now -- hitherto there has been an alarming paucity of lodgers.
Miss Parkes had a grand ball last night. I was asked, but refused to go. 100 I hug letters from you all with rapture -- do let me hear as often as you can. Madame D'Albert has sent me the sweetest letter just like herself and I feel grateful to have such a heart remembering and loving me on the other side of the Jura. They are very well and flourishing.
A thousand loves to Sara and Mr. Bray.
Your
Marian.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 27 February [1871]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1871. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | February 27.
My dear Cara
I am much obliged to you for sending me the Coventry paper containing the notice of Mr. Noel's publication 259 which I had not before known of. Even among those whose minds have been strenuously occupied with wider public troubles there can have been few who have not felt some sympathetic indignation on behalf of Mr. Frank Noel and his friends. It is altogether as felicitous a way of carrying out his vindication as one could imagine, to publish these letters, which must speak better for him than the finest eloquence apr'e8s coup. His father must have suffered heavily.
I hope that you have all weathered this winter pretty well and are entering bravely on the usual severities of spring. I have had more than my usual sense of bodily weakness, and Mr. Lewes has become headachy again of late, but otherwise all is well with our private lot.
The last time I saw Mrs. Call she told me the bad news about her Frank, which I felt to be very grievous for her. Since then I have remained in ignorance about her, but I shall beg Mr. Lewes to call some day soon, and find out any more cheering [The rest of this letter is lacking.]

My dear Cara
Though I am usually content with your silence, thinking much letter-writing a waste of time, it is a real delight to me when I do see your handwriting and have a few of your own words.
I write to say goodby. By a sudden decision, we start tomorrow, and you may be sure that I am busy with preparations. But I cannot go without a word of farewell to you, though a hasty one.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 26 December 1863
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, II, 373.
December 26. 1863.
Dear Cara
Your letter and Sara's are among the many pleasures of this happy Christmas. One of the chief is the great improvement we see in Bertie who is come from his Scotch farming to have a home holiday. It is a delight to see his face bright with a new interest in things, and his body getting stalwart as well as graceful.
We are enjoying our new house too, though it may not quite deserve Mr. Dallas's epithet -- enjoying its quiet and freedom from perpetual stair-mounting -- enjoying also the prettiness of colouring and arrangement, all of which we owe to our dear good friend Mr. Owen Jones. He has determined every detail, so that we can have the pleasure of admiring what is our own without vanity. And another munificent friend has given me the most splendid reclining chair conceivable, so that I am [in] danger of being envied by the Gods, especially as my health is thoroughly good withal. I should like to be sure that you are just as comfortable externally and internally. I daresay you are, being less of a cormorant in your demands on life than I am; and it is that difference which chiefly distinguishes human lots, when once the absolute needs are satisfied.
I hope you are getting as much satisfaction about your book as it deserves. Charlie has taken it out of my hands for the present, to get his share of good from it. With Longmans' abundant machinery for distribution, I should think it is sure to make its way. Reviews or newspaper notices are of less significance even than usual, in the case of an educational work.
Mr. Lewes wants to send you "Romola" as a Christmas present, and has written to order a copy to be sent to you. He does not like that my rule of not giving away my books 219 should prevent him from doing what he insists will give you pleasure. So pray lend the copy in large print to Mr. John Sibree, and save him from the long lines and misprints of the magazine copy.
I grieve to think that Mr. Bray's cough is become an evil that you only expect to be abated and not removed by favorable weather. Best love and wishes to him and you
Ever yours,
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 25 March 1874
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1874. Extracts published: Cross, III, 228-229.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 25. 74.
My dear Cara
Tracy has sent Mr. Lewes also a rigmarole to much the same effect as what he sent you. As to the objection that the anecdotes are taken from the Animal World -- that is ridiculous. As if boys were running about to select anecdotes for their own improvement!
I fear the fatal fact about your story is the absence of God and Hell. "My dear madam, you have not presented motives to the children!" It is really hideous to find that those who sit in the scribes' seats have got no farther than the appeal to selfishness which they call God. The old Talmudists were better teachers. They make Rachel remonstrate with God for his hardness, and remind him that she was kinder to her sister Leah than He to his people -- thus correcting the traditional God by human sympathy. However we must put up with our contemporaries since we can neither live with our ancestors nor with posterity.
Would not the respectable Partridge 60 publish [Paul Bradly]? I have just been looking again over the [tiny] Richard Barton, and the charm of the illustrations both in the story and in the pages of advertisement gives me quite an affection for that publisher. I am loth to have the tale cut up into parts until its publication as a whole is proved quite hopeless.
It is cheering to see the programme of your new Society. There certainly is an awakening of conscience about animals in general as our fellow-creatures -- even the vogue of Balaam's ass is in that sense a good sign. A lady wrote to me the other day that when she went to church in the island of Sark, the sermon turned on that remonstrant hero or heroine.
Thanks, I have been on the whole better this last week or two, though this morning it happens that I have a nasty headache.
Don't imagine that we have had any trouble which should vex you. There is nothing for you to be vexed about except the fact that it is difficult to get good wholesome teaching into print.
Always your loving
Marian.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 25 March 1867
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1867. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 25. 67.
My dear Cara
One of my wants on our return home is to know how you have all borne the severities of this terrible winter. We escaped them for the greater part, having lived chiefly in delicious summer during our long flight which reached as far as the South of Spain. After staying a month at Biarritz, we made our way to San Sebastian, Saragossa, and Barcelona; then by sea to Alicante and Malaga; then over the mountains to Granada, Cordova and Seville, returning homeward by Madrid.
Mr. Lewes says he never enjoyed a journey more and it has answered the great end of restoring him to comparative health. So you perceive that we are fortunate and altogether uninteresting people. I have nothing to tell except travellers' stories, which are always tiresome, like the description of a play which was very exciting to those who saw it.
But I want to know what you can tell me -- so be generous and let me know it. Health is the chief thing, and after that everything that can seriously affect your life.
Sara will perhaps like to hear that we saw R'e9nan in Paris, and had much of his conversation. He seemed to me very like an amiable dissenting minister. With best love to all
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 23 November 1877
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 23. 77.
My dear Cara
About Nelson's intention to [burke] your [Morals,] Mr. Lewes is incredulous. He thinks it does not lie in the sane publisher's nature to waste material in that way, after he has paid for it. But who shall say what does or does not lie in human stupidity, whether well or ill-intentioned?
Thank you very much for the accounts you have sent me of Mr. Bray's state of health and our friends Mrs. Pears and Mrs. Cash. I long that we may have a mild winter to save Mr. Bray and you from an increase of his bronchial trouble. But the prospect for poor Mrs. Pears seems to me more dismal than it can ever be for your husband with his mental activity and cheerfulness. 777
Please give my love to dear Mrs. Cash. I think one may reasonably hope that her constitution will surmount the present symptoms about the heart. Our landlady (for three years at Richmond) had a severe attack of angina pectoris and her physician said to me in a solemn tone -- "Ah, poor Mrs. Croft will not last long -- she has organic disease". But she did last long and in very comfortable health.
When I had read your letter to Mr. Lewes, he said, "What a pretty picture that is of Cara playing the Messiah every Sunday for forty years!" I see the picture as it used to be, in the dear old drawing-room at Rosehill.
Tell Mr. Bray he has not seized the drift of Mr. Lewes's chapter on Motion. 778 But we get along mainly by a pathway of misunderstandings -- proving good cases against somebody who has never questioned them.
Mrs. Merridew I think must be a very beautiful sight in her old age -- there was a nobleness of type in her face that years would not spoil. Yours always lovingly
M. E. L.
I enclose a note to Sara.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 23 November 1874
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 23. 74.
My dear Cara
I am delighted to have the good news about the books. Especially I enjoy thinking that the little darkies in Hindustan will be the better for the work of your dear fair head.
Yes, I should like to have a proof (if it can be had in pages, for slips are too irritating) of Paul Bradly, just for the chance of getting anything done with it in Mrs. Schwabe's direction. She is not forthcoming just now, and may be in Italy for what I know, but she has a house in Clarges St. Piccadilly to which she comes from time to time, and I dare say she will show herself by and by. She is a dear benevolent widow, up to her chin in wealth, I suppose, and wanting to do good with it.
The plan of getting illustrations is a very happy one. I think, in the case of a book about animals, they will really help the moral effect by giving the children more vivid images of the creatures written about.
As to the printing, that is to be paid for irrespective of proceeds or profits, and is my contribution to your Society for the protection of animals.
Please thank Sara from me for her delightful letter, telling me news in her nice easy way, just as of old. In haste,
Your always loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 23 August [1869]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1868. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 23.
My dear Cara
I am much easier now I have news of you. I beseech you not to let the lawyer's bill be in any way a trouble to you and Mr. Bray. If it is anything that in the least hampers you, let me meet it. You know I desire this.
"The true Story of Lady Byron's Life," you see, is to appear in the next "McMillan." 98 You will probably have that in your hands. If not, I will send you the loose sheet. I, in my total ignorance of the inner facts, was more prepared to feel with Lady Byron, than you seem to be, who know much of her through her intimate friends. 99 Byron and his poetry have become more and more repugnant to me of late years (I read a good deal of him a little while ago, 100 in order to form a fresh judgment). As to this story, I cannot help being sorry that it seemed necessary to publish what is only worthy to die and rot. After all Byron remains deeply pitiable, like all of us sinners.
I have thought with interest of poor Mrs. Dallas, 101 since I heard of her determination to go to America -- if she could raise £800! She seems to have shewn a praiseworthy energy under all her troubles, always doing what she could to earn an honest living. The Sp[anish] Gypsy has had a very large sale in America -- so she might possibly find some favour for it in an audience there. I should only be glad if it would give her readings a little acceptable novelty.
Our own health has been feeble lately -- and I have been at a lower ebb than usual. But otherwise, Thornie is our only trouble.
Please give my love to Miss Marshall, and tell her that I am always bearing her in mind as one of our kind friends. Best love to Sara -- and some headshaking at her tendency to work too hard. Ought she not rather to be thinking of an autumn holiday? Only write when you have something to tell me -- not simply to acknowledge.
Ever thine
Pollian.
Tell Mr. Bray that my head has much fellowship with those aches of his. I don't know anything about the article on Lady Byron in Blackwood. 102 It escaped my observation.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 22 March 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 22 March 1873
MS: Yale. Extract published: Mathilde Blind, George Eliot, 1883, p. 30.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 22. 73.
My dear Cara
I see at once that you must be right about the necessity for being simple and literal. In fact I have ridiculous impulses in teaching children, and always make the horizon too wide.
"The Wounded Bird" is perfect of its kind -- and that kind is the best for a longer work. You yourself see clearly that it is an exceptional case for any one to be able to write books for children without putting in them false morality disguised as devout religion. And you are one of the exceptional cases. I am quite sure, from what you have done, that you can do the thing which is still wanted to be done. As to imagination, the Wounded Bird is full of imagination. And by the way I wish Mr. Smithers were not a nasty man -- he does put delightful illustrations into his little books.
Then, further -- cheques must not be locked up in drawers, else the money they represent may vanish. You will do the work much better if your mind is swept clear of various other projects which you might think it right to entertain for the sake of earning something. And you have got no commercially minded publisher to please. You shall have no trouble about the book. Do, dear Cara, take my view of the matter. Have you not done a great deal of work -- really good work in that geographical survey, and never been paid for it? I cannot bear that you should go on in that way. And I look on this cheque entirely as public money which I am empowered to dispense. The other day I had £50 sent me for the right to reprint "The Spanish Gypsy" abroad. 758 It came quite unexpectedly -- I don't want it for myself or those who are immediately mine.
Even if I thought it was private money, you ought to do me this kindness of old friendship, this willingness to share with me. And, as I said before, I do not regard it as private money. Therefore, please get the cheque cashed without delay, and set your dear head to work on this duty that has come near to you.
Yours ever lovingly
Marian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1869. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
July 22. 69.
My dear Cara
Remembering your experienced sympathy, I cannot refrain from telling you that we are much happier about Thornie. Paget thinks him on the way to recovery, and the signs of this are very marked. His nights are usually passed quietly, and on most days he is carried down to the lawn, and lies out there for two or three hours. 90 You will imagine how glad we are of the warmer weather which makes this strengthening change possible for him.
I conclude that you are at home again by this time, though the weeks have passed so dreamily for me that I cannot tell how long it is since I saw you. With love to Sara
Always yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 22 December 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 22 December 1873
MS: Yale. Brief extracts published: Cross, III, 220-221.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 22. 73.
Dear Cara
Jubilate! The story, 897 I am convinced, will do more good in the hands of the Christian K. S. than in any other mode of distribution. And I am very glad that you at once see your way to a little "ornamental surgery" for the improvement of your clergymen. Indeed, if I had had to criticize your tale -- heaven forbid that I should ever have to criticize anybody's work! -- but if I had been obliged to say what seemed to me its least commendable quality, I should have mentioned certain parts concerning the schoolmaster and the clergyman which seem to be addressed to grown-up people and imply a shifting of the point of view from that of an appeal to the young, which is otherwise consistently and vigorously maintained.
As to the other objection, I know what you meant, but in writing any careful presentation of human feelings, you must count on that infinite stupidity of readers who are always substituting their crammed notions of what ought to be felt for any attempt to recall truly what they themselves have felt under like circumstances. Anyhow, the reader's demands are very mild, and you will hardly find any difficulty in meeting them.
But please dismiss from your "neural groups" any kind of reel or dance that may be going on there as to your not having done what you were asked to do. You have the proof now, that your story strikes those quite outside your circle of friends as being valuable for its purpose, and you have well-earned more money than perhaps you will ever get for your labour. So pray do not torment yourself to write anything which does not attract your imagination, or is in any sense a troublesome effort.
Please give my love to Sara, and tell her that I received her reassuring card. Also, that the other day Julia Wedgwood told me of Miss Alice Carter having said to her that she found much "help and healing" in Sara's Thoughts. These indirect tributes, uttered to third persons, are better than any direct assurances.
We are under the care of Dr. Andrew Clarke 898 who ministers to all the minds diseased 899 by telling them to diminish their allowances of pudding and draughts of tea -- and doubtless we shall be the better by and by. We are to spend Christmas Eve and Christmas Day with our friends at Weybridge, London being the least agreeable of Christmas scenery.
I am delighted that you have found "The Problems of Life and Mind" so clear and readable. We are surprized to find that 800 have been sold already 900 -- which for a hard philosophic book is a good sale, and implies that there is an increasing public for such things.
I am glad to hear that Mr. Bray's cough is better -- at least so I interpret Sara's statement that he is looking well.
Please send me word when the C. K. S. has finally accepted the manuscript. Our days are stuffed full of engagements, even with all our avoidance of the world, and you will not wonder if I write in a hasty way.
Your ever loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 21 December 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 21 December 1876
MS: Yale. Brief extract published: Mathilde Blind, George Eliot, 1883, pp. 172-173.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 21. 76.
Dear Cara
Your letter is quite precious to me, notwithstanding that there is much in it of a saddening kind -- I mean, about the bodily suffering and the prospect of more. But one would rather grieve with one's friends than have them grieving without one's knowing anything of it. -- I cannot quite agree that it is hard to see what has been the good of your life. It seems to me very clear that you have been a good of a kind that would have been sorely missed by those who have been nearest to you and also to some who are more distant. And it is this kind of good which must reconcile us to life -- not any answer to the question, [What would the universe have been without me?] The point one has to care for is, [Are A B and C the better for me?] And there are several letters of the alphabet that could not have easily spared you in the past and that can still less spare you in the present.
These returns of bronchitis must shake dear Sara very painfully and cannot but have a depressing effect on her mind as well as on her average bodily state. I trust that Mrs. Cash and other neighbours help you to cheer her by sympathetic attentions, but we have to face the terrible fact that, even where everything kind is done, there are periods in the majority of lives when pain dips the scale so low that comfort seems nought.
I am so glad to think that poor Frank Hennell's lot is brightened by his marriage and that the new niece's visit can be looked forward to with pleasure. A great load must have been lifted off Mrs. Call's mind, and she will perhaps now be able to settle down finally in England with a prospect of satisfaction. -- We too are thinking of a new settling down, for we have bought a house in Surrey about four miles from Godalming on a gravelly hill among the pine trees, but with neighbours to give us a sense of security. Our present idea is that we shall part with this house and give up London except for occasional visits. We shall be on the same line of railway with some good friends at Weybridge and Guildford.
George Dawson was strongly associated for me with Rosehill -- not to speak of the general Baptist Chapel where we all heard him preach for the first time (to us). And do you remember Mr. R. R. R. Moore? 581 His son has come to the border of my scenery as a friend of Madame Bodichon's. I have not seen him, but she thinks most highly of his character and powers. He is an anatomist. I have a vivid recollection of an evening when Mr. and Mrs. Flower dined at your house with George Dawson when he was going to lecture at the Mechanics' Institute, and you felt compassionately towards him because you thought the rather riotous talk was a bad preface to his lecture. We have a Birmingham friend 582 whose acquaintance we made many years ago in Weimar, and from him I have occasionally had some news of Mr. Dawson. I feared -- what you mention -- that his life had been a little too strenuous in these latter years.
The [Sir Charles Grandison] you are reading must be the series of little fat volumes you lent me to carry to the Isle of Wight, 583 where I read it at every interval when my father did not want me, and was sorry that the long novel was not longer. It is a solace to hear of any one's reading and enjoying Richardson. We have fallen on an evil generation who would not read [Clarissa] even in an abridged form. The French have been its most enthusiastic admirers, but I don't know whether their present admiration is more than traditional, like their set phrases about their own classics.
I don't know what you refer to in the [Jewish World.] Perhaps the report of Dr. Hermann Adler's Lecture on Deronda to the Jewish Working
Men, given in the Times. Probably the Dr. Adler whom you saw is Dr. Hermann's father, still living as Chief Rabbi. I have had some delightful communications from Jews and Jewesses both at home and abroad. Part of the club scene in D. D. is flying about in the Hebrew tongue through the various Hebrew newspapers which have been copying the [Magid,] in which the translation was first sent to me three months ago. The Jews naturally are not indifferent to themselves.
The other night 584 we went to hear the Bach Choir, a society of Ladies and Gentlemen got together by Jenny Lind, who sings in the middle of them, her husband acting as conductor. It is pretty to see people who might be nothing but empty fashionables taking pains to sing fine music in tune and time with more or less success. One of the baritones we know is a Grosvenor 585 who used to be a swell guardsman, and has happily taken to good courses while still quite young. Another is a handsome young Gurney 586 -- not of the unsatisfactory Co. but of the Russell Gurney kin. A soprano is Mrs. Ponsonby -- wife of the Queen's Secretary, General P. -- the granddaughter of Earl Grey and just like him in the face. And so on. These people of "high" birth are certainly reforming themselves a little.
Mr. Lewes has just come up to me after reading your letter and says, "For God's sake, tell her not to have the photograph reproduced!" -- and I had nearly forgotten to say that the fading is what I desired. I should not like the image to be perpetuated. It needs the friendly eyes that regret to see it fade, and must not be recalled into emphatic black and white for indifferent gazers. Pray let it finally vanish.
Please give my best love to Mrs. Cash and dear Mrs. Pears, who often returns to my thought because of my fear that she has had some heart-troubles about her daughter. Do let me know the good news when the Sydenham house is let, and do not forget your promise that you will not suffer any lack which I could hinder -- you know, I mean lack of comforts for that difficult breath, such as might come from a sense that expensiveness obliged renunciation. With much affection all round,
Yours always
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 21 August 1869
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 21 August 1869
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 21. 69.
My dear Cara
Since I wrote you a hasty note telling you that we were more hopeful about our poor Thornie, we have gone through many sad fluctuations. The apparently decided improvement lasted hardly a week, and since then he has had an attack of paraplegia which for a few days made the lower part of his body quite helpless. He has recovered the use of his limbs, contrary to the expectation of Sir H. Holland 95 who has been kindly giving us advice in Paget's absence. But the dear boy is more than ever wasted, and in all ways shows signs of reduced strength. We feel utterly in the dark as to the probabilities of his case, and must resignedly accept what each day brings, comforting ourselves with the thought that various sad predictions have been successively proved false. We have just had the misfortune of being obliged to part with our Nurse, whose health has broken down, but we have a promising substitute. 96 Such are our circumstances.
But I confess, I should not have been impelled to write to you of what is far from cheerful, if I had not wished to hear something of you. How are you all? And what external conditions are making life easier or harder for you? Pray let me have the satisfaction of knowing how things go with you.
Mrs. H. B. Stowe has just sent me from America an article which she has written for the next Atlantic Monthly 97 containing the "True Story of Lord Byron's Life" which she had entrusted to her by Lady Byron. It has been drawn from her by the Countess Guiccioli's wretched book. With best love to Sara
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

October 20. 69.
My dear Cara
Thornie is dead. He died last night, very gently. Nurse and I raised him and his last breathings were quite peaceful. When death comes, it always seems worse than anything else -- but it is not really so. I am too crushed now to feel that the dear boy is saved from a life of almost certain deprivation and helplessness.
Always your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 20 March 1877
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, III, 305-306.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 20. 77.
My dear Cara
Your letter on the breakfast table was just what I had long been wishing for, and I had not earned the good by writing to you only because I had rather dolorous news to tell of ourselves. At the beginning of February Mr. Lewes was seized with rheumatic gout, and for some time was either not able to leave his bed or else only able to move by the help of two sticks. Imagine my anguish in sight both of that present and the possible future -- for him whose light quick step has always been unlike every other to my ear. But at the end of three weeks he could get along without a stick and now he walks as well as ever. I was not well before his attack came, but of course I forgot all about my back-ache in running and carrying, standing and lifting, as a nurse must do -- and I suppose all this was the worst possible regimen for my body, so that as soon as my patient got well, I broke down with my old ailment which only began to mend greatly four or five days ago. However, I am able now to take a walk as well as a drive, and to sit through a long concert, 623 and unless I have a relapse into evil conditions I hope soon to be no weaker than usual.
Your good news really helps the cure. The relief to dear Mr. Bray's bodily suffering is the foremost good, but next to that I rejoice in your getting freedom from the greater part of the monetary anxieties which have worried you. I think Mr. Bray's mind will be much the easier, and this is so important when all one's energy is demanded to bear pain of body that I can't help longing for the sale of the Sydenham house too, seeing that Mrs. Winnall 624 might be provided with another by the help of her parents.
Please give my tender love to Sarah [sic] and tell her that the years make the memory of her always dearer to me. I grieve to think of this liability to bronchitis which I feel sure is a greater trial than anything I have known -- tearing chest and head at once. One can only long that the spring will be a gentle one and confirm her recovery.
You must read Harriet Martineau's Autobiography. While I was ill Mr. Lewes took my office of reader and for the most part read the first two volumes to me. The account of her childhood and early youth is most pathetic and interesting, but 'ablike'bb as in all books of the kind the charm departs as the life advances, and the writer has to tell of her own triumphs. One regrets continually that she felt it necessary not only to tell of her intercourse with many more or less distinguished persons -- which would have been quite pleasant to everybody -- but also to pronounce upon their entire merits and demerits, especially when, if she had died as soon [as] she expected, these persons would nearly all have been living to read her gratuitous rudenesses. But I rejoiced profoundly in the conquest of right feeling which determined her to leave the great, sad breach with her once beloved brother in almost total silence, and as I did not read Mrs. Chapman's volume (Mr. Lewes having glanced through it and told me that it was worthless) I was feeling hardly anything about the book but satisfaction in the picture of a life which was on the whole thoroughly virtuous, beneficent and dignified, until I found (what Mr. Lewes had not observed) that this wretched Mrs. Chapman has been so forsaken of all the good as to enter into details and accusations connected with that very quarrelling which Harriet Martineau had willed to bury in silence. Really there is nothing but imbecility to be pleaded as a reason why Mrs. Chapman's conduct should not be called wicked. Then again, she has published H.M's private letters -- at the end of the very book which begins with a solemn protest against any such publication!
Browning observed to me that Miss Martineau's procedure in demanding back her own letters, made it the more reprehensible for her to enter into statements about her relations with others, because her own letters being destroyed there remained no evidence to check her statements. And one cannot help being convinced that her representations are often false, not from any untruthfulness in her but from the extremely self-satisfied point of view with which she regarded her transactions with business acquaintances and her intercourse with friends.
Still, in spite of Mrs. Chapman, I hope the book will do more good than harm. Many of the most interesting little stories in it about herself and others she had told me (and Mr. Atkinson) when I was staying with her, almost in the very same words. But they were all the better for being told in her silvery voice. She was a charming talker, and a perfect lady in her manners as a hostess. It is a comfort to think -- looking back on the vile treatment she received from the Quarterly and Frazers, making people believe that she was a coarse-minded, repulsive woman 625 -- that such blackguardism in print could not be tolerated now, and that it would hardly enter into anybody's mind to conceive such sentences for any form of outward utterance.
I do hope that Rufa is coming home to some years of settled domestic enjoyment, now that her chief anxiety about Frank is removed. If you write to her again will you ask her to remember that we always think of her and Mr. Call with affection and hope to see them before we go into the country. That will not be till June. And we are only going to bivouac in our Surrey home for a few months, to try what alterations are necessary. We shall come back to this corner in the Autumn. [3 words deleted.] We don't think of giving up London altogether at present -- but we may have to give up life before we come to any decision on that minor point.
Your loving
Marian.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 20 March 1873
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1873. My little book. Marian's suggestion for story about animals. Published: Mathilde Blind, George Eliot, 1883, pp. 28-30.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 20. 73.
My dear Cara
Many thanks for the helpful things you have sent me. "The Wounded Bird" 754 is charming. But now something very much larger of the same kind must be written, and you are the person to write it -- something that will bring the emotions, sufferings, and possible consolations of the dear brutes vividly home to the imaginations of children: fitted for children of all countries, as Reineke Fuchs is comprehensible to all nations. A rough notion came to me the other day of supposing a House of Refuge, not only for dogs but for all distressed animals: the keeper of this Refuge understands the language of the brutes which includes differences only of dialect not hindering communication even between birds and dogs, by the help of some Ulysses among them who is versed in the various tongues and puts in the needed explanations. Said keeper overhears his refugees solacing their evenings by telling the story of their experiences, and finally acts as editor of their Autobiographies. I imagine my long-loved fellow-creature, the Ugly Dog, telling the sorrows and the tender emotions of gratitude which have wrought him into a sensitive soul. The Donkey is another cosmopolitan sufferer and a greater martyr than Saint Lawrence -- if one only knew what fine motives he has for his meek endurance and how he loves a friend who will scratch his nose.
All this is not worth anything except to make you feel how much better a plan you can think of. Only you must positively write this book which everybody wants -- this book which will do justice to the share our "worthy fellow-labourers" have had in the groaning and travailing of the world towards the birth of the right and fair.
But you must not do it without the "sustenance of labour" -- I don't say "pay," since there is no pay for good work. Let Mr. Smithers be -- blest with the blessing of the unscrupulous. I want to contribute something towards helping brutes and helping the children, especially the southern children, to be good to the creatures who are continually at their mercy. I can't write the needed book myself, but I feel sure that you can, and that you will not refuse the duty.
The cheque for £50 enclosed is only a necessary condition to your setting about a work which will for a time exclude other undertakings. Do not consider that it is my money; 755 it is money already devoted to the purpose which I plead with you that you may carry out.
Always your affectionate
Marian.
