Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 2 September 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 2 September 1873
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1873. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 2. 73.
My dear Cara
I am very glad to hear that the story 835 is finished. Will you send me the manuscript and let me read it? Then, if it is old enough for boys of ten or eleven, I will offer it to Mr. Macmillan. It would be an advantage to have it appear in the lists of so important a publisher, who has issued some of the most successful books for children.
We returned from the Continent only ten days ago. On Friday we go to the house we have taken in the country, on experiment only, to see if it will suit us as a permanent home. We shall break up nothing here, as we take the other house furnished and shall give it up without trouble if we find it undesirable to move thither finally. The address is Blackbrook, Bickley, Kent. So will you next week send the manuscript to me there?
Mr. Lewes did not flourish very well during our journey. He was troubled with an attack of deafness (which happily has proved to be due to a temporary cause) and he had continual colds, finishing with a cough which still lingers but is now less troublesome. We wandered quite away from our plan, and did not go to any place, except Fontainebleau, which we had set down in our programme. The reason was, that I felt too weak to venture on the amount of journeying by railway which our project of going to Geneva demanded, and we feared that the heat of July and August would be trying in that region. Moreover, I was running away from the fatigue of seeing too many acquaintances, and shrank from the excitement that Geneva would be sure to bring. So we went to the Vosges, the lovely scene of Erckmann-Chatrian's books; and travelled by easy stages. Monsieur d'Albert is living and still active. He is seven or eight years younger than Madame d'Albert, who is now dying gently of her more than seventy years. Their two handsome sons, who were little boys when I shared their home, are now married and eminently prosperous at Marseilles, and "Maman" has seen her two groups of grandchildren.
You say nothing of Sara or of Mr. Bray. I hope the silence means that the summer-time has been favourable to them. It is you only who are exempt from all the infirmities of age. You will live to bury us all -- I am thinking of the answer given by our friend's Irish servant when his master proposed to pension him off: "Nay, Sir, I'll stay to bury you." With best love to all
Your affectionate
Marian.
Mr. Chapman (Chapman and Hall) has not made any further communication about "The British Empire," since Mr. Lewes gave him the revised account of the Numbers sold. Whence it must be concluded that he has given up the notion of reprinting it.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 2 May 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 2 May 1864
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 2. 64.
Dear Cara
On Saturday I wrote to Sara telling her that we were about to start for Italy 260 -- not writing to you because I was uncertain as to your whereabout. This morning I have received a note from her telling me of your dear Nelly's severe illness, and I cannot rest without sending a word in sign of my deep sympathy with you in this trouble. I only hope that Sara's fears are naturally exaggerated by the fact of her absence: trouble always seems heavier when it is only one's thought and not one's bodily activity that is employed about it.
Sara writes that she has sent on my letter to her, so that I need tell you nothing further about our own destination. The object of this little note is only to vent some of the sadness I feel at the new weight that is pressing on you and Mr. Bray.
Ever yours, with love
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 2 June 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 2 June 1873
MS: Yale. Brief extracts published: Cross, III, 206-207.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 2. 73.
My dear Cara
Thanks for sending me word of poor Miss Rebecca's death. 811 It touches me deeply to think of her as having been long imbecile, for in spite of reason telling one that this is better than pain, the imagination not the less shrinks from it in association with a friend whom one once looked up to with reverence. She was always particularly good and affectionate to me, and I had much happiness in her as my teacher.
You see we are not in the country yet. And our failure to get such a retreat as we wanted has caused us to change our plans. We intend to go abroad in about a fortnight, taking our way slowly to Geneva, for the sake of seeing my old friends there. Madame d'Albert is very aged now, and has lately had an illness which threatened her life. If we can get so far as Geneva, I should like to see her again. But we mean to commit ourselves to nothing in the way of travelling, and so make no arrangements beforehand, beyond the determination of our starting point.
In September a house near Chiselhurst will be open to us -- a house which we think of ultimately making our sole home, turning our backs on London. But we shall be allowed to have it furnished for a year on trial.
Mr. Lewes received your letter containing the melancholy disillusion about the number sold of your "British Empire," and of course he straightway communicated the correction to Mr. F. Chapman, who undertook to reconsider the terms of publication on this new basis. 812 He has not yet sent word of the result, but Mr. Lewes will take an opportunity of seeing him, and will let you know of any definite issue. Necessarily, the terms offered will be less advantageous than before.
I am glad to hear that you are thinking of my friends the donkeys. I feel sure that something pretty will come out of your thinking. If one could but get children to begin feeling gratefully towards the dumb creatures that work!
I am sorry to hear of Sara's sore brain: we know something of the sensations which I imagine she means to describe by those words. She ought to rest completely, and be passive in the sunshine. My best love to her -- and trust in her affection, spite of long silence.
Frank 813 going to Peru! This is at least a temporary improvement in things, and I hope it will cheer Mrs. Call. She has lately written to her friend Mrs. Orr to get her information about Algiers, whence I conclude that she has a notion of passing the next winter in that region. I am very tired and sleepy --
Yours lovingly
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 2 December 1853
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 2 December 1853
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 318-319.
Cambridge Street | December 2. 1853.
Dear Cara
So you suspect me of benevolent hypocrisy. "Ut tute es, ita cense[a]s omnes esse," saith the Latin grammar. To prove to you that you are unjust, I am going to detail all my troubles to you. In the first place, the door of my sitting-room doesn't quite fit, and a draught is the consequence. Secondly, there is a piano in the house, which has decidedly entered on its second childhood, and this piano is occasionally played on by Miss Pitt with a really enviable aplomb. Thirdly, the knocks at the door startle me -- an annoyance inseparable from a ground-floor room. Fourthly, Mrs. Pitt 411 scolds the servants, stringendo e fortissimo, while I am dressing in a morning. Fifthly, -- there is no fifthly. I really have not another discomfort when I am well, which, alas, I have not been for the last ten days. Liver or stomach or some other agglomeration of cells has been "striking" like all other employ'e9s and has deranged everything else. So while I have been up to the chin in possibilities of enjoyment I have been too sick and headachy to use them. "One thing is needful" 412 -- a good digestion.
That quotation reminds me to tell Sara that if she feels inclined to abuse James Martineau I wish she would write me the worst she can say of him, for I am just now thoroughly disgusted with his article in the Prospective in reply to F. Newman's chapter on the Perfection of Jesus. 413 I am angry with Mr. Lewes for having said a word of compliment about it. 414 Love to all.
Your ever affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 18 March 1865
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 18 March 1865
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1865. Extracts published: Cross, II, 400-401.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 18. 65.
My dear Cara
You see I have let the weeks go by -- thinking of you, but not writing to you. I believe you are one of the few who can understand that in certain crises, direct expression of sympathy is the least possible to those who most feel sympathy. If I could have been with you in bodily presence, I should have sat silent, thinking silence a sign of feeling that speech, trying to be wise, must always spoil. The truest things one can say about great death are the oldest simplest things that everybody knows by rote, but that no one knows really till death has come very close. And when that inward teaching is going on, it seems pitiful presumption for those who are outside to be saying anything. There is no such thing as consolation, when we have made the lot of another our own as you did Nelly's. The anguish must be borne -- it will only get more and more bearable as other thoughts and feelings recover some power.
I don't know whether you strongly share, as I do, the old belief that made men say the gods loved those who died young. It seems to me truer than ever, now life has become more complex and more and more difficult problems have to be worked out. Life, though a good to men on the whole, is a doubtful good to many, and to some not a good at all. To my thought, it is a source of constant mental distortion to make the denial of this a part of religion, to go on pretending things are better than they are -- like talking of "your Majesty's happy reign" to a successful monarch whose reign has been one of blood and fire to half a population, who happen to be at a distance and out of sight. So to me, early death takes the aspect of salvation -- though I feel too that those who live and suffer may sometimes have the greater blessedness of being a salvation.
But I will not write of judgments and opinions. What I want my letter to tell you is that I love you truly, gratefully, unchangeably. And to show me you believe it, you must not write till you feel inclined -- not think I shall mind if you don't answer this at all, for indeed there is nothing to answer.
Sara spent an hour or two with us. She struck me as looking remarkably well in health, but with less ability than usual to receive impressions. I mean, that she seemed nervously absorbed, and dim of apprehension for everything outside her. I hope this stay at the coast will be a renovation for her.
It has been a grief to me to read in the parliamentary debates, the statement of Coventry distress, and the absence of any strong hope as to the revival of trade there. 324 I wish I had had some clothes to send, as Mr. Bray desired; but I really get rapidly fleeced of spare wool. The few things I could have parted with were rather for those who required to look "respectable."
With love to him, always, dear Cara, your old
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 17 February 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 17 February 1874
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 17. 74.
My dear Cara
I am thoroughly disappointed at this result of all your labour and long waiting. If it had been due to the behaviour of a single person or a firm, I should have said that you had been treated abominably, but I suppose that Christian Committees have no conscience, any more than other boards, and what their Secretary had said would have no binding power on them.
However, Mr. Lewes is not yet in despair, and I hope soon to write to you again. Meanwhile, revoke your very false conclusion that you "have no talent for this sort of thing." You have none, certainly, for enforcing such motives as the dread of devils and hell-fire -- a talent which might perhaps find a larger recognition. But the testimony of the Christian Knowledge reader should prove to you that your story seemed good enough to him to be recommended in spite of his objections to it.
That is depressing news about the "Humanity School Books," and is one of the many facts that are constantly turning up to check one's too hasty hopes about the improvement of public opinion. But we will not yet be quite downhearted about "Paul Bradly" at least, and I am sure that the book would interest boys and girls, if we could get it circulated.
Thank Sara for sending me the Coventry election news. I have been discussing it today with Mrs. Congreve, who was also puzzled as to the particular [Sam Carter] concerned and shared my identification of Mr. Jackson with the son of our old acquaintances. I remember hearing of Miss Jane Carter.
I am better now, and have not had any new attack of pain. With best love to all
Yours always
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 16 July [1867]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 16 July [1867]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
July 16.
Dear Cara
It was very good of you to write me a little news of yourself. I feel it a privation if I wait very long without a word or two from you or Sara, to give me some idea of the aspect life is bearing with you. Even if the aspect be grievous I prefer the pain of knowing it, to remaining ignorant and therefore indifferent while something is pressing hardly on you. I don't know whether you boil over, as I do, at the want of proportion in the denunciation of sins. That Sara should be one of the sufferers from the commercial baseness into which the nation is sinking helps to make me think with still more indignation at the comparative indulgence which that worst corruption of our society meets with, while our friend Professor Beesly is being persecuted for simply pointing out the unfairness with which crime is estimated. 648
Dear Sara -- I think a great deal, though she may not, of her income being reduced. And she is one among multitudes. An old friend of Mr.
Lewes's, 649 a man of distinguished intellectual refinement, who has been wealthy enough to live the life of a "country gentleman," unhappily some years ago, discovered a valuable sort of clay on his land, and thinking he ought to get money for daughters, entered into commercial schemes for working this clay. In the panic last year all turned out badly for him, and he has had to part with everything -- even to his library. A sickly, sensitive man, too, and no longer young.
That unmanageable Mr. Thornton is a grievous thorn in your sides -- the more so as I suppose it would be difficult, if not impossible to get quite rid of him.
I trust, dear Cara, that there is no friend to whom you would allow the privilege of giving you any help or comfort rather than to me. Change inevitably comes in many things as life advances, but of this I am sure, that my affection for you, my gratitude, my regret that I have not been a worthier friend to you, will never change while my mind lives. One needs to say these things now and then. But usually I feel with you that letters are unsatisfactory except as an occasional bulletin showing how and where one's friend is. It is a sad waste of life to write explanatory sheets that end in explaining nothing except the impossibility of mutual understanding.
You asked about my portrait. There has never been any portrait of me except the one now hung at the academy (by Mr. Burton in chalks) and another by Lawrence also in chalks, done many years ago, and now in the possession of Mr. Blackwood, at Edinburgh.
With best love to Sara
Your affectionate
Marian.

648 E. S. Beesly made a moderate speech  at a meeting of Trades-Unionists at Exeter Hall urging them to repudiate the accusation that the recent violence at Sheffield was a normal incident of Unionism. He was singled out for attack as an advocate of assassination and crime, and a serious attempt was made to deprive him of his professorship and expel him from the Headship of University College, London. See Frederic Harrison, Autobiographic Memoirs, 2 vols., 1911, 1, 316-321. Punch called him "Professor Beastly," as a name that describes the character of his speech. (13 July 1867, p. 14.)

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 15 April [1872]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 15 April [1872]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1872. Hitherto unpublished.
April 15.
Dear Cara
I shall be much obliged to you if you will put a paragraph on my behalf in your next letter to Mrs. Call. Pray tell her first of all, with my best love, that we have thought with much hardly earned fellow-feeling of that sad trouble -- Mr. Call's illness. And next, that I constantly recall her with gratitude for having trained Mrs. Dowling so well. Both she and Elizabeth have been comforts to us -- the only drawback being the feeble health of the latter.
As to our going abroad, there is no chance of it before the autumn, and then I think we shall not go further than Geneva. Our present desire is to get into the country, but we have not yet found a house. This warm weather has brought out the advertisements, however, and we shall probably soon be "accommodated," which, as Justice Shallow says, is a good phrase. 512 I have been better until today when I find the effects of some draught or other in face and neck ache.
It does seem a pity that Sara cannot come to hear music and have other varieties such as Sydenham would give her. I suppose the railway journeying would be impossible to her without some one to take entire charge of her.
I read Mrs. Pears's letter with pleasure, tell her: and assure her that I have a lively and grateful remembrance of her friendliness towards me in old days.
We have not seen Mr. Spencer since you were with us. He is often staying with friends in the country, and his time is much occupied.
Mrs. Call, if she has not yet heard of it, will be interested in your telling her that her excellent old friend Mr. William Smith -- the author of "Thorndale," has lately died. He had heart-disease, and was reduced to extreme weakness, but retained some of the brightness and all the gentleness of his charming nature to the last. He and his wife had had perfect happiness together for eleven years. Now she is suffering that heaviest sorrow which it is but mockery to try and console. They had been at Brighton for some time, and he died in the house of a niece there. He was a very old friend of Mr. Lewes's too, and always showed the most generous interest in his work, of whatever kind it might be.
Goodbye, dear Cara. I hope that you and Mr. Bray too will have nothing to mar your holiday -- not even a wet day, for surely the earth has had water enough for some time to come.
Yours ever lovingly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 14 November 1863
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1863. Extract published: Cross, II, 367.
The Priory, | North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 14. 1863.
Dear Cara
At last we are in our new home, with only a few details still left to arrange. An attack of influenza made both the prospect and reality of removal rather worse to me than it would otherwise have been; but in any case such fringing away of precious life in thinking of carpets and tables is an affliction to me and seems like a nightmare from which I shall find it bliss to awake into my old world of care for things quite apart from upholstery.
Sara, I suppose is away from you, paying her visit into Derbyshire. I hope she will get much good from it. Her letters seem to imply that enjoyment comes to her only in brief snatches, chiefly through her studies and writing, and that saddens me in thinking of her. How little we can do, even for those towards whom we feel the most tenderly.
I am wondering whether the Sydenham house is let, so that you and Mr. Bray may have a serene outlook on that side. Nelly, I hope, is ceasing to cause you anxiety about her health. Any news about you, written on a scrap of paper anyhow, will be welcome to
Your affectionate
M. E. Lewes.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 14 January 1875
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Mr. Fiske. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 14. 1875.
Dear Cara
Herewith the cheque for £28.10. 199 I am very glad to see the specimen of the Animal World. The portrait of the dear donkey on the right hand side I am sure must be edifying. The plan of getting illustrations in this way seems to me most fortunate.
Then about the Blood. Mr. Lewes says, [Yes, the red colour is rust] (until further notice).

Mr. Fiske used to come to us sometimes while he was in England. A large-headed man with rather a good-looking face -- what Milton might call a "bush with frizzy hair implicit" 200 -- staring at you as if in spellbound silence when he put out his hand to say goodbyes and altogether rather in the heavy style. Yet he is not at all a heavy writer.
I hope you got a card from me some time ago, correcting my omission to return dear Mrs. Pears's greeting in my [The second page has been cut away.]

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 13 June 1869
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1869. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 13. 69.
My dear Cara
We returned from Italy six weeks ago, but since then our time and feelings have been absorbed by our poor Thornie, who arrived three days afterwards -- two months sooner than we had thought it possible for him to get to us. We have been suffering much in seeing his suffering and our days have been broken into small fragments. The cause of his illness, which at the best must be long, was an injury of the spine.
It would be a pity to write only to tell a friend of such sadness; but I am unwilling to lose, by further silence, any chance of hearing from you or seeing you, since the years offer so few of such chances; and as we have not seen Mr. and Mrs. Call [three words deleted] I think you are likely to imagine us still away.
My motive for writing is to know as much as I can about you, so be sure that I shall be grateful for every detail on that subject. With love to all,
Ever, dear Cara, Your faithful and affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 13 January 1862
MS: Yale. Endorsed. 1862. Extract published: Cross, II, 330.
Blandford Sq. | January 13. 62.
Dear Cara
A few words straight from yourself are very precious to me, and if there is some anxiety mingled with the satisfaction they bring -- that is the way with all good things in this world, where even untroubled love is overhung by the shadow of death.
It is a great thing to have had so much delight in the return of an old friend, 9 and I am glad to think that his settling in London (I suppose for a year or so) gives you the promise of much helpful sympathy to light up the prospect of months to come.
I understand your disinclination to write about troubles. One has enough of them in the internal drama sometimes, without giving them outward voice. But I can't help wanting to know more. I am wondering whether you have finished that work 10 you were setting about when we saw you.
As for the brain being useless after fifty -- that is no general rule: witness the good and hard work that has been done in plenty after that age. I wish I could be inspired with just the knowledge that would enable me to be of some good to you -- I feel so ignorant and helpless.
The year is opening happily for us except -- alas, the exception is a great one -- in the way of health. Mr. Lewes is constantly ailing, like a delicate headachy woman. 11 But we have abundant blessings. Our Boys are all going on satisfactorily, and Charlie is the tenderest-hearted of brawny-armed youths: he shows the rare combination of thorough manliness and gentle purity. I am just emerging from a bog of colds and headache, in which I have been hopelessly tumbling of late.
God bless you, dear Cara. I have always one happy faith about you -- that you live too much for others, for life ever to be without its deep joys and comforts to you. Your loving
Marian
Love to Sara. I shall write to her tomorrow.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 12 September 1870
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 12 September 1870
MS: Mrs. Hennell Taylor. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 12. 70.
My dear Cara
Your letter this morning responds to what I have been feeling continually. Surely those human beings who have any love and value for each other should cling together now and keep the heavenly fire alive. We think of hardly anything but the War, and spend a great portion of our day in reading about it. 214 The deplorable demoralization of the French army and people divides one's sorrow with the horrible carnage. And every day now one shudders in expectation of what may happen in Paris: the people flying at each other's throats will be worse than the enemy's shells.
I am cheered this morning -- after a great deal of gloomy talk yesterday -- by your letter and the sunshine, which go well together. The news about your book 215 is very welcome. The thought of doing it was so felicitous, and now it seems to have found a good destination.
We are very well in health now, for such rickety furniture as we are. Mr. Lewes works a little in the mornings and is none the worse. We have had lately the (to our feelings) good news that Bertie is engaged [to be married] in due time, [one line at bottom of page cut out] among the Transval colonists, whose father has been long established in Bertie's neighbourhood. 216 Since Thornie's death we have especially desired this foundation of a lasting companionship.
We have not seen Mr. and Mrs. Call since our return, so that the news about Frank was unknown to us. One would have felt a more unmixed hope for his future if he had gone to America -- but where in the world can one feel quite easy about young creatures? [One line cut out.] Sara, I trust, is still feeling an afterglow from her sea-side enjoyment. I imagine you all taking, together or apart, delicious autumn walks over the fields, though the fields must be greatly changed towards Radford since the far-off days when I knew them.
Your mention of the Sheepshanks's and their share in that calamity of the wreck, has made me reflect that old Mr. Sheepshanks 217 must be dead now, and that the family would be more changed to my eyes than the Radford fields. Other Coventry people are more within reach of my imagination -- Mrs. Whittem and Mrs. Cash, for example, to whom I should like you to offer my affectionate remembrances when they happen to speak of me. -- You are as free from ailments as a goddess, so I never wonder how you are physically, but Mr. Bray is more assailable -- though not, I hope, suffering from his cough in this fine season.
Mr. Lewes's mother is 83 and is likely enough to outlive us, while a young girl who acts as her companion and attendant is threatened with life-long lameness from disease in the knee. 218 Such is the combination of things which according to Mr. Froude's philosophical remarks in his History "we owe first to Providence and next to accidents"! Ever, dear Cara,
Your affectionate
Marian.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 12 May 1862
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | May 12. 62.
Dear Cara
Alas, I am too feeble a creature to venture on engagements three days beforehand. I am compelled only to wish and be glad, if any friend will come to see me. There are still things to be done that oblige me to take care of myself not simply on selfish grounds.
You will I hope be coming to London, and I think you know that there is no one in the world whom I would more gladly have with me than you for as long as you could spare yourself to me. I wish I had a comfortable bedroom to offer you.
Always yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 11 October 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 11 October 1868
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 11. 68.
My dear Cara
Soon after we returned from the Continent, Mr. Lewes went to Mr. and Mrs. Call to deliver a book which had been entrusted to him, and they told him that you and Mr. Bray were at Sydenham, but very busy superintending re-arrangements. So I did not write, trusting that when you were at liberty to come to London you would not deny me the chance of seeing you -- since owing to our arrant rambling tendencies our being at home at a particular time could not be certified, so as to warrant my asking for more than a chance. I wonder whether you do think of coming to London at all before you go back to Coventry? If you could and would be so kind as to write me a note beforehand, saying that you and Mr. Bray would be with us on a given day and hour, I should answer immediately, according to my habit if I were at home. Not receiving an immediate word in reply you would conclude that I was not at home. I think our lunch-time -- 'bc to 2 -- is the time when Mr. Bray prefers to dine, and knowing beforehand I would have something warm and "comfortable."
We quite escaped the summer's heat in the Black Forest and in Switzerland, indeed we should have been glad there of more uninterrupted sunshine and of a temperature that would have made the heights more desirable. Since we came from abroad, Mr. Lewes has been to the Medical Assoc[iation] at Oxford, and we have been into Yorkshire. Our flights would perhaps be longer but they are restrained by the needs of Mr. Lewes's Mother, who is now so aged and fidgetty that she is never long satisfied in her son's absence. We are ill by turns, as usual. Just now the worseness is mine. In this way, you see, we are saved from being ashamed of our untroubled life in this troublous world. Love to Sara, when you write.
Always your faithfully affectionate
Marian.
We plunge into the country between Sundays, but it is for the sake of perfect peace in the wood and fields. Sydenham and back in one day would be too fatiguing to me. As acquaintances and solicitations tend to multiply I find it more necessary than ever to keep rigidly to my rule of paying no visits in or near London, and to renounce seeing any friends unless they will kindly come to me.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 11 July [1869]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 11 July [1869]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1868. 85 Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
July 11.
My dear Cara
I feel as if I had been indulging in cruel gossip last night, and I cannot rest without entreating you again not to let my needless mention of trivialities have any consequences that can reach our poor dear S. I shall always welcome her affectionately on her rare visits, for the old regard is much deeper than any new and transient irritations.
Pray excuse my want of thought in not asking you to go upstairs at once on your arrival. I must plead a certain flurry which was owing to my having talked and stood ever since dinner, a flurry which ended for me in a fit of diarrhaea after we got home. For, to tell the truth, my looks flatter if they seem to say that I am well.
I am unfortunately situated in relation to you, dear Cara. Words are good for nothing and may even seem repulsive when so many various conditions hamper a corresponding expression by deeds. But I am in no way false in what I say to you, though in our brief interviews I cannot enter into matter-of-fact statements which I should be able to make if we were in constant intercourse. I do not write these things apologetically, but that you may the less disbelieve in my gratitude and affection.
Yours ever
Marian.
Do not trouble yourself to write in reply.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 10 November [1865]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1865. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 10.
My dear Cara
When your kind letter came into my hands I had just returned from my first visit to Mrs. Congreve and Miss Bury. The poor patient is recovering, but still needs great care. Both Mr. and Mrs. Congreve have suffered less physically than I feared they would. You may imagine what the strain on Mr. Congreve is when I tell you that he expects in a month to undergo the Examination of his Medical Studies. 381
I wrote a long letter to you nearly a fortnight ago, and burnt it, because I hesitated whether I ought to say what I had said in it. Yet I think I will tell you that the gist of it -- of course confided to you with perfect trust in your loving discretion -- was to beg of you not to accept our dear Sara's statements about her friends' words or their condition, because I felt convinced that her mental habits were of a kind that absolutely forbid her getting any accurate impressions about things outside her own theoretic world. That word will suffice -- is perhaps more than enough -- by way of additional caution to your own indisposition towards hasty judgments. I had also told you in that burnt letter, that the best compensation for not seeing you was to hear that the reason was a Tenant. Gaudeamus!
Poor Harry's case is one of the most difficult to deal with. I have been hearing from Miss Marshall how long-suffering and kind Mr. Bray is towards him -- as usual to those whom everybody else would crush against the wall.
Mr. Lewes is in worse health than usual -- that is my only grief. You would find it difficult to imagine that he can be a cheerful, much-producing man with the amount of headache and nausea he endures.
I was glad to see Miss Marshall had recovered her former self so thoroughly except as to her sight. Unfailing memory, dear Cara, from
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 1 June 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 1 June 1863
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1863. Extracts published: Cross, II, 353.
Blandford Sq. | June 1. 63.
Dear Cara
My mind was very much in need of your letter, for I have been continually wondering what you would do, if you let your house furnished, our hurried talk not having made that clear to me. I hope the brightness of your face and your ready enjoyment of things have not given me a comforting impression about you which a less transient vision would rob me of. But health seems, to those who want it, enough to make daylight a gladness.
We were talking over that unpleasant fact of the Sydenham house 163 not letting, as we walked this afternoon. Mr. Lewes thinks the stronger presumption must be that the cause lies in the casualties which beset house-letting generally rather than in any false play of the agent, since he has hitherto served you well. But the explanation of evils is never consoling except to the explainer. Sara or you will be writing soon, I hope, to tell me that the house is let. Dear Sara -- I feel for her poor head! And a slight cough which is teazing me helps to make me think of her, for I see her shaken by that wearying depressing little hacking which is just now tormenting me.
We are just as we were -- thinking about the questionable house and wondering what would be the right thing to do -- hardly liking to lock up any money in land and bricks, and yet frightened lest we should not get a quiet place just when we want it. But I daresay we shall not have it, after all.
Charlie's words just after he first saw you were -- "a pretty little woman" -- so you perceive the admiration is mutual. And Mr. Lewes says you are a "femme de relations charmantes." It is much nicer to be admired than despised, in my opinion. Love to all.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 1 April 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, 1 April 1879
MS: Coventry and Warwickshire Collection, Coventry Public Libraries. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | April 1. 79.
My dear Cara
I have told Charles that I would myself answer your kind letter to him. For a long while I have been saying to myself that I would write to you, but I have shrunk from writing about myself needlessly though I have for the last month and more been answering all business letters.
I happen to have a headache today, but I have been generally better of late. I take the air every day and have no great bodily evil to complain of -- only a certain slowness and ineffectiveness of mind which may perhaps be counted as the worst form of bodily languor. The sorrow can't grow less -- the sense of the happiness that was, and the distaste for life that is and will be. I cannot yet resign myself to the cutting short of that happiness for him. He enjoyed it so intensely -- And we have had everything we wanted. I can bear my own privation, but I cannot yet bear submissively that he had not a few more years of joy. That was my first feeling and it is still the strongest. But we had 24 years of constantly growing love, and I have this comfort -- the belief that he never knew he was dying -- never felt that we were parting. But it is better not to write of these things.
I am so sorry that the winter has left sad effects on Mr. Bray's health, and that Sara felt its severity unintermittingly. It has been a dreadful time for all delicate frames. You say nothing of your own health, but I suspect that you have shared in the suffering physically as well as morally.
I want to tell you -- because perhaps it may allay some little anxiety in Mr. Bray, supposing there is any uncertainty about your other sources of income, that you will have by my Will £100 a year for your life. You once laughed at the idea that you should outlive me. That is not so unlikely. But at any rate, while I am here, think of me as a living Will, to provide for any want that you may feel. How is the letting of the Sydenham house going on?
I see no visitors yet -- only some gentlemen who are helping me in a matter of business which is near my heart. 208 I am going to found a Studentship of Physiology to be called by his name.
Our Bertie's widow, with her two children, is on her way to England, frightened out of Durban by the results of that wicked war. 209 I have plenty to think of, have I not? But my friends are so good and helpful that I am carried through everything. Love to all from your otherwise sadly changed
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [October 1851]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [October 1851]
MS: Benjamin Collection, Columbia. Hitherto unpublished.
Strand.
Of all things I wanted a note from you, dear Cara. Bless you for thinking of me and saying kind things just when I need them. I had a sight of the sky yesterday at Greenwich Park -- that too was cheering. On the whole I have everything -- that is -- every good thing compatible with an ill-conditioned soul and body. Dame Fortune is kinder to me than Dame Nature. Fortune does her part of the work as well as she can, seeing that she is in one perpetual wrestle with said step-dame Nature.
I have no courage to write much unless I am written to. I soon begin to think that there are plenty of other correspondents more interesting -- so if you all want to hear from me you know the conditions.
Mrs. Chapman is out still. Mr. Neuberg 1044 is here and a Mr. Birch is coming -- men of literary tastes and fat purses both. But alas! our subscription list has stood for the last week at Revd. F. J. Foxton.
Mr. Chapman is writing today to Mr. Bray I think telling him news that will a little surprize him.
My table is covered with books -- all to be digested by the editorial maw -- I foresee terribly hard work for the next 6 weeks. I gave Mr. C. your note to read. He keeps quoting your question "are they kind to you"? They outer barbarians he says.
I hope you look forward to your visitors 1045 with resignation at least. I fear I shall hardly be able to give myself any holiday before Christmas so I shall not tax your love, as I would willingly do.
Thine ever
Marian.
I am pronouncing a Commination on all dressmakers -- cursed be they in their needles and pins, cursed in their hooks and buttons, whereby you may know that my gowns all pinch and pull me.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [6 February 1862]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 1862. 1862-5. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
Thursday.
Dear Cara
I write in a hurry, that I may lose no time in telling you what Mr. Lewes says about Sara's business versus Manwaring. 17 He says that there is no danger of her stock being sold -- his bankruptcy meaning, for her, simply that if he happens to owe her anything she will only get a dividend on it. But, that she ought to take measures for removing her stock from under his hands. Poor Mr. Spencer will lose £50 by the affair, 18 after having had much vexation. He found Manwaring so unsatisfactory long ago that he was making arrangements to get clear of him before he was aware of bankruptcy being in the wind. There is clearly no happy conjunction of planets on behalf of that business in King William Street.
Tell Sara, with best love, that we can comprehend her head-troubles only too well. However, I am glad the sprain is better so that there is hope of her getting more and more fresh air.
Ever your loving
M. E. L.
Geo. Stevenson 19 is one of my great heroes -- has he not a dear old face?

By the end of 1861 it became obvious that Manwaring could not meet his obligations; his trustees hoped to get four to five shillings in the pound. Miss Hennell had invested in the business years before when Chapman was its head, and her books had been published under his imprint. See George Eliot and John Chapman, pp. 104, 110-111.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [4? March 1873]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [4? March 1873]
Text: Mathilde Blind, George Eliot, 1883, p. 28.
A very good, as well as very rich, woman, Mrs. S[chwabe], 744 has founded a model school at Naples, and has the sympathy of the best
Italians in her educational efforts. Of course a chief point in trying to improve the Italians is to teach them kindness to animals, and a friend of Mrs. S[chwabe] has confided to her a small sum of money -- fifty pounds, I think -- to be applied to the translation and publication of some good books for young people, which would be likely to rouse in them a sympathy with dumb creatures.
Will you kindly help me in the effort to further Mrs. S[chwabe]'s good work by sending me a copy of your book on animals, and also by telling me the periodical in which the parts of the book first appeared, as well as the titles of any other works which you think would be worth mentioning for the purpose in question?
Mrs. S[chwabe] (as indeed you may probably know) is the widow of a German merchant of Manchester, as rich as many such merchants are, and as benevolent as only the choicest few. She knows all sorts of good work for the world, and is known by most of the workers. It struck me, while she was speaking of this need of a book to translate, that you had done the very thing.
Dublin Core:Creator: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Publisher: George Eliot Archive, edited by Beverley Park Rilett. https://GeorgeEliotArchive.org

Dublin Core:Relation: 744 Mrs. Salis Schwabe (1818-96)  "called to consult Polly about Italian schools." (GHL Diary, 3 March 1873.) Her husband (1800-23 July 1853), "a wealthy and philanthropic German owner of a calico-printing works near Manchester," was one of the largest contributors of capital to the Leader. (Bookman, 3 [1892-93], 82.) His widow was "the confidant of Cobden, the worshipper of Gladstone, the admirer of Jowett, the intimate of Baron Bunsen, the guardian angel of Piatti, the nurse of the wounded Garibaldi at Caprera, and eventually the friend of our Princess Royal. Her Clarges Street house gathered a menagerie of mixed celebrities under its hospitable roof, while her enthusiasms public and private knew no bounds in their comprehensive if sometimes indiscriminate welcome. I remember her as a bright-coloured old lady with piercing blue eyes, in appearance resembling the great pianiste, Clara Schumann, whom, like Joachim, she knew so well; very generous, very emotional, most public-spirited. An educational enthusiast, she founded an excellent school at Naples and there were few good causes that appealed in vain not only to her purse, but her energies." GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [3 July 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 4. Brief extracts published: Cross, 1, 324.
Cambridge St. | Monday Morning.
Dear Cara
Pray consider the Strauss M.S.S. waste paper. I shall never want them again.
I dined with your old acquaintance Dr. Conolly 491 at Sir James Clark's the other day. After having been familiar with the large fat-looking portrait in your room, I was amazed to see a rather small unimpressive man. He took me down to dinner and we talked of you.
I spent last evening at Mr. Chapman's. There was a little party, and their new drawing-room looked very pretty.
Tell Sara I can imagine her shuddering at the "Cosmogonical Principal in God." 492 The disgusting ignorance and carelessness with which such things are managed are really exasperating. In haste
Ever yours
Marian.
Thanks for the Arabian Nights. They came quite safely.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [29 December 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Dec. 28. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, I, 319.
Cambridge St. | Thursday.
Dear Cara
I am to go to Chrissey on Monday the 2d, and to stay with her till the following Saturday, when I propose to inflict myself on you, since you are resigned. 423
How shall I thank you enough for sending me that splendid parcel of Beet-root, so nicely packed? I shall certainly eat it and enjoy it, which I fancy is the end you sought, and not thanks. Tell Mr. Bray that I was amused by the article on the cattle show and have quoted it to the amusement of others. 424 I had already had a copy of the Phrenological letter from Geo. Combe.
Don't suppose that I am looking miserable -- au contraire. My only complaints just now are idleness and dislike-to-getting-up-in-a-morningness, whereby the day is made too short for what I want to do. I resolve every day to conquer the flesh the next, and of course am a little later in consequence. I dined with Arthur Helps 425 yesterday at Sir James Clark's. Very snug -- only he and myself. He is a sleek man with close-snipped hair -- has a quiet, humorous way of talking, like his books. Love to Sara and all of you.
Ever your
Marian.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [28 June 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 'abJuly'bb 28 June. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 324.
Cambridge St. | Wednesday.
Dear Cara
As long as you can't afford the express, always come to London by the 12.30 train. It eventuates a spanker. I reached the E[uston] S[quare] Station 487 as dusty as an old ledger but with no other "incommodity" and a civil porter attended to me without delay. Yesterday Mr. Combe called. He and Mrs. C. set out on their journey on Sunday. Mr. Chapman is looking brighter, having got another letter of the alphabet, as Mr. Combe says, a G. or H. to satisfy the claims of E. and F. 488
I went to the Lyceum last night to see "Sunshine through the Clouds" 489 -- a wonderfully original and beautiful piece by Madame de Girardin, which makes one cry rather too much for pleasure. Vestris 490 acts finely the bereaved mother passing through all the gradations of doubt and hope to the actual recovery of her lost son.
My idea of you is rather bright just now and really helps to make me enjoy all that is enjoyable. That is part of the benefit I have had from my pleasant visit, which was made up of sunshine, green fields, pleasant looks and good eatables -- an excellent compound. Best love to all from
Your ever affectionate
Marian.
Will you be so kind as to send my books by railway, without the Shelley?

Dear Cara

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [19 May 1854]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 322-323.
Cambridge Street | Friday.
Dear Cara
My various aches determined themselves into an attack of rheumatism which sent me to bed yesterday; but I am better this morning and, as you see, able to sit up and write. My troubles are purely psychical
"Each in his hidden sphere of joy or woe, Our hermit spirits dwell and roam apart" -- 470 and this seclusion is sometimes the most intensely felt at the very moment your friend is caressing you or consoling you. But this gradually becomes a source of satisfaction instead of repining. When we are young we think our troubles a mighty business -- that the world is spread out expressly as a stage for the particular drama of our lives and that we have a right to rant and foam at the mouth if we are crossed. I have done enough of that in my time. But we begin at last to understand that these things are important only to one's own consciousness, which is but as a globule of dew on a rose-leaf that at mid-day there will be no trace of. This is no high-flown sentimentality, but a simple reflection which I find useful to me every day.
Tell Sara I did notice Hunt's picture, he being an immense admiration of mine, and that I did read Ruskin's letter. 471 I understand all the beauties Ruskin points out, and it is impossible to look at the picture without feeling the power there is in it -- but it is too mediaeval and pietistic to be rejoiced in as a product of the present age. At least that was my feeling on Monday; perhaps when I go again I may be more in harmony with it. There is one thing to make one laugh aloud at the Exhibition and that is a huge portrait of the Archb[isho]p of Canterbury 472 -- a head and face made all the more pitiably contemptible by the appareil of sanctified dignity which surrounds it. I wonder the clergy don't get up a "Society for the suppression of archiepiscopal portraits." They really are calculated to do as much harm to the Church as the Marquis of Blandford's bill. 473
Mr. Chapman has taken a house in Blandford Sq. 474 He had thought of a larger and more expensive one in Dorset Sq. which he would have taken if I would have become their lodger -- but I could not make up my mind to this for sundry reasons, though on many grounds I should like it.
I have had a nice letter from Chrissey this morning. Her two boys are suitably provided with situations, and Emily, the eldest girl is at school for a little while, so now she has only the three youngest at home.
Herbert Spencer is not quite recovered from his palpitations, but is better. He inquired after you all when he wrote.
I expect to see Mr. Lewes back again today. His poor head -- his only fortune -- is not well yet, and he has had the misery of being ennuy'e9 with idleness without perceiving the compensating improvement. Still I hope the good he has been getting has been greater than he has been conscious of.
Tell Sara I expect Feuerbach will be all in print by the end of next week and there are no skippings except such as have been made on very urgent grounds.
Mr. Atkinson called on Sunday and read me a letter of Harriet Martineau's denouncing "Vanity Fair" and reprobating his admiration of it. H.M. extols "Esmond" but thinks "Vanity Fair" a raking up of dirt and rotten eggs, a miserably mistaken criticism selon moi. The distinction drawn between Esmond and Vanity Fair seems to me quite unfounded. There is the same spirit -- there are the same characters in both -- Lady C. 475 is Amelia, Esmond is Dobbin, and Trix is Becky -- pure egoism -- in the one instance an adventures trying to become a great lady, in the other, a born great lady whose selfish duplicity consequently takes a different turn. There is not a pin to choose between them morally -- and yet they are as good as the mass of women -- only a little more clever and beautiful.
I don't think you will have read to the end, for the scribble is unreadable. But read and believe that I am ever
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [18 April 1854]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [18 April 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 18. 1854. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 321-322.
Cambridge St. | Saturday.
Dear Cara
I was delighted to have a letter from you, but I am not able to answer it as it deserves, for I am rather overdone with the week's work and the prospect of what is to come next. Poor Lewes is ill and is ordered not to put pen to paper for a month, so I have something to do for him in addition to my own work which is rather pressing. 455 He is gone to Arthur Helps in Hampshire 456 for ten days, and I really hope this total cessation from work in obedience to a peremptory order will end in making him better than he has been for the last year.
I am glad to hear that Mr. Noel is safe in spite of the disturbances 457 which were a reasonable ground of anxiety. -- I confess, however that I care more about Coventry ribbons than Greek insurrections, and I am not sure that a success against the Russians would cause me half as much joy as a satisfactory stocktaking. Chrissey writes me word that you are so good as to send her a paper constantly. Her two boys seem to be in prospect of satisfactory situations -- one at Birmingham and the other at Leicester, and I hope her eldest girl will go to school at Mid-summer. She will then have only Charlie who goes to the Grammar school and her two tiny pets at home. 458
Tell Sara that the MS.S. came all right. She must forgive me for omitting to say so. Mr. and Mrs. Pears I thought looking remarkably young and well. It was really a pleasure to see them.
Mr. Chapman has at length decided to leave his house at Midsummer. Mrs. C. came yesterday to look at a house in Cambridge St.! But I think it will be too expensive.
No opera and no fun for me for the next month! Happily I shall have no time to regret it. Plenty of bright sun on your anemone bed. How lovely your place must look with its fresh leaves!
Love to all from your ever affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Subject: MRS. CHARLES BRAY^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE TO MRS. CHARLES BRAY, LONDON, [12 MARCH 1851]
MS: Benjamin Collection, Columbia. Hitherto unpublished.
Strand.
Dearest Cara
Sundry matters have decided that I should stay here until Saturday week 942 -- resign yourself then to kissing and being kissed. You seem dearer to me every time I go back to you.
On Monday went to tea at Mr. Mackay's and called on Rufa by her invitation on our way home. Yesterday Mr. C. took me to Tottenham to see Mr. Windus's Turners. 943 On Friday we had a new man -- a Mr. Louis, 944 born a Jew -- believing in Christianity -- that is to say as a set of symbols expressing his philosophic creed. Very accomplished, played on the piano to Mrs. Chapman's utter disgust -- she hating Mendelssohnianism. Thornton Hunt 945 came again and to my vexation went away without my being introduced to him -- for which I reviled Mr. Chapman whereto he answers by revilings.
I hope you are all getting blooming again. I thought Rufa looking very pale -- and invalidish. She told us Mr. Bray had pronounced Frank the most spoiled of all children he had seen.
Ever thy
Pollian.
There are no Visitors -- i.e. who pay -- yet.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [12 January 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Jan. 12. | 1852. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 267-268.
Dearest Cara
With my wonted forgetfulness, I have left my small keys somewhere in my room -- at least I hope so, for they are not with me. Will you send me them by the post as soon as possible?
I had a comfortable journey -- all alone, except from 'abRugby'bb Weedon to Blisworth. When I saw a coated animal getting into my carriage, I thought of all horrible stories of madmen in railways, but his white neck-cloth and thin mincing voice soon convinced me that he was one of those exceedingly tame brutes, the clergy.
A kind welcome and a good dinner -- that is the whole of my history at present. Tell Mrs. C. Hennell the matter of the children is still undecided. Mrs. Bugden is coming tonight. 1 I am in anything but company trim or spirits. I can do nothing in return for all your kindness, dear Cara, but love you, as I do most heartily, you and all yours -- for their own sake first -- but if it were not so -- for yours. In haste and darkness
Your affectionate
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Relation: 1 Mrs. Bugden and Mrs. Charles  Hennell conducted a school for children from three to seven years of age. Chapman's daughter Beatrice had been a pupil there in May and June 1851, and Mrs. Bugden wanted his son Ernest also. Though their father favored the plan, Mrs. Chapman preferred to have the children at home. An advertisement of the school in the Leader, 17 July 1852, p. 692, shows that it was planned on "progressive" lines; obedience is enforced "by appealing to the understanding and the sympathies, by directing attention to the natural consequences of conduct, and by fostering a love of excellence . . . and while the teaching of dogmatic creeds on the assumption of their unquestionable truth is scrupulously avoided, as prejudicial to the due exercise and development of the intellectual faculties, the utmost endeavours are made to educe and strengthen those elements of character which are the foundation of true religious feeling. Knowledge is made attractive. . . . For reference, etc., apply to Mr. John Chapman, Publisher, 142, Strand."

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [11 November 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 10. 1852. Hitherto unpublished.
Strand | Thursday.
Dear Cara
After receiving your letter on Tuesday morning, I went to Mrs. Follen 221 to learn Miss Montgomery's address, not knowing even whether she had returned from the Continent.
I found that she had taken lodgings at 13, Upper Seymour Street, in order to be near Lady Byron who is nursing Lady Lovelace 222 in this sad ending of her career -- cancer. Miss M.'s time is almost entirely occupied with these friends and Mrs. Follen was doubtful whether I should be able to see her. However I trudged to 13, Seymour Street, having first written a note to leave in case I did not see Miss M. She was not at home and I left the note which told your news of Mr. Noel and asked her to send an account of her health etc. that I might transmit it to you. Last night came the note which I enclose. 223 She says nothing about herself, but I gathered from Mrs. Follen that she is as well as her general delicacy of health will allow her to be -- with no particular ailment or doctoring going forward.
Poor Mr. Chapman is under the cloud again, not seeing his way -- but Mr. Bray will be here soon and will hear all.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [10? May 1862]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [10? May 1862]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: May 1862. Extracts published: Cross, II, 339.
Blandford Sq. | Saturday Evening.
My dear Cara
Thank you very heartily for your kind service in printing a contradiction of the troublesome report about the "Carlingford" business. It is likely to be copied into other papers and will help to dissipate the error. I am sorry there was the misprint of Mr. Oliphant for Mrs. -- but there are plenty who will be able to correct it for themselves.
I suppose you are a widow by this time, with only Sara as a companion. But perhaps the change of being left at home in unusual quiet may be as good for you as the change to sea air will I hope be for Mr. Bray and Nelly. Miss Marshall called yesterday and told us she was going to join them. She seems in need of some such freshening influence, for she looks paler and more delicate than usual, I think.
Our life is the old accustomed duet this month, for Charlie is gone to spend his holiday at Geneva with my good friends the d'Alberts. We are fond of having our big boy, but yet we enjoy an interval of our double solitude.
I understand that you have not been able to get any decided answer about your book 64 in its present stage. You will not I hope deny me the pleasure of knowing when it is accepted -- or in the opposite case, I should like to learn all about it, if that were permissible.
Doesn't the Spring look lovelier every year to eyes that want more and more light? You have at least the happiness of being always near the fields, though the Coventry fields are not quite comparable to those round Dorking. It was rather saddening to leave the larks and all the fresh leaves to come back to the rolling of cabs and the "blacks," but in compensation we have all our conveniences about us.
Best love to Sara. Tell her she was wise to pay her London visit before the season. Baker Street is now crowded with carriages -- almost like Cornhill. Farewell, dear Cara -- you are always among the frequently suggested thoughts of your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [10 March 1868]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, London, [10 March 1868]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1868. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Tuesday Morning.
Dear Cara
Ever since I hurried away from you, I have been tormented with vexation and anxiety -- vexation that my ignorance of ways and omnibuses had led us into such blunders, and anxiety lest you should have been thoroughly overdone by the long walk and that weary parcel, which my stupid absence of mind allowed you to carry all the way. After all my original desire that you should stay to dine with us and take a cab home would have been the less evil for you as well as the greater pleasure for us. I should be glad of a line to say that you found Thurlow Road in some reasonable time.
I think I forgot to say that we go to the coast for a little while shortly. But if at any time in future you should want to say anything to me and are uncertain of my whereabouts, a letter addressed to 21 North Bank, and noted "To be forwarded" will reach me by the care of Charlie, who acts as secretary for us during our absence. Only you should always write on thin paper and use a thin envelope.
Ever yours lovingly
M. E. L.
Please not to repeat anything I may have said to you about letters written to me or other things in the nature of plaudits.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Gorey, 5 June 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Gorey, 5 June 1857
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 454-455.
Rosa Cottage | Gorey | Jersey | June 5. 57.
Dear Cara
I could have wished myself at Richmond even in this hot weather for the sake of seeing you, 880 but no pleasure short of that could have made me wish to be in the hazy atmosphere of London environs. Richmond is not fascinating in "the season" or through the summer -- it is hot, noisy and haunted with cockneys; but at other times we love the Park with an increasing love, and we have such a kind good landlady 881 there that it always seems like going home when we return to Park Shot. She writes to us "I hope you will make your fortune -- but you must always live with me," which, considering that she gets less out of us than other lodgers is a proof of affection in a landlady. We shall be obliged to return thither in the middle or at the end of July on business matters, but for a short time only; for at the end of August Mr. Lewes is going to take Bertie 882 the 'abeld'bb youngest boy to join his elder brothers at Hofwyl, and we shall if possible remain in Germany till the end of October. Yes! we like our wandering life at present; it is fructifying and brings us material in many ways; but we keep in perspective the idea of a cottage among green fields and cows, where we mean to settle down (after we have once been to Italy) and buy pots and kettles and keep a dog. The boys are going on so well at Hofwyl, and write charming letters. They are sweet-natured clever lads; the third, Bertie, has been sickly and stupid at books hitherto, but there is no knowing what boys and girls will turn into.
Wherever we are, we work hard -- and at work which brings present money; for we have too many depending on us to be dilettanti or idlers. By the way, before I leave talking about myself, your mention of Mr. Noel reminds me to say that Sara gave him a letter which I did not in the least intend him to see, 883 though I did not like to vex her by saying so at the time. He might infer from it that I invited him to come and call upon us. Now I should never invite any one, and it was only because Mr. Bray wrote me word that Mr. Noel had tried to find me at Richmond and expressed a wish to shake me by the hand again, that I thought it right to meet that friendliness by saying that I should be glad to see him, and to write to Sara a caution which, if he spoke of calling, she might communicate to him. The matter is of no importance, only I wish it to be understood, that I should never invite any one to come and see me who did not ask for the invitation.
Your gossip was very interesting to us, for we hear scarcely anything but what gets into the weekly newspapers, and not much of that. We had only heard of Miss Lynn, that she was going to marry Linton, the engraver. 884 Your description of her devotion to those seven children is very pretty. Her large-hearted energy is something to admire and love her for. I laughed heartily at the Brabantian 885 recitation which "sounds very grand on the other side of the wall."
Mrs. John Cash writes to me with such exquisite feeling that I can't help copying you a bit of her letter. She says -- "I hope you believe I value as highly as ever our dear neighbours. I could never have trusted such good fortune would befal me as to live next door to them, which is far more to me than living in this lovely garden. Of course I felt very much taking their place. It seemed as if the glory had departed to Ivy Cottage, but Mr. Bray is so beautifully generous through it all, takes such an interest in the place still and in our enjoyment of it, and does so fully appreciate my dear husband's character, that the change has not been so painful as friends at a distance might suppose." Is not that bien dit et bien senti? I write to her separately by the same post, for, having been out in a boat yesterday and made myself ill 886 I have a large amount of headache to bestow on correspondents. 887
You wonder how my face has changed in the last three years. Doubtless it is older and uglier, but it ought not to have a bad expression, for I never have anything to call out my ill-humour or discontent -- which you know were always ready enough to come on slight call -- and I have everything to call out love and gratitude. I seem to have said nothing, yet here I am at the end of my sheet. My best love and Mr. Lewes's kind regards to Mr. Bray. I must give the other sheet to Sara.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Foleshill, [25 May 1845]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Foleshill, [25 May 1845]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1845. Extracts published: Cross, I, 147, 129, 146.
Foleshill | Sunday.
My dear Friend,
I did think you slow to write, I confess, though I am not at all ready to answer you, for I can tell you nothing of Baby 558 or the Cow or the cleaning. On Friday I was busy all day, yesterday it rained incessantly and I was not well, and today I have been almost wet through since dinner in getting as far as Mr. Berry's 559 lime trees. I am afraid there is no chance of my being able to get to Rosehill this evening so I must make the house affairs the subject of my note to Mr. Bray tomorrow. So you are at Hastings! I cannot at all imagine your whereabout, you write so vaguely. I should like to know whether you have an upstairs room or a down-stairs one, whether there is a plenty or a paucity of easy chairs and sofas, what books you read together and what alone, and what was Mr. Hennell's last. Does a certain gentleman stretch and yawn frequently, or in Mr. D'Israeli's style, "extend his arms in the air and emit an exclamation indicative of weariness," or is he tolerably placid under the too great abundance of water? I wish it could be fair at Hastings and rain everywhere else for a few weeks that you might all get some good from the trip. I am sorry to hear that Sara wants it so much. She must have done herself harm with poring over my papers.
I have no news to tell you for I have scarcely heard any one speak since you left except Mr. and Mrs. Pears and a brace of clergymen at church this morning. I had a lecture from Mr. Pears on Friday, as well as a sermon this morning, so you need be in no alarm for my moral health. Do you never think of those Caribs who by dint of flattening their foreheads can manage to see perpendicularly above them without so much as lifting their heads? There are some good people who remind me of them. They see everything so clearly and with so little trouble, but at the price of sad self-mutilation.
Your books are come for the school and I have covered them, at least those that I think you will like for the children -- two or three are quite for grown-up people. [Hoary Head] seems to be a book against infidelity. [Three experiments of living] is all about a physician and his wife living too extravagantly, very good in its way, but not fit for our urchins. [The log cabin] 560 is another large book also very good but too mature. I cannot think how Miss A. G. 561 could recommend them for children. What an exquisite little thing that is of Harriet Martineau's -- The Crofton Boys. I have had some delightful crying over it. There are two or three lines in it that would feed one's soul for a month. Hugh's mother says to him, speaking of people who have permanent sorrows, "They soon had a new and delicious pleasure which none but the bitterly disappointed can feel -- the pleasure of rousing their souls to bear pain, and of agreeing with God silently, when nobody knows what is in their hearts." 562
Tell Mr. Bray I received Sybil 563 yesterday quite safely. I am not utterly disgusted with D'Israeli. The man hath good veins, as Bacon would say, but there is not enough blood in them. I shall get into disgrace for having a Committee book when I am no committee body. Mr. Bray forgets that I cannot enter it in my name without making worse of the matter but I suppose a forfeit is the extreme consequence and as Schiller's Capuchin says [Auf das Unrecht folgt das Uebel Wie Thr'e4nen auf den herben Schwiebel,] 564 which may be freely interpreted Sorrow follows wrong As tears the onion strong.
Do not stay longer than is necessary to do you good, lest I should lose the pleasure of loving you, for my affections are always the warmest when my friends are within an attainable distance, contrary to the general rule. I think I can manage to keep respectably warm towards you for three weeks without seeing you but I cannot promise more. Of Baby you shall hear to-morrow, but do not be alarmed. You will not have to chant "O ever thus" over her. Tell Sara I shall write to her on Tuesday. I have a great yearning of heart towards her that is my love-fit just now.
Love to everybody and Heaven bless you all. Tell Mr. Bray I am getting too amiable for this world, and Mr. Donovan's wizard hand would detect a slight corrugation of the skin on my organs 5 and 6: 565 they are so totally without exercise. Good bye, my dear love, and remember the duty of getting fat.
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, East Sheen, 4 September [1855]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, East Sheen, 4 September [1855]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1855. About her union with Mr. Lewes. Extracts published: Cross, I, 327-329.
Clarence Row | September 4.
Dear Cara
No one has better reason than myself to know how difficult it is to produce a true impression by letters, and how likely they are to be misinterpreted even where years of friendship might seem to furnish a sufficient key. And it seems the more probable to me that I misinterpreted your letter to me at Berlin 623 since I find that my answer to it produced totally false conclusions in your mind. Assuredly if there be any one subject on which I feel no levity it is that of marriage and the relation of the sexes -- if there is any one action or relation of my life which is and always has been profoundly serious, it is my relation to Mr. Lewes. If any expression or parallel in my letter bore an opposite construction it must have been, because you interpreted as of general application what I intended simply in answer to what I considered Mr. Combe's petty and absurd views about the effect on his reputation of having introduced me to one or two of his friends. Nothing that I said in that letter was intended as a discussion of the principles of my conduct or as an answer to your opinions on the subject.
It is, however, natural enough that you should mistake me in many ways, for not only are you unacquainted with Mr. Lewes's real character and the course of his actions, but also, it is several years now since you and I were much together, and it is possible that the modifications my mind has undergone may be in quite the opposite direction to what you imagine. No one can be better aware than yourself that it is possible for two people to hold different opinions on momentous subjects with equal sincerity and an equally earnest conviction that their respective opinions are alone the truly moral ones. If we differ on the subject of the marriage laws, I at least can believe of you that you cleave to what you believe to be good, and I don't know of anything in the nature of your views that should prevent you from believing the same of me. How far we differ I think we neither of us know; for I am ignorant of your precise views and apparently you attribute to me both feelings and opinions which are not mine. We cannot set each other quite right on this matter in letters, but one thing I can tell you in few words. Light and easily broken ties are what I neither desire theoretically nor could live for practically. Women who are satisfied with such ties do not act as I have done -- they obtain what they desire and are still invited to dinner. 624
That any unworldly, unsuperstitious person who is sufficiently acquainted with the realities of life can pronounce my relation to Mr. Lewes immoral I can only understand by remembering how subtle and complex are the influences that mould opinion. But I do remember this, and I indulge in no arrogant or uncharitable thoughts about those who condemn us, even though we might have expected a somewhat different verdict. From the majority of persons, of course, we never looked for anything but condemnation. We are leading no life of self-indulgence, except indeed, that being happy in each other, we find everything easy. We are working hard to provide for others better than we provide for ourselves, and to fulfil every responsibility that lies upon us. Levity and pride would not be a sufficient basis for that.
Pardon me, dear Cara, if in vindicating myself from some unjust conclusions, I seem too cold and self-asserting. I should not care to vindicate myself, if I did not love you and desire to relieve you of the pain which you say these conclusions have given you. Whatever I may have misinterpreted before, I do not misinterpret your letter this morning, but read in it nothing else than love and kindness towards me to which my heart fully answers yes. I should like never to write about myself again -- it is not healthy to dwell on one's own feelings and conduct, but only to try and live more faithfully and lovingly every fresh day.
I think not one of the endless words and deeds of kindness and forbearance you have ever shewn me has vanished from my memory. I recall them often, and feel, as about everything else in the past, how deficient I have been in almost every relation of my life. But that deficiency is irrevocable and I can find no strength or comfort except in "pressing forward towards the things that are before," and trying to make the present better than the past. But if we should never be very near each other again, dear Cara, do bear this faith in your mind, that I was not insensible or ungrateful to all your goodness, and that I am one amongst the many for whom you have not lived in vain.
Those dreadful sheets and pillow cases! Pray give them away if you won't use them, for I don't want them, and can never set up house-keeping on that small stock.
I am very busy just now, and have been obliged to write hastily. Bear this in mind, and believe that no meaning is mine which contradicts my assurance that I am your affectionate and earnest friend
Marian.
My love to Sara. I can't write more today but will write to her another day.
