Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Devizes, 30 November 1843
MS: Yale. Extract published: George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 24.
Devizes November 30th 1843.
My dear Friend,
We shall soon, I hope, be talking to each other [under your eyes,] for I have just written to my good Mary 498 telling her that I intend to be at the Coventry station by 9 o'clock on Monday evening, so prepare yourself to endure twenty kisses before Tuesday is over. I do not know whether to be glad or sorry, so I have come to a compromise with the contending feelings, and mean to indulge my grief at parting with my precious friends here till I reach home, and then let joy take complete possession. 499
I am going presently to meet a lady author, the only lion or rather lioness of the neighbourhood besides Tom Moore, 500 that I am likely to see, we having agreed in defiance of all the moralists to defer every expedition until my next visit. I must be like the Devizes poet who, Dr. B. tells me, thought it incumbent on him to mention what he did not seen in his description of the environs. Alike appear not to the view The house of Lansdowne and of Montagu.
This couplet reminds me that we had a new poem of Bernard Barton's at breakfast, printed for private circulation and sent as a present to Dr. Brabant one line of which is
Johnson and Beattie, Burke and Montagu, 501 so there are hopes for poetry yet, degenerate as the age may be.
Tell Mr. Bray there is a lady here who admires Fourier 502 and has lent me a book full of him and his isms, but heaven knows I shall have no time to read it; for the Dr. and I have meant to be very industrious. Every week I read Greek and read de omnibus rebus et quibusdam aliis, but the genius of sloth has possessed us and we have sent much new pavement to our future abode.
We are going to have a new book on the Immortality of the soul, the contents of which I shall have to report to you. I fear the carriage will be at the door in two or three minutes. Good bye till Tuesday, and then I will look at you as if I were what I truly am
Your affectionate
Mary Ann

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Devizes, 20 November [1843]
MS: Yale. Extract published: George Eliot and John Chapman, pp. 23-24.
Devizes. Monday | November 20th.
Thank you, meine Liebe for your kind letter, so much longer and earlier than you had allowed me to hope, but it was like you to be better than your promises. I am in a little heaven here, Dr. Brabant being its archangel, but it would be a less complete heaven if the recollection of you were not inwoven in the texture of my happy thoughts. All you tell me is interesting and I entreat that I may have another letter of details even to the health of the kitten. It is a grief that the principalities and powers of Coventry are not likely to smile on the allotment project, 492 but it will prosper in spite of them to their dishonour, or if otherwise you will surely not weep that your husband should work without wages in company with all the world's heroes be they clothed in steel or in superfine broadcloth. Dr. Brabant is gone to Chippenham to meet Mrs. Hennell, 493 and we shall see her probably within an hour. All will be better when the first meeting and parting are over.
Mrs. Brabant is a most affectionate amiable being, too forgetful of herself to talk of her loss, but really feeling it as much as any one. Of the Dr. what shall I say? for the time would fail me to tell of all his charming qualities. We read, walk and talk together, and I am never weary of his company. I have just written to Father to beg for a longer leave of absence than I had thought of when I came, but until I receive his answer I shall be uncertain about the time of my departure. If he should not wish for me sooner, I shall stay to the 13th of December. The journey will be rather formidable to a novice like me. Miss Hughes 494 advises me to go by Cheltenham and Birmingham and I should like the novelty of that plan, but I hope I have yet three weeks to consider about the matter.
I like to think that you are having all sorts of délices now I am away that you may recount them to me when I return to my Lares and yours. I mean to save all narrative for conversation and not forestall myself by telling you any of our sayings and doings in my letters.
The air of Devizes is very invigorating and I believe I am better than when I came, though I lost the first week in getting rid of my rakish languor. I am petted and fed with nice morsels and pretty speeches until I am in danger of becoming even more conceited than ever, and I shall want a month's mortification to make me endurable. Now then you know my whole status, and do you send me a letter just as full of Ichheit or I shall be wofully disappointed. I have written as fast as my pen

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Devizes, [8 November 1843]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1843. After C.C.'s marriage. Extract published: George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 23.
Devizes Wednesday.
My dearest Friend,
Alas! I like not to tell you of my pleasant journey yesterday 488 when I think that my parting from you was a beginning of sorrow to you.
I hated myself for sitting so snugly in the coach and driving away from you like a very impersonation of selfishness, but I know not what else to do. I will hope the best -- that neither you nor Mr. Bray took cold from your wet walk and that as Mr. Hennell would say, "Forsan et haec olim meminisse juvabit." 489 Perhaps as you are reading my note you will be seated so comfortably by your dining room fire that I should be discontented with my lot if I could have a picture of you. Should you like one of me? Well then, behold me at the table in Dr. Brabant's dining room with rather aching limbs which is not wonderful, and in perfect good humour which is wonderful. I should indeed have spleen enough to make me [one of the most remarkable women in this country] if I were not made happy by the warm welcome and the delicate attentions I receive here. I have nothing to talk of yet but kind words, kind looks, good fires and warm water, all which agrémens I have luxuriated in since 7 o'clock last evening, for we did not reach Devizes until that hour.
We staid at Reading three hours yesterday, and Dr. Brabant would tell you in the first place that we had an elegant luncheon at a very splendid house belonging to a Mr. Blandy: 490 I walked with the Adonis, as Sara calls him, alias cousin Frederick, to see the ruins of Reading Abbey, and O its sounding sequence! a pin manufactory. I of course had a wretched head-ache and was right glad that Dr. B's experienced eyes detected it, so that I was allowed to go to that best type of heaven, bed, soon after we reached Devizes.
I have been feasting my eyes on the Library this morning, and Dr. Brabant insists that I shall consider that my room. What name do you think I have been baptized withal? Rather a learned pun, Deutera, which means second and sounds a little like daughter. Both my host and hostess seem pleased with me, or simulate it so well, that their acting is as good as reality. I like Mrs. B. 491 She talks so neatly and is so perfectly polite. A dose of precision, not preciseness, will be the best thing in the world for me. Dr. B's habits are of that regular and simple kind that always indicate a healthy mind. He does not even sit in an easy chair; but here is luncheon and I shall have to walk presently. I have written in a great hurry and have not said one half of what I want to say, but I threaten you with a longer letter in a few days, and to atone for its length it shall be more legibly written.
I want nothing but a letter from Father to make me happy -- I have just been writing to him to ask him the reason of his silence. Mrs. Brabant is talking, so I must leave off scribbling.
Love, love love from your
Mary Ann
The people here are all so ugly! almost as ugly as I am.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Devizes, [24 November 1843]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Devizes, [24 November 1843]
MS: Yale. Brief extract published: George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 24.
My dear Friend,
Your thrice blessed letter, delivered last night, has put me on the worst terms with myself. Why did you not scold me for being so ungratefully silent? Then I should have felt saucy and have been not at all penitent, as I am now. I have but one excuse. Although I told you that the Devizes air was good for me, I have been anything but well since I came, and after reading German for two hours to the Dr. I have often felt so faint as to be obliged to lie on the sofa until walking time and so my writing hours have slipped away. I am better now and shall try to earn as many sweet letters from you as my small store of modesty will allow.
Mrs. Hennell has been with us all this week as you supposed and she means to send you a little note in my envelope to tell you how happily her visit has passed. She is an excellent creature and will be a real treasure to you all. I have been very glad to resign part of my interest in her papa for a week, only keeping up my prescriptive right by a little occasional reading and walking, and consoling myself with the prospect of being a pis aller by and bye.
So you are going to have Mr. Donovan 495 and I shall miss my lessons from the arch-phrenologist! Never mind, I shall miss, too, being told that I have some very bad propensities and that my moral and animal regions are unfortunately balanced, all which is too true to be heard with calmness. 496
We are going to dine at Mr. Hughes's 497 this evening, so I am doomed to indigestion and whist, the latter of which I choose as a smaller evil than trying to be agreeable in spite of dame Nature and circumstances. Dr. Brabant spoils me for every one else, and the Trennung from such a companion will be very painful. He really is a finer character than you think. Beautifully sincere, conscientious and benevolent and every thing besides that one would have one's friends to be. He is just come to invite me to walk as a reward for the good character I am giving him. Give my love to Mr. Bray and believe that you have as much of that worthless commodity as I can give to any one being. I hardly know what I am writing.
Lebe wohl,
Mary Ann.
Devizes. Friday.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Broadstairs, [4 July 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 4. 1852. Mostly published: Cross, 1, 285.
Chandos Cottage | Broadstairs.
Dear Cara
I warn you against Ramsgate which is a strip of London come out for an airing. Broadstairs is perfect, and I have the snuggest little lodgings conceivable with a motherly good woman and a nice little damsel of 14 to wait on me. There are only my two rooms in this cottage, but lodgings are plentiful in the place. Miss Field was once in these same lodgings and wanted to come here now, but that her medical man prescribed Ramsgate. I have a sitting-room about 8 feet by 9 and a bedroom a little larger, yet in that small space there is almost every comfort. Miss Field called last night with her brother, 138 but unfortunately I was out and so missed her. I pay a guinea a week for my rooms, so I shall not ruin myself by staying a month unless I commit excesses in coffee and sugar.
I am thinking whether it would not be wise to retire from the world and live here for the rest of my days. With some fresh paper on the walls and an easy chair I think I could resign myself. Come and tell me your opinion.
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Blackbrook, 10 October 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Blackbrook, 10 October 1873
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1873. Hitherto unpublished.
Blackbrook | Bickley | Kent | October 10. 73.
My dear Cara
I have just received the enclosed note from Macmillan. 848 I had hardly expected that he could publish "Paul Bradly" himself, but in any case I thought that we should get some suggestion from him; and both Mr. Lewes and I think that his notion of applying to the Sec[retary] of the C. K. S. 849 is a good one. This Society brings out some excellent books, and has not the stamp of slimy evangelicalism which belongs to the Religious Tract Society.
You see, Macmillan, after reading the story, takes for granted that there would be no religious objection to it -- and he is himself of a semi-or-quarter-Christian-Theistic colour. If one can get good doctrine about treating animals blown by a strong angel-trumpet, no matter from which of the four winds it is blown. The C. K. S.'s books are admirably got up. I confess I should never have thought of offering it to the Society if Macmillan had not suggested it -- but since he thinks the plan feasible, it smiles upon us as an advantageous one. But you may have some objection which I am unable to foresee.
I am asking M. to send the manuscript to you, that if you approve you may forward it to the Secretary. My interposition would do no good there. And after Macmillan, we have no relations with any publisher who undertakes other books for children than regular schoolbooks.
Your story is so good that it is sure of acceptance somewhere. I wanted to get you a fair share of money for it, as you would have done if it had been of a kind for Macmillan to publish. I hardly think it will do for the little Neapolitans or Florentines, but we shall see. When it is in print I shall give it to Mrs. Schwabe that she may judge. A lady who has visited the schools at Florence, says the little creatures there are as sharp as needles, and far beyond English pupils of the same age. If so, the English life would be no obstacle to their comprehending the story well enough for edification.
About your British Empire -- I fear that the misfortune of its having been sold off by Longmans as an encumbrance will hinder Chapman and Hall from entertaining its publication, notwithstanding your selfrenouncing willingness to revise it for nothing. I am very, very sorry.
We shall probably be in town again in the beginning of November. How are you all? We are much as usual -- rickety old things.
Always lovingly yours
Marian.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Blackbrook, [11 September 1873]
MS: Yale. Envelope: Mrs. Charles Bray | 3 Barr's Hill Terrace | Coventry. Postmarks: BICKLEY STATION | 6 | SP 11 | 73; COVENTRY | A | SP 12 | 73. Hitherto unpublished.
Blackbrook | Bickley | Kent.
Dear Cara
I have read through "Paul Bradley" and like it well. This morning I have written a letter to Macmillan in readiness for Mr. Lewes to take together with your beautifully legible manuscript, the first time he goes up to town. We prefer not trusting the manuscript to the post, unless it were absolutely necessary. When I hear from Macmillan in reply I will immediately let you know, and I only scribble this note now to make you understand the sources of delay, and to prevent you from thinking (as I should be inclined to do myself) that the quality of your work is in fault.
I daresay Macmillan may think it more suitable for a special publisher of children's books, but I have asked him to give me his advice, and he is sure to be obliging.
Yours always lovingly
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Wandsworth, 3? October? 1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Wandsworth, 3? October? 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Mrs. Charles Bray. Extracts published: Cross, II, 121-123.
Thank you, dear, dear Cara, for your words of sympathy. And the things you tell me at the end of your note 330 are just such as I need to know -- I mean, about the help my book is to the people who read it.
The weight of my future life -- the self-questioning whether my nature will be able to meet the heavy demands upon it, both of personal duty and intellectual production, presses upon me almost continually in a way that prevents me even from tasting the quiet joy I might have in the work done. Buoyancy and exultation, I fancy, are out of the question, when one has lived so long as I have. But I am the better for every word of encouragement, and am helped over many days by such a note as yours.
I often think of my dreams when I was four or five and twenty. I thought then, how happy fame would make me! I feel no regret that the fame, as such, brings no pleasure, but it is a grief to me that I do not constantly feel strong in thankfulness that my past life has vindicated its uses, and given me reason for gladness that such an unpromising woman-child was born into the world. I ought not to care about small annoyances, and it is chiefly egoism that makes them annoyances.
Tell Sara, I won't write to her today, but I know she will like to hear that I had quite an enthusiastic letter from Herbert Spencer the other day about "Adam Bede." He says he feels the better for reading it -- really words to be treasured up.
I can't bear the idea of appearing further in the papers. And there is no one now except people who would not be convinced though one rose from the dead, to whom any statement 'e0 propos of Liggins would be otherwise than superfluous. I daresay some "investigator" of the
Bracebridge order will arise after I am dead, and revive the story -- and perhaps posterity will believe in Liggins. Why not? A man a little while ago wrote a pamphlet 331 to prove that the Waverley Novels were chiefly written not by Walter Scott, but by Thomas Scott and his wife Elizabeth: the main evidence being that several people thought Thomas cleverer than Walter, and that in the list of the Canadian regiment of Scots to which Thomas belonged, many of the names of the W. Novels occurred -- among the rest Monk -- and in Woodstock, there is a General Monk! The writer expected to get a great reputation by his pamphlet, and I think it might have suggested to Mr. B. his style of critical and historical inference. I hope you appreciated the Z. Taft (author of some book) "doubtless Feyther Taft." 332 And I must amuse you by describing to you the Rev. Geo. Hake, the supposed "original" of Mr. Irwine. In the earlier letter, I read it Rev. G. Hole, and so missed the merit of the parallel.
The Rev. Geo. Hake was originally a soldier who entered the church rather late in life. He was an evangelical preacher; very ugly, stuttering, and rather obese; very poor, and unscrupulous about getting into debt, which he did to a considerable extent; supposed to conceal some meanness under a rather excessive air of benevolence; and generally disrespected by his Staffordshire parishioners: the resemblance to Mr. Irwine is obvious.
I feel almost vexed now that we ever noticed Mr. Bracebridge -- the whole affair is so contemptible. But Mr. Lewes will write to get a distinct statement from him, now that he has once entered on the matter.
Tell Sara, I leave the decision about the portrait to her -- but I do not like it to be in a public place. 333
Ever thine
Marian.
I must tell you, in confidence, that Dickens has written to me the noblest, most touching words about '91Adam'92 -- not hyperbolical compliments, but expressions of deep feeling. He says the reading made an epoch in his life. Mind, I tell you in confidence.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Wandsworth, 10 July 1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Wandsworth, 10 July 1860]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 10. 1860. Extracts published: Cross, II, 263-265.
Tuesday Morning.
Dear Cara
The little envelope 588 with its address of "Marian" was very welcome, and as Mr. Lewes is sending what a Malaproprian friend once called a "missile" to Sara, I feel inclined to slip in a word of gratitude -- less for the present than for the past goodness, which came back to me with keener remembrance than ever when we were at Genoa and at Como -- the places I first saw with you. How wretched I was then -- how peevish, how utterly morbid! And how kind and forbearing you were under the oppression of my company! I should like you now and then to feel happy in the thought that you were always perfectly good to me. That I was not good to you, is my own disagreeable affair: the bitter taste of that fact is mine, not yours.
Don't you remember Bellagio, or Lake Como? It is hardly altered much except in the hotels, which the eleven years have wondrously multiplied and bedizened for the accommodation of the English. We went to Sommariva, 589 because I had been before with you, and to the Serbelloni gardens (on the hill behind Bellagio, you remember) not altogether for the same reason, but partly for the sake of seeing the lake and mountains in the evening light.
But if I begin to recall the things we saw in Italy, I shall write as long a letter as Mr. Lewes's, which, by the by, now I have read it, seems to be something of a "missile" in another sense than the Malaproprian.
But Sara is one of the few people to whom candour is acceptable as the highest tribute. And private criticism has more chance of being faithful than public. We must have mercy on critics who are obliged to make a figure in printed pages. They must by all means say striking things. Either we should not read printed criticisms at all, (I don't) or we should read them with the constant remembrance that they are a fugitive kind of work which, in the present stage of human nature, can rarely engage a very high grade of conscience or ability. The fate of a book which is not entirely ephemeral is never decided by journalists or reviewers of any but an exceptional kind. Tell Sara her damnation -- if it ever comes to pass -- will be quite independent of Nationals 590 and Westminsters. Let half a dozen competent people read her book, and an opinion of it will spread quite apart from either praise or blame in reviews and newspapers. But my letter is running over. With love to Mr. Bray,
Ever yours
Marian.
Can you tell Mr. Lewes what is Mr. Spencer's present address?

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Richmond], 27 March [1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Richmond], 27 March [1858]
Text: Coventry Herald, 7-8 November 1919, p. 8. Mostly published: Haight, George Eliot, pp. 254-255.
March 27.
Dear Cara,
Your letter was very sweet to me, coming spontaneously, not a propos of a parcel. The feeling that you and Sara have been and always will be the women I have loved best in the world -- the women I have had most reason to love and admire -- strengthens instead of fading with time and absence. It is impossible ever to revive the past, and if we could recover the friend from whom we have parted we should perhaps find that we could not recover precisely the old relation. But that doesn't hinder the past from being sacred and belonging to our religion. I have some faith, too, that we should never lose our old fitness for each other, and that our talks together, and looks at each other must always be fuller of mutual understanding than we could find elsewhere.
In this faith I shall venture to recommend to you and Sara, a lady of my acquaintance in whom I have a peculiar interest. 382 She will present herself to you shortly, with a note from my hand, and I believe that for my sake you will receive her with indulgence. I can't say much that is good of her, but I am confident that she will not misconduct herself in your society. She will sit in modest silence, looking ready to enjoy any joke that is passing.
Marian.

Dear Cara

Marian.

Monday.
Impossible, my dear Cara, though I give you twenty spiritual kisses for wishing it. 1105 We set out next Monday, and there are all sorts of insuperable reasons why I couldn't leave home in the interim. In haste, ever your loving

Dear Cara

Love to all. 274

Saturday.
Dearest Cara
I have requested my Sister 27 to send to Rosehill a parcel containing some clothes which she has had made for me. Will you ask Sara to be so kind as to bring the said parcel with her luggage on Monday?
Mrs. C. Hennell brings me rather an unsatisfactory account of Mr. Bray -- that his chest is not well and that he still does not get sleep enough. I hope business is not helping to keep him awake. My love to him, and I want to see him very much.

Ever thine
Pollian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: May 30. 1853. Hitherto unpublished.
Monday.
Dear Cara
The hamper which you have had the trouble of packing for me, in addition to your other good deeds, has not yet made its appearance. I had a pleasant though rather fatiguing visit yesterday. Mr. Combe is looking well -- his eyes more terrible than ever -- but Mrs. Combe is quite ill with that horrid disease of the mucous membrane, which always makes people hypochondriacal. I made a very agreeable new acquaintance -- a Mrs. G. Taylor, 325 of whom I had heard from Kate Martineau.
I was little better than a "body" on Thursday and Friday, with head and back-ache, but I revived on Saturday evening and went to the opera to hear Ernani. I took the opportunity of judging whether Mr.
Bray could endure sitting through an opera in the pit, and I really think he may venture.
Rachel is to appear only once in Ph'e8dre 326 -- the part in which I most want to see her. Don't be having tooth-ache and lying awake this week as a preparation for enjoying London. 327 Love to all from
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 30 March 1852]
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, 1, 273-274.
Tuesday.
Dear Cara
I had two offers last night -- not of marriage, but of music -- which I find it impossible to resist. Mr. Herbert Spencer proposed to take me on Thursday to hear William Tell, 47 and Miss Parkes asked me to go with her to hear the Creation on Friday. 48 I have had so little music this quarter and these two things are so exactly what I should like that I have determined to put off, for the sake of them, my other pleasure of seeing you. So pray keep your precious welcome warm for me until Saturday, when I shall positively set off by the 2 o'clock train. 49 Miss Martineau (Harriet) has written me a most cordial invitation to go and see her 50 before July, but that is impossible. She has made me joint trustee with Mr. Atkinson of the fund for the publication of Comte. 51 I liked Atkinson very well the other day. You see I am cautious. Of new acquaintances one can never be sure because one likes them one day that it will be so the next. Of old friends one is sure that it will be the same yesterday, today, and forever.
Love to Mr. Bray and Sara. I have not written to the latter this long time because I have been busy -- but my heart has been inditing of many a good matter 52 to her.
Thy affectionate
Marian

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 30 June 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 1. 1852. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Cara
Good, delightful Miss Montgomery 137 has just been here and has been asking me for news of Mr. Noel. She is going to Germany in a week and I have promised to send her what news I can get from you as this must be before I go. Write at once that I may hear from you on Friday. She wishes to know if Mr. Noel gets the Papers etc. and anything else you can tell me about him. I think you have said nothing to me about him since I saw her before. Oceans of love. In great haste
Your
Marian.
Wednesday.

Dublin Core:Relation: 137 Mary Millicent Montgomery, described  in 1813 by Lady Byron as "my most valued friend," was one of the few intimates who survived her. Edward Noel, according to E. C. Mayne, had estranged himself from Lady Byron "for some obscure but violently resented reason, and left her appeals for reconciliation unanswered." Miss Montgomery, however, remained on friendly terms with him. In 1846 Lady Byron wrote: "It never seems to strike M.M., when he goes to her for aid and comfort, that heartily as I rejoice in his receiving that comfort, I am not quite so sublimated as to rejoice also in being cast aside." (The Life . . . of . . . Lady Noel Byron, 1929, pp. 374, 376.)

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 3 October 1851]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 3 October 1851]
MS: Benjamin Collection, Columbia. Hitherto unpublished.
Dearest Cara
By an oversight I have left behind the two volumes of Fl'fcgel's German Dictionary, which you will find in my room. Will you have the goodness to send them to me by Railway, as they are too bulky for anyone to carry. Also my scissors for want of which I am tormented.
Robert Chambers 1006 called yesterday -- a plain Scotchman with a strong Doric accent and small twinkling eyes. The Papers for the People are to be closed, not being so successful as some others of the Chambers publications -- only 35,000 have been sold.
Tell Mr. Noel that Mr. Chapman has been exerting himself about the work on mills -- I hope, with some good result. Meanwhile the terrible [Mill] hight John Stuart has ground F. Newman to powder in the Westm[inster]! 1007
When you send my Dictionary I wish you would ask Mr. Bray to let me have Mill's System of Logic which I don't suppose he wants at present. I shall be glad to have it by me for reference. I am training myself up to say adieu to all delights, I care for nothing but doing my work and doing it well.
Tell Sara especially that Greg wishes the writer of the notice in the Leader to know that he did not intend to omit Hennell for whose work he has a high esteem. 1008 I can't remember the exact words and have not his letter by me.
Frederika Bremer 1009 is not yet arrived. The house is only just exorcised of Dr. Brabant.
Ever thine
Marian.
I have no smaller envelope than this monster one.

1007 "Lectures on Political Economy, by  Francis William Newman," Westminster Review, 56 (October 1851), 83-101.

Toward the end GE pointed out that Charles Hennell's Inquiry concerning the Origin of Christianity has been a valuable aid to Greg, "though, doubtless through a temporary forgetfulness, he speaks in his preface as if he had no predecessor among laymen in the path of free but reverent inquiry into the claims of Christianity."

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 29 March 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 23. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Cara
I shall get into the train on Wednesday, nothing doubting that your arms will be open to receive me, as they have ever been at the end of my journeyings. I long to see you more than any one, for I have had no glimpse of you during the quarter.
I suppose the Herald came to me this morning that I might see the capital article about the City Mission. 45 Surely the sapient editor of the Standard is not Mr. Drake! 46
I had a call from Mr. Atkinson (of the firm Martineau and Atkinson) the other day -- of which more anon. I am busy today -- have three long letters to write, so good bye, dearest dear. I have three or four dearest dears -- they take it in turn week and week about. Love to Sara and the Pater.
Ever thy
Marian.
Dublin Core:Creator: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Publisher: George Eliot Archive, edited by Beverley Park Rilett. https://GeorgeEliotArchive.org
Dublin Core:Contributor: MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 23. Hitherto unpublished.
Dublin Core:Relation:
45 The Coventry Standard, a conservative  paper, opposed most of the reforms Bray was advocating in the Herald. The City Mission, established at Coventry in the autumn of 1851 "to help bring the Gospel to the neglected and debased districts of the city," had aroused objections from both churchmen and dissenters. E. H. Delf and John Sibree, the Independent ministers, wrote in defense of the work. Finally the Standard terminated the correspondence 26 March 1852. Thereupon Bray published Delf's rejected letter in the Herald, 26 March 1852, p. 3b, with an editorial defending the Mission. He accused the Standard of believing "that the main object of the Church is not to save souls, (except those who can afford to pay for it;) but to make money." (p. 4a.)
46 William Drake (1813-96) was at  this time Lecturer to St. John's Parish, Coventry, and Second Master at the Coventry Grammar School from 1841 to 1857, when he became Vicar of Holy Trinity. (Boase, Supplement.) A note in the Standard, 5 March 1852, announces new arrangements by which the editor will "only be responsible for the leading articles and occasional literary notices. The general compilation of the paper and the insertion of correspondence, will not be under his superintendance." There is no record of Drake's acting as editor.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 28 February 1852]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 28 February 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 20. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 272.
Saturday.
Dearest Cara
I long very much to see your hand-writing -- to have a word from your own self.
Sara writes that she is enjoying her visit extremely and is coming to us on Monday. But I suppose you have heard more than I have.
We went to the meeting of the Association for the Abolition of the Taxes on Knowledge on Wednesday -- I that I might hear Cobden 36 in whom I was wofully disappointed. George Dawson's speech, which the Newspapers don't report, was admirable. Dobson Collett, 37 too, was really clever.
I received a note from Miss Lynn last evening -- owing, it appears, to Mr. Bray's having mentioned my intention to leave here. She wished to mention to me some friends of hers in Cavendish Sq. who have two rooms to let. I called on her this morning and had a long talk. But the lodgings are not at all what I want, and altogether I think it undesirable to fix on a London residence at present as I want to go to Brighton for a month or two next quarter. I am seriously concerned at my languid body and feel the necessity of taking some measures to get vigour.
Mr. Bray will perhaps care to know that Miss Swanwick 38 called on me the other day. I mentioned my proposition that Mr. Bray should call on her with me when he next comes to town, and she expressed pleasure.
Lewes inquired for Sara last Monday in a tone of interest; he was charmed with her, as who would not be that has any taste. Do write to me, dear Cara -- I want comforting -- this world looks ugly just now, all people rather worse than I have been used to think them. Put me in love with my kind again, by giving me a glimpse at your own inward self since I cannot see the outer one. In haste
Ever your
Marian.

36 At St. Martin's Hall. Richard Cobden  (1804-65), M.P. for the West Riding of Yorkshire, was leader of the Anti-Corn Law League; his speech is reported at some length in the Leader, 28 February 1852, p. 192, with briefer accounts of the others.
37 Collet Dobson Collet (1812-98) was  Secretary of the London Committee for the Repeal of the Advertisement Duty and of the Newspaper Stamp Abolition Committee, which became An Association for Promoting the Repeal of Taxes on Knowledge 13 February 1851.

She was active in the work of establishing colleges for women, serving on the councils of Queen's College and Bedford College, London, and helping to found Girton College, Cambridge. Spencer lists her among the ladies he used to meet at Chapman's soirees. (Autobiography, 1, 347.)

MS: Yale. Last sentence published: Cross, 1, 284.
Friday Morning.
Dear Cara
Miss Montgomery's address is 76, Oxford Terrace, Hyde Park. I have extracted all about Mr. Noel from your letter of this morning and sent it to her, but I am sure she will be glad to have some later news, for she asks like one who really wants to know.
I am very jealous of Miss Field. You don't care about me in the least.
I am busy packing today and am going to Mr. Parkes's to dinner.
Ever thine
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 16 April 1853]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 16 April 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 16. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 308; George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 68.
Saturday Morning.
Dear Cara
My chief trouble is poor Chrissey. Think of her in that ugly small house with six children who are inevitably made naughty by being thrown close together from morning till night. To live with her in that hideous neighbourhood amongst ignorant bigots is impossible to me. It would be moral asphyxia and I had better take the other kind -- charcoal myself and leave my money, perhaps more acceptable than my labour and affection. Then I dare not incur the material responsibility of taking her away from Isaac's house and its attendant pecuniary advantages. My health might fail and other things might happen to make her, as well as me, regret the change.
Yet how odious it seems that I, who preach self-devotion, should make myself comfortable here while there is a whole family to whom, by renunciation of my egotism I could give almost everything they want. And the work I can do in other directions is so trivial!
The little Chapmans have whooping cough and from having been quite beautiful with healthy bloom they have become pale as death. I have an increasing regard for Mrs. Chapman. Her character has shewn some admirable phases lately, and indeed I think both he and she deserve far more respect than you are disposed to give them.
We had an agreeable soir'e9e last Wednesday. I fell in love with Helen Faucit. She is the most poetic woman I have seen for a long while. Her conversation is not remarkable in any way but there is the ineffable charm of a fine character which makes itself felt in her face, voice and manner.
I am taking doses of agreeable follies, as you recommend, dear Cara. Last night I went to the French Theatre and tonight I am going to the opera to hear William Tell. 316 People are very good to me. Mr. Lewes especially is kind and attentive and has quite won my regard after having a good deal of my vituperation. Like a few other people in the world, he is much better than he seems -- 'abhuman as [?]'bb a man of heart and conscience wearing a mask of flippancy.
Herbert Spencer means to quit his position as sub-editor of the Economist and trust to writing. This is entre nous. I rather tremble for him -- with his nature, article-writing for bread will be worse than he has just now persuaded himself to think. Still this editorship is a horrid g'eane and tethers him to London all the year, with the exception of a few days' holiday now and then.
By the bye, Kate Martineau and her Father 317 came on Wednesday. They were both very cordial and wish to see me at Highbury again.
I am going to write to George Combe to whom I am in debt two letters deep -- so, dear Cara, good bye -- and do not let my grumbling letters alarm you for me. Chrissey will never consent to go to Australia she says.
When the warm days come and the bearskin is under the acacia you must have me again. Love to Sara. Her letter about Hippolytus was read 'abaloud'bb to three gentlemen -- so she must not think her writing thrown away.
Ever your faithful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 11 September 1852]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [London, 11 September 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. 11. 1852. Extracts published: Cross, I, 290-291.
Saturday.
Dear Cara
The week has really yielded nothing worth telling you. I am a few degrees more wizened and muddle-headed, and the articles for the Review are on the whole unsatisfactory. I fear a discerning public will think this number a sad falling off. 180
This is the greater pity that said public is patronizing us well at present. Scarcely a day passes that some one does not write to order the Review as a permanent subscriber.
I should think Mr. Bray and Mr. C. have done corresponding now. I have not seen any letters between them lately. It was a vexation to me that Mr. Bray should have applied to Mr. Flower. I felt sure the result would be a negative. But God bless him for that and all his other good deeds.
You may as well expect news from an old spider or bat as from me. I can only tell you what I think of the Blithedale Romance, 181 of Uncle
Tom's Cabin, and the American Fishery Dispute -- all which I am very sure you don't want to know -- any more than Mr. Bray, who says he hates [intellectual gossip.] (I know he doesn't hate unintellectual gossip).
Do have pity on me and make a little variety in my life by all sending me a scrap -- never mind if it be only six lines apiece -- to-morrow. Perhaps something will befal me one day or other -- as it is, nothing happens to me but the ringing of the dinner bell and the arrival of a proof. I have no courage to walk out.
Love to all
Pollian.

180 GHL devoted two and a half columns  to this number in the Leader, 2 October 1852, pp. 949-950, beginning: "It is a matter of general remark, that the Westminster Review, since it passed into MR. CHAPMAN'S hands, has recovered the former importance it acquired when under the editorship of JOHN STUART MILL. It is now a Review that people talk about, ask for at the clubs, and read with respect. The variety and general excellence of its articles are not surpassed by any Review." The Critic, 15 October 1852, p. 538, though disagreeing wholly with the policy of "promoting infidelity in religion and radicalism in politics," praised the vigor of most of the articles.
181 It might be GE who reviewed Hawthorne's  Blithedale Romance in the "Contemporary Literature of America" section, Westminster Review, 58 (October 1852), 592-598, in which she calls it "unmistakably the finest production of genius in either hemisphere, for this quarter at least." But she finds that Hawthorne's moral faculty is "morbid as well as weak; all his characters partake of the same infirmity." Objecting to his failure to exhibit the working of the socialistic settlement, she says: "He confines himself to the delineation of its picturesque phases as a `thing of beauty,' and either has no particular convictions respecting its deeper relations, or hesitates to express them." (p. 597.) The rhetorical style makes GE's authorship doubtful.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Griff, 20 April 1842]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Griff, 20 April 1842]
MS: Parrish Collection, Princeton. Hitherto unpublished.
My dear Mrs. Bray,
I wish I had you as a companion in a ramble through a precious little dingle that I have as a resort here, instead of doing what is only second best to talking with you. Before I had your kind letter, one of the ravens that hovered over me in my Saul-like visitation, was the idea that you did not love me well enough to bestow any time on me more than what I had already robbed you of, but that same letter was a David's harp that quite charmed away this naughty imagination. 426 I know I am exposing myself very foolishly to contemptuous pity by telling such feelings, and the confessional too, according to the experience of all faithful Catholics is not the best check to frailty, but I am in earnest determining to o'er master this ugly habit of mind, that proceeds not from a want of self esteem, but a yearning for what is more than in sober reason and real humility I ought to desire.
You asked me in your first note to tell you about family matters -- they are rather clearer to me than they were. My sister-in-law here whose affection in spite of my excommunicated state I have been happy enough to win, having had some conversation with my Father wherein she represented to him what I have managed to make visible to herself -- that if he be actuated by a love of truth, and desire that I should return to the profession of what he regards as truth, he could not place a more effective barrier to my [conversion] than by making my apparent worldly interests in any way dependent on it. That the prospect of reinstalment in external comforts or in the good opinion of the world would be precisely the attendant on a change of opinion to create the most violent struggle in my mind ere I could confess such change, and that as regards society the attempt to interlace worldly interests with religious sentiment even more closely than in the present state of things is inevitable, would be an Ehud's homage to piety no other than a stab under the fifth rib. 427 My Father consented and said that I had better return to him after a time, but he is bent, at present, more determinedly than is usual with him, on leaving Foleshill. A most lugubrious looking place at Fillongley (!) 428 runs in his head as a desirable residence. Of course I shall not utter a word of discontent or claim a voice in the matter of a choice concerning his abode. I can quite appropriate Satan's sentiment, "What matter where if I be still the same." 429 Or rather if I be attaining a better autocratship than that of the Emperor of all the Russias -- the empire over self. But though disposed to be lamb-like in this matter, there is another on which I am warm and decided. When I came hither I did so in compliance with my Father's wish that I should retire for a time from a neighbourhood in which I had been placed on the very comfortable pedestal of the town gazing-stock and to be very plain but not less true, made a fool of by announcing my departure to everyone connected with me, but I never contemplated remaining here longer than a month, and I cannot be induced to prolong a visit farther than that. I must have a settled home if my mind is to become healthy and composed, and I shall therefore write to my Father in a week and request his decision. It is important, I know, for him as well as myself that I should return to him without delay, and unless I draw a circle round him and require an answer within it, he will go on hesitating and hoping for weeks and weeks. 430 It was a sacrifice in the first instance to take up my abode with any of my family, and though I have every kindness here, there are feelings which are incommunicable that render it impossible for me to continue long an adjunct to a family instead of an integral part. A very interesting yarn this, that I am spinning. Do forgive me I am extraordinarily dense and selfish this morning -- and the epistolary muse, if there were one, would disdain to unite her influence with those of Epsom salts, which are just now making my head dizzy. I do not make many knots an hour in mental progress here, for in-door attention to others and out-door loveliness are in league to make an idler of me. I would I knew something about any creature beside myself to write of -- as it is I can only beg you to reconcile me to my eternal egotism by copying it. I fear to read over my letter lest the silly things I have said should be engraven on my memory.
Thank you for the note and notes. I shall think of Miss Brabant 431 with grateful pleasure. Alas! I despair now of seeing your locks parted after my taste and like most other people (on other subjects) I am lost in astonishment that anyone can differ from me -- that my ideas of the elegant and becoming are not shared by all the world. Nevertheless I can love you just as well, and I venture to say shall always love you however you might travesty the exterior of that something that utters, looks, smiles, and writes wisely and lovingly.
Do manage to cheer me with another little note.
Ever your affectionate,
Mary Ann Evans.

427 See Judges 3:15-26.
428 Fillongley, about 6 miles northwest  of Coventry, a parish containing 212 houses in 1841. Mr. Evans's employer Lord Aylesford was one of the principal owners. (F. White, Warwickshire, 1850, p. 816.)

(M. Blind, George Eliot, 1883, p. 33.) The conflict with her father ended in a compromise: GE agreed to conform to custom by going to church, while her father was persuaded to let her hold what opinions she wished. MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1844. Hitherto unpublished.
My own dear Heart's Ease,
I am too selfish to be sorry that you took the trouble to write to me, your looks and words of love are so precious to me. I am altogether ashamed of myself -- do not tell any one that I am so silly as I appear to her whom I love best.
Dinner comes to take possession of the table and I cannot thank you half for your goodness but I will look my gratitude to-morrow afternoon, if you are inclined to finish the picture 442 then.
Yours ever truly
Mary Ann.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Foleshill, May? 1845]
MS: Yale. Address: Mrs. Bray | Rose Hill. Endorsed: 1845. Hitherto unpublished.
My dear Friend,
I hoped for a fine afternoon in which I could run over the fields to tell you the reason I could not have the pleasure of seeing you yesterday evening. Fanny staid until after tea and I had Father to entertain so that I had no choice in the matter. I expect to have Miss R. Franklin on Monday but I shall at least see you at the Mechanic's Institute and have one of your smiles to cheer me. It must be easier to die for the world than to live for it -- easier to die for a principle than to act up to it, and I should be quite glad of such a short cut to virtue.
Love to all
Mary Ann.

GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Foleshill, December 1842](2)
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, 1, 120-121, as part of the preceding letter to Mrs. Bray.
My dearest Friend,
I shall avenge myself on Fate by and bye for keeping me away from you so long, and you so poorly as I hear you are. I have had a visitor 466 ever since Saturday, and she will stay till Saturday again. I will tell you simple truth I could be with you to-morrow evening, that is if you would have my companion, but I should enjoy the pleasure much better another week.
I cannot desire that you should unask Violin and Flute, 467 unless a postponement would be in every way as agreeable to you and them. If you have them you will give them much more pleasure as Piano than I, so do not think of me in the matter for a moment. Good bye, and remember to nurse yourself 468 and treat your cold "as if it were an orphan's cold, or a widow's cold, or any one's cold but your own."
Your faithful
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Foleshill, December 1842](1)
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Foleshill, December 1842](1)
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1843. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 119-120.
As the apple tree among the trees of the wood so art thou my beloved, among the daughters, 458 and I only wish you would change houses with the Mayor, 459 that I might get to you when I would.
I send you the first part of Wallenstein 460 with the proposition that we should study that in conjunction with the Thirty years' war, as I happen to have a loose copy. We had better omit the Lager and begin Die Piccolomini. The other part is Wallenstein's Tod. You shall have Joan of Arc, my grand favourite as a bonne bouche when you have got through Wallenstein, which will amply repay you for any trouble in translating it, and is not more difficult than your reading ought to be now. I have skimmed Manzoni, who has suffered sadly in being poured out of silver into pewter. The chapter on Philosophy and Theology is worth reading. 461 Miss Brabant sent me my Hyperion 462 with a note the other day. She had put no direction besides Coventry and the parcel had consequently been sent to some other Miss Evans and my choice little sentimental treasures alas! exposed to vulgar gaze. Miss B. begs me to tell her all I know of Rosehill and the inhabitants of "that Paradise." I shall hope to see its Eve to-morrow; in the meantime will you tell your Adam, who [with front serene governs] 463 in your Paradise, with my compliments or respects or love, whichever is proper and all three are true, that the trees are condemned to fall and be sold to Mr. Webb. 464 Thank you for the Manual which I have had so long. I trust I did not bestow those scratches on the cover. I have been trying to find a French book that you were not likely to have read but I do not think I have one, unless it be Gil Blas 465 which you are perhaps too virtuous to have read, though how any one can opine it to have a vicious tendency I am at a loss to conjecture. They might as well say that to condemn a person to eat a whole plum pudding would deprive him of all future relish for plain food.
Vale,
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Foleshill, 6 March 1842]
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, I, 109-110.
My dear Friend,
I must relieve my conscience before I go to bed by entering a protest against every word or accent of discontent that I uttered this morning. 412 If I have ever complained of any person or circumstance I do penance by eating my own words. When my real self has regained its place I can shake off my troubles "like dewdrops from the lion's mane," 413 and then I feel the baseness of imputing my sorrows to others rather than to my own pitiful weakness.
I did not mean to give you an uncomfortable half hour this morning when I went to you, and I hope I shall never be guilty of inflicting such a jeremiad on any one again, least of all on you, my dearest love. But I do not write for your forgiveness -- that I know I have -- I only want to satisfy my indignation against myself.
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Foleshill, 18 June 1844]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Foleshill, 18 June 1844]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 128-129.
My dear Friend,
It was very kind of you to think of me among so many pleasant people and pleasant sights. 518 I am quite glad that you have Mr. Noel to double your enjoyment as well as have his own share. I went to your house as a marauder this morning, to carry off a book from the book-case, and I found Hannah brimful of a theft that has been committed at your neighbour's Mr. Carter's. 519 Some snapper up of unconsidered trifles from the fair I suppose, thought of running away with a silver fork and spoon but Jephcott has the glory of being the police officer in the case. Verily these are not days to hang up bracelets in the highways.
I do not think it was kind to Strauss (I knew he was handsome) to tell him that a young lady was translating his book. I am sure he must have some twinges of alarm to think he was dependent on that most contemptible specimen of the human being for his English reputation.
My love to Sara, and tell her I do not wish to distress her conscience with the purchase of an atheistic book, but I feel sure there is a [Bauer's Wesen des Christenthums] 520 published at Berlin.
By the way, I never said that the canons of the Council of Nice, or the Confession of Augsburg, or even the 39 articles are suggestive of poetry. I imagine no dogmas can be. But surely Christianity with its Hebrew retrospect and millennial hopes, the heroism and Divine sorrow of its founder and all its glorious army of martyrs might supply and has supplied a strong impulse not only to poetry but to all the fine arts.
Mrs. Pears is coming home from Malvern to-night, and the children are coming to tea with me so that I have to make haste with my afternoon matters. Beautiful little Susan has been blowing bubbles and looking like an angel at sport. I am quite happy, only sometimes feeling "the weight of all this unintelligible world." That is Wordsworth's idea, 521 and you must allow it to be vinous, not milk and watery as usual.
Love to Mr. Bray, although I am tremendously offended with his letter. Breakfast with you on Friday morning!
Mary Ann.
Tuesday afternoon.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Foleshill, 12 March 1842]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1842. Extract published: Cross, I, 104-105, dated January 1842.
My dear Mrs. Bray,
My guardian angel Mrs. Pears has just sent for me to hear your kind note, which has done my aching limbs a little good. I shall be most thankful for the opportunity of going to Leamington, 414 and Mrs. Pears is willing to go too. Since my morning's conversation with Mrs. P. I have been meditating on her kind plan of seeking an interview with my father, and owing to feelings and circumstances impossible for me to communicate fully, I am persuaded that the attempt to influence him would be unwise and could issue in no real good to any. I am unusually muddy to-night, and must wait for to-morrow to tell you more if even your benevolent ears are not weary of me and my woes -- but woes I will not call them, there is but one woe, that of leaving my dear Father. All else, doleful lodgings, scanty meals, and gazing-stockism 415 are quite indifferent to me. Therefore do not fear for me when I am once posited in my home, wherever it may be, and freed from wretched suspense.
Ever your grateful and affectionate
Mary Ann Evans.
We will be at your house by 10 o'clock.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Broadstairs, 19 August 1852]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, [Broadstairs, 19 August 1852]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I 287; George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 62.
Broadstairs | Thursday.
Dearest Cara
Are you really the better for having been here? Since you left I have been continually regretting that I could not make your visit pleasanter. I was irritable and out of sorts. But you have an apparatus for secreting happiness -- that's it.
Providence, seeing that I wanted weaning from this place, has sent a swarm of harvest-bugs and lady-birds to bite my legs. These, with the half blank, half dissipated feeling which comes on after having companions and losing them, make me think of returning to London on Saturday week with more resignation than I have felt before. Mr. Chapman writes to me in the hastiest fashion and tells me nothing of what he has been doing in business matters during the last week. The issue of the Cobden business is just what I expected. I find he is a churchman. 165
The sentence you quote is a good specimen of Mr. Chapman's skill in "the art of sinking," not in poetry, but in letter-writing. But it is nothing worse than bungling. He feels better than he writes, just as some other acquaintances of ours write better than they feel. I am sure I ought to have sympathy enough with people who mean well and do ill, for the grand occupation of my life has been contributing to hell-paving.
Thanks for the sermon -- it made us 166 laugh well over our tea on Monday.
I am very well -- minus the bites -- and [plucky,] a word which I propose to substitute for happy, as more truthful.
Best love to Sara and kind regards to your visitors. 167
Ever your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 1 September 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, London, 1 September 1863
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, II, 364-365.
Blandford Sq. | September 1. 63.
Dear Cara and Sara
Much love to you both on that far away coast! I think I get a little freshness from the breeze that blows on you -- a little lifting of heart from your wide sky and Welsh mountains. 192 And the edge of autumn on the morning air makes even London a place in which one can believe in beauty and delight. Delicate scents of dried rose-leaves and the coming-on of the autumnal airs are two things that make me feel happy before I know why. Make the best of your fortnight and let me know that you go home bright and strong.
The Priory is all scaffolding and paint, and we are still in a nightmare of uncertainty about our boys -- awaiting one letter here and another there, and feeling in many ways the wide gap between theoretic longing and possible practice. But then I have by my side a dear companion who is a perpetual fountain of courage and cheerfulness and of considerate tenderness for my lack of those virtues. And besides that, I have -- Roman History! Perhaps that sounds like a bitter joke to you who are looking at the sea and sky and not thinking of Roman History at all. But this too, read aright, has its Gospel and Revelation. I read it much as I used to read a chapter in the Acts or Epistles. Mommsen's Hist[ory] of Rome is so fine that I count all minds graceless who read it without the deepest stirrings of heart.
Farewell
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, [London, 17 June 1853]
Dublin Core:Subject: Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, [London, 17 June 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 17. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 309.
Friday Morning.
Dear Cara and Sara
Mr. Barclay 329 put an end to my pain in ten minutes by stopping my hollow tooth, and moreover consoled me by telling me that I need feel no anxiety about the state of my teeth in general. So I am radiant with benevolence, as it is so easy to be when one is perfectly comfortable. Not that I am quite that, for my cough has been worse again the last few days.
On Wednesday I dined at Sir James Clark's 330 where the Combes are staying and had a very pleasant evening -- nice Dr. Arnott 331 and Mr. Barton being the other guests. At 10 o'clock the Clarks went to the Queen's ball 332 and I had the amusement of seeing them in their court dresses.
The Combes have taken lodgings in Oxford Terrace where I mean to go, and where I hope Sara will come to stay with me some time. It is better than the Strand -- trees waving before the windows, and no noise of omnibuses.
Last Saturday evening I had quite a new pleasure. We went to see Rachel again, 333 and sat on the stage between the scenes. When the dropscene fell, we walked about and saw the green room and all the dingy, dusty paraphernalia that make up theatrical splendour. I have not yet seen the [Vashti] of Currer Bell 334 in Rachel, though there was some approach to it in Adrienne Lecouvreur.
We are going to have a party to-night to meet Mrs. Cornwallis 335 -- a lady who reads Egyptian hieroglyphs and for aught I know the arrow-headed and cuneiform characters to boot. I shall write again soon -- these few lines to thank you both for writing to me.
Your faithful
Pollian.

The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 2. 73.
My dear Mrs. Simpson
Many thanks for the lovely photograph.
You would have been less surprized at Mr. Lewes's outburst the other day 741 if you had been able to imagine what a feeble wretch I have been this winter, and how often he has seen me overdone by week-day appointments -- the "boiling over" of receptions beyond the rim of Sunday. My friends who are kept at home on Sundays usually send me a note or card to ask if I can see them on a particular afternoon. If at any time you think it worth while to do so, I will let you know whether there is any obstacle of illness or incompatible engagement; and thus you will be saved a journey in vain. I hope to be less good-for-nothing by and by. Believe me
Sincerely yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Bell, Venice, 8 June 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Bell^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Bell, Venice, 8 June 1860
MS: Mr. W. M. Matthews. Envelope: Mrs. Bell | Holly Lodge | Wandsworth | London S.W. | Inghilterra. Postmarks: VENEZIA | 9 | 6; LONDON | DN | JU 14 | 1860. Hitherto unpublished.
Venice June 8. 60.
Dear Mrs. Bell
It seems to me a long while since I wrote to you from Rome -- much longer, I dare say, than it seems to you, who have been leading a quiet monotonous life that leaves little trace in the mind. I hope it has been in no way an unpleasant life to you; indeed Mrs. Congreve has written me word that your report of your health was "very well for you" and that Martha has been very good -- news which it was a comfort to me to know.
The unfortunate letter you dispatched to Rome 556 has not reached us, but you need be in no trouble on that account, for if, as I imagine, you observed that the letter had been previously addressed to Smith and Elder with the intimation "To be forwarded," it is probably a letter of no importance from some person who did not know Mr. Lewes's address.
I am thankful to tell you that at last Mr. Lewes seems really the better for our holiday: there is no remnant of deafness, and he is certainly stronger in head and stomach. Our journey has been a continually increasing enjoyment to us both, and I hope will have good results for mind and body. We shall hardly manage to reach home before the end of this month, but of course I shall write again to let you know, as soon as possible after we know it ourselves, the exact day if not hour of our return to Holly Lodge.
In the mean time if you have not thought of it already, will you please see that the outside Spanish blind is put up over the drawing room window. Nicholson, 557 the builder, will be the best person to apply to. He has more than once sent carpenters to do work for us. And at the same time let it be seen that all the blinds are in order as to their rollers and cords. If the windows want cleaning, Nicholson will send men for that also. I think I mentioned that the muslin curtains should be put up in both rooms.
We shall be at Berne about the twentieth, so that if you or Mrs. Congreve should have any thing to say to me before our return, a letter to the Poste Restante, Berne, will not miss me.
Give my best love to Mrs. Congreve, and thank her for her last letter. I trust to her goodness not to demand another letter from me; for we are out of the house so continually during the day time, and I am so fatigued at night, that writing by candlelight is an oppressive prospect to me.
You have never sent us a word of news about Pug! 558 I hope no tragedy awaits us on our return. We have seen a pair of puppies -- brother and sister -- here at Venice that made us long to carry them home as companions for our very slow child.
The weather seems made on purpose for us. It is constantly brilliant, and yet not excessively warm, so that we have the pleasures of Venice in perfection -- without mosquitoes, and without head-scorching in our gondola. Remember me kindly to Martha, and believe me always
Your sincere friend
Marian Evans Lewes.
Pray think of everything within reach that will make Charles's room look comfortable and, if possible, pretty. Especially beg Martha to scrub away at the dirty paint, which is one of the dreariest things in a bed-room. Remember that the View of Scilly, over the drawing-room door, was to be put up in Charles's room.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Alfred Tennyson, Witley, 5 November 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Alfred Tennyson^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Alfred Tennyson, Witley, 5 November 1880
MS: Tennyson Research Centre, Lincoln.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
November 5. 80.
Dear Mrs. Tennyson
The regret I felt on finding your cards that my drive had happened when I might have had the pleasure of seeing you has been deepened by my inability to get to Aldworth.
I have been rather seriously ill, and am not allowed to be out in the open air for more than an hour in the scant sunshine. One seems to be making too much of such facts by writing about them; but I cannot bear to seem unmindful of any friendly sign made to me by you and yours.
Our friend Mrs. Greville has told me -- I hope quite correctly -- that you are in some respects better in health than you were last year, and that Mr. Tennyson is as energetic and bright as usual. You and he will I trust always believe in the high regard with which I am
Yours most sincerely
M. A. Cross.
Mr. Cross feels himself a loser, that he has missed this year's opportunity of making your and Mr. Tennyson's acquaintance. I am hoping that Mr. Hallam may find his way to us when we are in town at 4 Cheyne Walk, Chelsea.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist, Shottermill, 9 May [1871]
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist, Shottermill, 9 May [1871]
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library. Extracts published: H. H. Gilchrist, ed., Anne Gilchrist, 1887, pp. 216-217.
Brookbank | May 9.
My dear Madam
While I am writing this I trust you are already comforted by Mr. Lewes's last letter, which told you that our horizon was clearing. Some small articles which were missing at first were afterwards discovered by energetic Mrs. Larby's ferreting, and the entire extra expense that we shall have incurred in small purchases, mendings, and scourings and chimney-sweepings will apparently be under a pound.
The green blind is now working properly in the bedroom, and the only matter of furniture that I am at all anxious about now is the gauziness of the blinds in the drawingroom which is broadly exposed to the afternoon sun. But to this we must resign ourselves. The keys are not yet forthcoming, but the process of inquiry has not yet been lengthy enough. Everything goes on slowly at Shotter Mill, and the mode of narration is that typified in "This is the house that Jack built." But there is an exquisite stillness in the sunshine, and a sense of distance from London hurry, which encourages the growth of patience.
Mrs. Garland's pace is proportionate to the other slownesses, but she impresses me as a worthy person, and her cooking -- indeed, all her attendance on us -- is of satisfactory quality. But we find the awkwardness of having only one person in the house, as well as the advantage (this latter being quietude). The butcher does not bring the meat, everybody grudges selling new milk, eggs are scarce, and an expedition we made yesterday in search of fowls showed us nothing more hopeful than some chickens six weeks old which the good woman observed were sometimes "eaten by the gentry with asparagus." Those eccentric people, the gentry! But have we not been reading about the Siege of Paris all the winter, and shall we complain while we get excellent bread and butter and many et cetaeras? Mrs. Symonds 283 kindly sent us a dish of asparagus yesterday which we ate (without the skinny chicken) and had a feast.
You will imagine that we are as fond of eating as Friar Tuck -- I am enlarging so on our commissariat. But you will also infer that we have no great evils to complain of, since I make so much of the small.
If I ever steal anything in my life, I think it will be the two little Sir Joshua's over the drawingroom mantelpiece. I assure you I have thought much of the worry we may have caused you while you are in a state of health with which I can sorrowfully sympathize. I do hope that we shall not have reason to trouble you any more.
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist, Shottermill, 3 July 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist, Shottermill, 3 July 1871
MS: Parrish Collection, Princeton. Published: Cross, III, 133-134.
Brookbank | July 3. 71.
My dear Mrs. Gilchrist
We are greatly obliged to you for the trouble you have so sympathetically taken on our behalf. 310 But Mr. Smith is altogether reasonable, and I feel somewhat ashamed of our own outcries against an inconvenience which could only be got rid of by being shifted on to another.
As it is we resign ourselves, and we shall prepare to quit our quiet shelter on Wednesday, the 2d of August -- since Mr. Smith allows us grace for a day. During the first weeks of our stay I did not imagine that I should ever be so fond of the place as I am now. The departure of the bitter winds, some improvement in my health, and the gradual revelation of fresh and fresh [sic] beauties in the scenery, especially under a hopeful sky such as we have sometimes had -- all these conditions have made me love our little world here and wish not to quit it until we can settle in our London home. I have the regret of thinking that it was my original indifference about it (I hardly ever like things until they are familiar) that hindered us from securing the cottage until the end of September, for the chance of coming to it again after a temporary absence. But all regrets ought to be merged in thankfulness for the agreeable weeks we have had, and probably shall have till the end of July. And among the virtues of Brookbank we shall always reckon this -- that our correspondence about it has been with you rather than with any one else, so that along with the country we have had a glimpse of your ready quick-thoughted kindness.
Believe me always
Yours most sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist, Shottermill, 2 August 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist, Shottermill, 2 August 1871
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Anne Gilchrist, ed. H. H. Gilchrist, 1887, p. 219.
Cherrimans | Shottermill | Petersfield | August 2. 71.
Dear Mrs. Gilchrist
We parted from Brookbank yesterday and left it in the charge of good Mrs. Larby. I trusted that we should leave it in all respects not worse, but perhaps even better than we found it; but, after Mr. Lewes had written to you, I was made aware that a small dessert or bread and butter Dish had been broken. That arch-sinner, the cat, was credited with the guilt. I am assured by Mrs. Garland that nothing else has been injured during her reign, and Mrs. Larby confirmed the statement to me yesterday. I wish I could replace the unfortunate dish.
At last we have rather more promise of repose from wind and rain. But how cold it is! If only the corn can be ripened and the country not suffer from a damaged harvest, my chill sensations are of rather less importance, but I have been grumbling over them hitherto out of public spirit.
This note of course needs no answer, and is intended simply to make me a clean breast about the crockery. Hoping some day to shake you by the hand in our own home, I remain,
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
Mrs. Alex. Gilchrist.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist, London, 19 April 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Alexander Gilchrist, London, 19 April 1871
MS: Mr. Gordon S. Haight. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 19. 1871.
My dear Madam
We are very much obliged to you for your kind, methodical thoughtfulness as to all which is necessary for our accommodation at Brookbank, and also for your hints about the points of beauty to be sought for in our walks. That "sense of standing on a round world" which you speak of, is precisely what I most care for amongst out-of-door delights. The last time I had it fully was at St. M'e4rgen near Freiburg, on green hill-tops whence we could see the Rhine and poor France.
Mr. Ewens has written this morning to ask for a little more time, and Mr. Lewes will reply that he may stay until the 26th. Poor things, they seem sadly adagio in their movements, and are about to emigrate apparently with as much knowledge of America as they have of the lunar volcanoes.
The garden has been, and is being, attended to, and I trust that we shall not find the commissariat unendurable. Mr. Ewens wanted to stay till the last day of the month, but that would have been a serious annoyance and retardation for us, as the house cannot be well cleaned without the work of some days. Always, dear Madam,
Sincerely yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mrs. Albert Druce, Witley, 4 August 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Mrs. Albert Druce^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mrs. Albert Druce, Witley, 4 August 1880
MS: Miss Elsie Druce. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
August 4. 80.
My dear Anna
We shall be very glad to be with you on the 13th and I shall look forward delightedly to Johnnie's enjoyment of the tennis that Albert will provide for him besides the pleasure of the old companionship.
When I asked Johnnie how long he would think of staying with you, since you give us the generous invitation to stay as long as we can, he said "Till Monday." But I dared to plead that we should stay till Tuesday if that space were needed to cover the Spottiswood dinner. 461 I once met the Spottiswoods at Oxford and found them very agreeable.
"Phoebie" is a nice little body for anyone who wants a budding housemaid. Brett pronounces her clean, industrious and quick to learn. She is also rather pretty to look at.
We shall let you know the train by which we shall arrive on the 13th. Johnnie, I think, will meet Albert tomorrow at Weybridge, and will then have made up his mind on this point. [The rest of the letter has been cut away.]
