Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Geneva, 13 September [1849]
Dublin Core:Subject: Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^M, F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Geneva, 13 September [1849]
MS: Yale. Address: Charles Bray Esq | Rosehill | Coventry | Angleterre | Voie de France. Postmarks: GENEVE | 14 SEPT | 49 | 8'bdM; COVENTRY | SP 17 | 1849 | A. Extracts published: Cross, I, 221-222.
Plongeon September 13th.
Dear Friends
I have been expecting a letter from you for the last two or three days and I am just now hating you intensely because the postman has just been here and has brought nothing for me. My boxes arrived last Friday -- rather in disorder within, but otherwise safely enough. I miss some things which I thought I had put in, but I can hardly trust my memory on that head. I am chiefly distressed to find that there are no pocket handkerchiefs. The expense was 120 fr. -- perfectly horrible! Clearly I must give myself for food to the fowls of the air or the fishes of the lake. 832 It is a consolation to a mind imbued with a lofty philosophy that when one can get nothing to eat, one can still be eaten -- the evil is only apparent. It is quite settled that I cannot stay at Plongeon -- I must move into the town.
I have had a bilious attack, partly I believe from the way of living here -- long fasts etc. -- indeed I have never been well since I came. However I congratulate myself on this same bilious attack for I have had Dr. Lombard 833 to see me, a charming, frank person, who has studied in Edinburgh and speaks English well. He seemed to take a fancy to me and understood me at once -- tells me to send to him when I want anything -- said "I'll tell Prévost that I have seen you" -- and spoke to M. Prévost-Martin, 834 but he found that he, Mr. J.L.P., was gone to England again.
I thought of taking private lodgings in the town. I had fixed on some in the Terreaux de Chante-Poulet, but all the world says I must not go there. The Baronne de Ludwigsdorff, who is my chief friend here now, wants me to go to M. Gaussen-Huber's, 835 where she would go if she staid the winter in Geneva. M. Lombard too says he thinks that would be the best for me -- but, alas! I must pay 200 f. per month. If I were there I should see more conversable people than here. No one is received for less than a few months and there is never a larger number than 5 or 6. The Gaussen family is one of the most respectable (in the right sense) in Geneva. I think altogether that if I am to live through the winter I must go there. At private lodgings I should probably be robbed so as to make the expense greater even than in the other case.
Do you think any one would buy my Encyclopedia Britannica at 'bd price and my globes? If so I should not be afraid of exceeding my means and I should have a little money to pay for my piano and for some lessons of different kinds that I want to take. The Encyclopedia is the last edition 836 and cost £42, and the globes £8.10. The Enc[yclopedia] is in the oak-coloured chest, the globes in the chest with the padlock. I shall never have anywhere to put them, so it is folly to keep them if any one will buy them -- but do not teaze yourself about it unless you think it easy.
Mr. Sibree 837 called -- as perhaps you know by this time. I cannot say that I was in the least obliged to him as from the terms in which we are, it could be nothing else than a piece of impertinent curiosity. I beg you will neither give my address nor read my letters to any one else -- unless it be some one equal to yourselves in friendship for me or in refinement of mind. There are many people in whose happiness I take a great interest, whom yet I do not wish to interest themselves about me and my affairs. Miss Sibree has written to me and asks me to send my letters to her to Rosehill as she thinks her father would object to her corresponding with me. Please to give my love to her and tell her that I cannot carry on a correspondence with anyone who will not avow it. No one else has written to me, though I have written to almost all. I would rather have it so than feel that the debt was on my side. When will you come to me for help, that I may be able to hate you a little less? I shall leave here as soon as I am able to come to a decision as I am anxious to feel settled and the weather is becoming cold. This house is like a bird-cage set down in a garden. Do not count this among my letters. I am good for nothing today and can write nothing well but bitterness so that I will not trust myself to say another word except that you are dear good creatures and that I am
Your ever tiresome and seldom affectionate
Pollian.
There is a family of Forbes's 838 here -- related to Professor Forbes -- very strait-laced -- but very kind to me. M. de Herder is gone to the Pyrenees but will come again. Then there are a Mr. and Mrs. Wood, very rich people, who have lived in Italy chiefly, very commonplace but agreeable -- 3 raw-looking Germans who came yesterday -- a French family named Desaix, Parisians, husband and wife and two lovely boys, all interesting -- another French family just come. Mrs. Locke gone to Bex this morning. The Baroness de Ludwigsdorff whom I described to you -- she seems to have begun to like me very much and is really kind, taking upon herself, all the trouble about Madame Gaussen etc. -- so you see heaven sends kind souls, though they are by no means kindred ones. Poor Mrs. Locke is to write to me -- has given me a little ring -- says "take care of yourself, my child -- have some tea of your own -- you'll be quite another person if you get some introductions to clever people -- you'll get on well among a certain set, that's true" -- it is her way to say "that's true" after all her affirmations. She says, "You won't find any kindred spirits at Plongeon, my dear."

Dublin Core:Subject: Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^M, F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Geneva, [4 December 1849]
MS: Yale. Address: C. Bray Esq | Rosehill | Coventry | Angleterre. Postmarks: GENEVE | 4 | DECE | 49 | 8'bds; COVENTRY | DE 9 | 1849. Mostly published: Cross, I, 238-240.
Rue des Chanoines.
Dear Mr. Bray
I write at once to answer your questions about business. Spinoza and I have been divorced for several months. My want of health has obliged me to renounce all application. I take walks, play on the piano, read Voltaire, talk to my friends, and just take a dose of mathematics every day to prevent my brain from becoming quite soft. Therefore I am by no means eager to supersede any other person's labours, and Mr. Chapman is absolved from observing any delicacy towards me about Spinoza or his translators. 870 If you are anxious to publish the translation in question I could, after a few months, finish the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus to keep it company -- but I confess to you, that I think you would do better to abstain from printing a translation. What is wanted in English is not a translation of Spinoza's works, but a true estimate of his life and system. After one has rendered his Latin faithfully into English, one feels that there is another yet more difficult process of translation for the reader to effect, and that the only mode of making Spinoza accessible to a larger number is to study his books, then shut them and give an analysis. For those who read the very words Spinoza wrote, there is the same sort of interest in his style as in the conversation of a person of great capacity who has led a solitary life, and who says from his own soul what all the world is saying by rote, but this interest hardly belongs to a translation.
I am sorry to say that with a very great inclination to swear in your favour about the rent, I have not the slightest recollection of what you have paid or not paid. Dear Cara also. Your letter is very sweet to me, giving me a picture of your quiet life. How shall I enable you to imagine mine, since you know nothing of the localities? My good friends here only change for the better. Mde. D'Albert is all affection, M. D'Albert all delicacy and intelligence, the friends to whom they have introduced me very kind in their attentions. In fact I want nothing but a little more money to feel more at ease about my fires etc. etc. I am in an atmosphere of love and refinement -- even the little servant Jeanie seems to love me and does me good every time she comes into the room. I can say anything to M. and Mde. D'Albert. M. D'A. understands everything and if Madame does not understand she believes -- that is she seems always sure that I mean something edifying. She kisses me like a mother, and I am baby enough to find that a great addition to my happiness. Au reste, I am careful for nothing. I am a sort of supernumerary spoon, and there will be no damage to the set if I am lost. It is different with you, and I cannot help being saddened by the idea of losses and possible renunciations that may be required of you. My heart ties are not loosened by distance -- it is not in the nature of ties to be so -- and when I think of my loved ones as those to whom I can be a comfort or a help I long to be with them again. Otherwise I can only think with a shudder of returning to England. It looks to me like a land of gloom, of ennui, of platitude, but in the midst of all this it is the land of duty and affection, and the only ardent hope I have for my future life is to have given to me some woman's duty, some possibility of devoting myself where I may see a daily result of pure calm blessedness in the life of another.
Dear Cara -- carry my kindest remembrances to Clapton and Woodford. May you find our precious Mr. Hennell well enough to enjoy your visit thoroughly. 871 We have had some severe weather here but not more so than I have often felt in England. At present it is much milder. All possible Christmas pleasures and comforts to you all.
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Geneva, [28 January 1850]
Dublin Core:Subject: Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray^^M, F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Geneva, [28 January 1850]
MS: Yale. Address: Charles Bray Esq | Rose Hill | Coventry | England. Postmarks: GENEVE | 28 | JANV | 50 | 8'bdM; COVENTRY | JA 31 | 1850 | A. Extracts published: Cross, I, 243-244.
Rue des Chanoines.
Dear Friends
How are you? You leave me a long time without news of you, though I told you they were necessary as a counteractive to the horrors of this terrible winter. Are you really so occupied as to have absolutely no time to think of me? I console myself at least today, now we have a blue sky once more after two months of mist, with thinking that I am excluded by pleasanter ideas -- that at least you are well and comfortable, and I ought to content myself with that. Or was my last letter so shabby that you refuse to count it as one? That would be more just than kind. I do not mind how short your letters are, so that they tell me the essential about yourselves. The news does not interest me, and we can tell each other every thing of that sort much more quickly when I am with you. Long letters are only possible when one feels separated by a gulf of time as well as space. I like now to save everything that I may have all to tell you when I am in England. I am sure this reason ought to satisfy you -- it is a proof that I think a great deal of our reunion.
The fact is I am much of Touchstone's mind -- in respect my life is at Geneva I like it very well, but in respect it is not with you it is a very vile life. 882 I have no yearnings to exchange lake and mountains for Bishop Street and the Radford Fields, 883 but I have a great yearning to kiss you all and talk to you for three days running. But perhaps you are beginning to think differently, and I may as well spare myself all pains to convince you that I love you. At least write to tell me so. I do not think it will be possible for me to undertake the journey before the end of March. I look forward to it with great dread. I see myself looking utterly miserable, ready to leave all my luggage behind me at Paris for the sake of escaping the trouble of it.
We have had Alboni 884 here -- a very fat syren. There has been some capital acting of comedies by friends of M. D'Albert -- a M. Chancel, 885 an advocate, is superior to any professional actor of comedy I have ever seen. He reads vaudevilles so marvellously that one seems to have a whole troop of actors before one in his single person. He is a handsome man of fifty, full of wit and talent, and he married about a year ago an ugly old maid -- but this is less wonderful at Geneva than elsewhere.
Good bye, dear souls. I am persuaded that you are perfect and that I am good for nothing and I will not listen to what Satan says urging me to be angry with you.
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.

GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Geneva, [24 October 1849]
MS: Yale. Address: C. Bray Esq | Rosehill | Coventry | England. Postmarks: GENEVE | 24 OCTO | 49 | 11'bdM; COVENTRY | OC 27 | 1849 | A. Extracts published: Cross, I, 233-236.
Rue des Chanoines 107.
Dear Friends
I languished for your letter before it came and read it three times running -- judge whether I care less for you than of old. It is the best of blessings to know that you are well and cheerful, and when I think of all that might happen in a fortnight to make you otherwise, especially in these days of cholera and crises I cannot help being anxious until I get a fresh assurance that at least five days ago all was well. Before I say anything about myself I must contradict your suspicion that I paint things too agreeably for the sake of giving you pleasure. I assure you my letters are subjectively true -- the falsehood, if there be any, is in my manner of seeing things. But to satisfy Cara I will give you some "vérités positives" in which alas! poor imagination has hitherto been able to do little for the world. I have every day an excellent breakfast -- good coffee, delicious butter and confiture -- a good luncheon -- and a still better dinner -- for example, always two kinds of meat thoroughly well cooked, nice vegetables and pudding. Everything is on a generous scale without extravagance. Mde. D'Albert anticipates all my wants and makes a spoiled child of me. I like these dear people better and better -- everything is so in harmony with one's moral feeling that I really can almost say I never enjoyed a more complete bien-'eatre in my life than during the last fortnight.
For M. D'Albert I love him already as if he were father and brother both. You must know he is not more than 4 feet high with a deformed spine -- the result of an accident in his boyhood -- but on this little body is placed a finely formed head, full in every direction. The face is plain with small features, and rather haggard looking, but all the lines and the wavy grey hair indicate the temperament of the artist.
I have not heard a word or seen a gesture of his yet that was not perfectly in harmony with an exquisite moral refinement -- indeed one feels a better person always when he is present. He was educated for theology and did not become an artist -- did not even begin to draw till he was 21. He sings well and plays on the piano a little. It is delightful to hear him talk of his friends -- he admires them so genuinely -- one sees so clearly that there is no reflex egotism. His conversation is charming. I learn something every dinner-time.
Mde. D'Albert has less of genius and more of cleverness -- a really lady-like person, who says everything well. She brings up her children admirably -- two nice intelligent boys -- the youngest particularly has a sort of Lamartine expression with a fine head. I have not said half I feel about these good creatures because I am afraid you will laugh at me. But it is so delightful to get among people who exhibit no meannesses -- no worldlinesses that one may well be enthusiastic. For instance, I told you that Mde. D'Albert was to find me light for the 150 fr. She does this as if I were a visitor to whom she was anxious to be extremely polite. I have a large lamp and five bougies always in my room, 2 on the mantel-piece two on my piano and one on my dressing-table. She scolds me when she comes in and sees me reading by a single bougie. You will think me childish to talk of such things, but to me it is so blessed to find any departure from the rule of giving as little as possible for as much as possible. Their whole behaviour to me is the same spirit -- as if I were a guest whom they delighted to honour.
Last night we had a little knot of their most intimate musical friends -- a Mlle. Herpin 859 who plays admirably, a gentleman who has a splendid bass voice, and two really remarkable men, a M. Chaponni'e8re, 860 a physician, and his Father, a fine old man, quite a subject for a sculptor, who has written an infinity of clever poetry in the style of Thomas Hood, some of which M. D'Albert has read to me. He has also been a composer of music. The son is an antiquarian, has written a history of Bonnivard, is scientific, is full of all sorts of knowledge, with a delightful bonhommie. He has a fine tenor voice and sings with facility very difficult operatic music. M. and Mde. D'Albert introduce me to their friends as if they wished me to know them, as if they wished me to like their friends and their friends to like me. Mde. Chaponni'e8re, 861 the younger one's wife, is an amiable looking little woman who brings her work and listens to the music. The people and the evening would have been just after your own hearts. In fact I have not the slightest pretence for being discontented, not the shadow of a discomfort. Even the little housemaid Jeanie is charming -- says to me every morning, in the prettiest voice Madame a-t-elle bien dormi cette nuit? puts fire in my chauffe-pied without being told, cleans my rooms most conscientiously. There -- I promise to weary you less for the future with my descriptions. I could not resist the temptation to speak gratefully of M. and Mde. D'Albert.
Dear Mrs. Pears! How does she manage to endure her life with that poor monomaniac husband. Give my love to her -- my constant everfresh remembrance. My love to Miss R. Franklin -- tell her I have spun my web to Geneva -- it will infallibly carry me back again across the gulph -- were it twice as great. Tell Sara I shall write a little letter to her and enclose it in my next to you. In the meantime I am her faithful spouse. It is a comfort to hear of Mr. Hennell's being at all better. 862 Also it is good that Froude should marry a respectability 863 -- only if he preach the new word at Manchester I hope he will preach it so as to do without an after-explanation and not bewilder his hearers in the manner of Mephistopheles when he dons the doctor's gown of Faust. 864 I congratulate you on the new edition 865 and promise to read it with a disposition to admire when I am at Rosehill once more. I am beginning to lose respect for the petty acumen that sees difficulties. I love the souls that rush along to their goal with a full stream of sentiment, that have too much of the positive to be harassed by the perpetual negatives, which after all are but the disease of the soul, to be expelled by fortifying the principle of vitality. Mr. Bray wants a little letter all to himself, so I send him one full of sauciness that I dare not say to Cara. Kind regards to Miss Jenkins -- I hoped that her family circumstances would permit her to renounce her governess life.
Tell her I hear of her with interest. I am not well today. All my blood is in my head and Mde. D'Albert prescribes a walk before dinner, so I scribble to get done that I may put the letter in the post on my way.
Good-bye, dear loves -- shan't I kiss you when I am in England again -- in England! I already begin to think of the journey as an impossibility. Geneva is so beautiful now the trees have their richest colouring. Coventry is a fool to it -- but then you are at Coventry and you are better than lake trees and mountains to your affectionate
Mary Ann.

GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Geneva, [11 October 1849]
MS: Yale. Address: Charles Bray Esq | Rosehill | Coventry | Angleterre. Postmarks: GENEVE | 11 | OCTO | 49 | 8s; COVENTRY | OC 16 | 1849 | A. Extracts published: Cross, I, 230-231.
Rue des Chanoines No. 107.
Dear Friends
You do not want to hear from me again yet, but I want to hear from you -- that is the reason I write on this third day of my abode in my new lodgings. I like them very much. M. and Mde. D'Albert are really clever people, people worth sitting up an hour longer to talk to. This does not hinder Mde. from being an excellent manager, dressing scrupulously and keeping her servants in order. She has hung my room with pictures, one of which is the most beautiful group of flowers conceivable thrown on an open Bible -- painted by herself. I have a piano which I hire. There is also one in the salon. M. D'Albert plays and sings, and in the winter he tells me they have parties to sing masses and do other delightful things. There is at present a lady in the house who is studying crayons with M. D'Albert -- though she appears to be nearly fifty. I fancy she is doing it from some motive of duty. She will leave soon. M. D'A. is deformed with a face indicative of talent and feeling. 855 Mde. is a nice-looking woman -- the boys perfectly quiet, well-behaved and intelligent. In fact I think I am just in the right place. They appear to be evangelical and conservative, b[ut] 856 one finds these views in company with more breadth of cultu[re] here than one can
ever augur from them in England. I break[fast] in my own room at 'bd past eight, lunch at 'bd past 12, and dine at 4 or a little after, and take tea at 8. From the tea-table I have gone into the salon and chatted until bed-time. It would really have been a pity to have staid at Plongeon out of reach of everything and with people so little worth talking to. I have not found out the desagrémens here yet -- of course I shall, but I think they will not be more numerous than they would necessarily be in any sublunary lodgings.
Two unhappy newspapers 857 have cost each a franc and 20 centimes. The last however only cost 10 centimes. I do not know the reason of this but until the last came I was going to write to say that I must renounce the pleasure of having them -- since I am adopting Poor Richard's style of calculation, a franc a week etc. It is raining horribly here -- raining blue devils -- but this just saves me from the regret I should have felt at having quitted the chestnuts of Plongeon. That campagne looked splendid in its autumn dress. There are two good people there now -- a captain of the navy and his wife named Weavers, 858 whom I thought perfect nullities when they came, but it turned out that the husband is accustomed to the best scientific and literary society of London. We became capital friends and were sorry to part.
I have had a letter from Miss Sibree and am going to write to her to tell her that I think it right to abstain from correspondence with her. She is a sweet good girl, but her ideas want testing -- she should be let alone. I am by no means sure that she is prepared for the hardships of the new Protestantism. Also there is a strong leaven of Sibreeanism in her which I have tended to nourish by shewing a very strong interest in her. Sibreeanism is that degree of egotism which we call bad taste but which does not reach to gross selfishness -- the egotism that does not think of others, but would be very glad to do them good if it did think of them -- the egotism that eats up all the bread and butter and is ready to die of confusion and distress after having done it.
I am much obliged to Mr. Dawson for sending me so exceptional a proof of his regard -- tell him I only deserve it in consideration of my admiration for him. Dear souls I wish you had as great a freedom from care as I -- it is true my health has taken the place of all other cares or rather my want of health and I am sometimes ready to think that everybody is really prematurely worn out -- at other times I am more hopeful. Write to me soon.
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray, Edinburgh, 7 October 1852
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, I, 292-293.
Edinburgh | October 7. 1852.
Dear Friends
Here I am in this beautiful Auld Reekie once more -- hardly recognizing myself for the same person as the damozel who left it by the coach with a heavy heart some six years ago. 195
The Combes are all kindness and I am in clover -- an elegant house, 196 glorious fires, and a comfortable carriage -- in short just in the circumstances to nourish sleek optimism, convince one that this is "le meilleur des mondes possibles" and make one shudder at the impiety of all who doubt it. Last evening Mr. Robert Cox 197 came to tea, to be introduced to me as my cicerone through the lions of Edinburgh, and we are to set out on an expedition tomorrow morning. Mr. Williams, 198 too, the master of the Secular School was here, and I have been today to hear him give one of his lessons. The talk last night was pleasant enough, though of course all the interlocutors besides Mr. Combe have little to do but shape elegant modes of negation and affirmation like the people who are talked to by Socrates in Plato's dialogues -- [Certainly, that I firmly believe] etc. I have a beautiful view from my room window -- masses of wood, distant hills, the Firth, and four splendid buildings dotted far apart -- not an ugly object to be seen. When I look out in the morning it is as if I had waked up in Utopia or Icaria 199 or one of Owen's parallelograms. The weather is perfect -- all the more delightful to me for its northern sharpness which is just what I wanted to brace me. I have been out walking and driving all day and have only time before dinner to send this "paar worte" -- but I may have still less time to-morrow. Much love to you all.
Your ever affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, Edinburgh, 12 October 1852
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, I, 293-294.
Edinburgh | October 12. 1852.
Dear Friends
Between the beauty of the weather and the scenery, and the kindness of good people I am tipsy with pleasure. But I shall tell you nothing of what I see and do, because that would be taking off some of the edge from your pleasure in seeing me. One's dear friend who has nothing at all to tell one is a bore. Is it not so -- honour bright?
I enjoy talking to Mr. Combe -- he can tell me many things, especially about men in America and elsewhere, which are valuable, and besides I sometimes manage to get in more than a negative or affirmative. He and Mrs. C. are really affectionate to me, and the mild warmth of their regard, with the perfect order and elegance of everything about me, are just the soothing influence to do me good. They urge me to stay longer, but I shall adhere to my original determination of going to Miss Martineau's on the 20th, and I do not mean to stay with her longer than the 25th.
I shall probably not be at Rosehill more than a week or ten days -- so that I shall not interfere seriously with Mrs. C. Hennell's arrangements.
We are going to-day to Craig Crook (Jeffrey's place), 200 a beautiful spot which old October has mellowed into his richest tints. Such a view of Edinburgh from it! In haste
Your ever affectionate
Marian.
More another day.

GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London], 5 March 1853
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 307-308.
March 5. 1853.
Dear Friends
I send you a critique from the [Churchman] which will amuse you. Please to return it.
Mr. Chapman asked me the other day whether he had better send a copy of Newman's Horace 287 to the Coventry Herald. The work being published on commission, of course, he is bound to regulate its distribution to provincial papers with strict regard to Newman's interests. Should you notice it, and would the notice be at all influential on the Coventry public? Newman has honored me with a presentation copy.
I have been to Blandford Sq. (Leigh Smiths) 288 to an evening party this week. These soir'e9es are a terrible corv'e9e even without gas-lights -- especially when one gets introduced to a man who squints and one is haunted by the squint for an hour after getting home as one sometimes sees one's own eyes in the glass in an incipient bilious attack. Dined at Mr. Parkes's on Sunday, and am invited to go there again tonight to meet said Smiths, but I think I shall not go, the weather being wet and I ailing.
Better news of Harry, to-morrow I hope, and of Cara's tooth.
Dear Mr. Bray -- do you remember the "boiled mutton chops" in the Leader. 289 I don't think that dish would suit me.
I want to know what you think of Villette. Lewes was describing Currer Bell to me yesterday as a little, plain, provincial, sickly-looking old maid. 290 Yet what passion, what fire in her! Quite as much as in George Sand, only the clothing is less voluptuous.
Pray what does Sara mean by saying that my having plenty to do must be a great treat to me? I will trouble her to be more respectful to my serene editorship. The Review is to be stunning this time -- very superior to the last both in variety and general interest. I am going to write to Col. Thompson 291 who has asked leave to insert an article at the eleventh hour.
I am very jolly -- and ever your affectionate
Marian.

GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London, 6 November 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Nov. 6. 1852. Extracts published: Cross, I, 296.
Saturday.
Dearest Friends
To get into a first class carriage, fall asleep, and awake to find oneself where one would be, is almost as good as having Prince Hussein's carpet. This was my easy way of getting to London on Thursday. Good Mr. C. 215 at the station waiting for me and delighted to see me. By 5 o'clock I had unpacked all my boxes and made my room tidy, and then I began to feel some satisfaction in being settled down where I am of most use just now. After dinner came Herbert Spencer and spent the evening with me. 216 Yesterday morning Mr. Greg 217 called, on his way to Paris, to express his regret that he did not see me at Ambleside. He is very pleasing, but somehow or other he frightens me dreadfully.
Things seem to be going on tolerably well here. Mr. Chapman listens most amiably to my report of the fault people find with him. He is better than they think. I have read Kingsley's Phaethon 218 this morning, and long to cut it up. Kingsley provokes me more and more. I am going to plunge into Thackeray's novel 219 now, so good-bye.
God bless you all. 220

GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London, 5 June 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 5. Extract published: Cross, I, 282-283.
Saturday.
Dearest Friends
Many thanks for the books which came yesterday so nicely packed. We went to Mr. Mackay's on Wednesday evening, and met there Miss Marshall 107 and several other Misses. Mr. M. looked more cheery and smart in his own house as usual. Mrs. M. is disagreeably nervous and wanting in ease. One feels very glad when she has done her duty-talk.
On Thursday morning I went to St. Paul's to see the Charity Children assembled and hear their singing. 108 Berlioz 109 says it is the finest thing he has heard in England and this opinion of his induced me to go. I was not disappointed -- it is worth doing once especially as we got out before the sermon.
I had a long call from George Combe yesterday. They are going to the Continent after their stay in London. He says, he thinks the Westminster, under my management the most important means of enlightenment of a literary nature in existence -- the Edinburgh, under Jeffrey, nothing to it etc. etc!!! I wish I thought so too. A Mr. Bastard 110 has agreed to give £60 in the form of payment for articles, but no more extensive help has presented itself. Mr. Atkinson paid me a long visit the other day -- I can't help liking him though if one could feel ill naturedly towards him there is occasion if not matter for ridicule. He has no profession or occupation -- does not even mesmerize, as he has found it injure his health.
The Herald came to me this morning. Unless when there is something you particularly wish me to see, it seems a pity to send it, as I have no time to read it. A thousand loves to you all.
Your
Pollian.

GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London, 26 February 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 25. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 306-307.
Saturday.
Dear Friends
Do you observe that we are on the eve of having an American Copyright? 283 In which case the fortune of the Westminster is made, always supposing that periodicals are not excepted -- which would be a most unbecoming piece of envy in the Gods.
I suppose you got my last Saturday's note, which, it appears, was too late for the post. We had an agreeable evening on Wednesday -- a Mr. Huxley being the centre of interest. Since then I have been headachy and in a perpetual rage over an article that gives me no end of trouble and will not be satisfactory after all. I should like to stick red hot skewers through the writer whose style is as sprawling as his handwriting. I send Sara another Mazzini autograph to replace the one I took from her. 284
Dear Chrissey writes me letters that agitate me. People have offered to send her little ones to the Infant Orphan Asylum -- and the idea of the thing rends her heart. I think she ought to be provided for without any such measures.
For the rest, I am in excellent spirits, though not in the best health or temper. Mrs. Chapman knows that I am going to leave, and I think I shall manage it in the beginning of April. I am in for loads of work next quarter, but I shall not tell you what I am going to do. 285 Good-bye, dear souls. Write me some little scraps to-morrow.
Ever your
Pollian.
Forgive me if I forget anything for my head is distraught. I am most anxious to hear a more hopeful account of poor Harry. 286 Lameness seems worse than death for him. Mrs. C. Hennell was here last Sunday, looking, as you said, rather dejected.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London, 24 May 1852]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 281.
Monday.
Dearest Friends
I was very naughty not to write to you on Saturday, but I don't feel resigned to the punishment of hearing nothing from any of you this morning. My days have slipt away in a most mysterious fashion lately -- chiefly I suppose in long walks and long talks.
When shall you be out of hot water? I am tired of having all my friends at feud with somebody or other. The Gordon affair 95 I deeply regret -- and I must say that had you -- Mr. Bray -- been the author of the circular signed "a liberal churchman" -- his retort would have been richly deserved. You say nothing about Cara's tooth so I hope it has been quiet lately.
Our Monday evenings are dying off -- not universally regretted -- but we are expecting one or two people tonight. I have nothing to tell except that I went to the opera on Thursday and heard La Juive 96 -- and moreover fell in love with Prince Albert who was unusually animated and prominent. He has a noble, genial intelligent expression and is altogether a man to be proud of. As for the Queen, she is deplorable -- worse and worse the more one looks at her -- so utterly mean in contour and expression.
I am going next Thursday to see Grisi in Norma. 97 She is quite beautiful this season, thinner than she was and really younger looking. I know this is a stupid letter, but I will write when I am more in the vein. This is to assure you of my constant thought and love.
Pollian.

GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London, 19 September 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Sep. 19. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 312-313.
Monday.
Dear Friends
Your packet was a real treat to me this morning and made me enjoy my walk in the Park all the better. As for me, I am in the best health and spirits, with no cloud but the fact that Mr. Chapman seems a little more oppressed than usual just now, which causes me some regretful feeling about leaving.
I have had a letter from Mr. Combe today urging me to go to Edinburgh, but I have made an engagement with Mr. Chapman to do work which will oblige me to remain in London. I shall manage, however, to run away for a week to my sister and I hope I shall see you either going or returning.
Mrs. Perry 369 is a very bonny, pleasant looking woman, with a smart drawing-room and liberal opinions -- in short such a friend as self-interest well-understood 370 would induce one to cultivate.
I have not yet fixed on any lodgings, and I think of advertising, as a certain situation is a sine qu'e2 non. I find it difficult to meet with anything at once tolerable and cheap. My theory is to live entirely -- that is, pay rent and find food -- out of my positive income, 371 and then work for as large a surplus as I can get.
Cheap and pleasant lodgings are obtainable enough if one doesn't mind going 4 miles away from the centre, but not so when one must be within a reasonable distance at the West End.
The next number of the Review will be better than usual. Froude writes on the Book of Job! 372 He at first talked of an article on the three great subjective Poems -- Job, Faust and Hamlet. An admirable subject -- but it has shrunk to the Book of Job alone.
Herbert Spencer inquires after you. He made the pen with which I write. So you see he is a useful member of society.
Mr. Bray says, with dreadful truth, that my letters are uninteresting.
I'm very sorry, but it will be all the kinder of you if you will send me your interesting ones gratuitously. A visitor.
Your faithful
Marian.

GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London, 19 February 1853]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 301.
Saturday.
Dear Friends
What news of the ribbon trade? Pray tell me, for that is of as much consequence to me as the American Copyright. 275 Here is Harriet Martineau's pleasant letter to amuse you. I suppose you have seen Robert Owen's "Manifesto" 276 or I would send you that.
I am out of spirits about the W[estminster] R[eview]. The editorship is not satisfactory and I should be glad to run away from it altogether. But one thing is clear -- that the Review would be a great deal worse if I were not here. This is the only thought that consoles me.
We are thinking of sending Chrissey's eldest boy 277 to Australia. Mrs. Whichcote, 278 of Meriden, a patient of his father's, has offered to place him under suitable protection at Adelaide and I strongly recommend Chrissey to accept her offer -- that is, if she will let it be available a year hence. So I have bought Sidney's book on Australia 279 and am going to send it to Chrissey to enlighten her about matters there and accustom her mind to the subject.
Mrs. C. Hennell was here the other night, looking very well, but only in middling spirits -- I thought. What think you of Lord John's speech? 280 I suppose the answer to that question is already in the Herald. You are [jolly] I daresay, as good people have a right to be. Tell me as much of your happiness as you can, that I may rejoice in your joy -- having none of my own.
Ever your faithful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:

MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 12. 1852. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 284; George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 49.
Monday.
Dearest Friends
The opera, Chiswick Flower Show, the French play, and the Lyceum, 116 all in one week, brought their natural consequences of headache and hysterics all yesterday. At 5 o'clock I felt quite sure that life was unendurable and that I must consider the most feasible method of suicide as soon as the revises are gone to press. This morning, however, the weather and I are both better, having cried ourselves out and used up all our clouds, and I can even contemplate living six months longer. Was there ever anything more dreary than this June?
Pray what are Mr. and Mrs. Pears doing? I thought they were coming to town in May. My love to them, however. Tell Sara, the mysterious contribution is rejected and there will be no Independent in this number.
I shall write to her another day. The house is quite full -- the Brewitts, 117 Mrs. Chapman's relations, being here with the little deaf and dumb boy -- an interesting creature. 118
I am distressed to hear that you are all ailing with Influenza. I should like to see you very much -- nay, it is fast becoming a necessity to me -- so don't be surprized if I announce an intention of that sort by and bye. I told Herbert Spencer of your invitation, Mr. Bray, not mentioning that you asked him with me. He said he should like to accept it -- but I think it would be better for him to go down when I am with you. We certainly could not go together, for all the world is setting us down as engaged -- a most disagreeable thing if one chose to make oneself uncomfortable. [Tell it not in Gath] 119 however -- that is to say, please to avoid mentioning our names together, and pray burn this note, that it may not lie on the chimney piece for general inspection.
Your faithful
Marian.

GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London, 13 November 1852]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 296-297; George Eliot and John Chapman, pp. 64, 66.
Saturday.
Dear Friends
O this hideous fog! Let me grumble, for I have had headache the last three days and there seems little prospect of anything else in such an atmosphere. I am ready to vow that I will not live in the Strand again after Christmas. If I were not choked by the fog, the time would trot pleasantly withal, but of what use are brains and friends when one lives in a light such as might be got in the chimney?
I went to one of Jullien's concerts the other night and endured the Polkas for the sake of Zampa and Mendelssohn's Scherzo. 224 I amused myself with imagining Mr. Bray's curses if he had been there to hear the hop, skip, and jump of the dance music thundered by the drums and squealed by the pipes.
[Esmond] is the most uncomfortable book you can imagine. You remember, Cara, how you disliked [Fran'e7ois le Champi] (George Sand's). Well, the story of Esmond is just the same. The hero is in love with the daughter all through the book, and marries the mother at the end.
Mr. Chapman's affairs are just like the fog. Instead of a thousand, he wants £1200 now! The Lord have mercy on him!
You should read the debates on the opening of Parliament in the [Times.] Lord Brougham, [the greatest of English orators] perpetrates the most delicious non sequitur I have seen for a long time. "My Lords, I believe that any disturbance of the repose of the world is very remote, because it is our undeniable right and an unquestionable duty to be prepared with the means of defence should such an event occur." 225 These are thy gods O Israel! 226
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray, [London, 12 March 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 19. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 306.
Saturday.
Dear Creatures
It is nearly post time and I have only just remembered that it is my day for writing to you. I come from reading a letter of John Sibree's -- to me, not to my editorship, a very pleasing letter, telling of his doings, his aspirations, and his little daughters.
Many things have happened this week but I can't think of them in a trice. Mr. Chapman went with Mr. Neuberg to Carlyle's the other night. Carlyle said he had had a letter from Dr. Stamm 292 announcing an intended call -- a letter which made him expect nothing less than Elijah the Tishbite. I called on Miss Montgomery on Thursday and delivered Mr. Noel's message. She is a thoroughly nice person and I quite enjoy a chat with her. Mrs. Follen shewed me a delightful letter which she has had from Mrs. Stowe 293 telling all about herself. She begins by saying -- "I am a little bit of a woman, rather more than forty, as withered and dry as a pinch of snuff -- never very well worth looking at in my best days, and now a decidedly used up article." At 25 she married a man "rich in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, but alas! rich in nothing else." The proceeds of her first writings she devoted to buying her first feather bed! The whole letter is most fascinating and makes one love her.
Villette -- Villette -- have you read it?
Our next number is to be "grand, fundamental, and imposing." Mr. Bray deserves to be immortalized for inventing that phrase.
Herbert Spencer admires Mr. Hennell's portrait 294 greatly and sees "a resemblance to both sisters in it."
I must write three lines to Chrissey so there is no help for this stupid letter.
Ever your
Marian.
If you wanted to send a message would you send it by your eyes or by your nose? A dreadfully vulgar riddle. 295

MS: Yale. Endorsed: April 11. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 308.
Monday Morning.
Dear Creatures
Your letters this morning make sunshine for me and I shall go to Sydenham 311 in good spirits, though a quarter of an hour ago I was thinking the journey a bore. Only I am sorry to hear of Mr. Bray's lumbago -- after having had rheumatism myself I know how to sympathize with him.
The Times and the Athenaeum still speak confidently about the American Copyright, so perhaps there is no reason for desponding. 312
Please return H.M's letter.
The article on Schopenhauer is Oxenford's. That on Ruth and
Villette G. H. Lewes's! His, too, is the one on Alex. Smith. 313 "French Writers on Fr[ench] Policy" 314 is by Col. Perronet Thompson. There is an amusing article on Human Hair in the Quarterly. 315 The Edinburgh is a good number -- better than ours.
What do you think of my going to Australia with Chrissey and all her family? -- to settle them and then come back. I am just going to write to her and suggest the idea. When will Mr. Bray come to London? Not but that he is wise to keep away from it.
Bless you all. I can sing a Jubilate Deo when you are comfortable. One wants something to keep up one's faith in happiness -- a ray or two for one's friends if not for oneself. 'abLewes has been quite a pleasant friend to me lately.'bb
Much love from your ever affectionate
Pollian.

Dearest Friends
I like to remind you of me on Sunday morning when you look at the flowers and listen to music, so I send a few lines, though I have not much time to spare today. After Tuesday I will write you a longer letter and tell you all about everything.
Thank you for the Herald. Your quotations are conclusive but I wish you had left out the allusion to the "prophets" of the present day, and confined yourself to the illustration of the effect of italics. 70

Ever your
Marian.

'bd past 9. | Wednesday Morning.
Dear Friends --
Mr. Bury told us last night that he thought Father would not last till morning. I sat by him with my hand in his till four o'clock, and he then became quieter and has had some comfortable sleep. He is obviously weaker this morning and has been for the last two or three days so painfully reduced that I dread to think what his dear frame may become before life gives way. My Brother 791 slept here last night and will be here again tonight. What shall I be without my Father? It will seem as if a part of my moral nature were gone. I had a horrid vision of myself last night becoming earthly sensual and devilish for want of that purifying restraining influence. I write when I can but I do not know whether my letter will do to send this evening. Love to all -- Mrs. Hennell, Mr. and Mrs. C. Hennell, and my Siebenk'e4s. 792 By the bye, Siebenk'e4s, Cara is very Lenettish 793 about sundry things. Season your conversation with a little salt for her advantage and tell her to let me strip myself of my pewter and table-napkins without so many scruples. Dear Cara, love to you and yours.
Father is very, very much weaker this evening. 794

MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1846. Extracts published: Cross, I, 147-148.
Dearest Friends,
I cannot deny that I am very happy without you, but perhaps I shall be happier with you, so do not fail to try the experiment. 629 We have been to town only once and are saving all our strength to rake with you; but we are as ignorant as Primitive Methodists about any of the amusements that are going. All we know is that Judas Maccabaeus is to be performed at Exeter Hall on Friday Evening 630 just when we cannot hear it. But I am going to spend the day with Mr. and Mrs. Hennell tomorrow, and we will hunt in the M[orning] Chronicle. Do you the like in the Spectator, and please to come in a very mischievous, unconscientious, theatre-loving humour. Every body I see is very kind to me and therefore I think them all very charming, and having everything I want, I feel very humble and self denying. It is only rather too great a bore to have to write to my friends when I am half asleep, and I have not yet reached that pitch of amiability that makes such magnanimity easy.
Don't bring us any bad news or any pains, but only nods and becks and wreathed smiles. 631 Dear Sara is not at her strongest -- she is even knocked up with niaiseries and walks, but perhaps any other sort of excitement will be more endurable.
Your very insincere and unfaithful friend
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Subject: Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell^^M, F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, Wandsworth, [27 June 1859]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 1859. Mostly published: Cross, II, 116-117.
Holly Lodge | Monday Evening.
Dear Friends -- all three of you --
Thanks for your packet of heart-felt kindness. That is the best of your kindness -- there is no sham in it.
It was inevitable to me to have that outburst when I saw you for a little while after the long silence, and felt that I must tell you then or be forestalled, and leave you to gather the truth amidst an inextricable mixture of falsehood. But I feel that the influence of talking about my books even to you and Mrs. Bodichon has been so bad to me that I should like to be able to keep silence concerning them for evermore. If people were to buzz round me with their remarks, or compliments, I should lose the repose of mind and truthfulness of production without which no good healthy books can be written. Talking about my books, I find, has much the same malign effect on me as talking of my feelings or my religion.
I should think Sara's version of my brother's words concerning Adam Bede is the correct one -- "that there are things in it about my father" i.e. being interpreted, things my father told us about his early life, not a "portrait" of my father. There is not a single portrait in the book, nor will there be in any future book of mine. There are two portraits in the Clerical Scenes; but that was my first bit of art, and my hand was not well in -- I did not know so well how to manipulate my materials.
As for the incognito -- things must take their course. We can't help people saying now that the books are mine, but the one point to secure is that we and our friends make no categorical statement, which can be taken as absolute authority. As soon as the Liggins falsehood is annihilated of course there will be twenty new ones in its place; and one of the first will be that I was not the sole author. The only safe thing for my mind's health is to shut my ears and go on with my work.
So much, and no more. Think of me always as a sharer in your evil and your good.
Marian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: From Marian in 1851 -- from Dr. Chapman's -- her first year there. Hitherto unpublished.
Strand | November 21, 1851.
Dear Mr. Bray, Cara and Sara
Mr. Chapman thinks you will all be glad to know that he has had a very friendly letter from Mr. Lombe, dated before George Combe's despatch could have reached him. He writes to introduce a friend and makes no allusion to the Westminster business except that he hopes "Jemmy" 1058 will be up to the mark.
We have just had a long call from Mr. Conyngham, 1059 a disciple (not yet run mad) of Robert Owen's. He is a fine, handsome, tall fellow with an honest expression -- and a gentleman. His earnest simple talk was quite refreshing. He and Robert Owen called yesterday to propose that Mr. Chapman should let his front shop and first floor 1060 for the purpose of a society for the federation of England and America -- of course with an ultimate view to Socialism. I have been amused with the group we have just had in Mr. C's room -- Mr. Conyngham, Mr. Mackay, and Dr. Brabant. The last, seeing Mr. Conyngham was rather aristocratic, turned out his right leg 'e0 perfection, and good Mr. Mackay put his pocket handkerchief to his mouth and talked in an unusually minor key.
Mrs. C. Hennell was here the other night, but I didn't see much of her. Miss Bellamy 1061 is ill -- apparently sinking -- and there are four or five boarders in the house, so Mrs. Chapman is rather hurried, Miss Tilley 1062 being absent.
Dear Sara, I treasure all your notes, and do not forget that you write to me more than any one else, but I know you understand that I generally scribble my missives to Rosehill in a hurry.
Ever yours, all of you
Marian.

Strand | Friday Morning.
Dear Friends
I arrived here only yesterday. I had agreed with Chrissey that, all things considered, it was wiser for me to return to town -- that I could do her no substantial good by staying another week, while I should be losing time as to other matters. Isaac, however, was very indignant to find that I had arranged to leave without consulting him and thereupon flew into a violent passion with me, winding up by saying that he desired I would never "apply to him for anything whatever" -- which, seeing that I never have done so, was almost as superfluous as if I had said I would never receive a kindness from him. But he is better than he shewed himself to me and I have no doubt that he will be kind to Chrissey, though not in a very large way. The practice is sold for £1200, and we are hoping that with the interest of that and other money Chrissey will have about £100 a year independently of brothers and sisters. I trust I shall be able to add something to it. Chrisseyis is to live in a house of my brother's which was once her own 253 -- rent free, of course. That will be a great help, and the boys will go to a free grammar school. 254 But I am crossing my note by mistake -- so you will thank me to come to an end.
Your
Marian.

Dear <Friend> Creatures all
I was annoyed about the Combe affair 1038 before, and still more now I see his letter.
We have had three more £20 subscriptions since you left 1039 -- Newman, Robert Cox, 1040 and a Mr. Birch, 1041 without sending circulars.
Professor Forbes 1042 is to write us a capital scientific article whereat I rejoice greatly. The Peerage apparently will not [get itself done] as Carlyle says. I begin to fear that the Lombe patronage will be rather a bondage. The peerage is not an urgent question, nor does one see that, if the undue influence of the Peers on the elections for the Commons were done away with, there would be much mischief from the House of Lords remaining for some time longer in statu quo.
I have been reading Carlyle's life of Sterling with great pleasure -- not for its presentation of Sterling but of Carlyle. There are racy bits of description in his best manner and exquisite touches of feeling. Little rapid characterizations of living men too -- of Francis Newman for example, "a man of fine university and other attainments, of the sharpest cutting and most restlessly advancing intellect, and of the mildest pious enthusiasm." There is an inimitable description of Coleridge and his eternal monologue, "To sit as a passive bucket and be pumped into, whether one like it or not, can in the end be exhilarating to no creature." 1043
I can't write any more having to send an editorial missive to Greg. The business news is disquieting. Love to all from
Your
Pollian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, Geneva, 5 August [1849]
MS: Yale. Address: Charles Bray Esq | Rosehill | Coventry | Angleterre | Voie de France. Postmarks: GENEVE | 6 | AOUT | 49 | 11'bd M; COVENTRY | AU 9 | 1849 | D. Extracts published: Cross, I, 210-213.
Plongeon Sunday August 5.
Dear Friends
I hope my imagination paints truly when it shows me all of you seated with beaming faces round the tea-table at Rosehill. I shall be yearning to know that things as well as people are smiling on you -- but I am sure you will not let me wait for news of you longer than is necessary. Have you my letter written on Friday week to beg that you would send my passport by the first post after your arrival? I was as naughty as usual to forget it. My life here would be delightful if we could always keep the same set of people, but alas, I fear one generation will go and another come so fast that I shall not care to become acquainted with any of them. My good Mrs. Locke is not going -- that is one comfort. She is quite a mother to me -- helps me to buy my candles and do all my shopping -- takes care of me at dinner and quite rejoices when she sees me enjoy conversation or anything else. The St. Germains are delightful people -- the Marquise really seems to me the most charming person I ever saw, with kindness enough to make the ultra-politeness of her manners quite genuine. She is very good to me and says of me, "Je m'interesse vivement 'e0 Mademoiselle." The squinting Marquis is the most well-bred, harmless of men. He talks very little -- every sentence seems a terrible gestation, and comes forth fortissimo, but he generally bestows one on me, and seems especially to enjoy my poor tunes (mind you, all these trivialities are to satisfy your vanity -- not mine, because you are beginning to be ashamed of having loved me). The grey-headed gentleman who was here when I came was the Chevalier de Berray, the uncle of Mde. la Marquise. He got quite fond of talking philosophy with me before he went, but alas he and a very agreeable young man who was with him are gone to Aix-les-Bains.
The American ladies too are gone and in their place we have a lady from Frankfort with her daughter and governess. She arrived only yesterday so I have not yet said a word to her. The young German is the Baron de Herder -- the veritable grandson of the great Herder. I should think he is not more than two or three and twenty -- very good-natured, but a most determined enemy to all gallantry. I fancy he is a Communist, but he seems to have been joked about his opinions by Mde. de Valli'e8re and the rest until he has determined to keep a proud silence on such matters. He has begun to talk to me and I think we should become good friends -- but he too is gone on an expedition to M. Rosa. He is expecting his brother 807 to join him here on his return, but I fear they will not stay long. Mademoiselle Rosa is the only person who speaks English besides Mrs. Locke. She is about equally French and English -- rather a nice creature, but with a mere woman's head and mind. Mlle. de Phaisan 808 is a good old maid -- a native of Geneva -- she has spent three summers here -- but she goes into the town for the winter. Mlle. Elise, the gouvernante, is a German with a moral region that would rejoice Mr. Bray's eyes. Poor soul! she is in a land of strangers and often seems to feel her loneliness. Her situation is a very difficult one, and [die Angst] she says often brings on a pain at her heart.
Mde. de Valli'e8re is a woman of some reading, and considerable talent -- very fond of politics, a devourer of the journals -- with an opinion ready for you on any subject whatever. The poor woman has her share of anxieties -- her youngest child is not more than eighteen months old, her eldest son eighteen years -- and between these there are six more one of whom is an epileptic patient. It will be a serious loss to her to part with the St. Germain family -- there are three children and six servants, so that they occupy 6 or 7 rooms. I fear they will not stay longer than this month.
I should be quite indifferent to the world that comes or goes if once I had my boxes with all my books. A Mrs. Sydney, a Scotch lady who was here before I came, is gone to Bex, and has sent Mrs. Locke an account of the excellent living and accommodations to be had there for 3 francs a day. Mrs. Locke says she would go if there were an English clergyman there, but she does not feel good enough to do without a clergyman. So you see there is some use for these insipid sticks still. Last Sunday I went with Mde. de Valli'e8re to a small church near Plongeon 809 and I could easily have fancied myself in an independent chapel at home. The spirit of the sermon was not a whit more elevated than that of our friend Dr. Harris 810 -- the text "What shall I do to be saved" -- the answer of Jesus being blinked as usual. The people use books not larger than our little prayer-books containing the tunes of all the hymns they sing beautifully printed -- the clerk sets the tune and the singing is respectable though dronish. Today I have been to hear one of the most celebrated preachers, M. Me'fbnier. 811 His sermon was really eloquent -- all written down, but delivered with so much energy and feeling that you never thought of the book. It was very superior in its tone to what we usually hear in England. It is curious to notice how patriotism -- dévouement 'e0 la patrie -- is put in the sermons as the first of virtues, even before devotion to the church. We never hear of it in England after we leave school. After the sermon a form of prayer is read for the magistrates etc. -- nothing of this kind is introduced into the extempore prayer which is entirely spiritual. There is quite as great a majority of women in the churches here as in the Roman Catholic places and I am told this is invariable. The good Marquis goes with his family and servants all nicely drest to the Catholic church. They are a most orderly set of people -- there is nothing but their language and their geniality and politeness to distinguish them from one of the best of our English aristocratic families.
I am better, but not well. My limbs ache terribly sometimes, but I have everything to make me well. M. Prévost 812 has not been a second time. Mrs. Locke would insist on my writing to thank him for calling and to express my regret that I had not seen him, and I did so yesterday. I do not know whether you will approve of this. I have told you almost everything, but whatever I have omitted may be summed up in the one assurance that I am perfectly comfortable, that every one is kind to me and seems to like me. Your kind hearts will rejoice at this I know. Only remember that I am just as much interested in all that happens to you at Rosehill, as you are in what happens to me at Plongeon. Dear Sara, write to me. I am tired to death and can hardly fashion a sentence, so good-night dear souls. Pray that the motto of Geneva may become mine -- Post tenebras lux.
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE TO MR. AND MRS. CHARLES BRAY AND SARA SOPHIA HENNELL, GENEVA, 20 AUGUST [1849]
Dublin Core:Subject: MR. AND MRS. CHARLES BRAY AND SARA SOPHIA HENNELL^^M, F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE TO MR. AND MRS. CHARLES BRAY AND SARA SOPHIA HENNELL, GENEVA, 20 AUGUST [1849]
MS: Yale. Address: Charles Bray Esq | Rosehill | Coventry | Angleterre | Voie de France. Postmarks: GENEVE | 21 AOUT | 49 | 10'bd M; COVENTRY | AU 24 | 1849 | D. Extracts published: Cross, I, 213-216.
Plongeon August 20th. Monday.
Dear Friends
I have no head for writing today for I have been keeping my bed for the last three days -- but I must remember that writing to you is like ringing a bell hung in the planet Jupiter -- it is so weary a while before one's letters reach. I have been positively sickening for want of my boxes and anxiety to hear of my relations. Your kind letter of this morning has quieted the latter a little, but my boxes alas! have not appeared. Do not be alarmed about my health. I have only had a terrible headache prolonged in fact by the assiduities of the good people here -- for the first day I lay in bed I had the whole female world of Plongeon in my bedroom, and talked so incessantly that I was unable to sleep after it -- the consequence, as you may imagine, was that the next day I was very much worse -- but I am getting better, and indeed it was worth while to be ill to have so many kind attentions.
There is a fresh German family from Frankfort here just now -- Mde. Cornelius and her children. She is the daughter of the richest banker in Frankfort and, what is better, full of heart and mind with a face that tells you so before she opens her lips. She has more reading than the Marquise, being German and Protestant, and it is a real refreshment to talk to her for half an hour.
The dear Marquise is a truly devout Catholic -- it is beautiful to hear her speak of the comfort she has in the confessional -- for our t'eates-'e0-t'eate have lately turned on religious matters. She says, I am in a "mauvaise voie sans le rapport de la religion. Peut-'eatre vous vous marierez -- et le mariage, ch'e8re amie, sans la foi religieuse --" She says I have isolated myself by my studies -- that I am too cold and have too little confidence in the feelings of others towards me -- that I do not believe how deep an interest she has conceived in my lot. She says Signor Goldrini (the young Italian who was here for a week) told her when he had been talking to me one evening -- Vous aimerez cette demoiselle, j'en suis s'fbr -- and she has found his prediction true. Their residence is a short distance from Turin. They were obliged to escape from Piedmont because her brother-in-law the Duke de Visconti 813 was proscribed and the St. Germains were accused of harbouring him. An amnesty has been obtained and they are leaving for their own country on Wednesday. She hopes I shall go to Italy and see her, and when I tell her that I have no faith that she will remember me long enough for me to venture on paying her a visit if ever I should go to Italy again, she shakes her head at my incredulity. She was born at Genoa, where there are two palaces belonging to her family -- one close to the cathedral of Sta. Maria del Carignano from which we had the view of the city. Her father 814 was three years Sardinian Minister at Constantinople before she was married, and she speaks with enthusiasm of her life there -- C'est l'e0 le pays de la vraie poésie -- o'f9 l'on sent ce que c'est que de vivre par le coeur. The gouvernante of Mde. Cornelius's little girl is an excellent person, simple in her manners and very intelligent.
M. de Herder is returned from M. Rosa, with a face and mouth such as we had at Chamouni. He would be a nice person if he had another soul added to the one he has by nature -- the soul that comes by sorrow and love. I stole his book while he was gone -- the 1 volume of Louis Blanc's History of Ten Years. 815 It contains a very interesting account of the 3 days of July 1830. His brother is coming to join him, so I hope he will not go at present.
Two other young Germans 816 -- Prussians -- are here -- the eldest odious, with an eternal simper and a mouth of dubious cleanliness. He speaks French very little and has a miserable splutter between a grunt and a snuffle so that when he begins to speak to one one's brain begins to twist and one feels inclined to rush out of the room. His brother frowns instead of simpering and is therefore more endurable. I gave a description of them something like this to M. de Herder the first night he came back. I found to my dismay that he knew them -- however he disclaimed any friendship for them. After all they are very harmless young men and I fancy very rich -- [so the world will love its own.] 817 Then we have a family from Holland, gone now on an excursion to Chamouni, but coming back.
I hardly know yet whether I shall like this place well enough to stay here through the winter. I have been under the disadvantage of wanting all on which I chiefly depend -- my books, etc. When I have been here another month I shall be better able to judge. When you write, have the goodness to send me the names of McCracken's agents, 818 and also the number of Miss Massy's residence in the Rue St. Honoré. Mlle. Elise the housekeeper has been away on account of her health for the last fortnight and Mariane the housemaid has been sent away ill. Matters have gone on all the worse, for poor Mde. de Valli'e8re is not the best manager in the world. But perhaps there will be an alteration for the better by and bye.
Tell Fanny just the opposite of what you have told her -- tell her never to let her husband entertain any project of living on the continent. He would be miserable and by consequence she would too. There is just as much "world" here as in England -- just as many eyes are on you -- and one requires the utmost flexibility of mind and feeling to render intercourse tolerable. Poor Mrs. Locke, who is a thorough Englishwoman and can only speak French negro-fashion, begins to tire sadly of the bows and [Bonjours] and [Pardons.] Yet she has no intention of returning to England. She has had very bitter trials which seem to be driving her more and more aloof from society. She has not yet had courage to tell me herself what these trials are, but I have heard from Mlle. Rosa that her daughter married one of the French noblesse. 819 The match was in every way highly advantageous -- the husband excellent, fortune considerable. They lived happily for some time -- she had two little girls -- when an accursed cousin of the husband's came in the way and caused a separation within the last year. Mrs. Locke is one of the Heads -- the same family as that of Sir Francis Head. Her brother Major Head wrote an "Overland Journey from India" 820 which you may have seen. She has multitudes of relations in England, but I suppose shame at her daughter's disgrace makes all her old associations painful. No one likes her here -- simply because her manners are brusque and her French incomprehensible. She means to go to Bex for economy.
Why does Fanny say she trusts to Isaac's writing to me? Will not she write too? I shall be very ready to write to every one when every one has written to me, but I require warming up by letters first. Tell Miss Sibree my address and beg her to write to me all about herself, and to write on thin paper. Poor dear Cara -- to have had so much trouble about my muff and tippet -- after all I remember that they are in a chest of drawers lined with cedar which I have lent to Chrissey. I hope you managed to get in the black velvet dress. The people dress and think about dressing here more even than in England. You would not know me if you saw me. The Marquise took on her the office of femme de chambre and drest my hair one day. She has abolished all my curls and made two things stick out on each side of my head, like those on the head of the Sphinx. All the world says I look infinitely better so I comply, though to myself I seem uglier than ever -- if possible. Mr. Prévost has not been again -- but I do not care much about it. I have enough of monde here. In fact that becomes one of the disagreeables. If people like one they buzz round one like flies round a sugar basin, and neither one's heart nor one's vanity inclines one to make oneself odious for the sake of being left in quiet. I am fidgeted to death about my boxes, and that tiresome man not to acknowledge the receipt of them. I make no apology for writing all my peevishnesses and follies, because I want you to do the same -- to let me know everything about you, to the aching of your fingers -- and you tell me very little.
Dear Sara -- Thank you for your scrap of L.E.L. 821 I have been invoking the French muse for the Marquise's album -- since she would fain have something and it must not be in English which she cannot understand. It will make you smile -- so I write it.
As tu vu la lune se lever Dans un ciel d'azur sans voile? Mille gouttes de rosée réflechissent Sa lumi'e8re, comme autant d'étoiles. Un violet du printemps cueilles Et le caches bien dans ton sein, De la delicieuse odeur Tu et tes v'eatements seront pleins. Ainsi lorsqu'une belle 'e2me se montre Elle rev'eatit tant de ses charmes: -- Ainsi son souvenir gardons Quoique, hélas! il tire nos larmes.
I thought it would have done admirably to put in Moli'e8re's Misanthrope or Precieuses ridicules. But the thought, dear soul, is a very true one, above all when I apply it to you. Receive it as just what I am feeling and thinking about you. Love me ever in spite of everything, dear friends, and believe
Your loving
Pollian.
Dear Mr. Hennell! Give him my heartiest affectionate remembrances. Tell him I find no one here so spirituel as he -- there are no better jokes going than I can make myself. Mrs. Hennell and Mrs. C. Hennell too -- all are remembered -- if even I have only seen them in England.
A thousand loves to Mrs. Pears. Ask her to write to me. Tell her to write to me as she used to talk to me -- to fancy she is walking with me. My sympathy with Mr. P. under his heavy trials. Send some one to Geneva to call upon me, that I may have the pleasure of talking to one who is not a Plongeonite.
Many many thanks for the trouble you have taken about my luggage. I shall be particularly glad of the newspaper 822 for I never see anything here except daily French papers which one might spend one's day in reading. Have you heard anything of Froude 823 again or of any one else worth hearing about? I am afraid you have not received the German books since you say nothing about them.
I have been interrupted by the Marquise who has been talking to me for the last hour about going to Italy -- she is sure I should be happier in Italy than anywhere else -- that England is not good for me etc. etc. I am tired to death and can write no more. My boxes, my boxes! I dream of them night and day.

GE to Mr. Charles Bray and Caroline [Mrs. Charles] Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, Geneva, [22 December 1849]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Dec. 1849. Extracts published: Cross, I, 241-242.
Chez M. D'Albert Durade. | 107 Rue des Chanoines.
Dear Friends all
A thousand Christmas pleasures and blessings to you -- good resolutions and bright hopes for the New Year! Amen. People who can't be witty exert themselves to be pious or affectionate. Henceforth I tell you nothing whatever about myself, for if I speak of agreeables and say I am contented, Mr. Bray writes me word that you are all trying to forget me. If I were to tell you of disagreeables and privations and sadness, he would write that he should like me to go to hell for a few months that I might learn to be contented -- also Sara would write, [If you are unhappy now, you will be so 'e0 fortiori ten years hence.] Now since I have a decided objection to doses sent by post which upset one's digestion for a fortnight, I am determined to give you no pretext for sending me either blue pill or bitters. You shall not know whether I am well or ill, contented or discontented, warm or cold, fat or thin. But remember that I am so far from being of the same mind as Mr. Bray, that good news of you is necessary to my comfort. I walk more briskly and jump out of bed more promptly after a letter that tells me you are well -- comfortable -- that business is promising -- that men begin to speak well of you, etc. "I am comforted in your comfort" as saith St. Paul to his troublesome Corinthians. 874 When one is cabin'd, cribbed, confined 875 in oneself, it is good to be enlarged in one's friends. Good Mr. Marshall! 876 We wish to keep even unamiable people when death calls for them -- much more good souls like him. I am glad he had had one more pleasant visit to Cara for her to think of. Dear Sara's letter is very charming, not at all physicky -- rather an agreeable draught of vin sucré. I thank her for the extracts, and above all for the rejected leader 877 at which I have laughed aloud again and again, at the risk of being thought mad by Mde. D'Albert on the other side of the wall. The proposal to leave out the foreign news and advertisements is delicious
I do not know exactly the expense from Geneva to Paris, but I am told it is certainly about 90 frs. per malle poste. The newspapers come and do not cost more than 10 c. I have not inquired about the cause of the variations, but I think it was probably the omission of the printing office people to put on the stamps. Mde. de Ludwigsdorff had recommended Mr. Munroe to me -- in vain -- for I do not want grocery and if I wanted anything else that want would be extinguished by a greater -- the want of money.
I am attending a course of lectures on Experimental Physics by M. le professeur de la Rive, 879 the inventor amongst other things of the electro-plating. I do not tell you whether I enjoy them or not. The lectures occur every Wednesday and Saturday. 880 It is time for me to go. I am distressed to send you this shabby last fragment of paper and to write in such a hurry, but the days are really only two hours long, and I have so many things to do that I go to bed every night miserable because I have left out something I meant to do. Good bye dear souls -- Forget me, if you like, you cannot oblige me to forget you, and the active is worth twice of the passive all the world over.
Mary Ann. The earth is covered with snow and the government is levelling the fortifications. This last fact will do to put among your "Varieties." 881

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, [London], 21 June 1852
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 283.
June 21. 1852.
Dear Trio
Your joint assurance of welcome strengthens the centripetal force that would carry me to you, but on the other hand sundry considerations are in favour of the centrifugal force which I suppose will carry me to Broadstairs or Ramsgate. On the whole I prefer to keep my visit to you as a bonne bouche when I am just in the best physical and mental state for enjoying it. I hope to get away on Saturday or on Wednesday at the latest.
Who should walk in the other day but Mrs. Pears? I was delighted to have her for an hour -- though half the pleasure was destroyed by seeing her suffer from a bad headache.
I think the 3d number of the W.R. will be capital -- thoroughly readable and yet not frothy. Poor Mr. Chapman has been in agonies of anxiety about money matters, but there is a patch of blue visible between the clouds now. Nothing has happened worth telling you.
Pray is the opposition paper come out? 121 Mr. Beveridge told Mr. Chapman that it was -- indeed I think Mr. C. said he had seen a number of it, and moreover that it was partly printed in London!! Do you know that dodge? There is a printing office where the general news of provincial papers is done -- the other half of the space being filled up in the country with the local news.
I have nothing more to say -- so I had better say it.
Ever your true and loving
Marian.
