MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oc. 2. Extract published: Cross, I, 292.
Saturday.
Dear Trio
Pity me -- I have had the headache for four days incessantly. But now I am well and even the Strand seems an elysium by contrast.
I set off on Tuesday for Edinburgh -- by express. This is awfully expensive, but it seems the only way of reaching there alive with my frail body. I have had the kindest notes from the Combes and from Harriet Martineau.
I should think you have got the Review by this time. Let me know what you all think of it. I have no time for anything -- my headache has wasted so much. Of course I shall write when I have been at Edinburgh a day. A thousand loves to you all.
Your
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell^^M, F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mr. and Mrs. Charles Bray and Sara Sophia Hennell, [London, 2 June 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: June 2. Extracts published: Cross, I, 282; George Eliot and John Chapman, pp. 42-43.
Wednesday.
Dear Trio
No good news yet, but I have a Micawber-faith that something will turn up. Geo. Combe called yesterday while I was out, and by some chance he talked of Mr. Bray's affairs -- thinks the Editor of the Herald has too small a head to make the paper answer and that you should have a partner in the ribbon business. I suppose he came primed with all this to say to me and not finding me, let it off at Mr. Chapman. Don't of course let him (Geo. Combe) be aware that I have told you. Mrs. Combe 102 called the other day, looking perfectly beautiful -- a blooming complexion like a girl of fifteen and a smile as bright and cheery as a flower-garden.
We went to Miss Swanwick's for a stupid evening on Saturday -- 12 women and 2'bd men! The house is brimful of Americans with varying degrees of disagreeableness, but one is glad to think they pay well for their lodging. Good Mr. Mackay called on me yesterday, though I have not yet paid my wedding visit. He looked more miserable and ashamed of presuming to exist than I ever saw him. I asked him how they liked Weymouth (where they staid). "Not at all, not at all, but it was not the fault of the place"! I think I shall go this evening.
I am bothered to death with article-reading and scrap-work of all sorts -- it is clear my poor head will never produce anything under these circumstances, but I am patient while Mr. C. is in such a preliminary [predicament?] and only care to help him as much as I can.
I am ashamed to teaze you so -- but I must beg you to send me Geo. Sand's works (tomorrow or Friday if possible) and also I shall be grateful if you will lend me -- what I think you have -- an English edition of Corinne, and Miss Austin's "Sense and Sensibility." 103
Dear Sara, the Catalogue 104 is really coming out -- the wrapper is printed!
Disraeli is divinely handsome if one can trust his portrait 105 in the exhibition.
Harriet Martineau's article on Niebuhr will not go in the July number. 106 I am sorry for it -- it is admirable. After all she is a trump -- the only English woman that possesses thoroughly the art of writing. I am in such a hurry that you must not wonder at my hop skip and jump style -- By the bye, we met that odious Mrs. Richard Greaves at Miss Swanwick's. She is fearful -- her whole organization seems made for the sake of her teeth -- if indeed they are not false. Farewell, dear ones,
Your
Marian.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 2. Mostly published: Cross, 1, 270-271.
Monday.
Dear Friends all
Thanks for the budget of this morning, and congratulations on the success of the birthday festivities. We went to quite a gay party at Mr. Mackay's on Saturday -- Miss Rowan, 20 a learned lady in spectacles, Mr. Vansittart Neale, 21 and other small celebrities. Good Mr. Mackay has been taking trouble to get me to Hastings for my health -- calling on Miss Fellowes, daughter of the Religion of the Universe, 22 and inducing her to write me a note of invitation. But Mr. Chapman can't spare my head and hands this week.
Sara will be heartily welcome, and Mrs. C. said she would write and tell her so this morning. Unfortunately I had an invitation to the Parkes's 23 to meet Cobden on Saturday evening -- I was sorry to miss that. Miss Parkes is a dear, ardent, honest creature, and I hope we shall be good friends. 24
I have nothing else to tell you. I am steeped in dullness within and without. Heaven send some lions tonight to meet Fox, 25 who is coming. In haste,
Ever your
Marian.
I have opened my letter to send you an advertisement we found in the Times today. "To Gentlemen. A converted medical man, of gentlemanly habits, and fond of Scriptural conversation, wishes to meet with gentleman of Calvinistic views, thirsting after truth, in want of a Daily Companion. A little temporal aid will be expected in return. Address, Verus"! 26

Dear Trio
This week has yielded nothing to me but a crop of very large headaches. I hope it has been kinder to you -- that business is looking up and, like the paper, lengthening its cords and strengthening its stakes -- as they say at the Bible meetings. The pain is gone from my head at last, but I am feeling very much shattered and find it easier to cry than do anything else. With best love to you all, I am ever
Your faithful

Dear Friends
I shall set off from here on Tuesday morning and shall be due at the Coventry station, I believe, at 5.50. But I do not care about having any one to meet me there unless it be quite convenient to you.
We had a fine day yesterday and went to Borrowdale. I have not been well since I have been here -- still I manage to enjoy, certainly not myself, but my companions and the scenery.
Ever your faithful
Marian Evans.

GE to Mr. and Mrs. Bray, [Ambleside, 21 October 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oc. 22. 1852. Mostly published: Cross, I, 295.
Ambleside | Thursday Night.
Dear Friends
The coach brought me to Miss Martineau's gate at 'bd past 6 yesterday evening and she was there with a beaming face to welcome me. Mr. Atkinson joined us this morning, and is a very agreeable addition. There has been an intelligent gentleman visitor today who is interested in Miss Martineau's Building Society, 207 and we have all been trudging about looking at cottages and enjoying the sight of the mountains, spite of the rain and mist.
The weather is not promising -- that is the worst of it. Miss M. is charming in her own home -- quite handsome from her animation and intelligence. She came behind me, put her hands round me and kissed me in the prettiest way this evening, telling me she was so glad she had got me here. I hardly know yet whether I shall leave on the 25th (Monday), but I will write again and let you know. I send you her note that you may have an idea of "The Knoll."
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Mme Louis Belloc^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Mme Louis Belloc, Witley, 10 July [1877]
MS: The Countess of Iddesleigh. Envelope: Madame Belloc | 17 Wimpole Street | London | W. Postmarks: GODALMING | D | JY 11 | 77; LONDON.W | G7 | JY 12 | 77. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights | Witley | Godalming | July 10.
Dearest Bessie
Your letter this morning was a blessing, for the last account had thrown me into a state almost of despondency -- we thought the signs of nervous irritability so alarming. But now I can think of our dear Barbara with less of a pang, indeed with the comforting hope that since she has recovered thus far, she will at last be set entirely free from the fetters on her speech. You say nothing about the Doctor, 723 so I am wondering whether he is coming to England or not, and cannot tell myself what to wish on the subject.
I wonder too how you are feeling about French affairs. However, your two little ones and your two venerable ladies 724 connect themselves with interests and feelings happily more stable than forms of political life. I hope you will all prosper in the sunshine.
We delight in this region. It is more beautiful than I had imagined, having both wildness and culture in delightful alternation. I have been souffrante, but am content to bear my share of such trouble, or rather an amount which is much less than my share if there were equal division.
Mr. Lewes brought me in your letter which he had ventured to open seeing where it came from, and he said, "Famous news of Barbara!" with a radiant face. He had almost feared from the last account that some permanent injury had set in.
He sends his best regards and thanks with mine.
Yours ever lovingly
M. E. Lewes.

My dear Bessie

Dearest Bessie
Will you or can you come to lunch with us some day -- say Monday -- at 'bd past 1 o'clock? That is the only time of day on which I can make an appointment just now. But if that time is inconvenient to you, we shall always be at home between 5 and 6 except on a Saturday. It is so long a journey for you that I have a sort of compunction in writing easily to say [Come]. For Christmas we go to Sevenoaks to see some of the family, and I suppose you will then be at Slindon. 506
We have been here a fortnight but are not yet in thorough quietude and freedom from house arrangements. One reason is, that Mr. Cross was ill with a bilious attack one whole week. He is well again now, and I am quite flourishing again in my rickety fashion -- a mended piece of antique furniture.
I am deeply grieved to hear of Barbara's partial relapse. We should all feel life the sadder if she were to have another seizure which would narrow her powers still further.
I hope you will have found the children in a satisfactory state of progress, bodily and mentally.
Yours lovingly
M. A. Cross.

Text: Cross, New Edition, pp. 317-318.
Here, then, is the lock of hair which, now it is severed from its companions, may be mistaken for a lock from some youthful head, full of brightest hopes. 574 My hopes, you know, were never very bright, even in my youthful days, and it was always my fears that painted my future for me. That has, at least, saved me from some disappointment and has brought me some unexpected joys in life. For instance, I had never ventured to hope that you would bear me so tenderly in your mind through long years, and gladden my heart by such strong sympathy as your eyes and voice assured me of during our short stay with you.
Very few things have happened to me, apart from my domestic life, that have cheered me more than the feeling that you and M. D'Albert are woven into my outward practical existence, no longer as mere memories, however cherished, but as actual breathing friends, ready to share my thoughts and help me with your encouraging words. I will say nothing to you on the subject of Mr Lewes's letter to M. D'Albert, 575 because I am sure you know all the feeling that is implied in the wish he has expressed on behalf of us both. I am rather weighed down with anxiety now, dear Maman, and find life, even in the middle of my many blessings, still a difficult and sometimes a toilsome journey. I have always to struggle against a selfish longing for repose.
You will write to me, I know, and tell me now and then how it fares with you. 576 It is doubly pleasant to read details about a friend's life, when we know just how she looks, and where she sits through long, quiet days.
I fear I gave very feeble signs of the gratitude I felt towards you for your affectionate reception of me and mine, and all the delicate attentions you showed us. All speech was difficult to me just then, and especially on matters of feeling. Nevertheless, I have confidence that you interpreted me more kindly than any even of my unexpressed feelings deserved, and that you believe in me as your always true and grateful friend.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 8 July 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 8 July 1878
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
July 8. 78.
Dearest Barbara
I received this morning the carefully packed fan, which I feel renewed compunction for having teazed you about. I imagine poor Miss Marks having made explorations for it in your drawers or boxes and feel myself ignobly indebted as one who has been more considerate of her own small wants than of others' trouble. By post I return the beautiful Sandalwood Fan which was a too valuable object of barter for my old trumpery, the sole attraction of this latter being that it has the telescope structure now difficult to find and especially convenient to one of my dropping-all-things-from-hands-and-lap propensity, because it passes easily into my pocket.
Is it not a comfort for each of us separately and the country generally that the sunshine is come back? Mr. Lewes has been gouty and I bilious, so I dare say you have had the advantage of us lately and will soon make us look, as usual, pitiable by the side of you. With best love
Yours ever
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 7 November 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 7 November 1880MS: Parrish Collection, Princeton. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
November 7. 1880.
My dear Barbara
Three weeks ago I had a rather troublesome attack but I am getting well now, though still reduced and comparatively weak. We shall probably linger here till near the end of the month, for the autumnal landscape is very beautiful and I am not yet quite fit for the exertion of moving. Mr. Cross has nursed me as if he had been a wife nursing a husband, never leaving me except to get his walk. He has turned woodman lately and has been cutting away some of the too abundant fir trees which made an ugly mass and line against the sky. I think you will find the clearance an improvement.
Miss Marks' good prospect for her final examination is very good news to me. I wonder how her sister is going on? You will perhaps think of telling me when you happen to write again. 489
It is a comfort to think that you can be very snug through the winter in your nice house and with the maid who I hope is as suitable as ever. What a pity we are not within an easy, driving distance from you!
Mr. Hall is here today. He gave a lecture on Leclaire the house-painter in Paris who initiated an excellent plan of co-operative sharing for his workmen. 490 It has been printed, and when I have another copy
I will send it you. Leclaire is mentioned by John S. Mill in the notes to his Political Economy, but had not been otherwise taken much notice of. Still, you may know all about him.
Ever thine
Marian.
Mr. Cross is just gone out walking with Mr. Hall, else he would want to send a message.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 3 September 1879
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Brightling Road | Hawkhurst | Sussex. Postmarks: GODALMING | C | SP 4 | 79; HAWKHURST | B | SP 5 | 79; BURWASH | A | SP 6 | 79. Extracts published: Cross, III, 377-378.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
September 3. 79.
Dearest Barbara
Before I received your letter the other day I was intending to write to you to ask whether, now that I am stronger and the fine weather shows some signs of permanence, you feel any revival of the inclination to come and see me for a couple of days. I hardly like to propose your taking the journey now that you are not being brought near me by other visits, for the railway from you to me is, I think, rather tiresome. But if your inclination really lies towards coming you will be affectionately welcomed. Charles and Gertrude are to be here from next Saturday till Monday, but after that I am open to any arrangement you will fix upon.
About the sea-side I am hopeless. The latter part of October is likely to be too cold [4 words deleted] for me to move about without risk of chills, and I hope to be back in town before [1 word deleted] the end of the month. I am not very fond of the sea-side, and this year it is likely to be crowded with people who have been hindered by the bad weather from going earlier. I prefer the Surrey hills and the security from draughts in one's own home. The one attraction of a coast place to me is a great breadth of sand to pace on when it is in its fresh firmness after the fall of the tide. But the sea itself is melancholy to me -- only a little less so under warm sunlight with plenty of fishing smacks changing their shadows, and I hate lodgings. All this is to let you know why I do not yield to the attraction of being with you, when we could chat as much or as little as we liked. I feel very much your affectionateness in wishing to have me near you.
Write me word soon whether you feel able to come so far as this for my sake. Always, dear,
Your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 22 October 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 22 October 1879
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Robertsbridge | Sussex. Postmarks: GODALMING | C | OC 22 | 79; ROBERTSBRIDGE | OC | 79; HURSTGREEN SUSSEX | B | OC 23 | 79. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
October 22. 79.
Dearest Barbara
You see I am not yet in town, which will account to you for my delay in acknowledging your note -- posted apparently on the 18th but sent to me only this morning.
It is a grievous trial, this that has fallen on poor Miss Marks. 333 Right or not right, it is the hard fact, that those who are strong (or a little the stronger) have to bear the infirmities of those that are weak, and may not please themselves. I suppose it is as she declares -- that you see no means of hindering her departure from Girton at the end of this term and entering at once on the struggle for existence. I, of course, can know nothing about the conditions, with the Hartogs, etc.
You have enjoyed the beautiful, though cold, autumnal days, I feel sure, since you tell me that you are very well.
And you will be glad to hear that just the right man is found for the George Henry Lewes Studentship. He is named Roy, is an Edinburgh student, and not a pupil of Michael Foster's. But Dr. Foster says he thinks him by far the most promising of young physiologists, and what is most satisfactory is, that Dr. Roy was looking round to consider how he might maintain himself without dropping his physiological work.
I shall be in London on the 30th. In health I am very well.
Always thine lovingly
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 2 July 1879
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 371-372.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
July 2. 79.
Dearest Barbara
The sight of your handwriting on the pamphlet sent me by Madame Mario (whom please thank for me when you are sending to her) urges me to do the sooner what I should have already done but for a rather sharp illness which has kept me chiefly in bed for nearly a fortnight and from which I am not yet quite free.
I enclose a copy of Michael Foster's Draft of conditions for the Studentship, which I put into the lawyer's hands some ten or twelve days ago, and which is now come to me drawn up in legal form -- differing greatly from the original sketch as to wording, but agreeing with it in all essentials. 292 You said it would interest you to see the Draft and I have been bearing this in mind but have not been able to go to the desk where the copy lay.
I hope to hear that you have been going on well despite the cruel restless winds and sad intermittence of sunshine. Write me word when you return the copy. On the 12th I am going to have two daughters-in-law, five grandchildren, and servant, for a week -- if I can get well enough, as I have good hope now that I shall. The strawberries will be ripe then, and as I can't eat any myself it would be dolorous not to be able to have the children and see them enjoy the juicy blessing.
Always thine faithfully and lovingly
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 2 [August] 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 2 [August] 1877
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Poor House | Zennor | St. Ives | Cornwall. Postmark: GODALMING | D | AU 2 | 77. Mostly published: Cross, III, 312-313.
The Heights | Witley | Godalming | July 734 2. 77
Dearest Barbara
It was a draught of real comfort and pleasure to have a letter written by your own hand, and one so altogether cheerful. I trust that the warmer weather is salutary to you and that you will by and by be able to write me word of continued progress. Hardly any bit of the Kingdom, I fancy, would suit your taste better than your neighbourhood of the Land's End. You are not fond of bushy midland-fashioned scenery.
We are enjoying the mixture of wildness and culture extremely, and so far as landscape and air go, we would not choose a different home from this. But we have not yet made up our minds whether we shall keep our house or sell it.
Some London friends are also occasional dwellers in these parts. The day before yesterday we had Mr. and Mrs. Frederic Harrison, whose parents have a fine old Tudor house -- Sutton Place -- about 3 miles beyond Guildford. Mrs. Harrison asked with much interest about you, and was glad to hear of Madame Mario also, of whom Dr. Bridges had spoken very prettily to her. And do you remember Edmund Gurney? He and his graceful bride lunched with us the other day. She was very poor before her marriage and had worked in an exemplary way both to help her mother and educate herself -- her father having lost his property and left his family destitute.
And Miss Thackeray's married today to young Ritchie. 735 I saw him at Cambridge and felt that the nearly 20 years' difference between them was bridged hopefully by his solidarity and gravity. This is one of several instances that I have known of lately, showing that young men with even brilliant advantages will often choose as their life's companion a woman whose attractions are wholly of the spiritual order.
Do you care about this gossip? I am wondering how long Madame Mario will be able to remain with you. Please ask her to send me a line in case of her leaving you. But August is an inauspicious month for returning to Italy.
We are poor creatures -- headachy and feeble but not the less affectionate in our memories of our too far-off friend. I often see you enjoying your sunsets and the wayside flowers.
Always your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 19 August 1879
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
August 19. 79.
Dearest Barbara
How are you now? I should like to hear some more good news of you such as Miss Marks wrote me many weeks ago.
I am at last getting out of my trying illness and hope to go on without relapse. During the last fortnight I have been in tolerable ease and have been gathering strength.
The deed of the Studentship is now executed and Prof. Foster writes me that the Trustees will meet next week at Sheffield, when they will appoint the Director and proceed to advertise the fact of the Studentship being opened.
The continually recurring rain is terribly depressing to me. I hope you are more independent of that malignant influence -- though few can be independent of the thought that the rain means general calamity.
Since you liked some of the things in Theophrastus Such, you will perhaps also like to know that nearly 6000 of him have been sold, so that if he has told any needful truths the medicine has been taken by many.
I wish I had anything else to tell that would interest you, but I am a hermit.
Your ever loving
Marian.

MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Robertsbridge | Hawkhurst | Surrey. Postmark: GODALMING | C | 18 AU | 80. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
August 18. 1880.
My dear Barbara
I found your letter awaiting me yesterday evening on our return from Sevenoaks, where we have been spending a few days with Mr. Cross's sister, Mrs. Druce. This is the first of three family visits which we have engaged to pay, the other two being to Mr. and Mrs. Otter in Lincolnshire and to Mr. and Mrs. Hall (whom you know) in Cambridgeshire. We shall hardly get back from these till the second week in September, when we shall be obliged to attend to our house arrangements and other matters in town.
So this time we cannot do what we should both have enjoyed -- pay a little visit to you and Dr. Bodichon. We must wait for another time when you will like to have us. I am sorry that my absence hindered my sending you an immediate answer, as you wished me to do.
Please give my affectionate remembrances to Nanny and Miss Blythe. Also to our little dark-eyed friend who is "delightful to you." I dare say she would consider that a good final cause for her existence.
Mr. Cross sends his best regards. He would have been very much interested in paying a visit to Scalands Gate. Always, dear,
Yours lovingly
Marian.
Please thank Dr. Bodichon from me for wishing to see us. 468

The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
August 16. 78.
My dear Barbara
I hope I shall not be too troublesome in asking to have some news of your progress in health. It seems too long to me since my disposition to fear was checked by hearing that you were enjoying the summer and gathering strength. If Miss Marks is still with you I am sure that she will be kind enough to write me a little report about you. At present I imagine that the Doctor is with you and that your life may be too full of claims on your attention. But let this note be taken as a telegraphed question which some one else will answer with telegraphic brevity. An "all is well" would be a great satisfaction.
We are both ailing in body but otherwise well off in the world.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 15 October 1878
MS: Huntington Library. Extracts published: Cross, III, 340-341.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
October 15. 78.
Dearest Barbara
The days pass by without my finding time to tell you what I want to tell you -- how delighted I was to have a good account of you from Miss Marx, to whom I feel quite grateful for her nice letter. But every bright day -- and we have had many such -- has made me think the more of you and hope that you were drawing in strength from the clear, sweet air. I miss so much the hope I used always to have of seeing you in London and talking over everything just as we used to do -- in the way that will never exactly come with any one else. How unspeakably the lengthening of memories in common endears our old friends! The new are comparatively like foreigners, with whom one's talk is hemmed in by mutual ignorance. The one cannot express, the other cannot divine.
We have been a little better of late but the poor little man has still visitations of cramp and gout. Still he is as joyous as ever, 139 and we are intensely happy in our bit of country -- as happy as the cloudy aspect of public affairs will allow any one who cares for them to be, with the daily reading of the Times.
I hope that Miss Marx's companionship is replaced for you by some charming friend, and that you continue to like your sea-side abode. I unhappily mislaid the letter containing your address, but I imagine that this will find you without the number of your house in the Marina.
A neighbour 140 of ours was reciting to me yesterday some delicious bits of dialogue with a quaint Surrey woman -- e. g. "O ma'am, what I have gone through with my husband. He is so uneddicated -- he never had a tail-coat in his life!" Best love from us both.
Yours ever
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 14 September 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Witley, 14 September 1880
MS: Parrish Collection, Princeton. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Robertsbridge | Hawkhurst. Postmarks: GODALMING | C | 14 SP | 80; ROBERTSBRIDGE | A | SP 15 | 80; HAWKHURST | A | SP 15 | 80. Mostly published: Cross, III, 415-416.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
September 14. 80.
My dear Barbara
Your letter this morning is a welcome assurance about you. We have been away in Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire, paying visits to Mrs. Otter and the Halls. The weather, which is now broken, was glorious through all our wandering which we made very interesting by pausing to see Ely, Peterborough and Lincoln Cathedrals. The Otters have a very pretty happy household. He is a country gentleman now, called
[Squire] by his tenants, acting as a magistrate and glancing towards parliament. 476 But he keeps up his reading and is delightful to talk to. Emily looks very pretty in her matronly position, with three little children. The Halls too are very pleasant to behold in their home life. He has done wonders in building nice cottages and schools and sinking a well where it was wanted, and founding a cooperative store, and in general doing whatever opportunity allows towards slowly improving this confused world. We saw Mr. and Mrs. H. Sidgwick. Perhaps you know that they have had and have the admirable public spirit to let their house and arrange to live for a year in the new Nuneham House, in order to facilitate matters for the double institution.
We are very well. Mr. Cross gets stronger and brighter every day. We often mention you, because you are associated with so many of my memories. He goes to town only once or twice a week, and unhappily is gone today through the rain and cold wind. His unmarried brother and sisters are going to leave Weybridge and live in London. We shall go to our winter nest there at the end of October. Our only bugbear -- it is a very little one -- is the having to make preliminary arrangements towards settling ourselves in the new house (4, Cheyne Walk). It is a quaint house, and a Mr. Armitage of Manchester, of whom you may have heard has been superintending the decoration and furnishing, but not to the exclusion of old things which we must carry and stow, especially wallings of books. I am become so lazy that I shrink from all such practical work, and pine if I have only to think of furniture.
Charles and Gertrude are very prosperous and happy and are bringing up their three little girls very nicely. They have just come back from a five weeks' holiday in Switzerland.
Here is a gossiping letter! -- I wish I had more edifying things to tell you. Please give my kind remembrances to Dr. Bodichon, and my love to Miss Marks whose hand writing is a pleasant sign to me that she is with you.
Always your loving
Marian.

MS: Parrish Collection, Princeton. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Robertsbridge | Hawkhurst. Postmarks: GODALMING | C | 2 AU | 80; HAWKHURST | A | AU 3 | 80; ROBERTSBRIDGE | A | AU 3 | 80. Extracts published: Cross, III, 410-411.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
August 1. 80.
My dear Barbara
We arrived here in all safety last Monday, and if I had not had your welcome little note this morning I think I should soon have written to you without any such extra stimulus.
Mr. Cross had a sharp but brief attack at Venice -- due to the unsanitary influences of that wondrous city in the later weeks of June. We stayed a little too long there with a continuous Scirocco blowing and bad smells under the window of the H'f4tel de l'Europe, and these conditions found him a little below par from long protracted anxiety and excitement before our marriage. But ever since we left Venice (on the 23d of June) he has been getting strong again, and we have enjoyed a leisurely journey through Germany in constant warmth and sunshine, save for an occasional thunder storm. The climate in this beloved country of ours is a sad exchange, and makes one think of a second bad harvest time with all its consequences. Still it is a delight to be at home, and enjoy perfect stillness after the noisiness of foreign bells and foreign voices indoors and out.
It would be very pretty to pay you a visit next April if we are all alive, and I think Mr. Cross would like it very much. He sends you, hoping you will accept them, his best remembrances, which have been kept up by our often talking about you. Charles sent me word that the missing letter to you had been found, as you conjectured, in my drawer, and that he had forwarded it to you. He and Gertrude have just started on their five weeks' holiday in Switzerland.
I have been amazingly well through all the exertions of our travel, and in the latter half of the time have done a great deal of walking.
Please give my best love to Nanny (how long it is since I saw her!), and to Miss Marks. I shall long to hear that the latter has got well through her final examination. 458
Your ever loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 5 September 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 5 September 1860
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, II, 273-274.
Holly Lodge | September 5. 60.
Dear Barbara
My fingers have been itching to write to you for the last week and more, but I have waited and waited, hoping to be able to tell you that we had decided on our future house. This evening, however, I have been reading your description of Algiers and the desire to thank you for it moves me too strongly to be resisted. It is admirably written and makes me see the country. I am so glad to think of the deep draughts of life you get from being able to spend half your year in that fresh, grand scenery. It must make London and English green fields all the more enjoyable in their turn.
As for us, we are preparing to renounce the delights of roving and settle down quietly, as old folks should do, for the benefit of the young ones. We have let our present house, 626 and after endless searching and doubting, we have come at last to think it will be the best policy to buy a house, since we have found one near Regent's Park to suit our taste. It is a better house than I care to have, but as it is more shut out than anything we have seen, and as, by buying it, we shall be paying no more rent for it than for an inferior house of which we should only be tenants, I accept the luxury that I really am indifferent about. It is in Park Village West, close to Gloucester Gate. We have made an offer for it, 627 but the answer is not yet come, and moreover, the place must be surveyed by a builder before we can come to a final decision; so, after all, we may have to give up the plan and adopt another.
Is it not cheering to have the sunshine on the corn, and the prospect that the poor people will not have to endure the suffering that comes on them from a bad harvest? The fields that were so sadly beaten down a little while ago, on the way to town, are now standing in fine yellow shocks.
I wish you could know how much we felt your kindness to Charley. He is such a dear good fellow that nothing is thrown away upon him.
Write me a scrap of news about yourself, and tell me how you and the Doctor are enjoying the country. I shall get a breath of it in that way. I think I love the fields and shudder at the streets more and more every month.
George unites with me in all respect and affection to you and yours -- and in longing for some sign of your existence. Think of us as often as you can and cherish every spark of affection for
Yours ever
M. E. Lewes.
Thank you for sending me Mrs. Howitt's letter. Her suggestion of the triad of young men at Sydenham was not available.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 5 December 1859
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, II, 146-149.
Holly Lodge, December 5. 1859.
Dearest Barbara
"Better late than never" is true of all good things, and therefore of your letter; so I will not waste space in grumbling at its lateness. Dr. Bodichon's manuscript with your note 417 went yesterday to Mr. Smith (of Smith and Elder) enclosed with a letter from Mr. Lewes. It had been presented to Lucas, the editor of "Once a Week" and also to the editor of the "Constitutional Free Press," without success, which was a disappointment to both of us. You will recognize Mr. Lewes in the "Cornhill
Magazine"; he is writing for it a series of papers -- "Studies in Animal Life" -- which are to be subsequently republished as a book. 418 It is very pleasant work to him, in addition to his "Physiology," the writing for which is not quite finished yet. 419 Then, he has a new microscope, 420 of a first-rate class -- another source of fresh enjoyment. You would have been amused to see a scene in this room one night when he was expecting the new microscope. P.D.C. knocked at the door late, after the servant was gone to bed: George opened the door, and brought into the drawing-room a palpable tea-chest (he himself having ordered said chest of tea a few days before). Nevertheless, his perceptions were so completely drowned by intoxication about the microscope that he began to open the tea-chest with the firm persuasion that it contained that key to discovery and immortality. At last the obstinacy of the lid moderated his inflamed imagination, and he began to see the tea-chest. It is events like this that make up our drama -- a very quiet one: especially since I have resolutely closed my ears to all gossip, and have determined to let no one talk to me about my books.
A short time ago your kind sister 421 wrote to me announcing the blackberry jam, which came duly; and from her I learned that Chapman and Hall had written to ask your views about terms for the American Letters -- from which I gather that they will print them. I hope that little spec. will turn out well, and I would endure a few small torments if they would help to make the perverse race of Editors accept Dr. Bodichon's interesting papers. I do so thoroughly enter into your wishes on that subject. As to your pictures, there is surely solid ground for hope about them. This last season was one of progress as to status, though not in a monetary sense. I like to think of your glorious walkings together; and the sight of your sketches has enabled me to imagine them better.
The Englishwoman's Journal must be doing good substantially -- stimulating woman to useful work, and rousing people generally to some consideration of women's needs. A few mistakes, and rather a feeble presentation of useful matter, will not neutralize the good that lies in a great aim and an honest effort; and I heartily wish all connected with the Journal '91God speed'92 -- except the ignorant and unconscientious writer who sometimes figures as a reviewer of books. I wish Bessie felt more keenly about the immorality of such slack writing as is sometimes admitted into that department of the Journal.
I took no notice of the extract you sent me from a letter of Mrs. Gaskell's, being determined not to engage in any writing on the topic of my authorship, except such as was absolutely demanded of us, as in the case of the muddle-headed magistrate, Mr. Bracebridge. But since then I have had a very beautiful letter from Mrs. Gaskell and I will quote some of her words, because they do her honour, and will incline you to think more highly of her. She begins in this way: "Since I heard, on authority, that you were the author of "Scenes of Clerical Life" and "Adam Bede," I have read them again, and I must, once more, tell you how earnestly, fully, and humbly I admire them. I never read anything so complete and beautiful in fiction in my life before." Very sweet and noble of her, was it not? She went on to speak of her having held to the notion of "Liggins," but, she adds, "I was never such a goose as to believe that books like yours were a mosaic of real and ideal." 422
The "Seth Bede" 423 and "Adam Bede, Junior" are speculations of dishonest publishers, who are always ready to fasten themselves, like leeches, on a popular fame. 424 Such things must be endured: they are the shadow to the bright fact of selling 16,000 in one year. As to the silly falsehoods and empty opinions afloat in some petty circles, I have quite conquered my temporary irritation about them -- indeed I feel all the more serene now for that very irritation: it has impressed on me more deeply how entirely the rewards of the artist lie apart from everything that is narrow and personal. There is no peace until that lesson is thoroughly learned. I shall go on writing from my inward promptings
I am delighted to hear that Dr. Bodichon and you admire the "Physiology": 425 it really promises to be a useful book, and, I think, especially useful as an educator, even apart from the specific knowledge it conveys, because it looks at the questions discussed in a philosophic spirit -- a very rare quality in books on natural science. We have been reading Darwin's Book on the "Origin of Species" just now: it makes an epoch, as the expression of his thorough adhesion, after long years of study, to the Doctrine of Development -- and not the adhesion of an anonym like the author of the "Vestiges," but of a long-celebrated naturalist. The book is ill-written and sadly wanting in illustrative facts -- of which he has collected a vast number, but reserves them for a future book of which this smaller one is the avant-courier. This will prevent the work from becoming popular, as the "Vestiges" did, but it will have a great effect in the scientific world, causing a thorough and open discussion of a question about which people have hitherto felt timid. So the world gets on step by step towards brave clearness and honesty! But to me the Development theory and all other explanations of processes by which things came to be, produce a feeble impression compared with the mystery that lies under the processes.
It is nice to think of your reading our great, great favourite Moli'e8re, while, for the present, we are not taking him down from the shelves -- only talking about him, as we do very often. I get a good deal of pleasure out of the sense that some one I love is reading and enjoying my best-loved writers: Mrs. Congreve and her sister are reading Scott, now, and it quite gives me a flavour of reading him myself. I think the Misanthrope the finest, most complete production of its kind in the world. I know you enjoy the "Sonnet" scene and the one between Arsino'eb and C'e9lim'e8ne. 426 You make me tremble by what you say you observe of the French feeling towards us. 427 We live so out of the political world that the threatenings of war, which have in some degree subsided from the English newspapers, only reach us now and then. It is depressing to witness this reaction towards barbarism. One would like one's life to be borne on the onward wave and not the receding one -- the flow and not the ebb: yet somebody must live in the bad times, and there is no reason, I suppose, out of our own esteem for ourselves, why the best things in the lot of mankind should fall to us in particular.
"Where shall we be in May?" I don't know at all. Perhaps just where we are: for at present we expect Charlie, our eldest boy, to come to us at Easter, and we think of staying here, till it is quite settled what his destination is to be. My novel 428 will not come out till Easter, and until it is out of my hands, I shall think of no migration, unless it be to the coast for a week or two.
You are a vilely uncertain correspondent, and that's the truth. I don't mind about having long letters, but I don't like to be left in utter ignorance of you for months together. But follow your own promptings, and be disagreeable by silence rather than make me disagreeable to you, by forcing yourself to write when you have no inclination.
Mr. Lewes unites with me in heartiest respect and regard towards Dr. Bodichon, and in the desire to be always kindly remembered by him among the palms and olives. He sends his affectionate "duty" to you, leaving it to be defined by any commands you may have for him.
Ever yours affectionately,
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 27 April 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 27 April 1859
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | South Fields | Wandsworth | April 27. 59.
Dear Barbara
When you come to us on the third Sunday in June, come to the Putney Station, not to the Wandsworth Station. The walk is prettier and not longer, from Putney, and if we knew your hour of arrival we would meet you.
I sent on your letter about the unhappy Mary Jones to Dr. Blackwell, 123 not being able to act in consequence of it myself. I say no more by letter because, we shall have better opportunities of understanding each other.
But one little bit of news I must tell you because I know it will please you. Mr. Lewes lunched the other day with Toynbee the great aurist, 124 and in answer to the question whether he knew Dr. E. Blackwell, Toynbee said that she had been to his place to look over his apparatus and that there was more judgment and knowledge in her remarks than in any professional visitor's he remembered. That will please both your friendship and your theory, won't it?
No more at present, from your busy and affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 23 July 1859
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Brief extract published: Barbara Stephen, Emily Davies and Girton College, 1927, p. 38.
Holly Lodge | July 23. 59.
Dear Barbara
We reached home last night, and one of my first thoughts is naturally about you. Did you get your three volumes of American Letters? Mr. Lewes thought we had better send them even without your commands, and we sent them by the carrier accordingly.
I am wonderfully inspirited and strengthened by our rapid run -- Mr. Lewes less so, but still conscious of benefit. Some quiet days of talk with the Congreves, in sight of the Lucerne lake and mountains, was a soothing change to me, and I sit down to my desk with fresh courage and fresh enjoyment. You are getting the same sort of repose in the green country, I hope. Let me hear of it, and enrich my life with your pleasures.
The 4th edition of '91Adam Bede'92 (5000) sold in a fortnight! These are the results that give one fortitude to endure one's enemies -- even to endure one's friends. I will not call you a friend -- I will rather call you by some name that I am not obliged to associate with evaporated professions and petty egoism. I will call you only Barbara, the name I must always associate with a true, large heart. Some mean, treacherous Barbara may come across me, but she will only be like a shadow of a vulgar woman flitting across my fresco of St. Barbara.
Ever yours,
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 17-18 September [1859]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Mrs. Bodichon | 21 Alpha Road | St. John's Wood. Postmark: LONDON-S.W | 12 | SP 19 | 59. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Saturday Night, September 17.
Dear Barbara
If you ever write to me again through an earthly post, address to this place. We are settled at home again and are flourishing like the green bay tree. 299
I have just been reading, with deep interest and heart-stirring, the article on the Infant Seamstresses in the Englishwoman's Journal. 300 If, as I imagine, Bessie is the writer, just say to her when you happen to be writing to her or seeing her, that I am one among the grateful readers of that moving description -- moving because the writer's own soul was moved by love and pity in the writing of it. These are the papers that will make the Journal a true organ, with a function.
Of course you will go off to Africa without writing me a word, and I shall hear no more of you till you are amongst the palms and olives with six long months between us!
Well, God bless you, wherever you are, and fill your life full of joyful work. I am writing at the end of the day, on the brink of sleep, too tired to think of anything but that picture of the little sleeping slopworker who had pricked her tiny finger so. 301
Yours always
G. E.
Sunday. I see, from an allusion in another article, that the writer of "Infant Seamstresses" is not Bessie. 302 Is it Isa Craig? I love the writer, whoever she may be.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 11 August [1859]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge. August 11.
Dearest Barbara
I think we shall use the tickets ourselves, 248 since it is so easy to turn in at Pall Mall, when we are next in town.
An artist-friend of ours -- Mr. F. W. Burton 249 -- a nice creature, expressed high admiration of your pictures -- didn't care about the want of finish in some of them -- they had finer qualities than that of finish -- he felt they were done on the spot under true inspiration.
Thanks for the pictures of Nannie in the letters; they amused and interested us immensely. The '91bare legs'92 especially is a detail that delights me: the wind suddenly betraying them to the horror of an on-looking friend is a delicious touch.
I do wish much to see more of human life 250 -- how can one see enough in the short years one has to stay in this world? But I meant, that at present my mind works with the most freedom and the keenest sense of poetry in my remotest past, and there are many strata to be worked through before I can begin to use artistically any material I may gather in the present.
Curiously enough, 'e0 propos of your remark about '91Adam Bede'92 251 there is much less "out of my own life" in that book -- i.e. the materials are much more a combination from imperfectly known and widely sundered elements than the "Clerical Scenes."
I'm so glad you have enjoyed these -- so thankful for the words you write me.
It was my fault that the volume of the Phys[iology] 252 was brought back again. Come and fetch it. I am very tired and hotheaded at this close of the morning, so I find myself writing you nothing at all, when I meant to say a great deal.
Farewell. Write again before long, because it is cheering to hear of you --
Ever yours
Marian.

249 Frederick William Burton (1816-1900)  was born in Ireland, where in early life he made his reputation as a portrait painter. In 1851 he settled at Munich to study the old masters. He was out when GHL called on him there 25 April 1858, but he returned the visit next day and promised to put their names down for the Verein. Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, 1 July 1860
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, II, 255-256.
Holly Lodge | July 1. 60.
Dear Barbara
We reached home by starlight at one o'clock this morning, and I write in haste fear and trembling lest you should already be gone to Surrey. 567 You know what I should like -- that you and your husband should come to us the first day possible, naming any hour and conditions.
We would arrange meals and everything else as would best suit you. Of course I would willingly go to London to see you, if you could not come to me. But I fear lest neither plan should be practicable, and lest this letter should have to be sent after you.
It is from your note only that I have learned your loss. 568 It has made me think of you with the sense that there is more than ever a common fund of experience between us. But I will write nothing more now -- I am almost ill with fatigue, and have only courage to write at all, because of my anxiety not to miss you.
Affectionate regards from both of us to both of you.
Ever yours
M. E. Lewes.
Madame Bodichon.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [3 October 1859]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Monday.
Dearest Barbara
The words in your note this morning "off directly for Algiers" frighten me lest this farewell word should not reach you.
The hamper came on Saturday, with all the beautiful things -- the butter, such as Mrs. Poyser would not have scorned, the ferns, the cresses, the fruit, the mushrooms! I took it as a hamper full of love, expressed in all those sweet country things.
Tell the giver of the ferns -- which are special favourites with me -- that it happens, quite curiously, her Perizade has a mysterious resemblance for me, to the heroine of the book I am writing. It is not a formal outward resemblance, but an inward affinity felt through the attitude of Perizade and the expression of her face. "I don't know whether I make myself understood," as Mr. Curdle says, after his definition of the unities. 334
Heaven and earth bless you and take you safe to your husband to whom much loving respect from
Your ever affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [21? August 1860]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, Tuesday.
Dear Barbara
About the inscription. 615 The object is, to be as little wordy as possible, and we both think that there are some unnecessary words in the draught you sent us.
No. 1. Your meaning would be as well expressed if you were to say simply "of every measure which he held likely to promote political liberty and social well-being" leaving out "of his fellow-countrymen." 3. Mr. Lewes votes for leaving out "a constant friend to education." The specific deed that follows implies the general statement.
Strike out "hearty."
I would say simply, "He was untiring in his hospitality to exiled patriots."
I would say "kind and helpful."
I shall be very glad to see Miss Bayley with you on Sunday. But half past 5 is precisely our dinner hour: Can you come either before or after? At 4 o'clock -- or any time after one -- except this unfortunate dinner hour. Only send me word, that we may be in the house. Mr. Lewes is going to Professor Owen's on Sunday, but he will be back again by 4. I should like him to be at home, that he might see Miss Bayley.
Always yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [2 July 1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [2 July 1859]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
H. L. | Saturday Morning.
Dear Barbara
The pretty picture is come quite safely, and we will send back the useful packings. Thanks for the journal, which I shall look into eagerly -- and for the photograph of the '91Happy Valley.'92 I'm so glad you have such a paradise of your own to retreat to away from this hard noisy world. Thank God there is abundance of pure human feeling that makes no noise, else we might sink into the belief that it is but a devil's world.
Your letter, with its heart-warming words, came just after we had read the Athenaeum! 199 If one could be glad at any baseness, one would be glad that this is so bad -- it will carry no sympathy with it.
I would have written to your sister and enclosed the letter to you now, but that I [am] very poorly and trembling, and am only fit to sit in a heap with a warm water bottle at my feet. So no more now. Come again soon!
Yours ever
Marian.

Dublin Core:Relation: 199 The Athenaeum, 2 July 1859, p.  20, published a savage attack on GE in the "Weekly Gossip" column: "It is time to end this pother about the authorship of `Adam Bede.' The writer is in no sense a `great unknown'; the tale, if bright in parts, and such as a clever woman with an observant eye and unschooled moral nature might have written, has no great quality of any kind. Long ago we hinted our impression that Mr. Liggins, with his poverty and his pretensions, was a mystification, got up by George Eliot, -- as the showman in a country fair sets up a second learned pig to create a division among the penny paying rustics . . . Mr. Nicholas, it is true, answers for Mr. Liggins; but who answers for Mr. Nicholas? Liggins, Eliot, and Nicholas are like Sairy Gamp, Betsy Prig, and Mrs. Harris. Roll all three into one and you turn up a rather strong-minded lady, blessed with abundance of showy sentiment and a profusion of pious words, but kept for sale rather than for use. Vanish Eliot, Nicholas, Liggins, -- enter, (let us say, at a guess,) Miss Biggins! . . . The elaborate attempt to mystify the reading public, pursued in many articles and letters at the same time, but with the same Roman hand observable in all, is itself decisive of the writer's power. No woman of genius ever condescended to such a ruse, -- no book was ever permanently helped by such a trick."

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [18 August 1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [18 August 1860]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, II, 268.
Holly Lodge | Saturday Evening.
Dear Barbara
I am thoroughly vexed that we didn't go to Lawrence's today. We made an effort. but it was raining too hard at the only time that would serve us to reach the train.
That comes of our inconvenient situation, so far off the railway; and alas, no one comes to take our house off our hands! We may be forced to stay here after all. A Mr. Barry, son of Sir Charles, 613 seemed inclined to take it, but appears to have been deterred by the distance.
Yet, I can't help being glad that you and the Doctor went in vain to Lawrence's today -- it is so sweet to know that there are loving souls in the world, who really rejoice in our joy. Tell the Doctor, his act of human fellowship was not thrown away, since we know of it and are gladdened by it.
I don't wonder at your yearning to get away from town. Our movements are all in obscurity. George must run down to Edinburgh for a few days by and by, to see about a family with whom we can place Thorney, the second boy, who is going to study at the High School there, under Dr. Schmitz. That is the only thing we are certain about at present.
One of the things I shall count upon if we are able to get nearer London is, to see more of your schools 614 and other good works. That would help me to do without the fields for many months in the year.
I am glad to hear that poor Bessie is going to have a holiday. Give my love to her. And will you tell your sister Nannie, when you see her, that I was relieved to have her note telling me of the arrival in due time at Hampstead, after our feminine failure to catch the train. She is very charming, to my mind -- so clear and direct, and so modest in her strength. I hope I shall know her better.
God bless you, dear Barbara, we both say -- and both add, affectionate remembrances to the Doctor.
Ever yours
Marian.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [17 August 1860]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Brief extract published: Cross, II, 268.
Holly Lodge | Friday.
Dear Barbara
I know you will rejoice with us that Charley has won his place at the Post Office, having been at the head of the list in the examination. Magnificat anima mea! The dear lad is fairly launched in life now.
I trusted to your being frightened at the rain on Wednesday, 612 as I was. I am going to Lawrence's tomorrow at 'bd past 2, and can't help wishing you would meet me, for I long to see or hear something of you.
We go to Miss Bayley's to lunch today. In haste
Ever yours
M. E. L.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [12 August 1860]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Sunday.
Dear Barbara
I shall go to sit to Lawrence for the third time on Wednesday, about 'bd past 2. Should you like to come and meet me -- and judge of the painter? 609 He has one or two portraits in his atelier, which might serve as a ground of judgment: mine, of course, is not in a stage to be looked at just yet.
Have you not missed an umbrella which you left with me, taking my small sun shade instead? I will take your umbrella to Lawrence's for the chance of returning it to you. His atelier is at 6 Wells Street, Oxford St.
Kindest double remembrances to Dr. Bodichon.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Wandsworth, [1 October 1859]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Private.
Holly Lodge | Saturday.
Dearest Barbara,
The mushrooms -- there is poetry as well as scent in the bare word, -- are not yet come, but I don't wait for them before I thank you for this morning's note, containing the information about the P.O. It is everything we wanted to know.
Not a glorious morning for the wedding! 328 But the raindrops are a good omen, you know. We have not been without our wishes for all good to your sister, both for her sake and yours. Indeed your last letter but one, called up very deep feeling about you. 'abNo one you [six words indecipherable] anything else in the world.'bb I am scribbling in the greatest hurry, just before going into the fresh air. I can only say, '91Don't be vexed at anything in the note Mr. Lewes sent you yesterday.'92 It was best you should see just what the man said.
Ever thine
Marian.
This morning I have had quite an enthusiastic letter from Herbert
Spencer about '91Adam Bede.'92 329 Forgive him his trespasses! He says he has not changed towards us, and what a man is not conscious of he must not answer for.
Nulla dies sine linea.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Torquay, [28? March 1868]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Torquay, [28? March 1868]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 37-38, dated 6 April 1868.
Carclew | Hesketh Road | Torquay.
My dear Barbara
I did not write because you said you were going to Bromley, and seemed to imply that writing was needless.
It was a naughty piece of work to get a cold -- the thing of all others that you should guard against. We are very well, and are enjoying these perfect skies, sunshine all day, Venus and the crescent moon 733 in the evening. Torquay is getting too much like a London suburb, spreading out strands of half-built houses in all directions. But there are still a few quiet walks -- only a few -- and the soil has an almost Spanish richness of colour.
I think Ruskin has not been encouraged about women by his many and persistent efforts to teach them. He seems to have found them wanting in real scientific interest -- bent on sentimentalizing in everything.
What I should like to be sure of as a result of higher education for women -- a result that will come to pass over my grave -- is, their recognition of the great amount of social unproductive labour which needs to be done by women, and which is now either not done at all or done wretchedly.
No good can come to women, more than to any class of male mortals, while each aims at doing the highest kind of work, which ought rather to be held in sanctity as what only the few can do well. I believe -- and I want it to be well shown -- that a more thorough education will tend to do away with the odious vulgarity of our notions about functions and employment, and to propagate the true gospel that the deepest disgrace is to insist on doing work for which we are unfit -- to do work of any sort badly. There are many points of this kind that want being urged, but they do not come well from me, and I never like to be quoted in any way on this subject. But I will talk to you some day, and ask you to prevail on Miss Davies to write a little book which is much wanted.
We are uncertain whether we shall stay here more than a week
Ever thine
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Shottermill, 20 [August 1871]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Shottermill, 20 [August 1871]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands | Robertsbridge | Hawkhurst. Postmarks: PETERSFIELD | A | AU 20 | 71; HAWKHURST | B | AU 21 | 71; ROBERTSBRIDGE | A | AU 22 | 71. Hitherto unpublished.
Cherrimans | Shottermill | Petersfield | Sunday, 20.
Dearest Barbara
The irregularities of the Post here are exasperating, and George has been in a constant state of r'e9clamations. Your former letter dated Tuesday, I answered immediately on receiving it, telling you that we should be delighted to see you, that we could give you a bed (unless you preferred the inn), and that you must let us know if possible when you would arrive at Haslemere Station, that you might be duly met and that we might arrange our dinner-hour to suit you.
And lo! now on-this unhappy Sunday morning we get a second note from you, showing that on Friday you had not received my letter punctually written on the Wednesday.
Whether this will get to Scalands in time before you start for Tunbridge I am necessarily uncertain, and write with little more than a forlorn hope.
George says, if you will telegraph from Tunbridge to say when you will be at Haslemere Station, he will meet you and escort you hither. There is a palatial bedroom here, but if you reject that, there is a Railway Hotel, just opposite the station. We are 'bc of an hour or 20 m. beyond the station.
It is a vexatious business that you did not get my letter. 351
Always your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Shottermill, 18 July 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Shottermill, 18 July 1871
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Brookbank | Shottermill | near Petersfield | July 18. 71.
My dear Barbara
You will have thought that I must be dead. The fact is, that before your letter came, I was waiting for certainty about our habitation, intending to write to you immediately on getting that certainty. But we are still in treaty about the house opposite this, having unluckily told Mrs. Gilchrist that we should give up her cottage at the end of July, and she having forthwith got her old tenant, Mr. George Smith, the water-colour painter, to come into it on our departure. I have been waiting for precise knowledge before answering the question on your card, (and perhaps it may still come before I am obliged to close this,) but I cannot bear to go on any longer in total silence towards you. If we get the said house we shall remain in it till the end of August, and then go home at least for a few days, and possibly for good, though George dreams of a journey to Harrogate for a fortnight's cure.
It will be very sweet to see you and have a great talk about everything. I scribble these few words provisionally, hoping by and by to add the needful information.
Ever your loving
Marian. 
6 o'clock. The decision is not yet come. I will write you word tomorrow, or whenever I know. 326

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Shottermill, 17 June 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Shottermill, 17 June 1871
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 132-133.
Shotter Mill | near Petersfield | June 17. 71.
My dear Barbara
Our country P.O. has a disease and does not "fonctionner" quite properly, so that the longed-for pleasure of having a letter from you was delayed till this morning instead of coming yesterday. Consequently I had one more day than I need have had of slight internal swearing at you for not letting me hear anything of you.
I have been ill, but am now gaining strength and your news comes instead of my quinine which is exhausted. Delighted to know that the Doctor is safely through his journey and reposing in your green home! Nanny too is surely to be congratulated that she is in Blandford Square and not in Algiers. But the newspapers are so absolutely silent about the state of things there, that my conceptions on the subject are visionary and bred by fear rather than knowledge.
How about dear Madame Mohl and her husband? I have been wondering through all the horrors whether M. Mohl had returned to Paris, and whether their house, containing too probably the results of much studious work, lies buried among ruins. 294 But I will not further recall the sorrows in that direction.
I am glad to see the words "very satisfactory" in connection with the visit to Hitchin and Cambridge. Ely Cathedral I saw last year, but too cursorily. It has more of the massive grandeur that one adores in Le Mans and Chartres than most of our English Cathedrals -- though I am ready to recall the comparison as preposterous.
I don't know how long we shall stay here -- perhaps, more or less, till the end of August. For I have given up the idea of going to the Scott Festival at Edinburgh to which I had accepted the invitation. 295 The fatigue of the long journey with the crowd at the end would be too much for me.
Let us know beforehand when you are about coming. George is gloriously well, studying, writing, walking, eating, and sleeping with equal vigour. He is enjoying the life here immensely. Our country could hardly be surpassed in its particular kind of beauty -- perpetual undulation of heath and copse and clear veins of hurrying water, with here and there a grand pine wood, steep wood-clothed promontories, and gleaming pools.
If you want delightful reading get the 1/6 edition of Lowell's "My Study Windows," and read the essays called "My garden acquaintance" and "Winter." 296
I suppose Miss Edwards has returned, or will soon return to you. I hope she will be round-cheeked and strong. My love to her. Also, my best regards to the Doctor. I wonder how poor Bessie is going on. Ever, dear Barbara
Your faithfully affectionate
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Shottermill, 17 August [1871]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Shottermill, 17 August [1871]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Cherrimans, Shottermill, Petersfield. | August 17th.
Dearest Barbara
We shall be delighted to see you next Tuesday. There is an excellent bedroom here at your service. But if you really prefer the inn -- though that would be a pity -- you shall do as you like. We dine now at two o'clock, because, although this high place is much cooler than the rest of the world, it is still too hot for us to find walking agreeable in the middle of the day. Can you write and let us know at what time you will be able to arrive? -- since we could alter our dinner time to any hour, if we only knew what would suit you.
There is no luxurious living in this region -- tightness of butchers shops and unimaginative English cooking. But we have light bread, good butter and milk, and always a dinner not of herbs alone, but of some joint after the taste of the British-human carnivors.
I thought you never would write to say you were coming.
George went to town yesterday and heard of you from poor Owen Jones, whom you have helped a little in his sad suffering.
Always thine
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Rickmansworth, 13 August 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Rickmansworth, 13 August 1875
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Elms | Rickmansworth | August 13. 75.
My dear Barbara
As to weather you are better off than we are. The last ten days and nights have brought us frequent rain which we try to be thankful for because it is not continuous as it was in the calamitous time of July. Our nice old house is unfortunately in a valley much given to mists, and my health has I think been the worse for it. I am much satisfied with your news about yourself, which had been too long waited for.
We have had a trouble, prepared for by a long-standing anxiety. On the 29th of June our poor Bertie died at Durban, where he was staying for the sake of sea-air and medical attendance. The sad news only reached us last Sunday, when we were hoping that we might soon get a letter to tell us of his being able to rejoin his wife. He leaves two little children, the youngest an infant boy, born in May. It is a comfort that we are able to provide for the wife and children, but the consequent claims (in these next months when there will be debts and expenses of uncertain amounts) prevent me from doing what I should like to do, namely, to supply the needed £100 for the new rooms at Girton. 300
It will be worth while to send the information to Mrs. Alfred Morrison 301 -- it can do no harm. But she made no response at all when I sent former circulars to her; she is now ill, and her husband a most unsympathetic mortal. I am determined not to appeal to him again in any way. I lately gave an introduction to Gertrude that she might try to interest him in keeping open the Hampstead fields, and she found the interview a great crux.
I am glad to think that Miss Edwards has got into the right groove. -- But poor Mr. Sylvester! 302 It is saddening to think of him beginning anew at 64 -- driven from what he is first-rate in, and setting himself the difficult task of being second-rate in something else. One longs helplessly to be of use to such a man.
Poor Bertie had been suffering from the glandular disease of which he showed symptoms when a boy, but which he appeared to have completely outgrown. He had become a splendidly strong man before he went to Natal and continued so till about three years ago, when he began to complain of neuralgia. His death was immediately caused by an attack of bronchitis.
We return to town on September 23. but go off again in two or three days to the Coast -- Bournemouth I believe, till about the end of October.
Ever yours lovingly
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Publisher: George Eliot Archive, edited by Beverley Park Rilett. https://GeorgeEliotArchive.org

Dublin Core:Relation:
300 See Barbara Stephen, Emily Davies and Girton College, 1927, p. 303.
301 Alfred Morrison (1821-97), wealthy  collector of works of art and autographs, married in 1866 Mabel, daughter of the Rev. R. S. C. Chermside. They began to call at the Priory in 1872, and twice GHL records going to see their collections at 16 Carlton House Terrace: "Called on the Morrisons to see Houdon's bust of Voltaire and their pictures. Bored by being shown all their splendours and rarities: each the `finest in the world.'" (GHL Diary, 21 March 1872.) On the second visit, 9 May 1874, he and GE were shown a wonderful watercolor by Albrecht D 'fcrer of a bird's wing.
302 James Joseph Sylvester (1814-97),  mathematician, had resided at St. John's College, Cambridge, but as a Jew could not take his degree until after the passing of the Tests Act in 1872. Long before then he was recognized as one of the foremost mathematicians of the time. He was Professor of Mathematics at the University of Virginia, 1841-1845 and at the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich, 1855-1870. In the interval he practised law and worked as an actuary. In 1877 he went again to America as the first Professor of Mathematics at the Johns Hopkins University and in 1883 returned as Savilian Professor of Geometry at Oxford. The mistake about his age was Mme Bodichon's. See Hester Burton, Barbara Bodichon, [1949], p. 74.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Redhill, 6 July 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Redhill, 6 July 1872
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Road | Red Hill | July 6. 72.
Dearest Barbara
Good news of you was just what I wanted. I have often been saying, "Barbara must be settled in Sussex now," and I wondered that you sent me no word.
I had often thought of what you told me about Miss Elinor Carter, 556 so that the news of her happy engagement comes to me as something I had wished for. How many Diceys are there?
Nannie's account of Madame Mario 557 is delightful. What she says of the happiness between the husband and wife pleases me especially, because I had heard at Florence that he was 'e9goiste and allowed her to adore him. Remember me to Nannie when you write to her. I like to believe, from her saying nothing about health, that she has been gaining strength since I saw her.
It is a great comfort to me that you find good in "Middlemarch," and George will begin to like Trench 558 from henceforth. I am so used to hearing him called by that simple name that I hardly identify him with his new title.
We are going on comfortably, George having got rid of his ailments, and the warm weather being friendly to us both. Gertrude is very near her confinement, and a letter from Charlie today tells us that she is going on well. Her sister Emily is to be married to Edmund Maurice next month.
I suppose Bessie is in France now. She made no sign of herself to me after calling with her husband one Sunday in the early Spring. If Miss Edwards is with you give my love to her and tell her she should get the volumes of a very cheap publication -- the Deutscher Novellenschatz -- that is to say if she doesn't already know them as well as I do. Some of the tales are remarkably fine. I am reading aloud the last three volumes, which are even better than the others (George just tells me that he has already recommended this, so pray excuse me for the needless repetition.) I have just been so deeply interested in one of the stories "Diethelm von Buchenberg," 559 that I want everybody to have the same pleasure, who can read German.
We both desire to be remembered to the Doctor, who I hope is looking as well and handsome as he was last year. I of course am still anxious, as I always am when any work is not safely finished, and my days are very full with writing walking and reading aloud. My letters are written at night when I am tired and stupid.
Think of me as often as you can and believe me
Yours always affectionately
M. E. Lewes.
