Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Redhill, 4 June 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Redhill, 4 June 1872
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 158-159.
June 4. 72.
My dear Barbara
I am glad to know that you are having a time of refreshing in fine scenery, with entire freedom to paint. I am in a corresponding state of relief from the noises and small excitements that break up the day and scatter one's nervous energy in London.
We have been in our hiding place about twelve days now, 527 and I am enjoying it more and more -- getting more bodily ease and mental clearness than I have had for the last six months. Unhappily George is rather ailing, having slipped back a few degrees in the hurry and fatigue of book-packing etc. on our migration.
Our house is not in the least beautiful, but it is well-situated and comfortable, perfectly still in the middle of a garden surrounded by fields and meadows, and yet within reach of shops and "civilization."
We managed to get to the Academy Exhibition one day before leaving town. 528 I was delighted with Walker's picture -- were you? -- and Mason's unfinished Reapers, and a few, very few, others. Also, we went twice to the opera 529 in order to save ourselves from any yearnings after it when we should have settled in the country. We have taken our house only till the end of August, and have the option of quitting it at the end of July.
George, being a little heady, and unable to occupy his mornings with writing, is going tomorrow to see the aquarium at the Crystal Palace of which one sees such beautiful accounts.
We tell no one our address and have our letters sent on from the Priory. I have no other news to tell you. But I must say that it vexed me to miss having you with us to lunch that day when you could have come. We went to rather a grand luncheon 530 which was not a great delight to me -- and it is always something pleasanter than that to see you.
Your affectionate
Marian.
G. sends his love. When you see Julia Wedgwood do remember, if you can, to tell her that I thought of her much before leaving, but abstained from writing notes as a necessary part of hygiene.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Milan and Verona, 29 May -- 1 June 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Milan and Verona, 29 May -- 1 June 1880
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Robertsbridge | Hawkhurst | Sussex | England. Postmark: BOLOGNA-ALA | 1 | GIU | 80. HAWKHURST | A | JU 4 | 80: ROBERTSBRIDGE | J 4 | 80. Mostly published: Cross, III, 400-403.
'abMilan May 29'bb Verona, June 1. 80.
Dearest Barbara
The change I make in the date of this letter is a sign of the difficulty you well know that one finds in writing all the letters one wants to write while travelling. Ever since Charles forwarded to me your dear letter while I was in Paris I have been meaning to write to you. That letter doubly sweet to me because it was written before you received mine, intended to inform you of my marriage before it appeared in the newspaper. Charles says that my Friends are chiefly hurt because I did not tell them of the approaching change in my life. But I really did not finally, absolutely decide -- I was in a state of doubt and struggle until only a fortnight before the event took place and for a week of that time I was ill with influenza, so that at last everything was done in the utmost haste. However, there were four or five friends, of whom you were one, to whom I was resolved to write so that they should at least get my letter in the morning of the 6th.
I had more than once said to Mr. Cross that you were that one of my friends who required the least explanation on the subject -- who would spontaneously understand our marriage. But Charles sends me word that my friends in general are very sympathetic, and I should like to mention to you that Bessie is one whose very kind words he has sent to me, for you may have an opportunity of giving my love to her and telling her that it is very sweet to me to feel that her affection is constant to me in this as it was in other crises of my life.
I wish, since you can no longer come in and out among us as you used to do, that you already knew my husband better -- his character is so solid, his feeling is so eminently delicate and generous. But you will have inferred something of this from his desire to dedicate his life to the remaining fragment of mine. His family welcome me with the utmost tenderness, and they are of the best paste men and women can be made of. All this is wonderful blessing falling to me beyond my share after I had thought that my life was ended and that, so to speak, my coffin was ready for me in the next room. Deep down below there is a hidden river of sadness but this must always be with those who have lived long -- and I am able to enjoy my newly re-opened life. I shall be a better, more loving creature than I could have been in solitude. To be constantly lovingly grateful for the gift of a perfect love is the best illumination of one's mind to all the possible good there may be in store for man on this troublous little planet.
We leave Verona today, and stay a little at Padua on our way to Venice. The last two days we have had some greyness of sky and good rain which has laid the dust for us while cheering the richly cultivated plains around us. Hitherto we have had delightful weather and just the temperature we 'abboth'bb rejoice in. We are both fond of warmth, and could bear more heat than we have the prospect of at present. We came into Italy by way of Grenoble (seeing the Grande Chartreuse) Chamb'e9ry, and the Mont Cenis tunnel. Since then we have been staying at Milan and enjoying the Luini frescoes and a few other great things there. The great things are always by comparison few, and there is much everywhere one would like to help seeing after it has once served to give one a notion of historical progression.
We shall stay at Venice ten days or a fortnight, so if you have a scribe, or would write yourself, to tell me that all is going on well with you the letter would not, as the Scotch say, "go a-missing."
Your always loving
Marian.
Yesterday we had a drive on the skirting heights of Verona and saw the vast fertile plain around with the Euganean Hills blue in the distance, and the Appennines just dimly visible in the clear margin of the horizon. I am always made happier by seeing well-cultivated land.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 9 May 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 9 May 1867
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank | May 9. 67.
Dearest Barbara
The weather here is beautiful now -- warm and, in the country, brilliant. Your little Sussex home must be looking like a paradise. But I am magnanimous enough to wish that you should not come to England till there is no risk of your being overdone by affectionate friends. So many are interested in you that I feel a sympathetic fatigue at the idea of the kindness that would be poured out upon you; Bessie would be crushed in attempting to defend you from it.
Our good old Neuberg 626 had been much out of health before we left England at Christmas, and looked sadly worn and physically uneasy. Mrs. Frankau told me that he had a painful complaint which troubled him almost constantly. And about a month ago, all that trouble ended. I believe he had no great preparatory increase of illness, but I have not yet seen his sister as I hoped to do, and have only heard imperfect accounts. We should have liked him to live bodily amongst us much longer -- his life seemed so quietly beneficent, especially in his own family. But the thought that he was enduring frequent malaise makes death seem a good for him. I hope we shall cherish more and more the best memories of the dead and so be able to keep them with us -- living within us when they have ceased to live without us. [About six words deleted.]
George has finished his book and is very bright just now.
We went to see the collection of historical portraits at Kensington yesterday, and met your old friend Mr. Scharf there. It is a wonderful collection -- such Gainsboroughs and Sir Joshuas! a wonderful portrait of Sir Isaac Newton by that usually prosaic Sir Godfrey Kneller -- a Duchess of Queensberry, very old, very grand, by someone unknown, worth going to see if there were nothing else.
No more now, because I am called away. Best love to Bessie -- gratitude to her also, for being your Guardian Angel. George sends his best, most respectful love.
Always yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 9 April 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 9 April 1861
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square | April 9. 61.
Dear Barbara
The possibility of our not seeing you is almost the only regret I feel that we are going to run away from London for two months. I am only just able to tell you the exact time, for our departure has hitherto been dependent on unsettled matters, about our Edinburgh boy. 736 We are to set off on the 18th -- or, perhaps, the 19th Thursday or Friday week. That will be too early for any chance of our meeting you on the way, but I preserve a hope that you may still be in London on our return. We are almost sure to be at home again by, if not before, the end of June.
Bessie has sent me tickets for a private view of your pictures, 737 and I am particularly glad to be among the privileged, since we are to start so soon.
This morning there came a letter in an envelope with the Matlock postmark, and addressed in a handwriting strange to me. The letter was written by you to a certain "Dear Florence." I didn't read it, but seeing Bessie's name near the end, I have just sent it to her, hoping she may know what to do with it.
I think of you a good deal, dear Barbara -- sometimes with a mingling of sadness at some things that touch you nearly. But there are so many chords in your life, that some joy and consolation lies by the side of every grief. But your having any grief makes me all the more sorry not to be sure of seeing you.
Tell your sister, with my love, that I was very pleased to have the caricatures -- pleased to be remembered in that way, and amused with the images of dear Bessie. I feel a sort of sick longing at the faintest sketch suggesting a broad sky and a distance, this London life oppresses and depresses me so terribly.
What a story that is about the Frenchwoman and her dress! I see no immediate prospect for us but the spread of that mania. There is
everything at work to drive women's unsatisfied diseased longings into that channel, and I really feel almost guilty when I buy a gown or bonnet with any approximation to fashion in it. I am not sure that one ought not to rush into some sort of new Quakerism as a counteraction and a protest.
Mr. Lewes is gone to the Museum for me -- else he would send his love with mine to the Doctor and you. God bless you. You are very near to your affectionate
Marian.
P.S. It has just occurred to me that I have not told you where we are going. To Florence -- by the Corniche -- and then back through Switzerland, just to see Bertie the youngest boy, who is still at Hofwyl.
You did talk of going to Switzerland this summer. If you can't write to me so that the letter would reach me before the 18th, one addressed to the Post Restante, Florence, would find me. We shall probably stay at Thun for a day or two, and have Bertie there.
Miss Ellen Allen 738 called when I was away last week. I shall try to see her on Friday, but I am rather embarassed with engagements just now. I should like to go to the school on Friday morning, if I could, and hear those young voices.
Thanks for letting me see the letter to Miss Longdon. 739 Any scrap about you and yours has interest for us. We have no clouds -- except such as come from feebleness of body. All is well besides. Charlie will keep house alone, while we are away, and would feel himself honoured and happy if you and the Doctor would once shine on him when you come to town. He is only at home in the latter part of the day, you know -- after 'bd past four. He always seizes your name when we mention it, as an opportunity of saying something admiring about you; so that, if once, when you are passing the door, you could look at him and shake him by the hand, you would be doing a deed like yourself -- kind and pretty. He is going to work like a negro at his music while we are away, and have lessons, so that his time will be filled up.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 8 April 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 8 April 1879
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 354-355.
The Priory | April 8. 79.
Dearest Barbara
Your letter was very welcome this morning, for I do not like to be very long without having some picture of you, and your words of affection are always sweet.
The Studentship I mention is to supply an income to a young man who is qualified and eager to carry on physiological research and would not otherwise have the means of doing so. Mr. H. Sidgwick, Michael Foster, and other men of kindred mind are helping me in settling the scheme. I have been determined in my choice of the Studentship by the idea of what would be a sort of prolongation of His life. That there should always, in consequence of his having lived, be a young man working in the way he would have liked to work, is a memorial of him that comes nearest to my feeling. It is to be at Cambridge to begin with, and we thought at first of affiliating it to the University, but now the notion is that it will be well to keep it free, so that the Trustees may move it where and when they will. But the Scheme is not yet draughted.
I cannot tell yet when I shall be able to get down to Witley, for our daughter-in-law (Bertie's widow) with her two little children is on her way to England from Natal -- terrified into flight by the state of things there -- and as she comes in a sailing vessel, the time of her arrival is uncertain. I must stay to see her and the little ones.
I am going to bring out one of His Problems in a separate volume at the beginning of May, and am now correcting the proofs. 212
My going to Witley is an experiment. I don't know how I shall bear being there. But I hope there will be nothing to hinder my having you there if you will undertake the troublesome journey for my sake. It is a little melancholy to me that the Blandford Sq. house is let for so long, but that does not hinder it from being the wiser plan. It releases you from trouble about details.
My love to Nannie and Bessie when you write to them -- and to the dear dark-eyed Marquis 213 when she comes back to you.
I am better in health, but find seeing the few people I am obliged to see very fatiguing, and dare not say [I will do this or that] much beforehand.
Ever your loving grateful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 6 September 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 6 September 1876
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Hawkhurst | Sussex. Postmarks: LONDON-N.W | C I | SP 6 | 76; HAWKHURST | A | SP 7 | 76; ROBERTSBRIDGE | A | SP 7 | 76. Published: Cross, III, 289-290.
North Bank | September 6. 76.
My dear Barbara
We got home again last Friday, much strengthened by our journey, notwithstanding vicissitudes. I suppose you will not be in town for ages to come, but I let you know that I am here in case you have anything to say to me by letter -- about "objects."
We gave up going to the Maritime Alps. When we were on our way as far as Aix-les-Bains, I got ill, and we almost thought we must return home. We wended northward again, and by slow stages reached Ragatz, which answered for us both, especially for me. After leaving Ragatz we still kept in eastern Switzerland in high vallies unvisited by the English, and in our homeward line of travel we paused in the Schwarz-Wald, at St. Blasien which is a Luft-Kur, all green hills and pines with their tops as still as if it were the abode of the gods.
But imagine how we enjoy being at home again, in our own chairs, with the familiar faces giving us smiles which are not expecting change in franc pieces!
We are both pretty well, but of course not cured of all infirmities. Death is the only physician, the shadow of his valley the only journeying that will cure us of age and the gathering fatigue of years. Still, we are thoroughly lively and [spry.]
I hope that the hot summer has passed agreeably for you and not been unfavourable to your health or comfort. Of course a little news of you will be welcome, even if you don't particularly want to say anything to me.
Always your loving
Marian.

The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
February 6. 79.
Dearest Barbara
Bless you for your loving thought. But for all reasons, bodily and mental, I am unable to move. I am entirely occupied with his manuscripts and must be on this spot among all the books. 173 Then, I am in a very ailing condition of body -- cannot count on myself from day to day -- and am not fit to undertake any sort of journey. Your ever loving and grateful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 5 May 1880
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Robertsbridge | Hawkhurst. Postmarks: ST. JOHNS WOOD N.W. | A ZX | JY 7 | 80; [HAWKHUR]ST-GREEN [SUS]SEX | B | JY 8 | 80; [RO]BERTSBRIDGE | B | JY | 80. Endorsed: I have today found this in a drawer in the desk in the dining room. This explains the mystery. C.L.L. Written May 5. B.L.S.B. Mostly published: Cross, III, 391-392.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 5. 80.
My dear Barbara
I have something to tell you which will doubtless be a great surprize to you, but since I have found that other friends, less acquainted with me and my life than you are, have given me their sympathy, I think that I can count on yours. I am going to do what not very long ago I should myself have pronounced impossible for me, and therefore I should not wonder at anyone else who found my action incomprehensible. By the time you receive this letter 401 I shall (so far as the future can be matter of assertion) have been married to Mr. J. W. Cross, who you know is a friend of years, a friend much loved and trusted by Mr. Lewes, and who now that I am alone sees his happiness in the dedication of his life to me. This change in my position will make no change in my care for Mr. Lewes's family and in the ultimate disposition of my property. 402 Mr. Cross has a sufficient fortune of his own.
We are going abroad for a few months, and I shall not return to live at this house. Mr. Cross has taken the lease of a house in Cheyne Walk (No. 4), Chelsea, where we shall spend the winter and early spring, making Witley our summer home.
You will like to hear that Charles has shown a quite perfect feeling in relation to this unexpected event, and if you would like to write or in any way communicate with him your wish for further knowledge, he will I am sure readily respond to your wish.
I indulge the hope that you will some day look at the river from the windows of our Chelsea house which is rather quaint and picturesque.
Please tell Bessie for me, with my love to her. I cannot write to more than two or three 403 persons.
Ever yours lovingly
M. E. Lewes.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 5 March 1879
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Mostly published: Cross, III, 350-351.
N.B. | March 5. 79.
My dear Barbara
Your letter which tells me that you are benefiting by the "clear sunny air" is very welcome. Yes, here too the weather is more merciful and I drive out most days. I am better bodily, but I never feel thoroughly comfortable in that material sense, and I am incredibly thin. 192 As to my mind, I am full of occupation, but the sorrow deepens down instead of diminishing. I mean to go to Witley in a few months, that I may look again on the spots that he enjoyed, and that we enjoyed together, but I cannot tell beforehand whether I shall care to go again afterwards.
Everybody is very kind to me, and by and by I shall begin to see a few intimate friends. 193 I can do or go through anything that is business or duty, but time and strength seem lacking for everything else.
Give my love to Bessie. You and she must excuse my weakness, remembering that for nearly 25 years I have been used to find my happiness in his. I can find it nowhere else. But we can live and be helpful without happiness, and I have had more than myriads who were and are better fitted for it.
I am really very busy and have been sadly delayed by want of health. One project I have entered on is to found a studentship which will be called after my husband's name. I am getting help from experienced men. 194
Is Nannie in England still? Surely not. But when you write to her, assure her of my affectionate grateful remembrance.
Always your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 5 February 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 5 February 1880
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | February 5. 80.
My dear Barbara
I think you are happy not to be obliged to come to London where our climate is hideous, so for your sake I will not say that I regret my loss in not seeing you.
I should like very much to make Miss North's 368 acquaintance and I will write to Miss Ewart, since you think that she would be kind enough to bring her.
I saw all about Miss Scott's success 369 in the Times and was the more interested in it because Miss Marks had described her to me.
That failure of the Kinder-garten plan at Portsmouth made me very sorry for our sweet little friend. 370 It seemed to be everything one could desire for her sister's well-being so far as external effort could secure it.
I know how you feel the successive deaths of aged relatives -- changing the world for you and making it less and less like what it was in your earlier time, especially as to remaining associations with your Father. I do not know who is your Aunt Joanna: I suppose Mrs. Bonham Carter. 371
I have not yet seen Bessie. I hope she does not regard me as neglectful in not writing to ask her to come and see me. I don't know her address, and even if I did, I have made it a system not to write notes of invitation to my friends. One who has been to see me carries a message to another, and in this way they come gradually. So much of my time is taken up in correspondence that I cannot write gratuitous notes.
If you had come to town you would have liked to see the drawings at the Grosvenor Gallery, and the Old Masters at the Academy but perhaps you may yet come before they are removed.
It is some comfort to think that you and others in the country have been enjoying beautiful days when we have been wrapt in a darkness that not only might be but was felt. Keep getting better and believe ever in
Your faithfully loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 4 December 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 4 December 1863
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, II, 370-372.
The Priory, 21 North Bank | December 4. 1863.
Dearest Barbara
Your good news about your double self rejoiced us the other night and your letter was duly sent on to Lea Hurst. 209 Miss Hennell is staying there and writes me word that Miss Remond is a fellow guest lecturing (par parenth'e8se) on Slavery. I am rather ashamed to hear of anyone trying to be useful just now, for I am doing nothing but indulge myself -- enjoying being petted very much, enjoying great books, enjoying our new pretty quiet home and the study of Beethoven's Sonatas for piano and violin with the mild-faced old Jansa -- and not being at all unhappy, as you imagined me.
We had a house-warming celebration of Charlie's birthday on the 24th: it was a birthday extraordinary introducing a new era for him, for he became twenty-one! Our youngest lad Bertie seems to have had his wits a little sharpened by change of circumstances and writes as if he liked his Scotch farming and Scotch domesticity. Of Thornie we cannot well hear until the end of January or beginning of February, so that our parental minds are for the moment at ease.
The "Life of Goethe" is about to appear in one handsome volume, and George is correcting the proofs of the "Aristotle." The correction is a slow business, because the proofs are read by several people: our friend Mr. Clark 210 of Cambridge reads them to make us easy about the Greek accents, and Huxley and Tyndal read some of them for the sake of scientific criticism. Meanwhile George sits in a comfortable room delightfully free from irritation of organs and street cries, making further studies for his History of Science, and I sit in another room taking deep draughts of reading -- Politique positive, Euripides, Latin Christianity and so forth, and remaining in glorious ignorance of "the current literature." Such is our life: and you perceive that instead of being miserable, I am rather following a wicked example and saying to my soul, "Soul, take thine ease." 211
We have not seen or heard anything of the Websters and are wondering whether they have yet left Algiers. I am sorry to think of you without any artistic society to help you and feed your faith. It is hard to believe long together that anything is "worth while" unless there is some eye to kindle in common with our own, some brief word uttered now and then to imply that what is infinitely precious to us is precious alike to another mind. I fancy that, to do without that guarantee, one must be rather insane -- one must be a bad poet, or a spinner of impossible theories or an inventor of impossible machinery. However it is but a brief space either of time or distance that divides you from those who thoroughly share your cares and joys -- always excepting that portion which is the hidden private lot of every human being. In the most entire confidence even of husband and wife there is always the unspoken residue -- the undivined residue, perhaps of what is most sinful, perhaps of what is most exalted and unselfish.
All blessings on you and yours, dear Barbara. George is gone into town, or he would send his message.
Ever your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 4 April 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 4 April 1864
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | North Bank | April 4. 1864.
Dearest Barbara
At last we have a letter of Thornie's from the African land -- the event I had waited for before writing to you. We had heard twice from him during his voyage, which he enjoyed immensely, editing a paper on board, acting in comedies, and, I am afraid, rather scandalizing the clergyman by dressing up in blue tights and a tail to represent Mephistopheles -- etc., etc. This letter of today is dated January 28, and much may have happened since then, but let us trust in the good omen of a good beginning. He says "My plans for the present are these. On the 4th February I am going up country with Mr. Brickhill Junr. who is interpreter to the court, so we shall be a small party consisting of the judges etc. who are going on circuit -- I go, of course, to see the country and get information about it. We shall be 18 days away and when I come back, I start on the first week of March for the Free State (Trans Vaal Republic) on an excursion with a French trader. . . . I shall have to look after the waggon when he is at Dutchmen's houses, and to keep the books, and for this shall get £3 a month. Won't that be glorious? I would have gone willingly for nothing at all, as the shooting and butterfly catching will be quite enough payment. However £9 will go nicely into my pocket to fill up some of the holes that living and doing nothing makes. When I come back, I shall settle down quietly near Durban, or at least somewhere on the coast and shall join some coffee planter, where I can learn the business, and get my board and lodging in return for my work. I shall stay there 6 months or a year probably. So much for the next year of my life. . . .
"I delivered the only letter I had in Durban to Mr. Brickhill the manager of the Natal bank who was very kind to me. . . . Mr. David Buchanan 245 who lives up here (Pietermaritzburg) had told a Mr. John Sanderson 246 of Durban that I should arrive soon and asked him to look out for me, which he accordingly did, and I was soon quite at home with him and his wife. He is a very nice man and a great botanist -- not a very scientific one, but the other kind -- you know what I mean. -- His wife is a charming creature about 30, no children, and immensely fond of music, not that disgusting trash which is called music at home and here, but Beethoven! Mendelssohn etc. . . . So you may imagine the evenings we have together, sonatas, symphonies etc., while I howl German songs. Mrs. S. was delighted to find some somebody as congenial as I was, for there is nobody in Durban or Maritzburg either, as far as I can find, who cares for anything but dance music. . . . On Saturday the 9th I rode out with Mr. Sanderson 10 miles to the north, to see the coffee plantation of Mr. Lister, the crack one of the Colony and was much pleased with it. . . . I have been out shooting a little, principally with the rifle, with which I shot a sand piper walking at 70 yards, and a parson at 60 (a parson is a crow with a white band on his neck, which may be taken for a choker). . . . So much for life in Durban: the town is pretty, plenty of trees in it, but the soil is sandy so that walking is not of the easiest. The country round is beautiful, the wooded hills and the large flat called the Vley with a marsh on one side is very pretty, the birds and butterflies and flowers gorgeous. Birds of prey are abundant. I have seen 50 Buzzards at a time floating over Maritzburg. The climate is very fine -- better than I expected -- not unpleasantly hot to me -- there is almost always a delightful sea breeze. . . .
"On the 10th I left Durban and on the 12th got to Maritzburg. . . . I like many of the people very much indeed: The Buchanans (particular Ebenezer family) are very kind, and Mr. Smith's friend Warwick Brooks 247 and I get on very nicely. . . . Dr. Mann 248 was very cool, which was rather surprising, as he is usually much liked, and he had been very kind to a fellow passenger of mine -- but who, I imagine, had been setting him against me, as we were rivals on board the [Damietta,] he being editor of the [Herald,] about which you will have heard in my letter you got about Christmas. I am going out to see Pigott's friend at Blackhurron[?] on Saturday. The Governor 249 was very kind and had a long talk. Newcastle's 250 letter was not worth a rap: it is a lithographed one he gives to all new Colonists, but of course Sir E. B. Lytton's was of a good deal of use, and the Governor seemed to think very highly of it, and offered to introduce me to any person who could be of any service. . . . I also rode to Edendale to see Miss Annie Buchanan, and spent a day at Ebenezer B's farm and am constantly with young Ebenezer, who is a conveyancer etc., and in whose office this letter is written. . . . Give my kind regards to Mrs. Bodichon, whose letters have done me a deal of good. Miss Annie Buchanan, tell her, was delighted with her portrait."
I send you these extracts, dear Barbara, because they will give you a better idea of the lad and his doings than any version of mine. I wish I could send you his whole letter. It is very long -- stuffed full of details telling of high animal spirits and also of considerable good sense. His father is much comforted by the practical tone of the letter, and I shall not say -- because I could not say fully -- how grateful we are to her who helped us most in finding this new starting point for our nineteen-year-older.
Your last little letter was a great relief to me. Mrs. Peter Taylor had heard that you had been called to Rome because Nannie was worse; and my suspense on that subject made it impossible for me to write to you. Poor dear Bessie! I often think of her, but hear little. We are very well ourselves -- have just been on a wild rapid trip to Scotland for a week(!), having business in Glasgow and wanting also to see Bertie who is farming about an hour's distance from that rich noisy smoky whiskey drinking town. We were fortunate enough to see Helen Faucit at Glasgow in three of Shakspeare's plays -- a flash of real acting in the evening twilight of the stage. -- For the rest, you see all the papers, and know all the news, so I can give you no information that will not be stale to you, except of the domestic sort -- as that Charlie has just returned from his month's holiday [four lines deleted].
George unites with me in kindest regards to Dr. Bodichon and sends affectionate homage to the "charmante Mistress Barbara."
Ever thine lovingly
Marian.
This morning we went to see Leighton's pictures. There are two large ones -- Dante coming down the stairs of his host in exile -- the stairs so "hard to tread" -- and Orpheus and Eurydice from a fine moment in Gluck's opera, where Eurydice, not knowing the command that Orpheus is not to look at her, clings to him in pained wondering entreaty, while he turns his head away in anguish.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 30 September 1861
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Mrs. Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Brightling Road | Hurst Green. Postmark: Illegible. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
September 30. 61.
Dearest Barbara
Grace will go to her sister this evening, and you will have a letter by Wednesday morning with precise information. Grace believes that her sister is quite ready for you.
I do hope the change will turn out well, and that you will get almost as much comfort out of her as I do out of her honest sisters. 848 Quite as much you can hardly get, because you will be less dependent on her. Old Captain Willim is in a state of great bitterness about Mrs. Lee's 849 taking a situation, as she has been a sort of factotum for him, going into the city about money business, etc.
The oak leaves are a pleasant symbol of your enjoyment. I hope the Doctor is revelling in the absence of smoke and the endless obstruction of brick. Thornie has been at home the last week. He quits us for Edinburgh this evening.
Our double love to your double self.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 30 March 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 30 March 1876
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 275-276.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 30. 76.
My dear Barbara
Your letter was a most welcome assurance that no evil had befallen you on the voyage which was made in what to us was horribly blustering weather. I had said to Mr. Lewes, [She will perhaps send me a post card by and by] -- so that your letter with more details than a card could have carried, was doubly acceptable as something better than what I had counted on.
I am delighted to know that nature and the weather are enjoyable to you and your companions altogether sympathetic, still more that the Doctor was glad to receive you all and that your object in taking the journey is likely to be answered. Also, I am well pleased that Deronda touches you. I wanted you to prefer the chapter 435 about Mirah's finding, and I hope you will also like her history in Part III which has just been published.
We want very much to get away, but I fear we shall hardly be able to start till the end of May. At present we think of the Maritime Alps as a destination for the warm summer, if we have such a season this year, but we shall wander a little on our way thither and not feel bound to accomplish anything in particular. Meanwhile we are hearing some nice music occasionally, and we are going to see Tennyson's Play which is to be given on the 15th. 436 The occasion will be very interesting and I should be sorry to miss it.
I have not seen or heard anything of Miss Marks since you left. I trust that all is going on well with her. 437 Apropos of her and all other subjects, will you kindly remember that we shall be out of reach of ordinary letters after May?
We have been getting a little refreshment from two flights between Sundays to Weybridge, where Mr. and Mrs. Hall lent us their house and servants. But we have had the good a little drained from us by going out to dinner two days in succession. At Sir James Paget's I was much interested to find that a gentle-looking, clear-eyed, neatly-made man was Sir Garnet Wolseley and I had some talk with him which quite confirmed the impression of him as one of those men who have a power of command by dint of their sweet temper, calm demeanour and unswerving resolution. The next subject that has filled our chat lately has been the Blue Book on Vivisection, which you would like to look into. 438 There is a great deal of matter for reflection in the evidence on the subject, and some good points have been lately put in print and conversation that I should like to tell you of if I had time. Prof. Clifford told us the other Sunday that Huxley complained of his sufferings from "the profligate lying of virtuous women." 439 I am scribbling at the fag end of the day, being short of time not so much because of work as because of my feebleness which makes me incapable of getting through it.
Best, affectionate remembrances to your sister and Miss Blythe. And kind regards to the Doctor from both of us. George unites in love to you. I hope we shall hear of your being safe in England before we set off.
Yours always
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 30 August 1869
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | 5 Blandford Square. Endorsed: Aug. 1869.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 30. 69.
Dearest Barbara
I think no one but you could be the kind donor of the beautiful flowers and the bulrushes which were addressed to Thornie the other day. I delighted in them, but Thornie seemed to be grateful for the kindness only and not for the material signs of it. He is fond of flowers in the field and on the mountains, and, you know, was a great collector of them, but he says they do not affect him agreeably in a room. Du reste, he is strangly indifferent about everything now, in contrast with his former vivacity. I tell you the truth about the flowers, because I value the time and trouble and pretty thoughts you give to such efforts for others' pleasure, far too highly to be willing that you should bestow them -- if not in vain, at least with rather a different result from the one you contemplated.
Physically, Thornie has gone on suffering less and less pain, and acquiring comparatively good looks in the face. He moves himself better in the bed, but he has not quite recovered the power of standing, &unknown;still less&unknown; not to speak of walking. Usually he has ceased to care about conversation, unless it is with some male friend who is a rare or a new visitor. He eats fruit, and drinks milk chiefly, and seems to flourish on this diet.
I hope you are still thoroughly enjoying your country life. I am rather hungry to have a word from you that will give me some assurance of your being well and happy.
Ever your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 29 April 1879
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Robertsbridge | Hawkhurst. Postmarks: LONDON N.W | C 12 | AP 30 | 79; HAWKHURST | A | MY 1 | 79; ROBERTSBRIDGE | MY 1 | 79. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | April 29. 79.
Dearest Barbara
The grandchildren and their mother are come, and all today I have been occupied with them. I am a little oppressed just now with the claims on my time and thoughts and can long for nothing except to get away to my country home.
This I hope to do now in the second week of May. Hence I cannot see you in London when you come up on the 2nd of June; but if by "Miss Jekyll's house" you mean the one she built for her mother, it is almost within sight of Witley -- is certainly within a drive from our house. Can you not therefore come and see me on your way from that house, making the little round as part of your journey homeward? You know I am close to a railway station.
Send me word when and how you would like to come. I cannot go to you, dear. The world, in the shape of kind friends and creatures who have claims on my care, is crowding on me before I am quite prepared for it, though I am now determined to live as bravely as I can. 231
It is a happy thought to me that you are so enjoying the spring. The sense of it to me comes chiefly through the flowers which my friends send me abundantly. There is much that we could say to each other if we were face to face -- so little that one [can] say by letter.
Always your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 27 February 1865
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 27 February 1865
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
1 North Bank | February 27. 1865.
Dearest Barbara
Your letter, just received, has comforted me greatly. We did go to Paris, but did not go to the Hotel de Saxe, which perhaps was the reason that I lost the chance you had given me of hearing from you there. Not having had the Paris letter, I felt it long since I had had some assurance of your being at least well in health and able to enjoy some of the good things Fate has granted you. Your letter this morning is just what I wanted.
Gertrude and Charlie will be delighted with the Burnous -- and I will duly deliver your message. They are to be married on the 20th, and we shall be glad now when the epoch has come -- if one can really be glad at the lapse of time irrecoverable. We have loved Gertrude better and better as we have seen more of her, and we both feel that we could have desired no better lot for Charlie.
George and I enjoyed our ten days at Paris, making the most of our time in theatre-going and sight-seeing. I have lost my old dislike of Paris -- but, it must be confessed that the Paris of today is another Paris than the one I used to detest. What a delight it is to think of the precious Gothic remains being restored with Violet le Duc's perfection of knowledge and taste! 642 We reserved seeing St. Denis until we can go in better weather -- and S'e8vres and St. Cloud and Fontainebleau, and all the other summer places.
I see you have had your article on Pottery printed -- seen that fact, but not the article. I like to think of you as "th'e4tig" in all sorts of ways: it is the best remedy for one's own ills, and helps a little to remedy other people's. Mr. Theodore Martin 643 was telling us yesterday how he is changing the face of a neighbourhood in Hampshire, by building cottages, and a dining-room, and establishing a co-operative store, for the workmen engaged in new pottery or terra-cotta works there. I should have envied him, if I allowed myself to envy anyone, in a world where each has dire need of his share.
Will the doctor come with you to England this year, I wonder? And Nannie? 644 I heard good news of her from some friend or other a little while ago. I hope it was not false. It would do me good to know that she was once more able to walk about and find the hours something more than hours of endurance. O sadness -- that a sweet clear-eyed woman striving after all that is beautiful and best, should be taken away for so many precious years, from the active influences of the world.
George is pretty well now, and expects soon to be very busy about the new Fortnightly Review, which I think I mentioned to you. I am so so: dyspeptic and dismal occasionally, and had I been a Hebrew prophet near the time of the captivity I should doubtless have written Lamentations. Dyspepsia determines a great deal of literary production.
A carpenter, putting up brackets, wants me. You see, I am scribbling in a hurry -- because I want to let you know at once how pleased I was to hear of you.
Ever dear, Your true and affectionate
M. E. L.

MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 26. 74.
My dear Barbara
I want a housemaid with a first-rate character -- our nice little Charlotte having divined in herself a genius for cooking which makes her want to be a kitchen maid. Can you help me? I know you will, if you can.
We are just come home, and after a little ramble of two or three days we shall be settled here for the winter. 150 I imagine you at Blandford Square by this time, and think it safest to send my note there. We expect to leave town again on Thursday and to return on Saturday.
In any case I hope to see you soon and shall keep all gossip till then.
Always your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 26 November 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 26 November 1862
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, II, 343-344.
Blandford Sq. | November 26. 62.
Dear Barbara
First, thanks for the note from Marseilles. Since I had not the parting kiss in a regular way I was glad to have it in the commuted form of that pretty billet -- especially glad to know that your journey had not been too hurried.
Next, about your letter of this morning. I don't see what we can do towards making ourselves agreeable or useful to Mr. Allingham 115 just yet, but when we begin to receive visitors again, we will try and ask him to come on an evening when he will meet somebody worth talking to. Mr. Lewes has taken down his address and will write to him on the strength of your letter.
Miss Allen sat an hour with me a week ago, and I hope she will find it pleasant to come and speak to us or ask us for any book we can give her. I have said all I can to convince her of what is the truth -- that I like to see her very much.
Pray don't ever ask me again not to rob a man of his religious belief, as if you thought my mind tended towards such robbery. I have too profound a conviction of the efficacy that lies in all sincere faith, and the spiritual blight that comes with No-faith, to have any negative propagandism in me. In fact, I have very little sympathy with Freethinkers as a class, and have lost all interest in mere antagonism to religious doctrines. I care only to know, if possible, the lasting meaning that lies in all religious doctrine from the beginning till now.
That speech of Carlyle's, 116 which sounds so odious must, I think, have been provoked by something in the manner of the statement to which it came as an answer -- else it would hurt me very much that he should have uttered it.
Our big boy is gone to Mrs. P. Taylor's gathering to-night. He has been telling us a story of an old supplementary clerk at the P.O. who is called "maid of all work" in the Correspondence Branch. The waiter at the dining room offered him the newspaper; whereupon he replied, "I didn't come 'ere to 'ear the news. I came to heat!" -- It was the boy's twentieth birthday on Monday -- a very happy date to us, for we think he gets better with the years. He was rather discontented that he did not say goodby to you.
You left a handkerchief at our house. I will take care of it till next summer. I look forward with some longing to that time when I shall have lightened my soul of one chief thing I wanted to do, and be freer to think and feel about other people's work. We shall see you oftener, I hope, and have a great deal more talk than ever we have had before to make amends for our stinted enjoyment of you this summer.
We are very well and unspeakably happy. I know you care to think of other people's happiness -- therefore I tell you such private news. George is plunged in dingy books of science -- sends his loving remembrances to you both, nevertheless. God bless you, dear Barbara. You are very precious to us.
Ever yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 26 December 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 26 December 1860
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, II, 283-284.
Blandford Square | December 26. 60.
My dear Barbara
Your letter 677 came this evening and if I were a journalist, I should say that I "hailed it with delight."
I am not so wicked as I seem in this matter of not writing to you. First, after you left, I was so ailing for several weeks that I had no spirit to write an unnecessary line; then came the troubles of moving and infinite anxieties about pots and kettles; and afterwards, when I quite longed to write to you, I somehow felt it impossible to do so till I had heard some good news of Mrs. Ludlow. Your dear old Nurse, when she brought me your sister's letter (for which, thanks,) promised to come and tell me when the crisis was well over, as I expressed to her my wish to know this on your account; but I have not yet seen her -- I have only seen that there is straw before the door of No. 5. 678 So you perceive I have not been unmindful of what concerns you, though I have made no sign by post.
The bright point in your letter is, that you are in a happy state of mind yourself. For the rest, we must wait, and not be impatient with those who have their inward trials though everything outward seems to smile on them. 679 It seems to those who are differently placed that the time of freedom from strong ties and urgent claims must be very precious for the ends of self-culture, and good, helpful work towards the world at large. But it hardly ever is so. -- As for the "forms and ceremonies," I feel no regret that any should turn to them for comfort, 680 if they can find comfort in them: sympathetically, I enjoy them myself. But I have faith in the working-out of higher possibilities than the Catholic or any other church has presented, and those who have strength to wait and endure, are bound to accept no formula which their whole souls -- their intellect as well as their emotions -- do not embrace with entire reverence. The highest "calling and election" is to do without opium and live through all our pain with conscious, clear-eyed endurance.
You say nothing about the Doctor, so I hope he is flourishing and free from neuralgic pains. We are all right -- comfortable enough in our new house with the prospect of two old-maidish servants, who will want no looking after. And our dear boys are a joy to us -- Charley more good and loving every day -- Thornie prospering at Edinburgh, etc. etc. etc. -- In fact we have no sorrows just now, except my constant inward worret of unbelief in any future of good work on my part. Everything I do seems poor and trivial in the doing, and when it is quite gone from me and seems no longer my own -- then I rejoice in it and think it fine. That is the history of my life.
By the way, we have consulted a barrister, very accomplished in foreign and English law, about that matter broached by your friend Mrs. Brodie. 681 He pronounces it impossible. I am not sorry. I think the boys will not suffer, and for myself I prefer excommunication. I have no earthly thing that I care for, to gain by being brought within the pale of people's personal attention, and I have many things to care for that I should lose -- my freedom from petty worldly torments, commonly called pleasures, and that isolation which really keeps my charity warm instead of chilling it, as much contact with frivolous women would do.
I have been wanting to go to your school again to refresh myself with the young voices there, but I have not been able to do it. My walks have all been taken up with shopping errands, of late. But I hope to get more leisure soon.
Give my love to your sister and Bessie, whom you make me imagine always in a flower-garden -- a strange vision in the midst of our hard frost! Mr. Lewes sends you the love of an anatomist, which, he begs to state, is of a superior quality, quite unlike that of creatures ignorant of the vertebral structure.
God bless you, Think often of your affectionate Friend.
M. E. Lewes.
We both beg to offer our affectionate remembrances to the Doctor. Get Herbert Spencer's new work -- the two first quarterly parts. It is the best thing he has done.

677 From Algiers 22 December 1860.  (Yale.)
678 The Leigh-Smith house at 5 Blandford  Square, where Barbara's sister Bella, Mrs. Ludlow, was ill.
679 "Nanny is better but not well, so  irritable with everything and everybody. I am so sorry. She says herself she is better, but that life is nothing to her at all, nothing in it worth living for and nobody in it she cares to live with -- lively for a young woman of 29 with near  £1000 a year! . . . She ought to fall in love, but she will not, I think. I do not know what to do with her at all." (Mme Bodichon to GE, 22 December.)
680 "Nanny wants a religion with  forms and ceremonies, something present, something of routine, and how many do want it! and what is to give it them? I wish she could go to Mass every day. Now don't think I am going over with Bessie to the C.C. but I do see that the `golden rule' and the matins and vespers she attends do her daily good, make her more cheerful and bright. Bessie has not entered the CC, but really she is more Catholic than 900 out of every 1000 of the Pope's children. We talk very much of all the bearings of this question. B's great argument is what I wish for, that liberty, order, justice for all, and succour for the sick and poor is better supplied to the world by the CC than by any other organization. I don't agree to the argument; 1st if it is true of the past or present, it is no reason why it should be true in the future, and I deny that it is true." (Ibid.)
681 Wife of the chemist Benjamin Collins  Brodie, the younger (1817-80), was a daughter of John Vincent Thompson, serjeant-at-law. She and her husband were friends of Mme Bodichon. (B. Stephen, Emily Davies and Girton College, 1927, p. 363.) The reference to "foreign and English law" suggests that there had been some consideration of GHL's obtaining a divorce abroad.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 26 April 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 26 April 1880
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 26. 80.
My dear Barbara
Your cook-housekeeper's place would be a welcome one to many. If one could only bring the right person and the right place together! I have mentioned the possibility to my servants.
The news that you are going on well in health was most welcome. But I do not cease to be vexed that I did not see more of you when you were in London.
You must not tell Miss Marks to call upon me, for I shall probably not be in town. I have changed my plans and am going abroad for a little while. But I shall write to you again before long and tell you more. For the present adieu and bless you.
Yours ever
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 25 September 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 25 September 1868
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extract published: Cross, III, 60-61.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
September 25. 68.
Barbara carissima
Two minutes before your letter came this morning at breakfast, you had been in my mind. Alas, the fine weather is no more -- unless it rises again and makes a new Easter. One may hope for change to anything in this climate. Your kind pretty project would have been forbidden to us for next week, apart from the weather, because we have an indefinite engagement for one day or other in it to three people who are to come and dine with us. They were to have come this week and have been put off till next, and they are people we care about a great deal. Also, George has got a little bit of work to do for a friend and he is very anxious to get it finished. But under all these hindrances there remains to us the pleasure of being grateful to you for your affectionate wish to see us. I can imagine how delicious your country home has been under the glorious skies we have been having -- glorious even in London. Yesterday, we had Doctor and Mrs. Congreve with their two adopted children, 817 and went with them to the Zool. Gardens; and on our return about five o'clock I could not help pausing and exclaiming at the exquisite beauty of the light on Regents Park, exalting it into something that the young Turner would have wanted to paint.
We went to Leeds last week -- saw your favourite David Cox and thought of you the while. Certainly there was nothing finer there in landscape than that Welsh funeral. Among the figure painters Watts and old Philip are supreme. 818 We went on from Leeds to Bolton and spent a day in wandering through the grand woods on the banks of the Wharfe. Altogether our visit to Yorkshire was extremely agreeable, our host Dr. Allbut is a good clever graceful man, enough to enable one to be cheerful under the horrible smoke of ugly Leeds, and the fine hospital which he says is admirably fitted for its purpose is another mitigation. You would like to see the tasteful subdued ornamentation in the rooms which are to be the sick wards. Each physician is accumulating ornamental objects for his own ward -- Chromo-lithographs etc. -- such as will soothe sick eyes. But the Leeds work people, we were told, are sadly coarse beer-soaked bodies, with pleasures, mostly of the brutal sort, and the mill-girls "epicene" creatures that make one shudder.
It was quite cold in that northerly region, and we sat close to the fender every day when we were not out of doors. Yesterday I flaunted muslin and was warm -- this morning I am in a flannel dressing gown. Such is life!
Our best regards to the Doctor and thanks for his hospitable wish.
Always your affectionate
Marian.
Your picture keeps a memory of sunshine on my wall even on this dark morning.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 25 November [1869]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 25 November [1869]
MS: Huntington Library. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | November 25.
My dear Barbara
I am very glad to know where you are, and to know also that you are in enjoyable circumstances. We have been at home since the beginning of last week, having benefited greatly by the beautiful quietude of Limpsfield, a delicious spot in Surrey far away even from the sound of railways. The air of London is always depressing, by comparison, but we retain some of our country vigour -- George, especially, seems to have shown improvement since his return. We are beginning to see our friends again, and externally our life is becoming what it used to be. But I have a deep sense of change within, and of a permanently closer companionship with death.
The months pass so quickly that it will not seem long before you are with us again. Mr. Burton sent me a letter to Limpsfield in which he expressed his regret that he had not been able to see you before his departure. I shall write to him by and by, to Naples, where he expected to be at the end of the year. He seemed, the last time I saw him, to be much exhilarated by the prospect of his journey, and I do hope that nothing will happen to spoil his pleasure.
It delights me to hear that the Doctor enjoyed his summer, and his having an easy passage will perhaps defer the need for you to make new arrangements as to a summer residence.
We are not likely to move again during the winter. Mr. Lewes's mother is a tie that makes a distant journey uneasy to us.
Please to paint the afternoon sunlight gleaming on the sails of the fishing-boats, from under a lifted cloud.
Always your loving
Marian.
The Meltray book or pamphlet is not yet come.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 23 August 1873
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 23. 1873.
Dear Barbara
We are just come home, but we shall not be in town more than ten days before going into the country (to Blackbrook, near Bromley) for at least two months.
I am wondering what can have determined you to brave again the voyage to Algiers, but I trust that you are now strong enough to endure the evils both of sea and land. I will not tell you anything about the vicissitudes of our journeying, which ended only this morning. You will come to us and hear.
My best and affectionate regards to your sister and to Miss Edwards.
I am unable to interpret the "little pots" which are mysterious to me as the seven vials.
Yours always lovingly
Marian.

Educated at Downing College, Cambridge, he was for some time an assistant master at Wellington College. He was ordained deacon at Oxford, 21 December 1865, but never took further orders; in October 1867 he became Curate of Christ Church, Marylebone. He contributed articles on art, literature, and religion to the Pall Mall Gazette, Macmillan's, Vanity Fair and other periodicals. Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 22 October 1869
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 22 October 1869
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank. | October 22. 69.
Dearest Barbara
Thanks for your tender words. It has cut deeper than I expected -- that he is gone and I can never make him feel my love any more. Just now all else seems trivial compared with the powers of delighting and soothing a heart that is in need.
We go tomorrow morning to Limpsfield, in Surrey, to nice people in an old-fashioned farm house, that we knew of beforehand. 112 It is an unspeakable comfort to have an immediate retreat. Later on, we shall perhaps go to the Isle of Wight, but, just now we are unequal to journeying and arrangements with new people.
Ever yours affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 22 November 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 22 November 1877
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 22. 77.
Dearest Barbara
I was very glad to have your nephew's letter giving me some news of you, and I trust that if he were to write again now he could tell me of your more rapid progress in strength. Here the weather alternates daily from dismal raininess and mugginess to clear, sharp cheeriness. At Hastings I hope you are spared the dark days.
The day before yesterday we drove to Mrs. Allingham's to see her pictures -- a charming little collection. 773 We were heartily glad to see her looking healthy again, and there were also the children to admire, the boy a striking beauty from his rare tone of colour.
Everything is well with us according to the town standard, except that you are away and not yet robust. We have seen many pleasant friends on our Sundays, and now our Saturday concerts have begun to give us our weekly musical food. The sadder part of one's life is reading the Times reports about France, 774 and imagining the sufferings of the poor unglorified fellows in the ranks both Russian and Turkish.
By the way, have you read Tourgu'e9neff's Terre Neuve? 775 It is worth reading. But of course you take care -- or Miss Scott 776 takes care for you -- not to let your head get tired. And I too must take care not to tire you with too many suggestions.
God bless you, dear. Offer my best regards to Miss Scott.
Your ever loving
Marian.

December 21.
Dearest B.
O what a lovely basket! It is a little oasis in the dreariness of this morning's fog. Bless you for it -- and come up to town looking and feeling as well as you deserve -- or better if possible.
We are going to dine with our children on Christmas day, and to visit the grave at Highgate in the morning if the weather will let us. 121
I hope your Christmas will be very happy among the dear kith and kin. I cling strongly to kith and kin, even though they reject me.
Ever yours lovingly
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 2 October 1876
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | Scalands Gate | Roberts-bridge | Hawkhurst. Postmark: ST. JOHNS WOOD | C 5 | OC 2 | 76 | N.W; HAWKHURST | A | OC 3 | 76; ROBERTSBRIDGE | A | OC 3 | 76. Published: Cross, III, 290-291.
N.B. | October 2. 76.
My dear Barbara
My blessing on you for your sweet letter which I count among the blessings given to me. Yes. Women can do much for the other women (and men) to come. My impression of the good there is in all unselfish efforts is continually strengthened. Doubtless many a ship is drowned on expeditions of discovery or rescue, and precious freights lie buried. But there was the good of manning and furnishing the ship with a great purpose before it set out.
We are going into Cambridgeshire this week, and are watching the weather with private views.
I have had some very interesting letters both from Jews and from Christians about Deronda. Part of the scene at the club is translated into Hebrew in a German-Jewish newspaper. On the other hand a Christian (highly accomplished) thanks me for embodying the principles by which Christ wrought and will conquer. This is better than the laudation of readers who cut the book into scraps and talk of nothing in it but Gwendolen. 530 I meant everything in the book to be related to everything else there.
I quite enter into Miss Jekyll's 531 view of negative beauty. Life tends to accumulate [messes] about one, and it is hard to rid oneself of them because of the associations attached. I get impatient sometimes and long, as Andrew Fairservice would say, to "kaim off the fleas" 532 as one does in a cathedral spoiled by monuments out of keeping with the pillars and walls.
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 2 July [1869]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 2 July [1869]
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
The Priory, | North Bank, | Regents Park.
Friday July 2.
Dearest Barbara
It is difficult to say how Thornie is. He varies greatly, sometimes remaining a day or two without pain, and then having severe returns and taking more and more morphia; 868 sometimes seeming torpid and full of indescribable uneasiness, and at other times looking bright and showing his old spirits. The doctors seem to be as much in the dark as we are, but they all -- Dr. Bastian, in addition to the others -- concur in saying that the glandular disorder is more serious than the spinal. My chief anxiety now is that Mr. Lewes should get into a calm and ordered way of life, such as will make the least evil for him of this long trouble. His health was so wretched last week that Paget said to him "You must go away." So Gertrude and Charlie took our places on Monday, and we went to Sevenoaks, hoping to stay the whole week. But the gloomy sky and cold wind drove us back yesterday. However, George is better, and I hope has recovered from the bodily disturbance which he needlessly brought on by taking a too large dose of podophillin 869 -- if you know that important-sounding name.
I felt sure you would like to know how the boy was going on, and so I determined to overcome the obstacle of having nothing new or definite to say about him. I feel hopeful as to his ultimate recovery because he shows surprizing revivals of force and spirits.
I fear that your country pleasures are diminished by the cold winds and cloudy skies.
Always yours lovingly
Marian.
I have read Mill's Book, 870 and think the second chapter excellent; the 3d and 4th not so strong and well argued as they ought to have been coming from him.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 19 May 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 19 May 1877
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 19. 77.
My dear Barbara
I have been rather annoyed by Mr. Lewes having told me only yesterday that some unpleasantness had arisen between Miss Bernard and the students at Girton about the invitation sent to me. 679 This puts me in rather an unpleasant position, for in accepting the invitation (conditionally), I promised to write to Miss M'fcller 680 whenever I went to
Cambridge, and propose a day and hour for my visit. What am I to do now? We are engaged to go to Mr. Sidgwick's on the 31st. If I don't keep my word to Miss M'fcller, will she understand that you have communicated the state of the case to me? Or will you write to her and tell her why I remain silent?
Mr. Lewes says that you suggested my calling simply to see the college in the ordinary way, but this affair with Miss Bernard makes me disinclined to appear there at all. All I desire is to be set right with Miss M'fcller, towards whom I feel in danger of seeming to act very unscrupulously. I am sorry to trouble you, but I can see no way out of the disagreeable position I am in without learning more from you.
We are going to start for Oxford but shall be at home again on Tuesday evening.
Your loving
Marian.

"With much personal distinction and charm, Miss Bernard had a cool judgment and a manner of austere dignity, which was something of a bar to intimacy with the students, though beneath it there lay a real interest in their welfare." Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 19 August 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 19 August 1863
Text: Copy lent by the Countess of Iddesleigh. Extracts published: Cross, II, 363-364.
Blandford Sq. | August 19. 63.
Dear Barbara
Your letter brought me needful comfort. I seldom feel any emanation of sadness from you, but I had a little consciousness of that sort when you came to say goodby, looking so weary and telling us that the dear Doctor was ill.
I was at Worthing 182 when your letter came, spending all my daylight hours out of doors and trying with all my might to get health and cheerfulness. I will tell you the true reason why I did not go to Hastings. I thought you would be all the better for not having that solicitation of your kindness that the fact of my presence there might have caused. What you needed was precisely to get away from people to whom you would inevitably want to be doing something friendly, instead of giving yourself up to passive enjoyment.
Else, of course I should have liked everything you write about and invite me to -- especially the visit to Nannie in her imprisonment. I get a great deal of pleasure out of your assurance that the thought of seeing me brought some added brightness into her eyes.
We only got home last night and I suppose we shall hardly be able to leave town again till after the two younger boys have left us and after we have moved into the new house. Thornie's destination is still doubtful for us. His companions in failure are getting up a memorial to Sir Charles Wood, 183 showing that their case is peculiarly hard and unjust, since the announcement that the second examination, contrary to precedent, was to be final, was not made until it was too late for them to take the additional year they would otherwise have taken for study before presenting themselves for the first examination.
We have not yet received an answer from Mr. Heald, so that at present we do not even know whether he will still accept pupils.
Since I saw you I have had some sweet woman's tenderness shown me by Mrs. Hare, 184 the <wife> widow of Archdeacon Hare, and the sister of Frederick Maurice. This is between ourselves. I will tell you more when I see you.
I know how you are enjoying the country. I have just been having the joy myself. The wide sky, the not-London, makes a new creature of me in half an hour. I wonder then why I am ever depressed -- why I am so shaken by agitations. I come back to London, and again the air is full of demons. God bless you.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 18 March 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 18 March 1867
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
March 18th 1867.
Dearest Barbara
We got home only the day before yesterday (Saturday the 16th) and there I found Bessie's letter enclosing your own few words in pencil written from Marseilles. That was the first news I had had of your illness, and it was a painful shock to me -- all the more because the information I got left me still so ignorant as to the nature of your illness, and the reasons why you are moving northward into a horrible climate. 601 Pray let me hear somehow what has been the matter with you, and where you are going. I found also the sheet of your Spanish letters giving an account of your journeying from Malaga to Telems'e1n so that I have the whole now with the exception of the "Earthquake continued" which you sent to Bessie.
I know you will like to hear that our journey has been a great success in restoring George's health, but I have no heart to write about anything else while I think of you ill in the horrible cold of Paris. We find hard winter here after having hot summer and mosquitoes at Seville. It is snowing this morning and the wind is howling so as to make one pity every mortal who has to cross the Channel. We were as fortunate as possible, for even in summer we never had a finer passage than on Saturday.
We crowned our delights in Spain with the sight of the pictures at Madrid. They and the Cathedral at Seville are enough to justify western civilization, with all its faults, and transcend any amount of diaper patterns even if they were coloured as the Moors coloured. Not that I mean to be irreverent to the Orientals, but I am thankful that Europe has been filled with ideas over and above what they ever possessed.
But never mind what I think about all that -- I care now to know about you. Let me know what you can. Love to Bessie and thanks for her note. If you see Madame Mohl call me to her remembrance, and say that I wrote to her from Biarritz, before we set out for Spain.
Ever yours lovingly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Relation: 601 Mme Bodichon had fallen ill in  Algiers and her husband had sent her home earlier than usual. At Paris she met Bessie Parkes and suggested that they take a house in the country where Barbara could rest and paint. Mme Mohl told them of a house at La Celle St. Cloud to be let by Mme Hilaire Belloc, which they took at once. Bessie became attached to Mme Belloc's son Louis, and was married to him the following September. (Mrs. Belloc Lowndes, "I, Too, Have Lived in Arcadia," New York, 1942, pp. 1-6, 58.)

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 17 June 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 17 June 1867
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 17. 67.
Dearest Barbara
I was going to write to you, even if you had not sent me Mrs. Mohl's letter, just to send a word of love and to express my uneasiness that I was not able to enjoy your second visit as I should have done if my mind had not been distrait by the opera going. But thou knowest -- if not all things, at least -- that I love thee.
Tell Mrs. Mohl that what I am doing now is not suitable for translation by her friend, but that when, or if, I write another novel, I will remember her wish and let her know. I refused Hachette's offer for Adam Bede, 635 and he has not applied to me since. It has never seemed to me worth while to be ill-translated for the sake of £25 or £30, and on quite impersonal grounds I object to the encouragement of poor literary work. Poor writing is one of the things that ought never to be done and that everybody is morally the worse for.
Pray tell Madame Mohl that I shall be delighted to see her, and only hope we shall not have left town before she can come to me. Assure her that she is kept in a favourite corner of my memory, and that I am glad of any sign that she ever thinks about me.
Get well, dear thing and love always
Your
M. E. L.
