Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 17 January 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 17 January 1878
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 324-325.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 17. 78.
Dearest Barbara
I wish with all my heart that our house (at Witley, of course, you mean) could be ready to receive you at the end of March. But it will not be furnished -- I fear, even, it will not be dry by that time. Some building that is now going on will not, according to contract, be finished until February 3. 6 and after that there is colouring, papering, painting etc. to be done before beds, chairs, and tables can be got into it. I am very sorry. You said, I remember, that you would like to try that neighbourhood, and it seems to me that another house thereabout might be found for you by the time you will want it. There are various pretty houses to be let for months or seasons -- some of them frequently inhabited by artists -- about Haslemere, Godalming and Witley.
I was delighted to see your handwriting -- still more to read your cheerful news, which was a much needed bulletin, Miss Greatorex 7 not having yet made her appearance. Please give my love to Miss Marks, and grateful regards to Miss Scott for watching over you. Mr. and Mrs. Allingham were here the Sunday before last, both looking admirably well and in great force. Mrs. Allingham asked anxiously for news of you, but my latest then was Miss Marks's letter.
Yes -- it is a comfort to one in the midst of so many dispiriting European signs, that France has come so far through her struggle. And no doubt you are rejoicing too that London University has opened all its degrees to women.
On the other and gloomy side, poor Octavia Hill is peremptorily ordered away from her work by the doctor, and is going to start for Italy next Monday. 8
I think we know no reading more amusing than the Times just now. [Les 'c9preuves de Ra'efssa] by Henry Gr'e9ville, 9 is a French novel turning on Russian life which we have just had from the London Library, but it has no merit beyond theatrical cleverness. We are deep among the gravities now. I have been reading aloud Green's first vol. of his new, larger History of the English People, 10 and this evening have begun Lecky's Hist. of England in the XVIIIth century 11 -- in fact we are dull old fogies who are ill-informed about anything that is going on of an amusing kind. On Monday we took a youth to the Pantomime, but I found it a melancholy business. The dear old story of Puss in Boots was mishandled in an exasperating way, and every incident as well as pretence of a character turned into a motive for the most vulgar kind of dancing. I came away with a sick headache from which I am only today recovered. It is too cruel that one can't get anything innocent as a spectacle for the children!
If I have an opportunity of getting news about a house likely to suit you, I will let you have the information at once.
Mr. Lewes sends his best love, but is quite barren of suggestions about books -- buried in pink and lilac periodicals of a physiological sort, and preoccupied with the case of a man who has an artificial larynx with which he talks very well. 12 What do you say to the Phonograph, 13 which can report gentlemen's bad speeches with all their stammering?
Your always loving
M. E. L.

December 17.
My dear Barbara
Miss Julia Wedgwood 119 will probably be preoccupied now until after Christmas, but whenever she is sufficiently at liberty to write to me proposing to come on any day not earlier than 'bd past 3, I shall be very happy to see her. It is necessary for me to know beforehand to prevent disappointment.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 16 November 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 16 November 1874
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 16. 74.
Dearest Barbara
A prospective welcome to you! We will find you an edifying book when you come -- Tylor's Early History of Mankind, 158 if you have not read it, or something else as good. Meanwhile you ought to be in great mental vigour compared with your fellow-mortals who muddle and enfeeble themselves with reading.
I am delighted to hear so good an account of the Doctor, and I trust that your soul is at rest now from any gnawing anxieties.
I have hired a very promising housemaid, 159 found for me by our dear Mrs. Senior who -- did you know? -- is laid prostrate by illness and ordered to lay herself up for two or three years at least. She looks like a white angel in her little bed.
Please give my kindest remembrances to the beautiful little Aunt 160 -- or rather, ask her to remember me kindly -- for I think our forms of message are very conceited and ungraceful. How do we know that our kind remembrances are wanted? Whereas we do know whether we want the kind remembrances of others.
Come in for a bit of lunch at 'bd past 1 some day -- that is the best way of getting a chat. And then we will drive you on some errand.
Yours always
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 16 November 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 16 November 1868
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 65.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 16. 68.
Dearest Barbara
Thanks for your little note of notification. No oracle would dare to predict what will be our next migration. Don't be surprized if we go to the borders of the White Sea, to escape the fitful fast and loose, hot and cold, of the London climate.
The Chromo-lithograph awaited me on my return from Matlock. Many thanks. When you have occasion to write, tell me, if you can remember, what is the price. It is very pretty, though not what your words had foreshadowed.
We enjoyed our journey to the North. It was a great experience to me to see the stupendous iron-works at Sheffield, and then, for a variety, we went to the quiet and beauty of Matlock, and I recognized all the spots I had carried in my memory for more than five and twenty years. 836 I drove through that region with my Father when I was a young grig -- not very full of hope about my woman's-future. I am one of those perhaps exceptional people whose early childish dreams were much less happy than the real outcome of life.
G. is but so-so. He sends his love, which is always whole and sound in spite of dyspepsia. You will divine my sentences, if you can only half read them. I am scribbling on my lap, with a soft background.
Always yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 15 May 1877
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 15. 77.
Dear Barbara
We will ourselves certainly give £10 towards paying Miss Gr'fcner's 666 expenses, but we have not yet been able to think of anyone else who would do the same.
Pray bring Madame Mario to see us again. But bear in mind that on Sunday the 27th -- which probably will be our last Sunday in London -- Holmes 667 the violinist is coming to play, with Mrs. Vernon Lushington 668 to accompany him. They are to be here about 4 o'clock, and I beseech you to come in early -- between 3 and 4 -- so as not to disturb any music that may have been begun. For Mr. Holmes is nervous. And don't mention to anyone else that he and Mrs. L. are coming, lest the audience should be larger than he wishes.
Please tell Madame Mario that I have received an interesting parcel of books from Italy, with pretty words of her husband's on his card. I am much pleased to have such a present from her and him.
We are working a little too hard at [pleasure] just now. This morning we are going for the third time to a Wagner rehearsal, at 10 o'clock. 669
I could scribble a great deal of gossip to you, but I have another letter to write before we start.
Always your loving
Marian.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 15 May [1876]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory 21 N.B. | May 15.
My dear Barbara
I have not written to you this long while because I was uncertain about your movements. But yesterday Miss Rintoul 476 got me the information that you were in England and sent for letters to B[landford] Sq.
I would have followed your indication about Miss Marks, but for the continuous bad health which has made my inevitable engagements too much for me. (I don't know her address, but I could have sent a letter for her to Miss Townsend). 477 And now I have no time to make an appointment for her to come to me on a week-day, while the remaining Sundays before we go away are likely to be too crowded for me to have any conversation with her. Perhaps when you see her you will mention, if it seems desirable, that I should have wished much to see her if I had been in possession of health and leisure.
We want to get away at the beginning of June. I suppose you are not coming to town. So take my parting benediction, believe in my stedfast love, and send me word, if you can, that all things have gone on well from the last accounts up to the present time.
We go to Oxford on Saturday, for the Sunday. After that I should be glad if we had no more than one Sunday at home.
Always your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 15 March 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 15 March 1878
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Madame Bodichon | 6 Robertson Terrace | Hastings. Postmarks: ST JOHNS WOOD N.W | A 3 | MR 15 | 78; HASTINGS | D | MR 15 | 78. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 15. 78.
Dearest Barbara
It makes me rather unhappy this morning to think of your having had a new drawback. But perhaps no delicate person could escape something of the kind under the fluctuating severities of the weather. I too have been tormented with sore throats and seem to get a fresh one each time I go out.
Marquis's 28 letters are charming and thoroughly satisfactory in their indications of her moral nature. Be sure that I bear her in my mind with affectionate interest both for her sake and yours.
Dear Bessie came to see me one Sunday a little while ago. 29 I always get a fresh sense of her goodness and sweetness of nature whenever I have a glimpse of her.
Mrs. Allingham, who looks very blooming again and seems to be painting with great zest, asks for news of you with much feeling whenever I see her. And so does Mrs. Burne Jones.
But I will tell you what dissatisfies me in the scheme of the Universe: it is, that you are fixing yourself in Sussex while we are fixing ourselves in Surrey. And railways are no help for it. I wonder whether you have found a suitable house ad interim, as you desired to do.
God bless you, dear. Let somebody write us a card to say how you are by and by.
Yours ever lovingly
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 15 January 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 15 January 1866
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
1 North Bank | January 15. 1866.
My dear Barbara
My not writing is due rather to the want of health, which robs me of energy for things that are not peremptory, than to want of time. One can always find time to scribble a letter, if the spaces between work are not filled with malaise. George and I have both been more suffering than usual, 686 but we are always grumblers, so there is no use in dwelling on what is so far from exceptional. Your illness is much more of a case to inquire about. Why did you not tell me what was the matter with you? -- Palpitation -- or what else? And are you well again? I am terribly afraid that you are worrying yourself about the unchangeable -- looking for fowls' milk or some other impossibility -- when half the great lesson of life is to adapt one's soul to the irremediable.
Confess, and be healed by adopting the prescriptions you have had over and over again. There are no other. Certain human natures, and certain periods of life for some natures, have limits as immovable as the Jura. You may say that one can't help feeling anguish, and that is true enough. But the anguish is fed by false hope, as fire is fed by fuel. However, I will not go on preaching across France and the Mediterranean: perhaps by this time you are bright again, well in health and able to paint.
Life is very interesting to us in spite of disordered mucous membranes. Great subjects become greater to us, and for that reason smaller ones lose their power of tormenting. As soon as Bertie is gone to his farming again, we shall migrate to Tunbridge Wells for a fortnight and try the effect of the purer air to take our daily walks in. George gets thinner and thinner, and the less there is of him, as with the Sybil's papers, the more precious he becomes.
Poor Mr. Neuberg had a sad accident in driving his little carriage, about six weeks ago. His sister was pitched out and had a contusion of the head which has caused a prolonged state of feebleness. He says it made him feel twenty years older. But she is recovering without having incurred erisypelas, which was the great dread.
I have been delighted to know of Bessie's final decision against the marriage. She seems bright and happy, and courageous in the hope of working with her pen so as to eke out her income.
You remembered the beautiful-eyed, clever, amiable Lord Edward Seymour? 687 Did you see the account of his death -- after amputation of a leg, made necessary by a gunshot? I was grieved by his death. He was not one of the ordinary young Liberals, who echo the catchwords of a party. He had genuine opinions, and strove after their precise expression.
When you write again, remember to tell me particularly about the progress of Nannie's health. I want to hear that she is thoroughly restored to all the enjoyments of life -- that she can walk, ride, paint, and be active in the many valuable ways her nature prompts. Yesterday, Mr. Hamerton, whose books and (bad) pictures you are acquainted with, came to be introduced to me. 688 He is a very unaffected man, but not of transparent porcelain, rather of good honest earthenware. He really writes well, but I have been told by others as well as you that his pictures are a painful non sequitur to all his able theorizing. "So vast is art, so narrow human wit." 689
We were much interested by your account of all you gathered about Courbet, and after reading your letter I was less sceptical as to Proudhon's conception of his genius. Apropos of Proudhon, in the Revue Contemporaine, 690 there are four interesting papers by Sainte Beuve, giving a sketch of Proudhon from his correspondence which was unusually copious and representative of the man. If the last 4 Numbers of the Revue Cont[emporain]e come in your way, read them.
Always, dear Barbara
Your faithfully affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 15 February 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 15 February 1862
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | February 15. 1862.
My dear Barbara
If Miss Allen 22 had not given me good news about you, I should have been urged to write and ask you for a letter; but I think it is a reasonable law that the one who takes wing should be the first to write
Everything has gone well with us since you left, except -- a great, great exception! -- livers and stomachs. Mr. Lewes has had much suffering of the usual head-achy, indigestive kind, and I too have had my share. Otherwise we have had no troubles but the public troubles -- anxiety about the war with America, and sympathy with the poor Queen. It really distresses one more than most general questions, to read the evidence of the low moral conditions -- the barbarism of feeling made all the more hideous by the pretension to advancement -- which discloses itself in the acts and writing of the Americans. My best consolation is that an example on so tremendous a scale of the need for the education of mankind through the affections and sentiments as a basis for true development, will have a strong influence on all thinkers, and be a check to the arid, narrow antagonism which in some quarters is held to be the only form of liberal thought.
Charlie was pleased to be remembered by you with a message of love. He is more and more precious to us, growing in inward grace, and I think somewhat also in outward. Your friend Mr. Scharf 24 has taken to him quite affectionately, and often has him for a quiet evening at his own house. Thornie too seems to be working and in every way improving at Edinburgh, and we are hoping, though without too much confidence, that he will get well through the Indian Examination in July.
George, in spite of ailments, has done a great deal of work since we said goodby to you. He has fairly begun what we have long contemplated as a happiness for him -- a History of Science, and has written so thorough an analysis and investigation of Aristotle's Natural Science, that he feels it will make an epoch for the men who are interested at once in the progress of modern science and in the question, how far Aristotle went both in the observation of facts and in their theoretic combination -- a question never yet cleared up, after all these ages. This work makes him very "jolly," but his dear face looks very pale and narrow. Those only can thoroughly feel the meaning of death who know what is perfect love.
I think I have no news to tell you. We do not, at present, think of going abroad till the Autumn. Charlie has his holiday in May, but we shall arrange for him to spend it at Geneva with my friends the d'Albert's, who will make a pleasant home for him. -- I am glad to hear from Miss Allen that your sister 25 is enjoying her life at Rome, and still more glad that you have perfect comfort about Mrs. Ludlow and her boy. I imagine the General's bliss! 26
George sends his best love. He and I would fain have known a few details about the Doctor's life in these months. It will do us good to see his face beside yours in May. You are both mingled with very much that is constantly in our thoughts, and your names are often turning up even on the surface of our talk. I am in a furor of scribbling in order to get done and carry this to the post. If I dislike letter-writing, I am at least prompt in answering letters, am I not?
I hope the word "success," means many beautiful, or rather, a few beautiful pictures.
God bless you -- that is not a false word -- however many false ideas may have been hidden under it. No -- not false ideas, but temporary ones, caterpillars and chrysalids of future ideas.
Farewell -- Ever thine
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 12 May 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 12 May 1863
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | May 12. 63.
My dear Barbara
I was very much in want of that proof in black and white that you were not only "all right" but that part of the rightness consisted in sometimes thinking of me.
Yes! we shall be in town in June. Your coming would be reason good enough, but we have others -- chiefly, that we are up to the ears in Boydom and imperious parental duties. All is as happy and prosperous with us as heart can lawfully desire, except my health. I have been a mere wretch for several months past. You will come to me like the morning sunlight and make me a little less of a flaccid cabbage plant.
It is a very pretty life you are leading at Hastings with your painting all morning and fair mothers and children to look at the rest of the day. You will bring still better news, I hope, when you come to town. That about Nannie was especially gratifying to me, because in her letter, lively as it was, there were phrases that gave me rather a melancholy notion of her health.
The insects can be waited for a long while, as they will keep, and Mr. Lewes is not tempted to microscopy just now. I am terribly frightened about Mrs. W. 156 She wrote to me telling me that we were sure to suit each other, neither of us holding the opinions of the "moutons de Panurge." 157 Nothing could have been more decisive of the opposite prospect to me. If there is one attitude more odious than any other of the many attitudes of "Knowingness" it is that air of lofty superiority to the vulgar. However, she will soon find out that I am a very common-place woman.
I have been fasting so long from all news about you, that I shall have a voracious appetite for all you can tell of these six months.
Our boy, who brightens up at your name, is as good or better than ever, only his beard grows with a vicious rapidity -- the downy time forever gone!
George shares all my loves and cares, you know -- and not least those which concern you and the dear Doctor -- our image of human uprightness, bodily and spiritual.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 12 December 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 12 December 1868
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 68.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 12. 68.
Dearest B.
Since I wrote to you last we have not been anywhere away from home, where I think we shall stay till some time after Christmas, and then perhaps take a long journey.
I fear you had rather a doleful s'e9jour at Ventnor. In London the weather was, moderately speaking, hideous, for perhaps a fortnight, but of late we have been having some clear days with such delicate effects of high cloud and faint blue that even the squares and broader streets of London have seemed rather like Paradise by comparison with what had gone before. I am much better and am less than usually conscious of my body. George is variable -- quickly worse and quickly better, but always showing an inability to bear a long stretch either of work or recreative exercise.
I should like to know how you are, and also to hear from you some better prospects about Miss Edwards' health than I gathered from Miss Davies, who told me the other day of Miss E's consumptive symptoms. 845 I had imagined her to be a strong woman.
We have been having a little company, and are rejoicing to think that our duties of this sort are done for the present. We like our studies and our dual solitude too well to feel company desirable more than one day a week.
Nevertheless, I hope you will stray to London some time soon and interrupt us. I saw your house in Blandford Sq. lit up the other evening as we passed it, so I conclude that Mr. Hastings 846 is still inhabiting it, but I understood from you that he would be tenant for only a few weeks, so that if you are inclined to try London I suppose there will be no obstacle in your way.
Mr. Burton has been come back from Ireland some weeks. He looks exceedingly well in health -- quite robust. And he has painted a portrait in Ireland, so that I hope he has now made the beginning in a new era of work. I have not seen him except when other friends have been present, and have not been able to talk to him, except as one of a circle. G. has been to see his old friend W. B. Scott 847 and is delighted to see his achievements as a painter. Also he (Mr. Scott) has dined with us and has charmed me by his simplicity and genuine talk.
George sends his love, which this evening is happily not headachy love. I wish our affection may be with you as some little cheering influence through the dark months. We hardly estimate enough the difference of feeling that would come to us if we did not imagine friendly souls scattered here and there in places that make the chief part of the world so far as we have known it.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 12 August 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 12 August 1864
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library. Brief extract published: Haight, George Eliot, p. 377.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
August 12. 64.
Dearest Barbara
I am glad to think of you in your "cottage near a wood" under these fine skies. But it was a pity that we didn't see you that Sunday, and that you didn't see the Orang. She is more touching and amiable than the little chimpanzee at the Crystal Palace, but not so clever and dramatic. Chim has a great piece of heavy drapery in his cage, with which he drapes himself in a magnificent mysterious manner, as if he were trying to find his way to an art that would express his very big thoughts.
About dear Bessie, I will try to think that all will come right. 621 On these matters we outsiders can never judge otherwise than blunderingly. Relations that seem to us full of promise are the preparation of misery, and vice versa. That stanza you quote would serve as a motto for half the history of my life: what pain I have had from the ills that have never befallen me!
Apropos of that interesting subject, self, I have been having my likeness taken "positively for the last time" or rather by the last person, namely by Mr. F. W. Burton. 622 George saw it for the first time the other day, and was in raptures with it, whereupon Mr. Burton told him it was his (George's). I don't know myself whether it is good or not.
George has been very poorly -- Dr. Brinton 623 says solely from feebleness -- and he looks thinner and thinner. He is so good. You are one of those who guess how good he is. God bless you, Barbara, if only for that.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 11 November 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 11 November 1873
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 219-220.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 11. 73.
My dear Barbara
Glad to hear at last that you have arrived safely in Algiers. I imagined that you must have got there long ago. It is at least something to sing a Jubilate over, that one crossing is done.
We are altogether jolly, save and except that since our return to town on the 31st. Mr. Lewes has had one of his long headaches. 876 He had got much better during the latter part of our stay at Blackbrook, and we had become very fond of the neighbourhood. The walks and drives round us were delightfully varied -- commons, wooded lanes, wide pastures -- and we felt regretfully that we were hardly likely to find again a country house so secluded in a well-inhabitated region. But the house would not do in its actual state, and our landlord allowed us to give up the agreement by which we must have kept it for a year. We proposed to pay him double for our two months, and now the place is entirely off our hands. There is a chance that he may not let it, and may make repairs and alterations to suit us, in which case he will give us the refusal, unless we find another house to our minds beforehand.
But we mean to keep up this house in town, so that we may see people here and have none but choice visitors in the country.
I suppose Nannie has also arrived, or probably arrived before you. Please give my love to her and Miss Blythe, and tell Nannie that I valued much her last unanswered letter to me. I adore correspondents who write to me letters brimfull and running over without asking for any return. I also adore two or three who write me a scrap to say that they are safe and only demand a scrap of the same sort from me.
I was interested to see in last week's Spectator that there is a translation from the Doctor's writings in "Temple Bar." 877 Of course you know all about it. I wonder what he has thought of the Legitimist drama, and the fresh budding of Catholicism? 878
We have seen few people at present. The George Howards 879 are come from a delicious lonely s'e9jour in a tower of Bamborough Castle! -- and he has brought many sketches home. That lodging would suit you -- wouldn't it? -- The castle is in the hands of trustees, who let one tower to fortunate applicants. A castle on a rock washed by the sea seems to me just a paradise for you.
We have been reading John Mill's Autobiography, like the rest of the world. The account of his early education and the presentation of his Father are admirable, but there are some pages in the latter half that one would have liked to be different. 880
Goodbye, dear. Send me some word how you are by and by, because I shall be anxious about you.
G., I am sure, sends his love with mine -- which is that of your faithful
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 11 March 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 11 March 1862
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | March 11. 1862.
Dear Barbara
All my books have been translated by M. d'Albert, except the Clerical Scenes, and I am not certain that they have been translated. Mrs. Blackwell some time ago asked leave to translate them and Silas Marner. 39 I could not give the leave for the latter as M. d'Albert had already undertaken it, but I did, for the Clerical Scenes. Whether she acted on that leave, or gave up the whole affair because she could not have Silas Marner, I don't know. But since your account of the Algerian lady's powers is not encouraging I think you had better simply tell her that I cannot authorize any translation on her part. In strictness, I have no power to forbid it, after the first year of publication.
We shall be glad to see you safe across the waters once more. You may well bring brightness, living in perpetual summer as you do. We are come back this very evening from Englefield Green, where we have been staying, with much enjoyment, at the pretty little inn you recommended to us. The good Mrs. Bone there asked with interest about you. It is just the neighbourhood in which we should like to live: -- the air is true country air, clear from the London haze, which Richmond is not. But unhappily the railway is impracticably far-off and infrequent in its trains.
The Doctor's life looks very paradisaic in your description -- only there were no sick people in paradise. But the next best thing to seeing all the world healthy is to help and soothe the sick.
Pater and Charlie beg to send their love.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 11 March 1861
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | March 11. 61.
Dear Barbara
It seems to be the understood rule of our correspondence that I am always to write first even when I have written last; but I will quarrel with no rules if they will only allow me somehow or other to have news of you. I should have asked for them before if I had not been oppressed with bad health, dragging me back from all unnecessary writing. Since I had your letter, I have seen no creature who knows anything about you, and as my imagination is the reverse of sanguine, I have black fancies filling the blank. Pray disperse them, if you can.
We are going to freshen our minds and bodies at the coast for a fortnight, by gathering the harvest of molluscs brought with the Equinoctial winds. After that, there is a project of our going to Italy again -- perhaps at the end of April or beginning of May. I should be vexed if this caused us to miss you, in your visit to London. But our plans are not yet immovably fixed. -- We are as happy as creatures can be with imperfect digestions -- associating chiefly with the animals in the "Zoo," where we take our walks continually. Of other acquaintances, we have seen the Noels 713 lately, exchanging calls with them. The years have changed them a little since our old meetings, and I think those signs of our mortal lot made me all the more pleased to shake them by the hand again. -- I forget whether you told me that you liked Mrs. Hay (Miss Benham) 714 and her paintings, or the contrary. She came to see us when she was in town, and we saw her pictures. One of these -- a view near Florence with a foreground of stones (exhibited the year before last) pleased me highly. The figure of Old Tobit, also, in her last picture is admirable. She seems to be very ardent and thorough in her devotion to her painting, and altogether interested us a good deal.
I hope your sister and you are enjoying your painting as much as
ever. How is she now? The sunshine has got within her, I hope. And Bessie, too, is she still with you? My affectionate wishes to them both.
We had a blow on Hampstead Heath the other day 715 and brought home a jarful of microscopic wonders from the ponds, which are giving Mr. Lewes rapturous occupation. He is very busy with high scientific matters, but they do not prevent him from thinking and speaking of you, though our speech of late about you has been of the wondering conjecturing sort. I am so tired of such uncertainty that this very first evening on which I have dismissed some work that has absorbed my time hitherto, I write with rather heavy eyes and hands, to beseech you for some information about yourself and all your belongings. Perhaps if I had waited till tomorrow, I should have sent you a better-fed letter, but take the proof of anxious love as a substitute for all other merits.
Our united kind remembrances to the Doctor. We hope he is in better health. God bless you: George says, Amen.
Ever yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 11 July 1869
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 11 July 1869
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
July 11. 69.
Dearest Barbara
Mr. Lewes would delight in the vipers, but alas! he says he could not give the proper attention to them now. He thanks you for the kind thought. Dearest, don't get bitten in the heel.
On Saturday last, I received a letter from Madame Mohl saying that she was going to leave town on the following Friday, but did not like to go without asking me whether I could see her. I wrote immediately addressing to the Deanery, Westminster, 872 from which she dated her letter, and assured her that I should be very sorry not to see her, begging her, if she could, to come to me either on Tuesday or Wednesday at 4 o'clock. She did not come, and I have not heard from her. I wished very much to see her, and I cannot help being uneasy lest my letter should have missed her. She is one of the people whom I should most bitterly regret to have treated with apparent neglect. Will you try and ascertain the truth for me? I would not trouble you, but that I am ignorant of her present address.
I cannot write very cheerfully about the Boy. He gets no strength -- on the contrary, appears to lose some of his reduced store, and he has frequent attacks of pain. The alternations from discomfort to ease and brightness are as frequent as ever, but his spirits, though not depressed, seem to share in the increased feebleness. But one is so utterly in the dark, that it seems irrational either to be hopeful or fearful.
I will write in answer to your &unknown;other&unknown; letter, on the next sheet.
Yours lovingly
M. E. L.
We think of going to St. Alban's next week, Charlie and Gertrude taking our place again.
I have just re-read your letter and see that the nest is a wren's -- not formidable. I will not forget to write to you when we come back. Kind regards to Miss Edwards.
Ever thine lovingly
Marian.

MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
October 10. 70.
Dearest B.
Here we are! I was beginning to lose belief in your affection, but not to lose my affection for you. Do not come on Thursday or Saturday, because on one of those days -- I am not certain which -- we shall be having a family party.
O what a lovely autumn is shining on those hideous guns which are being hauled along to Paris! What novices in wickedness were Milton's devils! 223 We shall like very much to hear how you have been spending the months, and how the Doctor is, and whether he contemplates staying in England through the winter, and how Nannie is situated on the other extremity of the French dominions. Come and tell us. I am always
Your faithfully affectionate
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 10 April 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, 10 April 1866
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Mostly published: Cross, II, 425-426.
North Bank | April 10. 66.
My dear Barbara
The happiness in your letter was delightful to me, as you guessed it would be. See how much better things may turn out for all mankind, since they mend for single mortals, even in this confused state of the bodies social and politic.
George has read your Dr. Janetti's diagnosis and prescription, and says it does not inspire him with any confidence. It is vague. But I hardly know what would inspire confidence in cases of medical treatment.
We have been going on as usual -- both of us better and worse by turns. Yet happier and happier. As soon as we can leave, we shall go away, probably to Germany, for six weeks or so. But that will not be till June. I am finishing a book, which has been growing slowly like a sickly child, because of my own ailments; but now I am in the later acts of it. I can't move till it is done.
You know all the news public and private -- all about the sad Cattle Plague, and the Reform Bill 423 and who is going to be married and who is dead. So I need tell you nothing. You will still find the English world extremely like what it was when you left it -- conversation more or less trivial and insincere, literature just now not much better, and politics worse than either. Bring some sincerity and energy to make a little draught of pure air in your particular world. I shall expect you to be a heroine in the best sense now you are happier after a time of suffering. See what a talent I have for telling other people to be good!
Is it not pretty that excellent little Isa Craig is going to marry her not distinguished but solid cousin, 424 after her three years' engagement? She seems to me to have one of the soundest minds in one of the soundest bodies I ever met with in a woman who has made a business of literature.
Our children at Hampstead are gone for their month's holiday to the Isle of Wight. Dear Gertrude, who shows herself more and more of a treasure, has the joy now of expecting a little one -- but not till the autumn. We are getting patriarchal, and think of old age and death as journeys not far off -- all knowledge, all thought, all achievement seems more precious and enjoyable to me than it ever was before in life. But as soon as one has found the key of life "it opes the gates of death." 425 Youth has not learned the art of living, and we go on bungling till our experience can only serve us for a very brief space. That is the "external order" we must submit to.
I am too busy to write except when I am tired, and don't know very well what I say. So you must not be surprized if I write in a dreamy way.
Kind remembrances to all whom you know me to remember, especially to your sister. George sends his love with mine.
Always your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [September 1868]
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday.
My dear Barbara
The picture looks glorious this morning, now there is a better light in the room, and it will be the cause of many happy thoughts to me about many things -- beginning with your sweet friendship. Also, the plums were nice yesterday, and I am looking forward to the figs and peaches. Grace 811 begged me to look at her herbs this morning -- your bunches which she hung up proudly.
O dear, I know only one thing in the world better than being loved and petted -- and that is, loving others perfectly, without guile and without one mite of bitterness.
You see, my thanks consist in trying to let you know how much delight your goodness gives me. I see many, many things in the picture this morning, which I did not see yesterday, and I dare say I shall see more to-morrow.
Ever thine
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [November 1870]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [November 1870]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Published: Cross, III, 123-124, dated November 1870.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
Dearest B.
Lying awake early in the morning according to a bad practice of mine, I was visited with much compunction and self-disgust that I had ever said a word to you about the faults of a friend whose good qualities are made the more sacred by the endurance his lot has in many ways demanded. I think you may fairly set down a full half of my alleged grievances to my own susceptibility and other faults of mine which necessarily call forth less agreeable manifestations from others than as many virtues would do, if I had them. I trust to your good sense to have judged well, in spite of my errors in the presentation of any matter. But I wish to protest against myself, that I may as much as possible cut off the temptations to what I should like utterly to purify myself from for the few remaining years of my life 236 -- the disposition to dwell for a moment on the faults of a friend.
Always thine
M. E. L.
Tell the flower and fern-giver, whoever it may be, that some strength comes to me this morning from the pretty proof of sympathy.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [March 1873]
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library. Endorsed: March 1873.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Sunday.
Dearest Barbara
Mr. Lewes read your note this morning without sending it up to me -- else I should immediately have written a line to say, first how vexed I was to have missed you the other day. Next, I will remember your message to Mrs. B. Jones.
The word you send me of a life so bound up with your early years being suddenly brought to a premature close, 155 makes me imagine how your thoughts are saddened and solemnized in these first succeeding days. For her sake -- even for the children's -- the passing away seems a good. But every death that comes at all near to one makes one in some sense a mourner.
The precious flowers are duly cherished.
Your ever grateful
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [9] February 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [9] February 1874
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Feb. 2. 18 74.
My dear Barbara
Rejoiced to hear that you are coming home so soon! This note is simply to give the assurance that I am still alive to love you, and that we shall probably be on the old premises when you get home -- a moment which will be, I imagine, a little too early for the brief trip to Heidelberg and T'fcbingen which we contemplate.
I have been a sad invalid lately, and last week had a severe attack of a new sort -- neuralgia just above the left hip. I am so far better that I have had no fit of pain for several days, but I am still rather [done up,] and tired this morning by having received rather a large party of visitors yesterday -- the first day for a week that I have been beyond the door-sill. 19
Mr. Lewes is unusually well, so that between us we have nearly the usual share of health. But that doesn't serve me to write letters with, any more than the high average of food-consumption nourishes all the hungry.
Do you mind about the Conservative majority? 20 I don't.
I trust that your health is none the worse, since you seem to write in spirits -- and that on the whole I shall hear of your risky journey having been a success. Best love to Nannie.
Always your affectionate
Marian.

19 "Polly had bad attack of pain in  her left side, lasting five or six hours in spite of fomentations etc. Went to see Dr. Clark who prescribed temporary remedy till he could arrive. Sat with her all day and read Times and Dickens [Life] vol. III to her." (GHL Diary, 3 February 1874.) The next day Dr. Clark came; "fears concretion in the kidney, but not quite sure yet." Another attack followed 5 February, after which GE grew better. She was up 7 February and able to walk out a little Sunday, 8 February, when the company included Lady Colville, Mrs. Strachey, Clifford, Mr. and Miss Simcox, Mr. Champneys, Du Maurier, Lyulph Stanley, Mrs. Orr, Dr. Hughlings Jackson, Dr. Payne, Mr. Payne, Ralston, Ruskin, Appleton, and Charles Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [3 August 1865]
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday.
Dear Barbara
You did not come again, but the picture 664 came. We are both very much pleased with it and grateful to the soul and the hand that produced it for us. It is deliciously fresh and airy and happy. It is settled now that we go for a month's holiday in Normandy and Brittany starting next Thursday. So I am reading Villemarqu'e9 665 and setting my mind towards Celtic legends, that I may people the land with great shadows when there are no solid Bretons in sight.
Yesterday the two Trollopes 666 dined with us and we had a good deal of pleasant talk, or rather shouting. Also I sat for the last time for my portrait, and Mr. Burton was disappointed to find that you had left town before he had been able to call on you and see certain oil sketches. I gave him your address that he might write to you.
Let me know how you get on.
Ever yours
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [27 July 1867]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday.
Dearest Barbara
I was relieved to have a letter from you, for I had been wondering much about you. Pray thank Miss Blackwell 653 for taking the trouble to write me her opinion about you. I feel gladdened by knowing that you have someone well-instructed in hygiene -- I hope, staying with you.
I got your letter from Mrs. P. Taylor's, and answered it. Madame Mohl's report of the physician's opinion would, I should think, be conclusive for all rational people. I presume you give up the idea of pleasing all the world, rational and irrational.
We start on Monday evening, if I am well enough -- but I have been quite ill this week. 654 The nearest address I dare give you is Poste Restante, Dresden. We are almost sure to be there in the course of a fortnight.
The rainy weather is I fear very unfavourable to your comfort in your country nest. Don't overdo yourself with having visitors out of benevolence. You see Dr. Blackwell says you should be "quiet." Always
Your loving
Marian.

The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Dearest Barbara
The fruit came just in the nick of time -- when he was wanting a strawberry and the last supply was all gone.
Dr. Reynolds 82 met Paget last evening. The report given to George is that there is slight curvature of the spine, and inability to move the ribs in breathing -- these seeming to Paget to be new symptoms. Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [16 May 1878]
MS: Huntington Library. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Thursday Evening.
My dear Barbara
Thanks for the newspaper containing the letter from V'e9ra Zassoulitch. 63
My headache yesterday 64 made me oblivious of something I wanted to say to you. It was, that our friends Mr. and Mrs. Hall of Six Mile wish to get a governess for their nine year old boy. 65 She must know French, German and music, must be a lady in manners and general culture, and young enough to be a bright companion. The position, I imagine, would be as happy as such positions can be made by the amiability and rectitude of the parents. The boy is a beautiful, charming fellow. Mr. Hall mentioned you as one whom he would have consulted on the subject if it had been admissible for him to trouble you. I promised to tell you of his want, trusting that it will rather please than worry you if you happen to know of a suitable young lady, and if not -- of course you will dismiss the matter.
I did not remember when we were talking of the Goldsmids that I know the Julian who succeeds to the title 66 and lives at a beautiful place near Tunbridge. I dined with him one day at Mr. Goschen's. He is a handsome, vigorous man -- not like the poor Augustus.
I hope Sir W. Jenner 67 did not find you overdone yesterday. I again stayed too long.
Yours lovingly
M. E. L.
If you or Miss Scott know of a well-warranted woman who would take care of our house during our absence for the summer and autumn, will you ask the invaluable Miss Scott to write me word of her, and at the same time to let me know whether you have secured the delightful House in Sussex?

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [14 June 1869]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Monday.
My dear Barbara
I am always rather miserable when I have chanced to seem flippant and irreverent to one who deserves respect, and I felt yesterday that in speaking of Mr. 'abPattison'bb, my joking way of saying that he was a "general writer" 80 might have seemed a sarcasm on him personally, when in fact it was rather a spurt on the condition of the literary world in answer to Mr. Burton's query "what is he?" The Rector seems to me worthy of high esteem so far as I have seen anything of him, and his t'eate-'e0-t'eate talk is really valuable and unusually genuine.
Pardon me for troubling you with an explanation which is necessary rather for my own ease of mind than for any good of yours. Du reste, I have been so poorly for the last three days, that I was imbecile in conversation yesterday. 81
Yours ever
M. E. L.

80 Mark Pattison (1813-84), Rector of  Lincoln College, Oxford, was quite properly described as a "general writer." Under Newman at Oriel he had written lives of two English saints. Later he was a steady contributor to periodicals, among them the Quarterly, the National, the North British, Fraser's, the Saturday, the Fortnightly, Macmillan's, and the Times. For some time he wrote the "Theology and Philosophy" section of the Westminster. The breadth of his learning and the magnitude of his published work refute the assertion that he was the original of GE's Casaubon. His masterpiece, the life of Isaac Casaubon (the name has helped to spread the story), did not appear till 1875. See 22 May 1869.
81 The callers on Sunday, 13 June  1869 were "Barbara, Stanley, Mr. and Mrs. G. Howard, Alice Helps, Burton, Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Martin, Mr. and Mrs. Burne Jones, Colvin, Spencer, Mr. and Mrs. Bain, Sir H. Thompson; -- Deutsch to dinner." (GHL Diary.)

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, London, [10 January 1870]
MS: Berg Collection, New York Public Library.
Monday Morning.
Dearest Barbara
Now you are getting morbid and remorseful! I saw nothing on your part but the most perfectly graceful behaviour -- indeed I was struck with your immediate thoughtfulness on behalf of Rosetti, 894 that he should not be robbed of too much time by visitors. My own immediate feeling (knowing your old acquaintance with him) was that we should be interfering with both the artistic and friendly chat that would naturally occur between you. On all other grounds I was glad that we should all go together.
I am tormented with my teeth -- a depressing condition even for brave cheerful people, and I am not queen of them. So I can hardly bear seeing anybody. I hope to be better before Thursday. 895
Ever your loving
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Limpsfield, 25 August [1870]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Limpsfield, 25 August [1870]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Mostly published: Cross, III, 119-121.
Park Farm | Limpsfield | August 25.
My dear Barbara
We shall return to town on Monday, various small reasons concurring to make us resolve on quitting this earthly paradise.
I am very sorry for the sufferings of the French nation, but I think these sufferings are better for the moral welfare of the people than victory would have been. The war has been drawn down on them by an iniquitous Government, but in a great proportion of the French people there has been nourished a wicked glorification of selfish pride, which like all other conceit is a sort of stupidity, excluding any true conception of what lies outside their own vain wishes. The Germans, it seems, were expected to stand like toy-soldiers, for the French to knock them down. It was quite true that the war is in some respects the conflict of two differing forms of civilization. But whatever charm we may see in the southern Latin races, this ought not to blind us to the great contributions which the German energies have made in all sorts of ways to the common treasure of mankind. And who that has any spirit of justice can help sympathizing with them in their grand repulse of the French project to invade and divide them? If I were a French-woman, much as I might wail over French sufferings, I cannot help believing that I should detest the French talk about the "Prussiens." They wanted to throttle the electric eel for their own purposes.
But I imagine that you and the Doctor would not find us in much disagreement with you on these matters. One thing that is pleasant to think of, is the effort made everywhere to help the wounded. All this scribble is mere fringe to the information I wished to send you as to our whereabouts.
With best regards to the Doctor,
Yours always
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Earlswood Common, 23 September 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Earlswood Common, 23 September 1874
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
The Cottage | Earlswood Comm. | September 23. 74.
My dear Barbara
I have often been saying, [Barbara is gone on her sketching expedition] or, [This grey day will suit Barbara.] But somehow you had sent my imagination to Yorkshire. I should think Cornwall and its granite was the scenery most after your own heart.
Glad to hear good news of your establishment. Altogether you give me the impression that you have had a delightful summer. So have we.
We are not robust, but otherwise jolly -- are going up to town on Friday, then into Cambridgeshire for a few days, then to France. At the beginning of November we expect to be settled in town. 145
George has got his 2d volume ready for the press, and we have had daily drives in lovely scenery, looking at the country through the changing months as one looks at a dear face through the changing years. The children have been to us twice from Saturday to Monday, and we have had about eight other visitors 146 for a day or half a day at rare intervals. Otherwise we have had uninterrupted quiet. You know we are not social creatures, unlike you who have always the real, breathing, talking world about you. The sketch you give me of Numa Hartog's cousin 147 is very gratifying. To hear of good young things growing up is the best of news.
I dare say you wonder that I have not done more for Girton. The fact is that we have been devoting a considerable sum of late years to the help of individual needs which are not published to the world. 148 More and more of such needs disclose themselves to one -- old governesses and other beings having some claims through the memory of good received in one's youth, and who could only be helped by such special care. But you will let me know what is to be done for this nice girl.
George has had a good deal of headache but you know how elastic his nature is, and how soon he brightens when pain has left him. He sends his love with mine.
Always your affectionate
M. E. Lewes.
I was pleasantly surprised by Mr. Allingham's marriage. 149 I rejoice in his getting the editorship and in the indications that his bride is an accomplished industrious woman.
Dublin Core:Creator: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Publisher: George Eliot Archive, edited by Beverley Park Rilett. https://GeorgeEliotArchive.org
Dublin Core:Contributor: MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Dublin Core:Relation:
145 They returned to London Friday,  25 September; visited Mr. W. H. Hall at Six Mile Bottom, 28 September -- 1 October; and left for France 3 October. No letters have been found during their journey, which began with a week in Paris, 4-11 October, took them by way of Soissons, Rheims, Sedan, and Dinant to Brussels, where they stayed 14-18 October. They returned to the Priory 19 October.
146 In addition to Mrs. Stuart and  Roland, Mrs. Congreve, Mrs. Geddes, Lord Lytton, and John Cross are mentioned in GHL's Diary. 

147 Phoebe Sarah Marks (1854-1923),  afterwards Hertha Ayrton. Her cousin Numa Edward Hartog, (1846-71), son of Alphonse Hartog, French professor at Jew's College, Finsbury Square, was admitted pensioner at Trinity College, Cambridge without oath in 1865 and was Senior Wrangler in 1869, the first Jew to attain this honor. His failure to obtain a fellowship is said to have caused the removal of the disability.
148 Among her charities in 1874 were   'a3200 to Octavia Hill and  'a310 to Maria Lewis, her old governess. But the largest gifts were those to GHL's family. Agnes was given about  'a3200, and her children by Thornton Hunt, who died in 1873, received generous gifts from time to time; GHL's sister-in-law Mrs. Edward Lewes had  'a375; his children, especially Herbert, were helped, and a number of organizations like the Comte Fund, the Little Sisters of Hammersmith, and the Shakespeare Society were subscribed to regularly.
149 William Allingham married 22 August  1874 Helen Paterson (1848-1926), eldest child of Dr. Alexander Henry Paterson.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Earlswood Common, 16 July 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Earlswood Common, 16 July 1874
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 238-239, dated 17 July 1874.
The Cottage | Earlswood Common | July 16. 74.
Dearest Barbara
Your letter brings delightful news. I was in a resigned condition about you -- hoping as the best thing that you were gone on a painting expedition. But it is better that everybody should be good, and that there should be no ugly corners of anxiety in your mind. And the addition of the little Baby for you to rescue and befriend is also pretty. I like much better to hear of the children already born being taken care of, than to be asked to rejoice greatly because a new one is born.
Your picture of poor Miss E[dwards] 127 is deplorable. I cannot help thinking it a misfortune that she took to writing. But it seems that the only chance of her finding dignity and independence is that she should be left to extricate herself. That chlorale is a very pernicious thing to begin taking: the doctors say that women who begin with it never leave it off. 128
We enjoy our country peacefulness greatly, [5 lines deleted] George has had some headachiness, and for the last day or two it has been my turn to grumble, but I am very much stronger since I came into this pure air. I was a great wretch, you know, just before we left town.
And now I have two questions to ask of your benevolence. First, was there not some village near Stonehenge where you stayed the night? -- nearer to Stonehenge than Amesbury? -- Secondly, Do you know anything specific about Holmwood Common as a place of residence? It is ravishingly beautiful: is it in its higher part thoroughly unobjectionable as a site for a dwelling? I ask in reference to a house which is built on the higher part of the Common -- a thick-walled substantial house, but with no high trees round it. 129
We shall be very grateful if you will answer these questions, so far as you can, by a speedy post.
It seems that they have been having the heat of Tophet in London, whereas we have never had more than agreeable sunniness, this common being almost always breezy. And the country around us must I think, be the loveliest -- of its undulating woody kind -- in all England.
I remember when we were driving together last, something was said about my disposition to melancholy. I ought to have said then, but did not, that I am no longer one of those whom Dante found in a Hellborder because they had been sad under the blessed daylight. I am uniformly cheerful now -- feeling the preciousness of these moments in which I still possess love and thought.
I can't think who Mary Ewart 130 is. And do you know how our dear Mrs. Senior is tormented by the officials about her capital Report?
G. sends his love and I am
Always your faithful
M. E. L.

GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Cromer, 23 June 1870
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 114.
Albert House | Cromer | June 23. 70.
My Dear Barbara
We have been driven away from home again by the state of Mr. Lewes's health, for which there seems to be no more special name than debility. Dr. Reynolds recommended the Yorkshire coast, but we wanted to know Cromer, and so we came here first for the sake of variety. We shall go on to Whitby at the end of the month, and shall probably stay there till the end of July, unless something unexpected should call us home. Our letters are sent on to us, so that if you have anything to say to me you can write to the Priory.
I am glad that you enjoyed your sketching journey, and that you are now comfortably settled at your cottage. To me the most desirable thing just now seems to be to have one home, and stay there till death comes to take one away. I get more and more disinclined to the perpetual makeshifts of a migratory life, and care more and more for the order and habitual objects of home. However there are many in the world whose whole existence is a makeshift, and perhaps the formula which would fit the largest numbers of lives is, "a doing-without more or less patiently."
The air just now is not very invigorating anywhere I imagine, and one begins to be very anxious about the nation generally on account of the threatening drought. But George is certainly a little the better even for the one week of change and idleness. I have been very ailing also, and am a poor piece of feminine flesh.
It is all the pleasanter to know that you and others are well. We are very "jolly," in spite of weak heads, stomachs, etc. and have more than our share of happiness.
I shall be delighted to have any details about you, when you are inclined to ask for a little sympathy. George unites in love, and I am always
Your true
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Conway, 31 August [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Conway, 31 August [1859]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Envelope: Mrs. Bodichon | Mountfield Park Farm | Hurst Green | Sussex. Postmarks: D | CONWAY | AU 31 | 59; 2 J | LONDON | SP 1 | 59; HURST-GREEN | A | SP 2 | 59. Hitherto unpublished.
Conway | Wednesday Morning | August 31.
Dearest Barbara
The cruel winds are driving us from this northern coast, and I have just been packing up for our journey to Weymouth. 275 I write now, because, as we stay at Lichfield on our way, for the sake of seeing my nieces who are at school 276 there, we shall not arrive at Weymouth till tomorrow evening. If you have anything to say to us, address Poste Restante, Weymouth.
Your sister's 277 words are very sweet and helpful to me. Don't imagine that she can be troublesome to me, for she will understand that I am not able to be expansive as a letter writer, and any form of human love that comes near me does me unspeakable good.
Since feeble health sent us away from town, I'm glad you can't go there. It was my one regret that we should miss you.
Write as often as you can, and let me know all about you.
Ever your affectionate
Marian.
George says, "Tell her to date her letter to Chapman and Hall from Blandford Square." 278

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Bordeaux, [4 January 1867]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Bordeaux, [4 January 1867]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extract published: Cross, III, 1-2.
Hotel de Nantes, Bordeaux.
Sitting by the fire on a rainy morning with all our things packed and nothing particular to do.
Dearest Barbara
I am so delighted with your letters from Spain, that I want to try and get them printed in a good organ. I gave them to Madame Mohl to read, and she expressed the same wish, saying they were better than the usual printed Travels, and that she especially wished the testimony about the Bull-fights to be made public. What do you feel and think about my sending the letters (in confidence) to Mr. G. Smith, of whose judgment I have a good opinion, and asking him whether he will print them in the Pall Mall? They would go in at twice, or thrice at the most -- i.e. in the form of two or three letters. The last I got before leaving home was the sheet in which you speak of the Soeurs de St. Vincent de Paul at Malaga. I put this question first because it is the most important thing, and the only thing I have to say that demands an answer.
You have suggested delicious pictures to me. My favourite is that in the potter's workshop, on the Albajcin at Granada -- the still life of the pottery and the pans and the moving life of the dance and the music. But all through, I am ready to read over again and dwell on what you say. Of course, if the letters were printed the proof should be sent to you. But I should think there is nothing that need be left out except names, and a sentence about the people in Algiers. In one place, "traditional patterns" should be substituted for "legendary patterns." I hardly remember anything else that signifies.
We enjoyed our stay in Paris in order to see Madame Mohl, who was very good to us -- invited the Scherers and other interesting people to meet us at dinner on the 29th and tempted us to stay and breakfast with her on the 31st by promising to invite Renan, which she did successfully and so procured us a bit of experience that we were glad to have, over and above the pleasure of seeing a little more of herself and M. Mohl. I like them both, and wish there were a chance of knowing them better. We paid for our pleasure by being obliged to walk in the rain (from the impossibility of getting a carriage) all the way from the Rue de Rivoli, where a charitable German printer who had taken us up in his fiacre was obliged to set us down -- to the Hotel du Helder, through streets literally jammed with carriages and omnibuses carrying people who were doing the severe social duties of the last day in the year. The rain it raineth every day, with the one exception of yesterday: we can't travel away from it apparently. But we start in desperation for Bayonne in half an hour.
George got worse and worse, thinner and thinner, after you saw him, and was induced at last to leave his Hist[ory] of Philosophy unfinished. I hope you will not have written to me in England before you receive this, because then you will tell me everything in answering this -- which pray do at once and address Poste Restante, Biarritz. We contemplate staying a little while at Biarritz, if we like it. But as that is an uncertainty among uncertainties, your writing at once will simplify things, and prevent the risks of ordering letters to be sent on.
George sends his chivalrous love -- and I a great many unexpressed thoughts and wishes. Bless you, dear Barbara. Keep me always as
Your faithful loving friend
M. E. L.
You see, I have been writing on my knees.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Barcelona, 2 February 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, Barcelona, 2 February 1867
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Extracts published: Cross, III, 5-8.
Barcelona February 2. 1867.
It has been a vexing thought to me, dear Barbara, that I have been so long without writing to you after your last interesting packet, received at Biarritz. There have been constant hindrances: first, a journey to Pau to see our friend Mrs. Lehmann with whom we spent all our time there, leaving no intervals except for rest. Then a bilious attack at Biarritz, which made the one letter I was obliged to write a heavy burthen; and after that, incessant travelling and life in the open air -- and I am not able either to read or write in a railway carriage. I wrote to Mr. George Smith before I left Biarritz and told him about your letters, reserving them till my return. My George thought that would be the best plan, as all the matter in the letter is of a kind that will keep, and I don't want anyone to know about the proposition except ourselves until we find that it is accepted. So I have not written to Bessie, and I return you the envelope which will come in for one of your own letters.
Are you astonished to see our whereabouts? We left Biarritz for San Sebastian, where we stayed three days, and both there and all our way to Barcelona, our life has been a succession of delights. We have had perfect weather -- blue skies and a warm sun. George is much stronger and looks almost well; I think the interest of Spanish sights helps to do him good. We travelled from San Sebastian to Saragossa, where we paused two nights, then to Lerida, for one night, and yesterday to Barcelona. You know the scenery from San Sebastian to Alsasua, through the lower Pyrenees because it lies on the way to Burgos and Madrid. At Alsasua we turned off through Navarre into Aragon, seeing famous Pampeluna looking as beautiful as it did ages ago amongst the grand hills. At Saragossa the scene was thoroughly changed: all through Aragon as far as we could see, I should think the country resembles the highlands of central Spain. There is the most striking effect of hills, flanking the plain of Saragossa, I ever saw. They are of palish clay washed by the rains into undulating forms, and some slight herbage upon them makes the shadows of an exquisite blue. These hills accompanied us in the distance all the way through Aragon, the snowy mountains topping them in the far distance. The land is all pale brown, the numerous towns and villages just match the land, and so do the sheep-folds built of mud or stone. The herbage is all of an ashy green.
Perhaps if I had been in Africa, I should say as you do that the country reminded me of Africa: as it is, I think of all I have read about the East. The men who look on while others work at Saragossa also seem to belong to the East: with a great striped blanket wrapt grandly round them, and a kerchief tied about their hair. But though Aragon was held by the Moors longer than any part of northern Spain, the features and skins of the people seem to me to bear less traces of the mixture there must have been than one would fairly expect. Saragossa has a grand character still, in spite of the stucco with which the people have daubed the beautiful small brick of which the houses are built. Here and there we see a house left undesecrated by stucco and all of them have the fluted tiles and the broad eaves beautifully ornamented. Again, one side of the old Cathedral still shews the exquisite inlaid work which on the facade has been overlaid hideously. Gradually as we left Aragon, and entered Catalonia, the face of the country changed, and we had almost every sort of beauty in succession -- last of all between Monserrat and Barcelona a perfect garden, with the richest red soil -- blooms on the plum and cherry trees, olives thick in the hedges.
At present we are waiting for the Spanish hardships to begin. Even at Lerida, a place scarcely at all determined by foreign travellers, we were perfectly comfortable -- and such sights! The people scattered on the brown slopes of rough earth round the fortress, the women knitting etc. the men playing at cards. One wonderful family group; another of handsome gipsies.
We are actually going by steam-boat to Alicante, and from Alicante to Malaga. Then we mean to see Granada, Cordoba, and Seville. We shall only stay here a few days -- if this weather continues. George is on fire for the journey and now I am not afraid of it for him. So I shall not write again till we are in England. George sends his best of love to you and the Doctor. Remember me affectionately to your sister. Farewell, dearest Barbara.
Yours ever
M. E. L.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, [Wandsworth], 27 July [1859]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, [Wandsworth], 27 July [1859]
MS: Huntington Library. Hitherto unpublished.
Wednesday, July 27.
My dear Barbara
I sent you a note to Blandford Square the day after our return, but your letter from the Isle of Wight this morning gives me a delightful reason for writing again.
Come on Sunday, without fail. I shall not lose the sense that you are coming, all the week, in spite of a real pug, who is coming too -- a present to the Author of A.B. in compensation for lost friends. But don't look for me at the railway station, because that spoils my morning's work. By the time you get here (coming by your usual train) I shall be at liberty without pangs of conscience. But do come to us for the whole day.
From what I have gathered concerning Miss Bailey, 231 I think I should like to know her very much, but we will talk more of her on Sunday -- unless you wish to give her an answer before. In that case I think you may safely say '91yes,'92 for if you had thought I should not like her, you would have warned me.
Of course we shall go and see your pictures. 232 George told me the other day, when he had been in town, that he had seen your name in large letters on a walking "sandwich," and we were not without sensations at your having that honourable publicity. It is really a step to have your pictures hung together in a regular gallery where you have an illustrious predecessor. 233
Yes! I know Niton, and am glad to think that you have been so quietly there. I thought your time in the country was likely to be made less of a rest by family duties. Come!
Ever your affectionate
Marian.
Dublin Core:Creator: George Eliot^^F
Dublin Core:Publisher: George Eliot Archive, edited by Beverley Park Rilett. https://GeorgeEliotArchive.org
Dublin Core:Contributor: MS: Huntington Library. Hitherto unpublished.
Dublin Core:Relation:
231 Mme Bodichon wrote GE from  Niton 25 July [1859]: "My old friend Miss Bayley of Wimbledon says she knows Mr. Lewes, having met him at the Chadwicks, and wishes to know you. She asked if she might call. I said I would speak to you about it during the summer. She did not know anything about you at all until I told her, she having begun the conversation by saying, `Have you read A.B. -- it is quite Shakespearian! That man is one of the first intellects of the day, etc. etc. etc." (Yale.) Miss Bayley wrote Henry Crabb Robinson 5 August [1859] that Mrs. Bodichon feels privileged to overlook convention "in behalf of genius and both moral and intellectual worth." Miss Bayley intends to make GE's acquaintance. She once knew Lewes a little and was repelled by his rather coarse manners, but disliked his wife still more, who had been unfaithful to him long before their separation. (Dr. Williams's Library.)
232 At the French Gallery, 120 Pall  Mall. The Illustrated London News comments favorably on them, 30 July 1859, p. 105.
233 David Cox. See [30 June -- 1 July  1859].

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, [Wandsworth, 6 March 1860]
Dublin Core:Subject: Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Barbara [Mme Eugene] Bodichon, [Wandsworth, 6 March 1860]
MS: Mr. Philip Leigh-Smith. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Barbara
That was a charming way of letting us know what you were doing -- to send me the chapter of news written for your Father. Everything remains with me, from the Jackals and hypothetic Hyaena, to the designs for Oxford columns. O, I could write so much to you, if my nervous energy were not all going with a rush in the one channel of my fastclosing third volume. But now I don't mean to write anything directly to you; I am going to write to your sister through you. She will be with you, she tells me, next Monday. I want her to know that she has given me some very happy feelings by sending me some parting proofs that she has been thinking of me. First, a sketch of you, in which I learn to see more and more of you, as I keep it before me; and next, a sheet of caricatures that give me a merry sense of the merry vein there is in her. Looking at them when I was ill with a bad headache, the other day, I got some of the enjoyable breeze and freshness that is playing about that lucky artist with the streaming hair. Tell her, I thank her: no goodness is lost on me -- that is the only compliment I can pay myself.
I have been crying myself almost into stupor, over visions of sorrow. 498 So no more, except my love to you and yours.
Yes! one thing -- that I fancy we forgot to put stamps on our last letter to you -- slipping it into the box by mistake. I hope we don't often do those disgusting things.
Ever yours
Marian.
