Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 2[8] May 1840
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 2[8] May 1840
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, I, 66-67. Thursday was 28 May.
Griff May 26th 1840.
My dear Friend,
If you are in health it is well. I am also well. 201 I am so tired of artful simplicity, in modern vogue, that I have a mind to return to the antique fashion of simple formality. What if I should send you a matter of fact letter? Would you doubt the integrity of my signature? I have much that I could tell you and should like to convey to your ear, but I forbear to put down on paper, prospects that may yet after all pass by as the scenery of a Diorama. I will only hint that there seems a probability of my being an unoccupied damsel, 202 of my being severed from all the ties that have hitherto given my existence the semblance of a usefulness beyond that of making up the requisite quantum of animal matter in the universe. A second important intimation respecting my worthy self is one that I confess I impart without one sigh though perhaps you will think my callousness discreditable. It is that Seeley and Burnside have just published a Chart of Ecclesiastical History, doubtless giving to my airy vision a local habitation and a name. I console all my little regrets by thinking that what is thus evidenced to be a desideratum has been executed much better than if left to my slow fingers and slower head.
So you intend to cheat us by migrating in any direction rather than ours? I cannot be so selfish as not to wish that you should go where you can have the most invigorating breeze and the loveliest novelty, and I heartily echo your kind wish that we should be "like Juno's swans" 203 coupled together, though Brighton is not a name of stirring association with me. Give me a cliff that no tools have violated from whence to view the great deep, not a crowded splendid pier. My knowledge, conferred by my own pupillage, of the nearness of your holiday's commencement, has induced me to write you a hasty letter to-night, that I may have to expect a notification of your plans before your departure from Burton. I did hope to have the benefit of a little unfettered intercourse with you to have all those little plans and feelings to which recent circumstances have given birth passed through the crucible of your judgment, but it is good to see future disappointments in a camera obscura.
My dear Sister is in charming health with her darlings great and small. Can you imagine me domiciled at Meriden? Think you my elements are such as are likely to disturb the serenity of that atmosphere? or rather do you not think I shall be a stunted shrub? I desire to imitate my beloved father's calm endurance and humble gratitude and be quite free from anxiety respecting my destination. To be faithful to my theme, I fear I am laboriously doing nothing, for I am beguiled by the fascinations that the study of languages has for my capricious mind, and could e'en give myself up to making discoveries in the world of words. My pilot too is anything but uninteresting, all external grace and mental power, but "Cease ye from man" 204 is engraven on my amulet. And to tell you the truth I begin to feel involuntarily isolated, and without being humble, to have such a consciousness that I am a negation of all that finds love and esteem as makes me anticipate for myself -- no matter what; I shall have countless undeserved enemies if my life be prolonged, wherever my lot may be cast, and I need rigid discipline, which I have never yet had. Byron in his Childe Harold (which I have just begun the second time) checks reflections on individual and personal sorrows by reminding himself of the revolutions and woes beneath which the shores of the Mediterranean have groaned. 205 We may with more effectual comparison think of the dangers of the Great Ark of the Church in these latter times of the deluge of sin. I have written an almost unpardonably egotistical letter to say nothing of its other blemishes, but I believe you are the person that loves me well enough to bear with me. Send me word soon how you are and whither going, and think of me as your true and affectionate
Mary Ann.
Thursday Evening

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 17 September 1840
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 17 September 1840
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering | Northamptonshire. Postmark: COVENTRY | SE 17 | 1840. Extracts published: Cross, I, 72-73.
Griff | September 17th 1840.
My very dear Friend,
I believe it is Woman's privilege to give no reason for her actions and by parity of reasoning for her omissions, but I will not avail myself of this article of our Charter to one of my own sex. I will tell you that the cause of my silence has been partly excess of occupation, partly absence from home, 243 and, as the base part of the triangle a little sloth for I will not say that by better management it would have been impossible for me to write to you. I can say however that my thoughts have been more frequently with you than any of my absent female friends, and this the rather that my folly, to give it the mildest name, has placed me 'e0 la portée of certain dangerous powers, from whose injuries I have to be thankful that I have so early escaped. I have thought of you as the one who has ever shewn herself so capable of consideration for my weakness and sympathy in my warm and easily fastened affections. My imagination is an enemy that must be cast down ere I can enjoy peace or exhibit uniformity of character. I know not which of its caprices I have most to dread -- that which incites it to spread sack-cloth "above, below, around," or that which makes it "cheat my eye with blear illusion, 244 and beget strange dreams" of excellence and beauty in beings and things of only "working day" price. There is but one remedy -- and blessed thought! it is in the hands of One who, at least while we are willing to receive it is waiting to bestow it on us. The beautiful heavens that we have lately enjoyed awaken in me an indescribable sensation of exultation in existence and aspiration after all that is suited to engage our immaterial nature; but I feel that this is not pure, not chastened, and therefore not to be indulged. So much for self of which I believe you wish me to speak and so I will not even ask pardon. While I think of it the chart we have on the tapis is thus called: "A Chart of Ecclesiastical History from the commencement of the Christian Era to the present time," published by Seeley and Burnside.
I have not read very many of Mr. W. Bucknill's 245 poems, nor any with much attention. To waste one's time in conning such productions is like choosing to be fanned indoors when one can have the breath of Eolus and all his children for less exertion. I do not mean to be satirical, or affect the critic to which character I have not a shadow of right. I simply declare my determination not to feed on the broth of literature when I can get strong soup, such for instance as Shelley's Cloud, the five or six stanzas of which contain more poetic metal than is beat out in all Mr. B' pages. By the bye do recommend to all your married friends "Woman's Mission" 246 a 3.6d book and one you would like to read; the most philosophical and masterly on the subject I ever read or glanced over.
Mr. Harpur 247 told me you looked well when he was at Burton but
I cannot trust his eyes and you do not tell me anything about your health. All is in statu quo here. I think it probably will be so till spring -- then most probably I shall be transplanted, and that to Meriden. 248 This letter is only fit to be the avant courier of another, but in all simplicity its faults are like those of the Irishman's Horse, unavoidable misfortunes -- for my hand and mind are wearied with writing four pages of German and a letter of business. If you can scribble me a few lines before I am able to write again I shall be grateful. You must know I have had bestowed on me the very pretty cognomen of Clematis, which in the Floral language, means Mental Beauty. I cannot find in my heart to refuse it, though like many other appellations it has rather the appearance of a satire than a compliment. Addio!
Ever yours
Clematis.
I will send your Floral name in my next, when I have received my Dictionary.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 17 February 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 17 February 1841
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | FE 17 | 1841. Hitherto unpublished.
Griff | February 17th 1841.
My dear Veronica,
By answering your first enquiry I preclude the necessity of entering farther into the pros and cons of the Baginton situation -- boys are included, the number of children I suppose, causing it to be thought unnecessary to divide the labour of instruction. We will therefore dismiss the matter from our letters and our minds, and wait and watch for a more propitious opening.
I tremble lest you should allow your feelings, so suddenly shaken by a change of prospect, to operate unfavourably on your weak frame, but I am sure your confidence in Divine Guidance and protection, and your well-tried elasticity of spirits will cause you to resist that tendency. Probably this projected transportation may be to a Cape of Good Hope instead of a Siberia, and it is a real comfort to have sufficient time coolly to weigh all that presents itself.
Mrs. T. Bull is staying with me and requests me to say that Mrs. King's direction is Cheetham Hill, Manchester. 297 She also wishes me to ask that you will say to Miss Harper with her love, that she will write to her in a few days.
I am obliged to curtail my letter out of politeness to my visitor, but I hope to write again soon, though my power to do so is necessarily dubious.
Much love from your true
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 16 [March 1839]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 16 [March 1839]
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | Northamptonshire. Postmark: COVENTRY | M 18 | 1839. Extracts published: Cross, I, 49-54.
Griff February 118 16.
My dear Friend,
My thoughts are as apt to slip from my grasp as certain lubricous little inhabitants of fresh water that I need not name so I will commit them to paper immediately on their suggestion, not out of fear lest you should sustain a weighty loss by my forgetting them, but lest they should suddenly refuse to come a second time at my incantations because I suffered them to vanish without using them at their first appearance, and so leave me without a word today in answer to a question you have been so kind as to put to me. I am this morning hardly myself owing to the insuppressible rising of my animal spirits on a deliverance from sick head ache. I dare say therefore I shall scribble much nonsense but remember our letters were to be mere conversation, and if you were chatting with a silly girl of nineteen you would think yourself bound to excuse a considerable deal of froth.
In trying to guess as to the expedience of reading works of fiction I put out of the question all books of persons of perceptions so quick, memories so eclectic and retentive, and minds so comprehensive, that nothing less than omnivorous reading as Southey calls it can satisfy their intellectual maw, for (if I may parody the words of Scripture without profaneness), they will gather to themselves all facts and heap unto themselves all ideas. 119 For such persons we cannot legislate. Again I would put out of the question standard works whose contents are matter of constant reference, and the names of whose heroes and heroines briefly and therefore conveniently describe characters and ideas. Such are Don Quixote, Butler's Hudibras, Robinson Crusoe, Gil Blas, Byron's Poetical romances, Southey's do. etc. Such too are Walter Scott's novels and poems. Such allusions as "He is a perfect Dominie Sampson," "He is as industrious in finding out antiquities and about as successful as Jonathan Oldbuck," 120 are likely to become so common in books and conversation that always providing our leisure is not circumscribed by duty within narrow bounds, we should I think qualify ourselves to understand. Shakespeare has a higher claim than this on our attention but we have need of as nice a power of distillation as the bee to suck nothing but honey from his pages. However as in life we must be exposed to malign influences from intercourse with others if we would reap the advantages designed for us by making us social beings, so in books.
Having cleared our way of what would otherwise have encumbered us, I would ask why is one engaged in the instruction of youth to read as purely conscientious and self denying performance of duty, works, whose value to others is allowed to be doubtful? I can only imagine two shadows of reasons. Either that she may be able experimentally to decide on their desirableness for her pupils, or else that there is a certain power exerted by them on the mind that would render her a more efficient tutress by their perusal. I would not depreciate the disinterestedness of those who will make trial of the effect on themselves of a cup suspected poisonous, that they may deter another from risking life, but it appears to me a work of supererogation, since there are enough witnesses to its baneful effects on themselves already to put an end to all strife on the matter. The Scriptural declaration, "As face answereth to face in a glass, so the heart of man to man," 121 will exonerate me from the charge of uncharitableness or too high an estimation of myself if I venture to believe that the same causes which exist in my own breast to render novels and romances pernicious have their counterpart in that of every fellow-creature.
I am I confess not an impartial member of a jury in this case for I owe the culprits a grudge for injuries inflicted on myself. I shall carry to my grave the mental diseases with which they have contaminated me. 122 When I was quite a little child I could not be satisfied with the things around me; I was constantly living in a world of my own creation, and was quite contented to have no companions that I might be left to my own musings and imagine scenes in which I was chief actress. Conceive what a character novels would give to these Utopias. I was early supplied with them by those who kindly sought to gratify my appetite for reading and of course I made use of the materials they supplied for building my castles in the air. 123 But it may be said, "No one ever dreamed of recommending children to read them; all this does not apply to persons come to years of discretion, whose judgments are in some degree matured." I answer that men and women are but children of a larger growth; they are still imitative beings. We cannot, at least those who ever read to any purpose at all, we cannot I say help being modified by the ideas that pass through our minds. We hardly wish to lay claim to such elasticity as retains no impress. We are active beings too. We are each one of the Dramatis personae in some play on the stage of life -- hence our actions have their share in the effects of our reading.
As to the discipline our minds receive from the perusal of fictions I can conceive none that is beneficial but may be attained by that of history. It is the merit of fictions to come within the orbit of probability; if unnatural they would no longer please. If it be said that the mind must have relaxation, "Truth is strange -- stranger than fiction." When a person has exhausted the wonders of truth, there is no other resort than fiction; till then I cannot imagine how the adventures of some phantom conjured up by fancy can be more entertaining than the transactions of real specimens of human nature, from which we may safely draw inferences. I dare say Mr. James's Huguenot 124 would be recommended as giving an idea of the times of which he writes, but as well may one be recommended to look at landscapes for an idea of English scenery. The real secret of the relaxation talked of is one that would not generally be avowed; but an appetite that wants seasoning of a certain kind cannot be indicative of health. Religious novels are more hateful to me than merely worldly ones. They are a sort of Centaur or Mermaid and like other monsters that we do not know how to class should be destroyed for the public good as soon as born. The weapons of the Christian warfare were never sharpened at the forge of romance. Domestic fictions as they come more within the range of imitation seem more dangerous. For my part I am ready to sit down and weep at the impossibility of my understanding or barely knowing even a fraction of the sum of objects that present themselves for our contemplation in books and in life. Have I then any time to spend on things that never existed?
I have written at random and have not said all I wanted to say. I hope the frequent use of the personal pronoun will not lead you to think that I suppose it to confer any weight on what I have said. I used it to prevent circumlocution and waste of time. I am ashamed to send a letter like this as if I thought more highly of myself than I ought to think, which is alas! too true. I long for Midsummer that I may see you. Do not talk of glimpses. I am grieved that your poor head is a frequent sufferer. Pardon all I ought not to have said and believe me
Your very affectionate and sincere
Mary Ann Evans.
In reading my letter I find difficulties in understanding my scribble that I fear are hopelessly insurmountable for another. Sir Walter Scott's life, 125 of which I have read the 1st volume and here and there some pages of the succeeding ones, conveys some sad and useful lessons. The spiritual sleep of that man was awful; he does not at least betray if he felt any thing like a pang of conscience. All biography is interesting and instructive. Sir W.S. himself is the best commentary on the effect of romances and novels. He sacrificed almost his integrity for the sake of acting out the character of the Scotch Laird, which he had so often depicted. J'attends une réponse. Some persons are so provokingly phlegmatic that perhaps they should have stimulants.

Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 12 August 1840
MS: Yale. Address: The Revd L. Harper | Burton Latimer | near Kettering | For Miss Lewis. Postmark: COVENTRY | AU 13 | 1840. Extracts published: Cross, I, 70-71.
Griff | August 12th 1840.
My very dear Friend,
Although you seem to intimate that my parcel will be detained some time before it reaches you, I will enclose my letter in it, first, because its trivialities will offer themselves to you with a better grace in this more modest way of conveyance, and secondly, because I am expecting a young friend (Martha Jackson) to join me on Monday next, and it is therefore probable that the desire to render her stay with me agreeable, may, in addition to ordinary occupations, quite engross me. Although I could wish to hear that you are quite well, I will look at the right end of the beam, and be only glad that you are "getting better."
I have received "The Faerie Queen," and am trebly pleased with it, first for its clear type, next for its cheapness, and last, not least, for the tacit witness it gives to your anxiety to gratify my little wishes in the midst of your own far weightier anxieties. I am able to destroy your claims to vaticination by telling you that I am so well as to find both rest and labour sweet, and that I would pass several days of languor to behold some of those guileless wearers of purple and scarlet, which the Germans call summer birds, 238 but which have not justified that name in our country lately. I mean, moths and butterflies, yea and dragon flies. I have since last I wrote to you, been blessed with an unusual placidity of mind, partly perhaps attributable, though I hope in a slight degree, to those physical sensations by which a beneficent Creator shews kindness even to the unthankful and the evil; chiefly I trust I may assign my feelings to the far more precious rills of mercy that flow to the willing soul not only through the appointed channels which we are commanded diligently to keep open, but by an infinity of passages too narrow for the natural eye to discern.
Did you read Mr. Keble's hymn for the Sunday before last? That sweetly describes the way in which Jesus' love "can turn earth's worst and least, into a conqueror's royal feast." 239 Mr. Finney in his Lectures on Revivals 240 a powerful book but to be read with broad views of the differences in national character) says that the whole of religion is, simply to submit to God. The phrase is common enough but I doubt whether the idea, still less the act be fully comprehended and carried out by the majority even of professing Christians. The confession "we are not our own" is readily made but where is the vivid consciousness of it that can alone conform us to His image who sought not His own will? It is this that makes dwelling in God and He in us. The Christian realizes the apparent paradox of glorying in the possession of the very summit of honour, honour inconceivable until revealed, with the lowest self-abasement. With this man will I dwell, even with him who is of an humble and a contrite spirit and that trembleth at my word. "I send you the Comforter that He may abide with you forever. He dwelleth with you and shall be in you." 241
The Epistle to the Colossians is preeminently rich in the colouring with which it portrays the Divine fulness contained in the Saviour contrasted with the beggarly elements that a spirit of self-righteousness would in some way mingle with the light of life, the filthy rags it would tack round the "fine raiment" of His righteousness. I have been reading it in connexion with a train of thought suggested by the reading of "Ancient Christianity and the Oxford Tracts," by Isaac Taylor, 242 one of the most eloquent, acute, and pious of writers. Five numbers only have yet appeared. Have you seen them? If not I should like to send you an abstract of his argument. I have gulped it (pardon my coarseness) in a most reptile-like fashion; I must chew it thoroughly to facilitate its assimilation with my mental frame. You will think me interminably loquacious, and still worse you will be ready to compare my scribbled sheet to the walls of an Egyptian tomb for mystery, and determine not to imitate certain wise antiquaries or antiquarian wiseacres who "waste their precious years, how soon to fail?" in deciphering information which has only the lichen and moss of age to make it more valuable than the facts graphically conveyed by an upholsterer's pattern book.
When your pupils can relish Church History I venture to recommend the Chart lately published by Seeley and Burnside, only 7s. far superior in conception to mine, as being more compendious, yet answering the purpose of presenting epochs as nuclei round which less important events instinctively cluster. Much, much love and a request that you will write as soon as you can do so comfortably, from
Your affectionate
Polly.
Am I right in the sum I have sent? 12.6?
I was disappointed in my expectation of forwarding this letter with the parcel, I therefore send it with all its imperfections on its head to prevent your probable surprise at my silence. May Aaron's blessing which involves the sum total of human bliss be ever with you and your
Polly.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 11 March 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 11 March 1841
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Your letter this morning, my Veronica, was sweet to me as the early incense of the Jasmine, and sent a thrill from my heart to my finger ends that impels them at the risk of indigestion, to employ the half hour after dinner, being the only one at liberty, to thank you for the affection that same letter breathes. As well I am anxious to tell you that you have my young and poor judgment now entirely with you in your decision respecting Baginton. I was from the first tremulously alive to the contra of the matter, and was guided solely by what I imagined to be my duty to her whose welfare I have in my heart of hearts.
Thank you, my dear Veronica, for your admonition that I should spare my worthless self. It is true that I am weak, chiefly I believe from a cause that existed when you were with me and continues still, but which I fancy will in the end be beneficial, and must not therefore be checked. I have had considerable bodily exertion of late but I am now favoured with a short breathing time before our departure. My spirits are not exactly low, but my mind is nauseated by feeding on material trifles, and I even find my habit of immersing myself in a pursuit accompany me in engagements naturally repulsive. This is blameworthy, for I ought not to suppose a necessity under any possible circumstances for mere earthliness. I have to be grateful for the disappearance of some little black clouds that seemed to be steering their course towards me, and on the whole our family prospect is comfortable as it respects this nether stage.
Mrs. T. Bull won on my affections during her little stay with me, and I feel much interest in her happiness.
I am expecting four visitors to spend the afternoon with me! I must therefore put myself in company guise and say good bye to you, my Veronica, assuring you that I am as ever
Your affectionate,
Clematis.
Griff March 11th 1841.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff , 11 February 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff , 11 February 1841
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, I, 80.
Griff | February 11. 1841.
My dear Veronica,
There are three accidents of mortality very grievous to me, yea four from which my soul shrinketh -- a freezing northeast wind, foraging for that unsatisfiable animal, man, the din of his revelry, and -- bad writing tackle. 289 My condition at this moment is the product of enduring these evils either retrospectively, actually or prospectively, and I do you to wit that my letter will be matter-of-fact, as undiluted as after a progress through my unhappily transmutative brain any matter may be.
Imprimis -- I have a niece! 290 a healthy little baby, with its dear mamma preserved through her sufferings and as comfortable as ever she has been after her confinements. Here is matter for much thankfulness. I had the pleasure of delivering your nice present into Chrissey's hand last week, and was commissioned to tell you that they are just her desideratum and to tender to you her love and thanks. The baby's name will I think be Mary Louisa owing partly to my denunciation of everyday names before the plebeian monosyllabic surname to which her star has made her inheritor.
On Monday and Tuesday my Father and I were occupied with the sale of furniture at our new house 291 -- it is probable that we shall migrate thither in a month. It is not true that my Father has had much trouble about the Spon Street house. 292 I shall be incessantly hurried until and after our departure, but at present I have to be grateful for a smooth passage through contemplated difficulties. Sewing is my staple article of commerce with the hard trader Time -- now the wind has veered to the south I hope to do much more and that with greater zest than I have done for many months; I mean of all kinds.
My sister Fanny sent me word this morning that a head is wanted for the Baginton school, 293 which is managed entirely by a female. The salary is now £60 per annum and will be 80 at the death of the old schoolmistress, and as coals, brooms etc. are supplied as well as a pleasant and comfortable residence, my sister thinks the remuneration equivalent to a hundred. The number of children does not exceed 30 at the highest calculation, probably not more than 20. It is a situation that offers a permanent home as nothing but misconduct or death would occasion removal, and Fanny surmises that permission would be given to receive boarders. I send you an account of all this because you may probably know some one to whom such a situation would be a rich boon from its possessing the three blessings to which the letter p has the honour of being the initial, plenty, peace and permanence.
Dick has just returned from a journey in quest of R. Whadcock, whose wife gave birth to a triad of babes, 294 and who says that he had the parcel containing pinafores and stockings, but he asserts that there was no R. in the direction and that he therefore did not know whether the parcel was really meant for him. When Dick called at the house to leave the package R. Whadcock was not at home, but he delivered it to an elderly man who was in the house and promised to give it to Whadcock. It appears that he did so and I know not the reason that the sender of the parcel believes it to have miscarried. I should say, by the bye, that Dick found Whadcock had removed from the Coton Road into Abbey St.
My head is but poorly today and I am altogether in so low and flat a key that I fear I have committed treason against the Queen's English, but provided you can tell what my sentences should have been, it is enough. The words of one of Dr. Watts' sweet little hymns have been much in my mind today -- "Twill please us to look back and see, That our whole lives were thine." 295 Such a retrospect is indeed blissful, but how sad to look back on imperfectly used. 296

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 10 June [1840]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 10 June [1840]
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | 25. Gurnault Place | near Myddleton Street | Spa Fields | London. Postmark: COVENTRY | JU | 1840. Extract published: Cross, I, 67.
Griff Whitwednesday.
My own dear Friend,
I have very sufficient reason savoir mauvais gré towards myself for giving you reason to ruminate two moments on your supposed satire which was nothing more than a playful "mighty" attached to my labours. I will make use of the dernier report of non-eloquent people and tell you that the state of our house "transcends description" -- 'tis at the very climax of dirt and confusion, consequently it must now needs turn round and grow better. I do hope that in a fortnight we shall have a tolerable degree of tranquility, and I do beg, as a proof of your affection, that you will once more visit Griff while I am its mistress. The last sentence was not written for Doctor Johnson, who had a particular inveteracy against a certain little superfluous auxiliary that figures therein, 206 but for my friend, who will pity my little troubles when I tell her that in addition to already detailed perplexities, I have had Dr. Kittermaster 207 two days to amuse, and have been far from well since Saturday. I shall have I hope a little trip with my Father next week into Derbyshire, and this [lark] will probably be beneficial to me, so that do not imagine I am inviting you to come and hear moaning, when you need all attainable relaxation. I assure you I am exhilarated by my prospects in many points of view, though I seem to need chastisement so much as almost to anticipate its introduction by a change of circumstances.
So you are in London! a fact which I have happily recalled at this moment, for though in full possession of the contents of your letter I am so stultified as to be unable to use my knowledge, and was on the point of directing to you at Burton. May the London air be blest to the refreshment of your body and may you possess that peace which no exterior tumult can disturb! If you have not met with a little book called "Hours of Thought," by W. McCombie 208 and should happen to do so, make an effort if necessary to peruse it. It is well worth it. Please to offer my love to Mrs. Buchanan, 209 to imagine all excuses for this letter, so little worthy of you, and to believe me as ever,
Your affectionate
Mary Ann.
May I trouble you with a commission? It is to procure for me an Italian book recommended by Mr. Brezzi -- or probably I had better send you his list which he gave me to select from that I might have something containing familiar Italian. If you can get it I should like the first, Silvio Pellico, Le mie prigioni; if not, Storia d'Italia. 210 If they are cheap I should like both. I beg of you not to endeavor to procure the books unless you can do so quite easily and agreeably.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 1 October 1840
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, 1 October 1840
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd R. [sic] Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering | Northamptonshire. Postmark: COVENTRY | oc 2 | 1840. Extracts published: Cross, I, 73-76.
Griff | October 1st 1840.
My dear Veronica, which being interpreted, is [fidelity in friendship,] when I remember that there was an enquiry at the close of your last letter concerning the fate of your books, which are yet in my keeping, I feel some anxiety as to the effect of my silence of nearly a fortnight -- possibly it has been that of putting a troublesome mote, however minute, in your mind's eye; but without any prolix shewing of causes I beg of you to pardon an error which is not without mitigation from the variety of little matters that Michaelmas presents for my attention. Last week I was absent from home from Wednesday to Saturday, in quest of the "coy maiden" Pleasure -- at least nominally so, the real motive being rather to gratify another's feelings. 249 I heard the Messiah on Thursday morning at Birmingham and some beautiful selections from other oratorios of Handel and Haydn on Friday. With a stupid, drowsy sensation produced by standing sentinel over damson cheese 250 and a warm stove I cannot do better than ask you to read if accessible Wordsworth's short poem on the Power of Sound 251 with which I have just been delighted.
My prospects have been long fluctuating so as to make it unsafe for me to mention them; now I believe I may say that I am not to be dislodged from my present pedestal or resign my sceptre. The secession has devolved on another and the flutterer is to leave the nest -- that nest that will still have its most downy nook ready to receive you. I am as oriental in my style as if I were under the perpendicular darts of Apollo, you will think, in the land of the morning. I am really sorry to send you profitless babil such as my late letters have been filled with; however "les plus courtes erreurs sont toujours les meilleures" 252 and I hope to become more methodical once again in my occupations.
I have made an alteration in my plans with Mr. Brezzi, and shall henceforward take Italian and German alternately so that I shall not be liable to the consciousness of having imperative employment for every interstice of time. There seems a greater affinity between German and my mind than Italian, though less new to me, possesses. I am reading Schiller's Maria Stuart and Tasso. I was pleased with a little poem I learnt a week or two ago in German, and as I want you to like it I have just put the idea it contains into English doggrel which quite fails to represent the beautiful simplicity and nature of the original, but yet I hope will give you sufficiently its sense to screen the odiousness of the translation. Eccola:
Question and Answer. "Where blooms, O my Father, a thornless rose?" "That can I not tell thee, my child; Not one on the bosom of earth e'er grows, But wounds whom its charms have beguiled." "Would I'd a rose on my bosom to lie! But I shrink from the piercing thorn; I long, but I dare not its point defy, I long, and I gaze forlorn." "Not so, O my child, round the stem again Thy resolute fingers entwine -- Forego not the joy for its sister pain, Let the rose, the sweet rose, be thine!"
I was this morning deeply struck by a figure in I think the 31 chapter of Isaiah 253 where a picture is given of a young lion tearing the flock and fearlessly continuing his work of destruction though a multitude of shepherds be assembled against him -- this to shadow forth the works that God doeth, the desolations He maketh in the earth, unobstructed by all the mustered array of human power and skill. I must prepare for bed. Forgive my desultory nothings. Write as soon as you can and believe me
Your own
Clematis.
Would not a parcel reach you by railway?

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [6 July 1840]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [6 July 1840]
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | 12. Buenos Ayres | <Ramsgate.> | Try Margate. Postmarks: COVENTRY | Jy 7 | 1840; RAMSGATE | Jy 8 | 1840. Extract published: Cross, I, 70.
Griff Monday Evening.
My very dear Friend,
In this vestibule to life's theatre we must be content to accomplish all our projects and realize all our hopes imperfectly. I am going to give you a new illustration of this trite dictum by replying promptly indeed to your Saturday's letter, (and this part of my wishes my affection and sympathy will not let me forego) but with little of the composure and still less of the leisure that are required to speak of those subjects which alone are asbestian 223 and retain any substance in the fire of tribulation. I am afraid to imagine what may now be your circumstances. I can only renew my prayer that you may have the assurance that "your Father is at the helm" and find that an adequate support. I am a little tried, in my style of trial just now, but I need it.
I know you like to hear of the state of my thermometer, so I will tell you that though I am not in hot water I am in some that is slightly troublous. I believe it is decided that Father and I should leave Griff 224 and take up our residence somewhere in the neighbourhood of Coventry, if we can obtain a suitable house and this is at present a matter of anxiety. So you see I am likely still to have a home where I can independently welcome you. I am really so plunged in an abyss of books, preserves and sundry important trivialities that I must send you this bare proof that I have not cast the remembrance of you to a dusty corner of my heart. I beg you, if possible, to send me a bulletin by the earliest post. I promise to write more if it will be acceptable. Ever believe that "my heart is as thy heart" that you may rely on me as a second self, and that I shall with my usual selfishness lose no opportunity of gratifying my duplicate. Basta, you say, and I obey. Good bye.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [30 March 1840]
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | M 31 | 1840. Extracts published: Cross, I, 62-65.
Griff Monday Evening.
My very dear Friend,
If you go on conferring favours on me I shall be so hopelessly distanced in the race, that I must e'en as I have heard some grateful people systematically do, quarrel with my Friend to be quit of the sense of obligation. Seriously I do fully estimate your kind sacrifice of precious time to my gratification and I heartily wish I could give you a kiss with my thanks at this moment, though by the bye I am forgetting that our house is now, and will be for the next two months miserably noisy and disorderly with the musical operations of masons carpenters and painters. You know how abhorrent all this is to my tastes and feelings, taking all the spice out of my favorite little epithet "This working day world": 184 I can no longer use it figuratively. How impressive must the gradual rise of Solomon's Temple have been! Each prepared mass of virgin marble laid in reverential silence. I fancy Heber has compared it to the growth of a Palm. 185
Your nice miniature chart which I shall carefully treasure up has quite satisfied me that Dr. Pearson at least has not realized my conceptions, though it has left me still dubious as to my own power of doing so. I will just (if you can bear to hear more of the matter) give you an idea of the plan, which may have partly faded from your memory. The series of perpendicular columns will successively contain, the Roman Emperors with their dates, the political and religious state of the Jews, the bishops, remarkable men and events in the several churches, a column being devoted to each of the chief ones, the aspect of heathenism and Judaism toward Christianity, the chronology of the Apos[tolical] and Patristical writings, schisms and heresies, General Councils, eras of corruption, under which head the remarks would be general, and I thought possibly an application of the Apocalyptic prophecies, which would merely require a few figures and not take up room. I think there must be a break in the chart after the establishment of Christianity as the religion of the Empire, and I have come to a determination not to carry it beyond the first acknowledgment of the supremacy of the Pope, by Phocas 186 in 606 when Mahommedanism became a besom of destruction in the hand of the Lord, and completely altered the aspect of Ecclesiastical Hist[or]y. So much for this, at present, airy project, about which I hope never to teaze you more.
Mr. Harper 187 lent me a little time ago a work by the Revd W. Gresley, begging me to read it, as he thought it was calculated to make me a proselyte to the opinions it advocates. I had skimmed the book before ("Portrait of An English Churchman") but I read it attentively a second time and was pleased with the spirit of piety that breathes throughout. His last work is one in a similar style, "The English Citizen," 188 which I have cursorily read, and as they are both likely to be seen by you, I want to know your opinion of them. Mine is this: that they are sure to have a powerful influence on the minds of small readers and shallow thinkers, as, from the simplicity and clearness with which the author, by his beau idéal characters, enunciates his sentiments they furnish a magazine of easily wielded weapons for morning calling and evening party controversialists, as well as that really honest minds will be inclined to think they have found a resting-place amid the foot-balling of religious parties. But it appears to me that there is unfairness in arbitrarily selecting a train of circumstances, and a set of characters as a development of a class of opinions. In this way we might make atheism appear wonderfully calculated to promote social happiness. I remember, as I dare say you do, a very amiable atheist depicted by Bulwer in Devereux, 189 and for some time after the perusal of that book, which I read 7 or 8 years ago, I was considerably shaken by the impression that religion was not a requisite to moral excellence.
Have you not alternating seasons of mental stagnation and activity? Just such as the political economists say there must be in a nation's pecuniary condition -- all one's precious specie, time, going out to procure a stock of commodities while one's own manufactures are too paltry to be worth vending. I am just in that condition, partly I think owing to my not having met with any steel to sharpen my edge against for the last three weeks. I am going to read a volume of the Oxford Tracts and the Lyra Apostolica; 190 the former I almost shrink from the labour of conning, but the other I confess I am attracted towards by some highly poetical extracts that I have picked up in various quarters. I have just bought Mr. Keble's Christian Year, 191 a volume of sweet poetry that perhaps you know; if not it is a dish both in ingredients and cooking that would suit you. Not more than 2/6 or 3s. The fields of poesy look more lovely than ever now I have hedged myself in the geometrical regions of fact, where I can do nothing but draw parallels and measure differences in a double sense. I shall soon hate heretics as vehemently as any papist can desire, for both their wide uniformity and their narrow differences are as Chrissey would say, pestering. Certain divines enjoin us to consult ecclesiastical records for the settling of our faith, a result the very opposite to what they appear likely to produce, in my humble and narrow apprehension. I was struck yesterday with Mr. Hake's text, 2. Hosea 6 and 7 verses. They appeared partly an exact description of some of my experience. How exquisite the succeeding chapter is, the 3d I fancy, in which the Almighty covenants to bestow on His people all blessings for time and eternity! "I will betroth thee unto me" etc. Why do we yearn after a fellow mortal but because we do not live and delight in conscious union with Him who condescends to say, "Ye shall no more call me Baali or Lord, but ye shall call me Ishi, 192 my husband." Our Lord's words, "Henceforth I call you not servants but friends," 193 etc. seem to be an allusion to this text.
With respect to my own state of soul of which I have said nothing for some time, I fear that my sins or rather one particular manifestation of them, have forsaken me instead of my forsaking and abhorring them. I feel that a sight of one being whom I have not beheld except passingly since the interview I last described to you would probably upset all; but as it is, the image now seldom arises in consequence of entire occupation and, I trust in some degree, desire and prayer to be free from rebelling against Him whose I am by right, whose I would be by adoption. I endeavoured to pray for the beloved object to whom I have alluded, I must still a little while say beloved, last night and felt soothingly melted in thinking that if mine be really prayers my acquaintance with him has probably caused the first to be offered up specially in his behalf. But all this I ought not to have permitted to slip from my pen. 194
I am quite angry with those around you for letting your life be uninterrupted monotony, when they have the power of pleasantly varying it. Why does not Mr. Craig shew his superiority to the childishness and narrowness, that shew themselves in wayward jealousy on one side and stiff assumption on the other? You do not say anything of your health, hence I conclude you are tolerably well. Dear Chrissey has been staying at Warwick, a fact that will describe her state of health better than my rhetoric. Poor Mrs. Buchanan has been in anxiety about her little Anney, 195 who has been very ill. She desired me to tell you that Mrs. MacDonell has a son! The Attlebro Bazaar will take place in November next; but if you work for it, I shall blush. It is now twelve o'clock, and the obtuseness of my faculties has reached its climax. I would ask you to forgive all the nonsense and bad English I have scribbled, but that you have interdicted all such appeals. The sooner I see your handwriting the better for
Your affectionate
Polly.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [20 July 1840]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [20 July 1840]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: July 1840. Extract published: Cross, I, 69-70.
Griff Monday Morning.
My very dear Friend,
Twice before I have written an exordium for a letter to you, but as I generally let my feelings flow to the end of my pen as soon as I begin to write to you, I am obliged to reject both, as no longer containing a true representation of myself. Bodily debility has of late made me a slave to a train of morbid fancies -- from these I trust I am emerging, and I can this morning write to you with something of the calmness and cheerfulness that are the proper result of mercies more than I can even number. I have said thus much to account for my not sending you a letter as soon as I had reason to believe that you were settled at Burton. My heart has lately been with you more than ever and had I any magic at command it would certainly be used in transporting me to Burton for one day. My last accounts of the poor sufferer at Nuneaton 225 were favourable; but you will probably receive more regular and trustworthy information concerning him than I. I cherish hopes concerning the result of this scourging should God see fit in His immeasurable longsuffering, to uphold his life under such excruciating pain as he must endure. I long to know Mrs. B's spiritual state. It is an inexpressible mercy, enough to absorb our finite gratitude and leave none for other gifts, to feel that the "Lord God hath opened our ear" 226 to His voice, which is to be heard in every note of the scale to which His dealings in the Kingdom of Grace and of Providence are set; from the still and gently drawing whispers of His Spirit in the soul to the deep-toned and almost stunning thunder of his power when whole nations, while falling a sacrifice on the shrine of His incensed justice, subserve at the same time the designs of His compassion by putting others in fear that they may know themselves to be but men. We may so far agree with the Quietists 227 as to exercise that constant waiting on God for instruction and comfort which they make the sum total of religion but which we would unite with that active obedience that reasonable service, so prominently set forth in precept both figurative and literal and embodied in the conduct of God's saints, throughout the "lively oracles" 228 that have been committed to us. Our poor bodies are in league with our spiritual enemies within and without to make us weary in well doing, 229 we get troubled by reason of the way and we sit down weeping in the camp at the prospect of encountering the terrific giants 230 that stand between us and our promised Canaan, after all the trials of the traversed wilderness. What is the remedy in this case? Surely more of the grace that has subdued kingdoms wrought righteousness stopped the mouths of lions, out of weakness has produced strength, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens. 231 How replete with meaning for doctrine, for reproof, for instruction in righteousness is the historical part of Scripture. Is it not clear that strong faith in the promises, real appropriation of them, must be a fountain ever sending forth streams of love and joy? The greater our assurance of pardon, the more lively and active our gratitude. While enjoying the light of God's countenance and feeding on the supplies that His Spirit imparts through the word and works of God we shall scarcely miss inferior comforts when withdrawn. Blessed state! O that I could attain it -- and why not? Because I am straitened not in Christ but in my own bowels. 232 We are like poor creatures of whom I have read, who, for some cause or other, having been thrust out of a ship by their companions, try to grasp first one part of the vessel then another for support, until by the successive lashes that are given to make them loose their hold, they have no fingers left by which to venture another hopeless experiment on pitiless hearts. So we, having voluntarily caused ourselves to be cast out as evil by the world, are continually indicating a vacillation in our choice by trying to lean on some part of it within reach, and it is mercy that orders the lashing of our disobedient fingers, even though for a time we be faint and bleeding from the correction.
Do you not think that sufficient consideration will be felt towards you to make a short cessation from your occupations attainable some time during the half year? I really fear for your health, and I wonder some plan was not contrived to give you a rather longer respite, your circumstances being known.
I write with a very tremulous hand as you will perceive; both this and many other defects in my letter are attributable to a very mighty cause -- no other than the boiling of currant jelly. I have had much of this kind of occupation lately, and I grieve to say I have not gone through it so cheerfully as the character of a Christian who professes to do all even the most trifling duty as to the Lord 233 demands. My mind is consequently run all wild and bears nothing but dog roses.
I am truly obliged to you for getting me Spenser, amid all your anxieties. I have not yet received it. How shall I send to you Don
Quixote which I have quite finished? It is a charming passe-temps (a word by the bye that I ought to have outlawed long ago) full of philosophical wit. Isaac is in Paris! There has been a mist of suspense thrown round our prospects lately. My brother's marriage is at present uncertain, so I know not what will be our situation. Chrissey is very well and happy and the darlings healthy. Forgive all that needs forgiveness in my letter. Write soon, if only to tell me how you do.
Ever your affectionate
Mary Ann.
You will think my common sense has begged a furlough, that I should so badly manage my paper.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [18 August 1838]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Aug. 18. 1838. Address: Miss Lewis | Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | Northamptonshire. Postmark: COVENTRY | AU 18 | 1838. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 39-42.
Griff | Saturday Night.
My dear Friend /
My night thoughts are generally even more misty than my day thoughts; I would not therefore have inflicted them on you without good reason, especially as my letter writing is, like my chess playing, unpremeditated and quite at random, and so dependent on the immediate circumstances in which I write; but when I tell you that I have been to London, that neither my ménage nor my head is quite restored to order and quietude, that I have two correspondents besides yourself to whom I am anxious soon to reply, and a dozen other things of various kinds that must be done and that all require time, you will forgive me if of two evils I have chosen to write now at the risk of appearing extraordinarily stupid, rather than by delay to appear ungrateful for your kind remembrance of me.
I really feel for you, sacrificing as you are your own tastes and comforts to the pleasure of others, and that in a manner the most trying to rebellious flesh and blood, for I verily believe that in most cases it requires more of a martyr's spirit to endure with patience and cheerfulness daily crossings and interruptions of our petty desires and pursuits, and to rejoice in them if they can be made to conduce to God's glory and our own sanctification, than even to lay down our lives for the truth.
I trust that the expected union may ultimately issue in the spiritual benefit of both parties; for my part when I hear of the marrying and giving in marriage that is constantly being transacted I can only sigh for those who are multiplying earthly ties which though powerful enough to detach their heart and thoughts from heaven, are so brittle as to be liable to be snapped asunder at every breeze. You will think I need nothing but a tub for my habitation to make me a perfect female Diogenes, and I plead guilty to occasional misanthropical thoughts, but not to the indulgence of them; still I must believe that those are happiest who are not fermenting themselves by engaging in projects for earthly bliss, who are considering this life merely a pilgrimage, a scene calling for diligence and watchfulness, not for repose and amusement. I do not deny that there may be many who can partake with a high degree of zest of all the lawful enjoyments the world can offer and yet live in near communion with their God; who can warmly love the creature, and yet be careful that the Creator maintains His supremity in their hearts; but I confess that in my short experience and narrow sphere of action I have never been able to attain this; I find, as Dr. Johnson said respecting his wine, total abstinence much easier than moderation. 66 But I am as usual becoming egotistical, and you by the bye have naughtily encouraged the habit. I am in danger of imitating the frog in the fable vainly imagining herself a rival for the ox, and such pride generally has a similar catastrophe to hers.
You must let me tell you though that I was not at all delighted with "the stir of the great Babel," 67 and the less so probably owing to the circumstances attending my visit thither. Isaac and I went alone (that seems rather Irish) and staid only a week, every day of which we worked hard at seeing sights. I think Greenwich Hospital interested me more than anything else. We heard on Sunday morning a very animated and experimental sermon from the Revd T. Dale 68 of whom you may have heard. In the afternoon we went to St. Paul's where I grieve to say my strongest feeling was that of indignation (I mean during the sermon) towards the surpliced personages, chapters I think they are, who performed the chanting, for it appears with them a mere performance, their behaviour being that of schoolboys, glad of an opportunity to titter unreproved. If I am not mistaken we did not hear Mr. Craig 69 to advantage -- it was the common swing of Goliah's arm, and I have no doubt would only enable us to guess the real force of the giant. I do not wonder you are pleased with Pascal; his thoughts may be returned to the palate again and again with increasing rather than diminished relish. I have highly enjoyed Hannah More's letters; the contemplation of so blessed a character as hers is very salutary. 70 "That ye be not slothful but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises," 71 is a valuable admonition. I was once told that there was nothing out of myself to prevent my becoming as eminently holy as St. Paul, and though I think that is too sweeping an assertion, yet it is very certain we are generally too low in our aims, more anxious for safety than sanctity, for place than purity, forgetting that each involves the other, and that as Doddridge tells us to rest satisfied with any attainments in religion is a fearful proof that we are ignorant of the very first principles of it. O that we could live only for Eternity, that we could realize its nearness! I know you do not love quotations so I will not give you one but if you do not distinctly remember it, do turn to the passage in Young's "Infidel reclaimed" beginning O vain vain vain all else, Eternity! 72 and do love the lines for my sake.
I heard a few days ago from dear Miss Rebecca Franklin who is now in her turn indisposed. Miss Franklin 73 is in her old station again but not with equal strength for its duties; so that these dear friends as well as others are for a time "in heaviness." 74 My dear Sister is tolerably well and our dear baby still fatter than when you saw him. Isaac presumes to say that I must send his love to you. And now, last not least, for we save, you know, the choicest morsel till last, you tell me nothing about your own health which I fear is suffering from the confusion you describe. I beg you will not forget this when you write again, if I can hope that you will be magnanimous enough to forgive the trouble I fear my almost undecipherable letter will give you. Do not, pray write neatly to me, for I cannot undertake to correspond with any one who will not allow me to scribble, though this precious sheet has I think an extra portion of untidiness owing to my being from a cause I need not mention in a degree of perturbation that prevents my either thinking or writing as I should like. Men speak of the inequalities of this world, but I confess I think happiness very equally distributed. I speak of course of happiness as connected with externals, for those who have the Lord for their portion enjoy satisfaction utterly unknown to those without hope and without God in the world. 75 I feel unable to write more, and can only beg you to believe me
Your truly obliged and affectionate
Polly.
I beg you to believe that I know which way a letter should be directed, but that as in many more important cases I have failed to put my theory in practice. 76

GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [17 July 1839]
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | at Mr. Burbage's | Kenilworth. Postmark: COVENTRY | JY 17 | 1839. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 57-59.
Griff Wednesday Morning.
My dear Friend,
I thank you very heartily for your kind note, and I send you in return some doggrel lines, the crude fruit of a lonely walk last evening, when the words of one of our martyrs occurred to me. You must be acquainted with the idiosyncrasy of my authorship, which is that my effusions, once committed to paper, are like the laws of the Medes and Persians that alter not. 135 My attempt at poetry will serve to amuse you, if no more, and you love a laugh so well that it would be ungenerous to withhold the occasion of one.
I have a second little nephew! 136 A new call to thankfulness. Had Mr. Bull 137 gone to Kenilworth again before your departure I would have sent your book, which had my blood a "moral flow" I could not mention without blushing. May health and peace, the only earthly image of heaven, attend you wherever you may go! With much love,
Your sincere
Mary Ann Evans
"Knowing that shortly I must put off this tabernacle" -- 2 Pet. 1. 16. 138 As o'er the fields by evening's light I stray, I hear a still, small whisper -- "Come away! Thou must to this bright, lovely world soon say Farewell!" The mandate I'd obey, my lamp prepare, Gird up my garments, give my soul to pray'r, And say to earth and all that breathe earth's air Farewell!
Thou sun, to whose parental beam I owe All that has gladden'd me while here below, -- Moon, stars, and covenant confirming bow, Farewell! Ye verdant meads, fair blossoms, stately trees, Sweet song of birds, and soothing hum of bees, Refreshing odours, wafted on the breeze, Farewell! Ye patient servants of creation's lord Whose mighty strength is govern'd by his word, Who raiment, food and help in toil afford, Farewell! Ye feebler, freer tribes, that people air, Fairy like insects, making buds your lair, Ye that in water shine, and frolic there, Farewell! Books that have been to me as chests of gold, Which, miser like, I secretly have told, And for them love, health, friendship, peace have sold, Farewell! Blest volume! whose clear truth-writ page, once known, Fades not before heaven's sunshine or hell's moan, To thee I say not, of earth's gifts alone, Farewell! 139 Dear kindred, whom the Lord to me has given, Must the dear tie that binds us, now be riven? No! say I only till we meet in heaven, Farewell! There shall my newborn senses find new joy, New sounds, new sights my eyes and ears employ, Nor fear that word that here brings sad alloy, Farewell!

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [13 March 1840]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 62, under date 2 May 1840.
Griff Friday Evening.
My very dear Friend,
This is a business letter and will be written in business-like haste. I could not bear to send you such a one in return for your last which will be one of my treasured remembrances of an era in my existence but that I know you will be glad to think of me as thoroughly employed, as indeed I am to an extent that makes me fear I shall not be able to accomplish anything well. I have engaged if possible to complete the Chart, 171 the plan of which I sketched out last year, by November next, and I am encouraged to believe that it will answer my purpose to print it. The profits arising from its sale, if any, will go partly to Attleborough Church 172 and partly to a favorite object of my own. Mrs. Newdegate 173 is very anxious that I should do thus and she permits me to visit her library when I please in search of any books that may assist me. Now what I want to beg of you is that you will, if you have an opportunity, pump Mr. Craig on the subject, and obtain his opinion on the utility, feasibility for me, and best mode of executing the work. Will you ask him what he considers the best authority for the date of the apostolical writings? I should like to carry the chart down to the Reformation, if my time and resources will enable me to do so.
We are going to have a Clothing Club, the arrangement and starting of which are left to me. Naughty Mrs. Newdegate promised to send me rules which she has forgotten. I am ashamed to run the risk of troubling you, but I should be very grateful if you could send me an abstract of the rules by which yours is regulated. Now I hope I have done with self of which both you and I have reason to be weary. I do not tell you the cause of my silence after your permission that I should write again within last week, as that would lead me to subjects on which I cannot trust myself; I have felt grieved that I have not been able to entitle myself to a bulletin respecting your bodily and mental health. One circumstance connected with the trial you mentioned in your last was gratifying to me, namely that it gave occasion for the triumph of Christian friendship over a regard to your own comfort, for I am sure it must have been a task for you to write with your eyes and heart both sore. I am anxious to know that your persecutor 174 has had a thorough castigation for her own sake as well as yours.
Mrs. T. Bull has entrusted me with a message of love to you and this reminds me to tell you that I was invited to a party at her house last week. You know I had causes for anything but high spirits before-hand, and when I had been there some time the conviction that I was not in a situation to maintain the Protestant character of the true Christian, together with the oppressive noise that formed the accompaniment to the dancing, the sole amusement, produced first headache and then that most wretched and unpitied of afflictions, hysteria, so that I regularly disgraced myself. 175 Mrs. Bull was extremely kind. One good effect of a temporary annoyance and indisposition will be to render me more decided in rejecting all invitations of a dubious character.
You see I have rolled again on the centre to which I invariably gravitate. I wish I could make you amends for nearly four sides of uninteresting matter by sending you something worth reading before I say good bye. Perhaps something I wrote this morning to my useful little pocket-book (Brown's patent with a metallic pencil the marks of which are indelible) will amuse you. Wretched doggrel as the lines are, I would the sentiment they convey though obscurely were graven with an iron pen and lead in the too rocky heart within me. I will put them on the envelope. 176 I beseech you to pardon my trifling, my egotism, and much more that is perceptibly offensive to others though not to myself. I have not referred to realities that I desire to have nearest my heart, for several reasons. I hope soon to write a little more tolerably to you. I shall hug a letter from you, and I assure you I need one as much as ever. Tell me all about your dear self. I think you will be pleased to hear that Isaac is determinately busy, and altogether improving. It is time I came to an end for you see I forget even my nominative case. 177 Never, you will say when it is in the first person, and to this charge I plead guilty but have great confidence in the clemency of the court. Love and pray for your grateful and affectionate
Mary Ann.
I promise to write again very soon if that will be the least bait to you.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Griff, [13 February 1840]
MS: Yale. On inside of envelope. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering | Northamptonshire. Postmark: COVENTRY | FE 13 | 1840. Published: Cross, I, 81.
I have been reading the 3 volumes of the Life and Times of Louis the Fourteenth 161 and am as eagerly waiting for the 4th and last as any voracious novel reader for Bulwer's last. I am afraid I am getting quite martial in my spirit, and in the warmth of my sympathy for Turenne and Condé losing my hatred of war. Such a conflict between individual and moral influence is no novelty. But certainly war though the heaviest scourge with which the Divine wrath against sin is manifested in Time, has been a necessary vent for impurities and a channel for tempestuous passions that must have otherwise made the whole earth like the land of the devoted Canaanites to vomit forth the inhabitants thereof; 162 awful as such a sentiment appears it seems to me that in the present condition of man, and I do not mean this in the sense that Cowper does, such a purgation of the body politic is very likely essential to its health. 163 A foreign war would soon put an end to our national humours that are growing to so alarming a head. -- What do you think of the Progress of Architecture as a subject for Poetry?

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 4 October 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 4 October 1841
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: CONVENTRY | OC 4 | 1841. Hitherto unpublished.
Foleshill | October 4th 1841.
My beloved Friend,
To me, who am continually having to fear that I live in vain it was no [meagre] comfort to receive an assurance that with respect to you at least this is not the case. But my pleasure in this thought is much tarnished by the recollection of the silly nothings I sent you the other day when you must have been ill prepared to overlook their worthlessness. The use of the pen is even a more responsible possession than that of the tongue and I ought to blush when I remember my own defalcations as a steward of both these trusts.
Thank you for the real treat Mr. Henslowe's letters have given me. They deserve transcription, and have won for him my love and respect maugre a pre-existing distaste. The introduction to Mrs. Sumner 372 is a promising boon and such a person is likely to seize indications of integral character in your letter that will render the paucity of adjuncts a minor consideration. What has that coarse man of books 373 done to wound you? I have never liked that you should put yourself in the position of a recipient of favours from him, and quite agree with you that the absence of his testimony is a "breach" more honourable than an "observance" 374 at least to you. I shall this morning take an opportunity of lodging in my dear Friend Mrs. Pears's hands as good a description of your Gouvernante character as I am capable of giving (I hope you will not be angry with me for venturing to do so) that she may forward it to Miss Crump 375 of London, who has a flourishing school and has often been successful in obtaining situations for others.
You are not the only dear friend who is suffering. The Miss Franklins have been and are enduring a complication of trials. The refiner and purifier of silver 376 must see His own likeness in the metal ere he ceases the purging process. He will then make you glad according to the years wherein you have known adversity. 377 You will think it is a strange application of a text when I tell you that I have often used for comfort a passage in Joel when conscious of the desolating effects of back-sliding on my heart. "I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the canker worm, the caterpillar and the palmer-worm." 378 It will be a less strained interpretation of the words to make them symbolic of the power and intention (as I think we generally see it to be) of God to make the tearful sowing a prelude even to a rich harvest of peace and comfort on earth.
How joyful will it be to put my arms round you at Christmas! let us pray that our meeting may be fraught with much profit. I fear you will have some difficulty in reading this letter, but I know you will have none in believing that I am still though an unworthy yet a sincere, loving and I trust constant friend. If you can do so I should be glad if you would send me a few lines when you hear from Mrs. Sumner.
Your
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 31 July-2 August 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 31 July-2 August 1841
MS: Yale. Brief extract: Cross, 1, 89.
Foleshill Road | July 31st 1841.
My beloved Veronica,
Among all my queries I have never yet asked what is your destination after your holidays supposing you do not meet with a settled home. Are you to return to Burton? I am very anxious to know the answer to this question and I hope your poor eyes will by the time you receive this be free from tears, that writing may not be a grievance. Your tempting allusion to the half bed and your items of description would be a powerful loadstone if I were not already firmly fixed by a still mightier one. I am beginning to be interlaced with multiplying ties of duty and affection that, while they render my new home happier, forbid me to leave it on a pleasure-seeking expedition. I think indeed that both my heart and my limbs would leap to behold the [great and wide sea] 336 that old Ocean on which man can leave no trace; 337 but the emotions created by soul-stirring sights are more healthful and commonly stronger when duty leads us by them than when we go to them. You my Veronica have been thus led and I trust the breezes may invigorate your body while a more precious wind may blow on your soul's garden and call the spices forth. 338 I am instigated just now to increased -- o'clock. This letter my Veronica is written in odds and ends of time, and the thoughts will be equally fragmentary. I have forgotten or at least lost zest for the idea I was going to pursue, so I will take up another, in which I am very desirous that you should [jump with me.] It is a proposal that we should endeavour to think of each other and if possible lift up an ejaculation to our common Father on each other's behalf at Curfew time and that if no impediment exist we should take a glance at the firmament. I do not tax you with a long meditation on my worthless self; two minutes will suffice for my object. And will you choose one of the books of Scripture that we may each take the same morsel morning by morning, a verse at a time until we have reached the end?
If you return to town and make a prolongued stay there I really shall beg you to execute some commissions for me of the same kind as those you so nicely performed before. I can enclose the money in a letter as I should be rather extravagant if I had the opportunity. This is altogether a selfish letter, written to gratify my curiosity and obtain my own wishes. I shall so far persist in my self pleasing as to beg you to write me an answer as quickly as possible. Should a work, now I believe out of print entitled [Thoughts preparative or persuasive to private devotion] by John Sheppard 339 fall in your way, read it -- it is a sweet booklet of pious meditation adapted to accompany the Christian in all the windings of his experience. I am sorry to send you a letter that breathes no fragrance my Veronica but you will believe me when I tell you that I have much business for body and mind. Lebe wohl --
Your Clematis.
August 2d.
