Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 3[-4] September 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 3[-4] September 1841
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | SE 4 | 1841. Extracts published: Cross, I, 89-92.
Foleshill | September 3d 1841.
My beloved Veronica,
I have had many compunctious visitings for the reiteration of the word [write] in my last contribution to the revenue in the shape of a note to you. I was tickled the other day by a witty account of a statesman's and general's efforts to convince others that he was undismayed by certain untoward events. Since says the writer, to say [I am fearless] was equivalent to nothing he set about teaching the fact by way of induction, putting on airs of determination and authority, and a corresponding fierceness of action. Now I suppose I am in a similar situation as to the question of my selfishness and inconsideration. To say [I am really generous and would not have my Veronica spend her precious moments of leisure on me] is of little avail, so I must prove all this "per modo d'induzione." There is another truth I would have you enter on your creed which does not seem yet to be there -- viz. that to receive the mere outpouring of feeling from you is my chief consolation under inability to assist you more validly. Ergo never apologize for details about yourself, they being the gold dust for which I barter my large sheet of rag. And, anah, 349 my honey, why talk you in voice as hollow as that of a half-starved hermit, about plans for the future, their deceptiveness, impossibility etc. etc.? Know you not, you recreant daughter of the green isle, that you owe a debt to a friend who will not allow you to have the benefit of [habeas corpus] for next Christmas? Here you have infamously put off payment for a year and presume to have other thoughts in your head than that of honestly bringing her principal and interest when you will really have the means! I vow I will change your name for some brand of treachery, 350 if you do not quickly impetrate my mercy. I must now happily for you go to pay a morning visit to my poor dear neighbor 351 who has long been seriously ill. Of course my mood will be set to a different key when I begin to write again. -- --
I thought the other day that a mode of studying Scripture very beneficial to adults might be made equally so to your pupils. It is that of taking the parables or other portions of the New Testament for analyzation -- writing in words other than those of Scripture the general truths contained or implied in the passage. For a hasty example, the familiar but impressive parable of the Sower 352 might yield the following heads for reflection and perhaps many more. 1. Satan is watchfully active in counteracting the effects of the preached word. 2. A semblance of conversion is frequently produced under the means of grace which has not its foundation in principle. 3. The cares, pleasures, and riches of the world are essentially opposed to the heavenward progress of the soul. 4. There is a connection between the affections and the understanding causing the corruption of the one to issue in the perversion of the other. They who understand the word are said to receive it into an honest and good heart. 5. The saving reception of the word is invariably marked by strong effort on the part of the recipient to [hold fast] what he has heard. "Having heard the word, keep it." 6. There are different degrees of holiness even among those born again of the incorruptible seed. 7. The obedience of Christ involves circumstances calling for patience. The frequent and indeed constant use of this plan would I am convinced give a clearness and comprehensiveness to our knowledge of Scripture truths that I have not found common, and the lack of which I am earnestly desirous to supply in myself. Perhaps you have already used this or a superior method, but if I were conversing with you viv'e2 voce I should say all this, and you know my rule for letterwriting.
I have been revelling in Nichol's Architecture of the heavens and
Phenomena of the Solar system 353 and have been in imagination winging my flight from system to system, from universe to universe, trying to conceive myself in such a position and with such a visual faculty as would enable me to enjoy what Young enumerates among the novelties of the [stranger] man when he burst the shell, to Behold an infinite of floating worlds Divide the crystal waves of ether pure, In endless voyage without port. 354 "Hospitable infinity"! Nichol beautifully says. 355 How should I love to have a thoroughgoing student with me that we might read together! We might each alternately employ the voice and the fingers and thus achieve just twice as much as a poor solitary. I am more impressed than ever with a truth beautifully expressed in [Woman's Mission.] "Learning is only so far valuable as it serves to enlarge and enlighten the bounds of conscience." 356 This I believe it eminently does when pursued humbly and piously and from a belief that it is a solemn duty to cultivate every faculty of our nature so far as primary obligations allow. There is an exhortation of St. Paul's that I should love to take as my motto. Finally my brethren whatsoever things are honest (you know the continuation) -- if there be any virtue and if there be any praise think on these things. 357
I have had to lament lately my Veronica that mine is not a hard working mind -- that it requires frequent rests. How has your body served you in this particular? Have you been pretty well at Burton? I am violently in love with the Italian fashion of repeating an adjective or adverb and even noun to give force to expression. There is so much more fire in it than in our circumlocutory phrases, our dull verys and exceedinglys and extremelys. I strongly recommend Hallam 358 to you. I shall read it again if I live. When a sort of haziness comes over the mind making one feel weary of articulated or written signs of ideas does not the notion of a less laborious mode of communication, of a perception approaching more nearly to intuition seem attractive? Nathless I love words; they are the quoits, the bows, the staves that furnish the gymnasium of the mind. Without them in our present condition, our intellectual strength would have no implements. I have been rather humbled in thinking that if I were thrown on an uncivilised island and had to form a literature for its inhabitants from my own mental stock how very fragmentary would be the information with which I could furnish them. It would be a good mode of testing one's knowledge, to set one's self the task of writing sketches of all subjects that have entered into one's studies, entirely from the chronicles of memory.
I shall weary you out of your last infinites[i]mal of patience my Veronica, and I can fancy you shaking your head and saying to yourself [This poor girl's brain is fast losing its little specific gravity and is flying off to Milton's Limbo to keep company with all "the unaccomplished works of Nature's hand, abortive monstrous or unkindly mixed." ] 359 Well, my own I will spare you all further ground for solicitude, the rather as my father is just come in. Indeed dear Veronica my affections are not so easily evaporated as my wits, and my love to you grows by accretion not by expansion.
Ever your true
Clematis.
I have reopened my letter, my dear friend, conscious that it was written in an evening's delirium to which I am subject, and which this [sober-suited morn] 360 has dissipated. Indeed it is not a representative of the serious, earnest sympathy with which I think of you, nor do I attach more importance to my own vagaries than to the labouring yet onward steps of your pilgrimage.
I believe however that there is not at present reason for discouragement -- I feel assured that you will be guided towards some suitable provision. I perceive a reason for all this discipline when I read the sweet expression of your trust and submission. Once again let me thank you for all the trouble you have taken so generously for my sake. When you think of me remember Solomon's mode of characterizing a true friend, [born for adversity.] 361 Yes, I firmly believe our love is of a nature not to be changed by place or time, and though my path on earth should lie between the tropics and yours should still remain among these bleak latitudes, I humbly hope and pray that when the poor modicum of three score years and ten or far less is consumed we shall enter on a condition whose moral elements are all congenial to love, when having left all the reptile behind us, we shall mount up with wings like eagles, we shall run and not be weary, we shall walk and not faint. Glorious prospect of activity! In the meanwhile we will be mindful that this is promised to those "who wait on the Lord." 362

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 28 April 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 28 April 1841
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | A 28 | 1841. Extract published: Cross, 1, 87-88.
Foleshill Road, | April 28th 1841.
My dear Veronica,
No errors are strictly speaking retrievable, but those of omission more frequently appear to be so than the actual class -- if we have let the early seed time pass unimproved, we may have a late crop by relenting diligence, but when shall we cleanse our ground if we sow tares? After the proposition and illustration comes the practical application, namely that by a prompt reply to your kindly anxious enquiry I may possibly obtain your pardon, and repair the loss of speculating energy which my leaving you in doubt as to my health etc. has occasioned you. I have to be grateful for a greater degree of bodily strength than I had enjoyed for many months previous to my leaving Griff, 307 and this blessing I attribute to copious doses of Quinine as an instrument. Why then you will say did you not spend some of your newly acquired strength in thanking an affectionate friend for her letter and dissipating her undeserved fears? One of the penalties women must pay for modern deference to their intellect is I suppose that they must give reasons for their conduct after the fashion of men. The days are past for pleading a woman's reason. Well then my dear Veronica the truth is that the hindrances to my writing have been like the little waves of the brooks that look so lovely just now -- they have arisen one after another close to my side, but when I have looked back I have found the ripples too insignificant to be marked in the distance. My Father's longer séjours at home than formerly and multiplied acquaintances and engagements are really valid excuses for me hitherto, but I do not intend to need them in future; I hope to be a "snapper up of unconsidered" 308 moments.
I have just been interrupted by a visit from a lass of 14 who has despoiled me of half an hour, and I am going out to dinner, so that I cannot follow the famous advice [Hasten slowly.] I suppose you framed your note on the principle that a sharp and sudden sound is the most rousing, but there are addenda about yourself that I want to know though I dare not ask for them. I do not feel settled enough to write more at present -- this worthless sheet I send to assure you my dear Veronica that I am well and not less than ever
Your true and affectionate
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 20 August [1841]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Foleshill Road | August 20.
My very dear Veronica,
I received your note containing a receipt, but have not yet had the books; what can detain them I am unable to imagine.
I thank you warmly for this new proof of affection and only wish that I had an opportunity of shewing you that even my more sluggish body may become active under the influence of affection.
Have you never noticed the possession of a sort of intellectual conscience, that affrights one all of a sudden with the recollection of some crime against sense or syntax, quite unconsciously committed. I am convicted by this same monitor of having written in my last letter, [final cause] instead of [first cause,] thus doing innocently what is often done voluntarily, saying just the opposite to what I was thinking. I may be doing so now for I am in a hurry, but not so great that I cannot feel and say that I am ever my dear Veronica (and certainly Speedwell)
Your true and affectionate,
Clematis.
How did you get to Burton and how is your health?
Have you seen Mr. Henslowe?

Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 18 June 1841
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Foleshill Road | Coventry | June 18th 1841.
My very dear Veronica
Somnophilus was rowing his bark down the bosom of a glassy stream and saw in the distance a fair garden on its banks whose edge presented all manner of bright flowers and luscious fruits as if for the acceptance of the river nymphs. Suddenly his eye sparkled in the anticipation of gathering a rich store of these beauties, that seemed to have none of the coyness of earth, and he almost forgot his oars, as he gazed and dreamed till time and distance vanished and imagination seemed like actual enjoyment -- when lo! his neglected bark struck against the shore and roused the visionary -- where is the fair garden? lost in the distance behind him, and the ground he touches is but a marsh bordered with flags!
The conclusion to which this air balloon is to carry you is that while writing talking and thinking of the holidays I had as usual no definite idea of their when, and I am now alarmed lest you should depart from Burton without apprizing me of your destination. The object of this hasty scribbling before dinner is to beg that you will let me hear from you as soon as possible. How glad I should be to hear you!
By the bye I have not yet told you that Isaac is married, 324 that I officiated as a bridesmaid and that the pair are now in Scotland after visiting the lakes with most propitious weather. I already love my sister for her own sake as well as Isaac's and I trust she will make him a valuable partner.
I am particularly anxious to know all you can tell me of your plans and prospects, and if there be one recommendation of Foleshill as a place to visit pray put it in the scale and give it a fair trial before you decide not to come hither.
This is not a letter -- therefore do not mistake its attributes for faults -- it is a hybrid between that and a note and is half folly and half feeling with a little matter of fact and so a good type of its parent.
May Heaven bless you my Veronica as well as
Your own affectionate
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 18 February 1842
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 107-109.
Foleshill Road | February 18th 1842.
My dear Maria,
I dare say you have added subtracted and divided suppositions until you think you have a sure product -- viz. a good quantum or rather a bad one of indifference and forgetfulness as the representation of my conduct towards you. If so, revise your arithmetic, for be it known to you that, having had my propensities sentiments and intellect gauged a second time, 401 I am pronounced to possess a large organ of [adhesiveness,] a still larger one of [firmness,] and as large of conscientiousness -- hence if I should turn out a very weather cock and a most pitiful truckler you will have data for the exercise of faith maugre common sense, common justice, and the testimony of your eyes and ears. I have not been in your neighbourhood 402 since I wrote to you, though I imagine, from a message my sister Mrs. Isaac told me of, that you had the idea that I was at Griff when you received my parcel.
I am right glad to hear of your going on at least as well as you expected -- with so much material for cheerfulness I know you will need no exhortation to its exercise. Some day or other we shall have a chat and I shall know more of your plans and prospects. I commit this letter with your Estelle 403 and a piece of brown holland to the charge of my Aunt Evarard, who I have no doubt will allow her servant to convey it to you. 404 I am sorry I kept your worsted so long and your songs, of whose presence in my folio I was unaware.
How go you for society, for communion of spirit, the drop of nectar in the cup of mortals? But why do I say the drop? The mind that feels its value will get large draughts from some source if denied it in the most commonly chosen way. "Mid the rich store of nature's gifts to man Each has his loves, close wedded to his soul By fine associations' golden links. As the Great Spirit bids creation teem With conscious being and intelligence, So man His miniature resemblance gives To matter's every form a speaking soul, An emanation from his spirit's fount, The impress true of its peculiar seal. Here finds he thy best image, sympathy!"
Beautiful ego-ism! to quote one's own. But where is not this same ego? The martyr at the stake seeks its gratification as much as the court sycophant, the difference lying in the comparative dignity and beauty of the two egos. People absurdly talk of self-denial -- why there is none in Virtue to a being of moral excellence -- the greatest torture to such a soul would be to run counter to the dictates of conscience, to wallow in the slough of meanness, deception, revenge or sensuality. This was Paul's idea in the 1st chapter of 2d Ep[istle] to Timothy (I think that is the passage). 405
My dear Sister is as you may imagine, but poorly. I shall have my children 2nd week in March. If you have any little ones with whom you commence teaching to read, use I earnestly recommend, Mrs. Williams's Syllabic Method. 406 I have had a weary week and you have the fag end. At the beginning more than the usual amount of cooled glances, and exhortations to the suppression of self-conceit. The former are so many hailstones that make me wrap more closely around me the mantle of determinate purpose -- the latter are needful and have a tendency to exercise forbearance that well repays the temporary smart.
The heart knoweth its own whether bitterness or joy 407 -- let us, dearest beware how we even with good intentions press a finger's weight on the already bruised. The charity that thinketh no evil is loudly professed -- but where is it in persons who to nurse their reliance on their own sentiments positively as I have heard a lady do today attribute perseverance in lovely conduct to a proud determination to disappoint the expectation of a fall? O this masquerade of a world! But I shall weary you. May you be happy and healthy and continue to love
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 16 October 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 16 October 1841
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | OC | 1841. Hitherto unpublished.
Foleshill October 16th 1841.
My very dear Veronica,
The exhaustion following last night's unusually severe headache, renders writing to you a very pleasant remove from [rien faire,] and I am glad of the incitement Mrs. Pears has just given me to do so. She has forwarded my deposition concerning you to Miss Crump, who writes in return that she should be very happy to use her interest on your behalf. This interest, however, though unexceptionable in other respects to the most fastidious, lies among dissenters, and she is just now aware of a desirable situation in a family, which was vacant about a week ago, and for which she appears to think you suitable. But she proposes the question whether liberal spirited nonconformity would be an obstacle to your approval. I had mentioned that you were an attached member of the Establishment. Will you send me the reply by return of post?
I was very glad of your last little note -- only remember it was a little one. Mr. C[raig]'s expressions surpass in grossness all the conceptions my severity had formed about them. Why such behaviour in the days of chivalry would have been enough to bring upon him all the valour of all the Knights errant in existence. Whatever might be his opinion respecting you, the fact that this rendered him unable to accede to your request ought to have called up every particle of delicacy and tenderness he possessed to frame a reply not calculated to wound. But we must forgive and pity him. The immense superiority that endurance gives over the inflicter of a wound makes the sufferer well afford to pardon. But this is the heathen's motive -- the Christian's is far higher. I am strongly of opinion that a family in the most cultivated class of middle life would be the one where you would find most comfort (for a Governess among the aristocracy there is none) and the most profitable circulation of intelligence. Salary is the only thing that would be inferior. How large a one should you expect? These are all ugly accompaniments of our mundane existence, the very dross of life, but without this dross the gold of moral discipline is not to be found.
The prevalence of misery and want in this boasted nation of prosperity and glory is appalling, and really seems to call us away from mental luxury. O to be doing some little toward the regeneration of this groaning travailing creation! 379 I am supine and stupid, overfed with favours, while the haggard looks and piercing glance of want and conscious hopelessness are to be seen in the streets. Goodbye, dear Veronica. I fear this is almost unreadable. (I am tired of illegible). Write on Monday and believe me ever
Your true
Clematis.
May I call you Maria? I feel our friendship too serious a thing to endure even an artificial name. And restore to me Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 1 October 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, 1 October 1841
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | OC 1 | 1841. Extract published: Cross, I, 92.
Foleshill | October 1st 1841.
My very dear Veronica,
It seems a weary while since I indulged myself with sending you some scantlings of my thoughts and feelings, but I should not, to tell truth, have done it this afternoon but that I feel rather sad, and just as on a sultry day one thinks of the greenest, coolest nook one has ever enjoyed, I turn to the recollection of you for comfort. I wish to have good news of your prospects and if I cannot have these yet I wish to know the actual state of affairs with you. I am afraid of teazing you with letters, but as our new Ministry is thought likely to alter the postage 366 we ought to make use of our scribbling privilege while we have it. By the bye however poor a figure a paragraph about slippers may make on my first page I am determined to tell you while the matter is present with me that your plaid slippers worked for the Leamington bazaar have been in my care for more than 6 months, Mrs. Newdegate having returned them with other unsold things. What shall I do with them? Save them for an approaching Bazaar for the erection of Schools in our parish?
I want a letter from you all about yourself with a retraction of a very ambiguous reply to my statement of accounts between us. You do not really mean to refuse me a visit at least at Christmas? I am really quite unfit to write this afternoon, but as I expect full occupation, (fearing among other things a change of servants) I am afraid lest procrastination should deprive me another week of some information about you. My head and heart are both so sadly that I am reduced to copying to fill my sheet. Do you know these 3 little verses. What if the little rain should say So poor a drop as I Can ne'er refresh those thirsty fields I'll tarry in the sky? What if a shining beam of noon Should in its fountain stay, Because its feeble light alone Cannot create a day? Doth not each rain drop help to give The cool refreshing shower? And every ray of light to form And beautify the flower? 367
Is not this a true autumn day? Just the still melancholy that I love -- that makes life and nature harmonize. The birds are all consulting about their migrations, the trees are putting on the hectic or the pallid hues of decay, and begin to strew the ground that one's very footsteps may not disturb the repose of earth and air, while they give us a scent that is a perfect anodyne to the restless spirit. Delicious Autumn! my very soul is wedded to it, and if I were a bird I would fly about the earth seeking the successive autumns. Sweet day, so calm, so pure, so bright The bridal of the earth and sky
The dew will weep thy fall tonight For thou alas! must die! 368
"Pleasant is the joy of grief! It is like the shower of spring, when it softens the branch of the oak, and the young leaf rears its green head." I shall sicken you or infect you, either of which is undesirable, so dearest Veronica, I will assure you that you are continually sharing my warmest love and deliver you by a good bye from more of this trash.
Your
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [4 June 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [4 June 1841]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 86-87.
Foleshill Road | Friday Morning.
My very dear Veronica,
The whole of last week was devoted to a bridesmaid's duties, and each day of this has been partially occupied in paying or receiving visits. 318 Hence I have been unable earlier to acknowledge your affectionate attention, and even now I must write to you immediately after a meal with a hurry that my feelings towards you would always lead me, if possible, to avoid. I am inclined in my ignorance and impatience to grieve that want of health and other causes have detained you at Burton so long after the usual commencement of your holidays, but I doubt not that there is a wise purpose to be effected by the continued discipline through which you are passing. I hope to pray earnestly for you not only that your worldly prospects may assume a definite and promising shape but that as [the fining pot is to silver and the furnace to gold,] 319 even so may your trials be to you, that you may be more evidently a vessel fit for your Master's use. 320 I have no doubt that you have taken the wisest course that presented itself, and indeed you could hardly have chosen one that so united the means of bodily renovation with probabilities of profiting by the assistance of able and extensively connected persons.
Believe me my Veronica that prolonged separation from you will not diminish my love, which I trust will rather grow in intensity of colour than fade, as long as this tabernacle confines its exercise and limits its activity, and I beg you to pray with me that it may be purified and established in a world where kindred spirits will communicate without misunderstanding, and associate only to further their eternal progress in the knowledge adoration and performance of the will works and attributes of their common Father. 321
My dear Sister is tried even more than yourself -- her domestic life is one continued endurance. You remember Charles Clarke -- he is in a rapid consumption which seems to have reached a late stage and is under Edward's care, in his house. His father has not yet visited him. This is just now almost my only external trouble. I have a calm in sea and sky that I doubt not will ere long be interrupted. This is not our rest, if we are among those for whom there [remaineth one,] and to pass through life without tribulation, or as Jeremy Taylor beautifully says with only such a measure of it as may be compared to an artificial discord in music which nurses the ear for the returning harmony, would leave us destitute of one of the marks that invariably accompany salvation, and of that fellowship in the sufferings of the Redeemer which can alone work in us a resemblance to one of the most prominent parts of His Divinely perfect character, and enable us to obey the injunction, [In patience possess your souls.] 322 I have often observed how in secular things active occupation in procuring the necessaries of life renders the character indifferent to trials not affecting that one object. There is an analogous influence produced in the Christian by a vigorous pursuit of duty, a determination to work while it is day. Write my dear Veronica when you reach Margate and you shall hear again if she still live from
Your faithful and affectionate
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [27 May 1842]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [27 May 1842]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
My very dear Friend,
Several days alas! have flown away from me, without bearing on their wings any letter from me to you, since I saw the announcement of what, I am sure, causes you some sorrow. I fear your poor pupil, 432 from the period she lingered, must have suffered much bodily, and her mother mentally. You are always ready to exemplify the beautiful precept, "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep," 433 a blessed duty which like all others [is] its own reward.
I am anxious to know how you feel and how you are circumstanced in the near approach of your Vacation. I know you must be more than ordinarily busy, so I cannot expect to hear from you just yet, indeed I should like better to see you and be told by you viv'e2 voce that you were come to chat away some days of your holidays with us. You would be heartily welcomed if you could do so, by both the Master and Mistress of our mansion, and I do not know any one to whom I would rather [do the honours] or do honour, without technicality, than yourself. Chrissey will leave Meriden on the 21st June; 434 I wish you could take what I may almost anticipate will be a farewell peep at her. We do not at all like her departure from our vicinity for many reasons, but our duties in this instance, as in so many thousands of others, are passive, not active. You will want to come to Coventry on business, perhaps? I hope such may be the case, and we shall then be sure of you.
You remember Chrissey's third babe, Mary Louisa. She died a week or two ago, 435 after a little life of smiles and roses that seemed the promise of a healthy maturity. It is like the breaking off of a sweet melody to poor parents when these jewels are taken, but to spectators it is one of the beauties of this earth. The meltings of sorrow on such occasions are to the harder sex one of the surest means of subduing and refining the spirit. I am hurried, and am going to send you what is hardly worth the penny tax unless you would choose to give so much for the assurance that I am ever
Your truly affectionate
Mary Ann.
Foleshill | Friday.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [23 October 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [23 October 1841]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 85-86.
Foleshill Saturday Evening.
You are veritably an overreaching friend, my dear Maria, not content with my scribbling a couple of sheets to every quarter of the moon, you even insist on dictating the subjects of the same, and the one you now impose on me is at once so sterile, so incomprehensible and so unfascinating that I should be quite justified in refusing to descant thereon. If you complain that my letters become increasingly illegible, just take into consideration the necessary effect of having to write a few pages almost daily. This has been the case with me of late, and I am likely to be more and more busy, if I succeed in a project that is just now occupying my thoughts and feelings. There is no request of yours that I would deny on selfish grounds, therefore my dearest dear, albeit I would rather not reduce myself to the unhappy condition of certain writers of billets, who sit like Hamlet gazing apparently on vacancy 380 out of sheer destitution of matter, I will even do so for the sake of satisfying your ill deserved anxiety about me.
Your fears about my health I feel that I have been culpable in raising from a foolish habit both in writing and discourse of saying all the truth. What mortal has not occasionally headaches? and if there are exceptions in this case, I am sure there are none who have not sometimes heartaches. Both are salutary for us while we tread "this spacious globe" 381 and like ipecacuanha and juleps, though not good in se are often invaluable in their effects. In fine, my dear Veronica, I have seriously to be thankful for far better health than I have possessed I think for years, and I am imperatively called on to trade diligently with this same talent. I seem to be tried in a contrary mode to that in which most of my dearest friends are being tutored -- tried in the most dangerous way -- by prosperity. Solomon says in the day of prosperity be joyful but in the day of adversity consider 382 -- it seems to me that a transposition vice versa of the admonitions would be equally salutary and just. Truly as the prophet of Selwyn has told us "Heaven is formidable in its favours." 383 Not that a wise and grateful reception of blessings obliges us to stretch our faces to the length of one of Cromwell's [Barebones,] nor to shun that joyous bird-like enjoyment of things (which though perishable as to their actual existence will be embalmed to eternity in the precious spices of gratitude) that is distinct from levity and voluptuousness.
On referring to Mr. Brezzi's accompts I find that he has hitherto charged 3 guineas for 10 lessons of German and two for the same number in Italian -- whether his terms will continue to be the same I cannot tell. 7/6 seems to me an exorbitant charge for French. I know that such persons charge variously according to the rank etc. of the pupils. I wrote to Miss Crump immediately on receiving your letter but have not yet had any tidings from her.
I will write better to you, dearest, if I can by and bye, but I am really crowded with engagements just now, and I have added one to the number of my correspondents. I know you will judge indulgently and will rather have such letters as this, which really resembles the tree growing on Fair Rosamond's tomb, apparently full of nuts to crack, but lo! empty, than none at all. Please to remember I have just as longing a desire for regular despatches from you. My dear Sister is rather an object of solicitude on many accounts -- the troubles of married life seem more conspicuously the ordinance of God, in the case of one so meek and passive than in that of women who may fairly be suspected of creating half their own difficulties. Adieu, my very dear Maria, in the etymological sense of the word. Love and practically remember
Your affectionate
Mary Ann

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [21 June 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [21 June 1841]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Foleshill Road, | Coventry, | Monday.
My very dear Veronica,
I write impromptu on rising from the breakfast table lest new arrivals in the antechamber of intention should elbow out this first comer. You tell me that you have arrived at a decision respecting the situation described by Mr. Henslowe so that I will not by venturing a crude opinion check the confidence you may now have in the views of far more experienced judges. I strongly feel, myself, the difficulty of rejecting what has the appearance of a Providential offer, and the quality of fruit is so little to be judged of by the rind, that apparent disadvantages are not always a counterpoising argument. A week's visit can do you no mischief and will give you firm ground for a determination.
I am quite obliged to you for sending me Mr. Henslowe's letters -- they have an individuality that makes them worth preserving. His is evidently a character made up of natural crystallization, instead of one turned out of a mould. You remember Mr. Villiers 325 of Kenilworth -- he is leaving with his excellent curate, and we yesterday heard him preach his last Missionary sermon, a very inspiriting one. In the afternoon I heard a very valuable sermon on a subject dear to all Christians but to none more than those who for the time are in heaviness, [Ask and it shall be given you.] 326 Mary Jane Graham published a very ingenious and pious little work called the Test of Truth, 327 for the use of Spanish refugees who she learned were in the dreary plains of infidelity. Her argument is this -- Jesus has said [Ask and it shall be given you] -- here then is a test of His divinity -- if God, His promise will be fulfilled, if not you have demonstrated the contrary and impartially used the conditions -- but until you have asked sincerely and importunately you have no right to decide on the question. Do you know this little book? It is 6 years since I read it but I think from what I remember it would be invaluable as a present to sceptical persons. How blessed that we have not to obey this command hypothetically! Well might the Apostle say [All things are yours] 328 and we cannot escape the logical inference from this invitation and promise that every deficiency is in one sense voluntarily chosen by us! As my jewel Isaac Taylor says, The most exemplary and advanced Christians have only become such by allowing their full weight to motives that are involved in the profession of the weakest.
I am expecting the Bride and Bridegroom to return by the railway this evening. 329 They have had a delightful excursion amongst the lakes and in Scotland. Did I tell you that I have some rose-leaves from Wordsworth's garden? But why do I say anything about self. I am chiefly anxious to let you know my warm sympathy and affection towards you. In reply to the query at the close of your letter I give an unhesitating No! unless very rare conditions be annexed. Your feelings on the subject are such as God approves. A full reliance on His Wisdom and love and a firm faith that if really for our ultimate good such a protector as His laws will permit us to accept will be given is the state of mind I seek to obtain. I am convinced that every desire that relaxes this limitation is an inordinate one and will be an incubus checking the aspirations of the spiritual life. I have the firm belief that He who sits at the Helm is your Father and that your last anchorage will be in the shallows of an ocean of peace and bliss whence you shall plunge into a deep that knows no storm nor death nor danger.
In haste your own
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [21 July 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [21 July 1841]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
My very dear Veronica,
The contents of the letter bag had been a subject of interest and disappointment to me for several mornings previous to this on which I have just received your welcome little note. I think I see some advantage connected with your being driven to the apparently repulsive measure of advertising. The possession of friends able privately to serve you might have caused you to accept a settlement less propitious than perhaps may be presented in the wider range taken by an advertisement. My own natural aversion to the machinery of society, to that intercourse with my fellow creatures, whom I would fain regard as pictures from the hand of a Divine Artist, however torn and soiled, which makes one calculate about them as so much canvas and paint with a certain value of frame, united with my love for you, gives me a full comprehension and lively conception of all the little mortifications and disgusts that you have had and will have to endure in this trying stage of your education. Yes my Veronica your education, that cheering word refreshes I am sure your willingness to undergo all that the [Only Wise] sees to be a furtherance of your [growing up to Him in all things, who is the Head] 330 -- glorious portion! To feel the roots of faith strengthened by every blast, daily giving nourishment to the fair and joy-giving fruits of Love, Hope and Patience. That this is your experience is my [consolation in all my prayers for you.]
My beloved sister has gone through the trials incident to the rather sudden death of poor Charles 331 since I wrote to you. His interment took place yesterday. My two little nephews are with me.
Do you remember Cowper's Hymn beginning [I was a grovelling creature once.] 332 It is lovely and rich as the pomegranate and the vine. And the collect for last Sunday 333 -- was not that beautiful? Truly the night of sorrow brings to the ear "the sound of many fountains musical by day unheard," and in blessed freedom from troubles of my own I find those of my loved ones a sweet monitor to keep up my contemplation of that part of the Divine character expressed in the appellative "the Comforter." 334 Alas I need monitors and I need chastisement -- and God will send them in His own good time. May they never be in vain!
[God and good angels guard you,] 335 my Veronica.
Your affectionate
Clematis.
Foleshill. | Wednesday.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [21 August 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [21 August 1841]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
My very dear Veronica,
My precious books arrived last night, and I hasten to prevent your feeling the least anxiety about what has been too troublesome already. They are all beautiful -- just what I wished, and Rivingtons have very liberally allowed 15s/ discount, so that I have 6 volumes of Chalmer's Sermons. 346 How shall I ever repay you? I will make you some delicious extracts, if you are not intimate with Coleridge, or any of the other books. Tell me. I have now said enough about myself for many months to come -- I want to talk and hear of you. Write, write, write. Keep a sheet by you and scribble down thoughts as they occur. I have been reading 1 Pet. 5 this morning (the 2d lesson). You know the sweet, the elevating comfort it contains. I was impressed with the mode in which the Apostle speaks of the reversionary possessions of the Christian. [When the Chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.] [That He may exalt you in due time.] [The God of all grace hath called you to His eternal glory by Christ Jesus.] 347 Let us call up the image of the Grecian games -- the concourse of spectators, the noblest and most intelligent of the sons of the land. The ambition of those who strove for the mastery, an efficient motive for rigid discipline and strenuous agonizing exertion, their perseverance until the reaching of the goal and the bestowal of the crown amid the acclamations of the multitude. Here is a type that by its analogy illustrates, but by its infinite inferiority serves to exalt our conceptions of the arduousness of the spiritual race, the dignity of the cloud-like host of witnesses, and the transcendent glory the inappreciable value of the [crown] reserved for those who have finished the course and kept the faith. 348
Forgive hurry and almost incoherency -- believe me my beloved Veronica,
Your faithful,
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [20 May 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [20 May 1841]
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | MA 20 | 1841. One sentence published: Cross, 1, 85.
Foleshill Road | Coventry | Thursday.
[Is there no quiet lane in my Clematis's vicinity whose banks rival the intensest sapphire of the firmament from the luxuriance of my emblems, admonishing her to emulate the fidelity of which their name and colour are the representatives?] Yes, my Veronica, there is such a lane, and I have not only gazed at and gathered your bewitching namesakes, but I have talked of you more than, considering one's friends are multiplicands of self, an honest eschewing of egotism would allow. Last evening I mentioned you to my neighbour 309 who is growing into the more precious character of a friend, and she told me that Mrs. Sibley Whittem 310 wanted some little time ago a governess -- I presume for her whole family, consisting, I believe, of 3 or 4 boys and girls. She is not certain that such is the case now but that can be ascertained. The said lady is one of no common intellectual and moral worth. I should say the prima donna of Coventry in these respects, and I believe, a Christian, but -- O this ill-omened precursor, portending more disastrous facts than ever did croak and screech of owl or raven -- her husband is an ultra-liberal, a man who has never kept rank and file, a lecturer for the Mechanics' Institute, an ardent lover of science, an amiable being as to his fellowmen, the frequent description, strange to say, of one who, from orthodox profession, has apostatized, first to Socinianism, next to an ism that assumes itself competent and commissioned to supply the deficiencies of the Bible if not to supersede it. The whole family are dissenters -- Mr. Whittem's father, a holy man. Of course in
Mr. W's family perfect freedom of thought and action in religious matters would be understood as an unquestioned right, but as education, to be such, implies aggression on supposed error of every kind and incubation of truth it is probable you would not choose to put yourself in a position apparently requiring the anomalous conditions of neutrality and command. It is folly to talk of educating children without giving their opinions a bias. This is always given whether weak or strong, not always nor perhaps in a large proportion of cases, a permanent one, but one instrumental in determining their point of repose. So much on this head which I fear I am dilating unnecessarily.
With respect to your idea of putting on the responsibilities and anxieties of an independent housekeeper, I confess, little able as I am to judge on the subject I cannot consent to put it in the balance -- I feel utterly averse to it. It is invariably our feeling that precisely those things we have not are the very desiderata for our happiness, and I can fully understand your yearning for divi foci of your own, but just imagine an inventory of concomitants that might be drawn up -- rent, taxes, bad debts, servants untrustworthy, scarlet fever, panic of parents, imposing tradesmen, mortifying conjunctions with et ceteras all at present experimentally unknown to you. I have been let into a few secrets as to the trials of schoolkeeping of late and my inference is that it is one of the most fluctuating, dubious occupations beneath the changing moon.
I have not received a call from any of Mr. Stephenson's family, 311 though we have met and spoken on our way from church, when they have expressed the hope of seeing me often, whence I infer that they expect me to invert the common order of things and call on them. This I did not intend, young ladies being the animals that would possess the minimum of attraction for me in a menagerie of the varieties of the human race, and you know there are two in their family -- were there none but the two senior members I should certainly preserve their acquaintance, but if I can satisfy the coolest wish you possess by talking to them concerning Coventry openings, why, "my dearest dear, therefore it shall be done." 312 I spoke of you as a dear friend whom I was anxious to see comfortably situated to Mr. Brezzi and he in the tantalizing mode of words and things here below, immediately said that he had known shortly before of a situation just -- Alas whither shall I go to scribble further? crossing 313 would be death to the sense or nonsense of my letter and with this half sheet I shall make the packet heavy. Well Mr. B. had heard of a situation just suitable for you but in ignorance of your existence he had obtained it for another. He has kindly promised to bear you in mind, I hope to some purpose. But you have many more efficient friends than I or any one to whom I can apply. Mr. and Mrs. Henslowe I should think are likely to be serviceable.
I do not say come hither at Midsummer; you know that my bosom shall always be a leaning place for you while the heart beneath it beats. I can only say in accordance with your own view, go in the most useful direction. I have a world more to say, and am very fertile in thoughts that like many greater productions are born to die in unregretted obscurity, but I really think even your affection will not make the task of deciphering my letter easy. How is it that Erasmus could write volumes on volumes and multitudinous letters besides, while I whose labours hold about the same relation to his as an anthill to a pyramid or a drop of dew to the ocean seem too busy to write a few? A most posing query! Solved, after due thought by the very recondite fact that your poor friend is considerably inferior in mental profundity, power and fertility to the said Erasmus.
Adieu my dear Veronica. Write me a scrap when you have time and then you shall hear again from your
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [2 November 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [2 November 1841]
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | near Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | NO 2 | 1841. One sentence published: Cross, I, 92.
Foleshill | Tuesday Morning.
Like a true friend, my ain dearie, I am delighted to plunge you in blushes for not writing to me on Saturday by sending you a second packet within the week. This morning has brought the enclosed note and advertisement from Miss Crump -- they will explain themselves. You know better than I the importance of promptness in these matters, and except the proviso about furnishing pupils, there seems to be no obstacle to your obtaining the situation if that promptness be used. This to be sure is something like saying that a mountain might be climbed if it were not too steep, but impossibility is the only insurmountable barrier to human effort and that does not here exist. Effort! 'tis the very sound of the inspiriting trumpet, the hand that draws out all the rich tones from the lyre of human life.
Tell me what you think of the matter to-morrow, if possible and also tell me that you forgive my -- something between brusquerie and confusion in my last letter. The present one will not indeed compensate for its predecessor's faults, but must ask for the benefit of the same indemnity. I sat down after pork pie and coffee with the single intention to send you Miss C's prettily proffered aid, and though I cannot bear to send you one empty side of the sheet I seem just now not to have a peg in my mind on which to hang another idea. Not all the wonders of flood, fire, earth or air can avail me at this unpropitious hour. I might certainly moralize at some length on the [destructive conflagration] at the Tower, 386 or poetize on the loud laugh that the spirits of the elements are having at man's mimicry of power, or politically economize on the magic potency of law shewn in the conduct of the sentry -- the newspaper having furnished me with this ready change for the day, in common with other luckless mortals whose conversation purse needs such replenishment -- but I spare you the pains of doing what by others is often self-inflictingly done, unawares -- reading whole pages full of their own thoughts in another's livery.
I am going I hope to-day to effect a breach in the thick wall of indifference behind which the denizens of Coventry seem inclined to entrench themselves, but I fear I shall fail. 387 Hope in one scale, fear in the other, alternately preponderating -- such is the description of our microcosm within, to speak learnedly and sentimentally as it behooves a young lady what reads.
When my dear Maria, one's physical forces are occupied in digestion, it is obviously impossible according to the laws of matter that they should at the same time be ministering to the action of one's brain. Hence my folly -- and the enduring of this must have been a capital object in your unwise bargain to adopt as a friend
Your
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [13 November 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [13 November 1841]
MS: Yale. Address: Miss Lewis | The Revd L. Harper's | Burton Latimer | Kettering. Postmark: COVENTRY | NO 13 | 1841. Extracts published: Cross, I, 103.
Foleshill | Saturday.
My very dear Friend,
I fear you have thought me tardy in seeking further information about your prospects -- at least if your goodness have not permitted this, my own wish to know them has made me fancy the eight or nine days that have elapsed since I had your letter unusually long. My whole soul has been engrossed in the most interesting of all enquiries for the last few days, and to what result my thoughts may lead I know not -- possibly to one that will startle you, but my only desire is to know the truth, my only fear to cling to error. 388 I think Miss Chandler writes like a sincere, well-meaning person, and the situation she offers would very likely accord with your habits and feelings better than your present one; but are the Fates really to take you to the southern-most verge of the land? Eh bien! There are various preservatives for substances, vinegar, sugar, alcohol, a vacuum, and other things known to the scientific -- and so for love, ours I venture to say will not decompose under the influence of separation, unless you excommunicate me for differing from you in opinion. I was amused with your sharp remarks on the advertisement -- milksop as I am, I immediately perceived them to be vraisemblable. My dear Father has just returned rather sooner than I expected and has limited my allowance of time for writing.
Think -- is there any conceivable alteration in me that would prevent your coming to me at Christmas? I long to have a friend such as you are I think I may say alone to me, to unburthen every thought and difficulty -- for I am still a solitary, though near a city. But we have the universe to talk with, infinity in which to stretch the gaze of hope, and an all-bountiful, all-wise Creator in whom to confide -- He who has given us the untold delights of which our reason, our emotion, our sensations are the ever-springing sources. Hurry and darkness -- so goodbye dear one. Why may we not talk without so much circumlocution, 'tis a very great compliment to the understanding of one's hearers to speak elliptically.
Ever yours
Mary Ann.
"An answer by return will oblige."

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [12 August 1841]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [12 August 1841]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 88-89.
Foleshill | Thursday Morning.
My very dear Veronica,
Do not, I beseech you, think of crowding your half day in London with my [levities] and [ponderosities.] I am ashamed to have asked so much and certainly should not have done it had I supposed you would have taken such a bird's flight through London. I shall not be disappointed but rather relieved if you send me word that you have rested after sailing from Margate, instead of spending nerve and muscle for me. If however you determine to make some purchases for me the plan you mention for conveying them would be decidedly the best. I had some similarly conveyed last year.
How should I love to join you at Margate now that you are alone! A few days of conversation would I believe set my crazy body right. In consequence of its slight ailments I have of late felt a depression that has disordered the vision of my mind's eye, and made me alive to what is certainly a fact though my imagination when I am in health is an adept at concealing it, that I am alone in the world. I do not mean to be so sinful as to say that I have not friends most undeservedly kind and tender and disposed to form a far too favorable estimate of me, but I mean that I have no one who enters into my pleasures or my griefs, no one with whom I can pour out my soul, no one with the same yearnings the same temptations the same delights as myself. This I do not murmur under -- I am too conscious of utter unworthiness to be otherwise than astonished at the multitude of my blessings, but I merely mention it as the impression that obtrudes itself when my body tramples on its keeper (a metaphor borrowed from a menagerie of wild beasts, if it should happen to puzzle you). Mysterious [connexion exquisite of distant worlds] 340 that we present! A few drops of steel 341 will perhaps make me laugh at the simple objects that in gloom and mist I conjure into stalking apparitions.
But my Veronica I would not speak of such feelings with a self-compassionating spirit. With sins to confess, and graces to implore, and duties to be done, I have no time for sentimental sorrows, and I ought not to admit them. Neither do I like to see that I have scribbled so much about myself -- a self so bountifully provided for [compared] to you, my dearest friend, who have substantial difficulties wherewith to combat. Pray regard all I have written as cancelled in my own mind. Yes we will be cheerful in the contemplation of all but sin in ourselves and our fellow beings. I would reserve all my grief for my transgressions, and continually remember that all but these come from God. I have lately been much impressed with the truth that in Him we live and move and have our being 342 -- that He is the primal source of glory, holiness, beauty -- the final 343 cause (words often uttered and written but not fathomed) of all in the worlds of matter and mind. Our text today [Why do the heathen rage and the people imagine a vain thing?] 344 is rich in association, from the company of apostolic Christians into whom it breathed moral courage to the last anticipated contest between good and evil. What words could we, on whom the ends of the world are come, select as a better description of the persecutions of avowedly heathen Rome, the virtually heathen Papacy, or the wilfully heathen conspirators of infidelity, whose motto was [Ecrasez l'Infame,] 345 than those which the holy Seer, a thousand years before the signal was given for Satan's mightiest, despairing efforts, uttered under the inspiration of that Spirit [who shews things to come.] It is time I ceased to tax your patience my Veronica and I will do so. May you be enriched with heavenly blessings and if it please God with a greater degree of earthly peace than hitherto.
Ever your true
Clematis.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [1 January 1842?]
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, Foleshill, [1 January 1842?]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Foleshill Saturday Morning.
My dear Maria,
Come when it suits you best, and stay as long as your inclination and arrangements allow. I have no particular engagements in view but should any such occur I will apprize you. Please to send me word a day or so before you come that I may be at home to welcome you, as
I shall do with great pleasure. Thank you very much for your kind enquiries about my health. I have been but poorly since I saw you, but I am decidedly better, and I am taking some medicine that seems beneficial.
My Father returned from his journey to Hallam last evening, 396 and we have just breakfasted together for the first time since last Saturday, so that I have had a lonely week in which your company would have been very valuable, but it rather prevents one from being very urgent in giving invitations when one's own society is the only divertissement one has to offer. You however have kindly put up with me and my circumstances many times before this and will good naturedly do so again.
Goodbye and may Heaven bless you as it does by the sure laws of consequence 397 bless every one who does his work faithfully and lives in loving activity.
Ever your affectionate
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, 58 Griff, 6 January 1836
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, 58 Griff, 6 January 1836
MS: Parrish Collection, Princeton. Address: Revd L. Harper | Burton Latimer | Northamptonshire. | Miss Lewis. Postmark: COVENTRY | JA 7 | 1836. Published: B. C. Williams, George Eliot, New York, Macmillan, 1936, pp. 24-26, with a facsimile of the first page; brief extract, Cross, 1, 29-30.
Griff Wednesday | January 6. / 36.
My dear Miss Lewis,
I am grieved and ashamed that we should have appeared so unmindful of your kindly expressed desire to hear from us respecting our dear Mother's health. I will not say that our silence was altogether unavoidable, for had we borne in mind our promise we had many opportunities of forwarding a note to you previous to your departure from Nuneaton; but I trust that the entire occupation of our minds on other and painful subjects will be a sufficient plea for our seeming neglect. Since we saw you at Griff, [my] 59 dear Mother has suffered a great increase of pain, and though she has for the last few days been much relieved, we dare not hope that there will be a permanent improvement. Our anxieties on her account though so great have been since Thursday almost lost sight of in the more sudden and consequently more severe trial which we have been called to endure in the alarming illness of my dear Father. For four days we had no cessation of our anxiety, but I am thankful to say that he is now considered out of danger, though very much reduced by frequent bleeding and very powerful medicines. 60
My Mother and Sister unite with me in love to you, and my Brother 61 begs me to present his kind regards. We all hope that your health is established by change of air and scene. I need scarcely apologize for the disgraceful untidiness of my note, as you may well imagine that neither my hand nor my head is in a very favourable state for writing; but I must tell you that I am compelled to send you this paper that looks so poverty-stricken in consequence of Mr. Bucknill's 62 having drawn on my stock till it is quite exhausted.
Again begging you to accept my love and best wishes, I remain, my dear Miss Lewis
Yours very affectionately
Mary Anne Evans
We shall be glad to hear from you.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Maria Lewis, [Foleshill], 8 December 1841
Dublin Core:Subject: Maria Lewis^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Maria Lewis, [Foleshill], 8 December 1841
MS: Yale. Brief extract published: Cross, I, 103-104.
My dear Maria,
It is actually the 8th of December and little more than a fortnight to Christmas. Such being [the case] it is high time that I should know when your Gaol delivery will happen and when I may hope to kiss, yea, actually kiss you. I conclude you will come hither directly from Burton, and I shall at least have the first grasp of you, though how soon you will shake me off I cannot predict. I am regularly both head and leg-weary and so I very generously bestow these dullest moments of my dullardship on you. 389 Your last little kind note was unsatisfactory as to the situation. The illness of Miss R. Franklin has obliged her to renounce at least for the present, school duties but the eternal dragons of Church and dissent present themselves everywhere. 390 A partner is likely to be wanted (this entre nous) and one who would ultimately have the establishment left in her hands, but I think the Miss F's desire that the future principal should be a nonconformist. I advise the two parties to file off and divide the cities of the land between them -- to follow Abraham's example -- "If thou wilt go to the right hand I will go to the left." 391 Though by the bye that would not do for the odium theologicum would find abundant food under the generic names Church and Dissent and these would begin to bite and devour each other. What pity that while mathematics are indubitable, immutable, and no one doubts the properties of a triangle or a circle, doctrines infinitely important to man are buried in a charnel heap of bones over which nothing is heard but the barks and growls of contention. [Unto their assembly mine honour be not thou united.] 392 Here is a tolerably long coil that I have kept spite of aching limbs. No thanks, you will say. I ask none carissima. Loquacity with tongue or pen is its own reward -- or, punishment. Farewell. Please write me a scheme soon.
Ever your true
Mary Ann.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Lord Houghton, London, 9 April 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Lord Hough^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Lord Houghton, London, 9 April 1878
Text: T. Wemyss Reid, The Life, Letters, and Friendships of Richard Monckton Milnes, First Lord Houghton, 3d ed., 2 vols., 1891. II, 376.
The Priory, | North Bank, | Regent's Park, | April 9th, 1878.
Dear Lord Houghton,
I had a little chat with Mrs. M[oulton] 39 the morning I met her under your kind auspices, and I think we came to the understanding that I preferred the breach to the observance of such flattering intentions as calls from "Strangers." I have been so constantly declining to accept proposed visits of that kind from American ladies that it would be invidious on my part to make an exception, unless it were warranted by the prospect that I could render some needed service. But Mrs. M[oulton] is so well received and appreciated that I can add nothing to her advantages during her stay in London. Visits from friends and from those who are likely to become friends I am very fond of, but I have a horror of being interviewed and written about, and though I would not impute an intention of that sort to Mrs. M[oulton], my experience in relation to other American ladies has confirmed me in my churlish habits. Pray interpret me charitably, and believe me
Yours very sincerely,
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Lord Houghton, London, 13 May 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Lord Hough^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Lord Houghton, London, 13 May 1873
MS: Yale.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 13. 73.
My dear Lord Houghton
I think you know our friend Mr. Edward Pigott, for whom we have a respect founded on an acquaintance of twenty years.
It has been suggested that he might possibly obtain the Secretaryship of the Royal Academy which is about to be declared vacant and which is not to be given to any artist or art critic.
So far as I can imagine the Duties of the office, Mr. Pigott seems to me to have just the requisite qualifications. He has a perfect command of French both for conversation and correspondence -- not an ordinary accomplishment in an Englishman, as you have had reason to complain in a certain essay of yours -- and I suppose that this must be a chief demand on a Secretary to the Academy with its present cosmopolitan admissions. Then, he has the sympathetic manners which would make difficult business relations easier, and his letter-writing is peculiarly felicitous. He has a fine literary sense, and in spite of fourteen years' hard work at journalism, he retains his finesse of expressions and has not lost the discrimination of epithets.
If anybody asks whom he "boasts himself to be" 188 -- he is a younger son of a Somersetshire gentleman, made a good figure at Eton and Baliol (the present master of Baliol is one of his best friends), spent some time in France, and finally coming to London bought the Leader newspaper in which he sank all the portion that fell to him as a younger son. 189 He took this check of fortune very gracefully, put himself into heavy harness without grumbling, and has ever since been deepening the respect of his friends.
Those who know his value -- and among them are some of the best people both French and English -- must be heartily rejoiced at his getting a post which would give him both a comfortable maintenance and a suitable change of work. But his success of course depends on his recommendations being straightway made known to those who have the power in their hands. Every day is of importance.
If, from what you know, you believe that his appointment would be a good service to the Academy as well as to himself, will you be so kind as to write a letter to me expressing your favourable wishes on Mr. Pigott's behalf -- a letter which might be put in as an informal sort of testimonial? You may possibly have knowledge which would correct my uninstructed suppositions. In that case you will consider my request to be retracted. But I make no apology for trusting in your readiness to give help wherever you can.
I remain, my dear Lord Houghton
Yours very sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Leslie Stephen, London, 7 January 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Leslie Stephen^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Leslie Stephen, London, 7 January 1878
MS: Huntington Library. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 7. 78.
Dear Mr. Stephen
After you left, 1 it flashed upon me that my memory had dropt some stitches, or paragraphs, in fastening the unacknowledged age of Villemain on the innocent Mr. Mew who writes on Quevedo. The accused (by the Academy) is a writer on Marivaux. 2 I dare say you saw through my inaccuracy, but in case you did not, here is my correction.
This comes of neglecting [cerebral hygiene] by glancing over weekly newspapers and becoming loquacious on the strength or weakness of that [scrappy reading.]
By the way, readiness in accusation unverified or unverifiable is one of the points on which the general conscience wants rousing in relation to what has the pretension to be literature. But you know better than I the many ways in which all good is retarded by unscrupulous writing.
Always yours more or less blunderingly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Lady Lytton, London, 21 March 1874
Dublin Core:Subject: Lady Lyt^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Lady Lytton, London, 21 March 1874
MS: Lady Hermione Cobbold. Envelope: The Rt. Honble | Lady Lytton | English Embassy | Paris. Postmarks: LONDON N.W | 5 MR 21 | 74; ANGL. CALAIS | 22 MARS | 74.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
March 21. 74.
Dear Lady Lytton
I am perhaps the very last in writing to you, though since I knew of your trial 232 there has not been a day in which I have not called it to mind. It is so long since we saw each other that my usual spirit of distrust has taken possession of me, and thinking of you as surrounded by a world of nearer friends, I have hardly been able to persuade myself that there would not be some obtrusiveness in sending you my helpless words. Very helpless -- carrying only affectionate sorrow in your sorrow, and grateful sweet remembrance of you.
Those who have known you, though but briefly and interruptedly, cannot help counting you among their possessions -- caring much lest any harm should befal you -- wishing that you should not be quite loosed from them. And I cannot see my writing now in any other light than that of a self-indulgence which needs forgiveness. You will not deny me this.
I trust that your health has borne the pressure of grief, and that your life in Paris is not too arduous for you socially. I find the most effective source of resignation -- and resignation makes half our spiritual life -- in thinking of sorrow and pain as part of a sum which is shared among poor mankind. In that way one gets calmer about oneself, remembering others.
Please let me tell you of a pleasure I have had lately, namely, reading that page of your husband's which contains the stanzas to E.L. They are perfect, and give me a delight which includes you both.
Mr. Lewes unites with me in offering to yourself and Lord Lytton a deeply felt regard and sympathy. In this busy world we are obliged to live in all senses by faith in each other, which nullifies silence and separation.
Always, dear Lady Lytton,
Yours faithfully and affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Lady Holland, London, 26 April 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Lady Holland^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Lady Holland, London, 26 April 1880
MS: Fales Collection, New York University.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 26. 80.
My dear Lady Holland
I felt that I was unfortunate when I found that it was you and Sir Henry whom I had missed seeing on Saturday.
I was just getting ready to go to Weybridge, and the servant took it for granted that I could not see any one, but if I had known who was at the door I should have begged you to let me see you only for five minutes. It is rather hard that one should see many whom one does not care about seeing and should twice miss those who would be most welcome.
As our visiting is not of the formal sort I do not add one more to the multitude of formalities you are obliged to attend to, by calling at Rutland Gate 549 when you are sure to be preoccupied.
I have a wretched cold in the head which almost blinds me, after winning through the terrible winter without any such effect. I like to think you and Sir Henry gave me a proof that you are both well.
Yours most sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

GE to Lady Amberley, London, 2 June 1870
MS: The Bertrand Russell Archives, McMaster University.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
June 2. 70.
Dear Lady Amberley
I am very glad to have had an opportunity of reading your lecture in a more complete form than the report in the Times. 912
Now that I have read it at length I find little of which I cannot say that I both agree and keenly sympathize with it. I am glad to see your energetic protest in the beginning against that common position -- "I see nothing amiss in the world: I am very comfortable in it."
I have addressed the newspaper to Miss Octavia Hill. Her home is 14 Nottingham Place, N.W.
Mr. Spencer mentioned to us last Sunday that he was intending to go to Standish. 913
If we were seated quietly together this morning, I should say many things which a letter could not easily convey, even if one were industrious enough to write lengthily. There are "nuances" which require the eyes and voice.
Yours always truly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Kate Field, London, 21 May 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Kate Field^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Kate Field, London, 21 May 1872
MS: Boston Public Library. Published: Lilian Whiting, Kate Field: A Record, Boston, 1899, pp. 270-271.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
May 21. 72.
Dear Miss Field 520
Your letter finds me still here, but in the midst of arrangements for our departure. The weather, our ailments, and various other causes have made us put off our flight from one week to another, but now we are really fluttering our wings and making a dust about us.
I wish we had seen you oftener. I was placidly looking forward to your staying in England another year or more, and gave way to my general languor about seeing friends in these late months, which have been too full of small bodily miseries for me to feel that I had much space to give to pleasanter occupation.
The present of Autumn leaves which Col. T. W. Higginson 521 has brought will be very gratefully accepted if he will kindly send them to this house so that I may find them on our return in our coming autumn. Pray thank him on my behalf.
If Mrs. Mark Pattison is still in town, and if you are seeing her, will you say that I expected her to come the Sunday before last? -- since it had been agreed that if we left before the Sunday she was to have a card telling her the fact. I wish you had been here on that Sunday -- there was some pleasant singing of men's voices. 522
Mr. Lewes adds his hearty wishes to mine that your future may be a bright one. We trust that your visit to England has been at least a good seed-time in your experience, and you are young enough to make such sowing all-important.
Goodbye. Believe me, always, whether you come back to us in the flesh or not,
Yours with sincere friendliness
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Joseph Munt Langford, Wandsworth, 6 October 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Joseph Munt Langford^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Joseph Munt Langford, Wandsworth, 6 October 1859
MS: Mrs. Dorothy Hicks. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, South Fields | Wandsworth | October 6. 59.
My dear Sir
Some time ago, in a letter to Mr. Lewes, you spoke of certain hard-headed lawyers who were impressed by "Adam Bede."
Now a "hard-headed lawyer" is precisely the personage I am most in need of -- to consult about the affairs of my heroes and heroines (and a little also about my own). I would willingly pay a fee for the sake of avoiding legal blunders in my novels, and I have just now a question which I cannot solve to my satisfaction with the books at my command.
Is it quite an irrational supposition, that among the hard-headed admirers you alluded to, there may be one to whom you could mention my want, and who would not be too much disgusted by the painful certainty that the author of "Adam Bede" is a woman, to be willing to be consulted by her?
You would oblige me very much if you would turn this matter over in your mind, and let me know if you can help me in it.
Yours very truly
Marian Evans Lewes.
Joseph Langford Esq.

Dublin Core:Subject: Joseph Munt Langford^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Joseph Munt Langford, Wandsworth, 10 October 1859
MS: Mrs. Dorothy Hicks. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | October 10. 59.
My dear Sir
I am very much obliged to you for your ready suggestions in reply to my letter. The attorney 346 you mention, as a friend of your own, is precisely the kind of man I had in my mind when referring to your generic term, "hard-headed lawyers," and we shall by and by ask you to favour us with an introduction to him.
Meanwhile I enclose the simple questions I wish to have answered for the behoof of my authorship. They by no means require so accomplished a lawyer as the "Devil," to answer them, and I shouldn't wonder if your own amateur knowledge would suffice for the purpose. Simple questions, you know, are the last one gets answered by the exasperating race of compilers.
If you consult Mr. Welsby for me, I think I should prefer your dropping the questions in conversation, without formal introduction of them as the questions of an author, if that were possible. But I leave this to your judgment. I remain, my dear Sir
Yours sincerely
Marian Evans Lewes.
J. M. Langford Esq.
Over.
P.S. Mr. Lewes urges that a formal introduction of the questions to Mr. Welsby will be preferable, as the surest means of getting full and definite answers.
