GE to Frederic Harrison, London, 15 January 1870
MS: Tinker Collection, Yale. Envelope: Frederic Harrison Esq | 7 New Square | Lincolns Inn. Postmarks: LONDON-N.W | 2 | JA 15 | 70; LONDON-W.C | GN | JA 15 | 70. Mostly published: Cross, III, 103-104.
North Bank | January 15. 1870.
My dear Mr. Harrison
I am moved to write to you rather by the inclination to remind you of me, than by the sense of having anything to say. On reading "The Positivist Problem" 123 a second time, I gained a stronger impression of its general value, and I also felt less jarred by the more personal part at the close. Mr. Lewes would tell you that I have an unreasonable aversion to personal statements, and when I come to like them it is usually by a hard process of conversion. But -- to tell you all just for the sake of telling, and not because the matter can have any weight -- my second reading gave me a new and very strong sense that the last two or three pages have the air of an appendix added at some distance of time from the original writing of the article. Some more thoroughly explanatory account of your non-adhesion seems requisite as a nexus -- since the statement of your non-adhesion had to be mentioned after an argument for the system against the outer Gentile world. However, it is more important for me to say that I felt the thorough justice of your words, when in conversation with me, you said, "I don't see why there should be any mystification: having come to a resolution after much inward debate, it is better to state the resolution." Something like that you said and I give a hearty "Amen," praying that I may not be too apt myself to prefer the haze to the clearness. But the fact is, I shrink from decided "deliverances" on momentous subjects, from the dread of coming to swear by my own "deliverances" and sinking into an insistent echo of myself. That is a horrible destiny -- and one cannot help seeing that many of the most powerful men fall into it.
I should have scribbled this nothing-in-particular before now, but that bodily infirmities have hindered me.
Always yours most sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
I was very glad that you did not leave Fitzjames Stephen's wretched letter without notice.

Dublin Core:Subject: Frederic Harrison^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Frederic Harrison, London, 15 August [1866]
MS: Tinker Collection, Yale. Envelope: Frederic Harrison Esq. | Beckenham | Kent. Postmark: LONDON-N.W | 5 | AU 15 | 66. Mostly published: Cross, II, 440-443.
North Bank | August 15.
My dear Mr. Harrison
I have read several times your letter of the 19th 516 which I found awaiting me on my return and I shall read it many times again. Pray do not ever say, or inwardly suspect, that anything you take the trouble to write to me will not be valued. On the contrary, please to imagine as well as you can the experience of a mind morbidly desponding, of a consciousness tending more and more to consist in memories of error and imperfection rather than in a strengthening sense of achievement -- and then consider how such a mind must need the support of sympathy and approval from those who are capable of understanding its aims. I assure you your letter is an evidence of a fuller understanding than I have ever had expressed to me before. And if I needed to give emphasis to this simple statement, I should suggest to you all the miseries one's obstinate egoism endures from the fact of being a writer of novels -- books which the dullest and silliest reader thinks himself competent to deliver an opinion on. But I despise myself for feeling any annoyance at these trivial things.
That is a tremendously difficult problem which you have laid before me, and I think you see its difficulties, though they can hardly press upon you as they do on me, who have gone through again and again the severe effort of trying to make certain ideas thoroughly incarnate, as if they had revealed themselves to me first in the flesh and not in the spirit. I think aesthetic teaching is the highest of all teaching because it deals with life in its highest complexity. But if it ceases to be purely aesthetic -- if it lapses anywhere from the picture to the diagram -- it becomes the most offensive of all teaching. Avowed Utopias are not offensive, because they are understood to have a scientific and expository character: they do not pretend to work on the emotions, or couldn't do it if they did pretend. I am sure, from your own statement, that you see this quite clearly. Well, then, consider the sort of agonizing labour to an English-fed imagination to make art a sufficiently real back-ground, for the desired picture, to get breathing, individual forms, and group them in the needful relations, so that the presentation will lay hold on the emotions as human experience -- will, as you say, "flash" conviction on the world by means of aroused sympathy.
I took unspeakable pains in preparing to write Romola -- neglecting nothing I could find that would help me to what I may call the "Idiom" of Florence, in the largest sense one could stretch the word to. And there I was only trying to give some out of the normal relations. I felt that the necessary idealization could only be attained by adopting the clothing of the past. And again, it is my way, (rather too much so perhaps) to <teach> urge the human sanctities through tragedy -- through pity and terror as well as admiration and delights.
I only say all this to show the tenfold arduousness of such a work as the one your problem demands. On the other hand, my whole soul goes with your desire that it should be done, and I shall at least keep the great possibility (or impossibility) perpetually in my mind, as something towards which I must strive, though it may be that I can do so only in a fragmentary way.
At present I am going to take up again a work which I laid down before writing [Felix.] 517 It is -- but please let this be a secret between ourselves -- an attempt at a drama, which I put aside at Mr. Lewes's request, after writing four acts, 518 precisely because it was in that stage of Creation or "Werden," in which the idea of the characters predominates over the incarnation. Now I read it again, I find it impossible to abandon it: the conceptions move me deeply, and they have never been wrought out before. There is not a thought or symbol that I do not long to use: but the whole requires recasting, and as I never recast anything before, I think of the issue very doubtfully. When one has to work out the dramatic action for one's self under the inspiration of an idea, instead of having a grand myth or an Italian novel ready to one's hand, one feels anything but omnipotent. Not that I should have done any better if I had had the myth or the novel, for I am not a good user of opportunities. I think I have the right locus and historic conditions, but much else is wanting.
I have almost read through the "International Essays." 519 I hope they are selling enough to serve as leaven. We shall be very glad if you can spare us a sight of you before you go away. I have not, of course, said half what I want to say, but I hope opportunities of exchanging thoughts will not be wanting between us.
Always yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
F. Harrison Esq.

MS: Tinker Collection, Yale. Envelope: Frederic Harrison, Esq | 7 New Square | Lincoln's Inn. Postmarks: LONDON-N.W | 5 | JA 12 | 66. LONDON-W.C | KN | JA 12 | 66. Extracts published: Cross, II, 420.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
January 12. 1866.
My dear Mr. Harrison
The ample and clear statement you have sent me with kind promptness has put me in high spirits -- as high spirits as can belong to an unhopeful author suffering from a bilious attack. Your hypothetical case of a settlement suits my needs surprisingly well. I shall be thankful to let Sugden alone and throw myself entirely on your goodness, especially as what I want is simply a basis of legal possibilities and not any command of details. I want to be sure that my chords will not offend a critic accomplished in Thorough Bass -- not at all to present an Exercise in Thorough Bass.
I was going to write you a long story, but on consideration, it seems to me that I should tax your time less, and arrive more readily at a resolution of my doubts on various points not yet mentioned to you, if you could let me speak, instead of writing to you.
If you could let me know beforehand when it would be possible and convenient to you to give me an hour or two (I think I need not ask for more than one hour) whether in the afternoon or evening, I would take care to be disengaged.
On Wednesday afternoons I am always alone, 404 but on any other day when I could be sure of your coming, I would set everything aside for the sake of a consultation so valuable to me. After next week there is danger of our being out of town, as Mr. Lewes's state of health urges us to try whether he can find any additional strength in extra-London air.
Yours most gratefully
M. E. Lewes.
Frederic Harrison Esq.

The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 10. 66.
My dear Mr. Harrison
I feel all sorts of doubt and reluctance in troubling you again about my book, in which your advice has already been so precious to me. I hear that you are much occupied, and besides, since we have not had a glimpse of you since I gave you so much trouble, I fear you are weary of me -- a result eminently reasonable to expect, though not the less melancholy for poor me, who am very much in need of your help.
At this season, I know, your engagements must be thickening like other people's, but please tell me the truth in your own behalf, and do not let me be too troublesome.
My second volume, which has been much delayed by illness, is ready now for your correcting glance, and I feel sure that there are deficiencies if not absurdities in what the Germans call the Motivirung seen from a legal point of view. Unhappily there is a great deal of slow matter in the volume which is only indirectly necessary to the completeness of your revision. I wish I could with confidence write "Skip" to everything that does not touch on law. But the threads are so woven together that I do not know how to separate them without leaving you in a state of mystification as to my intentions.
If you are able to read this second volume, I think I shall perhaps not need to trouble you with the third. Can you read it? If you say "Yes" -- Mr. Lewes shall leave it at your address in Lincoln's Inn as soon as possible -- with your permission. I am not making any pretence when I say that I know I am asking a great deal from you.
It would have been a satisfaction to see you -- but I am afraid of asking you to come so far and add the length of the streets to the length of my MSS.
Yours most sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
Frederic Harrison Esq.

Dear Mr. Harrison
If you could some day this week or the beginning of next, allow me half an hour's quiet t'eate-'e0-t'eate, I should be very much obliged by such a kindness.
I could call on you at 3 o'clock on any day except Saturday, or if it would be easier for you to come to me, I should be at home always at 5 o'clock, again with the exception of Saturday.
The trivial questions I want to put could hardly be shapen in a letter so as to govern an answer that would satisfy my need. And I trust that the interview will hardly be more troublesome to you than writing.

GE to Frederic Harrison, London, [26 May 1866]
MS: Tinker Collection, Yale. Endorsed: May 28. 66. Envelope: Frederic Harrison Esq | 7 New Square | Lincolns Inn | W.C. Postmarks: LONDON-N.W | 9 | MY 28 | 66; LONDON-W.C | 5M | MY 28 | 66. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Saturday Evening.
My dear Mr. Harrison
I cannot help writing to you to tell you how much I feel your goodness in writing and coming to me today.
Now I have read your letter, I see there are one or two points which I might have used with advantage had I known them earlier. But the only thing that seems to impose an alteration in the nature of transposition is, that the witnesses to character should come last. This morning, in order to produce a certain slackening of interest before Esther comes in, I unfortunately just made the wrong transposition and put the <three> two witnesses who swear to a fact <concerning> -- the effort of Felix to make the mob go down Hobb's Lane -- last. But this can be altered in proof. 464 Alas -- I am a miserable wretch.
Always yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
I beseech you, do all you can with the proof.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Frederic Harrison, London, [25 May 1868]
Dublin Core:Subject: Frederic Harrison^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Frederic Harrison, London, [25 May 1868]
MS: Tinker Collection, Yale. Extract published: Cross, III, 51.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Monday.
Dear Mr. Harrison
Yes, indeed, I not only remember your letter, but have always kept it at hand, and have read it many times. Within these latter months, I have seemed to see in the distance a possible poem shaped on your idea. But it would be better for you to encourage the growth towards realization in your own mind rather than trust to transplantation.
My own faint conception is that of a frankly Utopian construction, freeing the poet from all local embarrassments. Great epics have always been more or less of this character -- only the construction has been of the past, not of the future.
Write to me Poste Restante Baden-Baden, within the next fortnight. My head will have got clearer then.
Ever yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
By the way, if you see Mr. Deutsch, as you are almost sure to do, will you kindly mention to him this address of Baden-Baden, in case he should have occasion to write to us. I have told our friends to write to this house, but our usual secretary (Charles) will be absent on his holiday, and there may be a difficulty in getting our letters sent on.

My dear Mr. Harrison

Will you cast your eyes over it and see if there is anything wrong or absurd? I found, in time to correct some allusions in the previous dialogue, that felons were not allowed to have counsel till 1836.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Frederic Harrison, London, [19 April 1880]
Dublin Core:Subject: Frederic Harrison^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Frederic Harrison, London, [19 April 1880]
MS: Yale. Envelope: Frederic Harrison Esq | 38 Westbourne Terrace | W. Postmarks: ST. JOHNS-WOOD | CX | AP 19 | 80 | N.W; PADDINGTON | Z | AP 19 | 80. Endorsed: A.P. 19.80. Wordsworth. Published: Cross, III, 388-389.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
Monday Morning.
Dear Mr. Harrison
I have found the spot in [The Prelude] where the passage I mentioned occurs. 385 It is in Book VIII 386 -- [The Retrospect] -- towards the end.
"The human nature unto which I felt That I belonged, and reverenced with love, Was not a punctual presence, but a spirit Diffused through time and space, with aid derived Of evidence from monuments, erect, Prostrate, or leaning towards their common rest In earth, the widely scattered wreck sublime Of vanished nations."
The bit of brick-work in the rock is "with aid derived from evidence." I think you would find much to suit your purpose in [The Prelude] -- such as
"There is One great society alone on Earth: The noble Living and the noble Dead." 387
Except for travelling, and for popular distribution, I prefer Moxon's one-volumed edition of Wordsworth to any selection. No selection gives you the perfect gems to be found in single lines, or in half a dozen lines, which are to be found in the "dull" poems.
I am sorry Matthew Arnold has not included 388 the sonnet beginning
"I griev'd for Buonaparte with a vain And an unthinking grief" -- and which has these precious lines --
"Tis not in battles that from youth we train The governor who must be wise and good, And temper with the sternness of the brain Thoughts motherly, and meek as womanhood. Wisdom doth live with children round her knees."
Has he the magnificent sonnet on Toussaint l'Ouverture? 389 I don't know where there is anything finer than the last eight lines of it.
Please don't acknowledge this note -- else you will neutralize my pleasure in sending it by making me feel that I have given you trouble.
Yours very sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Frederic Harrison, Granada, 18 February 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Frederic Harrison^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Frederic Harrison, Granada, 18 February 1867
MS: Tinker Collection, Yale. Envelope: Frederic Harrison, Esq | 7 New Square | Lincolns Inn | London. Postmarks: GRANADA | 19 | FEB | 67; MADRID | 21 | FEB | 67 | (1); LONDON-W.C | Y6 | FE 28 | 67. Extracts published: Cross, III, 8-10.
Granada, | February 18. 1867.
My dear Mr. Harrison
Your kind letter written on the 5th reached me here this morning. I had not heard of the criticism in the Edinburgh. Mr. Lewes read the article but did not tell me of the reviewer's legal wisdom, thinking that it would only vex me to no purpose. However I had felt sure that something of that sort must have appeared in one review article or another. I am heartily glad and grateful that you have helped justice in general as well as justice to me in particular by getting the vindication written for the Pall Mall. It was the best possible measure to adopt. Since we left Barcelona a fortnight ago we have seen no English papers, so that we have been in the dark as to English news.
Were you not surprized to hear that we had come so far? You inferred of course that Mr. Lewes had profited by our stay at Biarritz and had become much stronger before we ventured to enter Spain -- not without some trembling as to the result. The journey from San Sebastian by Saragossa and Lerida turned out to be so easy and delightful that we ceased to tremble, and determined to carry out our project of going by steamer to Alicante and Malaga.
You cannot do better than follow our example -- I mean, so far as coming to Spain is concerned. Believe none of the fictions that book-makers get printed about the horrors of Spanish hotels and cookery, or the hardships of Spanish travel -- still less about the rudeness of Spaniards. It is true that we have not yet endured the long railway journeys through Central Spain, but wherever we have been hitherto we have found nothing formidable even for our rickety bodies.
We came hither from Malaga in the berlina (coup'e9) of the diligence, and have assured ourselves that Mr. Blackburn's 585 description of a supposed hen-roost overturned in the Alameda at Malaga, which proved to be the Granada diligence, is an impudent invention. The vehicle is comfortable enough; and the road is perfect. And at the end of it we have found ourselves in one of the loveliest scenes on earth.
We shall remain here till Saturday the 23 and then go to Cordova first, to Seville next, and finally to Madrid, making our way homeward from thence by easy stages. We expect to be in the smoky haze of London again soon after the middle of March, if not before.
I dare say you will see Mrs. Congreve before I have -- shall I say the industry, the time, or the strength? -- to write to her again. Pray be so kind as to tell her of our whereabout and our projects, and to say that I found her letter awaiting me at Barcelona. She was not well when she wrote, but your sentence about our common friends makes me hope that she has recovered. I wish I could believe that you were all having anything like the clear skies and warm sun which have cheered our journeying for the last month. At Alicante we walked among the palm trees with their golden fruit hanging in rich clusters, and felt a more delightful warmth than that of an English summer. Last night we walked out and saw the towers of the Alhambra, the wide Vega, and the snowy mountains by the brilliant moonlight. You see we are getting a great deal of pleasure, but we are not working as you seem charitably to imagine. We tire ourselves, but only with seeing or going to see unforgetable things. You will say that we ought to work to better purpose when we get home. Amen. But just now we read nothing but Spanish novels, and not much of those. 586 We said goodby to philosophy and science when we packed our trunks at Biarritz.
Please keep some friendship warm for us that we may not be too much chilled by the English weather when we get back. Mr. Lewes sends his best regards to you and I am always
Yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Frau Karl von Siebold, Shottermill, [ June 1871]
Dublin Core:Subject: Frau Karl von Siebold^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Frau Karl von Siebold, Shottermill, [ June 1871]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
My dear Friend
I am very glad that you found an occasion for writing to me, and I assure you that the effort to help and comfort your wounded countrymen is one in which we gladly join now, as we did at the beginning of the War. As soon as I received your letter, Mr. Lewes wrote to Mr. Darwin 303 on your behalf, and I enclose two photographs of him together with his letter, which I think you will be glad to have because of the feeling which it expresses towards your husband. The two wives of illustrious men to whom he refers are yourself and the Freifrau v. Liebig.
I also enclose my husband's photograph, which I am sorry to say is a very unfavourable one. He has had much better likenesses of himself produced. But we are not now in town, and are obliged to send you what happens to be at hand. Since the beginning of May we have been residing in the country while our town house is being altered, and of course we have only necessary papers with us. Otherwise, Mr. Lewes would have been glad to send you a few more autographs of celebrated men. He has written a scrap from Hegel as a light and amusing extract.
Unhappily I can send you nothing on my own part, for I have resolutely declined to have my photograph taken.
We were delighted to have all the news of yourself and the Professor which you have kindly written in your letter, and the work on Parthenogenesis 304 will be very welcome when it comes. Another year we may perhaps have the pleasure of welcoming the writer in London, may we not? When we were at Munich, he held out the promise that he would come to England to see Richard Owen and Charles Darwin, and when he has gratified those chief desires, I hope he will not forget us.
We have very often spoken of the two days which you made happy for us at Munich last year, and of Prof. W'f6hler's agreeable conversation. 305 When we think of the melancholy account he gave us of Liebig's health, it is a pleasant wonder to us that his restoration is so complete.
Poor Heyse! 306 How much trouble he has had mingled with his gifts of genius and beauty! I think the boy whom he has lost must be the one I saw when I was first at Munich -- a tiny beautiful child then with a little sister.
I imagine you with a 'ablittle'bb young companion in your temporary separation from the Professor during his holiday rambles, the nice girl whom we saw come in from school being, I suppose, your constant inmate. But it is pleasant to think that you have a journey to Venice in prospect with your husband. I cannot imagine any more delightful plan for a holiday. -- We are enjoying quiet in the green country. Our retreat is in a very beautiful spot on the borders of Hampshire, and we find fresh long walks continually.
Do not be afraid of writing to me in German. I am as quick in reading foreign languages as I am slow to speak them, and every evening I read a German book of difficult science 307 to my husband, so that, you perceive, I am used to much less charming styles than yours in that venerable language.
The accounts we read of Paris are saddening for the whole world. The destruction there is the world's loss, 308 and the calamities of the unhappy French nation seem to be constantly opening fresh vistas.
I think you misconceive the state of English minds generally at the opening of the War. So far as our observation went, English sympathy was mainly on the German side. It was not till after the battle of Sedan, 309 that there was any widely-spread feeling on behalf of the French. Pray tell all those friends remaining at Munich who were kind to us when we made our long stay there, that not one of them is forgotten by us. Whenever we have been in Germany we have been treated with warm friendliness, and for this reason among many others we cherish a great love for Germany and the Germans, both North and South.
My husband unites with me in the best regards to your double self, and I am always
Yours affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Frau Karl Theodor Ernst von Siebold, London, 26 August 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Frau Karl Theodor Ernst von Siebold^^F
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Frau Karl Theodor Ernst von Siebold, London, 26 August 1861
MS: Yale. Endorsed: (George Elliot) Author of The mille on the flooth -- Adam Beed, etc. G. Elliot (Frau Lewes). Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square | London | August 26. 1861.
Dear Madame
I received this morning the little packet you sent by Mr. Ranke, and I am so pleased -- so grateful that you have thought of giving me this proof of your remembrance that I cannot satisfy my feeling without writing at once to thank you. The portrait, 836 which we shall prize very much, seems to us as good as a small photograph can be: the expression of the eyes is lost, but all the rest of the face is admirably characteristic. You know, I used to like particularly the slightly Demonic angle of the eyebrows. Women are seldom represented at all fairly by photographs; else I should have wished to have yours also. But I remember you very vividly, and if I were a painter I could make a sketch of you still, either under the bowering trees of your garden, or on your drawing room sofa with the vase of flowers before you.
I imagine your life is very nearly the same as when we had a glimpse of it; but ours has changed a good deal. We have no longer our complete solitude 'e0 deux, for two of our three boys (the cr'e9tins, you remember?) are now tall fellows, and the eldest has been at home with us for a year. He is between 18 and 19, and has a place in the General Post Office, which is an advantageous opening of a career for him. For his sake -- that is, to make a home for him -- we are living in London; a change which is a great sacrifice to me, who care more about the country than about all other outside enjoyments. But he is a dear, precious boy, worth a great deal of sacrifice for the sake of preserving the purity and beauty of his mind. He is very tender to us old people and pets us very much. The second boy is studying at Edinburgh, and we think of his passing the next year's examination for the Civil Service in India. He is of an active adventurous temperament, fond of Natural History, and of roving about in search of "specimens," so that a life of London work would not suit him at all. The third boy is still at Hofwyl.
You see, we have had a great many serious matters to think of since you saw us, and I dare say we should both look graver and older to you. But such a change is due rather to imperfect health than to cares, for we have been greatly blessed by prosperity in all other things. My dear husband's health troubles me more than usual just now: for years he has been delicate, but I think I have never seen him so weak and so frequently reduced to inactivity by headache and other ailments as he is now. We were in Italy in the spring, but instead of being benefitted by the change, he came back much shaken. I live in alternate hope and fear, for his bright, cheerful disposition makes his face often contradict in a few hours all the sad auguries of irrecoverably enfeebled health that I have been drawing from it. How I wish he had your husband within reach to cheer him with delightful talk about salamanders 837 and all the other charming creatures lately introduced into society! You who have only known that mixture of town and country which belongs even to a capital in Germany, can imagine nothing so ugly and oppressive as London. We are near Regent's Park and the Zoological Gardens, and in these we take our daily walk; but the sky above us is not the blue sky of Munich, and we can only vary our walk by going into streets and squares. I am in a grumbling mood, you see; but you must set all this down as so much wickedness. I wish there were many women who have so much good in life as I have. You know, as well as any one, how slight everything else is compared with a life of perfect love and a union that every year makes closer.
I have often thought of the Bodenstedts since you sent me that sad picture of them, and have wished I could know more about that sweet little suffering woman, who seemed to bear up under the difficulties of life with noble unostentatious spirit. I should be very glad, and so would Mr. Lewes, if you would give our kind remembrances to them, whenever it occurs to you to speak of us to them. They were among our kindest friends at Munich, and I regretted that the distance of our residence from town, at the time Prof. Bodenstedt was in London, prevented us from seeing him frequently. 838
Goodby, dear Madame. Thank you warmly for sending me a few kind words: they will make the thought of you brighter to me. We both echo your wish that we could meet again, and both unite in the highest, kindest regards to the Professor. You have always a chief place in my husband's gallery of charming women.
Ever yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Witley, 15 November 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Witley, 15 November 1880
MS: Harvard. Extracts published: Cross, New Edition, p. 627.
The Heights, Witley, | Nr. Godalming.
November 15. 80.
Dear Friend
I thank you with deep feeling for sending me an account of my revered Maman's peaceful falling asleep. Blessed are the dead, who rest from the struggles of this difficult life. The pitiable are those who survive in loneliness, and I feel sorrowfully that notwithstanding the numerous friends whose respectful regard you have won, your loneliness will press on you with a weight proportioned to the devoted care which has for years sanctified your life and made you cherish it in order that you might bless another life to its close. That Maman should have retained full possession of her sweet mind through all her increasing weakness will always give perfection to your remembrance of her. There will be nothing to blot out from the sacred record.
I trust that your health will continue to bear up and that you will be able to relieve the weary days by some gentle activity such as you have been accustomed to.
I have been rather ill lately but am getting well again. Believe me, dear Friend,
Your faithfully affectionate
M. A. Cross.
My address in London is Mrs. Cross (not Evans-Cross) | 4 Cheyne Walk | Chelsea, | where we shall be by the end of this month.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Witley, 1 August 1878
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Witley, 1 August 1878
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade at Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Heights, Witley | Nr. Godalming | August 1. 78.
My dear Friend
I think that I have not yet answered your kind letter of inquiry, which brought me welcome news of your well-being -- for so we mortals must call the exception from severe pain or the pressure of the myriad calamities which are wandering through the earth. Our lot is one of rare privileges, for, except the growing sense of age and consequent liability to ailment, we count for our private share nothing but joys. This spring we were much occupied in furnishing this country house, to which, however, we only came on the 20th of June. We return to town for the winter. And since then I have found the days full, if not of occupations then of malaise from headache. Our health has certainly not corresponded with our external ease. Mr. Lewes has been much troubled with gouty symptoms (!) which you may think an anomaly in one so temperate -- but we carry the penitential load of our forefathers.
I am surprised to hear that a Geneva publisher has the courage to print your translation of Romola. 105 I should have thought the few French speaking people who would care to read it would certainly be able to read it in English. But I hope the publication will have success enough to save you from the tacit reproach of a publisher who finds himself "out of pocket."
It is a comfort to think that Madame D'Albert has no increase of suffering as the months go by. Tell her that if my loving remembrance of her had wings, it would often be hovering round her and giving her caresses.
We are rejoicing in the prospect of European peace and of an abundant wheat harvest which will make a great difference to our artisans and labourers. I wonder whether you read our papers and notice the bad figure our liber[al] party has made of late on the Eastern Question. 106 You remember me as much less of a conservative than I have now become. I care as much or more for the interests of the people, but I believe less in the help they will get from democrats.
Yours always faithfully
M. E. Lewes.
Pardon me for my bad economy of space, which thrusts into the margin what is really the gist of my letter -- that with all my slowness to write notes with or [without] a reply, I am unchangedly full of affectionate memories.

GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Wandsworth, 7 February 1860
MS: The late Arthur Pforzheimer. Published: Cross, New Edition, p. 303.
Holly Lodge, South Fields | Wandsworth | February 7. 1860.
My dear Friend
I must be satisfied to send a very brief answer to your kind letter, 470 received this morning, that I may lose no time in giving you the authorization which I enclose.
I am deeply gratified by your consent to undertake the labour of translation, and I have more than a literary satisfaction in it: I have an affectionate pleasure in the thought that you and Madame d'Albert will talk over some of my pages together.
Mr. Lewes shares my feeling of gratification as an author, that I can have so much confidence in my translator. In spite of your disbelief in the veracity of my descriptions, I shall persist in thinking that he will not be disappointed if ever we have the pleasure of conversing in a quartett at Geneva. Your letters have already introduced you to him, apart from my descriptions.
We are quite of your opinion as to the dialect 471 in "Adam Bede." As simple, biblical French as possible will be the best vehicle, and I think Mrs. Poyser's epigrams will wed themselves very felicitously to the most epigrammatic of languages.
Mr. Lewes begs me to express the pleasure he feels in the revival of my correspondence with such valued friends. Give my affectionate remembrances to Madame d'Albert, and believe me
Always yours very sincerely
Marian Evans Lewes.
Monsieur d'Albert-Durade.

Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Wandsworth, 6 December 1859
MS: British Museum. Published: Cross, New Edition, pp. 297-299.
Holly Lodge, South Fields | Wandsworth | December 6. 59.
Dear Friend
Before your last letter 431 came, I was thinking of writing to you again to tell you of my real pleasure in once more knowing something of the way in which you and Madame d'Albert are passing your lives, and in being assured by you that you both remember me with kind feeling. I had so vivid a recollection of poor Madame Chaponni'e8re -- of her fair face and gentle manners, and of the affectionate relation there was between her and Madame d'Albert -- that I read your account of her trials and death with keen, sad interest. And now the husband, who, I used to think, had so many channels for the enjoyment of life, is gone too! 432 I can enter thoroughly into the sensitive state Madame d'Albert must be thrown into by going through so much experience of a kind to stir her deepest sympathies. I wish it might be any thing like a ray of sunlight -- a happy thought to her -- to know how I cherish the memory of her goodness to me, and all the words tones and looks which were the interpreters of her character. The years deepen the value of our past to us, and of our friends who were part of that past.
I can understand that there are many pages in "Adam Bede" in which you do not recognize the "Marian" or "Minie" of old Geneva days. 433 We knew each other too short a time, and I was under too partial and transient a phase of my mental history, for me to pour out to you much of my earlier experience. I think I hardly ever spoke to you of the strong hold Evangelical Christianity had on me from the age of fifteen to two and twenty and of the abundant intercourse I had had with earnest people of various religious sects. When I was at Geneva, I had not yet lost the attitude of antagonism which belongs to the renunciation of any belief -- also, I was very unhappy, and in a state of discord and rebellion towards my own lot. Ten years of experience have wrought great changes in that inward self: I have no longer any antagonism towards any faith in which human sorrow and human longing for purity have expressed themselves; on the contrary, I have a sympathy with it that predominates over all argumentative tendencies. I have not returned to dogmatic Christianity -- to the acceptance of any set of doctrines as a creed, and a superhuman revelation of the Unseen -- but I see in it the highest expression of the religious sentiment that has yet found its place in the history of mankind, and I have the profoundest interest in the inward life of sincere Christians in all ages. Many things that I should have argued against ten years ago, I now feel myself too ignorant and too limited in moral sensibility to speak of with confident disapprobation: on many points where I used to delight in expressing intellectual difference, I now delight in feeling an emotional agreement. On that question of our future existence, to which you allude, I have undergone the sort of change I have just indicated, although my most rooted conviction is, that the immediate object and the proper sphere of all our highest emotions are our struggling fellowmen and this earthly existence.
So much in reply to your questions on those matters. I hope I shall not have made myself more obscure by my explanation.
We are very anxious to get an accomplished translator for "Adam Bede," and a little while ago Mr. Lewes wrote to Emile Mont'e9gut whose answer we are expecting on the subject. Hitherto I have rejected propositions of translation, from the dread of having one's sentences metamorphosed into an expression of somebody else's meaning instead of one's own. I particularly wish my books to be well translated into French, because the French read so little English, and if there is any healthy truth in my art, surely they need it to purify their literary air!
I should love to go to Geneva again and walk about the old spots with you and introduce Mr. Lewes to you. He is already strongly interested in you not only through my conversation about you but through your letters, and begs me to present his compliments to you and Madame d'Albert. He is a person of the readiest, most facile intercourse -- thoroughly acquainted with French literature -- and of the most varied tastes. His great passion is now Biological Science, and he is publishing a work entitled the "Physiology of Common Life" in which he has compressed in a popular form much hard study and independent research. But he is a very airy, bright, versatile creature -- not at all a formidable personage.
I am writing a new work, which will not be published till next Easter, so that just now my hands and brain are full. At Easter our eldest boy will come home from school, and that will make a new epoch in our domestic life, for hitherto we have lived alone. I hope my heart will be large enough for all the love that is required of me.
I have written you an unconscionably long letter about myself; but it is not out of pure egoism. I feel with you under the recent trying scenes you have gone through -- perhaps these details, which carry you away, for a little while, from painful associations, may not be without their service to you. At least, let them assure you and Madame d'Albert that the thought of you is one over which I willingly linger, and that I like to find myself talking with you in imagination. I will not suppose that this assurance can be indifferent to you: it can never be indifferent to loving-hearted people to know that they are the means of creating some addition to the sum of happy thought and feeling in the world. Ever, dear Friend,
Yours with lasting regard
Marian Evans Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'albert-Durade, Wandsworth, 28 January 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'albert-Durade, Wandsworth, 28 January 1860
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge, South Fields | Wandsworth, Surrey | January 28. 60.
Dear Friend
Do you know anything of the abilities of a certain Madame Ad'e8le Roch, who writes to me from Geneva, asking permission to translate "Adam Bede"? As we have not succeeded in making any satisfactory arrangement with the Parisian publishers, I have no objection to giving her the permission she desires, if you [have] any ground for believing her a capable person, and if, as I gathered from your former letter, you yourself shrink from that troublesome office of translation. In that case, will you oblige me by forwarding the enclosed letter, which accords the permission to Madame Ad'e8le Roch? If, on the contrary, you think my unfortunate book would suffer under her hands, pray burn the said letter, and be so kind as to write me word that you have done so. 464 I will not apologize for asking [you] to take this trouble, for I believe your kindness will prevent you from feeling it burthensome.
I hope Madame D'Albert is recovered in some degree from the severe mental and bodily trial of sharing and soothing these sad last moments of her friends. February, I remember, was a very bright month at Geneva when I was there. It promises to be so this year with us who are generally shivering under cold at this time. The sun shines and the winds are mild.
I should not wonder if we pass through Geneva in the course of a few months, if we carry out our plan of going to Italy, as soon as my next book is out. You would not be very sorry, I hope, to receive a note from our hotel, telling you that we were there. But pray, write me your address in your next letter.
With my best remembrance, and deepest regard to Madame D'Albert, Always dear Friend
Yours sincerely and gratefully
Marian Evans Lewes.
If you have the [s]lightest inclination to translate "Adam Bede," pray understand that it would be a pleasure to me to see your name on the title page. I have signed the letter to Madame Roch with my nom de plume, and do not wish, of course, to have any more immediate relations with her. 465

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Wandsworth, 18 September 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Wandsworth, 18 September 1860
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Holly Lodge | Wandsworth | September 18. 60.
Dear Friend
I was really relieved to see your handwriting, for, remembering the wish you had expressed to send me a copy of your translation, 632 I feared that either a parcel from you might have miscarried, or that you might have supposed me neglectful because I had not yet written you word of our new address. I thought that no publishers and printers, out of Germany, would be so slow as yours at Geneva seem to be. A propos -- I have had requests for permission to translate the "Mill on the Floss" from France, in one case the proposed publisher was Hetzel. 633 Perhaps if you have not yet concluded your bargain with your Genevese publisher, 634 you may make use of this fact.
I could not write earlier, because we have always been thinking ourselves on the eve of a decision as to our future residence, and yet have never decided until today. At last I can tell you that our next address, probably for six months, will be 10 Harewood Square, London. We have taken a furnished house there, in order to try the experience of how far a town life will be endurable to us, since that seems on the whole the most desirable thing for Charles, who has a good place in the Post Office, after passing a government examination with high credit. His working hours are from 10 till 4, and of course we are anxious to provide a home for him that shall be the best moral education in the critical years between seventeen and twenty one. Thornton, the second boy, is coming from Hofwyl in a fortnight, to be immediately placed at Edinburgh. I quite understood the difficulty you were under, in your expensive house, with the inability to receive many boarders at once. At first it was a great regret to me that Thornton should not be placed with you; 635 but our observation of Charles, since he came home, has convinced us that, as we hope Thornton will be able to pass an examination for the Indian service, it will be best for him to be prepared in the routine of English teaching. The English methods, especially in mathematics, are not the best; but a boy whose intelligence is really more cultivated than that of the average, is still under a disadvantage in his native country, if native words and practices are not the readiest to him.
I hope you and dear Maman have had some comfort from your journey to Carlsruhe, and that your Charles 636 is making progress of a satisfactory kind. Our Charles is very precious to us. I think he must be quite an exceptional boy -- he is wonderfully sweet and gentle in disposition without any want of force and manliness; he is particularly tender and good to me and adds greatly to our happiness. Indeed, there can hardly be a woman in the world who has more blessings, outside herself, than I have. The leaf of ivy 637 will be duly treasured, dear friend. I have not yet seen Heidelberg, but Mr. Lewes has, in days long gone by. I like to think of your having enjoyed a holiday, after so long a time of uninterrupted labour -- and I like to think, too, that you have [had?] me in mind in the midst of that beautiful Rhine country.
Alas! for the harvest, and for the poor people whose lot is so deeply affected by its failure. Here, after two or three weeks of sunshine, in which, I trust, a good deal of corn has been gathered in, we have again wet, wet, wet! I feel for Maman in the irritation of nerves that painful teeth must cause her! Assure her of my deep and constant gratitude and affection, and believe me, dear friend, yours ever, with cherished memories,
M. E. Evans.
Mr. Lewes sends his very kind remembrances to you and Maman.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'albert-Durade, Wandsworth, 18 October 1859
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'albert-Durade, Wandsworth, 18 October 1859
Text: William Harris Arnold, Ventures in Book Collecting, New York, C. Scribner's Sons, 1923, pp. 306-311, with corrections from Cross, New Edition, pp. 289-291.
Holly Lodge, South Fields | Wandsworth, Surrey
October 18, 1859.
My dear Friend
Does it ever happen to you now to think of a certain Englishwoman, n'e9e Marian Evans? She seems perhaps to deserve that you should forget her, seeing that she has let years pass without making any sign of her existence. But in reality she is not so blameworthy. When, more than two years ago, I wrote you word that I and my husband were going to the coast, I could not give you our permanent address, not knowing what it would be; and it did not occur to me to mention any other address which would serve for all times and seasons. Having made this omission, I could not hear from you again, and I had not the courage to write again myself, not feeling that I had anything to tell you that would be worth sending over the Jura.
But in these last three years a great change has come over my life -- a change in which I cannot help believing that both you and Madame d'Albert will rejoice. Under the influence of the intense happiness I have enjoyed in my married life 358 from thorough moral and intellectual sympathy, I have at last found out my true vocation, after which my nature had always been feeling and striving uneasily without finding it. What do you think that vocation is? I pause for you to guess.
I have turned out to be an artist -- not, as you are, with the pencil and the pallet, but with words. I have written a novel which people say has stirred them very deeply -- and not a few people, but almost all reading England. It was published in February last, and already 14,000 copies have been sold. The title is "Adam Bede"; and "George Eliot," the name on the title page, is my nom de plume. I had previously written another work of fiction called, "Scenes of Clerical Life," which had a great literary success, but not a great popular success, such as "Adam Bede" [h]as had. Both are now published by Tauchnitz in his series of English novels.
I think you will believe that I do not write you word of this out of any small vanity: -- my books are deeply serious things to me, and come out of all the painful discipline, all the most hardly-learnt lessons of my past life. I write you word of it, because I believe that both your kind heart and Madame d'Albert's too, will be touched with real joy, that one whom you knew when she was not very happy and when her life seemed to serve no purpose of much worth, has been at last blessed with the sense that she has done something worth living and suffering for. And I write also because I want to give both you and her a proof that I still think of you with grateful affectionate recollection.
My books are such close and detailed pictures of English life, that I hardly know whether they will affect foreign readers strongly. Yet I cannot help wishing that Madame d'Albert could read them, for I think the views of life with which they are written would excite her sympathy.
I am very much changed from the Minie of old days: the years have altered me as much inwardly as outwardly. In some things, however, I am just the same -- in some of my failings, I fear: -- but it is not a failing to retain a vivid remembrance of past scenes, and to feel warmly towards friends whose kindness lies far back in the distance, and in these things I am the same as when I used to walk on La Treille 359 with you or Madame d'Albert.
Do I deserve that you should write me some word about yourselves? Everything you could tell on that subject would be interesting. Alphonse 360 and Charles are now bearded men, are they not? I remember them with the more interest, because Mr Lewes has three boys, the youngest of whom is about the age your Charles had reached when I was at Geneva. Our boys are all three at Hofwyl under Dr M'fcller, who has revived Fellenberg's 361 institute there. They went soon after I wrote to you on the subject of a foreign school, the Hofwyl school appearing to suit Mr Lewes' views better than that of the Genevese gentleman whom you kindly mentioned to me.
I almost fear to send my letter after the long lapse of time in which I have known nothing of you. What sad things may have happened! Yet I will hope that such fear is groundless, and that you and Madame d'Albert are leading the same peaceful pleasant life as ever, with excellent friends around you.
How I should love to see Geneva again. But that too is greatly changed, is it not? We were in Switzerland in the summer, but had not time then to go so far south as Geneva. Another time, when we go into Italy, I hope to revisit the dear old scene and show it to my husband.
Farewell, dear friend. Ask Madame d'Albert to accept my affectionate regards, and believe me faithfully yours
Marian E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Venice, 7 June 1860
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, Tinker Collection. Yale.
Venice | June 7. 60.
My dear Friend
I received your kind letter on our arrival here a few days ago, but I have been too busy enjoying the wonders of Venice to find any time for writing until this evening, when the rain has shortened our excursions in the gondola.
First, let me solve your literary difficulties. The Egyptian Sorcerer 551 is a personage much spoken of in modern books of travel, and for aught I know to the contrary, still living in Cairo. He professes to call a boy out of the street (having no previous knowledge of him); he then drops ink into the palm of the said boy, commands him to gaze earnestly into the black drop, and gradually elicits from him descriptions of persons or scenes chosen by the spectator -- for example, Napoleon the First, or some passage of his life -- which the boy is supposed to see in the ink drop through some magical influence exerted on him by the sorcerer. Accounts vary, some explaining the whole affair as "humbug," others as one of the phenomena of mesmeric influence. Thus "necromancier Egyptien" will be the right translation.
Your difficulty No. 2. is easily solved. "The Floss" is simply the name of a river.
When I wrote to you from Rome, 552 I think we did not contemplate extending our journey as far as Naples -- at least we hardly thought that we should not have ended our stay in Florence till the end of May. Once at Naples in delicious weather, the temptation to spend an additional week there for the sake of seeing at our leisure Salerno, Paestum, Amalfi, and Sorrento was made all the stronger because we both needed that more quiet pleasure for our health's sake, after the excitement of Rome.
And so it has turned out that we have robbed ourselves of another pleasure we had counted on, for Mr. Lewes tells me I must prepare myself to find that our time will not allow of our seeing Geneva on our way home. The disappointment is not absolutely certain yet; and it is still possible that we may find our remaining days of absence from home suffice for a flying visit. But that would hardly be for more than a day and a half, and it would be a pity on every account for us to disturb you by telegraphing or otherwise. I know how Maman's kind hospitality would make her desire to receive us, but in our uncertainty and in the scantiness of our time, it will [be] really the simplest and best plan for us to determine on going to the H'f4tel des Bergues, without preliminary question -- if indeed destiny should prove so friendly as to let us see Geneva after all. Mr. Lewes unites with me in thanking you and Madame D'Albert for your kind proposal, but he can only know from me how pleasant a home Maman makes for those whom she welcomes under her roof. I should love to be seated by her side once more! -- But do not expect us -- only be glad to see us if we do present ourselves and ask for two or three hours of your society. We shall have all the more freedom for enjoying that, if we give Maman no anxiety about luggage and other material affairs. We could hardly, in any case, arrive much before the 20th.
Pray, never write to me again about criticism or remarks in French journals or reviews. 553 I have desired my publisher not to forward any newspaper critiques to me, for I make it a rule never to read any, except such as occur in the "Times" or a leading quart[er]ly Review. Journalistic criticism does good to no author; it is written by incompetent men who are not even doing their best, and it is utterly indecisive as to the ultimate rank of any book. The Am'e9d'e9e Pichaud, who imparts his inaccuracies concerning English matters to the readers of la Revue Britannique, probably made his acquaintance with "Adam Bede" six months after it was published, i.e. nine months after it was written, and on that basis he jauntily affirms that I have been in a hurry to produce my new book for the sake of making capital out of the fame acquired by "Adam Bede." 554 The simple fact is that "The Mill on the Floss" has had much more time and labour bestowed on it than "Adam Bede." But the most ignorant journalist in England would hardly think of calling me a rival of Miss Mulock 555 -- a writer who is read only by novel readers, pure and simple, never by people of high culture. A very excellent woman she is, I believe -- but we belong to an entirely different order of writers. So much and no more for the sake of indicating what I dare say you already know, that the Revue Britannique is not to be swallowed without several grains of salt.
You will like to hear that the "Mill" sold 6000 of the three-volume edition in the first seven weeks after its appearance. I hope the French edition of "Adam Bede" will have its share of good fortune too. If there is any other question you wish to ask me, a letter addressed to Milan would find me, not later than the 15th.
I am writing in rather a headachy condition. Pray pardon me if I have left unsaid anything I ought to have said and beg Maman to accept my affectionate thanks.
Ever yours with faithful regard
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Rome, 17 April 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, Rome, 17 April 1860
Text: Cross, New Edition, pp. 310-311.
I think you have made rapid progress with the translation, 503 seeing that you can only use fringes of time for it. It is a very sweet thought to me that the work may be a source of some pleasure to you and Maman (I am very glad to be assured that I may still say "Maman," for that is the name by which she has always gone in my silent memory). 504 It will interest you, perhaps, to know that it is translated into Hungarian, and the first volume is fairly rendered into German -- possibly the second also by this time.
You see I am counting on your and Maman's interest in everything that belongs to me. I do not write about Rome: you have read much better things on that subject than I can tell you. But no one can tell you about myself, unless I take upon me that agreeable labour.
What a delight it would be to take the old walks in Geneva once more! But I fear there are many changes that would check the current of my memory. And the change from the old to the new is always painful to us who are getting old and living more and more in the past. Tell Maman I enter now into her conservative feelings, which I used inwardly to disapprove in my revolutionary mood -- the mood I was in when you knew me.
You will forgive me for writing hastily and briefly, and will understand that temporary preoccupation with the wonderful place I am in is not indifference to other things. With affectionate regards to Maman, I am always yours, with sincere and faithful friendship.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 9 March 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 9 March 1879
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | March 9. 79.
Dear Friend
I must beg you to excuse me for answering your kind letter very briefly. I am much obliged to my friends for writing to me, and I like to know of their welfare, but to answer their letters is a great burthen to me, my time and strength being just now much taxed.
How wonderfully Madame D'Albert endures the weight of years! Pray assure her of my reverential remembrance and affection.
I have no objection to your publishing the translation of "Amos Barton," by which you probably mean the three stories comprised under the title of "Scenes of Clerical Life," since you find a publisher willing to undertake the issue. 195
The translation of "Romola" 196 I have not looked into, finding no interest in my own work at present. The last bit of writing that my husband did at his desk was in sending a manuscript of a small work by me to the Messrs. Blackwood. This was on the morning of the 21st of November, the day on which he took the cold that was the proximate cause of the fatal illness. But of course I have not allowed the work to be published. You must pardon me, therefore, for neglecting your present of the French Romola. My appetite for life is gone.
Our son Charles gave you a very erroneous idea if he said that I was engaged in "finishing" a work of my husband. I am simply revising and putting in order for the press such portions of his manuscript as are at all in a state for publication. But this sacred task is necessarily accompanied with much anxiety, and my health has been a great hindrance to progress.
I am sorry that your Charles is less thoroughly prosperous as to income than I had imagined. But all through Europe there are sufferers from the long-standing commercial depression.
Your health I trust will bear up under your domestic cares. Believe me always, though silent, not forgetful of your friendship. I shall feel your kindness all the more if you will indulge me by not asking letters. You will perhaps be inclined to rebuke this apparent want of sympathy in me, but if you knew how many notes and letters I have to write, you might withdraw your condemnation. Formerly, there was one who saved me from correspondence by writing in my stead whenever it was possible. But now I am alone.
Yours with faithful regard
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 6 December 1860
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade,^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade,, London, 6 December 1860
MS: Huntington Library. Extracts published: Cross, New Edition, p. 328.
Harewood Square | London | December 6. 1860.
My dear Friend
The two copies of your '91Adam Bede'92 reached me in all safety two or three days ago. 666 Very pleasant they were to see in their pure white covers, which I greatly prefer to the favourite French yellow. At present
I have only read the chapters containing Hetty's wanderings 667 which I find faithfully rendered; but Mr. Lewes has read much more and declares himself well satisfied with the translation. It will never cease to be a happy thought to me, dear friend, that you and Maman have spent pleasant hours over my books.
I think it will be wise to adopt the title you suggest "le Moulin de Dorlcote" instead of "sur la Floss"; 668 but on this point I leave you to decide according to your final impressions, when the decision becomes necessary. Here in England the public is about equally divided in opinion about my two last books -- some preferring "Adam," some "The Mill"; but I agree with you that the French readers are likely to find the first volume of the latter too long. My delight in the pictures of childhood led me into what the Germans call an "epic breadth," which to many may perhaps be an epic tediousness. Altogether I should think my mind is one of those most remote from the French standard. What a detail that is which you mention, about the rejection of Maman's apt quotation, 669 lest the book should have a religious air!
I am grieved to hear that you have had sickness in your family. One enters into that trouble with more thorough sympathy when one's own body is not strong. But I am much better now, after a course of tonics, and I think it probable that I have now overcome the first effect of entering the more relaxing atmosphere of town. We shall soon be in our own house -- 16, Blandford Square: 670 so that if you write after the middle of this month, please to address to us there.
Our second boy, Thornton, is established at Edinburgh to our entire satisfaction, having just that mixture of stimulus to study, and social intercourse, which we desired for him. Charles is dearer every day. He often mentions you, and begs to be kindly remembered by you.
Mr. Lewes begs me to thank you for your kind attention to his request about the schools. Mr. Trollope is a friend of ours who has exerted himself so obligingly on behalf of our son Charles, that we should be glad to be able to procure him any useful information.
So you too have abominable weather! Here there is almost unintermittent rain and fog -- a perpetual blanket over our heads, and I irritate myself with thinking that in the country, though it might rain, I should still see some moving clouds. I languish sadly for the fields and the broad sky; but duties must be done, and Charles's moral education requires that he should have at once a home near to his business and the means of recreation easily within his reach. In three years, I hope, we shall be free to go beyond the smoke for ever. -- I wonder if you will come to London again some time, and let us have the pleasure of welcoming you to our home?
Give my tender love to Maman, and assure her that she does me good by the distant thought of her. My husband joins cordially in all affectionate wishes towards her and yourself, and I am always dear Friend,
Yours faithfully
Marian Evans Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 5 July 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 5 July 1862
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square | London N.W. | July 5. 1862.
Dear Friend
I am sure you will forgive me for not being prompt in letter-writing under my pressing occupations. If I had been quite at leisure I should have written before now to thank you and Maman for having made our son Charles's stay at Geneva so agreeable to him. The pretty little photograph of Maman which he brought me is very precious: it represents her air -- her Wesen, as the Germans call it -- to perfection. I wish I had not to think of her as delicate in health -- a thought which is inevitable after your account of her fainting in church.
It would be a gratification to me if you should have the official translation of my new book consigned to you, and it is perhaps not hopeless. The absence of dialect will make it more easy to render than my previous books have been -- at least, there will be one difficulty the less.
We have our second boy at home just now, and have a general impression that life is made up of large boys with robust voices and bright spirits. The weather too is of the most oppressive -- rainy and close. Nevertheless I am very well in health, and my only trouble after extreme anxiety about my work is to see my dear husband's constantly recurring feebleness of head and stomach. The comfort is that he rallies quickly and is ready to enjoy life the moment pain or sickness has left him.
We shall not I think be able to leave home until next year, when, if we live, we look forward to a long holiday. We keep out of the bustle of this tumultuous London season as much as possible, and have only been to the International Exhibition once. 89 There is no enthusiasm about this second World's fair, as there was about the first, and it is not comparable in beauty. But the picture galleries make me wish that you could see them. Nevertheless "this also is vanity" 90 compared with a quiet life of home love. With best love to Maman,
Ever yours faithfully
Marian E. Lewes.
Mr. Lewes, I know, would desire to send his special remembrances to both of you, if he were not gone up to bed with a bad headache. Alas!

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 5 April [1863]
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 5 April [1863]
Text: Cross, New Edition, p. 353, dated 5 April 1862.
The two volumes of [La Famille Tulliver] 148 have duly arrived, and some day, when I can afford to give myself that idle pleasure, I shall glance at the pages, that I may imagine the translator more vividly by reading phrases which have been in his mind -- a little too often for his patience, perhaps, in the long business of revision and proof-correcting. Yet I hardly need any help in bringing you and Maman before me, and hearing the tone of the two voices. I have the happiness of being able to recall beloved faces and accents with great clearness, and in this way my friends are continually with me.
Tell Maman that she never ceases to make one among those dearest human beings who have given me the blessedness of feeling perfect respect as well as love. I fancy I am kissing her soft cheek now, while you, dear friend, are saying something to make us smile. I wonder whether you are now as you used to be -- at once brightly cheerful and deeply sad.
Mr Lewes shares all things with me, except my failings, of which he only shares the inconveniences. And so, though I have no express message to deliver, I am quite truthful in saying that he shares my affectionate wishes towards you both.

Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'albert-Durade, London, 31 October 1872
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | October 31. 72.
My dear Friend
We arrived at home only a few hours ago, when I found your letter of the 19th awaiting me. It is the first letter from you for a long while which has had any sad news in it -- for that dear Madame D'Albert has had an illness is still very sad news to me, though you can tell me of her gradual recovering. 617 It was better that we could not carry out our intention of getting to Geneva, since we should have found you absorbed in anxiety. As it was, we got no farther than Stuttgardt on our way southward, having been hindered from setting out on our journey until the 17th just before the weather changed so unpropitiously. We were obliged to think chiefly of health in our destination, and we had been led to believe that Homburg -- for its air and water and not for its gambling tables -- would be the place to do us both good. We staid there three weeks, until we got used [to] seeing idle people and set off to Stuttgardt, as a town where at least we should see people going about some useful business. Here and at Carlsruhe we had ten days of beautiful weather and intense enjoyment of our dual solitude, but we were foolish enough to spoil our improved health by taking a night journey from Strasbourg to Paris, and this with a bad passage from Boulogne yesterday 618 has made us feel rather shattered than built up by our holiday. But on the whole, we are really stronger than when we set out.
I write at once both to send you my love and sympathy to Madame D'Albert and also to assure you that we shall be happy to receive your friend Mlle. Herzog, 619 whom you describe in a way to interest us. I fancy that she has already called, for our servant mentions [a lady] who declined to leave her name, saying that she would write.
I am very glad [that] you are interested in Middlemarch. The final number, the 8th, will appear here at the beginning of December, the 6th, 7th, and 8th, being brought out monthly instead of bi-monthly.
You say truly that the serious readers in France are few. It distressed us to see the show of trashy books everywhere in shop windows and in stalls at Paris, and the total absence of solid works either in science, history, or philosophy. The contrast [with] the German book shops is striking.
I am going now to plunge into my husband's manuscripts. But I have for some time been too much occupied to read. He is engaged in a long, long book on Psychology, which gives him great delight, perpetually opening fresh vistas of thought. For the last two years his health has been improving, and he is now far the stronger and more blooming of [us] two.
I used to tell you that I should never be happy, but life has almost falsified my prophecy. I have so many blessings and am so free from any trouble, except my own imperfection, that I feel life to be more a personal good -- something worth having seen for my own sake. I know that you will like to read this. My husband sends his best regards, and I am always with deep affection yours and Maman's till death.
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 30 January 1868
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 30 January 1868
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | January 30. 68.
My dear Friend
I was delighted to have your letter last night and to hear once more some tolerably good news about you and dear Madame D'Albert.
Of ourselves I have nothing but cheerful news to give, except that my health is just now troublesome. 723 Mr. Lewes has been better than usual for the last two or three months, which is a great happiness to me. He is intensely occupied with investigations into the nervous system and even made an expedition of a fortnight to Bonn and Heidelberg in the worst of our January weather for the sake of making researches with the professors of those Universities. In spite of my being rather ailing, I am much more cheerful than I used to be, and I enjoy the abundant blessings of my life in spite of the growing years. Mentally I feel even younger than I used to feel, with a keener interest in all subjects. I am writing a book quite different from anything I have done before. I hardly know whether it will please you at all, but I will send you a copy when it is published -- which may not be before next autumn.
Our family is very prosperous. Charles has just been promoted in his office and has double his former salary with a constant increase yearly, and the prospect of further promotion as the years go on. His married life is eminently happy, but there has not yet come another little one to replace the lost one. From Natal we have very gratifying letters. Our two boys there, in partnership of the farm they have bought, agree admirably and are very happy in their occupation.
We have braved the winter in London, where as you know from the newspapers the distress of people out of work is heart-rending.
Altogether, public affairs call on our sympathies very painfully. The position of our own count[r]y, as well as the hideous prospect of a European war, make life very grave to those who have any care beyond their domestic concerns. The want of public spirit is one of the crying defects in our countrymen, but we are all being urged into it now by painful pressure.
I enter deeply into dear Madame D'Albert's grief at the loss of Madame de Viny. I remember well the deep affection and esteem that bound them together, as it used to be expressed in Maman's words and tones when she spoke of her friend. Pray assure her of my constant love and beg her always to keep a little place for me in her kind thoughts. Mr. Lewes also begs to be remembered and sends, to her and you both, his kindest regards. Our frequent travels may perhaps take us through Geneva again, and then we shall have much to say to each other! Always, dear friend
Yours with grateful affection
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 29 January 1872
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 29 January 1872
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | January 29. 72.
My dear Friend
Thanks for your kind letter, so delightful to read as your letters have always been. The weather here, though remarkably mild, seems to be as unfavourable to health as its severer form with you. We have been both sufferers, Mr. Lewes perhaps not so much as myself, from the alternation of fog and rain, but I more than I remember in these later years. I was very ill prepared for the depressing influence of winter by a severe illness -- a gastric irritation which attacked me on our return from the country and robbed me of two months, during which I was a much petted patient, while Mr. Lewes was a perfect nurse. This want of health has retarded me in my work -- which would be a matter of no consequence if I had not begun to print. However I am advanced enough to make all things easy if I can keep well now.
The plan of publication is a new one, namely in [parts] each equal to half a volume which will appear every two months. The second part will appear on the 1st of February just coming. That part of the English edition costs 5 s. I would send it you as it appears, but that we have made arrangements with Cohn, the publisher of Berlin, to bring out an edition (in English) so that it will soon be at hand in Geneva, and Blackwood will be relieved from the attention [of] an additional detail to the already numerous despatches of proofs to various places abroad. There are to be eight of these bi-monthly parts, so you perceive it will be a frightfully long book. But I wanted to give a panoramic view of provincial life, which could not be done in small space.
We both desire very much to make a visit to Geneva as soon as my work is quite out of my hands. But that will hardly be until the autumn.
I trust that dear Madame D'Albert's health will be re-established when there is a change of season -- that change which I remember to have been delightful as early as February in the happy time of my stay with you. In the meantime, I shall think of her the more because her symptoms seem to be very much like what I am continually feeling. But for infirmity of body our happiness would be quite untroubled. It is hardly possible to have more of real peace and joy in each other than we two are blessed with. But if I live to see you again, you will be rather startled with the effect of the years upon me.
Mrs. Sartoris, a charming accomplished woman who was once Adelaide Kemble, tells me that she met a Mr. D'Albert, a son of yours, at Vichy last year, or rather the year before last, who spoke of me as having been in your house. He was alone, she said, and musical. I thence conclude that this son must have been Mr. Charles. 455
Give my best love to the ever dear Maman and pray accept for her and yourself Mr. Lewes's very high respects. You believe, I hope, that I am and shall always be till I die
Your affectionate friend
M. E. Lewes.
