Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 28 November 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 28 November 1863
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in the Tinker Collection, Yale. MS listed in W. V. Daniell Catalogue, July 1903, item 242. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regents Park, N.W.
November 28th 1863.
Dear Friend
Your letters are always so charming that I never forget when it is your [turn] to write and not mine. Now unless I am mistaken, it was you who were in debt in our correspondence until your letter came yesterday, and I was really beginning to feel rather hurt and sad at your long silence. But I forgot all such discontent when I read once more the delightful assurance that you have been thinking of me as usual.
Our life has been very eventful since I last wrote to you. During part of the summer we had our two younger boys at home, and were much occupied with thoughts and arrangements about their future destination. Thornton, our second boy, who is at once amiable and troublesome, easy and difficult to manage, has caused us considerable anxiety. Unknown to us he had during his last year in Edinburgh contracted a dislike to the thought of going to India and did not work heartily and thoroughly in preparation for the final examination. He failed, and we found that he had expected to fail; and this for a time was a great grief and disappointment to us. However, I will not trouble you with a narration of our various agitations and schemes on his account, since they have all ended happily enough in his willing departure for Natal with a first-rate rifle and revolver, excellent introductions to well known friends of our friends, and a very sanguine expectation of shooting lions. To give you an instance of the lad's nature, he had come from Edinburgh with a fixed idea of going to fight for the Poles against the hated Russians. His father felt that it would be a sin to allow a boy of nineteen to incur the demoralisation of joining [the] coarse men engaged in a guerilla warfare, to say nothing of Thornie's utter unfitness for military subordination and other inevitable hardships. But for some time it seemed as [if] he would take willingly to no other career. With all this he is the best-tempered lad in the world; intense, though narrow, in his mental activity and he may possibly [turn] out to be something useful and remarkable. Our other boy Bertie is in Scotland, learning agriculture, so that at last we have regained our quiet domesticity with no interruption in our t'eate 'e0 t'eate beyond the occasional presence of our eldest boy.
Besides these grave parental duties, we have had to think of our new residence and to decide on buying a house. You see our new address at the head of my letter and will be careful not to recur to the old one. At present we are well satisfied with our home, which is not at all like a London house with rooms piled one above the other after the fashion of boxes. It stands in a garden detached from all other houses; and the living rooms are all on [one] floor. Our drawing room has been decorated for us by an artistic friend, who has given himself with kind enthusiasm to make [the room] in which I sit thoroughly harmonious. We have not been in our new home quite a month yet, and on Tuesday we had our "house-warming" in celebration of Charlie's twenty-first birthday -- a great epoch. I am glad to tell you that he has been promoted in his official employment and is altogether a comfort to us from the growth in him of a manliness which does not in the least subtract from his child-like purity and affection. It is very pretty to us the worship he gives me, preparing him, I hope, for a yet more complete devotion to some Beatrice in store for him.
There! I have written a letter all about ourselves, and it would be a very poor sort of affectation for me to apologize. Because you and Maman are good, you care about us and care to know those small affairs which affect our daily life. I am very idle now -- indulging myself in mere reading and in study for no more express subject than to feed my soul. We have just finished correcting the proofs of "The Life of Goethe" which is coming out in a cheaper edition, and are still correcting the proofs of the volume on "Aristotle" which is to appear after Christmas. Mr. Lewes's health is much improved and mine since I got [rid] of a bad cough is also tolerable. A thousand imaginary kisses to Maman, and to yourself perfect regard from
Yours very [fai]thfully
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
Ge to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 28 November 1862
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in the Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square | November 28. 62.
Dear Friend
Before you receive this note you will probably have received another, which I wrote this morning to thank you for the copies of "Silas Marner."
As to the title of the Mill, I think your publishers reasonably fear that the enigmatic "Moulin sur la Floss" may be disadvantageous. I have no objection to that title being thrown overboard altogether and the substitution for it of "La Famille Tulliver" -- which, by the by, Charlie told me you had decided on when he was with you. I strongly object to "Amour et Devoir," but I have not any repugnance [to] a change for the better. Perhaps it would be well to put "Le Moulin sur la Floss" as the second title -- but do what you think best in the matter.
Only resist to the death anything of the same [genre as] "Amour et Devoir."
Your letter assures me of what I wanted to know -- that all is well with you and Madame D'Albert, and my letter of this morning will have carried the same news to you about ourselves.
Yes, "Silas" looks very pretty in its French dress. In England many of my readers prefer it to all my other writings; but it is intensely English.
I am glad you are translating the Scenes of Clerical Life, because Maman will know them [by] that means, and I love the thought of her knowing something I write. Once more best love to you both.
M. E. Lewes.
You will see that I too have written hastily.

Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 28 November 1862
MS: The late Arthur Pforzheimer. A copy by D'Albert-Durade is in the Tinker Collection, Yale. Extracts published: Cross, New Edition, pp. 356-357.
Blandford Square | November 28. 62.
Dear Friend
I have to thank you for two copies of Silas Marner, 120 which arrived the other day. I looked through the scene in the Village Tavern, and thought, so far as I am a judge of a French rendering, that you had given the spirit of the scene very charmingly. Here and there it was inevitable that, for want of the knowledge which only a native of England can have, you should mistake the meaning of a phrase.
I hope Maman and you are expecting Christmas and the New Year with a sense of family joys about you, as well as with tolerable health. With us at present the weather is mild, and we are hoping, for the sake of Lancashire weavers out of work, that the winter will not be severe.
Our life has been quite without incidents lately, and we have been absorbed in our work and our fire-side affections. In this world of struggle and endurance, we seem to have more than our share of happiness and prosperity, and I think this year's end finds me enjoying existence more than I ever did before, in spite of the loss of youth. Study is a keener delight to me than ever, and I think the affections, instead of being dulled by age, have acquired a stronger activity -- or at least their activity seems stronger for being less perturbed by the egoism of young cravings. I should like to know that your experience is the same.
My constant love to Maman. Mr. Lewes is down below in his study else I know he would want me to send his best remembrances to Madame d'Albert and you.
Generally I am very well, but this morning I am suffering from a sick headache, which I dare say, makes my letter briefer than it would otherwise be. Ever, dear friend,
Yours faithfully
Marian E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 28 March 1880
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 28 March 1880
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade at Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | March 28. 80
Dear Friend
Your kind letter with the photograph of your well remembered self reached me last night, and I thank you very much for bearing me affectionately in mind. I was not aware that I owed you a letter, and I beseech you not to attach any grave meaning to my abstinence from letter-writing, for the reasonable conclusion will be merely that I am a little oppressed with correspondents and visitors and find my time too much used up by these minor motives. I have escaped any severe consequences from the late trying winter and, though not robust, am not ailing otherwise than with an occasional headache.
It is a comfort to know that dear Madame D'Albert does not feel any positive suffering under the weight of years and that you have that treasure, a sympathetic servant to care for her in your absence.
I cannot answer your question about "Felix Holt". I know nothing of any translation, and if I have known, I have forgotten. I remember there used to be an unscrupulous adaptation of English novels in the "Revue des deux Mondes," 'abchiefly, I imagine, by Emile Forgues'bb. But whether "Felix Holt" was stolen in this way I am not aware. 378 Some time ago "Silas Marner" was printed in an Italian journal as an original Italian novel under another title. 379 Such is the standard of honour in literary matters!
I wish you could have had Mr. Alphonse and his family in Geneva with you for the remainder of your life. But you retain many warm friends, such as both you and Madame D'Albert used to make in the old days.
Your acquaintance "the youth Charles Lewes" celebrated the other day [the] fifteenth anniversary of his wedding. He is as happy as possible with his good wife and three nice little girls.
Assure the venerate[d] "Maman" of my continued grateful remembrance and believe me, dear friend
Yours always most truly
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 27 November 1877
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 27 November 1877
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | November 27. 77.
My dear Friend
I have just received and read aloud to my husband your kind letter and answer it at once that I may not again seem [un]mindful of my tenderly remembered and remembering friends.
Your account of Madame D'Albert comforts me. That she retains her soundness of mind and can enjoy this change of visiting you daily at your post 782 gives me a delighted sense that life is not a burthen to her. Assure her of my constant love and lively memory of her goodness. It seems rather astonishing that Mr. Alphonse has a grown up daughter! We realize our own age chiefly in the growth of the young ones who date from our latter time. Our now only son Charles, has a third little daughter who was christened Eleanor about three weeks ago. In these children and in all other conditions of our life we are thoroughly happy, and my health has of late been much improved. I hardly know whether I told you that we have bought a house in the loveliest part of Surrey for a summer residence, no longer liking so well to travel abroad as we used to do. Long railway journeys and crowded hotels are a heavy price to pay for that sight of out[-of-door] nature which we can get with more undisturbed benefit at home.
Yes! the state of affairs in France is a grief for all Europe, and many of us here are more deeply concerned about it than about the Eastern question. The arrest of trade, already in a depressed condition before the 16th May 783 is a deplorable, widely dispersed calamity. People here have greatly reduced their establishments and general expenditure, and here as with you artists find poor sale for their pictures.
We are settled in our London home for the winter and shall hardly be able to get into the country again before the end of May. That change is one which we both greatly enjoy. London, in spite of our utmost efforts to ward off visits and other engagements, is a place of continued unrest and interruption. Letters and other small claims eat away much time and leave no corresponding benefit.
You are quite right not to accede to the stupid suggestion of the publishers to reduce Romola. 784 You only have the means of judging whether "Brother Jacob" would find a welcome in any of your periodicals. I have no objection to your using it, now that you have taken the trouble to translate it, and am glad you so appreciate it. I have given the authorisation to translate "Daniel Deronda" to a Jewish writer, the brother-in-law of Calman Levy, and the translation is finished but has not yet appeared. 785
I have had so many letters at different times from French men and women asking leave to translate first one book and then another of mine! They seem ignorant that any of them has been translated. And I really am not anxious that those which are not yet put into French should ever receive that introduction. My French public must be small. It gratifies me that your Rabbi is gratified with my work, and I thank you for putting it within his reach.
Mr. Lewes is as usual very bright and happy, working industri[ous]ly at his favourite studies, though much checked by dyspeptic headache. He begs to be remembered in my messages and heartily reciprocates
yours and Madame D'Albert's friendly regards. With earnest wishes for her and your sustainment in strength and courage as the years become more and more taxing, I remain always, dear friend
Yours affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 27 January 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 27 January 1871
Text: Composite from Cross, New Edition, p. 468, W. V. Daniell Catalogue, (1906), item 365, and Raphael King, Ltd. Catalogue 42 (1945), item 99.
I had a great longing to hear from you, and I confess I had almost suspected you of having ceased to think of me. That was an unworthy suspicion, for since I had not ceased to think of you, I had the best reason for trusting in your faithful kindness as greater than my own. It is unspeakably sweet to me to have some intimation of what you and dear Madame D'Albert have been feeling and doing in these late months. Seventy-one! I imagine how beautifully venerable she must look now. Is it not nearly ten years since I saw her, with her fine figure as firm and upright as ever? I bless her from my heart. She is one of the sweet memories of my life.
This war has been a personal sorrow to every human creature with any sympathy, who has been within reach of hearing about it, still more to those who have gone out to see and help the sufferers. Several of our friends have been among these latter. 255 But even we who have stayed at home have seen as well as heard the effects of the great calamity, for the French who are among us are many of them half or wholly ruined. Last Sunday we had the eminent paysagiste D'Aubigny 256 to see us, -- a grave, amiable, simple-mannered man. His house on the Loire, full of his own painting and such objects as his daughter's bedstead and all such family memories, has been completely destroyed. He is now living with his parents in small lodgings at Kensington. This is but a mild sample of the myriad sorrows produced by the regression of barbarism from that historical tomb where we thought it so picturesquely buried -- if indeed we ought not to beg pardon of barbarism, which had no weapons for making eight wounds at once in our body, and rather call the present warfare that of the devil and all his legions. Enough! I like better to think how Madame D'Albert would exert herself in all helpfulness as long as she had strength to do it.
Mr. Lewes has lately prepared a new edition of his History of Philosophy with many changes and additions. 257 . . . I think my affections grow more intense and my interest in his studies increases rather than diminishes; but physically I feel old, and Death seems to me very near. The idea of dying has no melancholy for me, except in the parting and leaving behind which Love makes so hard to contemplate.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 26 August 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 26 August 1861
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, in the Tinker Collection. Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square | August 26. 61.
Dear Friend
I really have nothing particular to say to you, but I cannot rest without telling you and Maman how sincerely I rejoice in the prospect of the very best sort of happiness for your son Alphonse. 833 Surely nothing could have comforted Maman's heart more than this! I should have written sooner to say these few words, since I cannot give that pressure of the hand which would serve instead of them, but that I have been under the pressure of more thoughts and external solicitations than usual. Our boy Thornton, who is just now gone to spend a few weeks at his dear old Hofwyl, was with us at home for more than a fortnight and made me feel more maternally preoccupied than usual, and in addition to this there are so many things I want to do that every day is too short for me. So never be surprised if I am silent unless you have sent me some question which demands an immediate answer.
I wish I could send you better news of my dear husband. He is still in the same feeble fluctuating state as when I last wrote to you. One day he seems bright and well and the next he is oppressed by headache and unable to enjoy anything. In other respects all things go well with us, and our dear boy Charles is increasingly satisfactory to us, improving constantly and applying himself with admirable resolution and good sense to the everyday work of life. I suffer greatly from despondency and distrust of myself, 834 and I have need continually to summon to my aid all the deepest motives that can serve to make life seem worthy of the day's weariness -- a proof, if any were needed, that in the complex mystery of our organisation the influence of delicate invisible threads may serve to mar the effect of the richest blessings. For after some hours of despondency there will come hours of strength in which life seems glorious and the very pain I have had welcome as the means by which some special work is to be wrought out. My dear husband is so differently constituted, so constantly cheerful even in ill health, so perfect in temper and in the external estimate of facts, without any perceptible influence of changing moods! 835
Do not suppose that I expect you to write in notice of this letter. I only wanted to say my word of sympathy on this deeply affecting epoch in your life.
Mr. Lewes sends his kind regards, and I am ever with affectionate remembrances to Maman,
Your sincere friend
M. E. Lewes.
M. D'Albert-Durade.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 25 November 1879
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 25 November 1879
MS: Harvard. Mostly published: Cross, New Edition, pp. 603-604.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
November 25. 79.
My dear Friend
I am deeply obliged to you for your affectionate sympathy and to my dear venerable [Maman] for still bearing me in her heart.
I returned from the country at the beginning of this month, much restored in health after rather a painful illness which occupied most of the summer. I have nevertheless completed the two chief objects I had in view -- the editing of the final volume of my husband's work which will appear in December, and the founding of a Studentship of Physiology which bears his name and will perpetuate it in connection with the researches which most deeply interested him.
It seems wonderful to me that Madame d'Albert is more than 80 years of age! The years shrink as I look back through them and recal my first interview with her and you. It is very blessed that her mind is tranquil as well as clear. And your family is apparently a source of continual interest and satisfaction. What I should most dread for you is the solitude that will come when your beloved charge no longer needs your care. Imperative duties -- such as leave us in no doubt as to what we shall do next -- are the only condition that makes life easy, though we ignorantly rebel against those benignant bonds while we still have them.
Charles is very well and very happy, with an excellent wife and three little girls. He has an admirable moral character and is a useful man, but has not the least resemblance to his father intellectually. My friends are very good to me and I have many blessings. I try to interest myself in life and to keep my faculties in activity.
[Theophrastus Such] has had a very large sale in England and in the next edition will make the 20th volume of the Cabinet Edition of my works. I can well imagine that it is difficult to translate, and I rather shudder to think what the German translator will make of it -- probably turning the irony into heavy seriousness.
Pray give my reverent love to Madame d'Albert and believe me
Always yours with grateful affection
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'albert-Durade, London, 25 April 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'albert-Durade, London, 25 April 1871
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | North Bank | Regent's Park | April 25. 71.
My dear Friend
Mr. L'fcltze 267 has just been here, bringing your letter of introduction, and I hope that we have been able to furnish him with opportunities of making some valuable acquaintances in London. We ourselves have taken a house in the country that we may vacate our house here for the builders and painters who are going to make alterations. But we shall be at home one more Sunday, which is our day of reception, and we have asked Mr. L'fcltze to come on that day, whe[n] we hope to introduce him to a gentleman also interested in national legends who is attached to the British Museum and may help Mr. L. there. 268
I was startled to find that you were wondering at my silence; for I was under the impression that I was not in your debt as a correspondent. I trust that my letter last-written has not failed to reach you.
We enter with much fellow-feeling into your and Madame D'Albert's anxiety about your sons, settled as they are in unhappy France, alas, poor country! I love the French and am grateful to them for what they have contributed to the mind of Europe, feeling that the Good outweighs the Evil. The sad prospect of calamities yet to be heaped on what they have already endured makes the reading of the news and correspondence in the journals a daily grief.
We are much in need of repose and shall enjoy getting into the country among the peaceful Surrey hills and heaths.
I have your letter of the 12th of March before me in which you tell me much pleasant news about Mr. Charles and his elder brother. I trust no public events will long becloud their happiness.
Our children are also sources of satisfaction to us, and we feel that we have a large share in the moderate store of human happiness. I write as if in the dark, not knowing what I have told you before. But pray, dear friend, take this half letter as an assurance that I did not intend to neglect any letter of yours which seemed to ask an answer. For though I am not a diligent correspondent, I have a conscience about answering letters. Give my tender love to Madame D'Albert and assure her of Mr. Lewes's respectful remembrance; he bears all those persons in his heart who have been good to me. And you too are one of these, dear friend.
Believe me ever yours affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 24 June 1864
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 24 June 1864
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank | Regent's Park | June 24. 1864.
Dear Friend
Yes! We have been absent, and if this, your second letter 268 had come a day earlier, it would not have found us at home. We have been away seven weeks and have been like you, in Italy; moreover, twice -- on our way to and from Venice -- we spent some days in Milan. If either [of] those stays had happened to coincide with your visit and we had met at a turning of the street! But on Corpus Christi Day 269 we were in Venice, nearly at the end of our fortnight's sojourn there, which we enjoyed not at all the less because we had been there four years ago. In spite of the years that have made us older, Venice and her art seemed more beautiful to us than the images our memory had retained. We entered the more thoroughly into the art from having a friend with us who is like yourself, a brother of the brush, and having never been in Italy before felt an ardour of curiosity and enjoyment that was an added stimulus to his companions. Our route was from Paris to Turin, Milan, and Venice without pause at the intermediate Lombard towns, which we reserved to vary our return homewards. I had half set my heart on seeing Ravenna, but Mr. Lewes's health was too delicate for us to venture on the inconvenient journeying necessary to get to that out of the world place. So we returned from Venice in the easiest and most luxurious manner, pausing at Padova, Verona, and Brescia, and going from Milan by Lakes Como and Lugano over the St. Gothard to Lucerne, where we rested well, and so on to Paris again. You can imagine that London does not look pretty after such a journey, and the gratification we get in returning home must be such as comes from the sense of duties to be fulfilled there.
We have many such duties. Mr. Lewes has an aged mother who has lately become a widow 270 and makes large demands on his time, both for personal attentions and for the management of her monetary affairs. And our family prospects have complicated themselves even during our short absence in a way that will not, I think, be entirely without interest to Maman and you. Our "boy" Charles in this his twenty-second year has become engaged to a young lady, 271 for whom [we] had observed that he had a growing penchant, but who we suspected would hardly fall in love with our amiable bit of crudity. That was a mistake, a parental notion, however. She has fallen in love with him, and it is very pretty to see their fresh young happiness. She is in my opinion remarkably handsome and has the rare gift of a splendid contralto voice. She is 4 years older than Charles, which under all the circumstances is an advantage, for she seems to have been brought up in such a way as to have preserved all that is best in youthfulness while she has had much domestic experience. One never knows what to wish about marriage -- the evils of an early choice may be easily counter-balanced by the vitiation that often comes from long bachelorhood. So Mr. Lewes and I fix our minds chiefly on the good we see instead of the possible ills which we may never see.
I especially rejoice in the agreeable position of your Charles, 272 and I trust that Maman's heart is now quite at rest about those who are dearest to her. I should like to see her with her "fillette" -- to see her, in fact, anyhow and anywhere if only she were not in suffering. Give her my best love and assure her that the thought of her is very frequently a joy to me. Mr. Lewes begs me to offer both to Madame D'Albert and yourself his very kind regards, and I, dear friend, am as ever
Yours with affectionate memory
M. E. Lewes.
I have little doubt that MMrs. Smith and [Elder will] answer your letters favourably. 273

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 23 February 187[4]
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 23 February 187[4]
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | February 23. 76.
My dear Friend
In reply to your kind letter received on Saturday I can tell you without delay that Mlle. Herzog repaid the £30 only a few days after the sum had been transmitted to her. 43 Your suggestion that her pictures may be part of the property consumed with the Pantechnicon 44 makes me feel a pitying alarm on her account. I trust a little in the various possibilities that may have led her to some other place of deposit. She would indeed be an object of sympathy if her pictures were consigned to the Pantechnicon uninsured.
I am made the happier when I think of you by knowing that our mild winter has made life gentler to you by telling favourably on dear Madam D'Albert. Give her my tender love and assure her that Mr. Lewes always counts it a gain to him that our visit to Geneva gave him the true delightful image of her.
He is in great [form] just now from improved health and is writing and studying with much enjoyment. It will perhaps interest you to hear that that incalculable entity, the Public, seems enamoured enough of "Middlemarch" to go on spiritedly buying a guinea edition which came out last summer. But I am correcting the sheets for a new edition. 45
We enter thoroughly into the repose of mind which you find in the wellbeing of your sons, and the sense that in quitting life you will leave no hardship to press on those who are still at the early point of their journey. Believe me, dear Friend
Yours ever with grateful affection
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 21 September 1866
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 21 September 1866
MS: The late Mr. Arthur Pforzheimer. A copy by M. D'Albert-Durade is in the Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
North Bank | September 21. 66.
My dear Friend
I was glad to have some news of you and yours after the long silence, though the news is clouded by your prospect of a parting such as must become more frequent to most of us as life advances. I remember well Madame Covelle's 534 graceful person and pretty features. It must be a comfort to Madame d'Albert under this family sorrow to have her sister's presence with her.
With us, all is happy. We have just said goodbye, under cheerful circumstances, to our youngest son, who is gone to join his brother in Natal, according to their mutual wish. Charles expects to be a father at the end of this month, and our sweet daughter-in-law bears the malaise of her condition well enough to make us altogether hopeful. For ourselves we are, as usual, delicate in health, but we were reinforced by a long holiday on the Continent during the months of June and July. It was not a time when we should have chosen to be seeking pleasure, (for the war was making too many hearts heavy,) but that Mr. Lewes had been suffering so much during the winter and spring as to make change absolutely a duty for us, since it was not an impossibility. Accordingly when my new book "Felix Holt" was fairly through the press, we set out for Holland first, spending the larger part of our subsequent time among the Taunus Hills at Schwalbach, and then at Schlangenbad, which we left just in time to avoid witnessing the entrance of the Prussians and to get our passage down the Rhine to Bonn! On our way home we lingered a little in the famous old Belgian towns, and finished by tasting the sea breeze for a few days on the broad firm sands of Ostend. Mr. Lewes has certainly benefited by this holiday, and so have I -- who also was in a miserable condition beforehand. But for the frailty of our bodies, we should be as happy as it seems possible for two mortals to be in this confused state of human things; indeed, I think we have more than our share of good. Mr. Lewes continues to edit the "Fortnightly Review," but it is not improbable that he will give it up by and by, if he can do so without injury to the proprietors. His own studies are of course a good deal interrupted by the demands of editorial work, and besides, we are less free to move about and make flights away from London while he has such a responsibility upon him. "Felix Holt" has been a great success to me both in fame and money -- two things called good, but which vary much in quality according to their uses. I dare say you will not be able to read it, if you were inclined to take that trouble, as my publisher Blackwood has declined to sell it to Tauchnitz, finding by experience that the Tauchnitz editions are injurious to the cheaper English editions. 535
We shall be happy to welcome the young sculptor of whom you speak. I may just mention, in case you should wish to introduce any other friend of yours to us, that our day of reception is Sunday, from 2 o'clock till 5. We find it a great economy of time, and a means of saving our friends from calling in our absence, to have a fixed day of reception.
I hope you do not get all your conceptions of English journalism and the state of our literature from the Athenaeum, which is strong in its advertising interest and therefore impossible to supplant except by a scarcely possible application of capital and time, but is very low in character as a critical organ. The Saturday Review is the best weekly paper in point of talent -- the Pall Mall Gazette, the best of the daily evening papers. But the aspect of culture shown in journalism is never very lofty or cheering.
I like to imagine you at play with the little grand-daughter, and to believe that Madame d'Albert's life also is much cheered by these fresh objects of interest. I am afraid Mr. Lewes and I enjoy our t'eate-'e0-t'eate too much to be very open to the pleasures which may be found in our personal share of the grand-parents' joy. But we rejoice on behalf of our children, hoping that their life will be enriched.
Give my best and most affectionate regards to dear Madame d'Albert, and let me offer Mr. Lewes's kind remembrances both to her and yourself. For me, I am unchangeably yours with affectionate memory,
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 21 March 1873
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 21 March 1873
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | March 21. 1873.
My dear Friend
Some news of you we had in the long interval between your letters, from Mr. Charles Ritter whom you know. He told us that he had seen you and that dear Madame D'Albert's health was still in a sadly frail condition. How I wish that I could see her once more! Whether we shall travel out of England this year -- at least before the Autumn, is made uncertain by the fact that my husband has just begun to print the work on which he has long been engaged. He will publish at first only one volume, which is chiefly a discussion of fundamental questions introductory to the "Problems of Life and Mind" which furnish the matter and title of his work -- to consist ultimately [of] two or three volumes. The correction of the proof-sheets will probably keep us in England, and we shall only move so far as a country house, not very far from London. These are the probabilities of our programme, but they may possibly change.
If "Maman" really gets better as the spring advances, pray do not let me remain in ignorance of the good news. I can imagine her sweet placidity in the prospect of the final change, and I rejoice unspeakably that she and you have the comfort of seeing your children blest with a happy lot such as to make it a gladness to you that they were born and that the whole fruit of your wedded life has been good.
We can not understand why you have not received the last (8th) number of Middlemarch from Assher at Berlin. It was forwarded to us I think more than a fortnight ago. Some delay in packages can be the only cause.
No wonder you have little time for reading, with your life of devotedness to the small needs of others. It always requires some severity of resolution to keep up a course of orderly study, even when the solicitations are no more than those of ordinary society. I can only maintain some repose and intellectual self-possession by making a rule never to pay visits, never to return calls, or go out to dinners. Without that rule all my happiness would be absorbed by futile or rather hurtful occupation with the outsides of social life. As it is, I am compelled to see so many people and [with] the utmost chariness of correspondence to write so many notes that I always long for that retirement into the country which gives us long days of our sweet semisolitude.
Mr. Lewes's health has been greatly improving during the last two years, and his activity of mind has been borne unusually well by his susceptible body. On the other hand, I have been weaker even than usual, and "Middlemarch" was brought into the world under bad auspices, so far as my bodily health was concerned. But in the other great element of happiness it is hardly possible to be more blest than I am -- in the perfect love which cherishes me, and in the sympathy in my books which is constantly being expressed to me in letters from those whom I have never seen.
How long it seems, dear Friend, since we walked together in the old and now vanished walks on the fortifications at Geneva. I had no bright hopes about my life then. But your affectionate heart will delight -- has already delighted in the good that has been given to me -- and more [in] that chief gift of having one's life felt to be of some value by others. For the direct personal joy of living can never be intense with [me], though it is stronger now than when I was young.
I fall into this egotism because I am recalling old times. How vividly I still [see] Maman's entering my room and opening her arms to greet me -- my pleasant bed-room with the alcove in it, and with her painting of the Bible opened and the flowers hanging on the book.
Tell her that Minnie values that memory all the more as the years deepen her impressions of the goodness shown towards her in the past. Life, I find, seems to strengthen, not wither my affections of youth with a comparatively hard unsympathetic period. I dare say Maman remembers that I was always cold and burned an unconscionable amount of wood. I can not pretend that I have reformed in that respect.
Mr. Lewes begs to express his pleasure in being remembered by both you and Madame D'Albert, and he too would be glad if circumstances would accommodate themselves to our seeing you again. Always, dear friend, yours and Maman's,
With grateful affection
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 20 March 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 20 March 1875
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | March 20. 1875.
My dear Friend
Your words of affectionate remembrance are very sweet to me and rouse vivid pictures of that long past time 225 when I made my first severe acquaintance with sledge travelling, and when your admirable portrait of "Maman" won the agents of the Douane to a gracious behaviour. The March wind was less formidable to me then, and I had no fear of neuralgia from a moment's draught of air.
Your letter arrives propitiously in every way, except that it asks about my health at a moment when I happen to be unusually ailing. I had got through the harsh winter unusually well till about five weeks ago, when a state of malaise began which found its climax in sharp attacks of pain, attributed by my physician to gravel in the kidney.
The attacks have ceased, 226 but I am still out of health with occasional interruptions from headache.
I rejoice to know that dear Maman has an unclouded mind in the midst of her bodily feebleness. The sense that your life is passed beneficently for her and the others immediately around you must help to sustain you under the monotony and restriction which you enable me to imagine. I wish you happened to like whist, for in that case it would be a sedative for you equivalent to the cigar on which many men rely as a solace under all earthly trouble.
I heard of your son Alphonse from a Mrs. Sartoris who saw him at Vichy -- perhaps two or three years ago. 227 She was Adelaide Kemble -- a remarkable singer, who married after her first season -- the daughter of Charles Kemble and niece of Mrs. Siddons. Your handsome Italian-looking son seems to have struck her agreeably. But she, poor thing, has been beaten down by the sorrow of losing her son, who was brought home dead from hunting. 228 Sorrow and age are too strong for wealth and homage of which she has abundantly.
Mr. Lewes is very busy and happy in his writing and our happiness in common seems to grow continually in spite of bodily feebleness. I am also writing, but my work "hangs fire" just now.
I write this morning immediately on receiving your letter lest anything should happen to retard my answer if I deferred it to the uncertain morrow. Whenever you are wondering at my long silence, pray imagine me with claims that fill up my days and still leave me a defaulter. Writing notes is an occupation which I am disposed to reduce as much as possible, and well-meaning Americans who are ever and anon asking me for my autograph probably think me the most churlish of celebrities, for I systematically leave their requests unanswered.
Mr. Lewes begs you and Madame D'Albert to accept his warm regards and best wishes. Assure Maman of my unfailing affectionate remembrance and believe me
Yours with faithful friendship
M. E. Lewes.
Our son Charles is highly prosperous and blessed with two dear little girls as well as with one of the best wives in the world. He advances both in worldly position and in intellectual capabilities. Lately he has been promoted to a post of much responsibility in connection with the telegraphs which our government has now taken in hand. Our son in Africa is also happily married, but we hear bad accounts of his health.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 2 September 1876
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 2 September 1876
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | September 2. 76.
My dear Friend
While you have been wondering at my silence and explaining it by my occupation in writing, we have been far away, getting mountain air and drinking mineral waters, out of reach of all correspondents as well as all visitors. "Daniel Deronda" was finished several months ago, and we set off with the intention of going to a much recommended spot among the Maritime Alps, but the effect of the June heat on our way to Italy warned us to change our course and turn northward. We have found much benefit from our stay at Ragatz, Stachelberg and other places, not too much haunted by our fellow-countrymen, in the east of Switzerland and in the Schwarz Wald and are now in our usual place with a sense of more than usual strength. But we arrived only last night, and I have not yet attempted to read the heap of letters which lie awaiting me. Your writing, discerned on an uppermost envelope, gave me a reason for selecting it from the heap, and I hope that you will take this answer in the very first morning of my recovered home-life as a sufficient refutation of the demon's hint that I am in danger of forgetting you, especially as I see that your letter is dated only the 28th.
You perceive that we have been escaping the evil attendant on the exceptional heat, which I confess has given me a cheerful reassurance that this planet is not yet in circumstances too chilling to allow of summer heat any more. Meanwhile the harvest has profited by it. But
I can well imagine that you have found your imprisonment in the white heat of town houses particularly trying to you -- the languor consequent on it being likely to increase that depression you speak of. I feel for you, dear friend, in your life of monotonous effort. But still, you have what I regard as the very strongest motive -- the most fortifying consciousness under the difficult task of living, namely the sense that your life is absolutely necessary to the comfort of another and a cherished being.
Pray give my love to my venerated "Maman" and assure her that I am proud and thankful to be allowed a continual place in her memory. We are altogether happy and prosperous and must not in the midst of so many blessings beyond our share complain that we get more and more liable to infirmities of body and susceptible to the least disturbance.
I am glad that you have found some pleasure and interest in "Daniel Deronda." The writing of it was a great excitement to me and wore me down to a very low point. I had hardly a day of good health while it was in progress. But now it is all behind me, and when I open it again I shall seem to be making a fresh acquaintance with it.
You will not wonder that I write in a brief hasty way. I hardly now can write [a] letter otherwise -- correspondence being a claim that eats away too much time. My husband keeps Madame D'Albert and yourself in his best regard and remembrance, and I am always, dear friend
Yours with sincere affection
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 2 January 1862
MS: Yale. Extract published: Cross, New Edition, pp. 348-349.
Blandford Square | January 2. 1862.
Dear Friend
First of all, by way of explanation, I did not receive your letter despatched a month ago. It is very disagreeable, is it not? -- to have our faith in the Post Office shaken. I had been for many weeks rather wondering at your long silence, but I had tried to still all anxiety by believing that you and Maman were too busy and too happy with your son's marriage to have time for letter-writing. Still, I had been more than once on the point of satisfying myself by writing to you, when, on going down to lunch this morning, I was rejoiced by the welcome sight of your letter lying against my plate. All regret is quenched in the pleasure of finding that you really have been busy and happy as I had tried to imagine you. Pray give a hearty kiss to dear Maman for me, and tell her I feel maternal enough now, with our great boys, to enter at least into half her joy.
When I last wrote to you, Mr. Lewes was sadly out of health, and my heart was rather heavy about him. But for the last two months he has been so much better as to enjoy work. He has begun a long labour which we have been contemplating for him several years, as a thing to be undertaken when circumstances should make it possible -- a History of Science for which he feels that there is a vacant place in our scientific literature. He has been working very ardently on Aristotle, trying to give a complete estimate of what that greatest of ancients did in physical science; for, strangely enough after all the writing on the subject of Aristotle, there is no thorough analysis of his scientific works and no tolerable estimate of them -- the reason being that scholarship has hardly ever been accompanied by very deep acquaintance with physical science.
Our dear boy Charles is as great a comfort to us as ever in the sweetness of his disposition and conscientious discharge of his duties. And Thornton -- our second, you know -- is working hard at Edinburgh, trying earnestly, we think, to prepare himself for the Indian examination next summer. I have no special ailment, but I think I suffer a constant depression of vitality from this foggy air of London. The yearning for the blue sky and the fields haunts me constantly. For the rest, we have all blessings that are worth desiring.
My interest in everything that can, even but slightly, affect you and Maman, makes me sorry that your careful translations of my books should not bring something into that "budget" which has been drawn upon rather heavily of late. I have learned to take a very matter-of-fact view of money matters, and should like, of all things, to know that those I love are not in the least troubled about them. I fear that the widely spread knowledge of the English language gives "Tauchnitz" too overpowering an advantage for a publisher to venture on much risk for translations, beyond the cost of print and paper; but a small sum would be more cheering than blank nothing. I find, to my surprize, that I have admirers in France, and in some cases, where I least expected them -- Montalembert, for example, and -- Alexandre Dumas! (the Elder). 3 Count Arrivabene, 4 on his return from Naples told us that Dumas went off into rhapsodies about Adam Bede, and pronounced it the first novel of the age. After this, I will never guess who will admire or dislike me.
After the marriage of Alphonse, the news of your son Charles being at home with you, and actively employed, is a fact I shall like to think of, when I give my mind a holiday, by picturing what is going forward at Geneva. Such picturing is often done viv'e2 voce -- for Mr. Lewes and I like to talk of you both.
The treachery of the Post Office makes me beg you to send me a few lines, that I may know you have received this letter. Perhaps one additional precaution you might take in the address would be to write simply Madame Lewes, as the name Lewes which the postman associates with our house is sometimes obscured, owing to the double name, 5 by the Postmark.
Goodbye, dear Friend. Mr. Lewes shares in my hopes that we may all meet again, and that the coming year may be full of blessing to Maman and you. You have both the undying affection and esteem of
Your faithful Friend
M. E. Lewes.
No French translation of the "Physiology of Common Life" has yet appeared.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 18 July 1863
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 18 July 1863
Text: Cross, New Edition, pp. 364-365.
I am rather deaf and stupid this morning, for last night we went to hear Gounod's "Faust" for the second time. It is being performed at both our opera-houses, 172 and last night we heard it with the advantage, not only of some preparation by a first hearing, but also of a superior, well-conducted orchestra. My first impressions were not favourable, but last night I was converted to considerable admiration, -- converted by an intense enjoyment of certain moments. Faure, who is the Mephistopheles, acts and sings the part with a striking effect. Nevertheless, I still feel that the composer is wanting in the great power of wedding passion with melody; he seems to me to be comparatively feeble in the pathetic and tragic moments. But we have an accomplished critic, who says the garden duet is finer than the divine duet between Valentine and Raoul in the "Huguenots." That may be, but I have not yet felt it.
I have not seen Renan's book. He is a favourite writer of mine, but I care less about this [Vie de J'e9sus] than I should have cared years ago. It consists, as I gather from the notices I have seen, of conclusions, without any statement of the process by which they have been arrived at; and the conclusions, I imagine, have nothing novel in them for people who have been long acquainted with the results of modern criticism.
But I am surprised to hear that there is anything "cavalier" in Renan's treatment of religious belief: he has always seemed to me remarkable as a French mind that is at once "scientific" (in the German sense) and eminently tender and reverent towards the forms in which the religious sentiment has incarnated itself.
I fear you would hardly be likely to get adequate compensation for the labour it would cost you to translate the [Physiology of Common Life.] In money certainly not. And even the French now are becoming accomplished in foreign languages, so that the demand for translations from the English into French is probably lessening for works which address themselves to the cultured.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 17 December 1865
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 17 December 1865
MS: Morgan Library. Extracts published: Cross, New Edition, pp. 390-391.
The Priory, North Bank | St. John's Wood. | December 17. 1865.
My dear Friend
Your kind letter came to me yesterday. I wish there had been no family trouble to disturb the happiness of which your previous letter had given me an idea, and which I allowed myself to trust in as still continuing, notwithstanding your long silence. I sympathize with the indisposition to write letters: time becomes more precious as one gets older and in need of economizing all strength for the sake of not falling short towards immediate duties. We are altogether prosperous and happy in each other, as usual. Our one great want is health: we both remain delicate and liable to constant subtractions of time through headache and debility.
"The Fortnightly" is a great succ'e8s d'estime; the principle of signature, never before thoroughly carried out in England, has given it an exceptional dignity, and drawn valuable writers. It is a thoroughly serious periodical, intended for the few who will pay a high price, and is supported by proprietors unconnected with the publishing trade. It is still a question whether it will succeed commercially. I think I told you that Mr. Lewes accepted the editorship on urgent request, after having previously refused it, and has nothing to do with it as a speculation. He likes the work very well, now he has entered into it, finding that superior contributors present themselves and brave the supposed perils of signature. I am occupied, in a leisurely way, with my own writing, 391 and, as you know, am not in the habit of contributing to periodicals.
It grieves me that you have had your trouble in vain in translating Romola. I have had at least four applications from France for permission to translate it. But in fact the permission has always belonged to Smith and Elder; and now, no permission is needed. A short time ago we had a visit from Mlle. Bohn, the niece of Professor Sch'e9rer, 392 residing with him at Versailles. She says that, by herself and in her circle, Romola is valued more than any of my previous books. It is rather a cruel thing that she, like so many others, inquired whether my books had been translated into French -- I mean, it is cruel for you, that after your conscientious labour your publishers have not been able to make better arrangements for you with Parisian houses. I have received numerous letters asking me to give my authority to translations of the Clerical Scenes, or Silas Marner, or the Mill. I only tell you this as so much information that you might perhaps use, in your relations with your publishers.
Our eldest son Charles is extremely happy in his marriage, and we see more and more reason to rejoice in his early establishment. Thornton has had some calamities to encounter in Natal, owing to a monetary crisis in the colony and a war with the natives. But he is well in health and shows much spirit. These conditions in Natal cause us to waver in our intention of sending out the youngest who is now old enough to go, and is better fitted for colonial than for English life, at least as far as the means of pushing his fortune are concerned. He is a fine fellow physically, and has pleasant social qualities, but he is not suited to any other life than that of a farmer, and in England farming has become a business that requires not only great capital but great skill to render it otherwise than hazardous.
These are the chief points in our present circumstances. Besides these, perhaps it will interest you to know that what my friends consider a remarkably fine portrait of me (in crayons) has been executed by an artist named Frederick Burton, a friend of ours, and that the portrait is to be published by a process which professes to produce facsimiles of such drawings. 393 See how I chat about myself! But you wish me to do so.
Mr. Lewes unites with me in kindest feelings and wishes. Send my best love to Madame d'Albert when you write, and believe me dear friend -- with a thorough response to your wish that we may meet again --
Your true and affectionate friend
Marian E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 15 June 1861
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 15 June 1861
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | June 15. 1861.
Dear Friend
Only last night we returned from Italy, whither we started on the 19th of April! We went through France and along the coast of the Mediterranean, and for some time I entertained the hope that we should return by way of Geneva and see you and Maman. That was the reason I did not answer your letter, which was forwarded to me at Florence. I wished to wait until I could say absolutely that we should see you. But destiny said "No." We lingered too long at Florence, and were obliged to hasten home in order to meet a person 783 who had been awaiting us in London. We therefore took the shortest way -- across the St. Gothard, by Lucerne, to Bern -- where we saw our youngest boy (still at Hofwyl) -- and here we are at home again, and at an impossible distance from certain dear people whose letters of kind anxiety at my silence were among the first things that occupied me on my entrance into our dining room.
I have been written to by a French lady for permission to translate "Silas Marner." But I have told her that the right of translation was reserved for you. Since we returned, however, we have been made aware by a letter from the German publisher Duncker, 784 who had agreed to purchase the right to translate Silas Marner into German, that my publisher Blackwood has forgotten to have inserted the necessary formula reserving the right of translation on the title page. I am sorry for this on your account as it may interfere with your translation, [transactions?] about publishing, though indeed, according to the rate of procedure of publication of "Adam" and "The Mill," the year of possible reservation is likely enough to have elapsed with "Silas," as it had long done with "Adam" and "The Mill" before your translation can get published, so that the lapse of my English publishers may after all make no difference.
I quite forget what were the facts I wrote to you about Hetzel, having long dismissed the matter from my mind. As to the probability that Dentu has issued more copies of "Adam" than he has accounted for to Georg 785 -- nothing but an integrity very rare among publishers can secure a man against the fraud, when once he lets the printing go out of his own hands. I hope, however, that Georg will not be a positive loser. "Silas" has been very successful in England, and possibly its smaller size makes it seem a more tempting speculation to him. But I hate writing about the money aspect of my books. I am thankful, very thankful for the honest gain that comes with honest work, but I like to feel that I have done with my book when it is once fairly written, and happily my English publisher is a man of such high character that few authors can get their business transacted more simply than I do.
As to the "Physiology of Common Life" we are pleased to hear that you are interested in it. Some time ago my husband received a proposition for its translation into French, and the work may by this time be somewhat advanced. It has been translated into German by the eminent physiologist Victor Carus. 786 The second part, containing the considerations on the Nervous System, could hardly be translated by any one who was not well versed both in physiological and psychological science: accomplishment in language generally would not suffice without special knowledge.
We seem destined to give you fruitless trouble about schools. Mr. Trollope, since we wrote to you on his behalf, has changed his mind, having been dissuaded by the present tutor of his boys at Winchester from sending them abroad until they are much more matured. We are grateful to you for the trouble you have kindly taken, but feel some regret that you should have been led into asking it in vain.
I write under some hurry and much heat (of temperature, not of temper) this morning, and I half fear I may have scarcely said precisely what I mean. I have certainly not said half what I feel of affectionate regret that I have had to pass through Switzerland without seeing Maman and you. I am sure she will excuse my not answering her welcome letter directly under the flutter of my first morning at home. I decided not to delay answering you after my long silence, as a smaller evil than answering you with some hurry. Ever, dear Friend, with deep regard to Maman and yourself
Yours faithfully
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 13 September 1871
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 13 September 1871
Text: Cross, New Edition, pp. 476-477.
Your letters are always delightful to me, because I imagine you speaking while I read them: you have that power of easy description and narration in your letters and your talk which is exceedingly rare among us English. We are for the most part hesitating, clumsy talkers, and our letters are either curt or laboured.
You must know that I am very busy now, preparing a long, long book; but when I have finished it, one of my first plans will be to visit Geneva. My husband is equally inclined to make that our next journey -- in the first place, because he is always inclined to do what I wish; and in the next, because he will enjoy seeing not only you and Madame D'Albert, but certain scientific men of whom you can boast, as the fine writers say, though I fancy you have never used that privilege of boasting. I suppose I shall not be at liberty to get so far away from home until next year -- probably in July, if I live so long.
Your mention of Madame Chancel quite startled me, for I had believed that she was dead. It was very prettily done of the German Empress to visit her old governess incognita. 361 I have heard from those who know the Empress that she is a thoughtful and sympathetic woman, much subdued by experience. But you, of course, have heard abundant details about her from Madame Chancel. How one pities these royal people, who are necessarily human monstrosities, having little experience in common with the multitude of their fellow-men -- except in their diseases. I suppose a royal toothache is much like a bourgeois toothache. But the royal point of view about everything else, even the stars, changes the very quality of knowledge. The German princes, in some instances, have a better chance of being tolerably common human beings than any other royalties.
Pray pardon me for writing a hasty letter. I have been ill since we came back, and my strength will not permit me to write anything but my necessary, or rather my voluntary, author's work in the mornings. Even that I can only do irregularly, so I scribble my letters at night before going to bed.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 13 October 1875
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 13 October 1875
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade, Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | Regent's Park | October 13. 75.
My dear Friend
On my return to town the other day I found your kind letter with the volume obligingly presented to me by Mr. Gustave Revilliod. 320 Pray offer him my best thanks and say that I have an interest in oriental literature which makes the gift especially acceptable.
Your letter is a delightful assurance that you have been having much family happiness, and I can imagine the pretty picture made by the grandparents with the two younger generations. What a comfort that Madame D'Albert, in spite of bodily weakness, is able to share such joys of heart and mind!
To us the summer brought sorrow in the death of our son Herbert who, you may remember, was settled in South Africa. He had for some time been in delicate health, and we were afraid of urging him to come to England because his disease was of a nature to be encouraged by our fitful climate. This death is all the sadder because he was very happily married and has left a deeply attached young wife to sorrow for him. Hardly a month before his death she had had a second child -- a fine little boy. Our consolation is that we are at least able to provide for them in the worldly sense -- but for her, poor dear, there is no present consolation. They felt peculiarly united, leading unseparate[d]ly a retired life and being all in all to each other.
Apart from this loss our life has been as much blessed as usual, our son Charles and his family being a constant source of satisfaction to us and our own domestic joy having no flaw except the accustomed infirmities of health which we must not expect ever to be free from.
We spent the summer in the country according to our habit, but our situation was rather too low, and I think we suffered some depression of vitality from a rather close and over moist atmosphere. But we have been and are still very busy, Mr. Lewes being engaged on the third volume of Problems, and I on a long book, the first part of which will perhaps appear in the beginning of February.
We old people cannot help regretting the beautiful old Geneva, enclosed in its harmless fortifications. But the changes you describe are such as we have to witness in all prosperous towns -- in Dresden, for example -- which used to have a clear heaven above it and quiet amusements within the streets and beyond them where one could sit and hear the best music without being overcrowded. The last time we were there the times had changed all that. Everywhere there is a prosperous crowd to be amused, and the tastes of the crowd are not yet refined, so that Art must condescend to please the low average. This condescension is painfully marked in our huge rich London; but of late we have been a little cheered [by] a revived interest in the Shakespearean drama to counterbalance Offenbach.
Mr. Lewes begs me to offer his best remembrances to Madame D'Albert and yourself, and I am as ever both to her and you
Your affectionate friend
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 12 January 1865
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 12 January 1865
Text: Copy by D'Albert-Durade in the Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory | North Bank N.W. | January 12. 1865.
Dear Friend
Your letter was very welcome and remains especially cheering to me from the happy account it gives of your two sons. I rejoice sincerely that after your long anxieties you at length see your younger son in a position such as you have desired for him. Surely this fact, with the possession of a sweet little granddaughter, must make dear Maman's life brighter -- if, alas, illness does not come to spoil all delights. I fear the attack at Christmas of which you speak must have been a severe one.
We are exceedingly well prepared to sympathize both in joy about sons and in sickness, for we have had much of both those different experiences. Charles is to be married in April, and his engagement is an increasing source of satisfaction to us. We have good news from Thornie, who is happy and active at Natal; and our third son Bertie has just been with us for his Christmas visit, gratifying us highly by his improvement in health and morale. As for sickness, that has been an almost incessant companion with us since I last wrote to you. I do not mean sickness which creates alarm for life or keeps one in bed, but those wretched sensations of dyspepsia which suffuse life with cheerlessness and discomfort. Mr. Lewes was unusually enfeebled from that cause about the middle of September, and continued to suffer so much as to be unable to pursue his usual studies until November, when a visit to Malvern and medical application of the water cure with much walking on the hills restored him [to] his ordinary condition, which, as you know, is not robust. I too have been suffering in the same way, but since the fogs and close weather have given place to a more wintry sharpness of air, we have both been better. So I will not dwell longer on past grievances.
I never write in periodicals. That is to say, I have not done it for many years, and of late Mr. Lewes has not contributed to the Cornhill until this month, the number [for] which contains an article by him on "Shakspeare in France." I am now occupied with writing, but rather to please myself than the public, and I am not certain whether what I am doing will be published.
Mr. Lewes has been earnestly requested to take the editorship of a new periodical which is in some respects to form a sort of English "Revue des deux Mondes," and after decidedly refusing from fear of an undertaking which would make too great demand on his time, he is now inclined to consent under certain arrangements which will save him from excessive work.
Tomorrow we shall start for Paris 309 for a stay of about ten days, so I have written in haste this morning lest you should wonder at my silence if I deferred writing till my return.
You see, we are happy and prosperous and I shall feel all the happier now that I have had good news of you.
Pray give my best love to Madame D'Albert, and beg her to accept with you my husband's very high and kind regards. Believe me, dear Friend,
Ever yours gratefully and affectionately
Marian E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 12 April 1867
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, 12 April 1867
MS: Yale. A copy by D'Albert-Durade is in the Tinker Collection, Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 12. 67.
My dear Friend
Your letter, which came to me last evening, was a welcome assurance to me that you and dear Madame d'Albert still remember me and think of me kindly. Since I last wrote to you we have wandered far -- as far as the south of Spain. My dear husband's health had broken down so (to me) alarmingly, that I persuaded him to give up the editorship of "the Fortnightly," and to defer finishing the new edition of his History of Philosophy until he had had a long rest. He complied, and at the end of December we set off to the south of France. After passing a month at Biarritz, he was so much strengthened that we ventured to travel on, tentatively and slowly into Spain, which I longed to visit because I have for the last three years been interesting myself in Spanish history and literature. We went by Saint Sebastian, Saragossa and Lerida to Barcelona, and Mr. Lewes was so delighted with this first taste of Spain, that we had courage to take the steamer for Malaga by way of Alicante. From Malaga we went to beautiful Granada, where we made our longest stay, and from thence to Cordova, Seville, and Madrid.
We returned home only three weeks ago, after having had nearly three months of delicious summer, while our poor fellow-countrymen who were doing their hard duties at home were suffering from our horrible English winter. Are we not privileged creatures, and ought not something good to come out of us after all this indulgence? Mr. Lewes is in very fair health now -- not robust, which I hardly expect him to become, but well enough to enjoy both work and relaxation. Like you, we are quite disinclined to encounter the crush and excitement of the Paris exhibition, and our dread of the commencing crowd was great enough to hurry us home rather prematurely, as we were unable to contrive a route homeward that would not take us through Paris.
I like very much to read all the details you tell me about yourself and Maman. It was prettily done of the Duke of Weimar to write to the artist as well as the donor of a portrait, 607 but to have succeeded in a likeness painted from memory was something that deserved special recognition. I hope your loved ones at Lyons 608 will join you at Geneva in the summer, rather than attract you to them, for surely Geneva is a better residence than Lyons in all seasons, but especially in the summer. I hope we shall see it again -- and see you and Maman still well and happy there -- before many years are past. Some time, when we are going to Italy again, we may be able to make Geneva a part of our route.
We are quite without external trouble -- prosperous, at present, in all things, studying quietly and with increasing happiness in companionship. I hope you have not had any trouble to get Felix Holt. I would have sent it to you if I had thought you wished for it. But I believe Blackwood has now given permission to Tauchnitz to reprint it. It has produced a stronger impression on many minds than my previous books, and I am often cheered by letters from unknown men, often working men, telling me of its strong influence. I mention these things to you because I know of your kind sympathy in what touches me nearly.
Mr. Lewes unites with me in affectionate and respectful regards to yourself and Madame d'Albert. I shall add for my own part my most grateful love.
Always yours faithfully
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, [July 1868]
Dublin Core:Subject: Francois D'Albert-Durade^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Francois D'Albert-Durade, London, [July 1868]
MS: Harvard. Mostly published: Cross, New Edition, pp. 430-431.
The Priory | 21 North Bank | London.
My dear Friend
Your welcome letter was forwarded to me in Germany whither we had set out at the beginning of June. When we found ourselves as far south as Basle, we indulged ourselves with the project of returning home by Geneva, but we finally gave up that pleasure for this year, because we feared that the long railway journeying it involved would not be good for us at the end of our sanitary excursions among the pinewoods and mountains of the Black Forest. But we look forward with hope to some other continental journey which will give us a route through Geneva. I long to see you and always-loved "Maman" again, and Mr. Lewes, besides the delight he takes in seeing those who have shewn me so much sympathy and kindness, wishes to make the acquaintance of some men of science who are your fellow-citizens.
It is always charming to me to read your letters. You have the happy talent of remembering all the little details which have associations in my memory, and so making a little picture of the life around you. For example, that son of M. Heyer 800 whom you mention as an "'c9tudiant en th'e9ologie," I remember to have seen standing on the table in my room as a tiny, pretty boy! If the excellent parents remember me too, pray ask them to accept my kind regards. I have often spoken of them and described them to Mr. Lewes.
I imagine "Maman" looking beautiful with the beauty of age -- as upright as ever, and still a presiding genius of order and comfort in the household. It is very pretty that her sister can still travel all the way from Trieste to spend the summer months with her.
We are increasingly happy, although the years carry away with them some of our physical strength and buoyancy. Our life is absolutely untroubled, and I grow much more cheerful as I grow older. We have good news (though too rarely) from our exiled boys in S. Africa, and Charlie's lot is altogether satisfactory to us -- prospering outwardly, and with evidence of constant improvement in his mind and character.
We should often remain longer on the Continent than the two months which we usually allow ourselves at a time, but that Mr. Lewes's mother is now very aged (82) and does not of course like him to go very far beyond easy reach for months together. Otherwise, we should perhaps carry out a plan of going to the East, before we get too old for that daring enterprise.
My poem has been a great source of added happiness to me -- all the more, or rather principally because it has been a deeper joy to Mr. Lewes than any work I have done before. I seem to have gained a new organ, a new medium that my nature had languished for. The public, here and in America, has received it very kindly, and it has sold well.
I care for the sale, not in a monetary light (for one does not write poems as the most marketable commodity) [but] because sale means large distribution. We are so happy now as to be independent of all monetary considerations, and Mr. Lewes plunges at his will into the least lucrative of studies, while I on my side follow tastes not much in keeping with those of our noisy, hurrying, ostentatious times. Mr. Lewes begs to be included in all kind remembrances, and I am always, dear friend, both to you and "Maman"
Your grateful and affectionate
M. E. Lewes.
I feared that English verse could hardly be a pleasure to you, but my book will at least be a sort of imperfect conversation with me.
