GE to Charles Bray, St. Leonard's, 9 August [1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 310.
St. Leonard's August 9.
Dear Friend
Thanks many for the Herald, which one reads with avidity at St. Leonard's, whatever one may do in London. It would have been a satisfaction to your benevolence to see me sitting on the beach laughing at its many jokes (i.e. the Herald's) and sympathizing with your indignation against Judge Maule. 357
You always used to send me an account of the results of stock-taking, and I missed that proof of your understanding my affection very much. Do you mean that you gained £200 exclusive of housekeeping etc. or only that altogether? It always helps me to be happy when I know that you are so, but I do not choose to vindicate myself against doubts of that, because it is unworthy of you to entertain them. I am going on as well as possible physically -- really getting stout, and, as I have been telling Mrs. Chapman, being regenerated by baptism and -- beer drinking! This latter sacrament I have taken to for the last week and find it very efficacious.
If I had chosen to go to the Continent I should have gone with the Combes. I have had a letter from Mr. Combe today in which he says that Mrs. C. is much better. But perhaps you have heard this before.
I should like to have a good laugh with you immensely. How nice it would be to meet you and Cara on the beach this evening, and instead of sending you such a miserable interpreter of one's feelings as a letter, give you the look and the hand of warm affection! This British Channel really looks as blue as the Mediterranean today. What weather! Love to all from
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, St. Leonard's, [5 June 1848]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, St. Leonard's, [5 June 1848]
MS: Yale. Published: Cross, I, 186-188.
Victoria Hotel | Monday.
My dear Friend
Your words of affection seem to make this earthly atmosphere sit less heavily on my shoulders, and in gratitude I must send you my thanks before I begin to read of Henry Gow and Fair Catherine 739 for Father's delectation. In truth I have found it somewhat difficult to live for the last week -- conscious all the time that the only addition to my lot worth having must be more strength and love in my own nature -- but perhaps this very consciousness has an irritating rather than a soothing effect. I have a fit of sensitiveness upon me which after all is but egotism and mental idleness. The enthusiasm without which one cannot even pour out breakfast well (at least I cannot) has forsaken me. You may laugh and wonder when my enthusiasm has displayed itself, but that will only prove that you are no seer. I can never live long without it in some form or other. I possess my soul in patience for a time, believing that this dark damp vault in which I am groping will soon come to an end and the fresh green earth and the bright sky be all the more precious to me. But for the present my address is Grief Castle, on the river of Gloom, in the valley of Dolour. I was amused to find that Castle Campbell in Scotland was called so. 740 Truly for many seasons in my life I should have been an appropriate denizen of such a place, but I have faith that unless I am destined to insanity, I shall never again abide long in that same castle. I heartily say amen to your dictum about the cheerfulness of "large moral regions." 741 Where thought and love are active, thought the formative power, love the vitalizing, there can be no sadness. They are in themselves a more intense and extended participation of a divine Existence -- as they grow the highest species of faith grows too -- and [all things are possible.] I don't know why I should prose in this way to you. But I wanted to thank you for your note and all this selfish grumbling was at my pen's end. And now I have no time to redeem myself. We shall not stay long away from home I feel sure.
Your affectionate friend,
Mary Ann Evans.

She was of a most affectionate disposition, always requiring some one to lean upon, preferring what has hitherto been considered the stronger sex, to the other and more impressible. Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, St. Leondard's, [11 JUNE 1848]
Dublin Core:Subject: CHARLES BRAY^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, St. Leondard's, [11 JUNE 1848]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1848. Brief extract published: Cross, I, 191.
Marina | St. Leonard's | Sunday.
Alas! mon ami, Father is not better as you imagine -- on the contrary all his worst symptoms have returned -- a bad cough, shortness of breath, languor and aching of the limbs. I fear I shall have to take him home as great an invalid as ever. I thought you went to London last Thursday, and wrote a letter for the community there, supposing you to be a part of it. It is very charming to hear of all Cara's pleasures past and to come, 749 and it will be still better to think of them when you are sharing them. Her letter was as exhilarating to me as anything could be when Father's pale haggard looking face was opposite to me.
Thank you for your goodness in writing to me -- I take crumbs with gratitude, though I should be glad of a thorough meal of news about you. The kind words and thoughts of my beloved ones are so many little gauze wings which were of no avail to me when I had not inward strength to fly withal -- but now my native vigour is come again I flutter them joyously and soar with them into the Empyrean [in spite of sorrow.] 750 So give me more and more of these little wings, and judge of me as men judge of their divinities -- what you feel in your little half-drained puddle of a soul, I feel in my great Atlantic. There -- you see I have not kept your company in vain -- I am beginning to understand your doctrine of faith -- that it should be in inverse proportion to evidence.
Persevere in the Devonshire plan pray. 751 I think we shall surely have fine weather now. Today is crowned with the most beautiful of skies, light floating clouds setting off that perfect azure which must ever stand for hope in the language of colours.
I have read Jane Eyre, 752 mon ami, and shall be glad to know what you admire in it. All self-sacrifice is good -- but one would like it to be in a somewhat nobler cause than that of a diabolical law which chains a man soul and body to a putrefying carcase. However the book is interesting -- only I wish the characters would talk a little less like the heroes and heroines of police reports.
Do not curse my pale ink and send me an answer in the style of the Duke of Wellington to Mrs. M. 753
Yours in secula seculorum
Mary Ann.

MS: Yale. Address: Mr. Bray. Hitherto unpublished.

Dear Friend
I'm very glad you can put off your visit, for I want to enjoy it thoroughly. In a fortnight or so, we shall be more at liberty. But you must not just come and look at us and then run away again. Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 31 March 1856
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, I, 394.
Richmond | March 31. 56.
Dear Friend
My mind is more rebellious than yours, and I can't help being saddened by the idea of you and Cara being in any other home than the dear old one. 687 But I know that your cheerful courage is yet stronger in deed than in word.
Will not business or pleasure bring you to London soon, and will you not come to see us? We can give you a bed -- not a sumptuous one, but one which you will perhaps not find intolerable for a night.
I know the trip up the Thames is charming, and we should like to do it with you, but I don't think we can manage it this summer. We are going to send or take the boys 688 to school in Germany at Midsummer, and are at present uncertain about our arrangements. If we can send them, we shall go to the coast as soon as the warm weather comes and remain there for three months. But our plans are not yet crystallized.
I think the joke about the sauce and "cold shoulder" capital -- better than the famous mot "With this sauce, you might eat your grandmother."
Mr. Lewes sent kindest regards the last time I wrote, and I forgot to give them.
Ever yours faithfully
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 31 March [1858]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1858. Extracts published: Cross, II, 17-18.
Richmond | March 31.
Dear Friend
Thanks for your disclaimer. It shows me that you take a right view of the subject, and I feel sure that Sara too will on reflection see it in the same light. There is no undertaking more fruitful of absurd mistakes than that of "guessing" at authorship, and as I have never communicated to any one so much as an intention of a literary kind, there can be none but imaginary data for such guesses.
What these random shots of conjecture are worth, may be seen from Dr. Hodgson's success in this way. I have not read Guy Livingstone, 1106 but from the reviews I have seen, I imagine Mr. Lewes would be anything but gratified to have it fathered upon him.
If I withhold anything from my friends which it would gratify them to know you will believe, I hope, that I have good reasons for doing so, and I am sure those friends will understand me when I ask them to further my object -- which is not a whim but a question of solid interest -- by complete silence.
I can't afford to indulge either in vanity or sentimentality about my work. I have only a trembling anxiety to do what is in itself worth doing and by that honest means, to win very necessary profit of a temporal kind.
"There is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed" 1107 -- in due time. But till that time comes -- till I tell you myself "This is the work of my hand and brain" -- don't believe anything on the subject. There is no one who is in the least likely to know what I can, could, should or would write.
It would have been a great pleasure to me to see you all, but you perceive it was impossible. Goodbye, and love to all from
Yours ever affectionately
Marian Lewes.
I should have thought it might have been seen that Mr. Lewes is hardly in a vein for novel-writing. He is now engaged on a series of physiological papers for Blackwood, which are to be published separately as the "Physiology of Common Life."

GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 30 October 1857
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 467-468.
Richmond | October 30. 57.
Dear Friend
Thank you for sending me your pamphlet, 998 which I have read with much interest. It brings forward some important points for the consideration of our reformers. The picture you give of the results of female labour in factories is sad enough. How is it that the results have been so different at Lowell?
That passage you quote from Mrs. Bodichon's book about "doing small things badly" is mine. 999 She did me the honor to copy it from a letter I wrote to her, and that word -- "Conscience goes to the hammering in of nails" is my Gospel. There can be no harm in preaching that to women, at any rate. But I should be sorry to undertake any more specific enunciation of doctrine on a question so entangled as the "Woman Question." The part of the Epicurean gods is always an easy one; but because I prefer it so strongly myself, I the more highly venerate those who are struggling in the thick of the contest.
"La carri'e8re ouverte aux talen[t]s," 1000 whether the talents be feminine or masculine, I am quite confident is a right maxim. Whether "La carri'e8re ouverte 'e0 la sottise," be equally just, when made equally universal, it would be too much like [taking sides] for me to say.
Ever your affectionate Friend
Marian Lewes.
Charles Bray Esq.

GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 26 March [1856]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1856. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 393.
Park Shot | Richmond | March 26.
Dear Friend
It seems a long, long time since I heard from you, except indirectly, and though I have no other reason to urge for your writing me a few lines, I hope you will not think it a bad one, that you will be giving me a great pleasure. I want to know something more than a vague report of how things fare with you, for there is always a corner -- perhaps more than a corner -- of memory for Rosehill in my mind, and your joys and sorrows are always mine when you let me know them.
We are flourishing in every way, except in health. Mr. Lewes's head is still infirm, but he manages nevertheless to do twice as much work as other people. We feel very thankful for this degree of health, especially when we think of poor Herbert Spencer, who is still, from a complaint like Mr. Lewes's, unable even to read more than a quarter of an hour together. 683 I am always a croaker you know, but my ailments are of a small kind -- their chief symptom being a muddled brain, and as my pen is not of the true literary order which will run along without the help of brains, I don't get through so much work as I should like.
By the way, when Spinoza comes out, be so good as not to mention my name in connection with it. I particularly wish not to be known as the translator of the Ethics, for reasons which it would be "too tedious to mention."
Do write me a note, and tell me as many particulars about business as you can. You don't know what a severely practical person I am become, and what a sharp eye I have to the main chance. I keep the purse and dole out sovereigns with all the pangs of a miser. In fact, if you were to feel my acquisitiveness, I dare say you would find it in a state of inflammation, like the Veneration of that clergyman to whom Mr. Donovan said, "Sir, you have recently been engaged in prayer." 684
Have you heard that the Spectator newspaper is for sale? The circulation must have been going down of late, for Mr. Rintoul 685 has been doing that most injudicious thing for an old newspaper -- advertizing it and telling why the price can't be reduced.
I hope you recognized your own wit about the one-eyed dissenters, which was quoted in the Leader some time ago. 686 You always said, no one did so much justice to your jokes as I did. Best love to Cara and Sara.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 25 March [1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 25 March [1858]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Richmond | March 25.
Dear Friend
We send Buckle today -- glad to be able to make it useful to a friend. Never mind about stamps -- those things balance themselves in the long run. I am unable to pay for parcels by the railway, because there are two different lines between us.
Criticisms are never futile, so pray make them whenever they occur. But as to the celandines and dog violets I believe that, so far as my testimony is worth anything, I can vindicate Mr. Lewes's juxtaposition of them. 1099 About Ilfracombe I have no distinct image of those flowers -- I don't know whether he places them at Ilfracombe -- but at Scilly I distinctly remember noticing the fact that they were in blossom together. I have busied myself a good deal the last two years with Calendars of Natural History, and I find it quite futile to argue from one part of England to another as to the times of the phenomena in plants and animals.
I am so glad to see that pleasant word "I am as happy as it is possible." I'm sure it makes me the happier that you are so.
Ever your affectionate friend,
Marian.
Tell Cara I shall write to her shortly. Mr. and Mrs. Call are coming to see us shortly.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 25 December [1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 25 December [1858]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1858. Extract published: Cross, II, 73.
Park Shot | Christmas Day.
Dear Friend
The well-flavoured Molluscs came this morning. It was very kind of you, and if you remember how fond I am of oysters your good nature will have the more pleasure in furnishing my gourmandise with the treat. I have a childish delight in any little act of genuine friendliness towards us -- and yet not childish, for how little we thought of people's goodness towards us when we were children. It takes a good deal of experience to tell one the rarity of a thoroughly disinterested kindness.
Mr. Lewes is not quite so capable of appreciating oysters as I am, being a miserably moderate eater, unequal to the sublime excesses of a genius like me. In compensation, he will dissect a few.
He sends his kind regards to you, and will be as much interested as I shall be in knowing about the vicissitudes of Coventry journalism, 1249 when any new phase or crisis comes of which you can tell us. He is an old soldier, and cares for battles of that sort.
You understand that what I said about the Continent had reference only to a prolonged residence there -- a residence of five or six months; and would not apply to a visit of a month or two. One can rough it with enjoyment for a short time, but the pleasure of change is inherently short lived.
I hope you are all substantially happy this Christmas: the merriment perhaps will be chiefly of the sympathetic sort -- looking on at the fun of the young ones, or helping to create it.
Tell Sara I am glad to think that she is pleasantly absorbed, and am content with her silence under such circumstances. Love to her and Cara. Kind remembrances, too, to Mrs. John Cash, when it occurs to you to mention me in her company. Tell her, an Oxford clergyman who lately paid us a visit -- bringing a philosophic admiration of Mr. Lewes and, of course, MSS. of his own to be admired if possible -- spoke of Hegel's Philosophy of History as being read by himself and many other Oxford clergymen or students. I was not so rude as to ask him whether he read it in Mr. Sibree's translation, 1250 but as I gathered that he knew no German, I thought the symptoms justified such a conclusion. I dare say the majority of said readers prefer the [well of English undefiled] 1251 to the [puddle of German unclarified] as decidedly as Mr. A. is likely to have done; so that we may safely infer Mr. John Sibree's labours as a translator to have been acceptable at Oxford and elsewhere. Worth telling him perhaps this Christmas time, if he is paying family visits at Coventry?
All prosperity of soul and body attend you on this and every other day in the calendar. That, dear friend, is the sincere wish of
Yours affectionately
Marian Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 23 December 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 23 December 1857
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | December 23. 57.
Dear Friend
Thank you for sending me your pamphlet on the Currency. I have read your letter on the subject in the Leader, 1041 and so far as I am capable of judging, your views are the "sound" ones. But it has often appeared to me -- and your letter is, I think, open to a similar criticism -- that the opponents of the [gold-standard] do not make it sufficiently clear to their readers that they presuppose, as a necessity, some guarantee such as government security, as a basis for confidence; so that the holder of a bag of cowries for example, where cowries are the circulating medium, should not be liable, some fine morning, to discover that his cowries will purchase him nothing. That contingency, so far as I am able to see, is the one stronghold of those who maintain that the circulating medium should have an intrinsic value, and therefore all the emphasis of argument and illustration should storm them at that point. But whether I am talking "sanity or insanity," as Carlyle says of himself, 1042 is a perfectly equal chance, on a subject of which I know so little.
I heartily respond to your good wishes for Christmas and the New Year. I find there is nothing so heart-warming as happiness when it comes to those who have known what it is to suffer. But the human being can hardly be educated, at present, without the two. I'm sorry to hear from Sara that you have been having a little too much of the suffering lately, in the way of toothache and other bodily evils.
We should like to lend you "Buckle" ourselves very much, but I am sorry to say that Mr. Lewes is needing it for reference on some subjects on which he is engaged. But we shall be going to Germany early in the Spring, and by that time I have no doubt he will have done with it and will be able to leave it for you to read at your leisure, if you cannot obtain it before then. It is a book full of suggestive material, though there are some strangely unphilosophic opinions mixed with its hardy philosophy. For example, he holds that there is no such thing as race or hereditary transmission of qualities! I should tell you, at the same time, that he is a necessitarian, and a physiological-psychologist. It is only by such negations as these that he can find his way to the position, which he maintains at great length, that the progress of mankind is dependent entirely on the progress of knowledge, and that there has been no intrinsically-moral advance. However, he presents that side of the subject which has perhaps been least adequately dwelt on.
Mr. Lewes unites with me in kind regards, and I am always
Your affectionate Friend
Marian Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 21 November 1855
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 21 November 1855
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1855. Mostly published: Cross, I, 387-388.
Park Shot | Richmond | November 21. 55.
Dear Friend
You will receive by rail tomorrow a copy of the "Life and Works of Goethe" 643 which I hope you will accept as a keepsake from me. I should have been glad to send it you earlier, but as Mr. Lewes has sold the copyright of the 1st edition, he has only a small number of copies at his disposal and so I doubted whether I ought to ask for one. I think you will find much to interest you in the book. I can't tell you how I value it, as the best product of a mind which I have every day more reason to admire and love.
We have had much gratification in the expressions of individual opinion. The press is very favourable, but the notices are for the most part too idiotic to give us much pleasure, except in a pecuniary point of view.
Tell Sara we have not yet heard from H. Spencer, and can't think what has become of him.
How is business going on? And how are the colds? We have been doing our share of sniffing and coughing lately. I am going out today -- for the first time for nearly a fortnight. 644 With love to all,
Ever yours affectionately
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 2 December [1855]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 2 December [1855]
MS: Coventry City Libraries.
Richmond | December 2.
Dear Friend
I have just read your kind letter and write now, while I think of it, to ask you to give my kind regards to Mr. Noel 269 and say that if ever his excursions bring him near us again, I shall be very glad to see him.
You know that you will be always welcome, and we have such comfortable lodgings and such a charming cook, that I can put you in clover.
I don't think my sister is in any anxiety about me, since we often write to each other, and I am going to see her at Christmas.
Mr. Lewes sends his kind regards. We are both flourishing.
I have just been spilling my ink, and am in a quandary -- writing this in the interval of hindrance, while the damage is being remedied.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 15 November 1857
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 15 November 1857
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 471-474.
Park Shot | November 15. 57.
Dear Friend
It is pleasant to have a kind word now and then when one is not near enough to have a kind glance or a hearty shake by the hand. It is an old weakness of mine to have no faith in affection that does not express itself, and when friends take no notice of me for a long while I generally settle down into the belief that they have become indifferent or have begun to dislike me. That is not the best mental constitution; but it might be worse, for I don't feel obliged to dislike them in consequence. I, for one, ought not to complain if people think worse of me than I deserve, for I have very often reason to be ashamed of my thoughts about others. They almost always turn out to be better than I expected -- fuller of kindness towards me, at least.
I don't make out quite clearly what is the point on which you ask my opinion -- whether it is the desirability of republishing the Phil[osophy] of Necessity, or the degree in which I share its doctrines. To any one who is not bound to consider authorship from the pecuniary point of view, the question about republication is not -- [Will the book find a large public?] but [Will it find any public?] Your book has found a public, since the first edition sold at last, though slowly, and you have had indications that the book has been thought valuable by some earnest readers. I should not think a second edition would find a different kind of public, but it would very likely enlarge your circle of readers, especially if it were cheap. But that is an expensive mode of doing good. 1011
In the fundamental doctrine of your book -- that mind presents itself under the same condition of invariableness of antecedent and consequent as all other phenomena (the only difference being that the true antecedent and consequent are proportionately difficult to discover as the phenomena are more complex) -- I think you know that I agree. And every one who knows what science means must also agree with you that there can be no Social Science without the admission of that doctrine. As to the more detailed contents of the book, I have not any longer a vivid recollection of them, but I think it is very likely that I should be unable to agree with much that you say in relation to the religious ideas and the moral tendencies. For I dislike extremely a passage quoted by Sara 1012 in which you appear to consider the disregard of individuals as a lofty condition of mind. My own experience and development deepen every day my conviction that our moral progress may be measured by the degree in which we sympathize with individual suffering and individual joy. The fact that in the scheme of things we see a constant and tremendous sacrifice of individuals is, it seems to me only one of the many proofs that urge upon us our total inability to find in our own natures a key to the Divine Mystery. I could more readily turn Christian and worship Jesus again than embrace a Theism which professes to explain the proceedings of God. But I don't feel at all wise on these matters. I have a few strong impressions which serve me for my own support and guidance but do not in the least qualify me to speak as a theorist.
Mr. Lewes sends you his kind remembrances and will not like you any the worse for cutting him up. 1013 He has had to perform that office for his own friends sometimes. I suppose Phrenology is an open question, on which everybody has a right to speak his mind. Mr. Lewes, feeling the importance of the subject, desired to give it its due place in his History of Philosophy, and doing so, he must of course say what he believes to be the truth not what other people believe to be the truth. If you will shew where he is mistaken, you will be doing him a service, as well as phrenology. His arguments may be bad, but I will answer for him that he has not been guilty of any intentional unfairness. I dare-say I expressed myself very ill in my letter to Sara, for I had a bad headache then, and may have written nonsense, for what I know. But in anything I said about sectarianism I meant no [fling] at you, though I cannot except you from my general experience of phrenologists. With regard to their system, they seem to me to be animated by the same sort of spirit as that of religious dogmatists and especially in this -- that in proportion as a man approximates to their opinions without identifying himself with them, they think him obnoxious and contemptible.
It is amusing to read, from the opposite side, complaints against Mr. Lewes for giving too high a position to phrenology, and a confident opinion that "phrenologists, by their ridiculous pretensions, merit all the contempt that has been thrown on them." Thus doctors differ!
But I am much less interested in crusades for or against phrenology than in your happiness at Ivy Cottage. Happiness means all sorts of love and good feeling, and that is the best result that can ever come out of science.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian Lewes.
Do you know Buckle's History of Civilization? 1014 I think you would find it a suggestive book.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 13 October [1858]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 13 October [1858]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1858. Hitherto unpublished.
Richmond | October 13.
Dear Friend
We had not thought of the stamps, but so far as I know, Sara is right in thinking they had not been sent. However, as there is no arriving at certainty on the subject, pray do not be so uncomfortably scrupulous about the next parcel we send, but let us pay for it without receiving stamps in return. Ten to one we forget to pay you in that way, and it would be better to leave such debts to adjust themselves.
It will be very pleasant if business brings you within reach of us. Do come, and if possible, let us know the day beforehand, that we may not be out of the house when you come. We will not live in community, but of course, like all enthusiastic friends, give you our [best wishes.] Come, and tell us about the penny paper, and let us know better how things fare with you.
Tell Sara, the charming article on Travel 1205 is Harriet Martineau's, but the exchange of cheque and receipt is understood to be the last communication between her and the editor. A pity for the Review, I think.
Mr. Lewes sends kind regards, and we are both glad you find the Biog[raphical] History of Philosophy a useful text-book. He is extremely happy in his work just now -- is dissecting every animal he can get in furtherance of his investigation into the nervous system, 'e0 propos of which a paper of his was read at the British Association. But I suppose I am making him a "more definite object of contempt" by telling you this -- as Helps says of the builders of the Pyramids.
Ever your affectionate friend
Marian Lewes.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 1 September [1856]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 1 September [1856]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | September 1.
Dear Friend
I have this minute laid down Sara's kind letter -- which distresses me, however, for it tells me that she has been suffering much discomfort of body -- and your postscript, which rather vexes me. I will tell you why. Last Monday Mr. Lewes started with the boys to Hofwyl, and I expect him home tomorrow or Wednesday. 740 I had counted on this space of solitary time to get an article written which I had promised to let Mr. Chapman have for his next number. 741 But lo! on Tuesday came seven large devils of toothache in place of one little devil that had been teazing me now and then, and from Tuesday till Saturday I was nothing but a frightful energumen. 742 The doctor came and said it was neuralgia, and dosed me with quinine. That didn't do so we sent for the dentist, who decided that it was simply my good-for-nothing wisdom tooth. So I was chloroformed twice, and at last -- on Saturday evening -- the tooth was got out.
I had written to Mr. Chapman begging him to let me off and get a substitute, but he cruelly wrote back that he must have the article. So here am I on this blessed 1st of September, with this odious article to write in a hurry and with Mr. Lewes coming home to reduce my writing time to the minimum. That is why I am vexed you are coming on the 6th, for we MUST see you, if everything else goes wrong. Send me word exactly when you shall be here. Love and thanks to Sara. I will write to her another day. I am not yet well, and unable to begin my work. If it were not for the work I should be in excellent spirits at the idea of having got through this nasty business of chloroform and forceps while Mr. Lewes is away. Excuse incoherence.
Ever yours
Marian.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 1 January 1856
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, 1 January 1856
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Marian's letters 1856. Hitherto unpublished.
Park Shot | Richmond | January 1. 56.
Dear Friend
A happy New Year to you and yours!
I have never answered your note in which you invited me to call at your house on my way to my sister's. I am sure that note was written with the kindest intentions, but if you had thought twice you would have seen that I was not likely to take a journey twice as long as necessary and walk all through Coventry in order to make a call where I had only the invitation of the master of the house. I went straight from London to Nuneaton by express in two hours and a half, and returned in the same way. In this season one likes to abridge railway journeying as much as possible.
You will be glad to hear that I found my sister and her children very well and comfortable. She mentioned your kindness in sending her a newspaper. I, as well as she, am obliged to you. While I have been away Mr. Lewes has I hope been getting a great deal of good from a visit to his friend Mr. Helps at his pleasant place in Hampshire. 655 He returns to me on Friday or Saturday. Meanwhile I am trying to fill up the gap his absence makes by being as industrious as possible. 656
I hope you have enjoyed your Christmas and are beginning the year with pleasant prospects. With kind remembrances to all, visitors 657 included, I am
Always yours affectionately
Marian E.

MS: Yale. Addressed: Mr. Bray. Endorsed: 1856. Hitherto unpublished.
Dear Friend
I am so glad to see you can make use of anything I have done. And thank you for letting me know it.
I don't know quite the bearing of your remark on Mr. Lewes's citation of "Love your enemies" etc. but certainly to call that an axiom was a slip of the pen. Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, [15 October 1855]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, Richmond, [15 October 1855]
MS: Yale. Mostly published: Cross, I, 386.
Richmond | Monday.
Dear Friend
Since you have found out the "Cumming," 632 I write by to-day's post just to say, that it is mine, but also to beg that you will not mention it as such to any one likely to transmit the information to London, as we are keeping the authorship a secret. The article appears to have produced a strong impression, and that impression would be a little counteracted if the author were known to be a woman. [Six words deleted.] I have had a letter addressed to "the author of article No. 4." begging me to print it separately for "the good of mankind in general." It is so kind of you to rejoice in anything I do at all well.
Tell Cara I am very pleased to have her nice long letter, which I shall answer another day, when I have more time. I am dreadfully busy again, for I am going to write an article for the W. R. 633 again, besides my other work. We enjoy our new lodgings very much -- everything is the pink of order and cleanliness.
I am grieved to hear of Cara's cold -- I know how terrible her colds are. Mr. Lewes is pretty well -- but his head is still infirm. All other news to Sara another day.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian.

Richmond | Tuesday.
Dear Friend
After I wrote you yesterday morning, we had a letter from Germany which has made Mr. Lewes incline to defer sending the boys thither till next year. Yours faithfully
Marian.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, 6 OCTOBER [1851]
MS: Benjamin Collection, Columbia. Hitherto unpublished.
Strand | October 6.
Dear Friend,
I don't advise you to come to see Frederika Bremer -- she is old -- extremely ugly, and deformed -- I should think she is nearly sixty. 1015 Her eyes are sore -- her teeth horrid. I tell you this, not because I have no veneration for the earthen vessel of such an inspiration as hers, but because I think a pilgrimage to see her would end in disappointment. I have not been introduced to her yet, having been out of the way. Yesterday I dined at Mr. Ellis's at Champion Hill. 1016 Mrs. Ellis delightful -- Sharon Turner's daughter, you know -- Mr. very good, but a bore. Mrs. E. and her son and daughter are going to see George Combe.
I shan't tell you how I cried about you all the other night and how I have felt like an [orfling] ever since you were gone. 1017 But every one is very kind and attentive to me and my only real lasting trouble is my own emptiness. Thank Cara for the parcel and note -- eke Sara. Who is J.N.W.J.? who sends me respectful comp[limen]ts.
I think Hickson's article very poor in argument. There is throughout the article 1018 a miserable confusion of the universal with the particular -- see first in the 3d page where [he] speaks of the worn out machine, the motive power remaining -- and the conclusion too, which he puts in large type -- Blanco White's sonnet 1019 is better than all the rest -- indeed as Dr. Hodgson says, the subject is better dealt with in poetry than in prose. In haste -- ever
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, 6 February [1854]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 320.
Cambridge Street | February 6.
Dear Friend
In the last number of the Scotsman which I send you, there was a report of a speech by Dr. Guthrie at the Education Meeting, containing a passage which I meant to have copied. He is speaking of the impossibility of teaching morality with the "Bible shut" and says that in that case the teacher would be obliged to resort to "congruity and the fitness of things," about which the boy knows nothing more than that the apple is fit for his mouth. What is wanted to convince the boy of his sin is "Thou, God, seest me" and "Thou bleeding Lamb, the best morality is love of thee"!! This is too good to be lost. I want it to go into the Leader, 434 and I write to beg of you -- I know it is troublesome, but, as Mr. Chapman says, "the cause demands it not I" -- to send me this passage either cut out of the paper or copied.
Tell Cara she is pronounced to be quite wrong about Miss Martineau's rendering of Comte. Herbert Spencer, who never praises but upon compulsion and who has no knowledge of the original to help him, 435 says that it appears to him perfectly lucid, and that the difficulty lies in the matter, not in the form.
Mr. Lewes came a few minutes after you left, and desired me to tell you that he was sorry to miss you. With love to Cara,
Ever yours affectionately
Marian Evans.

434 Thomas Guthrie (1803-73), Scottish  preacher and leader in the Free Church secession of 1843, was known for his work in establishing the Ragged Schools of Edinburgh; but insistence on his right to teach the whole Bible to all the scholars led to the withdrawals of some of his supporters. He and other opponents of purely secular education are ridiculed in the article heading the "Literature" section of the Leader, 18 February 1854, p. 163. Though apparently written by GHL, the article is of interest as an early example of GE's collaboration.

He protested against being considered an adherent of Comte both in "The Genesis of Science," British Quarterly Review, 20 (July 1854), 108-162, and in The Classification of the Sciences, a pamphlet published in 1864; the latter was the cause of a brief coolness between Spencer and GHL.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, 4 December 1880
MS: Coventry and Warwickshire Collection, Coventry City Libraries. Envelope: Charles Bray Esq. | 3 Barrs Hill Terrace | Coventry. Postmark: CHELSEA S.W | 4 | DE 4 | 80. Endorsed: Dec. 5th. The last. 1880. Hitherto unpublished.
Cheyne Walk, | Chelsea, S.W.
November 497 4. 1880.
Dear Mr. Bray
Most certainly you shall have the remaining two volumes of [Problems.] I had not failed to think of you in connection with them, but I was not at all sure that you would like to have them, and in such cases questions defeat their proposed end. But will you excuse a delay of a few days in your getting them from the Publisher? For I am overwhelmed with details just now. We only got into this house to dinner yesterday evening, and notwithstanding the much that is done, chaos still prevails behind the surface. This morning I find myself with the usual penance on my hands for neglecting letters -- the feeling of hurry in making up for the neglect.
As to your other request, Mr. Cross has no photograph of himself. But I think you would be satisfied with his coronal arch which finishes a figure six feet high. If his head does not indicate fine moral qualities, it must be phrenology that is in fault. He is exceedingly acute, accustomed to deal with men in matters where their characters are inevitably betrayed, well aware of all our human humbug but charitable towards it withal as a quality or manifestation in which we have everyone of us some brother -- or -- sisterhood. All this is more than you would learn from a carte de visite of the photographic kind, even if he could give it you.
I suppose we may consider 70 -- not the normal length of human life according to the mistaken view of the Psalmist 498 but -- a comparatively youthful epoch, since we have our Prime Minister on the one hand doing more work than he is obliged to do, and Dean Close on the other marrying at 84. 499
I am writing to Sara this morning.
Yours very sincerely
M. A. Cross.

GE to Charles Bray, London, 3 November [1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1853. Extract published: Cross, I, 317.
Cambridge Street | November 3.
Dear Friend
Eh bien! I will welcome the Bookcase. Please to add to your other goodness that of letting me know when it will arrive, as the impenetrability of matter positively forbids my having two Bookcases in my room at once. Poor Mr. Chapman has just left me, looking fagged to death from having, as a bit of extra work yesterday, run along the Strand after a thief who had managed to get into the house and out of it with £8 worth of plate! 387
Hitherto I have been spending £9 per month -- at least after that rate -- but I have had frequent guests. I am exceedingly comfortable and feel quite at home now. Harriet Martineau has been very kind -- called again on Tuesday, and yesterday sent to invite me to go to Lady Compton's, 388 where she is staying, on Saturday evening. This, too, in spite of my having vexed her by introducing Mr. Lewes to her, which I did as a desirable bit of peacemaking. 389
Pray let me know of any opening in the clouds. Love to Cara and Sara.
Yours affectionately
Marian Evans.

387 The Leader, 12 November 1853, p.  1087, gives the following account: "An impudent thief, who gave the name of Henry Devine, but withheld his address and occupation `out of regard for his family,' was brought up at Bow-street on Saturday, charged with stealing a quantity of plate from Mr. J. Chapman, the bookseller, 142, Strand. About two o'clock one day the housemaid saw the prisoner coolly walk down from the drawing-room, and out into the street; she called out to her master, who at once set off after him. The prisoner ran off at full speed, but Mr. Chapman, attracted by the glitter of his own plate, with which the thief in his flight was now strewing the street, ran faster after him, and eventually tripped him up on his face on the pavement. On appearing before the magistrate, prisoner said, with the greatest effrontery, he `merely took the plate to enable him to raise money sufficient to go to Australia, and intended to reimburse Mr. Chapman when he got to the gold diggings.' He considered he had been very badly used by Mr. Chapman, who, instead of offering him a glass of ale after his fall, had seized him by the throat, and nearly choked him. He considered `such conduct anything but gentlemanly, but was willing to forget and forgive, if Mr. Chapman on his part would do the same.' Mr. Henry committed him for trial."
388 At 3 Leinster Terrace, Bayswater.
389 GHL won Miss Martineau's dislike  in 1851 by two devastating reviews of her Letters on the Laws of Man's Nature and Development (Leader, 22 February 1851, p. 178, and 8 March, p. 227). A few weeks later the Leader printed without comment an absurd extract from the book headed "Experiences of a Deaf Person," which began: "I fainted one day from having, in a freak, put a musical snuffbox on my head." (5 April 1851, p. 326.) Her enmity was intensified by rivalry over Comte. GHL's papers in the Leader in 1852 were expanded and published in September 1853 as Comte's Philosophy of the Sciences: Being an Exposition of the Principles of the Cours de Philosophie Positive of Auguste Comte in Bohn's Scientific Library, 1853. Miss Martineau's abridged translation, The Positive Philosophy of Auguste Comte in Chapman's Quarterly Series, announced as "nearly ready" 24 September, did not appear until 19 November. The review in the Leader, 3 December 1853, pp. 1171-1172, has none of GHL's sparkle, but is more reminiscent of GE's style in the Analytical Catalogue of Mr. Chapman's Publications. Her peacemaking was not successful.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, London, 29 December 1862
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, 29 December 1862
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1862. Extract published: Cross, II, 347-348.
Blandford Sq. | December 29. 62.
Dear Friend
I obey your instructions literally, and send a pound, but another is ready whenever you will tell me to send it. I have been fearing that Coventry would be minus of help, from the concentration of effort in Lancashire. 129
Poor "Lizzie"! I am disappointed with that clause "no wittles" -- I had hoped she was well off.
I am not quite sure what you mean by "charity" when you call it humbug. If you mean that attitude of mind which says "I forgive my fellow-men for not being so good as I am," I agree with you in hoping that it will vanish, as also the circumstantial form of almsgiving. But if you are alluding to anything in my letter to Sara, I meant there what charity meant in the elder English and what the translators of the Bible meant in their rendering of the XIIIth chapter of I Corinthians -- Caritas, the highest love or fellowship, which I am happy to believe that no philosophy will expel from the world.
My health has mended since I grumbled to Sara, and so has Mr. Lewes's. Cara's sign manual was very welcome at the end of your letter. I hope her geographical labours are nearly over.
Ever yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.
C. Bray Esq.

MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1861. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Square, | N.W.
August 21. 61.
Dear Friend
Mrs. Bodichon is away, visiting her sister in Wales, but she will be at home again in a few days and I will tell her about the important subject of your letter. I know nothing could interest her more, in the way of public effort, than an Industrial Girls School, and if she has any special hints to give, you may be sure of having them. Yours ever
M. E. Lewes.
C. Bray Esq.

The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 19. 68.
My dear Mr. Bray
I am moved to congratulate you on writing against the Ballot, with such admirably good sense -- having just read your "slip" at the break-fast table.
It has been a source of amazement to me that men acquainted with practical life, can believe in the suppression of Bribery by the Ballot, as if Bribery in all its Protean forms could ever disappear by means of a single external arrangement! Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, 17 April [1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1852. Extract published: Cross, 1, 275.
Strand | April 17.
Dear Friend
I send you your share of Geo. Combe's missive. Mine contains a sequel to the mesmeric case which is very interesting and which I will send you when I have done with it.
A very kind letter is come from James Martineau this morning. shewing his thorough willingness to write for us, and his appreciation of the subject proposed to him, but one of his daughters is seriously ill and he cannot pledge himself to prepare anything by July. 53
There was an article on the Bookselling affair in the Times of yesterday 54 which must be the knell of the Association. Dickens is to preside at a meeting in this house on the subject some day next week. Mr.
Chapman called on him yesterday with Bentley, 55 and found him very straight-forward and agreeable. Splendid library, of course, with soft carpet, couches etc. such as become a sympathizer with the suffering classes. How can we sufficiently pity the needy unless we know fully the blessings of plenty?
I am longing for the arrival of my wardrobe, for my clothes are all helter-skelter. Pray keep an account of all the expenses, Mr. Simms 56 and the carpenters etc.
The one source of my low spirits was the parting with you in the midst of such bad news about everything, and the thought I can do nothing but cry when sorrows come. However, I came home and went to sleep from sheer want of spirit to do anything else, and Providence in an hour or two took pity on me and sent Herbert Spencer to ask me to go to the Lyceum and see [The Chain of Events.] 57 It is a very long chain and drags rather heavily. No sparkle, but a sort of Dickens-like sentimentality all through -- in short, I think it might please you. As a series of tableaux I never saw anything equal to it. But to my mind it is execrable moral taste to have a storm and shipwreck with all its horrors on the stage. I could only scream and cover my eyes. It was revolting to hear the cheers and clapping of the audience. But perhaps all that was pure philosophy, and they were so thoroughly imbued with your beloved optimism 58 that they felt more than ever reconciled to the scheme of things.
I am sorry to have lost these few days with you, but not sorry to have come, for there are various things to be done which I am more satisfied to have the doing of.
Of course this letter is for all. My blessings on you all.
Your affectionate
Marian.
The opinions on the various articles in the Review are, as before, ridiculously various. The Economist calls the article on Quakerism "admirably written." Greg says the article on India is "very masterly": while he calls Mazzini's "sad stuff" -- "mere verbiage." 59

GE to Charles Bray, London, 16 February [1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Feb. 16. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 271-272.
Dear Friend
I have not merely had a headache -- I have been really ill, and feel very much shattered. I must tell you this to account for my not writing on Saturday after your dear letter which came to comfort me in bed.
I am a hideous hag now, but if I don't get up some better looks before next Tuesday week, seeing you will at least make me look brighter. Do come on Monday and be with us in the evening. Why not? as Bunsby says. 30 I want to introduce you to somebody. 31
Sara is the dearest creature, ready to find pleasure in the smallest things, else she would have had little pleasure in this visit. We dined yesterday at Mr. Peter Taylor's, 32 at Sydenham. I was not fit to go, especially to make my d'e9but at a strange place, but the country air was a temptation. Sara seemed to like it. This morning she is sitting quietly by my fire reading Social Statics with many interjections. Miss Parkes is very pretty in her attentions, called yesterday to see how I was and looked affectionately at me.
I was quite interested in Cara's letter -- the description of the Stratford visit 33 etc., but I think it is very healthy for you to be alone a little while, much as I should enjoy breaking your solitude. The thick of the work is just beginning and I am bound in honour not to run away from it, as I have shirked all labour but what is strictly editorial this quarter. But we will talk of this when you come.
I wish I could hear some better news about business -- do remember what God made man for. 34 I had a long letter from Geo. Combe the other day in which he too inquires about Thornton Hunt and asks me if possible to remove him from "the category of the reckless." 35
Much love to Cara and you from your ever affectionate
Marian.
Strand | February 16th.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, London, 16 April [1863]
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, 16 April [1863]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | April 16. 62. 149
Dear Friend
I had seen Mr. Trollope's letter in the Athenaeum. 150 Any statement of his on that question is interesting and valuable, since it is the statement of a man whose nature is of quite remarkable simplicity and integrity. But one of the most striking facts about his evidence to us has been, that in our repeated conversations with him on the subject he -- being too sober-minded to "see double" and to[o] honest to wish to astonish his hearers by what is not true -- never tells anything of which no ordinary explanation is conceivable. The "higher phenomena" have been seen, as he hears, by his acquaintances, but for his part, he has only seen etc. etc. His deep interest in the subject arises from the confirmation it appears to him to bring to his yearning belief in a future life, and therefore in his theory of the manifestations, he keeps constantly before him the idea that the hidden cause is the action of departed spirits. He is not in the least a credulous man, but his mind is strongly swayed by moral beliefs. He is a Free-thinker with an ardent spirit of reform. His brother Mr. Anthony Trollope, on the other hand, is a Church of England man, clinging to whatever is, on the whole, and without fine distinctions, honest, lovely and of good report. I mention these points, although you may know them, lest, not knowing them, you should fall into some confusion of personalities and opinions.
We happen to have made arrangements for taking a short flight next week. On Saturday, if I am well enough -- if not, on Monday -- Mr. Lewes will take me to Dorking, and on his return to town will start for Hofwyl to see our third youngster and arrange about the time of his (Bertie's) return home. In the meanwhile, the servants will clean the house, and Charlie will tinkle on his piano with a chorus of scrubbing brushes and pails. If there were not matters of business which oblige us to make this plan absolute, I should wish to defer it for the sake of seeing Cara, who is as rare as a black swan, before inconvenient modern discoveries robbed us of that figure. With love to her and Sara
Always yours truly
M. E. Lewes.
Please to thank Sara for her last letter to me. I take her at her word by not writing -- knowing that she is one of the people who mean what they say.

GE to Charles Bray, London, 15 March 1854
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge St. | March 15. 1854.
Dear Friend
I shall be delighted to see you next Tuesday in all the copiousness of your "flesh." I am even for once glad to hear of the said copiousness, because I have noticed that anxiety makes you thin, and if you are not so, I hope I may take that as a proof that business is not desperate.
I thought it right to let you know the worst side of Gerald Massey, for his sake as well as yours, for Atheneums and Savage Landors can only lead him to perdition. 449 Otherwise I should be sorry to expose a "fellow-sinner."
Best love to Cara. In haste,
Your affectionate
Marian Evans.

Dublin Core:Relation: 449 William Hepworth Dixon praised  Massey extravagantly in the Athenaeum, 4 February 1854, p. 139: "In him we have a genuine songster. The faculty divine is there . . . here is another poet." Walter Savage Landor was even more enthusiastic in a letter to the Morning Chronicle, 24 February 1854, p. 8. Cf. the severe notice in the Westminster Review, 61 (April 1854), 627-628, probably by Mrs. Sinnett. The low opinion of Gerald Massey that GE reveals in these letters should dispel the absurd story that he was the original of Felix Holt: "No one indeed can go through the two volumes of Mr. Massey's poems without being struck with what struck George Eliot when, as she made no secret, she drew the portrait of their author in Felix Holt -- the innate nobility of the character impressed on them." Sir Sidney Lee's repetition of the error in his account of Massey in the DNB, Second Supplement (1912), gave it currency.

GE to Charles Bray, London, 15 December 1864
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1864. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
December 15. 64.
My dear Mr. Bray
I think we have given away all available scraps of old clothing to various claimants, but I am very glad to send my mite towards relieving the poor Radford weavers 296 in the shape of a cheque for £1.0.0. I will not fail to give your "scientific doubt" to Mr. Spencer when I next see him. His present address is 88 Kensington Gardens Square W. Of late he has been interesting himself in the fortunes of the Reader, which he thinks important as a journal that takes special note of scientific progress. It (the Reader) has been changing its proprietorship, and the scientific portion is edited by Huxley and Tindal. You read, I dare say, the article on Spiritualism by Tindal in the last number. 297
Mr. Lewes and I are recovering from our dyspeptic miseries. Until the last week I think I was rather the worse invalid of the two, but now I am brisk again. I think I had disordered myself by taking tonics that disturbed the liver -- by trying to be better than Nature meant me to be.
I have seen people much changed by the Banting system. 298 Mr. A. Trollope is thinner by means of it, and is otherwise the better for the self-denial. Best love to Cara and Sara and all sympathetic wishes for Nelly.
Ever yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
April 14. 73.
My dear Mr. Bray
I quite understand the impulse which made it necessary to you to write that little explanation. We must always allow for the unrevised condition of winged words, and I did so in your case.
I think all the king's horses and all the king's men would not draw Mr. Lewes to an expedition beyond the necessary search for a country house 765 which is occupying us just now. We have long been getting hardened in our arrogant habit of going to see nobody, and asking all our friends to take the trouble of coming to see us.
Your departure from town will probably happen before ours (at the end of May), so that there is no danger of my missing the happy promise of seeing Cara? The Sydenham house I trust will soon be let, and then you will both come within easy reach.
Thanks for the prospective gift of your book, 766 which will be one side of an exchange to be completed I hope next November. With best love to Cara
Yours always sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, 13 July [1861]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: 1861. Hitherto unpublished.
Blandford Sq. | July 13.
Dear Friend
Thanks many, from Mr. Lewes and me too, for your kind proposition, but it is not practicable. In the first place, there would be no cure for either of us away from each other, unless the sense of absolute duty made absence endurable. And in the second place, he is too ailing and delicate to find repose in being with people who are unfamiliar to him. He would not be able to use the "four hours" for work: there are few mornings at present on which he is able to write. He has had abundance of change, you know, so that he is not suffering for want of that. He is taking quinine, and I hope he will by and by be himself again. Alas, that "self" is not particularly robust, but I think he has never been so thin and feeble as he is now. Still, there has been some advance in the last few days.
Once again -- thank you. I don't forget how comfortable you and Cara make all your guests, and how you have the art of leaving them without constraint, and yet making them feel that they are attended to.
Ever yours affectionately
M. E. Lewes.

GE to Charles Bray, London, 12 July [1867]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
The Priory, | 21. North Bank, | Regents Park.
July 12.
My dear Mr. Bray
Is it true that your letter was a joke, and that the worthy Mrs. Bray you proposed to bring was really Cara? Mr. Lewes said so, on reading your letter (which I had already answered), and I almost wished he had been as stupid as I was, so that I might have been saved the vexatious disappointment of knowing that I had missed my unexpected chance of seeing Cara with you.
My dulness has an apology in the fact that I answered my letters just before I began my morning's work, and at that time I am always in haste to have done with letters. O dear, O dear, I am unfortunate, and, like many unfortunate people, feel spiteful, almost wishing that you were serious, and guilty of proposing to bring some strange Mrs. Bray to see me.
We returned from Niton on Wednesday. I did not write before lest you should still be away from home.
Always yours sincerely
M. E. Lewes.

GE to Charles Bray, London, 12 January 1854
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | January 12. 1854.
Dear Friend
Mr. Lewes tells me that he has written to you about your contemplated second letter to the Leader. 427
As to the other point, he has heard nothing of it from Thornton Hunt, but, on receiving my letter in which I said that your copy had not been sent to you as usual, he "blew them up at the Office," supposing it to be an irregularity. The functionaries there told him that you were on the Free list and had therefore shared the fate of your compeers. He thinks that Thornton Hunt's delay in answering your letter is probably owing to his wanting to consult Pigott 428 about the matter. He is "very delicate about the paper" -- that is, I suppose, he dislikes interfering in anything that can have a pecuniary bearing.
Herbert Spencer is just come in, and asks me to send his kind regards to you. I think you will be quite touched, as I was, to read the enclosed letter of Mr. Combe's. My love to Cara, and thanks to her and you for all your kindness and indulgence towards my bad habits.
Ever yours affectionately
Marian Evans.

Dublin Core:Title: GE to Charles Bray, London, 1 May 1855
Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, 1 May 1855
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
V. G. Terrace | May 1. 55.
Dear Friend
We go tomorrow to our new home at East Sheen, a charming village close to Richmond Park. If you write to me, please to enclose the letter to G. H. Lewes Esq. | 7 Clarence Row | East Sheen | Richmond | Surrey. When you come to London again, I hope you will pay us a visit, for I think, apart from any regard for me it will be a pleasure to you to see that pretty place, and it is far less trouble to get there than to Bayswater. You have only to jump into the train at the Waterloo Bridge Station and in ten minutes you will be at Mortlake where you must get down. Mortlake, as I daresay you know, is a lovely village on the banks of the Thames, and East Sheen is its twin sister lying close to it. Ask the way to East Sheen and in three minutes you will be at our door. Then you shall have a nice dinner and a nice snooze after it, and then a stroll, along the river or in the Park, such as you can't get at Coventry even by the help of a carriage.
And pray, when I see you again, don't misquote something I said two or three years ago, which something you seem to have converted into a supercilious, impertinent expression of disapprobation on my part. If the discipline of years has taught me anything, it has taught me to be reverent to all good in others and perpetually mindful of my own need of tolerance, and surely few people can have had more opportunity than I have had for knowing the good in you, and still fewer can have put that goodness to an equally severe test.
We are panting to be in the country and resume our old habits of undisturbed companionship and work. Mr. Lewes has been much worse since he returned to town and the other evening he alarmed me terribly by fainting. Imagine that I had never seen any one faint before, and that I thought he was dead! You will be able then to understand my condition for three or four minutes until he returned to consciousness. However we hope that when we are far away from the roar of omnibii (as poor Joseph Hume 588 is accused of calling them) we shall have no more of such attacks.
Mrs. Hennell called on me the other day, very kindly and nobly. I respect her for it. I was so stupified and heated by having sat in-doors writing all day, that she must have carried away anything but a charming image of me, but that was of slight consequence -- it was enough that she did a good action.
Best love to Cara and Sara for whom, of course, I write as well as for you.
Ever your affectionate friend
Marian.
Poor Mr. Chapman seems in an uncomfortable state both physically and mentally.

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, [9 December 1853]
MS: Yale. Hitherto unpublished.
Cambridge Street | Friday Morning.
Dear Friend
If you went to the Haymarket on Wednesday I hope you didn't carry away the impression that that stupid play -- the "Hope of the Family" -- was by Slingsby Lawrence. 416 I confess, the theatre is generally a very dreary amusement to me. The wit is generally threadbare as well as vulgar -- the actors and actresses are neither men and women nor gentlemen and ladies. I mentally resolved last night that it should be a long while before I wasted another evening there.
I rescued the letter I enclose from the flames the other day, thinking it might amuse you all. It shows a phase of human nature of which only editors have the full enjoyment.
The weather is brightening and making life easier.
By the bye, last night two young men -- cattle show comers, I think -- were chatting behind me, and one of them said -- "I remember being at a dinner at Coventry, where one man said in reply to some accusation "I never said you was." "No," answered another fellow, "I'm sure you couldn't possibly have said anything so ungrammatical!" "That is the smartest thing I ever heard in my life," said my narrator.
Ever yours affectionately,
Marian Evans.

Some of his remarks about the man who has what Mrs. Slipslop calls a "fondling" palmed off on him as his son glance at the situation in GHL's own family: "One is always the son of somebody; but, happily, one is not always the father of somebody. GE to Charles Bray, London, [8 OCTOBER 1851]
MS: Yale. Extracts published: Cross, I, 261.
Strand | Wednesday.
Dear Friend
The works on Mills etc. are for Mr. Noel's inspection. If he should not want any of them, you or he can return them when you come to London.
I don't know how long Miss Bremer will stay, but you need not wish to see her. She is to me a repulsive person, equally unprepossessing to eye and ear. I never saw a person of her years who appealed less to my purely instinctive veneration. I have to reflect every time I look at her that she is really Fred[rik]a Bremer.
Fox is to write the article on the Suffrage, 1020 and we are going to try Carlyle for the Peerage, 1021 Ward refusing, on the ground that he thinks the improvement of the physical condition of the people so all-important that he must give all his energies to that. Ward, you know, is the man of the Sewers. 1022 He says "Life is a bad business, but we must make the best of it" -- to which philosophy I say Amen.
Dr. Hodgson is gone, 1023 and all the fun with him. He found in the Minutes of Council on Education the following rhymes, used as copies in one of the schools: God made bees, Bees make honey; God made man, Man makes money;
God made Satan, Satan made sin; God made a place To put Satan in.
Kate Martineau 1024 has just been here. She inquires with great interest about Cara. Love to this last and to Sara. Kind thoughts and wishes to all.
I was introduced to Lewes the other day in Jeff's shop -- a sort of miniature Mirabeau in appearance. 1025
Your
Marian.

Cambridge St. | Hyde Park | Saturday.
Dear Friend
I have made arrangements to replace my present Bookcase by a Library Table and Desk, so the sooner the other comes, the better. Will you when you write, remember to send me the address of the London agent for the Fire-lighters?
I think you would find some capital extracts for the Herald in the article on Church Parties in the Edinburgh. The Record is attempting a reply to it -- in which it talks of the "truculent infidelity of Voltaire and Robespierre!" Has Robert Cox sent you his book on the Sabbath? 390 If ever I write a book I will make a present of it to nobody -- it is the surest way of taking off the edge of appetite for it, if no more.
I am as well as possible -- and certainly when I put my head into the house in the Strand I feel that I have gained, or rather escaped, a great deal physically by my change.
Love to Cara and Sara. I have no news this morning.
Yours affectionately
Marian Evans.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, [30 March 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: March 31. Hitherto unpublished.
Wednesday.
Dear Friend
I think your offer about the ribbons would have been very acceptable if it had come a little earlier -- but now the luggage is all gone to
Glasgow whence the vessel starts and Miss S. Tilley herself goes tonight. I forget whether I told you that she accompanies Mr. Syme 303 and his family.
The Times 304 speaks of the American Copyright as a fait accompli -- so I suppose there is no doubt that the Senate will ratify the treaty.
Tell Sara I would rather not disclose the authorship of the articles until they have been read. I consider -- no -- I will not say which I think the poorest.
I am right glad to hear that you are flourishing under extra work. Why did you send last week's Herald to Herbert Spencer? We could neither of us make out. I am better than I was -- the Spring moving in my veins a little, I suppose.
Your affectionate

Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, [29 October 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Oct. 29. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, I, 315.
Cambridge St.
Dear Friend
If you find your proposition about the Bookcase a feasible one, I shall be very glad to have it put in practice soon, as I wish to exchange my present one for a Library Table, of which I am sorely in need.
I had a great deal of chat yesterday with Sir John Forbes, 381 and found him, as you might expect from his books of travel, a very pleasant, unaffected man. Everybody is talking of the article on the Church in the Edinbro' Review. 382 Forbes is immensely tickled by your story about saddling the prophet instead of the ass, which the writer of said article has put in a note. You should read the article in the Quarterly on Electro-Biology -- it is by Dr. Carpenter 383 -- a "naked neddy" in your esteem, but still the first physiologist in England.
Last night I saw the first fine specimen of a man in the shape of a clergyman that I ever met with -- Dawes, the Dean of Hereford. 384 He is the man who has been making the experiment of mingling the middle and lower classes in schools. He has a face so intelligent and benignant that children might grow good by looking at it. [Four words deleted.]
Mr. and Mrs. Chapman are just gone, and have brought me the bit of ribbon which Mr. C. forgot to give me the other day. Thanks. Harriet Martineau called yesterday -- looking fatter than ever. She is going to her Brother's 385 at Birmingham soon. Mrs. Wills 386 came with her -- a nice little Scotch woman, a small edition of Robert Chambers, her brother. Love to Sara and Cara.
Yours ever
Marian Evans.

GE to Charles Bray, London, [27 May 1854]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: May 23. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 322; George Eliot and John Chapman, p. 74.
Cambridge St. | Saturday.
Dear Friend
Thanks many for the pretty bit of ribbon which came to me this morning.
I have finally decided not to live with the Chapmans. The consideration that determined me was, that I could not feel at liberty to leave them after causing them to make arrangements on my account, and it is quite possible that I may wish to go to the continent or twenty other things. At all events, I like to feel free. Apart from the comfort of being with people who call out some affection there would be no advantage in my living with the C's -- at least none that I take into account.
It was very good of you to come so far away from London pleasures for the sake of seeing me, 476 and I quite appreciate the good deed.
Mr. Lewes is going on a walking excursion to Windsor to-day with his doctor, 477 who pronounces him better, but not yet fit for work. However he is obliged to do a little and must content himself with an approximation to his doctor's directions -- in this world all things are approximations, and in the system of the Dog-star too, very probably, in spite of Dr. Whewell. 478
I get up with fresh rheumatism every morning, and the weather, to my sensations is more than wintry in coldness. 479 I want your garment of fat and a "fleecley" into the bargain. Best love to all from
Your ever affectionate
Marian.
I am obliged to send you this Brobdignag 480 envelope because I have no stamp for a smaller.

GE to Charles Bray, London, [22 January 1853]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Jan. 1853. Extracts published: Cross, 1, 302.
Dear Friend
Will you be so kind as to tell me in a few words, what are your objections to Mr. Chapman's letter to Mr. Combe? Mr. Chapman and I differ in our opinions -- or rather feelings -- on this subject, and I should be glad to check my own judgment by that of a third person.
I will ask Mr. Atkinson more about Lady Monson. 262 All I know of her at present is that she gives literary soir'e9es. I am very glad to hear that Miss Lynn has a kind friend in her. I am sure she needs friends, and I begin to feel for other people's wants and sorrows a little more than I used to do. Heaven help us! said the old religions -- the new one, from its very lack of that faith, will teach us all the more to help one another.
I am so sorry to hear that Cara has been having toothache again. Love to her and to Sara. Tell the latter she is as good as a group of spice islands to me -- she wafts the pleasantest influences even from a distance. I will write to her to-morrow, if possible.
Couldn't "Jane" 263 tell you what ribbons will be worn this spring?
Your affectionate
Marian.

Dublin Core:Subject: Charles Bray^^M
Dublin Core:Description:
GE to Charles Bray, London, [22 January 1852]
MS: Yale. Endorsed: Jan. 22. Extracts published: George Eliot and John Chapman, pp. 45, 66.
Strand.
Dear Friend
On opening the mysterious-looking letter you have sent me I find it addressed to "Dear Matilda." I have not read farther than the first sentence, and return it to you that you may enclose the cards you speak of with it and send it to the P.O. again.
I had headache yesterday. I have burnt my hand so that I am not in the best condition imaginable, especially for writing. Mr. Chapman's hearing is not worse than usual, but he looks horribly ghastly and wants change, of which he has had none at all for months. I have declared my resolution to leave at the end of this quarter -- but say nothing about it. Mrs. Chapman is increasingly polite and attentive, and I have many comforts here that I could hardly expect elsewhere, but --
There is an article in the last Quarterly on [Physiognomy] which you should read. It is by Lady Eastlake -- Miss Rigby that was. 13 On the whole our number is very superior even in attractiveness to either the Edinburgh or the Quarterly. In the Edinburgh there is a famous shewing up of Bishop Philpotts. The sketch of his history begins thus: "Bp P. is probably descended from the celebrated Archdeacon Philpotts who in the reign of Ed[ward] VI published his [Reasons for spitting upon an Arian.]" There is also an article on Parliamentary Reform, which I have not yet read. It is better written than ours, they say, but not so practical.
Please to thank your Mr. Spencer 15 for his letter to me in answer to a question I put to him. God bless you, make you happy, and keep you thin. I wish you the utmost thinness compatible with your happiness. I have several other letters to write so good bye.
Marian.
